units.tr: To the most noble and most distinguished man, Lord Hieronymus van Beveringh, Doctor of Laws, Lord of Theiling, Curator of the Academy of Leiden, Consular man of the Republic of Gouda, who has discharged many embassies for the United Netherlands with great prudence: illustrious sir.

units.la: QUod jam pridem votis omnibus optaveram, Vir Amplissime, ut daretur mihi aliquando locus, publicè testificandi quantum tibi debeam, id in hujus opellæ limine mihi tandem videor utcunque consecuturus, si me meumque munusculum, non pro prætio operæ, sed pro dignitate operis, proque sinsingulari meo, summoque in te studio sub tuis au-fpiciis prodire sinas, & hanc Inter Victrices hederam tibi serpere lauros: Quæque vidi in Regno Cœlorum perlustrando, quæque ex felicissimâ illa Regione viventium attuli, nobilissimo tibi viro & amplissimo offerenda, benevolè & amanter excipias. Age, paucis enarrabo.
units.tr: Since I have long desired with all my heart, most distinguished sir, to be given at some time an opportunity of openly bearing witness to how much I owe you, I seem at last, on the threshold of this little work, to be able to achieve it in some measure, if you allow me and my modest gift to come forth under your auspices. I offer it not in proportion to the labour expended but in proportion to the dignity of the work, and in keeping with my singular and very great devotion to you. Graciously and kindly receive this Ivy to creep among the victorious laurels for you, and the things I saw in my tour of the Kingdom of Heaven, and which I brought back from that most happy region of the living, to be offered to you, most noble and distinguished man. Come, I shall relate it in a few words.

units.la: Cum primùm animum ad demandatum mihi ab annis quadragenis officium, de Regno Cœlorum promovendo, appuli, id mihi negotii credidi solum dari perspectum clara in luce scriptu-rarum ut haberem, admirabile illud sanctorum Regnum in luce, & omnium primùm inconcussa illius fundamenta, quis jecerit, quibus modis posuerit; quâque auctoritate, quibusve viribus fultus tantum illud & vel angelis stupendum opus, fuerit aggressus.
units.tr: When I first turned my mind to the task entrusted to me forty years ago, of advancing the Kingdom of Heaven, I believed that I had been given this business only so that I might have it set out plainly in the clear light of the Scriptures: that admirable kingdom of the saints in the light. And, first of all, I wanted to see who laid its unshaken foundations, in what ways he laid them, and by what authority and with what powers he undertook so great a work, one that would astonish even the angels.

units.la: Videbam Regnum Dei primo ereptum Homini nefariis artibus Satanæ illius Giganteæ procéritatis Anak, Principisque tenebrarum tyrannicum in morem dominantis in malè sanos posteros victi sibique mancipati primi Parentis. Verùm ecce gratulabundus vidi Filium Hominis, tantæ calamitatis misertum sanctè pollicitum fore se semen mulieris contriturum caput serpentis יהוה איש מלחמה Do-
units.tr: I saw that the Kingdom of God was first snatched from man by the wicked arts of Satan, that giant of Anakite stature, and by the Prince of darkness, who, like a tyrant, ruled over the ill-minded posterity of the first parent, which he had conquered and made his own. But behold, with rejoicing I saw the Son of Man, who, moved with pity by so great a calamity, solemnly promised that he would be the seed of the woman who would crush the head of the serpent: Yahweh is a man of war [יהוה איש מלחמה] Do-

units.la: EPISTOLA.
units.tr: LETTER.

units.la: Dominum Bellatorem illustrem יהוה צבא טר, Principem exercitus Domini, qui post velitariæ pugnæ in deferto præludium, pugnam cruentam & decretoriam pugnaret, principatus & potestates, superbos illos Anakim spoliaret, Diabolum mortis imperatorem destrueret, foras illum mundi principem ejiceret, finibusque regni Dei, quod nefariè occupaverat, penitus exterminaret, idola profligaret, idololatriam emaciaret & deartuaret, suâ fultus æternâ potentissimâque Divinitate, suâque tergeminâ auctoritate, pontificiâ, qua numen generi humano infensum placaret, factâ per se ipsum criminum purgatione: Prophetica, qua sua crimina, suamque miseriam miseros mortales doceret & in spem certissimam salutis erigeret: Regali, qua leges justitiæ cordibus inscriberet, rebelles πεϑυναγκὴ & vorticordiâ spiritus sui efficaciâ potenter, sed & spontanea voluntate, funibus dilectionis in Dei obsequium pertraheret, eâdemque operâ divinissimè demonstraret, quàm sapientissimo consilio tremendo illo sui indigitamento יהוה Erit, totum id quantum quantum erat luculenter portendisset, futurus in plenitudine temporum Deus Amen, idolorum eversor, Deus Judæorum & gentium, Legislator, Judex, Rex, & Dominus universæ terræ. Ita Filius Hominis infelicissimi pa-renrentis Adami jaƈturam felicissimè reparavit. Hæc vidi in regno cœlorum, Vir Amplissime, quis enim perviderit profunda jacti illius fundamenti mysteria, non quæ cernit acutum aquila, non Serpens Epidaurius, non oculatus Argus, non animalia sacra intus & extus plena oculis, sunt enim εἰς ἃ [illegible, ~12 letters] ἄγγελοι [illegible, ~9 letters]. Nec vana fuit mea illa regni Cœlorum lustratio, manipulum hinc pro mea tenuitate attuli אשכול ענבים, Bo-trum uvarum, quem tibi, Vir Amplissime, gustandum offerrem, nihil quicquam in eo acerbi, nihil amari, nihil venenati, non enim est ex vinea Sodomæ, vel ex propagine Go-morrhæ; sed ex vinea Henguedi, tribus Judæ regione amœnissima אשכול הכפר Botrus propitiatio-nis, ex quo presso torculari Dei, fluxit ille san-guis uvæ, hominos aræ, lætitia Dei, hominum-que novorum, vinumque novum, quod pleno poculo Filius Hominis amicis suis se propi-naturum recipit in regno patris sui. In eo tibi offerendo, Vir Amplissime, ne te quæsiverim extra, juxta sapiens illud tuum lemma Persianum, in-tra orbem modestiæ tuæ totum me continebo. Ne te quæsiverim extra, de gente vetustâ illustrique famâ nobili prognatum te non recensebo, nec avorum stemmata, nec eorum tumulis manibus dabo dabo lilia plenis, nec purpureos spargam flores, nec fungar inani munere.
units.tr: To the illustrious Warrior Lord [יהוה צבא], Commander of the Lord's army, who, after the skirmish that served as a prelude in the wilderness, fought the bloody and decisive battle; who plundered the principalities and powers and those proud Anakim, destroyed the Devil, the lord of death, cast out that prince of the world, and utterly drove him from the borders of God's kingdom, which he had wickedly seized; who overthrew idols and wore down and broke the strength of idolatry, supported by his eternal and most mighty Divinity and by his threefold authority: the priestly, by which he appeased the Deity, now hostile to the human race, by a purification of sins accomplished through himself; the prophetic, by which he taught wretched mortals their sins and their misery and raised them to a most certain hope of salvation; and the kingly, by which he wrote the laws of justice on hearts and drew rebels, compelled by persuasion [πειθανάγκη] and by the powerful efficacy of his Spirit turning the heart, but also by their own willing consent, to obedience to God with cords of love; and who, by the same work, most divinely showed with what most wise counsel, through that fearful self-designation I Am [יהוה], Erit, he had clearly foretold all of this, being destined in the fullness of time to be God, Amen, the destroyer of idols, the God of Jews and Gentiles, Lawgiver, Judge, King, and Lord of the whole earth: thus the Son of Man most happily repaired the loss suffered by the most unhappy parent Adam. These things I have seen in the kingdom of heaven, most distinguished Sir. For who could behold the deep mysteries of that foundation once laid? Not the eagle, sharp of sight, not the Epidaurian serpent, not the watchful Argus, not the living creatures full of eyes within and without, for they are into which [illegible] angels [illegible]. Nor was my survey of the kingdom of heaven in vain: I have brought from there, as far as my slight powers allow, a cluster of grapes [אשכול ענבים], a cluster of grapes, which I offer you, most distinguished Sir, to taste. There is nothing bitter in it, nothing harsh, nothing poisonous, for it is not from the vineyard of Sodom or from the vine of Gomorrah, but from the vineyard of Engedi, the most pleasant region of the tribe of Judah, [אשכול הכפר], a cluster of the henna-flower, the Cluster of atonement, from which, when God's winepress was pressed, there flowed that blood of the grape, the wine of the altar, the joy of God and of new men, and the new wine, which the Son of Man receives to pour out for his friends in a full cup in the kingdom of his Father. In offering it to you, most distinguished Sir, I will not seek you outside yourself, according to your wise Persian motto, but will keep myself wholly within the sphere of your modesty. Not seeking you outside yourself, I will not recount that you are sprung from an ancient people and a noble and famous line, nor the genealogies of your ancestors, nor will I give lilies with full hands to their tombs, nor scatter purple flowers, nor perform an empty gift.

units.la: Stemmata quid faciunt? quid prodest Pontice longo Sanguine censeri, pictosque ostendere vultus Majorum?
units.tr: What do pedigrees achieve? What good is it to be counted by a long line of blood, or to display the painted faces of one's ancestors?

units.la: Nec te quaesiverim extra, decem legationibus apud exteras nationes, functum felicissimè in honorem gentis Batavæ, patriæque charissimæ felicitatem, nec in spretis generosè, muneribus Regiis, invio illo tuo potentissimis intentato illecebris, fortissimoque pectore, ut tui moveris non mediocrem apud gentem superbissimam admirationem. Nec te quaesiverim extra, in præclaris illis magistraturis honorificis, in civitate patriâ, in consessu ordinum, in præfecturâ Ærariâ, in agundis negotiis publicis, ubi eluxit summa illa tua ἀγχίνοια, ἔρτχία, sapientia, justitia, æquitas & φιλοτιμία, ut dynastis reipublicæ admirationi, omnibus in oculis & deliciis fueris. Ne te quaesiverim extra, sinas rogo etiamnum & obsecro, in te ipso ut quaesiverim spontaneam illam, & stupendam generositatem, quâ abdicatis omnibus illis ambitiosorum hominum titulis, vitam privatam in Tusculano tuo prætulisti, uni Deo ut servires, omnibus procul negotiis publicis, famigeratissimæ Universitati Lugduno Batavæ
units.tr: Nor would I seek you outside yourself as one who has most happily discharged ten embassies to foreign nations, in the honour of the Dutch nation and the happiness of your dearest fatherland; nor as one who nobly spurned the royal gifts, and with that invincible and most powerful heart, unassailed by allurements, and with great strength of mind, has won no small admiration among that most proud people. Nor would I seek you outside yourself in those distinguished and honourable offices, in your native city, in the assembly of the estates, in the superintendence of the treasury, in the conduct of public affairs, where your great quick-wittedness, [ἔρτχία] (virtue), wisdom, justice, fairness, and [φιλοτιμία] (public spirit) shone forth, so that you became the admiration of the rulers of the commonwealth and the delight and the eye of all. Do not let me seek you outside yourself; I beg and entreat you to allow me, even now, to seek within yourself that spontaneous and astonishing generosity by which, having renounced all the titles of ambitious men, you preferred a private life in your Tusculan villa, to serve God alone, far from all public business, in that most famous University of Leiden,

units.la: * * væ; indefessus Curator ut invigilares, & investigandis regni cœlorum mysteriis, in honesto tuo otio litterario perdius & pernox incumberes. Nec te quæsiverim extra, si tuam illam profundam eruditionem in Græcis & Latinis Poëtis, Oratoribus, Historicis, Philosophis, Jureperitis, & Theologis recensuero, ut uni Salomoni in plantarum utriusque orbis notitia, ab hyssopo horti ad Cedrum Libani, secundus videaris. Eam non quæro in te, miror magis, sapientiam, qua me ex ore tuo suspensum Sylvæ-Ducis tenuisti olim, & fere in stuporem dedisti. Nec te quæsiverim extra, si in te suspexero,
units.tr: * * væ; as tireless Curator, to keep watch, and to devote yourself by day and by night, in your honourable literary leisure, to the investigation of the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven. Nor would I seek you outside yourself, if I were to recount your profound learning in the Greek and Latin poets, orators, historians, philosophers, jurists, and theologians, so that, like Solomon alone in his knowledge of plants of both worlds, from the hyssop of the wall to the cedar of Lebanon, you appear second to none. I do not seek this in you; I rather marvel at that wisdom by which, long ago, you held me hanging on your words at Sylvaeducis, and almost struck me dumb. Nor would I seek you outside yourself, if I have looked up to you,

units.la: Compositum jus, fasque animi, sanctosque recessus Mentis, & incoctum generoso pectus honesto.
units.tr: The right and the just of a composed mind, the holy recesses of the spirit, and a breast steeped in noble honour.

units.la: Hoc tuum est, quia gratia Dei, quæ tecum est. Nec te, demum, quæsiverim extra, si grata mente recoluero collata tua in me beneficia, benevolo illo animo, quo te suffragatorem suum, te studiorum fautorem, te bonorum conciliatorem, te Mæcenatem erudyti omnes agnoscunt. Deus optimus maximus, pro talibus digna tibi rependat præmia, Patriæ & Academiæ diu te servet incolumem, tuo sub patrocinio, tuoque sub umbraculo, Botrus noster uvarum ab Harpyis & fœdis tenebrarum volucribus, tutus sit & incolumis
units.tr: This is yours, because the grace of God is with you. Nor, finally, would I seek you outside yourself, if I, with a grateful mind, recall the benefits you have conferred on me, with that kindly spirit by which all learned men acknowledge you as their supporter, the patron of studies, the friend of good men, and their Maecenas. May God, best and greatest, render you worthy rewards for such deeds, may he keep you long safe for your fatherland and Academy, and under your protection and your shade, may our cluster of grapes be safe and unharmed from the Harpies and the foul birds of darkness.

units.la: EPISTOLA.
units.tr: EPISTLE.

units.la: Semper honos nomenque tuum laudesque manebunt Quo me cumque vocant terrae. – –
units.tr: Always your honour and your name and your praises will remain, wherever the lands call me. – –

units.la: Vale, Vir Amplissime, vive Nestora totum eruditorum ocelle, perge porrò amare
units.tr: Farewell, most distinguished sir, live a Nestor through and through, the eye of the learned; go on, I pray, to love

units.la: Amplissimi tui Nominis observantissimum
units.tr: Most observant of your most distinguished name,

units.la: JACOBUM GAILLARDUM.
units.tr: JACOBUS GAILLARDUS.

units.la: INDEX Quæstionum, quæ hocce in libro enodantur.
units.tr: Index of the questions explained in this book.

units.la: QUÆSTIO I.
units.tr: QUESTION I.

units.la: Cur Iesus in Novo Instrumento passim, ὁ υἱὸς τ ἀνθρώπου appellari voluerit? pag. I
units.tr: Why did Jesus so often want to be called ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου [ho huios tou anthrōpou, the Son of Man]? p. I

units.la: QUÆSTIO II.
units.tr: QUESTION II.

units.la: Cur Iesus in Novo Instrumento se titulo Filii Hominis passim insignire voluerit, ut eo se esse Messiam, seu Christum significaret? p. 19
units.tr: Why did Jesus so often mark himself with the title Son of Man, so as to signify that he is the Messiah, or Christ? p. 19

units.la: QUÆSTIO III.
units.tr: QUESTION III.

units.la: Cur Iesus interdixerit discipulis suis, ut nemini dicerent eum esse Christum, cùm ipse se Filium Hominis passim appellaverit, ut se esse Christum significaret? p 62
units.tr: Why did Jesus forbid his disciples to tell anyone that he is the Christ, when he himself so often called himself the Son of Man in order to signify that he is the Christ? p. 62

units.la: QUÆSTIO IV.
units.tr: QUESTION IV.

units.la: Quem intellexerint, David Psalm. 8. vers. 5, 6, 7. & Paulus Hebr. 2. vers. 6, 7, 8. quid est Homo, quòd recorderis ejus, aut Filius Hominis, quòd visites eum, &c. p 81
units.tr: What did David (Psalm 8:5–7) and Paul (Hebrews 2:6–8) understand by "What is man, that thou art mindful of him, or the son of man, that thou visitest him," etc.? p. 81

units.la: QUÆSTIO V.
units.tr: QUESTION V.

units.la: Cur vates Psalm. 8. vers. 5. & Apostolus Hebr. 2. vers. 6. per contemptum dixerint, quid est Filius Hominis, ut visites eum? cùm Filius Hominis sit Christus? p. 105
units.tr: Why did the psalmist (Psalm 8:5) and the apostle (Hebrews 2:6) speak with contempt, "What is the son of man, that thou visitest him?" since the Son of Man is Christ? p. 105

units.la: QUÆSTIO VI.
units.tr: QUESTION VI.

units.la: Quid significat videro cœlum apertum Act. 7. ad Filium Hominis? p. 128
units.tr: What does it mean to see the heavens opened (Acts 7) over the Son of Man? p. 128

units.la: QUÆSTIO VII.
units.tr: QUESTION VII.

units.la: Quid significet ascensus & descensus Angelorum Dei ad Filium Hominis? Item. quì & quando discipuli Angelos Dei viderint ascendentes & descendentes ad Filium Hominis? p. 152
units.tr: What does the ascending and descending of the angels of God upon the Son of Man signify? Likewise, where and when did the disciples see the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man? p. 152

units.la: QUÆSTIO VIII.
units.tr: QUESTION VIII.

units.la: Quomodo visio Cæli aperti & Angelorum Dei ad Filium Hominis ascendentium atque descendentium, majora sint iis, quæ Nathanael de Christo viderat? p. 166
units.tr: In what way is the vision of the open heaven and of the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man greater than what Nathanael had seen of Christ? p. 166

units.la: QUÆSTIO IX.
units.tr: QUESTION IX.

units.la: Cur inter tot majora, quæ Christus de se videnda exhibuit, destinato seligere voluerit visionem cæli aperti, &c. p. 179
units.tr: Why, among so many greater things which Christ showed as worthy of being seen in himself, did he deliberately choose the vision of the open heaven, etc.? p. 179

units.la: QUÆSTIO X.
units.tr: QUESTION X.

units.la: Quomodo, quam Iacob in somnio vidit scalam, typus fuerit Filii Hominis? p. 208
units.tr: In what way was the ladder that Jacob saw in a dream a type of the Son of Man? p. 208

units.la: QUÆSTIO XI.
units.tr: QUESTION XI.

units.la: Cur Christus solemni isthac loquendi formula, Amen, Amen, dico vobis, &c. promissionem visionis cæli aperti, caeterasque passim roborare voluerit? p. 231
units.tr: Why did Christ, with the solemn formula of speech "Amen, amen, I say to you," etc., confirm the promise of the vision of the open heaven and his other sayings? p. 231

units.la: QUÆSTIO XII.
units.tr: QUESTION XII.

units.la: Cur Iohannes Christum constanter exhibuerit ingeminantem Amen, Amen, cum contrà cæteri Euangelistæ Christum uno Amen perpetuò usum memoraverint? p. 239
units.tr: Why does John consistently show Christ repeating "Amen, amen," whereas the other evangelists record that Christ always used a single Amen? p. 239

units.la: QUÆSTIO XIII.
units.tr: QUESTION XIII.

units.la: Cur Christus Dei Filius dictus fuerit ὁ Amen, Apoc. 3. verf. 14. p. 242
units.tr: Why was Christ, the Son of God, called ὁ Ἀμήν [ho Amēn, the Amen] in Revelation 3:14? p. 242

units.la: QUÆSTIO XIV.
units.tr: QUESTION XIV.

units.la: Virum nomen יהוה Dei proprium, Moisi primum innotuerit, ut ante Mosem ignotum, & inauditum fuerit? p. 256
units.tr: Was the proper name of God, יהוה [YHWH], first made known to Moses, so that it was unknown and unheard of before Moses? p. 256

units.la: QUÆSTIO XV.
units.tr: QUESTION XV.

units.la: Vtrum nomen יהוה sit ita Deo proprium, ut nulli nisi Deo competat? p.262
units.tr: Is the name יהוה [YHWH] so proper to God that it belongs to no one but God? p. 262

units.la: QUÆSTIO XVI.
units.tr: QUESTION XVI.

units.la: Quomodo nomen יהוה primitùs fuerit pronuntiatum & lectum? Item quomodo hodie sit legendum, & pronunciandum? p.264
units.tr: How was the name יהוה [YHWH] originally pronounced and read? Likewise, how is it to be read and pronounced today? p. 264

units.la: QUÆSTIO XVII.
units.tr: QUESTION XVII.

units.la: Quid proprie, directè, & per se Deus significaverit, & de se revelare voluerit nomine proprio יהוה? p.270
units.tr: What did God properly, directly and of himself intend to signify, and wish to reveal about himself, by the proper name יהוה [YHWH]? p. 270

units.la: QUÆSTIO XVIII.
units.tr: QUESTION XVIII.

units.la: Vtrum Deus יהוה nomen proprium sibi fecerit, ut proprie, directè, ac per sese significaret æternam essentiam suam, quatenus auctor & causa est rerum omnium? p.276
units.tr: Did God make the name יהוה [YHWH] his own proper name so that he might properly, directly and through himself signify his eternal essence, insofar as he is the author and cause of all things? p. 276

units.la: QUÆSTIO XIX.
units.tr: QUESTION XIX.

units.la: Vtrum Deus nomen יהוה proprium sibi fecerit, fidelitatem suam, hoc est, constantiam in exequendis promissionibus & minis, proprie, directè, & immediatè, ut significaret? p.291
units.tr: Did God make the name יהוה [YHWH] his proper name so that he might signify, properly, directly and immediately, his faithfulness, that is, his constancy in carrying out his promises and threats? p. 291

units.la: QUÆSTIO XX.
units.tr: QUESTION XX.

units.la: Quid Deus ignotum antea Patriarchis, vel à mundi conditu, suo illo proprio indigitamento יהוה Mosi, populoque Israeli suo, proprie, ac directè, significare voluerit? p.300
units.tr: What did God, who was unknown before to the patriarchs, or from the creation of the world, wish to signify properly and directly to Moses and to his people Israel by that proper designation יהוה [YHWH]? p. 300

units.la: אשכול ענבים HOC EST SPECIMEN QUÆSTIONUM IN NOVUM INSTRUMENTUM DE FILIO HOMINIS.
units.tr: A Cluster of Grapes [אשכול ענבים]: This Is a Specimen of Questions on the New Testament Concerning the Son of Man.

units.la: QUÆSTIO PRIMA.
units.tr: QUESTION ONE.

units.la: Cur Iesus in Novo Instrumento passim, ὁ Υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου appellari voluerit?
units.tr: Why did Jesus so often wish to be called ὁ Υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου [the Son of Man] throughout the New Testament?

units.la: HAud mediocrem nobis movet admirationem, quòd Paulus instituta collatione Adamum inter & Christum, Adamum vocat πρῶτον ἄνθρωπον, primum hominem, Christum verò ἔσχατον Ἀδὰμ εἰς δεύτερον [?], ultimum & secundum hominem, 1 Cor. 15: 45. 47. Adamum quidem in animam viventem creatum, primum fuisse hominem, nec est ad intelligendum difficile, nec ad edisserendum prima fronte, cum & nullus exstiterit ante Adamum ἄνθρωπος χοϊκός, homo terrenus, unde Adam originem duceret, & nemo mortalium non sit ex Adamo oriundus. Intuenti verò in penitissimum Scripturæ sensum, non ita facile intellectu dictuve videtur. Qui enim fieri potest, ut Adam & sit, & perhibeatur πρῶτος, quandoquidem ἐν τύπῳ τοῦ μέλλοντος [?], typus est futuri Adami, scilicet Christi, Rom. 5: 14? Typus verò cum exsculpta sit ἐκ τύπων ἀνθρώπων figura, in quavis materia durabili, natura & origine posterior est τῷ τυ- πωθέντι, exemplari suo. Posterior est, facebor enim, natura & origine: sed & ipso tempore, cum typus est manu finita excusus: sed ut ut natura & origine sit posterior, nihil vetat esse tempore, suo exemplari priorem, cum utrumque omnipotens atque æterna Dei manus in dias luminis oras producit, veluti Melchisedec Dei filio assimilatus, Heb. 7: 3. tempore fuit prior, reali Melchisedeco Christo: fuit vero natura posterior, sicut res assimilata quævis, suo exemplari. Idem esto de Adamo & Christo judicium, primus fuit Adamus, habita ratione temporis, Christus vero posterior, & ab Adamo secundus, ratione temporariæ suæ nativitatis: sed itidem primus & Adamo antiquior, natura, in mente scilicet & consilio Dei, veluti exemplar, cujus Adamus typus erat futurus. Qui vero Christus ἔσχατος ultimus Adam, fuerit, & ab Adamo secundus, non ita planum, vel intellectu facile explicatuve? Christus homo ultimus, quem millenæ myriades myriadum hominum excepere, suntque demum exceptura, ad sæculorum consummationem? Christus ab Adamo δεύτερος secundus, quem millenæ myriades hominum interpositæ, procul distermi-nant ab Adamo? Est vero Christus hominum ultimus, sicuti Adamus mortalium primus: ut enim nemo Adamum in animam viventem, hoc est in vitam animalem cretum, antevertit, unde Adamus traxerit originem: sed omnes χοϊκοὶ, & in vita animali creti homines, ex protoplasmate Adamo originem ducunt: non secus & Christus ultimus est homo, ex quo omnes cœlestes homines oriundi sunt, quia nullus homo, cui cœlestes & spiritu vivifico regeniti homines, vitam suam spiritualem & cœlestem ferre debeant acceptam, Christum excepturus est. Est vero itidem Christus secundus ab Adamo, Adam, sicut Adam est primus homo: nam 1°. sicut Adam in Hebræorum phrasi, est אדם quia unus, vel primus fuit homo, ex quo cæteri vitam animalem ducerent, ita Christus eadem phraseologia, quam novi scriptores amant, est אדם δεύτερος secundus, scilicet ab Adamo, quia nullus est præter Christum, nec ex decessoribus, nec ex successoribus, ex quo homines in vita spirituali creti duxerint originem suam. 2°. Sicut Adamus est primus homo, quia omnes homines terreni in Adamo unum sunt, natura scilicet & conditione: ex Adamo enim, ejusque posteris, unum exsurgit genus humanum terrenum & peccaminosum; ita Christus est ab Adamo secundus homo, quia in Christo omnes qui de candido ejus nomine vere censentur fideles, unum pariter sunt natura & conditione vitæ cœlestis ac sanctæ, quandoquidem ex Christo & posteris ejus, semine spirituali ipsius regenitis, nitis, unum effloresćit genus humanum coeleste ac sanctum: unde si cum animo tuo reputaveris omnes, quotquot vixere in terris homines, duo tantum hominum genera ob oculos tuos posita animadvertes, primum genus in Adamo, secundum vero genus humanum in Christo. Denique Adamus est primus homo, Christus vero secundus, quia secundus est ab Adamo filius Adami seu hominis: Deus enim neglectis cæteris ךְ נִי אָדָם & pro nihilo habitis, utpote imparibus liberando Adamo cum posteris ejus, unum Jesum Adami filium, qui tantum opus effectum daret, dignum habuit ac reputavit: Christus igitur est secundus homo, quia filius Adami, seu hominis: sed secundus atque ultimus, si omnes recensueris Adami filios, qui lamentabilem parentis Adami, fratrumque miserorum jacturam, magnificum in modum repararet.
units.tr: It does not little surprise us that Paul, in drawing a comparison between Adam and Christ, calls Adam πρῶτον ἄνθρωπον [the first man], primum hominem [the first man], but calls Christ ἔσχατον Ἀδὰμ εἰς δεύτερον [the last Adam, the second], ultimum & secundum hominem [the last and second man] (1 Cor. 15:45, 47). That Adam, created as a living soul, was the first man is neither hard to understand nor hard to explain at first sight, since there was no earthly man, ἄνθρωπος χοϊκός [earthy man], homo terrenus [an earthly man], before Adam from whom he could derive his origin, and no mortal is not descended from Adam. But to one who looks into the deepest sense of Scripture, it does not seem so easy to understand or to say. For how can Adam both be and be called the first, since he is ἐν τύπῳ τοῦ μέλλοντος [a type of the one to come], typus est futuri Adami [a type of the Adam who was to come], namely Christ (Rom. 5:14)? A type, however, when a figure is carved ἐκ τύπων ἀνθρώπων [from human moulds] in any durable material, is in nature and origin later than the thing it represents, its exemplar. It is later, I shall grant, in nature and origin; but also in time, since the type is finished and shaped by hand later. Yet, however much it is later in nature and origin, nothing prevents it from being earlier in time than its exemplar, since the almighty and eternal hand of God brings both into the light of day. Thus Melchizedek, made like the Son of God (Heb. 7:3), was earlier in time than the real Melchizedek, Christ; but he was later in nature, as any likeness is later than its exemplar. The same judgment holds for Adam and Christ: Adam was first, reckoning by time, and Christ was later, and second from Adam, by reason of his temporal birth; but in the same way Christ is first and older than Adam in nature, namely in the mind and counsel of God, as the exemplar of which Adam was to be the type. But how Christ is the last Adam, and second from Adam, is not so plain, nor easy to explain by understanding? Christ is the last man, whom thousands of myriads of men have followed, and who are yet to follow, until the consummation of the ages? Christ is the second from Adam, whom thousands of myriads of men, lying between, separate far from Adam? Christ is, indeed, the last of men, just as Adam is the first of mortals. For just as no one preceded Adam, who was created as a living soul, that is, in animal life, from whom he drew his origin, but all earthly men, created in animal life, derive their origin from Adam as the first protoplast, so also Christ is the last man, from whom all heavenly men have sprung, since no man, to whom heavenly men regenerated by the life-giving Spirit must owe their spiritual and heavenly life, will come after Christ. Christ is also the second from Adam, just as Adam is the first man. For first, just as Adam in the Hebrew idiom is אדם [adam] because he was the one, or first, man from whom the others would draw their animal life, so Christ, in the same phraseology that the newer writers love, is אדם δεύτερος [adam, the second], namely from Adam, because there is no one besides Christ, neither among predecessors nor successors, from whom men created in spiritual life have drawn their origin. Second, just as Adam is the first man, because all earthly men are one in Adam, in nature and condition, for from Adam and his posterity there rises one earthly and sinful human race; so Christ is the second man from Adam, because in Christ all who are truly counted faithful by his sacred name are equally one in nature and in the condition of heavenly and holy life, since from Christ and his posterity, regenerated by his spiritual seed, there springs one heavenly and holy human race. Hence, if you consider in your mind all who have lived as men on earth, you will see that only two kinds of men are set before your eyes: the first kind in Adam, and the second kind, the human race, in Christ. Finally, Adam is the first man, but Christ the second, because he is the second, namely the son of Adam, or of man: for God, neglecting and counting for nothing the others, as unequal to the task, judged that one Jesus, son of Adam, who would accomplish so great a work, was worthy to deliver Adam with his posterity. Christ is therefore the second man, because he is the son of Adam, or of man; but he is second and last if you count all the sons of Adam, whom he would restore in a wonderful way from the sad loss of the parent Adam and of his wretched brothers.

units.la: Mirari equidem subit Novum Instrumentum legenti ac meditanti, inter tot nomina, quibus Jesus Dei filius insignitur, nullum æque frequenter occurrere, atque istud ὁ υἱὸς τῆς ἀνθρώπου, quo Jesus ubivis fere sese amat appellitare apud quatuor Euangelistas, ut serio computanti istius nomenclationis vices, ultra octogies repetitæ videantur. Mirari præterea subit, ea se solum appellatione Christum insigniisse, si loca exceperis, quæ ad tempus claræ manifestationis Messiæ, spectant: ut Act. 7: 56. Heb. 2: 6. Apoc. 1: 13. & 14: 14. Nam quod plebeia Judæorum multitudo regerit, Joh. 12: 34. Quis est ille Filius hominis? Mero meridie clarius liquet, hanc ex ore Christi appellationem mutuasse: Judæi enim aversantes durum hunc sibi Jesu sermonem, scilicet Filium hominis sublatum iri in crucem, utpote contrarium præconceptæ suæ de Messia perpetuum duraturo ac glorioso, opinioni, irridentes reponunt, Quis est ille Filius hominis? Novimus quidem ex lege Filium hominis perpetuo duraturum, Filium vero hominis in crucem ignominiosè dandum, non novimus. Mirari denique subit cum in veteri Instrumento, omnes plebei homines ךְ נִי אָדָם filii hominis, & nobiles ךְ נִי אִישׁ filii viri audiant: ut Psal. 49: 3. & 62: 10. In Prophetis vero singulari ratione Ezechiel de nomine Filii hominis censeatur, & Daniel semel: Dan. 8: 17. Nemo tamen in novo Instrumento Filii hominis nomenclatione insignitur, uno excepto Jesu Christo. Hinc nemo non conjectabit, siquidem præ oculis Scripturæ sapientiam habuerit, reconditum aliquod latere mysterium in isto Filii hominis titulo, ita Christo proprio ἀχοινωνήτως, ut nulli mortalium sub novo fœdere contigerit. Anne amabo tibi fit, Lector, vero simile, Jesum, quâ erat divina sapientia, se Filium hominis & passim in novo Instrumento appellasse, & hominibus cognoscendum propositisse, ista nomenclatione emphatica singulari, absque deliberato consilio magni alicujus mysterii revelandi? Agedum adspirante coelestis spiritus flamine, ac luce Scripturarum praeeunte, latens salutare mysterium, in ea Domini nostri nomenclatione, investigemus. Verum enim vero, ut propositæ quæstioni, pro modulo nostro fiat satis, illustrium virorum sententias audire ac perpendere liber, & si quid caespitatum lapsumve fuerit, modeste notare, aurei dicti memores, ὀντοῖν ἀμφοῖν φιλοῖν ὅσιον προλιμάν τὴν ἀληθειαν.
units.tr: Truly, when one reads and meditates on the New Testament, one is moved to wonder that among so many names by which Jesus is marked out as the Son of God, none occurs as often as this, ὁ υἱὸς τῆς ἀνθρώπου [the Son of Man], by which Jesus, among the four Evangelists, almost everywhere loves to call himself, so that, if one counts seriously the instances of this designation, it appears to be repeated more than eighty times. One is moreover amazed that he has marked out Christ by this title alone, except in passages that concern the time of the clear manifestation of the Messiah, such as Acts 7:56, Heb. 2:6, Rev. 1:13, and 14:14. For what the common multitude of the Jews replies, John 12:34, Quis est ille Filius hominis? [Who is this Son of man?], is clearer than midday, showing that they borrowed this designation from the mouth of Christ. For the Jews, shrinking from this hard saying of Jesus, that the Son of Man would be lifted up on the cross, as contrary to their preconceived and lasting opinion of a glorious Messiah, reply mockingly, Quis est ille Filius hominis? We indeed know from the law that the Son of Man will endure forever, but we do not know that the Son of Man is to be given up to a shameful cross. Finally, one is amazed that in the Old Testament all common men are called filii hominis [sons of man, Hebrew בני אדם], and nobles filii viri [sons of man of rank, Hebrew בני איש], as in Psalm 49:3 and 62:10. Among the Prophets, Ezekiel is singularly called by the name Son of Man, and Daniel once (Dan. 8:17). Yet no one in the New Testament is marked with the title Son of Man, except Jesus Christ alone. Hence anyone who has wisdom from Scripture before his eyes will conjecture that some hidden mystery lies in this title Son of Man, belonging to Christ in such an unshared way that it has fallen to no other mortal under the New Covenant. Surely, dear reader, is it likely that Jesus, being divine wisdom, called himself the Son of Man so often in the New Testament and set this emphatic and singular designation before men to be known, without a deliberate purpose of revealing some great mystery? Come now, with the breath of the heavenly Spirit inspiring us and the light of the Scriptures going before, let us search out the hidden saving mystery in this name of our Lord. Indeed, so that the question proposed may be answered to the measure of our ability, I ask you to hear and weigh the opinions of illustrious men, and, if anything has been stumbled over or slipped, to note it modestly, mindful of the golden saying, ὄντοιν ἀμφοῖν φίλοιν ὅσιον προτιμᾶν τὴν ἀλήθειαν [since both are dear, it is holy to prefer the truth].

units.la: Veteres Ecclesiæ Doctores Jesum, se titulo Filii hominis insigniisse, ut ostenderet se vere esse hominem, asseveranter pronunciant, ut Epiphanius adversus Noetianos haeresi 57. & Theodoretus in Comment. in caput 7. Dan. & Tertullianus in libro de carne Christi cap. 15. Quando quod ad omnes dictum est, si humana non fuit, nec ex homine, non video ex qua substantia? si Christus hominem & filium hominis pronunciarit: nunc autem vultis occidere hominem veritatem ad vos locutum: & Filius hominis est Sabbati Dominus. Augustinus Epistola 174. Filium autem hominis eundem dicimus, quem filium Dei, non tamen propter formam Dei, in qua est aequalis Deo Patri: sed propter acceptam formam servi, qua Major est Pater. Et libro 5. contra Faustum Manichæum cap. 4. Satis apparet, quemadmodum Christum Filium hominis credere debeamus, qui filius Dei, per quem facti sumus, etiam Filius hominis per assumptionem carnis factus est, ut moreretur propter delicta nostra & resurgeret propter justificationem nostram, ideo utrumque se dicit, & Filium Dei & Filium hominis. Patrum sententia scripturæ phrasibus niti videtur, ubi homo & filius hominis pro uno eodemque promiscue usurpantur: ut Num. 23:19. Deus non est homo ut mentiatur, nec Filius hominis ut poeniteat eum. Consentiunt Patribus Doctissimi Viri, & in iis literarum decus, Clarissimus Grotius, in cap. 12. Matth. Comm. 8. Quia, inquit, Hebraeis notissimum est אדם hominem quemvis significare, quamquam interdum ad minus illustres restringitur, & Syri ad quemvis hominem designandum dicunt nash bar nasch[o]. At assensum nostrum sibi demereri non potuerunt: 1°. quia Judaeorum nemo unquam vocavit in dubium, Jesum esse verum hominem: eum enim noverant, & natum ex Maria, & cum iis versatum, omnibus humanis infirmitatibus innocuis obnoxium: nihil igitur opus erat Jesum se Filium hominis passim venditare, ut Judaeos doceret, se vere esse hominem. 2°. Quia non se vocat Filium hominis simpliciter, sed emphaticè, ὁ Υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, qua singulari emphasi, nec Ezechiel, nec Daniel, uspiam insigniuntur, sed sine emphasi utrumque Υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου dicitur. Καὶ εἶπε πρὸς με Υἱὲ ἀνθρώπου Ezech. 2: 2. & 3:1. & sic passim. Gemina est Danielis nomenclatio, ᾧ εἶπε πρὸς με μὲ σωμὲς υἱὲ ἀνθρώπου Dan. 8: 17. Et sicut apud septuaginta nusquam comparet articulus ὁ demonstrativus: ita nec in textu Hebraeo ה emphaticum & demonstrativum. Unde concludere in promptu est, singularem Jesu hanc appellationem ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, alio tendere, quam ad designandum tantummodo, Jesum esse hominem. 3o. Quia Joh. 1. cum Philippus Nathanaeli significasset, se, & Andream, & Petrum invenisse Jesum, Filium Josephi e Nazareth, eundemque negantem boni aliquid ex Nazareth oriundum, ad Jesum duxisset, ut ipsum videret: Jesus colloquium suum cum Nathanaele concludit his verbis, Amen Amen dico vobis, ab hoc tempore videbitis coelum apertum, & Angelos Dei ascendentes & descendentes ad filium hominis. Quisquamne in animum suum inducat, Jesum se filium hominis appellasse, ut Nathanaelem doceret se esse hominem? cum Nathanael, & Jesum hominem videret, & a Philippo didicisset, Jesum esse Filium Josephi, & ex urbe Nazareth prodiisse: ita sane persuasum erat Nathanaeli Jesum esse hominem, ut eum pro vili ac despicabili homuncione, utpote Nazarethanum, haberet, quod & sua illa interrogatione, An ex urbe Nazareth potest aliquid boni esse? satis superque contestatus fuerat. Alio igitur tendit solemnis ille Christi titulus, ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, quam ut eo significet, se esse vere hominem.
units.tr: The ancient Doctors of the Church assert confidently that Jesus adopted the title Son of man to show that he was truly a man. So Epiphanius against the Noetians, heresy 57, and Theodoret in his commentary on Daniel chapter 7, and Tertullian in his book on the flesh of Christ, chapter 15: "Since what was said to all, if he was not human nor of man, I do not see from what substance? If Christ pronounced himself man and son of man: but now you want to kill the man who has spoken the truth to you: and the Son of man is Lord of the Sabbath." Augustine, Letter 174: "We say that the Son of man is the same as the Son of God, yet not on account of the form of God, in which he is equal to God the Father, but on account of the form of a servant which he took, in which the Father is greater." And in book 5 against Faustus the Manichaean, chapter 4: "It is plain how we ought to believe Christ to be the Son of man: he who is the Son of God, through whom we were made, was also made the Son of man by taking on flesh, so that he might die for our sins and rise again for our justification. Therefore he calls himself both the Son of God and the Son of man."* The opinion of the Fathers seems to rest on the phrases of Scripture, where man and son of man are used interchangeably for one and the same thing, as in Num. 23:19: "God is not a man, that he should lie, nor a son of man, that he should repent." Learned men agree with the Fathers, and among them the great glory of letters, the most famous Grotius, in his commentary on Matthew chapter 12: "Because," he says, "it is well known to the Hebrews that [אָדָם] signifies any man whatever, although at times it is restricted to lesser men; and the Syrians, to designate any man, say nash bar nasha." But they could not win our assent, for these reasons. First, because none of the Jews ever called into doubt that Jesus was a true man: they knew him, born of Mary, who had lived among them, subject to all human weaknesses apart from sin. There was therefore no need for Jesus to call himself the Son of man everywhere, in order to teach the Jews that he was truly a man. Second, because he does not call himself simply Son of man, but emphatically, ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου [the Son of man]; and with this special emphasis neither Ezekiel nor Daniel is ever so designated, but in them without emphasis both are called υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου [son of man]. Καὶ εἶπε πρὸς με Υἱὲ ἀνθρώπου [And he said to me, Son of man], Ezek. 2:2 and 3:1, and so everywhere. Daniel's name is twin: εἶπε πρὸς με σύνες υἱὲ ἀνθρώπου [he said to me, Understand, son of man], Dan. 8:17. And just as in the Seventy the demonstrative article ὁ never appears, so in the Hebrew text the emphatic and demonstrative ה is absent. Hence it is easy to conclude that this unique appellation of Jesus, ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, aims at something other than merely designating Jesus as a man. Third, because in John chapter 1, when Philip had told Nathanael that he and Andrew and Peter had found Jesus, the son of Joseph from Nazareth, and Nathanael, denying that anything good could come from Nazareth, had been led by Philip to Jesus to see him, Jesus concludes his conversation with Nathanael with these words: "Amen, amen, I say to you, from now on you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man." Would anyone suppose that Jesus called himself the Son of man in order to teach Nathanael that he was a man? Nathanael saw that Jesus was a man, and had learned from Philip that Jesus was the son of Joseph and had come out of the town of Nazareth. Nathanael was so persuaded that Jesus was a man that he regarded him as a worthless and contemptible little man, being a Nazarene; and his own question, "Can anything good come out of Nazareth?" had sufficiently and more than sufficiently testified to this. That solemn title of Christ, ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, therefore aims at something other than indicating that he is truly a man.

units.la: Plerique omnes, qua Orthodoxi, qua Pontificii, in quibus Jesuita Maldonatus in Matth. 8: 10. & clarissimus Grotius, existimant, Jesum hoc titulo Filii hominis, se ipsum designasse, ad significandum statum suum humilem, de quo Psal. 22. ait, se esse vermem, opprobrium hominis, non vero hominem: nec aliud esse יִּ֫ υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, quam Christi κένωσιν, de qua Phil. 2:7. & Jes. 53:3. Despectus & abjectus inter viros, vir dolorum, & notus afflictione, & abscondimus facies ab eo, adeo despectus erat. Vectantur hac ratione, quod in Scriptura Veteris Instrumenti hominem contemptae sortis designat: ut Gen. 6: 2. filiae hominum, opponuntur filiis Dei, & Psal. 82:7. Magistratus vocati filii excelsi, morituri tamen dicuntur sicut homo, & Psal. 49:3. filii hominis, opponuntur filiis viri illustris, nec non Ezechiel & Daniel ab Angelis, eos alloquentibus vocantur, filii hominis, ut suae vilitatis & infirmitatis humanae memores, modesti & humiles, agerent cum gloriosis Angelis, virili illustrique forma vestitis. Unde Prophetae ad hanc vocem fili hominis in terram procumbunt, metu perculsi, & fatiscentes sub pondere gloriae fortis & illustris Angeli Gabrielis. Hinc concludunt, Jesum, hoc titulo Filii hominis, se passim designasse ad suam abjectionem & formam servilem significandam.
units.tr: Almost all, both Orthodox and Papists, among whom are the Jesuit Maldonatus, on Matthew 8:10, and the most famous Grotius, think that by this title Son of man Jesus designated himself, to signify his humble state, of which Psalm 22 says that he is "a worm, the reproach of men, and not a man"; and that the title υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου [son of man] is nothing other than the kenosis of Christ, of which Phil. 2:7 and Isa. 53:3 speak: "Despised and rejected of men, a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief; and we hid as it were our faces from him, so despised was he." They support this view by arguing that in the Old Testament man designates a person of despised condition: thus in Gen. 6:2 "daughters of men" are set against "sons of God"; and in Psalm 82:7 magistrates, called "sons of the Most High," are nevertheless said to die like a man; and in Psalm 49:3 "sons of men" are set against "sons of the great man." Likewise Ezekiel and Daniel are called by the angels, when they address them, "son of man," so that, mindful of their own lowliness and human weakness, they might behave modestly and humbly before the glorious angels, clothed in manly and splendid form. Hence the prophets, at this address "son of man," fall to the ground, struck with fear, and faint under the weight of the glory of the mighty and splendid angel Gabriel. From this they conclude that Jesus, by this title Son of man, everywhere designated himself to signify his abasement and servile form.

units.la: Verum multa vetant, quominus viris doctissimis hac in parte adstipulemur, 1° quia aliud est Filius hominis, aliud ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, h.e. filius hominis κατ' ἐξοχὴν. Jesus vero nunquam dixit, se esse υἱὸν ἀνθρώπου, sed emphaticè, constanter ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, quod singularem inter Filios hominum excellentiam significat. Si regeras cum doctissimo Grotio, articulum ὁ non semper excellentiam significare; sed saepe signum esse generalitatis, ut ὁ ἐθνικὸς Matth. 18:17. τῷ ἱερεῖ, Marc. 1:44. τὰ τέκνα, Apoc. 2:23. Respondemus, locis laudatis articulum esse distinctivum, & excellentiam significare, vel improbitatis & infamiae, vel officii: ut qui nec fratrem audit, nec Ecclesiam, habendus est ὁ ἐθνικὸς, id est excellenter nefas, & infamis, veluti gentilis, extra Ecclesiam positus. Ita homo lepra sua purgatus, jubetur se ostendere τῷ ἱερεῖ, id est, vel summo sacerdoti: vel illi singulari sacerdoti, qui tunc officio suo fungebatur in templo: ut ex Lev. 13:2. & 14:11. evidenter apparet. Filii vero Jezabel scorti spiritualis, dicuntur τὰ τέκνα, ut distinguantur articulo distinctivo, tanquam famosi & exosi, à Filiis Ecclesiae sponsae, pudicae, ac fidelis Christo sponso suo. Si regeras sicut בן אדם filius hominis, hominem sortis contemptae significat in Scriptura veteri, non secus & Jesum per excellentiam dici ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, ut vilissimam ac despicatissimam sortem suam significet. Christus, fatebor enim, in forma servi, vas & sponsor, vel vilissimorum peccatorum, hominum fuit abjectissimus: ut liquet ex Psalmo 22. & Es. 53. sed quominus voluerit hac sua filii hominis appellatione emphatica, sortem suam contemtissimam significare, obstat haec secunda ratio; nimirum haud decet summam Christi sapientiam, sortis contemptissimae appellationem cum summa gloria sua consociare; sapientissimè tamen & nomenclationem filii hominis, & exercitium infinitae majestatis, amicè consociavit, dum enim summa authoritate peccata remittit, & infinitam potentiam in sanando miraculosè paralytico exerit, se filium hominis amat nuncupare, Mat. 9:6.7. Cum se & templo Hierosolymitano majorem, & omnibus sacris ceremoniis superiorem docere intendit, infit ad Pharisaeos, κύριός ἐστι καὶ τοῦ σαββάτου ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, Dominus etiam sabbati est filius hominis, Mat. 12:8. Cum supremam, & ἀνεύθυνον orbem universum judicandi potestatem, sibi vindicat, ore rotundo asserit, Patrem sibi authoritatem dedisse judicium exercendi quia est filius hominis, & horam venire, quâ omnes, qui sunt in monumentis, audient vocem ejus, sc. filii hominis, & prodibunt qui bona fecerint in resurrectionem vitae, qui vero mala egerint in resurrectionem condemnationis, Joh. 5: 27. 28. 29. Cum futuram illam gloriam suam praenunciat, ciat, qua mortalibus conspicuum fiet, ipsum esse Deum & Dominum, vel ipsorum Angelorum, se filii hominis titulo insignire amat, Amen amen dico vobis, ab hoc tempore videbitis cœlum apertum, & Angelos Dei ascendentes & descendentes ad Filium hominis, Joh. 1: 51. ut significaret, Israelitas vigilantes visuros, quod Jacob eorum parens tantum in somnio viderat, se nimirum esse Deum illum Israelis, cui se præbent Angeli obsequiosos, Gen. 28:12. cum vigilantes, & propriis oculis, Angelos ad ejus nutum ascendentes & descendentes, admirabundi contemplabuntur, in agone montis Olivarum, in resurrectione, & triumphali ejusdem in cœlum ascensione. Cum denique supremam suæ divinitatis gloriam in ascensu atque triumpho de Diabolo, peccato, morte, & mundo futuro, mortalibus conspicuam prænunciat, signanter se filium hominis, atque sapienter dixit, Joh. 6:62. hoccine vos offendit, quid si igitur spectaveritis ☩ υἱὸν τῦ ἀνθρώπου, filium hominis eò ascendentem ubi erat prius? 3°. Cum omnes pro comperto & indubitato habeant, Jesum per resurrectionem, ascensum triumphalem, & sessionem ad dextram majestatis in excelsis, servi formam, & carnis abjectam conditionem deposuisse, ut Paulus pronunciare nullus dubitaverit, se non amplius nosse Christum secundum carnem, 2. Cor. 5:16. Christus semel ingressus in gloriam suam, honore ac gloria coronatus, nec foret nec diceretur filius hominis, siquidem ea nomenclatione uteretur, ad abjectissimam dierum carnis conditionem indigetandam. Secus tamen se res habet, Jesus enim vel dum in culmine gloriosæ suæ exaltationis apparebit, & est, & dicitur ὁ υἱὸς τῦ ἀνθρώπου, Mat. 16: 27. futurum est ut Filius hominis veniat cum gloria Patris sui, cum Angelis suis, & tunc retribuet unicuique secundum opera ipsius, & Mat. 24: 27. Sicut fulgur exit ab oriente, & apparet usque in occidentem, ita etiam erit adventus τῦ υἱῦ τῦ ἀνθρώπου, filii hominis, & verf. 30. 31. tunc apparebit signum τῦ υἱῦ τῦ ἀνθρώπου, filii hominis in cœlo, & tunc omnes tribus terræ plangent & videbunt ☩ υἱὸν τῦ ἀνθρώπου, filium hominis, venientem in nubibus cœli cum potestate & gloria multa, & mittet Angelos suos cum tuba voce magna, & cogent electos ejus ex quatuor ventis. Hic vero omnia divinæ majestatis insignia cernere est, 1°. summam authoritatem, orbem judicandi, 2°. nubem Dei currum ac magnificentiam Deut. 33: 26. Ps. 104:3. 3°. Angelorum satellitium; 4°. Electorum à quatuor mundi cardinibus collectionem. Sambucam vero citius caloni aptaveris alto, quam tot supremi numinis insignia, vermi non homini, probro & retrimento hominum, Jesu vilissimæ ac despicatissimæ conditionis, in quam indigetandam unicè, collimasse contendunt hanc filii hominis nomenclationem. Denique Proto-
units.tr: Yet many things prevent me from agreeing with these learned men on this point. First, the phrase Filius hominis is one thing, and ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου [the Son of Man] is another, that is, the son of man par excellence [κατ' ἐξοχήν]. Jesus never said that he was υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου [a son of man], but always, emphatically, ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου [the Son of Man], which signifies his unique excellence among the sons of men. If you object with the learned Grotius that the article ὁ does not always signify excellence but is often a sign of generality, as in ὁ ἐθνικὸς [the Gentile] in Matt. 18:17, τῷ ἱερεῖ [to the priest] in Mark 1:44, and τὰ τέκνα [the children] in Rev. 2:23, we reply that in the passages cited the article is distinctive and signifies excellence, either of wickedness and infamy or of office. He who will not hear the brother or the Church is to be regarded as ὁ ἐθνικὸς [the Gentile], that is, pre-eminently a villain and infamous, like a heathen placed outside the Church. So the man cleansed of his leprosy is ordered to show himself τῷ ἱερεῖ [to the priest], that is, either to the high priest or to that particular priest who then discharged his office in the temple, as is plain from Lev. 13:2 and 14:11. The sons of Jezebel, the spiritual harlot, are called τὰ τέκνα [the children], so that they may be distinguished by the distinctive article, as infamous and hateful, from the children of the Church, the chaste and faithful bride of her spouse Christ. If you object that בן אדם [ben adam], son of man, in the Old Testament denotes a man of despised condition, and that in the same way Jesus is called by excellence ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου [the Son of Man] to signify his most vile and despised lot, I shall admit that Christ, in the form of a servant, a surety and bearer of the sins of the vilest sinners, was the most abject of men, as is clear from Psalm 22 and Isaiah 53. But the second reason stands in the way of thinking that he wished by this emphatic title "Son of Man" to signify his most contemptible condition: it is not fitting that the supreme wisdom of Christ should join the title of the most contemptible lot with his own supreme glory. Yet most wisely he joined the name Son of Man with the exercise of infinite majesty in a friendly way. For when with supreme authority he forgives sins, and exerts infinite power in miraculously healing the paralytic, he loves to name himself the Son of Man (Matt. 9:6–7). When he intends to teach that he is greater than the temple of Jerusalem and superior to all the sacred ceremonies, he says to the Pharisees: κύριός ἐστι καὶ τοῦ σαββάτου ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου [the Son of Man is Lord also of the sabbath], the Son of Man is also Lord of the sabbath (Matt. 12:8). When he claims for himself the supreme and unaccountable power of judging the whole world, he declares with full voice that the Father has given him authority to execute judgment because he is the Son of Man, and that the hour is coming in which all who are in the graves will hear his voice, that is, the voice of the Son of Man, and those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil to the resurrection of condemnation (John 5:27–29). When he foretells that future glory of his, by which he will become visible to mortals, that he is God and the Lord even of the angels themselves, he loves to mark himself with the title Son of Man: Verily, verily, I say unto you, hereafter you shall see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man (John 1:51). By this he meant that the Israelites, awake, would see what their father Jacob had seen only in a dream, namely that he is that God of Israel to whom the angels show obedience (Gen. 28:12), when they, awake and with their own eyes, will marvel at the angels ascending and descending at his nod: in the agony on the Mount of Olives, in the resurrection, and in his triumphal ascent into heaven. Finally, when he foretells the supreme glory of his divinity, visible to mortals, in his ascent and his triumph over the devil, sin, death and the world, he marks himself especially and wisely as the Son of Man, saying: Does this offend you? What if then you shall see the Son of Man ascending where he was before? (John 6:62). 3. Since everyone holds it as established and beyond doubt that Jesus, through the resurrection, his triumphal ascent and his session at the right hand of majesty on high, laid aside the form of a servant and the abject condition of the flesh, as Paul did not hesitate to declare, that he no longer knew Christ according to the flesh (2 Cor. 5:16), then Christ, once he had entered into his glory and been crowned with honour and glory, would neither be nor be called the Son of Man, if he were to use that name to designate the most abject condition of the days of his flesh. Yet the matter stands otherwise: Jesus, both when he appears in the height of his glorious exaltation and in being so, is and is called ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου [the Son of Man]. Matt. 16:27: The Son of Man is going to come in the glory of his Father, with his angels, and then he will render to each according to his deeds. Matt. 24:27: As lightning comes out of the east and shines even to the west, so also will be the coming of the Son of Man. Verses 30–31: Then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven, and then all the tribes of the earth will mourn and will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory, and he will send his angels with a loud trumpet voice, and they will gather his elect from the four winds. Here indeed one may see all the marks of divine majesty: first, supreme authority to judge the world; second, God's cloud as his chariot and his magnificence (Deut. 33:26; Ps. 104:3); third, the retinue of angels; fourth, the gathering of the elect from the four corners of the world. You would sooner fit a sambuca to a lofty ... than fit all these marks of the supreme Deity to a worm and not a man, to a disgrace and refuse of men, to Jesus of the most lowly and despised condition, for whose sake alone, they contend, this name Son of Man was aimed at. Finally, the first-

units.la: Proto-Martyr Stephanus, intentis in coelum oculis, gloriam Dei cernit, & filium hominis adstantem ad dexteram Dei, Act. 7: 55.56. Conveniunt quidem rebus nomina saepe suis, quae homines haud tamen semper acutum cernentes, indidere. Ast conveniunt rebus nomina semper suis, quotquot sapientissimum numen rebus significandis adhibuit. Qui vero conveniet in gloria Dei constituto Domino nostro, filii hominis nomen, siquidem ad designandam formam servi ipsius, ac sortem contemptissimam dierum carnis institutum fuerit? Si regeras Jesum ad gloriam evectum, Filium hominis eo consilio Spiritum sanctum appellasse: ut significaret eundemmet Jesum, qui sortis fuit contemptissimae, jam vicibus commutatis, ad sortem gloriosissimam & supremam Majestatem evectum: haeret sane tibi aqua: laudati enim textus διαρρήδην pronunciant, Jesum gloria & honore coronatum, vel in ipsa gloria esse filium hominis, non enim dicit Martyr, se eum videre qui fuit filius hominis, sed ipsum filium hominis adstantem ad dexteram Dei, & Christus ipse testis fidelis asserit, fore ut homines videant filium hominis venientem in nubibus coeli, cum potestate & gloria multa. Unde libet argumentari, vel Jesus erit revera filius hominis, cum veniet in nubibus cum gloria Patris, vel non erit revera filius hominis: si posterius, non verum est filium hominis venturum, nedum homines visuros filium hominis, eorum enim quae non sunt, nulla sunt accidentia, nedum adventus. Si vero sit revera filius hominis, cum veniet stipatus omnibus supremae ac gloriosae majestatis insignibus, hinc quam evidentissime sequitur, Filium hominis nec significare abjectam Jesu conditionem, nec ipsum se hoc titulo insignitum voluisse, ad formam servi despicatissimam indigetandam, nulla enim in Jesu Angelorum myriadibus stipato, & veniente in nubibus coeli, apparebunt vestigia despicabilis formae servi.
units.tr: Proto-Martyr Stephen, with his eyes fixed on heaven, beholds the glory of God and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God (Acts 7:55–56). Names often agree with things, though men, who do not always see keenly, have assigned them; but names always agree with the things they signify, whenever the most wise Deity has employed them. How then could the name Son of Man, if it were established to designate the form of a servant and the most contemptible lot of the days of the flesh, agree with our Lord, now placed in glory? You may say that Jesus, raised to glory, by that design called the Holy Spirit the Son of Man, so that the same Jesus, who was of the most contemptible lot, now with the roles reversed, is raised to the most glorious lot and to supreme Majesty: your water indeed sticks fast. For the cited texts expressly declare that Jesus, crowned with glory and honour, is the Son of Man, or is the Son of Man in glory itself. The Martyr does not say that he sees him who was the Son of Man, but the Son of Man himself standing at the right hand of God, and Christ himself, the faithful witness, affirms that men will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and much glory. Hence one may argue: either Jesus will truly be the Son of Man when he comes on the clouds with the glory of the Father, or he will not truly be the Son of Man. If the latter, it is not true that the Son of Man is coming, much less that men will see the Son of Man, for there are no accidents of things that are not, much less of a coming. But if he truly is the Son of Man when he comes attended by all the marks of supreme and glorious majesty, it follows most evidently that the Son of Man signifies neither the abject condition of Jesus nor that he chose this title to designate the most despised form of a servant; for no trace of the despicable form of a servant will appear in Jesus, surrounded by myriads of angels and coming on the clouds of heaven.

units.la: Hinc colligas, quam aeque sit futilis Johannis Despaigne quaestio ac responsio, in Gallicis observationibus suis novellis, in symbolum fidei, nimirum cur Jesus Christus post suam resurrectionem non se amplius filium hominis appellaverit, sicut antea: Nam 10 Stephanus eodem quo Jesus Spiritu plenus, Jesum Christum non e mortuis modo excitatum, sed & in coelum evectum & ad dexteram Dei astantem, filium vocat hominis, Act.7:55.56. 2°. Ipse Christus ad finem mundi respiciens cum novissima die vivos ac mortuos judicabit, longo post suam resurrectionem intervallo, se filium hominis appellare amat, Mat. 13: 38. 39. 40. 41. 42. 43. Messis est consummatio saeculi, messores autem Angeli sunt. In consummatione saeculi hujus mittet filius hominis Angelos suos, qui colligent ex ipsius regno omnia offenoffendicula, & eos qui faciunt iniquitatem, & mittent eos in fornacem ignis, ibi erit fletus & stridor dentium, tunc justi fulgebunt sicut sol in regno Patris sui. Sed virum acris sane ingenii falsum habuit, male præconcepta opinio significationis & sensus nomenclaturæ τῷ υἱῷ τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ. Fuit enim in ea sententia, filium nempe hominis designare statum exinanitionis & passionum Christi, hinc putavit observatu dignum, Jesum non dixisse sicut antea, oportet filium hominis pati: sed oportuit pati Christum, & intrare in gloriam suam, Luc. 24:26. Verum ipse Christus qui dixerat, oportuit Christum pati, dixit, futurum est ut filius hominis tradatur in manus hominum & trucidabunt eum, sed tertia die resurget, Mat. 17:22. 23. & verf. 9. Nemini dixeritis visionem, donec filius hominis à mortuis resurgat, se igitur à mortuis resurgentem, vocat filium hominis. Est igitur vel in ipsa resurrectione, qua infirmitates omnes ac passiones deposuit vere filius hominis. Denique lubens scisciterer, num Christi nomenclatura, statum infirmitatis & passionum filii Dei includat nec ne? Si posterius, perperam dixerat Jesus, oportuisse Christum pati, nec Jesus qua Christus, fuerit sacerdos & victima afflictionibus consecrata, quod est plane ἀθεόλογον. Si prius, cum judice novello observatore nostro, Jesus post resurrectionem sese abstinuerit ab appellatione filii hominis, quod ea statum infirmitatis & passiones includat ac consignificet, eadem de causa & sese ab appellatione Christi, post resurrectionem abstinuisset.
units.tr: Hence you may see how equally futile is the question and answer of Jean Despaigne, in his new Gallic observations on the creed: namely, why Jesus Christ, after his resurrection, did not call himself the Son of man any more, as he had before. For (1) Stephen, full of the same Spirit as Jesus, calls Jesus Christ, not only raised from the dead but also taken up into heaven and standing at the right hand of God, the Son of man (Acts 7:55, 56). (2) Christ himself, looking to the end of the world, when on the last day he will judge the living and the dead, long after his resurrection, likes to call himself the Son of man (Matt. 13:38–43): The harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are angels. At the end of this age the Son of man will send out his angels, who will gather out of his kingdom all the stumbling blocks and those who do iniquity, and will cast them into the furnace of fire; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. But that acute man was mistaken, through a badly preconceived opinion about the meaning and sense of the name τῷ υἱῷ τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ [the Son of man]. He held the view that the title Son of man denotes the state of humiliation and sufferings of Christ. Hence he thought it worth noting that Jesus did not say, as before, the Son of man must suffer, but said that Christ had to suffer and enter into his glory (Luke 24:26). But Christ himself, who had said that Christ must suffer, also said: The Son of man is going to be delivered into the hands of men, and they will kill him, but on the third day he will rise (Matt. 17:22, 23), and in verse 9: Tell the vision to no one until the Son of man is raised from the dead. So he calls himself the Son of man when rising from the dead. Therefore the Son of man is truly so even in the resurrection itself, by which he laid aside all infirmities and sufferings. Finally, I would gladly ask whether the name Christ includes the state of infirmity and sufferings of the Son of God or not. If not, Jesus spoke wrongly when he said that Christ had to suffer, and Jesus as Christ would not have been a priest and victim consecrated by afflictions, which is plainly ἀθεόλογον [contrary to sound theology]. If so, then, according to our new judge and observer, Jesus after his resurrection would have refrained from the title Son of man, because it includes and co-signifies the state of infirmity and sufferings; for the same reason he would also have refrained from the title Christ after his resurrection.

units.la: Aliis, in quibus Camero ὁ μακαρίτης, in contrariam delapsis ὑπερξολὴν, Filium hominis, nunquam dici de Christo per contemptum, visum est: sed constanter significare illustrem Christi personam, sublimi munere mediatorio ornatam. Verum equidem est, Jesum non ea mente se filium hominis appellasse, ut contemptam sortem suam hoc titulo significaret: sicut solidis hactenus rationibus addiximus: sed ne, ad illustrem personam suam significandam usurpasse, ut sentiamus, hæc rationum momenta vetant. 1°. Quia Christus in forma servi, gloriosa formâ Dei evacuatus, pauperrimus, despicatissimus, vermis, non homo, crucifixus, vas & sponsor vilissimorum peccatorum, sub eo sane schemate non sese offert contemplandum, ut illustrem personam: veruntamen supra vidimus, Iesum in statu despicabili humilitatis ac κενώσεως suæ, ad maledictam ac ignominiosam usque mortem crucis, consideratum, titulo filii hominis insignitum, quasi diceret se inter omnes filios hominis, unum esse ὁ ἐξοχὴν, τὸν υἱὸν τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ, filium hominis, miserrimum ac despicatissimum. 2°. Quia per contemptum, filius hominis appellatur: Psal. 8:5. & Heb. 2:6. Quod infra quæstione ad id deputata, solidis rationibus σὺν Θεῷ addicemus.
units.tr: Others, in whom Camerarius, of blessed memory, has seen fit to fall into the opposite excess, have held that the Son of man is never said of Christ with contempt, but always signifies the illustrious person of Christ, adorned with the lofty mediatorial office. It is true, indeed, that Jesus did not call himself the Son of man with the intention of signifying by this title his despised lot, as we have hitherto argued with solid reasons. But that he used it to signify his illustrious person, so that we should understand it that way, these weighty considerations forbid. (1) Because Christ, in the form of a servant, emptied of the glorious form of God, most poor, most despised, a worm and not a man, crucified, the vessel and surety of the most vile sinners, does not under that aspect present himself to be contemplated as an illustrious person. Yet we have seen above that Jesus, considered in the despised state of his humiliation and κένωσις [emptying], even to the cursed and shameful death of the cross, was marked with the title Son of man, as if to say that among all the sons of men he was, ὁ ἐξοχήν [pre-eminently], τὸν υἱὸν τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ [the Son of man], the most wretched and most despised. (2) Because the Son of man is used with contempt: Psalm 8:5 and Heb. 2:6. We shall add solid reasons, with God's help, to this point below in the question devoted to it.

units.la: B
units.tr: B

units.la: 3°. Quia ut ut filius hominis Christum, h. e. Iesum, munere mediatorio functum, significet, non sequitur tamen ad illustrem suam personam designandam, titulum filii hominis sibi tribuisse: nam ut ut filius Dei, secundum æternam personam suam spectatus, sit Dominus gloriæ, non sequitur tamen personam Christi mediatoris, quà vices personamque probrosorum peccatorum gerebat, vas atque sponsor eorum, factus peccatum & maledictio pro iis, & sub schemate hirci expiatorii, ἀποπομπαῖος, sub lege repræsentatus, illustrem fuisse personam, sed vile potius ac despicabile caput, maledictioni ac supplicio crucis addictum & obnoxium.
units.tr: (3) Although the Son of man signifies Christ, that is, Jesus, who performed the mediatorial office, it does not follow that he assumed the title Son of man to designate his illustrious person. For although the Son of God, considered according to his eternal person, is the Lord of glory, it does not follow that the person of Christ the mediator, who in place and person of the reproached sinners, becoming their vessel and surety, made sin and curse for them, and under the figure of the scapegoat, ἀποπομπαῖος [sent away], was represented under the law, was an illustrious person; rather he was a vile and despicable head, given over to curse and to the punishment of the cross, and liable to it.

units.la: Quorsum igitur tendit hæc Filii hominis appellatio? Ad quid tandem designandum identidem repetita ac inculcata fuit ab ipso Iesu? Respondemus filium hominis non modò hominem significare, sed & hominem qui ab homine originem duxit, ut medicorum filii, non modo medicos sonat, sed & qui derivatam ab aliis medicis scientiam medicinam in se traduxerunt: Iesum tamen Dei filium se fere semper appellasse ὁ υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, non ut Iudæis indigetaret se esse hominem, sed verum Messiam, seu Christum promissum, ab ipso hominis lapsu, & identidem Abrahamo ac Davidi repromissum, ut & per Prophetas creberrimè prænunciatum. Nostra sententia hisce nititur fundamentis. Primum, Sternitur ex collatione quatuor Euangelistarum, quæ nos aperte docet Iesum nomine Christi ac nomine τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου tanquam nominibus ἱσοδυναμοῦντι usum fuisse. Pontifici Maximo Iesum in Synedrio adjuranti per Deum viventem, ut diceret num esset Christus filius Dei? respondet Iesus, tu dixisti: quin etiam dico vobis ab hoc tempore videbitis filium hominis sedentem ad dexteram potentiæ Dei, & venientem in nubibus cæli, Mat. 26: 64. Rursum Pontifex Maximus eum interrogavit & dixit; tune es Christus Filius benedicti? Iesus autem dixit, ego sum, & videbitis Filium hominis sedentem ad dexteram potentiæ, & venientem in nubibus cæli. Mar. 14: 61. 62. Si tu es Christus dic nobis? quibus Iesus, si vobis dixero non credetis: ab hoc tempore filius hominis sedebit ad dexteram potentiæ Dei, Luc. 22: 67. 69. Audiatur & Johannes. Cum Andreas fratri Simoni dixisset, invenimus Messiam, quod est interpretatum Christus, & Philippus Nathanaeli, invenimus illum de quo Moses scripsit in lege & Prophetæ, Nathanaeli confesso Iesum esse Messiam, Rabbi tu es Filius Dei, tu es Rex Israël, insignibus ut liquet elogiis, quibus & Prophetæ & Iudaica gens Messiam ornabat 1. Chron. 17: 13. Ps. 2: 7. & 89: 27. Iesus illico reponit, Quia dixi tibi, vidi te sub ficu credis, majora ipsis videbis. Amen amen dico vobis, ab hoc tempore videbitis cœlum apertum tum & Angelos Dei ascendentes & descendentes ad filium hominis. Joh. 1: 42. 46. 49. 50. 51. Hinc mero meridie clarius liquet Christum & filium hominis, nomina esse ejusdem plane valoris ac significationis; quaerentibus enim ac loquentibus de Christo, Jesus reponit se esse filium hominis. Secundum Fundamentum praestruitur ex consideratione locorum ubi Jesus se filium hominis, appellare amat, cum ea sibi tribuit quae Prophetae Messiam praestiturum, passurum, vel ex passione reportaturum praedixerant, ut fidem de Messia venturo facerent, & totidem velut illustribus characteribus dum veniret cognoscendum exhiberent. Prophetae praedixerant Messiam fore pauperrimum, Surculus exibit ex trunco Isai, & virgultum ex radicibus ejus, Es. 11: 1. Ascendit ut surculus coram Jehova, & ut radix e terra siticulosa, sine forma, sine pulchritudine eum vidimus, nec aliquid aspectabile vidimus, cur eum desideraremus, despectus fuit, homo dolorum, &c. Es. 53: 2. 3. Jesus dum eo respicit & paupertatem suam ac statum despicabilem Scribam docet, diserte se filium hominis appellare amat, Vulpes, inquit, habent lustra, & volucres coeli nidos, at filius hominis non habet ubi caput reclinet, Mat. 8: 20. Dum Christus miracula ipsamet edit, quibus fore ut inclaresceret Messias, Esaias vaticinatus fuerat. Es. 35: 4. 5. 6. & quaerentibus Johannis discipulis, num sit Christus venturus, titulo, filii hominis ad multitudinem conversus seipsum condecorat, Mat. 11: 5. 19. Prophetae Messiae passiones, genus & circumstantias mortis praedixerant. Ps. 22: 17. 18. 19. Es. 53: 4. 5. 6. 7. 8. 9. Jesus vero mortem suam crucis praenuncians, diserte sese filium hominis vocat. Mat. 26: 2. Joh. 3: 14. Prophetae Messiam e mortuis resurrecturum vaticinati erant. Ps. 16: 9. 10. 11. Es. 53: 10. Iesus vero suam e mortuis resurrectionem praenuncians, filii hominis elogio se ipsum insignit, Mat. 17: 9. Prophetae Messiae sepulturam praedixerant, Es. 53: 9. Jesus vero sepulturam suam dum praenunciat, titulo filii hominis gaudet, sicut Jonas fuit in ventre ceti tres dies & tres noctes, ita filius hominis erit in corde terrae tres dies & tres noctes, Mat. 12. 40. Prophetae Messiam in coelum ascensurum pompa triumphali vaticinabantur, Ps. 68: 19. Iesus vero dum ascensionem suam futuram memorat, titulo filii hominis iterum gaudet, Quid igitur si videritis filium hominis eo ascendentem ubi erat prius? Ioh. 6: 62. Sessurum ad dexteram Dei Messiam, Prophetae promiserant. Ps. 110: 1. Iesus vero, sessionem suam ad dexteram Dei futuram dum praemonet, titulo filii hominis sese commendat, Praeterea dico vobis in posterum videbitis filium hominis sedentem ad dexteram Majestatis & venientem in nubibus coeli, Mat. 26: 64. Mar. 14: 62. Luc. 22: 69. Hinc evidentissime paret Iesum se filium hominis constanter appelappellare, ubivis docet, impleta iri in sese quotquot momentosa Prophetæ de Christo prædixerant, ut Christum & filium hominis synonyma plane nomina juremerito dixeris. Unde nihil admirationis subest, cum in novo Instrumento filii hominis nomenclatura, modo cum passionibus ac statu humili & despicabili Christi; modo cum gloria & majestate ipsius conjuncta videtur, prædixerant enim sacri vates, quia res erat futura necessario, filium hominis, seu Christum sub statu duplici, contemptus nimirum & gloriæ, alternis vicibus futurum. Non minus igitur à veritatis tramite abiere doctissimi viri, qui filii hominis nomenclaturam in humilitatem & contemptam Christi sortem unicè collimare, quam qui delapsi in contrariam hyperbolen, in magnitudinem ac gloriam Christi personalem commendandam respicere, sunt opinati. Tertium, Sententiæ nostræ fundamentum exstat, Ioh. 12: 34. ubi Iudæorum multitudo, audita filii hominis futura in crucem elatione, admirabunda reponit, audivimus ex lege, Christum manere in æternum, quomodo igitur tu dicis oportere tolli filium hominis? quis est iste filius hominis? unde concludere tam est in proclivi, quam imber dum pluit, & Iesum & Iudæorum multitudinem, Christum atque filium hominis pro uno eodemque usurpare.
units.tr: Toward what, then, does this title Son of man tend? To what end was it repeatedly stated and impressed by Jesus himself? We reply that the Son of man means not only man but a man who derives his origin from man, as sons of physicians means not only physicians but those who have taken over into themselves the medicine they derived from other physicians. Yet Jesus almost always called himself the Son of man, ὁ υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου [the Son of man], not so as to tell the Jews that he was a man, but to show that he was the true Messiah, or the promised Christ, promised from the very fall of man, and repeatedly promised to Abraham and David, and very often foretold by the prophets. Our view rests on these foundations. First, it is established by comparing the four Evangelists, which plainly teaches us that Jesus used the name Christ and the name τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου [of the Son of man] as names ἰσοδυναμοῦντα [of equal force]. When the High Priest adjured Jesus in the Sanhedrin by the living God to say whether he was the Christ, the Son of God, Jesus answered: You have said it; moreover I tell you that from now on you will see the Son of man sitting at the right hand of the power of God and coming on the clouds of heaven (Matt. 26:64). Again the High Priest questioned him and said: Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed? And Jesus said: I am; and you will see the Son of man sitting at the right hand of power and coming on the clouds of heaven (Mark 14:61, 62). If you are the Christ, tell us? To whom Jesus said: If I tell you, you will not believe; from now on the Son of man will sit at the right hand of the power of God (Luke 22:67, 69). Let John also be heard. When Andrew said to his brother Simon, We have found the Messiah, which is interpreted Christ, and Philip to Nathanael, We have found him of whom Moses wrote in the law and the prophets, and Nathanael confessed that Jesus was the Messiah, Rabbi, you are the Son of God, you are the King of Israel, these are, as is clear, the distinguished titles with which both the prophets and the Jewish nation adorned the Messiah (1 Chron. 17:13; Ps. 2:7; 89:27). Jesus at once replied: Because I said to you, I saw you under the fig tree, do you believe? You will see greater things than these. Amen, amen, I say to you, from now on you will see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man (John 1:42, 46, 49–51). Hence it is clearer than midday that Christ and Son of man are names of plainly the same value and meaning; for when people asked about and spoke of Christ, Jesus answered that he was the Son of man. The second foundation is laid by considering the passages where Jesus likes to call himself the Son of man, when he claims for himself what the prophets had foretold the Messiah would do, suffer, or obtain from his suffering, so as to make faith in the coming Messiah and to present them, as it were, as illustrious marks by which he might be recognised when he came.
