As if he said: afflicted nation of the Jews, raised by God to hope for the promised son, the seed of the woman who was to be born, dry your tears, rejoice, exult; behold the child, expected through long ages since the fall of Adam, the promised Son, is at last born to us, given to us by God. Do not doubt, I beg you: he will be wonderful by the manner of his birth from a virgin without a man, and by the wonderful personal union of the divine and human natures; but he will also be Mighty God, so that he may crush the head of the serpent and deliver us from the harsh bondage of the devil, of sin, and of death. And from this memorable victory and so great a deliverance he will bring back an eternal kingdom, for the government was laid upon his shoulder. He will reign, but as counsellor to his subjects in unblemished obedience and in faithfulness unbroken even unto death, as prince and author of immortal life and eternal happiness. Believe me, for this is why he will be called Counsellor, Everlasting Father, and Prince of Peace.

units.la: Observa 6°. Quò tempus nasciturî promissi feminis benedicti accedebat propiùs, hoc Judæos ardentius ejus adventum exspectasse, eo ipso tempore, quo Jesus noster in mundum venit, persuasos scilicet Messiam proximè venturum, tum quia sceptrum Judæ, hoc est, Judaicæ gentis suprema authoritas, inclinabat in finem: tum quia Danielis hebdomades, præstitutum Messiæ tempus, non procul aberant à complemento. Hanc de Messia proximè venturo Judæorum certitudinem, tum historia Johannis Baptistæ, tum frequentissimus ad ipsius baptisma Judæorum concursus, luculenter demonstrant. Et 1°. quidem supremum Judæorum Synedrium, Sacerdotes ac Levitas è secta Pharisæorum, ad Johannem mittunt scisci-tatum, quis esset? num Elias? num Propheta? ipsi vero neganti reponunt, Cur baptizas, cum nec Christus sis, nec Elias, nec Propheta? Joh. 1: 19. 21. 24. 25. Quid verò frequentissimum, ac fervidissimum concursum universæ gentis Judaicæ ad Johannis baptisma exciverat? Respondet Evangelista, ut fugerent iram futuram, h. e. sæverum Dei judicium, quod Prophetæ nationi sub Messiæ adventum interminabantur, Joel. 2: 10. 11. 30. 31. Verum & Simeon & Anna prophetissa tunc demum Israelis consolationem præstolabantur. Hinc Pharisæi à Jesu quærunt quo tempore adveniet regnum Dei? Luc. 17: 20. Denique ita Judæi persuasi erant de impleto tempore adventus Messiæ, ut sub imperatore Adriano anno quinquagesimo simo secundo à templi vastatione, impostor vaferrimus בר כוכב filius stella, & se Messiam superciliosè venditaverit, & sub speciosò Messiæ titulo ab ipso Rabbi Akibha, qui viginti quatuor millia discipulorum habuit, palam promulgatus fuerit, his verbis חיינו מלכא משיחא En ipsum Regem Messiam. Impostura sua miseram gentem æternum irretiisset, ni Imperator Adrianus male feriatum impostorem cum sectariis suis funditus delevisset, unde eum mutato pauxillum nomine בר כוזבא vel כזיבא, filium mendacii, vel falsum & mendacem Messiam, quàm primùm suum sensit errorem, delusa natio, appellitavit.
units.tr: Observe, sixthly, that as the time of the promised blessed seed of the woman drew nearer, the Jews awaited his coming the more eagerly; and at the very time when our Jesus came into the world they were persuaded that the Messiah would come soon, both because the sceptre of Judah, that is, the supreme authority of the Jewish nation, was declining toward its end, and because the weeks of Daniel, the appointed time for the Messiah, were not far from their fulfilment. The history of John the Baptist and the very large crowds of Jews who came to his baptism clearly show this certainty of the Jews about the Messiah being soon to come. First, indeed, the supreme Jewish council sent priests and Levites from the sect of the Pharisees to ask John: who are you? Are you Elijah? Are you the prophet? And when he denied it, they replied: Why do you baptize, if you are neither the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the prophet? (John 1:19, 21, 24, 25). What indeed had drawn such a very large and fervent crowd of the whole Jewish nation to John's baptism? The Evangelist answers: that they might flee from the coming wrath, that is, the severe judgment of God, which the prophets had threatened upon the nation at the coming of the Messiah (Joel 2:10, 11, 30, 31). Indeed Simeon and the prophetess Anna were then waiting for the consolation of Israel. Hence the Pharisees ask Jesus: when will the kingdom of God come? (Luke 17:20). Finally, the Jews were so persuaded that the time of the Messiah's coming had been fulfilled that in the fifty-second year after the destruction of the temple, under the emperor Hadrian, the most crafty impostor Bar Kokhba [בר כוכב], that is, son of the star, proclaimed himself the Messiah with arrogance, and was openly announced under the specious title of Messiah by Rabbi Akiba himself, who had twenty-four thousand disciples, with these words: Behold our King the Messiah [חיינו מלכא משיחא]. His imposture would have ensnared the wretched nation forever, had not the emperor Hadrian utterly destroyed the most cunning impostor together with his followers. Afterwards, when the deluded nation perceived its error, it called him, with a slight change of name, Bar Kozeba or Kziba [בר כוזבא, כזיבא], that is, son of a lie, or the false and lying Messiah.

units.la: Observa 7o. Judæos de Messia proximè venturo, dum Jesus in terris ageret persuasos, fluctuasse incertos de origine ac modo adventus ejus, num scilicet oriundus esset è vivis, num è mortuis, quod paret 1o. quia Judæi hac potissimum ratione ducti, Jesum Messiam confiteri nolunt quod nossent unde, & ex quibus parentibus oriundus: nonne ipse est ille Iesus, Filius ille Iosephi, cujus nos novimus patrem ac matrem, Joh. 6: 42. Sed novimus unde hic sit, cùm autem venerit Christus, nemo noverit unde sit, Joh. 7: 27. 2o. Ex Talmude Hierosolymitano in Berachot, sol. 5. his verbis, Post hæc convertentur Filii Israëlis, & requirent Dominum Deum suum, & Davidem Regem suum, Hos. 3: 5. Rabbini nostri dicunt: si è vivis sit ille, David est nomen ejus: si è mortuis sit ille, David est nomen ejus. Et Talmud. Babylon. in Sanedrin, sol. 98. Rab dicit, si Messia sit è vivis Rabbenou Hakkadosch ille est. Et Glossa, si Messia sit ex iis qui jam vivunt, certè Rabbi noster Sanctus ille est, quippe, qui portet infirmitates. Nec eos modò exercitos habuit modus ac ratio adventus Messiæ: sed & modus atque ratio adventus prodromorum ipsius, cum enim ex Malachia, Eliam futurum Messiæ prodromum didicissent, penduli hærebant, num è vivis vel è mortuis in Messiæ adventum Elias, vel Jeremias, vel singularis alius Propheta esset excitandus, unde Jesu nostro percunctanti, quem me dicunt esse homines, discipulorum nomine Petrus reponit, alii Iohannem Baptistam, alii Eliam; alii Jeremiam, aut unum ex Prophetis; Mat. 16: 14.
units.tr: Observe, seventhly, that while Jesus was on earth, the Jews, persuaded that the Messiah was soon to come, wavered uncertain about the origin and manner of his coming: whether, namely, he would be from among the living or from among the dead. This appears, first, because the Jews, led chiefly by this consideration, refuse to confess Jesus as the Messiah, since they knew whence he was and from what parents: Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? (John 6:42). But we know where this man is from; but when the Christ comes, no one will know where he is from (John 7:27). Second, from the Jerusalem Talmud in Berakhot, folio 5, with these words: After these things the children of Israel will return and seek the LORD their God and David their king (Hos. 3:5). Our rabbis say: if he is from among the living, David is his name; if he is from among the dead, David is his name. And the Babylonian Talmud in Sanhedrin, folio 98: Rab says, if the Messiah is from among the living, that one is our Rabbi the Holy One. And the Gloss: if the Messiah is from among those who are now living, certainly our Holy Rabbi is that one, since he bears our infirmities. Not only the manner and the reason of the Messiah's coming troubled them, but also the manner and reason of the coming of his forerunners. For since they had learned from Malachi that Elijah would come as the forerunner of the Messiah, they were in doubt whether Elijah, or Jeremiah, or some other singular prophet, was to be raised from the living or from the dead for the Messiah's coming. Hence when our Jesus asked, who do men say that I am?, Peter answered in the name of the disciples: some say John the Baptist, others Elijah, others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets (Matt. 16:14).

units.la: Observa 8o. Judæos persuasos de Messia proximè venturo, Iesu nostro in terris πολλευομένῳ, fluctuasse tamen incertos, num unus foret Messias, an duo: ut tandem in hanc ultimam delapsi sententiam, Messias ambos statuerint, alterum Iosephi filium, vilem ac despicabilem, asinoque vehentem, quem in Talmude Babylonico tractatu Sanedrim. cap. 11. Ad portam Romæ jacentem inter ægrotos ac leprosos, fabulantur. Alterum Davidis Filium, Regem præpotentem ac magnificum, quod scilicet Scriptura Messiam exhibeat modo vilem, despicabilem, ac afflictum hominem, nem, Pf.22:7.8. Ef.53: 3.4. Et asino vehentem Zach.9: 9. Interdum virum magnificum, victorem præpotentem, ac Regem triumphantem in nubibus. Ef.63: 1. 2. 3. 4. Dan. 7: 23. 24.
units.tr: Observe, eighthly, that the Jews, persuaded that the Messiah was soon to come while our Jesus lived on earth [πολιτευομένῳ], nevertheless wavered uncertain whether there would be one Messiah or two. At last they fell into this final opinion, that the Messiah was both: one, the son of Joseph, a base and despised man who rode on an ass, whom the Babylonian Talmud in tractate Sanhedrin, chapter 11, fables as lying at the gate of Rome among the sick and the lepers; the other, the son of David, a mighty and magnificent king. This was because Scripture presents the Messiah sometimes as a man only base, despised, and afflicted (Ps. 22:7, 8; Isa. 53:3, 4), and riding on an ass (Zech. 9:9), and sometimes as a magnificent man, a mighty victor and a king triumphing in the clouds (Isa. 63:1, 2, 3, 4; Dan. 7:23, 24).

units.la: Observa 9o. Judæos de proximo adventu Messiæ persuasos: sed & addictos rebus sensibilibus, divitiis ac pompæ sæculi, heu nimium inhiantes, sibi finxisse Messiam Regem præpotentem, qui & exercitus duceret, & gentium reges ac Judæorum hostes per orbem universum profligaret, victorias illustres reportaret, triumphos ageret, & regnum Israelis instauraret florentissimum, regnoque Davidis ac Salomonis quàm simillimum, quique lauta subditis convivia instrueret, & carnem Behemot, & avis Zis immensæ magnitudinis, dapes regias apponeret, & generosissimum vinum ex uvis paradisi terrestris propinaret bibendum. Hinc Christus scisscitantibus Pharisæis, quando venturum erat Dei regnum, reddidit: regnum Dei non veniet μετὰ παρατηρήσεως, cum observatione, Luc. 17: 20. Hinc Judæorum multitudo, miraculosa panum multiplicatione satiata, Iesum sequitur, & in Regem sibi constituere affectat, deliberato consilio, eum esse spectatum sibi Messiam, rata, ut vitam bonis omnibus cumulatissimam vivat sub ejus imperio, quem penes erat, tenuem panum hordeaceorum annonam, solo nutu in victum multis hominum millibus sufficientissimum multiplicare, Ioh. 6: 25. Hinc nata inter Christi discipulos, animique contentione exagitata quæstio, Quisnam eorum maximus in regno cœlorum futurus? Mat. 18: 1. Hinc mater filiorum Zebedæi, ad pedes Christi provoluta, vehementer efflagitat, ut daret filiis suis sedere, alteri ad dextram, alteri ad sinistram in regno suo, Mat. 20: 21.
units.tr: Observe, ninth, that the Jews, convinced of the Messiah's imminent coming but also devoted to sensible things and eagerly longing for riches and worldly pomp, imagined a mighty king as Messiah. He would lead armies, crush the kings of the nations and the enemies of the Jews throughout the whole world, win brilliant victories, celebrate triumphs, and restore a most flourishing kingdom of Israel, very like the kingdom of David and Solomon. He would set up lavish banquets for his subjects, serve royal dishes of the flesh of Behemoth and of the birds Ziz, of immense size, and pour out for them the finest wine from the grapes of the earthly paradise to drink. Hence, when the Pharisees asked when the kingdom of God was coming, Christ answered that the kingdom of God does not come μετὰ παρατηρήσεως [with observation] (Luke 17:20). Hence the multitude of Jews, satisfied by the miraculous multiplication of the loaves, followed Jesus and eagerly wanted to make him their king, having decided deliberately that he was the Messiah they had looked for, since they thought that under his rule they would live a life heaped with every good, he who had at hand the power to multiply, by a mere nod, the meagre supply of barley loaves enough for many thousands of people (John 6:25). Hence arose among Christ's disciples the question, sharpened by their contention of spirit, "Which of them would be the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?" (Matt. 18:1). Hence the mother of the sons of Zebedee, falling down at Christ's feet, urgently begged that he would grant that her sons sit, one at his right hand and the other at his left, in his kingdom (Matt. 20:21).

units.la: Observa 10. Judæos gloriosum Messiæ adventum ac regnum, in unam gentis Judaicæ liberationem ac felicitatem ratos ita spectare ἀκοινωνήτως, ut cæteras orbis nationes, non illius modò extorres ac exsortes futuras: sed & eodem pessundandas, ac funditus delendas opinarentur. Hinc illa discipulorum Emmaünticorum lamentabilis quærimonia, sperabamus Iesum Nazarenum illum esse, qui redempturus esset Israelem, Luc. 24: 21. Hinc nata hæc importuna Discipulorum ad Christum quæstio, num hoc tempore restitues regnum Israeli? Act. 1: 16. Hinc anxia Petri cunctatio, confirmataque animi aversio annunciandi Euangelium Romano Cornelio, cæterisque Ethnicis, quos uti immunda animantia, impuros habebat ac abominabatur, ut ter repetito miraculo vasis cœlitus delapsi, ad curandam male præconceptam de seclusis æternum regno cœlorum gentibus, opus fuerit, Act. 10: 14. 16. Errandi occasionem dederat, sinistre ac perperam intellectum Danielis vaticinium, de regno Messiæ, contrituro omnia regna, Dan. 2: 44. Fabulantur enim Regem Messiam armis, copiisque terrenis, Regem Idumæum aspero bello persecuturum, h. e. Imperatorem Romanorum, ejusque regnum destructurum & desolaturum, latamque hostium stragem editurum: unde Targum Hierosolymitanum, Ef. 63: 1. 2. 3. sic explicat, Messias occidet Reges & Principes, facietque fluvios sanguine occisionis eorum rubros: vestimenta ejus erunt sanguine imbuta. At Christi regnum non est hujus mundi, nec venit ut regna Regibus eriperet, qui homines constanter docuit, tribuenda esse Cæsari, quæ sunt Cæsaris. Regnum tamen Christi, quod præpotenti sceptro verbi ac Spiritus, in medio inimicorum suorum stabilitum venit, regna terrena conteret. 1°. Quia firmum, ac ineluctabile omnibus adversariorum insultibus permanebit, dum cætera Regum terrenorum imperia contrita dirutaque evanescent. 2°. Quia injustitiam, crudelitatem, violentiam ac impietatem, quibus ut plurimum stabiliuntur regna terrena, ac conservantur, ita conteret ac abolebit, ut qui ejus gratiâ pii Reges dominabuntur in populos, pietate ac justitia regnare in posterum videantur. Cæterum Regis Messiæ victoriæ, liberatio, benedictio ac felicitas, ad omnes terrarum orbis gentes spectant ac pertinent. Numen enim mentiri nescium, in semine Abrahami Christo, fore, ut omnes terræ nationes benedicerentur, sanctè recepit: Gen. 22: 18. Nec obstat, quod dixerit Christus, non sum missus nisi ad oves perditas domus Israëlis, Mat. 15: 24. Loquitur enim de sua ad Euangelium, in diebus carnis annunciandum missione, quæ ad gentem Judaicam unicè spectabat, unde minister circumcisionis dicitur, propter veritatem Dei, ad confirmandum datas Patribus promissiones, Rom. 15: 8. De cætero ipse Christus asserit se habere alias oves, quæ non sunt ex hac caula, h. e. ex natione Judaica. Illas quoque, inquit, oportet me adducere, (Apostolorum scilicet ministerio) nam vocem meam audient, fietque unus grex, & unus Pastor, Ioh. 10: 16.
units.tr: Observe, tenth, that the Jews, supposing the glorious coming and kingdom of the Messiah to be the liberation and happiness of the Jewish nation alone, viewed it ἀκοινωνήτως [akoinōnētōs, without fellowship], so that they thought the other nations of the world would not only be excluded and deprived of it, but would also be destroyed and utterly wiped out by the same means. Hence that sorrowful complaint of the disciples on the road to Emmaus: "We hoped that it was Jesus of Nazareth who would redeem Israel" (Luke 24:21). Hence this troublesome question of the disciples to Christ: "Will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?" (Acts 1:6). Hence Peter's anxious hesitation and the firmly rooted reluctance to announce the gospel to the Roman Cornelius and the other Gentiles, whom he regarded and loathed as unclean animals, so that the thrice-repeated miracle of the vessel let down from heaven was needed to cure this ill-conceived notion that the Gentiles were shut out for ever from the kingdom of heaven (Acts 10:14, 16). The occasion for error had been given by a prophecy of Daniel, wrongly and perversely understood, about the kingdom of the Messiah, which would crush all kingdoms (Dan. 2:44). For they imagined that the Messiah would pursue the Idumaean king, that is, the emperor of the Romans, with bitter war, armed with earthly forces, and would destroy and lay waste his kingdom and inflict a great slaughter on his enemies. Hence the Targum of Jerusalem explains Isaiah 63:1–3 thus: "The Messiah will kill kings and princes, and will make rivers red with the blood of their slaughter; his garments will be soaked in blood." But the kingdom of Christ is not of this world, nor did he come to snatch kingdoms from kings; he constantly taught men that the things that are Caesar's are to be given to Caesar. Yet the kingdom of Christ, which came established with the mighty sceptre of the Word and Spirit in the midst of its enemies, will crush earthly kingdoms. First, because it will remain firm and unshaken against all the assaults of its adversaries, while the other empires of earthly kings, broken and overthrown, will vanish. Second, because it will so crush and abolish injustice, cruelty, violence and impiety, by which earthly kingdoms are for the most part established and maintained, that pious kings who rule over peoples for its sake will appear to reign in future by piety and justice. Moreover, the victories, deliverance, blessing and happiness of the Messiah King pertain to and concern all the nations of the world. For God, who cannot lie, faithfully promised that in the seed of Abraham, that is Christ, all the nations of the earth would be blessed (Gen. 22:18). Nor does it stand in the way that Christ said, "I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel" (Matt. 15:24). For he speaks of his mission, in the days of his flesh, to proclaim the gospel, which pertained solely to the Jewish nation, "whence he is called a minister of the circumcision, for the sake of the truth of God, to confirm the promises given to the fathers" (Rom. 15:8). Elsewhere Christ himself asserts that he has other sheep which are not of this fold, that is, of the Jewish nation. "Those also," he says, "I must bring (namely by the ministry of the apostles), for they will hear my voice, and there will be one flock and one Shepherd" (John 10:16).

units.la: Observa 1°. Judæos Iesum nostrum non modò pro mero habuisse homine: sed & pro filio Josephi ac Mariæ, vilissimoque homuncione Nazarethano, Math. 13: 55. Mar. 6: 3. Luc. 4: 22. Ioh. 6: 42.
units.tr: Observe, first, that the Jews not only regarded our Jesus as a mere man, but also as the son of Joseph and Mary, and as a most base little man of Nazareth (Matt. 13:55; Mark 6:3; Luke 4:22; John 6:42).

units.la: Præmissis observationibus. Primæ quæstioni respondemus, Danielem, triumphantem Messiam in nubibus, ac in regnum suum venientem, appellasse בר אנוש filium hominis, ægritudine ac peccati miseriis laborantis, duabus imprimis de causis. 1°. Quia prophetiam suam scripsit in Chaldæa: est verò solemnis Syris ac Chaldæis, vernacula dialecto hominem vocare בר נושא, vel בר אנוש. 2°. Eò lubentius Prophetam, Messiam triumphantem, familiari genti Chaldæae, ubi tunc degebat, dialecto בר אנוש nuncupasse, ut Israelitarum è transmigratione animos ad primam Messiæ promissiomissionem, quae exstat Gen. 3:15. recolendam eveheret. Caph enim praefixum ב̇ non est Caph Hebraeorum כ similitudinis: sed Caph אמיתת veritatis, quasi diceret, se verum vidisse filium hominis: & signanter dixit בר אנוש, non בן אדם, vel בן איש, quia respexit ad hominem, aegritudine labis, ac peccati miseriis laborantem, cùm Deus illum Filium hominis, seu semen mulieris, h. e. Messiam, promisit. אנוש enim est ab אנש, aegrum esse, aegritudine affici, & hominem peccatorem utriusque sexus significat, ut: Dan. 2: 43. & 4: 14. Verum quia ille Filius אנוש hominis aegritudine laborantis, promissus fuerat, ut contriturus caput serpentis, h. e. planè debellaturus Diabolum, ejusque regnum pessundaturus, divino planè consilio eum Daniel vocat אנוש, ubi ipsum contemplatur in nubibus triumphantem de Diabolo, peccato, ac morte, extrema peccati miseria, ut significet ipsummet esse verum ac genuinum semen mulieris, seu filium hominis aegritudine laborantis, quem Deus à lapsu promiserat, caput serpentis contriturum, & de ipsius regno triumphaturum. Cohaeret igitur quam sapientissimè בר אנוש elogium, cum triumphali Messiae apparatu. Hinc sponte suboritur nobis praecipuae quaestionis solutio, nimirum, cur Iesus se passim filium hominis dixerit, ut significaret se esse Christum? Respondemus igitur, Iesum prae omnibus aliis Messiae elogiis, hoc unum filii hominis selegisse, quo unus Daniel, aut alter David Messiam insignierant, eodem planè animo ac consilio atque Daniel & Psalmographus, ut scilicet Judaeorum animos ad recolendam primam de Messia promissionem excitaret, ac doceret, hoc elogio, se esse illum בן filium mulieris, seu hominis, quem Daniel triumphantem in nubibus in exstasi viderat, ac Numen Adamo promiserat, dum diabolo capitis per eum contritionem, ac regni abolitionem interminaretur. Sententia nostra hisce nititur fundamentis.
units.tr: With these observations set out, we answer the first question: Daniel, when he called the Messiah coming triumphant in the clouds into his kingdom, named him בר אנוש [bar enosh, son of man], suffering from sickness and the miseries of sin, chiefly for two reasons. First, because he wrote his prophecy in Chaldea, and it is customary among the Syrians and Chaldeans, in their vernacular dialect, to call a man בר נושא [bar nosha] or בר אנוש [bar enosh]. Second, the prophet was all the more willing to name the triumphant Messiah in the dialect of בר אנוש [bar enosh] familiar to the Chaldean people among whom he then lived, so that he might lift up the minds of the Israelites, after the exile, to recall the first promise of the Messiah, which is found in Genesis 3:15. For the Caph prefixed to ב is not the Hebrew Caph כ [kaph] of likeness, but the Caph of truth [אמיתת], as if he meant that he had truly seen the son of man. And he deliberately said בר אנוש [bar enosh], not בן אדם [ben adam] or בן איש [ben ish], because he looked to man, suffering from the sickness of the fall and the miseries of sin, when God promised him as the Son of man, or seed of the woman, that is the Messiah. For אנוש [enosh] comes from אנש [anash], to be sick, to be afflicted with sickness, and signifies a sinful man of either sex, as in Daniel 2:43 and 4:14. But since that Son of man, who was אנוש [enosh], suffering from sickness, had been promised to crush the head of the serpent, that is, to completely subdue the devil and overthrow his kingdom, by a truly divine plan Daniel calls him אנוש [enosh], when he contemplates him triumphing in the clouds over the devil, sin and death, the utmost misery of sin, so as to show that he himself is the true and genuine seed of the woman, or son of man suffering from sickness, whom God had promised after the fall would crush the head of the serpent and triumph over his kingdom. Thus the title בר אנוש [bar enosh] fits most wisely with the triumphal state of the Messiah. Hence the solution of the chief question arises naturally for us, namely why Jesus so often called himself the Son of man, so as to signify that he is the Christ? We answer, therefore, that Jesus chose from all other titles of the Messiah this one alone, Son of man, by which Daniel alone, or David another time, had marked the Messiah, with exactly the same mind and purpose as Daniel and the psalmist: namely, to stir up the minds of the Jews to recall the first promise concerning the Messiah, and to teach that by this title he is that בן [ben], son of the woman, or of man, whom Daniel saw in an ecstasy triumphing in the clouds, and whom God had promised to Adam, when he threatened the devil with the crushing of his head through him and the abolition of his kingdom. Our opinion rests on these foundations.

units.la: Primo ubi Iesus suum cum Nathanaële colloquium absolvit his verbis, Amen, amen dico vobis, ab hoc tempore videbitis coelum apertum, & Angelos Dei ascendentes & descendentes ad filium hominis, signanter se [?]υἱὸν [?]ἀνθρώπου, filium hominis dixit, Ioan. 1: 52. 1°. Ut Nathanaelem doceret; se, aliosque Israelitas sine fraude, vigilantes visuros impletum in se filio hominis, quod tantum in somnio Iacob eorum parens, è supplantatore per Patriarchalem benedictionem in sincerum Israelem mutandus, viderat, in celebri illa visione, quam sacer Moses memorat, Gen. 28. Nam & coelum apertum viderat Patriarcha, unde in hanc exclamationem erumpebat, hæc est domus Dei, hæc est porta coeli, verf. 17. Viderat praeterea Angelos Dei ascendentes & descendentes in scala: sed & viderat filium hominis, & Angelos Dei ascendentes & descendentes ad eum: nam τὸ ἐπί, quo Iesus explicat τὸ ἐπὶ quod exstat in visione scalæ, Gen. 28: 12. non modò significat super, sed & aliquando ad, ut Luc. 7: 13. & 10: 9. Hic vero vident, qui oculos habent τὸ ἐπί non significare super: nam Angeli Dei, nec super Christum descenderunt, nedum super Christum ascenderunt: sed equidem ad Filium hominis Christum, sive in cœlo, sive in terra spectatum, Angeli Dei ascenderunt & descenderunt, mandata ipsius prompti ac alacres executuri. Vidit igitur Patriarcha in somnio, non modò cœlum apertum, & Angelos Dei ascendentes & descendentes: sed & ipsum filium hominis vidit. Quod ut sentiamus, scopus Christi necessario efflagitat, & vel invitis extorquet; quandoquidem planum est & in confesso apud omnes, hanc Iesu solemnem promissionem, complementum continere symbolicæ visionis Patriarchæ Iacobi. Cum igitur Iesus solemni, sibique propria hac asseveratione, Amen, amen dico vobis, recipiat fore, ut Nathanael, cæterique discipuli Israelitæ sine fraude, cœlum apertum videant, Angelosque Dei ascendentes ac descendentes ad filium hominis, non in somnio sicuti Iacob, sed reapse. Exacta typi cum antitypo convenientia sanè efflagitat, ut Iacob in somnio filium hominis viderit. Quipote vero? Quia vidit scalam altera parte cœlum, altera terram attingentem. Ita quidem sentiunt plerique omnes doctissimi viri, qui per scalam, Christi personam ex natura divina suprema, & humana infima coalescentem intellexere: quâ fit, ut cœlum ac Deus, terra & homo, amicè consocientur: per Deum vero adstantem supernæ parti scalæ, Dei Patris personam, & per Iacobum ad infimam scalæ partem jacentem, hominem Deo fidelem ac reconciliatum per Christum scalam mysticam. Sed assensum nostrum sibi promereri non potuerunt. 1o. Quia si virorum undecunque doctorum sententia semel obtinuerit, symbolica hæc Patriarchæ visio ad Christum unicè non spectaverit; sed & ad Deum Patrem & ad Iacobum: nam & Deus Pater & Patriarcha, pars erunt maximè memorabilis istius visionis: Iesus verò, Ioh. 1: 52. evidenter nos docet, integram hanc visionem ad filium hominis, seu Christum, unicè respectasse. 2o. Quia si pars scalæ suprema, naturam divinam, seu personam Filii significaverit: hinc colligas, Deum, seu naturam divinam, per manu & arte factum aliquid, puta scalam, fuisse repræsentatam, quod abhorret quàm maximè à genio symbolorum, quibus Numen æternum voluit repræsentari: corpora quidem naturalia, quæ ab arbitrio libituque humano non pendent, nubem, ignem, ventum, aerem, rorem, aquam, pluviam, in suæ divinitatis symbola adhibuit: sed arte-facta facta haud quaquam, ut se Numen æternum, & ab arbitrio libituque humano independens, à fictitiis & manu factis gentium Diis discerneret. 3º. Quia Numen quod Iacobum è scalæ fastigio alloquitur, Ego sum Jehova Deus Abrahami Patris tui, & Deus Isaaci, Gen. 28:13. est filius Dei, qui Mosem è rubo iisdemmet verbis alloquitur, Act. 7:30.31;32. Idemmet mero meridie clarius paret ex Gen. 31: 11.13. Nam qui in somnio Iacobo dicit, ego sum Deus fortis Bethel, vocatur Angelus Dei, verf. 11. At Deus Pater nunquam ac nusquam Angelus Dei dicitur, mittit enim filium; sed à filio vicissim non mittitur. Unus filius & Deus fortis est æterna sua divinitate, & Angelus Dei, officio: Missus enim fuit in forma carnis peccati, ut foret propitiatio pro peccatis nostris; & peccatum condemnaret, h. e. destrueret, in carne, Rom. 8: 3. 1. Ioh. 4: 9.10. Scala igitur mystica, cœlum ac Deum suprema parte, terram vero & Iacobum infima attingens, typus, fuit tum unionis naturæ divinæ ac humanæ in Christo, tum muneris mediatorii Christi, in quo gradus admirabiles humiliationis ac exaltationis, sicut in scala mystica, cernere est. Deus vero in cœlo, & scalæ fastigio visus, fuit persona divina filii Dei: Jacob vero humi jacens ad pedes scalæ, typus naturæ humanæ, personali unione filio Dei unitæ, & integra visio scalæ Dei atque Iacobi, typus fuit filii hominis, seu Christi Mediatoris inter cœlum & terram, coalescentis ex natura divina & humana, unione personali conjunctis. Nam sicut in symbolica visione, Deus & homo Iacob, per scalam mediam conjuncti, in unum coalescebant, quo cœlum & terra, Deus & homo, amicè ac sapienter conjuncti videbantur: ita ut Deus, dum erat in cœlo simul in homine Jacobo erat in terra. Non secus & in Iesu filio hominis, seu Christo, Deus & homo, cœlum & terra tam arcta unione copulabantur, ut dum filius hominis versaretur in terris, simul foret in cœlo. Eò respiciebat Christus, Ioh. 3:14. Nemo ascendit in cœlum, nisi qui e cœlo descendit, filius hominis qui est in cœlo. Hic adverte arcanorum Sacrorum studiose. 1º. Exactam convenientiam typi cum antitypo: nam filius hominis Christus in terram descenderat, contentus scilicet in lumbis Iacobi, utpote futurus Iacobi semen, Gen. 28: 14. Sed & idemmet simul in cœlo erat positus, & conspiciendus in fastigio scalæ, uti Deus fortis Bethel, & Angelus Dei. 2º. Iudica quàm longè abierint à tramite veritatis, qui Iesum, filium hominis, dictum opinantur in contemptam, vilissimamque ipsius sortem designandam: nam filius hominis in cœlo, felicitatis ac gloriæ domicilio, ubi reatus, maledictio, miseria, mors, quæ tristi suo ambitu, sors Christi contempta complectitur, nunquam stabulantur. bulantur. Hic vero, ut se explicet oculis vis ac robur rationis nostrae, duo quaestionum momenta nobis veniunt perstringenda. 1o. Cur inter majora illa, quae Nathanaelem visurum Jesus promittit, destinato eligit visionem coeli aperti, & Angelorum Dei ascendentium ac descendentium ad filium hominis, tanquam complementum, ac reale τυπωδὴς symbolicae visionis Patriarchae Jacobi. 2o. Quamobrem visio coeli aperti, & Angelorum Dei ascendentium ac descendentium ad filium hominis, res major est ac mirabilior, eo quod jam Nathanael noverat, scilicet, Jesum esse Filium Dei, ac Regem Israelis, quia eum sub ficu viderat. Ad primum quaestionis momentum, quod attinet. Respondemus, Jesum ex compacto, hanc futuram admirabilem visionem coeli aperti, &c. uti complementum symbolicae visionis Jacobi selegisse. 1o. Quia ad Nathanaelem sine fraude Israelitam, h. e. filium Jacobi supplantatoris: sed per benedictionem Patriarchalem, mutandi in Israelem sine fraude, sermonem ac promissionem suam dirigebat, utique par erat, ut Israelita sine fraude Nathanael, caeterique sinceritatis ipsius imitatores, ac genuini filii, non Iacobi supplantatoris: sed Israelis per benedictionem sanctificati, vigilantes, cum penitissimo sensu consolationis ac gaudii, in Christo & per Christum, realem filium hominis, complementum cernerent laetabundi, typicae ac symbolicae visionis, quam in somnio benedictus: sed adhuc supplantator eorum parens contemplatus fuerat. 2o. Quia promissa coeli aperti visio, & Angelorum Dei ad obsequium filii hominis accinctorum, pernecessaria erat, vel ad errorem, quo fides Nathanaelis laborabat corrigendum: confessus enim Nathanael, Iesum esse filium Dei, & Regem Israelis, h. e. Messiam: vel eum esse Dei Filium, sicut Reges terrae; etsi nobiliori & excellentiori praerogativa, & futurum hominum ac populorum tantummodo dominatorem, cum sua natione Judaica consentiebat: Iesus vero, qua erat summa charitate ac sapientia, docere eum voluit, se esse filium Dei, non umbratili quadam cum Deo conformitate, sicut praepotentes terrae Reges: sed vere atque proprie, se esse filium Dei, ac Deum fortem Bethel, quem parens ipsius Iacob in somnio viderat, & Regem Israelis, ad cujus nutum & obsequium, non modo homines terrae incolae; sed & ipsi Angeli Dei, ascenderent ac descenderent, ut homines, viso coelo aperto, & fideli Angelorum Dei obsequio, Iesum filium hominis ac Regem Israelis, summum esse coeli ac terrae, orbisque universi dominatorem, ore uno confiterentur. Vel sin minus fides Nathanaelis hoc vulgari errore laborabat, tenella adhuc, omnia ad credendum necessaria, de Christo, non pervidebat. Hinc adeo factum ut hanc coeli aperti visionem promittendam selegerit. 3°. Quia erat complementum symbolicæ visionis Iacobi, h. e. realis visio cœli aperti, & Angelorum Dei ascensus ac descensus ad filium hominis, finis certè erat ac plena consummatio, tum omnium super Messia promissionum, tum eorum omnium, quotquot Messia passurus ac præstiturus erat. Quicquid enim nativitatis, vitæ, miraculorum, passionum ac victoriarum Messiæ fuit, in hoc unum collimabat, ut cœlum hominibus aperiret, apertumque ostenderet, & Deum placatum audiendum eis exhiberet, dicentem, ero Deus tuus, & semini tui: & Angelos reconciliatos ac amicos, ad nutum Christi ascendentes & descendentes, non dormientibus atque somniantibus: sed expergefactis ac vigilantibus hominibus, conspiciendos proponeret. Iure merito igitur inter majora multa, cognitione, qua jam imbutus erat Nathanael de Messia Rege Israelis, hoc unum selegit sapientissime Iesus, visionem puta cœli aperti, ac Angelorum Dei ascendentium ac descendentium ad filium hominis. Hinc nobis facilis patet aditus ad secundum quæstionis momentum, scilicet, quamobrem promissa isthæc visio cœli aperti, &c. majus ac mirabilius fuerit spectaculum, eo, quod intuebatur Nathanael, scilicet Iesum esse Dei Filium ac Regem Israelis, quia eum sub ficu opaca viderat.
units.tr: First, when Jesus concluded his conversation with Nathanael with these words, Amen, amen I say to you, from now on you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending to the Son of man [υἱὸν ἀνθρώπου], he deliberately called himself Son of man, John 1:52. First, he meant to teach Nathanael that he and the other Israelites without guile, who keep watch, would see fulfilled in him the Son of man, which their forefather Jacob, who was to be changed from a supplanter into a true Israel by the patriarchal blessing, had seen only in a dream, in that famous vision which holy Moses records, Gen. 28. For the patriarch also saw heaven opened, and from this he broke out in the exclamation, This is the house of God, this is the gate of heaven, v. 17. He further saw the angels of God ascending and descending on the ladder, but he also saw the Son of man, and the angels of God ascending and descending to him. For the Greek ἐπί, by which Jesus explains the ἐπί found in the vision of the ladder, Gen. 28:12, does not only mean upon, but sometimes also to, as in Luke 7:13 and 10:9. Here those who have eyes see that ἐπί does not mean upon: for the angels of God neither descended upon Christ, much less ascended upon Christ, but rather the angels of God ascended and descended to the Son of man Christ, whether he is regarded in heaven or on earth, ready and eager to carry out his commands. Therefore the patriarch in his dream saw not only heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending, but also saw the Son of man himself. That this is the right understanding, the purpose of Christ necessarily demands, and even against our will forces it upon us, since it is plain and admitted by all that this solemn promise of Jesus contains the fulfilment of Jacob's symbolic vision. Since Jesus, with this solemn assertion, peculiar to himself, Amen, amen I say to you, declares that Nathanael and the other Israelites without guile will see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending to the Son of man, not in a dream as Jacob did, but in reality, the exact correspondence of type with antitype certainly requires that Jacob saw the Son of man in his dream. But why so? Because he saw a ladder, one end reaching heaven and the other earth. Indeed, most very learned men hold this view, who understood by the ladder the person of Christ, joined together from the supreme divine nature and the lowest human nature, whereby heaven and God, earth and man, are amicably joined: by God standing above on the upper part of the ladder they understood the person of God the Father, and by Jacob lying on the lowest part of the ladder, man reconciled to God through Christ, the mystical ladder. But they have not been able to win our assent. First, because if the opinion of men learned from every quarter were once to prevail, this symbolic vision of the patriarch would not refer solely to Christ, but also to God the Father and to Jacob: for God the Father and the patriarch would be the most notable parts of that vision; yet Jesus, in John 1:52, clearly teaches us that the whole of this vision referred solely to the Son of man, or Christ. Second, because if the upper part of the ladder signified the divine nature, or the person of the Son, you would infer that God, or the divine nature, was represented by something made by human hand and skill, namely a ladder; and this is most strongly contrary to the character of the symbols by which the eternal Godhead chose to be represented. He used natural bodies, which do not depend on human will and pleasure, such as cloud, fire, wind, air, dew, water and rain, as symbols of his divinity; but by no means artifacts, so that the eternal Godhead, independent of human will and pleasure, might be distinguished from the fictitious gods of the nations, which are made by hand. Third, because the Lord who addresses Jacob from the top of the ladder, I am Jehovah the God of Abraham your father, and the God of Isaac, Gen. 28:13, is the Son of God, who addresses Moses from the bush in the same words, Acts 7:30, 31, 32. This appears even more clearly at midday from Gen. 31:11, 13. For he who says to Jacob in a dream, I am the God of Bethel, is called the Angel of God, v. 11. But God the Father is never and nowhere called the Angel of God, for he sends the Son; the Son, in turn, is not sent by him. The one Son is the mighty God by his eternal divinity, and the Angel of God by his office: for he was sent in the form of sinful flesh, to be a propitiation for our sins, and to condemn sin, that is, to destroy it, in the flesh, Rom. 8:3; 1 John 4:9, 10. The mystical ladder, reaching heaven and God with its upper part, and earth and Jacob with its lower part, was therefore a type both of the union of the divine and human natures in Christ and of the mediatorial office of Christ, in which admirable degrees of humiliation and exaltation are to be discerned, as on the mystical ladder. The God seen in heaven at the top of the ladder was the divine person of the Son of God; Jacob lying on the ground at the foot of the ladder was a type of human nature, united to the Son of God in personal union; and the whole vision of the ladder of God and Jacob was a type of the Son of man, or Christ the Mediator, between heaven and earth, joined together from the divine and human natures in personal union. For just as in the symbolic vision God and man, Jacob, were joined by the middle ladder and coalesced into one, whereby heaven and earth, God and man, appeared amicably and wisely joined, so that God, while he was in heaven, was at the same time in the man Jacob on earth; in the same way, in Jesus the Son of man, or Christ, God and man, heaven and earth, were joined in so close a union that while the Son of man was dwelling on earth he was at the same time in heaven. Christ had this in view in John 3:14: No one has ascended into heaven except him who came down from heaven, the Son of man who is in heaven. Here note, as a careful student of the sacred mysteries: first, the exact correspondence of type with antitype: for the Son of man Christ had come down to earth, contained, of course, in the loins of Jacob, as one who was to be Jacob's seed, Gen. 28:14; yet at the same time he himself was placed in heaven, and to be seen at the top of the ladder, like the God of Bethel and the Angel of God. Second, judge how far from the path of truth those have strayed who think that the name Son of man was given to Jesus to designate his despised and most base condition: for the Son of man in heaven, the dwelling place of happiness and glory, where guilt, curse, misery and death, which with their sad circuit embrace the despised lot of Christ, never dwell. Here, however, so that the force and strength of our reason may reveal itself to the eyes, two points of the question come to us that must be touched on. First, why among those greater things which Jesus promises Nathanael will see, he chose for this purpose the vision of heaven opened and of the angels of God ascending and descending to the Son of man, as the fulfilment and real typical [τυπωδὴς] fulfilment of the symbolic vision of the patriarch Jacob. Second, why the vision of heaven opened and of the angels of God ascending and descending to the Son of man is a greater and more wonderful thing, in that Nathanael already knew that Jesus was the Son of God and King of Israel, because he had seen him under the fig tree. As to the first point of the question, we answer that Jesus by agreement chose this future wonderful vision of heaven opened, etc., as the fulfilment of Jacob's symbolic vision. First, because he directed his speech and promise to Nathanael, an Israelite without guile, that is, a son of Jacob the supplanter, who was to be changed by the patriarchal blessing into an Israel without guile; so it was fitting that Nathanael, an Israelite without guile, and the other imitators of his sincerity and true sons, not of Jacob the supplanter but of Israel sanctified by the blessing, should keep watch and see, joyfully, with the deepest sense of consolation and joy, in Christ and through Christ, the real Son of man, the fulfilment of the typical and symbolic vision which the blessed patriarch had seen in a dream, but which their forefather, still a supplanter, had contemplated. Second, because the promised vision of heaven opened, and of the angels of God girded for the service of the Son of man, was most necessary, either to correct the error by which Nathanael's faith was troubled: for Nathanael had confessed that Jesus was the Son of God and King of Israel, that is, the Messiah; yet he agreed with his Jewish nation that he was the Son of God just as earthly kings are, though with a nobler and more excellent prerogative, and would be only a ruler of men and peoples. Jesus, however, in his great love and wisdom, wished to teach him that he was the Son of God, not in some shadowy conformity with God, as the mighty kings of the earth are, but truly and properly the Son of God, the mighty God of Bethel whom his forefather Jacob had seen in a dream, and the King of Israel, at whose nod and service not only the men who dwell on earth but also the angels of God themselves would ascend and descend; so that men, having seen heaven opened and the faithful service of the angels of God, would with one voice confess Jesus the Son of man and King of Israel to be the supreme ruler of heaven and earth and of the whole universe. Or, if Nathanael's faith was not suffering from this common error, it was still tender and did not yet clearly see all the things about Christ necessary for belief. Hence it came about that he chose this vision of heaven opened to be promised. Third, because it was the fulfilment of Jacob's symbolic vision, that is, the real vision of heaven opened and of the ascent and descent of the angels of God to the Son of man, it was certainly the end and full completion both of all the promises concerning the Messiah and of all that the Messiah was to suffer and accomplish. For whatever belonged to the birth, life, miracles, sufferings and victories of the Messiah aimed at this one thing, that he might open heaven to men, and, having opened it, show them God reconciled, to be heard by them saying, I will be your God and the God of your seed; and that he might present to men, awake and watching, not sleeping and dreaming, the reconciled and friendly angels ascending and descending at the nod of Christ. Rightly, therefore, among many greater things which Nathanael, already imbued with the knowledge of the Messiah as King of Israel, could have been told, Jesus most wisely chose this one: the vision, namely, of heaven opened and of the angels of God ascending and descending to the Son of man. Hence an easy path lies open for us to the second point of the question, namely, why this promised vision of heaven opened, etc., was a greater and more wonderful spectacle, in that Nathanael had grasped that Jesus was the Son of God and King of Israel, because he had seen him under the shady fig tree.

units.la: Et 1°. quidem majus ac mirabilius futurum erat spectaculum, in habitudine ad cognitionem ac fidem præsentem Nathanaelis: Nathanael enim, quòd Iesus absens eum sub ficu latentem viderat, vel credebat eum esse Filium Dei ac Regem Israelis, qualem scilicet Messiam fore credebat universa Iudæorum natio, h. e. Filium Dei ac Regem, sicut Reges Israelis, merum hominem: sed eximia ac singulari prærogativa, quæ tamen vires humanas non excederet, præpotentem ac excellentem Regem, quique βασιλεὺς, regiæ suæ dignitatis, ac excellentiæ terrenæ ergò, filius Dei diceretur. Vel si Iesum verè & reapse filium Dei æternum credebat. Nondum tamen noverat, quæ filius hominis Deus & homo, in humani generis redemptionem, ut verum semen mulieris, præstiturus erat. At visio cœli aperti atque descensus nec non ascensus Angelorum ad filium hominis, uti complementum visionis symbolicæ Iacobi, majora erat super filio hominis Christo, edoctura Nathanaelem, cæterosque sine fraude Israelitas. Ecquid verò? scilicet filium hominis Christum esse simul Deum ac hominem, Dei cum homine reconciliatorem, cœli clausi apertorem, & secundum cœlestium Angelorum cum hominibus pacificatorem: atque ea propter Diaboli mortis imperatoris, & justitiæ divinæ carnificis ac tortoris, peccati ac mortis debellatorem: uno verbo generis humani, in ruinam per Adamum pessundati gloriosum liberatorem ac reparatorem. Re enim vera cum Iacob in somnio filium hominis viderit, ut supra solidis rationibus addiximus, & Nathanael, caeterique Israelitae sine fraude, visuri essent coelum apertum, & Angelos Dei ascendentes ac descendentes ad filium hominis. Hac solemni promissione futura in complementum visionis symbolicae Patriarchae, Iesus luculentam oppositionem instituit inter se ac Adamum parentem suum, & simul necessario animos discipulorum suorum efficaciter excitat ad recolendam primaevam promissionem de semine mulieris, seu hominis, contrituro caput serpentis, quod paret, 1°. Ex circumstantiis historiae Adami, & historiae Nathanaelis: nam sicut Moses, dum lapsi Adami historiam recitat, unam ex omnibus paradisi arboribus ficum, proprio nomine indigetat, quod scilicet, latis densisque prae caeteris omnibus & nuditati tegendae, omnium maxime opportunis foliis ficulneis, pudibundus homo tegmen sibi confuerit. Non secus & sacer Euangelista, unius ficus in isthac Nathanaelis historia meminit. Insuper sicut Adam, dum nuditati, pudori ac horrori suo, idonea quaerit inter paradisi arbores latibula, exuberantissimas luxuria foliorum ac opacissimas elegit arbores, ficus scilicet, quarum latis foliis, jam suae nuditati consuluerat, palmas, myrthos, oleas, quarum omnium propter luxuriam foliorum, usus fuit perpetuus in tabernaculis aedificandis, Nehem. 8: 15. Tum in tuguriolis instruendis in hortis locisque amoenis arcendo aestui, ad laetitiam agitandam idoneis: unde vinea ac ficus Iudaeis ita erant in deliciis, ut passim in Scriptura audias sedere ac habitare sub vinea & ficu, 1. Reg. 4: 25. Mich. 4: 4. & vocare amicos sub vineam ac ficum, Zach. 3: 10. Ad pacifica laetaque tempora significanda. Solebant enim se recipere Iudaei sub opaca tuguriola, ex opacis ficubus ut impervii radiis solaribus umbraculi, frigore se reficerent. Viderat igitur Numen Adamum sub ficu latentem. Non secus & Iesus Nathanaelem videt sub umbraculo opacae ficus, vel ipsis radiis solaribus abscónditum; unde haec admirabundi Nathanaelis exclamatio, Rabbi tu es filius Dei. Novi me sub umbraculo opacae ficus, ita corporeos hominum oculos, nedum tui absentis latuisse, ut nemo me sub ea deprehendere potuerit, praeter unum Deum, qui Adamum sub opacis Edenis ficubus latitantem deprehendit. Nunc igitur credo, te hominem esse vere filium Dei. 2°. Eadem oppositio filium hominis inter & Adamum, paret, ex ipsa Adami historia. Adamus enim integer vitae, scelerisque purus, mentis oculis apertum coelum contemplabatur: etsi enim Moses id silentio sapienter praeteriit, nec Deum, vel Angelos e coelo ad Adamum descendentes memoravit, (ut eo silentio Adami in animam viventem creti, felicitatem in terra, non in coelo positam doceret: altùm enim Scriptura silet de Adami integri in cœlum translatione) descensum tamen Dei, Angelorumque ad Adamum integrum, necessariò colligendum relinquit. Cum enim Deum memorat Adamum in terra creantem, & in Paradisum introducentem, & alloquentem, sat evidenter innuit, Deum è cœlo venisse in terram, & in cœlum ascendisse, tantisper dum rediret in Paradisum terrestrem, & serpentem juxta atque Adamum, reos nefandi criminis perageret. Quod spectat ad Angelos Dei, ad Adamum descendisse, & iterum in cœlum ascendisse liquet, quia par erat ut creaturæ sanctæ, & Deo communi creatori obsequiosæ amicam societatem colerent, qua sortem beatam, sanctitatem parem, cultum Numinis, ac mutuam felicitatem, sibi invicem gratularentur. Cum enim animum ad scribendam historiam creationis post exitum ab Ægypto, Moses appulit, cœlum esse Dei, ac Angelorum domicilium, Israelitæ habebant pro comperto. Hinc in promptu colligere est, Adamum sceleris purum, mentis oculis cœlum sibi apertum vidisse, dum beatâ frueretur cum Numine, Angelisque Dei ascendentibus atque descendentibus communione. Verum nefanda sua rebellione primævam cum Numine Angelisque Dei dissolvit communionem, & Deum iratum, Angelosque Dei, sibi exosos expertus, & paradiso depulsus, clausum sibi & paradisum terrestrem, & cœlum animadvertit. Sed filius hominis reparatum venit hominis parentis ruinam, ipse enim pugnâ decretoriâ caput serpentis contrivit, & suâ ad mortem crucis obedientiâ, rebellis Adami parentis inobedientiam expiavit, & pretioso calcanei sui sanguine extinxit inimicitias, & quæ in cœlo, sicut & quæ sunt in terra reconciliavit, & cœlum clausum aperuit, & infensorum Angelorum amicitiam hominibus conciliavit, quod eximium opus in visione somnii Jacobo ostentaverat, & vigilantibus suis fidelibus se reapse ostensurum recipit, ut dum cœlum apertum viderint, & Angelos Dei ascendentes ac descendentes ad filium hominis, necessaria demonstratione sciant, Jesum esse illum filium hominis, seu mulieris, promissum, ut contriturum caput serpentis, & talo suo conterendum, Deum juxta ac hominem, ex Adamo oriundum plenè ac cumulatè perfunctum munere mediatorio, cum prostrato ac contrito Satana, peccato ac morte, cœlum hominibus aperuerit, quod sibi, suisque posteris clauserat Adam, & in Angelos Dei, nedum in omnem carnem, supremum dominium obtinuerit, ut det vitam æternam electis suis, Ioh. 17: 2.
units.tr: And first, the spectacle would indeed be greater and more wonderful in relation to Nathanael's present knowledge and faith. For Nathanael, because Jesus, though absent, had seen him hiding under the fig tree, either believed that he was the Son of God and King of Israel, the kind of Messiah the whole Jewish nation believed would come, that is, a Son of God and King like the kings of Israel, a mere man, but endowed with a special and singular prerogative, one that did not exceed human powers: a most mighty and excellent king, who, on account of his royal dignity and earthly eminence, would be called son of God (βασιλεύς). Or, if he believed Jesus to be truly and really the eternal Son of God, he did not yet know that the Son of Man, God and man, would accomplish the redemption of the human race as the true seed of the woman. But the vision of the open heaven and the descent and ascent of the angels to the Son of Man, as the fulfilment of Jacob's symbolic vision, was greater than what it was concerning the Son of Man Christ, and it would teach Nathanael and the other Israelites without guile. And what was it? That the Son of Man, Christ, is at once God and man, the reconciler of God with man, the opener of the closed heaven, and the peacemaker between the heavenly angels and men; and therefore the conqueror of the Devil, the emperor of death, and the executioner and torturer of divine justice; in a word, the glorious deliverer and restorer of the human race, which had been cast into ruin through Adam. For indeed, since Jacob saw the Son of Man in a dream, as we argued above on solid grounds, so Nathanael and the other Israelites without guile were to see the heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending to the Son of Man. By this solemn promise, to be fulfilled as the completion of the Patriarch's symbolic vision, Jesus sets up a clear contrast between himself and Adam, his parent, and at the same time he necessarily and effectively stirs the minds of his disciples to recall the first promise concerning the seed of the woman, or of man, who would crush the serpent's head. This appears, first, from the circumstances of the history of Adam and the history of Nathanael. For as Moses, in recounting the fall of Adam, names one tree of all the trees of paradise, the fig, by its proper name, because its broad and dense leaves were, of all others, most suitable for covering nakedness, so the sacred Evangelist mentions the one fig tree in this history of Nathanael. Further, just as Adam, when seeking fitting hiding places among the trees of paradise for his nakedness, shame and dread, chose the most luxuriant and shadiest trees, namely the fig, whose broad leaves he had already used to cover his nakedness, so also the palms, myrtles and olives, all of which, because of the abundance of their foliage, were used perpetually for building tabernacles (Neh. 8:15), and for furnishing little booths in gardens and pleasant places to keep off the heat and to promote gladness. Hence the vine and the fig were so delightful to the Jews that in Scripture you hear everywhere of "sitting and dwelling under the vine and the fig" (1 Kings 4:25; Mic. 4:4), and "calling friends under the vine and the fig" (Zech. 3:10), to signify peaceful and joyful times. For the Jews used to withdraw under shady booths, and under the shady fig trees, which were impervious to the sun's rays, to refresh themselves in the cool. The Deity therefore saw Adam hiding under the fig tree. In the same way Jesus sees Nathanael under the shade of the shady fig, hidden even from the sun's rays themselves; whence came Nathanael's astonished exclamation, "Rabbi, you are the Son of God." You have known me under the shade of the shady fig, so that my bodily eyes, let alone yours, though you were absent, were hidden, and no one could detect me there except the one God, who detected Adam hiding under the shady figs of Eden. Now therefore I believe that you are truly the Son of God. Second, the same contrast between the Son of Man and Adam appears from the history of Adam itself. For Adam, whole in life and pure of wickedness, contemplated the open heaven with the eyes of his mind. Although Moses wisely passed this over in silence, and did not mention God or the angels descending from heaven to Adam, (so that by this silence he might teach that the happiness of Adam, created into a living soul, was placed on earth and not in heaven, for Scripture is silent on the translation of the upright Adam into heaven), nevertheless he leaves us to conclude necessarily the descent of God and of the angels to the upright Adam. For when he records God creating Adam on earth, leading him into paradise, and speaking to him, he quite clearly indicates that God came from heaven to earth, and ascended into heaven, while he returned to the earthly paradise, and called the serpent and Adam to account as guilty of a dreadful crime. As for the angels of God, that they descended to Adam and ascended again into heaven is plain, because it was fitting that holy creatures, obedient to God their common Creator, should cultivate friendly fellowship, rejoicing with one another in their blessed lot, their equal holiness, the worship of the Deity, and mutual happiness. For when Moses turned to write the history of creation after the exodus from Egypt, the Israelites regarded it as established that heaven is the dwelling of God and of the angels. Hence it is easy to infer that Adam, pure of wickedness, saw heaven open to him with the eyes of his mind, while he enjoyed blessed fellowship with the Deity and with the angels of God ascending and descending. But by his impious rebellion he dissolved the primeval communion with God and the angels of God; and having found God angry and the angels of God hostile to him, and having been driven from paradise, he perceived that both the earthly paradise and heaven were closed to him. But the Son of Man came to repair the ruin of the human parent. For he himself crushed the serpent's head in the decisive battle, and by his obedience unto the death of the cross he atoned for the disobedience of the rebellious parent Adam, and by the precious blood of his heel he quenched the enmity, and reconciled the things in heaven as well as the things on earth, and opened the closed heaven, and won for men the friendship of the angels, who had been hostile; this excellent work he had displayed to Jacob in the vision of the dream, and he receives it as something he will really show to his faithful ones while they are awake, so that when they see the heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending to the Son of Man, they may know by a necessary demonstration that Jesus is that Son of man, or of the woman, promised as the one who would crush the serpent's head and bruise it with his heel; God as well as man, sprung from Adam, fully and abundantly endowed with the mediatorial office, who, with Satan, sin and death laid low and crushed, has opened to men the heaven which Adam had closed to himself and his posterity, and has obtained supreme dominion over the angels of God, and indeed over all flesh, so that he may give eternal life to his elect (John 17:2).

units.la: Secundum sententiæ nostræ fundamentum sternitur, ex collatione, Dan. 7: 13. 14. cum Ioh. 5: 22. 23. 27. Cum Daniel in visionibus noctis, filium hominis honiinis venientem cum nubibus coeli ad Antiquum dierum contemplatur, & accipientem dono datam dominationem, & gloriam & regnum, in populos omnes, nationes, ac linguas, dominationem aeternam, ac regnum immutabile, Dan. 7: 13. 14. Messiae praenunciat triumphalem in coelum ascensionem, post victricem resurrectionem, & contritum per mortem suam, mortis imperatorem Diabolum, abolitam mortem, legis maledictionem, expiatum ac victum peccatum. Consentientibus Hebraeorum Magistris, & Jesu ipso declarante, Ioh. 6: 62. Mat. 26: 64. Praeterea dico vobis in posterum videbitis filium hominis, sedentem ad dexteram Majestatis, & venientem in nubibus coeli. Daniel vero Messiam in nubibus coeli ad dexteram Majestatis ascendentem, signanter vocat בר אנש [?], quia respicit ad primam de Messia semine mulieris, caput serpentis contrituro promissionem. Nam triumphum in nubibus celebrare Messiam non decuit, nec sapientia, ac divina justitia sustinuit, nisi post reportatam gloriosam victoriam de serpente Diabolo, peccati ac mortis authore. Jesus vero, ubi Judaeos his verbis alloquitur, Pater neminem judicat: sed omne judicium dedit filio, ut omnes honorent filium, sicut honorant Patrem, qui non honorat filium non honorat Patrem qui misit illum, & potestatem dedit ei etiam judicium exercendi. ὅτι υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου ἐστί , quia filius est hominis. Ioh. 5: 22. 23. 27. Signanter ac sapienter filii hominis elogio se insignit, cum de suprema sua majestate ac authoritate, orbem universum judicandi sermonem instituit, aperte respiciens, tum ad visionem Danielis, tum ea propter ad primam de Messia filio hominis, contrituro caput serpentis promissionem: nam quod filius Dei factus fuit [filius hominis, & pugnam iniit cum Diabolo decretoriam, in qua passus est calcanei sui contritionem, & sua illa contritione calcanei, h. e. morte cruenta, Diaboli imperium abolevit, & homines e Satanae servitute, peccati & mortis liberavit, ille filius hominis, quia est filius hominis, id est, Christus, munere functus mediatorio, dignus equidem est qui omne judicium exerceat in omnes creaturas, Diabolos prostratos & victos, pugna sua cruenta, ac gloriosa resurrectione, & homines suo sibi acquisitos sanguine, & a Diaboli tyrannide deliberatos, ac legis maledictione, ac terribili Dei justitia exemptos. Hoc nos docet Paulus, dum ex eo quod Christus assumpta servi forma obsequiosus fuerit ad mortem: imo vero ad mortem maledictam Crucis, sapienter concludit: Quapropter eum summe Deus evexit, eique dedit nomen supra omne nomen, ut ad nomen Jesu omne genu flectatur; eorum quae sunt in coelis & in terra & sub terra, & omnis lingua confiteatur Jesum Christum esse Dominum ad gloriam Patris, Phil. 2: 9. 10. 11. & Hebr. 2: 9. units.tr: The foundation of our opinion is laid by comparing Daniel 7:13-14 with John 5:22-23, 27. When Daniel, in his night visions, contemplates the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days, and receiving dominion, glory and kingdom given to him, an everlasting dominion over all peoples, nations and languages, and an unchangeable kingdom (Dan. 7:13-14), he foretells the Messiah's triumphal ascension into heaven after his victorious resurrection, and the Devil, the emperor of death, crushed by his death, death abolished, the curse of the law, and sin expiated and conquered. The Hebrew teachers agree, and Jesus himself declares it (John 6:62; Matt. 26:64): "Moreover I say to you, hereafter you shall see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Majesty, and coming in the clouds of heaven." Daniel indeed calls the Messiah, ascending in the clouds of heaven to the right hand of Majesty, by the phrase "bar enash" [?], expressly, because he looks back to the first promise concerning the Messiah, the seed of the woman, who would crush the serpent's head. For it was not fitting for the Messiah to celebrate triumph in the clouds, nor did wisdom and divine justice permit it, unless after gaining the glorious victory over the serpent, the Devil, the author of sin and death. But when Jesus addresses the Jews with these words, "The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, that all may honour the Son as they honour the Father; he who does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him; and he has given him authority to execute judgment also, because he is the Son of Man" (John 5:22-23, 27; hoti huios anthrōpou estin, because he is the Son of Man), he distinguishes himself wisely and expressly with the title Son of Man, when he is speaking of his supreme majesty and authority to judge the whole world, clearly looking both to Daniel's vision and to the first promise concerning the Son of Man, the seed who would crush the serpent's head. For he who became the Son of God [the Son of Man, and entered upon the decisive battle with the Devil, in which he suffered the bruising of his heel, and by that bruising of his heel, that is, by his bloody death, abolished the dominion of the Devil and freed men from the servitude of Satan, sin and death; that Son of Man, because he is the Son of Man, that is, Christ, having discharged the mediatorial office, is indeed worthy to exercise all judgment over all creatures: the Devils laid low and conquered by his bloody battle and glorious resurrection, and men acquired for himself by his own blood, delivered from the tyranny of the Devil, and freed from the curse of the law and the terrible justice of God. Paul teaches us this, when from the fact that Christ, taking the form of a servant, was obedient even unto death, yes, unto the accursed death of the cross, he wisely concludes: "Therefore God has highly exalted him, and given him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of the Father" (Phil. 2:9-11; and Heb. 2:9). Unde in promptu concludere est, Iesum se elogio filii hominis insigniisse, semper respectantem ad primam promissionem de semine mulieris, seu filio hominis, contrituro caput serpentis, & victoriam gloriosam ac solemnem triumphum celebraturo de Diabolo, peccato, & morte, in nubibus, per gloriosam in coelum ascensionem.
units.tr: Thus it is easy to conclude that Jesus gave himself the title Son of man, the one who was "crowned with glory and honour, who was made a little lower than the angels," namely Jesus, through the suffering of his death. crowned with glory and honour, who was made a little lower than the angels, namely Jesus, through the suffering of his death. He always looked back to the first promise about the seed of the woman, or the son of man, who would crush the serpent's head and celebrate a glorious victory and solemn triumph over the Devil, sin and death, in the clouds, through his glorious ascent into heaven.

units.la: Tertio. Iesum, intentis in primam de Messia promissionem oculis, se filium hominis dixisse, quam evidentissimè paret ex Joh. 12: 23. 24. 27. 31. 32. 33. Venit hora illa, ut filius hominis glorificetur. Amen, amen dico vobis, nisi granum frumenti cadens in terram mortuum fuerit, ipsum solum manet, si vero mortuum fuerit, multum fructum adfert. Nunc anima mea turbata est, & quid dicam? Pater libera me ab hac hora: sed propterea veni in hanc horam. Nunc judicium adest mundi hujus: nunc Princeps ille hujus mundi ejicietur foras. Et ego si sublatus fuero e terra, omnes traham ad me ipsum. Hoc autem dicebat, significans qua morte esset moriturus. Hic, Lector Christiane, filium hominis cernis, inimicitiam exercentem, & pugnam decretoriam cum potestate tenebrarum, principe hujus mundi, serpente Diabolo, pugnantem cominus: cernis & eventum pugnae memorabilis. Hinc filium hominis e terra in crucem sublatum, & morte cruenta ac maledicta in terram cadentem: sed multum fructum ex morte ferentem, instar grani tritici, ubi puta calcaneum tritum seminis mulieris, vi ac lethali impetu serpentis Diaboli. Illinc victum & foras ejectum principem hujus mundi, imperio suo mortis expoliatum, & mundum judicatum, hoc est, condemnatum, ac internecioni addictum. Ubi puta contritum caput, hoc est, robur ac regnum serpentis Diaboli, ad internecionem deletum ac abolitum. Unde istius promissionis, Inimiciam ponam inter te & inter mulierem, inter semen tuum, & inter semen ejus: ipsum conteret tibi caput, & tu conteres ei calcaneum, Gen. 3: 15. complementum efflorescere, ut fateacalcaneum ris, necesse est: Nam serpens Diabolus tunc princeps erat hujus mundi, hoc est, hominis, generisque humani, quod victum & ereptum Dei imperio, suo peccati, maledictionis, & mortis imperio, obnoxium fecerat. In hac enim promissione 1°. Cernis semen mulieris. 2°. Serpentem Diabolum, hujus mundi principem, & ipsius semen, spirituale scilicet, Daemonum legiones, malignos ac facinorosos homines, Deo exosos ac inimicos, morti ac maledictioni obnoxios: mali enim Angeli, & homines nequam, genuinum sunt ac germanum semen serpentis Diaboli: Beelzebul enim Diabolorum princeps, parens est omnium Angelorum tenebrarum: tum quia suam in Deum rebellionem in eos propagavit, pelleſtos in suam apostasiam nefandam: tum quia est eorum caput ac princeps: princeps vero suorum subditorum parens perhibetur: unde Augusti Cæsares Patres patriæ, & authores aliis, artis vel scientiæ, eorum parentes jure merito habentur: unde Jabal Pastorum stabulantium in tabernaculis, & Jubal pulsantium cytharam & organum Pater dicitur, Gen. 4: 20. 21. Eadem plane de causa, serpens Diabolus parens est omnium nequam hominum; tum quia illis author peccati, maledictionis & mortis, ex quibus exsurgit imago Diaboli: tum quia eorum princeps suam in iis efficacem exercet potestatem, tanquam in filiis rebellionis. Unde peccato ac Diabolo mancipati, & progenies viperarum, & filii Diaboli non immerito dicuntur, Vos ex patre Diabolo estis, & cupiditates Patris vestri vultis exequi, Ioh. 8: 44. Hinc Judas Iscariota Diabolus dicitur, Ioh. 6: 70. Hinc filii Dei, & filii Diaboli opponuntur, 1. Ioh. 3: 10. Et Magum Elymam plenum omni dolo & omni fallacia, inimicum omnis justitiæ, & filium Diaboli Paulus pronunciat, Act. 13: 10. Hic 3°. cernis inimicitiam irreconciliabilem ac fatalem, in pugnam ad lethum prorumpentem, inter semen mulieris, serpentem ac semen ejus. 4°. Denique pugnæ eventum disparem. Hinc tritum seminis mulieris calcaneum: illinc caput serpentis Diaboli, ac seminis ejus contritum. Hæc vero omnia exacte adimpleta, tibi ponit ob oculos Jesus in loco quem habemus præ manibus. Hic enim cernis, 1°. filium hominis, promissum nempe semen mulieris. 2°. Principem hujus mundi, Diabolum, ejusque semen, seu mundum. 3°. Inimicitiam ac fatale odium, tum principis hujus mundi, tum ejus seminis in filium hominis, cum effectu æstuantissimi odii, morte cruenta ac ignominiosa crucis, in quam datur filius hominis, authore Diabolo principe hujus mundi: (nam Diabolus Judæ Iscariotæ author est proditionis ac traditionis Christi, Luc: 22.3. Ioan. 13: 2. 27. Et Scribæ ac Pharisæi cum Sectariis Judæis nequissimis, filium hominis in crucem dant, Ioh. 8: 28.) 4°. Inimicitiam filii hominis adversus Diabolum hujus mundi principem, ac semen ejus mundum. Effectum denique ac eventum hujusmodi inimicitiæ, judicium scilicet mundi, & Diaboli e suo principatu ejectionem. Filius enim hominis Christus, morte sua abolevit Diabolum mortis imperatorem, Hebr. 2: 14. & mundum vicit, Ioh. 16: 33. Cum igitur Jesum vides signanter se ὁ υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου appellantem, dum ea prænunciat, quæ plenum continent complementum primæ promissionis de Messia, semine mulieris contrituro caput serpentis, & vicissim in talo suo à serpente conterendo, hanc filii hominis nomenclationem sibi Jesum tribuisse, buisse, ut Judæorum animos, ad recolendam primam de Messia promissionem, excitaret, fatearis necesse est.
units.tr: Third, that Jesus, with his eyes fixed on the first promise about the Messiah, called himself the Son of man, which is most evidently shown by John 12:23, 24, 27, 31, 32, 33. The hour has come that the Son of man should be glorified. Truly, truly I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. Now my soul is troubled, and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour; but for this reason I came to this hour. Now is the judgement of this world; now the prince of this world shall be cast out. And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all men to myself. But he said this, signifying by what death he would die. Here, Christian reader, you see the Son of man carrying on enmity and a decisive battle with the power of darkness, the prince of this world, the serpent the Devil, fighting at close quarters. You also see the outcome of this memorable battle. Here the Son of man is lifted from the earth onto the cross, and falling to the earth by a bloody and accursed death, yet bearing much fruit from his death, like a grain of wheat, where, namely, the heel of the seed of the woman is bruised by the force and deadly assault of the serpent the Devil. There the prince of this world is conquered and cast out, stripped of his power over death, and the world is judged, that is, condemned and given over to destruction. There, namely, the bruised head, that is, the strength and kingdom of the serpent the Devil, is destroyed and abolished to ruin. Hence it is necessary that you admit the fulfilment of that promise, I will put enmity between you and the woman, between your seed and her seed; he shall crush your head, and you shall bruise his heel (Gen. 3:15), to blossom forth. For the serpent the Devil was then the prince of this world, that is, of man and the human race, which he had made subject to his own power of sin, curse and death, after it had been conquered and snatched from the rule of God. For in this promise (1) you see the seed of the woman; (2) the serpent the Devil, prince of this world, and his seed, namely the spiritual seed, the legions of demons, wicked and criminal men, hateful and hostile to God, subject to death and curse. For evil angels and worthless men are the genuine and true seed of the serpent the Devil. Beelzebul, prince of the devils, is the father of all the angels of darkness, both because he spread his rebellion against God to them, enticing them into his wicked apostasy, and because he is their head and prince; and a prince is called the father of his subjects. Hence the Caesars of Augustus are rightly regarded as fathers of the fatherland and authors of other arts or sciences, and so they are rightly considered their fathers. Thus Jabal is called the father of those who dwell in tents with flocks, and Jubal the father of those who play the harp and organ (Gen. 4:20, 21). For exactly the same reason the serpent the Devil is the father of all wicked men: both because he is the author of sin, curse and death, from which the image of the Devil arises, and because their prince exercises his effective power over them as over sons of rebellion. Hence those who are enslaved to sin and the Devil are not undeservedly called a brood of vipers and children of the Devil: You are of your father the Devil, and you want to carry out the desires of your father (John 8:44). Hence Judas Iscariot is called a devil (John 6:70). Hence the sons of God and the sons of the Devil are set in opposition (1 John 3:10). And Paul pronounces the magician Elymas, full of all deceit and all trickery, an enemy of all righteousness and a son of the Devil (Acts 13:10). Here, third, you see an irreconcilable and deadly enmity breaking out into a battle to the death between the seed of the woman and the serpent and his seed. (4) Finally, you see the unequal outcome of the battle: on one side the heel of the seed of the woman is bruised, on the other the head of the serpent the Devil and of his seed is crushed. All these things, precisely fulfilled, Jesus sets before your eyes in the passage we have in hand. For here you see (1) the Son of man, the promised seed of the woman; (2) the prince of this world, the Devil, and his seed, or the world; (3) the enmity and deadly hatred both of the prince of this world and of his seed against the Son of man, with the effect of a most fierce hatred: a bloody and shameful death on the cross, to which the Son of man is handed over by the author, the Devil, prince of this world (for the Devil was the author of the betrayal and handing over of Christ by Judas Iscariot, Luke 22:3; John 13:2, 27; and the scribes and Pharisees, with the most wicked Jewish sectaries, hand the Son of man over to the cross, John 8:28); (4) the enmity of the Son of man against the Devil, prince of this world, and against his seed, the world. Finally, you see the effect and outcome of this kind of enmity: the judgement of the world and the casting out of the Devil from his principality. For Jesus Christ the Son of man, by his death, abolished the Devil, the ruler of death (Heb. 2:14), and conquered the world (John 16:33). Since, therefore, you see Jesus expressly calling himself ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου [the Son of man] while he foretells those things which contain the full fulfilment of the first promise about the Messiah, the seed of the woman who would crush the serpent's head and in turn would be bruised by the serpent in his heel, you must admit that Jesus gave himself this name of Son of man in order to stir the minds of the Jews to recall the first promise about the Messiah.

units.la: Quarto. Cum Euangelista Matthæus Christi genealogiam pertexuit ab Abrahamo ad Josephum Mariæ sponsum, ex qua natum Jesum Christum asserit, Jesum illum filium mulieris per Johannis baptisma, & cœli apertionem, & vocem Dei inclamantis, Tu es filius meus dilectus, & Spiritus sancti sub specie columbæ descensum in ejus caput, palam ac miraculosè in munus mediatorium inauguratum exhibet sub finem capitis tertii, continenter capite quarto, Jesum memorat ductum spiritu in desertum, ut tentaretur à Diabolo dies quadraginta: sed & eum cominùs pugnantem cum vaferrimo illo serpente, eumque tandem in celebri illa μονομαχία expugnantem. Cæcutiat oportet, qui non videt sacrum Spiritus sancti amanuensem, quâ erat divinâ sapientiâ, animos nostros è Jesu filio mulieris, palam in Messiam inaugurato, sapienter deducere ad solemnem illam promissionem seminis mulieris, inimicitias cum serpente agitaturi, ac cominùs pugnaturi, donec tandem caput illius contereret. Re enim vera in deserto serpentem mysticum cum Jesu filio mulieris, iisdemmet artibus ac armis pugnantem nobis proponit, quibus Adamum ac mulierem aggressus, hominem expugnaverat, victumque imperio suo mancipaverat: nimirum concupiscentia oculorum: nam fructus arboris scientiæ erat ad videndum amabilis: concupiscentia carnis, nam erat ad comedendum bonus: superbia vitæ, erat enim ad scientiam desiderabilis, ejusque comestione sperabat homo, se fore Deo parem, sorte sua humana ac terrena, in sortem supremam Numinis, magnificum in modum commutata. Paribus armis at dispari successu expugnandum si pote, filium mulieris aggreditur tentator vaferrimus. Concupiscentia carnis, Si tu es filius Dei, dic ut lapides isti panes fiant: sed malè suada fame, & adversus Deum timidâ diffidentiâ, armata carnis concupiscentia, telum fuit imbelle in filium mulieris purissimum.
