Ad vitæ superbiam, arma validiora se convertit callidissimus Satan: assumptum igitur Iesum in Sanctam civitatem, super pinnaculum templi statuit, infitque ad eum, dejice te ipsum deorsum: nam scriptum est, Angelis suis præcipiet de te, & attollent te in manus, ne forte offendas ad lapidem pedem tuum: Sed irritum expertus conatum suum, confugit ad concupiscentiam oculorum, & assumpto in montem sublimem Iesu, ostendit ei omnia regna mundi, & gloriam eorum, dixitque hæc omnia tibi dabo, si prostratus adoraveris me: sed nec successit insultus ultimus: Victus enim vel in ipso deserto serpens, missum fecit filium mulieris, Angelorum lucis famulitio colendum. Hanc de serpente, sed tractu temporis, leone, aspide, ac dracone, reportandam illustrem victoriam, sacer Vates praedixerat, Psal. 91. contemplatus enim Satanam solemni abusurum promissione, quae extat versiculo 11. ac 12. uti telo, in superbiam inflammandam opportuno, quod in Messiam vibraret, extemplo subnectit versiculo 13. super leonem & aspidem calcabis, leunculum conculcabis, & Draconem. Hic vero mirari subit, cur Iesus luculentam hanc promissionem, futurae Messiae victoriae praenunciam, ad Satanam repellendum non reposuerit. Mirari tamen nolito: noluit enim Christus triumphum ante victoriam celebrare, maluit tentatoris vaferrimi subdole promissionis, qua abutebatur haec verba reticentis; Ut te custodiant in omnibus viis tuis, latebras detegere, vim ac os hosti suo retundere, hocce sui responsi, inevitabili telo; Non tentabis Dominum Deum tuum: nam dare sese praecipitem, ac per aerem volitare, non sunt viae hominis, nedum pientissimi filii hominis Christi.
units.tr: Fourth. When the evangelist Matthew traced Christ's genealogy from Abraham to Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom he says Jesus Christ was born, he openly and miraculously presents this Jesus, the son of the woman, as installed in the mediatorial office at the close of the third chapter, through John's baptism, the opening of heaven, the voice of God crying out, You are my beloved Son, and the descent of the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove upon his head. Then, continuing in the fourth chapter, he records that Jesus was led by the Spirit into the desert to be tempted by the Devil for forty days; and also that he fought at close quarters with that most crafty serpent and finally overcame him in that famous single combat. Someone must be blind who does not see that the holy amanuensis of the Holy Spirit, by divine wisdom, wisely leads our minds from Jesus, the son of the woman, now openly inaugurated as Messiah, to that solemn promise of the seed of the woman, who would wage enmity with the serpent and fight with him at close quarters until at last he would crush his head. For in truth, in the desert, he sets before us the mystical serpent fighting with the son of the woman by the very same arts and weapons with which he had attacked Adam and the woman and conquered man and subjected him to his power: namely, the lust of the eyes, for the fruit of the tree of knowledge was pleasing to the sight; the lust of the flesh, for it was good for eating; and the pride of life, for it was desirable for knowledge, and by eating it man hoped to become equal to God, his human and earthly lot being exchanged, in a magnificent way, for the supreme lot of the Deity. The most cunning tempter attacks the son of the woman, trying to overcome him with equal weapons but with unequal success. By the lust of the flesh: If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread. But this was a feeble weapon against the most pure son of the woman, the lust of the flesh armed with a persuasion of hunger and a timid distrust of God. Turning to weapons of greater strength, the most crafty Satan turned to the pride of life: Then the devil took him to the holy city and set him on the pinnacle of the temple, and said to him, throw yourself down; for it is written, He will give his angels charge over you, and they will bear you up in their hands, lest you strike your foot against a stone. But having found his attempt useless, he fled to the lust of the eyes, and taking Jesus up to a very high mountain, he showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, and said, All these things I will give you, if you fall down and worship me. But even this final assault did not succeed. For the serpent, conquered even in the desert itself, gave up the son of the woman to be worshipped by the service of the angels of light. The sacred prophet had foretold this famous victory over the serpent, which would be obtained, in the course of time, over the lion, the asp and the dragon (Ps. 91). For when he saw that Satan would abuse the solemn promise found in verses 11 and 12 as a weapon suited to kindle pride, which he would hurl against the Messiah, he immediately added in verse 13: You shall tread upon the lion and the asp; the young lion and the dragon you shall trample under foot. Here one is moved to wonder why Jesus did not bring out this splendid promise, a forecast of the future victory of the Messiah, to repel Satan. Yet do not wonder: for Christ was unwilling to celebrate a triumph before the victory. He preferred to uncover the hiding places of the most cunning tempter, who abused the promise by quietly omitting these words, that they may keep you in all your ways, and to blunt his force and mouth against his enemy with this unavoidable weapon of his reply: You shall not tempt the Lord your God. For to cast oneself headlong and to fly through the air are not the ways of man, much less of Christ, the most devoted Son of man.

units.la: 5°. Euangelista Lucas, ubi capite tertio Iesum muneri mediatorio praepositum exhibuit, solemni Dei proclamatione, ac pompa miraculosa coeli aperti, & descensus spiritus Sancti, visibili columbae specie, extemplo Jesu genealogiam pertexit, ascendendo a Iosepho ad Adamum, eumque nobis exhibet contemplandum, ut filium Adami, seu hominis. Eccur vero? nimirum sacer spiritus sancti amanuensis, consilii Christi sui plane conscius, facto suo sapienti clare innuere voluit, Iesum eo consilio se filium hominis, seu Adami, ubivis fere insigniisse, ut Judaeorum animos, ad recolendam primam de Messia Mediatore ac liberatore, filio mulieris, seu Adami promissionem, sapienter ac efficaciter excitaret. Et ne cuiquam subsit de scopo, tum Euangelistae, tum Christi, dubitatio; protinus capite quarto sequenti, Euangelista sacer subnectit historiam tentationis Christi filii Adami, ut nos doceat, 1°. se non in consulto Iesum legitima serie genealogica exhibuisse filium Adami, illum scilicet, quem Deus a lapsu Adamo promiserat, passurum a serpente calcanei contritionem, & vicissim caput serpentis contriturum ex mutuo odio, ac implacabili inimicitia. Dubitare enim qui pote, Iesum esse semen mulieris, seu filium hominis, hostilem inimicitiam cum serpente Diabolo exercituram, quem videt a serpente in deserto tentatum & oppugnatum: ex quo solemni Dei declaratione, Mediator ac liberator hominum promulgatus fuit? 2°. Ut nos doceat, Iesum ab assignato sibi munere, ut ut laboriosio, & telis lethiferis venenati serpentis expositio, se non subduxisse: sed alacrem accinxisse ad pugnam, & in arenam, ductu proprii spiritus, desertum horridum, descendisse, cum satana hoste infensissimo seminis mulieris, cominus pugnaturum, donec pugnam decretoriam in cruce iniret, passurus calcanei sui contritionem, & per eam, mortem scilicet cruentam suam, Diabolum mortis imperatorem aboleret, ejusque caput, peccatum, legis maledictionem, mortem, robur ac regnum contereret. Denique Christum iisdem telis petitum a satana, haud inconsulto memorat, quibus Adamus a serpente satana prostratus ac victus succubuerat, nimirum concupiscentia carnis, concupiscentia oculorum, ac vitae superbia, Luc. 4: 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. 8. 9. 10. Noverat enim hostis vaferrimus, hinc peccatum omne in mundum profluxisse, 1. Joh. 2: 16. Jac. 1: 14. 15.
units.tr: Fifth, the evangelist Luke, having presented Jesus in the third chapter as installed in the mediatorial office, with the solemn proclamation of God and the miraculous spectacle of the opened heaven and the descent of the Holy Spirit in the visible form of a dove, immediately traces Jesus' genealogy, ascending from Joseph to Adam, and sets him before us to be considered as the son of Adam, that is, of man. Why? Surely the sacred amanuensis of the Holy Spirit, fully aware of Christ's purpose, wished to show clearly by his act that Jesus, with this aim, had almost everywhere marked himself as the Son of Man, or son of Adam, so that he might wisely and effectively stir the Jews to recall the first promise concerning the Messiah, the Mediator and Deliverer, the seed of the woman, or son of Adam. And lest anyone doubt the purpose of either the evangelist or Christ, the sacred evangelist in the following chapter four adds the account of Christ's temptation, the son of Adam, to teach us, first, that he did not present Jesus in a genealogical sequence without purpose as the son of Adam, that is, the one whom God had promised after Adam's fall, who would suffer the bruising of his heel by the serpent and in turn would crush the serpent's head, through mutual hatred and implacable enmity. For who could doubt that Jesus, the seed of the woman or Son of Man, would wage hostile enmity against the serpent, the devil, when he sees him tempted and attacked by the serpent in the desert, from which solemn declaration of God the Mediator and Deliverer of men was proclaimed? Second, to teach us that Jesus did not shrink from the task assigned to him, however laborious and exposed to the deadly weapons of the poisonous serpent. Rather, he girded himself eagerly for the fray and, led by his own Spirit, descended into the arena, the dreadful desert, to fight at close quarters with Satan, the most hostile enemy of the seed of the woman, until he joined the decisive battle on the cross, suffering the bruising of his heel, and through that, his own bloody death, would abolish the devil, the lord of death, and crush his head, sin, the curse of the law, death, power and kingdom. Finally, the author notes that Christ was assailed by Satan with the very weapons by which Adam, struck down and conquered by the serpent Satan, had succumbed: namely, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes and the pride of life, Luke 4:3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10. For the most cunning enemy knew that all sin had flowed into the world from these sources, 1 John 2:16; James 1:14, 15.

units.la: 6°. Jesum hac sua frequenti Υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, nomenclatione, ad primam de semine mulieris propheticam promissionem respectasse, vel hinc evidentissime liquet, quòd nimirum se filium hominis dixerit, ubi ea se praestiturum, vel passurum recipit, quae aperte continentur in solemni isthac promissione. Et 1°. quidem, si in ea inimicitiam inter serpentem Diabolum & semen mulieris exercendam cernimus. Cum Christus fatum in agro lolium ex Diaboli inimici sui odio, proponit, se filium hominis insigni illi inimico oppositum, insignire amat, Qui seminat bonum semen est filius hominis, ager autem est mundus: bonum vero semen sunt filii regni, zizania vero sunt filii illius mali: inimicus autem, qui seminavit ea, est Diabolus, Matth. 13: 37. 38. 39. Dum vero reponit mutuam suam inimicitiam exercendam in semen Diaboli, quâ fore ut id perdat consumatque aeterno exitio, praenunciat, signanter se iterum filium hominis dixit, Mittet filius hominis Angelos suos, qui colligent ex ipsius regno omnia offendicula; & eos qui faciunt iniquitatem, projicientque eos in fornacem ignis, illic erit fletus stridorque dentium, verf. 41. 42. 2°. Si in solemni, quae exstat Gen. 3: 15. promissione, contritum filii mulieris, infensissimo odio serpentis ac seminis ejus calcaneum cernimus. Iesus dum authores mortis suae memorat, ipsamque maledictam mortem crucis praenunciat, signanter ac sapienter se filii hominis nomenclatione insignire amat: Iesus autem dixit ei, Iuda, osculo τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, filium hominis prodis? Luc. 22: 48. Ecce ascendimus Hierosolyma, & filius hominis tradetur primariis sacerdotibus ac Scribis, & condemnabunt eum morte, tradentes eum gentibus, ut illudant, & flagellent, & crucifigant, Matth. 20: 18. 19. 3°. Si in celebri illa promissione, victoriam cernimus seminis mulieris, quâ contriturum est caput serpentis. Iesus dum victoriam suam, quam de serpente ac semine ejus, peccato ac morte per resurrectionem, amplam reportabit praenuntiat, signanter se dixit filium hominis, Filius hominis tertia die resurget, Matth. 20: 19. Cum sustuleritis filium hominis, tunc cognoscetis me eum um esse, & à me ipso nihil facere, scilicet per meam è morte resurrectionem, cognoscetis, Ioh.8:28. Venit hora, ut glorificetur filius hominis: nunc iudicium adest mundi: nunc princeps ille mundi huius ejicietur foras; & ego si sublatus fuero è terra, omnes trabam ad me ipsum, Joh. 12: 23. 31. 32. 4º. Si in celebri promissione ex victoria seminis mulieris, & contrito serpentis capite, oriundam cernimus liberationem generis humani ab imperio serpentis Satanæ, æternamque salutem. Christus dum finem adventus sui in carne, discipulos docuit, salutem puta generis humani, iterum se filii hominis nomenclatione commendat, Venit enim filius hominis, ut servet quod perierat, Matth. 18: 11. 5º. Denique si in solemni promissione modum durum quidem, sed & admirabilem, quo semen mulieris, & contritu-rum erat caput Serpentis, & genus humanum liberaturum, contritum puta ipsius calcaneum, cernimus. Jesus vicissim, dum mortem suam futurum docet pretium redemptionis, modumque liberationis, se filium hominis appellare amat, Filius hominis non venit, ut sibi ministretur: sed ut ministret, detque animam suam redemptionis pretium pro multis, Matth.20:28. Verum enim vero, quæstioni, quam suscepimus perstringendam, plenè ut fiat satis. In causam inquirendum est; cur Jesus huc illuc vagantes Judæorum animos, hac solemni sua filii hominis nomenclatione, in primam super Messia semine mulieris promissionem direxerit? Respondemus igitur tribus imprimis de causis. 1º. Quia perspecta hæc de venturo Messia promissio, præsentissimum erat male præconceptis omnibus super Messia Judæorum opinionibus remedium. 2º. Opportunum ac efficax alexipharmacum, ad purgandos Judæorum errores, adversus Jesum Nazarethanum, heu nimium debacchantes. 3º. Divinum planè collyrium, quo detersō glaucomate, in Jesum, sanis & apertis oculis, uti verum Messiam à lapsu prænunciatum ac promissum, nisi mens læva fuisset, eis intueri daretur. Agedum, hæc tria responsionis momentosa capita, non omninò indiligenter perstringenda, aggrediamur.
units.tr: Sixth, that Jesus, by this frequent name "Son of Man [υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου]", was looking back to the first prophetic promise concerning the seed of the woman, is evident from this: namely, that he called himself the Son of Man whenever he speaks of what he will do or suffer, things plainly contained in that solemn promise. And first, indeed, if we see in it the enmity to be waged between the serpent, the devil, and the seed of the woman. When Christ, from the hatred of his enemy the devil, presents the parable of the tares in the field, he likes to mark himself as the Son of Man, set against that notable enemy: "He who sows the good seed is the Son of Man; the field is the world; the good seed are the children of the kingdom, but the tares are the children of the evil one; and the enemy who sowed them is the devil", Matt. 13:37, 38, 39. And when he foretells that his mutual enmity will be exercised against the devil's seed, by which it will be destroyed and consumed in eternal ruin, he again pointedly calls himself the Son of Man: "The Son of Man will send his angels, who will gather out of his kingdom all stumbling blocks and those who do iniquity, and will cast them into the furnace of fire; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth", vv. 41, 42. Second, if we see in the solemn promise found in Gen. 3:15 the bruised heel of the seed of the woman under the most hostile hatred of the serpent and its seed. When Jesus mentions his betrayers and foretells his own death by the accursed death of the cross, he pointedly and wisely likes to mark himself with the name Son of Man: "But Jesus said to him, Judas, do you betray the Son of Man [τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου] with a kiss?" Luke 22:48. "Behold, we go up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn him to death, and hand him over to the Gentiles to mock, scourge and crucify him", Matt. 20:18, 19. Third, if in that famous promise we see the victory of the seed of the woman, by which the serpent's head is to be crushed. When Jesus foretells his victory, which he will win broadly over the serpent and its seed, sin and death, through the resurrection, he pointedly calls himself the Son of Man: "The Son of Man will rise on the third day", Matt. 20:19. "When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he, and that I do nothing of myself", namely, you will know it through my resurrection from the dead, John 8:28. "The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified; now is the judgment of this world; now the prince of this world will be cast out"; and "I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all men to myself", John 12:23, 31, 32. Fourth, if in the famous promise we see arising from the victory of the seed of the woman and the crushed head of the serpent the deliverance of the human race from the dominion of the serpent Satan, and eternal salvation. When Christ, teaching his disciples the purpose of his coming in the flesh, sets forth the salvation of the human race, he again commends himself by the name Son of Man: "For the Son of Man came to save what was lost", Matt. 18:11. Fifth, finally, if in the solemn promise we see the manner, hard indeed but also admirable, by which the seed of the woman, who was to crush the serpent's head and deliver the human race, would be bruised in his heel. Jesus, in turn, when he teaches that his coming death will be the price of redemption and the manner of deliverance, likes to call himself the Son of Man: "The Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many", Matt. 20:28. But, to be sure, the question we have undertaken to treat must be fully answered. We must inquire into the reason why Jesus, by this solemn name Son of Man, directed the wandering minds of the Jews to the first promise concerning the seed of the woman and the Messiah. We answer, then, chiefly for three reasons. First, because this promise concerning the coming Messiah, clearly understood, was the most ready remedy for all the false preconceived opinions of the Jews about the Messiah. Second, an opportune and effective antidote for purging the errors of the Jews, who, alas, raged too wildly against Jesus of Nazareth. Third, a truly divine eye-salve, by which, the cataract being removed, they would have been granted to look upon Jesus with sound and open eyes as the true Messiah foretold and promised from the fall, unless their mind had been perverse. Come, let us take up these three weighty heads of the answer, not to be treated carelessly.

units.la: Primo quidem frequentissima hæc ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, filii hominis, nomenclatio, tota in animos Judæorum ad primam de Messia promissionem dirigendos comparata, erat quam maximè opportuna, ad sistendam fluctuationem Judæorum, de origine ac modo adventus Messiæ. Eccur dubitatis Judæi, incerti, num Messias è vivis, num è mortuis sit oriundus? An vos fugit, Messiam esse illum filium illius hominis, quem datum in ruinam præcipitem, Numen consolatum est, promisso semine mulieris? cur male sana capita, cum venerit Christus, nemo noverit unde sit, identidem reponitis? An obliti estis Numen mentiri aut fallere nescium, fidem suam obstrinxisse, fore, ut Messias ex muliere originem ducat, futurus semen mulieris, contriturum caput serpentis? An vos fugit, Danielem Messiam contemplatum ipsummet, quem Deus à lapsu promiserat filium hominis, venientem in nubibus cœli? Apage stuporem vestrum, insanam fluctuationem super origine ac modo adventus Messiæ apage. Messiam esse carnis ac sanguinis participem, hominem ex homine, filium hominis, ut pote semen mulieris, Numen veracissimum fore, recepit. 2. Solemnis filii hominis emphatica nomenclatio, tota ad animos, in primam de Messia promissionem, uti in unam scripturarum, ac sapientiæ divinæ cynosuram, dirigendos comparata, quam opportunum erat remedium, ad Judæorum errorem de gemino Messia curandum. Quid furentes Messiam geminum, vilem ac despicabilem alterum ægrum & afflictum Josephi filium: alterum Regem terrenum præpotentem ac bellatorem Davidis filium somniatis? Quò ducit frequens hæc mea filii hominis nomenclatio, sequimini, ad primam de Messia semine mulieris propheticam promissionem animum advertite seduli. Hæc una vos, unum Messiam ex uno homine oriundum, unum filium mulieris, afflictum modò, modò præpotentem bellatorem, ac Regem victorem luculenter docebit. Anne decet semen mulieris ægræ peccati miseriis, vile esse, miserum, ac despicabile caput? Anne decet semen mulieris, ex seminis serpentis æstuantissimo odio, ac furore Diaboli implacabili, calcanei sui passurum contritionem, ægrum esse ac afflictum homunculum? Ulterius vero promissionem audite, miserum illud, ac afflictum mulieris semen, fore ut Serpentis caput conterat, Numen sanctè recepit. Anne decet invictum filium mulieris, contriturum Diaboli robur, ac regnum toto orbe potentissimum; pro tanta liberatione ac victoria, de mortis ac mundi imperatore reportata, Regem fore orbis universi supremum, honore ac gloria coronatum? Quid igitur ambos somniatis Messias, distinctos origine, statu, ac conditione, invicem perpetuum disterminatos? Ecce me unum filium hominis, nunc pauperem, afflictum, hominemque dolorum, mortem ignominiosam oppetiturum. At ecce memet in posterum calcanei mei contritione, caput serpentis contriturum, è mortis dominio exiturum, peccatum, maledictionem, mortem victurum, triumphum de postratis, ac deletis hostibus in excelsis celebraturum: venturum ad Antiquum dierum in nubibus, sessurum ad dextram Majestatis, longè latèque in omnes nationes, orbem universum dominaturum. Ecce me in posterum omni ex parte futurum, qualem promissum à lapsu filium mulieris, Daniel contemplatur in visionibus noctis. 3o. Allucente primæ promissionis veritate, in cujus intuitum tutò dirigit solemne filii hominis elogium, cispellitur vægrandis error, quo etiamnum laborat vniversa Judæorum natio, de Messia Rege præpotenti terreno, & affictis ipsi hostibus carnalibus, regnoque, divitiis, delitiis, ac pompa seculari florentissimo. Quid Christum Regem terrenum, quid regnum ejus somniatis regni Salomonis ad instar florentissimum? Quid debellandos hostes carnales, copiis, bello, ac secularibus armis, carnales ac superciliosi Judæi, ipsi malè affingitis? Quo usque tandem fumosis affectibus ac superbiæ in poenam & ruinam indulgebitis? Mutate tandem mentem insanam: ex scriptura θεοπνεύστῳ sapite: intuemini in primam super Messia semine mulieris, propheticam promissionem. Hostes equidem habet expugnandos, calcandos, ac conterendos: sed spirituales, Serpentem Diabolum, ejusque semen: inimicitiam enim posuit Numen ad internecionem exercendam, inter Serpentem, ejusque semen, filios de natura parentis spirituales censendos, & Messiam mulieris semen. Diabolum verò, tenebrarum potestatem, & quos conscripsit exercitus. peccatum, mundum ac mortem, armis, copiisque carnalibus prosternere, expugnare, conterere, quipote? Ex natura & ingenio hostium Messiæ spiritualium, naturam liberationis ac victoriæ, putate ac colligite: regni Messiæ, ruinis imperii Satanæ diruti atque contriti, inædificandi naturam, æqui rerum æstimatores, si cor sapiat, æstimate. Cœleste sanè ac spirituale regnum sibi comparabit semen mulieris, Rex Messias, ex hostibus spiritualibus Serpente Diabolo, ejusque semine spirituali, fusis ac fugatis, pessundatis ac contritis: victoriam cœlestem ac spiritualem reportabit: trophæa æternùm perennatura eriget spiritualia; ex amplis eorum spoliis: cœlestem triumphum celebrabit, Rex cœlestis ac spiritualis Messias. Hoc vos Daniel docuit filium hominis contemplatus in cœli nubibus triumphantem, usque dum ad Antiquum dierum veniret. Hoc vos docet hæc mea filii hominis nomenclatio: eò tandem vos ducit, solemnis in quam tendit, prima de semine mulieris, inimicitiam cum Serpente ejusque semine agitaturo, ejusque tandem caput contrituro, promissio. 4o. Primæ promissionis intuitus, in quem duxit Judæorum animos insignis hæc Christi, filii hominis appellatio, opportunum erat remedium, ad errorem de gentibus, regno cœlorum Messiæ æternùm exterminandis, curandum, quasi benignissimum Numen, electa sibi una Israelitarum natione, indignas cæteras orbis terrarum gentes habuisset, quæ fierent participes victoriarum, liberationis, ac gratiarum regni Messiæ. Quid, Judæi, inquit Christus, Regem Messiam in unam vestrum salutem, tem, felicitatem ac gloriam venturum, vobis gratulamini? Quid caeteras orbis nationes הנה־ prae contemptu, ac terrae populos, appellitare amatis? Quid eas aeternum abs Dei foederibus, ac regno coelorum Messiae extorres fabulamini? Quid in unum Israelis regnum restituendum Messiae adventum praestolamini? Quin potius in Dei regnum longe lateque per orbem universum constabiliendum, ex prima de semine mulieris, serpentis caput contrituro, promissione, putatis? Numen equidem, Messiam semen Abrahami, filiumque Davidis fore recepit. Verum ne vos insana caperet superbia, ipsummet verax ac fidele Numen omnium primum recepit, Messiam fore semen mulieris, Matris omnium viventium, filiumque Adami, dati in ruinam praecipitis. Est igitur Messias omnium hominum, gentium ac populorum frater, ex homine communi mortalium parente, ex una eademque muliere, omnium viventium matre, oriundus. Eccur vero? ut scilicet ipso Deo, fidem suam astringente, calcanei sui patiatur contritionem, conteratque caput Serpentis, unius generis humani ruinae authoris, destruat opera Diaboli, benignus ac potens generis humani liberator, nullo habito discrimine Judaei aut Graeci, Scythae aut Barbari, liberi aut servi, maris aut foeminae, in omnes, qui de candido ejus nomine vere censebuntur fideles subditi, filius mulieris e potestate Diaboli liberatos, dominabitur. Hoc vos docuit Daniel, intentis in primam promissionem de Messia oculis: vidit enim בר אנוש filium hominis, venientem in nubibus ad Antiquum dierum, ut dominationem, gloriam & regnum dono datum acciperet, ut populi omnes, nationes & linguae serviant illi, Dan. 7: 13. 14.
units.tr: First of all, this very frequent designation son of man [ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου], which is directed entirely at the minds of the Jews, so as to fix their attention on the first promise concerning the Messiah, was most fitting for halting the Jews' wavering about the origin and manner of the Messiah's coming. Why do you Jews doubt, uncertain whether the Messiah will spring from the living or from the dead? Does it escape you that the Messiah is that son of that man whom God comforted when he was given over to headlong ruin, by the promised seed of the woman? Why, you dull-witted people, do you keep repeating when Christ comes, no one will know where he is from? Have you forgotten that God, who cannot lie or deceive, pledged his faith that the Messiah would trace his origin from a woman, being the seed of the woman who would crush the serpent's head? Does it escape you that Daniel contemplated the Messiah himself, whom God had promised from the fall as the son of man, coming on the clouds of heaven? Away with your stupidity, away with your mad wavering over the origin and manner of the Messiah's coming! He received that the Messiah would be a sharer in flesh and blood, a man born of a man, the son of man, as the seed of the woman, and that God would be most truthful. 2. The solemn and emphatic designation son of man, directed entirely at minds, as at the one guiding star of the Scriptures and of divine wisdom, fixed on the first promise concerning the Messiah, was a fitting remedy for curing the Jews' error about a twofold Messiah. Why, in your madness, do you dream of two Messiahs, one a worthless and contemptible son of Joseph, sick and afflicted, the other a mighty earthly king and warrior, a son of David? Follow where this frequent designation of mine, son of man, leads you; attentively consider the first prophetic promise about the Messiah, the seed of the woman. This one promise will clearly teach you that there is one Messiah, born of one man, one son of a woman, who is at one time afflicted, at another a mighty warrior and victorious king. Is it fitting that the seed of a woman, sick with the miseries of sin, should be a base, wretched and contemptible head? Is it fitting that the seed of a woman, who would suffer the bruising of his heel from the raging and implacable hatred and fury of the Devil, the seed of the serpent, should be a sick and afflicted little man? Hear further the promise that God solemnly gave: that this wretched and afflicted seed of the woman would crush the serpent's head. Is it fitting that the invincible son of a woman, who would crush the power of the Devil and a kingdom most mighty over the whole world, should, for so great a deliverance and victory won over the lord of death and of the world, be made the supreme king of the whole world, crowned with honour and glory? Why then do you dream of two Messiahs, distinct in origin, condition and state, forever cut off from one another? Behold, I, one son of man, now poor, afflicted, and a man of sorrows, shall undergo a shameful death. But behold, in the future I shall crush the serpent's head by the bruising of my heel, I shall come forth from the dominion of death, I shall overcome sin, curse and death, and I shall celebrate on high a triumph over prostrate and destroyed enemies; I shall come to the Ancient of Days on the clouds, sit at the right hand of the Majesty, and rule far and wide over all nations, over the whole world. Behold, in the future I shall be in every respect such as Daniel contemplates in the visions of the night, the son of woman promised from the fall. 3. As the truth of the first promise shines forth, and with it the solemn saying son of man guides us safely, the error that still holds the whole Jewish nation is dispelled, the error about a Messiah who is a mighty earthly king, with his enemies, the carnal foes, cast down, and with a kingdom flourishing in riches, pleasures and worldly pomp. Why do you dream of Christ as an earthly king, and of his kingdom as flourishing like the kingdom of Solomon? Why do you yourselves wrongly imagine that carnal and haughty Jews will crush their carnal enemies with troops, war and worldly arms? How long, at last, will you indulge in smoky passions and pride, to your own punishment and ruin? Change your mad mind at last: be wise from the God-breathed [θεοπνεύστῳ] Scripture; look upon the first prophetic promise about the Messiah, the seed of the woman. Indeed, he has enemies to be overcome, trodden down and crushed, but they are spiritual: the Serpent, the Devil, and his seed. For God set enmity between the Serpent and his seed, to be carried on to mutual destruction, and the seed of the woman, the Messiah. But who can cast down, overcome and crush by carnal arms and forces the Devil, the power of darkness, and the army he has enrolled: sin, the world and death? From the nature and character of the Messiah's spiritual enemies, consider and infer the nature of the deliverance and victory; and, if your heart is wise, judge the nature of the building up of the Messiah's kingdom, once the empire of Satan has been overthrown and crushed, as impartial judges of things. The seed of the woman, the king Messiah, will win for himself a heavenly and spiritual kingdom, having routed, put to flight, overthrown and crushed the spiritual enemies, the Serpent the Devil and his spiritual seed: he will win a heavenly and spiritual victory, he will set up spiritual trophies that will last forever from their rich spoils; the heavenly King, the spiritual Messiah, will celebrate a heavenly triumph. Daniel taught you this when he contemplated the son of man triumphing in the clouds of heaven until he came to the Ancient of Days. This my designation son of man teaches you this; it leads you at last to that solemn promise, the first, about the seed of the woman, which will wage enmity with the Serpent and his seed, and will at last crush his head. 4. Looking to the first promise, to which this distinctive appellation of Christ, son of man, led the minds of the Jews, was a fitting remedy for curing the error that the Gentiles were to be forever excluded from the kingdom of heaven of the Messiah, as if the most kindly God, having chosen for himself the one nation of the Israelites, had regarded all the other nations of the earth as unworthy to share in the victories, the deliverance and the graces of the kingdom of the Messiah. Christ says: Jews, why do you rejoice that the Messiah is coming for the salvation, happiness and glory of you alone? Why do you love to call the other nations of the world, and the peoples of the earth, הנה [hinneh] in contempt? Why do you fable that they are forever cut off from God's covenants and from the kingdom of heaven of the Messiah? Why do you await the Messiah's coming to restore the kingdom to Israel alone? Do you not rather think that the kingdom of God is to be established far and wide over the whole world, from the first promise about the seed of the woman, who will crush the serpent's head? God indeed received that the Messiah would be the seed of Abraham and the son of David. But lest mad pride should seize you, the true and faithful God first received that the Messiah would be the seed of the woman, the mother of all living, and the son of Adam, who was given over to headlong ruin. The Messiah is therefore the brother of all men, nations and peoples, sprung from the common parent of mortals, from one and the same woman, the mother of all the living. Why indeed? Namely, so that, God himself pledging his faith, he might suffer the bruising of his heel, crush the serpent's head, and destroy the works of the Devil, as the kindly and powerful deliverer of the human race, with no distinction made between Jew and Greek, Scythian and barbarian, free and slave, male and female; the son of the woman will rule over all who are rightly counted among his faithful subjects by his bright name, having freed them from the power of the Devil. Daniel taught you this, his eyes fixed on the first promise about the Messiah: for he saw the son of man [בר אנוש], coming on the clouds to the Ancient of Days, to receive dominion, glory and a kingdom given by gift, so that all peoples, nations and tongues should serve him (Dan. 7:13, 14).

units.la: Ad secundum responsionis momentum quod spectat, frequentem hanc filii hominis, qua se Christus insignire amavit, nomenclaturam, ad curandos omnes errores, quibus in Jesum Nazarethanum praepediti Judaei impotenter debacchabantur, quam opportunam fuisse, inficiabitur nemo, siquidem in animum suum induxerit, errores hujusmodi ad tria imprimis capita, commodum referri posse. 1o. Ad opinionem de Jesu Christi origine ac natalibus. 2o. De vili ac contempta ipsius sorte. 3o. De ipsius syncretismo, & occulta cum Daemonibus amicitia. Nolebant enim Judaei, Jesum Nazarethanum habere & confiteri Messiam, sibi promissum à Numine, quod apprime nosse se existimarent, unde duxisset originem, quòd vilis, pauperrimus, ac contemnendus iis videretur, plebeis aliquot stipatus discipulis, & cum exosis sibi telonibus, ac violentis exactoribus, & nullius frugis homunculis, frequenter conversaretur: quod denique occultam coleret cum Daemonibus amicitiam, & authoritate Beelzebul, principis Diabolorum, daemoniacos curaret. Haec vero ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, filii hominis, appellatio, in animos Judaeorum, ad primam de Messia promissionem, dirigendos comparata, omnes hujuscemodi male praeconceptas de Jesu, Judaeorum opiniones, radicitus evellere, nisi mens laeva fuisset, valebat. Quae vos, inquit Christus, male occupavit dementia. O Judaei, ut me carnali conjugio ex Josepho fabro, & Maria ortum putetis? ego sum filius hominis, quem Deus a lapsu Adami promisit, quem vidit Daniel in coelum ascendentem in nubibus, cujus pedibus subjecit omnia Deus. Reputate amabo cum animis vestris; sapientissimum Numen Messiam vocasse filium hominis, ac eundem, uti semen mulieris, promisisse: non vero semen viri & mulieris: ut ut Serpens non mulierem modo, sed & Adamum ipsius virum in errorem pellexerat, dederatque in ruinam praecipitem. Hocine factum absque divina sapientia existimatis, quod sapientissimum Numen non dixerit, Messiam fore semen viri & uxoris: sed signanter semen mulieris? semen sane mulieris Messiam fore dixit, ut singularem & exortem illius nativitatem, ex sola muliere, significaret. En me illum filium hominis, quod Numen Serpenti ruinam interminatum, Adamo promisit. Nolite igitur in posterum existimare, me ex carnali ortum conjugio, filiumque Josephi fabri ex Maria matre mea susceптum. Nolite in posterum me prae odio ac contemptu homulum habere, vestro dignum ludibrio: sum equidem, fatebor enim, hominum pauperrimus, passurus scilicet, in hominum salutem, a serpente Diabolo calcanei contritionem, sed & ea propter dignus, quem homines in amore habeant ac deliciis; nam filius hominis ego, promissum illud benedictum semen mulieris, caput Serpentis conteram, hominesque abs dura ipsius exemptos tyrannide, asseram in libertatem ac salutem gloriosam. Quid putatis me occultam colere cum Daemonibus amicitiam, quem videtis & Serpenti Diabolo, & femini ejus Daemoniis ac mundo, infensissimum? Opera Diaboli ubivis terrarum diruo ac destruo, morbos, languores ac miserias, generis humani misertus, passim curo: famelicos populos miraculosa panum multiplicatione nutrio ac reficio: incurvatos paralyticos, aegrotos omne genus, pristinae sanitati restituo: mortuos, vel foetentes ad vitam revoco: Daemonia passim ejicio: inimicitiam exerceo, ac bellum sine induciis, cum Serpente Diabolo agito: mundum Serpentis semen, cum suis operibus diabolicis, blasphemiae, hypocriseos, injustitiae, superbiae, avaritiae, reum perago. An sano cuiquam fit verisimile, me occultam colere cum Daemonibus amicitiam? Ad opera mea attendite. Quis vestrum me arguat sceleris, vel peccati cujusvis reum jure peragat? An filius hominis, vitæ integer, scelerisque purus, sine fraude, sine mendacio, occultam colit amicitiam, cum impurissimo Serpente, mendacissimoque Diabolo, aut mundo semine ejus in malitia posito? Attendite in primam Messiæ seminis mulieris promissionem. Ego sum ille filius hominis, inimicitiam ad necem usque cum Serpente ac semine ejus exerciturus. Hoc clamat vita mea: hoc mea clamant patrata, vobis spectantibus, adversus Diabolum præclara facinora: hoc meum clamat, filii hominis, nomen. Nolite igitur me syncretismi, & occultæ cum Dæmonibus insimulare amicitiæ. Nolite amplius in spiritum sanctum, tot præclara miracula in mei filii hominis ac Messiæ testimonium exhibentem, peccare. Nolite accepta referre Diabolo, filii hominis hosti infensissimo opera, quæ spiritus sanctus edidit, Deo unicè referenda.
units.tr: As to the second point of the answer, that the frequent name Son of Man, by which Christ loved to designate himself, was well suited to correcting all the errors with which the Jews, hindered by their opposition to Jesus of Nazareth, raged without restraint, no one will deny, if he considers that such errors can conveniently be traced to three main heads. First, to the opinion about Jesus Christ's origin and birth. Second, to the view of his base and despised condition. Third, to the charge of a syncretism and a secret friendship with demons. For the Jews did not want to have or confess Jesus of Nazareth as the Messiah promised by God, whose origin they thought they knew very well. He seemed to them lowly, very poor and contemptible, attended by a few common disciples, and often in the company of tax collectors, whom they hated, and of violent extortioners and worthless little men. Finally, they held that he cultivated a secret friendship with demons and cured the demon-possessed by the authority of Beelzebul, the prince of demons. But the appellation ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου [filii hominis, the Son of Man], was fitted to direct the minds of the Jews to the first promise concerning the Messiah, and it could have torn out by the roots all such preconceived opinions of the Jews about Jesus, had their minds not been perverse. "What madness," Christ says in effect, "has seized you? O Jews, do you suppose that I was born of carnal marriage, from Joseph the carpenter and Mary? I am the Son of Man, whom God promised after Adam's fall, whom Daniel saw coming in the clouds, and to whose feet God subjected all things. Consider, I beg you, with your minds: the most wise Deity called the Messiah the Son of Man, and promised him, as the seed of the woman, and not the seed of man and woman, although the Serpent had led astray not only the woman but Adam, her husband, and had thrown him into headlong ruin. Do you think this happened without divine wisdom, that the most wise Deity did not say the Messiah would be the seed of man and wife, but pointedly the seed of the woman? Surely he said the Messiah would be the seed of the woman to signify his singular birth, free of man, from the woman alone. Behold, I am that Son of Man, whom God promised to Adam when he threatened ruin to the Serpent. Do not therefore suppose henceforth that I was born of carnal marriage, or that I am the son of Joseph the carpenter received from my mother Mary. Do not from now on look upon me with hatred and contempt as a poor little man, worthy of your mockery. I am indeed, I will confess, the poorest of men, destined indeed to suffer, for the salvation of men, the bruising of my heel by the serpent, the devil; yet for this very reason I am worthy to be loved and delighted in by men. For I am the Son of Man, the promised blessed seed of the woman, who will crush the head of the Serpent and rescue men from his harsh tyranny and assert them into liberty and glorious salvation. Why do you think I cultivate a secret friendship with demons, when you see that I am utterly hostile both to the serpent, the devil, and to his seed, the demons and the world? Wherever on earth I overthrow and destroy the works of the devil, out of pity for the human race I heal diseases, sicknesses and miseries everywhere; I feed and restore hungry peoples by the miraculous multiplication of loaves; I restore the crippled and paralytics, and the sick of every kind, to former health; I call the dead, or those already stinking, back to life; everywhere I cast out demons; I wage hostility and war without truce against the serpent, the devil. I prosecute the world, the serpent's seed, with its diabolical works of blasphemy, hypocrisy, injustice, pride and avarice. Is it at all plausible to anyone that I cultivate a secret friendship with demons? Look at my works. Which of you can accuse me of wrongdoing, or prosecute me rightly as guilty of any sin? Does the Son of Man, whole in life, pure of crime, without deceit, without lying, cultivate a secret friendship with the most impure serpent and the most lying devil, or with the world that lies in wickedness, his seed? Attend to the first promise concerning the Messiah, the seed of the woman. I am that Son of Man, who will wage enmity to the death against the Serpent and his seed. My life cries this out; my notable deeds, performed before your eyes against the devil, cry this out; my name, the Son of Man, cries this out. Do not therefore accuse me of syncretism and of a secret friendship with demons. Do not sin any longer against the Holy Spirit, who has shown so many notable miracles as the testimony to me, the Son of Man and the Messiah. Do not attribute to the devil, the most bitter enemy of the Son of Man, the works which the Holy Spirit has performed, which are to be referred to God alone."

units.la: Hæc denique filii hominis nomenclatio, primæ de Messia promissionis memoriam refricans, præ cæteris Messiæ elogiis, ad momentosa quævis super Messia capita, Judæos docenda, omnium erat maximè opportuna. Et 1º. quidem Messiam esse ex muliere, sine viro virgine oriundum, uti genuinum ac singulare semen mulieris. 2º. Non modò singularem nativitatem: sed & vitam Messiæ laboriosam, serpenti Diabolo, ejusque semini mundo, infensissimam, explicabat ob oculos Judæorum: filius enim mulieris, caput Serpentis contriturus, vitam erat victurus, in Diaboli perniciem, ac ruinam operum ipsius. 3º. Statum Messiæ afflictum, ac mortem crudelissimam ex serpentis insidiis, ac venenatis insultibus per calcanei contritionem, oculis explicabat considerandam. 4º. Messiæ filii mulieris, illustrem victoriam de Serpente, ac semine ipsius, peccato, maledictione, ac morte, per mortem ac resurrectionem reportandam, non innuebat modò, sed & evidenter docebat. 5º. Ascensionem in cælum, triumphum victore Messia dignum, ut commodum vitæ spirituali, ex maledictione ac morte emergenti, adiret & ingrederetur domicilium, colligendam necessario proponebat. Denique dum recolendam procurabat primam super Messia promissionem propheticam, tria filii hominis Christi munera, haud obscurè ob oculos Judæorum exponebat. Et 1º. quidem propheticum: nam sicut serpens caput Adami contriverat, eumque innocentiâ, sanctitate, ac dominio in creaturas expoliaverat, falsâ suâ prophetiâ de erciscunda suprema gloria Creatoris, in errorem ac inobedientiam pellectum. Non secus & Messias filius mulieris, munere Prophetæ veracis functus, vias Dei ac regni cœlorum hominibus aperiens, illâ verâ suâ prophetiâ, caput serpentis erat contriturus. turus. Hinc dum reversi è præconio regni cœlorum septuaginta cum gaudio discipuli, Christo renunciant, etiam Dæmonia subjiciuntur nobis in nomine tuo: exultans Jesus in spiritu, lætabundus exclamat: spectabam Satanam ut fulgur è cœlo cadentem; ecce do vobis potestatem calcandi serpentes & scorpiones, & supra omnem vim inimici, & nihil vos lædet, Luc. 10: 17. 18. 19. 20. Sacerdotale in trito calcaneo, morte nimirum cruenta ac maledicta, quâ & se obtulit in sacrificium, & divinam justitiam placavit, & peccata expiavit, in credituri feminis sui ex Serpentis tyrannide, liberationem ac salutem. 3°. Denique regale munus in pugna, ac reportata victoria per contritum caput Serpentis, robur ac imperium Diaboli mortis imperatoris, dirutum ac abolitum. Regis enim pugnare est, debellar hostes superbos, trophæa è manubiis eorum erigere, triumphum celebrare, ac dominari longè latèque in victos, subditosque populos. Non igitur absre, sed sapientissimo ac plane divino consilio, posthabitisferè cæteris Messiæ elogiis, unum amavit filii hominis nomen, quod primam recolendo de Messia promissionem, opportunum erat & ad curandos malè præconceptos de Christo venturo Judæorum errores, & iniquissimas de Jesu Nazarethano opiniones radicitùs evellendas, & maximè memorabilia momenta aperienda, de Messiæ nativitate, vita, pugna, morte, victoria, resurrectione, ascensione, dominio supremo, nec non ad homines, de ejusdem muneribus, prophetico, sacerdotali, ac regio, commonefaciendos ac erudiendos.
units.tr: Finally, this name Son of Man, recalling the memory of the first promise concerning the Messiah, was of all the titles of the Messiah the most opportune for teaching the Jews the most important points about the Messiah. First, indeed, that the Messiah would be born of a woman, a virgin without a man, as the true and singular seed of the woman. Second, it set before the eyes of the Jews not only his singular birth but also the laborious life of the Messiah, most hostile to the serpent, the devil, and to his seed, the world; for the seed of the woman, who was to crush the serpent's head, was to live a life that would bring ruin to the devil and the destruction of his works. Third, it set before their eyes the afflicted state of the Messiah and his most cruel death from the serpent's snares and venomous assaults, by the bruising of the heel, to be considered. Fourth, it not only hinted but clearly taught that the Messiah, the seed of the woman, was to win a famous victory over the serpent and his seed, over sin, curse and death, through death and resurrection. Fifth, it necessarily proposed his ascension into heaven, a triumph worthy of the victorious Messiah, so that, as a benefit to spiritual life emerging from curse and death, he might enter and take up his dwelling there. Finally, while it brought back to mind the first prophetic promise about the Messiah, it displayed clearly before the eyes of the Jews the three offices of the Son of Man, Christ. First, indeed, the prophetic office: for just as the serpent had bruised Adam's head, and stripped him of innocence, holiness and dominion over creatures, having led him into error and disobedience by his false prophecy of equality with the supreme glory of the Creator, so too the Messiah, the seed of the woman, discharging the office of a true Prophet and opening to men the ways of God and of the kingdom of heaven, was to crush the serpent's head by that true prophecy of his. Hence, when the seventy disciples returned from preaching the kingdom of heaven with joy and reported to Christ, even the demons are subject to us in your name, Jesus, exulting in the Spirit, cried out joyfully: I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven; behold, I give you power to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing will harm you (Luke 10:17, 18, 19, 20). Second, the priestly office, in the bruised heel, namely a bloody and cursed death, by which he offered himself as a sacrifice, appeased divine justice, and expiated sins, so that he might obtain for the believers of his seed liberation and salvation from the tyranny of the serpent. Third, finally, the kingly office: in the battle and the victory won through the crushed head of the Serpent, the power and dominion of the devil, the emperor of death, were overthrown and abolished. For it belongs to a king to fight, to subdue proud enemies, to raise trophies from their spoils, to celebrate a triumph, and to rule far and wide over conquered and subject peoples. Therefore, not without reason, but by a most wise and altogether divine counsel, he loved the name Son of Man above almost all the other titles of the Messiah, because by recalling the first promise concerning the Messiah it was suitable both for correcting the Jews' errors about the coming Christ, which were ill-conceived, and for tearing up by the roots their most unjust opinions about Jesus of Nazareth, and for disclosing the most memorable moments concerning the Messiah's birth, life, battle, death, victory, resurrection, ascension and supreme dominion, and also for reminding and instructing men about his offices, the prophetic, priestly and kingly.

units.la: Non erat par ratio cæterarum Judæis notissimarum Messiæ nomenclationum, v. gr. filii Dei, vel filii Davidis. Etsi enim Judæi Prophetarum edocti oraculis, Messiam existimarent fore filium Dei, mentem tamen Prophetarum minus assecuti, Messiam opinabantur fore Dei filium, jure adoptionis, sicut cæteros orbis Reges, modo tamen excellentiori. Si Jesus frequentissimè filii Dei elogio se insigniisset: (quandoquidem non reputavit rapinam esse Deo æqualis) tantum aberat ut mederetur falsò præconceptis Judæorum de Messia Rege potentissimo ac opulentissimo opinionibus, ut errorem potius fovisset, & sibi tunc despecto homini conflatum odium exacerbasset, ac prorsus præclusisset aditum ad annunciandas eis, mysteria regni cœlorum. Hinc factum ut sapienter raro, & maximè cum privatim aliquem alloqueretur, se elogio filii Dei insignierit. Eadem planè ratio fuit, cur se se ferè abstinuerit ab elogio filii Davidis: cum enim David & Rex fuisset bellicosissimus atque potentissimus, & crebras instructis carnalibus copiis, de hostibus Israëlitarum reportasset victorias, & dum Jesus in Judæa versaretur, Judæi exspectarent Messiam Davidis filium, potentissimum ac magnificum victoriarum Davidis æmulum. Si Jesus se Davidis filium frequentissimè venditasset, non medicinam errori Judæorum de Messia tulisset: quin potius robur ac pondus maximum addidisset. Nihil hujusmodi sibi erat metuendum ab elogio filii hominis, quem in prima promissione à serpente modò contritum, modò caput serpentis conterentem, Judæis intueri licebat, si modò allubuisset, ut inde certò colligerent, futuras Messiæ filii mulieris spirituales victorias, ac regnum planè cœleste, & à pompa seculari, quantum cœlum distat à terra, disterminatum.
units.tr: There was no parallel reason for the other titles of the Messiah that were well known to the Jews, for example "Son of God" or "Son of David." Although the Jews, taught by the oracles of the Prophets, thought the Messiah would be the Son of God, they did not grasp the Prophets' meaning. They supposed that the Messiah would be God's Son by right of adoption, as the other kings of the earth are, though in a more excellent way. If Jesus had very often marked himself with the title Son of God (since he did not consider it robbery to be equal with God), he would have done far less to correct the Jews' mistaken preconceptions about a most powerful and wealthy Messiah-King. Rather, he would have fed their error and inflamed the hatred they already felt toward him, a man they despised, and would have completely closed the way to announcing to them the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven. Hence it came about that he wisely used the title Son of God rarely, and mostly when speaking privately with someone. Exactly the same reasoning explains why he largely refrained from the title Son of David. David had been a most warlike and most powerful king, who with well-equipped carnal armies had won many victories over the enemies of Israel. While Jesus was in Judea, the Jews were waiting for a Messiah, the son of David, a most powerful and magnificent rival of David's victories. If Jesus had frequently advertised himself as David's son, he would not have brought a remedy to the Jews' error about the Messiah; he would instead have added the greatest strength and weight to it. There was nothing of this kind to fear from the title Son of Man, which the Jews could see in the first promise, where the seed of the woman is sometimes bruised by the serpent and sometimes crushes the serpent's head, if only they cared to look. From this they could surely gather that the Messiah, the son of the woman, would win spiritual victories, and that his kingdom would be wholly heavenly, separated from worldly pomp as far as heaven is from earth.

units.la: Hinc non modò in promptu colligere est, usitatissimum filii hominis elogium, in primam de Messia promissionem collineasse, ex mente & consilio Christi: sed & ratio sese nobis aperit sapientissimæ dispensationis Spiritus sancti, in usu vel præteritione istius filii hominis nomenclaturæ: nam ex quo Jesus resurrexit è mortuis, plenè determinatus filius Dei, per victricem, resurrectionem, ministri ejus Apostoli, & testes αὐτόπται perpessionum ac gloriæ ipsius, eum quidem frequentissimè appellarunt filium Dei, Dominum gloriæ, Christum, Jesum Christum, λόγον, seu sermonem Dei, magnum Deum nostrum ac servatorem: sed ex compacto ac destinato consilio, quâ erant divinâ sapientiâ, eum fere nusquam, (si unum aut alterum locum exceperis) filium hominis, appellavere. Eccur verò? An quia Jesus post suam resurrectionem non fuit amplius filius hominis? Contrarium supra solidis rationibus addiximus: nam filius hominis novissima die venturus est cum gloria Patris, Angelorum myriadibus stipatus. Unde igitur adeò constans frequentissimi filii hominis elogii præteritio? Unde? Nimirum dum finem obtinuimus, nullus est mediorum usus: filii verò hominis nomenclatura, medium erat, quo Christus sapientissimè abutebatur, ad refricandam Judæorum memoriam, primæ de Messia promissionis in usus salutiferos, quos non omninò ofcitanter supra aperuimus. Verum post victricem Christi è mortuis resurrectionem, ascensionem in cœlum, sessionem ad dexteram Majestatis, & Spiritus sancti abundantissimam die Pentecostes effusionem, eventus comprobaverat, & in clara luce posuerat, quidquid Judæos in diebus carnis, hac sua filii hominis nomenclatura, Jesus docere intendebat. Tunc igitur & passus calcanei sui contritionem, & victor Diaboli, peccati, mundi ac mortis, & triumphator in nubibus & orbis universi è solio suo cœlesti dominator, testibus perpessionum ac gloriæ ministris fidelibus imperavit, ut eum palam promulgarent æternum Dei filium, Dominum gloriæ, imaginem Dei invisibilis, characterem & splendorem gloriæ patris, magnum Deum ac servatorem nostrum. Si regeras, Stephanum, Jesum in gloria coelesti constitutum, vocasse filium hominis, Act. 7: 56. Respondeo, quòd protomartyr Stephanus, Jesum hoc elogio insignierit, nihil plane causæ nostræ incommodare: nam singularis suberat lapidato martyri ratio, abutendi isthoc elogio filii hominis. Et 1°. quidem, quia vel in ipsa morte (morientis verò verba magni sunt apud superstites ponderis) docere voluit Judæos, Jesum illum, quem in crucem dederant, exiisse e mortis potestate, ac coelo se vivum intulisse, ut ipse eum cerneret, intentis in coelum oculis, pro se adstantem ad dexteram Majestatis Dei. 2°. Jesum revera esse ipsummet filium hominis, quem Daniel curru triumphali nubis in coelum vehentem, pluribus retrò seculis intuitus fuerat. 3°. Denique, Jesum veracem esse ac fidelem Prophetam, utpote cujus prophetia, de ascensione sua in coelum, & statione ad dexteram Majestatis supremæ, suum complementum in totum obtinuerat. Eadem prorsus de causa Paulus Hebr. 2. Jesum dixit filium hominis, cujus pedibus omnia Deus subjecerat, ut Hebræos doceret propheticam Davidis exclamationem, in uno Iesu Christo, plenum suum sortitam complementum. Idem esto judicium de Iohanne, Apoc. 1: 13. & 14: 14. Nam præterquam quod Iohannes phrases Ezechielis ac Danielis imitari amat, in suo illo libro prophetico, hac filii hominis nomenclatura, quâ Iesum bis insigniit, Iudæos docere voluit, Iesum e mortuis excitatum, esse verum illum filium hominis, quem in Chaldæa Daniel, venientem in nubibus coeli, contemplatus fuerat.
units.tr: From this it is not only easy to conclude that the most common title, Son of Man, was aimed at the first promise of the Messiah, according to the mind and purpose of Christ. We also see the reason behind the wisdom of the Holy Spirit's dispensation in using or omitting this title, Son of Man. For since Jesus rose from the dead, and was fully determined to be the Son of God by his victorious resurrection, his ministers the Apostles, who were eyewitnesses [αὐτόπται] of his sufferings and glory, very often called him the Son of God, the Lord of glory, Christ, Jesus Christ, the Word [λόγος] or Speech of God, our great God and Saviour. Yet by a settled and deliberate plan, shaped by divine wisdom, they almost nowhere called him the Son of Man, except in one or two places. Why then? Was it because Jesus was no longer the Son of Man after his resurrection? We have already shown the opposite on solid grounds, for the Son of Man is to come on the last day in the glory of the Father, surrounded by myriads of angels. Why then is the very frequent title Son of Man so consistently passed over? Why? Clearly, when the end has been reached, there is no further use for the means. The title Son of Man was a means, which Christ used most wisely to refresh the Jews' memory of the first promise of the Messiah, for saving purposes, which we have set out above not carelessly. But after Christ's victorious resurrection from the dead, his ascension into heaven, his sitting at the right hand of the Majesty, and the most abundant outpouring of the Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost, the events had confirmed and placed in clear light whatever Jesus intended to teach the Jews in the days of his flesh by this title, Son of Man. Then, therefore, the Apostles, who were witnesses of his sufferings and glory, commanded faithful ministers to proclaim openly that he was the eternal Son of God, the Lord of glory, the image of the invisible God, the express image and brightness of the Father's glory, our great God and Saviour: he who had suffered the bruising of his heel, the victor over the Devil, sin, the world and death, the triumphant one in the clouds, and the ruler of the whole world from his heavenly throne. If you object that Stephen, when he saw Jesus placed in heavenly glory, called him the Son of Man (Acts 7:56), I answer that the first martyr Stephen's marking of Jesus with this title does not harm our case at all. For the stoned martyr had a special reason for using this title of the Son of Man. First, indeed, even in his death (and the words of a dying man carry great weight with those who survive) he wanted to teach the Jews that this Jesus, whom they had handed over to the cross, had come out of the power of death and had entered heaven alive, so that he himself could see him, standing at the right hand of the Majesty of God, with eyes fixed on heaven. Second, he wanted to show that Jesus was truly that very Son of Man whom Daniel had long before seen being carried to heaven in a triumphal chariot of cloud. Third, and finally, he wanted to show that Jesus is a true and faithful Prophet, since his prophecy about his ascension into heaven and his station at the right hand of supreme Majesty had been fully fulfilled. For the same reason, Paul in Hebrews 2 called Jesus the Son of Man, to whose feet God had subjected all things, so as to teach the Hebrews that David's prophetic exclamation had received its full completion in the one Jesus Christ. The same judgment applies to John in Revelation 1:13 and 14:14. For apart from the fact that John loves to imitate the expressions of Ezekiel and Daniel in that prophetic book of his, by this title Son of Man, with which he twice marks Jesus, he wanted to teach the Jews that Jesus, raised from the dead, is that true Son of Man whom Daniel contemplated in Chaldea, coming in the clouds of heaven.

units.la: USUS.
units.tr: USE.

units.la: 1°. Admirandam hîc, & plane divinam, mirari iubit veteris & novi fœderis harmoniam. Ambos jure dixeris Cherubim mysticos, mutuis hinc inde defixos admirabundis aspectibus, sed in propitiatorium ex compacto cernuos. Duo sunt, sed vox una, quia unus spiritus; quod Pater promittit, filius implet, & filius hominis, plenum est implementum promissi feminis mulieris, caput serpentis contrituri.
units.tr: 1. Here one is bidden to marvel at the admirable and truly divine harmony of the Old and New Covenants. Rightly might you call them both the mystical cherubim, gazing at each other with wondering looks, yet bowing together toward the mercy-seat by agreement. They are two, yet one voice, because there is one Spirit. What the Father promises, the Son fulfils, and the Son of man is the full accomplishment of the promise of the seed of the woman who would crush the serpent's head.

units.la: 2°. Hîc Christi divina pellucet sapientia, in uno filii hominis elogio; hoc unum, neglectis ferè aliis, sibi selegit proprium ἀκοινωνήτως, quòd, factâ velut anacephalæosi, totum contineat Euangelium, quia implementum habet primæ de Messia promissionis: & quæ cætera ex parte exhibent, Servatoris mysteria, hoc unum ἀθρόως, & affatim, producit consideranda. Miraculosam ex virgine Messiæ nativitatem, est enim filius muliemulieris, quia filius est hominis, (& homo utrumque sexum, sequiorem & nobiliorem significat:) duas naturas; humanam, calcaneum contritum, & divinam, caput illæsum & illibatum: vitam & actiones, pugnam cruentam, & perpessiones: mortem, tritum filii mulieris calcaneum: resurrectionem ac victoriam, caput Serpentis conterentem: tria denique officia, propheticum, sacerdotale, regium. Nec mirum, cum filius hominis sit semen mulieris & Christus, unus, Deum inter & homines mediator. In uno filii hominis elogio, absconditi in prima de Messia promissione, omnes sapientiæ ac intelligentiæ thesauri, aperti sese explicant, ut de eo jure merito usurpaveris, quod de legis litteris Hebræorum Magistri, אין בתורה אפילו אות אחת שאין הרים גדולים תלויין בה, Non est in lege vel una littera, ex qua non dependeant magni montes. Magni sanè montes sapientiæ & potentiæ Christi, ex uno filii hominis elogio, pendent. Agedum sacrorum, studiosè, arcanorum, scripturas veteres & novas nocturnâ, diurnâ versato manu, invicem contendito, ut aperta intuearis regni cœlorum mysteria, γραφῶν γὰρ ἀνάγνωσις, ὑρανῶν ἄνοιξις, Scripturarum enim lectio, cœlorum est apertio, ut aureum os loquitur.
units.tr: 2. Here Christ's divine wisdom shines forth in the single title Son of man. Neglecting almost all the others, he chose this one as his own, uniquely [ἀκοινωνήτως], because, as in a summary recapitulation, it contains the whole Gospel, since it holds the fulfilment of the first promise concerning the Messiah. The other titles show some of the Saviour's mysteries in part, but this one alone sets before us, all at once and in abundance, things to consider [ἀθρόως]. It sets forth: the miraculous birth of the Messiah from a virgin, for he is the son of the woman because he is the son of man (and "man" signifies both sexes, the weaker and the nobler); his two natures, the human, whose heel is bruised, and the divine, whose head is unhurt and unblemished; his life and actions, the bloody battle and the sufferings; his death, the bruised heel of the seed of the woman; his resurrection and victory, crushing the serpent's head; and finally his three offices, prophetic, priestly and royal. Nor is this surprising, since the Son of man is both the seed of the woman and Christ, the one mediator between God and men. In the single title Son of man, all the treasures of wisdom and understanding hidden in the first promise of the Messiah are opened and displayed. So you may rightly apply to it what the Hebrew masters said of the letters of the Law: "Not even one letter is in the Law from which great mountains do not hang" [אין בתורה אפילו אות אחת שאין הרים גדולים תלויין בה]. Indeed, great mountains of Christ's wisdom and power hang upon the single title Son of man. Come now, study the old and new Scriptures diligently, turning them over by night and by day, comparing them with one another, so that you may behold the open mysteries of the kingdom of heaven. As the golden-mouthed one says: "The reading of the Scriptures is the opening of the heavens" [γραφῶν γὰρ ἀνάγνωσις, οὐρανῶν ἄνοιξις].

units.la: 3°. Miraris nec immerito, Christum morti proximum, uno verbo ego sum, armatas cohortes retrorsum agitasse ac prostravisse. Quid miraris? Magni montes potentiæ Christi, ex verbulo illo pendebant. Mirare potentiæ ac sapientiæ montes, ex uno filii hominis elogio, in caput Adversariorum ejus, ita confertim procidere, ut profligandis omnibus Iudæorum erroribus, multisque novitiorum hæreticorum hæresibus, fuerit quam sufficientissimum. Eo profligatur error de incerta Messiæ origine: eo somnium de Messia gemino fugatur: eo regnum Messiæ seculare, terrenisque opulentum divitiis, difflatur: eo Iudæorum superbia sibi in solidum, seclusis gentibus, Messiæ liberationem ac felicitatem vindicantium, prosternitur: eo retunduntur vibratæ in Iesum calumniæ: eo salutifera Christi pandun-tur mysteria: eo pestilentissimorum Socini sodalium, hæresis jugulatur; eo Pontificiorum male sana doctrina in Christi contemptum, confoditur. Agedum, quid & quantum in Socinianos & Pontificios, hæc Christi filii hominis nomenclatura valeat, sigillatim experiamur.
units.tr: 3. You marvel, and not undeservedly, that Christ, close to death, drove back and laid low armed cohorts with a single word, I am. Why marvel? Great mountains of Christ's power hung upon that little word. Marvel that mountains of power and wisdom fall so thickly, from the single title Son of man, upon the heads of his adversaries, that it has been most sufficient for overthrowing all the errors of the Jews and the many heresies of recent heretics. By it the error about the uncertain origin of the Messiah is overthrown; by it the dream of a twofold Messiah is put to flight; by it the worldly kingdom of the Messiah, rich in earthly wealth, is blown away; by it the pride of the Jews, who claimed for themselves alone, to the exclusion of the Gentiles, the Messiah's deliverance and happiness, is cast down; by it the calumnies hurled against Jesus are beaten back; by it the saving mysteries of Christ are laid open; by it the heresy of the most pestilent companions of Socinus is throttled; by it the unsound doctrine of the Papists, to the contempt of Christ, is run through. Come now, let us test one by one what, and how much, this title Son of man avails against the Socinians and the Papists.

units.la: 4°. Quid, Socini sodalis, Christum profiteris non ante exstitisse, quam ex beata virgine nasceretur? Censen' ingloriæ Deo Servatori, tuæ illi opinioni, ex filii hominis elogio, commodum adsuturas suppetias? Est equidem Christus filius hominis, quia filius est mulieris virginis, filius à lapsu promissus, inimicitiam cum serpente ejusque semine, Dæmonibus ac mundo fatalem, exerciturus. Si igitur Christus noster filius est hominis, quia implementum est primæ de Messia propheticæ promissionis, fracta concidit tua opinio coram filio hominis. Et 1o. quidem filius hominis, ut prophetia & ipse eventus clamat, caput serpentis Diaboli, & seminis ejus spiritualis mundi contrivit. Ex contritione capitis, mors, & plena destructio Diaboli ac mundi consequitur, ἐx πάσης ἀνάγκης. Qui vero moritur Diabolus immortalis, ut ut malus spiritus? Qui moritur mundus semen spirituale ipsius? Mortem sane naturalem, qua rei viventis existentia profligatur, quaque mortuum definit existere, intellexerit nemo, cui sanum fuerit synciput. Ergo serpentis ac seminis ejus caput conteritur, quia imperio suo peccati, maledictionis, ac mortis, exspoliatur; robur ac regnum, quo in mundum truculenter dominabatur, perimitur. Venit igitur filius hominis, vidit serpentem ac mundum ipsius semen, hostes infensissimos in sui perniciem conjuratos, vicit Diabolum, principatus ac potestates, mundum integrum: & tu, Sociniane, credideris, filium hominis fuisse φίλον ἄνθρωπον, nudum ac merum hominem? Unus equidem Imperator cunctando Romanam restituit rem: sed unus filius hominis, pugnam cruentam pugnando, principatus ac potestates exspoliavit; caput serpentis Diaboli contrivit, regnum abolevit: mundum vicit, ipsius semen. Hoccine est humanum factum? Meri unius hominis vires, viribus Diabolorum, & mundi integri profligandis, pares fuisse, quis, nisi insaniente ac furente ratione, crediderit? Nec regeras, Deum vim suam omnipotentem in filio hominis exeruisse, singulari plane ratione, ut tantam victoriam de Diabolo, peccato, maledictione, mundo ac morte, reportaret. Multum jam promovimus: verum dixisti, si sano sensu. Exeruit sane Deus omnipotentem suam virtutem in filio hominis illustri bellatore, singulari ratione: quia ipse filius hominis, dum pugnam victricem pugnaret, Deus erat in secula benedictus. Tu vero, Socini sodalis, ore rotundo inficiaris. Dic sodes igitur, quænam est illa singularis ratio, qua Deus omnipotentem virtutem in filio hominis, tantam ut reportaret victoriam, exeruit? Anne exeruerat Numen potentissimum, & ratione singulari, omnipotentem suam virtutem in Prophetis, per stupenda multa infinitæ virtutis miracula? Anne eamdem demum in filii hominis Apostolis virtutem, exeruit, Ubivis contestatum signis, & portentis, & variis virtutibus, & Spiritus sancti distributionibus, juxta voluntatem suam, veram esse salutem, cujus mundo pracones erant, Hebr. 2: 4. Qui factum igitur, ut nullus Propheta, nullus Apostolus, nec caput serpentis contrivisse, nec mundum vicisse perhibeatur? Qui tantum opus, uni filio hominis acceptum refert Spiritus sanctus? Qui factum ut nullus Propheta, nullus Apostolus, capitis serpentis contritionem, ac mundi victoriam sibi vindicaverit? Qui amabo unus filius hominis, eximium hujuscemodi opus, sibi sine rapina & blasphemia tribuere, ausus est? Vel Deus in filio hominis unione personali conjunctissimus, Diabolum vicit ac mundum: vel Deus Pater extra Christum, tantum separatus, quantum creator distat à creatura, per filium hominis, tanquam per organum finitum, hoc opus effectum dedit? Si prius fatearis, causâ cecidisti, vicit veritas. Si posterius, errori tuo, uti clypeum pertendas. Non igitur filius hominis caput serpentis contrivit; sed Deus per filium hominis, tanquam per finitum organum. Sed ipsi filio hominis audacter contradicis, exclamanti laetabundo, Torcular calcavi לבדי ego solus, & de populis, non vir mecum: & calcavi eos in ira mea, & conculcavi eos in excandescentia mea, Quia dies ultionis in corde meo, & annus redemptorum meorum venit, & aspexi, & nullus mihi auxiliator, & obstupui; quia nullus fulciens: sed salvavit me brachium meum, & excandescentia mea fulcivit me, Esa. 63: 3. 4. 5. Confidite, ego vici mundum, Joh. 16: 33. Contradicis & Paulo, uni Christo in totum, tantam victoriam tribuenti; Exspoliavit principatus & potestates, in spectaculum produxit, triumphum agens de illis, in se ipso, Col. 2: 15. Qui factum tandem, ut tanta haec victoria, cui reportandae impares erant, quotquot erant creaturae finitae vires, Deo patri authori & causae uni, (siquidem tua obtineat sententia) nunquam: filio vero hominis Christo, finito tantum organo, semper & ubique attribuatur? 2o. Perpendas oportet paulo pensiculatius, rationem & modum, quo filius hominis, serpentis & mundi caput contrivit. Pugnam scilicet iniit cum serpente & mundo, ubi calcanei sui passus est contritionem, h. e. mortem cruentam & maledictam crucis, Tu illi conteres calcaneum serpens. Mors igitur filii hominis, caput serpentis ac mundi contrivit: seu mavis, filius hominis in cruce moriens, robur ac regnum Diaboli & mundi vicit & abolevit. Hoc nos docuit Paulus, Et ipse, filius nempe hominis, particeps fuit carnis & sanguinis, ut per mortem aboleret eum, qui robur & imperium mortis obtinebat, id est Diabolum, Hebr. 2: 14. Hic vero nihil causam tuam juvat, si de more confugias ad martyrium & exemplum: nam Christi mors, nec ut martyrium, nec ut exemplum, Diabolum mortis imperatorem abolevit: martyrium enim, & exemplum mortis Christi, spectant ad homines, non vero ad Diabolum. Valet equidem mors Christi, ut martyrium & exemplum, uti causa moralis, ad persuadendam hominibus, doctrinae Christi veritatem, ac sanctitatem in eorum animos transfundendam, efficacia exempli, suavi ac voluntario amoris illicio: sed in Diabolum conterendum, & mortis imperio exspoliandum, nihil quicquam valet sub σχέσῃ martyrii & exempli: nam nec iis persuadetur Satan, ut volens ac lubens imperio suo se abdicet, & vi externa, ac contraria, non persuasione morali, conterendum erat serpentis caput, & Diaboli imperium abolendum. 3o. Contritus filii mulieris calcaneus, juxta oppositionem quam habet ad caput serpentis, te, Sociniane, vel invitum trahit, in confessionem naturæ divinæ, reapse existentis in filio hominis, vel dum calcanei pateretur contritionem: nam sicut serpens, ita & caput serpentis, allegoricè intelligitur: ita sanè exacta calcanei filii hominis oppositio postulat, & vel invitis extorquet, ut calcaneus allegoricus intelligatur. Re enim vera, proprie dictus Christi calcaneus, nec fuit, nec memoratur contritus à serpente & mundo, in crucifixione & morte filii hominis: sed tota natura humana Christi, morte fuit contrita & extincta. Hæc igitur natura crucifixa, calcaneus fuit filii hominis. Jam vero, Sociniane, dic sodes, quodnam fuit caput istius calcanei contriti? Caput ne humanum dixeris? Sed vetat, 1o. Exacta ratio divinæ allegoriæ: nam sicut calcaneum, non proprie, sed allegoricè intelligendum esse, solidis rationibus addiximus: ita & caput istius calcanei, in filio hominis, allegoricum ut sit, necesse est. 2o. Quia Christo mortuo, caput humanum filii hominis, morte lethali telo Serpentis, contritum fuit, seu extinctum. Verùm semen mulieris, ipso Numine attestante, non capitis sicut Serpens: sed calcanei, tantum passurum erat contritionem. Ecquid tandem fuit in filio hominis caput triti sui calcanei, illæsum & illibatum ad venenatos Serpentis insultus? Dic sodes, Sociniane? Fortean anima Christi? Apage errorem θεήλατον, lethalia sensit Serpentis spicula anima filii hominis sanctissima, Undiquaque tristis est anima mea usque ad mortem, Matth. 26: 38. Hinc grumi sanguinis in terram defluentes: hinc tristia lamenta, preces ac supplicationes filii hominis iteratæ: hinc timor ille, non mortis quidem, eam enim lubens oppetiit, nec ex ea exanditus fuit: sed truculentissimæ tentationis, ac ingruentis Dei maledictionis, sub cujus pondere, ne tandem satisceret anima sua, vehementer pertimuit: sed exauditus fuit, quia liberatus ex suo illo timore, Hebr. 5: 7. Superest igitur, caput filii hominis, contrito calcaneo suo respondens: sed ad insultus Satanæ illæsum & illibatum, divinam fuisse filii hominis naturam, ut tandem, Sociniane, confitearis necesse est. Disce igitur Mysterium elogii filii hominis, passi calcanei sui contritionem, in morte maledicta ac ignominiosa crucis, & duas in filio hominis naturas, humanam atque divinam, in salutem æternam discès, & ore meliore confitebere. 5o. Pon-
units.tr: 4. What do you mean, companion of Socinus, by professing that Christ did not exist before he was born of the blessed Virgin? Do you think that your opinion can gain any useful support from the title "Son of Man", which is no glory to God the Saviour? Christ is indeed the Son of Man, because he is the son of a virgin woman, the son promised after the fall, who was to wage enmity against the serpent and its seed, the demons and the world, and bring them to ruin. If then our Christ is the Son of Man because he is the fulfilment of the first prophetic promise concerning the Messiah, your opinion collapses and is broken before the Son of Man. And first, the Son of Man, as the prophecy and the event itself proclaim, crushed the head of the serpent, the Devil, and of his spiritual seed, the world. From the crushing of the head there follows the death and complete destruction of the Devil and of the world, [ex pases anankes] by all necessity. But who can say that the Devil, even though he is an evil spirit, is immortal? Who can say that the world, which is his spiritual seed, does not die? Surely no one of sound mind would understand the natural death by which the existence of a living thing is destroyed and by which the dead cease to exist. Therefore the head of the serpent and of its seed is crushed, because it is stripped of its power over sin, curse and death, and the strength and kingdom by which it savagely ruled over the world are destroyed. The Son of Man came, he saw the serpent and the world, its seed, sworn together to his destruction as the most hostile enemies, and he conquered the Devil, the principalities and powers, and the whole world. And you, Socinian, would believe that the Son of Man was a [philon anthropon] mere friend of man, a bare and simple man? Indeed one emperor by delaying restored the Roman state; but one Son of Man, by fighting a bloody battle, stripped the principalities and powers, crushed the head of the serpent, the Devil, abolished his kingdom, and conquered the world and its seed. Is this a human deed? Who, unless reason were raving and frenzied, would believe that the powers of one mere man were equal to the powers needed to overthrow the Devils and the whole world?
