We would be foolish and silly if we put faith in clear miracles and in witnesses to Jesus' resurrection and ascension into heaven, while holding guilty of worthless faith and false testimony those whom we had already known to be most conspicuously attested by miracles. (4) If the disciples had proclaimed that Jesus of Nazareth was the Christ in the sense they themselves believed, namely the Messiah expected by the Jews, an earthly King who would crush the enemies of his nation, they would either have fostered the Jews' error about the Messiah, or they would have exposed themselves to the ridicule and hissing of the Pharisees, who saw nothing in Jesus of Nazareth that smelled of the worldly pomp of their expected Messiah. (5) That absurd preaching of the disciples would have persuaded no one among the Pharisees and scribes that Jesus of Nazareth was the Christ, both because the disciples were common folk and because they were disciples of Jesus. For, I ask you, what preaching by a few most despised little men, ignorant of the law, could have overcome the most obstinate unbelief of the Pharisees, which not even the miracles by which the prophets had marked out the Messiah, and by which Jesus then commended himself, could overcome? The disciples' preaching would have been utterly futile, since the malicious princes of the age would have suspected a conspiracy and would have believed without fail that the disciples, in giving such testimony, were colluding with Christ, whom they used to accuse, while he worked miracles, of a secret alliance and a nefarious conspiracy with Beelzebub, the prince of devils. (6) At that time the Jews regarded Christ as King of the Jews rather than as Prophet, and certainly not as High Priest who would lay down his soul as a sacrificial victim and an offering for sin. If the disciples, by proclaiming that Jesus of Nazareth was that King, had drawn the Jewish people into this opinion, the princes of the Jewish age and the Romans would have conceived such envy and hatred against Jesus that they would have sought to have him, as one guilty of rebellion against Caesar and of seeking a kingdom, destroyed by force and arms wherever he was found. From this one of two things would necessarily seem to follow: either Jesus would exercise his omnipotent power to restrain the hostile violence of both the Pharisees and the Romans, who were raging for his destruction, since the time of Christ's death had not yet come, or he would not. But the prophecies forbade Christ to exercise his omnipotent power at that time in crushing his enemies: Isa. 42:1, 2, 3, 4; Matt. 12:18. The purpose of Christ's coming forbade it, since he came to save men, not to destroy them; so did the condition and state of humility and suffering, and, finally, the wisdom of Christ. For the exercise of his omnipotent power in restraining and crushing his enemies would not only have fostered but would have confirmed the disciples' error about Christ himself, and the nation of the Jews' error about a mighty earthly King Messiah. Therefore it was necessary that the other consequence of that absurd preaching of the disciples follow, namely that Christ would close off for himself and for the disciples every way of proclaiming the kingdom of heaven and of performing miracles for the good of the Jewish nation, which are the marks of the true Messiah. (7) Since Christ did not flee from it, the disciples, moved by love toward him, would have preached that Jesus of Nazareth was the Christ, and from that preaching the hatred of the Pharisees would have been enormously inflamed, so that they would have hastened his death with all their strength. In his wisdom Christ did not want that holy love of his disciples to be directed to another end, altogether the opposite of what they intended, namely to hasten the death of their venerable teacher. (8) Since, according to the most wise counsel of God, the Son of Man Christ was to suffer a dreadful death from the enmity of the serpent, the Devil, and of his seed, the world, Christ did not want his disciples, his spiritual seed, to contribute anything, even unwittingly, to the death of the Son of Man. Yet that absurd preaching would have contributed weight and force, kindling the envy and hatred of the Pharisees against Christ. (9) By this prohibition the wise and good Teacher wished to spare his disciples the future affliction. He knew that his disciples would be struck down by the most severe affliction when they saw him given over to the shameful cross, and how much more deeply and bitterly they would have grieved over the shameful death of their Lord, knowing that by their own preaching they had provoked and inflamed the hatred of the Pharisees, the immediate cause of Christ's death. (10) When the testimony about Jesus as the Son of Man, or the Christ, would have stirred up a Vatinian hatred in the minds of the princes of the Jews, it would have exposed the disciples, the heralds of that truth, to insults and many kinds of death, the disciples being as yet unable to bear so great a temptation, as their flight and the sorrowful denial of Peter, who had confessed Christ, showed. Therefore Jesus, in his wisdom and goodness, did not want to expose his disciples by this preaching to dangers and atrocious punishments, lest, weakened by fear of death, they be driven to recantation, which would have undermined both the truth of the Mediatorial office and the glory of Christ. Nothing of this kind was to be feared from the disciples when they bore witness that Jesus of Nazareth was the Christ, after his death, resurrection and ascension into heaven, and the solemn outpouring of the Holy Spirit upon them. For both the outcome and the full outpouring of the Spirit as Teacher had purged their minds of their false and mistaken preconceptions about Christ, and had made it thoroughly known to them and to all the Jews that the true Christ of God had come not as an earthly king, nor to restore the worldly kingdom of Israel, but to free men from the tyranny of the Devil and from the slavery of sin, the curse, the law and death, and to establish the kingdom and worship of God far and wide throughout the whole world, the Prince of this world, the Devil, having been cast out. Nor was there any need to fear that the Pharisees might pretend, on any legitimate pretext, that the disciples of Christ were bearing false testimony that Jesus had been in collusion with anyone. For the disciples, who had seen with their own eyes what they proclaimed, were fearless, though it was hateful and odious to the Pharisees and the Romans, and they preached even under the whip and in many forms of dreadful death, being overcome, of course, by the evidence of the truth. They expected from it neither worldly dignities, nor the comforts of life, nor riches, but on the contrary they bore and suffered reproach, poverty, and every kind of disgrace, whippings and punishments. Again there was no need to fear that, thoroughly imbued with saving truth and strengthened and fortified by the power of the Holy Spirit, they would grow weak from fear of death and be driven to recantation. It remained, therefore, that Jesus himself, while awaiting his glorious resurrection, ascension, and the full outpouring of his Spirit upon the disciples, alone proclaimed that he was the Son of Man and the Christ, because he feared nothing for himself, knowing well that he was the Christ whom the prophets had foretold, who would undergo a cursed and shameful death on the cross, by that death crush the head of the serpent, come forth from curse and death through the resurrection, ascend into heaven, and live and reign over all flesh. For having come into the world by the impulse of his eternal love toward God and the elect, he would render himself obedient to God unto the death of the cross, and redeem the Church with his own blood. So far was he from being deterred by fear of death from proclaiming this truth about himself as the Messiah, that he gave this illustrious confession before Pilate, although he knew that a cursed and shameful death awaited him there with certainty. Matt. 27:11; John 18:37; 1 Tim. 6:13.

units.la: Secundo. Sapientissimè ex parte ipsius Christi. Ille enim quâ Christus, & singularis Propheta erat, & singularis author ac doctor Euangelii. Unde Paulus, Hebr. 1: 2. asserit, Deum ultimis hisce temporibus, nobis locutum esse per filium suum; & cap. 2: 3. Salutem, h. e. Euangelium salutis, cujus summa est, Jesum esse Christum, primum annunciatam fuisse per Dominum. Utraque sanè de causa necesse erat, ut ipse doceret, se esse Christum, qualem scilicet Prophetæ venturum prædixerant, altùm silentibus tunc temporis ejus discipulis. 1°. Quâ singularis Propheta erat: nam si ejus discipuli prædicassent, Iesum esse Christum, seu filium hominis, passurum calcis contritionem, contriturum caput serpentis, è mortuis resurrecturum, in cœlum ascensurum, & ad dexteram Dei sessurum, priusquam eventus rem comprobasset, nec Christus visus esset singularis Propheta, ad id prænunciandum à Deo missus, & ejus discipuli partiti essent cum Christo apud homines, gloriam illius muneris prophetici, & tantæ, tamque incredibilis prædictionis veritatem. Hinc factum, ut Jesus, quos miserat discipulos ad urbes Israëlis, annunciatum proximum adventum regni cœlorum, ut Iudæorum animos ad ipsius perceptionem præpararent, Matth. 10: 5. 7. non constituerit annunciatores & testes de se Christo, nisi tandem post suam resurrectionem, quâ declaratus plenè fuerat filius Dei in potentia, h. e. Christus, Act. 1: 8.
units.tr: Second, it was most wisely done on Christ's own part. As Christ, he was the singular Prophet and the singular author and teacher of the Gospel. Hence Paul says, Heb. 1:2, that God has spoken to us in these last times through his Son; and at 2:3, "salvation" (that is, the gospel of salvation, whose sum is that Jesus is the Christ) was first announced through the Lord. For both reasons it was necessary that he himself should teach that he is the Christ, such as the prophets had foretold would come, while his disciples kept silent at that time. First, because he was the singular Prophet. If his disciples had preached that Jesus is the Christ, or the Son of man, who would suffer the bruising of his heel, crush the head of the serpent, rise from the dead, ascend into heaven and sit at the right hand of God, before the event had confirmed the matter, then Christ would not have appeared as a singular Prophet sent by God to foretell it, and his disciples would have shared with Christ, in men's eyes, the glory of his prophetic office and the truth of so great and so incredible a prediction. Hence it came about that Jesus, when he sent his disciples to the cities of Israel to announce the approaching coming of the kingdom of heaven, so that they might prepare the Jews' minds to receive it (Matt. 10:5, 7), did not appoint them as heralds and witnesses concerning himself as Christ, except finally after his resurrection, by which he was fully declared the Son of God in power, that is, Christ (Acts 1:8).

units.la: 2°. Quâ author & primus Euangelii doctor: nam, magistro docente, audire, discere, & silere, discipulos decet: doctores verò agere, haud quaquam.
units.tr: Second, because he was the author and first teacher of the Gospel. For while the teacher teaches, disciples ought to listen, learn and keep silent; it is by no means fitting for them to play the teacher's part.

units.la: 3°. Interdixit sapientissimè, habita ratione muneris sui sacerdotalis: Jesus enim quâ Christus erat, sacerdos erat, & victima, animam suam sponte oblaturus in sacrificium propitiatorium pro peccatis. Cum enim Jesus ultrò docuerit, se esse filium hominis, seu Christum, non nescius hinc sibi conflandum Judæorum odium internecinum, quo tandem ageretur in crucem. Hac sua voluntaria & generosa confessione, unde mortem se manere certissimam, & ignominiosam noverat: luculenter sanè testatus est, se solo ductu & impulsu φιλανθρωπίας, & amoris justitiæ, libenter ire ad mortem maledictam crucis.
units.tr: Third, he forbade it most wisely, given his priestly office. For Jesus, as Christ, was also priest and victim, about to offer up his soul of his own accord as a propitiatory sacrifice for sins. Since Jesus of his own accord taught that he is the Son of man, or the Christ, knowing well that from this a deadly hatred of the Jews would be kindled against him, by which he would at last be driven to the cross, he clearly showed by this voluntary and noble confession, knowing that death was most certainly awaiting him and an ignominious one, that he went willingly to the accursed death of the cross, moved solely by his philanthropy [φιλανθρωπία] and his love of righteousness.

units.la: Verum si Jesus, vel mandasset discipulis, ut annunciarent eum esse Christum: vel ni etiam severè interdixisset, ut nemini dicerent. Discipuli, sua illa de Jesu prædicatione, Judæorum odium, proximam causam mortis Christi, tantò exacerbassent vehementius, quò plures fuissent invisæ illius veritatis præcones, unde causa mortis Christi aliundè, quam ex proprio & libenti ipsius testimonio, duxisset originem, & mors quam Christo peperit hujusmodi odium, aliundè, quam ex plena voluntate Christi, & perfecto amore in electos suos, ortum traxisse, videretur.
units.tr: But if Jesus had either commanded the disciples to announce that he is the Christ, or had not even strictly forbidden them to tell anyone, the disciples, by their preaching, would have inflamed the hatred of the Jews, the immediate cause of Christ's death, all the more fiercely, the more heralds there were of that hated truth. The cause of Christ's death would then have arisen from some source other than his own free testimony, and the death which brought him such hatred would seem to have arisen from something other than Christ's full will and his perfect love for his elect.

units.la: 4°. Christus, quâ Rex, pugnam cruentam erat pugnaturus, cum serpente in cruce, in ea enim expoliavit principatus & potestates, & de iis triumphum egit. Pugnare verò, vincere, hostes profligare ac triumphare, Regis est: sed Christo Regi potentissimo, & soli pugnandum erat, sicut & soli vincendum, nihil quicquam in pugnam illam & victoriam conferentibus ejus subditis.
units.tr: Fourth, as King, Christ was about to fight a bloody battle with the serpent on the cross, for there he stripped the principalities and powers and triumphed over them. But to fight, to conquer, to overthrow enemies and to triumph belongs to the king; yet Christ, the most powerful King, had to fight alone, just as he alone had to conquer, none of his subjects contributing anything to that battle and victory.

units.la: Fac verò, discipulos, sua de Christo prædicatione. Diabolum & Pharisæos Christi hostes, proritasse & lacessisse in Christum oppugnandum ad mortem, in pugnam & victoriam Christi, ex suo aliquid contulisse viderentur. Sapientissimè igitur iis interdixit, ne cuiquam dicerent, eum esse Christum, ut agitatæ cum serpente, ejusque semine inimicitiæ, pugnæ ac victoriæ gloria, uni Christo in totum accepta referretur.
units.tr: But suppose the disciples, by their preaching about Christ, had provoked and goaded the devil and the Pharisees, Christ's enemies, into attacking Christ to the death. Then they would seem to have contributed something of their own to Christ's battle and victory. Therefore he most wisely forbade them to tell anyone that he is the Christ, so that the enmity between him and the serpent and its seed, and the glory of the battle and the victory, might be credited wholly to Christ alone.

units.la: Si quis verò regerat, contrariam colligi posse istius interdicti rationem, ex Matth. 16: 20. 21. & 17: 9. Marc. 8: 30, 31. & 9: 9. Luc. 9: 21. 22. Ipse verò interminatus eis, præcepit ut nulli hoc dicerent, dicens, ὅτι δεῖ τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου πολλὰ παθεῖν, quia oportet filium hominis multa pati, & reprobari à senioribus, & principibus sacerdotum, & Scribis, & interimi, & tertia die suscitari. Hinc enim colligi posse videtur, discipulorum prædicationem, quâ Jesum Nazarenum esse Christum palam evulgassent, futuram impedimento, ne Christus reprobaretur à senioribus, & Principibus sacerdotum, & Scribis, & ne interimeretur. Tum quia tres discipuli, uno ore contestantes, se Mosem & Eliam, verba commutantes cum Jesu in monte, & gloriosæ ipsius transfigurationis Majestatem, vidisse, & vocem audivisse Dei e nube, inclamantis, Hic est filius meus dilectus, in quo ego conquievi, eum audite. Judaicæ plebi persuasissent, Jesum Nazarenum esse verum Messiam, Regem illum Iudæorum desideratum & expectatum, ut plebs, vel vi aperta, invidiam, & falsas Principum sacerdotum in Jesum criminationes ita coercuisset, ut qui vix Jesum, durante solemni festivitate, audebant apprehendere, nunquam ausi essent eum dare ignominiosè in crucem: tum quia hæc discipulorum, miraculis spectatorum, constans prædicatio, ignorantiam, quâ præpediti seculi Iudaici Principes, Jesum morte ignominiosa mulctarunt, tandem expugnasset atque vicisset. Victâ verò semel Principum sacerdotum, Pharisæorum & Scribarum ignorantiâ, unde eorum obstinata adversus Jesum incredulitas & malitia profluxerat, nunquam de eo in crucem dando in posterum cogitassent, sicut nos docet Apostolus, Proponimus sapientiam Dei, in mysterio abscónditam, quam nemo principum hujus seculi novit: si enim novissent, nunquam Dominum gloriæ crucifixissent, 1. Cor. 2: 7. 8. Nam si per principes seculi intellexerimus primarios sacerdotes, & judices magni Sanedrin, seculi Iudaici principes; sive Herodem atque Pilatum. Neutri Dominum gloriæ Christum, planè cognitum, in crucem ignominiosè dedissent. Non primi quidem, quia Regem suum Jesum, ex plena persuasione confessi, mala facinorosorum morte perdere noluissent, desideratum inquam, suum Regem, unde & liberationem & regni Israëlis restaurationem expectassent. Non postremi, nam Dominum gloriæ, orbis universi judicem, judicare, & morti servorum ignominiosæ addicere non sustinuissent, quem sibi supremum judicem constitutum credidissent. Nihil vero ejusmodi metuendum erat ex testimonio, quod sibi ipsi Jesus perhibebat, dum se filium hominis, id est, Christum, profitebatur. 1º. Quia proprium Jesu testimonium nullius erat ponderis apud Iudæos, tu de te ipso testaris, testimonium tuum non est verum, Ioh. 8: 13. 2º. Quia cum se filium hominis passum insigniret, ut significaret se esse semen mulieris, passurum calcis contritionem, & caput serpentis contriturum, necessariam sui contritionem, seu mortem, evidenter docebat, sicut & gloriosam de Diabolo conterendo per mortem, victoriam. Si igitur Pharisæi ex Jesu solemni illa prædicatione intellexissent, eum esse Christum, promissum semen mulieris, conterendum à serpente, & vicissim caput serpentis contriturum, necessitatem mortis Messiæ intuiti in solemni filii hominis nomenclatione, & prima de Messia prophetica promissione, Christi mortem, quavis demum ratione contigisset, nunquam impediissent, dicturi sicut Caïphas, sed meliori mente, præstat unum hominem mori pro populo, quam totam gentem perire. Joh. 11: 50. & 18: 14.
units.tr: If anyone should reply that a contrary reason for this prohibition can be drawn from Matt. 16:20, 21; 17:9; Mark 8:30, 31; 9:9; Luke 9:21, 22, where it says: "But he strictly charged them to tell this to no one, saying that the Son of man must suffer many things [ὅτι δεῖ τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου πολλὰ παθεῖν], and be rejected by the elders, chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised up." For from this it seems one may gather that the disciples' preaching, by which they would openly have spread abroad that Jesus of Nazareth is the Christ, would have stood in the way of Christ's being rejected by the elders, chief priests and scribes, and of his being killed. Also, three disciples, testifying with one voice that they had seen Moses and Elijah talking with Jesus on the mountain, and the majesty of his glorious transfiguration, and had heard the voice of God from the cloud crying out, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him," had persuaded the Jewish people that Jesus of Nazareth is the true Messiah, the desired and expected King of the Jews. Then the people, by open force, would have checked the envy and the false accusations of the chief priests against Jesus, so that those who scarcely dared to seize Jesus while the solemn festival lasted would never have dared to hand him over to an ignominious cross. Also, this constant preaching of the disciples, attested by miracles, would at last have overcome and conquered the ignorance by which the rulers of the Jewish age, being hindered by it, punished Jesus with an ignominious death. Once the ignorance of the chief priests, Pharisees and scribes was overcome, from which their obstinate unbelief and malice against Jesus had flowed, they would never afterwards have thought of giving him to the cross, as the Apostle teaches: "We speak the wisdom of God, hidden in a mystery, which none of the rulers of this age knew; for if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory" (1 Cor. 2:7, 8). For if by the rulers of this age we understand the chief priests and the judges of the great Sanhedrin, the rulers of the Jewish age, or Herod and Pilate, neither group would have ignominiously handed the Lord of glory, Christ, over to the cross, had they clearly known him. Not the former, indeed, for being fully persuaded that Jesus was their King, they would not have been willing to destroy him by the evil death of malefactors; their desired King, I say, from whom they hoped for both deliverance and the restoration of the kingdom of Israel. Nor the latter, for they would not have dared to judge the Lord of glory, the judge of the whole world, nor to consign him to the ignominious death of slaves, when they believed him to be set over them as their supreme judge. But nothing of this kind was to be feared from the testimony which Jesus himself gave when he professed that he was the Son of man, that is, Christ. First, because Jesus' own testimony carried no weight among the Jews: "You bear witness about yourself; your testimony is not true" (John 8:13). Second, because when he marked himself as the Son of man to signify that he is the seed of the woman, who would suffer the bruising of his heel and crush the head of the serpent, he was plainly teaching the necessity of his own bruising, that is, his death, just as he taught the glorious victory over the devil through death. If, therefore, the Pharisees had understood from Jesus' solemn proclamation that he is the Christ, the promised seed of the woman, to be bruised by the serpent and in turn to crush the serpent's head, and had they, having regard to the necessity of the Messiah's death, implied in the solemn title Son of man and in the first prophetic promise about the Messiah, never hindered Christ's death, however it came about, they would have spoken as Caiaphas did, but with a better mind: "It is better for one man to die for the people than for the whole nation to perish" (John 11:50; 18:14).

units.la: Hæc quidem aliquam habent veritatis speciem: sed ut primo obtutu speciosa verisimilitudo videatur, quominus eâ dimoveamur à nostra sententia, vetant, 1º. Quia firmis rationibus hactenus addiximus, prædicationem, quâ discipuli, Jesum Nazarenum esse Christum annuntiassent, magis ad inflammandum odium Pharisæorum in Jesum Christum, quam ad eos in fidem pertrahendos, valituram. 2º. Quia si constans ejusmodi discipulorum prædicatio, vulgus incertum Iudæorum in hanc sententiam pertraxisset, videlicet Jesum esse Christum, seu regem gentis expectatum. Plebs tamen timida, & in horas mutabilis, non ausa fuisset palam obsistere Pharisæis, & sacerdotum primariis, & Jesum apertè profiteri Christum, verita sibi, ne eorum authoritate fieret ἀποσυνάγωγος, Ioh. 1: 42. 3º. Quia plebs discipulorum prædicatione vel plane persuasa, Jesum esse Judæorum regem, imperii Romani hostem, ac præpotentem gentis liberatorem, qualem universa somniarat natio, & ipsi hactenus credebant discipuli, in horas mutabilis, ut fieri assolet, facilis in contrariam manibus pedibusque ivisset sententiam, quamprimum vidisset, Jesum apprehensum, vinctum, flagris cæsum, & in crucem ignominiosè datum, dum & se illusam discipulorum prædicatione, & spem suam decollasse, sensisset: nam quò plures, victi miraculis Christi, in eum credebant, hoc vehementius in Jesum perdendum Pharisæi, cæterique Judæorum principes, æstuabant ac validius obsirmabantur, veriti videlicet, ne Romani, & Jerusalem, & gentem delerent, Joh. 4: 48. & 12: 19. 4°. Non fit verisimile plebem Judaicam, aut Pharisæos, vel constanti discipulorum prædicatione, vera fide crediturōs, Jesum esse Christum, sed tantum persuasione, ex affectibus carnalibus oriundā, quia vera ac germana in Christum fides originem ducit ex appulsu veræ doctrinæ ad rationales facultates efficaciā Spiritus sancti, intus intellectum trahentis in assensum verae doctrinæ Euangelicæ. Verum discipulorum prædicatio, quā Jesum esse Christum, Regem terrenum, qualem ipsi esse credebant, annuntiassent, maximam partem falsa ac erronea, non habuisset comitem efficaciam Spiritus sancti, eam enim veritatis spiritus in falsæ doctrinæ confirmationem, nunquam ac nusquam adhibet. Eccur igitur Jesus, interdicto de non evulgando se esse Christum, & visione transfigurationis, quā filius Dei voce coelesti declaratus fuerat, nemini aperiendā, mentionem attexuit futurae suæ perpessionis ac mortis, quam nefario conatu Pharisæorum, Scribarum & seniorum populi, passurus erat? Respondeo, Jesum non nescium discipulos suos, eum esse Christum confessos, credere tamen eum esse Judæorum regem, qualem obcæcata præjudiciis carnalibus, universa credebat natio, quā erat sapientia ac bonitate, præsentem ac opportunam eorum erroribus medicinam ferre voluisse, aperta declaratione necessariæ ac futurae mortis suæ. Eò quidem sapientius, quod noverat, electos tres discipulos vidisse quidem gloriam corporeæ suæ transfigurationis, & Moysis ac Eliæ miraculosam præsentiam: sed sommo correptos, ac metu, nec audiisse, nec intellexisse colloquium de exitu, seu morte, quæ eum manebat Ierosolymis. Luc. 9: 32. 34. Hinc futurum erat, si per Christum illis licuisset annuntiare, quæ viderant, ut visione illa, pompa corporea aspectabili, magis magisque persuasi de futuro regno Christi terreno, quippe tabernacula terna instruere in monte gloriosō cogitabant ac satagebant, cum Christo, Moyse, ac Elia inibi mansuri. Eò alacrius prædicassent, Jesum esse Regem Iudæorum terrenum, quò efficacius in hac sua perperam præconcepta opinione, terribili illa visione confirmati fuerant, ignari de cætero colloquii de futura Christi morte, quod sommo ac metu correpti, nec audierant, nedum intellexerant.
units.tr: These considerations have a certain appearance of truth; but that a specious likelihood may seem to exist at first glance, which should not move us from our view, is forbidden by the following. First, because we have hitherto shown by firm reasons that the preaching by which the disciples would have announced Jesus of Nazareth as the Christ would have been more likely to inflame the Pharisees' hatred of Jesus Christ than to draw them to faith. Second, because if the constant preaching of such disciples had drawn the uncertain crowd of the Jews to this opinion, namely that Jesus is the Christ, that is, the expected king of the nation, the common people, timid and changeable from hour to hour, would not have dared to openly oppose the Pharisees and the chief priests and to profess Jesus openly as Christ, fearing that by their authority they would be made ἀποσυνάγωγοι [put out of the synagogue] (John 1:42). Third, because the crowd, even if fully persuaded by the disciples' preaching that Jesus is the King of the Jews, the enemy of the Roman empire and the mighty deliverer of the nation, as the whole nation had dreamed and as the disciples had hitherto believed, being changeable from hour to hour, as usually happens, would easily have turned with hands and feet to the contrary opinion as soon as they saw Jesus seized, bound, scourged and ignominiously given over to the cross, feeling both that they had been deceived by the disciples' preaching and that their hope had been cut off. For the more who, overcome by Christ's miracles, believed in him, the more vehemently the Pharisees and the other rulers of the Jews raged to destroy Jesus and hardened themselves the more firmly, fearing, of course, that the Romans would destroy both Jerusalem and the nation (John 4:48; 12:19). Fourth, it is not likely that the Jewish crowd or the Pharisees would believe with true faith, through the constant preaching of the disciples, that Jesus is the Christ, but only through a persuasion arising from carnal affections. For true and genuine faith in Christ arises from the impact of true doctrine on the rational faculties, by the efficacy of the Holy Spirit drawing the intellect inwardly to assent to the true evangelical doctrine. But the disciples' preaching, by which they would have announced Jesus as Christ, an earthly king such as they themselves believed him to be, being for the most part false and erroneous, would not have had the efficacy of the Holy Spirit as its companion; for the Spirit of truth never and nowhere lends his aid to confirm false doctrine. Why, then, after forbidding them to make known that he is the Christ, and after the vision of the transfiguration, in which he had been declared the Son of God by a heavenly voice and which was not to be disclosed to anyone, did Jesus add mention of the suffering and death which he was to undergo through the wicked attempt of the Pharisees, scribes and elders of the people? I answer: Jesus was not unaware that his disciples, who had confessed that he is the Christ, still believed him to be the King of the Jews, as the whole nation, blinded by carnal prejudices, believed. With wisdom and goodness he wished to apply a remedy present and suited to their errors, by an open declaration of his necessary and coming death. All the more wisely, because he knew that the three chosen disciples had indeed seen the glory of his bodily transfiguration and the miraculous presence of Moses and Elijah, but, overcome by sleep and fear, had neither heard nor understood the conversation about his departure, or death, which awaited him at Jerusalem (Luke 9:32, 34). Hence it would follow, if it had been permitted them through Christ to announce what they had seen, that, persuaded ever more by that visible bodily spectacle of a earthly kingdom of Christ, since they were planning and busily arranging to build three tabernacles on the glorious mountain for Christ, Moses and Elijah to remain there, they would have preached all the more eagerly that Jesus is the earthly King of the Jews, the more effectively they had been confirmed in this preconceived opinion by that terrifying vision, ignorant from then on of the conversation about Christ's future death, which, overcome by sleep and fear, they had neither heard nor understood.

units.la: USUS.
units.tr: Use.

units.la: 1o. HInc colligere in promptu est, quantus, quàm purus, quamque constans Jesu fuerit adversus veritatem amor. Veritatem annunciatum venit, videlicet se esse filium hominis Christum, unde se certò manere maledictam ac ignominiosam mortem sciebat: sed ab ea annuncianda, nec Pharisæorum odio, nec vultu, verbisque Pilati minacibus, nec mortis metu deterreri potuit. Clamat Pilatus, An nescis me habere potestatem & crucifigendi te, & liberum dimittendi? Joh. 19: 10. Nec Jesum tamen ab hac præclara confessione absterret, Ego sum Rex Judæorum, & ideo natus, & veni in mundum, ut perhibeam testimonium veritati: Joh. 18: 37. Sed sanctus ejusmodi, purus ac illibatus veritatis amor Christi nostri, ex alio amore originem duxit, eo videlicet æternum celebrando amore, quo Ecclesiam suam dilexit. Illius ductu ac pondere sese ad formam servi dimisit, ut morte maledicta crucis, delicta ejus expiaret, & profunda suâ obedientia, dilectæ Ecclesiæ suæ inobedientiam ac rebellionem repararet. Eo impellente amore, fatalem sibi veritatem imperterritus palam prædicavit, ut redemptam proprio suo sanguine Ecclesiam, exemplo omni exceptione majore doceret, quanto sibi habenda sit in pretio veritas salutaris Christi sui, vitæ commodis, divitiis, delitiis, dignitatibus, vel vitæ ipsi anteferenda. Agedum Ecclesia, imitare Christum tuum, caput, Regem, sponsum tuum, illibatam retine veritatem ipsius, nullis seculi pollicitationibus, minis nullis, non amore mundi, non metu mortis terribilis, ab ea te dimoveri patiare. Hanc unam si retineas, omnia habes ad felicitatem æternam necessaria; hanc unam si amiseris, pretiosum sponsi tui monile, & sponsæ elogium, & jus ad hæreditatem cœlestem, omnia perdidisti misera, quia amorem Christi tui, cum amore ipsius veritatis, propudiosè repudiasti.
units.tr: 1. From this one may readily gather how great, how pure, and how steadfast was Jesus' love for the truth. He came to announce the truth, namely that he, Christ, is the Son of Man, whence he knew he was certainly to remain under a cursed and ignominious death. Yet neither the hatred of the Pharisees, nor the threatening look and words of Pilate, nor the fear of death could deter him from announcing it. Pilate exclaims, Do you not know that I have power to crucify you, and power to release you? John 19:10. Nor did this deter Jesus from that noble confession: I am a King of the Jews, and for this I was born and came into the world, that I should bear witness to the truth. John 18:37. But this holy, pure, and unblemished love of the truth in our Christ arose from another love, namely that eternal love with which he loved his Church. Driven by that love and its weight, he took on the form of a servant, so that by the accursed death of the cross he might expiate her sins, and by his deep obedience might repair the disobedience and rebellion of his beloved Church. Impelled by that love, he fearlessly preached openly the truth that was fatal to himself, so that by his example, greater than any exception, he might teach the Church, redeemed by his own blood, how highly the saving truth of Christ is to be prized, above life's comforts, riches, pleasures, dignities, and life itself. Come now, Church, imitate your Christ, your Head, King, and Bridegroom; keep his truth undefiled, and suffer yourself to be moved from it by no promises of the world, no threats, not by love of the world, not by fear of terrible death. If you keep this one thing, you have everything necessary for eternal happiness; if you lose it, you have lost the precious jewel of your Bridegroom, the mark of a bride, and the right to the heavenly inheritance, and, wretched one, you have shamefully rejected, together with the love of Christ, the love of truth itself.

units.la: 2o. Eccur profani Christi contemptores ipsius mortem, vel incerto casui, vel cæcæ, suisque nescia fortunæ in miserum hominem truculenter sævienti, adscribitis? Christus libentissimus, pleno mentis assensu, & voluntario ductu amoris in Deum & Ecclesiam suam, ad mortem ivit, nemo tollit vitam à me, sed ego depono eam per me ipsum, potestatem habeo ponendi eam, & potestatem habeo rursus eam assumendi, Ioh. 10: 18. Ecquid, profane, quæris, ut mortem Christi, omni ex parte voluntariam, confiteare? Vis filium Dei hominem ac filium hominis fieri, ut passus calcis contritionem moriatur? Lubens ac volens formam servi assumpsit, particeps factus carnis & sanguinis, ut per mortem suam, mortis imperatorem aboleret, Hebr. 2: 14. Noluisti Deus sacrificium & oblationem pro peccato: sed aptasti mihi corpus, tunc ego dixi, ecce me, veni ut faciam voluntatem tuam. Psal. 40: 7. Hebr. 10: 5. 6. 7. Vis Christum nihil quicquam reluctantem, cum paratissimas haberet legiones Angelorum in sui tutelam accinctorum, si voluisset, apprehendi, vinciri? sicut agnus ad occisionem ductus, & sicut ovis coram tondentibus eam obmutuit, neque aperuit os suum, Iesr. 53: 7. Matth. 26: 63. & 27: 14. Act. 8: 32. Verum si Iesus, factus semen mulieris, vitam obscuram degisset in angulo, nemini dictitans, se esse filium hominis Christum, nec invidiam, nec odium internecinum Pharisaeorum sibi conflasset, nec mortem passus esset, nedum ignominiosam mortem crucis. Quid superest igitur, ut confitearis, Iesum lubentem ac volentem in diram hanc iviste mortem? Ut inimicitiam agitet cum serpente Diabolo, Daemonia ejiciat, Diaboli opera passim diruat, miracula veri Messiae, Pharisaeis exosa, ubivis edat, se filium hominis Christum, ore rotundo profiteatur, conscius hinc certam se manere mortem? Haec omnia unus praestat, vel dum interdixit discipulis, ne cuiquam de se eadem annunciarent. Nec minus volens ad mortem iverit, quod deprecatus fuerit, Pater mi, si possibile est, transeat a me calix iste, Matth. 26: 39. Nam & volens voluntati Patris acquievit. Verum tamen, non ut ego volo: sed ut tu. Fiat voluntas tua. Matth. 26: 39. 42. Et quanti sibi salus nostra constiterit, suo illo ad calicem plenum divinae maledictionis pavore, quanti denique nobis facienda sit voluntaria ejus ad mortem, non communem, sed terribilem, & maledictam, obedientia, nostrae salutis ergo, luculenter docuit. O stupendam Christi obedientiam, incomparabilem adversus Ecclesiam suam amorem! An te pudebit, Ecclesia Christo dilecta, benedictam ac gloriosam obire mortem pro Christo tuo, quem nec puduit, nec piguit, promptissimo animo mortem ferre maledictam & ignominiosam, pro te ab inferis redimenda, Deoque aeternum conciliandā.
units.tr: 2. Why, profane despisers of Christ, do you ascribe his death either to chance, or to a blind fortune that knows nothing of us and rages cruelly against wretched man? Christ went to death most willingly, with full assent of mind and by the free impulse of his love for God and his Church: No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it up again. John 10:18. Profane man, what more do you seek, that you should confess his death to be voluntary in every respect? Do you want the Son of God to become man and the Son of Man, so that, suffering, he might die crushed under a heel? Gladly and willingly he took the form of a servant, made a partaker of flesh and blood, so that through his death he might destroy him who had the power of death. Hebr. 2:14. You did not desire sacrifice and offering for sin; but you have prepared a body for me. Then I said, Behold, I come to do your will. Ps. 40:7; Hebr. 10:5, 6, 7. Do you want Christ, who could have called upon innumerable legions of angels, girded for his protection, if he had wished, to be seized and bound without resisting in any way? He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearers is dumb, so he opened not his mouth. Isa. 53:7; Matt. 26:63; 27:14; Acts 8:32. But if Jesus, made the seed of the woman, had led an obscure life in a corner, declaring to no one that he was the Christ, the Son of Man, he would not have stirred up envy and deadly hatred of the Pharisees against himself, nor would he have suffered death, much less the ignominious death of the cross. What remains, then, but that you confess that Jesus went willingly and gladly to this dreadful death? That he should wage enmity with the serpent, the Devil, cast out demons, everywhere overthrow the works of the Devil, perform everywhere the miracles of the true Messiah, hateful to the Pharisees, and openly profess with frank voice that he is the Christ, the Son of Man, knowing that he would thereby certainly remain under death? One thing alone accomplished all this, even when he forbade his disciples to announce these things about him to anyone. Nor did he go to death any the less willingly because he prayed: My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me. Matt. 26:39. For he also willingly submitted to the will of the Father: Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will. Your will be done. Matt. 26:39, 42. And how dearly our salvation cost him, by that dread of the cup full of divine curse, and how greatly we ought to render to him a voluntary obedience to death, not a common death but a terrible and accursed one, for our salvation's sake, he has clearly taught us. O stupendous obedience of Christ, incomparable love toward his Church! Will you, Church beloved of Christ, be ashamed to undergo a blessed and glorious death for your Christ, when he was not ashamed nor reluctant, with the most ready mind, to bear a cursed and ignominious death, to be redeemed for you from the dead and reconciled to God forever?

units.la: 3°. Cum Iesum cernimus solum annunciantem, se esse filium hominis Christum, altum tunc silentibus ipsius discipulis. Cum vero vicibus commutatis, Iesu per ascensionem in coelum, intra velum recepto, discipulos factos Apostolos, Iesu altum silente, cernimus, late per orbem universum praedicantes, Iesum esse Christum. Admirandam mirari subit sapientiae ac charitatis Christi oeconomiam. Ipse solus doctrinam annunciat, sibi ex malitia, odio, & invidia Pharisaeorum mortem certo illaturam, tutis interdum ipsius discipulis. Cum vero Apostoli, Iesum esse Christum, palam docent universum orbem, doctrinam annunciant, vitam & salutem aeternam credicrediturisí collaturam, sed præconibus ipsis, ex mundi malitia, invidia, & odio, ignominiam & mortem multifariam, tuto interdum Jesu Christo in solio suo cœlesti. Eccur vero ejusmodi discrimen? Eccur? Voluit Christus solus annunciare doctrinam, unde mortem sciebat se manere certissimam, quia unus cum serpente conterendo pugnare, & justitiam divinam placare mortis pretiosissimæ suæ λύτρῳ potuit, & tunc unus par fuit sustinendis imperterritus Satanæ ac mundi insultibus. Verum mutatis vicibus, Apostolos suos doctrinam de se Christo, vitam & salutem æternam credituris collaturam, ut annunciarent, jussit, quia meriti mortis suæ efficaciam, hominum ministerio applicare voluit, ut homines in sui fidem & amorem alliceret opportunius, perficiens potentiam suam in organorum infirmitate, ut gloria potentiæ hominies eruentis è potestate tenebrarum, Dei, non hominum, foret & videretur, munitis interim ministris suis vi ac robore, cunctis Satanæ ac mundi fluctibus procellosis immersabili.
units.tr: 3. When we see Jesus alone announcing that he is the Christ, the Son of Man, his disciples are then silent in the highest degree. But when, the roles having been reversed, after Jesus was received into heaven by the ascension, within the veil, we see the disciples made apostles, with Jesus silent in the highest degree, they preach far and wide throughout the whole world that Jesus is the Christ. We are moved to wonder at the admirable plan of Christ's wisdom and love. He alone announced the doctrine, knowing that death would surely come upon himself from the malice, hatred, and envy of the Pharisees, while his disciples were at times safe. But when the apostles openly teach the whole world that Jesus is the Christ, announcing a doctrine that would bestow life and eternal salvation on those who would believe, they, the heralds themselves, are at times exposed, while Jesus Christ sits safe on his heavenly throne, to ignominy and death in many forms, from the malice, envy, and hatred of the world. But why such a difference? Why? Christ wished to announce the doctrine alone, since he knew that death would certainly remain for him, because he alone could fight with the serpent, crushing it, and could appease divine justice by the ransom [λύτρῳ] of his most precious death, and so he alone was fearless enough to endure the assaults of Satan and the world. But when the roles were changed, he ordered his apostles to announce the doctrine about himself, which would bestow life and eternal salvation on those who were to believe, because he wished to apply the efficacy of his merited death through the ministry of men, so that he might more opportunely draw men to faith and love in himself, displaying his power in the weakness of the instruments, so that the glory of rescuing men from the power of darkness might be and be seen to be God's and not men's, while in the meantime he strengthened his ministers with power and might, so that they could not be submerged by any of the stormy waves of Satan and the world.

units.la: 4º. Quam irreconciliabilis sit Euangelii veritas, cujus summa est, Jesum esse Christum, non modò cum mendacio, sed & cum falsitate, ex Christi interdicto evidentissimè paret. Norunt ac credunt discipuli, Jesum esse Christum, filium Dei viventis: sed eorum fides multis errorum naevis hactenus laborat. Non norunt qualis revera sit, sed qualem exoptant, qui sapiunt quæ sunt hominum, non quæ sunt Dei. Non finit igitur Christus, infallibilis veritatis doctor, ut quod norunt annuncient, ne errore quo laborant hactenus, agnitam veritatem vitient, ne verum & falsum, calidum & frigidum, eodem ore flare videantur. Non finit intempestiva illa praedicatione, falsâ ex parte, ut fidem in totum dictis suis auferant, cum purgata erroribus mente, & regni coelorum imbutâ plane mysteriis, verum omni ex parte ferendum erit Christo testimonium. Hinc docemur, 1º. Euangelii veritatem non se tueri, aut commendare falso testimonio, nedum piis, ut Patres aliquot locuti sunt, fraudibus, & perperam affictis Sibyllarum carminibus, & oraculis, quasi Euangelium, potentia Dei, in salutem omni credenti, siculneis indigeret infirmae carnis dolis, technis & artibus Patris mendacii fallacibus. 2. Quanta sit habenda fides praedicationi Apostolorum, & Scripturæ, quam Ecclesiæ pretiosum κειμήλιον reliquere. Nec locuti sunt de Christo, nec de eo quicquam scripsere, tantisper dum eum plane cognitum ac perspectum habuere, ipsis revelante spiritu veritatis, post ipsius mortem, resurrectionem & ascensionem in coelum. Antehac non idonei doctores, vel Iudaeorum, vel mundi, erronei ipsi, ipso Magistro Iesu jubente, perpetuam ἐχεμυθίαν, Pythagorae discipulorum ad instar, observarunt. Agedum eorum Scripturam, uti veritatis normam irreformabilem
units.tr: 4. How irreconcilable the truth of the Gospel is, whose sum is that Jesus is the Christ, not only with a lie but also with falsehood, is most evidently shown by Christ's prohibition. The disciples knew and believed that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God; but their faith has hitherto labored under many blemishes of error. They did not know what he really was, but what they wished him to be, who mind the things of men, not the things of God. Christ, the infallible teacher of truth, therefore did not allow them to announce what they knew, lest by the error under which they still labored they might spoil the truth they had recognized, lest truth and falsehood, hot and cold, might seem to flow from the same mouth. He did not allow that untimely preaching, false in part, lest they should take away faith entirely from his words, when, with minds purged of errors and fully imbued with the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, the testimony to Christ would be wholly acceptable. From this we are taught: first, that the truth of the Gospel does not defend or commend itself by false testimony, much less by pious frauds, as some of the Fathers have said, nor by badly fabricated Sibylline verses and oracles, as if the Gospel, which is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes, needed the tricks of frail flesh, the devices and arts of the deceitful Father of lies. Second, how great the trust is to be placed in the preaching of the Apostles and in Scripture, which they left to the Church as a precious treasure [κειμήλιον]. They did not speak of Christ, nor write anything about him, so long as they did not have him fully known and clearly perceived, which was after his death, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, when the Spirit of truth revealed him to them. Before that, the teachers, not fit ones, whether of the Jews or of the world, themselves erroneous, observed, at the command of their Master Jesus, a perpetual silence [ἐχεμυθίαν], like the disciples of Pythagoras. Come now, let us embrace their Scripture as the irreformable rule of truth,

units.la: K 3 amplectamur, nocturnâ diurnâ manu versemus, bona fide, tutaque conscientia scriptam putemus: nam nec quæ affectus carnales, & malè præconcepta judicia dictabant, prædicarunt, vel scripserunt: sed quæ propriis oculis usurpaverant, quæ contemplati fuerant, quæ audiverant, quæ propriis manibus contrectaverant, de verbo vitæ Christo, è mortuis excitato, intus docente spiritu veritatis, fallere nescio, annunciarunt, & sacris literarum monumentis legenda, & ad salutem credenda, mandarunt & Ecclesiæ reliquerunt.
units.tr: Let us embrace them, let us turn them over by night and by day, let us regard them as written in good faith and with a clear conscience. For they did not preach or write what carnal desires and badly preconceived judgments dictated; rather, what they had seen with their own eyes, what they had contemplated, what they had heard, what they had handled with their own hands, concerning the Word of life, Christ raised from the dead, they announced—taught within by the Spirit of truth, whom I cannot deceive—and they handed on to the Church, to be read in the sacred monuments of letters and to be believed for salvation.

units.la: 5º. Hinc facilè dirimi potest, diu vexata, & multa animi contentione agitata controversia super legitima vocatione prædicandi Euangelii, & ministrorum verbi Christi. Omnes, ut ut sectis variis disterminati, & in partes distracti Christiani, legitimam Euangelii prædicandi vocationem, ac missionem ἀκοινωνήτως sibi propriam vindicant, valere jussis, ac æternùm silere aliis. Quid causæ præjudiciis occæcati, & horsum illorsum abrepti, serram infelicem tamdiu reciprocatis? Quærendus est judex, & vocationis legitimæ, norma infallibilis, adeunda. Præsto adsunt Christi discipuli & Apostoli, principes Euangelii præcones. Agedum vestram, ad eorum vocationem legitimam, exigite. Profundum Jesus discipulis suis imperat silentium, ut ut norint credantque eum esse Christum, quamdiu non norunt creduntve, ut par est, errores multos veritati admixturi, si vera prædicandi tunc à Christo concederetur. Verum legitima vocatione ad Euangelium prædicandum mittuntur, ubi purgatis mentis erroribus, & carnalibus præjudiciis abdicatis, nihil incerti, falsi nihil, veritati Euangelicæ de Christo sunt admixturi. Legitimam igitur vocationem & missionem ad Euangelium de Christo annunciandum obtinent, non modò, qui Iesum esse Christum crediderunt: sed & qui eum plane perspectum ac cognitum annunciant, qualem se ipsum in Euangelio revelavit, absque ulla mixtura affectuum ac præjudiciorum carnalium, vanarum hominum traditionum, commentitiarum doctrinarum, quæ pleno ore redolent, sapiuntque quæ sunt hominum, non quæ Dei sunt. Ad hanc normam legitimæ vocationis infallibilem, si exigatur Episcopi Romani, Cardinalium, Metropolitanorum, Archiepiscoporum, Episcoporum, Abbatum, Sacerdotum missaticorum, Monachorum, vocatio, corruit plane; quia eorum omnium doctrina ac prædicatio de Iesu Christo, admixtas habet innumeras, non falsas modò, sed novitias, & ex carnalibus præjudiciis natas, doctrinas innumeras: supremam & ἀγεύθωμον Episcopi Romani authoritatem in Ecclesiam universam, errandi immunitatem, intolerabilem in Reges unctos Dei, authoritatem, Missæ sacrificium, transsubstantiationem, sanctorum, reliquialiquiarum, imaginum, religiosam adorationem, purgatorii figmentum superciliosum operum meritum, Angelorum ac sanctorum mediationem, & quas non?
units.tr: 5th. From this the long-vexed controversy, debated with much contention of mind, about the lawful calling to preach the Gospel and the ministers of Christ's word can easily be settled. All Christians, however divided into various sects and split into parties, claim for themselves, to the exclusion of others, a lawful calling and mission to preach the Gospel, and they bid others farewell and keep silent forever. Why, blinded by prejudices and dragged this way and that, do you keep up the unhappy saw so long? The judge must be sought, and the infallible rule of lawful calling must be approached. The disciples of Christ and the Apostles, the chief heralds of the Gospel, are at hand. Come then, demand your calling from their lawful calling. Jesus commands his disciples to keep deep silence, although they knew and believed that he was the Christ; while they did not yet know and believe as they ought, they would mix many errors with the truth, if they were then permitted by Christ to preach true things. But they are sent with a lawful calling to preach the Gospel when, the errors of the mind having been purged and carnal prejudices laid aside, they will mix nothing uncertain, nothing false, with the Gospel truth concerning Christ. Therefore a lawful calling and mission to proclaim the Gospel of Christ is held not only by those who believed that Jesus is the Christ, but also by those who proclaim him, having been plainly perceived and known as he revealed himself in the Gospel, without any admixture of affections and carnal prejudices, of vain human traditions and invented doctrines, which breathe out the full mouth and savour of what is of men, not of God. If the calling of the Roman Bishop, of Cardinals, Metropolitans, Archbishops, Bishops, Abbots, mass-priests, and Monks were examined by this infallible rule of lawful calling, it would plainly collapse; for the teaching and preaching of all of them concerning Jesus Christ has countless admixtures, not only false but novel doctrines born of carnal prejudices: the supreme and unerring authority of the Roman Bishop over the whole Church, the immunity from error, the intolerable authority over the anointed kings of God, the sacrifice of the Mass, transubstantiation, the cult of saints, relics, images, religious adoration, the superstitious fiction of purgatory, the merit of works, the mediation of angels and saints, and what not?

units.la: 6o. Quod noluerit Jesus imbutos discipulos seculi praejudiciis, ut ut coloribus ex Prophetiis male intellectis, speciosis, Euangelium, cujus summa est, Jesum esse Christum, annunciare. Quàm sedulò abdicanda sint legitimis Euangelii praeconibus, carnalia, vel speciosissima seculi praejudicia, summus doctor veritatis Christus nos evidentissimè docuit. Non sunt equidem ordinarii Euangelii praecones testes αὐτόπται perpessionum & gloriae Christi, quales futuri erant primi ejus discipuli ac Apostoli. Nec metuendum est, si abrepti carnis affectibus, & occaecati seculi praejudiciis, quae sanae doctrinae minus conveniunt, populo Christiano venditent, ne fides Euangelii laboret, vel quid decedat firmae ipsius veritati. Ne patiantur tamen, se furiis illis transversos abripi à veritatis salutaris tramite.
units.tr: 6th. That Jesus did not want disciples steeped in the prejudices of the age to proclaim the Gospel, whose sum is that Jesus is the Christ, even with specious colours drawn from prophecies badly understood. How carefully carnal or most specious prejudices of the age must be renounced by the lawful heralds of the Gospel, the supreme teacher of truth, Christ, taught us most clearly. Ordinary heralds of the Gospel are indeed not eyewitnesses (αὐτόπται) of the sufferings and glory of Christ, as his first disciples and Apostles were to be. Nor need we fear, if, carried away by fleshly affections and blinded by prejudices of the age, which agree less with sound doctrine, they hawk such things to the Christian people, that the faith of the Gospel will suffer or that anything will be lost from the firm truth itself. Yet let them not suffer themselves to be swept aside from the path of saving truth by those frenzies.

units.la: 1o. Quia Domino, ipsiusque salutari Euangelio, non pravis nostris affectibus serviendum est, ne se ipsos transformet in idola, Euangelii praecones, suaeque vanitati, magis quam Christi veritati morigerentur. 2o. Quia suum verbi ministerium in Ecclesiae aedificationem, & sanctificationem totum dirigere, ex Christi instituto, tenentur: at Spiritus sanctus vorticordi sua efficacia, nunquam ac nusquam prosequitur verbum hominum, nedum verbum, quod affectus carnales, & seculi praejudicia inspirarunt atque dictarunt. Cogitent igitur Euangelii praecones, qui sese student placere hominibus, petitis è trivio Poetarum fabulis, crebrisque è sinu Ethnicorum historiolis, quibus praegnant, quas parturiunt molles & effoetae ad populum conciones: num Jesum Christum praedicent in salutem omni credenti, num animorum consolationem, ac sanctificationem satagant, num potius seculi praejudiciis, carnisque Dei inimicae affectibus, mancipiorum ad instar, ducantur. Vah vani, catique Euangelii Christi mangones! Itane Christum didicistis, & veritatem, quae est in Jesu? si quis illi fundamento ligna, faenum, stipulam superstruxerit, male multabitur, & opus ejus exuretur, 1. Cor. 3: 12. 15.
units.tr: 1st. Because we must serve the Lord and his saving Gospel, not our depraved affections, lest the heralds of the Gospel make themselves idols and comply with their own vanity rather than with the truth of Christ. 2nd. Because they are bound, by Christ's institution, to direct their whole ministry of the Word to the building up and sanctification of the Church; but the Holy Spirit never and nowhere follows with his efficacy the word of men, much less a word which carnal affections and the prejudices of the age have breathed in and dictated. Let the heralds of the Gospel, who strive to please men, consider this: with the fables of the poets picked up from the crossroads and the frequent little stories from the bosom of the heathens, with which they are pregnant and which the soft and effete preachers bring forth to the people, do they preach Jesus Christ for salvation to everyone who believes? Are they careful for the consolation and sanctification of souls, or are they rather led, like slaves, by the prejudices of the age and by the affections of the flesh, which is hostile to God? Vain men, cheap hucksters of the Gospel of Christ! Have you so learned Christ and the truth that is in Jesus? "If anyone builds on that foundation wood, hay, or stubble, he will suffer loss, and his work will be burned up," 1 Cor. 3:12, 15.

units.la: 7o. Praeterea discipulorum, quibus prohibitum est, ne Jesum esse Christum annunciarent, quia eum non habebant, plane perspectum ac cognitum, exemplo docentur legitimi Euangelii praecones, gregumque pastores, quam sedulò ipsis incumbendum est, ut plena ac distincta Christi, in Euangelio revelati, cognitione, imbuantur, ne thesauro illo animarum vacui, ad vanas seculi divitias, puram putam pauperiem confugere, ad restim tandem redacti, male cogantur. Ne pabulo illo coelesti destituti, molles & otiosi œconomi Christi, gregem fame spirituali perire tandem videant, vel seipsum alere lethali secularium concupiscentiarum pabulo. Ne armis spiritualibus denudati, & lapidibus è torrente perpolitis destituti, terrenis ac secularibus Saulis armis gravati & male accincti, veritatis victoriam prodituri, cum Gigante mystico inauspicatò, congredi aggrediantur. Vel sileant, Christi interdicti memores, quia discipulorum ad instar, nondum veritatem, quæ est in Jesu, plenè ac distinctè didicerunt, vel Jesum Christum apertè nobis revelatum in mysterio pietatis fervida prece, lectione Scripturarum assidua, attenta ac profunda meditatione, discere contendant, ut Scribæ in regno cœlorum periti, è bono cordis thesauro, vetera è veteri, novaque è novo Instrumento promant, in sanctificationem & salutem gregis sibi commissi.
units.tr: 7th. Moreover, from the example of the disciples, who were forbidden to announce that Jesus is the Christ because they did not yet have him plainly perceived and known, lawful heralds of the Gospel and shepherds of the flock are taught how earnestly they must labour to be imbued with a full and distinct knowledge of Christ revealed in the Gospel, lest, empty of that treasure of souls, they flee to vain worldly riches for pure and bare poverty, and at last, reduced to the rope, are forced against their will. Lest, deprived of that heavenly food, the soft and idle stewards of Christ see the flock perish at last of spiritual hunger, or feed themselves on the deadly pasture of worldly lusts. Lest, stripped of spiritual weapons and without the smooth stones from the brook, burdened and badly girded with the earthly and worldly armour of Saul, they venture to engage the mystical Giant ill-omened and so betray the victory of truth. Or let them keep silent, mindful of Christ's prohibition, since, like the disciples, they have not yet fully and distinctly learned the truth that is in Jesus; or let them strive to learn Jesus Christ, revealed to us openly in the mystery of godliness, by fervent prayer, assiduous reading of the Scriptures, and attentive and deep meditation, so that, like scribes instructed in the kingdom of heaven, they may bring forth from the good treasure of the heart old things from the Old and new things from the New Testament, for the sanctification and salvation of the flock committed to them.

units.la: 8°. Interdictum factum discipulis de non annunciando Jesum esse Christum, mutatum vero imperium post ipsius resurrectionem, & solemnem die pentecostes Spiritus sancti in eosdem illapsum, ex æquo nos docent, Iesum neminem dignatum fuisse, sua, ad Euangelium annunciandum, vocatione, haud satis instructum necessariis ad id muneris obeundum, dotibus. Utinam ad hanc normam Euangelii præconum vocatio, seriò exigeretur. In ordinariis, fatebor enim, Euangelii præconibus, constituto jam Christi regno, dotes illæ extraordinariæ ac miraculosæ Apostolorum non desiderantur: sed ordinariæ, non ad libitum nostrum: ducimur enim, heu nimium, corpusculi terreni affectibus: sed ad sapientissimam Spiritus sancti normam, quæ prostat in Paulinis ad Titum & Timotheum epistolis, matura ætas, prudentia, mores compositi, boni, bonum vel exterorum testimonium, scientia in mysterio Iesu Christi non levis, sed longo Scripturarum sacrarum exercitio, distincta & obfirmata: nam si semel oppido multi ordinariis, sed & necessariis hisce dotibus vacui, in sacrum verbi Christi ministerium irrepserint, permetuendum sane est, ne similes sibi adsciscant operarios, gregariisque gaudeant commilitonibus, eos quippe dolebit atque pudebit, se meliores ac doctiores in sacrum verbi presbyterium ac præconium cooptare.
units.tr: 8th. The prohibition laid on the disciples not to announce that Jesus is the Christ, and the command changed after his resurrection, and the Holy Spirit's solemn descent upon the same disciples on the day of Pentecost, teach us alike that Jesus did not deign to call anyone to announce the Gospel without the gifts necessary for discharging that office. Would that the calling of the heralds of the Gospel were seriously examined by this rule. In ordinary heralds of the Gospel, I will admit, now that Christ's kingdom is established, those extraordinary and miraculous gifts of the Apostles are not required; but the ordinary ones are required, and not at our pleasure: for, alas, we are led too much by the affections of our earthly body; rather they are required by the wisest rule of the Holy Spirit, which is set out in the Pauline epistles to Titus and Timothy: mature age, prudence, composed and good morals, a good testimony even from outsiders, a knowledge of the mystery of Jesus Christ that is not slight but distinct and confirmed by long exercise in the sacred Scriptures. For if once very many men, lacking these ordinary and yet necessary gifts, have crept into the sacred ministry of the word of Christ, it must indeed be greatly feared that they will take on similar workers and rejoice in comrades-in-arms of their own sort, since they would surely grieve and be ashamed to co-opt into the sacred presbytery and herald's office of the word men better and more learned than themselves.

units.la: QUÆSTIO
units.tr: QUESTION

units.la: QUÆSTIO IV.
units.tr: QUESTION IV.

units.la: Quem intellexerint, David Psal. 8:5.6.7. & Paulus Hebr. 2:6.7.8. Quid est homo, quòd recorderis ejus, aut filius hominis, quòd visites eum, &c.
units.tr: Whom did David (Ps. 8:5, 6, 7) and Paul (Heb. 2:6, 7, 8) mean? "What is man, that thou art mindful of him, or the son of man, that thou visitest him?" etc.

units.la: EN familia Stoïcorum, Seneca Philosophus non ignobilis, veteres omnes Philosophos sub unum veluti oculorum conjectum reduxit, ubi eos lepidè confert, cum contendentibus ad ludos Olympicos. Eò tendebant alii, ut spectatores agerent, & vana spectaculorum curiositate oculos suos pascerent. Non secus & nonnulli Philosophi animum suum ad naturæ contemplationem appulere, ut avidum scientiæ animum suum explerent, nuda rerum naturalium cognitione. Istos verò in sapientibus non habet celebris Stoïcus. Eò alii, non spectatum modò, sed ut ipsi spectarentur, convolabant frequentissimi: parili planè modo, & Philosophi non pauci se totos dedidere studio rerum naturalium, ut famam sibi conciliarent, & auram popularem captarent, gloriolæ aucupes cupidissimi, quibus semper arrisit illud, pulchrum est digito monstrari, & dicier, hic est. Nec hos inter sapientes computavit Stoïcus. Eò tandem generosiores proficiscebantur alii, nec spectaturi, nec spectandi: sed acturi ac pugnaturi. Nihilo secius & Philosophi cæteri sese addixere contemplationi mundi, ut ex contemplatione agerent, & ad virtutem sibi potentissimum facerent incitamentum, quos Stoicus dignos reputat illustri elogio sapientis. Sed nec ipsa Stoïcorum Porticus ejusmodi nobis exhibet Philosophos sapientes. Severam quidem virtutem colere visi sunt: sed superciliosam tantum virtutis umbram amplexi, in Deum ipsum injurii ore sacrilego, scita, fulmine quovis & tartaro digna, effutivere. Una Dei Ecclesia, germanæ virtutis schola & Academia, sapientes ad salutem alumnos habet cœli contemplatores, qui invisibilia Dei intuiti, potentiam nempe ipsius æternam ac divinitatem, bonitatem ipsius, admirabundi ore pleno celebrant. Audiatur unus è choro Sancto sapientum præcentor David, Cum cœlos tuos video, opus digitorum tuorum, lunam & stellas, quas disposuisti; quid est homo, quod recorderis ejus, & filius hominis, quod visites eum?
units.tr: In the school of the Stoics, the philosopher Seneca, no obscure man, gathered all the ancient philosophers as if into one field of view, and compares them wittily to those who competed at the Olympic Games. Some went there to be spectators and to feed their eyes with the empty curiosity of the show. In the same way, some philosophers turned their minds to the contemplation of nature, to satisfy their greedy minds with the bare knowledge of natural things. The famous Stoic does not count these among the wise. Then many others rushed there, not only to watch but to be watched. In just the same way, not a few philosophers devoted themselves entirely to the study of natural things in order to win fame for themselves and catch popular applause, most eager hunters of glory, for whom that saying always pleased: it is a fine thing to be pointed at with the finger and to be said, "there he is." The Stoic did not count these among the wise either. Finally, others, more noble, set out there, neither to watch nor to be watched, but to act and to fight. Likewise the other philosophers gave themselves over to the contemplation of the world, so that they might act from that contemplation and make it the most powerful spur to virtue. The Stoic judges these worthy of the distinguished name of wise man. But not even the Stoic Porch itself shows us such wise philosophers. They seemed to cultivate a stern virtue, but, embracing only the haughty shadow of virtue, they uttered with a sacrilegious mouth, against God himself, insulting opinions worthy of any thunderbolt and of Tartarus. The one Church of God, the school and academy of true virtue, has as its wise pupils for salvation the contemplators of heaven, who, looking upon the invisible things of God, namely his eternal power and divinity and his goodness, celebrate them with wondering mouths. Let us hear one from the holy choir of the wise, the precentor David: When I see thy heavens, the work of thy fingers, the moon and the stars which thou hast ordained; what is man, that thou art mindful of him, and the son of man, that thou visitest him?

units.la: Locus illustris, sed difficilis, etsi lucem intulit Paulus, toto fere secundo capite ad Hebræos, varie à variis intelligitur. Alii enim dictum volunt de homine in statu creationis & innocentiæ gloriosæ, quòd de dominio à Numine in eum collato, Gen. 1: 26. 28. In aves cœli, pisces Oceani, greges, armenta, & bruta omnia, mentionem Psaltes attexuerit. Alii de genere humano, seu natura humana in universum spectata, quatenus singularibus inexistit, absque applicatione & determinatione ad quemvis singularem hominem, vel ex ipso peccato, quod Paulus tamen per sapientem aliquam accommodationem Christo tribuerit, sicuti ad justitiam fidei, Rom. 10: 6. 7. accommodavit, quod Moses de legis præceptis dixerat Deut. 30: 12. Ne dicas in corde tuo, quis ascendet in cœlum, &c. Quasi verò Paulus usus fuerit quadam accommodatione ad justitiam fidei, non verò exacta applicatione & explicatione, ut vident qui oculos acutos habent. In iis tamen fuit Calvinus ὁ μακαρίτης. Alii denique supponunt, 1°. Hominem & filium hominis esse ἰσοδυναμοῦντα nomina, & pro uno eodemque usurpari. 2°. Juxta Apostoli mentem de Christo unicè dictum volunt, in quibus est Camero eximius Theologus: sed ut sese expediat difficultate, quâ hæc sua laborat hypothesis, scilicet filium hominis nunquam dici de Christo per contemptum: sed constanter significare illustrem Christi personam, sublimi munere mediatorio ornatam, ut se inquam expediat evidente difficultate, quam illi parit hic textus Psalmographi, ubi evidenter per contemptum ipsius de quo sermo habetur, hæc vehemens interrogatio instituitur, Quid est homo, ut memineris ejus, aut filius hominis, ut visites eum? Tandem commentus est, & ut ajunt, κατὰ τὴν δεύτερον πλῆν secunda velificatione, Davidis interrogativam admirationem intelligendam esse de natura humana, non unitâ quidem, sed uniendâ Christo. Verum ultima hac sua interpretatione, proprias, ut ajunt, vites sibi cædere, nobis videtur, & inconsideratè demoliri, quæ superius de Christo sapienter struxerat, & à scopo Apostoli longissimè aberrare. Si nobis igitur minimis, inter tot Ecclesiæ lumina & collumina, fari liceat quod sentimus, nullus hactenus, (quorum quidem facta nobis est copia) plenè assecutus Spiritus sancti mentem videtur.
units.tr: This is a notable but difficult passage. Although Paul has thrown light on it, across nearly the whole of the second chapter of Hebrews, it is understood in various ways by various people. Some want the words to be said of man in the state of creation and of glorious innocence, with reference to the dominion conferred on him by the Deity (Gen. 1:26, 28), and they hold that the Psalmist added mention of the birds of the air, the fish of the sea, the flocks, herds and all beasts. Others take it of the human race, or of human nature considered in general, insofar as it exists in individuals, without application or restriction to any single man, and even of sin itself. Paul, they say, applied this to Christ by a clever accommodation, just as he applied to the righteousness of faith (Rom. 10:6, 7) what Moses had said of the precepts of the law (Deut. 30:12): Do not say in your heart, who shall ascend into heaven? etc. As if Paul had used some accommodation to the righteousness of faith, and not an exact application and explanation, as those with sharp eyes see. Calvin, of blessed memory (ho makaritēs), was among those holding this view. Finally, others assume: (1) that "man" and "son of man" are equivalent names [isodynamounta] and are used for one and the same thing; (2) that, according to the mind of the Apostle, the words are said solely of Christ. Camero, an outstanding theologian, belongs to these. But in order to extricate himself from the difficulty which afflicts this hypothesis of his, namely that "son of man" is never said of Christ in contempt but always signifies the illustrious person of Christ, adorned with the high mediatorial office, he (I say) tries to escape the obvious difficulty which this text of the Psalmist creates for him. Here, clearly, in contempt of the very one who is the subject of discourse, this vehement question is raised: "What is man, that thou art mindful of him, or the son of man, that thou visitest him?" At last he has devised, and as they say, by a second tack [kata tēn deuterēn plēn, secunda velificatione], that David's interrogative exclamation must be understood of human nature, not as united, indeed, but as to be united to Christ. But to us this last interpretation seems, as they say, to cut the very vines that support it, and to demolish inconsiderately what he had wisely built up above concerning Christ, and to stray very far from the Apostle's aim. If then we, the least among so many lights and lesser lights of the Church, may be allowed to say what we think, none hitherto (of whom we have had a supply) seems to have fully grasped the mind of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Observa igitur 1°. Psalmographum rem ipsam quod attinet, verbis tantum paululum immutatis, admirabundum in geminam exclamationem errumpere, Psal. 144: 3. nam cum Psal. 8:5. dixerit Quid est homo, quòd recorderis ejus, & filius hominis quod visites eum? Mutatis Epithetis, Psal. 144: 3. sic infit quid est homo, & cognovisti eum, filius hominis, & reputasti eum. Nec mirum, nam res eòdem redit, siquidem homo à lapsu, non modò fuit qualis ante lapsum, utpote ex terra cretus: sed & potiori jure, utpote in terram & pulverem ex reatu morte rediturus: sed & praeterea fuit אנוש lethali peccati ægritudine miseriisque omne genus conflictatus. Non immerito igitur David eum Psal. 8:5. vocavit אנוש, & Psal. 144:3. אדם, & filium ipsius, de quo loquitur modò בן אדם, modò בן אנוש ut sapienti illa epithetorum commutatione nos doceret, illius filium factum fuisse participem, tum naturæ, in terram reditu-ræ per mortem, tum maledictionis, ægritudinis, ac miseriæ parentis, ut nemo jure ullo ambigere posset, Christum (de eo enim utrobique sermo instituitur, ut solidis infra addicemus rationibus) verè ac reapsè fuisse Adami filium.
units.tr: Observe therefore, first, that as regards the matter itself, with the words only slightly changed, the Psalmist breaks out into a double exclamation of wonder (Ps. 144:3). For whereas in Ps. 8:5 he said, "What is man, that thou art mindful of him, and the son of man, that thou visitest him?", in Ps. 144:3, with the epithets changed, he begins thus: "What is man, that thou hast known him? The son of man, that thou hast regarded him?" Nor is this surprising, for the matter comes to the same thing. Man since the fall was not only what he was before the fall, namely formed of earth, but with a stronger right, since he was to return to earth and dust by death as the penalty of guilt; and moreover he was an enosh [אנוש], struggling with every kind of misery and the deadly sickness of sin. Not without reason, then, David called him enosh [אנוש] in Ps. 8:5, and adam [אדם] in Ps. 144:3, and his son, of whom he speaks now as ben adam [בן אדם] and now as ben enosh [בן אנוש]. By this wise change of epithets he teaches us that the son of this man was made a partaker both of the nature which returns to earth through death, and of the curse, sickness and misery of his parent, so that no one could doubt by any right that Christ (for it is of him that the discourse is held on both occasions, as we shall show below by solid reasons) was truly and in fact a son of Adam.

units.la: Observa 2o. אנוש & אדם significare 1o. Adamum ab Eva distinctum, Gen. 2: 19. & 3: 8. & 4: 1. Job. 9: 2. 2o. Adamum & Evam simul, Gen. 1: 26. 27. & 3: 22. & 5: 1. 2. Psal. 144: 3. & passim, ubi quotquot nascuntur & denascuntur homines, dicuntur בני אדם 3o. Genus humanum in peccatum prolapsum, quia de nomine primorum parentum, eorum ac miserorum, universa ipsorum progenies censetur, ut: Job. 33:26. Psal. 9: 20.21. Dan. 2: 43. & 4: 14. Psal. 22: 7. & 36:7. & 39: 6.
units.tr: Observe, second, that enosh [אנוש] and adam [אדם] signify: (1) Adam as distinct from Eve (Gen. 2:19; 3:8; 4:1; Job 9:2). (2) Adam and Eve together (Gen. 1:26, 27; 3:22; 5:1, 2; Ps. 144:3, and often), where all the men who are born and die are called bene adam [בני אדם]. (3) The human race fallen into sin, because the whole progeny of the first parents, who are wretched, is reckoned by the name of them (Job 33:26; Ps. 9:20, 21; Dan. 2:43; 4:14; Ps. 22:7; 36:7; 39:6).

units.la: Observa 3o. Cum homo & filius hominis conjuncta occurrunt, non esse nomina ἰσοδυναμοῦντα, nec unum idemque significare, ut viris undiquaque doctis visum est: sed diversa planè subjecta, distincta statu & conditione, ut Numer. 23:19. לא איש אל ויכזב ובן אדם ויתנחם Non est vir Deus ut mentitus sit, & filius hominis, ut pœnituerit eum. Nam cum איש & אדם opponuntur, איש virum illustrem, vel munere & authoritate, vel virtute & divitiis, & אדם è fœce plebis hominem, infimum, vilem & despectum, humique jacentem, ut: בני איש בני אדם, filii viri illustris, filii hominis, Psal. 49:3. Bileamus significare voluit, non unum quemvis singularem hominem: sed universum genus humanum, in ambas classes distinctum, illustres scilicet viros & plebeios homines: nam non est quod ingratiis ad pleonasmum confugiamus, cum vel ipsa nomina, quibus utitur Spiritus sanctus, frequenti atque solemni sua significatione, distincta qualitatibus & conditionibus, ὑποκείμενα significent. Si quando verò איש & בן אדם ad unum idemque singulare subjectum referuntur, id equidem respiciunt distinctum qualitatibus statu & conditione, ut: Psal. 80: 18. תהי ידך על איש ימינך על בן אדם אמצת לך Sit manus tua super virum dexterae tuae, super filium hominis quem roborasti tibi. Quae dicta de Messia, & Paraphrastes Chaldæus Josephus Cæcus fatetur, dum ita παραφράζει, על מלכא משיחא, Super Regem Messiam, & Aben-Esra fatetur hoc posse intelligi de משיח בן אפרים, Messia filio Ephraim. Et ratio ipsa suadet: nam vates sacer, defixus in contemplationem illustrium beneficiorum, quæ Deus in populum suum, è servitute Ægyptiaca assertum in gloriosam libertatem, effuderat, gradatim assurgit ad contemplationem constitutae reipublicae, & regni Davidis e tribu Judae, & tandem ducente Spiritu sancto ad Regem Messiam, cujus David typus erat illustris. Christum vero dum contemplatur sedentem ad dexteram Majestatis in excelsis, vocat virum illustrem dexterae Dei: eundem vero dum intuetur in diebus carnis suae, versantem in terris, vocat filium hominis, quem Deus sibi ipsi roboravit.
units.tr: Observe, third, that when "man" and "son of man" occur together, they are not equivalent names, nor do they signify one and the same thing, as seemed right to men learned on every side. They are plainly different subjects, distinguished by rank and condition, as in Num. 23:19: לא איש אל ויכזב ובן אדם ויתנחם [lo ish El weyechzav, uven adam veyitnachem], "God is not a man [ish], that he should lie, nor a son of man, that he should repent." For when ish [איש] and adam [אדם] are set in contrast, ish [איש] signifies an illustrious man, either by office and authority, or by virtue and riches, while adam [אדם] signifies a man of the dregs of the people, the lowest, vile and despised, lying on the ground, as in bene ish, bene adam [בני איש בני אדם], "sons of men of high degree, sons of men of low degree" (Ps. 49:3).
