Balaam wished to signify not any single individual man, but the whole human race, divided into the two classes, namely illustrious men and common people. For there is no reason for us to take refuge in a pleonasm in vain, since the very words used by the Holy Spirit, in their frequent and solemn meaning, signify subjects distinguished by qualities and conditions. If at any time ish [איש] and ben adam [בן אדם] are referred to one and the same singular subject, they indeed look to a distinction of qualities, rank and condition, as in Ps. 80:18: תהי ידך על איש ימינך על בן אדם אמצת לך [tehi yadcha al ish yeminecha al ben adam ametzta lach], "Let thy hand be upon the man of thy right hand, upon the son of man whom thou madest strong for thyself." These words are said of the Messiah, and the Chaldee paraphrast, Joseph the Blind, admits this when he paraphrases thus: על מלכא משיחא [al malka meshicha], upon the King Messiah; and Aben Ezra admits that this can be understood of משיח בן אפרים [meshiach ben Ephraim], the Messiah son of Ephraim. Reason itself also persuades this. For the sacred seer, fixed on the contemplation of the illustrious benefits which God poured out on his people, rescued from Egyptian servitude into glorious liberty, rises step by step to the contemplation of the established commonwealth and of the kingdom of David of the tribe of Judah, and at last, the Holy Spirit leading him, to King Messiah, of whom David was an illustrious type. But when he contemplates Christ sitting at the right hand of the Majesty on high, he calls him the illustrious man of God's right hand; and when he looks on him in the days of his flesh, living on earth, he calls him the son of man, whom God made strong for himself.

units.la: Observa 4o. Psalmum octavum, ut prima fronte ad meram Dei bonitatem, creationem & dominium, quod Deus in Adamum contulit, spectare videatur: revera tamen in opus redemptionis, & gloriam divinae misericordiae celebrandam, totum collimare; quod & Christus & Paulus, infallibiles Spiritus sancti interpretes, & ratio ipsa nobis persuadent. Et Christus quidem, Matth. 21: 16. Indignantibus enim sacerdotibus & Scribis, quod pueri clamarent in templo Hosanna filio David, ut os obturaret, repositit, Nunquam legistis ex ore infantium & lactentium perfecisti laudem? Ex versiculo tertio Psalmi octavi. Revera enim puerorum illorum testimonio, Christus sacerdotum & scribarum hostium suorum capitalium, vim & odium coercuit. Nec quis regerat, Christum usum quadam accommodatione: nam vel Spiritus sanctus ore Davidis respexit ad pueros testimonium Christo perhibentes, eumque Regem solemni acclamatione Hosanna, salutantes: vel non respexit: sed tantum ad infantes proprie dictos, via naturali genitos & ubera fugentes. Si posterius respondeas, sophistam egerit Christus, & plane abusus fuerit textu sacri Vatis, cum ex tua responsione Spiritus sanctus locutus ore Prophetae, non respexerit ad pueros dignitatem Jesu Christi celebrantes in templo. 2o. Cum in statu creationis Adami, ubi Deus eum condecoravit dominio, in pisces maris, volucres aeris, armenta, & bestias agri, Gen. 1. 26. 28. nondum essent infantes, nec ubera fugentes. Qui, amabo, potuit sacer Vates Dei bonitatem celebrare, effusam in creatione Adami, quod tunc gloriam suam fundaverit per os infantium, & ubera fugentium ad coercendos adversarios, & cessare faciendum inimicum se ulciscentem, cum nulli tunc forent Dei adversarii, nedum infantes ubera fugentes? 3o. Ex instinctu infantium & fugentium ubera, argumentum quidem divinae providentiae depromi potest, non vero Achilleum argumentum, & omni majus exceptione, quod compescat & cessare faciat Atheos Dei adversarios, & inimicum Diabolum, & mundum se ulciscentem adversus Deum. 4o. Nulla dari potest ratio, cur Spiritus sanctus prius elegerit exemplum instinctus puerorum & infantium ubera fugentium, ad laudem Dei ex eorum ore stabiliendam, quam exemplum instinctus longe admirabilioris, bilioris, quem cerninus in brutis animantibus, non minus ab utero ubera fugentibus, cum minoris sit admirationis, animal ratione præditum ab ipso utero, vel quam fari valeat prius, in ubera materna ferri, quam pullos ab ovo pinsere, & catulos ferri ad mammas. Hinc efficitur ad mysticum sensum sacrum Vatem respexisse, & pueros intellexisse primâ Christi cognitione imbutos, oppositos scilicet sapientibus principibusque seculi Judaici, infensissimis Dei & Christi adversariis. Reapse enim & primam Christi notitiam sub schemate lactis non semel nobis exhibet Spiritus sanctus, sicut & imbutos primâ illâ notitiâ sub schemate infantium: unde Propheta, emite sine argento & sine pretio vinum & lac, Jef. 55: 1. Et Paulus, Lacte vos potavi, non escâ, nondum enim poteratis ferre. 1 Cor. 3: 2. & Petrus, sicut modo geniti infantes lac rationale sine dolo concupiscite, ut per id crescatis. 1 Pet. 2: 2. Inclamantes verò ad Jesum Hosanna pueri in templo, non ætate modò: sed & Christi notitiâ, lacte rationali primùm imbuti, pueri erant. Præterea Paulus, 1 Cor. 15: 27. Eph. 1: 22. Hebr. 2: 6. 7. 8. 9. ad Christum refert, non accommodatione: sed proprie & ἀπολόμως versum 6um. & 7um. Psalmi 8i, ut ad Adamum, juxta mentem Apostoli, versus illi proprie trahi nequeant. Christo & Paulo sapienter concinunt Hieronymus & Augustinus in enarrationibus suis in Psalmum 8um, quem integrum in Dei misericordiam, Christum, & opus redemptionis constanter referunt. Accedat & ratio, petita ex consideratione initii & finis istius Psalmi, eum enim sacer vates à sonora admiratione exorditur, eademque claudit admiratione sonora, Jehova Domine noster יהוה אדונינו, Quam illustre, seu admirabile nomen tuum in universa terra! Si nullum foret Dei opus magnificentius, vel admirabilius opere creationis, admiratione Vatis, opus hujusmodi dignum videretur: sed cum opus redemptionis, Dei magnificentiam & gloriam, nobis exhibeat contemplandam, magnificentiâ ac gloriâ creationis innumeris parasangis superiorem, par est, ut Vatis admirabundi exclamationem ad magnificentiam gloriamque Dei, in opere redemptionis in clara luce revelatam, referamus. Præterea, cum Dei nomen in scriptura significet, vel Deum ipsum, quia nomen cum sit rei signum, pro re significata usurpatur, ipsiusque locum obtinet in sermone, imprimis cum res est absens, vel quasi absens, qualis est Deus, ut pote infinitus atque invisibilis, ut 2 Chron. 2. 4. Psal. 115: 1. Es. 29: 23. Joel. 2: 32. Vel Dei claram & distinctam revelationem ac notitiam, quia nomen cum sit rei signum, & eam facit innotescere, & distinguit ab aliis, ut, Psal. 22: 23. Matth. 4: 5. Joan. 17: 6. vel famam, & gloriam Dei; tum, quia nomine proprio, dum personæ innotescunt, famam sibi conciliant, tum, quia famâ illustres per ora circumferuntur, & identidem nominominantur, ut: Psal. 48: 11. & 76: 2. & 111:9. Vel potentiam, authoritatem & majestatem Dei, 1 Sam. 17: 45. Psal. 54:3. Matth. 18:20. Vel denique regnum Dei & Euangelium, ut: Matth. 19: 29. collato cum Marc. 10: 29. & Luc. 18: 29. Reputet Lector cum animo suo, quomodo sit intelligendum Dei nomen in vehementi isthac exclamatione admirabundi Davidis, quam illustre est nomen tuum Jehova Domine noster in universa terra! Si Deum ipsum vel ipsius revelationem intellexerit, Deusne Dominus Davidis, erat admirabilis & illustris in universa terra tempore Davidis? Qui, obsecro, illustris & admirabilis ἀγνως Θεὸς? annunciat verba sua Jacobo, & judicia sua Israeli, non sic fecit omni genti, & judicia ejus non agnoscunt, Psal. 147: 19. Effunde iram tuam ad gentes, quae non te cognoverunt, & super regna, quae non invocaverunt nomen tuum, Psal. 79: 6. Si famam Dei & gloriam, h. e. laudem, & virtutum divinarum celebritatem intellexeris. Qui, amabo, illustre & admirabile erat Dei nomen in universa terra, quandoquidem fere universa terra sub luce maligna & umbra mortis jacens, idololatriae & cultui Diabolorum mancipata, Deum verum ignorabat? nam mundus non novit Deum per sapientiam in mundi nempe Systemate revelatam, 1 Cor. 1: 22. vel per lucem creperam, cognitum nec ut Deum glorificarunt, nec debitis gratiis hostierunt, Rom. 1: 21. Si potentiam, authoritatem & majestatem Dei intellexeris. Qui illustre & admirabile erat Dei nomen in universa terra, quandoquidem universa fere Ethnicorum terra Deum & Dominum Israelis, propudiose repudiabat, mancipata Baalim falsis ac fictitiis numinibus ac idolis? Superest igitur, ut Vates sacer in futurum prospexerit, & Dei nomen in clara luce prophetiae, h. e. Deum ipsum, claram ipsius revelationem & notitiam, famam & gloriam, potentiam, authoritatem & majestatem in regno Dei, seu coelorum, per Euangelium, longe lateque per universam terram, magnificum in modum extensum, illustrem & admirabilem intuitus, in haec verba praesentis temporis propter infallibilem visionis certitudinem eruperit, Iehova Domine noster, quam illustre, quam admirabile est nomen tuum in universa terra!
units.tr: Observe, fourthly, that Psalm 8 at first sight seems to look only to God's mere goodness, to creation, and to the dominion which God conferred on Adam. In truth, however, the whole of it aims at the work of redemption and at celebrating the glory of divine mercy. Christ and Paul, the infallible interpreters of the Holy Spirit, and reason itself persuade us of this. Christ indeed, at Matt. 21. 16, when the priests and scribes were indignant that the boys cried out in the temple "Hosanna to the son of David", silenced them by replying: Have you never read, "Out of the mouth of infants and sucklings you have perfected praise"? This is from verse 3 of Psalm 8. For by the testimony of those boys Christ restrained the power and hatred of the priests and scribes, his chief enemies. Nor may anyone reply that Christ used the verse by some accommodation. Either the Holy Spirit, speaking through David's mouth, looked to boys bearing witness to Christ and greeting him as King with the solemn acclamation Hosanna, or he did not look to them but only to infants properly so called, born naturally and sucking the breast. If you answer the latter, Christ played the sophist and plainly abused the text of the sacred Bard, since on your answer the Holy Spirit, speaking through the mouth of the prophet, did not look to boys celebrating the dignity of Jesus Christ in the temple. Second, in the state of Adam's creation, when God adorned him with dominion over the fish of the sea, the birds of the air, the cattle and the beasts of the field (Gen. 1. 26, 28), there were not yet any infants or sucklings. Pray, how could the sacred Bard of God celebrate God's goodness poured out in the creation of Adam, in that God then founded his glory through the mouths of infants and sucklings, to restrain adversaries and make the avenging enemy cease, when at that time there were no adversaries of God at all, let alone sucklings? Third, from the instinct of infants and sucklings a proof of divine providence can indeed be drawn, but not an Achilles' argument, greater than any objection, that would restrain and make cease the atheists, the adversaries of God, the devil the enemy, and the world avenging itself against God. Fourth, no reason can be given why the Holy Spirit should have chosen first the example of the instinct of boys and infants sucking the breast, to establish praise of God from their mouths, rather than the example of a far more admirable instinct, which we see in brute animals that likewise suck from the womb. For it is less remarkable for a rational creature to be carried from the womb itself to its mother's breasts before it can speak, than for chicks to peck from the egg and puppies to be carried to the teats. Hence it follows that the sacred Bard looked to a mystical sense, and understood the boys to be imbued with the first knowledge of Christ, opposed, that is, to the wise men and princes of the Jewish age, the most hostile adversaries of God and Christ. Indeed the Holy Spirit more than once sets before us the first knowledge of Christ under the figure of milk, just as those imbued with that first knowledge under the figure of infants. Whence the Prophet: Buy wine and milk without money and without price, Isa. 55. 1. And Paul: I gave you milk to drink, not food, for you were not yet able to bear it, 1 Cor. 3. 2. And Peter: As newborn infants, desire the rational milk without guile, so that by it you may grow, 1 Pet. 2. 2. The boys crying Hosanna to Jesus in the temple were boys not only in age but also in the knowledge of Christ, first imbued with rational milk. Moreover Paul, at 1 Cor. 15. 27, Eph. 1. 22, and Heb. 2. 6, 7, 8, 9, refers Psalm 8 to Christ, not by accommodation but properly, and [simply] refers the sixth and seventh verses to him, so that those verses cannot properly be drawn to Adam according to the mind of the Apostle. Jerome and Augustine agree wisely with Christ and Paul in their commentaries on Psalm 8, which they consistently refer in its entirety to God's mercy, to Christ, and to the work of redemption. Let reason also be added, drawn from consideration of the beginning and end of this Psalm. For the sacred Bard begins with a resounding exclamation of wonder and closes with the same resounding wonder: Jehovah, our Lord [יהוה אדונינו], how illustrious, or admirable, is your name in all the earth! If there were no work of God more magnificent or admirable than the work of creation, the Bard's wonder would seem fitting to that work. But since the work of redemption sets before us God's magnificence and glory to contemplate, a magnificence and glory far superior to those of creation by countless parasangs, it is right that we refer the Bard's exclamation of wonder to the magnificence and glory of God, revealed in clear light in the work of redemption. Furthermore, since in Scripture the name of God signifies either God himself (because a name, being the sign of a thing, is used for the thing signified and takes its place in speech, especially when the thing is absent or as good as absent, as God is, being infinite and invisible: 2 Chron. 2. 4; Psal. 115. 1; Es. 29. 23; Joel 2. 32); or the clear and distinct revelation and knowledge of God (because a name, being the sign of a thing, makes it known and distinguishes it from others: Psal. 22. 23; Matth. 4. 5; Joan. 17. 6); or the fame and glory of God (because by a proper name, when persons become known, they win fame for themselves, and because famous men are carried about on the lips and are constantly named: Psal. 48. 11; 76. 2; 111. 9); or the power, authority and majesty of God (1 Sam. 17. 45; Psal. 54. 3; Matth. 18. 20); or finally the kingdom of God and the Gospel (Matth. 19. 29, compared with Mark 10. 29 and Luke 18. 29). Let the reader consider in his own mind how the name of God is to be understood in this vehement exclamation of the wondering David: how illustrious is your name, Jehovah our Lord, in all the earth! If he understood God himself, or his revelation, was the God of David then illustrious and admirable in all the earth, in the time of David? Pray, how was the unknown God [ἄγνωστος Θεός] illustrious and admirable? He declares his word to Jacob, his statutes and judgments to Israel. He has not done so for any other nation, and they do not know his judgments, Psal. 147. 19. Pour out your wrath on the nations that do not know you, and on the kingdoms that do not call upon your name, Psal. 79. 6. If you understood the fame and glory of God, that is, praise, and the renown of his divine virtues, pray, how was the name of God illustrious and admirable in all the earth, since almost the whole earth, lying under the evil light and the shadow of death, given over to idolatry and the worship of devils, did not know the true God? For the world did not know God through wisdom (wisdom revealed in the system of the world itself), 1 Cor. 1. 22; or, known through the dim light, they neither glorified him as God nor gave him the thanks due, Rom. 1. 21. If you understood the power, authority and majesty of God, pray, how was the name of God illustrious and admirable in all the earth, since almost the whole land of the Gentiles shamefully rejected God, the Lord of Israel, being given over to Baal, false and fictitious deities and idols? It remains, therefore, that the sacred Bard looked forward into the future, and in the clear light of prophecy, that is, looking upon God himself, his clear revelation and knowledge, his fame and glory, his power, authority and majesty in the kingdom of God, or of heaven, extended through the Gospel far and wide throughout the whole earth in a magnificent manner, illustrious and admirable, burst out in these words of the present tense, because of the infallible certainty of his vision: Jehovah, our Lord, how illustrious, how admirable is your name in all the earth!

units.la: Haec praefati, distinctis aliquot theorematis, sententiam nostram promere, & in clara luce constituere, visum est.
units.tr: Having said these preliminary things, it seemed good to set out our opinion by means of several distinct theorems, and to place it in clear light.

units.la: Theorema primum.
units.tr: The first theorem.

units.la: Textus sacri Vatis non est intelligendus de homine in statu creationis & innocentiae gloriosae.
units.tr: The text of the sacred poet is not to be understood of man in the state of creation and glorious innocence.

units.la: 1. Theorema hisce nititur fundamentis. Primum sternitur ex observatione quarne quarta, quâ firmis addiximus rationibus, Psalmum integrum prospexisse in futurum, nec vehementem Vatis admirabundi exclamationem in Adamum competere, vel in Dei bonitatem effusam in opus creationis. Secundum sternitur ex consideratione verborum textus. Primùm אנוש occurrit, אנוש, inquit Psaltes, אנוש verò est ab אנש, ægrum esse, & hominem significat, sed lethali ægritudine peccati & miseriarum laborantem. Unde Seth, tertius Adami filius, restitutus in locum Abelis, filium suum vocavit אנוש, ut in eo monumentum haberet lethalis ægritudinis peccati, Gen. 4: 26. & Ecclesia, ubi vindictam efflagitat in gentes idololatriæ mancipatas, quâ afflictæ & prostratæ reatum & miseriam suam persentiscant & confiteantur, judicentur, inquit, gentes, ut sciant, quod ipsæ sint אנוש, Psal. 9: 20. 21. Nec in toto veteri Instrumento legas, Adamum in statu innocentiæ vocatum אנוש, id demum nominis obtinuit, ex quo lethalis ægritudo peccati, in homines invecta fuit. Cum igitur sacer Vates sermonem habeat de homine אנוש, certo certius est, non spectasse hominem in statu innocentiæ gloriosæ. 2°. Occurrit verbum זכרו, quod meminerit ejus. Metaphora ducta ab amicis, qui amicorum afflictorum meminisse solent, & memoria, circa res præteritas, & quæ sunt, dum nobis absunt, versatur, & Deus meminit quidem eorum qui jam sunt, uti dicitur meminisse Noë, Gen. 8: 1. Sed proprie nusquam legitur meminisse eorum qui nondum sunt: at nondum erat Adam, antequam crearetur, non igitur proprie Adami meminisse, dum eum conderet ad imaginem suam, Numen sapientissimum dici potest: sed optimè meminisse dicitur hominis peccatoris miseri, cum ei filium hominis, seu Christum redemptorem destinavit, promisit, deditque. 3°. Occurrit בן אדם, filius hominis, constat vero Adamum in statu innocentiæ, vel dum crearetur, fuisse quidem aliquatenus filium Dei, utpote ad ejus imaginem cretum, filium vero hominis, haud pote. 4°. Occurrit תפקדנו, Visites eum, Visitatio verò Dei in Scriptura proponitur consideranda, vel ut fons & origo vindictæ, Exod. 20: 5. Psal. 59: 6. Vel ut fons & origo amoris, miserricordiæ, gratiæ & felicitatis, ut Job. 7: 17. & 10: 12. Psal. 65: 10. Luc. 1: 68. 78. Hic intelligendam visitationem Dei favorabilem, gratiarum & benedictionum omne genus scaturiginem, paret: addit enim extemplò sacer Vates, eum coronasti gloriâ & honore, omnia subjecisti pedibus ejus. Deum verò Adamum in puncto creationis eâ visitatione dignatum fuisse ut sentiamus, non patitur historia sacra creationis; Deum enim nobis exhibet creantem Adamum, & nullâ interposità morâ, vel dum ipsum crearet, ornantem imagine suâ, positâ in justitia & sanctitate, & dominio in omnes creaturas subcœlestes. Deus enim in Scriptura dicitur visitare hominem jam existentem, stentem, vel visitatione justitiæ & vindictæ; vel visitatione amoris & gratiæ. Nunquam vero visitare dicitur, quod nondum est, cum se ad id creandum & ornandum accingit. Est enim metaphora ducta à visitatione hominum, qui vel hostes dicuntur visitare, cum eorum fines armis invadunt, & regiones depopulantur: vel amicos amicitiæ, vel honoris, vel consolationis, vel beneficiorum ergò. Adamum igitur non visitavit Deus, cum eum condidit ad gloriosam suam imaginem, innocentem, sanctum, dominatorem, ac beatum. Denique cum in hanc admirationem admirabundus Vates erupit, Quid est homo, &c. evidenter loquitur per contemptum de homine. Tantine homo est, ut tu Deus immensus ac gloriosissimus eum visitare dignaris? Indignum igitur hominem immensi Dei visitatione, putat & docet evidenter sacer Vates. Verum homo ad imaginem Dei conditus, justus & sanctus, orbis universi inferioris dominus, beatus ac gloriosus, dignus sanè erat favorabili & amicâ Dei visitatione, ea equidem dignitate, quæ non merētum: sed sapientem inter duo convenientiam, in Scriptura significat: reapse enim sicuti Deus se ipsum necessariò amat, amat & pariter imaginem suam, quæ justitiam ac sanctitatem refert sui Creatoris: dignus igitur erat Adamus ad imaginem Dei conditus amore ac visitatione favorabili Dei sui. Deum suo amore, ac memoria favorabili, suos Angelos dignari, nihil equidem admirationis incessit: sancti enim sunt æquè ac insontes, beati, & obsequiosi Deo. Verum sanctitatis Deum, hominem reum, labe peccati coinquinatum, Diaboli mancipium, infamem & miserum, favorabili sua recordatione, & amica visitatione dignatum fuisse, non mediocrem movet admirationem Angelis ipsis, nedum hominibus. 5º. Occurrit [?], quod proprie significat, minuisti, decurtasti eum: est enim 2a. perf. fut. [?], destituit, defraudavit, minuit, deficere fecit. Unde paret, significare mutationem conditionis in pejus, illius videlicet, qui minuitur, decurtatur, & defraudatur. Mutatio vero conditionis, rei, quæ mutatur, existentiam supponit necessariò. Nondum vero existebat Adam, ut mutaretur in pejus. Et cum primùm Numen Adamum condidit, terram rubram, ipsius materiem, in melius commutavit. 6º. Occurrit [?], paucillum pro Angelis. [?] verò, veteris testamenti stylo, vel ad quantitatem molis discretam, vel continuam refertur, ut [?], pauci homines, Nehem. 2: 12. [?] paululum mellis, 1. Sam. 14: 29. Vel ad quantitatem temporis, seu durationis, ut: [?], & adhuc paululum, & non erat impius, Psal. 37: 10. [?], quasi momento inimicos eorum prostravissem, Psal. 81: 15. Græcum verò βραχύ τι, aliquando tenuem rei quantitatem significat, ut Joh. 6: 7. frequentissimè verò breve tempus, ut Act. 5: 34. [?] verò, modò Deum significat, ut Gen. 1: 1. & passim, non quidem ad indigetandam personarum pluralitatem: nam Deus dicitur אלהים, vel dum Dei unitas asseritur in scriptura, ut: אתה יהוה אלהים לבדך, tu Jehova solus Deus, 2. Reg. 19:19. sed compendio sermonis, & per Ellipsin אל, vel אלוה, quia Deus & est & dicitur, Deus Deorum, Deut. 10: 17. Psal. 50: 1. Dan. 2: 47. & 11: 46. 2o. Significat Angelos: nam beatæ intelligentiæ, Angeli sunt officio atque ministerio: sed sanctitate, potentia & gloria, quâ præ se ferunt Dei imaginem, dicuntur אלהים, ut Psal. 97:7. 3o. Principes, summosque magistratus, quia & virtutis ὑπεροχή, ἡ δυνάμει, ἡ ἐξουσία, potentia & authoritate, Dei imaginem referunt, ut Psal. 82: 6. Quovis modò intellexeris שם & אלהים, nequit referri ad Adamum in statu creationis, & felicis innocentiæ. Deum si interpreteris, non verum est, Numen minuisse Adamum, vel modicum, vel ad breve tempus infra Deum: nam 1o. Qui nondum existebat Adamus, non potuit dum conderetur decurtari aut minui infra Deum: quandoquidem imminutio, & in pejus mutata conditio, mutati præexistentiam supponit. 2o. Quia non modicum, nec ad modicum tempus: sed infinitè & in infinitum Adamus, creatura finita, conditus fuit Deo inferior. Si principes summos, & magistratus intellexeris, longè falsum est, Adamum fuisse conditum, vel modicum, vel breve tempus, principibus summis, atque magistratibus inferiorem, eum enim coronavit Deus supremo dominio, non montibus, non saltibus, non fluviis aut oceano circumscripto: sed longè latèque per orbem universum in omnes creaturas inferiores diffusò, Gen. 1: 26. ut sine fine prærogativâ imaginis Dei, si modò in ea perseveraret, æternum beatus ac gloriosus, in eas dominaretur. Si denique Angelos intellexeris, ut Septuaginta Interpretes, παρ' ἀγγέλως reddidere, & Paulus ὁ Θεόπνευστος, Hebr. 2:7. longè a veritatis tramite, abire nobis videris: nam ut Angeli sint immortales, prærogativa substantiæ spiritualis, mutabiles tamen conditi, in lapsum & ruinam non pauci se dederunt præcipites, ut Adamus, vel par Angelis, vel etiam superior ac dignior creatus fuerit. Quod liquet, 1o. Quia non est absimile vero, partem Angelorum, ab obedientia Creatoris defecisse, ex invidia in Adamum, eumque lapsos, ad defectionem sollicitasse: invidia vero non æstuat in inferiores: sed in pares, vel virtute aut dignitate superiores. 2o. Quia Adamus erat typus Christi, tum quatenus fuit caput & princeps generis humani, statum & conditionem suam, vel felicem, vel miseram, in suam progeniem propagaturus, sicut Christus caput est atque princeps electorum & fidelium, conditionem & vitam suam spiritualem, cœlestem & immortalem, in eos vivifico Spiritu propagaturus, 1. Cor. 15: 45. Tum quia divinæ malemaledictioni ultrò sese exposuit, ductu amoris, quo Evam suam prosequebatur, sicut Christus factus est κατάρα, execratio, pro Ecclesia sua, Gal. 3: 13. Angeli verò, nunquam ac nusquam exhibentur ut typus Christi. Unde liquet, sub illa ἀγγέλ, Adamum fuisse Angelis ipsis superiorem. 3o. Adamus ita fuit ad Dei imaginem conditus, ut Dominium in omnes creaturas inferiores obtinuerit, quod nunquam ac nusquam legeris, Angelis tributum. 4o. Super formationem Adami, tanquam in praecellentissimum Dei opus, S.S. Trias deliberavit, quod de Angelis creandis, nunquam ac nusquam memoratum legeris. Cum igitur Dei dominium, illustris sit gloriae Dei gradus, in promptu concludere est, Adamum, praevia Trinitatis consultatione cretum, & imagine dominii supremi Numinis, ornatum, nobiliori ac excellentiori modo prae Angelis, ad Dei imaginem fuisse conditum. Nobis igitur, Pauli probaturi excellentiam Christi prae Angelis, methodum secutis, liceat argumentari. De quo Angelorum dixit Deus, faciamus Angelum ad imaginem & similitudinem nostram? De quo Angelorum dixit Deus, & dominetur in pisces maris, & in volucres caeli, & in jumentum, & in omnem terram? Gen. 1: 26. Tertium Theorematis fundamentum praestruitur ex consideratione magnitudinis dominii, quod sacer Vates tribuit, versu 7o. subjecto, de quo loquitur כל שתה תחת רגליו, omnia posuisti sub pedibus ejus. Quis verò omnia Adami pedibus subjecta asserere sustinuerit? Ut enim Deus Adami dominio obnoxias fecerit subcoelestes creaturas, coeli volucres, oceani pisces, brutasque animantes, Gen. 3: 26. Angelos tamen Adami pedibus non subjecit: nec facile crediderint, qui Adamum volunt paulò Angelis inferiorem creatum. Praeterea Paulus interpres ἀναμάρτητος Spiritus sancti, omnia, sic interpretatur, ut nullam creaturam eximat abilla subjectione, unum Deum Patrem excipit, qui ei omnia subjecit, 1. Cor. 15: 27. Cum verò mundus futurus, h. e. Ecclesia, seu populus Messiae, in nobilissimis Dei creaturis sit annumerandus, & Deus nunquam ac nusquam legatur, subjecisse Adami pedibus mundum futurum Messiae Ecclesiam, cum omnibus partibus mundi renovati per liberationem à servitute corruptionis, Rom. 8: 20. In promptu concludere est, sacrum Vatem non prospexisse in Adamum, in statu innocentiae gloriosae constitutum, cum in haec verba erupit, omnia posuisti sub pedibus ejus.
units.tr: 1. This theorem rests on the following foundations. The first is drawn from the fourth observation, by which we have adduced firm reasons for holding that the whole Psalm looks forward into the future, and that the vehement exclamation of the admiring poet does not apply to Adam, or to God's goodness poured out in the work of creation. The second is drawn from a consideration of the words of the text. First, enosh [אנוש] occurs. The Psalmist says enosh [אנוש], and enosh [אנוש] comes from anash [אנש], to be sick, and means a human being, but one labouring under the deadly sickness of sin and its miseries. Hence Seth, the third son of Adam, who was given in place of Abel, called his son enosh [אנוש], so that he might have in him a memorial of the deadly sickness of sin (Gen. 4:26). And the Church, when it calls for vengeance on the nations given over to idolatry, so that they, afflicted and prostrate, may perceive and confess their guilt and misery, says: let the nations be judged, that they may know that they themselves are enosh [אנוש] (Ps. 9:20, 21). Nor will you read anywhere in the whole Old Testament that Adam, in the state of innocence, was called enosh [אנוש]; that name was acquired only from the time when the deadly sickness of sin was brought upon mankind. Since, then, the sacred poet is speaking of man as enosh [אנוש], it is more than certain that he was not looking at man in the state of glorious innocence. Second, the word zikhro [זכרו] occurs, that he may remember him. This is a metaphor taken from friends, who are wont to remember afflicted friends; and memory is concerned with things past and things present while they are absent from us. God indeed remembers those who now exist, as it is said that God remembered Noah (Gen. 8:1). But properly speaking, one never reads of remembering those who do not yet exist. Adam did not yet exist before he was created, so it cannot properly be said that the most wise Deity remembered Adam when He formed him in His own image. Rather, it is rightly said that He remembered sinful and wretched man when He destined, promised and gave him the Son of Man, that is, Christ the Redeemer. Third, ben adam [בן אדם], son of man, occurs. But it is clear that Adam, in the state of innocence, or while he was being created, was indeed in some sense a son of God, as having been made in His image, but he was not a son of man. Fourth, tifqedenu [תפקדנו], visit him, occurs. But the visitation of God in Scripture is to be considered either as the source and origin of vengeance (Exod. 20:5; Ps. 59:6), or as the source and origin of love, mercy, grace and happiness (Job 7:17; 10:12; Ps. 65:10; Luke 1:68, 78). Here the favourable visitation of God is to be understood, the fountain of every kind of grace and blessing; for the sacred poet immediately adds: you have crowned him with glory and honour, you have put all things under his feet. That God visited Adam with such a visitation at the very moment of creation, the sacred history of creation does not allow us to think. For it presents God creating Adam without any intervening delay, adorning him, while He was creating him, with His own image, placed in righteousness and holiness, and in dominion over all creatures under heaven. In Scripture God is said to visit a man who already exists and stands, either with a visitation of justice and vengeance, or with a visitation of love and grace; but He is never said to visit what does not yet exist, while He is preparing to create and adorn it. For the metaphor is taken from the visiting of men, who are said to visit enemies when they invade their borders with arms and lay waste their lands, or to visit friends for the sake of friendship, honour, consolation or benefits. God, therefore, did not visit Adam when He formed him to be His glorious image, innocent, holy, a ruler, and blessed. Finally, when the admiring poet broke out into this wonder, What is man? etc., he clearly speaks of man with contempt. Is man so great that you, O immense and most glorious God, deign to visit him? The sacred poet therefore thinks and clearly teaches that man is unworthy of the visitation of the immense God. Yet man, created in the image of God, just and holy, lord of the whole lower world, blessed and glorious, was certainly worthy of the favourable and friendly visitation of God, a dignity which he did not earn; but Scripture signifies a fitting agreement between two parties. For just as God necessarily loves Himself, so He equally loves His image, which reflects the justice and holiness of its Creator. Adam, therefore, made in the image of God, was worthy of the love and favourable visitation of his God. That God should deign to remember His angels with love and favour does not indeed cause any wonder, for they are holy and, like the innocent, blessed and obedient to God. But that God, who is holy, should have deigned to remember sinful man, defiled with the stain of sin, the slave of the devil, infamous and wretched, with a favourable remembrance and a friendly visitation, moves not a little wonder even in the angels themselves, let alone in men. Fifth, [?] occurs, which properly means you have made him less, you have diminished him. It is the second person of the perfect/future of [?], he left destitute, defrauded, diminished, caused to fail. From this it is clear that it signifies a change of condition for the worse, namely of one who is diminished, lessened and defrauded. But a change of condition supposes necessarily the existence of the thing that is changed. Adam, however, did not yet exist, so that he could be changed for the worse. And when God first formed Adam, He changed the red earth, his matter, for the better. Sixth, [?] occurs, a little for the angels. [?], in the style of the Old Testament, refers either to a discrete or continuous quantity of bulk, as [?], few men (Neh. 2:12), [?], a little honey (1 Sam. 14:29); or to a quantity of time or duration, as [?], and yet a little while, and the wicked is not (Ps. 37:10), [?], as if I had in a moment laid low their enemies (Ps. 81:15). The Greek brachy ti [βραχύ τι] sometimes signifies a slight quantity of a thing (John 6:7), but most often a short time (Acts 5:34). [?], however, now signifies God (Gen. 1:1 and passim), not indeed to point out a plurality of persons, for God is called Elohim [אלהים] even when the unity of God is asserted in Scripture, as: you, O Jehovah, are God alone [אתה יהוה אלהים לבדך] (2 Kings 19:19); but by a shortening of speech, and by ellipsis, El [אל] or Eloah [אלוה], because God both is and is called the God of gods (Deut. 10:17; Ps. 50:1; Dan. 2:47; 11:36). Second, it signifies the angels: for angels, being blessed intelligences, are so by office and ministry; but by holiness, power and glory, by which they bear the image of God, they are called Elohim [אלהים], as in Ps. 97:7. Third, princes and the highest magistrates, because by the eminence of virtue, power and authority they bear the image of God, as in Ps. 82:6. Whichever way you understand shem [שם] and Elohim [אלהים], it cannot be referred to Adam in the state of creation and happy innocence. If you interpret it as God, it is not true that God diminished Adam, either slightly or for a short time, below God. For, first, Adam, who did not yet exist, could not be lessened or diminished below God while he was being created, since diminution, and a condition changed for the worse, presupposes the prior existence of the thing changed. Second, because he was not diminished slightly, nor for a short time, but Adam, a finite creature, was made infinitely and forever inferior to God. If you understand the highest princes and magistrates, it is far from true that Adam was made, even slightly or for a short time, inferior to the highest princes and magistrates; for God crowned him with supreme dominion, not circumscribed by mountains, woods, rivers or ocean, but spread far and wide throughout the whole world over all lower creatures (Gen. 1:26), so that, by the prerogative of the image of God, if only he persevered in it, he might rule over them, blessed and glorious for ever without end. Finally, if you understand the angels, as the Seventy translators rendered it, para angelous [παρ' ἀγγέλους], and Paul, who was inspired by God (Heb. 2:7), you seem to me to depart far from the path of truth. For although angels are immortal, by the prerogative of a spiritual substance, yet, being created mutable, not a few of them threw themselves headlong into fall and ruin, so that Adam was either made equal to the angels, or even created superior and more worthy. This is clear: first, because it is not unlikely that a part of the angels fell away from obedience to the Creator out of envy toward Adam, and enticed him, once fallen, to revolt; but envy does not burn against inferiors, but against equals, or those superior in virtue or dignity. Second, because Adam was a type of Christ, both inasmuch as he was the head and prince of the human race, about to propagate his own condition, whether happy or wretched, into his offspring, just as Christ is the head and prince of the elect and faithful, about to propagate into them, by the life-giving Spirit, His own spiritual, heavenly and immortal condition (1 Cor. 15:45); and also because he voluntarily exposed himself to divine curse, moved by the love with which he cherished his Eve, just as Christ was made katara [κατάρα], a curse, for His Church (Gal. 3:13). But angels are never and nowhere exhibited as a type of Christ. Hence it is clear that under that angel [ἀγγέλ], Adam was superior to the angels themselves. Third, Adam was made in the image of God in such a way that he obtained dominion over all lower creatures, a thing which you will never and nowhere read was attributed to the angels. Fourth, over the formation of Adam, as over the most excellent work of God, the Most Holy Trinity took counsel; of the creation of angels, you will never and nowhere read anything like this. Since, then, the dominion of God is an illustrious degree of the glory of God, it is easy to conclude that Adam, created after a prior consultation of the Trinity and adorned with an image of the supreme dominion of the Deity, was made in the image of God in a nobler and more excellent way than the angels. Therefore, following the method of Paul, who sought to prove the excellence of Christ above the angels, let us be allowed to argue thus: To which of the angels did God ever say, Let us make an angel in our image and likeness? To which of the angels did God ever say, and let him have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the heaven, and over the cattle, and over all the earth? (Gen. 1:26). The third foundation of the theorem is laid from a consideration of the greatness of the dominion which the sacred poet ascribes to man, in verse 7, where he speaks of the subject: kol shat tachat raglav [כל שתה תחת רגליו], you have put all things under his feet. But who would dare to assert that all things were subjected to the feet of Adam? For although God made the creatures under heaven subject to Adam's dominion, the birds of the heavens, the fishes of the ocean and the brute animals (Gen. 1:26), He did not, however, subject the angels to Adam's feet; nor would those easily believe it who want Adam to have been created a little inferior to the angels. Moreover, Paul, interpreting the anamartetos [ἀναμάρτητος] of the Holy Spirit, all things, so explains it that he exempts no creature from that subjection, excepting only God the Father, who put all things under him (1 Cor. 15:27). But since the future world, that is, the Church or people of the Messiah, is to be counted among the most noble creatures of God, and since God is nowhere and never read to have subjected to Adam's feet the future world, the Messianic Church, along with all the parts of the renewed world, delivered from the bondage of corruption (Rom. 8:20), it is easy to conclude that the sacred poet did not have in view Adam, constituted in the state of glorious innocence, when he broke out into these words: you have put all things under his feet.

units.la: Theorema Secundum.
units.tr: Theorem Second.

units.la: Textus sacri Vatis non est intelligendus de genere humano corrupto.
units.tr: The text of the sacred prophet is not to be understood of corrupt humankind.

units.la: Theorema hisce nititur fundamentis. 1°. Cum Deus non fecerit hominem peccatorem, nedum genus humanum, quod de nigro nomine parentis corrupti & maledicti, jure censetur. Equidem dici nequit, vel Adamum, vel genus humanum fecisse breve tempus Angelis inferius: nam cum homini peccatoris conditio deterior, vel ex amissione sanctitatis: vel ex amissione felicitatis sit æstimanda. Deus neutro modo genus humanum corruptum, fecit breve tempus Angelis inferius. Et 1°. quidem, non ratione amissionis sanctitatis. Deus enim non decurtavit aut minuit genus humanum, auferendo sanctitatem: unus Diabolus vi & efficacia suæ tentationis hominem deficere fecit à sanctitate, & homo sibi ipsi posterisque suis sanctitatem abstulit ἀταξία enormi desiderii sui. 2°. Non ratione amissionis felicitatis. Etsi enim Deus justo suo judicio ab homine reo, & labe peccati contaminato felicitatem abstulit; ita abstulit, ut genus humanum non ad breve tempus, vel paucillum dignitate sit inferius bonis Angelis: quippe quod immenso fere intervallo ab iis disterminatur, ipsis Dæmonibus inferius, vile ac despicabile caput, mancipium Diaboli & peccati, non ad breve tempus: sed in æternum, ni victrix Dei gratia, maledictum, infame ac miserum genus humanum è tristiilla servitute eruat, asseratque in gloriosam libertatem. Præterea Vates sacer asserit, Deum omnia posuisse sub pedibus ejus, de quo loquitur. Verum, nec omnia subjiciuntur dominio generis humani corrupti, ut ipsum Tros, Rutulusve suat in universum subjiciatur pedibus Diaboli, principis hujus mundi, efficaciter operantis in filiis contumacibus, Eph. 2: 2. Qui, obsecro, Deus omnia generis humani corrupti pedibus subjecerit, cum genus humanum nefaria rebellione dominio in creaturas exciderit, easque quotidie adversas ac infestas experiatur? Qui bonos Angelos posuerit Deus sub pedibus rei hominis, cum ipse prostratus ac victus jaceat sub pedibus potestatis tenebrarum? Qui denique Deus mundum futurum, Ecclesiam primogenitorum, novorum hominum cœtum, pedibus generis humani corrupti subjectum voluerit, cum mundum illum futurum, Messiæ populum, assiduè protegat ac tueatur adversus generis humani corrupti insultus, ut ne quidem inferorum portæ, h. e. potestas mortis & sepulchri, adversus Ecclesiam suam sint prævalituræ? 3°. Denique Deus dicitur gloria & honore eum coronasse, de quo sacer Vates sermonem instituit, genus verò humanum corruptum, ruptum, maledictioni, infamiæ ac probro æterno, quæ gloriæ & honori è diametro opponuntur, Numen ob violatum fœdus operum, jure meritissimo addixit.
units.tr: This theorem rests on the following grounds. (1) God did not make man a sinner, much less the human race, which by right is judged from the dark name of a corrupt and cursed parent. Indeed, it cannot be said that either Adam or the human race was made for a short time inferior to the angels, for the condition of a sinner must be judged worse either by the loss of holiness or by the loss of happiness. God has made the corrupt human race inferior to the angels for a short time in neither way. And first, certainly, not by reason of the loss of holiness. For God did not diminish or lessen the human race by taking away holiness. The Devil alone, by the force and efficacy of his temptation, caused man to fall from holiness, and man took holiness away from himself and his posterity by the disorder [ἀταξία] of his immense desire. (2) Nor by reason of the loss of happiness. For although God, by his just judgment, took happiness away from man, who was guilty and stained with the defilement of sin, he took it away in such a way that the human race is not inferior to the good angels for a short time or by a small degree of dignity. Indeed it is separated from them by an almost immense distance, and is placed even below the demons themselves: a vile and despicable head, a slave of the Devil and of sin, not for a short time but for eternity, unless the victorious grace of God rescues the cursed, infamous and wretched human race from that sad servitude and asserts it into glorious liberty. Moreover, the sacred prophet asserts that God has put all things under the feet of him of whom he speaks. But truly, not all things are subject to the dominion of the corrupt human race, so that the Trojan or the Rutulian himself should be subjected to the feet of the Devil, the prince of this world, who works effectively in the disobedient sons (Eph. 2:2). I beg you, what God would have subjected all things to the feet of the corrupt human race, since the human race, by its wicked rebellion, has fallen from dominion over the creatures, and daily experiences them as hostile and hurtful? What God would have put the good angels under the feet of guilty man, when he himself lies prostrate and conquered under the feet of the power of darkness? Lastly, what God would have wished the future world, the Church of the firstborn, the assembly of new men, to be subject to the feet of the corrupt human race, when he constantly protects and guards that future world, the people of the Messiah, against the assaults of the corrupt human race, so that not even the gates of hell, that is, the power of death and the grave, shall prevail against his Church? (3) Finally, God is said to have crowned with glory and honour him of whom the sacred prophet speaks, while the corrupt human race, which is directly opposed to glory and honour, he has, by right and most deservedly, assigned to curse, infamy and everlasting reproach, because of the violated covenant of works.

units.la: Theorema Tertium.
units.tr: Theorem Third.

units.la: Textus sacri Vatis non est intelligendus de natura humana Christo unienda.
units.tr: The sacred Poet's text is not to be understood of the human nature to be united to Christ.

units.la: Theorema hisce nititur fundamentis, 1°. Natura humana Christo unienda non est homo: sed futura hominis natura. Verùm sacer Vates loquitur de homine. 2°. Natura humana Christo unienda, futura erat sanctissima, eximiis dotibus, ac illustri Dei imagine condecoranda, amore & æstimatione Dei dignissima, ut enim Deus se ipsum necessariò amat, sibique complacet, ita & necessariò amore complectitur purissimam sanctitatis suæ imaginem: sed Vates sacer per contemptum loquitur de homine, Quid est homo, quod memineris ejus? tantine est misella isthæc creatura, ut tua eam digneris recordatione? 3°. Vates loquitur de filio hominis: sed natura humana Christo unienda, non futura erat filius hominis. Verùm tota Christi persona ex natura divina & humana, ὑποστατικῶς unitis, coalescens. 4°. Vates asserit, Deum minuisse illum de quo loquitur, & Angelis ad breve tempus fecisse inferiorem, mutata nempe ejus conditione in pejus. Deum verò Naturam humanam Christo uniendam, cum non præexisteret, minuisse, & in pejus mutasse, non sustinet recta ratio. At enim cum primùm Christo coepit inexistere, eam Deus non minuit, fecitve Angelis inferiorem: sed longè excellentiorem, quandoquidem eam per unionem ad gloriosam filii sui personalitatem evexit, mutata ejus conditione in melius, quam si personalitate ψιλὴ ἀνθρώπῳ, meri hominis, eam donasset. 5°. Sacer Vates diserte docet, Deum fecisse מעט βραχύ τι, ad breve tempus Angelis inferiorem eum, de quo loquitur. Deus verò naturam humanam Christo uniendam, non fecit Angelis inferiorem, nedum ad breve tempus. 6°. Vates docet, Deum omnia posuisse sub pedibus ejus, de quo sermonem habet: sed Deus non posuit omnia sub pedibus naturæ humanæ Christo uniendæ: verùm ipsi jam unitæ, & ad gloriam supremæ Majestatis evectæ in cœlum. 7°. Vates asserit, Deum coronasse gloria & honore illum, de quo loquitur, ut hac gloriosa coronatione significet augustam majestatem regni illius, eumque exhibeat nobis in omnia regnantem. Verùm naturam humanam Christo uniendam nemo sanus dixerit in omnia regnare, nec ipsam quidem jam unitam, nam munera non sunt partium aut naturarum: sed personarum: regia enim authoritas, ritas, non corporis, sed animæ regis est; sed totius personæ, quæ regnare dicitur. Denique, cum Natura humana Christo unienda, non foret Christus: sed futura Christi natura, quod Vates sacer tribuit subjecto, de quo sermonem habet: vel pertinebat ad Christum: vel ad naturam humanam Christo uniendam. Si posterius, cum hujusmodi natura non foret Christus: sed natura futura in Christo, male argumentatus fuerit Apostolus, Hebr. 2: 9. dum ea refert ad Jesum, quem, inquit, jam videmus gloria & honore coronatum. Si vero ad Christum pertineat: non pertinet igitur ad naturam humanam Christo uniendam, illa enim natura non erat Christus: sed tantum destinatione Dei, futura Christi natura.
units.tr: This theorem rests on the following foundations. (1) The human nature to be united to Christ is not a man, but the future nature of a man; yet the sacred Poet speaks of a man. (2) The human nature to be united to Christ was to be most holy, adorned with excellent gifts and with the illustrious image of God, and most worthy of God's love and esteem; for just as God necessarily loves himself and takes pleasure in himself, so too he necessarily embraces with love the most pure image of his holiness. But the sacred Poet speaks of man with contempt: "What is man, that you should remember him? Is this wretched creature so worthy that you should deign to think of him?" (3) The Poet speaks of the son of man; but the human nature to be united to Christ was not going to be the son of man. Rather, the whole person of Christ coalesces from the divine and human natures, united hypostatically. (4) The Poet affirms that God made lower than he who is spoken of, and for a short time lower than the angels, that is, by changing his condition for the worse. But that God should have made lower, and changed for the worse, the human nature to be united to Christ, which did not yet exist, is something right reason does not allow. For when it first began to exist in Christ, God did not make it lower or inferior to the angels; rather he made it far more excellent, since through the union he raised it to the glorious personhood of his Son, changing its condition for the better, far more than if he had given it a mere personhood, that of a mere man. (5) The sacred Poet plainly teaches that God made him of whom he speaks lower than the angels for a little while [מעט, βραχύ τι]. But God did not make the human nature to be united to Christ lower than the angels, much less for a little while. (6) The Poet teaches that God put all things under the feet of him of whom he speaks; but God did not put all things under the feet of the human nature to be united to Christ, but under that nature already united and raised to the glory of supreme Majesty in heaven. (7) The Poet affirms that God crowned him of whom he speaks with glory and honour, so that by this glorious crowning he might signify the august majesty of that kingdom and present him to us as reigning over all things. But no sane person would say that the human nature to be united to Christ reigns over all things, nor even the nature already united; for offices belong not to parts or natures but to persons. Royal authority belongs not to the body but to the soul of the king, and indeed to the whole person who is said to reign. Finally, since the human nature to be united to Christ was not Christ, but would be the future nature of Christ, the attribute the sacred Poet gives to the subject of which he speaks must either pertain to Christ or to the human nature to be united to Christ. If the latter, then, since such a nature was not Christ but a nature future in Christ, the Apostle argued badly when he referred this to Jesus, Heb. 2:9, where he says, "whom we now see crowned with glory and honour." But if it pertains to Christ, then it does not pertain to the human nature to be united to Christ, for that nature was not Christ but only, by God's designation, the future nature of Christ.

units.la: Theorema Quartum, & Quæstionis solutio.
units.tr: Fourth Theorem, and the solution of the question.

units.la: Textus sacri Vatis intelligendus est, juxta membrorum διχοτομίαν. Primum interrogationis membrum de genere humano corrupto: Postremum de filio hominis, seu Christo, par est, ut intelligatur.
units.tr: The text of the sacred Bard must be understood according to its division into two members. The first member of the question, concerning the corrupted human race, and the last, concerning the Son of Man, or Christ, ought to be understood in that way.

units.la: Theorema hisce nititur fundamentis. Primum sternitur ex consideratione bimembris exclamationis admirabundi Vatis. Atenim, nemo opinor infitiabitur, Vatem admirabundum duo quaerere. Alterum de homine lethali ægritudine, miseriis peccati laborante, quid est homo, quod recordaris ejus? Hæc verò plena admirationis interrogatio, apprimè competit in Adamum, ejusque posteros, peccati reos, miseriisque omne genus conflictatos. Alterum de filio hominis, peccati reatu, ac miseriis Adami onerato, quem Deum dignari sua favorabili visitatione, quâ imminutum breve tempus infra Angelos, gloria ac honore coronavit, non immeritò sacer Vates miratur. Secundum præstruitur ex præcedentibus theorematis, ubi firmis rationibus addiximus, textum integrum sacri Vatis, non esse intelligendum de Adamo in statu creationis, & innocentiæ gloriosæ, vel de genere humano corrupto: vel de natura humana Christo unienda. Unde sponte sua sequitur, textum Psalmographi integrum bimembrem esse, ut primum membrum prospiciat in Adamum, & ipsius progeniem, genus humanum, corruptum ac miserum: alterum in filium hominis, Christum, quatenus est secundus Adamus, caput & princeps electorum ac fidelium suorum. Agedum, utrumque Theorematis membrum sigillatim probatum demus. 1°. Adamum peccati reum, ejusque posteros genus humanum, quis infitiabitur, esse lethali ægritudine peccati infectum, ac saucium? Quis iverit infitias, Adamum exstitisse, ejusque posteros reapse [illegible, ~12 letters] num exstare, ut Dei recordationis objectum sint opportunum? Quis infi-tiabitur, argumentum esse cujusvis admirationis dignissimum, Adamum, ejusque posteros, reos violatæ legis, maledictioni ac morti obnoxios, dignosque, quorum Deus recordetur, ea recordatione justitiæ suæ vindicatricis, quæ fons est ultionis atque poenarum: ipsorum tamen benignissimum Numen recordari gratiosa recordatione, quæ in salutem eorum prospicit, ut immerentibus illis, filium hominis destinet in redemptorem, & eum in forma Dei gloriosissima existentem, vestitum forma servi vilissimi, & carnis peccatricis, imminuere ac decurtare voluerit ad breve tempus, infra Angelos? Hinc Vates, illam Dei recordationem explicaturus, mentionem attexit filii hominis, quem scil. Deus juxta fidelitatem promissionis, quæ exstat, Gen. 3:15. in gratiam hominis [illegible, ~4 letters], lethali peccati ægritudine laborantis, factum e filio Dei semen mulieris, imminuit atque depressit ad breve tempus infra Angelos. Quis denique negare sustinuerit, hanc interrogationem, quid est homo miser, quod recordéris ejus? competere in Adamum, ejusque posteros, maledictionis ac mortis reos? Si à sapiente Moyse percunctatus fueris, quid est homo? Illico respondebit, Et vidit Deus multam esse malitiam hominis in terra, & omnem imaginationem cogitationum cordis ejus, nihil esse præter malum omni die, Gen. 6:5. & 8:21. Si abs Davide? Non est justus, neque unus, non est intelligens, non est requirens Deum, omnes declinaverunt, simul inutiles facti sunt, non est faciens benignitatem, ne quidem ad unum usque. Sepulchrum patens guttur eorum, linguis suis dolose egerunt, venenum aspidum sub labiis eorum, quorum os maledictione & amaritudine plenum est, non est timor Dei præ oculis eorum, Psal. 14:1. Psal. 5:10. & 140:4. Psal. 10:7. & 36:1. Si abs sapiente Salomone? Veloces pedes eorum ad effundendum sanguinem, Prov. 1:16. Si ab Jeremia? Numquid æthiops mutabit pellem suam, & pardus maculas suas? Numquid vos etiam poteritis benefacere, edocti malefacere? Jer. 13:23. Si ab Jesaia? Omne caput est ægrum, & omne cor infirmum à planta pedis usque ad caput, non est in eo integritas, vulnus, & livor, & plaga saniosa, Jes. 1:6. Ipse vir pollutus sum labiis, & in medio populi labiis polluti habito, Jes. 6:5. Si ab Ezechiele? Pater ejus Amorreus, & mater Chittæa, in die nativitatis umbilicus ejus non fuit præcisus, in aquis non fuit lotus, projectus fuit ad superficiem agri, dum abjiceretur vita ejus, in die, quo nasceretur, Ezech. 16:4. 5. 6. Si à Daniele? Peccavimus, & perverse egimus, impie fecimus, & rebellavimus recedendo à præceptis tuis, & à juribus tuis, penes te, Deus, est justitia, at penes nos pudor faciei, penes viros Jehudæ, & penes habitatores Hierosolymorum, & penes omnes Israelitas, propinquos & longinquos, penes reges nostros, penes principes nostros, & penes patres patres nostros, quia peccavimus in te, Dan. 9: 5. 6. 7. 8. Sià Paulo? A'άτεκνος ἀμάζλωλος, ἀσεβὴς, viribus cassus, peccator, impius, Rom. 5: 6. 7. 8. Mortuus in delictis & peccatis, filius rebellionis, natura filius irae, h. e. servus, Eph. 2: 1. 2 3. Quid igitur est אנוש, reus homo atque miserellus, ut tu Deus ipsius recorderis? Indignus sane est, quem Numen favorabili sua dignetur recordatione. Deus tamen ipsius meminit benignissimum in modum, ut communionem nectat aeternam insolubilem cum afflictissimo illo homulo, seque in carnem miseram & afflictam ipsius induat, evehatque naturam ejus ad gloriosam filii sui σαρκωθέντος personalitatem, vel dum Angelos ipsos spernit, aut recordatur, ut rebelles plectat aeternis obscuritatis vinculis, dirisque cruciatibus inferorum. Meminit infensissimi hujus inimici, ut foedus pacis cum eo pangat, sibi reconciliato per sanguinem crucis: recordatur istius caeci, ut oculos aperiat: hujus servi, ut eum asserat in gloriosam libertatem: meminit conspurcati istius ac leprosi, ut mundet: stulti, ut coelesti sapientia donet: sepulchri, ut in sanctuarium, templumque sacrum commutet: mortui, ut vivificet, & sedere faciat aeternum cum ipso in excelsis. Concludamus igitur, primum interrogationis Vatis admirabundi membrum, apprime competere in Adamum, ejusque posteros, genus humanum, corruptum, reum, miseriisque omne genus ad mortem usque conflictatum.
units.tr: The theorem rests on these foundations. The first is laid down by considering the twofold exclamation of the admiring Bard. For, I think no one will deny that the admiring Bard asks about two things. The first is about man, afflicted with deadly sickness and suffering from the miseries of sin: what is man, that you are mindful of him? This question, full of wonder, applies most fittingly to Adam and his posterity, guilty of sin and worn down by every kind of misery. The second is about the Son of Man, burdened with the guilt of sin and the miseries of Adam, whom God deigned to crown, by his favourable visitation, with glory and honour, having made him for a short time lower than the angels. It is not without reason that the holy Bard marvels at this. The second foundation is laid by our preceding theorems, where by firm arguments we have shown that the whole text of the holy Bard is not to be understood of Adam in the state of creation and glorious innocence, nor of the corrupted human race, nor of human nature to be united to Christ. From this it follows of its own accord that the whole text of the Psalmist has two members: the first looks to Adam and his offspring, the corrupt and wretched human race; the second looks to the Son of Man, Christ, insofar as he is the second Adam, the head and prince of his elect and faithful. Come, let us prove each member of the theorem separately. First, who will deny that Adam, guilty of sin, and his posterity, the human race, are infected and wounded by the deadly sickness of sin? Who will deny that Adam existed, and that his posterity actually exists [illegible], so as to be a fitting object of God's remembrance? Who will deny that it is a matter most worthy of any wonder that Adam and his posterity, guilty of violating the law, liable to curse and death, and deserving that God should remember them, should be remembered by God's avenging justice, which is the source of vengeance and punishments; and yet that the most kind Divinity of these same people should remember them with a gracious remembrance, which looks to their salvation, so that, though they deserve nothing, he should appoint the Son of Man as their Redeemer, and should be willing to lessen and shorten him, existing in the most glorious form of God, clothed in the form of a most base servant and of sinful flesh, for a short time, below the angels? Hence the Bard, about to explain that remembrance of God, adds a mention of the Son of Man, whom God, according to the faithfulness of the promise which stands in Gen. 3:15, made from the Son of God the seed of the woman, for the sake of man [illegible], who labours under the deadly sickness of sin, and lowered and depressed him for a short time below the angels. Finally, who would venture to deny that this question, what is wretched man, that you are mindful of him? applies to Adam and his posterity, guilty of curse and death? If you ask the wise Moses, "what is man?", he will at once answer, And God saw that the malice of man was great on the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil every day, Gen. 6:5 and 8:21. If you ask David? There is none righteous, no, not one; there is none that understands, there is none that seeks after God. They have all turned aside, they are together become unprofitable; there is none that does good, no, not one. Their throat is an open sepulchre; with their tongues they have used deceit; the poison of asps is under their lips; whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness; there is no fear of God before their eyes, Ps. 14:1; Ps. 5:10; Ps. 140:4; Ps. 10:7; Ps. 36:1. If you ask the wise Solomon? Their feet are swift to shed blood, Prov. 1:16. If Jeremiah? Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? Then may you also do good, who are accustomed to do evil? Jer. 13:23. If Isaiah? The whole head is sick, and the whole heart faint, from the sole of the foot even to the head there is no soundness; but wounds, and bruises, and putrifying sores, Isa. 1:6. I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips, Isa. 6:5. If Ezekiel? Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite. As for your nativity, in the day you were born your navel was not cut, nor were you washed in water; you were cast out into the open field, when your life was abhorred, in the day that you were born, Ezek. 16:4, 5, 6. If Daniel? We have sinned, and have done perversely, and have committed wickedness, and have rebelled, departing from your precepts and your judgments. Righteousness belongs to you, O Lord, but to us confusion of face, to the men of Judah, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and to all Israel, those near and those far off; to our kings, our princes, and our fathers, because we have sinned against you, Dan. 9:5, 6, 7, 8. If Paul? Without strength [ἀσθενεῖς], sinners [ἁμαρτωλοί], ungodly [ἀσεβεῖς], Rom. 5:6, 7, 8. Dead in trespasses and sins, a son of disobedience, by nature a child of wrath, that is, a slave, Eph. 2:1, 2, 3. What then is man [אנוש], a guilty and wretched creature, that you, O God, should be mindful of him? Indeed he is unworthy to be remembered by the Divinity with favour. Yet God remembers him in the most kind manner, so that he might bind an eternal, indissoluble communion with that most afflicted little man, and clothe himself in his wretched and afflicted flesh, and raise his nature to the glorious personhood of his Son made flesh [σαρκωθέντος]; whether he despises the angels themselves or remembers them, in order to bind the rebels with eternal chains of darkness and the dreadful torments of hell. He remembers this most hostile enemy, in order to make a covenant of peace with him, reconciled to himself through the blood of the cross. He remembers this blind man, to open his eyes; this slave, to set him free in glorious liberty; he remembers this defiled and leprous man, to cleanse him; this fool, to endow him with heavenly wisdom; this sepulchre, to change it into a sanctuary and a holy temple; this dead man, to make him alive and to make him sit with himself on high for ever. Let us conclude, then, that the first member of the Bard's question applies most fittingly to Adam and his posterity, the corrupted human race, guilty, and worn down by every kind of misery even to death.

units.la: Secundum vehementis interrogationis Vatis admirabundi membrum, quod attinet, in Christum competere in solidum, multis invictisque argumentis possumus demonstrare. 1°. Ex interpretatione Pauli, 1 Cor. 15: 27. Eph. 1: 22. Hebr. 2: 6. 7. 8. Infallibilis enim Spiritus sancti interpres, hunc textum sacri Vatis, non accommodatione quadam: sed ἀπολύμως, ac proprie, unice ubivis ac constanter refert ad Christum. 2°. Ex consideratione verborum: nam Jesus & est filius hominis, & ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, uti proprio nomine, caeterisq; in novo instrumento incommunicabili, passim indigetatur: nam ut raro peccatores ex Adamo oriundi, filii hominis, seu hominum, h. e. Adami & Evae, aliquando dicuntur, nemo tamen singularis homo in toto novo testamento, υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου, nedum ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου καὶ ἐξοχὴν, & praefixis articulis emphaticis & characteristicis, appellatur. Unus Jesus hac gaudet nomenclatione insigni: unus ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, filius hominis, ut significet, se esse Christum, appellitatur. Pergamus, Deus proprie Jesum aeternum filium suum imminuit, eum enim qui erat in forma Dei, nec rapinam ducebat se esse Deo aequalem, natura divina, instructa infinitis virtutibus, omnibus divinae majestatis ac gloriae insignibus, praeditum, evacuavit, & ad vilissimam usque servi formam dimisit, quousque nunquam Angelos, gloriae suae ministros dimiserat. Hinc in Christum filium hominis apprime primè competit τὸ מעש מאלהים, nam sive per אלהים Deum, sive reges, principesque summos, sive Angelos cum Paulo intellexeris, certò certius est, Deum filium hominis, Christum suum, Deum in secula æterna benedictum מעש, βραχύ τι, breve tempus, imminuisse, ac fecisse Deo, principibus, Angelisque inferiorem: fecit enim Deus eum, qui non noverat peccatum, peccatum pro nobis, 2. Cor. 5: 21. & benedictum suum κατάραν maledictionem pro nobis, Gal. 3: 13. Jesum fecit ad breve tempus, scil. per passionem suæ mortis, ut interpretatur Apostolus, Hebr. 2:9. Angelis inferiorem. Quippe qui in agone montis olivarum, opis indiguit Angeli, e coelo venientis, ut eum consolaretur, Luc. 22: 43. Christum unum Deus visitavit illa visitatione favorabili, quæ fons est bonorum inexhaustus, Psal. 65: 10. 11. 12. 13. 14. Christum unum Deus coronavit gloria & honore, propter passionem mortis, ut conserta Christi corona ex gloria & honore mortalium nemini jure mitti valeat: quippè coronam Jesu, ex gloria & honore, sicut ex binis floribus amarantinis, contextam, ubi Paulus interpretatur, Phil. 2: 9. 10. 11. sic infit, Propterea enim Christum Deus summè evexit, eique dedit nomen supra omne nomen, ut ad nomen Jesu omne genu flectatur, eorum quæ sunt in cœlis, & in terra, & subter terra, & omnis lingua confiteatur, Jesum Christum esse Dominum, ad gloriam Dei Patris. Denique uni Christo convenit, quod asserit Vates, Deum omnia posuisse sub pedibus ejus. Dedit enim illi potestatem omnem in cœlo & in terra, Matth. 28: 18. Eum collocavit in dextera sua in cœlestibus, supra omnem principatum & potestatem, & virtutem, & dominationem, & omne nomen, quod nominatur, non solum in hoc seculo: sed etiam in futuro, Eph. 1: 21. Christus est in dextera Dei, profectus in cælum, subjectis illi Angelis, & potestatibus, & virtutibus, 1 Pet. 3: 22. Eum fecit Deus hæredem omnium, per quem & secula condidit, Hebr. 1:2. Illi dedit gentes hæreditatem suam, & possessionem suam terminos terræ, Psal. 2: 8. Omnes populi, nationes, & lingua servient ipsi, dominatio ejus est dominatio æterna, quæ non transibit, & regnum ejus non corrumpetur, Dan. 7: 14. Cum enim omnia sub pedibus ejus subjecerit Deus, Paulo interprete, nihil dimisit ei non subjectum, Hebr. 2: 8. Nempe Christi dominio subditi sunt Dæmones & mundus, quos vicit: Angeli, quos habet spiritus servientes, nuntios ac ministros: peccatum quod expiavit, & Spiritus efficacia abolebit: mors & sepulchrum, e quorum potestate, vivus & victor exiit: creaturæ mundi visibilis, quas condidit, in libertatem gloriosam filiorum Dei propediem asserturus, & denique οἰκουμένην μέλλοσα, mundus futurus, seu Ecclesia, cujus caput est, atque rex in secula victurus ac regnaturus.
units.tr: As for the second member of the Bard's earnest question, we can demonstrate by many unanswerable arguments that it applies wholly to Christ. First, from the interpretation of Paul, 1 Cor. 15:27; Eph. 1:22; Heb. 2:6, 7, 8. For the infallible interpreter of the Holy Spirit refers this text of the sacred Bard not by some accommodation, but absolutely [ἀπολύτως], and properly, uniquely, everywhere and consistently, to Christ. Second, from a consideration of the words. For Jesus is both the son of man and the Son of Man [ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου], as a proper name, and is passim designated by this title, which is incommunicable in the New Testament. For although sinners descended from Adam are sometimes called sons of man, that is, sons of men, that is, of Adam and Eve, rarely; yet no single man in the whole New Testament is called the son of man [υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου], much less the Son of Man [ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου] by eminence, with emphatic and characteristic articles prefixed. Jesus alone enjoys this distinguished name; he alone is called the Son of Man [ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου], so as to signify that he is Christ. Let us go on. God truly diminished his eternal Son Jesus; for he who was in the form of God, and did not think it robbery to be equal with God, endowed with divine nature, furnished with infinite powers, and endowed with all the marks of divine majesty and glory, emptied himself and was sent down even to the lowliest form of a servant, to a degree that he had never sent down the angels, the ministers of his glory. Hence the words [מעט מאלהים] (a little less than God) apply most properly and first of all to Christ the Son of Man. For whether you understand by Elohim [אלהים] God, or great kings and princes, or angels, with Paul, it is most certainly true that God made his Christ, the Son of Man, blessed for ever, a little less [βραχύ τι] for a short time, and made him inferior to God, to princes, and to angels. For God made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, 2 Cor. 5:21; and his blessed one to be a curse [κατάρα] for us, Gal. 3:13. He made Jesus a little lower for a short time, namely through the suffering of his death, as the Apostle explains, Heb. 2:9: lower than the angels. Indeed, in the agony in the Mount of Olives he needed the help of an angel coming from heaven to comfort him, Luke 22:43. God visited Christ alone with that favourable visitation which is an inexhaustible fountain of blessings, Ps. 65:10, 11, 12, 13, 14. God crowned Christ alone with glory and honour, because of the passion of his death, so that no one can rightly claim a share in the crown of Christ, woven from the glory and honour of mortals; for Paul, explaining the crown of Jesus, which is woven of glory and honour as of two amaranth flowers, begins thus at Phil. 2:9, 10, 11: For this reason God highly exalted Christ and gave him a name above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father. Finally, what the Bard asserts applies to Christ alone: that God put all things under his feet. For he has given him all power in heaven and on earth, Matt. 28:18. He set him at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every principality and power, and virtue, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this world, but also in the world to come, Eph. 1:21. Christ is at the right hand of God, gone into heaven, with angels, powers, and virtues made subject to him, 1 Pet. 3:22. God has made him heir of all things, through whom he also made the worlds, Heb. 1:2. He gave him the nations for his inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for his possession, Ps. 2:8. All peoples, nations, and languages shall serve him; his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed, Dan. 7:14. For since God, as Paul interprets, has put all things under his feet, he left nothing that is not subject to him, Heb. 2:8. Indeed the demons and the world, which he conquered, are subject to the dominion of Christ; the angels, whom he has as serving spirits, messengers and ministers; the sin which he expiated and which the efficacy of the Spirit will abolish; death and the grave, from whose power he came forth alive and victorious; the creatures of the visible world, which he made, and which he will soon assert in the glorious liberty of the children of God; and finally the world to come [οἰκουμένην μέλλουσαν], that is, the Church, of which he is the head and the king, who will live and reign for ever.

units.la: 1º. DUo hîc sacer Vates miratur, alterum cur Deus hominis meminerit: alterum cur filium hominis visitaverit. In utroque admirationis membro in causam admirationis inquirendum est, & in primo quidem spectanda occurrunt. 1º. Ipsa Vatis admiratio oriunda ex cognitione juxta ac ignorantia. Ex cognitione status hominis, recordationis Dei, scopi, & effectus hujuscemodi recordationis. Ex ignorantia rationis, quae Deum in hanc hominis recordationem impulit. 2º. Status hominis, quid est homo? 3º. Recordatio Dei adversus illum hominem. 4º. Finis & effectus illius recordationis. In altero admirationis membro inquirendum pariter est in causam admirationis. Ubi spectanda occurrunt. 1º.Ipsa Vatis admiratio oriunda partim ex cognitione, partim ex ignorantia: Ex cognitione status & conditionis filii hominis, visitationis Dei, scopi & effectus illius visitationis. Ex ignorantia rationis quae Deum ad illam filii hominis visitationem impulit. 2º. Status filii hominis. 3º. Visitatio Dei, ad illum filium hominis. 4º.Finis & effectus illius visitationis. Verùm haec momentosa capita, quae spectant ad secundum admirationis membrum, proximâ quaestione perstringemus σιω θεῷ. Age igitur momenta primi membri admirationis, in usus nostros conferamus.
units.tr: 1. Here the holy seer wonders at two things: first, why God remembers man; second, why he visited the Son of man. In each part of this wonder we must inquire into the cause of the wonder. In the first part, the following points present themselves for consideration. 1. The seer's wonder itself arises both from knowledge and from ignorance: from knowledge of the state of man, of God's remembrance, of the purpose of such remembrance and its effect, and from ignorance of the reason that moved God to this remembrance of man. 2. The state of man: what is man? 3. God's remembrance of that man. 4. The end and effect of that remembrance. In the second part of the wonder, we must likewise inquire into the cause of the wonder, where the following points present themselves. 1. The seer's wonder arises partly from knowledge and partly from ignorance: from knowledge of the state and condition of the Son of man, of God's visitation, and of the purpose and effect of that visitation; from ignorance of the reason that moved God to that visitation of the Son of man. 2. The state of the Son of man. 3. God's visitation of that Son of man. 4. The end and effect of that visitation. But we shall deal with these weighty heads, which concern the second part of the wonder, in the next question, [in the presence of God]. Come, then, let us apply the points of the first part of the wonder to our own use.

units.la: 2º. Quem Vates sacer intuetur hominem, heu quantùm est mutatus ab illo, quem condiderat optimum juxtà ac sapientissimum Numen! Conjiciamus oculos in Adamum è terra cretum ad imaginem Dei. Nostrum neminem haec incesserit admiratio: sanus, beatus ac eximius Adami status, neminem in hanc sollicitabit interrogationem, Quid est homo, ut tu Deus memineris ejus? Deus Adami meminit, ut incolam Paradisi faciat, ut non sinat vitam vivere solitariam, ut uxorem ipsi similem, in laetum auxilium procreandae sanctae soboli, condat. Nec mirum, ut quis jure dixerit, Quid est homo, ut tu Deus memineris ejus? Quaeris divinae bonitatis ignare, quid est homo? Sanctum est juxtà ac divinum animal, Dei imago, justitia, sanctitate ac immortalitate, si velit juste ac sancte Deo vivere, abundè locupletatus, orbis universi Dominus, ad cujus nutum & obsequium componunt sese animalia cuncta, sanctitate Angelis par, dominio ac felicitate superior, praerogativâ imaginis secundi Adami, quam prae se fert, major. Tu verò miraris, cur Deus meminerit ipsius, & male sanus percunctaris, quid est homo, quod Deus ipsius recordetur? Sanctus Deus meminit sancti sui hominis, sui Deus amantissimus, suae meminit imaginis, quam laetus intuetur in Adamo suo.
units.tr: 2. Look at the man whom the holy seer contemplates: alas, how far he has changed from the one whom the most good and most wise Godhead made! Let us cast our eyes on Adam, formed from the earth in the image of God. None of us will be struck by this wonder. Adam's healthy, blessed and outstanding state would prompt no one to ask, What is man, that you, God, should remember him? God remembers Adam so as to make him a dweller in Paradise, so as not to let him live a solitary life, so as to create for him a wife like himself, as a joyful helper in begetting holy offspring. Nor is it surprising that someone might rightly say, What is man, that you, God, should remember him? Do you, ignorant of divine goodness, ask what man is? He is a holy and divine creature, the image of God, richly endowed with righteousness, holiness and immortality, so long as he chooses to live righteously and holily before God; the lord of the whole world, at whose nod and obedience all the animals arrange themselves; equal to the angels in holiness, superior in dominion and happiness, and greater in the prerogative of bearing the image of the second Adam. Yet you wonder why God should remember him, and in your unhealthy state you ask, what is man, that God should be mindful of him? The holy God remembers his holy man; the most loving God remembers his own image, which he gladly beholds in his Adam.

units.la: 3o. Nec Vates sacer, liberatum intuetur hominem beneficio Christi Servatoris, in assertum istum in gloriosam libertatem filiorum Dei, hominem, isthæc Vatis admirabundi interrogatio non cadit. Eximius sanè est novus homo in Christo suo conditus, à Deo præcognitus ineffabili beneficentiæ amore, prædestinatus ad fidem & gloriam, vocatus vorticordi gratia, Deo fidelis, justificatus, alta pace animi ex sensu suæ reconciliationis donatus, adoptatus in filium, Dei hæredem, cohæredem Christi, Spiritus Sancti templum, particeps divinæ naturæ, transformatus ad imaginem Dei de gloria in gloriam per Spiritum Sanctum, Deo Sacerdos & Rex per sanguinem Christi & unctionem Spiritus, obsignatus in diem redemptionis. Tu verò de novo isthoc homine imprudenter percunctareris, quid est homo, ut tu Deus ipsius recorderis? Meminit sanè Deus fidelis sui novi hominis, ut oculos providentiæ suæ in eum conjiciat, servetque illæsum & incolumem in virtute sua per fidem, ut salutem tempore novissimo plenè revelandam, obtineat.
