Meminit ipsius Deus, ut fidem ipsi augeat, spem roboret, inflammet charitatem. Meminit, ut sanctificationem ejus in dies promoveat, gratiæ & pacis novam mensuram indulgeat. Meminit, ne sinat, tentari ultra vires ac virtutes Spiritus indultas: sed ut lætum ab omnibus Satanæ, mundi & peccati insultibus sortiatur exitum, exeatque victor, & plus quam victor, novo sanctitatis incremento. Meminit, ut in agone mortis roboret, mortuum in dias luminis oras reducem faciat, & vita spirituali donatum, curru triumphali nubis, immortalitatis candidatum in cœlum rapiat, æternùm victurum & regnaturum. Nec mirum, ut Deus ipsius meminerit, sui enim amantissimus, imaginem suam amat atque præclaram sobolem sanctitatis suæ, quam lætus cernit in homine sibi ac Christo fideli. Mutatum igitur miserandum in modum, sacer Vates contemplatur hominem, indignum planè quem Deus amica sua recordatione dignetur. Conditus fuit sanctus, nunc peccato sordidus; innocens, nunc reus: liber, nunc servus, prudens juxta ac sapiens, nunc cæcus ac stultus: pius, obsequiosus & Deo amicus, nunc impius, rebellis, & Deo inimicus: dignus amore Dei, nunc maledictioni obnoxius: immortalis, nunc morti æternæ addictus: orbis universi Dominus, nunc vile Satanæ mancipium, miseriis omne genus conflictatus, indignus sanè est, cujus Deus recordetur. Quis sanus misellum istud scelus dignum judicaverit favorabili Dei recordatione? Anne jure potius cum Davide clamaverit, Quid est homo, ut tu Deus memineris ejus? Una infanda peccati lues effectam dedit hanc mutationem. Agedum fideles, quibus perspecta est lues peccati pestifera, inexhaustus calamitatis lamentabilis fundus obvius, heu fugite gite peccatum, uni Deo benigno vivite, conscīique statūs miserrimi unde vos eruit misericors Numinis recordatio, admirabundi ingeminate ad laudem gloriosæ ipsius misericordiæ, Quid est homo, ut tu Deus ipsius memineris?
units.tr: 3. Nor does the holy seer, looking at man freed by the benefit of Christ the Saviour, and brought into the glorious liberty of the sons of God, find this question of the admiring seer fitting. Truly the new man, founded in his Christ, is outstanding: foreknown by God through the inexpressible love of his kindness, predestined to faith and glory, called by the grace of God, faithful to God, justified, granted by the sense of his reconciliation a deep peace of mind, adopted as a son, an heir of God, a fellow-heir with Christ, a temple of the Holy Spirit, a partaker of the divine nature, transformed into the image of God from glory to glory by the Holy Spirit, a priest and king before God through the blood of Christ and the anointing of the Spirit, sealed for the day of redemption. Would you then foolishly ask about this new man, what is man, that you, God, should remember him? Surely the faithful God remembers his new man, so as to turn the eyes of his providence upon him, and to keep him unharmed and safe in his power through faith, so as to obtain for him the salvation to be fully revealed at the last time. He remembers him to increase his faith, strengthen his hope, and kindle his love; he remembers him to advance his sanctification day by day and to grant him a new measure of grace and peace; he remembers him so that he does not allow him to be tempted beyond the strength and powers of the Spirit given to him, but so that he may obtain a joyful outcome from all the assaults of Satan, the world and sin, and come out a conqueror, and more than a conqueror, with a new increase of holiness. He remembers him, so that he strengthens him in the agony of death, brings him back from death to the regions of light, and, endowed with spiritual life, snatches him up to heaven in a triumphal chariot of cloud, a candidate for immortality, to live and reign for ever. Nor is it surprising that God should remember him, for he loves himself most dearly, and loves his own image and the splendid offspring of his holiness, which he gladly sees in the man who is faithful to himself and to Christ. The holy seer, then, contemplates man changed in a most pitiable way, plainly unworthy that God should deign to remember him with a friend's remembrance. He was made holy; now he is defiled by sin. He was innocent; now he is guilty. He was free; now he is a slave. He was prudent and wise; now he is blind and foolish. He was pious, obedient and a friend of God; now he is impious, rebellious and an enemy of God. He was worthy of God's love; now he is liable to curse. He was immortal; now he is given over to eternal death. He was lord of the whole world; now he is the vile slave of Satan, afflicted with every kind of misery. Surely he is unworthy that God should remember him. What sane person would judge such a wretched and guilty creature worthy of God's favourable remembrance? Would not one rather say with David, What is man, that you, God, should remember him? One deadly plague of sin brought about this change. Come, faithful ones, to whom the destructive plague of sin has been made plain, and who see before you the bottomless pit of lamentable calamity: alas, flee sin, live to the one kind God. Acknowledge the most wretched state from which the merciful remembrance of the Godhead has rescued you, and in wonder repeat again, to the praise of his glorious mercy, What is man, that you, God, should remember him?

units.la: 4º. Recordatur Numen Sapientissimum, dum plectit pariter ac miseretur, dum iram suam effundit, peccati meminit, violatæ legis & spretæ majestatis suæ recordatur in vindictam, Ne recorderis iniquitatum nostrarum priorum, Psal. 79:8. Recordare Domine filiorum Edom, diei Jerusalem dum dicebant, denudate, denudate ad fundamentum eam, Psal. 137:7. Meminit, & ut faveat benignissimum, suisque mactet beneficiis, uti Noe meminit, Gen. 8:1. Rachelis & Annæ, ut victa sterilitate admirandum in modum, utramque fœcundaret, Gen. 30:22. 1 Sam. 1:19. Nihil Vates admirabundus, scisciraretur, Quid est homo? Siquidem vindicatricem Numinis recordationem animo suo putaret: Sed præsentem intuitus in genere humano vitiorum lernam & inexhaustam criminum lethalem scaturiginem, humillimè veniam deprecaretur, & conscientia contestante hominem esse ab ortu ipso iræ filium, rebellem, contumacem, Deo inimicum, fœdifragum, reum multifarii criminis, maledictioni ac morti obnoxium, nullus abs Deo quæreret quid est homo? Verum totus in contemplationem benignæ Numinis recordationis defixus, haud immeritò scisicitatur, Quid est homo? Abundat divitiis, diffluit delitiis, pollet dignitate, authoritate, latè dominatur in populos, sibi plaudit suffenus, ac gratulatur. Ecquid tandem homo est, ut tu Numen adorandum, tua illum favorabili recordatione dignéris? Quid est homo præ te, in cujus conspectu tremebundi Seraphim ambabus alis facies obnubunt ac pedes. Præ te cœlum non est purum: præ te omnes nationes guttula è situla, minutissimus bilancis pulvillus ac denique nihil: Præ te homo cinis, umbra, somnium, scelus, Quid igitur homo ut tu memineris ejus?
units.tr: 4. The most wise Godhead remembers, while it both punishes and shows mercy, while it pours out its wrath; it remembers sin, and recalls the violated law and the scorned majesty for vengeance: Remember not against us our former iniquities, Ps. 79:8. Remember, O Lord, the children of Edom, the day of Jerusalem, when they said, Raze it, raze it to its foundations, Ps. 137:7. It remembers, and so that it may show favour and bless its own, it remembers Noah, Gen. 8:1; it remembers Rachel and Hannah, so that, barrenness overcome in a wonderful manner, it made both of them fruitful, Gen. 30:22; 1 Sam. 1:19. The seer in wonder would ask nothing, What is man?, if he thought of the Godhead's remembrance as avenging in his mind. But looking upon the present fountain of vices and the inexhaustible deadly spring of crimes in the human race, he would humbly beg for pardon; and with conscience bearing witness that man from birth is a son of wrath, rebellious, stubborn, an enemy of God, a breaker of covenant, guilty of manifold crimes, liable to curse and death, no one would ask God, what is man? But fixed entirely on the contemplation of the gracious remembrance of the Godhead, he asks, not without reason, What is man? He abounds in riches, overflows with pleasures, excels in dignity and authority, lords it widely over peoples, applauds himself in his self-satisfaction and rejoices. What, then, is man, that you, O Godhead to be adored, should deign to remember him with your favour? What is man in comparison with you, before whose sight the trembling seraphim cover their faces and feet with both wings? Compared with you, heaven is not pure; compared with you, all nations are a drop from a bucket, the smallest dust on the scales, and in the end nothing. Compared with you, man is ash, shadow, dream, crime. What then is man, that you should remember him?

units.la: 5º. Non verò quærit Vates sacer, vel ab Ethnicorum sapientibus, vel à quovis homine è massa generis humani, suæ disquisitioni responsum, omnes novit, ne uno quidem excepto, in peccatis esse mortuos, cæcos ac stultos. Non quærit ab Angelis, quia ut purissimæ sint intelligentiæ, cordis humani momenta haud pervident, (& ex corde non ex facie æstimari debet humanum genus) exosos habent peccatores Deo suo inimicos, imparesque sunt, tum propter finitam cognitionem, tum propter constans in peccatores odium, qui æquum ferant de genere humano judicium. Unum igitur adit Deum, infallibile veritatis oraculum, qui omnia pervidet, & vel secretissima cordis latibula, sunt ipsius oculis τετραχηλι Cηδοα, tum denique quia unus ipse suæ recordationis benignæ rationem novit, valetque perhibere. Dic igitur, obsecro, Numen benignissimum, cujus rectum semper judicium, fallere aut falli nescium, quid est homo, quod memineris ejus? Num aliquid boni in Adamo perduelli, in ejus posteris genere humano stabulatur, quod tibi dignum gratiosa tua recordatione videatur? Aliter videt gubernator navim: aliter medicus ægrotantem: aliter pictural pictor, quam imperitorum rudes oculi. O tu igitur Deus, qui providentia tua humanum genus regis ac moderaris, quod in tui similitudinem primum finxisti, & ex uno sanguine cretum confervasti, dic oro, quid, & quale nunc est opus illud manuum tuarum, ut favorabilem in modum ipsius recorderis? Meo quidem judicio boni plane nihil habet, cujus illicio pellectus fueris in amicam illam ejus recordationem.
units.tr: 5. The holy seer does not ask the wise men of the heathen, nor any man from the mass of the human race, for an answer to his inquiry, for all of them, not one excepted, he knows to be dead in sins, blind and foolish. He does not ask the angels, because, although they are of the purest understanding, they do not see the depths of the human heart (and humankind must be judged by the heart, not by the face); they hold sinners in abhorrence as enemies of their God, and they are unequal to judging the human race fairly, both because of their finite knowledge and because of their constant hatred of sinners. He therefore goes to the one God, the infallible oracle of truth, who sees all things, and to whom even the most secret recesses of the heart are laid bare [τετραχηλισμένα] before his eyes; and finally because he alone knows, and is able to declare, the reason for his kindly remembrance. Tell me then, I beg you, most kind Godhead, whose judgement is always right, who can neither deceive nor be deceived: what is man, that you remember him? Is there anything good in the rebel Adam, or in his posterity, the human race, that seems worthy to you of your gracious remembrance? The helmsman sees his ship one way, the physician sees his patient another way, and the painter sees his picture differently from the crude eyes of the unskilled. O you, then, God, who by your providence rule and govern the human race, which you first formed in your own likeness and preserved, created from one blood, tell me, I pray, what and of what sort is now that work of your hands, that you should remember it in such a favourable way? In my judgement it certainly has nothing good, by whose allurement you were drawn to that friendly remembrance of it.

units.la: 6°. Vatis admirabundi vehemens isthæc interrogatio, quid est homo ut memor sis ejus? innatum peccatoris deprimit supercilium, & corruptum genus humanum præ oculis Dei nihil esse, nos luculenter docet. Hæc sane Vatis interrogatio fervida, præfractæ æquivalet boni cujusvis in homine corrupto negationi, huic ejusdem haud absimilis, Quis ego, & qua vita mea, & familia patris mei in Israel, quod futurus sim gener Regis? 1 Sam.18: 18. Hæc fuit mens Hieronimo, quale, inquit, meritum sit hominis, ut memor ejus factus, pro ejus redemptione suscipias carnem. Hæc mens Augustino. Utique cum Pelagius dicit facilius, quid vult intelligi, nisi & gratia si desit, posse per liberum arbitrium, vel facile vel etiam difficile, quæ divinitus jubentur, impleri? Ubi est ergo, quid est homo, quod memor es ejus? Nisi adjuvet gratia, nihil pietatis atque justitiæ sive in opere, sive etiam in ipsa voluntate, habere possumus. Unde interrogat Apostolus, quis enim te discernit? 1 Cor. 4. Ubi si dixerit homo, fides mea, voluntas mea, bonum opus meum. Quid enim habes quod non accepisti? si autem & accepisti, quid gloriaris quasi non acceperis? Si quaerere voluerit ante gratiam, quid meruerit, ut acciperet eam, mala sua poterit homo invenire, non bona, etiamsi eum unius diei vitam habentem super terra, gratia Salvatoris invenerit, quia si aliquid operatur homo, ut gratiam mereatur, non ei merces imputatur secundum gratiam, sed secundum debitum. 7°. Quàm lato distent limite, vel in ferendo judicio, vir pius sicuti David, cui cor ut sapiat dedit Spiritus sanctus, & impius nec sui, nec Dei sui conscius, collata hæc Davidis sententia, quam sua isthac promit interrogatione, quid est homo, quod memor sis ejus, cum adversa Stoicorum, Pelagianorum, & Semi-Pelagianorum Pontificiorum sententia superciliosa, neminem finit dubitare. Stoicorum nemo contemptim quæsivit, uti David, quid est homo? Omnes enim sapientem habent Deo parem. Sapiens, inquit Seneca, Seneca, plenus gaudio, hilaris & placidus, inconcussus cum Deo ex pari vivit. Solebat Sextius dicere Jovem plus non posse quam virum bonum. Plura Iupiter habet quae praestet hominibus: sed inter duos bonos non est ille melior, qui locupletior. Est aliquid quo sapiens antecedat Deum, ille naturae beneficio, non suo sapiens est. Ecce res magna, habere imbecillitatem, hominis, securitatem Dei. Deus sapientem non vincit felicitate, etiamsi vincat aetate. Faciunt cum Stoicis, Pelagiani superciliosi, & hominem ab ortu ipso ab omni labe peccati purissimum, atque praegnantem virtutum omnium seminibus, superbe orbi Christiano venditant. Quis fecit homini Spiritum? inquit Pelagius, sine dubio Deus. Carnem quis creavit? Idem credo Deus. Bonus est qui utrumque creavit Deus? nulli dubium est. Et utrumque quod bonus author creavit bonum est? Confitendum est. Si igitur spiritus bonus & caro bona, ut a bono authore condita, qui fieri potest, ut duo bona possint sibi esse contraria? Est in animis nostris naturalis quaedam, ut ita dixerim, sanctitas, quae velut in arce animi praesidens, exercet mali bonique judicium, & ut honestis rectisque actibus favet, ita siniistra opera condemnat. Quam multos enim Philosophorum audivimus & legimus & ipsi vidimus castos, patientes, modestos, liberales, abstinentes, benignos, & honores mundi simul & delicias respuentes, & amatores justitiae non minus quam scientiae. Unde quasi hominibus alienis a Deo ista quae Deo placent? Julianus Pelagianus purum putum esse naturae bonum explicat, ubi pronuntiat ore rotundo, Alienos a fide Christi abundare virtutibus, in quibus sine adjutorio gratiae, solum esse naturae bonum, qui solis libertatis ingenitae viribus, & misericordes crebro, & modesti & casti inveniuntur & sobrii. Causam vero istius naturae boni, dum aperit Julianus, sic infit, Cunctarum origo virtutum in rationabili animo sita est, & affectus omnes per quos aut fructuose aut sterliter boni summus, in subjecto sunt mentis nostrae, prudentia, justitia, temperantia, fortitudo. Ne quis vero existimaverit Fabricios, Camillos, Regulos, Scipiones, naturae humanae beneficio, virtutum umbras, non genuinas virtutes obtinuisse, id diserte Julianus negat. Si dicatur, inquit, quia castitas infidelium, castitas non est, eadem fronte dicetur, quia corpus Paganorum corpus non sit, & oculi Paganorum sensum non habeant intuendi, & frumenta quae in Paganorum nascuntur agris, frumenta non sint, & multa alia, quae tanta absurditatis sunt, ut risum possint intelligentibus commovere. Objicientibus vero istud Jobi, nemo mundus a sorde, &c. Respondebat Pelagius, sordes pannorum significari in infantia, non vitia peccatorum. Ipsam Stoicorum arrogantiam ex parte Pelagiani superant, vel dum cum Stoicis faciunt mortalitatem & infirmitatem hominis, quam Stoici confitebantur, ridentes. Sed tu, inquit Augustinus ad Julianum, tanquam in coelo, jam inter Angelos immortaliter habitans, verba infirmitatis & mortalitatis irrides. Faciunt cum Stoïcis & Pelagianis Pontificii, dum liberum arbitrium in bonum & in malum ex æquo homini inesse naturaliter proterve docent, faucium, non mortuum, sopitum, non extinctum ad bonum supernaturale clamant, quod adjutorio gratia, sine quo non fit cum Pelagio; non vero adjutorio gratia, quo fit libenter ac necessario cum Augustino, indigere tantum pertendunt. Dum merita ex congruo in homine constituto in statu corruptæ naturæ, & merita ex condigno, & opera supererogatoria ex gigantea superbia in homine sub gratia constituto, crepant. Heus quàm superbi isti gigantes ab humilitate Davidis procul abesse videntur! Quem istorum suffenorum cum viro pio audiveris interrogantem, O Deus, quid est homo, ut memineris ejus? Eum ne humiliter interrogantem, quem proterve, si percunctteris, quid est homo? respon-santem cum Stoïcis audiveris, homo est sapiens, liber, peccare nescius, Rex, beatus, Deo par, Deo major, suo beneficio sapiens, cum Deus sit sapiens naturæ beneficio, non voluntatis arbitrio sicut homo. Cum Pelagianis: Homo ab ipso ortu purus est, ampla virtutum omnium semente instructus, ingenitis liberi arbitrii viribus, sine adjutorio gratiæ prudens, justus, temperans, fortis. Habet igitur homo si Stoïcis, Pelagianis, Pontificiis credere fas est, bona non contemnenda, quibus bonum sanctumque Numen in favorabilem sui recordationem pelliciat. A page proterviam diabolicam cæcæ ac stultæ creaturæ, fulmine quovis ac tartaro dignam! Nobis uni Deo loquenti, conscientiæ contestanti, humilique Davidi interroganti, quid est homo? credere fas est, ut omnis caro sileat, obturetur os omne superbi hominis, & intemerata laus, misericordis recordationis, in unum Deum patrem misericordiarum transfundatur.
units.tr: Sixthly, this exclamation of the admiring prophet, "What is man, that you are mindful of him?", clearly shows that the innate pride of the sinner is brought low and that the corrupt human race is nothing in the sight of God. Indeed, this earnest question of the prophet is equivalent to a flat denial that anything good is to be found in corrupt man. It is not far from that other denial: "Who am I, and what is my life, and my father's family in Israel, that I should be son-in-law to the King?" (1 Sam. 18:18). Jerome held this view: "What, he says, is the merit of man, that you, mindful of him, should take on flesh for his redemption?" Augustine held it too: "Indeed, when Pelagius says that it is easier, what does he want us to understand, except that, without grace, by free will alone, the things that are commanded by God can be fulfilled either easily or even with difficulty? Where then is 'What is man, that you are mindful of him?' Unless grace helps, we can have no piety or righteousness, either in work or even in the will itself." Hence the Apostle asks, "For who makes you to differ?" (1 Cor. 4:7). "Where if a man should say, my faith, my will, my good work... For what do you have that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you glory as if you had not received it?" If man wishes to ask, before grace, what he merited to receive it, he will be able to find his own evils, not good things, even if he has found the grace of the Saviour while living on earth for only one day; for if a man does anything in order to merit grace, the reward is not imputed to him according to grace but according to debt. Seventhly, how far apart are the two in their judgement: on the one hand the godly man, such as David, to whom the Holy Spirit gave a heart to be wise; on the other the impious man, who knows neither himself nor his God. Set David's judgement, which he expresses in this question, "What is man, that you are mindful of him?", against the arrogant opinion of the Stoics, Pelagians and Papist Semi-Pelagians, and no one will doubt which is which. No Stoic ever asked contemptuously, as David did, "What is man?" For they all hold that the wise man is equal to God. "The wise man," says Seneca, "full of joy, cheerful and calm, lives unshaken with God on equal terms." Sextius used to say that Jupiter can do no more than a good man. Jupiter has more things to bestow on men, but between two good men he is not better, if he is richer. There is something by which the wise man surpasses God: God is wise by the benefit of his nature, the wise man by his own. Behold a great thing: man has weakness, God has security. God does not surpass the wise man in happiness, even if he surpasses him in age. The arrogant Pelagians agree with the Stoics, and they proudly peddle to the Christian world a man who from his very birth is most pure from every stain of sin, and pregnant with the seeds of all virtues. "Who made the Spirit of man?" says Pelagius. "Without doubt God. Who created the flesh? I believe it is the same God. Is God, who created both, good? No one doubts it. And is what the good author created good? It must be confessed. If then the spirit is good and the flesh is good, since they were founded by a good author, how can it be that two good things should be contrary to each other? There is in our souls a certain natural holiness, so to speak, which, sitting like a guard in the citadel of the mind, exercises the judgement of good and evil, and as it favours honest and right actions, so it condemns wicked works." For how many philosophers have we heard, read about, and seen ourselves who were chaste, patient, modest, generous, temperate, kind, and who rejected the honours and pleasures of the world, and loved justice no less than knowledge! Whence then do these things that please God come, if men are alien to God? Julian the Pelagian explains that the good of nature is pure and simple, when he pronounces with full voice: "Those who are alien to the faith of Christ abound in virtues, in whom, without the help of grace, there is only the good of nature, who by the powers of innate freedom alone are often found merciful, modest, chaste and sober." When Julian sets out the cause of this good of nature, he begins thus: "The origin of all virtues lies in the rational soul, and all the affections by which the good are either fruitfully or sterilely good lie in the subject of our mind: prudence, justice, temperance, fortitude." Lest anyone should think that Fabricius, Camillus, Regulus and Scipio, by the benefit of human nature, obtained shadows of virtues and not genuine virtues, Julian expressly denies it. "If it is said," he says, "that the chastity of unbelievers is not chastity, then with the same face it will be said that the body of pagans is not a body, and that the eyes of pagans have no sense of sight, and that the grain which grows in the fields of pagans is not grain, and many other things which are so absurd that they could move those who understand them to laughter." When the objection of Job is raised, "No one is clean from filth," etc., Pelagius answered that "the filth of rags is signified in infancy, not the vices of sins." They even surpass the arrogance of the Stoics themselves, in part, when they agree with the Stoics about the mortality and weakness of man, which the Stoics acknowledged, but mocked. "But you," Augustine says to Julian, "as if already dwelling immortally in heaven among the Angels, mock the words of weakness and mortality." The Papists agree with the Stoics and Pelagians when they shamelessly teach that free will, for good and for evil, is naturally present in man in equal measure; they cry out that the good is not dead but only drowsy, not extinct, and that it needs supernatural good, which, with Pelagius, "needs the help of grace without which it does not happen," but not, with Augustine, "the help of grace by which it happens willingly and necessarily." They insist only on that. They rattle on about merits of congruity in man placed in the state of corrupt nature, and merits of condignity, and works of supererogation, in man placed under grace, out of gigantic pride. Oh, how far these proud giants seem from the humility of David! If you were to hear one of these bloated men with the godly man asking, "O God, what is man, that you are mindful of him?", you would not hear him humbly asking it; but if you asked him arrogantly, "What is man?", you would hear him answer with the Stoics: man is wise, free, unable to sin, a king, blessed, equal to God, greater than God, wise by his own benefit, whereas God is wise by the benefit of his nature, not by the choice of his will, as man is. With the Pelagians: man is pure from his very birth, furnished with an ample seed of all virtues, prudent, just, temperate, brave, by the innate powers of free will, without the help of grace. Therefore, if it is right to believe the Stoics, Pelagians and Papists, man has good things not to be despised, by which the good and holy Deity may be lured into a favourable remembrance of him. Away with the devilish impudence of this blind and foolish creature, worthy of any thunderbolt or of Tartarus! For us it is right to believe the one God speaking to us, bearing witness in our conscience, and asking, with humble David, "What is man?", so that every flesh may be silent, every mouth of proud man be stopped, and the unblemished praise of merciful remembrance be poured out upon the one God, the Father of mercies.

units.la: 8o. Meminit igitur misericors Deus hominis, ut eum eruat e statu miserrimo peccati, criminis, maledictionis, & mortis. Ut vero finem benignæ suæ adversus hominem recordationis consequatur, filium hominis illi destinat & mittit in redemptorem. Hinc Vates, ubi miratus est Numen meminisse hominis, extemplo mentionem attexit filii hominis: eccur vero? Quia filius hominis finis est & effectus favorabilis illius recordationis Dei, sicut & causa unica per quam Deus eruit hominem e statu miserrimo. Meminit enim Deus hominis favorabilem in modum, quia illi filium hominis destinavit & dedit in Redemptorem. Re enim vera in Christo filio hominis, homo Deo inimicus, Mediatorem habet quàm maximè opportunum. In filio enim hominis, homo à Deo dissitus, Dei naturæ unitur indissolubili vinculo, est enim filius hominis Immanuel Deus & homo. Per filium hominis homo inimicus, Deo reconciliatur, filio hominis plane functo Mediatoris & reconciliatoris officio. Reus multifarii criminis homo, in filio hominis purpurgationem habet, & plenam criminum suorum expiationem; In Christo enim habemus redemptionem per sanguinem ipsius, hoc est, peccatorum remissionem, ipse enim fecit per se ipsum purgationem peccatorum nostrorum, Iesus Christus est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris. Hinc per filium hominis, homo reus liberatur ab omni condemnatione, à legis maledictione, & obligatione ad mortem, Christus nos redemit à maledictione legis, factus maledictio pro nobis: Et Deus fecit peccatum pro nobis; id est, victimam piacularem pro peccato, qui non noverat peccatum, ut nos efficeremur justitia Dei in ipso. In filio hominis homo caecus ac stultus, per fidem obtinet Spiritum illuminationis & sapientiae. Per filium hominis, homo peccati servus, obtinet Spiritum sanctificationis & libertatis: nam Spiritus vita qui est per Iesum Christum, nos liberavit à lege peccati & mortis. Per filium hominis, homo despicabile ac infame Satanae mancipium, Spiritum consequitur adoptionis, qui contestatur Spiritui nostro nos esse filios, haeredes Dei, & coharedes Christi. Per filium hominis, homo afflictus, & dirum in modum vexatus, metu maledictionis & mortis, pacem habet apud Deum. Per filium hominis, homo filius & imago Diaboli, in imaginem Dei sancti, de gloria in gloriam transformatur per Spiritum Domini. In filio & per filium hominis, homo morti obnoxius, in vitam spiritualem & immortalem tùm animae, tùm corporis, potentissimum in modum transfertur: est enim Christus vita princeps, & Adamus è coelo, factus in spiritum vivificum, qui per manifestationem suam in carne, vitam & immortalitatem in claram lucem posuit per Euangelium: si autem Spiritus illius qui Iesum excitavit è mortuis habitat in nobis, qui Christum suscitavit à mortuis, vivificabit & mortalia corpora nostra propter inhabitantem ejus spiritum in nobis. Meminit igitur hominis benignissimum in modum Deus, quia illi filium hominis dedit in potentissimum juxtà ac beneficentissimum redemptorem.
units.tr: Eighthly, then, the merciful God remembers man, so as to rescue him from the most wretched state of sin, guilt, curse and death. But to achieve the end of his kindly remembrance towards man, he appoints and sends to him the Son of man as Redeemer. Hence the prophet, when he marvelled that God was mindful of man, immediately added mention of the Son of man. Why? Because the Son of man is the end and the effect of that favourable remembrance of God, and also the sole cause through which God rescues man from his most wretched state. For God remembers man in a favourable manner because he has appointed and given him the Son of man as Redeemer. Indeed, in Christ the Son of man, man, an enemy of God, has a most suitable Mediator. For in the Son of man, man, far removed from God, is united to the nature of God by an indissoluble bond, since the Son of man is Immanuel, God and man. Through the Son of man the enemy man is reconciled to God, the Son of man having clearly discharged the office of Mediator and Reconciler. Man, guilty of many crimes, has in the Son of man purification and full expiation of his crimes: "For in Christ we have redemption through his blood, that is, the forgiveness of sins; for he himself made purification of our sins by himself, Jesus Christ is the propitiation for our sins." Hence, through the Son of man, guilty man is freed from all condemnation, from the curse of the law, and from the obligation to death: "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us; and God made him sin for us, that is, a sin-offering for sin, though he knew no sin, so that we might be made the righteousness of God in him." In the Son of man, blind and foolish man obtains through faith the Spirit of illumination and wisdom. Through the Son of man, man the slave of sin obtains the Spirit of sanctification and liberty: "for the Spirit of life which is in Jesus Christ has freed us from the law of sin and death." Through the Son of man, man, a despised and infamous slave of Satan, obtains the Spirit of adoption, "who bears witness with our spirit that we are children, heirs of God, and joint heirs with Christ." Through the Son of man, man, afflicted and dreadfully harassed by fear of curse and death, "has peace with God." Through the Son of man, man, a child and image of the Devil, "is transformed into the image of the holy God, from glory to glory, by the Spirit of the Lord." In the Son of man and through the Son of man, man, subject to death, is transferred most powerfully into spiritual and immortal life, both of soul and of body: for Christ is "the Prince of life," and "the last Adam, from heaven, made a life-giving spirit, who through his manifestation in the flesh has brought life and immortality into clear light through the Gospel; and if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in us, he who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to our mortal bodies, because of his Spirit dwelling in us." God therefore remembers man in the most kindly manner, because he has given him the Son of man as the most powerful and at the same time most beneficent Redeemer.

units.la: 9º. Utinam homo Dei sui meminisset, sicut & Deus hominis meminisse dignatus est. Meminerat Deus Adami in imaginem suam conditi, ut paradisum & uxorem & dominium in omnes creaturas toto orbe beneficentissimus conferret: noluit verò ingratus homo sui Creatoris meminisse: sed plane oblitus Majestatis supremae conditoris, eximiorum beneficiorum inexhaustae ipsius liberalitatis, oblitus sanctitatis legis, oblitus debiti naturalis & aeterni obsequii, oblitus maledictionis & mortis intentatae in ipsum, si leges sibi positas proterve transiliret, oblitus denique vitae suae beatissimae ac immortalis si voluisset, in nefandam rebellionem, & ruinam lamentabilem sese praecipitem dedit. Sed verò nec quicquam obstante abominandâ illâ hominis oblivione, ipsius ut ut contumacis, rebellis & inimici iterum meminit benignissimum Numen meliorem in modum. Prima adadversus purum hominem Numinis recordatio, Paradisum terrenum derat, & fructum arboris vitæ vescendum in medio Paradisi. Secunda Numinis recordatio dedit filium hominis, vitæ cœlestis arborem fructibus sapientiæ, justitiæ, sanctificationis & redemptionis divitem, & foliis in sanitatem gentium indutam salutiferis. Prima Numinis recordatio uxorem homini dederat in auxilium opportunum. Secunda Numinis recordatio, homini scorto putidissimo, virum dedit filium hominis, in auxilium gratiæ, quo fit libenter juxta ac necessario, ut præclaram ferat sobolem, gratosque Deo justitiæ ac sanctitatis fructus. Prima Numinis recordatio amplum contulerat in hominem dominium in orbem universum. Secunda vero cum filio hominis, miserrimo dedit homini, æternum dominium in omnes, nulla excepta, creaturas, omnia enim nostra sunt, sive Apollos, sive Cephas, sive mundus, sive vita, sive mors, sive præsentia, sive futura, omnia nostra sunt, nos autem Christi, Christus autem Dei. Tui Deus meminit homo miselle, tu vero, oblivioni parentis tui Adami, filius nequissimus, Deum tuum oblivisceris, ut tibi vivas sine Deo. Oblitus supremæ Majestatis Numinis, te Deum geris superciliosum in modum; oblitus bonitatis Dei, times & expavescis ad miseriam, confidis divitiis, & propriæ litas bonitati; oblitus potentiæ Numinis, tuis fidis viribus & potentiæ valentioris adversæ occursu, totus horrore contremiscis: oblitus sanctitatis Numinis, peccato servis, oblitus justitiæ scelerum vindicatricis, scelera cumulas sceleribus, sine metu mortis æternæ, quæ manet impios omnes. Nefandum crimen ingrati pariter ac obliviosi hominis! Eccur injuria hæc male te cepit, oblivio. Omnia Deum clamant, quæcunque cernis Deum ingeminant, cœli enarrant gloriam Dei, & expansum opus manuum ipsius; ortus & occasus solis, lunæ incrementum & decrementum, accessus & recessus Oceani, indefessæ tempestatum vices, æquinoxia, solstitia, dies & nox, ver, æstas, autumnus, hyems, Deum omnia clamant & ingeminant: tu vero Deum oblivisceris, vel prava colis recordatione. Si Deus tibi in mentem venit, stulte, Dei meminineris, sed ut dicas in corde tuo, non est Deus. Si Deus in mentem venit, Dei vel invitus meminisiti: sed ut Deum sua expolies gloria, quam conferas in creaturas: sed ut Deum infinitum multiplices, & portenta Deorum fingas cum animo tuo. O inexhaustam Numinis misericordiam! nec quicquam obstante tua Numinis oblivione, vel prava recordatione, tui Deus meminit, ut annunciet verbum Euangelii, & te per læti nuncii prædicationem, in cognitionem & rectam Dei tui memoriam, illicio charitatis, pelliciat.
units.tr: 9. If only man remembered his God, as God has deigned to remember man! God remembered Adam, created in his own image, and most generously bestowed on him paradise, a wife, and dominion over all creatures throughout the world. But ungrateful man was unwilling to remember his Creator. Forgetting the supreme majesty of his maker, the outstanding benefits of God's inexhaustible liberality, the holiness of the law, the natural and eternal obedience he owed, and the curse and death threatened against him if he defiantly broke the laws set for him, and finally forgetting that he could have had a most blessed and immortal life, he hurled himself headlong into a monstrous rebellion and a lamentable ruin. Yet, despite that abominable forgetfulness of man, however stubborn, rebellious and hostile he was, the most kind Divinity remembered him again, and in a far better way. God's first remembrance of pure man provided an earthly paradise and the fruit of the tree of life to be eaten in the middle of the garden. God's second remembrance gave the Son of Man, a tree of heavenly life rich in the fruits of wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption, clothed in leaves that bring health and salvation to the nations. The first remembrance gave man a wife as a fitting help. The second, to a most foul harlot of a man, gave the Son of Man as a husband, a helper of grace, through whom it comes about, willingly and necessarily, that he bears a splendid offspring and fruits of righteousness and holiness pleasing to God. The first remembrance granted man a broad dominion over the whole world. But the second, by giving the Son of Man to wretched man, gave him an eternal dominion over all creatures without exception: for all things are yours, whether Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or the present or the future; all are yours, and you are Christ's, and Christ is God's. God remembers you, poor man; but you, forgetful of your father Adam, most wicked son, forget your God, so that you may live for yourself without God. Forgetting the supreme majesty of the Divinity, you behave with arrogance towards God; forgetting God's goodness, you fear and tremble at misery, trust in riches, and take pleasure in your own goodness; forgetting the power of the Divinity, you are utterly terrified, relying on your own weak strength and on confronting a stronger power; forgetting the holiness of the Divinity, you serve sin, and forgetting the justice that avenges crimes, you heap crime upon crime, without fear of eternal death, which awaits all the wicked. What a monstrous crime of the ungrateful and forgetful man! Why, forgetfulness, has this wrong taken such hold of you? Everything cries out God, everything you see proclaims God: the heavens declare the glory of God and the work of his hands; the rising and setting of the sun, the waxing and waning of the moon, the ebb and flow of the ocean, the tireless changes of the weather, the equinoxes, solstices, day and night, spring, summer, autumn, winter, all cry out and proclaim God. Yet you forget God, or worship him only in a corrupt remembrance. If God has come into your mind, you fool, you remember God only so that you may say in your heart, "There is no God." If God has come into your mind, you have remembered him, though unwillingly, not so as to honour his glory, which you spread among creatures, but so as to multiply the infinite God and to fashion monsters of gods in your own mind. O inexhaustible mercy of the Divinity! Despite your forgetfulness of God or your corrupt remembrance of him, your God remembers you, in order to announce the word of the Gospel and, through the preaching of the joyful message, to draw you by the enticement of love into the knowledge and right remembrance of your God.

units.la: 10. Agedum fideles, quibus innotuit benignissima Dei in hominem recordatio, mementote Dei vestri, mementote Creatoris, ut vitam quam contulit, conservavit & auxit ad maturam ætatem, ad cultum & obsequium Creatoris totam fideliter componatis: Mementote Redemptoris, ut empti emptori vestro sitis usui, & redempti pretio sanguinis Dei, illi uni serviatis in timore & tremore: Mementote illius præsentiæ, ut coram Deo & cum Deo Enochi ad instar ambuletis: mementote ejus misericordiæ, ut vos misereat miserorum: charitatis Dei erga vos, ut eum toto corde, toto animo, totis viribus diligatis: potentiæ, ut sit fidei fulcrum adversus Satanæ, mundi & mortis insultus; sapientiæ, ut eâ ducente ac dirigente lucem visdeatis oriundam ex tenebris, consolationem ex afflictionibus, ex ignominia gloriam, & vitam è sinu mortis: mementote filii hominis, quem vobis dedit redemptorem amica Dei recordatio, ut posito recte calculo cum Paulo liceat colligere, si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? qui etiam proprio filio non pepercit: sed pro nobis omnibus illum tradidit, quomodo etiam cum illo omnia nobis non gratificabitur? Rom.8:31. Qui dedit plus, non abnuet minus; qui filium salutis authorem dedit; & plenam dabit cum eo salutem, sanctitatem consummatam, vitam & immortalitatem cœlestem, gloriam & felicitatem, nullo miseriarum telo deterendam, ut cum eo æternum vivamus, regnemus ac triumphemus. AMEN.
units.tr: 10. Come now, faithful, to whom the most kind remembrance of God toward man has become known, remember your God, remember your Creator, so that you faithfully devote your whole life, which he has given, preserved and extended to mature age, to the worship and obedience of your Creator. Remember your Redeemer, so that, having been bought, you may be useful to your buyer, and, having been redeemed with the price of God's blood, you may serve him alone in fear and trembling. Remember his presence, so that you may walk before God and with God, like Enoch. Remember his mercy, so that he may have pity on you in your wretchedness; remember God's love towards you, so that you may love him with your whole heart, your whole soul and all your strength; remember his power, so that it may be a support to your faith against the assaults of Satan, the world and death; remember his wisdom, so that, under its guidance and direction, you may see light arising out of darkness, consolation out of afflictions, glory out of shame, and life out of the bosom of death. Remember the Son of Man, whom God's kind remembrance gave you as Redeemer, so that, having reckoned rightly, you may conclude with Paul: If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how will he not also with him freely give us all things? Rom. 8:31. He who gave the greater will not refuse the lesser; he who gave the Author of salvation will also give with him full salvation, perfect holiness, heavenly life and immortality, glory and happiness, not to be struck down by any dart of misery, so that we may live, reign and triumph with him for ever. AMEN.

units.la: QUÆSTIO V. Cur vates Psal. 8: 5. & Apostolus Hebr. 2: 6. per contemptum dixerint, quid est filius hominis ut visites eum? Cum filius hominis sit Christus.
units.tr: Question V. Why did the prophet (Ps. 8:5) and the Apostle (Heb. 2:6) say disparagingly, "What is the son of man, that you visit him?" Since the son of man is Christ.

units.la: INfantem nobis natum, filium Dei videlicet atque virginis nobis datum, nomen admirabilis sortiturum, merito jure, Jesaias vaticinatus est: Christus enim manifestatus admirabilis visus est Angelis pariter atque hominibus. Angelis quidem, nam Cherubim gloriæ, in Christum propitiatorium cernui, mutuus velut ex compacto aspectibus, mutuam ex Christi intuitu admirationem suam significabant. Hinc Petrus, stupenda planè Christi per Euangelium revelata mysteria ea dicit esse, quæ Angeli prospicere desiderant, eorum ad instar, qui procumbunt in genua, ut in locum profundum & obscurum summâ ocu-lorum lorum contentione introspiciant. Admirabilis hominibus, ut ipsemet significavit Manoah, ut quid interrogas de nomine meo, est enim admirabile? Admirabilis equidem est, si personam ipsius intuitus fueris, propter admirandam naturarum, divinae ac humanae personalem in eo unionem: unus enim Christus in terra & in coelo fuit ac etiamnum est Immanuel; Deus & homo eximiâ ac singulari praerogativâ, quâ insigni suo charactere, ab omnibus aliis divinis, angelicis & humanis personis distinguitur; in hoc uno naturarum, sed non naturalem, personalem, sed non personarum unionem, ut te ejus incessat admiratio, cernis. Admirabilis, si generationem geminam, aeternam alteram, ex patre sine matre, temporariam alteram, ex matre sine patre, in eo contuearis. Admirabilis, si modum generationis temporariae, ex matre ac virgine simul, ex virgine à viro, sed non à partu, sedulò circumspicias. Admirabilis, si munus ipsius mediatorium Deum inter & homines, ut pacem aeternam Deo hominibusque conciliet, quam Moses Mediator nullus potuit conciliare. Admirabilis, si ternum istius mediatoris amicè conjunctum simul ac exercitum munus, propheticum, sacerdotale ac regium cum animo tuo reputaveris. Admirabilis, si doctrinam & miracula, quibus unus Christus inclaruit quâ Propheta; admirabilis si templum, altare, victimam & sacerdotem unum & idem in ejus sacrificio, quo iram divinam propitiavit, peccata expiavit, Diabolum mortis imperatorem destruxit, mortem abolevit, salutem & felicitatem aeternam electis ac fidelibus suis, quâ summus Pontifex obtinuit. Admirabilis, si majestatem, vim & modum regnandi in omnes creaturas, sed cum primis in Ecclesiam suam, ut par est, reputaveris. Admirabilis denique Christus est, si commutatum ipsius statum exinanitionis, cum statu gloriae & honoris haud ofcitanter cum sacro vate & divino Paulo contenderis. Ita profecto tibi videbitur admirabilis filius hominis Christus, ut pari perculsus admiratione in hanc crumpas interrogationem fervidam, Quid est filius hominis, ut tu Deus eum visitaveris?
units.tr: Surely the infant born to us, the Son of God, given to us from the virgin, who would bear the name wonderful, was rightly foretold by Isaiah. For Christ, once manifested, appeared wonderful both to angels and to men. To the angels, indeed, since the Cherubim of glory, bending over the mercy seat toward Christ, as if by mutual agreement in their gaze, signified their shared wonder at the sight of Christ. Hence Peter calls the stupendous mysteries of Christ, revealed through the gospel, those which angels desire to look into, like men who kneel down to peer with the utmost strain of their eyes into a deep and dark place. Wonderful to men, as Manoah himself indicated: Why do you ask about my name, seeing it is wonderful? He is indeed wonderful, if you look at his person, on account of the marvellous personal union of the divine and human natures in him. For one Christ was, and still is, Immanuel on earth and in heaven, God and man with a singular prerogative, by which he is distinguished by his own distinctive character from all other divine, angelic and human persons. In him you see a union of natures, not natural but personal, and a union of persons, not of persons in the ordinary sense, so that wonder at it steals over you. He is wonderful if you contemplate in him the twofold generation, one eternal, from the Father without a mother, the other temporal, from the mother without a father. Wonderful, if you carefully consider the manner of the temporal generation, from a mother who was also a virgin, from a virgin, not through a man, yet not through ordinary childbirth. Wonderful, if you reflect on his mediatorial office, by which he reconciles God and men in an eternal peace, which Moses the mediator could not bring about. Wonderful, if you consider with your mind the threefold office of this mediator, prophetic, priestly and kingly, exercised together in harmony. Wonderful, if you consider his teaching and the miracles by which Christ alone shone forth as Prophet. Wonderful, if you see one and the same temple, altar, victim and priest in his sacrifice, by which he appeased divine wrath, expiated sins, destroyed the Devil, the ruler of death, abolished death, and obtained salvation and eternal blessedness for his elect and faithful, as the high priest. Wonderful, if you rightly consider his majesty, power and manner of reigning over all creatures, but above all over his Church. Finally, Christ is wonderful if you set his changed state of humiliation against his state of glory and honor, and do not hesitate to compare it with the holy prophet and the divine Paul. Surely the son of man Christ will seem so wonderful to you that, struck with equal wonder, you burst out in this fervent question: What is the son of man, that you, O God, should visit him?

units.la: Vatem sacrum de filio hominis hic contemptim locutum, inficiabitur nemo, qui seriem interrogationis, & membrorum cohaerentiam attente consideraverit: sic enim infit uno tenore, Quid est homo, ut memineris ejus, & filius hominis, ut cum visitaveris? Hic vero Prophetam de homine, miseriis omne genus conflictato, ex lethali peccati aegritudine maledictioni ac morti obnoxio, contemptim rogasse, Quid est homo, ut Deus minimerit ejus? nihil equidem causae est, ut quis miretur. Rogasse vero Prophetam de filio hominis, cur eum Deus visitare fuerit dignatus, plenum est admirationis argumentum: non enim par ratio videtur hominis atque filii hominis: homo enim multifarii criminis reus, maledictioni, miseriis ac morti obnoxius ob violatam Numinis majestatem, jure merito indignus erat favorabilis Dei recordationis: sed vero filius hominis, Christus sanctus juxta ac dilectissimus, proprius ac unigenitus Dei filius, vel in ipso exinanitionis & perpessionis statu, ita dignus fuit amicâ Dei visitatione, quae eum gloriâ & honore coronavit, ut ipse nullus pronunciare dubitaverit, Oportuit Christum pati, & intrare in gloriam suam, Luc. 24: 26. Haec sane tantam magno Cameroni peperere difficultatem, ut postquam solidis rationibus adstruxit, filium hominis significare Christum apud Vatem nostrum & Paulum, palinodiam cecinerit, dum pronunciavit, verba haec Psaltis, Quid est filius hominis, ut respicias eum? non usurpari ab Apostolo de Christo naturâ humanâ pradito, quasi hic esset eorum sensus, Quid est Christus, filius hominis, ut eum respicias? Sed ea dici de natura humana in genere, cum relatione tamen ad Christum, quatenus in eo erat natura divina conjungenda. Quàm incautè & parum appositè ad mentem & scopum Apostoli, superiori quaestione demonstravimus. Nec mirum, si Camero in has inciderit angustias cum ore rotundo docuerit, Christum se titulo filii hominis insigniisse, ob eximium Mediatoris munus ipsi à Deo impositum, & singularem excellentiam, quâ reliquos homines superat, & longo post se relinquit intervallo, & nunquam Christum hunc titulum sibi tribuere, nisi cum de munere suo mediatorio agit, atque personam suam ex eo commendare, sibique conciliare authoritatem, studet, hanc denique filii hominis appellationem, non abjectam & humilem naturam ejus humanam significare: sed sublime munus mediatorium, seu personam illo munere illustrem. Hinc vero nulla nobis succrescit difficultas, supra enim addiximus, nomenclaturâ filii hominis Christum significari, sub statu utroque exinanitionis & gloriae. Exinanitionis, fuit enim Christus Filius hominis, vel dum ageretur in crucem mancipii ad instar despectissimi Joan.8:28.&12:34. Gloriae fuit enim Christus filius hominis, vel dum nube currù triumphali ascenderet in coelum, Dan.7:13. estque etiamnum filius hominis, ad dexteram majestatis & in gloria Dei constitutus, Act. 7; 55. 56. Estque tandem futurus filius hominis, cum veniet in gloria Patris, Angelorum myriadibus stipatus, Matth. 16: 27. Una igitur difficultas nobis expedienda, ejusque cardo versatur in hoc, cur de filio hominis Christo, Domino gloriae, sanctissimo juxta ac delectissimo Dei filio, pariter atque de homine flagitioso, reo ac misero, contemptim Propheta dixerit, Quid est filius hominis ut visites eum? Quasi talis ac tantus filius hominis indignus sit ae videatur amicâ illâ Dei visitatione, quae eum gloriâ & honore coronavit.
units.tr: No one who attentively considers the sequence of the question and the coherence of its clauses will deny that the sacred prophet spoke here disparagingly of the son of man. For it runs in one breath: What is man, that you are mindful of him, and the son of man, that you visit him? That the prophet asked disparagingly about man, afflicted with every kind of misery, liable to curse and death from the deadly sickness of sin, What is man, that God should think of him? gives no cause for anyone to wonder. But that the prophet asked why God had deigned to visit the son of man is a matter full of wonder. For the case of man and of the son of man does not seem to be the same. Man, guilty of many crimes, liable to curse, misery and death because he had violated the majesty of the divine Name, was rightly unworthy of God's favorable remembrance. But the son of man, Christ, holy and most beloved, the proper and only-begotten Son of God, even in his state of humiliation and suffering, was so worthy of God's friendly visitation, which crowned him with glory and honor, that he himself did not hesitate to declare: It behoved Christ to suffer and to enter into his glory, Luke 24:26. These matters caused great difficulty for the great Camero. After he had established with solid reasons that the son of man signifies Christ in our prophet and in Paul, he sang a palinode, declaring: "These words of the Psalmist, What is the son of man, that you regard him? are not used by the Apostle of Christ endowed with human nature, as if the sense were, What is Christ, the son of man, that you regard him? but they are said of human nature in general, with reference, however, to Christ, insofar as the divine nature was to be joined with it in him." How incautiously and how little to the purpose this is, against the mind and aim of the Apostle, we demonstrated in the previous question. Nor is it surprising that Camero fell into these straits, when with smooth-tongued confidence he taught that Christ adorned himself with the title son of man on account of the singular office of mediator imposed on him by God and the singular excellence by which he surpasses other men and leaves them far behind; that Christ never claims this title for himself except when he speaks of his mediatorial office and strives to commend his person from it and win authority for himself; and finally, that this appellation son of man does not signify his lowly and abject human nature, but the sublime mediatorial office, or the person made illustrious by that office. From this, however, no difficulty arises for us, for we have above shown that by the name son of man Christ is signified in both states, of humiliation and of glory. Of humiliation: for Christ was the Son of man when he was being handed over to the cross like the most despised slave, John 8:28; 12:34. Of glory: for Christ was the Son of man when he ascended into heaven in a cloud, in a triumphal chariot, Dan. 7:13; and he is still the Son of man, seated at the right hand of majesty and in the glory of God, Acts 7:55, 56. And he will finally be the Son of man when he comes in the glory of the Father, surrounded by myriads of angels, Matt. 16:27. There is therefore one difficulty for us to resolve, and its hinge lies in this: why did the prophet speak disparagingly of the son of man Christ, Lord of glory, most holy and most beloved Son of God, just as of a sinful, guilty and wretched man, asking, What is the son of man, that you visit him? as if so great a son of man were unworthy, and seemed unworthy, of that friendly visitation of God which crowned him with glory and honor.

units.la: Quaestionem igitur & difficultatem ut perstringamus, operae pretium est perperpendere. 1o. Vatis admirationem. 2o. Statum filii hominis. 3o. Dei visitationem. 4o. Finem & effectum hujuscemodi visitationis: Deus enim visitavit filium hominis, ut eum coronaret gloria & honore, & omnia pedibus ejus subjiceret, uno Deo Patre excepto, qui pedibus ejus omnia subjecit. 1 Cor. 15. 27.
units.tr: To set out the question and the difficulty, it is worth weighing carefully: (1) the prophet's wonder; (2) the state of the son of man; (3) God's visitation; (4) the end and effect of such a visitation. For God visited the son of man in order to crown him with glory and honor and to subject all things to his feet, God the Father alone excepted, who subjected all things to him. 1 Cor. 15:27.

units.la: Si filius hominis magnifica dignus fuit Dei visitatione, nihil equidem causae erat, cur Vates sacer miraretur, Deum pro sapientia sua & aequitate filium hominis visitasse, ubi eum coronavit gloria & honore. Trahit enim originem suam quaevis admiratio, vel ex rei magnitudine atque excellentia, quae captum nostrum superat: vel ex rei insolentia, cum sociata videmus, quae nobis haud quaquam consocianda videbantur, ut si e sacce plebis homunculum evectum intueamur ad regiam majestatem, ut 1Sam. 18:23. 2Sam. 7:18. 1 Chron. 17:16. Vel denique ex ignorantia, cum perspecto effecto, fugit nos ratio & causa ipsius, unde iris coloribus variegata Thaumantis filia dicitur, propter admirationem, quam parit in animo, vel ex colorum formaeque excellentia, vel ex ignorantia causae proximae multiformis coloris. Re enim vera quaelibet admiratio partim ex cognitione ὅτι quod res sit, partim ex ignorantia διὰ ὅτι cur res sit, in animis nostris originem ducit. Hinc arcessenda sacri Vatis admiratio: miratur enim illum filium hominis, quem Deus minuerat infra conditionem Angelorum, evectum tamen ad majestatem supremam, in omnes creaturas exercendam, & vel supra Angelos ipsos gloria & honore coronatum: videt enim consociata stupendo plane modo, quae minus socianda videbantur, filium nempe hominis, infra Angelos Dei ministros novissime dejectum, constitutum in solio majestatis supremae, & in ipsos Angelos regnantem, & dum commutati status filii hominis, ab infimo humilitatis & exinanitionis gradu, in supremum majestatis & gloriae gradum, rationem se fugere sentit, causam rogat stupendae adeo commutationis istius, Quid est filius hominis, ut visites eum?
units.tr: If the son of man was worthy of a magnificent visitation of God, there was indeed no cause why the sacred prophet should wonder that God, in his wisdom and justice, visited the son of man and crowned him there with glory and honor. Every wonder arises either from the greatness and excellence of a thing, which surpasses our grasp; or from the strangeness of a thing, when we see things joined together that seemed by no means to belong together, as when we see a little man lifted from the dunghill of the common people to royal majesty, as in 1 Sam. 18:23; 2 Sam. 7:18; 1 Chron. 17:16. Or finally it arises from ignorance, when the effect is plain but reason and its cause escape us. Thus Iris, the daughter of Thaumas, is said to be variegated with colors, on account of the wonder she produces in the mind, either from the excellence of her colors and form, or from ignorance of the proximate cause of her many-coloured hue. For indeed every wonder arises in our minds partly from knowledge that the thing is [ὅτι], and partly from ignorance of why the thing is [διὰ ὅτι]. Hence the wonder of the sacred prophet is to be derived from this source. For he wonders at that son of man whom God had lowered beneath the condition of the angels, yet raised to supreme majesty to be exercised over all creatures, and crowned with glory and honor even above the angels themselves. He sees things joined together in a truly stupendous manner that seemed least fitting to be joined: the son of man, lately cast down beneath the angels, God's ministers, set on the throne of supreme majesty and reigning over the angels themselves. And while he feels that the reason for this change in the state of the son of man, from the lowest step of humility and humiliation to the highest step of majesty and glory, escapes him, he asks the cause of so stupendous a change: What is the son of man, that you visit him?

units.la: Statum in quem Vates dejectum cernit filium hominis, Paulus explicat his verbis, eum breve tempus minuisti infra Angelos, διὰ τὸ πάθημα τοῦ θανάτου, propter mortis perpessionem, quae ultima verba, vel ad imminutionem filii hominis, tanquam finis ad medium, referri possunt, ut sit sensus, quia filius hominis perpessurus erat mortem pro omnibus credituris salvandis, ideo Deus eum breve tempus imminuit infra Angelos: vel ad haec, quae proxime sequuntur, videmus Jesum gloria & honore coronatum, propter perpessionem mortis, ut perpessio mortis causa sit & ratio, cur Deus Jesum gloria & honore coronaverit, ut Phil. 8:9. Jesus Christus factus fuit obediens usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis, quapropter etiam Deus ipsum in summam extulit sublimitatem, limitatem, ac largitus est ei nomen, quod est supra omne nomen: Vel denique ad utrumque commodè referri possunt: certum enim est, filium hominis, Deum infra Angelos breve tempus imminuisse, ut perpeteretur mortem ignominiosam crucis, & quia perpessus est mortem illam eximiâ & incomparabili obedientiâ adversus Deum, sicut & immenso amore adversus genus humanum perditum, ea propter Deum, (nempe illustrem illam ac sibi pergratam ut remuneraretur obedientiam) eum gloriâ & honore coronasse. Hic verò quærere licet, cur non dixerit sacer Vates, eum minuisti infra homines, quandoquidem ipse filius hominis dum conditionem suam, & statum perpessionis ad vivum pingit, confitetur, se esse vermem non virum, opprobrium hominum, & contemtum populi, Pf. 22:7. Respondemus, filium hominis in diebus carnis perpessionis & exinanitionis suæ, fuisse quidem imminutum atque dejectum infra conditionem ac sortem non illustrium modo virorum: sed & plebejorum ac contemtissimorum hominum, qualem nempe sortiuntur quilibet mortales in mundo: sed non fuisse imminutum & dejectum infra illam sortem, quæ eos manet ex justo Dei judicio, utpote reos, maledictioni, miseriis omne genus, ac dirissimæ morti obnoxios. Non dixit igitur sacer Vates filium hominis, pro genere humano misero ac maledicto, miserrimum, dejectum fuisse infra sortem hominum miserorum, quia eum intuebatur loco & bono generis humani credituri in ipsum, mortem gustantem pro omnibus electis ac crediturìs vice eorum. Sed verò cùm Christus ait se esse vermem non virum, sortem suam contulit cum sorte virorum, ac quorumvis mortalium, quâ fruuntur in mundo, non cum illa sorte, quæ eos manet peccatores ac maledictos ex justo Dei judicio. Cæterùm hæc filii hominis imminutio infra Angelos, 1°. sub schemate vermis, opprobrii, & contemptus hominum ab ipso Christo proponitur consideranda. 2°. Ab Esaïa sub schemate surculi ex radicibus Isaï, Jes. 11: 1. & rami languidi succrescentis e terra siticulosa, Jes. 53: 2. 3°. Sub schemate viri languidi, afflicti & despecti. 4°. agni ad occisionem, & oviculæ obmutescentis coram tondentibus eam, Jes. 53: 3. 7. 5°. sub schemate servi, seu mancipii vilissimi, Psal. 40: 7. Philip. 2: 7. 6°. sub schemate victimæ piacularis, in cujus caput Deus fecit occurrere iniquitates, h. e. poenam iniquitatum, & maledictionem hominum contulit, sicut per manuum impositionem, Israelita reus ac confessus reatum suum, maledictionem & mortem, in caput victimæ suæ piacularis, ex instituto divino conjiciebat, Jes. 53: 6. 2 Cor. 5: 21. Gal. 3: 13. 7°. sub schemate carnis peccati, id est juxta Hebræorum phraseologiam, carnis peccatricis, Rom. 8: 3. 8°. sub schemate serpentis æneï, quem Moses in lignum ligaum extulit, pendulum, & ab Israelitis contemplandum, Joh. 3: 14. & 12: 32.
units.tr: Paul explains the state into which the seer sees the Son of man cast down, in these words: you made him a little lower than the angels, on account of the suffering of death [διὰ τὸ πάθημα τοῦ θανάτου]. These last words may be referred to the lowering of the Son of man as end to means, so that the sense is: because the Son of man was to suffer death for all believers who would be saved, God lowered him a little below the angels. Or they may be referred to what immediately follows, we see Jesus crowned with glory and honour, so that the suffering of death is the cause and reason why God crowned Jesus with glory and honour, as in Phil. 2:8-9: Jesus Christ was made obedient unto death, even the death of the cross; wherefore God also highly exalted him, and gave him a name which is above every name. Or finally, both can fitly be referred to: it is certain that God lowered the Son of man a little below the angels so that he might suffer the shameful death of the cross, and because he suffered that death in singular and incomparable obedience toward God, as well as in immense love toward the lost human race, therefore God crowned him with glory and honour (namely, to reward that illustrious obedience, which was most pleasing to him). Here one may ask why the sacred seer did not say you made him a little lower than men, since the Son of man himself, when he portrays his condition and state of suffering to the life, confesses that he is a worm and not a man, a reproach of men and despised by the people, Ps. 22:7. We answer that the Son of man, in the days of his fleshly suffering and humiliation, was indeed lowered and cast down beneath the condition and lot not only of illustrious men, but also of common and most despised men, such as all mortals in the world have; but he was not lowered and cast down beneath that lot which remains for them by the just judgment of God, namely that of being guilty, subject to curse, miseries of every kind, and most dreadful death. The sacred seer therefore did not say that the Son of man, on behalf of the wretched and cursed human race, was lowered beneath the lot of wretched men, because he regarded him in the place and for the good of the human race, as one who would believe in him, tasting death for all the elect and believers in their stead. But when Christ says that he is a worm and not a man, he compared his lot with the lot of men and of any mortals, which they enjoy in the world, not with that lot which awaits sinners and the accursed by the just judgment of God. Moreover, this lowering of the Son of man beneath the angels is to be considered as proposed by Christ himself, 1. under the figure of a worm, a reproach and contempt of men. 2. By Isaiah, under the figure of a shoot from the roots of Jesse, Isa. 11:1, and of a feeble branch springing up out of a dry ground, Isa. 53:2. 3. Under the figure of a man who is sickly, afflicted and despised. 4. Of a lamb led to slaughter, and a little sheep dumb before its shearers, Isa. 53:3, 7. 5. Under the figure of a servant, or the most base slave, Ps. 40:7; Phil. 2:7. 6. Under the figure of a sacrificial victim, upon whose head God caused the iniquities to meet, that is, the punishment of iniquities, and laid upon it the curse of men; just as, by the laying on of hands, the Israelite who was guilty and confessed his guilt transferred his curse and death, by divine institution, onto the head of his sacrificial victim, Isa. 53:6; 2 Cor. 5:21; Gal. 3:13. 7. Under the figure of sinful flesh, that is, according to the Hebrew idiom, sinful flesh, Rom. 8:3. 8. Under the figure of the bronze serpent, which Moses lifted up on a pole and hung up for the Israelites to look upon, John 3:14; 12:32.

units.la: Constitutum in illo statu contemptissimo filium hominis, Deum ea visitatione, quæ fons est gratiæ atque gloriæ visitasse, asserit & miratur Vates. Nec immeritò : Deus enim filium hominis in mortis agone reliquerat: hinc lamentabilis ipsius querimonia, Deus mi, Deus mi, quid me dereliquisti? Ps. 22: 2. hinc deprecationes & supplicationes, clamor validus, & lachryma Christi in diebus carnis, apud Deum qui poterat ipsum servare, Hebr. 5:7. Verum sicuti Deus filium hominis pendulum è cruce reliquerat, non ratione sanctitatis, quam semper illibatam retinuit & intemeratam: sed ratione gloriosi gaudii, quod naturaliter ex sanctitate efflorescit, estque memorabilis felicitatis gradus. Ita & Deus filium hominis visitavit, cùm reddita luce radiantissimâ placati vultus paterni, eum excitavit è mortuis, evexit in cœlum, sedere fecit ad dextram majestatis ac gloriæ, unde gaudium ineffabile in animo Christi effloruit. Hinc sapientissimè Vates hanc Dei visitationem per finem & effectum, in quem collimavit, ut explicet, extemplò attexit, eum gloriâ & honore coronasti, omnia subjecisti pedibus ejus.
units.tr: The seer, affirming and marvelling, declares that God visited the Son of man, placed in that most despised state, with that visitation which is the source of grace and glory. And not undeservedly: for God had left the Son of man hanging in the agony of death; hence his mournful complaint, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? Ps. 22:2; hence the prayers and supplications, with strong crying and tears, which Christ offered in the days of his flesh to God, who was able to save him from death, Heb. 5:7. But just as God had left the Son of man hanging from the cross, not on account of holiness, which he always kept unimpaired and undefiled, but on account of the glorious joy which naturally blossoms from holiness and is a memorable degree of happiness, so too God visited the Son of man, when the most radiant light of his father's favourable countenance was restored, and raised him from the dead, carried him up into heaven, and made him sit at the right hand of majesty and glory, whence an unspeakable joy blossomed in the mind of Christ. Hence the seer very wisely, to explain this visitation of God by its end and effect toward which it aimed, immediately adds: You crowned him with glory and honour, and you put all things under his feet.

units.la: Hinc mero meridie clarius paret, quàm longè abierint à tramite veritatis, qui gloriam, florem alterum coronæ Christi, sapientiam, justitiam, uno verbo, sanctitatem, interpretantur: honorem verò, coronæ Christi florem alterum, majestatem & authoritatem ἀνυπεύθυνον, cum illustribus, insignibus, tantâ dignis majestate, intelligunt. Cùm enim sapientiâ, justitiâ & sanctitate nunquàm ac nusquàm, vel in ipso perpessionum ac mortis momento, filius hominis caruerit, sanus nemo intelligere potest, Deum coronasse sapientiâ, justitiâ ac sanctitate filium hominis Christum, ubi eum sua visitatione favorabili, gloriâ dicitur coronasse. Gloriam hic significare rectæ rationi consentaneum est, supremam majestatem, & regnandi ἀνυπεύθυνον authoritatem in omnes omninò creaturas, unà cum illustrissimis, dignisque tantâ majestate insignibus, immortali nempe ac gloriosò corpore, nube curru Dei, triumphali in cœlum ascensione, Angelorum satellitio, cœlo Dei domicilio atque throno, Angelorum ministerio, dono spiritus sancti in orbem mittendi ad Euangelium prædicandum, & Ecclesiam Christo, in quam regnet, colligendam. Sed verò per honorem alterum florem coronæ Christi amarantinum, par est, ut intelligamus, 1°. Favorabilem Dei adversus filium hominis acceptionem & tractationem. Cùm enim Deus filium hominis antea non tractaret honorificum in modum: sed flagris contumeliosis, paupertate, fame, cruce ac dira morte, servi ad instar, vilisque mancipii, ignominiosum in modum dum exciperet atque tractaret, functum eundem vili illo ad mortem usque crucis servitio, honorificentissimum in modum excepit atque tractavit, lata primum sententia judiciaria, qua plenam eum praestitisse divinae justitiae satisfactionem, ac placationem declaravit, ubi filium hominis Deus qua mundi judex excitavit e mortuis, eum honoravit dono currus sui, Angelorum satellitio & fideli ministerio, domicilio suo ac throno coelesti, jure denique exercendi supremi ac immensi dominii uti Mediatorem, in omnes omnino creaturas, sicut Pharao Josephum honoravit, & Assuerus Mardocheum, & Salomo matrem suam, ubi eos summi illi Monarchae honorifice exceperunt atque tractarunt. 2°. Per honorem, quo Deus filium hominis coronavit, cultum intelligimus, quem Deus Christo suo exhibitum voluit, ad finem usque seculorum, ab Angelis, hominibus, vivis atque mortuis, & ut summatim dicam, ab omnibus, nulla excepta, creaturis. Florem utrumque gloriosissimae ac honoratissimae Christi coronae, explicat Paulus ob oculos nostros, Phil. 2: 9. 10. 11. Dedit illi nomen supra omne nomen; en tibi florem gloriae, summam Christi majestatem & authoritatem regnandi: ut ad nomen Jesu, omne genu flectatur, coelestium, terrestrium, & infernorum, & omnis lingua confiteatur, Jesum Christum esse Dominum ad gloriam Dei Patris; en tibi alterum florem, nempe honoris, ex quo conserta radiat gloriosa Christi corona. Hinc Vates ut gloriam & honorem explicet ac interpretetur, extemplo attexit, omnia subjecisti pedibus ejus: universalis enim isthaec omnium creaturarum pedibus Christi subjectio, & Christi gloriam, supremam nempe & immensam majestatem, & regnandi authoritatem, sicut & honorem, nempe cultum debitum, & ab omnibus creaturis exhibitum, aperte ac luculenter significat. Hinc factum quam sapientissime, ut in regia Christi corona, gloria primum locum, honor secundum obtineat; quippe naturae ordine Regum majestas ac summa authoritas, quae gloria Regum est, honorem & cultum debitum & exhibitum a subditis, jure merito antevertit.
units.tr: Hence it is clearer than midday that those have strayed far from the path of truth who interpret glory, the other flower of Christ's crown, as wisdom, justice, and in a word holiness; and who understand honour, the other flower of Christ's crown, as majesty and authority ἀνυπεύθυνον [anypeuthynon, unaccountable], together with illustrious and distinguished marks worthy of such majesty. For since the Son of man never and nowhere lacked wisdom, justice and holiness, not even at the very moment of his sufferings and death, no sane person can understand that God crowned Christ the Son of man with wisdom, justice and holiness, when it is said that he crowned him with glory by his favourable visitation. It accords with right reason that glory here signifies supreme majesty and the authority ἀνυπεύθυνον [unaccountable] to reign over absolutely all creatures, together with the most illustrious marks worthy of such majesty: namely an immortal and glorious body, a cloud as the chariot of God, the triumphal ascension into heaven, the escort of angels, heaven as God's dwelling and throne, the ministry of angels, the gift of the Holy Spirit to be sent into the world to preach the Gospel, and the gathering of the Church, over which he is to reign. But by the second flower of Christ's crown, the amaranth, honour, we must rightly understand, first, God's favourable reception and treatment of the Son of man. For whereas God did not previously treat the Son of man in an honourable manner, but received and treated him in a shameful manner, with abusive scourgings, poverty, hunger, the cross and a dreadful death, like a servant and a base slave, and that same man, who had performed that base service even to the death of the cross, God then received and treated in the most honourable manner: first by pronouncing a judicial sentence by which he declared that the Son had rendered full satisfaction and propitiation to divine justice; then, when God as judge of the world raised the Son of man from the dead, he honoured him with the gift of his own chariot, the escort and faithful ministry of angels, his heavenly dwelling and throne, and finally the right to exercise supreme and boundless dominion as Mediator over absolutely all creatures. In this he honoured him as Pharaoh honoured Joseph, and Ahasuerus Mordecai, and Solomon his mother, when those supreme monarchs received and treated them with honour. Second, by the honour with which God crowned the Son of man we understand the worship which God willed to be paid to his Christ, by angels, men, the living and the dead, until the end of the ages, and, to sum up, by all creatures without exception. Paul sets before our eyes both flowers of the most glorious and most honoured crown of Christ, Phil. 2:9-11: He gave him a name above every name: behold for you the flower of glory, the highest majesty and authority of Christ to reign; that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, things on earth, and things under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father: behold for you the other flower, namely of honour, from which the glorious crown of Christ shines in combined splendour. Hence the seer, in order to explain and interpret glory and honour, immediately adds: you put all things under his feet: for this universal subjection of all creatures under the feet of Christ clearly and plainly signifies Christ's glory, namely supreme and immense majesty and authority to reign, as well as his honour, namely the worship due to him and rendered by all creatures. Hence it is most wisely arranged that in the royal crown of Christ glory holds the first place and honour the second; for in the natural order, the majesty and supreme authority of kings, which is the glory of kings, rightly precedes the honour and due worship rendered by subjects.

units.la: Haec praefati ad quaestionis solutionem propriius ut accedamus, observare operae pretium est, filium hominis, seu Christum, cum sit unus mediator, Deum inter & homines, tum naturarum communione, tum officio, spectandum nobis proponi in Scriptura. 1°. Quatenus est Immanuel, Deus & homo. 2°. Quatenus officio mediatorio fungitur, & vel partes & causam hominum agit apud Deum, eorum loco ac bono: vel partes & causam Dei agit apud homines. Haec vero momentosa capita pensitanda veniunt ad quaestionis resolutionem.
units.tr: Having said these things beforehand, it is worth observing, so that we may come more directly to the solution of the question, that the Son of man, or Christ, since he is the one Mediator between God and men, is set before us in Scripture to be considered both by the communion of natures and by his office. 1. As he is Immanuel, God and man. 2. As he discharges the mediatorial office, and either acts the part and cause of men before God, in their place and for their good, or acts the part and cause of God before men. These weighty heads must be weighed for the resolution of the question.

units.la: Primo. Filium hominis Christum ubi Scriptura, uti Deum considerat, eum vocat Deum supra omnia aeternum benedictum, Rom. 9: 5. magnum Deum nostrum & servatorem Jesum Christum, Titi 2: 13. Filium Dei unigenitum. Joh. 1: 14. proprium Dei filium, Rom. 8:32. imaginem Dei invisibilis, Col. 1:15. primogenitum omnis creatura, id est, Dominum; haeredem omnium, Hebr. 1:2. splendorem gloriae Patris, & Characterem existentiae Dei, Hebr. 1: 3. Dominum gloriae, id est, gloriosum, 1 Cor. 2: 8. Principem vitae, Act. 3: 15. Principem salutis, Hebr. 2: 10. Regem seculorum immortalem, invisibilem, solum sapientem Deum, cui debetur honor & gloria in secula seculorum, 1 Tim. 1: 17. De filio hominis Christo sub hac σχέσει aeternae ac gloriosissimae naturae divinae, nec David, nec Spiritus S. uspiam contemptim locutus est.
units.tr: First. Where Scripture considers the Son of man Christ as God, it calls him God over all, blessed for ever (Rom. 9:5); our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ (Titus 2:13); the only-begotten Son of God (John 1:14); the proper Son of God (Rom. 8:32); the image of the invisible God (Col. 1:15); the firstborn of every creature, that is, the Lord; the heir of all things (Heb. 1:2); the brightness of the Father's glory and the express image of God's substance (Heb. 1:3); the Lord of glory, that is, the glorious one (1 Cor. 2:8); the Prince of life (Acts 3:15); the Prince of salvation (Heb. 2:10); the eternal, immortal, invisible King, the only wise God, to whom be honour and glory for ever and ever (1 Tim. 1:17). Neither David nor the Holy Spirit has anywhere spoken contemptuously of the Son of man Christ under this aspect of his eternal and most glorious divine nature.

units.la: Secundò.
