Filius hominis Christus, spectatur ut homo purissimus juxta ac sanctissimus, innocens sine macula, & à peccatoribus separatus, ut nulla fraus in ejus labiis inventa fuerit, Deo semper charissimus pariter atque dilectissimus fuit, ut dum à Johanne baptisaretur, Deus clara voce super eo pronunciaverit, & cum in monte transfiguraretur, facie solis ad instar coruscante, dixerit, Hic est filius meus delectus, in quo complacui, Math. 3: 17. & 17: 5. Nec de filio hominis sub hac secunda σχέσει hominis purissimi, sanctissimi, Deoque dilectissimi, David & Spiritus sanctus per contemptum locutus est.
units.tr: Second. The Son of man Christ is regarded as a man most pure and most holy, innocent and without spot, separated from sinners, so that no deceit was found in his lips; he was always most dear and beloved to God, so that when he was baptised by John, God pronounced from heaven with a clear voice concerning him, and when he was transfigured on the mountain, his face shining like the sun, God said, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased (Matt. 3:17; 17:5). Nor has David or the Holy Spirit spoken contemptuously of the Son of man under this second aspect, as the most pure and most holy man, beloved of God.

units.la: Tertiò. Filius hominis Christus, ubi spectatur quatenus agit causam Dei, ejusque partes sustinet apud homines considerandus venit. 1°. ut summus propheta, voluntatem Dei, mysteria salutis aeternae ac regni coelorum docens homines, tum praeconio Euangelii foris; tum intus Spiritu revelationis & illuminationis: 2°. Qua patrans miracula propria & infinita virtute in missionis suae atque doctrinae confirmationem: 3°. ut Martyr ἀυλόγης doctrinae ac mysteriorum, quae apud Patrem viderat, quaeque ipse annunciabat & docebat, unde se venisse in mundum, ut testimonium perhiberet veritati coram Pilato profitebatur, Joh. 18: 37. obsignans proprio sanguine quae de Deo Patre, de se Rege Messia, Propheta & Pontifice, & salute docuerat, nullo enim mortis metu potuit ab hac vera professione dimoveri: sed sanguinem fudit, mortemque oppetiit ignominiosam, ut testis locupletissimus fidem faceret doctrinae suae: 4°. Filius hominis spectandus venit, quatenus partes Dei agebat apud homines, ut exemplar absolutissimum virtutum omnium: nobis enim reliquit exemplum, ut sequamur vestigia ejus. 1 Pet. 2:21. 5°. Quatenus Rex in solio majestatis constitutus in coelo, orbem universum moderatur ac regit, dona regalia Spiritus sui largitur, Ecclesiam subditos fideles sibi colligit, participes naturae divinae potentissimè efficit, transformatque de gloria in gloriam in imaginem suam per Spiritum suum, adversus Satanæ, mundi, peccati ac mortis insultus protegit, servatque incolumes, ut tandem salutem æternam obtineant, adeantque hæreditatem incorruptibilem ac immarcescibilem, ipsis in cœlo reservatam. Atque de filio hominis sub hac tertia σχέσει considerato, quatenus causam Dei partesque agit apud homines, nunquam ac nusquam Spiritus Sanctus ore Davidis, alterius viri Θεοπνεύστῳ, contemptim loquutus est.
units.tr: Third. The Son of man Christ comes to be considered where he is regarded as acting the cause of God and sustaining God's part before men. 1. As the highest prophet, teaching men the will of God and the mysteries of eternal salvation and of the kingdom of heaven, both outwardly by the proclamation of the gospel and inwardly by the Spirit of revelation and illumination. 2. By working miracles by his own infinite power, in confirmation of his mission and teaching. 3. As the martyr of the truth [ἀληθείας] of the doctrine and mysteries which he had seen with the Father, and which he himself proclaimed and taught; whence he professed that he had come into the world to bear witness to the truth before Pilate (John 18:37), sealing with his own blood what he had taught concerning God the Father, concerning himself as the Messiah, King, Prophet and Priest, and concerning salvation. For he could be moved from this true profession by no fear of death, but shed his blood and underwent a shameful death, so that as the most complete witness he might give credence to his teaching. 4. The Son of man is to be considered as he acted the part of God before men, as the most perfect example of all virtues: for he has left us an example, that we should follow in his steps (1 Pet. 2:21). 5. As the King seated in the throne of majesty in heaven, he governs and rules the whole world, bestows the royal gifts of his Spirit, gathers to himself a church of faithful subjects, makes them most powerfully partakers of the divine nature, and transforms them from glory to glory into his own image by his Spirit; he protects them against the assaults of Satan, the world, sin and death, and keeps them safe, so that at last they may obtain eternal salvation and enter the incorruptible and unfading inheritance reserved for them in heaven. And concerning the Son of man considered under this third aspect, as he acts the cause and part of God before men, the Holy Spirit has never and nowhere spoken contemptuously, by the mouth of David, that divinely inspired man of another kind.

units.la: 4º. Superest quarta habitudo, sub qua filius hominis Christus spectandus proponitur in Scriptura: nimirum quatenus causam reorum hominum partes ac personam agit atque sustinet apud Deum, estque ἔγγυος vas & sponsor Novi Testamenti, Hebr. 7: 21. Atque sub hac σχέσει, multifariam iterum spectandus proponitur, pro multifaria habitudine reorum hominum & peccati ad Deum, 1º. ut summus Pontifex; nam omnis pontifex ex hominibus assumtus, pro hominibus constituitur ad ea peragenda apud Deum, quæ ab ipsis requiruntur, ut offerat dona atque victimas pro peccatis, Hebr. 5: 1. peccatum enim cum sit divinæ majestatis ac legis contemptus nefarius, divinam læsit majestatem & justitiam, quæ ira Dei est, inflammat, & proritat in vindictam, nec expiatur, nisi placatione divinæ justitiæ, per plenam satisfactionem. Hinc Christus filius hominis constitutus est pontifex apud Deum pro hominibus, ut foret propitiatio & placamen divinæ justitiæ pro peccatis nostris, Hebr. 5: 5. Rom. 3: 25. & 1 Joh. 2: 2. 2º. Quatenus victima purissima, sanctissima, infinitæ dignitatis, valoris ac pretii immensi, placans suo sanguine divinam justitiam, & faciens purgationem peccatorum nostrorum. 3º. Quatenus obediens Deo Patri ad mortem, mortem usque crucis, h. e. obediens assumendo carnem, & formam carnis peccati, & formam servi, obsequiosi Deo & legi, & tandem mandato moriendi morte ignominiosa ac maledicta crucis, obediens, pono animam a me ipso, potestatem habeo ponendi eam, & potestatem habeo iterum sumendi eam, hoc mandatum accepi a patre meo, Joh. 10: 18. Aptasti mihi corpus, tunc dixi ecce veni, ut faciam, Deus, voluntatem tuam, per quam voluntatem sanctificati sumus per oblationem corporis Jesu Christi, semel factam, Hebr. 10: 5. 9. 10. 4º. Filius hominis Christus considerandus proponitur, ut illustris bellator, Exod. 15: 3. pugnam cruentam pugnans adversus principatus & potestates, id est, Diabolum & infernas ipsius copias, mundum, peccatum & mortem, Col. 2: 15. adversus justitiam Dei, legis obligationem atque maledictionem, Col. 2: 14. quia, peccatum, quatenus ad pœnam obligat: Diabolus, quatenus divinæ justitiæ minister crudelissimus atque peccatorum tyrannus; mundus, quatenus Diaboli satellitium: litium: mors quatenus poena peccati: justitia Dei, quatenus vindex acerrima majestatis ac juris Numinis: Lex, quatenus chirographum obligatorium ad mortem; Legis maledictio, quatenus peccatoris condemnatio, & irae divinae telum lethiferum, omnia haec velut armatus hostilis exercitus adversa sunt & contraria peccatoribus. Verùm filius hominis partes agens, & peccatorum quotquot in eum crediturí sunt, personam sustinens, pugnâ suâ cruentâ hostilem illum exercitum prostravit, vicit, expoliavit, & de iis triumphum egit in cruce, ubi fortiter bellator imperterritus ad victoriam usque pugnavit. De filio hominis summo pontifice ac victima sacrificio mortis suae justitiam Dei placante, obediente, vel de ipso forti bellatore, pugnâ suâ cruentâ hostes crediturorum suorum profligante in plenam victoriam, nunquam ac nusquam ore Davidis, vel alterius Spiritus sancti amanuensis, Numen contemptim loquutum est. 5°. Filius hominis Christus proponitur spectandus ut ἐπικατάρατος, execrabilis, seu κατάρα, execratio, loco & bono credentium & crediturorum hominum peccatorum, Gal. 3: 13. Quatenus scilicet poenam peccatoribus debitam tulit in ligno crucis: peccatum enim debitum est, quod peccatorem morti maledictae necessario obligat, facitque obnoxium. 6°. Quatenus poenam ferendo credentibus ac crediturisǀ peccatoribus debitam, debitum solvit, pleneque expunxit infinitae obedientiae suae merito ac pretio, unde animam suam vocat λύτρον, pretium redemptionis pro multis, Matth. 20: 28. Nec de Filio hominis sub hac ultima σχέσει vadis ac fidejussoris, debitum redemptionis pretium sponte sua plane solventis, Spiritus sanctus uspiam contemptim loquutus est: Sed contrà ipse asserit, propter hoc pater me diligit, quia ego pono animam meam pro ovibus meis, Joh. 10: 15. 17. 7°. Denique, Filius hominis spectandus venit, uti functus partibus generis humani maledicti, per plenam solutionem debiti maledictionis & mortis, partes agit & sustinet aeternae majestatis Dei adversus homines, vel hominum adversus Deum, constitutus in solio coelesti, Propheta, Rex & Pontifex, vivus comparens & intercedens pro fidelibus suis. Nec de filio hominis sub hac σχέσει spectato, usquam per contemptum locutus est Spiritus sanctus in Scriptura.
units.tr: Fourth. There remains a fourth relation under which the Son of man Christ is set before us in Scripture to be considered: namely, as he acts and sustains the cause, the part and the person of guilty men before God, and is the surety [ἔγγυος] and guarantor of the New Testament (Heb. 7:21). Under this aspect he is again presented in many ways, according to the many relations of guilty men and of sin to God. 1. As the highest Priest; for every high priest taken from among men is appointed for men in things pertaining to God, that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins (Heb. 5:1). For sin, since it is a wicked contempt of divine majesty and law, has injured the divine majesty and justice, which is the wrath of God, kindles it and provokes it to vengeance, and it is not expiated except by appeasing divine justice through full satisfaction. Hence Christ the Son of man was appointed a priest before God for men, that he might be the propitiation and appeasement of divine justice for our sins (Heb. 5:5; Rom. 3:25; 1 John 2:2). 2. As the most pure and most holy victim, of infinite dignity, worth and immense price, appeasing divine justice with his blood and making purification for our sins. 3. As obedient to God the Father unto death, even the death of the cross; that is, obedient in assuming flesh and the form of sinful flesh and the form of a servant, compliant to God and to the law, and at last obedient to the command to die the shameful and accursed death of the cross: I lay down my life of myself; I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again; this commandment I have received from my Father (John 10:18). Thou hast prepared a body for me; then I said, Behold, I come to do thy will, O God, by which will we are sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all (Heb. 10:5, 9, 10). 4. The Son of man Christ is set forth to be considered as a famous warrior (Exod. 15:3), fighting a bloody battle against the principalities and powers, that is, the Devil and his infernal forces, the world, sin and death (Col. 2:15), and against the justice of God, the obligation and curse of the law (Col. 2:14). For sin, as it binds to punishment; the Devil, as the most cruel minister of divine justice and tyrant over sinners; the world, as the Devil's retinue; death, as the punishment of sin; the justice of God, as the most fierce avenger of the majesty and right of the Deity; the Law, as the binding bond unto death; the curse of the law, as the condemnation of the sinner and the deadly weapon of divine wrath: all these, like an armed hostile army, are adverse and opposed to sinners. But the Son of man, acting the part and sustaining the person of all the sinners who are to believe in him, by his bloody battle overthrew that hostile army, conquered it, stripped it, and triumphed over it on the cross, where as a brave and undaunted warrior he fought on to victory. Concerning the Son of man, the supreme priest and the victim of sacrifice by his death appeasing the justice of God, obedient, or concerning him as the brave warrior who by his bloody battle routed the enemies of his believers into complete victory, the Deity has never and nowhere spoken contemptuously by the mouth of David, or of another amanuensis of the Holy Spirit. 5. The Son of man Christ is set forth to be considered as accursed [ἐπικατάρατος], execrable, or as a curse [κατάρα], an execration, in the place and for the good of believing and future-believing sinful men (Gal. 3:13). That is, he bore in the wood of the cross the punishment due to sinners; for sin is a debt which necessarily binds the sinner to the cursed death and makes him liable. 6. As by bearing the punishment due to believing and future-believing sinners he fully paid the debt and entirely cancelled it by the merit and price of his infinite obedience; whence he calls his soul a ransom [λύτρον], the price of redemption for many (Matt. 20:28). Nor has the Holy Spirit anywhere spoken contemptuously of the Son of man under this last aspect, as surety and guarantor who of his own accord fully paid the price of the debt of redemption; but on the contrary he himself affirms: For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life for my sheep (John 10:15, 17). 7. Finally, the Son of man is to be considered as having discharged the part of the accursed human race: by the full payment of the debt of curse and death, he acts and sustains the part of the eternal majesty of God against men, or of men against God, being seated in the heavenly throne as Prophet, King and Priest, appearing alive and interceding for his faithful ones. Nor has the Holy Spirit anywhere in Scripture spoken contemptuously of the Son of man considered under this aspect.

units.la: Superest igitur, ut de filio hominis spectato sub σχέσει fidejussoris, personam sustinentis Adami, generisque humani corrupti, crediturí in ipsum, quatenus luebat poenas peccato debitas ἐπικατάρατος ἡ κατάρα, execrabilis & execratio factus, contemptim sacer Vates dixerit, Quid est filius hominis? Sed vero, ut clare innotescat vera ratio, tum admirationis, tum contemptus istiusmodi, quatuor cum primis observanda sunt. 1°. Status & conditio filii hominis sub hac σχέσει. 2°. Voluntate, mandato & jussione Dei filium hominis ad vilissimum atque contemptissimum statum istum descendisse. 3°. Infimus iste juxta ac despicatissimus status, cum statu gloriæ & honoris est contendendus. 4°. Denique stupendam hanc statuum extremorum, filii hominis commutationem, factam fuisse per visitationem, hoc est, voluntatem ac mandatum Dei.
units.tr: It remains, then, to consider the Son of man under the relation of surety, sustaining the person of Adam and of corrupted mankind, as one who is believed on, insofar as he bore the penalties due to sin, made "accursed, the curse" [ἐπικατάρατος ἡ κατάρα], "execrable and an execration." The holy Psalmist, speaking with contempt, said, "What is the son of man?" But so that the true reason for this kind of wonder and contempt may be clearly known, four points above all must be observed. (1) The status and condition of the Son of man under this relation. (2) That by the will, command and order of God, the Son of man descended into this most vile and most contemptible state. (3) That this lowest and most despised state must be set against the state of glory and honour. (4) Finally, that this astonishing exchange of the two extreme states of the Son of man came about through the visitation, that is, the will and command of God.

units.la: Ad primum quod attinet, monuimus supra vilissimum filii hominis statum significari, tum ipsius imminutione infra angelos, tum formâ servi, tum similitudine carnis peccati, tum victimâ piaculari, morti ac maledictioni devotâ per manuum impositionem, tum homulo reo blasphemiæ, idololatriæ ac criminis publici, quique ea propter fiebat ἐπικατάρατος [?], execrabilis, & maledictio Dei in ligno, Deut. 21:23. Filium hominis in hunc statum vilissimum descendisse, consilio, voluntate ac mandato Dei, Scriptura διαῤῥήδην [?] asserit, Joh. 10:18. Actor. 4:28. Rom. 8:3. Phil. 2:7.8. Hebr. 10:5.7. Ut Status exinanitionis & demissionis Christi vilissimus rite contendatur cum statu gloriæ ac honoris ipsius, ponamus obsecro ob oculos nostros formam servi, quam filius Dei assumpsit, hæc vero cum primis quatuor significat. 1°. Hominem. 2°. Hominem, qui non est sui juris: sed alieno plane vivit, nempe domini sui arbitrio, ut vel durissima imperanti, in omnibus obsequi teneatur. 3°. Hominem vilissimæ conditionis, qui nihil proprium possidet, victu ac vestitu despicabilem. 4°. Denique hominem, quem crudelissimum ac probrosissimum manebat crucis supplicium, ex domini legumque gentium constitutione, si reus haberetur. Hujusmodi fuit filius hominis Christus, personam agens atque sustinens reorum ac maledictorum hominum. 1°. Quidem fuit homo, non vir eximius; sed plebeius, pariter atque pro plebeio habitus. 2°. Non fuit sui juris: sed totus ad libitum, voluntatem ac mandatum Dei patris compositus, non veni, inquiebat, ut faciam voluntatem meam: sed voluntatem Patris, qui misit me, Joh. 6:38. Fuit subditus legi morali, politicæ, ceremoniali, ejusque maledictioni, durissimum Patris ac Domini mandatum executus est, ad mortem ipsam maledictam; bona nulla propria possedit, factus pauperrimus, ut non haberet ubi caput reclinaret, fame, siti laboravit; habitu fuit, victu & vestitu despicabilis, sortis contemptissimæ, injuriis, contumeliis, flagris expositus ac lascessitus, supplicio denique crucis, servi vilissimi ad instar addictus, ignominiosissimum in modum. Præterea putemus cum animis nostris similitudinem carnis peccati, qua indigitatur status filii hominis contemptissimus. Sermo quidem factus fuit caro, Joh. 1:14. Sed non fuit factus caro peccati: sed vero ubi fuit factus caro, factus & missus fuit in similitudine carnis peccati, hoc est, quod ad speciem externam attinet, simi-lis holis hominibus peccatoribus, tam justa ac exacta conformitate, ut in ea qua peccatores referebat similitudine, unum duntaxat peccatum quà lues est, reapse abesset: fuit nimirum homo, oriundus ex homine, infirmus, Dei & legis servus, miseriis omnibus innocuis, per peccatum invectis obnoxius, ipsi maledictioni & morti, quatenus est peccati poena, sicut homines peccatores, addictus, ut, qui eum juxta speciem illam externam considerabant, facile judicarent, eum esse sicut alios peccatores, & pro peccatore habe-rent, unde Esaias, cum prævaricatoribus numeratus est, Ef. 53: 12. Hunc filii hominis statum dum sacer Vates animo complectitur, contenditque cum statu gloriosissimo ejusdem, gloria & honore coronati, jure eum incessit admiratio, qua ducente contemptim quærit, quid est filius hominis, ut dignus tibi, o Deus, gloria & honore videatur? Nihil equidem admirationis subesset, si Cacodæmones, & male feriati homines in malitia positi, filium hominis male haberent, injuriis, probris & suppliciis afficerent. Sed cum tu justus juxta ac sapiens Deus, contumeliis, flagris, crucis supplicio, maledictioni ac morti dirissimæ, eum uti ἐπικαλάρατον addixeris, & in prævaricatoribus juste annumeraveris, qui fieri potuit, ut eundem met tuo consilio, tua voluntate, gloria & honore coronares? Qui dignus est summa Dei majestate, & authoritate suprema in omnes creaturas, quem tu vilissima ac contemptissima sorte servi, alieno viventis arbitrio, dignum judicasti, atque adeo vermem fecisti non hominem? Qui dignus est filius hominis gloriosissimis insignibus, Dei ac Domini orbis universi, quem tu exinanitum vilissimis notis, habitu, victu ac vestitu pauperrimi servi, deformatum voluisti? Qui solio supremæ majestatis donasti, quem cruce ignominiosa arbore infelici plexum ac pendulum exhibueras, latronis, blasphemi, ac execrabilis ad instar idololatræ? Qui dignum judicasti honore & cultu Angelorum hominum, omniumque creaturarum humili servitio, quem flagris, sputo, contumeliis, probris ac maledictis hominum, judiciaria tua sententia addixeras? Tantine est filius hominis reorum fidejussor hominum, tibique eorum loco maledictus atque maledictio, infra conditionem Angelorum, & fortem terrenam vilissimorum capitum, tuo decreto dejectus & positus, ut omnia, vel Angelos ipsos pedibus suis subditos, & ad nutum suum compositos & obsequiosos videat ac sortiatur? Contemptim igitur nec immerito Vates de filio hominis Christo sub σχῆμα servi, & similitudinis carnis peccati & execrabilis, loco & bono hominum reorum, merito jure locutus est, quandoquidem Deus ipsum, sub hujusmodi σχῆμα, contemptissimum in modum habuit atque tractavit.
units.tr: As to the first point, we have said above that the most vile state of the Son of man is signified both by his being made less than the angels, and by the form of a servant, and by the likeness of sinful flesh, and by being a sacrificial victim, devoted to death and curse through the laying on of hands, and by being a poor man guilty of blasphemy, idolatry and public crime, who for that reason became "accursed" [ἐπικατάρατος], "execrable, and the curse of God on the tree" (Deut. 21:23). That the Son of man descended into this most vile state by the counsel, will and command of God, Scripture expressly affirms (John 10:18; Acts 4:28; Rom. 8:3; Phil. 2:7-8; Heb. 10:5, 7). So that the lowest state of Christ's emptying and humiliation may be properly set against his state of glory and honour, let us, I beg, place before our eyes the form of a servant which the Son of God took on; this chiefly signifies four things. (1) A human being. (2) A human being who is not his own master, but lives entirely at another's disposal, bound to obey in all things his lord's will, however harsh the command. (3) A human being of the most lowly condition, who possesses nothing of his own, and is despised for his food and clothing. (4) Finally, a human being who, if he were held to be a criminal, faced the cruellest and most shameful punishment of the cross, by the decree of his master and the laws of the nations. Such was Christ the Son of man, who bore and sustained the person of guilty and accursed men. (1) Indeed he was a human being, not an outstanding man, but a plebeian, and was regarded as one. (2) He was not his own master, but wholly disposed to the pleasure, will and command of God the Father: "I have not come," he said, "to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me" (John 6:38). He was subject to the moral, civil and ceremonial law and to its curse; he carried out the Father's and Lord's hardest command, even to death itself, which was accursed. He possessed no goods of his own; having become most poor, so that he had nowhere to lay his head, he suffered hunger and thirst; he was despised in his dress, food and clothing, of the most despised lot, exposed and harassed by injuries, insults and scourges, and finally, like the most abject slave, given over to the punishment of the cross in the most ignominious manner. Moreover, let us consider in our minds the likeness of sinful flesh, which marks the most contemptible state of the Son of man. "The Word was made flesh" (John 1:14), but he was not made sinful flesh; rather, when he was made flesh, he was also made and sent in the likeness of sinful flesh, that is, as far as outward appearance goes, like sinful human beings, in such exact conformity that in the likeness which he bore to sinners only sin itself, which is the plague, was truly absent. He was, of course, a man born of a man, weak, a servant of God and of the law, subject to all the innocent miseries introduced by sin, and given over, like sinful men, to the curse and death, which are the punishment of sin, so that those who looked at him in that outward appearance would easily judge him to be like other sinners and would hold him to be one. Hence Isaiah said, "He was numbered with the transgressors" (Isa. 53:12). When the holy Psalmist embraces this state of the Son of man and sets it against his most glorious state, crowned with glory and honour, he is rightly seized with astonishment, and in that astonishment he asks with contempt, "What is the son of man, that he should seem worthy to you, O God, of glory and honour?" There would be no cause for wonder if evil demons and wicked men, set in malice, treated the Son of man badly and subjected him to injuries, reproaches and punishments. But since you, O God, just and wise, have appointed him to insults, scourges, the punishment of the cross, and to curse and most dreadful death, and have justly counted him among the transgressors, how could it be that you yourself, by your counsel and your will, crowned him with glory and honour? Is he worthy of the highest majesty of God and of supreme authority over all creatures, whom you, in the most vile and contemptible lot of a servant, living at another's will, judged fit, and so made him a worm and not a man? Is the Son of man worthy of the most glorious marks of God, the Lord of the whole world, whom you willed to be emptied of all honour, disfigured by the outward marks, food and clothing of a most poor servant? You who gave him the throne of supreme majesty, when you had exhibited him hanged and suspended on the ignominious cross, a sad tree, like a thief, a blasphemer, and an idolater, execrable? You who judged him worthy of the honour and worship of the angels and of the humble service of men and all creatures, when by your sentence of judgment you had given him over to the scourges, spitting, insults, reproaches and curses of men? Is the Son of man so great a surety of men, accursed and a curse in their place for you, cast down and placed by your decree beneath the condition of the angels and in the earthly lot of the most vile of criminals, that he should see and obtain all things, even the angels themselves, subject to his feet and compliant and obedient to his nod? Therefore the Psalmist, not undeservedly, spoke contemptuously, and rightly and justly, of the Son of man Christ under the form of a servant, the likeness of sinful and accursed flesh, and in the place and for the good of guilty men, since God himself treated and regarded him in such a form in the most contemptible manner.

units.la: Si regeras, sacrum Vatem Spiritu sancto plenum, perspectum habuisse filium hominis, uti Deum super omnia benedictum, hominem justum, purissimum, omnibusque virtutibus sanctitatis cumulatissimum, Mediatorem, partes Dei gloriosissimi agentem adversus homines, obedientia sua eximia, ac dignitatis infinitæ, justitiam Dei placantem, juxta & dignissimum, quem Deus gloria & honore coronaret; bellatorem illustrem hostes Dei ac hominum salvandorum pugna sua cruenta proterentem ac proculcantem in plenam victoriam, lætumque triumphum. Atque adeo plenum Vatem gloriosissimis istis filii hominis ideis, non facile a sese impetrare potuisse, ut de eo ita contemptim loqueretur. Respondeo, finitam mentem sacri Vatis sub unum oculorum conjectum reducere non potuisse omnia isthæc simul & semel: nam si ipsius Christi anima infinitæ divinitatis suæ intelligentiæ, conjunctissima, uno oculorum obtutu simul & semel completi non potuit, dirum Dei poculum, plenum maledictione ad hauriendum propositum, & Dei decretum ratum fixumque, & salutem hominum, & sequuturas glorias. Nempe finita mens, ut ut purissima, jam occupata & plena aliquo objecto, cum non sit infinitæ capacitatis, impar est simul ac semel diversum plane objectum putare atque comprehendere. Nihil equidem mirari subit, si Vatis sacri finita mens, occupata ac plena conceptu status contemptissimi filii hominis ἐπικαλαρᾶτυ, nec non conceptu ejusdem gloria & honore coronati; minus simul & semel potuerit, eundem filium hominis perspectum habere sub idea gloriosissima magni ac benedicti Dei juxta ac hominis purissimi obedientia infinita ac λύτρω mortis, justitiam Dei placantis, debitaque creditorum solventis, partesve Dei gloriosi agentis adversus homines, cæteraque id genus, quæ animo pervia, omnem a filio hominis contemptum amoliuntur.
units.tr: If you should object that the holy Psalmist, full of the Holy Spirit, had a clear view of the Son of man as God blessed above all, as a just and most pure man, endowed with every virtue of holiness, as Mediator acting for the most glorious God against men, by his outstanding obedience and his infinite dignity appeasing the justice of God, and as one most worthy whom God should crown with glory and honour; as an illustrious warrior who by his bloody fight crushed and trampled underfoot the enemies of God and of men who were to be saved, and led them to complete victory and a joyful triumph; and that therefore the Psalmist, filled with these most glorious ideas of the Son of man, could not easily have brought himself to speak of him so contemptuously: I answer that the finite mind of the holy Psalmist could not take in all these things together and at once under one glance of the eyes. For if the very soul of Christ, most closely joined to the understanding of his infinite divinity, could not at one glance of the eyes and at once take in the dreadful cup of God, full of curse, which was set before him to drink, and the decree of God, fixed and sure, and the salvation of men, and the glories that would follow, then a finite mind, however pure, already occupied and filled with one object, since it is not of infinite capacity, is unable to think of and grasp at once a quite different object. Indeed, it is no wonder if the finite mind of the holy Psalmist, occupied and filled with the concept of the most contemptible state of the Son of man, accursed, and with the concept of the same man crowned with glory and honour, could less at once have seen the same Son of man under the most glorious idea of the great and blessed God, and of the infinite obedience and the ransom of death of the most pure man, appeasing the justice of God, paying the debts of creditors, and acting for the glorious God against men, and other things of this kind, which, once admitted to the mind, drive out all contempt for the Son of man.

units.la: 1°. Quod Vates sacer hîc rogat, Quid est filius hominis, ut visites eum? Quodque rogat ipse filius hominis, Deus meus, Deus meus! quare me dereliquisti, longinquus a salute mea, a verbis rugitus mei? Psal. 22: 2. Matth. 27: 46. Non levem habent speciem contradictionis. Miratur nempe Vates, cur Deus favens & amicus ad filium hominis accesserit ubi eum visitavit. Contrà verò ipse filius hominis queritur æque ac miratur, cur Deus eum reliquerit, iratusque ab eo recesserit, longinquus a salute, & verbis rugitus ipsius: nec immeritò sanè queritur atque miratur, cum Deus sit ipsius Deus, hoc est, fidei reverentiæ, amoris, pietatis, cultusque unicum objectum, sicut & liberator potentissimus, ac largitor beneficentissimus. Cum te Deum unicè coluerim mandato tuo ut ut durissimo obsequiosus ad mortem, tuque mutuo fidem tuam mihi adstrinxeris fore te in omnibus mihi Deum, liberatorem in adversis, & largitorem beneficientissimum, ut quid igitur præter fidem tuam, & exspectationem meam, ut quid me reliquisti? Contrà non de nihilo: sed solida de causa, ut supra demonstravimus, rogat & miratur Vates, cur Deus filium hominis visitaverit. Nec Vates & Jesus, filium hominis in statu diverso: sed eodem plane constitutum spectare videntur: nam Vates contemplatur eum, factum breve tempus angelis inferiorem, in passione scilicet mortis, formâ servi indutum, exinanitum, & inter ambos latrones è cruce pendulum. Sed verò filius hominis, actus in crucem, factusque ἱπναλάρα, & piaculum in arbore infelici, queritur, rogat, & ingeminat, Deus meus, Deus meus! ut quid me reliquisti? Haud contemnenda isthæc difficultas ex iis quæ edisseruimus in perstringenda quæstione, facilis ad expediendum videtur. Si responderimus, filium hominis Christum in eodem statu mortis maledictæ ac ignominiosæ constitutum, sub gemina σχέσει spectatum fuisse. Sub altera abs Vate sacro: sub altera verò ab ipso filio hominis. Et quidem à Vate sacro sub σχέσει vadis & fidejussoris generis humani, rei ac maledicti, quatenus indutus erat crimine, hoc est, obligatione ad pœnam generis humani redimendi, ἱπναλ- ἀράλ⊙ & piaculum publicum, non propriam suam, sed alienam reorum, nempe redimendorum λύτρῳ & solutione maledictionis & pœnæ, personam ferebat æque ac agebat: quando enim sub ea persona dignus erat justitia Dei vindicatrice, odio, quo Numen sanctissimum æstuat in scelera, maledictione ac morte crudelissima & probrosissima, sub illa nempe habitudine indignus erat amore ac favorabili visitatione Numinis. Verum enim verò filius hominis, ubi rogat cur Deus eum reliquerit, & lamentabilem in modum queritur, Deum longinquum recessisse à salute sua, spectatur sub altera σχέσει propriæ scilicet personæ, Deo suo ad mortem usque crucis obsequiosæ & pientissimæ. Atque hanc suam propriam personam innocentem ac sanctam quam intuetur, luculenter declarat hac ingeminatâ invocatione, Deus meus, Deus meus! quæ fidem, fiduciam roboratam, pietatem, reverentiam, cultumque fidelem ac intemeratum spirat. Atque sub hac habitudine propriæ ac sanctissimæ suæ personæ, dignissimus erat filius hominis; non quidem iratâ Dei derelictione, quæ nihil hujusmodi commeritum, lætitiâ ac gloriâ consummatissimæ sanctitatis nativa comite, eum privabat: sed potius amicâ lætâque Dei visitatione eum gloriâ ac honere coronatura.
units.tr: 1°. The sacred Prophet asks here, What is man, that you visit him? and the Son of Man himself asks, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me, far from my salvation, from the words of my roaring? Ps. 22:2; Matt. 27:46. These do not have a slight look of contradiction. The Prophet marvels why God, favourable and friendly, came to the Son of Man and visited him. On the contrary, the Son of Man himself complains and marvels just as much why God has left him, withdrawn from him in anger, far from his salvation and from the words of his roaring. And not undeservedly does he complain and marvel, since God is his God, that is, the sole object of faith, reverence, love, piety and worship, as well as his most powerful deliverer and most bountiful giver. Since I have worshipped you alone as God, obedient to your most harsh command even unto death, and you have bound yourself to me by a pledge that you would be God to me in all things, my deliverer in adversity and my most bountiful giver, why then, beyond your faith and my expectation, have you forsaken me? On the contrary, the Prophet asks and marvels, and not without solid cause, as we have shown above, why God visited the Son of Man. Nor do the Prophet and Jesus seem to regard the Son of Man as being in different states, but in the very same state: for the Prophet contemplates him, made for a short time lower than the angels, namely in the passion of death, clothed in the form of a servant, emptied, and hanging on the cross between two thieves. But the Son of Man, nailed to the cross and made accursed [ἐπικατάρατος] and an expiatory sacrifice on the unhappy tree, complains, asks, and repeats, My God, my God! why have you forsaken me? This difficulty, not to be despised, seems easy to resolve from what we have set out in examining the question. If we answer that Christ the Son of Man, placed in the same state of cursed and shameful death, was regarded under a twofold relation: under one by the sacred Prophet, under the other by the Son of Man himself. And indeed the sacred Prophet regarded him under the relation of surety and guarantor of the human race, guilty and accursed, in so far as he bore the crime, that is, the obligation to pay the penalty in order to redeem the human race, an accursed and public expiation; he bore and acted out not his own person but that of others, namely of the guilty who were to be redeemed by his ransom and by the removal of the curse and the penalty. For under that person he was worthy of the avenging justice of God, of the hatred with which the most holy Divinity burns against sins, and of the most cruel and disgraceful curse and death; under that aspect, namely, he was unworthy of the love and favourable visitation of the Divinity. But the Son of Man, when he asks why God has forsaken him, and complains in a lamentable manner that God has withdrawn far from his salvation, is regarded under the other relation, that of his own person, obedient and most devoted to his God even unto the death of the cross. And this his own innocent and holy person, which he has in view, he plainly declares by this repeated invocation, My God, my God! which breathes faith, a strengthened trust, piety, reverence, and a faithful and unblemished worship. And under this aspect of his own most holy person the Son of Man was most worthy; not indeed of the angry abandonment of God, which, since he had deserved nothing of the kind, deprived him of joy and glory, the native companions of most perfect holiness; but rather of the friendly and joyful visitation of God, which would crown him with glory and honour.

units.la: 2º. Ambæ istæ quæstiones super Messia adversis velut frontibus concurrentes, Quid est filius hominis ut visites eum? Deus meus, Deus meus! ut quid me, filium nempe hominis Christum, dereliquisti? divinum ac præsentissimum Deo ipso propinante in scriptura, Judæis erant remedium, si mens non læ-va & immedicabilis planè fuisset. Jesum Christum à cruce pendentem ludibrio & contemptu excepisti misera natio, benè erat, nam & Spiritus Sanctus eum contemptim tractat, habetque ἐπικατάρατος [?]: maledictus enim quis-quis pendet è ligno. Eccur verò summo eum non habuisti in precio, quando ipsum auditis Deum vestrum summa fide ac fiducia, uti Deum suum valido clamore & παῤῥησία [?] invocantem? Jurene an injuriâ queritur se à Deo derelictum? Quis verò pronunciare non erubuerit, eum injuria conqueri se à Deo derelictum, qui Deum unicè colit ac reveretur, habetque Deum, Deum suum, fœderatus scil. Deo fidelis, ejusque mandato obsequiosus ad servitium durissimum, vel ad ipsam mortem, Psal. 40: jure igitur, non injuriaMessias conquestus est, se à Deo derelictum: Ergo dignissimus erat, quem Deus diligeret, & amica sua lætaque dignaretur visitatione. Quid verò vos Jesum Christum è cruce pendentem odio etiamnum prosequimini & contemptu, quem videtis præ exquisitissima sua pietate, fide in Deum & fiducia, sicut & obsequio suo fidelissimo, dignum, quem Deus amet, visitet, coronet gloria & honore? Age igitur, odium ponite & contemptum, quo Jesum Christum prosequimini incredula natio, adductus in contemptum & ludibrium impulsu amoris sui, ut pœnas ferret vestro in Deum contemptui debitas, dignissimus sanè fuit, estque etiamnum præ sua adversus Deum pietate, & amore in vos perditos flagrantissimo, quem toto corde diligatis. Contemptim tractatum videtis morte dirissimâ juxta ac durissimâ plexum: sed eundemmet, vel dum contemptissimum in modum tractatur, amore Dei, æstimatione ac honoratissimâ visitatione simul videtis dignissimum: qui pote verò si propriam pœnam lueret, supplicioque commerito afficeretur? Age igitur, oculos aperite, & propriam sanctitatem, qua dignus fuit amico Numinis accessu, abs crimine vestro nostroque, quo procurante divina justitia à Deo relictus est, in eo oculati, discernite, ut crimen vestrum sedulò fugiatis, & Christi purissimam sanctitatem integrum vitæ curriculum imitemini; ita tandem fiet, ut purgati criminibus pretioso filii hominis fuso in cruce sanguine, facessat vester contemptus, quo hactenus laborastis, dignique tandem habeamini amica & honoratissima Dei visitatione, uti gens sancta & sacerdotium regale. Interim anima mea agnosce sanctitatem Christi tui, pendentis è cruce, imitare fidem, fiduciam, pietatem & obsequium ejus, ut in adversis, dum pacem tuam & lætitiam obscura intercipiet nubes afflictionis, jure valeas cum Christo ingemi-nare, Deus meus, Deus meus! ut quid me dereliquisti? Sed verò dum filium ho-minis minis Christum unigenitum Dei filium, contemptissimum in modum tractatum cernis ob crimina tua, peccatum odi, fugito crimen, funde lachrymas, & veniam supplex precare peccatorum anteactorum.
units.tr: 2º. These two questions about the Messiah, running against each other like opposing foreheads, What is man, that you visit him? My God, my God! why have you forsaken me, namely Christ the Son of Man, forsaken me? which God himself offers in Scripture as something divine and most present, would have been a remedy for the Jews, had their mind not been perverse and utterly incurable. You, wretched nation, received Jesus Christ hanging from the cross with mockery and contempt; that was well, for the Holy Spirit also treats him with contempt, and says he is accursed [ἐπικατάρατος]: for cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree. But why did you not hold him in the highest esteem, when you heard him invoking his God with the greatest faith and trust, calling on him with loud cries and with boldness [παῤῥησία]? Does the Messiah complain of being forsaken by God justly or unjustly? Who would not blush to say that he complains unjustly of being forsaken by God, he who worships and reveres God alone, and has God as his God, that is, is bound to God in faith and obedient to his command even to the harshest service or to death itself? Psalm 40. Therefore the Messiah complained justly, not unjustly, that he was forsaken by God: therefore he was most worthy to be loved by God and deemed worthy of his friendly and joyful visitation. But why do you still pursue Jesus Christ, hanging from the cross, with hatred and contempt, when you see that he, on account of his most exquisite piety, his faith and trust in God, and his most faithful obedience, is worthy to be loved by God, visited, and crowned with glory and honour? Come then, lay aside the hatred and contempt with which you, unbelieving nation, pursue Jesus Christ, who, led to contempt and mockery by the impulse of his love, that he might bear the punishments due to your contempt of God, was most worthy indeed, and still is, on account of his piety towards God and his most ardent love for you, who are lost; you ought to love him with your whole heart. You see him treated with contempt, bound by the most dreadful and harsh death; yet at the same time, even while he is treated with the greatest contempt, you see that he is most worthy of the love of God, of esteem, and of the most honourable visitation. How could he be so, if he were paying his own punishment and suffering a deserved execution? Come then, open your eyes, and discern in him that his own holiness, by which he was worthy of the friendly approach of the Divinity, was that from which, by the crime of you and of us, by which divine justice was at work, he was forsaken by God; so that you may carefully flee your crime, and imitate the most pure holiness of Christ throughout the whole course of life. Thus at last it will come about that, cleansed of crimes by the precious blood of the Son of Man poured out on the cross, your contempt, under which you have hitherto laboured, will vanish, and you will at last be counted worthy of the friendly and most honourable visitation of God, as a holy nation and a royal priesthood. Meanwhile, my soul, acknowledge the holiness of your Christ, hanging from the cross; imitate his faith, trust, piety and obedience, so that in adversity, when a dark cloud of affliction cuts off your peace and joy, you may rightly be able to repeat with Christ, My God, my God! why have you forsaken me? But when you see the Son of Man, Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, treated with the utmost contempt because of your sins, hate sin, flee crime, shed tears, and humbly pray for pardon for your past sins.

units.la: 3°. Contemptus, in quem adducitur filius hominis ubi se vadem & fidejussorem stitit reorum mortalium, quanto digni sint contemptu & opprobrio ipsi peccatores, luculenter nos docet. Nempe si lignum viride contemptim exceptum fuit atque tractatum, quid fiet ligno arido? Filius hominis Christus, Deus super omnia benedictus, imago Dei invisibilis, splendor gloriae, & character aeternae ὑποστάσεως patris, primogenitus omnis creaturae, innocens, purissimus, agnus sine macula, indutus formam peccatoris, reatu redimendorum lubens volensque implicitus, in extremum venit contemptum, non modo apud homines, quorum pravum & iniquum judicium: sed & apud Numen sanctissimum juxta ac aequissimum: quanto, obsecro, ipsi peccatores, pulvis, umbra, somnium, rebelles, Deo inimici, foedifragi, peccato ab utero conspurcati, vilissima Diaboli mancipia, maledictioni & morti obnoxii, digni videbuntur contemptu & ludibrio? Re enim vera, cum contemptus sit latum de re contempta judicium, eam nempe carere virtute, germano honoris fundamento, imparemque esse boni juxta ac mali cujusvis inferendi, quae summa est apud homines injuria. Anne mortales peccatores in peccatis sati, nati & educati, ἀξιενεῖς, viribusque in bonum omne genus casti, atque adeo mortui, summo digni habebuntur contemptu, quippe qui bonum vel malum in Deum, Angelos lucis & fideles inferendum, impares sunt pariter atque imparati? Nocent fateor, malum inferunt: Sed sibi tantum caeterisque malis perditisque sociis suis. Gaudeant honore, quem sibi parant in mundo posito in nequitia, fucato fruantur honore: germanum quippe honorem penes inhonestos & famosos vitii, Diabolique servos stabulari, nemo sanus dixerit. O stupendam peccatorum ἀξιλεψίαν! O lamentabilem caecitatem! peccatores immensus tenet laudis amor, quavis via ad honorem grassantur, interim, dum Diabolo & peccato vilissime serviunt: unde extremum sibi parant apud Deum judicem, aequumque rerum aestimatorem, contemptum. Agedum mortales, quibus naturae humanae sensus odisse dedit & aversari contemptum, fugite peccatum, fugite crimen inexhaustum contemptus & opprobrii fundum, putate serio in quantum adducentur opprobrium vasa coinquinata peccato, cum filius hominis vas sanctissimum, ubi vadimonium suscepit pro peccatoribus, nulla eorum lue, uno tantum reatu constrictus, propria dignitate excidit, princeps Angelorum factus inferior angelis, contumeliosum & contemptum in modum habitus atque tractatus. Age igitur, poenitentiam agite, solidam colite virtutem, pietatem in Deum, justitiam & charitatem in homines, temperantiam & honestatem in vos ipsos, ut difflato contemptu honos & laus è choro illo sanctissimarum virtutum vobis succrescat & efflorescat.
units.tr: 3°. The contempt into which the Son of Man is brought when he stands as surety and guarantor of mortal sinners shows clearly how worthy of contempt and disgrace the sinners themselves are. For if a green tree was received and treated with contempt, what will be done to the dry tree? Christ the Son of Man, God blessed above all, the image of the invisible God, the brightness of glory and the express image of the eternal substance of the Father, the firstborn of all creation, innocent, most pure, a lamb without spot, clothed in the form of a sinner, willingly and gladly entangled in the guilt of those to be redeemed, came to the utmost contempt, not only among men, whose judgment is perverse and unjust, but also before the most holy and most equitable Divinity. How much more, I beg you, will the sinners themselves, dust, shadow, dream, rebels, enemies of God, covenant-breakers, defiled by sin from the womb, the most base slaves of the Devil, liable to curse and death, seem worthy of contempt and mockery? For in truth, since contempt is a judgment passed on a thing despised, namely that it lacks virtue, the true foundation of honour, and is unable to inflict either good or evil of any kind, which among men is the greatest insult. Will mortal sinners, born and bred in sins, unworthy, and so chaste in no good kind of powers, and therefore dead, be held in the highest contempt, since they are equally unable and unprepared to inflict good or evil upon God, the angels of light and the faithful? I admit they do harm, they inflict evil; but only on themselves and their other evil and lost companions. Let them rejoice in the honour which they prepare for themselves in a world lying in wickedness; let them enjoy a false honour: that real honour should dwell among the dishonourable and infamous, the servants of vice and of the Devil, no sane person will say. O amazing unworthiness of sinners! O lamentable blindness! The immense love of praise holds sinners; they rush by any road to honour, meanwhile, while they serve the Devil and sin most basely; and so they prepare for themselves, before God the judge and the equitable assessor of all things, the utmost contempt. Come, mortals, whom the sense of human nature has taught to hate and shun contempt: flee sin, flee crime, the inexhaustible source of contempt and disgrace; consider seriously to what extent the vessels defiled by sin are brought to disgrace, when the Son of Man, the most holy vessel, taking upon himself the surety for sinners, though free of all their stain and bound only by the guilt of others, fell from his own dignity, was made lower than the angels, the prince of angels, and was treated and handled in a contemptuous and insulting manner. Come then, repent, cultivate solid virtue: piety towards God, justice and charity towards men, temperance and honour towards yourselves; so that, with contempt dispelled, honour and praise may spring up and blossom for you out of that company of most holy virtues.

units.la: 4°. Cum, necquicquam obstante forma servi vilissimi & ἐπικαλαρὰτς publici, Deus filium hominis visitaverit, amica illa visitatione, quae eum gloria & honore coronavit, evidentissimè paret, 1°. Filium hominis perpessum mortem crucis probrosissimam, poenam & contemptum proprium non luisse apud Deum: nam qui sanctissimo Numini dat poenas proprii peccati, indignus sane est amica Dei visitatione, nedum gloria & honore: cum enim dignissimus sit inimica visitatione justitiae vindicatricis, contemptu & ignominia, quibus praegnat famosum supplicium, eum equidem sana mens nulla, dignum judicaverit amica Dei visitatione, gloria & honore: & hoc quidem minus, quod ferendo poenas sceleri suo debitas, solvit quod debet justitiae, & in ordinem naturalis dependentiae invitus cogitur, unde gratiam, bonumve ex Numine jure non potest expectari. Quam enim gratiam ineas apud me, dum solvis quod mihi debes, non volens, lubensque, sed aversus atque coactus? 2°. Hinc liquet, filium hominis non fuisse merum hominem, sed Immanuelem, Deum ac hominem simul: nam merus homo oritur ex Adamo, vel via generationis naturali; iste vero caro est: nam quicquid natum est ex carne, est caro, Joh. 3: 6. hoc est, peccato conspurcatum, dignumque Dei odio, atque ideo irae filius, dignusque maledictione & morte: nec non indignus favorabili Dei visitatione, qua gloria & honore coronetur: vel oritur ex Adamo via supernaturali absque contagio carnis & peccati, ut Christus. Sed vero merus homo, ut ut sanctissimus, si volens lubensque contemptum poenasque ferret, aliis non sibi debitas, aeternum ferret, quia nunquam esset plane ac cumulate solvendo, cum ipsius poena, finitae utpote creatae perfectionis foret: peccatores vero infinitam debent infinito Numini laeso poenam ac mortem, infinitam inquam dignitate atque valore, rei nempe violatae Majestatis dignitate infinitae. Merus homo igitur ut sanctissimus, & ab omni labe peccati quam alienissimus, cum non sit solvendo poenam dignitate infinitam, sub poena mortis aeternum jaceret, cum nunquam esset solvendo, quod solvendum pro aliis suscepisset. Experiretur igitur Deum aeternum maledicentem sibi Vadi & fidejussori aliorum iratum, nec unquam amica Dei visitatione, eum poenae vinculis solventis gloria & honore coronantis, gauderet ac laetaretur. Sed vero, filium hominis Christum, perpessum mortem maledictam crucis, Numen benignissimum visitavit, gloria & honore coronavit. Unde concludere cludere in promptu est, filium hominis Christum non fuisse merum hominem: sed Immanuelem, Deum & hominem simul.
units.tr: 4°. Although the form of a most vile servant and a public accursed [ἐπικατάρατος] man stood in the way, God visited the Son of Man, and that friendly visitation, which crowned him with glory and honour, makes it most clearly evident: 1°. The Son of Man, who suffered the most shameful death of the cross, did not bear the punishment and contempt due to himself before God. For whoever pays the penalty of his own sin to the most holy Godhead is certainly unworthy of a friendly visitation from God, let alone of glory and honour. Since he is most worthy of the hostile visitation of avenging justice, that is, of the contempt and disgrace with which the infamous punishment is pregnant, no sound mind would judge him worthy of God's friendly visitation, of glory and honour. And this is all the more so because, by bearing the punishments owed to his crime, he pays what he owes to justice and is unwillingly forced into the order of natural dependence, from which no grace or good can rightly be expected from the Godhead. For what grace would you win from me when you pay what you owe me, not willingly and gladly, but reluctantly and under compulsion? 2°. From this it is clear that the Son of Man was not a mere man, but Immanuel, God and man at once. For a mere man comes from Adam either by natural generation; but such a one is flesh, for whatever is born of flesh is flesh, John 3:6, that is, polluted by sin and worthy of God's hatred, and therefore a son of wrath, worthy of curse and death, and not worthy of God's favourable visitation, by which he is crowned with glory and honour. Or he comes from Adam by a supernatural way, without the contagion of flesh and sin, as Christ did. But a mere man, however holy, if he willingly and gladly bore contempt and punishments not owed to himself, would bear them for ever, because he could never pay fully and abundantly, since his punishment would be that of finite, created perfection; sinners, however, owe to the infinite Godhead whom they have injured an infinite punishment and death, infinite I say in dignity and worth, namely by the infinite dignity of the violated majesty. A mere man, therefore, however holy and however far removed from every stain of sin, since he could not pay a punishment infinite in dignity, would lie under the penalty of death for ever, since he could never pay what he had undertaken to pay for others. He would experience God cursing him for ever as surety and God angry with those whom he stood for, and would never rejoice and exult in God's friendly visitation, crowning with glory and honour the one who loosed the bonds of punishment. But, on the contrary, the most benevolent Godhead visited Christ, the Son of Man, who suffered the accursed death of the cross, and crowned him with glory and honour. Hence it is easy to conclude that Christ the Son of Man was not a mere man, but Immanuel, God and man at once.

units.la: 5°. Contemptus ad mortem usque maledictam & ignominiosam crucis, in quem filium hominis & filium Dei simul, Christum æternum benedictum, ipse Deus pater adduxit, argumentum præbet necessarium, quo satisfactionis pro peccato necessitas absoluta demonstratur: Sedulò enim perpendenti & reputanti apud se causam seu rationem, quæ Deum Patrem impulit, ut filium suum unigenitum sorti contemptissimæ addiceret, factum in forma carnis peccatricis, & in crucem ignominiosissimam datum, una occurrit necessitas satisfaciendi pro peccatoribus justitiæ Dei vindicatrici, hoc est, pœnas peccatoribus debitas loco & bono eorum solvendi. Novimus quid respondeant Socini sodales, Deum scilicet filium hominis Christum adduxisse in hunc contemptum luctuosissimum, ut ferendo contemptum istiusmodi suam confirmaret doctrinam, & credentibus in se absolutissimum virtutum exemplar præberet, nempe ut credentes in ipsum, ducti pœnitentia veniam peccatorum consequerentur. Verum enim vero, præterquam quod in statu contemptissimo, filius hominis ea egit, quæ nec in doctrinæ suæ confirmationem, nec in exemplum virtutum ullomodo spectant, quin scopo ejusce modi contraria plane videntur, ut cum cœpit contristari & angi gravissimè, dicitque tristis undique est anima mea usque ad mortem, & mortem deprecaturus procidit in faciem, orans & dicens, pater mi, si possibile est, transeat à me calix iste, Matth. 26: 37. 38. 39. & manavit sudore sanguineo defluente in terram, Luc. 22:44. quæ plane nihil faciunt in doctrinæ confirmationem, vel in exemplum virtutis. Unum impræsentiarum perpendere libet, nempe, Deum commendasse charitatem suam adversus nos, quoniam adhuc nobis existentibus peccatoribus, Christus pro nobis mortuus est, Rom. 5: 8. Si Socinianorum Euangelium audias, Deus non eo nomine commendavit charitatem suam erga nos peccatores, quod Christus pro nobis mortuus sit, Deus enim commendat charitatem suam erga peccatores, ubi veniam peccatorum eis credentibus & pœnitentibus facit, datque eisdem vitam æternam: non vero suam illam charitatem commendat, quod Christus pro peccatoribus mortuus sit, quia, absque Christi morte fuisset, Deus & veniam peccatorum & vitam æternam credentibus & pœnitentia ductis dare poterat: si minus placanda fuisset ipsius justitia, & pax peccatoribus peccati expiatione procuranda, seclusa enim necessitate placandi divinam justitiâ sacrificio expiatorio Christi, fidem & pœnitentiam peccatorum cordibus, sicut & charitatem cæterasq; virtutes inde poterat Numen benignissimum, juxta ac potentissimum: nec tamen in contemptum mortis ignominiosissimæ adducere filium hominis Christum. Quid enim vetabat, quominus Deus inderet fidem secundum excellentem magnitudinem potentiæ suæ, & per fidem, pœnitentiam cæterasque virtutes ingeneraret salvandis, & absque morte ignominiosissima Christi, charitatem suam adversus eos testatam faceret? Si respondeat Socini sodalis, Deum addixisse filium hominis morti crucis ignominiosæ ac maledictæ, ut hac ratione magis charitatem suam adversus peccatores commendaret. Benè est, sed orthodoxo sensu, non Sociniano. Nempe in eo elucebit charitas Dei adversus peccatores, quod eos è maledictione & morte liberaverit, vitaeque æternæ participes fecerit: sed non elucebit charitas Dei in conferendâ æternâ illâ salute per mortem Christi, siquidem mors ignominiosa Christi non fuerit necessaria, ut numen benignissimum tantam salutem conferret in peccatores. Vel igitur Socitiani confiteantur, necessariam fuisse contemptissimam filii hominis mortem, ut Deus commendaret charitatem suam adversus peccatores in conferenda ipsis salute, per mortem Christi, erigantque suâ confessione triumphum necessariæ cruci Christi: vel ore rotundo Apostolo obloquantur, dicenti, Deum commendasse charitatem suam erga nos peccatores, eo quòd Christus pro nobis mortuus est. Fac verò, ut orthodoxa doctrina obtineat, scilicet, Deum, vetante ipsius justitiâ, fidelitate, sapientia, peccatoribus veniam peccatorum facere, & vitam æternam conferre haud potuisse, nisi intercederet supplicium ignominiosissimæ mortis Christi, λύτρον pro peccatis sufficientissimum, evidentissimè liquet, Deum commendasse charitatem suam adversus peccatores, non modò quod veniam peccatorum fecerit, dederitque vitam æternam: Sed imprimis, quòd, cum tantam gratiam, vetante sapientia, justitia & fidelitate, facere non poterit, ni intercederet λύτρον sufficientissimum mortis Christi, maluerit, filium hominis dilectissimum, Dominumque gloriæ Christum, in extremum probrosissimæ mortis contemptum adducere, quàm jacentes sub maledictione & morte æterna, miseros relinquere peccatores.
units.tr: 5°. The contempt, even to the accursed and shameful death of the cross, into which God the Father himself led the Son of Man and at the same time the Son of God, the eternal and blessed Christ, supplies a necessary argument by which the absolute necessity of satisfaction for sin is demonstrated. For whoever carefully weighs and considers within himself the cause or reason which moved God the Father to deliver his only-begotten Son to the most contemptible lot, made in the form of sinful flesh and given over to the most shameful cross, will meet one necessity: to satisfy for sinners the avenging justice of God, that is, to pay in their place and for their good the punishments owed by sinners. We know what the fellow Socinians answer: that God led the Son of Man Christ into this most dismal contempt so that by bearing such contempt he might confirm his doctrine, and offer to those who believe in him the most perfect pattern of the virtues, namely so that those who believe in him, led by repentance, might obtain forgiveness of sins. But truly, apart from the fact that in this most contemptible state the Son of Man did things that in no way serve to confirm his doctrine or as an example of the virtues, and indeed seem plainly contrary to that purpose, such as when he began to be grieved and to be in great anguish, and said, "My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even unto death," and, about to pray against death, fell on his face, praying and saying, "O my Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me," Matt. 26:37-39, and his sweat was like drops of blood falling to the ground, Luke 22:44. These things plainly do nothing to confirm the doctrine or serve as an example of virtue. For the present, it is worth considering one thing: that God commended his love toward us, because while we were still sinners, Christ died for us, Rom. 5:8. If you listen to the gospel of the Socinians, God did not commend his love toward us sinners on this ground, that Christ died for us. For God commends his love toward sinners when he grants forgiveness of sins to those who believe and repent, and gives them eternal life; but he does not commend that love by the fact that Christ died for sinners, because without Christ's death God could have granted both forgiveness of sins and eternal life to those who believe and are led to repentance, if his justice, to be appeased, did not need to be satisfied, and peace for sinners did not need to be procured by the expiation of sin. For, setting aside the necessity of appeasing divine justice by Christ's expiatory sacrifice, the most benevolent and at the same time most powerful Godhead could have worked faith, repentance and the other virtues in the hearts of sinners, and yet not have brought the Son of Man Christ into the contempt of the most shameful death. For what prevented God from working faith according to the excellent greatness of his power, and through faith producing repentance and the other virtues in those to be saved, and from displaying his love toward them without the most shameful death of Christ? If a Socinian fellow answers that God delivered the Son of Man to the shameful and accursed death of the cross so that by this means he might commend his love toward sinners more strongly, that is well, but in an orthodox sense, not a Socinian one. For the love of God toward sinners shines forth in this, that he freed them from curse and death and made them partakers of eternal life; but God's love does not shine forth in conferring that eternal salvation through the death of Christ, since the shameful death of Christ was not necessary for the most benevolent Godhead to confer so great a salvation on sinners. Therefore either let the Socinians confess that the most contemptible death of the Son of Man was necessary, so that God might commend his love toward sinners in conferring salvation on them through the death of Christ, and by their confession raise up a triumph for the necessary cross of Christ; or let them with open mouth gainsay the Apostle, who says that God commended his love toward us sinners in that Christ died for us. But suppose the orthodox doctrine prevails, namely that God, since his justice, faithfulness and wisdom forbade it, could not grant sinners forgiveness of sins and confer eternal life unless the punishment of the shameful death of Christ intervened, as a ransom [λύτρον] most sufficient for sins. It is most clearly evident that God commended his love toward sinners not only in that he granted forgiveness of sins and gave eternal life, but above all in that, since wisdom, justice and faithfulness forbade him to make so great a gift unless the most sufficient ransom of Christ's death intervened, he preferred to bring his most beloved Son and the Lord of glory, Christ, into the utmost contempt of a most shameful death, rather than leave sinners wretched, lying under curse and eternal death.

units.la: 6º. Hic declaratur illustri indicio amor filii hominis Christi adversus genus humanum redimendum. Nullum simile amoris exemplum reperias in tota seculorum serie. Fieri equidem potest, ut quis pro justo illustrive benefactore vel amico, mortis periculum subeat, ipsamve mortem oppetat: Sed filius hominis Christus sorti abjectissimæ sese addixit, morti ignominiosissimæ sese tradidit pro peccatoribus famosis rebellibusque inimicis. Adam equidem ipsius typus amoris ergò, quo Evam suam deperibat fecit sese obnoxium iræ atque maledictioni Numinis, miseriisque omne genus: sed pro sponsa charissima, conjuge dilectissima, carne ex carne sua, osse ex ossibus suis, sibi data in laetum juxta ac foecundum abs Numine auxilium. Sed vero filius hominis Christus pro peccatoribus a se sanctissimo quantum maxime distitis, Satanae mancipiis, superbis & acerrimis inimicis. Eja age quotquot filius hominis contemptissima sua forte servili, in gloriosam asseruit liberorum ac Dei filiorum conditionem: redamate filium hominis, omnium filiorum hominum pulcherrimum, amabilem vestrum liberatorem, qui vestri ergo spreto contemptu, crucem ignominiosam passus est, ut coronam gloriae contemptissima sua spinarum corona texeret vobis & concinnaret in coelo. Nullum non subeatis periculum, nullum non contemptum mundi, ipsius ergo alacres adeatis, ut palam fiat omnibus, vos prae omnibus Deum filiumque hominis sincere diligere, nec non ipsius gloriam deliciis, dignitatibus, gloriae mundi, vitaeque propriae volentes atque lubentes ante ferre, si quis filium hominis Jesum Christum non dilexerit sit anathema maranatha.
units.tr: 6º. Here the love of the Son of Man Christ for the redemption of the human race is declared by a most illustrious sign. You will find no similar example of love in the whole sequence of the ages. It may indeed happen that someone undergoes the danger of death, or even dies, for a just and illustrious benefactor or friend. But the Son of Man Christ delivered himself to the most abject lot and gave himself over to the most shameful death for sinners, infamous rebels and bitter enemies, who were most remote from his holiness. Adam, indeed, his type, by reason of the love with which he loved his Eve, made himself liable to the wrath and curse of the Godhead, and to every kind of misery; but that was for a most dear bride, a beloved spouse, flesh of his flesh and bone of his bones, given to him as a help, joyful and fruitful, by God. But the Son of Man Christ died for sinners who were Satan's slaves, proud and fierce enemies, very far from his holiness. Come then, all you whom the Son of Man has freed from his most contemptible servile lot and restored to the glorious condition of free men and children of God: love the Son of Man, the fairest of all the sons of men, your beloved deliverer, who for your sake, having despised contempt, suffered the shameful cross, so that from his most contemptible crown of thorns he might weave for you and fashion in heaven a crown of glory. Undergo every danger, and spurn every contempt of the world, approaching them eagerly for his sake, so that it may be made plain to all that you sincerely love God and the Son of Man above all, and that you willingly and gladly prefer his glory to the delights, dignities and glory of the world and to your own life. If anyone has not loved the Son of Man Jesus Christ, let him be anathema maranatha.

units.la: 7°. Quod Deus filium hominis despectissimum ac maledictum visitaverit amica illa visitatione, unde corona gloriae & honoris effloruit, argumento est omni exceptione majore, filium hominis Christum suo statu contemptissimo iram placasse Numinis, Deumque reconciliasse peccatoribus pro quibus mortem gustavit. Iratus Deus acerrimusque vindex peccatorum, filium hominis visitaverat ea visitatione terribili, qua visitat iniquitatem parentum in liberos, ut parentis Adami iniquitatem plecteret in filio Adami Christo: sed ecce visitationem acerbam justitiae & vindictae, admirabilem in modum in amicam ac remuneratricem visitationem commutatam. Filium hominis Deus visitaverat tristi illa visitatione, quae poculum amarae plenum maledictionis ipsi propinabat bibendum: sed ecce ipsemet Deus filium hominis visitavit laeta illa visitatione, quae poculum salutis & exultationis propinavit ad hauriendum, unde eum laetabundum audias exclamantem, Jehova est pars hereditatis meae & calicis mei, funes in jucundis cecidere mihi, & pulchra est hereditas mea, Psal. 16: 5.6. Filium hominis Numen visitaverat, ut infra angelos abjectum, durissimum juxta ac vilissimum servitium serviret, fami, siti, paupertati, legi, maledictioni & morti obnoxius: sed vero vicibus mutatis, idemmet Numen filium hominis visitavit, ut erepti dura illa servitute, omnia subjiceret pedibus ejus. Filium hominis Deus visitaverat, ut opprobrio hominum, Diaboli ludibrio expositus, corona spinea redimitus, mortalium omnium contemptissimus foret & videretur. Ast tandem post nubila Phoebus, Deus sol beneficentissimus filium hominis visitavit, ut gloria & honore coronaret. Eum equidem Numen sanctissimum, ut in ejus scelera animadverteret, nunquam ac nusquam visitaverat: erat enim sanctissimus sine labe & macula, Deo fidentissimus juxta ac obsequentissimus ad diram usque mortem crucis: eum igitur visitaverat tanquam vadem Novi foederis, caput & principem salutis, adducentem in gloriam filios multos per passiones consummatum, Hebr. 2: 10. Quod igitur Numen postmodum eum visitavit amico ac benefico accessu; sua illa amica visitatione luculenter declaravit, filium hominis sua perpessione contemptissima cumulatè satisfecisse justitiæ suæ vindicatrici, iram placasse Numinis, Deumque reconciliasse iis, quorum princeps est authorque salutis: hinc Christus dicitur propitiatorium per fidem in sanguine suo, Rom. 3: 25. Propitiatio pro peccatis nostris & totius mundi, 1 Joh. 2: 2. Pax nostra Ephes. 2: 14. Princeps pacis, Es. 9: 5. Melchisedec, Rex justitiæ atque pacis, Heb. 7: 2. Age igitur quotquot in filium hominis à Deo amicè visitatum creditis, ponite metum: nulla enim est condemnatio iis qui sunt in Christo Jesu, Rom. 8: 1. nempe Deum habent in filio hominis amicè visitato, reconciliatum & amicum. Circumspicite quoquoversum, undenam oro mali metus ingruere potest? Ex Deo? Sed verò sicut Deus in filio hominis ignominiosam mortem perpessso, terrifico vos in poenam & vindictam accessu visitaverat, ita & in filio hominis è morte maledicta ac ignominiosa eruto in vitam gloriosam, placatus & amicus, vos visitavit. Unde nam oro mali horror ingruit? Ex parte creaturarum? Absit: Deus enim omnia subjecit pedibus filii hominis, potentissimi vestri liberatoris: Quis nos separabit à charitate Christi? Tribulatio? an angustia? an persecutio? an fames? an nuditas? an periculum? an gladius? Sed in his omnibus superamus plus quam victores propter diligentem nos, Rom. 8: 35. 37.
units.tr: 7. That God visited the lowly and cursed Son of man with that friendly visitation from which the crown of glory and honour blossomed is proof beyond all exception that Christ the Son of man, in his most contemptible condition, appeased the anger of the Godhead and reconciled God to the sinners for whom he tasted death. God, angry and the most fierce avenger of sins, had visited the Son of man with that terrible visitation by which he visits the iniquity of the parents upon the children, so that he might punish the iniquity of the parent Adam in the son Adam, Christ. But behold, the bitter visitation of justice and vengeance was changed, in a wonderful manner, into a friendly and rewarding visitation. God had visited the Son of man with that sad visitation which offered him a cup full of bitter curse to drink; but behold, God himself visited the Son of man with that joyful visitation which offered him a cup of salvation and exultation to drink, so that you hear him crying out in gladness, The LORD is the portion of mine inheritance and of my cup: thou maintainest my lot. The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage, Ps. 16: 5, 6. The Godhead had visited the Son of man so that, cast down beneath the angels, he should serve the harshest and vilest servitude, subject to hunger, thirst, poverty, the law, curse and death; but with the scene changed, the same Godhead visited the Son of man so that, once he was rescued from that hard servitude, he might put all things under his feet. God had visited the Son of man so that, exposed to the scorn of men and the mockery of the Devil, crowned with a crown of thorns, he might be and seem the most contemptible of all mortals. But at last, after the clouds, the sun, the most bountiful God, visited the Son of man so that he might crown him with glory and honour. Indeed, the most holy Godhead never and nowhere visited him to take vengeance for his sins; for he was most holy, without stain or spot, most trusting in God and most obedient even unto the dreadful death of the cross. Therefore God visited him as the surety of the New Covenant, the head and prince of salvation, who, bringing many sons into glory, was made perfect through sufferings, Heb. 2: 10. That God afterwards visited him with a friendly and beneficent approach therefore clearly showed that the Son of man, by his most contemptible suffering, had fully satisfied his avenging justice, appeased the anger of the Godhead, and reconciled God to those of whom he is the prince and author of salvation. Hence Christ is called a propitiation through faith in his blood, Rom. 3: 25; a propitiation for our sins, and also for the sins of the whole world, 1 John 2: 2; our peace, Eph. 2: 14; the Prince of peace, Isa. 9: 5; Melchizedek, King of righteousness and of peace, Heb. 7: 2. Come then, all of you who believe that the Son of man was kindly visited by God, put away fear. For there is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, Rom. 8: 1; that is, they have God in the kindly visited Son of man, reconciled and friendly. Look around on every side: from where, I pray, can the fear of evil come upon you? From God? But truly, just as God, in the Son of man who suffered an ignominious death, visited you with a terrifying approach to punishment and vengeance, so too, in the Son of man raised from the accursed and ignominious death to a glorious life, he visits you, placated and friendly. From where, I ask, does the horror of evil rush upon you? From the part of creatures? Far from it: for God has put all things under the feet of the Son of man, your most powerful liberator. Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword? Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us, Rom. 8: 35, 37.

units.la: 8o. Sicut in amica Dei visitatione ad filium hominis, solidum habemus fidei fundamentum, quo nitatur persuasio de expiatione reatus nostri, & placato nobis Numine: non secus & in effectu istiusmodi amicae visitationis, omnium nempe subjectione pedibus & dominio filii hominis, inconcussum sese aperit alterum fidei nostrae fundamentum, quo plenè persuadeamur, fore ut nihil impediat quo minus vitae & salutis æternæ fiamus participes, cum omnia, nulla excepta creatura, obnoxia sint & addicta dominio filii hominis servatoris nostri. Si voluntatem & amorem, ut velit nos efficere salutis suæ participes, in filio hominis desideraveris? Præstò est: qui enim nos dilexit amore, contemptu & morte dirissima fortiore, ut peccatores suo sanguine Deo reconciliaret, anne nos diliget jam Deo reconciliatos, & sibi pretiosò suo sanguine acquisitos? Si authoritatem, qua jure possit hostes nostros compescere, mala cuncta avertere, bona cumulatæ felicitatis procurare? Deus eum coronavit. Si demum potentiam sufficientissimam, ut valeat effecta dare quotquot necessaria sunt bona in nostram felicitatem conferenda? En præsto adest filio hominis robur sufficientissimum, Deus omnia subjecit pedibus ejus. Hinc isthæc gloriatio Pauli, persuasus sum, neque mortem, neque vitam, neque angelos, neque principatus, neque potestates, neque præsentia, neque futura, neque altitudinem, neque profunditatem, neque aliquam aliam creaturam, posse nos separare à charitate Dei, quæ est in Christo Jesu Domino nostro, Rom. 8: 38. 39.
units.tr: 8. Just as in God's friendly visitation of the Son of man we have a solid foundation of faith on which the persuasion of the expiation of our guilt, and of the Godhead being appeased toward us, may rest, so too in the effect of such a friendly visitation, namely the subjection of all things to the feet and dominion of the Son of man, there opens up another unshaken foundation of our faith, by which we may be fully persuaded that nothing will hinder us from becoming partakers of eternal life and salvation, since all things, no creature excepted, are subject to and given over to the dominion of the Son of man, our Saviour. Do you look for his will and love, that he wishes to make us partakers of his salvation? He is at hand: for he who loved us, so that by his blood he might reconcile sinners to God, amid contempt and the most dreadful death, will he not love us, now reconciled to God and acquired for himself by his precious blood? Do you look for the authority by which he can rightly restrain our enemies, avert all evils, and procure for us the goods of a complete happiness? God has crowned him. Do you finally look for the most sufficient power to give the effects, that is, all the good things which are needed to be conferred for our happiness? Behold, the most sufficient strength is at hand for the Son of man: God has put all things under his feet. Hence that boast of Paul: I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord, Rom. 8: 38, 39.

units.la: 9°. Sed & ista omnium subjectio pedibus filii hominis Christi, vobis omnibus fidelibus potentissimum præbet ad obsequium incitamentum: dominatur enim in omnes creaturas princeps salutis vestræ filius hominis, tum quia Deus est super omnia benedictus, tum vestræ felicitatis procurandæ ergo. Et 1°. quidem, filium hominis esse Deum, non factitium, ut blasphemant Socinian: sed verum & æternum, ex ista omnium creaturarum ipsius dominio subjectione pellucet. Qui enim, obsecro, mera creatura finitæ necessariò potentiæ, omnes, nullâ exceptâ, creaturas, vel ipsam mortem, & angelos omnes, continere pedibus suis subditos & obnoxios potis esset? virtus major ac superior virtute omnium creaturarum, non potest non esse increata & infinita. Potentia denique in mortem, qua mortui debellata morte vocantur in dias luminis oras, infinita sit necesse est: quandoquidem nulla vis finita mortuum potest in vitam denuò revocare.
