Cave verò ne filium hominis factitium Deum, cum Socinianis blasphemaveris: nam non minus impossibile est Deum fieri infinitum, quàm creaturam non esse factam finitam ac dependentem. Præterea, quia filius hominis per mortem contemptissimam Deum propitiavit, & peccata expiavit, eum Deus honore & gloria coronavit, subjectis omnibus pedibus ejus, Hebr. 2: 9. Erat igitur Deus, ubi perpessione contemptissimæ mortis, peccata expiavit, & redemit Eeclefiam; unde Paulus, Deus acquisivit Ecclesiam proprio suo sanguine, Act 20: 28. Ipsi igitur filio hominis, quia Deus erat, & Dominus gloriæ crucifixus, Deus omnia subjecit, ut in remunerationem spontaneæ ad mortem crucis obedientiæ, jus exercendi dominium uti Mediator in omnes creaturas referret. Dignus itaque est filius hominis, Deus in secula benedictus, cui omnes obsequiosæ ac reverenter pareant creaturæ. Sed vero, quòd supremum ac universum exerceat dominium, ut felicitate beet electos suos fideles, dedisti enim, inquit ipse, ô Pater, filio potestatem in omnem carnem, ut det vitam æternam omnibus quos illi dedisti, Joh. 17: 2. potentissimus est stimulus omnibus fidelibus in obsequium alacre filio hominis exhibendum. Dominatur in Angelos; sed non ut vitam æternam conferat in ipsos; angeli tamen utut expertes salutis filii hominis, in mandata ejus capessenda volant ambabus alis. Age igitur fideles, mandata filii hominis exequimini, quippe habet omnia subjecta pedibus suis, ut vitam vobis conferat æternum beatam. Cacodæmones, mors, infernus, omnia subjiciuntur ejus pedibus, ut tremebunda ipsi pareant, dum vestram curat felicitatem. Quid vos redemptos & acquisitos infinito proprii sui sanguinis pretio, amicæ suæ voluntati, reluctantes & obnitentes haberet?
units.tr: 9. But this subjection of all things under the feet of the Son of man Christ also offers to you all, the faithful, a most powerful incitement to obedience: for the Son of man, the Prince of your salvation, rules over all creatures, both because he is God over all, blessed for ever, and for the sake of procuring your happiness. And first, that the Son of man is God, not a made God, as the Socinians blaspheme, but true and eternal, shines forth from this subjection of all creatures to his dominion. For what mere creature of necessarily finite power, I ask, could hold all creatures, none excepted, and even death itself and all the angels, subject and bound beneath its feet? A power greater and higher than the power of all creatures cannot but be uncreated and infinite. Finally, the power over death, by which the dead, death having been conquered, are called to the shores of light, must necessarily be infinite, since no finite force can recall the dead to life again. Beware, then, lest with the Socinians you blaspheme the Son of man as a made God: for it is no less impossible for God to become infinite than for a creature not to have been made finite and dependent. Moreover, because the Son of man, by his most contemptible death, appeased God and expiated sins, God crowned him with honour and glory, all things being subjected to his feet, Heb. 2: 9. He was therefore God, when by suffering the most contemptible death he expiated sins and redeemed the Church; hence Paul says, God purchased the Church with his own blood, Acts 20: 28. To the Son of man himself, therefore, because he was God and the Lord of glory who was crucified, God subjected all things, so that, as a reward for his voluntary obedience unto the death of the cross, he might exercise the right of dominion as Mediator over all creatures. Worthy therefore is the Son of man, God blessed for ever, to whom all creatures obediently and reverently submit. But truly, that he exercises supreme and universal dominion so that he may make his faithful elect happy, for you have given him, he says himself, O Father, power over all flesh, that he should give eternal life to as many as you have given him, John 17: 2; this is a most powerful spur to all the faithful to render eager obedience to the Son of man. He rules over the angels, but not so as to confer eternal life upon them; yet the angels, although they have no share in the salvation of the Son of man, fly with both wings to take up his commands. Come then, faithful, carry out the commands of the Son of man, for he has all things subject to his feet so that he may confer on you eternal and blessed life. Evil demons, death, hell: all things are subject to his feet, so that, trembling, they obey him while he cares for your happiness. What would it be like for him to have you, redeemed and purchased at the infinite price of his own blood, resisting and struggling against his friendly will?

units.la: 10. Uti filius hominis loco & bono nostro in sortem usque adeò contemptam adductus est, ut merito Sacer Vates rogaverit, Quid est filius hominū? Portavit nempe languores nostros, & bajulavit dolores nostros, vulneratus propter prævaricationes nostras, & attritus propter iniquitates nostras, Ef. 53:4.5. pariter & loco & bono nostro à Deo fuit visitatus: nos igitur in filio hominis Deus visitavit, pedibus nostris in hoc capite gloriosō omnia subjecit, nos in ipso gloria & honore coronavit. Unde divinus Paulus, Deus nos vivificavit cum Christo, & resuscitavit cum eo, & consedere fecit in cœlestibus in Christo Jesu, Eph. 2: 5.6. Hinc fideles vocantur prædestinati in conformitatem imaginis filii Dei, ut sit primogenitus inter multos fratres, Rom. 8:28. Hæc verò conformitas atque imago duo habet momenta & veluti lineamenta. Alterum contemptum habet & perpessiones varias: alterum exaltationem & gloriam. Hinc conformitatis ejuscemodi nec non communionis ergò, Ecclesia dicitur Jehova Ezech. 48:35. semen mulieris, hoc est filius hominis, Apoc. 12:17. Christus 1. Cor. 12:12. Hæres Dei & cohæres Christi, Rom. 8:17. hoc est, hera adoptionis jure omnium Dei bonorum. Unde Paulus: Omnia vestra sunt, sive Paulus, sive Apollos, sive Cephas, sive mundus, sive vita, sive mors, sive præsentia, sive futura, omnia vestra sunt; vos autem Christi, Christus autem Dei, 1. Cor. 3: 21.22. Hinc fore recipit ut propediem Deus pacis conterat Satana sub pedibus nostris, Rom. 16:20. Hinc Ecclesia regale dicitur sacerdotium 1 Pet. 2:9. Societas regum & sacerdotum Apoc. 1:6. habetque coronam incorruptibilem gloriæ vitæ & justitiæ, h. e. salutis, quam præstolatur Paulus tribuendam à Domino justo judice non sibi modò: sed & omnibus diligentibus apparitionem ipsius. 2 Tim. 4:8. Filio hominis Christo domino gloriæ, qui nos in imaginem suam transformat de gloria in gloriam per spiritum suum, quique demum hocce vile corpusculum nostrum in imaginem corporis sui gloriosi, omnipotenti sua efficacia transformabit, simulatque patri ac Spiritui sancto sit laus, honos & gloria sempiterna. Amen.
units.tr: 10. Since the Son of Man was brought down to a state so despised, for our sake and for our good, the holy prophet rightly asked, What is the Son of Man? He surely bore our griefs and carried our sorrows, he was wounded for our transgressions and bruised for our iniquities, Isa. 53:4, 5. In the same way, for our sake and for our good, he was visited by God. God therefore visited us in the Son of Man, placed all things under our feet in this glorious Head, and crowned us with glory and honour in him. Hence the divine Paul says: God hath quickened us together with Christ, and hath raised us up together, and made us sit together in heavenly places in Christ Jesus, Eph. 2:5, 6. Hence believers are called predestinated to be conformed to the image of the Son of God, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren, Rom. 8:28. This conformity and image has two aspects, as it were two outlines. The one carries contempt and various sufferings; the other, exaltation and glory. Hence, on account of this kind of conformity and communion, the Church is called Jehovah, Ezek. 48:35; the seed of the woman, that is, the Son of Man, Rev. 12:17; Christ, 1 Cor. 12:12; God's heir and co-heir with Christ, Rom. 8:17, that is, by the right of adoption, the heir of all God's goods. Hence Paul: All things are yours; whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come; all are yours; and ye are Christ's; and Christ is God's, 1 Cor. 3:21, 22. Hence she may expect that the God of peace will shortly bruise Satan under your feet, Rom. 16:20. Hence the Church is called a royal priesthood, 1 Pet. 2:9, a society of kings and priests, Rev. 1:6, and she has the crown of incorruptible glory, of life and righteousness, that is, of salvation, which Paul looked for to be given by the Lord, the righteous judge, not to himself only, but also to all who love his appearing, 2 Tim. 4:8. To the Son of Man, Christ the Lord of glory, who transforms us into his image from glory to glory by his Spirit, and who at last will transform this vile body of ours into the image of his glorious body by his almighty power: to him, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be praise, honour and everlasting glory. Amen.

units.la: QUÆSTIO VI. Quid significet videre coelum apertum & ad Filium Hominis?
units.tr: QUESTION VI. What does it mean to see the heavens opened and the angels ascending and descending upon the Son of Man?

units.la: Respondit Jesus & dixit illi, quia dixi tibi videbam te sub ficu credis, majora his videbis. Amen, Amen dico vobis, posthac videbitis coelum apertum & Angelos Dei ascendentes & descendentes ad filium Hominis.
units.tr: Jesus answered and said to him, Because I said to you, I saw you under the fig tree, do you believe? You will see greater things than these. Truly, truly, I say to you, hereafter you will see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man.

units.la: Vti paradisus terrestris, typus fuit illustris coeli, verae felicitatis domicilii. Unde Christus coelestem fœlicitatem fideli & poenitentia ducto latroni polliciturus, Hodie inquit mecum eris in paradiso Luc. 23: 43. Non secus & clausus Adamo reo armatis flammante gladio Cherubim paradisus, expressus fuit ad vivum typus, cœli peccatoribus præclusi, quò prohibente justitia vindicatrice, nullus patet aditus & accessus reis & impuris Adami filiis. Unde divinus Paulus nondum via sanctorum erat propalata stante priore Tabernaculo Heb. 9:8. & Joannes nihil quicquam impurum & faciens abominationem & mendacium in eam (Civitatem nempe sanctam) intrabit Apoc. 21:27. Ignorantia, malitia, crimen, paradisum juxta ac coelum, miseris præclusere mortalibus: sed & latam aperuere abyssi voraginem in quam ruant præcipites, tenebrosis mortis funibus, ferreis pessulis æneisque clastris, luctuosum in modum, coercèndi. Ponite metum & desperationem miserorum ratio. En vobis opportunum solatium, Filius hominis Christus, clavem habet Davidis, aperiens, & nemo claudet, præcludens & nemo aperiet. Apoc. 3:7. Si ignorantiæ tenebris impliciti cæcorum ad instar errabundi cespitatis. Filius hominis Christus clavem habet scientiæ, qua cispelluntur ignorantiæ tenebræ, portaque aperitur lucis, quà latus patet è miseria exitus, lætus in æternam felicitatem ingressus, clavem nempe regni cælorum, quam tradidit Apostolis, ut viam qua itur ad cælum quietam sedem fœlicitatis, fideliter vos docerent. Si nequitiæ vinculis undiquaque irretiti propudiosam servitutem in peccati ergastulo servitis. Filius hominis Christus, clavem habet sanctimoniæ Spiritum sanctum, qui exemptis lege peccati, portam libertatis aperiet, munietmunietque puram viam sanctitatis. Ipse enim via & porta reliquit vobis absolutum virtutum exemplar, ut sequamini vestigia ipsius 1 Pet. 2: 21. Si mortis mancipia, ad ferreum murmur claustrorum inferni, toti horrore contremiscitis, Filius hominis Christus clavem habet inferni & mortis. Noli, inquit, timere; nam mortuus sum, & ecce vivens sum in saecula saeculorum, & habeo claves mortis & inferni, Apoc. 1: 18. Porta inferorum non praevalebunt adversus Ecclesiam meam. Matth. 16: 18. Si coelum, sanctitatis & felicitatis domicilium, vobis in peccatis mortuis juxta ac miseris clausum intuemini; Filius hominis Christus clavem habet coeli: mortuus quippe est ipse justus pro nobis injustis, ut nos duceret ad Deum 1 Pet. 3: 18. libertatem habemus ingrediendi sanctuarium per sanguinem Jesu, viam, quam dedicavit nobis recentem & vivam, per velum, hoc est, per carnem suam. Heb. 10: 19. 20. abundanter vobis subministrabitur introitus in aeternum regnum Domini nostri & Servatoris Jesu Christi. 2 Pet. 1: 11. Nolite obsecro dubitare; ipse enim filius hominis, Amen, testis fidelis & verax, asseveranter pronuntiat, recipitque fore, ut qui credunt, hum esse filium Dei ac regem Israelis, videant coelum apertum ad filium eominis. Respondit Jesus & dixit illi; quia dixi tibi, videbam te sub ficu, credis: majora his videbis. Amen, amen dico vobis, posthac videbitis coelum apertum & Angelos Dei ascendentes & descendentes ad filium hominis.
units.tr: Just as the earthly paradise was an illustrious type of heaven, the dwelling-place of true happiness, so Christ, when he promised heavenly happiness to the faithful and penitent thief, said: Today you will be with me in paradise, Luke 23:43. In the same way, when Adam was guilty, paradise was shut and guarded by cherubim with a flaming sword, a lively picture of heaven closed to sinners, where, with justice exacting vengeance, no entrance or access lies open to the guilty and impure sons of Adam. Hence the divine Paul says: the way into the holy places was not yet made manifest while the first tabernacle still stood, Heb. 9:8; and John: nothing unclean, and nothing that works abomination or lies, shall enter into it (namely the holy city), Rev. 21:27. Ignorance, wickedness and crime have closed paradise, and heaven too, to wretched mortals; they have also opened a wide abyss into which they fall headlong, bound with the dark cords of death, shut in with iron bars and bronze bolts, in a mournful manner. Put away, you wretched ones, your fear and despair. Behold a fitting comfort for you: Christ, the Son of Man, has the key of David, opening and no one shall shut, shutting and no one shall open, Rev. 3:7. If you are caught in the darkness of ignorance and wander like the blind, stumbling about: Christ, the Son of Man, has the key of knowledge, by which the shadows of ignorance are dispelled and the gate of light is opened, through which there is a broad way out of misery and a joyful entrance into eternal happiness; namely the key of the kingdom of heaven, which he gave to the apostles so that they might faithfully teach you the way that leads to heaven, the quiet seat of happiness. If you are bound on every side by the chains of wickedness and serve in shameful slavery in the prison of sin: Christ, the Son of Man, has the key of holiness, the Holy Spirit, who, freeing you from the law of sin, will open the door of liberty and will fortify the pure way of holiness. For he himself is the way and the door; he has left you a perfect pattern of virtues, that you should follow in his steps, 1 Pet. 2:21. If you are slaves of death and tremble with dread at the iron clatter of the bolts of hell: Christ, the Son of Man, has the key of hell and death. Fear not, he says, for I am dead, and behold I am alive for evermore, and I have the keys of death and of hell, Rev. 1:18. The gates of hell shall not prevail against my church, Matt. 16:18. If you look upon heaven, the dwelling of holiness and happiness, as closed to you who are dead in sin and wretched: Christ, the Son of Man, has the key of heaven. For the just died for the unjust, that he might bring us to God, 1 Pet. 3:18. We have boldness to enter into the sanctuary by the blood of Jesus, by a new and living way which he has consecrated for us through the veil, that is, through his flesh, Heb. 10:19, 20. An entrance shall be abundantly supplied to you into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, 2 Pet. 1:11. Do not doubt, I beg you. For he himself, the Son of Man, the faithful and true witness, Amen, solemnly declares and promises that those who believe that he is the Son of God and the King of Israel will see heaven opened upon the Son of Man. Jesus answered and said to him: Because I said to you, I saw you under the fig tree, do you believe? You will see greater things than these. Truly, truly, I say to you, hereafter you will see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man.

units.la: Magnifica isthaec Christi promissio dextre ut elucidetur, haec quaestionum momenta elucidaturis praestringenda videntur. 1°. Cur Jesus Filii hominis nomenclatione sese insignire voluerit. Sed vero functi isthoc labore hactenus, verbum hic non addimus, ne actum agere videamur. 2°. Quid significet videre coelum apertum ad filium hominis. 3°. Quid videre Angelos Dei ascendentes & descendentes ad eum. 4°. Qui coelum apertum videre & Angelos Dei ascendentes & descendentes ad Filium hominis, majora sint iis, quae Nathanael, caeterique discipuli hactenus viderant, hoc est, noverant de Jesu. 5°. Cur inter tot majora, quae de se Jesus revelaverat, visionem simul coeli aperti, simul Angelorum Dei ascendentium & descendentium ad Filium hominis seligere; 6°. denique cur hanc promissionem Jesus duplici Amen, sigillo uti gemino, ratam firmamque esse voluerit.
units.tr: So that this magnificent promise of Christ may be explained well, the following points should be set out, since they will help clarify it. 1. Why Jesus chose to mark himself with the title Son of Man. But since we have so far completed this labour, we will add no further word here, lest we seem to be doing what is already done. 2. What it means to see heaven opened upon the Son of Man. 3. What it means to see the angels of God ascending and descending upon him. 4. Why those who see the heavens opened and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man are greater than what Nathanael and the other disciples had seen until then, that is, had known about Jesus. 5. Why, among so many greater things which Jesus had revealed about himself, he chose to single out the vision of the heavens opened and of the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man together. 6. Finally, why Jesus wanted this promise to be confirmed and made firm with a double Amen, as with a twofold seal.

units.la: Primum, quod attinet promissionem Posthac videbitis coelum apertum magnifica juxta ac difficilis ad intelligendum sedulo perpendenti videtur. Magnifica quidem. 1°. si ipsius Epocham ἀπαρχὴ, ab hoc tempore, attenderimus. Jesus enim extraordinarium quid, & toto seculorum decursu inexpectatum hactenus, promittere se evidenter docet. Viderant, fatebor enim, patriarchae coelum apertum, ut Gen. 28: 17. Viderant & prophetae, ut Ezechiel cap. 1: 1. Viderant & Israelitae in deserto. Deus nempe aperuerat coeli januas, & manna coelitus depluerat. Psal. 78: 23. 24. Coelum vero apertum, quomodo Jesus fore recipit ut discipuli videant, hactenus nemo viderat. Nempe per visionem coeli aperti nec patriarchae, nec prophetae, nec Israelitarum natio noverant, Jesum esse Dei filium & Regem Israelis ea evidentiae luce, qua futurum recipit ut discipuli videant, & credant. Sin secus, promptum erat Nathanaeli reponere: ut quid promittis, nos ab hoc tempore visuros coelum apertum, ut pleniore cognitione imbuti, simul cognoscamus & credamus, te esse filium Dei & regem Israelis; cum patriarchae, prophetae & patres nostri coelum apertum viderint, quorum tamen cognitio & fides de te Messia venturo, infra plenam tui revelationem, in cujus spem nos adducis, longe plane substiterit? 2o. Magnificam jure dixeris promissionem, siquidem cum animo tuo putaveris, hanc coeli aperti visionem, qua futura significatur plena Jesu Filii Dei & regis Israelis revelatio, ingens civisse & inflammasse desiderium Prophetis simul ac Regibus. Unde Petrus: Prophetae scrutati sunt, in quod, aut quale tempus praenuntiu ille, qui erat in ipsis, Christi spiritus, declararet, eventuras Christo perpessiones, & gloriam illas consequuturam. 1 Pet. 1: 11. Et Christus: Dico vobis, multos prophetas & reges cupivisse videre, quae vos videtis, nec vidisse; & audire, quae auditis, nec audivisse. Luc. 10: 24. Quid, quod & Angelorum Dei inflammavit desiderium, movit & meruit admirationem? Unde Petrus ea esse docet, quae Angeli procumbentes in genua avent introspicere. 1 Pet. 1: 12. Unde Paulus in maximè memorabilibus mysterii pietatis articulis & hunc memorat, Deum nempe in carne conspicuum conspectum fuisse Angelis. 1 Timoth. 3: 16. & denique ipse Jesus: Videbitis Angelos Dei ascendentes & descendentes ad Filium hominis. 3o. Magnificam nec immerito dixeris, si coeli aperti visionem pro dignitate putaveris. Admiranda sane coeli aerii apertio, quam Graeci χάσμα, hiatum Latini dixere, (cum nempe obscura profunditas lumine circumfusa sublimis apparet in aere,) non raro mortales in stuporem dedit. Admiranda simul ac miraculosa fuit coeli clausi, tres annos & dimidium ad preces Eliae, apertio. Hinc Rabbinorum scitum, nempe coeli clavem fuisse penes Eliam. Sed vero neutrum Christus hic pollicitus esse videtur. 1o. quia nullae coeli aetherii apertiones, Christum, nedum Jesum esse filium Dei & regem Israelis docuerunt. 2o. quia coelum aerium, cacodaemonum domicilium, non est sedes opportuna Angelis Dei, ut eo ascendant ad Filium hominis, hincve descendant iterum, ut jussa ejus exequantur. Multo igitur admirabilioris, tertii nempe coeli, nobiliorem apertionem Nathanaeli, caeterisque discipulis conspiciendam pollicetur. Quam vero magnifica sint, quae patefactum factum coelum, Dei domicilium, conspicienda exhibet, infitiabitur nemo, siquidem cum animo suo pro dignitate putaverit Majestatem Numinis infinitam, sacrosanctas Divinitatis personas, thronum gloriae, Angelorum myriadas, aeternae mysteria sapientiae, quae oculus non vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in cor hominis ascenderunt, civitatem Dei viventis sanctam Jerosolymam, arborem, fluvium, coronam vitae, manna absconditum, immortalem Dei viventis primogenitorum familiam, haereditatem, quae nec corrumpi potest, nec contaminari, nec marcescere, inexhaustos felicitatis thesauros. Esse vero ad intelligendum difficillimam promissionem, paret 1°. quod Filius hominis, qualem visum intellexerit, corporis, animi, vel utrumque simul, expresse haud declaravit. 2°. quod nec edixit, num realem, num metaphoricam coeli apertionem videndam polliceretur. 3°. quod τῷ ἀπαρχῇ [?], unde quidem implementi promissionis initium sit arcessendum, luculenter significavit; ipsius vero finem ne verbulo quidem designasse videtur. Unde orta sententiarum divortia, aliis in diem transfigurationis, aliis in ascensionis, in descensus Spiritus sancti aliis, aliis in ultimum adventus Christi diem, plenum promissionis implementum, protrahentibus. 4°. quod Euangelistarum, Apostolorum nullius, tantae, tamque magnificae promissionis istiusmodi, complementum memorasse videtur, qui de caetero exacte memoraverint tempestatem, diemque impletarum Christi caeterarum promissionum. Si Christus, se tertia die e mortis potestate exiturum, si se in coelum ascensurum, si missurum Spiritum sanctum, recipit; narrant simul Euangelistae & Apostoli, Jesum primo die hebdomadis exiisse vivum ac victorem potestate mortis, quadragesimo a resurrectione e Bethania in coelum ascendisse, die pentecostes Spiritum sanctum effudisse coelitus in Apostolos. Ubi vero, quando & quomodo coelum apertum discipuli viderint, omnes ex compacto siluisse videntur. Memorant, fatebor enim, Euangelistae, coelum fuisse apertum, ubi Jesus baptismate tingeretur: sed vero haec coeli apertio & jamdiu praeterierat, cum primum hanc coeli aperti visionem utique futuram promitteret; ab hoc tempore videbitis coelum apertum: nec Angeli visi sunt ad Christum descendere: sed Spiritus sanctus sub specie columbae. Caeterum nolito existimare, fidem suam Jesum liberasse, ubi protomartyr Stephanus coelum vidit apertum, & gloriam Dei, & filium hominis adstantem ad dexteram Dei. Act. 7: 55. 56. Nam & haec fuit Martyris singularis praerogativa, & Jesus sancte receperat fore, ut Nathanael, Philippus, caeterique discipuli coelum apertum viderent. 5°. Sententiarum divortia, quam sit ad intelligendum difficilis promissa isthaec coeli aperti visio, neminem sinunt dubitare; aliis realem & corpoream coeli aperapertionem & visionem: aliis vero spiritualem juxta ac metaphoricam præferentibus. Quos equidem si audire malueris, hunc sensum tibi resundet. Futurum est, ut ab hoc tempore liquidè vobis pareat, tanta me pollere rerum divinarum cognitione, adeoque intima frui cum Deo admissione, quasi mihi simul ac vobis cœlum apertum videretis.
units.tr: First, as for the promise Hereafter you will see heaven opened, it seems magnificent, and at the same time difficult to understand, to anyone who weighs it carefully. Magnificent indeed: 1. if we consider its beginning [aparchē], from this time onward. For Jesus clearly teaches that he is promising something extraordinary and hitherto unexpected through the whole course of the ages. The patriarchs, I grant, saw heaven opened, as in Gen. 28:17; the prophets saw it too, as Ezekiel in chapter 1:1; and the Israelites saw it in the wilderness: God had indeed opened the doors of heaven and rained manna from above, Ps. 78:23, 24. But that heaven should be opened in such a way that Jesus promises his disciples will see it, no one had seen until now. For by the vision of an opened heaven neither the patriarchs, nor the prophets, nor the nation of Israel had come to know that Jesus is the Son of God and King of Israel with that clear light of evidence by which he promises that his disciples will see and believe. Otherwise, Nathanael could easily have answered: why do you promise that we, from this time, shall see heaven opened, so that, being filled with fuller knowledge, we may at the same time know and believe that you are the Son of God and King of Israel; when the patriarchs, the prophets and our fathers saw heaven opened, yet their knowledge and faith concerning you, the Messiah to come, fell far short of the full revelation of you, into whose hope you lead us? 2. You may rightly call the promise magnificent, if you think in your mind that this vision of the opened heaven, which signifies the full revelation of Jesus, the Son of God and King of Israel, has kindled and inflamed a great desire in the prophets and kings alike. Hence Peter: The prophets searched what or what manner of time the Spirit of Christ which was in them did signify, when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ and the glories that should follow, 1 Pet. 1:11. And Christ: I tell you, many prophets and kings have desired to see what you see, and have not seen it; and to hear what you hear, and have not heard it, Luke 10:24. What of the fact that this also inflamed the desire of the angels of God, and won their admiration? Hence Peter teaches that these are the things which the angels long to look into, bending down to them, 1 Pet. 1:12. Hence Paul too, in the most memorable articles of the mystery of godliness, mentions this, that God was seen manifest in the flesh by the angels, 1 Tim. 3:16. And finally Jesus himself: You will see the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man. 3. You may rightly and not without reason call the promise magnificent, if you think of the vision of the opened heaven as it deserves. The opening of the aerial heaven, which the Greeks called chasma and the Latins hiatus (when, namely, a dark depth surrounded by light appears high up in the air), has often struck mortals with amazement. Wonderful and miraculous indeed was the opening of the heaven that had been shut for three years and a half at the prayer of Elijah. Hence the saying of the rabbis, that the key of heaven was in the hands of Elijah. But Christ seems to promise neither of these here. 1. Because no opening of the ethereal heaven has taught that Christ, and still less Jesus, is the Son of God and King of Israel. 2. Because the aerial heaven, the dwelling of evil demons, is not a fitting seat for the angels of God, that they should ascend to the Son of Man and then descend again to carry out his commands. He therefore promises his disciples, Nathanael and the others, to behold a far nobler opening of the third heaven, which is more admirable. Nobody will deny how magnificent are the things which the opened heaven, the dwelling-place of God, displays to be seen, if he thinks as he should of the infinite majesty of the Deity, the most holy persons of the Godhead, the throne of glory, the myriads of angels, the mysteries of eternal wisdom which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man; the holy city of the living God, Jerusalem, the tree, the river, the crown of life, the hidden manna, the immortal family of the firstborn of the living God, the inheritance which can neither corrupt nor be defiled nor fade away, the inexhaustible treasures of happiness. That the promise is most difficult to understand is clear: 1. because the Son of Man did not expressly declare what kind of vision he meant, whether of the body, the soul, or both together. 2. because he did not state whether he promised a real or a metaphorical opening of heaven to be seen. 3. because, although he plainly indicated [aparchē], the point from which the beginning of the fulfilment is to be taken, he does not seem to have designated its end even by a single word. Hence arose the divergent opinions, some deferring the fulfilment to the day of the transfiguration, others to the ascension, others to the descent of the Holy Spirit, others to the last day of Christ's coming, the full accomplishment of the promise. 4. because the Evangelists and Apostles seem to have recorded the fulfilment of no such great and magnificent promise, although they have recorded exactly the time and day of the fulfilment of Christ's other promises. If Christ promises that he will come out from the power of death on the third day, that he will ascend into heaven, that he will send the Holy Spirit, the Evangelists and Apostles relate at the same time that Jesus came out alive and victorious over the power of death on the first day of the week, that forty days after his resurrection he ascended from Bethany into heaven, and that on the day of Pentecost he poured out the Holy Spirit from heaven upon the apostles. But when, where and how the disciples saw heaven opened, they all seem by agreement to have kept silent. The Evangelists do record, I grant, that heaven was opened when Jesus was baptized; but this opening of heaven had long since passed, when he first promised that this vision of the opened heaven would come: from this time you will see heaven opened; nor were angels seen descending to Christ, but the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove. Yet do not think that Jesus fulfilled his promise when the first martyr Stephen saw heaven opened, and the glory of God, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God, Acts 7:55, 56. For this was the singular privilege of the martyr, while Jesus had solemnly declared that Nathanael, Philip and the other disciples would see heaven opened. 5. The divergence of opinions shows, and leaves no one in doubt, how difficult this promised vision of the opened heaven is to understand: some prefer a real and bodily opening and vision of heaven, others a spiritual and metaphorical one. If you prefer to hear them, the sense of the promise would be this: It will come to pass that from this time it will become clear to you that I am endowed with so great a knowledge of divine things, and enjoy such intimate admission to God, as if you and I together were seeing heaven opened.

units.la: Nobis, si potè fœliciter eruturis sensum genuinum ejusmodi promissionis, scopus Christi promittentis primùm omnium ob oculos nostros constituendus videtur. Intendit igitur Filius hominis discipulos in spem adducere, fore nempe, ut clariùs intelligant, credantque efficacius, se esse Filium Dei & Regem Israëlis. Sed verò in hunc finem selegit, uti medium opportunum, futuram cœli aperti visionem. Cæterùm cùm prophetæ prænuntiassent, venturum Messiam benedictum fore Dei filium. 2 Sam. 7:14. Psal. 2:7. & 89: 27.28.29.31. summum prophetam, Deut. 18:15.18. pontificem adinstar Melchisedeci. Psal. 110: 4. Regem Psal. 2: 6. & 110: 1. 2. Zach. 6: 13. Jesu in terris agitante, Judæi Messiam quidem prophetam juxta ac Regem præstolabantur: pontificem verò vix ac ne vix quidem putabant. Quod verò Reges, prosapia Davidis orti, prophetas & pontifices simul pompa seculari, simul authoritate præcelluissent; & regia dignitas præconceptis malè Judæorum opinionibus magis allubesceret: ipsi tunc spreto fere Messiæ prophetandi munere, eum modò Regem crepabant. Unde Nathanael ad Jesum: Tu es Filius Dei, tu es Rex Israël. Jam in expedito concludere est, Jesum, qua erat bonitate atque Sapientia, eam cœli aperti visionem discipulis promisisse, qua efficeretur, ut extra dubitationis aleam cognoscerent, ac crederent, eum esse non more quidem regum cæterorum; sed reapse Dei filium & Messiam: non Regem modo; sed & prophetam summum juxta ac pontificem: non Israëlis duntaxat; sed & orbis universi Regem, prophetam, pontificem. Concludamus igitur, Jesum ejusmodi aperturam cœli & visionem fuisse pollicitum, quæ maxime in hunc scopum collimaverit. Posito jam in clara luce Jesu promittentis scopo, ad rem ipsam aggrediamur.
units.tr: Since we hope to bring out successfully the genuine sense of this promise, we must first of all keep before our eyes the aim of Christ in promising it. Christ, the Son of man, therefore intended to bring his disciples into hope: that they would understand more clearly and believe more firmly that he is the Son of God and the King of Israel. To achieve this end he chose, as a suitable means, the future vision of an opened heaven. The prophets had foretold that the blessed Messiah would be the Son of God (2 Sam. 7:14; Psalm 2:7; 89:27–29, 31), the greatest prophet (Deut. 18:15, 18), a priest after the order of Melchizedek (Psalm 110:4), and King (Psalm 2:6; 110:1–2; Zech. 6:13). While Jesus was living on earth, the Jews looked for the Messiah indeed as prophet as well as King, but they hardly thought of him as priest at all. Moreover, since the kings descended from David had excelled in worldly pomp and authority, and also in prophecy and the priesthood, and since the royal dignity was more pleasing to the preconceived and mistaken opinions of the Jews, they then, having almost rejected the prophetic office of the Messiah, proclaimed him only as King. Hence Nathanael said to Jesus: You are the Son of God, you are the King of Israel. It is now easy to conclude that Jesus, in the goodness and wisdom that were his, promised his disciples that vision of an opened heaven by which they would come to know and believe, beyond any shadow of doubt, that he is not merely a king in the manner of other kings, but in truth the Son of God and the Messiah: not only King, but also the greatest prophet and priest; not only King of Israel, but King, prophet and priest of the whole world. We conclude, then, that Jesus promised such an opening of heaven and such a vision as would be most directed to this aim. With the aim of the promising Jesus now in clear light, let us turn to the matter itself.

units.la: Particula ἐπὶ prima omnium pensitanda videtur. Ut enim primo obtutu ad Angelos ascendentes & descendentes unicè referenda judicatur; nihil tamen causæ est, cur quis negaverit, simul ad cœlum apertum, simul ad Filium hominis spectare. Quando enim cœlum beatum est Angelorum Dei domicilium, Angelos in cœlum ascendere, vel è cœlo descendere super filium hominis, quisquam non facile intelliget, quin cœlum esse apertum super filio hominis, & pariter intellexerit. Merito igitur particula ἐπὶ simul ad Angelos ascendentes & descendentes, simul ad cœlum apertum, simul ad Filium hominis spectare nobis videtur. Hinc in promptu concludere est, in multis particulae significationibus, eam esse ad intelligendum hic loci seligendam, quae ad memorata tria, vi procul ac vitilitigatione opportune accommodatur. Plærique omnes ἐπί, super, interpretantur: infeliciter sane. Nam ut crebro usu hunc sensum fundat in novo Instrumento, multa vetant, quominus hic loci hanc valeat significationem sortiri. Et 1°. quidem si coelum apertum super filio hominis intellexeris, etsi verum est, coelum fuisse visum apertum super filio hominis agitante in terris, vel ascendente in coelum: non fuit tamen apertum super filio hominis, quatenus Deus est & filius Dei: est enim vel tertio coelo sublimior, utpote infinitus, & coelum ipsum est ipsius thronus. Isef. 66:1. 2°. Si ad Angelos Dei, ut fieri assolet, particulam referre malueris; verum equidem est, visos fuisse Angelos descendentes super filium hominis, hominem agitantem in terris: ascendentes vero super Filium hominis quipote? Ratione dignitatis? Neutiquam. 1°. quia Angelorum ascensus & descensus juge, quo sunguntur adversus Filium hominis, ministerium significat. Ministros vero Angelos dignitate ascendere super dominum suum, est plane ἀπροσδιόνυσον. 2°. quia haec interpretatio pugnat e diametro cum scopo Christi. Nempe Angelorum ascensu & descensu expedito, discipulos suos docere intendit, se non Israelis modo: sed & Angelorum Dei dominum esse & Regem. Subditos vero super Regem suum reapse ascendere, ut est grande nefas, ita & putare summa est absurditas. 3°. quia profectus in coelum Filius hominis est ad dexteram Dei, subjectus ipsi Angelis, & potestatibus, & virtutibus. 1 Pet. 3:22. Locine ratione visi sunt Angeli ascendisse super Filium hominis? Nihil minus. 1°. quia Filius hominis, vel dum homines alloqueretur in terris, in coelo erat. Joan. 3:13. 2°. quia Filius hominis humanam suam naturam nube vehens, in tertium coelum intulit. 3°. quia dum in coelum ascenderet, Angeli, aurigarum ad instar currui Christi triumphali adstantes, in coelum ascenderunt, ut Filio hominis, sedenti in solio suo, accincti ad obsequium adstarent, ejus mandata prompti & alacres executuri. Nec quicquam causae est, ut cum doctissimo Grotio ad συλλῆψιν confugiamus, ut ἐπί proprie ad καταβαίνουσας referatur. Nempe τὸ ἐπί non super modo; sed & solemni in novo codice biblico usu, ad frequenter significat; ut, ἐπὶ ἔ τόπῳ, ad eum locum Luc. 22:40. εἵλκυσε τὸ δίκτυον ἐπὶ τ γῆς, traxit rete ad terram. Joan. 21:11. Et junctum accusativo, ut hic loci; ut, ἐπὶ τὰ ὄρη, ad montes. Matth. 18:12. ἤγγικεν ἐφ' ὑμᾶς ἡ βασιλεία Θεοῦ, appropinquavit ad vos regnum Dei. Luc. 10:9. ἀναχάμψει ἐφ' ὑμᾶς, revertetur ad vos. Luc. 10:6. ἐπὶ τὰς ἀρχὰς, ad magistratus. Luc. 12:11. τὰ τείχη Ἱεριχὼ ἔπεσε, κυκλω-ῶντα θύντα ἐπὶ ἑπτὰ ἡμέρας, mœnia Iericho conciderunt, circumdata ad dies septem. Heb. 11: 30. προσεκυνήσεν ἐπὶ τὸ ἄκρον τῆς ῥάβδου αὐτοῦ· Et inclinavit se ad extremum virga ejus, nempe Iosephi. Hic enim functum Iacobum adoratione religiosa quominus sentiamus multa vetant. 1°. natura rei: agitur enim de promissione Iosephi. Rogaverat eum obnixè pater longævus, ut ossa ex Ægypto in Canaan adsportaret, conderetque in sepulchro patrum suorum. Quod cum se facturum solemni jurejurando Iosephus recepisset, Iacobus, gratias Filio Iosepho dignas rependens, caput suum ad Iosephi virgam seu sceptrum inclinavit. 2°. quia morti proximus longævus senex & lecto decumbens nihil opus habebat baculo, ut Deum adoraret super fastigio ejus. Quid enim baculo cum lecto senis morituri? Adorationem igitur civilem par est ut intelligamus. 1°. quia voti & postulationis vehementis compos Iacobus, gratias pro beneficio promisso, & juramento firmato, rependere voluit filio suo. 2°. quia necesse fuit, ut divinum plane Iosephi somnium de Sole & Luna ac undecim stellis, ante se procumbentibus, implementum suum sortiretur. Gen. 37: 9. 10. Qui vero, ni hanc Iacobi, Solis mystici, ad Iosephum inclinationem, adorationem civilem intellexeris? Nusquam enim legas, Iacobum procubuisse ante Iosephum, ut somnium plene adimpleretur, si hunc locum Gen. 47: 31. excipias. Nec est insolens in sacro codice, ut virgâ dignitas & authoritas tribuum significetur, ut Gen. 49: 10. Num. 24: 17. Psal. 45: 7. Jerem. 48: 13. Inclinavit igitur caput suum Iacobus ad Iosephum & virgam ejus, simul ut debitas gratias promittenti rependeret, simul ut ejus tribum, ma&ctatam dupla portione hæreditatis terræ Canaan, & primogenituræ honorem, partitam cum tribu Judæ & Levi, solemnem in modum veneraretur. Verùm è diverticulo in viam. Si ἐπί, ad interpreteris, convenit quàm optimè, sive in Filium hominis, sive in cœlum apertum, sive in angelos ascendentes & descendentes referas. Visum nempe est cœlum apertum ad Filium hominis, & visi sunt angeli ascendentes & descendentes ad Filium hominis.
units.tr: The particle ἐπί seems to deserve weighing first of all. At first glance it is judged to refer solely to the angels ascending and descending; yet there is no reason why anyone should deny that it refers at once to the opened heaven and to the Son of man. For since heaven is the blessed dwelling-place of the angels of God, no one would easily fail to understand, and would equally understand, that the angels ascending into heaven or descending from heaven upon the Son of man means that heaven is opened over the Son of man. Rightly, therefore, the particle ἐπί seems to us to refer at once to the ascending and descending angels, to the opened heaven, and to the Son of man. Hence it is easy to conclude that, among the many meanings of the particle, the one to be chosen here is the one that fits these three things suitably and without any strained or contentious argument. Almost all interpret ἐπί as over, and certainly to no good effect. For many things forbid its having this meaning here, though it commonly bears this sense in the New Testament. First, if you understand heaven to be opened over the Son of man, then, although it is true that heaven was seen to be opened over the Son of man while he was living on earth or ascending into heaven, it was not opened over the Son of man insofar as he is God and the Son of God; for he is higher than the third heaven, being infinite, and heaven itself is his throne (Isa. 66:1). Second, if you prefer to refer the particle to the angels of God, as is commonly done, it is indeed true that the angels were seen descending upon the Son of man while he was living on earth; but who would say that they were seen ascending over the Son of man, in respect of dignity? By no means. (1) Because the ascent and descent of the angels, continually carried out on behalf of the Son of man, signify service; and for servant angels to ascend in dignity over their Lord is plainly absurd. (2) Because this interpretation flatly contradicts the aim of Christ. For by the ascent and descent of the angels he intended to teach his disciples that he is not only the Lord and King of Israel, but also of the angels of God. But for subjects to ascend in reality over their King is as great a wickedness as it is an absurdity to suppose. (3) Because the Son of man, having gone up into heaven, is at the right hand of God, made subject to him the angels, and authorities, and powers (1 Pet. 3:22). Were the angels seen to ascend over the Son of man in any sense of place? Nothing less. (1) Because the Son of man, even while he was speaking to men on earth, was in heaven (John 3:13). (2) Because the Son of man, carrying his human nature on a cloud, bore it into the third heaven. (3) Because, while he was ascending into heaven, the angels, standing about the triumphal chariot of Christ like charioteers, ascended into heaven so that they might stand, ready for service, before the Son of man seated on his throne, prompt and eager to carry out his commands. Nor is there any reason, with the most learned Grotius, to take refuge in a συλλῆψις so that ἐπί should be referred properly to καταβαίνοντας. For τὸ ἐπί means not only over but, by the customary usage of the New Testament, frequently means to; as ἐπὶ τὸν τόπον, to that place (Luke 22:40); εἵλκυσε τὸ δίκτυον ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν, he drew the net to the land (John 21:11). It is likewise used with the accusative, as here; as ἐπὶ τὰ ὄρη, to the mountains (Matt. 18:12); ἤγγικεν ἐφ' ὑμᾶς ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ Θεοῦ, the kingdom of God has drawn near to you (Luke 10:9); ἀναχάμψει ἐφ' ὑμᾶς, it will return to you (Luke 10:6); ἐπὶ τὰς ἀρχάς, to the magistrates (Luke 12:11); τὰ τείχη Ἰεριχὼ ἔπεσε, κυκλωθέντα ἐπὶ ἑπτὰ ἡμέρας, the walls of Jericho fell, having been encircled for seven days (Heb. 11:30); προσεκύνησεν ἐπὶ τὸ ἄκρον τῆς ῥάβδου αὐτοῦ, and he bowed himself to the top of his staff, namely Joseph's. For many things prevent us from understanding this to be a religious adoration paid by Jacob. (1) The nature of the matter: for it concerns a promise made to Joseph. His aged father had earnestly asked him to carry his bones out of Egypt into Canaan and bury them in the sepulchre of his fathers. When Joseph had solemnly sworn that he would do so, Jacob, repaying his son with thanks worthy of him, bowed his head to Joseph's staff or sceptre. (2) Because an aged man near death and lying in bed had no need of a staff in order to worship God upon the head of his bed. For what has a staff to do with the bed of a dying old man? We ought therefore to understand a civil reverence. (1) Because Jacob, having obtained his vehement prayer and request, wished to repay his son for the promised benefit and the confirmed oath. (2) Because it was necessary that Joseph's dream about the Sun and Moon and eleven stars bowing down before him should receive its fulfilment (Gen. 37:9–10). But if you do not understand this inclination of Jacob, the mystical Sun, toward Joseph as civil reverence, what will you understand it to be? For you will nowhere read that Jacob bowed down before Joseph, so that the dream might be fully fulfilled, unless you except Gen. 47:31. Nor is it unusual in Holy Scripture for dignity and authority of the tribes to be signified by a staff (Gen. 49:10; Num. 24:17; Psalm 45:7; Jer. 48:17). Jacob therefore bowed his head to Joseph and his staff, both to repay the promised thanks due, and to reverence in the solemn manner the tribe of Joseph, which was favoured with a double portion of the inheritance of the land of Canaan and the honour of the firstborn, sharing this with the tribes of Judah and Levi. But back from the byway to the road. If you interpret ἐπί as to, it agrees most perfectly, whether you refer it to the Son of man, or to the opened heaven, or to the ascending and descending angels. For it was seen that heaven was opened to the Son of man, and angels were seen ascending and descending to the Son of man.

units.la: Explicandum occurrit secundò videre cœlum apertum. Significat verò in utroque instrumento. 1°. in extraordinariam Numinis è cœlo revelationem admitti, qua rerum cœlestium supernaturali cognitione imbuuntur, quotquot sorte divina quovis modo contigit cœlum apertum cernere. Ita Iacob visa per somnium scalâ è cœlo in terram protensâ, Deoque largam benedictionem promittente è summo scalæ fastigio, angelisque Dei ad eam Scalam ascendentibus juxta ac descendentibus, expergefactus extemplò clamat; hic locus est domus Dei, hæc est porta cœli. Gen. 28: 17. Sic Ezechiel, admissus in visionem magnifici currus hominis nempe Christi, vehentis quadrigis Cherubim alatis, oculatis & flammantibus, cœlum apertum fuisse pronunciat Ezech. 1: 1. Sic Stephanus vigilans intentus in cœlum oculis vidit gloriam Dei, & Iesum adstantem ad dexteram Dei & dixit; Ecce video cœlos apertos, & Filium hominis adstantem ad dexteram Dei. Act. 7: 55. 56. Sic Petrus, inter orandum raptus in extasim, conspexit cœlum apertum, ac descendens ad se vas, ut linteum magnum, quatuor extremis devinctum, in quo erant quadrupedia terræ & reptilia, &c. Act. 10: 10. 11. 12. 13. Sic Joannes, ubi admittitur in visionem, visioni Ezechielis plane geminam, portam fuisse apertam in cœlo, ore rotundo pronuntiat Apoc. 4: 1. Denique ubi equum album intuetur, & insidentem equo, vocatum fidelem atque veracem, se cœlum apertum vidisse, asserit Apoc. 19: 10. 11. Non secus & Sathan, nefarius Numinis simiolus, fictis ostentis gentes ut illuderet, cœlum apertum fertur ostentasse. Hinc Servius in illud Æneidos 8. discedere cœlum; In augurali libris, inquit, inter ostenta etiam cœlum discessisse dicitur. Et Livius; Faleriis cœlum findi visum velut magno hiatu, quaque patuerit, ingens lumen effulsisse. Hinc adeo factum, ut ascendere in cœlum scripturæ stylo significet admitti in cognitione rerum supernaturalium. Ita Christus, ut innuat, se unum vel ipso Moyse seclusò, scire cœlestia mysteria, quæ homines doceat; Nemo, inquit, ascendit in cœlum, nisi qui descendit è cœlo, Filius hominis, qui est in cœlo Joan. 3: 13. Moyses, ut præceptum Dei, hoc est justitiam fidei Paulo interprete Rom. 10: 6. non esse occultam & mortalibus inaccessam & imperviam doceat; præceptum hoc, quod ego præcipio tibi hodie, non est occultum, nec longinquum à te. non est in cœlo, ut dixeris; quis ascendet pro nobis in cœlum, qui sumet nobis & annuntiabit illud, ut faciamus. Deut. 30: 11. Secundo cœlum hominibus apertum dicitur, cum Numen benignissimum largas simul & extraordinarias benedictiones cœlitus in eos effundit. Aperiet tibi Jehova thesaurum suum optimum cœlum, dando pluviam terræ tuæ tempore suo, benedicendo cuique operi manus tuæ Deut. 28. 12. Deus Ianuas cœli aperuerat deplueris super eos manna, ut comederent; dederatque frumentum cælorum ipsis, Psal. 78: 23. 24. Hinc Tribunus regis Israelis, quam præNUNTIAVERAT Elizæus futuram abundantiam, ubi incredulitatis vitio negat; Vel si Deus, inquit, faceret fenestras in cælis, an posset esse res ista? 2 Reg. 7: 2. 19. Jam vero si quis in rationem inquirat, cur videre cœlum apertum perhibeantur, qui in extraordinariam Numinis revelationem, rerumque supernaturalium cognitionem admittuntur, & larga vel miraculosa gratiarum affusione donantur? causa in expedito esse videtur. Quando enim naturali lumine omnibus vel Ethnicis compertum fuit, 1°. cœlum esse numinis domicilium, Deumque sapientissimum unum esse arcanorum revelatorem. Dan. 2: 47. Authorem largitorem benedictionis & boni summi; unde Aristoteles fœlicitatem dixit Θεόσδοτον καὶ Θεόπεμπτον. 1 Eth. cap. 10. omne nempe bonum donum supernè descendit à patre luminum. Iacob. 1:17. 2°. omnibus liquidò constat, quæcunque sunt in cœlo reposita, mortalium esse cognitione exempta, velis nempe ambobus occulta, nimirum aërio ac cœlo stellifero; quod Sapientissimum Numen innuere voluit, ubi Templi sanctuarium & cœli extremi typum, gemino velo clausum esse jussit. Cùm igitur, quæ cœlum ambitu suo complectitur, occulta sint mortalibus, in terris agitantibus; rectæ equidem rationi consentaneum est, ut cœlum apertum ii cernere dicantur, quibus simul Numen, simul Numinis Sapientia, voluntas, gratiæ extraordinariæ, cæteraque id genus, quæ cœli ambitu & complexu in totum occultabantur, contrà jam conspicua fiunt atque comperta. 3°. Quando solemni tum veteris, tum novi Instrumenti phrasi, cœlum apertum prophetis dicitur, ut supra audivimus ex Ezechiele & Apocalypsi; nempe quia futurorum cognitione per somnium, visionem vel extasim imbuuntur, arcana Dei & singulari revelatione: meritissime sanè cœlum apertum eos cernere dixerimus, quibus forte divina contingit prophetiarum, typorum & figurarum implementum in clara luce intueri. Matth. 13:17. 4°. Denique si cum animis nostris putaverimus, cœlum, Numinis beatum domicilium, mortalibus homulis inaccessum esse juxta ac clausum, quia nulla intercedit communio lucem inter & tenebras, justitiam & injustitiam. 2 Cor. 6:14. Et caro & sanguis, id est, natura hominis χοϊκὸς καὶ ψυχικὸς, terreni & animalis, non adibunt hæreditatem regni Dei. 1 Cor. 15:46. 47. 50. merito illi cœlum apertum videre perhibentur, simul qui cœlo recipiuntur, ut Elias curru vehens flammeo; simul, qui eos in cœlum ascendentes & admittendos contemplantur, & suspiciunt, ut Elisæus intentis in cœlum oculis raptum & cœlo receptum Eliam intuitus. Hinc Paulus asserit, fideles sortitos libertatem ingrediendi sanctum sanctorum per sanguinem Jesu, viam, quam iis dedicavit recentem & vivam per velum, hoc est, per carnem suam. Heb. 10:19. 20. Et Petrus; Introitum abundanter iis subministratum in æternum regnum Domini & Salvatoris nostri. 2: Pet. 1:11. Et Ioannes; portas Sancta Civitatis, hoc est, cœlestis Ierusalem, nunquam claudendas interdiu Apoc. 21:25. nempe ut semper & undecumque recipiant fideles, in Domino morientes. Superest perpendendum τὸ videre. Vident nempe homines oculis corporeis, quicquid colore vel luce tinctum, vel ex utroque conflatum, oculis solet obversari. Vident & animæ rationalis oculis, intellectu utique speculativo & practico, quotquot sensus corporeos non occupant, causas puta & effecta, finem atque media, virtutem & vitium, rerum σχέσεις ac necessitudines, proportiones tiones & discrimina. Vident & oculis fidei, (quos illustratos intellectus oculos dixit divinus Paulus) quæ animalis homo percipere nequit, divitias nempe hæreditatis in sanctis locis, Eph.1:18. gloriam Domini reteEta facie, 2 Cor.3:18. Vident & oculis prophetiæ, quæ in futurum prospiciunt. Unde prophetæ videntes appellitantur 1 Sam.9:9. 2 Sam.24:11. 2 Reg.17:13. Bileamus, ubi vatem se perhibet, hominem esse se renuntiat, qui oculum habet apertum, Num.24:4. Vident denique oculis gloriæ faciem Dei in justitia, Psal.17:15. & Deum, sicuti est, ad nos videlicet, illustri omnium divinarum promissionum implemento, 1 Joan.3:2.
units.tr: Second, I must explain what it means to "see the heaven opened." This phrase occurs in both Testaments. (1) It signifies an extraordinary revelation of God from heaven, by which those whom God's lot happens to reach in any way, and who see the heaven opened, are filled with supernatural knowledge of heavenly things. Thus Jacob, having seen in a dream a ladder stretched from heaven to earth, with God promising him large blessings from the top of the ladder and the angels of God ascending and descending it, awoke and at once cried out: this place is the house of God, this is the gate of heaven (Gen. 28:17). So Ezekiel, admitted to a vision of a magnificent chariot bearing a man, namely Christ, drawn by winged, eyed and flaming Cherubim, declares that the heaven was opened (Ezek. 1:1). So Stephen, looking intently into heaven, saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand of God, and said: Behold, I see the heavens opened and the Son of man standing at the right hand of God (Acts 7:55, 56). So Peter, while praying, fell into a trance and saw the heaven opened, and a vessel descending to him like a great sheet, bound at the four corners, in which were the four-footed beasts of the earth and creeping things, etc. (Acts 10:10-13). So John, when he is admitted to a vision, very like that of Ezekiel, declares that a door was opened in heaven (Rev. 4:1). Finally, when he looks at a white horse and at the one sitting on it, called Faithful and True, he asserts that he saw the heaven opened (Rev. 19:10, 11). Not otherwise, Satan, that wicked little ape of God, is said to have displayed the opened heaven to deceive the nations with false portents. Hence Servius on the passage of the Aeneid, book 8, the heaven parting: "In the augural books," he says, "among the portents, it is also said that the heaven parted." And Livy: "At Falerii the sky was seen to split as if with a great gaping, and through the opening a huge light shone out." Hence it came about that, in the style of Scripture, to ascend into heaven signifies to be admitted to the knowledge of supernatural things. Thus Christ, to hint that he alone, apart even from Moses, knows the heavenly mysteries which he teaches to men, says: No one has ascended into heaven, except him who descended from heaven, the Son of man, who is in heaven (John 3:13). Moses, teaching that the commandment of God, that is, the righteousness of faith, as Paul interprets (Rom. 10:6), is not hidden, inaccessible and unreachable to mortals, says: This commandment which I command you today is not hidden from you, nor far off. It is not in heaven, that you should say: who will ascend into heaven for us, and take it and announce it to us, that we may do it (Deut. 30:11). (2) Secondly, the heaven is said to be opened to men when God, most kindly, pours out from heaven large and at the same time extraordinary blessings upon them. The Lord will open to you his good treasure, the heaven, giving rain to your land in its season, blessing every work of your hand (Deut. 28:12). God had opened the doors of heaven, and had rained down manna upon them to eat, and had given them the grain of heaven (Ps. 78:23, 24). Hence the captain of the king of Israel, when he denied, through the vice of unbelief, the abundance that Elisha had foretold, said: Even if God were to make windows in the heavens, could this thing be? (2 Kings 7:2, 19). Now, if anyone inquires into the reason why those are said to see the heaven opened who are admitted to an extraordinary revelation of God and to the knowledge of supernatural things, and are endowed with a large or miraculous outpouring of graces, the cause seems plain. For, since it has been known by natural light even to the Gentiles: first, that heaven is the dwelling of the Deity, and that the most wise God alone is the revealer of secrets (Dan. 2:47); second, that he is the giver and bestower of blessing and of the highest good, whence Aristotle called happiness given by God and sent by God [Θεόσδοτον καὶ Θεόπεμπτον] (Nicomachean Ethics, book 1, ch. 10); namely, that every good gift descends from above from the Father of lights (James 1:17). Third, it is clear to all that whatever is laid up in heaven is excluded from the knowledge of mortals, hidden from both eyes, namely by the air and by the starry heaven. This the most wise Deity wished to indicate when it ordered the sanctuary of the Temple, the type of the farthest heaven, to be closed by a double veil. Since, then, what heaven embraces in its compass is hidden from mortals who dwell on earth, it is surely consonant with right reason that those are said to see the heaven opened to whom, at the same time, the Deity, the wisdom of the Deity, his will, extraordinary graces and everything of that kind, which were wholly hidden within the compass and embrace of heaven, now become manifest and known. Third, when in the solemn phrase of both the Old and the New Testament the heaven is said to be opened to the prophets, as we have heard above from Ezekiel and from the Apocalypse, namely because they are filled with knowledge of future things through dream, vision or trance, and with the secrets of God by singular revelation, we may rightly say that they see the heaven opened to whom it happens by divine favour to behold in clear light the fulfilment of prophecies, types and figures (Matt. 13:17). Fourth, finally, if we think in our minds that heaven, the blessed dwelling of the Deity, is inaccessible to mortal creatures and closed, since there is no communion between light and darkness, righteousness and unrighteousness (2 Cor. 6:14), and flesh and blood, that is, the nature of man, earthly [χοϊκὸς] and natural [ψυχικὸς], will not inherit the kingdom of God (1 Cor. 15:46, 47, 50), then those are rightly said to see the heaven opened who are received into heaven, like Elijah carried in a fiery chariot, and at the same time those who behold and look up at them ascending into heaven and being admitted there, like Elisha, who, with his eyes fixed on heaven, saw Elijah taken up and received into heaven. Hence Paul asserts that the faithful, having obtained freedom to enter the holy of holies through the blood of Jesus, have a way which he has dedicated to them, new and living, through the veil, that is, through his flesh (Heb. 10:19, 20). And Peter: an entrance will be richly provided for them into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Saviour (2 Pet. 1:11). And John: the gates of the holy city, that is, of the heavenly Jerusalem, are never to be shut by day (Rev. 21:25), namely so that they may always and from every side receive the faithful who die in the Lord. It remains to weigh the verb videre. Men see with bodily eyes whatever is tinged with colour or light, or made up of both, as usually presents itself to the eyes. The rational soul also sees with the eyes of the intellect, both speculative and practical, whatever does not occupy the bodily senses: causes and effects, end and means, virtue and vice, the relations and connections of things, proportions and distinctions. Men see also with the eyes of faith (which the divine Paul called the eyes of the enlightened understanding) what the natural man cannot perceive: the riches of the inheritance among the saints (Eph. 1:18), the glory of the Lord with unveiled face (2 Cor. 3:18). They see also with the eyes of prophecy, which look forward into the future. Hence the prophets are called seers (1 Sam. 9:9; 2 Sam. 24:11; 2 Kings 17:13). Balaam, when he presents himself as a seer, declares that he is a man who has his eye opened (Num. 24:4). Finally, they see with the eyes of glory the face of God in righteousness (Ps. 17:15), and God as he is, that is, to us, in the clear fulfilment of all divine promises (1 John 3:2).

units.la: Jam vero percunctanti, quomodo Christus discipulos cœlum apertum visuros recepit, omnibus in scopum Christi promittentis rite libratis, nos non piget respondere; omnimodis fore, ut discipuli posthac cœlum apertum videant, hic loci sancte & asseveranter Christum fuisse pollicitum. In hanc vero sententiam gravissima isthæc rationum momenta nos pertraxere. 1°. Par utique est, ut Christus ea notione videre usurpaverit, qua versiculo præcedenti usurpat, dum infit: quia dixi tibi, te videbam sub ficu, credis? majora hisce videbis. Sed vero Nathanael Christum viderat oculis corporeis, viderat & oculis mentis, eum pectoris momenta abditissima pervidentem; viderat & oculis fidei, eum esse Dei filium & Regem Israelis, hoc est, crediderat; credis, infit ad eum Christus. Ad oculos prophetiæ quod attinet, etsi visio prophetica non est per se in salutem prophetæ videntis, est tamen in aliorum salutem perpetuo comparata. Sed vero discipuli Christi non in salutem propriam modo, sed & in salutem aliorum visuri erant cœlum apertum, ut suo de Christo, cœloque aperto, fideli testimonio electos in fidem & salutem sollicitarent & denuo pertraherent. Hinc adeo factum, ut Filius hominis extraordinariis Spiritus e cœlo aperto donis instructos eos, non Apostolos modo; sed & Prophetas & Euangelistas crearit, Eph.4:11. 2°. Quia isthæc cœli aperti visio finis erat juxta ac implementum insigne præteritarum omnium cœli aperti visionum, quæ in hanc ultimam unice proluserant, & uti umbræ in corpus & figuræ in veritatem collineabant. Quod cum Deo demonstrabimus, ubi ventum erit ad hanc quæstionem, cur Christus inter tot majora, quæ videnda, & cognoscenda & credenda de se, discipulis exhibuit, destinato selegerit cœli aperti visionem, &c. 3°. Quia necesse erat, ut discipuli oculis corporeis, mentis, fidei, prophetiæ & gloriæ cœlum apertum viderent ad Filium hominis, ut modis omnibus, quibus fides astruitur rei summi momenti, clare & distincte cognoscerent simul in salutem propriam, simul in aliorum salutem, quod umbratiliter hactenus levique experimento rimento noverant, Jesum nempe esse Dei filium & Regem Israelis, hoc est, Messiam, Prophetam, Pontificem, Regemque, non Israelis modò: sed & totius universi. 4°. Denique si res in experimentum vocetur, clarum fiet atque compertum, Jesu discipulos, cælum apertum vidisse ad Filium hominis, vel etiamnum visuros ad seculorum consummationem memoratis modis omnibus. Atque hic est ultimus labor, nobis impositerum exantlandus ad plenam quæstionis resolutionem.
units.tr: Now, if anyone asks how Christ received the disciples who would see the heaven opened, I am not reluctant to answer, since everything has been correctly weighed against the aim of Christ's promise: that the disciples would henceforth in every way see the heaven opened, Christ having promised this here solemnly and assuredly. Indeed, the following very weighty grounds have drawn us to this view. First, it is fitting that Christ used the word to see in the sense in which he uses it in the preceding verse, where he begins: Because I told you that I saw you under the fig tree, do you believe? You will see greater things than these. But Nathanael had seen Christ with bodily eyes; he had seen him also with the eyes of the mind, perceiving the most hidden movements of the heart; he had seen him also with the eyes of faith, that he was the Son of God and King of Israel, that is, he had believed. Do you believe? Christ says to him. As far as the eyes of prophecy are concerned, although prophetic vision is not in itself for the salvation of the prophet who sees, it is nevertheless always provided for the salvation of others. But the disciples of Christ were to see the heaven opened not only for their own salvation but also for the salvation of others, so that by their faithful testimony concerning Christ and the opened heaven they might stir up the elect to faith and salvation and draw them back again. Hence it came about that the Son of man, having instructed them with the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit from the opened heaven, created not only Apostles but also Prophets and Evangelists (Eph. 4:11). Second, because this vision of the opened heaven was both the end and the remarkable fulfilment of all the earlier visions of the opened heaven, which had merely foreshadowed this last one, and which pointed like shadows to the body and like figures to the truth. We shall show this with God when we come to the question why Christ, among so many greater things to be seen, known and believed about himself, chose for the disciples, as his appointed sign, the vision of the opened heaven, and so on. Third, because it was necessary that the disciples should see the heaven opened to the Son of man with bodily eyes, with the mind, with faith, with prophecy and with glory, so that, by all the means by which faith is established in a matter of the highest moment, they might know clearly and distinctly, both for their own salvation and for the salvation of others, what until then they had known only dimly and by slight experience: that Jesus is the Son of God and King of Israel, that is, the Messiah, Prophet, Priest and King, not of Israel only but of the whole universe. Fourth, finally, if the matter is brought to the test, it will become clear and certain that the disciples of Jesus saw the heaven opened to the Son of man, and that they will still see it, in all the aforementioned ways, until the consummation of the ages. And this is the last labour, to be undertaken by us, for the full resolution of the question.

units.la: Primò, quandoquidem Scripturæ stylo videre cælum apertum significat admitti in consortium & colloquium cum Numine, quo modo Prophetæ memorantur cælum apertum vidisse, & Moyses singulari prærogativa Deum vidisse, non in somnio aut ænigmate, sicut cæteri Prophetæ, sed facie ad faciem & verba cum Deo commutasse, uti fieri assolet inter amicos, Num. 12: 8. Discipuli sane cælum apertum viderunt ad Filium hominis. Nam sensibus corporeis, mentis perceptione & fide clare & distincte noverunt, Christum cum Deo non semel, sed iterum atque iterum familiari usum colloquio & consortio; ubi Numen e cœlo testimonium clara voce perhibere audierunt, Jesum nempe esse Filium suum unigenitum & unice carum, atque ea propter se eum gloria & honore propediem coronaturum, Joh. 11: 41. 42. & 12: 28. 30. Matth. 17: 2. 3. 4. 5. Hinc Johannes; Deum nemo vidit unquam: unigenitus ille filius, qui est in sinu Patris, ille nobis exposuit, Joh. 1: 18. Hinc Christus; Patrem nemo vidit, nisi is, qui est à Deo; hic vidit Patrem, Joh. 6: 42. Hinc Discipuli; oculis nostris aspeximus majestatem illius: acceperat enim à Deo Patre honorem & gloriam, voce ad eum delata hujusmodi à magnifica illa gloria; hic est filius ille meus dilectus, in quo acquiesco. Et hanc vocem nos audivimus e cœlo delatam, cum essemus una cum illo in monte illo sancto, 2 Pet. 1: 16. 17. 18. Contemplati sumus gloriam ejus, gloriam ut unigeniti à Patre, pleni gratia ac veritatis, Joh. 1: 14. Nos credidimus & novimus, te esse Christum illum, filium Dei viventis, Joh. 6: 69. Jesum vero recepisse fore, ut discipuli hoc modo cœlum apertum viderent, liquet 1°. Quia ejusmodi visione clare & distincte intellexerunt, Jesum esse Dei filium, non adoptionis prærogativa, vel tenui similitudinis umbra, uti reges cæteros; sed Dei filium proprium, unigenitum & unice charum, propria essentiæ divinæ communione. 2. Quia isthac cœli aperti visione clare & distincte perspectum habuerunt, Filium hominis, quem Deus e cœlo aperto amice, interdiu, palamque alloqueretur & magnificis futuræ gloriæ promissionibus convenire, verum esse & reale implementum visionis, qua Numen Jacobum solatum ita fuerat, ut lætæ admirationis plenus Patriarcha inclamaret extemplo; templo; hæc est porta cæli. 3o. Quia isthac visione factum est, ut distincte Discipuli noverint, Jesum esse non unigenitum modo Dei Filium; sed & summum Prophetam, quem Moyses audiendum prædixerat, Deut.18:15. Quippe summos viderunt Prophetas ambos Moysem & Eliam e cœlo venisse, ut eum audirent, & Deum audierunt e cœlo imperantem; eum audite, sicuti Moyses prædixerat.Deut.18:15. Præterea isthac cœli aperti visione factum est; ut discipuli clare & distincte intellexerint, Jesum esse summum Pontificem, alba veste summi Pontificis ad instar die solemni expiationum indutum,Lev.16:4. ubi de sacrificio mortis, exitu videlicet, quem habiturus erat Hierosolymis, dissereret. Sed & ea visione compertum fuit discipulis, Jesum esse regem, non modò Israelis, sed cœlestem ipsorum cœlicolarum, Moysis & Eliæ, supremum dominum, admiratis nempe miraculosam gloriam faciei ipsius, solis ad instar coruscantis, vestiumque magnificarum & plane regalium, splendore divino fulgentium instar lucis. Ita enim factum est, ut de Filio hominis, sive ipsius personam, sive munera consideraverint, ea clare & distincte viderint, quæ hactenus mente parum assecuti fuerant, ut longe majore rerum majorum cognitione imbuti in hunc assensum & confessionem pertraherentur, Jesum nempe esse Dei filium, Prophetam, Pontificem & Regem Israelis.
units.tr: First, since in the style of Scripture to see the heaven opened means to be admitted into fellowship and conversation with the Deity, as the prophets are recorded to have seen the heaven opened, and Moses, by a singular prerogative, saw God, not in a dream or a riddle as the other prophets did, but face to face, speaking with God as friends customarily do (Num. 12:8). The disciples certainly saw the heaven opened at the Son of Man. For by their bodily senses, by the perception of the mind and by faith, they clearly and distinctly knew that Christ had not once but again and again enjoyed familiar converse and fellowship with God. There they heard the Deity bear witness from heaven with a clear voice that Jesus was his own only-begotten Son and uniquely beloved, and that for this reason he would soon crown him with glory and honour (John 11:41, 42; 12:28, 30; Matt. 17:2-5). Hence John: "No one has ever seen God; that only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has made him known to us" (John 1:18). Hence Christ: "No one has seen the Father, except he who is from God; he has seen the Father" (John 6:42). Hence the disciples: "We were eyewitnesses of his majesty; for he received honour and glory from God the Father, when such a voice was conveyed to him from that magnificent glory: this is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. And we heard this voice brought from heaven when we were with him on that holy mountain" (2 Pet. 1:16-18). "We have beheld his glory, the glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth" (John 1:14). "We have believed and know that you are that Christ, the Son of the living God" (John 6:69). That the disciples did see the heaven opened in this way is clear, first, because by this vision they understood clearly and distinctly that Jesus is the Son of God, not by the privilege of adoption or a faint shadow of likeness, as other kings are, but the proper Son of God, only-begotten and uniquely beloved, by a proper communion of the divine essence. Second, because by this vision of the opened heaven they clearly and distinctly perceived that the Son of Man, whom God from the opened heaven addressed kindly, by day and openly, and to whom the magnificent promises of future glory belong, was the true and real fulfilment of that vision by which God had comforted Jacob, so that the patriarch, full of joyful wonder, immediately cried out: "This is the gate of heaven." Third, because by this vision the disciples distinctly knew that Jesus is not only the only-begotten Son of God but also the supreme Prophet whom Moses had foretold must be heard (Deut. 18:15). Indeed, they saw the two greatest prophets, Moses and Elijah, come from heaven to hear him, and they heard God commanding from heaven: "Hear him", as Moses had foretold (Deut. 18:15). Moreover, by this vision of the opened heaven the disciples clearly and distinctly understood that Jesus is the supreme Priest, clothed in the white garment of the high priest on the solemn day of atonement (Lev. 16:4), when he discoursed about the sacrifice of his death, namely the departure he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem. By that vision it was also made known to the disciples that Jesus is King, not only of Israel but the supreme Lord even of the heavenly inhabitants, Moses and Elijah. They admired, namely, the miraculous glory of his face, shining like the sun, and his magnificent and truly royal garments, gleaming with divine splendour like light. Thus it came about that, whether they considered the person or the offices of the Son of Man, they clearly and distinctly saw things which until then they had grasped only dimly in mind, so that, imbued with a far greater knowledge of greater things, they were drawn to this assent and confession: that Jesus is the Son of God, Prophet, Priest and King of Israel.

units.la: Secundò, quandoquidem phrasi, in Scriptura solemni, videre cœlum apertum significat admitti in arcana sapientiæ Numinis consilia, quæ Deus iis aperit, quos suo dignatur singulari consortio & alloquio; certo certius est, Discipulos ea nomenclatione vidisse cœlum apertum ad Filium hominis. Perculsi enim profunda admiratione eum viderunt tanta mysteriorum voluntatis Dei imbutum notitia, ut nihil eum fugeret eorum, quæ spectarent vel ad genus mortis, vel ad resurrectionem, vel ad ascensum ipsius in cœlum, vel ad Spiritus Sancti missionem, vel ad generis humani redemptionem, vel ad legis impletionem & abrogationem, vel ad Judæorum rejectionem, vel ad Hierosolymorum & templi excisionem, vel ad Satanæ & idololatriæ abolitionem, vel ad salutarem Ethnicorum vocationem, vel ad cœli mansiones & gloriam immortalem, electis repositam in sanctuario cœlesti: ut non cœlum duntaxat ipsi foret apertum; sed & ipse dum ea revelaret atque doceret, cœlo præsens adesset in sinu ipsius Numinis. Hæc autem Filii hominis clara rerum futurarum & Numinis mysteriorum notitia vel Ethnicos ultro in hanc confessionem adduxit; Nunquam ita locutus est homo, ut homo iste, Joh. 7:46. & discipulos; Nemo Deum vidit unquam; unigenitus ille filius, qui est in sinu Patris, ipse nobis enarravit, Joh. 1:18. Hinc Jesus, ut nemo dubitet, eum esse admissum in arcana sapientiæ Numinis consilia ; Nullus, inquit, ascendit in cœlum, nisi qui descendit è cœlo, nempe Filius hominis, qui est in cœlo, Joh. 3:13. Nemo Patrem vidit, nisi is, qui est à Deo; hic vidit Patrem, Joh. 6:46. Amen, amen, dico vobis; quod scimus, loquimur, & quod vidimus, testamur, Joh. 3:11. Qui è cœlo venit, supra omnes est; & quod vidit & audivit, hoc testatur, Joh. 3:31. 32. & 8:26. Non amplius dicam vos servos, quia servus nescit, quid faciat ipsius Dominus. Vos autem dixi amicos, quia omnia, quæ audivi à Patre meo, nota feci vobis, Joh. 5:15.
units.tr: Second, since in the solemn phrase of Scripture to see the heaven opened means to be admitted into the secret counsels of the wisdom of the Deity, which God discloses to those whom he deigns to honour with special fellowship and converse, it is most certain that the disciples saw the heaven opened at the Son of Man in this sense. Struck with profound wonder, they saw him so imbued with the knowledge of God's mysterious will that nothing escaped him of those things which concern either the kind of death, or the resurrection, or his ascent into heaven, or the mission of the Holy Spirit, or the redemption of the human race, or the fulfilment and abrogation of the law, or the rejection of the Jews, or the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple, or the overthrow of Satan and idolatry, or the saving calling of the Gentiles, or the mansions of heaven and immortal glory laid up for the elect in the heavenly sanctuary. So the heaven was not only opened to him, but he himself, while he revealed and taught these things, was present in heaven, in the bosom of the Deity itself. This clear knowledge of future things and of God's mysteries possessed by the Son of Man even drew the Gentiles, unprompted, into this confession: "No man ever spoke like this man" (John 7:46). And the disciples said: "No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he himself has declared him" (John 1:18). Hence Jesus, so that no one should doubt that he was admitted into the secret counsels of the wisdom of God, says: "No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, namely the Son of Man, who is in heaven" (John 3:13). "No one has seen the Father, except he who is from God; he has seen the Father" (John 6:46). "Truly, truly, I say to you, we speak what we know, and we testify to what we have seen" (John 3:11). "He who comes from heaven is above all; and what he has seen and heard, of this he testifies" (John 3:31, 32; 8:26). "I will no longer call you servants, for the servant does not know what his lord is doing; but I have called you friends, because all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you" (John 15:15).

units.la: Concludamus igitur, discipulos, quam sensibus corporeis, tam mentis ac fidei oculis cœlum apertum ad Filium hominis vidisse. Sed vero hanc cœli aperti visionem Jesum discipulis suis fuisse pollicitum, paret 1°. Quia sic eos docuit, se esse reapse & naturæ æternæ prærogativa alumnum & intimum in sinu Patris filium, utpote cui omnia Numinis arcana forent plane perspecta. 2°. Se esse summum Prophetam, ipso Moyse, nedum omnibus aliis Prophetis superiorem, utpote omnium futurorum plane conscium, atque ea propter verum Messiam. 3°. Quippe ist hac cœli aperti visione ad Filium hominis discipuli clare & distincte intellexerunt, & se & Filium hominis majora videre iis, quæ hactenus viderant. Miraris, Nathanael, & jure quidem merito miraris, me Filium hominis absentem & procul remotum te sub opaca ficu latentem vidisse, penitissima tui, mihi hactenus ignoti, & secreta cordis cogitata penetrasse ac pervidisse. Majora equidem tuque, cæterique discipuli mei videbitis. Terrena hactenus patere mihi latibula vidisti, & arcana cordis πνεύματος esse mihi pervia; universam terram jam mihi cernis apertam. Crede mihi, futurum est, ut in posterum cœlum ipsum mihi esse apertum intueamini, & omnia non hominis, sed & æterna Numinis arcana consilia & secretissimæ voluntatis decreta mihi esse usque adeo pervia, ut singula declarem & aperiam eadem facilitate & perspicuitate, qua significavi, quid & quando sub ficu agitares, quæque sentires clausa in corde tuo sine dolo.
