units.tr: We conclude, therefore, that the disciples saw the heaven opened at the Son of Man not only with their bodily senses but also with the eyes of the mind and of faith. Moreover, that Jesus had promised them this vision of the opened heaven is evident, first, because he taught them that he is in truth, by the prerogative of his eternal nature, the Son who is the intimate one in the Father's bosom, to whom all the secret counsels of the Deity were fully known. Second, that he is the supreme Prophet, superior not only to all other prophets but even to Moses himself, as one fully aware of all future things, and for that reason the true Messiah. Indeed, through this vision of the opened heaven at the Son of Man, the disciples clearly and distinctly understood both that he himself and the Son of Man were seeing greater things than those they had seen until then. "You marvel, Nathanael, and rightly do you marvel, that I, the Son of Man, though absent and far away, saw you hiding under the shady fig tree, and penetrated and fully perceived the innermost things of you, unknown to me until now, and the secret thoughts of your heart. Indeed you and my other disciples will see greater things than these. Hitherto you have seen the hidden places of earth open to me, and the secrets of the heart [πνεύματος] to be accessible to me; now you see the whole earth already open to me. Believe me, it will come to pass that henceforth you will see the heaven itself opened to me, and all the eternal counsels of the Deity, and the most secret decrees of his will, not only of man, to be so accessible to me that I shall declare and reveal each thing with the same ease and clarity with which I indicated what you were doing under the fig tree and what you were feeling, closed in your heart, without deceit."

units.la: Tertiò, siquidem videntes Prophetæ cœlum apertum vidisse memorantur Ezech. 1:1. Apoc. 4:1. & 19:10. 11. & Apostoli ipsi Act. 10: 10. 11. 12. 13. nempe quia per somnium, visionem & extasin futura memoranda in signis, typis & figuris contemplati sunt: jure sane potiori illi cœlum apertum videre censendi sunt, qui implementum Prophetiarum, Typorum & Figurarum liquida in luce ipsarum rerum intuentur. Hujusce modi visionem cœli aperti Jesum promisisse discipulis suis, nemo iverit inficias, qui Johannem audiverit pronunciantem; lex per Mosem data est; gratia & veritas per Jesum Christum præstita est, Joh. 1:17. Gratia & veritas; hoc est, Euangelium, seu gratiosum Fœdus, quod gratia est καὶ ἐξοχὴν, quia veritas est; & veritas, quia finis Legis est, & implementum Prophetiarum, typorum & figurarum, quarum Christus corpus est, Col. 2:17. sicut omnes Dei promissiones, quae in Lege & Prophetiis, umbris & figuris continebantur atque delineabantur implendae olim, in Christo sunt vai ᾿ᾳμὴν, ita & amen; hoc est, sicut in Christo & propter Christum factae sunt, ita in Christo, per Christum & propter Christum ratae & impletae vel demum implendae sunt, 2 Cor. 1:20. Jesum sane recepisse fore, ut discipuli impostorum isthoc modo coelum apertum viderent, nemo prudens negare sustinuerit, quando verissimum est, istiusmodi visionem coeli aperti in scopum Christi promittentis recta tendere & collineare, 1o. quia isthac coeli aperti visione demonstratum est, Jesum esse verum Messiam. Nempe genti Judaicae altum pridem insederat haec sententia, omnes prophetias, promissiones, umbras & ceremonias mysticas in Messia impletum iri juxta nobile Angeli Gabrielis ad Danielem vaticinium, Dan. 9: 24. 25. 26. 27. Nam scripta Mosis & Prophetarum Christo praebent testimonium, Luc. 24: 46. Johan. 5: 39. & 6: 4. Hinc mulier Samaritana; scio, Messiam venturum, qui dicitur Christus. Cum venerit ille, nobis annunciabit omnia, Joh. 4: 25. Hinc Rabbi Schelomo Jarchi in haec verba, hoc fac & vives, Lev. 18: 5. vita, inquit, intelligitur in mundo futuro. Sed vero τὸν οἰκουμένην τὸν μέλλοντα, mundum futurum, regnum esse Messiae apud Judaeos, nemo nescit, Heb. 2: 5. Hinc divinissime factum, ut Christo, loquenti de exitu, qui eum manebat Hierosolymis, Moyses & Elias, legem & prophetas referentes, adstiterint. 2o. quia isthac Coeli aperti visione demonstratum est, Jesum esse summum Prophetam, qui & praedixerit, impletum iri in se, quotquot lex & Prophetae adumbraverant & praenunciaverant, & suam illam praedictionem pleno eventu ipse adimpleverit. 3o. Jesum esse summum Pontificem, qui uno mortis sacrificio peccata expiavit, Numen propitiavit, coelum, Dei sanctuarium, aperuit, quo & ipse intulit sese & viam muniit populo suo, & in se reapse exhibuit, quotquot delineata & adumbrata fuerant in legali Pontifice, victimis, sacrificiis & umbratilibus expiationibus legis. 4o. Jesum esse Regem non Israelis modo; sed & orbis universi, qui potentissima Spiritus sui efficacia, sicuti sceptro potentiae suae regalis perficeret & impleret, quidquid Prophetae praedixerant, typi & ceremoniae adumbraverant, Reges Judae, Israelis, & extranei Cyri, aliique expresserant de Rege Messia, a sole oriente ad occidentem dominaturo. 5o. denique isthac Coeli aperti visione, uti argumento ἀποδεικτικῷ, demonstratum est, Jesum esse reapse Dei filium, qui & polleret potentia infinita, idque daret effectum, quod vires merae creaturæ immane superat, absolutum nempe implementum omnium prophetiarum, typorum & figurarum.
units.tr: Thirdly, the prophets who saw the heavens opened are recorded as having seen them (Ezek. 1:1; Rev. 4:1; 19:10, 11), and so are the Apostles themselves (Acts 10:10–13). They did so because they contemplated future events through dream, vision and ecstasy, recorded in signs, types and figures. By a much stronger right, surely, are those to be judged to see the heavens opened who look on the fulfilment of the prophecies, types and figures in the clear light of the realities themselves. That Jesus promised his disciples a vision of this kind will be denied by no one who has heard John declare: "the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ" (John 1:17). Grace and truth: that is, the Gospel, or the gracious covenant, which is grace by eminence [καὶ ἐξοχὴν] because it is truth; and truth, because it is the end of the Law and the fulfilment of the prophecies, types and figures, of which Christ is the body (Col. 2:17). Just as all the promises of God, which were contained and outlined in the Law and the Prophets, in shadows and figures, to be fulfilled in time, are in Christ yea and amen [ναὶ καὶ ἀμήν]: that is, as they were made in Christ and on account of Christ, so in Christ, through Christ and on account of Christ they have been ratified and fulfilled, or are yet to be fulfilled (2 Cor. 1:20). No sensible person would deny that Jesus intended his disciples to see the heavens opened in this way, since it is most true that this vision of the opened heaven is directed straight at the aim of Christ in promising it. First, because by this vision of the opened heaven it was shown that Jesus is the true Messiah. The Jewish nation had long held the view that all the prophecies, promises, shadows and mystical ceremonies would be fulfilled in the Messiah, according to the noble prophecy of the angel Gabriel to Daniel (Dan. 9:24–27). For the writings of Moses and the Prophets bear witness to Christ (Luke 24:46; John 5:39; 6:4). Hence the Samaritan woman said: I know that the Messiah is coming, who is called Christ. When he comes, he will declare all things to us (John 4:25). Hence Rabbi Solomon Jarchi, on these words, do this and you shall live (Lev. 18:5), says: "life" is understood to mean in the world to come. But that the world to come, the world to come [τὴν οἰκουμένην τὴν μέλλουσαν], is the kingdom of the Messiah among the Jews, no one is ignorant (Heb. 2:5). Hence it was most fittingly arranged that Moses and Elijah, speaking of the departure which awaited him at Jerusalem, stood by Christ, referring to the Law and the Prophets. Second, because by this vision of the opened heaven it was shown that Jesus is the supreme Prophet, who foretold that all that the Law and the Prophets had shadowed and foretold would be fulfilled in himself, and who himself fulfilled that prediction in full outcome. Third, that Jesus is the supreme High Priest, who by the one sacrifice of his death expiated sins, propitiated the Divine Majesty, and opened heaven, the sanctuary of God, by which he himself entered and prepared the way for his people, and actually displayed in himself all that had been outlined and foreshadowed in the legal high priest, the victims, the sacrifices and the shadowy expiations of the Law. Fourth, that Jesus is King not of Israel alone but of the whole world, who by the mighty efficacy of his Spirit, as with the sceptre of his royal power, would perfect and fulfil whatever the prophets had foretold and the types and ceremonies had foreshadowed, and whatever the kings of Judah and Israel, and foreign kings such as Cyrus and others, had expressed concerning the Messiah King, who would rule from the rising of the sun to the west. Fifth and finally, by this vision of the opened heaven, as a demonstrative argument, it was shown that Jesus is truly the Son of God, who possessed infinite power and brought about an effect which far surpasses the strength of a mere creature: namely, the complete fulfilment of all the prophecies, types and figures.

units.la: Quartò, quandoquidem videre Cœlum apertum significat, non omne modo bonum sed & extraordinarium & miraculosum, à patre luminum superne descendens, experiri & persentiscere; quis discipulos simul sensibus corporeis, simul mentis ac fidei oculis vidisse Cœlum apertum ad Filium hominis, cùm in terris, tùm in cœlo agitantem, negare sustinuerit? Nam 1o. quidem, dum Christus in terris versaretur, effusam cœlitus ad Filium hominis divinam benedictionem viderunt, qua omnia ipsis necessaria ad victum & vestitum sufficeret, Luc. 22: 35. stupenda abundantia panes multiplicaret, numerosum populum aleret, ægros omne genus verbo, tactu, nutuque sanitati restitueret, paralyticos firmaret, leprosos mundaret, claudos erigeret, dæmoniacos liberaret, lunaticos, mentisque impotes sui, mentisque compotes faceret, cæcos illuminaret, mortuos vel fœtentes in vitam revocaret, tempestates sonoras, fluctusque furentes componeret, eximeret periclitantibus metum, & sublatis in cœlum manibus benedictionem & Spiritum sanctum iis discessurus impertiretur. 2o. ad Filium hominis, in solio Majestatis sedentem, Cœlum iterum apertum viderunt, ubi abundantissimam Spiritus sancti plenitudinem, è cœlo descendentis die Pentecostes, oculis, sensibusque corporeis hauserunt, eumque experti sunt illuminantem mentis oculos, imbuentem divina ac præpotenti sapientia, donum linguarum, &c. id genus præclara munera in bonum & salutem orbis universi illuminandi, sanctificandi & salvandi conferentem, 1 Cor. 12: 9. 10. Denique Cœlum apertum viderunt ad Filium hominis, ubicunque fusis precibus, manibusque impositis Spiritum sanctum ad nomen Jesu credentes in Christum invadere admirabundi senserunt, & huic quidem conferre sermonem sapientia, alteri sermonem intelligentia, alii fidem, alii donum sanationum, alii virtutum operationem, alii prophetiam, alii discretionem Spirituum, alteri genera linguarum, alii vero earum interpretationem, experti sunt. 1 Cor. 12: 8. 9. 10. Hinc Johannes; ex plenitudine ipsius omnes accepimus & gratiam pro gratia, Joh. 1: 16. & Paulus; dona dedit hominibus, alios quidem dedit Apostolos, alios vero Prophetas, alios autem Euangelistas, alios Pastores & Doctores, ad aedificationem corporis Christi, donec deveniamus omnes in unitatem Fidei & agnitionis Filii Dei, in virum adultum ad mensuram plena statura Christi, Eph. 4: 8. 11. 12. 13. Deus benedixit nobis omni benedictione spirituali in cœlestibus in Christo, Eph. 1: 3. Denique ad Filium hominis, in gloria constitutum, Cœlum apertum viderunt, ubi eum gloria conspicuum modo ad dexteram Dei adstanadstantem contemplati sunt, Act. 7: 55. modo splendore coruscantem & verba referentem è cœlo, ut eos Apostolatu donaret, & luce cœlesti perfunderet, Act. 9: 4. 5. &c. 22: 6. 7. &c. 26: 12. 13. &c. modo Angelos suos mittentem liberatores è carceribus, erutores è periculis, monitores in perplexis, Act. 12: 7. 8. &c. revelationum Christi tabellarios & futurorum eventuum ad ejus nutum prænunciatores fideles, Apoc. 1: 1. Sed verò hanc Cœli aperti visionem hic loci Cristum promittere suis discipulis, nemo prudens negaverit, siquidem in scopum Christi promittentis animum adverterit. Nam in eum perquam opportune conducit. 1°. eos docuit, Jesum esse proprium Dei filium, cœli, sali, solique creatorem ac dominum, ubi omnes creaturas ad nutum ejus componi obsequiose, ubi benedictiones & bona quævis terrena & cœlestia è sinu ejus largiter & jugiter fluere, ubi eum manu omnipotenti mala omnia averruncare, serio apud se reputaverunt. 2°. Jesum esse summum Prophetam ad instar Mosis, ex cujus Spiritu Deus lautam portionem effunderet in homines ad stabiliendam Ecclesiam, novam Israelis secundum Spiritum rempublicam. 3°. Jesum, filium hominis summum esse Pontificem, qui post peractum sacrificium suum finem & complementum jugis sacrificii Levitici, cæterorumque sacrificiorum, pretiosa ac divite benedictione in gratiam & pacem æternam, discipulos suos, Deoque fœderatos, impertiretur; sicuti Aaron, summus Pontifex, post peracta omnia sacrificia sublatis in populum manibus illi benedixerat, Lev. 9: 22. Num. 6: 23. Hinc audias Apostolos, legatione pro Christo, summo Pontifice Novi Fœderis, sungentes, fideles hac benedictione Apostolica impertientes; gratia sit vobis & pax à Deo, Patre nostro & Domino nostro Jesu Christo. 4°. Jesum esse regem non Israelis modo; sed & orbis universi, qui dona sua regalia ex munificentia regali primum in Judæos, postmodum in gentes omnes effunderet, eas in gentem sanctam & regale Sacerdotium evehiceret, vocaretque efficaciter, subditas in regnum admirabilis suæ lucis.
units.tr: Fourthly, since to see the heavens opened means to experience and perceive not merely some good thing, but something extraordinary and miraculous, descending from above from the Father of lights, who could deny that the disciples saw the heavens opened over the Son of Man, active both on earth and in heaven, with their bodily senses and with the eyes of the mind and of faith? For, first, while Christ was living on earth, they saw the divine blessing poured down from heaven upon the Son of Man, by which everything necessary for food and clothing was supplied to them (Luke 22:35); he multiplied bread in wonderful abundance, he fed a great crowd, he restored the sick of every kind to health by word, touch and nod, he strengthened the paralytic, cleansed the lepers, raised the lame, freed the demoniacs, made the lunatics and those without control of their minds sane, gave sight to the blind, called the dead, even those already stinking, back to life, calmed roaring storms and raging waves, removed fear from those in danger, and, with his hands lifted to heaven, bestowed a blessing and the Holy Spirit upon them as he was about to leave. Second, they saw the heavens opened again over the Son of Man sitting on the throne of majesty, where they drank in with their eyes and bodily senses the abundant fullness of the Holy Spirit descending from heaven on the day of Pentecost, and they experienced him enlightening the eyes of their minds, imbuing them with divine and all-powerful wisdom, and bestowing the gift of tongues and the like, splendid gifts conferred for the good and salvation of the whole world, to enlighten, sanctify and save it (1 Cor. 12:9, 10). Finally, they saw the heavens opened over the Son of Man wherever, with prayers poured out and hands laid on, they felt with wonder the Holy Spirit fall upon those who believed in Christ in the name of Jesus, and they experienced that to one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another faith, to another the gifts of healing, to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the discerning of spirits, to another various kinds of tongues, and to another the interpretation of tongues (1 Cor. 12:8–10). Hence John: from his fullness we have all received, and grace upon grace (John 1:16); and Paul: he gave gifts to men: some indeed he gave as apostles, some as prophets, some as evangelists, some as pastors and teachers, for the building up of the body of Christ, until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a mature man, to the measure of the full stature of Christ (Eph. 4:8, 11–13); God has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ (Eph. 1:3). Finally, they saw the heavens opened over the Son of Man, set in glory, where they contemplated him, now standing visibly in glory at the right hand of God (Acts 7:55), now shining with brightness and speaking from heaven, as he gave them the apostolic office and filled them with heavenly light (Acts 9:4, 5, etc.; 22:6, 7, etc.; 26:12, 13, etc.); now sending his angels as deliverers from prisons, rescuers from dangers, and counsellors in perplexities (Acts 12:7, 8, etc.), as faithful bearers of Christ's revelations and announcers of future events at his command (Rev. 1:1). But that Christ, here, promises this vision of the opened heaven to his disciples, no sensible person will deny, if he considers the intention of Christ in promising it. For it leads most fittingly to his purpose. First, it taught them that Jesus is the proper Son of God, the creator and lord of heaven, air and sun, where all creatures obediently stand at his nod, where blessings and all good things, earthly and heavenly, flow abundantly and continually from his bosom, and where he with almighty hand averts all evils; they seriously considered these things among themselves. Second, that Jesus is the supreme Prophet like Moses, from whose Spirit God would pour out a rich portion upon men, to establish the Church, the new commonwealth of Israel according to the Spirit. Third, that Jesus, the Son of Man, is the supreme High Priest, who, after completing his sacrifice, the end and fulfilment of the continual sacrifice of the Levites and of the other sacrifices, would bestow upon his disciples, who were bound in covenant with God, a precious and rich blessing of grace and eternal peace; just as Aaron, the high priest, after all the sacrifices were finished, had lifted his hands over the people and blessed them (Lev. 9:22; Num. 6:23). Hence you may hear the Apostles, serving as ambassadors for Christ, the supreme High Priest of the New Covenant, bestowing this apostolic blessing on the faithful: grace be to you and peace from God our Father and our Lord Jesus Christ. Fourth, that Jesus is King not of Israel alone but of the whole world, who from royal generosity poured out his royal gifts first upon the Jews and afterwards upon all nations, raised them into a holy nation and a royal priesthood, and effectively called them, bringing them into the kingdom of his wonderful light.

units.la: Quintò denique, quando certum est, eos Cœlum apertum videre, tùm qui cœlo recipiuntur, ut Enochus & Elias, tùm qui raptos illos in Cœlum vehentes admirabundi contemplantur, tum denique qui vocem, è cœlo venientem, vel Spiritum, è cœlo descendentem specie visibili, vel cœlicolas, Moysem & Eliam, in terris aliquantisper agitantes, vel Deum Patrem è cœlo loquentem percipiunt, Matth. 3: 16. 17. Matth. 17. 3. 5. ecquis jure negaverit, Christi discipulos vidisse Cœlum apertum ad Filium hominis, qua sensibus corporeis, qua mentis & fidei oculis, ubi Jesum, nube vehentem in cœlum, intentis oculis contemplati sunt, Act. 1: 9. 11. vel demum visuros cœlum apertum ad Filium hominis, ubi descendet cum nubibus, potentia & gloria summa, stipantibus angelorum myriadibus, ut unicuique retribuat secundum opera sua? Matth. 24: 30. 31. Hic vero loci Jesum promisisse hanc Cœli aperti visionem, liquido paret è scopo Christi promittentis, sive visionem Cœli aperti ad Filium hominis ascendentem quadragesimo à resurrectione die, sive futuram novissimam visionem Cœli aperti ad Filium hominis descendentem, judicaturum vivos atque mortuos, cum animis nostris serio putaverimus. 1°. Ubi enim viderunt Cœlum apertum ad Filium hominis, vehentem in nubibus cœli, nulli dubitare potuerunt, quin Jesus foret & Deus & filius Dei, de quo Psaltes; Deus, ascendisti in altum, captivam duxisti captivitatem, dona accepisti hominibus, Psal. 68: 19. 2°. Iesum esse ipsum Messiam, Filium hominis, quem Daniel in visionibus noctis, venientem in nubibus Cœli ad Antiquum dierum viderat, Dan. 7: 13. 3°. Regem non tantum Israelis, sed & omnium gentium, sedentem ad dexteram Dei, Psal. 110: 1. mactatum dominatione, gloria & regno in omnes populos, gentes & linguas, dominioque æterno & ἀπραγέσκατω, nunquam abolendo, Dan. 7: 14. 4°. Summum Pontificem, qui post peractum sacrificium suum propitiatorium, solemni sacrificio expiationum adumbratum, in sanctum sanctorum haut manufactum ingrederetur, adeptus suo sacrificio redemptionem æternam. Summum denique Prophetam ad instar Mosis, qui non in montem aliquem terrenum, sicuti Moses; sed in cœlum, Dei thronum atque domicilium, ascenderet, ut Deum videret facie ad faciem; intima Dei communione non dies quadraginta, sed ad seculorum consummationem fruiturus. Novissimam vero Cœli aperti visionem die decretoria futuram, cum Filius hominis descendet ad ultimum judicium, ad Christi promittentis scopum apprime conducere, nemo non videt. Nam 1°. Cœli aperti visio omni oculo demonstrabit, Iesum esse Messiam. Descendet enim cum nubibus cœli sicuti cum nubibus cœli ascenderat, Act. 1: 9. 2°. Esse Deum. Veniet enim satellitio angelorum Dei & suorum stipatus, veniet sedens in throno gloriæ suæ, Matth. 25: 31. veniet in nube, curru Dei, veniet orbem universum judicaturus, Act. 17: 31. veniet unicuique retributurus secundum opera sua, Matth. 24: 30. 31. erunt igitur illi aperta atque πτεραχηλισμένα intima cordium momenta, ut judicium ferat de fide simul atque incredulitate, charitate adversus Deum vel inimicitia, veneratione & contemtu Numinis, deque cæteris omnibus humani cordis latebris, quæ puram putam creaturam latent. 3°. Novissima isthæc ad Filium hominis Cœli aperti visio omnibus facit compertum, Jesum esse regem omnium creaturarum, angelorum, lorum, quos habebit ministros & apparitores ad omnes homines judicandos, quos à dextris & sinistris suis constituet. Tunc enim rex dicet iis, qui ad dexteram ipsius erunt; adeste, benedicti patris mei, &c. Matth. 25: 34. 4°. Esse summum Prophetam, vel ex ipso implemento prophetiæ suæ de adventu in judicium, Matth. 24: 30. 31. 5°. Denique esse summum orbis universi Pontificem, adumbratum in Pontifice Levitico, qui in sanctuarium cœleste ingredietur non cum nominibus populi sui, exaratis in lapillis pretiosis; sed cum universa Ecclesia sua in apertum Cœlum, verum sanctuarium intromittenda. Rapiemur enim simul cum mortuis excitatis in nubes in occursum Domini in aëra, & ita semper cum Domino erimus, 1 Thess. 4: 17.
units.tr: Fifthly and finally, since it is certain that they saw the open heaven, both those who are received into heaven, like Enoch and Elijah, and those who wonderingly watch those carrying them up into heaven, and also those who perceive a voice coming from heaven, or the Spirit descending from heaven in visible form, or the heavenly inhabitants, Moses and Elijah, staying on earth for a while, or God the Father speaking from heaven (Matt. 3:16, 17; Matt. 17:3, 5), who could rightly deny that Christ's disciples saw the open heaven over the Son of Man, both with their bodily senses and with the eyes of mind and faith, when they gazed intently as Jesus was carried up into heaven on a cloud (Acts 1:9, 11)? Or who could deny that they will see the open heaven over the Son of Man at last, when he comes down with the clouds, in great power and glory, with myriads of angels attending him, to repay each one according to his works (Matt. 24:30, 31)? Now that Jesus promised this vision of the open heaven here is clear from the purpose of Christ in promising it, whether it is the vision of the open heaven when the Son of Man ascended on the fortieth day after the resurrection, or the future final vision of the open heaven when the Son of Man comes down to judge the living and the dead, which we have seriously thought about in our own minds. First, when they saw the open heaven over the Son of Man, coming in the clouds of heaven, they could not doubt that Jesus was both God and the Son of God, of whom the Psalmist says: "God, you have ascended on high, you have led captivity captive, you have received gifts for men" (Ps. 68:19). Second, that Jesus is the Messiah himself, the Son of Man, whom Daniel saw in his night visions coming with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days (Dan. 7:13). Third, that he is king not only of Israel but of all nations, sitting at the right hand of God (Ps. 110:1), granted dominion, glory and kingdom over all peoples, nations and tongues, and an eternal dominion [ἀπραγέσκατον] that will never be abolished (Dan. 7:14). Fourth, that he is the high priest who, after completing his propitiatory sacrifice, prefigured by the solemn sacrifice of atonement, entered the holy of holies not made with hands, having obtained eternal redemption by his sacrifice. And finally, that he is the great Prophet like Moses, who ascended not to some earthly mountain, as Moses did, but into heaven, the throne and dwelling place of God, so that he might see God face to face and enjoy intimate communion with God not for forty days but until the consummation of the ages. Now, that the final vision of the open heaven will take place on the day of judgment, when the Son of Man comes down to the last judgment, is very much to the purpose of Christ's promise; no one fails to see this. For, first, the vision of the open heaven will show to every eye that Jesus is the Messiah, for he will come down with the clouds of heaven just as he went up with the clouds of heaven (Acts 1:9). Second, that he is God. For he will come attended by the host of God's angels and his own, he will come sitting on the throne of his glory (Matt. 25:31), he will come in a cloud, the chariot of God, he will come to judge the whole world (Acts 17:31), he will come to repay each one according to his works (Matt. 24:30, 31). Therefore the innermost movements of hearts will be open and laid bare, so that he may pass judgment on faith and unbelief, love or enmity toward God, reverence and contempt for the divine majesty, and on all the other hiding places of the human heart, which hide a mere creature. Third, this final vision of the open heaven over the Son of Man will make clear to all that Jesus is king of all creatures, of angels, and of men, whom he will have as ministers and attendants to judge all people, and whom he will set at his right hand and left. For then "the king will say to those who are at his right hand: Come, blessed of my Father," etc. (Matt. 25:34). Fourth, that he is the great Prophet, even from the very fulfilment of his prophecy about his coming to judgment (Matt. 24:30, 31). Fifth, and finally, that he is the great High Priest of the whole world, prefigured in the Levitical high priest, who will enter the heavenly sanctuary not with the names of his people engraved on precious stones, but with his whole Church, to be brought into the open heaven, the true sanctuary. For "we shall be caught up together with the dead raised in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord" (1 Thess. 4:17).

units.la: Hactenus explicata Cœli aperti visio viam nobis munit facilem ad solvendam dextre geminam quæstionem, secus ad solvendum difficilem, nempe 1°. Cur Christus ἐπουρανίων quidem nobilissimæ promissionis fixerit τῷ ἀπ' ἀρχῆς, ab hoc tempore; finem vero ipsius & complementum nuspiam significasse videatur. 2°. Cur Euangelistarum, vel Apostolorum nullus magnificæ istius promissionis uspiam complementum expresse declaraverit, cum cæterum exacte memoraverint καιρον, diemque impletarum Christi cæterarum promissionum. Respondemus igitur, memorabilis istius differentiæ nobis hanc videri rationem genuinam, nempe quia præstitutum tempus implemento cæterarum promissionum, v.g. resurrectionis Christi, ascensionis in cœlum, missionis Spiritus sancti in proximo erat futurum propediem. Sed vero implementum hujusce promissionis; ab hoc tempore videbitis cœlum apertum & angelos Dei ascendentes & descendentes ad Filium hominis, non intra angustos temporis limites coercebatur: sed totum complectebatur seculorum decursum, per varios atque multiformes gradus ad seculorum consummationem extendendum.
units.tr: The vision of the open heaven explained so far prepares for us an easy way to resolve two questions, the one from the right side and the other, which is harder to solve, from the left. The first is: why did Christ set the time of this most noble promise [ἀπ' ἄρτι], "from now on", yet nowhere seems to indicate its end and completion? The second is: why did none of the Evangelists or Apostles expressly declare anywhere the fulfilment of this magnificent promise, although they otherwise carefully recorded the time and day of the fulfilment of Christ's other promises? We answer, then, that the genuine reason for this notable difference seems to us to be this: the appointed time for the fulfilment of Christ's other promises, for example his resurrection, ascension into heaven, and the sending of the Holy Spirit, was soon to come. But the fulfilment of this promise, "from now on you will see the open heaven and the angels of God ascending and descending to the Son of Man", was not confined within narrow limits of time; rather it embraced the whole course of the ages, extending through various and manifold stages until the consummation of the ages.

units.la: USUS.
units.tr: USE.

units.la: 1°. Cœlum apertum ad Filium hominis, ut è splendido divinitatis domicilio suo Numen Christum dignetur amico consortio & alloquio, ut è palatio majestatis æternæ Angeli lucis prodeant, Filio hominis debita cum reverentia ministraturi, ubi terra ipsi clauditur, & propudiosum mittit ubique repudium; simul traducit stupendam hominum cœcitatem, flagitiosè spernentium, quem cœlum apertum honore summo afficit & prosequitur, simul diffiat obscuram ignominiæ, probrique nubem, qua Filii hominis intemerata sanctitas & nativa gloria ausu nefario temerata rata obscurabatur. Apage mundum, in malo positum, Deo exosum & inimicum. Cogitationes tuæ non sunt Dei cogitationes, consilia tua, viæque tuæ non sunt consilia aut viæ Dei. Quantum cœlum sublime terræ eminet, tantum supereminent cogitationes, consilia & viæ Dei cogitationibus, consiliis & viis tuis. Ut quid, insane, odisti, quod Cœlum amat impensissime? ut quid temnis, quod Deus honorat? ut quid Christi refugis alloquium, quem Numen consortio & amico dignatur alloquio? ut quid pro vili capite habes, quem angeli, immortales Dei ministri, humiles colunt & venerantur?
units.tr: 1. The heaven was opened to the Son of man so that God, from the bright dwelling of his divinity, would deign to speak with Christ in friendly companionship, and so that the angels of light would come forth from the palace of eternal majesty, ready to minister to the Son of man with the reverence due to him. Where the earth shuts him out and sends him away with shameful rejection everywhere, the open heaven shows him the highest honour and attention. It also disperses the dark cloud of disgrace and reproach by which the spotless holiness and native glory of the Son of man were obscured, having been profaned by wicked daring. Away with the world, which lies in evil, hateful to God and hostile to him. "My thoughts are not God's thoughts, and my ways are not God's ways. As the heaven is higher than the earth, so are God's thoughts, counsels and ways higher than your thoughts, counsels and ways" (Isa. 55:8-9). Why, madman, do you hate what heaven loves most intensely? Why do you despise what God honours? Why do you shun the speech of Christ, whom God deigns to address in friendly companionship? Why do you count as a worthless head the one whom the angels, the immortal ministers of God, worship and venerate in humility?

units.la: 2o. Cœlum apertum ad Filium hominis, ut adorandum Numen è throno majestatis æternæ Christum declaret Filium suum unigenitum, ἀγαπητὸν & unice carum, ut hinc præpetes angeli, eum culturi perpetuo famulitio, descendant & convolent, ut ad ipsius nutum cœlestes omne genus benedictiones affatim in homines diffluant & corriventur; argumentum est omni exceptione majus, Christum esse unigenitum Dei filium, angelorum Dominum, cunctorum Numinis bonorum hæredem, supremum & legitimum cœli possessorem. Christus igitur, vel dum in terris agitaret, jus & autoritatem ἀνυπόδικον habuit simul promittendi, simul dandi cœlum omnibus, fide ἀνυπομένῳ eum requirentibus, ut vel è cruce, infimo suæ ignominiæ gradu, ducto pœnitentia latroni dixerit; amen dico tibi, hodie mecum eris in paradiso, Luc. 23: 43. Cœlum, sibi apertum, omnibus suis discipulis, sincerisque fidelibus Christus sancte pollicitus est, quia ardenti flagrabat desiderio, ut forent omnes in cœlo aperto, ubi ipse est, admissi in contemplationem gloriæ, quam apud Patrem habuit ante mundum conditum. Dicant igitur omnes fideles cum Paulo; Novi, cui credidi-rim, & mihi persuasum est, eum posse depositum meum in illum diem servare, 2 Tim. 1: 12. Certamen præclarum decertavi, cursum ad finem perduxi, fidem servavi. Quod reliquum est, reposita est mihi justitia corona, quam reddet mihi Dominus in illo die justus judex; non solum autem mihi, sed & omnibus iis, qui diligunt illustrem illius adventum, 2 Tim. 4: 7. 8.
units.tr: 2. The heaven was opened to the Son of man so that the adorable God, from the throne of eternal majesty, would declare Christ his only-begotten Son, [ἀγαπητόν] beloved and uniquely dear. Thus the angels, swift to fly down and gather, would serve him with perpetual service, and at his nod heavenly blessings of every kind would flow and pour out abundantly upon men. This is an argument greater than any objection: that Christ is the only-begotten Son of God, the Lord of the angels, the heir of all the good things of God, the supreme and lawful possessor of heaven. Therefore Christ, even while he walked upon the earth, had an unchallengeable [ἀνυπόδικον] right and authority both to promise and to give heaven to all who seek him with faith [ἀνυπομένῳ]. So, even from the cross, the lowest step of his shame, he said to the penitent thief: "Truly I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise" (Luke 23:43). Christ solemnly promised heaven, opened to himself, to all his disciples and sincere faithful, because he burned with the desire that they all should be admitted, where he himself is, into the contemplation of the glory which he had with the Father before the world was made. Let all the faithful therefore say with Paul: "I know whom I have believed, and I am persuaded that he is able to guard what I have entrusted to him until that day" (2 Tim. 1:12). "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day; and not to me only, but also to all who have loved his appearing" (2 Tim. 4:7-8).

units.la: 3o. Cœlum, apertum ad Filium hominis vel dum versaretur in terris, argumentum fuit, Christo pervia fuisse quotquot cœlum ambitu suo complectitur secreta naturaliter & impervia mortalium animis, ut consilia, decreta, voluntatem Dei, sanctitatem & beatitatem cœlestem, omnium plane conscius, & eloqui & docere infallibiliter homines potuerit. Quid igitur vos tenet admiratio, mortalium miserorum natio, cum primum Filium hominis auditis de rebus cœlestibus summa cum παῤῥησίᾳ edisserentem? Omnes perlustravit domicilii parentis sui mansiones cœlestes, divitias inviolabiles thesauros, delicias inexhaustas, gloriae intemeratae coronas immortales, immensas gazas & supellectilem infinitam haereditatis, quae nec contaminari potest, nec marcescere, fidelibus reservatae in coelis. Videt nempe coelum sibi apertum vel dum habitat nobiscum in hocce terreno tabernaculo, & vos vidistis & etiamnum visuri estis coelum apertum ad Filium hominis. Nolite igitur dubitare de veritate doctrinae Christi. Certa sunt, quotquot annunciavit vobis de arcana Dei voluntate, amore paterno Numinis in vos, de divitiis, voluptatibus, coronis & gloria, in salutem vestram perennaturis. Coelum & terra transibunt; sed verbum Christi firmissimum, aeternum permanebit, implemento glorioso veritatem simul ac certitudinem suam omni oculo demonstraturum.
units.tr: 3. The heaven was opened to the Son of man even while he dwelt on earth, which was a sign that everything that heaven encloses within its compass was open to Christ. The secrets which are by nature inaccessible to mortal minds, such as the counsels, decrees and will of God, and the heavenly holiness and blessedness, were fully known to him, so that he could speak of them and teach men infallibly. Why then, wretched race of mortals, do you wonder when you first hear the Son of man speaking of heavenly things with great [παῤῥησίᾳ] boldness? He surveyed all the heavenly mansions of his Father's house, the inviolable riches, the inexhaustible delights, the immortal crowns of undefiled glory, the immense treasures and the infinite inheritance, which cannot be defiled or wither and which are reserved in heaven for the faithful. Indeed, he saw heaven opened to himself even while he dwelt among us in this earthly tabernacle. You have seen, and you are yet to see, the heaven opened to the Son of man. Do not doubt, then, the truth of the teaching of Christ. Certain are all the things he has announced to you concerning the hidden will of God, the fatherly love of God towards you, and the riches, pleasures, crowns and glory that will endure for your salvation. Heaven and earth will pass away, but the most firm word of Christ will remain for ever, and by its glorious fulfilment will show its truth and certainty to every eye.

units.la: 4º. Coelum apertum ad Filium hominis; ut Numen eum e coelo aperto alloqueretur, ut argumentum est, veritatem & religionem, quam Christus instituit, divinam plane esse atque coelestem, ita & argumentum est, nostri esse officii, doctrinae & religioni Christi ita adhaerescere ἀπερι-σπάσως, ut ne latum unguem ab ea unquam discedere sit nobis animus. Si enim Judaei doctrinae & religionis Moysis cultores fuere addictissimi, & observatores tenacissimi hac comprimis ratione, quod scirent, Deum esse locutum Moysi, Joh. 9:29. quam potiori jure nos decet esse Christi discipulos, cui Deum locutum esse à coelo aperto scimus, quando certum est, Deum duntaxat e coelo aerio verba commutasse cum Moyse. Unde Paulus asserit, Deum in tradenda lege locutum esse in terra, Heb. 12:25. quia vel in monte Sinai, vel ab aere, montem ambiente, tum temporis loquebatur. Christum vero filium suum e coelo tertio aperto allocutus est, ut Christi doctrina & religio tanto sublimior sit doctrina & religione Moysis, quanto Coelum, thronusgloriae, aere, montisque cacumine eminet sublimius. Age igitur videte, ne recusetis eum, qui loquitur. Nam si illi non effugerunt, qui recusarunt divinitus loquentem in terra; multo magis nos, qui de coelis loquentem aversemur, Heb.12: 25.
units.tr: 4. The heaven was opened to the Son of man so that God would speak to him from the open heaven. It is an argument that the truth and religion which Christ established are wholly divine and heavenly. It is also an argument that it is our duty to cling to the doctrine and religion of Christ so [ἀπερισπάστως] undistractedly that we never have the intention of departing from it by so much as a hair's breadth. For if the Jews, the most devoted followers and the most tenacious observers of the doctrine and religion of Moses, held fast to it chiefly for this reason, that "we know that God spoke to Moses" (John 9:29), how much more rightly ought we to be disciples of Christ, to whom we know God has spoken from the open heaven? For it is certain that God only changed words from the aerial heaven with Moses. So Paul asserts that God spoke in giving the law on the earth (Heb. 12:25), because at that time he was speaking either on Mount Sinai or from the air surrounding the mountain. But he spoke to his Son from the third heaven, which was opened, so that the doctrine and religion of Christ are as much higher than the doctrine and religion of Moses as the heaven, the throne of glory, rises above the air and the summit of the mountain. "See to it, then, that you do not refuse him who speaks. For if those who refused him who warned them on earth did not escape, how much less shall we escape if we turn away from him who speaks from heaven" (Heb. 12:25).

units.la: 5º. Coelum apertum ad Filium hominis, ut multifariam visum est, ter comprimis apertum in Euangelio memoratur, ut Numen ab aperto coelo ternum Christo ferret testimonium, & multis spectantibus simul & audientibus declararet, Christum esse Filium suum, & primo quidem ad Jordanem, ubi Johannis baptismate tingeretur, Matth. 3:17. secundo in monte sancto, ubi spectantibus selectis tribus discipulis aspectabilem in modum transfiguraretur, Matth. 17:1. &c tertio quinque dies ante ultimum Pascha suum σωρόσιμον[?], Joh. 12:28. Ut quid vero ternum e coelo aperto latum Christo, uti filio Dei, testimonium? Nempe ut tergemino e coelo aperto testimonio abunde Filius Dei & Messias declarareretur, & ternum testimonium terno Christi muneri sapienter responderet, exacte commensuratum. Primum ad Jordanem testimonium, cum in aquam descenderet & totus immergeretur, eum declaravit summum Pontificem, in abyssum maledictionis & mortis ad populum Dei sanctificandum & eruendum e maledictione Dei descensurum. Rom. 10: 7. Quod liquet 1°. quia perhibitum accepit hujusmodi testimonium ineunte anno tricesimo, cum Jesus esset ὠσεὶ ἐτῶν τριάκοντα, Luc. 3: 23. ipso nempe tempore, quo sacerdotes Levitici muneri sacerdotali inaugurabantur, Num. 4: 3. &c. Coll. cum Deut. 24: 8. Josh. 21: 4. 2°. Quia vox Patris e cœlo tum reddita, dixit quidem; tu es filius meus ille dilectus, in quo acquiesco, Luc. 3: 22. sed non addidit; eum audite. Secundum e cœlo aperto testimonium in monte sancto discipulis audientibus Christo perhibitum, eum declaravit Prophetam, Moysi similem, quem Israelitæ audire debebant. Hinc vox Patris extemplo attexuit hoc imperium; eum audite; quod in lato ad Jordanem testimonio desideratur, Deut. 18: 15. Sed vero, quia Moyses, Christi figura, non Propheta modo, sed & rex fuit in Jeschurun, Deut. 33: 5. & summus Pontifex, Psal. 99: 6. qui & victimas immolavit, & Aaronem in Pontificem unxit & consecravit Exod. 29. hinc adeo factum est, quo τυπωθὲν typo suo usque quaque responderet, ut Christus non Propheta duntaxat e cœlo aperto declaratus fuerit; sed & vestium transfiguratione in albedinem nivis æmulam summus Pontifex, Lev. 16: 4. & splendore atque majestate vultus rex creatus fuerit, Matth. 17: 1. &c. Luc. 9: 28. &c. Tertium e cœlo aperto ante ultimum Pascha σωτρόσιμον perhibitum Christo solemne testimonium regem eum declaravit, solemnemque acclamationem popularem, Hosanna, benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini, rex Israelis, confirmavit. Nam cum primum Christus dixit; venit hora, ut glorificetur Filius hominis, Patremque obsecravit his verbis; Pater, glorifica nomen tuum, venit vox e cœlo dicens; & glorificavi, & rursus glorificabo, Joh. 12: 23. 28. Nempe eum Pater in monte sancto glorificaverat. Sed & eum iterum glorificavit, declaratum Filium Dei per resurrectionem e mortuis & curru nubis vehentem, triumphalem in modum cœlo receptum, & in throno majestatis collocatum, ut regnet in omnem carnem, donec omnes inimici facti fuerint scabellum pedum ipsius.
units.tr: 5. As has been shown in many ways, the open heaven is recorded in the Gospel three times, so that God would bear a threefold testimony to Christ from the open heaven and, with many watching and listening, would declare that Christ is his Son. The first time was at the Jordan, where he was baptised by John (Matt. 3:17). The second time was on the holy mountain, where, with three chosen disciples looking on, he was transfigured in a visible manner (Matt. 17:1 etc.). The third time was five days before his last Passover (John 12:28). But why was this threefold testimony from the open heaven given to Christ as the Son of God? Clearly so that the Son of God and the Messiah might be sufficiently declared by a threefold testimony from the open heaven, and so that the threefold testimony would wisely and exactly correspond to the threefold office of Christ. The first testimony, at the Jordan, when he went down into the water and was wholly immersed, declared him to be the high priest who would descend into the abyss of curse and death, to sanctify the people of God and to rescue them from the curse of God (Rom. 10:7). This is clear: first, because he received this testimony at the beginning of his thirtieth year, when Jesus was [ὡσεὶ ἐτῶν τριάκοντα] about thirty years old (Luke 3:23), at the very time when the Levitical priests were inaugurated into their priestly office (Num. 4:3 etc.; compare Deut. 24:8; Josh. 21:4). Second, because the voice of the Father, which was then given from heaven, said indeed: "You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" (Luke 3:22), but did not add: "Hear him." The second testimony from the open heaven, given to Christ in the hearing of the disciples on the holy mountain, declared him to be the Prophet like Moses whom the Israelites ought to hear (Deut. 18:15). Hence the voice of the Father immediately added this command: "Hear him", which is lacking in the testimony at the Jordan. But since Moses, the figure of Christ, was not only a prophet but also a king in Jeshurun (Deut. 33:5) and a high priest (Ps. 99:6), who both offered sacrifices and anointed and consecrated Aaron as priest (Exod. 29), it followed that Christ, in every way corresponding to his [τυπωθέν] type, was declared from the open heaven not only as a prophet, but also as a high priest by the transfiguration of his garments into whiteness rivalling snow (Lev. 16:4), and as a king by the brightness and majesty of his face (Matt. 17:1 etc.; Luke 9:28 etc.). The third solemn testimony given to Christ from the open heaven, a few days before his last Passover, declared him king and confirmed the solemn popular acclamation: "Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the king of Israel." For when Christ first said: "The hour has come for the Son of man to be glorified", and besought the Father with these words: "Father, glorify your name", a voice came from heaven saying: "I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again" (John 12:23, 28). Indeed, the Father had glorified him on the holy mountain. But he glorified him again, by declaring the Son of God through the resurrection from the dead, and by receiving him into heaven in triumph, carried on a cloud, and setting him on the throne of majesty, so that he may reign over all flesh until all his enemies become a footstool for his feet.

units.la: 6°. Sed vero Cœlum ad Filium hominis, ut ter eum Numen palam Filium Dei, supremum Prophetam, Pontificem, Regemque declararet; etiamnum apertum visum est, eum eo nomine ut admitteret in templum, sanctuarium & palatium, Filio Dei Propheta, Pontifice, Regeque æterno uniuniversi dignum : iterumque apertum visum est ad Filium hominis, terno illo è cœlo aperto fungentem officio, Prophetam, Spiritum revelationis mittentem, omnem veritatem docturum Apostolos, orbemque universum in symbolo linguarum ignearum; cœlestem Pontificem, populum suum post peractum solemne propitiationis sacrificium omnigena benedictione cœlesti impertientem; Regem, donis suis regalibus cumulantem subditos, sceptrum potentiæ regiæ è cœlo exserentem, ut orbem suæ ditionis legitimæ faceret, & in medio inimicorum ab oriente in occasum dominaretur.
units.tr: 6. But heaven was opened over the Son of Man so that, three times, the Deity would openly declare him the Son of God, the supreme Prophet, Priest and King. It was also seen that heaven was opened to him for this purpose: that he should be admitted into the temple, the sanctuary and the palace, as one worthy of the eternal Prophet, Priest and King, who is Son of God and worthy of the whole universe. And again it was seen that, for the Son of Man, the opened heaven performed its threefold office: sending the Prophet, the Spirit of revelation, who would teach the Apostles all truth and the whole world by the sign of fiery tongues; the heavenly Priest, bestowing on his people every kind of heavenly blessing after the solemn sacrifice of propitiation had been completed; and the King, heaping his royal gifts upon his subjects and stretching out from heaven the sceptre of royal power, so that he might make the world his lawful dominion and rule in the midst of his enemies from east to west.

units.la: 7°. O terque, quaterque beatos Apostolos, quibus forte divina videre contigit, quæ reges & prophetæ multi, ut ardenter videre cupiverint, nulli tamen viderunt! Luc. 10: 23. 24. Maximus inter natos mulierum Johannes Baptista fuit, nempe quia Christum oculis usurpavit præsentem, dixitque; hic est; Prophetarum ultimus, & Euangelizantium primus, ut eum confinium & horizontem Prophetas inter & Apostolos jure dixeris. At quanto majores Johanne Baptista fuere Apostoli, qui Cœlum apertum viderunt ad Filium hominis, ut in clara luce Cœli aperti, eum esse Dei Filium & Messiam exspectatum, Prophetam, Pontificem, Regemque supremum edocerentur, simul omnium prophetiarum, typorum & figurarum ultimum finem, absolutissimumque implementum?
units.tr: 7. O thrice and four times blessed Apostles, to whom it happened to see divine things which many kings and prophets, however eagerly they desired to see them, never saw! (Luke 10:23, 24.) John the Baptist was the greatest of those born of women, namely because he saw Christ present with his own eyes and said, behold. He was the last of the Prophets and the first of the evangelists, so that you may rightly call him the boundary and horizon between the Prophets and the Apostles. But how much greater than John the Baptist were the Apostles, who saw heaven opened over the Son of Man, so that in the clear light of the open heaven they were taught that he is the Son of God and the expected Messiah, the supreme Prophet, Priest and King, and at the same time the final end and most complete fulfilment of all prophecies, types and figures?

units.la: 8°. Viderunt utique oculis corporeis, mentis & fidei perceptione, ut plene persuasi ipsi omnibus certam fidem facerent & Filii hominis, salutisque, partæ per ipsum, scientiam universum mundum docerent. Hinc eos audias summa cum παῤῥησίᾳ pronunciantes; quod audivimus, quod propriis oculis vidimus, quod contemplati sumus & manus nostræ contrectarunt de sermone vitæ; id annunciamus vobis, Joh. 1: 3. Incassum sane & Christus recepe-rit, eos cœlum apertum visuros ad Filium hominis & sanctis promissis sancte steterit, & fidem suam liberaverit, & Numen è cœlo aperto ter frustra locutum fuerit ipsis audientibus, & spectantibus Filium hominis in cœlum apertum admiserit, & ipsi testes αὐτόπται viderint, contemplati fuerint, manibusque contrectaverint, Jesum Dei Filium, Prophetam, Pontificem, Regemque palam abs Numine declaratum; ni fidem eorum testimonio indubiam habuerimus, eorumque doctrinam, cultumque Christi, uti doctrinam & religionem veram, divinam atque cœlestem, amplexi fuerimus.
units.tr: 8. They saw him with their bodily eyes and perceived him with mind and faith, so that, being fully persuaded, they might give everyone sure faith and teach the whole world the knowledge of the Son of Man and of the salvation obtained through him. Hence you hear them declaring with boldness [παῤῥησίᾳ]: what we have heard, what we have seen with our own eyes, what we have looked upon and our hands have handled, concerning the word of life, that we proclaim to you (John 1:3). Surely Christ would have received in vain, and held firm to his holy promises, that they would see heaven opened to the Son of Man; and he would have freed their faith; and the Deity would have spoken three times from the opened heaven to no purpose in their hearing; and he would have admitted the Son of Man into the opened heaven while they watched; and the eyewitnesses [αὐτόπται] would have seen, looked upon and handled with their hands Jesus, the Son of God, openly declared by the Deity as Prophet, Priest and King, unless we hold their testimony to be certain and embrace their doctrine and the worship of Christ as the true, divine and heavenly doctrine and religion.

units.la: 9°. Re enim vera ideo Cœlum apertum est, ut Filium hominis, Adamum cœlestem admitteret, & sua illa apertione eum Prophetam, Pontificem, Regemque cœlestem declararet, & Spiritum sanctum Numen è cœlo aperto effunderet, ut religionem Christianam cœlitus homines doceret, quò hinc liquido pareret omnibus, doctrinam Euangelii, cultumque Christi, & Numinis, Apostolorum ministerio & præconio constitutum, esse plane spiritualem atque cœlestem. Siquæ igitur doctrina, siquæ religio nomine Christi & Apostolorum veniat, induta veste & specie Ethnicæ vel Mosaicæ religionis, addicta locis, festis, temporibus, carnalibus & mundanis onerata ceremoniis, rebusque terrenis, usu & tempore perituris; facessat ea cum templis suis & altaribus, terrenis sacrificulis, aquis lustralibus, oleis, acerris, suffitibus, cæterisque egenis mundi elementis. Nempe venit hora & nunc est, cum genuini cultores Deum adorabunt in Spiritu & veritate, Joh. 4: 24. juxta formam doctrinæ sanæ, quam è cœlo aperto hausere Apostoli, Christusque Propheta, Pontifex simul ac Rex cœlestis eos docuit; ubi cœlum apertum ad Filium hominis, ascendentem ad dexteram majestatis & Spiritum in terras mittentem, sicut ipse receperat, pleni lætitia non semel, sed iterum, iterumque viderunt.
units.tr: 9. Indeed heaven was opened for this reason: that it might admit the Son of Man, the heavenly Adam, and by that very opening declare him the heavenly Prophet, Priest and King; and that the Deity, the Holy Spirit, might pour out from the opened heaven, so as to teach men the Christian religion from heaven. Thus it might be clear to all that the doctrine of the gospel and the worship of Christ and of God, established through the ministry and proclamation of the Apostles, is altogether spiritual and heavenly. If therefore any doctrine or religion comes in the name of Christ and the Apostles, clothed in the form and appearance of the Gentile or Mosaic religion, bound to places, festivals and times, and burdened with carnal and worldly ceremonies and earthly things destined to perish with use and time, let it depart together with its temples and altars, its earthly little priests, lustral waters, oils, censers, incense, and the other needy elements of the world. Indeed the hour comes, and now is, when true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth (John 4:23). This is in accordance with the form of sound doctrine which the Apostles drew from the opened heaven, and which Christ, the Prophet, Priest and heavenly King, taught them. There they saw heaven opened over the Son of Man, ascending to the right hand of majesty and sending the Spirit into the earth, just as he himself had received him; full of joy, they saw it not once but again and again.

units.la: io°. Verum enim vero isthæc Apostolorum prærogativa omnium Christi discipulorum, quotquot sunt vere fideles, prærogativa singularis est. Nempe oculis corporeis, mentis, fideique perceptione cœlum vident apertum ad Filium hominis, in medio Scripturarum Novi Testamenti. Hinc meritissimo jure, quod Psaltes regius cœlo tribuit Psal. 19: 5. non accommodatione quadam, sed proprio sensu Paulus in sermonem transfudit Apostolorum, Rom. 10: 18. Scilicet Novi Instrumenti Scriptura cœlum nobis apertum est, ubi Pater Christum, Filium suum, amico suo dignatur alloquio, omne ei declarat æternæ suæ voluntatis consilium, ubi cœlum illi aperit nube vehenti triumphalem in modum, ubi eum gloria & honore coronat, ubi Filius hominis Spiritum suum effundit, ubi amorem & pacem reconciliati Numinis nobis aperit, ubi sanctitatem & cœlestem beatitatem ostentat in clara luce. Age igitur, Fideles, Christi discipuli, cœlum apertum in feria lectione & meditatione Scripturarum intueamini, ut gloriosi cœli aspectu rerum cœlestium cognitione imbuti, quotquot mundus ambitu suo complectitur pro vilibus ac despicabilibus retrimentis habeatis. Itaque, si resurrexisti cum Christo, superna quærite, superna sapite, non terrestria: nam vita vestra abscondita est cum Christo in Deo, Col. 3: 1. 2. 3. Age mundus ostentet vobis, quidquid habet pretiosum in divitiis, gratum & amœnum in voluptatibus, gloriosum & æstimabile in dignitatibus suis; ecquid tandem id rei est, ut cum bonis cœli aperti comparari, nedum æquiparari mereatur? Terra vitam animalem, brevi perituram, umbram, somnium, fugacem figuram aperit & ostentat; cœlum vero apertum ad Filium hominis vitam angelicam, æternùm perennaturam promit, atque promittit: terra homulorum societatem, miserorum nationem, Dei inimicorum, Diaboli mancipiorum, in horas mutabilem; cœlum apertum ad Filium hominis Angelorum legiones, filiorum Dei, regum & sacerdotum myriadas, sanctum beatorum & immortalium chorum: terra caducas divitias, fluxas & lutulentas voluptates, honorum fumos, umbrasque fugaces; cœlum vero apertum ad Filium hominis inviolabiles thesauros, puras putas & ab omni dolore secretas, sanctas voluptates, immortales vitæ coronas, hæreditatem, quæ nec contaminari, nec marcescere potest, reservatam nobis in cœlis, ponit ob oculos nostros. Age igitur τὰ ἄνω φρονεῖτε, sit anima vestra in cœlo aperto tota, ubi thesaurus vester in Deo & apud Deum perennans stabulatur. Scutum illud fidei vestræ impenetrabile & imperium cunctis Maligni telis ignitis generosi opponite, ut vita vestra Spiritualis sub illo clypeo illæsa & incolumis sit in tuto. Pollicitationibus bonorum terrestrium, telis ignitis ad inflammandam oculorum, carnisque concupiscentiam, vitæque superbiam oportunis, fidem bonorum cœlestium objicite, obsecro: minarum ignito telo, ad metum inflammandum comparato, auxilium Dei omnipotentis, nunquam è cœlo aperto vobis defuturum: morti denique, extremo & φωσφορωτάτῳ Diaboli telo, vitam spiritualem & gloriosam, repositam vobis in cœlo, milites Christi, generosi, objicite, ut cadant sine ictu omnia mundi & inferni tela ignita. Ut quid, mundus, vana ostentatione fluxorum bonorum eum aggrederis, cui Filius hominis è cœlo aperto æterna bona promittit? Ut quid minis tuis, ad terrorem comparatis, eum tentas & de statu dejicere frustra speras, cui potentissimum Numen è cœlo aperto auxilium suum præsentissimum in tempore oportuno sancte pollicetur? Vocem Filii hominis è dextera majestatis audio ingeminantem; ne metuas: fui quidem mortuus; & ecce vivo in secula seculorum: & habeo claves inferorum & mortis, Apoc. 1: 18. Quis nos separabit à charitate Christi? Num afflictio, num angustia, num persecutio, num fames, num nuditas, num periculum, num gladius? Imo in his omnibus amplius quam victores sumus per eum, qui dilexit nos. Nam mihi persuasum est, neque vitam, neque mortem, neque Angelos, neque principatus, neque potestates, neque præsentia, neque futura, neque sublimitatem, neque profunditatem, neque ullam rem aliam creatam posse nos separare à charitate Dei, quæ est in Christo Jesu, Domino nostro, Amen.
units.tr: 10. Truly, this prerogative of the Apostles is a singular one, belonging to all the disciples of Christ, as many as are truly faithful. With bodily eyes, by the mind and by the perception of faith, they see heaven opened over the Son of Man in the midst of the Scriptures of the New Testament. Hence, by the most fitting right, what the royal Psalmist attributes to heaven (Ps. 19:5), Paul transferred to the words of the Apostles, not by some loose application but in its proper sense (Rom. 10:18). Surely the Scripture of the New Testament is heaven opened to us, where the Father deigns to address his friend, his Son Christ, declares to him the whole counsel of his eternal will, where he opens heaven to him, with a cloud bearing him in triumph, where he crowns him with glory and honour, where the Son of Man pours out his Spirit, where he reveals to us the love and peace of the reconciled Deity, where he displays holiness and heavenly blessedness in clear light. Come then, faithful disciples of Christ, look upon the opened heaven in the daily reading and meditation of the Scriptures, so that, imbued with the knowledge of heavenly things by the sight of glorious heaven, you may count as worthless and despicable refuse all that the world embraces within its compass. So if you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, set your minds on things above, not on earthly things; for your life is hidden with Christ in God (Col. 3:1, 2, 3) [τὰ ἄνω φρονεῖτε: set your minds on things above]. Come, let the world display to you whatever it holds precious in riches, pleasant and delightful in pleasures, glorious and esteemed in its dignities: what, pray, is that thing that deserves to be compared, let alone equated, with the goods of the opened heaven? The earth reveals and displays an animal life, soon to perish, a shadow, a dream, a fleeting figure; but heaven opened over the Son of Man promises and holds out an angelic life, to endure for ever. The earth offers the company of mortals, the nation of wretched people, enemies of God, slaves of the Devil, changeable by the hour; but heaven opened over the Son of Man offers the legions of angels, the sons of God, the myriads of kings and priests, the holy choir of the blessed and immortal. The earth offers fading riches, flowing and muddy pleasures, the smoke of honours and fleeting shadows; but heaven opened over the Son of Man sets before our eyes inviolable treasures, pure and clean, free from all pain, holy pleasures, crowns of immortal life, and an inheritance that can neither be defiled nor fade, reserved for us in the heavens. Come then, set your minds on things above [τὰ ἄνω φρονεῖτε], let your soul be wholly in the opened heaven, where your treasure dwells and abides in God and with God for ever. Hold up against all the fiery darts of the Evil One that impenetrable shield of your faith, so that your spiritual life, safe under that shield, may be unharmed and secure. Against the promises of earthly goods, the fiery darts suited to inflame the lust of the eyes and of the flesh and the pride of life, I beg you, set the faith of heavenly goods; against the fiery dart of threats, prepared to kindle fear, set the help of almighty God, which will never fail you from the opened heaven; and finally, against death, the last and most fiery [φωσφορωτάτῳ] weapon of the Devil, set, O soldiers of Christ, the spiritual and glorious life laid up for you in heaven, so that all the fiery weapons of the world and of hell may fall without a blow. Why, O world, do you attack with vain display of fleeting goods one to whom the Son of Man promises eternal goods from the opened heaven? Why do you try him with your threats, prepared to terrify, and hope in vain to cast him down from his state, when the most powerful Deity holily promises him his most present help from the opened heaven at the right time? I hear the voice of the Son of Man from the right hand of majesty repeating: Fear not; I was dead, and behold, I am alive for evermore, and I have the keys of hell and of death (Rev. 1:18). Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword? Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us. For I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. Amen.

units.la: QUAESTIO VII.
units.tr: QUAESTIO VII.

units.la: Quid significet assensus & descensus Angelorum Dei ad Filium hominis? item qui, & quando discipuli Angelos Dei viderint ascendentes & descendentes ad Filium hominis?
units.tr: What do the ascent and descent of the Angels of God to the Son of Man signify? Likewise, who among the disciples saw the Angels of God ascending and descending to the Son of Man, and when?

units.la: IN admirandis omnibus naturæ operibus primum locum occupat occulta & inviolabilis rerum naturalium ἀπλανὴς χία & sympathia. Longe lateque illa diditur & effunditur. Pervadit & permovet universam fere naturam. Quòd præter naturam gravia sursum feruntur impetu rapidissimo, leviaque corpora infima petunt & invadunt quàm citissime, opus sympathiæ est, ut vitetur vacuum, exitialis lacuna cohærentiæ & occultæ rerum sympathiæ. Quòd fluit, refluitque accessu, recessuque perpetuo Oceanus, opus sympathiæ est, quam colit arctè cum cœlo suo. Quòd succinum paleas, & magnes ferrum, & Septemtrio magnetem, eique affrictam pyxidis lingulam pellicit & pertrahit, occultæ simul & admirandæ sympathiæ opus est, quæ simul vulgus, simul doctos hactenus in stuporem dedit. Nimium, mortales, naturæ occultis dediti, nimium contemplationi causarum sympathiæ naturalis vacastis. Cœlum apertum ad filium hominis longè præstabiliorem & vestra digniorem contemplatione sympathiam promit. Filius hominis, magnes universalis est, qui occulta sua virtute & dignitate pervadit & permovet, allicit & pertrahit mobilissimas quasque creaturas. Quam se mundo manifestaret prius, votis calidissimis inflammata corda regum & prophetarum permovit, traxitque ad sese sui videndi desiderio. Et Ecclesia, eum per cancellos intuita, ad eum exarsit, & in calidissimum hoc votum erupit: utinam disrumpens cœlum descenderes, & montes diffluerent à facie tua! Jef. 64:1. Cuumprimum cœlo descendit Deus, in carne manifestatus, carnis infirmæ humilitas despicabilis nulla tardavit divinissimam Christi vim magneticam. Cœlum sui perculsit admiratione, commovit & aperuit, Angelorum exercitus ad sese allexit, atque pertraxit. Pastorum Bethlehemiticorum tuguria aperuit, & flagranti inflammatos desiderio rapuit ad præsepe suum. Remotum Orientem pervasit & per longa viarum itinera in sui adoraadorationem Magos simul sollicitavit, simul potenter adduxit. Cumprimum baptismate fuit Israeli manifestatus, vim illam suam sympatheticam in tertium cœlum exseruit, id velut admiranda clavis reseravit, cor Patris, vocemque inclamantis, hic est filius meus ille dilectus, pertraxit, deduxit Spiritum sanctum in columbæ speciem, descendentem & recumbentem in caput suum. Transfiguratus in monte sancto cœlum iterum aperuit, Moysem & Eliam, summos prophetarum, gloriæ suæ testes locupletissimos advocavit. Spiritu divinitatis vivificatus Angelos pertraxit in sepulchrum suum ostiarios, vivus mortisque victor triumphalis multorum sepulchra nequicquam obstantibus æneis mortis pessulis ut reseravit potentissime, ita & sanctorum corpora in dias luminis oras viva secum pertraxit. Triumphum suum ubi celebravit in nube, angelos in sui famulitium in vestibus albis sollicitavit comites& satellites immortales, eosdem demum in gloriam celebrandam allecturus, ubi veniet in nubibus judex è cœlo descendens, vivos simul & mortuos ad augustum tribunal suum stupenda sua virtute stiturus. Nolite cunctabundi hærere super tanto spectaculo: Christus ipse, Amen, testis fidelis & verax, id quam testatissimum facit his verbis; amen amen dico vobis; ab hoc tempore videbitis cœlum apertum & Angelos Dei ascendentes & descendentes ad Filium hominis.
units.tr: Among all the admirable works of nature, the first place is held by the hidden and inviolable attraction and sympathy of natural things, the ἀπλανὴς χία [unerring sympathy]. It spreads and pours itself out far and wide; it pervades and moves almost the whole of nature. That heavy bodies, contrary to their nature, are carried upward with the most rapid impetus, and that light bodies seek and invade the lowest place as quickly as possible, is the work of sympathy, so that the void, that deadly gap in cohesion, may be avoided, by the hidden sympathy of things. That the ocean flows and ebbs in constant advance and retreat is the work of a sympathy which it keeps closely with its heavens. That amber draws straws, and the magnet draws iron, and the north star draws the magnet, and the needle of the compass that has been rubbed against it, is the work of a hidden and admirable sympathy, which until now has struck the common people and the learned alike with amazement. Mortals, you have been too much devoted to the hidden things of nature; you have given too much leisure to the contemplation of the causes of natural sympathy. The open heavens offer you a sympathy far more excellent and more worthy of your contemplation, that of the Son of Man. The Son of Man is a universal magnet, who by his hidden virtue and dignity pervades and moves, attracts and draws to himself the most mobile of all creatures. Before he made himself manifest to the world, he moved the hearts of kings and prophets, inflamed with the most ardent prayers, and drew them to himself by the desire of seeing him. And the Church, gazing at him through the lattice, burned toward him and broke out into this most fervent wish: Oh that you would rend the heavens and come down, that the mountains might flow down at your presence! Isa. 64:1. As soon as God came down from heaven, made manifest in the flesh, the lowly and despised humility of weak flesh did not delay the most divine magnetic power of Christ. He struck the heavens with wonder, moved and opened them, drew the host of Angels to himself and attracted them. He opened the cottages of the shepherds of Bethlehem and, inflamed with burning desire, snatched them to his manger. He pervaded the distant East and, through long journeys, both stirred up and powerfully drew the Magi to his adoration. As soon as he was made manifest to Israel at his baptism, he put forth that sympathetic power of his into the third heaven; as if with a wonderful key he unlocked it, drew the heart of the Father and his voice crying out, This is my beloved Son, and led down the Holy Spirit in the likeness of a dove, descending and resting upon his head. Transfigured on the holy mountain he opened the heavens again and summoned Moses and Elijah, the chief of the prophets, as most abundant witnesses of his glory. Quickened by the Spirit of divinity, he drew the Angels to himself as gatekeepers of his tomb; living and victor over death, he opened the tombs of many with power, though the bronze bars of death stood against them in vain, and so he drew the bodies of the saints along with him, living, into the regions of light. Where he celebrated his triumph in a cloud, he summoned the Angels in white robes to be his attendants and immortal guards, intending at last to draw them to the celebration of his glory, when he will come in the clouds, the Judge descending from heaven, to set the living and the dead before his august tribunal by his wonderful power. Do not hesitate, lingering over so great a spectacle: Christ himself, the Amen, the faithful and true witness, makes this most certain by these words: Verily, verily, I say unto you, hereafter you shall see heaven opened, and the Angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man.

units.la: Functis explicatione visionis Cœli aperti ad Filium hominis explicandum sequitur 1o. quid ascensus & descensus Angelorum Dei ad Filium hominis significaverit, 2o. qui & quando discipuli viderint Angelos Dei ad eum ascendentes & descendentes.
units.tr: Having completed the explanation of the vision of the open heaven over the Son of Man, there follows, for its explanation, (1) what the ascent and descent of the Angels of God to the Son of Man signified, and (2) who and when the disciples saw the Angels of God ascending and descending to him.

units.la: Primam quæstionem dextere elucidaturis 1o. inquirendum est in Angelos Dei, quando & ministri Dei homines Angeli Dei sunt, ut Sacerdos Angelus Jehova exercituum dicitur Mal. 2:7. & Joannes Malach. 3:1. & ministri verbi Angeli dicuntur Ecclesiæ, Apoc. 2:1.8. & 3:1. & κατ' ἐξοχὴν cœlestes intelligentiæ, Seraphim & Cherubim, principatus & potestates, angeli lucis & angeli Dei crebro in Scriptura appellantur. 2 Cor. 11:14. Matth. 22:30. Hinc Paulus discriminis ergo Angelum è cœlo nominavit, nempe quia se nominaverat, collegasque suos Apostolos insinuaverat Angelos omnes è terra, Dei nuncios & Euangelii præcones, Gal. 1:8. Hinc merito quæritur, quos Dei Angelos Christus videndos receperit ad Filium hominis ascendentes & descendentes num è terra, num è cœlo Dei Angelos?
units.tr: In order to elucidate the first question skilfully, we must first inquire into the Angels of God: when and how ministers of God are also called Angels of God. Thus the priest is called the Angel of the LORD of hosts, Mal. 2:7, and John is called the messenger, Mal. 3:1, and the ministers of the Word are called the Angels of the Churches, Rev. 2:1, 8, and 3:1. Above all, the heavenly intelligences, the Seraphim and Cherubim, the principalities and powers, the angels of light and the angels of God, are often named in Scripture. 2 Cor. 11:14; Matt. 22:30. Hence Paul, by way of contrast, named an angel from heaven, namely because he had named himself, and had included his fellow apostles, as angels from earth, messengers of God and heralds of the gospel, Gal. 1:8. Hence it is rightly asked which Angels of God Christ intended should be seen ascending and descending to the Son of Man: are they angels of God from the earth, or angels of God from heaven?

units.la: Augustinus tract. 7. in Joh. ascendentes & descendentes Angelos, bonos prædicatores, Christum prædicantes, interpretatur, sicut & eorum ascensum metaphoricum, nescio quem, intelligit, modo mentis excessum, cessum, ubi grandia loquuntur Regni coelorum mysteria, modo Christi imitationem; descensum vero modo, ubi loquuntur humilia, & captui auditorum accommodata, modo Christi praedicationem. Sed praestat, Augustinum ipsum audire loquentem: Quomodo ascendunt, & quomodo descendunt? Ex uno habemus exemplum. Vide Paulum ascendentem: scio hominem in Christo ante annos quatuordecim raptum fuisse usque in tertium coelum, sive in corpore, sive extra corpus, nescio, Deus scit; & audivit ineffabilia verba, quae non licet homini loqui. Ascendentem audistis; descendentem audite. Non potui loqui vobis, quasi spiritalibus, sed quasi carnalibus; quasi parvulis in Christo lac vobis potum dedi, non escam. Ecce descendit, qui ascenderat. Quare, quo ascenderat? Usque ad tertium coelum. Quare, quo descenderit? Usque ad lac parvulis dandum. Hanc vero suam interpretationem, lepidumve commentum dixerim, exemplo nutricum & matrum primum, postmodum vero exemplo parentis Oratoris illustrare satagit his verbis: disertus aliquis pater si sit tantus Orator, ut lingua illius fora concrepent & tribunalia concutiantur, si habeat parvulum filium, cum ad domum redierit, seponit forensem eloquentiam, quo ascenderat, & lingua puerili descendit ad parvulum. Sed pace magni Augustini dixerim, hic loci eum dormitasse, aut somniasse. Nam 1°. Christus hic respexit evidentissime ad visionem mysticam scalae Patriarchae Jacobi. Nempe ipsa verba recitat, quae exstant Gen. 28: 12. Quis vero nisi somnians non Jacobi, sed delirantis somnium, asserere sustinuerit, Patriarcham vidisse homines, Dei ministros, ad scalam ascendentes & descendentes? 2°. Augustini interpretatio a scopo Christi toto coelo aberrat. Intendit nempe Servator, hac Angelorum Dei ascendentium & descendentium futura promissione declarare, se esse ampliorem, & augustiorem rege illo Israelis, quem Judaei hactenus somniaverant, verum puta Dei filium, & regem non hominum modo, sed & coelestium Dei Angelorum. Fac vero promisisse, praecones Euangelii imitatione & praedicatione ascendisse & descendisse ad Christum; Christus haut quaquam futurus erat major, illustriorve regibus Israelis, qui & suos habuere praecones & ministros homines, ascendentes & descendentes ad capessenda & exsequenda mandata sua. 3°. Quia discipuli, Christique Apostoli Petrus, Andreas, Philippus visuri erant Angelos Dei, ascendentes & descendentes ad Filium hominis, ut tanto spectaculo scirent certo certius, Jesum esse verum Messiam & comprimis regem aeternum omnium vel coelestium creaturarum. Cum vero ipsi futuri erant Christi e terra nuncii & Angeli, Christus pollicitus fuerit, eos visuros se ipsos Christi praecones: Quae frigida est oratio, & nullius plane ponderis ad futuram illam de Christi gloria persuasionem ingenerandam. Denique cum certissimum sit coelum apertum proprie significare hic loci Dei domicilium, & pariter ascendentes proprio sensu Angelos Dei videndos recepit. At nemo discipulorum, Apostolorum nemo in coelum ad Christum ascendere visus est, una haec fuit Pauli singularis ut & occulta praerogativa.
units.tr: Augustine, in tractate 7 on John, interprets the angels ascending and descending as good preachers who proclaim Christ, and he understands their ascent in a figurative sense, I know not what: now as a rapture of the mind, when they speak of the great mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, now as the imitation of Christ; and their descent, now when they speak lowly things suited to the capacity of their hearers, now as the preaching of Christ. But it is better to hear Augustine himself speaking: How do they ascend, and how do they descend? We have one example. See Paul ascending: I know a man in Christ, who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven, whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows; and he heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter. You have heard the one ascending; hear the one descending. I could not speak to you as to spiritual people, but as to fleshly people; as to infants in Christ I gave you milk to drink, not food. Behold, he who had ascended came down. Why? To where had he ascended? Up to the third heaven. Why, to where did he descend? To the milk to be given to infants. He tries to illustrate this interpretation of his, or pleasant invention, first by the example of nurses and mothers, and afterward by the example of an orator who is a parent, in these words: If some eloquent father is so great an orator that his tongue makes the forums resound and the tribunals shake, yet if he has a little son, when he returns home he sets aside his forensic eloquence, to where he had ascended, and with a childish tongue he descends to the little one. But with respect to the great Augustine, I would say that here he was nodding off or dreaming. For, first, Christ here clearly looked to the mystical vision of Jacob's ladder. Indeed he recites the very words that stand in Gen. 28:12. Who but a dreamer, not Jacob's, but the dreamer of a delirious dream, would venture to assert that the patriarch saw men, the ministers of God, ascending and descending on a ladder? Second, Augustine's interpretation is wide of the mark of Christ's purpose. The Saviour intended, by this promise of the future ascent and descent of the Angels of God, to declare that he is greater and more exalted than that king of Israel whom the Jews had hitherto dreamed of, namely that he is the Son of God, and king not only of men but also of the heavenly angels of God.
