But suppose he had promised that the heralds of the gospel would ascend and descend to Christ by imitating and preaching him; Christ would by no means have been greater or more illustrious than the kings of Israel, who also had their heralds and ministers, men, ascending and descending to receive and carry out their commands. Third, the disciples, and the apostles of Christ, Peter, Andrew and Philip, were to see the Angels of God ascending and descending to the Son of Man, so that by so great a sight they might know more certainly than certain that Jesus is the true Messiah and above all the eternal king of all creatures, both heavenly and earthly. But since they themselves were to be the messengers and angels of Christ from the earth, Christ would have promised that they would see themselves, his heralds; what a cold speech this is, and of no weight at all for producing persuasion about the future glory of Christ! Finally, since it is most certain that the open heaven properly signifies here the dwelling of God, and likewise ascending, in its proper sense, Christ promised that the Angels of God would be seen. But none of the disciples, none of the apostles, was seen to ascend into heaven to Christ; this alone was the singular and hidden prerogative of Paul.

units.la: Superest igitur, efflagitante visionis mysticae scalae indole, cujus hic complementum est, & Christi Regis universi propalanda gloria, ut cum Chrysostomo Angelos Dei e coelo Christo ministrantes intelligamus. Nec mirum, sunt Angeli Dei λειτουργικὰ πνεύματα, Heb. 1: 14. & Angeli Filii hominis, Matth. 13: 41. quippe qui & Deus est in saecula benedictus, Rom. 5: 9. & Angelorum creator. Nam per eum condita sunt omnia, quae in coelis sunt, & quae in terra, visibilia & invisibilia, & throni, & dominatus, & imperia, & potestates; omnia per ipsum & in ipsum condita sunt, Col. 1: 16. Et primogenitus, id est caput & princeps, omnis creatura, Col. 1: 15. Filius, quem pater constituit haeredem, id est herum, omnium; per quem etiam mundum condidit, Heb. 1: 2. Ascensus igitur & descensus Angelorum, quo alacres perpetesque adversus Filium hominis funguntur, ministerium significat. Hinc apud Jesaiam adstantes throno Christi & alati graphice repraesentantur, quo eorum promptitudo & celeritas ad ejus mandata capessenda & exsequenda significetur, Jes. 6: 2. Joh. 12: 41. Cur vero Angelorum ministerium eorum ascensu & descensu Christus significatum voluerit, hae nobis causae oportunae videntur, 1°. quia respexit ad scalam mysticam, cujus ipse in sese luculentum exhibuit implementum. Inibi vero ministrantes Angeli Jacobo visi sunt ascendentes & descendentes. 2°. Ad significandam Angelorum multitudinem variaque ipsorum ministeria; quorum alii descendunt missi coelitus ad exsequenda imperata in terris officia alii ascendunt, factorum rationem Deo Domino suo reddituri, seque denuo ad nova capessenda imperia Deo, Domino pro solio suo sedenti, adstantes & obsequiosos stituri, 1 Reg. 22: 19. Job. 1: 6. 3°. quia ut in multis, probavit sese adversus Filium hominis Angelorum Dei ministerium, dum agitaret in terris, comprimis praebuit sese conspicuum, dum in coelum ascenderet, illustri eorum satellitio stipatus. Psal. 97: 7. Act. 1: 10. Heb. 1: 6. ut denuo se probabit illustre cum descendet e coelo in gloria patris sui cum Angelis suis, Matth 16: 27. & 25: 31. 2 Thessal. 1: 7. Sed vero hic mirari subit, cur Christus in describendo Angelorum per ascensum & descensum addicto sibi ministerio Angelos prius ascendentes quam descendentes ad Filium hominis exhibuerit. Quando enim certum est, coelum esse Angelorum domicilium; vident enim in coelo faciem Patris nostri coelestis, Matth. 18: 10. uti ministri adstantes folio Dei, in obsequium paratissimi; unde & coelestes exercitus, Luc. 2: 13. & Angeli e coelo dicuntur, Gal. 1: 8. opportunius & commodius ad statum & conditionem Angelorum videbatur, eos primum descendentes, postmodo vero ascendentes ad Filium hominis exhiberi. Sed vero nihil causae est, cur Christus verborum Moysis in visione scalae mysticae ordinem mutare debuerit. Nam cum ascensus & descensus Angelorum 1o. in genere significaverit eorum ministerium, Dei Filio olim exhibitum, ex quo functus est munere Mediatorio Deum inter & homines, fueritque Dei Filius ab aeterno in coelo regnans cum Patre, & inde angelos in terras miserit, quam in terris manifestatus in carne prius agitaret; angelos sane ad eum ascendentes, factorum rationem reddituři, exhiberi par erat, priusquam descendentes ad Filium hominis, versantem in terris. Hinc factum, ut Patriarcha Jacob memoretur Angelos vidisse primum ascendentes & postmodum descendentes; ascendentes nempe ad Filium hominis, quatenus Deus erat in scalae fastigio, descendentes postmodum ad eundem, humi jacentem in lumbis Jacobi. 2o. Supponit Christus, quod erat verissimum, nempe Dei Angelos descendisse jam dudum ad Filium hominis, in mundo manifestatum, cum Bethlehemi nasceretur, illiqúe adstitisse custodes, in excubiis positos. Unde Angelus Dei Josephum in somnio monuit, ut clam in Ægyptum secederet, Matth. 2: 13. cum in deserto a diabolo tentaretur, cum in monte Olearum sudore manaret sanguineo, Matth. 4: 11. Luc. 22: 43. cum vivus exiret e mortuis, Matth. 28: 2. 3. &c. cum denique in coelum ascenderet, Act. 1: 10. Sed vero quia hujusmodi angelorum ministerium clam & remotis arbitris Christo fuerat exhibitum, vel paucissimis significatum, & eorum, quae non sunt, & quae non apparent eadem sit ratio; supererat, ut Christus discipulorum animum in nobile & illustre angelorum ministerium, ad eum & cum eo in coelum ascensurorum, dirigeret. Hinc, videbitis angelos Dei ascendentes ad Filium hominis. 3o. Quandoquidem in caeteris ministerii angelorum adversus Christum gradibus duo sunt momenta illustrissima, ex quibus Scriptura aestimanda nobis relinquit caetera ministerii angelorum capita, alterum nempe ministerium, quo functi sunt erga Christum, in coelum ascendentem triumphalem in modum (Unde Paulus, in memorabilibus gloriae Dei, manifestati in carne, articulis & hunc memorat, nempe eum visum fuisse ab Angelis, 1 Tim. 3: 16. & probaturus Christi prae Angelis dignitatem, Heb. 1: 6. laudaverit ex Psal. 97: 7. hoc Dei Patris imperium; omnes angeli Dei adorent eum. Nam sicut Psaltes regnum Messiae celebrat Psal. 91: 1. & deinceps in Psalmis serie ingressum Messiae in regnum suum describit: ita Paulus Heb. 1: 6. loquitur de introductione Christi in regnum suum per ascensionem in coelum. Quod liquet 1o. quia eum vocat primogenitum, h. e. principem & supremum dominum. 2o. quia de introductione in mundum futurum loquitur, h. e. in Ecclesiam, cujus caput & regem Deus Christum constituit, cum per ascensionem eum ad dexteram majestatis suae locavit, Heb. 1: 6. collato cum 2: 5.) alterum vero illustrissimum ministerii Angelorum adversus Filium hominis momentum, situm in obsequio fidelissimo, quod angeli sunt Christo exhibituri, ubi descendet e coelo, stipatus myriadibus angelorum ad ultimum judicium, Matth. 16: 27. & 25: 31. 2 Thess. 1: 7. Judae comm. 14: utique quam sapientissime Christus angelorum ministerium exhibuit, quo adversus Filium hominis perfuncturi erant, primo per ascensum & postmodo per descensum.
units.tr: It remains, then, since the nature of the mystical vision of the ladder demands it (of which this is the completion) and the glory of Christ as King of the whole universe must be made known, that we understand with Chrysostom that the Angels of God, ministering to Christ, come from heaven. Nor is this surprising: the Angels of God are ministering spirits [λειτουργικὰ πνεύματα], Heb. 1:14, and the Angels of the Son of man, Matth. 13:41, since he is also God blessed for ever, Rom. 5:9, and the Creator of the Angels. For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created by him, and for him, Col. 1:16. And he is the firstborn, that is, the head and prince, of every creature, Col. 1:15. He is the Son, whom he hath appointed heir, that is, lord, of all things, by whom also he made the worlds, Heb. 1:2. The ascent and descent of the Angels, by which they eagerly and constantly serve the Son of man, therefore signifies ministry. Hence in Isaiah the attendants of Christ's throne are depicted as winged, so that their readiness and speed in receiving and carrying out his commands may be signified, Isa. 6:2; John 12:41. Why Christ wished the ministry of the Angels to be signified by their ascent and descent, the following causes seem fitting to us: (1) because he had regard to the mystical ladder, whose fulfilment he himself displayed in himself. In that vision the ministering Angels were seen by Jacob ascending and descending. (2) To signify the multitude of the Angels and their various ministries. Some of them descend, sent from heaven to carry out the duties commanded on earth; others ascend, to render an account of their deeds to God their Lord, and then, standing by and attending upon God seated on his throne, to receive new commands, 1 Kings 22:19; Job 1:6. (3) Because, as in many things, the ministry of the Angels of God towards the Son of man proved itself, so especially while he was living on earth it showed itself conspicuously, and when he ascended into heaven he was attended by their glorious retinue, Ps. 97:7; Acts 1:10; Heb. 1:6; and so it will show itself again, when he descends from heaven in the glory of his Father with his Angels, Matth. 16:27; 25:31; 2 Thess. 1:7. But here it is a wonder why Christ, in describing the ministry of the Angels bound to him by ascent and descent, presented the Angels as ascending before descending to the Son of man. For since it is certain that heaven is the dwelling of the Angels, for they see in heaven the face of our heavenly Father, Matth. 18:10, standing as ministers before the throne of God, ready for service in every way; whence they are also called the heavenly hosts, Luke 2:13, and Angels from heaven, Gal. 1:8, it seemed more suitable and fitting to the state and condition of the Angels to present them first descending and afterwards ascending to the Son of man. But there is no reason why Christ should have been bound to change the order of Moses' words in the vision of the mystical ladder. For since the ascent and descent of the Angels signify, first in general, their ministry once displayed to the Son of God, from the time when he discharged his mediatorial office between God and men; and since the Son of God, reigning from eternity in heaven with the Father, sent the Angels from there to earth, before he was made manifest on earth in the flesh and lived there, it was indeed fitting that the Angels should be shown ascending to him, to render an account of their deeds, before descending to the Son of man dwelling on earth. Hence it happened that the patriarch Jacob records that he saw the Angels first ascending and afterwards descending: ascending, namely, to the Son of man, inasmuch as he was God at the top of the ladder, and descending afterwards to the same one, lying on the ground in the loins of Jacob. (2) Christ presupposes what was most true, namely that the Angels of God had long since descended to the Son of man, made manifest in the world, when he was born at Bethlehem, and that guardians, posted on watch, stood by him. Hence an Angel of God warned Joseph in a dream to flee secretly into Egypt, Matth. 2:13; when he was tempted by the devil in the desert, Matth. 4:11; when in the Mount of Olives he sweated drops of blood, Luke 22:43; when he came alive out of the dead, Matth. 28:2, 3, etc.; and finally when he ascended into heaven, Acts 1:10. But since this kind of ministry of the Angels had been displayed to Christ in secret and with witnesses removed, or signified to very few, and since the reason is the same for things that do not exist and things that do not appear, it remained that Christ should direct the minds of his disciples to the noble and illustrious ministry of the Angels, which would accompany him and them into heaven. Hence, you shall see the Angels of God ascending to the Son of man. (3) Since, among the other stages of the Angels' ministry towards Christ, there are two most illustrious moments, from which Scripture leaves us to judge the remaining heads of the Angels' ministry: the one, namely, the ministry by which they served Christ as he ascended into heaven in triumph (whence Paul, in his memorable articles on the glory of God manifested in the flesh, also records this, namely that he was seen by the Angels, 1 Tim. 3:16; and, wishing to prove the dignity of Christ above the Angels, Heb. 1:6, he quoted from Psalm 97:7 this command of God the Father: let all the Angels of God worship him). For as the Psalmist celebrates the kingdom of the Messiah, Ps. 91:1, and afterwards in the series of Psalms describes the Messiah's entrance into his kingdom, so Paul, Heb. 1:6, speaks of the introduction of Christ into his kingdom by his ascension into heaven. This is clear: (1) because he calls him the firstborn, that is, the prince and supreme lord; (2) because he speaks of his introduction into the coming world, that is, into the Church, whose head and king God appointed Christ, when by his ascension he placed him at the right hand of his majesty, Heb. 1:6, compared with 2:5. The other most illustrious moment of the Angels' ministry towards the Son of man lies in the most faithful service which the Angels are to render to Christ, when he descends from heaven, attended by myriads of Angels, to the last judgment, Matth. 16:27; 25:31; 2 Thess. 1:7; Jude, v. 14. Surely Christ most wisely set out the ministry of the Angels, which they were to perform towards the Son of man, first by ascent and afterwards by descent.

units.la: Recipit igitur Christus fore, ut omnes discipuli sui videant, Filium hominis ascendentem in coelum apertum & angelos Dei ad eum, ut illustre famulitium, ascendentes comites; postmodum vero videant eundem Filium hominis e coelo aperto descendentem, & ad eum angelos Dei, illustre ipsius famulitium, descendentes assectas & comites, ad capessenda ipsius mandata, sistendosque vivos atque mortuos ad gloriosum ipsius tribunal, reportaturos in corpore suo secundum opera sua.
units.tr: Christ therefore affirms that all his disciples will see the Son of man ascending into the open heaven, with the Angels of God ascending with him as his illustrious retinue and companions; and afterwards they will see the same Son of man descending from the open heaven, and the Angels of God, his illustrious retinue, descending with him as attendants and companions, to receive his commands, and to bring the living and the dead before his glorious tribunal, to repay each one in his body according to his works.

units.la: Ascensus igitur angelorum Dei ad Filium hominis hic a Christo promittitur, modo aspectabili videndus, sicuti & eorundem descensus hic loci a Christo promittitur discipulis, ut appendix & consectarium quoddam ipsius ascensus in coelum apertum, & ultimi demum ipsius descensus e coelo aperto. Promittit igitur 1o. futurum suum ascensum in coelum, & ab eodem aperto descensum aspectabilem atque tremendum; 2o. verum, & veluti consectarium quoddam, visionem angelorum & ascendentium & descendentium ad ipsum promittit. Ratio est, quia magnifica isthaec promissio Filii hominis, ascensuri in coelum, & ab eodem descensuri, angelis Dei ascendentem & descendentem ministris comitantibus summopere confert in scopum Christi promittentis. Intendebat nempe, ut praecedente quaest. notavimus, declarare discipulis fore, ut in posterum illis palam innotesceret, qualis revera erat, Filius nempe Dei naturae aeternae praerogativa, non adoptionis jure & umbratili quadam similitudine, sicut reges terrae; verusque Messias, non rex modo Israelis; sed & propheta, pontifex, rexque aeternus orbis plane universi. Ut finem hunc sapienter assequatur fore recipit, ut videant, 1o. Filium hominis ascendentem in coelum apertum tum & angelos Dei ad eum ascendentes ministros & assecias. Ita enim eos docet, 1°. se esse revera Deum, cui angeli serviunt obsequiosi, dum ascendit in cœlum, domicilium, thronumque Dei viventis. 2°. se esse Prophetam æternum & universalem, qui non in angulo mundi, non in monte, vel e monte Sinai, sicut Moses; sed in cœlo & e cœlo, templo æterno & universali, Dei voluntatem doceat populos omnes per Spiritum suum. 3°. æternum & universalem Pontificem, qui non in terrenum, sicut Pontifex Leviticus ingreditur sanctuarium ad intercedendum pro uno carnali populo Israelitico; sed in cœleste, nec manufactum sanctuarium, ut pro universo spirituali & æterno electo Dei populo, ex orbe universo collecto & colligendo, intercedat. 4°. denique se esse regem, non Israelis duntaxat; sed regem æternum, cœlestem & universalem omnium creaturarum, populorum, linguarum & nationum, & vel ipsorum Angelorum Dei, quandoquidem ipsos visuri sunt ascendentes ad Filium hominis, ubi nube vehens ingredietur in regnum & gloriam suam. Sed & descensu suo e cœlo aperto, ut ferat in omnes ultimum & irrevocabile judicium, stipatus angelis Dei, ministris suis, discipulos docuit, 1°. se esse æternæ divinitatis prærogativa Deum & Filium Dei, cui aperta sint & pervia omnium hominum judicandorum momenta cordis abditissima, quique summa autoritate alios morti & ignominiæ, alios vitæ & gloriæ æternæ sit addicturus. 2°. Prophetam veracissimum, qui tantam promissionem & prophetiam sit ad umbilicum perducturus. 3°. Pontificem, qui e cœlo, sanctuario suo, plenissima benedictione cœlesti populum suum sit impertiturus. Regem denique mundi universi & ipsorum Dei angelorum, quorum tuba atque ministerio citabit, sistetque ad gloriosum suum tribunal omnes & singulos homines, unicuique secundum opera sua retributurus.
units.tr: The ascent of the Angels of God to the Son of man is therefore promised here by Christ, to be seen in a visible manner, just as their descent is also promised here by Christ to the disciples, as a kind of appendix and consequence of his own ascent into the open heaven, and finally of his own descent from the open heaven. He therefore promises, (1) his future ascent into heaven, and his visible and dreadful descent from the open heaven; (2) and, as a true and, as it were, a certain consequence, he promises them the sight of the Angels both ascending and descending to him. The reason is that this magnificent promise of the Son of man, who will ascend into heaven and descend from it, together with the Angels of God accompanying him as ministers ascending and descending, contributes greatly to the aim of Christ in promising. He intended, as we noted in the previous question, to declare to the disciples that it would become plain to them in the future what he truly was: the Son of God, possessing the prerogative of eternal nature, not by the right of adoption and some shadowy likeness, as the kings of the earth; and the true Messiah, not only king of Israel, but also prophet, priest and eternal king of the whole world. That he may wisely attain this end, he undertakes that they will see (1) the Son of man ascending into the open heaven, and the Angels of God ascending to him as his ministers and attendants. For thus he teaches them, (1) that he is truly God, whom the Angels serve obsequiously as he ascends into heaven, the dwelling and throne of the living God. (2) That he is the eternal and universal Prophet, who does not teach the will of God to all peoples through his Spirit in a corner of the world, nor on a mountain, nor from Mount Sinai as Moses did; but in heaven and from heaven, the eternal and universal temple. (3) That he is the eternal and universal High Priest, who does not enter an earthly sanctuary, as the Levitical high priest does, to intercede for the one carnal people of Israel; but enters a heavenly sanctuary, not made with hands, to intercede for the whole spiritual and eternal people of God, gathered and to be gathered from the whole world. (4) Finally, that he is king, not of Israel alone, but the eternal, heavenly and universal king of all creatures, peoples, tongues and nations, and even of the Angels of God themselves, since they are to be seen ascending to the Son of man, when he, riding on a cloud, enters into his kingdom and glory. But also by his descent from the open heaven, to bring the final and irrevocable judgment upon all, attended by the Angels of God, his ministers, he taught the disciples (1) that, by the prerogative of eternal divinity, he is God and the Son of God, to whom the deepest secrets of the hearts of all men to be judged lie open and accessible, and who with supreme authority will consign some to death and shame, and others to life and eternal glory. (2) That he is the most truthful Prophet, who will bring so great a promise and prophecy to its end. (3) That he is the Priest, who from heaven, his sanctuary, will bestow on his people the fullest heavenly blessing. Finally, that he is king of the whole world and of the Angels of God themselves, whose trumpet and ministry he will summon, and will bring all and each of men before his glorious tribunal, to repay each one according to his works.

units.la: Fidem suam liberavit Christus fidelissimus; quod in perstringenda secunda quæstione qui & quando discipuli angelos Dei viderint ascendentes & descentes ad Filium hominis, probatum damus. & 1°. quidem quando certissimum est, ascensum & descensum Angelorum in genere significare ministerium, ducta ex regibus metaphora, qui nutu, & verbo ministros & subditos mittunt & revocant, & experiuntur dicto suo obsequiosos; unde ἐκαλόνταρχῷ; habeo, inquit, sub me milites, & dico huic; proficisçere, & proficiscitur: & alteri; veni, & venit; & servo meo: hoc fac & facit, Matth. 8:9. viderunt equidem discipuli mentis, fideique perceptione angelos Dei, Christo famulantes. Nam Christus per Spiritum suum aperte eis revelavit omnia, quæ angeli Dei ipsi exhibuerant, ministeria ab ipsa natinativitate sua cum illa perspicuitate & certitudine, qua Euangelistæ illa narrant in historia Christi nascentis & tentati in deserto, quasi ipsi fuerint testes αὐτόπται. Viderunt igitur mentis & fidei oculis ministrum Christi angelum, annunciantem ejus natales Bethlehemiticis pastoribus, & cœlestes angelorum exercitus, Deum celebrantes hoc cantico; gloria in altissimis Deo, & in terra pax, in homines benevolentia, Luc. 2: 9. 13. 14. Viderunt & angelos Dei Christo victori de Diabolo ministrantes in deserto, Matth. 4: 11. 2º. Oculis corporeis simul mentis perceptione viderunt angelum e cœlo Christum corroborantem in monte Olearum, Luc. 22: 43. Viderunt perceptione mentis angelum e cœlo descendentem, & saxum ab ostio sepulchri cum terræ motu avolventem, sicut mulieres oculis corporeis angelos, in vestibus albis fulgurantes perceperunt, Matth. 28: 2. 3. 4. Luc. 24: 4. Joh. 20: 12. 13. 3º. quando ascensus & descensus angelorum Dei peculiari ratione significat angelorum ministerium, quo functi sunt adversus Christum, in cœlum ascendentem, quoque functuri denuo sunt, ubi descendet in nubibus cœli stipatus angelorum myriadibus; certo certius est, discipulos vidisse tum oculis corporeis, tum mentis, fideique perceptione, Dei angelos ascendentes ad Filium hominis, ubi e tractu montis Olearum, qui Bethania dicitur, nube vehens ascendit in cœlum. Nam ut duo tantum memorantur viri adstitisse illis in vestibus albis, qui dixerunt; viri Galilæi, quid statis intuentes in cœlum? evidenter tamen colligitur ex iis, quæ sequuntur, discipulos simul & apostolos vidisse angelos ascendentes ad Filium hominis. Addunt enim angeli sub specie virorum illustrium & cœlestium; hic Jesus, inquiunt, qui sursum receptus est a vobis in cœlum, ita veniet, quemadmodum spectastis eum proficiscentem in cœlum, Act. 1: 10. 11. Atqui descendet Christus novissimo die, non modo in nubibus cœli; sed & cum gloria Patris & angelis suis, Matth. 16: 27. & 25: 31. 2 Th. 1: 7. Jud. comm. 14. Viderunt igitur Christum ascendentem in nube & angelos ad eum ascendentes, sicuti omnes Christi discipuli eum denuo venientem nubibus, & angelos Dei ad eum descendentes visuri sunt, Apoc. 1: 7.
units.tr: Most faithful Christ kept his promise, as we shall show in treating the second question, who and when the disciples saw the angels of God ascending and descending to the Son of man. First, it is quite certain that the ascending and descending of angels generally signifies ministry. The metaphor is taken from kings, who by a nod or a word send out and recall their servants and subjects, and find them obedient to their command. Hence the centurion [ἑκατοντάρχης] says: I have soldiers under me, and I say to one, go, and he goes; and to another, come, and he comes; and to my servant, do this, and he does it, Matt. 8:9. The disciples indeed saw, by the perception of mind and faith, the angels of God serving Christ. For Christ, through his Spirit, plainly revealed to them all the ministries which the angels of God had performed for him from his very birth. He did so with the same clarity and certainty with which the Evangelists relate them in the history of Christ's birth and of his temptation in the desert, as if they themselves had been eyewitnesses (αὐτόπται). They therefore saw with the eyes of mind and faith the angel of God, a minister of Christ, announcing his birth to the shepherds of Bethlehem, and the heavenly hosts of angels praising God with this song: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men, Luke 2:9, 13, 14. They also saw the angels of God ministering to Christ, the conqueror of the Devil, in the desert, Matt. 4:11. Second, with their bodily eyes, and at the same time by the perception of mind, they saw the angel from heaven strengthening Christ on the Mount of Olives, Luke 22:43. They saw by the perception of mind the angel descending from heaven and rolling away the stone from the door of the sepulchre with an earthquake, just as the women with their bodily eyes perceived the angels in white garments shining brightly, Matt. 28:2, 3, 4; Luke 24:4; John 20:12, 13. Third, when the ascent and descent of the angels of God signifies in a particular way the ministry which they performed toward Christ ascending into heaven, and which they will perform again when he descends on the clouds of heaven attended by myriads of angels, it is more than certain that the disciples saw, both with their bodily eyes and by the perception of mind and faith, the angels of God ascending to the Son of man, when he, carried up on a cloud from the slope of the Mount of Olives, which is called Bethany, ascended into heaven. For although only two men are recorded as standing beside them in white garments, who said: Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? it is nevertheless clearly gathered from what follows that the disciples and apostles saw the angels ascending to the Son of man. For the angels, in the appearance of illustrious and heavenly men, add: This Jesus, they say, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you have seen him going into heaven, Acts 1:10, 11. But Christ will descend on the last day not only on the clouds of heaven, but also with the glory of the Father and his angels, Matt. 16:27; 25:31; 2 Thess. 1:7; Jude 14. Therefore they saw Christ ascending in a cloud and the angels ascending to him, just as all Christ's disciples will see him coming again on the clouds, and the angels of God descending to him, Rev. 1:7.

units.la: USUS.
units.tr: USE.

units.la: 1º. QUod Apostoli, cæterique discipuli oculis corporeis Filium hominis viderint ascendentem in cœlum apertum, stipatum angelis, Dei ministris, ad eum, nube, curru Dei vehentem, ascendentibus, argumentum est omni exceptione majus, Filium hominis esse Deum, non sublesta fide Proculi alicujus: qui ubi renunciavit, se vidisse Romulum, scandentem cœlum, ut Deus à Romanis haberetur, id sibi negotii credidit solum dari, Pop. senatuiqüe Rom. sua illa commentitia renunciatione ut placeret. Colligamus, Filium hominis esse Deum in secula benedictum, non ludicra pompa ἀποθέωσεως, ut vita functos Imperatores Romanos, sed divino plane spectaculo nubis & bona fide, tutaque conscientia simul quingentorum fratrum, qui eum contemplati sunt vivum post crucis probrosum supplicium, simul centum & viginti discipulorum, qui, juxta ac ipse receperat, angelos Dei viderunt ad eum ascendentes, ubi scanderet cœlum apertum. Age igitur Filio hominis templa viva, aras sanctas, hostias vivas, vota dicemus ac nuncupemus, sacros thuris mystici adoleamus honores angelorum Dei conservi, angelorum æmuli supplices eum omnes adoremus.
units.tr: 1. That the apostles and the other disciples saw the Son of man with their bodily eyes ascending into the open heaven, attended by angels, the ministers of God, and carried up to him in a cloud, in the chariot of God, is a proof greater than any objection that the Son of man is God. It does not rest on the shaky faith of some Proculus, who, when he reported that he had seen Romulus ascending to heaven, so that the Romans would regard him as a god, believed that his only business was to please the people and the Roman senate with that invented report. Let us conclude that the Son of man is God, blessed for ever. This is no mock pageant of apotheosis [ἀποθέωσεως], such as was staged for the Roman emperors when they died, but a truly divine spectacle, seen with a sure eye and a sound faith, and with a conscience that is safe, as five hundred brethren who beheld him alive after his shameful death on the cross can attest, together with the hundred and twenty disciples, who, as he himself had received, saw the angels of God ascending to him as he went up into the open heaven. Come then, let us dedicate and vow to the Son of man living temples, holy altars, living sacrifices; let us kindle the sacred honours of mystical incense; and let us, as fellow-servants of the angels of God and rivals of the angels, worship him as suppliants, all of us together.

units.la: 2º. Quando ut Christus receperat, oculis corporeis eum discipuli in cœlum ascendentem viderint, sicut omnis oculus eundem gemina cum pompa descendentem visurus est, in expedito colligere est; Filium hominis naturam suam humanam visibilem in modum intulisse in cœlum apertum. Nempe sicut è cœlo descenderat naturæ humanæ assumptione & ejusdem signi præsentiæ suæ exhibitione in terris, & ascendit pariter, ubi naturam humanam, singulare præsentiæ suæ signum, terris abstulit, intulitque cœlo; in promtu colligere est, naturam humanam Filii hominis non amplius terris esse præsentem, quandoquidem fideles visuri sunt oculis corporeis Filium hominis descendentem, ubi terris reddet præsentem & oculis corporeis intuendam suam illam naturam humanam, altum interea tacente Scriptura sacra quemvis alium occultum & invisibilem Filii hominis secundum naturam humanam descensum. Apage igitur commentitiam humanæ Filii hominis naturæ in terra præsentiam, apage portentosam Pontificiorum Transsubstantiationem. Christus nempe recepit fore, ut discipuli videant angelos Dei descendentes ad Filium hominis, quando nimirum descendet, ut terris sistat humanam naturam, quam cœlo intulit, quando angeli Dei visi sunt ad eum ascendentes. Ostendant igitur nobis angelos Dei descendentes ad Filium hominis in templis & altaribus suis, & sidem extemplo habebimus eis. Sin secus sinant nos potius Christo credere, asserenti: (ubi de decensu ad adstruendam præsentiam humanæ suæ naturæ in terris loquitur) videbitis angelos Dei ad Filium hominis descendentes.
units.tr: 2. From the fact that the disciples saw Christ with their bodily eyes ascending into heaven, as every eye will see him descending with the same twofold pomp, it is easy to gather that the Son of man carried his human nature, visibly, up into the open heaven. Just as he came down from heaven by assuming human nature and by showing the sign of his presence on earth, and likewise ascended, when he took away from the earth the human nature, the unique sign of his presence, and carried it up to heaven, so it is easy to conclude that the human nature of the Son of man is no longer present on earth. For the faithful are to see the Son of man descending with their bodily eyes, when he will make that same human nature present on earth again and offer it to be looked upon with bodily eyes, while holy Scripture is silent about any other hidden and invisible descent of the Son of man according to his human nature. Away then with the fictitious presence of Christ's human nature on earth! Away with the monstrous Transubstantiation of the Papists! Christ promised that his disciples would see the angels of God descending to the Son of man, namely when he descends to set on earth the human nature which he carried up to heaven, just as the angels of God were seen ascending to him. Let them show us, then, the angels of God descending to the Son of man in their temples and at their altars, and we shall at once give them credit. But if it is otherwise, let them rather allow us to believe Christ, who, speaking of the descent that proves the presence of his human nature on earth, says: You will see the angels of God descending upon the Son of man.

units.la: 3º. Quem discipuli viderant oculis יריה, βραχύτι, ad breve tempus angelis inferiorem, nempe per passionem mortis, eundem viderunt oculis corcorporeis angelis Dei longe superiorem, ubi angelos ascendentes ad Filium hominis oculis usurparunt ministros. Heu quantum in nube vehentem, heu quantum viderunt ab illo mutatum, quem nuper viderant probris hominum expositum, a satellitibus vinctum, sputis conspurcatum, alapis impetitum, flagris servi ad instar vilissimi caesum; nunc vident aperte declaratum Dei filium, victorem mortis, inferni triumphatorem, angelorum dominum in palatium divinae majestatis euntem, comitantibus & ad eum ascendentibus Dei angelis. Quam Deo Patri praestitit obedientiam ad mortem crucis, causa germana est mutatae ab ignominia in supremam gloriam conditionis. Eia, fideles quotquot praedestinati fuistis in conformitatem imaginis Filii Dei, Christi sorti haut absimilis sors laeta vos manet. Crucem fertis post Christum, mundi injuriis undiquaque lacessiti. Vilia mundi purgamenta infra terrenos homullos, nedum, Dei Angelos, per reliquias passionum Christi descenditis, & hoc mundus videt, ridet & laetatur. Sors olim mutanda in melius mundo dato in pudorem vos exhibebit in coelum ascendentes ad Filium hominis. Videbit mundus angelos Dei ad vos, Filium hominis Christum mysticum ascendentes. Sed interim patientia opus est, opus obedientia, qualem Christus exhibuit Dei voluntati ad mortem.
units.tr: 3. The one whom the disciples had seen, with their eyes, made "a little lower than the angels" [יריה, βραχύτι] for a short time, namely through the suffering of death, they saw with their bodily eyes far above the angels, when they used the angels ascending to the Son of man as their attendants. Alas, how much they saw him changed as he was carried up in the cloud! He whom they had lately seen exposed to the scorn of men, bound by soldiers, defiled with spittle, struck with blows, and beaten with whips like the lowest slave, they now see plainly declared the Son of God, the conqueror of death, the triumpher over hell, the Lord of angels, going into the palace of the divine majesty with the angels of God accompanying him and ascending to him. The cause of the change in his condition from shame to supreme glory was the obedience he rendered to God the Father, even to the death of the cross. Come, all you faithful who have been predestined to be conformed to the image of the Son of God, a happy lot, not unlike Christ's, awaits you. You bear the cross after Christ, assailed on every side by the injuries of the world. The world's filthy refuse, you go down beneath earthly men, let alone the angels of God, through the remnants of Christ's sufferings; and the world sees this, laughs, and rejoices. Your lot, one day to be changed for the better, will put the world to shame, when you ascend into heaven to the Son of man. The world will see the angels of God ascending to you, the mystical Christ, the Son of man. But meanwhile patience is needed, and obedience, such as Christ showed to the will of God even unto death.

units.la: 4o. Ut quid, miserorum natio, felicitatem in hoc mundo quaeritis & speratis. Si germana felicitas stabularetur in terris, Filius hominis excitatus e mortuis, ad felicitatem & gloriam terram, felicitatis domicilium, utique non reliquisset, Angeli Dei, fideles Christi ministri & apparitores in terris permansissent accincti ad Christi obsequium. Quod Filius hominis mundum reliquerit, quod in coelum ascenderit, quod ad eum Angelorum Dei famulitium ascenderit in coelum, certissimo argumento est, nullam veram felicitatem sedem suam posuisse in terra. Et vos, animae nostrae, inhiantes & addictae terrae eritis? Age studia vestra ad Filium hominis, in coelum ascendentem convertite. Placent honores, placet gloria? Coelum, quo se Filius hominis intulit, quo angeli Dei ad eum convolarunt ascendentes, vitae coronas habet, quae nec contaminari possunt, nec marcescere, thronos & divinos honores. Placent divitiae? Coelum, quo Filius hominis, angelique Dei ascenderunt, thesauros habet inviolabiles, divitias, quas nec tinea rodit, nec situs corrumpit, nec manus furis surripit. Placent deliciae? Coelum, quo Filius hominis ascendit, amoenum habet paradisum, deliciarum fluvium, puras & aeternum perennantes, ad dexteram Dei voluptates. Placet sapientum virorumque illustrium societas? Coelum, quo angeli ad Filium hominis ascenderunt, sociesocietatem habet æternam Personarum S. S. Τρίαδ⊙, angelorum myriadas, Enochorum, Eliarum, sanctorumque cœlicolarum chorum. Age igitur conversatio nostra sit conversatio civium cœlestium, mente, corde, toto animorum impetu ascendamus in cœlum ad Filium hominis. Sed ea mente, eo consilio ascendamus, quo ascenderunt angeli Dei, nempe ad eum colendum & adorandum, laudandum & celebrandum.
units.tr: 4. Why, you wretched race of men, do you seek and hope for happiness in this world? If true happiness had its home on earth, the Son of man, raised from the dead, would surely not have left the earth, the home of happiness, for heaven, and the angels of God, the ministers and attendants of Christ, would have remained on earth, girded for Christ's service. That the Son of man left the world, that he ascended into heaven, and that the service of the angels of God ascended with him into heaven, is a most certain argument that true happiness has not placed its seat on earth. And will you, our souls, stay gaping after the earth and wedded to it? Come, turn your pursuits to the Son of man, ascending into heaven! Do honours please you, and glory? Heaven, into which the Son of man entered and to which the angels of God flew up to him, has crowns of life that cannot be stained or fade, and thrones and divine honours. Do riches please you? Heaven, into which the Son of man and the angels of God ascended, has treasures that cannot be violated, riches which neither moth gnaws, nor rust corrupts, nor the hand of a thief steals. Do pleasures please you? Heaven, to which the Son of man ascended, has a pleasant paradise, a river of delights, and pleasures at God's right hand that are pure and flow for ever. Does the company of wise and illustrious men please you? Heaven, to which the angels ascended with the Son of man, has the eternal fellowship of the Persons of the Holy Trinity [Τριάδα], myriads of angels, the choirs of Enoch and Elijah, and of the saints who dwell in heaven. Come then, let our conversation be the conversation of citizens of heaven; with mind, heart, and the whole force of our souls, let us ascend into heaven to the Son of man. But let us ascend with the same mind and the same purpose with which the angels of God ascended, namely to worship and adore him, to praise and celebrate him.

units.la: 5º. Quandoquidem Angeli Dei ascenderunt ad Filium hominis, ut Christo ministrarent obsequiosi, traducenda simul ac deploranda hominum vesania est, qui angelorum Dei, Christum colentium exemplum haut quaquam secuti, relicto Filio hominis, ad colendos religiose ministros ejus angelos devotum animum appulere. Dicite obsecro mortales, ubi & quando Numen vobis imperaverit angelorum λατρείαν, cultumque religiosum. Adorabis Dominum Deum tuum, & illi soli servies, Matth. 4: 10. Angeline cultum religiosum ab hominibus efflagitarunt? Contra vetuerunt præfracte; vide, inquit Angelus, vide, Johannes; ne feceris, noli prostratus me adorare: ego sum conservus tuus; Deum adora. Apoc. 19: 10, 22: 9. Angeli Dei Spiritus sunt administratorii, missi in ministerium propter eos, qui hereditatem capient salutis, Hebr. 1: 14. Et vos, Christiani propter quos serviunt ipsi angeli, angelis servire induxistis in animum vestrum? Num filii servis parentis sui ministrant? Alterutrum igitur fateamini, vel vos non esse Dei filios, fratresque Christi, unigeniti Dei filii; vel haut quaquam decere, vos Dei filios esse servos angelorum, servorum Dei parentis vestri. Atenim proh dolor nequicquam obstante angelorum ministerio & gloria Christianorum, sese filios Dei, fratresque Christi profitentium, sub ipsis Pauli oculis Christiani non pauci in provincia Phrygiæ & Pisidiæ cultum religiosum angelis exhibuerunt. Hanc Paulus damnavit abominandam hæresim; nemo adversus vos rectoris partes sibi sumat in submissione animi & religioso cultu angelorum, Col. 2: 18. Damnavit & hanc hæresim Laodicena Synodus, habita Laodiceæ, Phrygiæ metropolis, anno Christi 364. hoc canone 139. in cod. Can. Ecclef. univerf. ὅτι ἡ δεῖ χριστιανὰς ἐγκαλεῖσθαι τῷ ἐκκλησίᾳ τοῦ Θεοῦ, ἢ ἀπένας, ἢ ἀγγέλας ὀνομάζειν, ἢ σωτηρίας ποιεῖν, ἄπερ ἀπεγόρευσαν. εἴπερ οὖν εὑρεθῇ ταύτῃ τῇ κεκρυμμένῃ εἰδωλολατρείᾳ σχολάζων, ἔστω ἀνάθεμα. ὅτι ἐγκατέλιπεν τὸν κύριον ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν, τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ, ἢ εἰδωλολατρείᾳ προσέλθειν. Quod non oportet Christianos Ecclesiam Dei relinquere & abire, & angelos nominare & congregationes facere; quod est prohibitum. Siquis igitur inventus fuerit huic occultæ idololatriæ serviens, sit anathema, quia reliquit Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum, filium Dei, & ad idololatriam accessit. Ita Theodoretus in locum laudatum Pauli ad Colossenses. Qui legem, inquit, defendebant, eos etiam ad angelos colendos inducebant, dicentes legem per eos datam. Mansit autem diu hoc vitium in Phrygia & Pisidia. Quocirca Synodus quoque, qua convenit Laodicea, quae est Phrygiae metropolis, lege prohibuit, ne precarentur angelos, & ne relinquerent Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum. Cultum hunc angelorum religiosum Tertullianus, Patrum Latinorum vetustissimus, Idololatriam vocat Simonianorum haereticorum: Simonia, inquit, magia disciplina Angelis serviens utique & ipsa inter idololatrias deputabatur. Sed vero nequidquam obstante angeli praefracta objurgatione, qua Johannis proclivitatem in cultum creaturae castigavit concisa oratione; vide ne feceris, nequidquam obstante veritate Pauli salutari, angelicorum ἐθελοθρησκείας traducentis, & orthodoxae Ecclesiae perpetua abs cultu angelorum abstinentia; Pontificii in eam usque adeo ruere praecipites, ut Petavius Iesuitarum Coryphaeus, ore rotundo fateatur, Romanam Ecclesiam Angelos colere, quod primo eorum praesidium & patrocinium precibus & votis ambit, quod nihil, inquit, est aliud quam eos mediatores ad Deum allegare, tum quod secundo oratoria & basilicas in illorum honorem excitat, ac festos dies & hilares eorum dicat cultui. Sed & quod omnem absurditatem superat, angelorum reliquias cultu religioso veneratur, ut Michaelis Archangeli nobilem scutum & clypeum ad ejus in littoribus Neustriae extremis fanum. Nam Marcus l'Escarbotus, vir Pontificius, suum ad illum Michaelis montem, in quo fanum exstat, iter susceptum narrans, angeli clypeum inter caeteras, quae isthic ostentantur reliquias sacras, antehac ostendi solitas, memorat: sed sese hoc armorum coelestium spectaculo fraudatum, quia Abrincensis Episcopus quinquennio ante, ne deinceps ostenderetur Angeli clypeus, vetuerat. Cum vero Lescarbotus fanum S. Michaelis lustraverit A.D.CIↄ Iↄ c vii. evidenter sequitur, Pontificios anno hujus seculi secundo sacra Angelorum scuta coluisse. Alia longe sane, alia mens Ecclesiae Christianae fuit S. Augustini seculo, quinto nempe à Christo nato. Ille enim ut Spiritus S. divinitatem probet adversus Maximinum Arrianorum Episcopum, eum praesentem in haec verba compellat: nonne si templum alicui S. angelo excellentissimo de ligno & lapidibus faceremus, anathematizaremur à veritate Christi & ab Ecclesia Dei, quoniam creatura exhiberemus eam servitutem, quae uni tantum debetur Deo? Si ergo sacrilegi essemus faciendo templum cuicunque creaturae, quomodo non est Deus verus, cui non templum facimus, sed nos ipsi templum sumus? Mente sane & animo usque adeo procul aberat Orthodoxa Ecclesia abs cultu angelorum religioso, ut nequidem crediderit cuiquam angelum alloqui fas fuisse, nisi qui Spiritu prophetico donatus esset. Invenies, inquit, Origines, in plurimis locis & maxime
units.tr: 5. Since the angels of God ascended to the Son of man in order to minister to Christ with obedience, the madness of men must be exposed and lamented, for they have not at all followed the example of the angels of God, who worship Christ; they have abandoned the Son of man and turned their devoted minds to worshipping his ministers, the angels, with religious reverence. Tell me, I beg you, mortals, where and when has the Divinity commanded you to offer the worship [λατρείαν] and the religious cult of angels? You shall worship the Lord your God, and serve him alone (Matt. 4:10). Did the angels demand religious worship from men? On the contrary, they stubbornly forbade it. See, says the angel, see, John, do not do it; do not fall down to worship me: I am your fellow-servant; worship God (Rev. 19:10; 22:9). The angels of God are ministering spirits, sent to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation (Heb. 1:14). And you Christians, for whose sake the angels themselves serve, have you brought yourselves to serve angels? Do sons serve the servants of their father? Therefore admit one of two things: either you are not sons of God and brethren of Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, or it is by no means fitting that you, the sons of God, should be servants of the angels, the servants of your Father God. Yet, alas, despite the ministry of the angels and the glory of the Christians, who profess themselves sons of God and brethren of Christ, not a few Christians in the province of Phrygia and Pisidia gave religious worship to angels right under the eyes of Paul himself. Paul condemned this abominable heresy: Let no one take upon himself the role of judge against you in humility of mind and in the religious worship of angels (Col. 2:18). The Synod of Laodicea also condemned this heresy; it was held at Laodicea, the metropolis of Phrygia, in the year of Christ 364, and its 39th canon, in the collection of the canons of the universal Church, reads: ὅτι οὐ δεῖ χριστιανὰς ἐγκαταλείπειν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν τοῦ Θεοῦ, καὶ ἀπέρχεσθαι, ἢ ἀγγέλους ὀνομάζειν, ἢ συνόδους ποιεῖν, ἅπερ ἀπηγόρευσαν. εἴπερ οὖν εὑρεθῇ ταύτῃ τῇ κεκρυμμένῃ εἰδωλολατρείᾳ σχολάζων, ἔστω ἀνάθεμα, ὅτι ἐγκατέλιπεν τὸν κύριον ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν, τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ, καὶ εἰδωλολατρείᾳ προσέρχεσθαι. That Christians ought not to abandon the Church of God and go away, and call upon angels, or hold assemblies, which things have been forbidden. If therefore anyone is found devoting himself to this hidden idolatry, let him be anathema, because he has forsaken our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, and has resorted to idolatry. So Theodoret, on the passage of Paul to the Colossians cited above. Those who defended the law, he says, also led people to worship angels, saying that the law had been given through them. This vice remained for a long time in Phrygia and Pisidia. Therefore the Synod that met at Laodicea, the metropolis of Phrygia, also forbade by law that they should pray to angels and abandon our Lord Jesus Christ. Tertullian, the most ancient of the Latin Fathers, calls this religious worship of angels idolatry, belonging to the Simonian heretics: Simonian magic, he says, a discipline serving angels, was certainly also counted among the idolatries. But indeed, despite the angel's stern rebuke, by which he checked John's inclination to worship a creature in a few words, see that you do not do it, despite the saving truth of Paul, who condemns the self-chosen worship of angels, and despite the constant abstinence of the orthodox Church from the worship of angels, the Papists rush headlong into it so far that Petavius, the leader of the Jesuits, admits with a round mouth that the Roman Church worships angels, first because it seeks their protection and patronage with prayers and vows, which, he says, is nothing other than appointing them as mediators with God, and then because it builds oratories and basilicas in their honour and dedicates feast days and festivals to their worship. Even more absurdly, which surpasses every absurdity, they venerate the relics of angels with religious worship, such as the famous shield and buckler of the Archangel Michael at his shrine on the far coast of Normandy. For Marc Lescarbot, a Papist, describing his journey to that Mount of Michael where the shrine stands, records that among the other sacred relics displayed there was the shield of the angel, which had been shown in former times; but he was deprived of the sight of this heavenly armour, because the Bishop of Avranches, five years earlier, had forbidden the angel's shield to be shown any more. But since Lescarbot visited the shrine of St Michael in the year 1607, it clearly follows that the Papists were venerating the sacred shields of the angels in the second year of this century. Quite different was the mind of the Christian Church in the time of St Augustine, that is, in the fifth century after the birth of Christ. For when he wishes to prove the divinity of the Holy Spirit against Maximinus, the Arian bishop, he addresses him present in these words: Would we not be anathematized from the truth of Christ and from the Church of God, if we made a temple of wood and stone to some most excellent holy angel, since we would be offering to a creature that service which is due to God alone? If then we would be sacrilegious in making a temple to any creature, how is not God true, for whom we make not a temple, but are ourselves the temple? Indeed the Orthodox Church was so far, in mind and spirit, from religious worship of angels that it did not even believe it right to address an angel to anyone, unless he had been endowed with the prophetic Spirit. You will find, he says, Origen, in very many places and especially

units.la: Tertull. de Praescript. cap. 33. maxime in Psalmis, & ad angelos sermonem fieri data homini potestate; ei tamen qui Spiritum S. habet, ut & Angelos alloquatur. Cum vero de allocutionibus, quae exstant in libris sacris & praecipue in Psalmis sermonem instituat, evidentissime paret, eum intelligere Prophetas, qui extraordinario Spiritus S. dono praediti erant. Quid vero senserit de angelis Dei ministris seculo tertio Orthodoxa Christi Ecclesia, non finit dubitare Origines, ubi de bonis angelis sermonem habet. Εὐφημοῦμεν οὖν ὡς τὸ μακαρίζομεν, ἐγκεκριμένους ὑπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ τὰ χρήσιμα τῷ γένει ἡμῶν. ἃ μὲν τὴν ὀφειλομένην πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν τιμὴν τούτοις ἀπονέμομεν. ὅτε γὰρ ὁ Θεὸς τοῦτο βούλεται, ὅτε αὐτοὶ οἱ τοιαῦτα ἐγχειρισμένοι. Eos, inquit, laudamus, beatosque illos praedicamus, quibus ea a Deo commissa sunt, quae nostro generi utilia sunt: non tamen honorem, Deo debitum, iis reddimus. Id enim neque Deus vult, neque illi ipsi, quibus haec talia commissa sunt. Templa vero, suffitus, religiosas preces, corporis prostrationem, &c. id genus honores esse Deo debitos, ne ipsi quidem Pontificii negant.
units.tr: Tertull. de Praescript. cap. 33. Especially in the Psalms, and that speech is addressed to angels, is a power granted to man, but only to one who has the Holy Spirit, so that he may also address the angels. Since he is discussing the addresses found in the sacred books, and above all in the Psalms, it is quite evident that he means the prophets, who were endowed with the extraordinary gift of the Holy Spirit. What the Orthodox Church of Christ thought in the third century about the angels, the ministers of God, Origen leaves no room to doubt, where he speaks of the good angels: "We bless them, and call them blessed, as those whom God has entrusted with things useful to our race [Εὐφημοῦμεν οὖν ὡς τὸ μακαρίζομεν, ἐγκεκριμένους ὑπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ τὰ χρήσιμα τῷ γένει ἡμῶν]. Yet we do not render to them the honour due to God, for God does not will this, nor do those very angels to whom such things are entrusted [ἃ μὲν τὴν ὀφειλομένην πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν τιμὴν τούτοις ἀπονέμομεν. ὅτε γὰρ ὁ Θεὸς τοῦτο βούλεται, ὅτε αὐτοὶ οἱ τοιαῦτα ἐγχειρισμένοι]." Temples, incense, religious prayers, prostration of the body, and such like honours, which are owed to God: even the Papists themselves do not deny this.

units.la: 6º. Age igitur angelos laudemus, beatosque praedicemus vel eo nomine, quod Filio hominis famulentur obsequiosi, ascendentes & descendentes ad eum; eosdem, uti conservos nostros imitemur hoc animo alacriori, quod fortiori vinculo in Christi obsequium constricti teneamur. Re enim vera, uti Christus est angelorum creator & conservator, creator pariter & conservator hominum est. Per eum enim creata sunt & invisibilia, Col. 1: 16. Sed vero Christus est hominum redemptor, non angelorum. Christus est Filius hominis, utpote semen mulieris; sed non est filius angeli, dignatus naturam humanam honore summo nempe evectam in unionem hypostaticam ὁ Θεάνθρωπος, naturam angelicam tanto honore non dignatus est. Non enim utique angelos assumpsit, sed semen Abrahami assumpsit, Hebr. 2: 16. Angelorum natura nusquam memoratur templum divinitatis Christi; haec una est naturae humanae excellentissima praerogativa. Joh. 1: 14. Christus non inhabitat per fidem angelicis Spiritibus; sed per fidem habitat in cordibus nostris, Eph. 3: 17. Christus ne guttam quidem pretiosissimi sanguinis profudit pro Angelis; sed mortuus est oportuno tempore pro nobis, cum adhuc essemus peccatores, Rom. 5: 6. 8. Christus coelum angelis non aperuit. Nam intemeratae sanctitatis angelis coelum semper apertum fuit. Nobis miseris peccatoribus coelum, Dei sanctuarium, aperuit, mortuus nempe justus pro nobis injustis, nos ad Deum ut adduceret, 1 Pet. 3: 18. Ad coelum non ascendit, beatam sedem angelis paraturus. Vident enim semper in coelo faciem Patris nostri coelestis, Matth. 18: 10. nobis in coelum ascendit locum praeparaturus, Joh. 14: 2.
units.tr: 6. Let us therefore praise the angels and call them blessed, if for nothing else, because they serve the Son of man obsequiously, ascending and descending to him. Let us imitate them, as our fellow servants, with a more eager mind, since we are bound by a stronger tie to the obedience of Christ. For just as Christ is the creator and preserver of the angels, so too he is the creator and preserver of men: For by him were created even the invisible things, Col. 1:16. But Christ is the redeemer of men, not of angels. Christ is the Son of man, as the seed of the woman; but he is not the son of an angel. He deigned to take human nature, raised to the highest honour in the hypostatic union, the God-man [ὁ Θεάνθρωπος]; he did not deign to take the angelic nature with such honour. For he took not on him the nature of angels, but he took on him the seed of Abraham, Heb. 2:16. The nature of angels is nowhere mentioned as the temple of the divinity of Christ; this is the single most excellent prerogative of human nature, John 1:14. Christ does not dwell by faith in angelic spirits, but dwells by faith in our hearts, Eph. 3:17. Christ did not shed one drop of his most precious blood for the angels; but he died in due time for us, while we were yet sinners, Rom. 5:6, 8. Christ did not open heaven to the angels. For heaven was always open to the angels of unstained holiness. For us miserable sinners, he opened heaven, the sanctuary of God, the just dying for the unjust, that he might bring us to God, 1 Pet. 3:18. He did not ascend into heaven to prepare a blessed seat for the angels: for they always behold the face of our heavenly Father in heaven, Matt. 18:10. He ascended to heaven for us, to prepare a place for us, John 14:2.

units.la: Non ascendit in coelum pro angelis comparituros. Sed vero pro peccatoribus nobis in coelum ascendere visus est, semper vivus, ut compareat pro nobis, Heb. 7: 25. Advocatum enim habemus apud Patrem, Jesum Christum Justum, 1 Joh.2:1. Angeli vero ut minoribus beneficiis eos Christus beaverit, nullo tamen invidiae aestro afflati zelo ardentissimo in Christi obsequium convolant, ascendunt alacres, descenduntque ad Filium hominis. Ab hoc tempore videbitis angelos Dei ascendentes, &c. Age igitur, fideles, Filium hominis, prophetam nostrum colamus, ipsius doctrinae addictissimi; Filium hominis, pontificem nostrum veneremur plena in ejus sacrificium & intercessionem fiducia recumbentes; Filium hominis, regem nostrum, fideli obsequio prosequamur, ab ipsius nutu & arbitrio pendentes, sanctisque legibus obnoxii atque subditi.
units.tr: He did not ascend into heaven to prepare for the angels to come there. But he has indeed seemed to ascend into heaven for us sinners, ever living to make intercession for us, Heb. 7:25. For we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, 1 John 2:1. As for the angels, though Christ has bestowed on them lesser benefits, they nevertheless, free from any sting of envy, hasten with the most ardent zeal into the obedience of Christ; they ascend eagerly and descend to the Son of man. Hereafter you shall see the angels of God ascending and descending, etc. Therefore, faithful people, let us honour the Son of man, our prophet, most devoted to his teaching; let us revere the Son of man, our high priest, resting on his sacrifice and intercession in full trust; let us follow the Son of man, our king, with faithful obedience, depending on his nod and his will, and subject and bound to his holy laws.

units.la: 7o. Quod angeli Dei simul ascendunt, simulque descendunt ad Filium hominis, argumentum est luculentum, nullum esse obsequii genus usque adeo multiforme & varium, ad quod obsequiosissimi non sese accingant, componantque pro colendo Christo Dei angeli. Si ad Filium hominis, in coelum apertum ascendentem, angeli Dei modo ascendentes viderentur, obsequium sane facillimum, gratissimumque exhiberent. Angeli lucis in coelum, lucis immortalis domicilium, naturae propriae impulsu tenderent; angeli sancti & beati, laetam sanctitatis atque beatitatis sedem, cum Christo & ad Christum hilares peterent, nec tam Christi gloriam, quam commodum suum proprium suo illo ad Christum ascensu quaerere viderentur. Hac equidem lege, mortales, rerum propriarum solliciti, Christo servire volupe est. Re enim vera, ubi Filio hominis servire videmini, dum interea bonis, commodisque propriis vestris egregie consulitur, ceu zelo sancto inflammati & prae laetitia gestientes Seraphinorum ad instar in Christi obsequium non ire modo, sed & volare vos, mundus, qui fuco & fallacia pascitur, non assereret modo, sed & juraret. Si inter serviendum Christo licet & ascendere vobis ad honorum fastigia, divitiarum cumulos, culmenque ambitionis, en vos extemplo alacres & expeditos ad Christi obsequium. Ecquid vero vestri ipsius obsequii est, nempe purum putum non Christo, sed carni ac φιλαυτία exhibitum servitium? Exemplo angelorum Dei discite, homulorum carnalium natio, alio consilio, alioque animo Filio hominis esse ministrandum. Angeli Dei non ascendunt duntaxat ad Filium hominis, coelumque apertum: sed & plane diversi ministerii genere ad eum, ubi & quando par est praeter naturam suam expediti praepetesque descendunt. Relicto coelo, sanctitatis juxta ac felicitatis domicilio, futurum est, ut ad terram, peccati, mortis & miseriae sedem luctuoluctuosissimam, descendentes videantur, ut tuba clangant, mortuos, & sepulchro exeuntes, celeusmate jucundo aliis, terribili caeteris, cunctos nullo discrimine citent ad Christi tribunal. Ita Christo serviendum est ad exemplum angelorum Dei, mortales, quotquot vultis digni haberi laude fidelis obsequii. Ascendendum ad Christum in coelum apertum meditatione, amore, desiderio boni superni, sanctitatis & felicitatis: sed & ad Christum & cum Christo descendendum est ad infimum humilitatis, afflictionis, pauperitatis & miseriae gradum. Ascendendum cum Christo in montem gloriosum Ithabyrium; sed & ad eum in montem Golgotha, Calvariaeque eundum. Age igitur Filium hominis, agnum Dei, sequamur quocunque eat cum Ecclesia sua tantisper dum in terris versatur, pugnam fidei gloriosam pugnatura cum carne & sanguine, cum principatibus & potestatibus seculi. Sed vero quia luctam carnis experimur, studium prompti spiritus in Christi obsequium tardantem, age vota convertamus nostra in regem nostrum, sponsumque dilectissimum, dicamus & ingemi- nemus; trahe nos, & concurremus ad te, trahe nos vinculis amoris tui & plenis deliciarum funibus, & pertrahemur tibi aeternum addictissimi, prompti & expediti in sempiterna secula ministraturi cum angelis tuis, & universo redemptorum, & beatorum choro, amen.
units.tr: 7. That the angels of God ascend together and descend together to the Son of man is clear proof that there is no kind of obedience so manifold and varied that the most obedient do not gird themselves for it and prepare themselves to worship Christ. If the angels of God were seen only ascending to the Son of man as he ascends into the open heaven, they would surely render a very easy and very welcome obedience. The angels of light would make for heaven, the home of immortal light, by the impulse of their own nature; the holy and blessed angels would seek the joyful seat of holiness and blessedness, cheerfully going with and to Christ, and would seem to seek not so much the glory of Christ as their own advantage in that ascent to Christ. Indeed, mortals anxious about their own affairs find it pleasant to serve Christ on this condition. For in truth, where you seem to serve the Son of man, while meanwhile your own goods and advantages are excellently looked after, as if inflamed with holy zeal and exulting with joy, like the Seraphim you not only go, but fly into the obedience of Christ. The world, which feeds on deceit and falsehood, would not merely assert this but swear to it. If it is permitted, while serving Christ, to climb to the heights of honours, to heaps of riches and the summit of ambition, behold, you are at once eager and ready for the obedience of Christ. But what is this your obedience, namely a service offered purely and simply not to Christ but to the flesh and self-love [φιλαυτία]? Learn from the example of the angels of God, you race of carnal little men, that the Son of man must be served with a different purpose and a different mind. The angels of God do not merely ascend to the Son of man and the open heaven; they also, by a wholly different kind of ministry, descend to him, readily and eagerly, beyond their own nature, when and where it is fitting. Having left heaven, the home of holiness and happiness alike, they seem to descend to the earth, the most sorrowful seat of sin, death and misery; they sound the trumpet, they call the dead out of the tombs, joyfully to some and terrifyingly to others, and summon all without distinction to the tribunal of Christ. Thus, mortals, all of you who wish to be counted worthy of praise for faithful obedience, you must serve Christ after the example of the angels of God. You must ascend to Christ into the open heaven in meditation, love and longing for the good things above, for holiness and happiness; but you must also descend with Christ and to Christ to the lowest level of humility, affliction, poverty and misery. We must ascend with Christ to the glorious mountain of Tabor, but also go to him on the mount of Golgotha and Calvary. Therefore, let us follow the Son of man, the Lamb of God, wherever he goes with his Church while he dwells on earth, about to wage the glorious battle of faith against flesh and blood, against the principalities and powers of this world. But since we experience the struggle of the flesh, which delays our ready spirit's obedience to Christ, let us turn our prayers to our king and most beloved bridegroom, and say and repeat again and again: draw us, and we will run after thee. Draw us with the bonds of your love and with cords full of delights, and we shall be drawn to you, forever devoted, ready and prepared to minister for ever and ever with your angels and the whole choir of the redeemed and blessed. Amen.

units.la: QUAESTIO VIII.
units.tr: QUESTION VIII.

units.la: Quomodo Visio coeli aperti & Angelorum Dei ad Filium hominis ascendentium atque descendentium, majora sint iis, quae Nathanael de Christo viderat?
units.tr: How the vision of the opened heaven and of the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man is greater than what Nathanael had seen concerning Christ

units.la: Cumprimum regina Sabae regis Schelomonis nominis celebritatem audivit, ut perculsa fama nobili non credidit tamen, vera esse quae fando audiverat de sapientia, & magnificentia Schelomonis. Cumprimum Nathanael Philippum audivit, narrantem, Jesum, Josephi ex Nazaretha filium, esse Messiam de quo Moses & prophetae scripserant; non credidit pariter vera esse, quae de eo narrabantur, vel loci obscuritate deterritus; ex Nazaretha, inquit, potest ne aliquid boni esse? Sicut regina Austri, excita curiositate sua, e finibus Aethiopiae ad Schelomonem accessit, acutis aenigmatis illius sapientiam sollicitatura: ita & Nathanael venit ad Jesum, ut videret, experin eutum facturus, num vera essent, quæ Philippus de ipso narraverat. Regina Sabæ, ubi sapientiam Salomonis tantam esse experta est, ut nihil haberet in animo perplexis ænigmatum ambagibus propositum, quod regem sapientem lateret, exclamavit admirabunda: verum est illud, quod audiveram in terra mea de rebus tuis & sapientia tua. Non credidi tamen usque dum venirem & viderent oculi mei. Sed ecce non indicatum fuerat mihi ejus dimidium. Superas sapientia & bonitate famam illam quam audiveram. Beati homines tui, beati servi tui isti, qui stantes coram te, jugiter audiunt sapientiam tuam: non secus & Nathanael, ubi primum audivit Jesum, de se dicentem; ecce vere Israelita, in quo non est dolus; priusquam te Philippus vocabat, cum esses sub ficu, videbam te; conscius tunc temporis, nihil se habere in animo clausum, quod Jesum vel remotum lateret, admirabundus in hanc erupit confessionem; Rabbi, tu es filius Dei, tu es rex Israëlis. 1 Reg. 10: 6. 7. 8. Joh. 1: 49. Ut quid, regina Austri, per longa viarum itinera remota petiisti Hierosolymam, expletura nempe animum studiosum videndi regem, cujus sapientia perplexa explicat, solvitque ænigmata? Hic hic est major rege Schelomone; Jesus, æterna Dei sapientia, regni cœlorum aperit mysteria illa profunda, quæ oculus non vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in cor hominis ascenderunt. Hic pacis princeps renes scrutatur, cuncta cordis humani momenta pervidet, omnia oculis ejus sunt τετραχηλισμένα, Heb. 4: 13. Tumet nosti, Nathanael, propria tua experientia, Jesum superare famam, nec fuisse tibi narratum dimidium illius sapientiæ, qua pollet Christus ὁ χρηστολογ-ούμενος. Sed præstolare paulisper & longe majora videbis iis, quæ hactenus percepisti de Jesu, filio Dei, regeque Israëlis. Quanto cœlum, splendidum Dei palatium, thronusque gloriæ, regium superat Schelomonis palatium, thronumque suffultum duodecim leonibus, insigne familiæ Judæ; quantò è terra in cœlum ascensus superbo supereminet Schelomonis ædes regales ascensui; quantò angeli Dei, Christi ministri splendore glorioso servos Schelomonis antecellunt: tantò majora de Christo, filio Dei, regeque Israëlis, deinceps visurus es. Quia dixi tibi; vidi te sub ficu, credis? majora istis videbis. Nam ab hoc tempore videbitis cœlum apertum, & angelos Dei ascendentes ac descendentes ad Filium hominis.
units.tr: As soon as the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of King Solomon's name, she was struck by the report but nevertheless did not believe that what she had heard by report about the wisdom and magnificence of Solomon was true. Likewise, when Nathanael heard Philip telling him that Jesus, the son of Joseph from Nazareth, was the Messiah of whom Moses and the prophets had written, he did not believe that what was said about him was true, being deterred partly by the obscurity of the place: "Can anything good come out of Nazareth?" As the queen of the South, roused by her curiosity, came from the ends of Ethiopia to Solomon, meaning to test his wisdom with subtle riddles, so Nathanael came to Jesus, intending to find out by experience whether what Philip had told him about him was true. When the queen of Sheba had found Solomon's wisdom so great that nothing she had proposed in the tangled ambiguities of her riddles lay hidden from the wise king, she cried out in wonder: The report is true which I heard in my own land about your affairs and your wisdom. I did not believe it until I came and my eyes saw it. But behold, the half was not told me. Your wisdom and goodness surpass the fame which I had heard. Happy are your men, happy are these your servants, who stand before you and continually hear your wisdom. In the same way Nathanael, as soon as he heard Jesus speaking about him, Behold, truly an Israelite in whom there is no guile; before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you, being aware at that moment that he had nothing hidden in his mind which could lie concealed from Jesus, broke out in wonder into this confession: Rabbi, you are the Son of God, you are the King of Israel. (1 Kings 10:6, 7, 8; John 1:49.) Why, O queen of the South, did you travel by long and distant roads to Jerusalem, surely to satisfy your eager desire to see the king whose wisdom unravels and solves riddles? Here is one greater than King Solomon: Jesus, the eternal wisdom of God, opens the deep mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man. Here is the Prince of Peace who searches the reins, who sees all the movements of the human heart, to whom all things are laid bare (Heb. 4:13) [τετραχηλισμένα]. You yourself, Nathanael, know from your own experience that Jesus surpasses his fame, and that the half of that wisdom with which Christ, the one who is called good [ὁ χρηστολογούμενος], excels was not told you. But wait a little, and you will see things far greater than those you have so far perceived about Jesus, the Son of God and King of Israel. As heaven, the splendid palace of God and throne of glory, surpasses the royal palace of Solomon and his throne supported by twelve lions, the emblem of the house of Judah; as the ascent from earth to heaven far exceeds the ascent to Solomon's royal house; as the angels of God, the ministers of Christ, surpass the servants of Solomon in glorious splendor, so greatly will you hereafter see greater things concerning Christ, the Son of God and King of Israel. Because I said to you, I saw you under the fig tree, do you believe? You will see greater things than these. For from now on you will see the heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man.

units.la: Ubi Christus recipit, Nathanaelem, Philippum, cæterosque discipulos majora visuros iis, quæ de eo hactenus noverant, nempe quia visuri erant cœlum apertum, & angelos Dei ascendentes & descendentes ad Filium hominis, locutus paradoxum videtur. Nathanael enim tria hactenus de Jesu noverat, duo quidem ut principia, tertium denique ut conclusionem, ex ambobus illis principiis cognitis elicitam. Noverat videlicet Natha-
units.tr: When Christ tells Nathanael, Philip and the other disciples that they will see greater things than those they had so far learned about him, namely that they would see the heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man, he seems to speak a paradox. For Nathanael had so far known three things about Jesus: two indeed as principles, and a third finally as a conclusion drawn from both of those known principles. Namely, he knew

units.la: Nathanael 1°. Jesum vel oculis corporeis secreta, longeque remota & occulta cognoscere, quia eum remotum viderat sub ficu latentem. 2°. Jesum vel intima cordis momenta atque sinceritatem acutum cernere. Dixerat nempe Jesus de accedente Nathanaele, sibi ignoto; hic est Israelita, in quo non est fraus. Hinc 3um. ignotum prius, ex notis illis ambobus veluti principiis uti conclusionem deduxerat; tu es filius Dei, tu es rex Israëlis. Unde liquet, Nathanaelem hunc in modum ratiocinatum esse. Qui homo secreta aliorum momenta cordis pervidet, ut ei sint nuda atque τελεια cuique semota; occultaque oculis corporeis aperta sunt & pervia, non homo modò, sed & filius Dei est, verusque Messias rex Israëlis. Atqui Jesus Nazarethanus occulta cordis momenta pervidet, novitque, quæ sunt in homine, habetque pervia quotquot sunt oculis corporeis secreta & occulta: Ergo Jesus, homo Nazarethanus; est Dei filius, rexque Israëlis. Sed vero hæc tanta videntur, ut vixdum majora de Jesu cognoscenda in mentem venire queant, nedum cœli aperti visio, ascensus & descensus angelorum ad Filium hominis jure ullo legitimo cum iis de magnitudine certare possint, aut æquiparari. Qui enim novit Jesum hominem simul esse Dei filium, Immanuelem novit, Deum & hominem, infinitum & finitum, immortalem & mortalem, æternum atque temporarium, Creatorem cum creatura in una eademque persona unione prorsus ἀρρήτῳ, insolubili, & æterno conjunctum vinculo; natum tempore Augusti & Herodis hominem, Deumque ante sæcula benedictum; natum ex Virgine hominem, atque adeo filium Adami, & Deum ex Deo, φῶς ἐκ φωτός, genitum ante mundum conditum; sine forma & specie hominem, despectum hominibus, vermem, non hominem, probrum populorum, Deum simul & Dominum gloriæ, qui renes scrutatur & corda, quique ventis & Oceano imperat, quemque Angeli Dei colunt & adorant, vel dum homines temnunt & vilipendunt. Qui Jesum, Dei filium, videt, novitque esse regem Israëlis, fide contemplatur, usurpatque mentis oculis imaginem Dei invisibilis, splendorem gloriæ & characterem hypostaseos Dei; ut Jesus asserere nullus dubitaverit; Philippe, qui me vidit, vidit & patrem meum. Joh. 14: 9. Hinc adeo oritur proposita quæstio, nempe qui videre cœlum apertum, & angelos Dei, &c. majora sint iis, quæ Nathanael hactenus de Jesu noverat, atque adeo crediderat.
units.tr: Nathanael (1) that Jesus could know, even with bodily eyes, secrets and things far away and hidden, because he had seen him from afar lurking under the fig tree. (2) That Jesus could discern the inner movements of the heart and sincerity; for Jesus had said of Nathanael, who was approaching and unknown to him: Here is an Israelite in whom there is no deceit. Hence (3), the thing previously unknown, he had deduced as a conclusion from those two known things, as if from principles: You are the Son of God, you are the King of Israel. From this it is clear that Nathanael reasoned in this way: whoever sees through the secret movements of the hearts of others, so that they are naked and perfect [τελεια] and laid open to him, and whatever is hidden from bodily eyes is open and transparent to him, is not only a man but also the Son of God and the true Messiah, King of Israel. But Jesus of Nazareth sees through the hidden movements of the heart, knows what is in a man, and has open to him all things hidden and concealed from bodily eyes. Therefore Jesus, a man of Nazareth, is the Son of God and King of Israel. But these great things seem so great that scarcely any greater thing about Jesus can come to mind, much less can the vision of the opened heaven and the ascent and descent of the angels upon the Son of Man, by any lawful right, contend with them in greatness or be considered equal to them. For whoever knows that Jesus is at once man and Son of God, knows Immanuel, God and man, infinite and finite, immortal and mortal, eternal and temporal, the Creator joined with the creature in one and the same person by an unspeakable [ἀρρήτῳ], indissoluble and eternal bond; man born in the time of Augustus and Herod, yet blessed God before the ages; man born of the Virgin, and thus son of Adam, and God from God, light from light [φῶς ἐκ φωτός], begotten before the world was made; a man without form or comeliness, despised by men, a worm and not a man, the reproach of the people, at once God and the Lord of glory, who searches the reins and hearts, who commands the winds and the Ocean, whom the angels of God worship and adore, even while men scorn and vilify him. Whoever sees Jesus, the Son of God, and knows him to be the King of Israel, contemplates him by faith and uses with the eyes of his mind the image of the invisible God, the brightness of the glory and the express image of the substance of God; so that Jesus did not hesitate to assert: Philip, he who has seen me has seen my Father also. (John 14:9.) Hence arises the question proposed: whether those who see the opened heaven, and the angels of God, etc., have greater things than those which Nathanael had so far known about Jesus, and therefore believed.

units.la: Ut dicto Christi veritas sua, fidesque illibata asseratur, eorum, quæ diximus in perstringendis ambabus quæstionibus de visione cæli aperti, deque ascensu Angelorum Dei ad Filium hominis, comprimis meminisse juvat, simulque observare, cœli aperti ascensus descensusque angelorum visionem nem, quam Christus futuram pollicebatur, bifariam contendi posse cum duobus illis memoratis, quæ de Jesu Nathanael noverat. Et 1o. quidem absolute spectatam in sese, 2o. spectatam sub σχέσει & necessitudine medii ad fidem faciendam de Jesu, filio Dei, veroque Messia. Et de prima quidem consideratione prudens nemo multum laboraverit, quandoquidem ex S. contextus serie perliquidum est, Jesum futuram aperti cæli visionem promisisse uti rem longe majorem, sub σχέσει & habitudine medii ad fidem faciendam de se, filio Dei, veroque Messia. Opponit nempe Christus visionem cæli aperti &c. visioni, seu cognitioni Nathanaelis, qua tanquam principio & medio collegerat, Jesum esse filium Dei, regemque Israelis. Ita enim Christus ratiocinatur; quia dixi tibi; te sub ficu videbam, credis. Majora videbis inposterum, quibus nempe credas fide majori & evidentiori, me esse filium Dei & Messiam. Hinc in expedito est, Christi scopum secuturis visionem cæli aperti, &c. comparandam esse cum visione, seu cognitione Nathanaelis, quatenus ambæ istæ visiones, seu cognitiones super Jesu, principia sunt atque media, è quibus hæc conclusio elicitur; Jesus, homo Nazarethanus est filius Dei, verusque Messias. Age igitur in hac comparatione instituenda in hunc Christi scopum, velut in certam Theologicæ istius navigationis cynosuram, mentis nostræ oculos dirigamus & defigamus, ut promissionis Christi veritas in clara & aperta luce constituatur.
