units.tr: So that the truth of Christ's word and his unimpaired faithfulness may be asserted, it is especially helpful to recall what we have said in setting out the two questions, concerning the vision of the opened heaven, and concerning the ascent of the angels of God to the Son of Man, and at the same time to observe that the vision of the opened heaven and of the ascent and descent of angels, which Christ promised would come, can be compared in two ways with the two things mentioned which Nathanael had known about Jesus. First, considered absolutely in itself; second, considered under the relation and connection of a means of producing faith in Jesus, the Son of God and true Messiah. Concerning the first consideration no sensible person will labour much, since it is perfectly clear from the sequence of the context that Jesus promised the future vision of the opened heaven as a thing far greater, under the relation and habitude of a means of producing faith in himself, as Son of God and true Messiah. Christ sets the vision of the opened heaven, etc., against the vision, or knowledge, of Nathanael, by which, as by a principle and a means, he had gathered that Jesus was the Son of God and King of Israel. For Christ reasons thus: Because I said to you, I saw you under the fig tree, do you believe? You will see greater things hereafter, by which you may believe with a greater and clearer faith that I am the Son of God and the Messiah. Hence it is plain that the vision of the opened heaven, etc., is to be compared, in accordance with Christ's aim, with the vision or knowledge of Nathanael, insofar as both of these visions or knowledges concerning Jesus are principles and means from which this conclusion is drawn: Jesus, the man of Nazareth, is the Son of God and the true Messiah. Come then, in instituting this comparison, let us direct and fix the eyes of our mind upon this aim of Christ, as upon a sure guiding star of this theological voyage, so that the truth of Christ's promise may be established in clear and open light.

units.la: Primò quidem Nathanaelis ratiocinium, quod supra formatum exhibuimus, sano nemini Theologo ἀχρι-ξεστάτῃ demonstratio videbitur. Nam prima propositio nec est necessaria, nec necessario semper vera. Nam ut Deus sit unus ὁ καρδιογνώστης, renum & cordium scrutator, non paucis φιλοῖς ἀνθρώ-ποις Numen indulsit benignissimum, ut non ἀμέσως, mediate tamen intueri cordis humani secreta. Danieli enim revelavit secretum Nabuchodonosoris somnium, vel dum plane cognitioni & memoriæ regis effugerat, Dan. 2:5. 30. Nec non Elisæo funestum Jorami regis Samariæ consilium, 2. Reg. 6:32. Quid cum Prophetæ futura omne genus prædixerint, quæque ex mero Dei pendebant, hominumque arbitrio; nonne Numen eis hominibus revelavit secreta cordis Dei, hominumque momenta? Quod igitur Jesus homo momentum cordis Nathanaelis perviderat, non erat oportunum, nedum necessarium medium, quo Nathanael concluderet, Jesum non esse merum hominem, sed Deum atque adeo Dei filium, super omnia benedictum. Quidni enim Deus Jesu, vel mero homini revelare potuit cor sincerum Nathanaelis, quando Danieli figmentum cordis Nabuchodonozoris, & Elisæo, mero homini, perniciosum Jorami consilium aperte revelaverat? Nec cognitio Nathanaelis, quâ persentiscebat remota, clausaque oculis corporeis, esse Iesu pervia, magis erat oportunum, necessariumve medium, quo Israelita sine fraude concluderet, Iesum hominem esse filium Dei, verumque Messiam, quando percompertum est, hanc non fuisse Iesu singularem, propriamve prærogativam. Nempe merus erat homo Elisæus. Vidit tamen, quæ ab oculis corporeis remota clam agebat Gehasi, ubi à Nahaamane duo talenta argentea, & ambas vestes acciperet: non abierat, inquit Elisæus, animus meus, cum converteret se vir à curru suo obviam tibi. An tempus erat accipiendi argentum aut vestes, 2. Reg. 5:26. Sed vero ad unum Iesum cœlum apertum visum est modo plane singulari, cæterisque hominibus incommunicabili. Unum Iesum è cœlo aperto Deus suo dignatus est alloquio, unum Iesum palam è cœlo aperto filium suum unice carum declaravit, unum Iesum audiendum imperavit, ut nunquam ac nusquam vox isthæc è cœlo reddita mortalium ulli audita fuerit; hic est filius meus dilectus, in quo complacui; eum audite. Unus Iesus visus est in cœlum apertum ascendere, vehens nube triumphali, non ab uno discipulo, uti Elias ab Elisæo raptus flammeo curru; sed ab omnibus discipulis ultra centenarium numerum, ut ab iis, qui familiari Iesu consortio usi fuerant à Johannis baptismate ad eum usque diem, quo sursum receptus est, unus in testem resurrectionis ejus, Apostolorum collegio allegeretur, Act.1:21,22. Unus Iesus cœlum aperire visus est & è cœlo aperto Spiritum S. mittere & effundere die solemni Pentecostes. Unus denique Iesus è cœlo aperto descendere videndus est, Angelorum myriadibus stipatus. Unde in expedito concludere est, cœli aperti visionem, quam hic Iesus futuram recipit, majus esse atque illustrius spectaculum in fidem faciendam de eo Filio Dei, veroque Messia, quam illud quod exhibuerat, dum remotum, clausumque, oculis corporeis Nathanaelem vidisse se sub ficu latentem probaverat, & cordis ejus sinceritatem ignoto sibi jam diu perspectam fuisse, vel solemni declaratione fecerat contestatum.
units.tr: First, Nathanael's reasoning, as we set it out above, will seem no demonstration at all to any sound theologian [ἀκριβεστάτῃ, most exact]. For the first proposition is neither necessary nor always necessarily true. Although God alone is the searcher of hearts [ὁ καρδιογνώστης], the scrutiniser of kidneys and hearts, the most gracious Deity has granted to not a few dear men the power to discern the secrets of the human heart, not immediately but by means of mediation. For he revealed to Daniel the secret of Nebuchadnezzar's dream, even when it had wholly escaped the king's knowledge and memory (Dan. 2:5, 30), and to Elisha the deadly counsel of Jehoram, king of Samaria (2 Kings 6:32). Since the prophets foretold every kind of future event, both those which depended on God alone and those which depended on human choice, did not God reveal to these men the secrets of the divine heart and the movements of human hearts? Therefore, that Jesus, a man, perceived the movement of Nathanael's heart was neither a fitting nor a necessary means by which Nathanael could conclude that Jesus is not a mere man but God, and so the Son of God, blessed above all. For why could God not reveal the sincere heart of Nathanael to Jesus, even as a mere man, when he had plainly revealed the figment of Nebuchadnezzar's heart to Daniel, and the pernicious counsel of Jehoram to Elisha, also a mere man? Nor was Nathanael's knowledge, by which he sensed that Jesus could see into what was remote and shut off from bodily eyes, a more fitting or necessary means by which an Israelite could rightly conclude that Jesus is a man, the Son of God and true Messiah, since it is well established that this was not a peculiar or distinctive prerogative of Jesus. Elisha was, after all, a mere man, yet he saw what Gehazi secretly did, remote from bodily eyes, when Gehazi took from Naaman two talents of silver and two garments. Did not my heart go, said Elisha, when the man turned from his chariot to meet you? Was it a time to receive silver or garments? (2 Kings 5:26). But the opened heaven was seen in a wholly singular manner by Jesus alone, which cannot be shared with other men. God deigned to address Jesus alone from the opened heaven. From the opened heaven he openly declared his only beloved Son, Jesus alone, and commanded that Jesus alone be heard, so that this voice from heaven was never heard by any mortal, at any time or place: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him. Jesus alone was seen ascending into the opened heaven, carried on a triumphal cloud, not with one disciple, as Elijah was taken up by Elisha in a fiery chariot, but with all the disciples, more than a hundred in number, so that from those who had enjoyed familiar fellowship with Jesus from John's baptism until the day he was taken up, one might be chosen as a witness of his resurrection and added to the college of Apostles (Acts 1:21, 22). Jesus alone was seen to open heaven and, from the opened heaven, to send and pour out the Holy Spirit on the solemn day of Pentecost. Finally, Jesus alone is to be seen descending from the opened heaven, surrounded by myriads of angels. Hence it is easy to conclude that the vision of the opened heaven, which this Jesus will receive in the future, is a greater and more illustrious spectacle for establishing faith in that Son of God and true Messiah than the one he displayed when he proved that he had seen Nathanael under the fig tree, hidden and shut off from bodily eyes, and when he attested by a solemn declaration that he had long known the sincerity of Nathanael's heart, which had been unknown to him.

units.la: Secundò, quando certum est, videre Cœlum apertum aliisque exhibere contemplandum & cognoscendum, majus esse & illustrius, quam terræ secreta & occulta penetrare ac pervidere; majora equidem & illustriora de se Iesus docuit discipulos, ubi iis clare, solideque comprobavit, cœlum sibi esse apertum, ut omnia nosset Dei mysteria, eisque in clara luce exhiberet aperta, quam ubi, viso Nathanaele sub ficu terrena latitante, eos docuerat sibi aperta & pervia esse, quotquot sunt in terra latibula.
units.tr: Second, since it is certain that to see the opened heaven, and to be shown it for contemplation and knowledge, is greater and more illustrious than to penetrate and see through the secrets and hidden places of the earth, Jesus did indeed teach his disciples greater and more illustrious things about himself when he clearly and solidly proved to them that heaven was open to him, so that he knew all the mysteries of God and set them forth in clear light. This was greater than when, having seen Nathanael hiding under the earthly fig tree, he taught them that all the hiding-places on earth, however many, are open and visible to him.

units.la: Tertiò, majus equidem est & quavis humana cognitione superius percontari & penetrare ipsum Dei cor, mentem nempe, consilium, nec non arcanam Numinis voluntatem, quam secreta cordis humani momenta & affectus ètus intimos rimari & pervidere. Atqui Iesus, ubi cœlum apertum Nathanaeli, cæterisque discipulis suis exhibuit, cor cœli, h. e. Dei mentem, consilia, mysteria, nec non voluntatem arcanam eadem opera iisdem aperuit. Vos autem dixi amicos, quia omnia quæ audivi a Patre meo, nota feci vobis, Ioh. 15:15. Majora igitur & illustriora de Christo viderunt, ubi cœlum apertum ad Iesum, mysteria cœli revelantem, viderunt, quam ubi intellexere cor & sinceritatem Nathanaelis esse Iesu apertam atque perspectam.
units.tr: Third, it is certainly greater than any human knowledge to inquire into and penetrate the very heart of God, that is, his mind, his counsel, and also his hidden will, than to search out and see through the secret movements and innermost affections of the human heart. Yet Jesus, when he showed the opened heaven to Nathanael and his other disciples, at the same time disclosed to them the heart of heaven, that is, God's mind, counsels, mysteries, and hidden will. But I have called you friends, because all things that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you (John 15:15). Therefore they saw greater and more illustrious things about Christ when they saw heaven opened to Jesus, revealing the mysteries of heaven, than when they understood that the heart and sincerity of Nathanael were open and clear to Jesus.

units.la: Quarto, cum Nathanael ex gemino documento cognitionis Iesu Nazarethani, tertium hoc, sibi antea ignotum, uti distincte cognitum collegerat, nempe, Iesum esse filium Dei; vel eum credebat Dei filium, more modoque regum atque magistratuum, qui filii Altissimi appellantur, Ps. 82:6. sed singulari & excellentiori prærogativa, quæ Messiam, regum maximum, decebat, quæ erat tunc temporis Iudæorum fere omnium de Messia sententia; vel credebat esse Dei filium æternæ divinitatis prærogativa, creaturæ incommunicabili; utrumvis sane dixerimus, majora vidit, credidit que de Christo Nathanael una cum cæteris discipulis, ubi cœlum apertum, & angelos Dei ascendentes & descendentes ad Filium hominis viderunt. Primum si dixerimus; credebat igitur Nathanael Iesum esse regem terrenum, regnaturum in Iudæam, subditosque Iudæos, populum sibi peculiarem, lateque dominaturum in orbem, vi & armorum strepitu vincendum & subigendum. Sed vero ubi cœlum apertum viderunt, Filiumque hominis nube, Dei curru vehentem, & stipatum Angelis, ministris, subditisque suis, ad thronum majestatis supremæ euntem; viderunt sane & crediderunt, Iesum esse regem cœlestem, cui parerent omnia longe lateque dominanti, non in orbem modo terrarum, sed & in ipsos cœlicolas, angelos Dei sibi subditos, ministrosque obsequiosos. Viderunt in clara Spiritus S. luce Iesum non Iudæos modo, sed & omnes terrarum gentes, sibi fecisse populum peculiarem, subditosque fideles, comprimunt illapsu Spiritus S., venientis e cœlo aperto, Apostolorum præconio regnum Christi late per orbem prædicatum, & gentes baptizatas in fidem Christi regis, excusso Diaboli regno, cui hactenus male feriatæ servierant, clare ac distincte viderunt ac cognoverunt. Secundum si dixerimus (ut non fiat valde verosimile, quandoquidem nondum datus erat Spiritus S. quia nondum Christus erat e mortuis excitatus, Ioh. 7:39.) non minus tamen verum est, Nathanaelem cæterosque discipulos majora & illustriora vidisse, seu credidisse de Iesu, ubi cœlum apertum ad eum, excitatum e mortuis, & ascendentem viderunt. Nam 1º. credere Iesum esse Dei filium æterna naturæ divinæ communione cum Patre, non est per se salutiferum: nam & hoc ipsi Diaboli norunt: sed credere dere Jesum Dei filium mortuum pro expiandis peccatis nostris, excitatum e mortuis & coelo receptum, in argumentum solidissimum placatae justitiae Dei, & peractae expiationis nostrorum peccatorum, id demum est salutiferum. Sed & hoc nondum credebat Nathanael, caeterive intelligebant discipuli. Quod liquet vel ex isthoc carnali Petri consilio; propitius tibi esto, Domine, nequaquam tibi erit istud, Matth. 16: 22. Hoc demum discipuli viderunt & crediderunt, ubi Jesum excitatum e mortuis nube, in coelum apertum euntem contemplati sunt, & spiritu Christi induti facti martyres intrepidi passionis & gloriae Christi coram regibus & populis in salutem omni credenti. 2o. Ut ut Nathanael noverit, crediderit que Jesum esse Dei filium & Messiam liberatorem, modum tamen & rationem, qua erat aeternam populo suo redemptionem consecuturus, necdum videbat aut credebat. Id denuo illi, caeterisque revelatum est, cum coelum illud, quod in ipsius morte horribilem in modum obscuratum fuerat, apertum viderunt, quo Jesum regem gloriae, mortis & inferni victorem, reciperet collocandum in solio aeternae majestatis Dei viventis.
units.tr: Fourth, since Nathanael had gathered from the twofold evidence of his knowledge of Jesus of Nazareth this third thing, previously unknown to him but now clearly known, namely that Jesus is the Son of God, he either believed him to be the Son of God in the manner and sense in which kings and magistrates are called sons of the Most High (Ps. 82:6), but with the singular and more excellent prerogative which befitted the Messiah, the greatest of kings, which at that time was the opinion of almost all the Jews concerning the Messiah; or he believed that he was the Son of God by the prerogative of eternal divinity, which is incommunicable to any creature. Whichever of these we say, Nathanael, together with the other disciples, saw and believed greater things about Christ when they saw the opened heaven and the angels of God ascending and descending to the Son of man. If we say the first: then Nathanael believed that Jesus was an earthly king who would reign over Judea, with the Jews as his subjects, a people peculiar to himself, and would rule far and wide over the world, to be conquered and subdued by force of arms and the clamour of war. But when they saw the opened heaven, and the Son of man borne on a cloud, on God's chariot, and going to the throne of supreme majesty, surrounded by angels, his ministers and subjects, they certainly saw and believed that Jesus is a heavenly king, to whom all things obey, who rules far and wide, not only over the world's lands but also over the heavenly inhabitants themselves, the angels of God, his subjects and obedient ministers. In the clear light of the Holy Spirit they saw that Jesus had made for himself a peculiar people, not only of the Jews but of all the nations of the earth, and faithful subjects, who are gathered by the descent of the Holy Spirit coming from the opened heaven. They clearly and distinctly saw and understood that the kingdom of Christ was proclaimed far and wide through the world by the preaching of the Apostles, and that nations baptized into faith in Christ the king, having cast off the kingdom of the Devil, which they had served until then in wretched bondage, had been brought in. If we say the second (although this is not very probable, since the Holy Spirit had not yet been given, because Christ had not yet been raised from the dead, John 7:39), it is nonetheless no less true that Nathanael and the other disciples saw and believed greater and more illustrious things about Jesus when they saw heaven opened to him, raised from the dead and ascending. For, first, to believe that Jesus is the Son of God by eternal communion of the divine nature with the Father is not in itself saving, for the Devils also know this. But to believe that Jesus, the Son of God, died to expiate our sins, was raised from the dead and received into heaven, as the most solid proof of God's satisfied justice and of the completed expiation of our sins, this indeed is saving. Nathanael did not yet believe this, nor did the other disciples understand it, as is clear even from Peter's carnal counsel: Be it far from you, Lord; this shall never happen to you (Matt. 16:22). The disciples saw and believed this only when they contemplated Jesus raised from the dead, going up into the opened heaven on a cloud, and, clothed with the Spirit of Christ, became fearless martyrs of his passion and glory before kings and peoples, for the salvation of every believer. Second, although Nathanael knew and believed that Jesus is the Son of God and the liberating Messiah, he did not yet see or believe the manner and the means by which he would obtain eternal redemption for his people. This was again revealed to him and to the others when they saw that heaven, which had been darkened in a dreadful way at his death, opened, by which they received Jesus, the King of glory, victor over death and hell, to be seated on the throne of the eternal majesty of the living God.

units.la: Quinto, ut Nathanael ex stupenda Iesu cognitione sibi persuaserit, Iesum esse regem Israelis, nullus tamen vidit, Iesum esse Messiam, qualem Prophetae praedixerant, non Regem modo, sed simul summum Prophetam, simul summum Pontificem, non Israelis modo, sed & totius mundi. Ut enim splendida regiae dignitatis idea Iudaeis allubescebat quam maxime, vix de Prophetia Messiae, ac ne vix quidem de ipsius dignitate sacerdotali cogitabant. Verum enim vero ubi coelum apertum viderunt ad Filium hominis, excitatum e mortuis eo ascendentem, & e coelo aperto Spiritum S., qui eos duceret in omnem veritatem, doceretque omnia, scitu & creditu ad salutem necessaria, viderunt & exceperunt; tunc demum illis clare innotuit, Iesum esse Messiam, qualem Prophetae praedixerant, omnium nempe creaturarum Regem supremum, summum Pontificem, qui post oblatum realis propitiationis sacrificium per velum coelestis sanctuarii intraret & compareret coram Deo, intercessurus pro populo suo fideli, eumque aeterna benedictione e locis coelestibus mactaturus. Tunc demum illis innotuit, Iesum esse summum Prophetam, qui per Spiritum S. suum scrutatur τὰ βάθη τοῦ Θεοῦ, profunda Dei, eaque revelat suis Apostolis, sanctisque Prophetis mundo praedicanda atque docenda.
units.tr: Fifthly, Nathanael, from the amazing knowledge of Jesus, was persuaded that Jesus is the king of Israel, but none of them yet saw that Jesus is the Messiah the prophets had foretold: not only King, but at the same time the chief Prophet and the chief Priest, and not of Israel alone but of the whole world. For while the splendid idea of royal dignity pleased the Jews exceedingly, they hardly thought about the prophecy concerning the Messiah, and scarcely even about his priestly dignity. But truly, when they saw heaven opened over the Son of Man, raised from the dead and ascending thither, and from the opened heaven the Holy Spirit, who would lead them into all truth and teach them everything necessary for salvation to know and believe, they saw and received it. Then at last it became clear to them that Jesus is the Messiah the prophets had foretold: the supreme King of all creatures, the High Priest who, after offering the sacrifice of real propitiation, would pass through the veil of the heavenly sanctuary and appear before God, interceding for his faithful people and blessing them with eternal blessing from the heavenly places. Then at last it became known to them that Jesus is the supreme Prophet, who through the Holy Spirit searches the depths of God [τὰ βάθη τοῦ Θεοῦ], the deep things of God, and reveals them to his apostles and holy prophets to be preached and taught to the world.

units.la: Sexto, ut Nathanael viderit, Iesum esse regem Israelis, nondum tamen viderat, Iesum esse dignum contemplatione, amore & reverentia Angelorum. Sed ubi coelum apertum vidit, Angelosque Dei ad eum ascendentes, tunc demum vidit atque credidit, Iesum esse dignum spectaculum, quod Angeli contemplarentur, admirarentur & velata facie tremebundi venerarentur. Hinc Paulus in memorandis pietatis articulis & hunc memorat, Deum nempe in carne manifestum, fuisse ab Angelis visum, 1. Tim. 3: 16. Eccur vero ? nempe Angeli Dei noverant fore, ut filius Dei caro fieret, mortemque oppeteret in redemptionem generis humani. Sed ubi sortem suam illam beatam, qua ab Angelis tenebrarum gloriosum in modum secernuntur, mente sagaci pensabant, cum utrimque paria originis momenta viderent, ut liberum Dei beneplacitum adorabant cernui, ita & filium Dei, futurum Ecclesiæ redemptorem, causam suæ perseverantiæ esse subodorabantur. Deus nempe eos fecerat Angelos electos, ut forent πνεύματα λειτουργικά, cum Christi, tum eorum, qui per Christum salutis hæreditatem sunt adituri. Hinc flagrans illud Angelorum desiderium, videndi Deum in carne manifestatum, & introspiciendi per eum, tum in mysteria redemptionis, tum in mysterium perseverantiæ suæ. Angeli tenebrarum, inquiebant, Angeli lucis sancti, beati, æque ac nos conditi, reliquere domicilium suum, facti Angeli rebelles, & Angeli tenebrarum miserrimi, dum nos in statu nostro sancto ac glorioso perstitimus. Undenam, obsecro, stupenda isthæc differentia nos inter & illos ? Unum Dei beneplacitum id fecit discriminis, qui nos selegit Christo, filio suo, in carne manifestato addicendos obsequiosos ministros Matth. 16:27. & 26:53. Age igitur ad statorem nostrum volemus, eum contemplemur, veneremur. Non equidem redemit nos, sed stabilem fecit nobis beatam sortem. Id autem mysterii Nathanaeli, caeterisque discipulis hactenus incognitum, clare & distincte innotuit, ubi cœlum apertum & angelos Dei ad filium hominis ascendentes viderunt. Concludamus igitur Nathanaelem caeterosque discipulos majora & illustriora vidisse nec non credidisse de Christo, ubi cœlum apertum viderunt, iis omnibus, quæ hactenus de ipso noverant, ubi terræ secreta & cordium momenta sibi esse pervia, luculenter demonstrabat.
units.tr: Sixthly, Nathanael saw that Jesus is the king of Israel, yet he had not yet seen that Jesus is worthy of the contemplation, love and reverence of the angels. But when he saw heaven opened and the angels of God ascending to him, then at last he saw and believed that Jesus is a sight worthy of the angels' contemplation, wonder and trembling veneration with veiled faces. Hence Paul, in recalling the articles of godliness, also mentions this: that God, manifest in the flesh, was seen by the angels, 1 Tim. 3:16. Why so? Namely, the angels of God knew that the Son of God would become flesh and undergo death for the redemption of the human race. But when they weighed with a keen mind their own blessed lot, by which the angels of darkness were gloriously separated from them, and saw on both sides equal grounds of origin, they bowed down and adored the free good pleasure of God; and so they suspected that the Son of God, who would be the Redeemer of the Church, was the cause of their perseverance. For God had made them chosen angels, that they might be ministering spirits [πνεύματα λειτουργικά], both for Christ and for those who are to obtain the inheritance of salvation through Christ. Hence their burning desire to see God manifest in the flesh, and to look into through him both the mysteries of redemption and the mystery of their own perseverance. The angels of darkness, they said, the holy and blessed angels of light, created like us, left their dwelling and became rebel angels, and the most wretched angels of darkness, while we have continued in our holy and glorious state. Whence, I ask, this amazing difference between us and them? One thing made the distinction, the good pleasure of God, who chose us to be bound as obedient ministers to Christ, his Son made manifest in the flesh, Matt. 16:27 and 26:53. Come, then, let us look to our Keeper, let us contemplate and venerate him. He did not indeed redeem us, but he made our blessed lot secure for us. This mystery, hitherto unknown to Nathanael and the other disciples, became clear and distinct to them when they saw heaven opened and the angels of God ascending to the Son of Man. Let us conclude, then, that Nathanael and the other disciples saw and believed greater and more illustrious things about Christ when they saw heaven opened, than all those things they had known about him so far, when he clearly showed that the secrets of the earth and the movements of hearts lay open to him.

units.la: Sed vero si cœli aperti ad Filium hominis & Angelos Dei eò ascendentes visio, majora fuere iis quæ hactenus discipuli noverant de Filio hominis, longe utique majora iis ac illustriora merito dixerimus, quæ omnibus exhibebit videnda, ubi demum è cœlo aperto descendet angelorum myriadibus stipatus. Nam Dominus cum hortationis clamore, cum voce Archangeli, & cum Dei tuba descendet è cœlo 1 Thessal. 4: 16. Descendet cum Angelis suis potentibus, cum igne flammante infligens ultionem iis, qui Deum nesciunt, neque auscultant Euangelio Domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui poenam pendent æterni exitii a facie Domini & a gloria roboris ipsius. 2. Thessal. 1:7.8.9. Descendet mortuos è sepulchris excitaturus, populos omnes ad tremendum suum tribunal validO lido tubæ clangore convocaturus & stituros, consilia cordium abditaque pectorum momenta, res tenebris occultatas manifestaturus 1. Cor. 4: 5. Vivos simul ac mortuos, orbem universum judicaturus, Act. 17: 31. Ut unusquisque reportet quæ in corpore fecerit, congruenter ad id quod fecerit sive bonum sive malum. 2. Cor. 5: 10. Descendet ut glorificetur in sanctis suis, & admirandus fiat in credentibus omnibus 2. Thessal. 1: 10. Descendet ut gloria adventus sui cœli cum stridore prætereant, elementa afluantia solvantur, terraque & quæ in ea sunt opera exurantur. Descendet creaturam liberaturus è servitute corruptionis, & in libertatem gloriæ filiorum Dei asserturus. Rom. 8: 21. Descendet cœlos novos & novam terram, in quibus justitia inhabitat, productURUS. 2. Pet. 3: 10. 13. Descendet Rex gloriæ alios à dextris, alios à sinistris suis collocaturus. Tunc dicet Rex iis, qui ad dextram ipsius erunt, adeste benedicti patris mei, possidete regnum paratum vobis à jacto mundi fundamento. Tunc dicet etiam iis qui ad sinistram erunt, execrandi abite à me in ignem illum æternum paratum Diabolo & Angelis ejus Matth. 25: 34. 41. Veniet rursum & fideles discipulos assumet ad seipsum ut & illi sint ubi ipse erit. Joan. 14: 3. rapiemur simul cum iis in nubes in occursum Domini in aera, & ita semper cum Domino erimus. 1. Thes. 4: 17.
units.tr: But if the vision of heaven opened and the Son of Man with the angels of God ascending thither was greater than the things the disciples had so far known about the Son of Man, then we may rightly say that the things which he will show to all to be seen, when at last he descends from the opened heaven surrounded by myriads of angels, are far greater and more illustrious. For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a shout of command, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trumpet of God, 1 Thess. 4:16. He will descend with his mighty angels, with flaming fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ; they shall suffer the punishment of eternal destruction from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his might, 2 Thess. 1:7-9. He will descend to raise the dead from their graves, to summon all peoples to his dread tribunal with a mighty blast of the trumpet, and to reveal the counsels of hearts, the hidden thoughts of breasts, and things hidden in darkness, 1 Cor. 4:5. He will judge the whole world, both the living and the dead, Acts 17:31. So that each may receive what he has done in the body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil, 2 Cor. 5:10. He will descend to be glorified in his saints and to be marvelled at in all who believe, 2 Thess. 1:10. He will descend so that, at the glory of his coming, the heavens will pass away with a roar, the elements will be dissolved by fire, and the earth and the works in it will be burned up. He will descend to deliver the creation from the bondage of corruption and to lead it into the liberty of the glory of the sons of God, Rom. 8:21. He will descend to bring forth new heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness dwells, 2 Pet. 3:10, 13. The King of glory will descend to place some on his right and some on his left. Then the King will say to those on his right, Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. Then he will also say to those on his left, Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels, Matt. 25:34, 41. He will come again and take his faithful disciples to himself, that they may also be where he is, John 14:3. We shall be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord, 1 Thess. 4:17.

units.la: Ecquis vero iverit infitias, stupenda isthæc cœli aperiendi Christique descensuri spectacula majora iis futura, quæ Nathanael hactenus noverat de Filio hominis? Age vero utraque ἐκ παραλληλης paulo fusius contendamus, quando opposita juxta posita magis elucescunt. 1º. Ubi Christus cœlum quo ascenderet apertum monstravit Apostolis placasse se divinam justitiam, quæ ipsi Numinis sanctuarium reseraret, argumento omni majus exceptione probavit. Sed vero ubi cœlum denuo apertum ostendet hinc descendens in nubibus cœli, simul Deum justitiæ simul orbis universi judicem, omni oculo tremendum in modum se revelabit. 2º. Ubi cœlum apertum quo se reciperet discipulis conspiciendum exhibuit, stiturum se & comparituram ad Dei tribunal coram probavit: Contra ubi cœlum apertum in ultimum suum descensum dabit, simul vivos simul mortuos omnes nullo discrimine sistendos ad tremendum suum tribunal ut quisque ferat in corpore suo, ut bene vel male egerit, magno celeusmate & Archangeli voce citabit. 3º. Ubi in cœlum apertum se intulit angelis suis stipatum, se esse hominem cœlestem dubio procul & clara in luce constituit: sed contra ubi denuo dimoto spansi velo cœlum apertum exhibebit, veniens cum innumeris sanctorum myriadibus, se simul potentia, simul potestate summa præditum, qua animales & terrenos homines, in cœlestes & immortales stupenda plane metamorphosi ad oculi nictum commutet, neminem sinet dubitare. 4º. In cœlum apertum ascendens, ascensus sui spectaculo paucorum discipulorum oculos pavit; vit; ubi vero e coelo aperto descendet, omnibus orbis nationibus sese conspiciendum dabit. 5o. In coelum apertum nube vehens comites habuit Dei angelos: sed vero e coelo aperto descendens, totam Ecclesiam e quatuor mundi cardinibus congregatam, uti triumphantem exercituum, nubibus coeli vehentem, habebit comitem ascensus sui triumphalis. 6o. Coelum apertum ubi primum exhibuit, se super thronum majestatis intulit, regnaturum ad dexteram Dei. Ubi vero iterum e coelo aperto conspicuum in modum descendet, omnes electos & fideles unice charos secum trahet in thronis aeternum paratis constituendos. Ut autem visio coeli aperti & filii hominis descendentis cum angelis majus & spectabilius spectaculum, primo Filii hominis ascensui est, quem tamen magnitudine superasse omnia quae de sese hactenus videnda exhibuerat, solidis rationibus addiximus. In proclivi concludere est, visionem Filii hominis e coelo aperto cum Angelis demum descendentis, longe superaturam eorum magnitudinem quae Nathanael hactenus de Christo viderat & crediderat. Vidisti Nathanael Jesum scrutari cor unum & acutum cernere momenta tui intima. Sed vero ubi coelum apertum videbis & ad Filium hominis descendentes Angelos, clare & distincte comperies, Filium hominis corda omnia percontantem & eorum consiliia in apertam lucem producentem. Quam primum Christus specimen sui dederat, cor Nathanaelis reseratum videratis sine fuco, syncerum fraudis: Verum ubi coelum apertum ad filium hominis descendentem videbitis, futurum est ut fraudem occultam cordium in clara luce positam admirabundi videatis. Insignis synceritatis laudem Nathanaeli tribuentem Filium hominis, tunc temporis audivistis. Impositerum vero, ubi coelum apertum denuo conspicietis ad Filium hominis descendentem, cum simul vobis, simul fidelibus omnibus laudem exploratae fidei tribuentem, futurum est ut audiatis, nam fides vestra auro pretiosior, vobis cedet in laudem, honorem & gloriam, quum Jesus Christus e coelo revelabitur. 1. Pet. 1: 7. Jesum tunc scrutantem cor sine fraude Nathanaelis, necquiquam obstante despecta conditione vilissimi Nazarethani, Filium Dei & regem Israelis confessi utcunque celebrasti. At ubi e coelo aperto descenderit nec quicquam obstante ignominia crucis, & probro servilis supplicii, eum vitae principem, Deum super omnia benedictum, Angelorum dominum, Regem regum, Rectorem & universi orbis judicem, cum Angelorum ac sanctorum myriadiabus, celebrabitis concinentes. Magna & mirabilia sunt opera tua Domine Deus omnipotens, justa & vera sunt via tua Rex sanctorum, quis non metuet te Domine & glorificabit nomen tuum? Apoc. 15: 3.
units.tr: Yet who would deny that these marvellous spectacles of heaven opened and of Christ about to descend will be greater than those which Nathanael had so far known about the Son of Man? Come now, let us set the two side by side a little more fully, for opposites placed side by side shine out more clearly [ἐκ παραλληλης]. (1) When Christ showed the heaven to which he would ascend opened to the apostles, he proved beyond all objection that he had appeased the divine justice, which would unlock the sanctuary of the Deity for him. But when heaven is opened again and he shows himself descending from it in the clouds of heaven, at once the God of justice and the judge of the whole world, he will reveal himself in a manner dreadful to every eye. (2) When the opened heaven showed him to the disciples to be seen as he withdrew to it, he proved that he would stand and appear before the tribunal of God. On the contrary, when the opened heaven gives him his final descent, he will at the same time summon all, living and dead, without distinction, to stand before his dread tribunal, that each may bear in his body whether he has acted well or badly, with a great shout and the voice of the archangel. (3) When he entered the opened heaven surrounded by his angels, he doubtless established beyond question that he is the heavenly Man; but when, the veil being drawn back, he shows heaven opened, coming with countless myriads of saints, he will leave no one in doubt that he is endowed at once with power and supreme authority, by which he will change animal and earthly men into heavenly and immortal ones in a wonderful metamorphosis in the blink of an eye. (4) Ascending into the opened heaven, he fed the eyes of a few disciples with the sight of his ascension; but when he descends from the opened heaven, he will show himself to be seen by all the nations of the world. (5) Ascending into the opened heaven on a cloud, he had the angels of God as companions; but descending from the opened heaven, he will have as the companion of his triumphal descent the whole Church gathered from the four corners of the world, carried up on the clouds of heaven like a triumphant army. (6) When he first displayed the opened heaven, he entered upon the throne of majesty, to reign at the right hand of God. But when he descends visibly again from the opened heaven, he will draw all the elect and faithful, his own dear ones, with him, to be seated on thrones prepared for them forever. Now, that the vision of heaven opened and of the Son of Man descending with the angels is a greater and more conspicuous spectacle, we have shown by solid arguments, first for the ascension of the Son of Man, which nevertheless surpassed in greatness all that he had so far shown to be seen. It is easy to conclude that the vision of the Son of Man descending with the angels from the opened heaven at last will far surpass the greatness of what Nathanael had so far seen and believed about Christ. You saw, Nathanael, that Jesus searches a heart and perceives the innermost movements of yours. But when you see heaven opened and the angels descending to the Son of Man, you will clearly and distinctly discover that the Son of Man examines all hearts and brings their counsels into open light. As soon as Christ gave a sample of himself, you saw Nathanael's heart laid open, free of deceit and sincere; but when you see heaven opened and the Son of Man descending, it will come to pass that you will look with wonder on hidden deceit set in clear light. You heard the Son of Man at that time bestowing on Nathanael the praise of remarkable sincerity. But when you see again heaven opened and the Son of Man descending, bestowing praise on you and on all the faithful for tested faith, you will hear, for your faith, more precious than gold, will turn to your praise, honour and glory when Jesus Christ is revealed from heaven, 1 Pet. 1:7. You have somehow celebrated Jesus, who searched Nathanael's heart without deceit, and who, despite the despised condition of the most humble Nazarene, you confessed as the Son of God and King of Israel. But when he descends from the opened heaven, and no disgrace of the cross or reproach of servile punishment stands in the way, you will sing together with the myriads of angels and saints, celebrating him as the Prince of life, God blessed above all, Lord of the angels, King of kings, Ruler and Judge of the whole world: Great and marvellous are your works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are your ways, King of the saints. Who will not fear you, Lord, and glorify your name? Rev. 15:3.

units.la: 1°. QUandoquidem Christus minora primùm de se revelavit discipulis, longe majora postmodum ipsismet revelaturus. Argumento est, Christum eamdem instituisse viam, ac geminam plane adhibuisse methodum in veteri ac nova salutaris revelationis dispensatione, ut enim obscurius olim Christus revelatus est, mox tractu seculorum clarius & distinctius revelandus, donec tandem affulgente novæ revelationis luce nox umbrarum legis, & Joannis Baptistæ diluculum, præterierint & loco cesserint ipsi corpori solique justitiæ Christo. Non secus & Christus in carne Deus manifestatus, gradatim sui fecit revelationem & notitiam, minora primum, majora longè impositerum in sui cognitionem infundendam animis discipulorum manifestavit. Discamus hinc unum & eumdem Dei filium in carne manifestandum & revelatum, Doctorem fuisse Ecclesiæ & mysteriorum Dei revelatorem, ut sit idem heri, hodie & æternum propheta Ecclesiæ, ut idem est pontifex, Rexque Deusque in secula benedictus.
units.tr: 1. Since Christ first revealed smaller things about himself to his disciples, intending afterwards to reveal far greater things to them himself, the argument is that Christ followed the same path and used a twofold method in the old and new dispensations of saving revelation. For just as Christ was revealed more obscurely in former times, and was to be revealed more clearly and distinctly as the centuries passed, until at last the new light of revelation shone forth and the night of the shadows of the law and the dawn of John the Baptist passed away and gave place to the body itself, Christ, the sole righteousness, so too Christ, God manifested in the flesh, gradually made himself known. He first revealed smaller things and only later greater things, to pour the knowledge of himself into the minds of his disciples. Let us learn from this that the one and same Son of God, manifested and revealed in the flesh, was the Teacher of the Church and the revealer of the mysteries of God, so that he is the same yesterday, today and forever, the prophet of the Church, just as he is the high priest, King and God, blessed forever.

units.la: 2°. Ut quid vero gradatim lucem sui salutarem intulit? nempe objecta salutifera mentibus hominum sapienter ut attemperaret, scite enim annotavit Aristoteles, ὥσπερ τὰ τῶν νυκτερίδων ὄμματα πρὸς τὸ φέγγος τῆς ἡμέρας, οὕτω καὶ τὸ τῆς ψυχῆς ὀμμα πρὸς τὰ τῇ φύσει φανερώτατα πάντων. Vt se habent vespertilionum oculi ad lumen diei, ita & intellectus animae nostrae ad ea, quae manifestissima omnium sunt. Erat igitur sensim administranda lux objectorum supernaturalium, ne sub immenso pondere gloriosæ lucis lumen naturale fatiscens, obrueretur & occæcaretur. 2°. ne laudem comparatæ Christi salutaris scientiæ superbi mortales sibi tribuerent: sed contra uni Christo illuminatori & dispensatori liberrimo vel inviti acceptam ferrent. 3°. quando omnibus innatum est sciendi desiderium, ut id desiderii inflammaret & potenter ad sese pelliceret, facta spe & fide data, ulterioris ac potioris cognitionis.
units.tr: 2. But why did he bring his saving light gradually? Certainly so that he might wisely adapt the objects of salvation to the minds of men. For Aristotle rightly observed: just as the eyes of bats are to the light of day, so the eye of the soul is to the things that are by nature most manifest of all [ὥσπερ τὰ τῶν νυκτερίδων ὄμματα πρὸς τὸ φέγγος τῆς ἡμέρας, οὕτω καὶ τὸ τῆς ψυχῆς ὀμμα πρὸς τὰ τῇ φύσει φανερώτατα πάντων]. The light of supernatural objects therefore had to be administered gradually, lest the natural light, failing under the immense weight of the glorious light, should be overwhelmed and blinded. Second, so that proud mortals should not claim for themselves the praise of the saving knowledge of Christ, but should rather acknowledge it, even unwillingly, as received from Christ alone, the most free illuminator and dispenser. Third, since the desire to know is innate in all, he would inflame that desire and draw it powerfully to himself by holding out the hope and the assurance of a further and more excellent knowledge.

units.la: 3°. Sed verò ut numen benignissimum nullum finit extare in natura vacuum, ita nec patitur vacuum & inutile sanctum cordis desiderium, famem sitimque restinguit impletu suarum promissionum, minora qui dedit benignus & confert majora oportuno quæque suo tempore, majora hisce videbis, nempe cælum apertum & Angelos Dei ascendentes ad Filium hominis, viderunt & discipuli quæ impositerum illustriora videnda promiserat, nempe Christus ὁ Ἀμὴν, testis fidelis & verax, fidem suam gloriosum in modum liberavit. Inex-haustam salvatoris benignissimi charitatem! Parva lucis & fidei rudimenta novo lucis affulsu mactas, ellychnium fumigans non extinguis & arundinem quassatam non frangis, habenti das: arrham & spiritus primitias, redemptione acquisitæ possessionis, & plena messe cumulas in laudem gloriosæ gratiæ tuæ. Macti animo Christi fideles discipuli, ac cœli interpretes: Nunc ex parte cognoscimus, videmus enim per speculum & per ænigma. Futurum est, ut majora olim facie ad faciem videamus. Si in Jesum Christum credimus, ut eum nulli oculis corporeis viderimus, cum videbimus, sicuti est, intimo sensu amoris, quo nos dilexit & impletu omnium promissionum pretiosarum, futuri illi similes absoluta suis numeris sanctitate, & consummata felicitate. Nunc quidem temporis Christi potentiam cernimus illuminatis mentis oculis; nempe dedit nobis ut crederemus, juxta supereminentem potentiam, pro efficacitate roboris virium ipsius: sed vero imposterum majora videbimus, victam Judæorum incredulitatem, fidem Christi potenter creatam in obduratis cordibus, universum Israelem e morte in vitam excitatum ac servatum, Christi potentiam, cœlum terramque novam creantem, & creaturas servituti corruptionis obnoxias, anhelantes & gemebundas, assertas in gloriosam filiorum Dei libertatem. Nunc temporis inexhaustam videmus Christi misericordiam, condonantem peccata, & lapillum album, cui novum nomen inscriptum est, clam suis fidelibus tribuentem: ast majora imposterum videbimus, nempe Christum pro solio majestatis sedentem, & nos Dei benedictos filios ad cernendam hereditatem Regni ore amico vocantem, ut æternum cum ipso victores vivamus & triumphemus. Nunc temporis oculis fidei ac mentis perceptione filium hominis morientem cernimus, e mortuis resurgentem propter nostram justificationem, in cœlum apertum euntem nobis sedem paraturum, sedentem ad dexteram majestatis, & pro nobis interpellantem: at imposterum majora videbimus, nempe oculis corporeis cœlum apertum, Filium hominis redeuntem in nubibus, non vermem & opprobrium hominum; sed regem augustum, forma Dei indutum, mortem ultimum hostium proterentem, mortuos vitæ & immortalitati addicentem, impios in tartarum detrudentem, omnes peccati & miseriæ reliquias ab universo; in melius immutato, fugantem. Nunc quidem eminus & in symbolis verbi sacramentorum involucris, umbrisque thronorum, divitiarum, & voluptatum terrenarum, velatam fœlicitatem videmus: at enim imposterum majora videbimus, germanam felicitatis fruendæ formam & nativam indolem; nempe non per fidem, sed per visionem ambulabimus, quia videbimus cœlum apertum & Angelos Dei ad Filium hominis descendentes, ces, ut glorificetur in sanctis suis, & admirandus fiat in credentibus suis.
units.tr: 3. But just as the most kind Deity allows no void to exist in nature, so he does not allow a holy desire of the heart to be empty and useless. He quenches hunger and thirst by fulfilling his promises. He who kindly gave smaller things also bestows greater things, each in its proper time. You will see greater things than these, namely the heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man; and the disciples saw what he had promised they would see more clearly afterwards, namely that Christ, the Amen, the faithful and true witness [ὁ Ἀμὴν, μάρτυς πιστὸς καὶ ἀληθινός], had gloriously kept his faith. O inexhaustible charity of the most kind Saviour! You kindle the small beginnings of light and faith with a new outpouring of light; you do not quench the smoking wick, nor break the bruised reed. To him who has, you give the pledge and the firstfruits of the Spirit, the redemption of the acquired possession, and you heap up a full harvest, to the praise of your glorious grace. Be encouraged, faithful disciples of Christ and interpreters of heaven: Now we know in part, for we see through a glass darkly. It will come about that we shall one day see greater things face to face. Though we believe in Jesus Christ without having seen him with bodily eyes, when we see him as he is, we shall, with the inward sense of the love with which he loved us and the fulfilment of all his precious promises, be like him, with holiness complete in all its parts and happiness perfected. Now indeed we perceive the power of Christ with the enlightened eyes of the mind, for he has given us to believe, according to the working of his mighty power [κατὰ τὴν ἐνέργειαν τοῦ κράτους τῆς ἰσχύος αὐτοῦ]; but hereafter we shall see greater things: the Jews' unbelief overcome, faith in Christ powerfully created in hardened hearts, all Israel raised from death to life and saved, the power of Christ creating a new heaven and a new earth, and creatures subject to the bondage of corruption, groaning and travailing, brought into the glorious liberty of the sons of God. Now we see the inexhaustible mercy of Christ, forgiving sins and secretly giving the white stone on which a new name is written to his faithful people; but hereafter we shall see greater things, namely Christ sitting on the throne of majesty, and calling us, the blessed sons of God, with a friendly voice to behold the inheritance of the kingdom, so that we may live and triumph with him forever as victors. Now by the eyes of faith and the perception of the mind we see the Son of Man dying, rising from the dead for our justification, going up into the opened heaven to prepare a place for us, sitting at the right hand of majesty and interceding for us; but hereafter we shall see greater things, namely with bodily eyes the opened heaven and the Son of Man returning in the clouds, not as a worm and reproach of men, but as the august King, clothed in the form of God, destroying death, the last enemy, bringing the dead to life and immortality, casting the wicked down into hell, and driving away from the whole world every remnant of sin and misery, which will be changed for the better. Now indeed we see happiness veiled from afar and in the symbols of the word and the sacraments, in the shadows of thrones, riches and earthly pleasures; but hereafter we shall see greater things, the true form and native character of the happiness to be enjoyed: we shall walk not by faith but by sight, because we shall see the opened heaven and the angels of God descending to the Son of Man, so that he may be glorified in his saints and admired in all who believe.

units.la: 4. Nempe quòd Christus primam partem promissionis adimpleverit, fidem simul ac spem certam facit, fore ut alteram impleat præstituto tempore ac die novissimo adventus sui gloriosi. Ut enim fidem suam liberet, urget ipsius intemerata veritas, integra fidelitas, potentia gloriosa, justitia scelerum accerrima vindex. & æternus amor, quo prosequitur Ecclesiam suam. Ascendit in cœlum apertum, ut mundum argueret de sua justitia: sed verò descendet, ut justitiam exerceat in inundum incredulum & obduratum in malo. Ascendit, ut gloriam à patre acciperet; descendet, ut suam illam gloriam omnibus faciat conspicuam: ascendit, ut regni exercendi habenas suscipiret; descendet, ut mortem & infernum, hostes regni sui potentissimos, proterat & aboleat: ascendit, nobis sedem paraturus in domo patris; descendet, ut nos in sedes paratas evehat. Ascendit à laboribus partæ salutis pugnâ cruentâ quieturus; descendet, ut nos requietis suæ participes faciat, ascendit, ut victor de peccato, morte & Sathana triumpharet; descendet, ut nos, vehentes in nubibus cœli, triumphi sui faciat participes: ascendit cum Angelis lucis; descendet, ut nos faciat ἰσαγγέλους, filiosque beatæ resurrectionis, ascendit intercessurus pro suis electis, descendet ut fructus suæ intercessionis gustandos exhibeat & sartos tectosque patri sistat incolumes, quotquot illi pater electos dedit servandos, ut sine mediatore, extinctis penitus peccato & morte, Deus sit omnia in omnibus.
units.tr: 4. Indeed, that Christ has fulfilled the first part of the promise makes us certain, in faith and hope alike, that he will fulfil the second at the appointed time, on the last day of his glorious coming. For his own unbroken truth, his perfect faithfulness, his glorious power, his most stern justice as avenger of sins, and the eternal love with which he pursues his Church, all urge him to keep his promise. He ascended into the opened heaven to convict the world of its unrighteousness; but he will descend to execute justice upon the unbelieving world, hardened in evil. He ascended to receive glory from the Father; he will descend to make that glory visible to all. He ascended to take up the reins of his kingdom; he will descend to trample down and abolish death and hell, the most powerful enemies of his kingdom. He ascended to prepare a place for us in his Father's house; he will descend to carry us up to the prepared mansions. He ascended to rest from the labours of the salvation he had won by bloody battle; he will descend to make us sharers in his rest. He ascended to triumph as victor over sin, death and Satan; he will descend to make us, carried up in the clouds of heaven, sharers in his triumph. He ascended with the angels of light; he will descend to make us equal to the angels [ἰσαγγέλους], and sons of the blessed resurrection. He ascended to intercede for his elect; he will descend to show us the fruits of his intercession to be enjoyed, and to present to the Father, safe and sound, all whom the Father gave him to keep, so that, with sin and death utterly destroyed, without a mediator, God may be all in all.

units.la: 5º. Quales igitur decet nos esse in sancta conversatione, ut digni habeamur visione cœli aperti & Filii hominis, descendentis in consummandam salutem nostram? Si nos tenet amor videndi majora illa, quæ Dominus revelabit è cœlo, aperto spectaculo, age festinemus in adventum Domini; nempe citò venit cum sua mercede magna. Beatum nobis, terribilem impiis adventum novissimum Domini votis ardentissimis sollicitemus, dicat Spiritus & sponsa; etiam veni, domine Jesu, tædet nos istius exilii, patriam cœlestem quærimus, ad eam exardescimus. Lucem vidimus candelabri aurei, majora illa cœli aperti, lucem agni videre ulterius speramus & expectamus. Da, quando futurum recepisti, ut lucem gloriosæ tuæ faciei videamus: primitias spiritus tui vidimus in consolationem & sanctificationem animarum, da, quando futurum recepisti, ut majora in plenitudine messis & salutis consummatæ videamus. Tabernaculum tuum vidimus, da nobis, ut majora videamus cœli aperti, sanctuarium & Jerusalem tuam civitatem fundatissimam, thesauris refertissimam, sedem quietissimam beatorum. Te sponsum dilectissimum per cancellos vidimus, per speculum verbi & ænigmata promissionum; da, majora ut videamus, nempe tuam faciem in justitia, & satiemur imagine tua in complemento sanctitatis & immortalitatis, quum ad tubam archangeli è somno & sepulchro excitabimur; ut te descendentem è cœlo aperto videamus, veneremur, amplectamur & æternum fruamur. Amen.
units.tr: 5. What manner of people, then, ought we to be in holy conduct, so that we may be counted worthy of the vision of the opened heaven and of the Son of Man descending to bring our salvation to completion? If the love of seeing those greater things, which the Lord will reveal from heaven in an open spectacle, holds us, then let us hasten towards the coming of the Lord; for he comes quickly, and with his great reward. Let us seek with most ardent prayers the last coming of the Lord, blessed for us but terrible to the wicked, as the Spirit and the bride say: Even so, come, Lord Jesus. We are weary of this exile; we seek the heavenly homeland and burn to reach it. We have seen the light of the golden lampstand, the greater things of the opened heaven, and we hope and look to see further the light of the Lamb. Grant, as you have promised for the future, that we may see the light of your glorious face. We have seen the firstfruits of your Spirit for the consolation and sanctification of souls; grant, as you have promised for the future, that we may see greater things in the fulness of the harvest and of perfected salvation. We have seen your tabernacle; grant us to see greater things of the opened heaven: the sanctuary and your city Jerusalem, most firmly founded, most richly stored with treasures, the most peaceful dwelling of the blessed. We have seen you, our most beloved bridegroom, through the lattice, through the mirror of the word and the enigmas of the promises; grant that we may see greater things, namely your face in righteousness, and be satisfied with your image in the perfection of holiness and immortality, when at the trumpet of the archangel we are raised from sleep and the grave; so that we may see you descending from the opened heaven, and worship, embrace and enjoy you forever. Amen.

units.la: QUÆSTIO IX. Cur inter tot majora, quæ Christus de se videnda exhibuit, destinatò seligere voluerit visionem cœli aperti, &c.
units.tr: Question IX. Why, among so many greater things which Christ showed to be seen concerning himself, did he deliberately choose to show the vision of the open heaven, etc.

units.la: VNum Immanuelis elogium, quo Propheta Esaias Messiam insigniit, diversa & plane opposita, quæ Sacri vates Messiæ attribuunt, simul amicè conciliare potuit, ut Judæis nihil opus fuerit geminum læva mente Messiam comminisci, alterum afflictum & miserum Josephi filium, cum ægris atque leprosis ad portas Romæ jacentem; alterum Davidis filium, Regemque potentissimum, victoriis ac triumphis illustrissimum: simul demonstrare in clara & aperta luce, Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum illum esse germanum Messiam, quem prophetæ multiformibus illis characteribus olim delineaverant. Reapse enim, quia Messias Immanuel est Deus nobiscum, hoc est, Deus & homo in una eademque persona, humilitatem servi, & excelsam Domini dignitatem in sese amicè consociavit. Servum, cui Deus aurem perforavit, propheta Regius eum exhibet Psal. 40: 7. Quippe homo nobiscum est, qui venit, ut voluntati Dei pareret obsequiosus ad mortem, mortem usque crucis Philip. 2: 8. Sed & idem David ipsum Regem & Dominum, cui Deus dixit; sede à dexteris meis, donec ponuero inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum, nobis intuendum proponit Psal. 110: 1. Quippe qui Immanuel est, Deus nobiscum, in secula benedictus. Rex filiæ Sion afflictus & humilis, pullo asinæ vehens, apud Zachariam est, Zach. 9: 9. nempe homo nobiscum est, homo dolorum & conscius afflictionum, contemptus & abjectissimus virorum, Es. 53: 3. Sed cum nubibus cœli vehens ad antiquum dierum pervenit, & datus est ei dominatus, gloria & regnum, ut omnes populi, nationes & linguæ ei serviant, Dan. 7: 13.14. quippe qui Immanuel Deus nobiscum est, Deus for-tis, tis, princeps pacis, & pater æternitatis, cujus humero imperium fuit impositum, Esa. 9:6. Sed verò Christus Dominus noster sese verum Immanuelem probavit vel in ipsis diebus carnis, amicè consociatâ hominis & servi humilitate cum Dei Majestate & potentiâ infinitâ. Natus est ex matre pauperrima, sed ex matre virgine, stirpe regia fata: natus in præsepi stabuli; sed natalium humilitatem stellæ novæ exortus, Angelorum chorus, magorum adoratio, & præclara munera, rumor Hierosolymis, famaque nobilis personans & Herodi superbi tremor, abundè & gloriosè pensavit. Altùm dormivit in navicula homo nobis simillimus: sed fluctus tempestatesque sonoras nutu & verbo composuit, Deus, Creator & Dominus cœli juxta ac Oceani. Baptismate tinctus Johannis Baptistæ ministerio, aquis fuit immersus; nempe homo fuit, afflictionibus consecratus, descenditque in abyssum maledictionis pro nobis: sed simul atque caput extulit undis, cœlum ipsi apertum est, & Spiritus Sanctus sub specie columbæ in caput ejus delapsus, & vox è cœlo aperto reddita Deum inclamantem exhibuit; hic est Filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi complacui. Didrachma solvit simul Cæsari, simul sanctuario templi: sed staterem, quo solveret ex ore piscis exegit, quia Filius erat Regis Regum & supremus orbis Dominus. Nazarethæ, despectissimæ Galileæ urbecula, in officina fabri lignarii despectissimè educatus, Nazarethanus per contemtum crebrò audiit, ut ipse sine dolo Nathanael nauci eum fecerit, eoque nomine contemptim petierit, ex Nazaretha potest aliquid boni esse? Sed verò contemptum istiusmodi gloriosum in modum ut à sese amoliretur, non modo Deum & Regem Israëlis abundè sese probavit, quia latentem longèque remotum sub ficu Nathanaelem vidit, & impervia hominibus momenta cordis sine dolo ignoti sibi hominis, pervidit; sed & majora in posterum se Nathanaeli, cæterisque discipulis, ostensurum recepit, nempe cœlum apertum & angelos Dei ascendentes & descendentes ad Filium hominis.
units.tr: One could easily reconcile the title Immanuel, with which the prophet Isaiah marked the Messiah, with the diverse and plainly opposed things that the holy prophets attribute to the Messiah. So the Jews would have had no need to invent, with a perverse mind, a twofold Messiah: one afflicted and wretched, the son of Joseph, lying with the sick and the lepers at the gates of Rome; the other the son of David, a most powerful king, renowned for victories and triumphs. At the same time, it shows in clear and open light that Jesus Christ our Lord is that true Messiah whom the prophets long ago portrayed in those many-shaped characters. For indeed, because Immanuel the Messiah is God with us, that is, God and man in one and the same person, he has harmoniously joined in himself the humility of a servant and the lofty dignity of the Lord. The royal prophet presents him as the servant whose ear God pierced, Ps. 40:7. Indeed, the man is with us, who came to obey the will of God, obedient even to death, the death of the cross, Phil. 2:8. But the same David also sets before our eyes the King and Lord to whom God said sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet, Ps. 110:1. Indeed he is Immanuel, God with us, blessed for ever. The king of the daughter of Zion, afflicted and humble, riding on the foal of an ass, is in Zechariah, Zech. 9:9. Indeed the man is with us, a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief, despised and rejected of men, Isa. 53:3. But coming with the clouds of heaven, he reached the Ancient of Days, and dominion, glory and kingdom were given to him, that all peoples, nations and languages should serve him, Dan. 7:13–14. Indeed he who is Immanuel, God with us, is the mighty God, the Prince of Peace, the Father of eternity, on whose shoulder the government was laid, Isa. 9:6. But Christ our Lord proved himself the true Immanuel even in the days of his flesh, when the humility of man and servant was joined harmoniously with the majesty and infinite power of God. He was born of a most poor mother, yet of a virgin mother, sprung from royal stock; he was born in a manger of a stable. But the humility of his birth was abundantly and gloriously made up for by a new star rising, a chorus of angels, the worship of the magi, splendid gifts, the rumour in Jerusalem and the noble fame that sounded abroad, and the trembling of proud Herod. The man most like us slept deeply in a little boat, but God, the Creator and Lord of heaven as well as of the ocean, calmed the waves and the roaring storms by a nod and a word. Dipped in baptism by the ministry of John the Baptist, he was immersed in the waters; he was indeed a man, consecrated by afflictions, and he descended into the abyss of the curse for us. But as soon as he lifted his head out of the waves, heaven was opened to him, the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove upon his head, and a voice from the open heaven, proclaiming God, showed him: this is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. He paid the didrachma to Caesar and to the sanctuary of the temple at the same time; but he demanded the stater, with which he paid, from the mouth of a fish, because he was the Son of the King of kings and the supreme Lord of the world. Brought up most contemptibly in the workshop of a carpenter at Nazareth, a little town of despised Galilee, he was often called the Nazarene in scorn, so that Nathanael, not without guile, despised him for this very reason and said with contempt, can anything good come out of Nazareth? But not only did he prove abundantly that he was God and the King of Israel, so that he might remove such glorious contempt from himself, because he saw Nathanael hidden and far away under the fig tree, and perceived the secret movements of the heart of a man unknown to him, whose heart was without guile, which are impenetrable to men; but he also promised that in future he would show Nathanael and the other disciples greater things, namely heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man.

units.la: Ex quo Christus recepit fore, ut Nathanael cæterique discipuli majora de se viderent, h. e. cognoscerent ac crederent, iis, quæ hactenus viderant collegerantque ex stupenda ipsius cognitione, multa palam ipsis patefecit, quæ magnitudine simul ac multitudine utique longè superant revelationem Nathanaelis sub ficu latentis, ipsiusque cordis sine dolo; & ea quidem in totum comparata, ut omninò tenderent ad fidem faciendam, Jesum esse Dei Filium, Regemque Israëlis, h. e. verum Messiam. Nam & miracula edidit multiformia, h. e. infinitæ potentiæ opera, non alienâ, sicut Prophetæ & Apostoli; sed insitâ propriâque virtute patravit, quod non obscurè ipse innuit, dum diceret in patrando hæmorrhoisæ miraculo, quis me retigit, nam virtus ex me effluxit, Luc. 8:46. Miraculorum verò productio opus est unius Dei proprium; nempe opus est præter & supra naturæ finitæ leges, & sphæram, ut loquuntur, activitatis finitæ: sed verò latentem sub ficu opaca hominem videre, aut ingenium ejus corculumque sine fraude percontari & exploratum habere, haut quaquam superat finitam angeli intelligentiam; ille enim invisibilis latentem cernere potest sub arbore hominem, ut & invisibili consortio, suaque vi ςοχασιχὴ admirabili, fraudulentum vel sincerum ejus animum certò explorare. Præterea, Jesus, ubi versaretur cum discipulis suis, totum Dei consilium & certam de salute voluntatem non semel eis aperuit palamque revelavit, Joan. 15. 15. Verùm revelare, quæ oculus non vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in cor hominis ascenderunt, & profunda Dei scrutari, longè utique majus est, quàm cor unius Nathanaelis percontari atque rimari. Denique quicquid volvunt in animo, quantumvis occultum, multi homines, exploratum habere, utique majus est, quàm sincerum cor unius hominis perspectum tenere: Jesus autem non credebat semet ipsum Judæis, eo quod nosset omnes, nec opus esset, ut quisquam ei testaretur de homine; ipse enim sciebat, quid esset in homine, Joh. 2: 24: 25. Ut quid igitur Jesus non dixit discipulis; majora in posterum videbitis, nempe Filium hominis ambulantem super aquas, fluctus & tempestates nutu & verbo compescentem, ægros omne genus sanantem, dæmonia ejicientem, paralyticos firmantem, leprosos purgantem, mortuos excitantem, cæcos illuminantem, surdis auditum liberum, mutisque loquelam expeditam tribuentem, arcanum Dei consilium & voluntatem revelantem, secreta cordium momenta pervidentem, mysteria regni cœlorum, in quæ vel Angeli prospicere cupiunt, hominibus aperientem? Filium hominis in posterum videbitis miraculosum in modum transformatum in monte, gloriam ejus contemplabimini, tanquam unigeniti ex patre, pleni gloria & veritate, Joh. 1: 14. Ut quid, obsecro, inter tot majora, quæ Jesus de se videnda exhibuit, destinatò seligere voluit conspiciendum cœlum apertum, & Angelos Dei ascendentes & descendentes ad Filium hominis? Quæstio equidem nobilis est, dignaque sapientiâ Christi, scituque ad salutem & pietatem necessaria.
units.tr: From this, Christ indicated that Nathanael and the other disciples would see greater things concerning him, that is, would come to know and believe them, from what they had hitherto seen and gathered from his amazing knowledge. He openly revealed to them many things which by far exceed, in both magnitude and multitude, the revelation of Nathanael hidden under the fig tree, and of his guileless heart. And these things were all so arranged that they tended entirely to producing faith that Jesus is the Son of God and the King of Israel, that is, the true Messiah. For he also performed manifold miracles, that is, works of infinite power, not by a borrowed power, as the prophets and apostles did, but by his own inherent virtue; which he hinted at plainly when, in working the miracle on the woman with the issue of blood, he said, someone has touched me, for power has gone out from me, Luke 8:46. But the production of miracles is a work proper to God alone; it is a work beyond and above the laws of finite nature, and, as they say, the sphere of finite activity. But to see a man hidden under an opaque fig tree, or to inquire into and know by experience the disposition and secret heart of a man without deceit, by no means surpasses the finite understanding of an angel; for that invisible being can perceive a man hidden under a tree, and can surely test by an invisible fellowship and by his admirable stochastic [στοχαστική] power of conjecture whether a man's mind is deceitful or sincere. Moreover, Jesus, wherever he dwelt with his disciples, more than once opened to them and openly revealed the whole counsel of God and his sure will concerning salvation, John 15:15. But to reveal what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered the heart of man, and to search the deep things of God, is surely far greater than to inquire into and examine the heart of a single Nathanael. Finally, to have a clear knowledge of whatever many men turn over in their minds, however hidden, is surely greater than to hold in view the sincere heart of one man: but Jesus did not trust himself to them, because he knew all men, and he had no need that anyone should bear witness about man; for he himself knew what was in man, John 2:24–25. Why then did Jesus not say to the disciples: you will see greater things in future, namely the Son of Man walking on the waters, calming the waves and storms by a nod and a word, healing the sick of every kind, casting out demons, strengthening the paralytic, cleansing the lepers, raising the dead, giving sight to the blind, giving free hearing to the deaf and an unhindered tongue to the dumb, revealing the secret counsel and will of God, seeing through the hidden movements of hearts, and opening to men the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, into which even the angels desire to look? You will see in future the Son of Man transfigured in a wonderful manner on the mountain; you will behold his glory, as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth, John 1:14. Why, I ask, among so many greater things which Jesus showed to be seen concerning himself, did he deliberately choose to set before them the open heaven, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man? The question is indeed a noble one, worthy of the wisdom of Christ, and one whose knowledge is necessary for salvation and piety.

units.la: Respondemus igitur 1º. per negationem, Jesum, quæ editurus erat in posterum, miracula seligere noluisse, ut ut sibi ex virtute insita, singularia, utpote sibi cum Prophetis & Apostolis communia ex captu vulgi, quando modus ea edendi ex propria virtute, singularis, erat occultus; nec in illa carnis infirmitate, quâ Jesus tunc conflictabatur, Judæi ex miraculis plus illi tribuissent; quàm Moysi & Prophetis sibi eximiis. Reapse enim quicquid miraculorum Christus edidit, Moyses & Prophetæ edidisse videntur. Nempe si Christus aquam transformavit in vinum; Moyses Ægypti flumina mutavit in sanguinem: si Christus super aquas ambulavit, fluctusque lacus compescuit; Moyses mare rubrum divisit, & ductum per undas Israelem in tuto locavit: si Christus, in monte transfiguratus, faciei splendore refulsit; Moyses in monte pariter transfiguratus faciem, usque adeo splendoris gloriâ fulgentem, prætulit, ut Israel faciei coruscantis radios sustinere perstrictus haut potuerit: si Christus leprosos curavit; Elisæus Naamanem Syrium leprosum mundavit: si Christus panes stupenda benedictione multiplicavit; Elias oleum & farinam viduæ Sareptanæ tractu continuo auxit, 1. Reg. 17:14. si Jesus quinque panibus hordeaceis numerosam multitudinem pavit; Elisæus centum homines panibus viginti ex abundanti pariter nutrivit, 2. Reg. 4:42. Ut sit finis, si Christus mortuos vitæ restituit; Elias viduæ Sareptanæ filium, & Elisæus filium Sunamitidis mortuum pariter vitæ reddidit. Sed vero cœli apertura & ascensus in cœlum, sicut e cœlo aperto descensus stipante numerosissimo Angelorum satellitio, usque adeo singularis est Messiæ character, ut nulli Patriarcharum, Prophetarum nulli, in veteri Scripturarum codice uspiam tribuatur.
units.tr: We therefore reply, first, by denial: Jesus did not want to choose the miracles which he was going to perform in future, since by his inherent power they were singular, yet, as to their kind, shared with the prophets and apostles, in the judgement of the common people, whereas the manner of performing them by his own power was hidden and unique. Nor, in that weakness of the flesh in which Jesus then struggled, would the Jews have ascribed more to him from the miracles than to Moses and the prophets, who were distinguished to them. For indeed, whatever miracles Christ performed, Moses and the prophets seem to have performed too. If Christ turned water into wine, Moses turned the rivers of Egypt into blood. If Christ walked on the waters and calmed the waves of the lake, Moses divided the Red Sea and placed Israel, led through the waves, in safety. If Christ, transfigured on the mountain, shone with the splendour of his face, Moses likewise, transfigured on the mountain, showed a face shining with such radiance of glory that Israel, struck by it, could not endure the rays of his shining face. If Christ cured lepers, Elisha cleansed the Syrian leper Naaman. If Christ multiplied loaves by a wonderful blessing, Elijah increased the oil and meal of the widow of Zarephath by a continual flow, 1 Kings 17:14. If Jesus fed a large crowd with five barley loaves, Elisha likewise fed a hundred men with twenty loaves, with some left over, 2 Kings 4:42. Finally, if Christ restored the dead to life, Elijah restored to life the son of the widow of Zarephath, and Elisha likewise restored to life the dead son of the Shunammite woman. But the opening of heaven and the ascent into heaven, as well as the descent from the open heaven accompanied by a very numerous retinue of angels, is so singular a mark of the Messiah that it is ascribed to none of the patriarchs or prophets anywhere in the ancient codex of the Scriptures.

units.la: At enim profundus Theologus, scientiâque miraculorum peritus, hic reponet haut immeritò, certa esse quædam miracula, nempe apertos cæcorum oculos, aures surdorum patefactas, & solutas linguas mutorum, quæ & proprii sunt Messiæ characteres, Jes. 35:5.6. Ps. 146:8. imo usque adeo proprii ἀχοινωνήτως, ut nunquam ac nusquam Moysi, Prophetis vel Apostolis totâ Scripturâ tribuantur. Nam quod narratur Ananias Sauli visum restituisse, Act. 9:17. ex ipsa historia sat liquet, Saulem non fuisse cæcum, nedum ab ortu; sed splendore lucis ita perstrictum, ut plenum glaucoma oculi ejus contraxerint: nam ab oculis ejus quasi squamæ deciderunt, Act. 9:18. Quod verò narrat de Vespasiano Suetonius, plebejo cuidam, luminibus orbato, oculos restituisse, cum inspuisset, vel ex ipsa historia liquidò paret, malignam fuisse, sed apparentem Serapidis, h. e. dæmonii nefarii simulioli, miraculorum Christi imitationem. Nam orbatus luminibus homo dici potest bifariam, vel quia extincta plane est facultas visiva in oculo cæcitate proprie dicta, vel quia densa quadam pellicula obducta & sepulta est videndi facultas integra latens: quæ ut arte medica abstergi vel acu dextrâ oculistæ deprimi, ita & vi dæmonis curari potest. Quod verò de Adriano Spartianus retulit, mulierem cæcatam & restitutam visui, ubi monito per insomnium paruisset; item de cæco nato, qui ex Pannonia venit, ut febrientem Adrianum contingeret, quo facto & ipse oculos recepit, & Adrianum febris reliquit: ipse Marius Maximus apud Spartianum, hæc per simulationem facta fuisse commemorat.
units.tr: But a profound theologian, skilled in the science of miracles, will reply, not without reason, that certain miracles are indeed peculiar to the Messiah: the opening of the eyes of the blind, the unstopping of the ears of the deaf, and the loosing of the tongues of the dumb (Isa. 35:5, 6; Ps. 146:8). These are so exclusively his [ἀκοινωνήτως] that they are ascribed to no one, neither to Moses, nor to the Prophets, nor to the Apostles, anywhere in the whole of Scripture. As for the story that Ananias restored Saul's sight (Acts 9:17), the narrative itself makes it fairly clear that Saul was not blind, much less from birth. Rather, he was so dazzled by the brightness of the light that a thick film grew over his eyes, for "something like scales fell from his eyes" (Acts 9:18). As for what Suetonius reports of Vespasian, that he restored sight to a certain common man who had been deprived of his eyes, by spitting on them, the story itself plainly shows that this was a wicked act, a mere counterfeit of Christ's miracles, performed by the apparent power of Serapis, that is, by a wicked little demon. A man may be said to be deprived of his eyes in two ways: either the faculty of sight is entirely extinguished, which is blindness properly so called, or the faculty of sight remains whole but is hidden and buried beneath a dense film. The latter can be wiped away by medical skill, or cured by an oculist's right hand with a needle pressing it down, and so it can also be cured by the power of a demon. As for what Spartianus relates of Hadrian, that a woman who had been struck blind was restored to sight when she obeyed a command given to her in a dream, and likewise of a man born blind who came from Pannonia to touch the feverish Hadrian, whereupon he himself received his sight and Hadrian's fever left him: Marius Maximus himself, cited by Spartianus, records that these things were done by pretence.

units.la: Hic autem mirari subit memorandum sane discrimen, nempe cur Scriptura Prophetarum & Apostolorum ministerio multa memoret edita miracula, quæ & Christus edidit; hæc vero tria nominatim, nempe cæcos illuminare, surdorum aures patefacere, mutorumque linguas solvere, uni Christo propria addixerit? Non equidem quòd majori virtute opus sit in cæcis illuminandis, &c. quam in firmandis solutis paralysi membris, aut mortuis vitæ restituendis: utrumque enim ex æquo opus infinitæ virtutis est. Eccur ergò institutum sapienter, (ut nemo sanus negaverit) memorandum discrimen istiusmodi? Vel alto silentio hic adoranda est Dei sapientia πολυπoικίλῳ, vel mysticum discrimen arcescendum videtur ex significatione mystica morborum corporeorum, qui adhibentur in typos peccatorum, morborum spiritualium, Jes. 53:4. collato cum Matth.8:17. Cæcitas igitur corporea typus est cæcitatis spiritualis, quâ peccatores omnes laborant, Ef. 42:18.19. Matth. 15:14. surditas typus incredulitatis & cordis obdurati in malitia & os mutum typus ingrati animi, cui nullûs inest amor laudis & confessionis nominis Dei, Ef. 6:10. Joh. 12:40. Hinc Zacharias, quòd incredulitate laborasset, factus est mutus, Luc. 1:22. Nempe increduli surdi spirituales ad vocem & promissionem Dei sunt, muti ad invocationem, confessionem & laudem divini nominis, ut spiritualis surditas causa sit muti spiritualis, non secus atque corporea surditas ab ortu, causa est muti corporei.
