Hinc malignus quidam Spiritus surdus & mutus metonymicè dicitur, Marc. 9:25. quòd surdum & mutum efficeret hominem. Nempe qui loquentem non audit quòd surdus sit, nec eloqui potest, atque adeò mutus est: pariter & incredulus, quia non novit quæ Dei sunt, quia cæcus & surdus spiritualis est, nec ea potest eloqui in laudem gloriosæ gratiæ Dei. Ut verò lepra, paralysis, morsque, typi sunt in Scriptura status peccatoris & moralis corruptionis innatæ & inolitæ omnibus peccatoribus, non secus atque cæcitas, surditas & loquendi facultatis privatio; ordo tamen naturalis in illis omnibus observandus est. Nam mentis cæcitas,& cordis obduratio, quæ surditas spiritualis est,& germana incredulitas, quodque eam comitatur ingratranimi crimen defectusque confessionis in ore, causa sunt lepræ, paralysis, & mortis spiritualis, quia peccatorum omnium colluvies originem trahit ex errore intellectus practici. Unde Christus; si autem oculus tuus malus fuerit, totum corpus tuum tenebrosum erit. Ergo si lumen quod in te est, tenebræ sunt, ipsæ tenebræ quantæ erunt? Matth. 6:23. Luc. 11:34. Hinc Paulus peccatores tenebras vocat, Eph. 5:8. ignorantes & errantes pro peccatoribus usurpat, Hebr. 5:2. peccata vocat ignorantiæ, Heb. 9: 7. Et scitè in hanc rem Philosophus; ἀγνοῦν μὲν πᾶς ὁ μοχθηρὸς, ὰ δεῖ πράττειν, ignorat igitur improbus omnis, quæ oportet agere. Arist. Eth. 3. c. 2. Respondemus igitur, tria isthæc miracula, nempe cæcorum illuminationem, aurium surdarum apertionem & linguæ mutorum solutionem, Spiritum Sanctum uni addixisse Messiæ, cùm cætera illius Prophetarum & Apostolorum communia fecerit, quo significaret unum Messiam, uti una causa est expiationis reatus, & propitiatæ Numinis justitiæ, pariter & causam esse sanctificationis, quæ originem trahit ex mentis illuminatione, cordisque ad auscultandum voci Dei apertione & confessione nominis Dei, h. e. Domini Jesu. Nam si ore tuo confessus fueris Dominum Jesum, & credideris in corde tuo, quòd Deus eum suscitaverit ex mortuis, salvus eris; corde enim creditur ad justitiam, fit autem ore confessio ad salutem, Rom. 10:9. 10. Depulsâ verò cæcitate simul ac surditate spirituali per fidem, & os mutum aperitur ad confessionem miseriæ, & divinæ misericordiæ & sacrificium laudis: sed & gradus fit necessarius ad resurrectionem & vitam spiritualem, quia justus ex fide vivit, Habac. 2: 4. Hebr. 10: 38. & Christo consepulti per baptismum, in eo etiam resurreximus per fidem efficacitatis illius virtutis Dei, qui excitavit eum ex mortuis, Col. 2: 12. Fit & ex fide gradus necessarius ad sanctificationem, quæ lepræ purgatione adumbrabatur: nam fide purificantur corda, Act. 15: 9. & per fidem, quæ est in Christum, gentes apertos obtinent oculos, & convertuntur a tenebris ad lucem, & potestate Satanæ ad Deum, & remissionem peccatorum, & sortem inter sanctificatos accipiunt, Act. 26: 18. Sed & gradus fit necessarius ad ambulationem in viis Domini, quæ paralyticorum sanatione adumbrabatur: nam fides per charitatem operatur Gal. 5: 6. sumus enim servati per fidem, & opus Dei creati in Christo Jesu ad opera bona, quæ præparavit Deus, ut in eis ambularemus, Eph. 2: 8. 10.
units.tr: Here one is moved to wonder at a distinction that is certainly worth noting. Why does Scripture, through the ministry of the Prophets and Apostles, record many miracles that were also performed by Christ, yet mention these three by name, namely the illumination of the blind, the opening of the ears of the deaf, and the loosing of the tongues of the dumb, and assign them to Christ alone? Not, indeed, because greater power is needed to give sight to the blind, and so on, than to strengthen the limbs of the paralysed, or to restore life to the dead; for each of these is equally a work of infinite power. Why then has this distinction been made wisely, as no sane person will deny? Either the manifold wisdom of God [πολυποικίλῳ] must be adored here in deep silence, or the mystical reason for the distinction must be sought in the mystical meaning of the bodily diseases, which are used as types of the spiritual diseases of sin (Isa. 53:4, compared with Matt. 8:17). Thus bodily blindness is a type of the spiritual blindness under which all sinners labour (Isa. 42:18, 19; Matt. 15:14). Deafness is a type of unbelief and of a heart hardened in wickedness, and the dumb mouth is a type of an ungrateful mind, in which there is no love of praise and no confession of the name of God (Isa. 6:10; John 12:40). Hence Zechariah, because he had laboured under unbelief, was made dumb (Luke 1:22). Indeed, unbelievers are spiritually deaf to the voice and promise of God, and dumb in calling upon, confessing and praising the divine name. Spiritual deafness is thus the cause of spiritual dumbness, just as bodily deafness from birth is the cause of bodily dumbness. Hence an unclean spirit is called, by metonymy, deaf and dumb (Mark 9:25), because it made the man deaf and dumb. For he who does not hear the one speaking is deaf, and cannot speak, and so is dumb; likewise the unbeliever, because he does not know the things of God, because he is spiritually blind and deaf, cannot speak them to the praise of the glorious grace of God. Yet, just as leprosy, paralysis and death are types in Scripture of the state of the sinner, of the moral corruption innate and ingrained in all sinners, and just as blindness, deafness and loss of the power of speech are likewise types, still the natural order must be observed in all of them. For blindness of mind and hardening of heart, which is spiritual deafness, and genuine unbelief, together with the sin of ingratitude that accompanies it and the failure to confess with the mouth, are the causes of leprosy, paralysis and spiritual death, because the whole mass of sins arises from an error of the practical intellect. Hence Christ says: if your eye is bad, your whole body will be dark. If then the light that is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness be? (Matt. 6:23; Luke 11:34). Hence Paul calls sinners darkness (Eph. 5:8), uses ignorant and erring for sinners (Heb. 5:2), and calls sins of ignorance (Heb. 9:7). The Philosopher also says well on this matter: every wicked man is ignorant of what he ought to do [ἀγνοῦν μὲν πᾶς ὁ μοχθηρὸς, ἃ δεῖ πράττειν] (Aristotle, Ethics, bk. 3, ch. 2). We reply, therefore, that these three miracles, namely the illumination of the blind, the opening of the ears of the deaf, and the loosing of the tongues of the dumb, the Holy Spirit assigned to the Messiah alone, while he made the rest common to the Prophets and Apostles. By this he signified that there is one Messiah, just as there is one cause of the expiation of guilt and of the propitiation of God's justice, and likewise that there is one cause of sanctification, which arises from the illumination of the mind, the opening of the heart to hear the voice of God, and the confession of the name of God, that is, of the Lord Jesus. For if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation (Rom. 10:9, 10). When blindness and spiritual deafness are removed through faith, the dumb mouth is opened to confess its misery, the divine mercy and the sacrifice of praise. But a step is also made necessary toward resurrection and spiritual life, because the just lives by faith (Hab. 2:4; Heb. 10:38), and having been buried with Christ in baptism, you were also raised with him through faith in the working of the power of God, who raised him from the dead (Col. 2:12). A step through faith is also necessary to sanctification, which was foreshadowed by the cleansing of the leper, for by faith their hearts are purified (Acts 15:9), and through the faith that is in Christ the Gentiles receive opened eyes, and turn from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan to God, and receive forgiveness of sins and a place among those who are sanctified (Acts 26:18). But a step is also necessary to walking in the ways of the Lord, which was foreshadowed by the healing of the paralytics, for faith works through love (Gal. 5:6); for by grace you have been saved through faith, and we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand that we should walk in them (Eph. 2:8, 10).

units.la: Quando igitur tria isthæc miracula Christi filii hominis propria sunt ἀχονωμάτως, haut abs re quæri potest, cur Christus inter tot majora, quæ de se videnda erat in posterum exhibiturus, ut fidem de se Messia certam faceret, seligere noluerit insignia isthæc Messiæ miracula propria, quando ipsi visum fuerit istis miraculis, velut nativis suis coloribus graphicè se ipsum pingere & exhibere oculis discipulorum Johannis Baptistæ; ite & renunciate Iohanni; quæ auditis & conspicitis: cæci visum recipiunt & claudi ambulant, leprosi purificantur & surdi audiunt, mortui suscitantur & pauperibus evangelizatur? Matth. 11: 4. 5.
units.tr: Since, therefore, these three miracles of Christ the Son of Man are peculiar to him exclusively [ἀκοινωνήτως], it may well be asked why Christ, among so many greater works that he was to display for them to see in the future, in order to make his messiahship certain to faith, did not choose to select these distinctive miracles of the Messiah. Why did he not, when it pleased him, use these miracles, as if painting and presenting himself to the eyes of John the Baptist's disciples in their own natural colours: go and report to John what you hear and see: the blind receive sight and the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear, the dead are raised and the poor have good news preached to them (Matt. 11:4, 5)?

units.la: Respondemus 1º. singularium istiusmodi miraculorum visionem solidè quidem demonstrasse, Jesum esse Deum & verum Messiam, Psal. 146: 8.
units.tr: First, we reply that the sight of these singular miracles has solidly demonstrated that Jesus is God and the true Messiah (Ps. 146:8).

units.la: Sed vero propria isthæc Messiæ miracula 1o. haut quaquam docebant modum & rationem, qua Messias futurus erat Jesus, hoc est Redemptor, quaque jus erat ex divina justitia consequuturus cæcos illuminandi, & aures surdorum spiritualium aperiendi, ut in salutem verbum Dei audirent. Unus Christi in cœlum apertum ascensus postquam descenderat in abyssum maledictionis & mortis, factus breve tempus Angelis inferior, modum & rationem, qua Christus Jesus & Redemptor factus est, comparata per mortem redemptione æterna palam omnibus declarabat. 2o. istiusmodi miraculorum visio, ut opportuna fuerit ad fidem hanc faciendam, Jesum esse Dei filium & verum Messiam, non fuisset tamen satis opportuna ad fidem salutarem in eum ingenerandam: nam Diaboli simul crediderunt, simul confessi sunt, Jesum esse Christum & filium Dei. Matth. 8: 29. Luc. 4: 41. Atenim ut fides in Christum salvifica cordibus ingeneretur omnino credendum est, Christum fuisse traditum propter peccata nostra, & e mortuis suscitatum ad justificationem nostram. Rom. 10: 9. 10. Nempe Christi resurrectio palam docet, ipsius morte placatam fuisse divinam justitiam & solutum ipsius sanguine plenum nostræ redemptionis λύτρον. Unus autem post mortem maledictam crucis Filii hominis in cœlum apertum ascensus, stipante numeroso Angelorum Dei famulitio, hæc omnibus palam probavit. Hinc Christus concludit, Spiritum Sanctum παράκλητον, advocatum, suum convicturum mundum de justitia, eo quod ad Patrem abeat, Joh. 16: 10. Quando igitur Christus ea promittebat discipulis suis videnda, quæ opportuna forent ad fidem salutarem eorum animis ingenerandam, inter tot majora, quæ in posterum illis erat exhibiturus, quam sapientissimo consilio visionem cœli aperti & Angelorum Dei, ascendentium & descendentium ad Filium hominis, selegit. 3o. Ut sit finis, quandoquidem de futura rerum majorum exhibitione agebatur, nemini non compertum est, visionem cœli aperti & Filii hominis eò ascendentis, illincque denuò descendentis in futuro beati seculi complemento, comitante simul ascendentem, simul descendentem numeroso Angelorum Dei exercitu, majus utique ac splendidius spectaculum esse, quam visionem trium istiusmodi miraculorum, quæ Spiritus Sanctus propria Messiæ fecit. Id equidem non erat nescius Paulus mysteriorum Regni cœlorum scriba peritissimus. Is enim selecturus magni pietatis mysterii illustrissimos arti-culos, nullus meminit cæcorum illuminatorum, apertarum surdis aurium, solutorumve mutis linguæ retinaculorum; atenim nobilem magni pietatis mysterii articulum ut constitueret, oculos mentis conjecit in ascensum gloriosum Dei, in carne manifestati, Angelis Dei contemplantibus, bus, simul augustum triumphatorem stipantibus: magnum, inquit, est pietatis mysterium, Deus conspicuus factus in carne, justificatus in Spiritu, conspectus ab Angelis, prædicatus gentibus, fides illi habita in mundo, sursum receptus in gloriam, 1 Tim. 3: 16.
units.tr: But these proper miracles of the Messiah, first, by no means taught the manner and method by which Jesus, that is, the Redeemer, would be the Messiah, or the right he would obtain from divine justice to open the eyes of the blind and the ears of the spiritually deaf, so that they might hear the word of God to their salvation. Christ's single ascent into the opened heaven, after he had descended into the abyss of curse and death and been made for a short time lower than the angels, plainly declared to all the manner and method by which Christ Jesus became the Redeemer, eternal redemption having been obtained through death. Second, the vision of such miracles, however suitable it was for producing the faith that Jesus is the Son of God and true Messiah, would not have been suitable enough for engendering saving faith in him, for the devils also believed and at the same time confessed that Jesus is the Christ and Son of God. Matth. 8:29; Luke 4:41. But for saving faith in Christ to be engendered in hearts, it must be fully believed that Christ was delivered up for our sins and raised from the dead for our justification. Rom. 10:9, 10. Indeed Christ's resurrection plainly teaches that divine justice was appeased by his death, and that the full ransom [λύτρον] of our redemption was paid with his blood. Moreover, the single ascent of the Son of man into the opened heaven after the accursed death of the cross, attended by the numerous host of God's angelic servants, proved these things plainly to all. Hence Christ concludes that the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete [παράκλητον], his advocate, would convict the world of righteousness, because he goes away to the Father, John 16:10. When Christ therefore promised his disciples things to be seen that would be suitable for engendering saving faith in their minds, among so many greater things which he would later show them, with most wise counsel he chose the vision of the opened heaven and of the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man. Third, since the matter concerned the future display of greater things, it is known to everyone that the vision of the opened heaven and of the Son of man ascending there and descending again at the completion of the blessed age to come, with a numerous army of God's angels accompanying him as he ascends and descends, is surely a greater and more splendid spectacle than the vision of those three kinds of miracles which the Holy Spirit performed as proper to the Messiah. Paul, the most skilled scribe of the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, was certainly not unaware of this. For when he was about to select the most illustrious articles of the great mystery of godliness, he mentions none of the blind made to see, the ears of the deaf opened, or the fetters of the tongues of the mute loosed. Rather, to set out the noble article of the great mystery of godliness, he turned the eyes of his mind to the glorious ascent of God, manifested in the flesh, with the angels of God looking on and attending the august triumphant one: "great," he says, "is the mystery of godliness: God manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen by angels, preached to the Gentiles, believed in the world, taken up into glory," 1 Tim. 3:16.

units.la: His ita demum complanatis ad quæstionem profligandam nunc temporis propius accedimus. Respondemus itaque, tot inter ac tanta, quæ deinceps de se videnda Christus palam exhibuit, visionem cœli aperti & Angelorum Dei ascendentium, &c. Jesum signanter ac sapienter selegisse simul in habitudine ad se Filium hominis; quia evidenter demonstrat, quàm verè unus Jesus in Novo Instrumento singulari prærogativa isthoc elogio insigniatur, habetque admiranda isthæc cœli aperti & Filii hominis ascendentis & descendentis visio luculentum implementum illustrissimarum de Messia prophetiarum, visionum, typorum & figurarum: simul in habitudine ad Nathanaelem, cæterosque Israelitas, ut non desiderio & expectationi Judaicæ gentis solum facere satis valeat; sed & eam gravi vetustissimoque errore liberare ac docere, Jesum esse verum illum Messiam, quem Prophetæ venturum prædixerant, visiones & figuræ illustrissimæ adumbraverant, & Judæorum natio avidè exspectabat præfinito illo tempore venturum; ut nil quicquam aliorum (quæ sanè Jesus maxima de se cognoscenda palam exhibuit) siquidem seorsim spectetur, illustres germani Messiæ characteres æque confertim exhibeat, atque stupenda cœli aperti cùm ad se, tùm ad homines, visio, quam se deinceps hominibus exhibitum ire sanctè recipit. Age igitur, quæ summatim edisseruimus, enucleatè magis jam temporis edisseramus.
units.tr: With these matters thus made plain, we now come closer to resolving the question. We answer, therefore, that among so many and such great things as Christ openly showed would be seen of himself afterwards, he chose, wisely and deliberately, the vision of the opened heaven and of the ascending angels of God, etc., in relation to himself as the Son of man; because it clearly demonstrates how truly Jesus alone is marked with this title, by a singular prerogative, in the New Testament, and because this admirable vision of the opened heaven and of the Son of man ascending and descending gives a brilliant fulfilment of the most illustrious prophecies, visions, types and figures concerning the Messiah. Also in relation to Nathanael and the other Israelites, it is able not only to satisfy the longing and expectation of the Jewish people, but also to free them from a grave and most ancient error, and to teach that Jesus is that true Messiah whom the prophets foretold would come, whom the most illustrious visions and figures foreshadowed, and whom the Jewish nation eagerly awaited at the appointed time. So, if considered on their own, none of the other things that Jesus openly showed as very great things to be known about himself presents the illustrious genuine marks of the Messiah as equally well as the wonderful vision of the opened heaven, both toward himself and toward men, which he sacredly undertakes to display to men thereafter. Come, then, let us now set out more fully what we have summarised.

units.la: Primò. Quidem stupendam isthanc visionem signanter & sapienter selegit in habitudine ad se, quatenus Filius hominis, h. e. Adami, erat. Nempe isthæc cœli aperti visio omnibus palam demonstravit, Jesum esse promissum illud semen mulieris, contriturum caput serpentis. Adamus nempe ipsius parens Paradisum, cœli typum, nefaria sua rebellione sibi filiisque suis usque adeò præcluserat flammato gladio Cherubim, ut omni aditu & accessu ad paradisum Deumque, & quovis locorum, ubi immortalis Deus extraordinaria in posterum præsentiæ suæ symbola exhibuit, interdiceretur. Unde mons Sinai, extraordinarium Numinis adytum, clau-stris ac repagulis undiquaque munitus est, ne eò populus perrumpere attentaret, Exod. 19: 12. Hebr. 12: 20. Et Sanctum simul ac Sanctum Sanctorum τῶ ναῶ, Dei habitaculum, clausum velo gemino, vel ipsum populum Dei Sanctum ab aditu & accessu ad Numen immortale procul removit. Sapienter itaque Christus visionem cœli sibi ac hominibus postmodum aperiendi riendi selegit, ut futura illa cœli apertione & visione significaret, se clara in luce demonstraturum, quàm verè esset Filius hominis, qui luctuosissimum damnum, quod sibi posterisque suis, ex carne satis, Adamus parens creaverat, ubi paradisum terrestrem cæteraque locorum secreta, quotquot Deus gloriosa præsentia sua dignabatur, æternum præcluserat & inaccessa fecerat, magnificè ita repararet, ut contrito serpentis capite & propitiatâ Numinis justitiâ & extincto Angeli flammato gladio & abolità penitus inimicitiâ, sibi & omnibus creditur is ad cœlum apertum & Deum aditus liber & accessus pateret. Hæc fuit mens prisicis Hebrærum Doctoribus. Illi enim in septem, quæ Messiam ostensurum sperant Israeli, duo isthæc numerant, nimirum paradisum Eden & arborem vitæ. Ita Rabbi Elias Ben-Mosis in Sepher Reschit Chocmah, etiam in hæc verba Cantic. 1: 1. 4. Rex me admisit in conclavia sua, ita commentatur: Doctores nostri beatæ memoriæ dixerunt, quod hæc sunt conclavia horti Eden. hoc est etiam quod dicunt de arbore vitæ, eam non esse frustra creatam sed homines resurrectionis epulaturos de ipsa & æternum victuros. Rabbi Menachem in cap. 3. Gen. Et Paraphrastes Chaldæus in Cantic. 4: 12. sic commentatur: Sicut paradisus Eden, in quem nemini ingredi fas est, nisi justis, quorum animæ eò feruntur per manus Angelorum. Hæc vero non de terreno paradiso, sed de cœlesti mysticè intelligenda, Rabbinorum summus, qui primus nugari desiit, Moses Maimonides palam docet in Misna tractatu de pœnitentia c. 3. sect. 2. dum sic divine commentatur de mundo futuro: Hic nec editur nec bibitur, nec alia sunt illa necessaria corporibus filiorum Adami in hoc mundo, ut sedere, stare, dormire, mori, tristari & similia. Sic nostri sapientes dixerunt in mundo futuro non editur, non bibitur non usus est conjugii: sed justi sedebunt cum coronis suis in capitibus suis & fruentur gloriâ Majestatis Dei. Christus autem qua erat infinita scientia harum rerum & opinionum sapientum gentis Judaicæ callentissimus, ut demonstraret esse se illum Messiam, quem præstolabantur jacturam Adami reparaturum, recipit, se ostensurum cœlum apertum, atque adeo lætum accessum ad Deum crediturus omnibus propediem muniturum. Hinc Christus; ego sum via, veritas & vita, nemo venit ad patrem nisi per me, Joh. 14: 6. & Petrus, Christus semel pro peccatis passus fuit, justus pro injustis, ut nos ad Deum adduceret, morte quidem affectus carne, vivificatus autem Spiritu, 1 Petr. 3: 18. & Paulus, utrique, Judæi nempe & Ethnici, per ipsum habemus aditum per unum Spiritum ad Patrem. In Christo habemus loquendi libertatem & aditum cum fiducia per fidem ipsius. Ephes. 2: 18. & 3: 12. Cum igitur fratres habemus libertatem ingrediendi Sanctum Sanctorum per sanguinem Jesu, ea via, quam dedicavit nobis recentem & vi& vivam per velum, h. e. per carnem suam, accedamus cum vero corde per plenam certiorationem fidei, aspersione purgati cordibus à conscientia mala, Hebr. 9:19.20.22.
units.tr: First. He chose this wonderful vision wisely and expressly in relation to himself, insofar as he was the Son of man, that is, of Adam. This vision of the opened heaven plainly showed to all that Jesus is that promised seed of the woman who would crush the serpent's head. Adam, his parent, by his wicked rebellion had so closed off Paradise, a type of heaven, to himself and his sons with the flaming sword of the cherubim, that every approach and access to Paradise and to God, and to any place where the immortal God would in future display extraordinary symbols of his presence, was forbidden. Hence Mount Sinai, the extraordinary sanctuary of the Deity, was fortified on every side with barriers and bars, lest the people attempt to break through there (Exod. 19:12; Heb. 12:20). Likewise the Holy and the Holy of Holies [τῶ ναῶ], the dwelling of God, closed by a double veil, and the holy people of God itself, were kept far away from access to the immortal Deity. Wisely, therefore, Christ chose the vision of the heaven opened for himself and afterwards for men, so that by that future opening and vision of heaven he might signify that he would demonstrate in clear light how truly he is the Son of man, who would so magnificently repair the most grievous loss which Adam, the parent, had brought upon himself and his posterity through the flesh, when he had eternally closed off the earthly paradise and the other secret places, all those which God deigned to honour with his glorious presence, and had made them inaccessible. Thus, with the serpent's head crushed, divine justice propitiated, the angel with the flaming sword extinguished, and enmity wholly abolished, a free approach and access to the opened heaven and to God would lie open for himself and for all who believe in him. This was the mind of the ancient teachers of the Hebrews. For among the seven things which they hope the Messiah will show Israel, they count these two, namely the Paradise of Eden and the tree of life. So Rabbi Elias ben Moses, in the Sepher Reschit Chocmah, commenting on these words of Song of Songs 1:4, "The king has brought me into his chambers," says: "Our teachers of blessed memory said that these are the chambers of the garden of Eden. This is also what they say about the tree of life, that it was not created in vain, but that men will eat of it at the resurrection and live for ever." Rabbi Menachem, on Gen. chap. 3, and the Chaldee paraphrast on Song 4:12 comment thus: "Like the Paradise of Eden, into which none may enter except the just, whose souls are carried thither by the hands of angels." But that these things are not to be understood of the earthly paradise but mystically of the heavenly one, the chief of the rabbis, who first ceased to trifle, Moses Maimonides, plainly teaches in the Mishnah, treatise on repentance, chap. 3, sect. 2, when he comments thus divinely on the future world: "Here neither is eaten nor drunk, nor are those other things needful to the bodies of the sons of Adam in this world, such as sitting, standing, sleeping, dying, being sad and the like. Thus our wise men have said that in the future world they neither eat, nor drink, nor use marriage; but the just sit with their crowns on their heads and enjoy the glory of the Majesty of God." But Christ, who had infinite knowledge of these things and was most skilled in the opinions of the wise men of the Jewish nation, in order to show that he is that Messiah who was to repair the loss of Adam, undertakes to show the opened heaven, and so promises that he will shortly provide all with a joyful access to God. Hence Christ: "I am the way, the truth and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me," John 14:6. And Peter: "Christ once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh but made alive in the Spirit," 1 Pet. 3:18. And Paul: "through him we both, Jews and Gentiles, have access by one Spirit to the Father. In Christ we have boldness of speech and access with confidence through faith in him," Eph. 2:18; 3:12. "Since therefore, brothers, we have confidence to enter the Holy of Holies through the blood of Jesus, by the way which he has dedicated for us, new and living, through the veil, that is, through his flesh, let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience," Heb. 9:19, 20, 22.

units.la: Secundò. Stupendam istam Filii hominis in cœlum apertum ascendentis, comitante Angelorum ascendentium famulitio, visionem, sepositis cæteris destinato selegit, quia celeberrimarum de Messia ascendente prophetiarum, quæ Judæis erant in oculis & osculis, implementum luculentum habet. Unus Psalmographus multa habet eximia; Attollite, porta, capita vestra, attollite vos, ostia aterna, ut ingrediatur Rex gloriæ. Antiphonæ verò reponenti, quis est iste Rex gloriæ ? Antiphona altera extemplò respondebat; Jeheve robustissimus & potentissimus, Jeheve potentissimus bellator. Attolite, porta, capita vestra, attollite, inquam, ostia aterna, ut ingrediatur Rex gloriæ. Scisncitanti iterum alteri Antiphonæ Sanctorum citharistarum, Quis est iste Rex gloriæ ? alternis Antiphona reponebat, Jeheve exercituum is est Rex gloriæ summus, Psalm. 24: 7.8.9.10. Ut enim isthæc de Philistæis triumphanti, & in montem Sion ascendenti arcæ, David cæteraque gens sancta cecinerint; in honorem tamen Regis Messiæ, triumphum celebrantis ad cœlum de victis & prostratis hostibus suis diabolo, peccato, mundo & morte, sonora voce pronunciata fuisse, liquidò paret. 1°. Quia ostia palatii Davidis, nedum ostia tabernaculi, jure nullo audire possunt ostia aterna: hæc cœli Dei sanctuarii prærogativa est, ostia æternum duratura habere. 2°. Quia Christus Deus & Dominus gloriæ est, qui unus nube, sedente pro solio, ex alis Cherubim affabrè concinnato, adumbrabatur: is enim Angelus est faciei Jeheve. Jes. 63: 9. qui cum Israelitas duxit in deserto, tum throno suo super arca insedit. Unde Moses, ubi nubes præiret & arca proximè cœlestem illam viæ ducem sequeretur, ingeminare solebat; surge, Jeheve, & inimici tui dispergentur, Num. 10: 35. Id nos docent Jesaias cap. 6: 1. 2. &c. coll. cum Ioh. 12: 41. & Jeremias vehementissima isthac Dei Patris interrogatione, Quid est dilecto meo domi meæ ? Jerem. 11: 15. Christus autem dilectus ille est Dei filius, Exod. 23: 20. 21. & 33: 14. Eccles. 5: 6. Jos. 5: 1. Ezech. 1: 26. 28, & 10: 1. 2. 19. 20. Matth. 3: 17. & 17: 5. & denique Ezechiel, Tollens me Spiritus deducit me in atrium intimum. ecce autem plena erat gloria Jehevé domus. Et audivi sermocinantem aliquem mecum è domo: vir enim adstabat mihi, dicebat autem mihi; Fili hominis, locum solii mei neque locum plantarum pedum meorum, ubi habitaturus sum inter filios Israëlis in seculum, neque nomen sanctitatis mee contaminaturi sunt amplius domus Israëlis, ipsi & reges ipsorum fornicatione sua, & cadaveribus regum suorum & excelsis suis. Ezech. 43: 5. 6. 7.
units.tr: Secondly. Of that stupendous vision of the Son of man ascending into the opened heaven, accompanied by the service of ascending angels, he chose this one deliberately, setting the others aside, because it has a clear fulfilment in the most famous prophecies about the ascending Messiah, which were constantly in the mouths and eyes of the Jews. The psalmist alone has many striking passages: Lift up your heads, O gates, lift yourselves up, eternal doors, that the King of glory may come in. When one choir answered, who is this King of glory?, the other choir at once replied: Jehovah, most strong and mighty, Jehovah, mighty in battle. Lift up your heads, O gates, lift up, I say, eternal doors, that the King of glory may come in. When the other choir of holy singers asked again, Who is this King of glory?, the first answered in turn: Jehovah of hosts, he is the supreme King of glory (Ps. 24:7, 8, 9, 10). For although David and the other holy people may have sung these words about the ark triumphing over the Philistines and ascending to Mount Zion, it is plain that they were proclaimed with a loud voice in honour of the Messiah King, who celebrates his triumph into heaven over his enemies, conquered and laid low: the devil, sin, the world and death. First, because the gates of David's palace, let alone the gates of the tabernacle, cannot rightly be called eternal doors; to have doors that will last forever is a prerogative of the sanctuary of God in heaven. Second, because Christ is God and Lord of glory, who was foreshadowed by the cloud sitting as a throne, fashioned skilfully from the wings of the cherubim. For he is the angel of the face of Jehovah (Isa. 63:9), who led the Israelites in the desert and then sat enthroned above the ark. Hence Moses, when the cloud went before and the ark followed close behind that heavenly guide of the way, used to repeat: Arise, Jehovah, and let your enemies be scattered (Num. 10:35). Isaiah ch. 6:1, 2, etc., compared with John 12:41, teaches us this, and so does Jeremiah, with that most vehement question of God the Father: What is my beloved doing in my house? (Jer. 11:15). But Christ is that beloved, the Son of God (Exod. 23:20, 21; 33:14; Eccl. 5:6; Josh. 5:1; Ezek. 1:26, 28; 10:1, 2, 19, 20; Matt. 3:17; 17:5). And finally Ezekiel: The Spirit lifted me up and brought me into the inner court; and behold, the glory of Jehovah filled the house. And I heard someone speaking to me out of the house, for a man was standing beside me, and he said to me: Son of man, this is the place of my throne and the place of the soles of my feet, where I will dwell among the children of Israel for ever; and the house of Israel shall no more defile my holy name, they nor their kings, by their whoredom and by the corpses of their kings and their high places. (Ezek. 43:5, 6, 7).

units.la: En tibi simul gloriam Jeheve & virum abstantem Ezechieli. Hic igitur qui loquitur, Immanuel est, Deus & homo in unitate personæ: sed verò templum vocat locum solii sui, & recipit se hic loci habitaturum inter Israelitas in seculum. Filius itaque hominis, idemque Rex Messias, habitabat in Sanctuario, quia is unus symbolis divinæ præsentiæ super arca & propitiatorio divinissimè adumbrabatur. Concludamus itaque, Davidem & Levitas triumphalem Regis gloriæ ascensum in cœlum cecinisse Psal. 24. Pergunt & Psal.47: 2. 3. 6. 7. 8. 9. Omnes populi, plaudite manu, clangite Deo voce canora. Ascendit Deus cum clangore, Jeheve cum sono buccinæ, psallite Deo, psallite: psallite Regi nostro, psallite: nam Rex totius terræ Deus est. Psallite, regnat Deus super gentes, Deus insidet solio Majestatis suæ. Hic primum arcam vides in civitatem Davidis, vel in templum Salomonis ascendentem, 2 Sam. 6: 12. 1 Reg. 8: 4. Hic thronum vides; nempe arca thronus erat Majestatis Jeheve, 1 Chron. 28: 18. Psalm. 80: 2. & 99: 1. Sed verò Deus sedens, pro solio arcæ, nondum Deus erat universæ terræ, in cujus honorem gentes omnes lætæ psallerent: id demum adventu Messiæ plenum implementum habuit post Christi ascensum in cœlum & Spiritus Sancti abundantem effusionem, quâ armati præcones Euangelii idololatriam falsaque gentium Numina ubique terrarum pessundederunt. Tunc enim Deus non jure duntaxat, sed & rebus ipsis Deus & Rex fuit universæ terræ: quia Christus ascendit in cœlum, quod solium gloriæ est & Hebræorum Doctoribus & Paulo Hebr. 8: 1. & 12: 2. Pergunt 68: 19. 20. 21. 22. Curruum Dei duo sunt myriades, millia multiplicia: Dominus cum illis Sinai in Sanctuario. Ascendens in sublime captivam fecisti captivorum multitudinem, accipiens dona hominibus, etiam rebelles habitando Jah Deus. Benedictus Dominus, qui quotidie nos onerat donis. Deus ille fortis salus nostra excellentissima, Deus ille fortis nobis fortis ad salutem omnimodam & Jeheve Domino exitus mortis. Quàm proprie & ad literam Christo Filio hominis hæc conveniant, simul triumphalis ipsius in cœlum ascensus & magnifica regalium donorum effusio die Pentecostes solemni probavit, simul Paulus docuit. Eph. 4: 8.
units.tr: Here you see at once the glory of Jehovah and the man standing beside Ezekiel. He who speaks here, therefore, is Immanuel, God and man in the unity of person; yet he calls the temple the place of his throne, and declares that he will dwell there among the Israelites for ever. The Son of man, therefore, who is also the Messiah King, dwelt in the sanctuary, because he was most divinely foreshadowed by the one thing that symbolised the divine presence above the ark and the mercy seat. Let us conclude, then, that David and the Levites sang of the triumphal ascent of the King of glory into heaven in Psalm 24. Psalm 47 goes on: All you peoples, clap your hands, shout to God with a voice of song. God has gone up with a shout, Jehovah with the sound of the trumpet. Sing praises to God, sing praises; sing praises to our King, sing praises; for God is King of all the earth. Sing praises: God reigns over the nations; God sits upon his holy throne. Here you see first the ark going up into the city of David, or into the temple of Solomon (2 Sam. 6:12; 1 Kings 8:4). Here you see the throne; for the ark was indeed the throne of the majesty of Jehovah (1 Chron. 28:18; Ps. 80:2; 99:1). But God sitting upon the ark as a throne was not yet God of the whole earth, in whose honour all the nations would rejoice and sing praise. That was fully fulfilled only at the coming of the Messiah, after Christ's ascent into heaven and the abundant outpouring of the Holy Spirit, by which the armed heralds of the gospel overthrew idolatry and the false deities of the nations everywhere on earth. For then God was the God and King of all the earth not only by right but in fact, because Christ ascended into heaven, which is the throne of glory, as both the Hebrew teachers and Paul affirm (Heb. 8:1; 12:2). Psalm 68 goes on: The chariots of God are twice ten thousand, thousands upon thousands: the Lord is among them, as at Sinai in the sanctuary. You ascended on high, you led captive a multitude of captives, you received gifts for men, even for the rebellious, that Jah God might dwell among them. Blessed be the Lord, who daily loads us with benefits. That God who is our strong salvation, that God who is strong for us to save us completely; and to Jehovah the Lord belong the issues of death. How properly and literally these words apply to Christ the Son of man, his triumphal ascent into heaven and the magnificent outpouring of royal gifts on the solemn day of Pentecost have together proved, and Paul has taught the same (Eph. 4:8).

units.la: Tertiò. Quia stupenda hæc cœli aperti & Filii hominis, comitantibus Dei Angelis, eò ascendentis, visio, implementum habet eximiarum de Messia Rege, Propheta & Pontifice visionum, quæ exstant apud Prophetas. Nonnullas nunc temporis perpendere libet. Prima visio Jesaiæ est cap. 6: 1. 2. 3. 11. &c. Anno, quo mortuus est Rex Hozias, vidi, inquit Propheta, Dominum, insidentem solio celso & elevato, cujus fimbriæ complebant templum ipsum. Seraphim adstantes superne ei, senis alis unusquisque, quarum binis tegebat faciem suam, & binis tegebat pedes suos, ac binis volabat. Et clamans alter ad alterum dicebat; Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus Jehove exercituum, implet totam terram gloria ejus. Tum commoti sunt postes liminum à voce inclamante, & domus ipsa impleta est fumo. Jesaiam vidisse filium hominis Christum, neminem quemquam Christianum Johannes dubitare finit, Joh. 12:41. Sed verò os simul Judæorum, simul hæreticorum, Socini sodalium, ut retundatur, age perpendamus 1o. personam, quam Propheta vidit. 2o. Munera, quibus fungebatur. 3o. Locum, ubi vidit. 4o. Tempus. 5o. Gloriam ipsius, quam Seraphim celebrant. Hæc verò omnia in Filium hominis, ascendentem in cœlum apertum volantibus ad eum Dei Angelis recta collineant.
units.tr: Thirdly. Because this stupendous vision of the opened heaven and of the Son of man ascending there, accompanied by the angels of God, fulfils the remarkable visions of the Messiah as King, Prophet and Priest that are found among the prophets. Let us now weigh some of them. The first vision of Isaiah is in ch. 6:1, 2, 3, 11, etc.: In the year that King Uzziah died, the prophet says, I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and lofty throne, and his train filled the temple itself. Seraphim stood above him, each with six wings: with two they covered his face, with two they covered his feet, and with two they flew. And one called to another and said: Holy, holy, holy is Jehovah of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory. Then the posts of the doorways shook at the voice of the one calling, and the house was filled with smoke. That Isaiah saw the Son of man, Christ, no Christian at all doubts, as John affirms (John 12:41). But in order to silence both the Jews and the heretics, the companions of the Socinians, let us weigh: first, the person whom the prophet saw; second, the offices he performed; third, the place where he saw him; fourth, the time; fifth, the glory of his which the seraphim celebrate. All these things point directly to the Son of man, ascending into the opened heaven, with the angels of God flying to him.

units.la: Personam quod attinet, simul Deus simul homo est. Deus quidem; nam & יהוה צבאות/ Jehove exercituum, dicitur proprio & singulari Dei nomine, quo olim ab Angelis, idolis & hominibus simul discerni, simul futuram suam revelationem, qua fusis & deletis gentium Numinibus latè in orbem dominaretur, polliceri voluit; & אדני Κύριος, Dominus, & Dominus universæ terræ, plenæ ipsius gloriâ, appellatur. Id verò nominis proprium Dei Israelis est, Josu. 3:13. Nehem. 10:29. Psalm. 8:2. & 68:21. & 97:5. Mich. 4:13. Hab. 3:19. Præterea Deus est, quia sedet non solum in templo; sed & in adyto pro solio celso, nempe in arca, quæ thronus Dei dicitur. 1 Chron. 28:18. & proprium Dei Israelis est sedere inter Cherubim. Psalm. 80:2. & 99:1. Deus denique est, quia Seraphim, h. e. Angeli, accincti in ejus obsequium, adstantes ipsi serviunt, eumque adorant, & binis alis faciem præ reverentia, & pedes, h. e. pudenda corporis, nubunt; & binis alis ad mandata ipsius capessenda volant. Sed verò & homo est. 1o. Quia Pontifex est, & sacra peragit in templo suo: est enim plenum fumo, nempe suffitus ex altari thymiamatum & victimæ propitiatoriæ ex altari holocaustorum, motis loco suo postibus templi. Omnis verò pontifex, ex hominibus assumptus, pro hominibus constituitur in iis, quæ apud Deum peragenda sunt, ut offerat dona & victimas pro peccatis, Hebr. 5:1. 2o. Homo est, quia veste sacerdotali indutus, sacræ vestis fimbriis templum replet. Atqui etsi Deus pater sub schemate viri & regis rarenter admodum in scriptura repræsentatur; ipse tamen vel Spiritus Sanctus nunquam ac nusquam ut Deus & homo pontifex videndus exhibetur. Unus Filius hominis Christus Immanuel est Deus, & homo in una eademque persona, unus Filius hominis Dominus ἐξοχὴν est, 1 Cor.8:16. & 12:5, Eph.4:5. & Dominus gloriæ, 1 Cor.2:8. & Deus in carne manifestatus, 1 Tim.3:16. qui Ecclesiam redemit proprio sanguine, Actor. 20:28. Munera, quibus fungitur Jeheve exercituum, omnino tergemina sunt, pontificium, regale & propheticum: est enim Pontifex, Rex & Prophe-ta, quem canit divinus Vates. Est Pontifex quidem 1o. quia cernitur in secretissimo adyto, quod unum Pontificem summum semel in anno admittebat; plebem vero, caeterosque sacerdotes arcebat. 2o. Quia indutus cernitur non utique veste regali, cujus fimbriae in Scriptura nullibi memorantur: sed veste sacerdotali, cujus mysticas fimbrias late persequitur Moses, Exod. 28:33. & 39:24. 3o. Sacra peragit solemnis propitiatio-nis: nam tota domus repletur fumo, quod in solemni propitiationum festo contigisse Moyses divine innuit Levitic. 16:13. & Philo notavit, lib. περὶ μοναρχίας, dum infit: atqui huic ipsi pontifici, quum quotannis duntaxat intrare, fas sit, non tamen omnia cernere licet. Rationem exemplo attexit; πυρεῖον μὲν γὰρ ἀνθρακῶν πληρες ἡ θυμιάματα αἰσχεμίζει. πολλῆς δ' ἀναλίσκομένης, ὡς εἰκὸς, ἀτμιδῶν κατέχεσθαι τὰ ἐν κύκλῳ πάντα· ἡ ἡ ὄψις διαπιαζεσθαι ἡ ἀναπτυλῶν ἰχθύ, πέσσω χωρεῖν ἀδυνάτως. Etenim thuribulum ignitis carbonibus & odoramentis plenum illuc infert. omnia autem circumcirca tenentur multo fumo, qui ut consentaneum est excitatur, tum vero & visus quoque obtenebratur, inhibeturque, neque longius sese ferre quit. 4o. Quia ministerio Seraphim pruna ex ara sua immunda purgat prophetae labia: purgare vero immundorum spurcitiem sacerdotis est. Sed vero & Rex cernitur; nam primo augusto illo nomine appellatur. Secundo, sedet super solio celso & elevato, Dominus universae terrae. Tertio, ministros habet adstantes, & accinctos ad obsequium Seraphim, ut regiam majestatem suam, qua late dominatur in orbem, Prophetae exhibeat contemplandam. Denique simul Prophetarum summus cernitur: nam 1o. prophetiam fundit de futura Judaeorum induratione & occaecatione. 2o. quia Jesaiam creat mittitque Prophetam. Sed vero tergemino illo simul fungitur munere Rex, simul propheta ac Pontifex, quae tempore Jesaiae ita erant distincta munia, ut Rex Ozias ubi thuribulum attrectare & sacros adolere aris honores aggressus fuit, repentina lepra ex vindice Numinis justitia correptus, e medio populi immundus secesserit. Haec quam exacte in Christum Dominum conveniant, non Johannes tantum diserte nos docet, Joh. 12:41. sed & ipsa experientia & universa Scriptura clamat. Nam Deus Pater, vel Spiritus Sanctus nusquam tota Scriptura munere sacerdotali, regali & prophetico functi memorantur. Unus Jesus Filius hominis Pontifex est, Psalm. 110:4. Rex, Psalm. 2:6. Pontifex Rexque simul, Psalm. 110:1.4. Unus Messias
units.tr: As to his person, he is at once God and man. He is God, for he is called by the proper and singular name of God, Jehovah of hosts [יהוה צבאות], the name by which of old he wished to be distinguished from angels, idols and men alike, and by which he promised his future revelation, through which the gods of the nations would be overthrown and destroyed and he would rule widely over the world. He is also called Lord [אדני, Κύριος], and the Lord of the whole earth, full of his glory. This is indeed the proper name of the God of Israel: Josh. 3:13; Neh. 10:29; Ps. 8:2; 68:21; 97:5; Mic. 4:13; Hab. 3:19. Moreover, he is God because he sits not only in the temple but in the inner sanctuary, on a lofty throne, namely the ark, which is called the throne of God: 1 Chron. 28:18. It is characteristic of the God of Israel to sit between the cherubim: Ps. 80:2; 99:1. Lastly, he is God because the seraphim, that is, angels girded for his service, stand by and minister to him and worship him, covering their face with two wings out of reverence, and their feet, that is, the parts of the body that should be covered, and with two wings they fly to carry out his commands. But he is also man. First, because he is a high priest who performs sacred acts in his temple; for it is filled with smoke, namely the incense of the altar of incense and the sacrifice of atonement from the altar of burnt offerings, the posts of the temple having been moved from their place. Every high priest, taken from among men, is appointed for men in the things pertaining to God, that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins: Heb. 5:1. Second, he is man, because clothed in the priestly vestment, with the hems of his sacred robe filling the temple. Yet although God the Father is rarely represented in Scripture under the form of a man and king, the Holy Spirit himself is never and nowhere shown to be seen as God and high priest. The one Son of Man, Christ Immanuel, is God and man in one and the same person; the one Son of Man is the Lord [κύριος] par excellence, 1 Cor. 8:16; 12:5; Eph. 4:5; the Lord of glory, 1 Cor. 2:8; God manifested in the flesh, 1 Tim. 3:16; who redeemed the Church with his own blood, Acts 20:28. The offices which Jehovah of hosts exercises are altogether threefold: priestly, royal and prophetic. For he is priest, king and prophet, as the divine seer sings. He is priest, indeed: (1) because he is seen in the most secret inner sanctuary, which admitted only the one high priest, once a year, and kept away the people and the other priests; (2) because he is seen clothed not in royal robes, whose hems are nowhere mentioned in Scripture, but in priestly vestments, whose mystical hems Moses describes at length: Exod. 28:33; 39:24; (3) because he performs the sacred acts of the solemn atonement, for the whole house is filled with smoke, which Moses indicates happened divinely at the solemn feast of atonement: Lev. 16:13. Philo also noted this in his book On the Monarchy [περὶ μοναρχίας], when he begins: Now, though it is lawful for this very high priest to enter only once a year, it is not permitted to see everything. He adds the reason by an example: For a censer full of burning coals and incense sends up a cloud, and since a great deal is burnt, as is likely, everything around is enveloped in vapour; so the sight is darkened and blocked, and cannot carry further [πυρεῖον μὲν γὰρ ἀνθρακῶν πλῆρες ἢ θυμιάματα ἀποκαπνίζει. πολλῆς δ' ἀναλισκομένης, ὡς εἰκὸς, ἀτμιδῶν κατέχεσθαι τὰ ἐν κύκλῳ πάντα· ἡ δὲ ὄψις διαπίπτειν ἢ ἀναπτυσσομένη ἰχθύς, πέρα χωρεῖν ἀδυνάτως]. (4) He is priest because, through the ministry of a seraph, he cleanses the prophet's lips with a live coal from his altar; for to purge the filth of the unclean is the work of a priest. But he is also seen as king: first, he is called by that majestic name; second, he sits on a lofty and elevated throne as Lord of the whole earth; third, he has ministers standing by, girded for service, the seraphim, so that he may show the prophet his royal majesty, by which he rules widely over the world. Finally, he is seen as the greatest of the prophets: for (1) he utters a prophecy about the future hardening and blinding of the Jews; (2) he creates and sends Isaiah as prophet. Yet this threefold office is exercised by the one king who is at once prophet and priest. In Isaiah's time these offices were so distinct that King Uzziah, when he took up the censer and undertook to offer the sacred honours at the altar, was struck with sudden leprosy by the avenging justice of God and withdrew unclean from the midst of the people. How exactly these things agree with the Lord Christ, not only does John teach us plainly, John 12:41, but experience itself and all of Scripture proclaim. For God the Father, or the Holy Spirit, is nowhere in all Scripture mentioned as exercising the priestly, royal and prophetic office. The one Jesus, the Son of Man, is priest, Ps. 110:4; king, Ps. 2:6; priest and king at once, Ps. 110:1, 4. The one Messiah

units.la: Rex simul & Pontifex sedet in solio suo, ut Zacharias vaticinatus est; sedebit & dominabitur super solio, & erit Sacerdos super solio suo. Zach.6:13. Non secus atque hic Jeheve exercituum, summus Pontifex Rexque simul, sedens cernitur super solio celso, singulari & eximia prærogativa, quæ merum hominem haud decet, sed unum Immanuelem Deum & hominem simul. Nempe Sacerdotum nemini, ne summo quidem Pontifici sedere in toto templi atrio fas jusve erat: stabant enim quotquot erant Sacerdotes, Deo ministrantes nudis pedibus in pavimento templi frigido. Hinc venarum inflatio & corporis languor. Unde Juvenalis in causa non absimili,
units.tr: is at once king and priest, sitting on his throne, as Zechariah prophesied: He shall sit and rule upon his throne, and he shall be a priest upon his throne: Zech. 6:13. Just so, Jehovah of hosts is seen as the supreme priest and king at once, sitting on a lofty throne, by a singular and remarkable prerogative which does not befit a mere man but the one Immanuel, God and man together. For it was lawful for no priest, not even the high priest, to sit anywhere in the whole court of the temple: all the priests, ministering to God, stood with bare feet on the cold pavement of the temple. Hence the swelling of the veins and the weariness of the body; whence Juvenal, in a not dissimilar case:

units.la: Varicosus fiet arujpex.
units.tr: The soothsayer will become varicose.

units.la: Uni quidem Regi Davidi & regibus è Davidis familia, si quando ingrederentur, nisi ubi solemni ritu consulerent oraculum Urim & Tummim, in atrio sancto sedere fas erat, 2 Sam. 7: 18. 1 Chron. 17: 16. Unde Maimonides in Halacha Beth Habbechira, cap. 7. Si intret atrium & sit de familia Davidis, sessio ei est. Nulli homini fas fuit in toto templi atrio sedere, præterquam Regi, qui ex familia Davidis esset. Ast nec regi e prosapia Davidis sedere fas fuit in Sancto Sanctorum, nedum eo prorumpere, quanto minus summo Pontifici: is enim astabat ad arcam cum suffitu & sanguine, septies aspergendo. Eccur vero? Nempe uno illo sacrificio propitiationis quotannis iterando, haud placabat justitiam Numinis, nec ipsi quiescendum erat ab iterandis sacrificiis: stabat igitur extemplo redituru s ad populum, mox ministraturus & sacrificia quotidie oblaturus. Contrà Christus futurorum bonorum summus pontifex, placatā λύτρῳ sanguinis sui justitiā Numinis, quievit ab opere consummato, seditque pontifex in solio suo. Id memorandi discriminis signanter notavit Paulus, ubi Sacerdotii Christi excellentiam demonstraturus, contendit eum cum Sacerdote Levitico. Purificatione peccatorum nostrorum per seipsum facta, consedit ad dexteram Majestatis in locis excelsissimis. Hebr. 1: 3. Caterum eorum, quæ diximus summa est, talem nos habere pontificem, qui consedit ad dexteram throni majestatis in cœlis, sanctuarii minister ac veri Tabernaculi, quod fixit Dominus & non homo. Hebr.3: 1. 2. Omnis igitur Sacerdos stat quotidie, sacram functionem obiens, & easdem sæpius offerens hostias, quæ numquam possunt auferre peccata. Hic vero, nempe Christus, una pro peccatis oblata in perpetuum victima consedit ad dexteram Dei. Hebr. 10: 11. 12. Audi & sedulo discrimen animadverte. Sacerdos Leviticus stat, quotidie nempe in templo sacram functionem obiens: Christus vero, pontifex futurorum bonorum, consedit ad dexteram Dei. Sacerdos Leviticus stat quotidie offerens. Eccur? Nempe hostias offert, quæ nunquam possint peccatum auferre; stet igitur in procinctu necesse est, ut quotidie offerat, iteretque sua sacrificia. Sed vero Christus consedit ad Dei dexteram una pro peccatis oblata in perpetuum victimâ, eâ nempe in perpetuum consummavit quotquot sanctificantur Heb. 10: 14. Sedet igitur, quia quiescit ab opere plenè consummato. Christus denique propheta est, Deut. 18: 15. 18. 19. Sed propheta ad instar Mosis, cui uni sicut Mosi singulari prærogativa fas fuit sancta sanctorum ingredi & ad arcam sanctuarii & ad operculum propitiatorium verba cum Numine commutare, Exod. 25: 22. Num. 7: 89. Concludamus itaque, Filium Hominis Christum summum prophetam, pontificem Regemque simul, unum illum esse, quem Jesaias propheta vidit.
units.tr: Only the king David and the kings of David's family were permitted to sit in the holy court, when they came in, except where they consulted the oracle of the Urim and Thummim by solemn rite: 2 Sam. 7:18; 1 Chron. 17:16. Hence Maimonides, in Halacha Beth Habbechira, ch. 7: If he enters the court and is of the family of David, he has the right to sit. No man was permitted to sit in the whole court of the temple except the king who was of the family of David. But not even a king of David's line was permitted to sit in the Holy of Holies, much less to rush into it, and still less the high priest: for he stood by the ark with incense and blood, sprinkling it seven times. Why was this? Because by repeating that one sacrifice of atonement each year he did not appease the justice of God, nor was he to rest from repeating the sacrifices; so he stood, expecting to return straight to the people, and soon to minister and offer sacrifices daily. By contrast, Christ, the high priest of good things to come, having appeased the justice of God by the ransom of his blood, rested from his finished work, and sat down as priest on his throne. Paul noted this difference with particular care when, intending to show the excellence of Christ's priesthood, he compared him with the Levitical priest: When he had by himself made purification of our sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high: Heb. 1:3. Now the sum of what we have said is this: we have such a high priest, who has sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven, a minister of the sanctuary and of the true tabernacle, which the Lord pitched and not man: Heb. 3:1, 2. Every priest therefore stands daily, performing sacred service and offering again and again the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But this one, namely Christ, having offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down at the right hand of God: Heb. 10:11, 12. Listen and carefully observe the difference. The Levitical priest stands, namely performing sacred service daily in the temple; but Christ, the high priest of good things to come, has sat down at the right hand of God. The Levitical priest stands, offering daily. Why? Namely, because he offers sacrifices which can never take away sin; he must therefore stand ready, so that he may offer and repeat his sacrifices daily. But Christ sat down at God's right hand, having offered one victim for sins for ever, by which indeed he has perfected for ever all who are sanctified: Heb. 10:14. He sits, therefore, because he rests from a work fully finished. Lastly, Christ is a prophet: Deut. 18:15, 18, 19. But he is a prophet like Moses, to whom alone, by a singular prerogative like Moses, it was lawful to enter the Holy of Holies and to exchange words with God at the ark of the sanctuary and at the mercy seat: Exod. 25:22; Num. 7:89. Let us conclude, therefore, that the Son of Man, Christ, the supreme prophet, priest and king at once, is that one whom the prophet Isaiah saw.

units.la: Locus, ubi apparet, domus & templum dicitur, & templi insignibus decoratur, nempe altari, prunis impositis, suffitu, fumo, pontifice summo & vestis sacerdotalis fimbriis, quæ nusquam nisi in templo usui erant: sed templum erat interius, quod in Novo instrumento discriminis ergò ὁ ναὸς appellatur, cùm contrà universa templi fabrica atrio populi significata τὸ ἱερὸν audiat discriminis ergò. Ratio est, quia fumo, nimirum altaris, tota domus repleta est. Atenim fumo altaris holocaustorum, qui, columnæ adinstar, sursum ferebatur per aërem liberum, templum haud facile repleri potuit, nisi motis loco suo postibus ϛ ναῦ: fumo itaque aræ suffituum, quæ erat in loco sancto operto coram arca, templum utique repletum fuit. Sed & in intimo templi adyto visus est Rex & Pontifex Jeheve exercituum: nam in sancto sanctorum super arca thronus erat ex alis Cherubim concinnatus, unde arca simul Dei thronus, simul scabellum pedum ejus dicitur, 1 Chron. 28: 2. 18. Psal. 99: 5. & 132: 7. & Rex visus est pro solio sedens excelso. Sed vero templum intimum oppanso gemino velo mortalibus præclusum erat, ut eorum nemini excepto pontifice summo semel quotannis eo penetrare sese jus fasve esset. Vidit itaque Propheta, princepsque nobilissimus e tribu Judæ, templum interius apertum, ut aram suffituum, fumum, thronum, Regem & volantes Seraphim inibi intueretur. Hic vero haud immeritò quæritur, templumne Hierosolymitanum fuerit, coelumve templo mysticè adumbratum. Respondemus, templum esse spirituale æde sacra Hierosolymorum præfiguratum. Nam hic aperte cernere est, quæ erant in Sancto Sanctorum, nempe duo Seraphim alis expansis (clamant enim קדוש קדוש קדוש ipse ad ipsum, sicuti duo Cherubim gloriæ alis expansis propitiatorium obumbrantes in Sanctuario videbantur) thronus gloriæ, qualis erat super arca: Rex Jeheve exercituum, pro celso illo solio sedens, sicut Numen sanctissimum sedere inter Cherubinos in arca dicebatur, Psal. 80: 2. & 99: 1. דביר oraculum, seu locutorium, 1 Reg. 6: 19. Deinde audivi vocem Domini, dicentis; quem missurus sum, & quis iturus est nobis? Tum dixit; dicas populo isti: audite indesinenter, at ne intelligatis, videte indesinenter, neque cognoscatis, &c. Jes. 6: 8 9. Hic iterum cernere est pontifex, veste sacerdotali, cujus fimbriæ templum replent, indutus, rex, sedens pro solio celso, summusque Propheta, fundens oracula, creans & mittens Jesaiam Prophetam. Non secus atque in adyto tria isthæc videbantur in solemni propitiationum festo: nempe summus pontifex ad arcam, Rex Deus in nube pro solio sedens, & summus Propheta λόγια divina fundens; unde locus iste sanctissimus de nomine דביר, oraculi, censebatur. Hic denique cernere est, quæ in loco Sancto oculis usurpabantur, ara, pruna, suffitus, fumus totum adytum replens. Atenim sub schemate ϛ vaῳ, sanctuarii mundani, excellentius hic & structuræ nobilioris templum, nimirum spirituale & celeste, Jesaiæ apertum exhibetur. 1°. Quia ut thronus arcæ celsus fuerit in habitudine ad arcam inferiorem, non tamen erat tanta cum emphasi thronus celsus & elevatus, qui thronus erat mundanus atque terrenus. 2°. Quia hic Angeli non Cherubim, h. e. alati boves, sed Seraphim, urentes ob Zeli ardorem, ducta nomenclatione non à mortiferis Seraphim, h. e. serpentibus deserti urentibus; sed à Saraph, mystico Christi typo: erant enim salutiferi: nam eos vidit & sensit Jesaias prunis ex ara purgantes spurcitiem labiorum suorum. 3°. Hic Seraphim clamant alter ad alterum: sed ambo Cherubim arcæ inanimes ac mutæ figuræ erant. 4°. Hic una, eademque persona simul Deus & homo est, simul Pontifex, Rex & Propheta; sed vero in sanctissimo Hierosolymorum adyto isthæc omnia distincta erant. 5°. Voce clamantis Templi superliminaria & postes moti sunt loco, vehementi ut isthac commotione aditus in loca sancta apertus fuerit: id vero tempore Jesaiæ Templo Hierosolymitano nusquam contigisse memoratur. Id memorandi eventus Christo offerente mortis sacrificio, demum contigit: nam simul terra tremuit, simul velum ϛ vaῳ, templi interioris, è summo ad imum fissum est, sicut ab Christi ad cœlum apertum ascensu magna porta orientalis Templi ex ære Corinthiaco sponte aperta Festo paschatis visa est, & vox distincte audita, quæ inclamaret; migremus hinc. Josephus de Bello Jud. lib. 7. cap. 12. Nempe Christus pascha reale cœlum, τῷ vaῳ adumbratum, sibi & crediturus Sanguine suo aperuerat. Vidit itaque Propheta sub schemate templi interioris terreni cœlum reale templum apertum: sed & vidit Seraphim, hoc est, Dei Angelos alis sursum elatis ad Filium hominis ascendentes, & ad ipsum propitiatorio adumbratum, cernuos ac descendentes.
units.tr: The place where the vision occurs is called the house and the temple, and it is adorned with the marks of the temple: namely the altar with coals placed on it, the incense, the smoke, the high priest, and the fringes of the priestly garment, which were used nowhere but in the temple. But the temple meant was the inner one, which in the New Testament is called the sanctuary [ὁ ναὸς] for the sake of distinction, whereas the whole building of the temple, signified by the court of the people, is called the temple [τὸ ἱερὸν] for the sake of distinction. The reason is that the whole house was filled with the smoke of the altar. For the smoke of the burnt offerings, rising like a column through the open air, could not easily have filled the temple unless the posts had been moved from their place. The smoke of the altar of incense, which stood in the holy place behind the veil before the ark, certainly filled the temple. But also in the innermost sanctuary the King and High Priest, Jehovah of hosts, was seen. For in the Holy of Holies, above the ark, there was a throne made of the wings of the cherubim, whence the ark is called at once God's throne and the footstool of his feet (1 Chron. 28:2, 18; Ps. 99:5; 132:7), and the King was seen sitting on a lofty throne. But the innermost temple was closed off from mortals by a double veil, so that no one was permitted or allowed to enter it except the high priest, once a year. The prophet, then, and the most noble prince of the tribe of Judah, saw the inner temple opened, so that he might behold the altar of incense, the smoke, the throne, the King, and the flying seraphim there. Here it is rightly asked whether this was the temple at Jerusalem or heaven mystically shadowed by the temple. We reply that it is the spiritual temple, of which the sacred house at Jerusalem was a type. For here one can clearly see what was in the Holy of Holies: namely two seraphim with outstretched wings (for they cry Holy, holy, holy [קדוש קדוש קדוש], one to another, just as two cherubim with outstretched wings overshadowing the mercy seat were seen in the sanctuary); the throne of glory, such as was above the ark; the King, Jehovah of hosts, sitting on that lofty throne, just as the most holy Godhead was said to sit between the cherubim on the ark (Ps. 80:2; 99:1); the oracle, or inner chamber [דביר] (1 Kings 6:19). Then: I heard the voice of the Lord saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then he said, Go, and tell this people: Hear indeed, but do not understand; see indeed, but do not perceive (Isa. 6:8-9). Here again one sees the priest, clothed in priestly garments whose fringes fill the temple, the king sitting on a lofty throne, and the chief prophet, uttering oracles, creating and sending the prophet Isaiah. Just so, in the sanctuary, these three things were seen at the solemn festival of atonement: the high priest at the ark, God the King sitting on a throne in the cloud, and the chief Prophet uttering divine oracles. Hence that most holy place was named from the word dabir, the oracle. Here, finally, one sees what was used in the holy place before the eyes: the altar, the coals, the incense, and the smoke filling the whole inner sanctuary. For under the figure of the earthly sanctuary, the temple of a more excellent and nobler structure, namely the spiritual and heavenly one, is shown opened to Isaiah. First, because although the throne above the ark was high in relation to the lower ark, it was not with such emphasis a high and lofty throne, and that throne was earthly and worldly. Second, because here the angels are not cherubim, that is, winged oxen, but seraphim, burning with the heat of zeal. They are named not from the deadly seraphim, that is, the fiery serpents of the desert, but from saraph, a mystical type of Christ; for they were life-giving, since Isaiah saw and felt them cleansing the uncleanness of his lips with coals from the altar. Third, here the seraphim call out one to another, whereas the two cherubim on the ark were lifeless and mute figures. Fourth, here one and the same person is at once God and man, at once priest, king and prophet; but in the most holy sanctuary at Jerusalem all these were distinct. Fifth, at the voice of the one calling, the thresholds and posts of the temple were moved from their place, so that by this violent shaking an entrance into the holy places was opened. Yet it is not recorded that this ever happened in the temple at Jerusalem in Isaiah's time. This memorable event happened at last when Christ offered the sacrifice of his death: at that moment the earth trembled, and at the same time the veil of the inner temple was torn from top to bottom. Just as the great east gate of the temple, made of Corinthian bronze, was seen to open of its own accord at the feast of Passover when Christ ascended to heaven, and a voice was distinctly heard crying out, Let us depart from here (Josephus, Bell. Jud. 7.12). Indeed Christ, our true Passover, had opened heaven, which was shadowed by the temple, for himself and for those who would believe, by his blood. So the prophet saw, under the figure of the earthly inner temple, the real heavenly temple opened; and he also saw the seraphim, that is, the angels of God, with wings raised upward, ascending to the Son of man, and bowing down and descending to the propitiatory which was shadowed in him.

units.la: Tempus visionis mysticæ anno mortis Hosiæ Regis insignitur; anno, quo mortuus est Rex Hosias, vidi Dominum, sedentem super solio excelso & elevato, inquit Propheta. Eccur vero mortuo Hosia rege potius, quam rege Ezechia, vel Josia? Ratio est, quia Rex Hosias singulari planè ratione typus fuit Regis Messiæ, itaque sublato è vivis umbratili rege, verus rex Messias apparet. Nempe unus Hosias è regibus Judæ sacerdotale, regiumque munus consociare aggressus adolevit aris honores in altari suffitum. Ita Christus Rex simul & Pontifex sacerdotale, regiumque munus consociavit. Sicut Rex Hosias nec quicquam obstante summo Pontifice, familiaque sacerdotali permansit in consilio offerendi suffitum: non secus & Christus, à propósito offerendi Deo sacrificium suavis fragrantiæ, quicquid in contrarium obluctarentur Summus Pontifex Leviticus cum universa gente sacerdotali dimoveri se haud passus fuit. Sicut rex Hosias lepræ plaga, quæ immunditiem legalis erat, ad mortem usque percussus est, quod insolitum planè facinus attentasset: non secus & Christus plaga crucis, quæ immunda Judæis erat, ad mortem usque percussus est, Jes. 53: 4. quod sacrificium Deo offerre voluerit. Sicut Hosias simul templo, simul regali palatio ejectus est & omni Judæorum consortio penitus exterminatus, quod divinitus lepra percussus pro immundo haberetur: non secus & Christus non semel pro immundo habitus, ἀποσωαγωγῷ factus, templo, urbe, & vita denique uti κατάρα exterminatus est. Sicut rex Hosias regiæ authoritatis exercitio spoliatus, jus tamen regnandi in Judæos retinuit: ita & Christus ut jam in Judæos, nefariè repudiatus non dominetur; in eos tamen regnandi jus illibatum sibi retinet, demum in Judæos regnaturus, ubi gentium plenitudo in Fœdus Gratiosum ingressa fuerit. Tempus autem, quo jure postliminii ad exercitium regni rediturus est ad finem obdurationis Judaicæ gentis præstitutum fuit: nam quando velum cordis amovebitur, futurum est, ut ad Dominum convertantur, & videant, quem transfixerunt, Zach. 12: 10. & totus Israel salvetur. 2 Cor. 3: 16. Rom. 11: 26.
units.tr: The time of the mystical vision is marked by the year of the death of King Uzziah: In the year that King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, says the prophet. But why at the death of King Uzziah rather than in the reign of Hezekiah or Josiah? The reason is that King Uzziah was a type of the Messianic King in a quite singular way, so that, once that shadowy king was removed from the living, the true King Messiah appears. Indeed Uzziah alone, of the kings of Judah, undertook to combine the priestly and the royal office, and grew proud and offered incense on the altar. So Christ, the King and at the same time the Priest, combined the priestly and the royal office. Just as King Uzziah, though the high priest and the family of priests opposed him, persisted in his plan of offering incense, and was not moved by any objection, so Christ, purposing to offer to God a sacrifice of sweet fragrance, was not moved away, whatever the high priest and the whole priestly nation strove against him. Just as King Uzziah was struck with leprosy, which was a legal uncleanness, even to death, because he had attempted a quite unusual deed, so Christ was struck with the plague of the cross, which was unclean to the Jews, even to death (Isa. 53:4), because he willed to offer a sacrifice to God. Just as Uzziah was cast out both from the temple and from the royal palace and utterly excluded from all fellowship of the Jews, because, struck by leprosy by God, he was held to be unclean, so Christ, not once but repeatedly held to be unclean, was made an outcast and, as a curse, was excluded from the temple, the city, and at last from life. Just as King Uzziah, though stripped of the exercise of royal authority, retained the right to reign over the Jews, so Christ, though now shamefully rejected by the Jews and not ruling over them, nevertheless keeps for himself the untouched right to reign over them, and will at last reign over the Jews when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered into the gracious covenant. But the time when he will return by right of restoration to the exercise of his kingdom has been appointed for the end of the hardening of the Jewish nation. For when the veil is taken away from their heart, they will turn to the Lord and look upon him whom they pierced (Zech. 12:10), and all Israel will be saved (2 Cor. 3:16; Rom. 11:26).

units.la: Gloria Regis augustissimi, Pontificis & Prophetæ, quam Seraphim celebrant, gemino lineamento describitur, essentiali altero, altero accidentali, ut primum ad naturam ipsius gloriæ, secundum ad ejus amplitudinem spectet. Nempe essentiale lineamentum in summa sanctitate consistit; clamat enim alter ad alterum, Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus Jehovè exercituum: jure meritissimo; quandoquidem Sanctitas eximia separatio est propter excellentiam. Nempe augustissima persona, quam contem-platur platur Propheta, simul ab omnibus personis divinis, simul ab omnibus creaturis, Angelis & hominibus eximiâ excellentiâ separatur; est enim Deus & homo, Pontifex, Rex atque Propheta. Quando verò munera nituntur virtutis ὑπερoχῆς, suam quæque habent singularem sanctitatem. Is autem unus Pontifex est, qui & purgationem fecit peccatorum per se ipsum, & realem propitiationem pro omnibus orbis universi hominibus, ut sanctitate sua lato limite abs Pontificibus Leviticis disterminetur, qui peccata solum typica per alienam victimam purgaverint, & umbratilem propitiationem egerint pro una gente Israelitarum. Is unus suam habet singularem sanctitatem, uti Propheta est, qua ab omnibus aliis prophetis quam excellentissimè separetur. Sedet enim doctorum summus non in cathedra Mosis; sed in solio Majestatis excelso & elevato, Prophetam creat, mittitque Jesaiam & labiorum spurcitem aræ suæ sacerdotalis prunâ Seraphim ministerio purgat. Is denique unus singularem sanctitatem habet, qua rex est. Sedet enim inter Seraphim & Dominatur in Angelos & terram universam replet gloriâ suæ majestatis, quod nemini usquam contigit regum terrenorum. Τρισάγιον igitur, quo Seraphim celebrant Dominum, regemque exercituum, non adeo refertur ad tres personas Sacrosanctæ Τριάδος, ut vulgò creditum est, ut unicè ad Christum, cujus gloriam vidit Jesaias, in totum collineet & ad terna ipsius munera ter repetita sanctitas, iis, qui oculos habent, spectare videatur. Amplitudinem gloriæ, quod alterum est ipsius lineamentum, si spectaverimus, uni Christo competit: tota enim terra, Seraphinorum mysticorum præconio repleta, fuit gloria personæ Christi Immanuelis, Pontificis, Regis & Prophetæ summi.
units.tr: The glory of the most august King, Priest and Prophet, which the seraphim celebrate, is described by a twofold outline, one essential, the other accidental, so that the first regards the nature of that glory itself and the second its extent. The essential outline consists in supreme holiness, for one cries to another, Holy, holy, holy is Jehovah of hosts, most rightly and deservedly; since holiness is an outstanding separation because of its excellence. For the most august person whom the prophet contemplates is set apart with outstanding excellence both from all the divine persons and from all creatures, angels and men; for he is God and man, priest, king and prophet. Moreover, when offices strive toward a supreme excellence, each has its own singular holiness. He alone is the Priest who both made purification of sins by himself, and made a real propitiation for all men of the whole world, so that by his holiness he is divided by a wide margin from the Levitical priests, who purified only typical sins by another's victim and performed a shadowy propitiation for one nation of Israelites. He alone has his own singular holiness as Prophet, by which he is separated from all other prophets in the most excellent way. For he, the highest Teacher, sits not in the chair of Moses but on a lofty and elevated throne of majesty; he creates the prophet, sends Isaiah, and by the ministry of a seraph cleanses the uncleanness of his lips with a coal from his priestly altar. Finally, he alone has the singular holiness by which he is King. For he sits among the seraphim and rules over the angels, and fills the whole earth with the glory of his majesty, which has never happened to any earthly king. Therefore the Trisagion [τρισάγιον], with which the seraphim celebrate the Lord and King of hosts, does not refer so much to the three persons of the most holy Trinity, as is commonly believed, but wholly and solely to Christ, whose glory Isaiah saw; and the holiness repeated three times seems to look to his threefold offices, to those who have eyes to see. If we consider the extent of his glory, which is the second outline of it, this belongs to Christ alone. For the whole earth, filled with the proclamation of the mystical seraphim, was the glory of the person of Christ Immanuel, the supreme Priest, King and Prophet.

units.la: Hactenus liquidò paret, magnificam istam Jesaiæ visionem totam collineasse in Filium hominis Christum. Age nunc temporis demonstremus, visionem cœli aperti ad Filium hominis, quam Jesus effectam dedit præstituto tempore, implementum esse exactissimum propheticæ visionis. 1o. Quidem discipuli cœlum, sanctuarium cœleste, apertum viderunt, sicut Jesaias cœlum apertum contemplatus fuerat. 2o. Viderunt Filium hominis, sedentem & vehentem in nube sicuti in throno suo, Deum atque hominem; non secus atque Jesaias Regem Jehevé exercituum viderat עבת, nube, symbolo Divinitatis suæ, super solio arcæ sedentem. 3o. Eum ascendentem in cœlum apertum clara in luce viderunt Pontificem, Regem & Prophetam summum: Pontificem, sanctuarium cœleste simul per velum carnis suæ, simul per velum cœlorum, in sancta sanctorum, haud manufacta, euntem post oblatum in atrio primi cœli aerii sacrificium suum propipropitiatorium. Eum viderunt Regem, sedentem in solio majestatis in excelsis apertis, donariis suis regalibus, solemni Spiritus Sancti effusione, magnificè donantem populum suum. Prophetam denique summum, supremos orbis terrarum doctores creantem, & in orbem universum mittentem, qui ea docerent, quæ nec oculus vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in cor hominis ascenderunt; sicut propheta, in templo viderat Jeheve exercituum pontificem, fimbriis vestis Sacerdotalis templum replentem; Regem totius terræ, sedentem pro solio excelso, & Prophetam, fundentem oracula, creantem & mittentem Jesaiam Prophetam. Viderunt Christum peracto sacrificio propitiatorio interpellantem pro nobis in cœlo, sicut Jesaias Deum Pontificem regium viderat, replentem suffitu aræ totum templum. Viderunt angelos ascendentes & descendentes ad Filium hominis, h. e. accinctos ad obsequium omne genus sursum deorsum, dextrorsum sinistrorsum euntes, sicut Jesaias viderat Seraphim supernè stantes, & quoquoversum volantes binis alis ad thronum Regis Jeheve exercituum. Viderunt totam terram, plenam gloriâ sacerdotii, regiæ majestatis & prophetiæ Christi; sicut Propheta viderat totam terram plenam gloriæ Jeheve exercituum Regis, Pontificis & Prophetæ. Viderunt denique occæcatam & incredulam Judæorum gentem, ubi Filius hominis tergemino suo fungeretur munere: non secus atque Jesaias viderat pinguefactum, induratum & occæcatum cor Judæorum.
units.tr: It is now clear that Isaiah's magnificent vision was wholly directed at the Son of Man, Christ. Let us now show that the vision of the open heaven, which Jesus granted to the Son of Man at the appointed time, is the most exact fulfilment of that prophetic vision. (1) The disciples saw the heaven opened, the heavenly sanctuary, just as Isaiah had gazed on the opened heaven. (2) They saw the Son of Man, God and man, sitting and riding on a cloud as on his throne, just as Isaiah had seen the King, the LORD of hosts, sitting upon the throne above the ark, with the cloud [עבת], the symbol of his divinity. (3) They saw him ascending into the open heaven in clear light as High Priest, King and supreme Prophet. As High Priest he was entering the heavenly sanctuary, through the veil of his flesh and the veil of the heavens, into the holy of holies not made with hands, after offering his propitiatory sacrifice in the court of the first aerial heaven. They saw him as King, sitting on the throne of majesty in the high heights, bountifully bestowing his royal gifts on his people in the solemn outpouring of the Holy Spirit. Finally they saw him as supreme Prophet, appointing the supreme teachers of the world and sending them out into the whole earth to teach those things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man. So the prophet had seen in the temple the High Priest, the LORD of hosts, filling the temple with the hem of his priestly robe; the King of all the earth sitting on a lofty throne; and the Prophet pouring out oracles, appointing and sending the prophet Isaiah.
