They saw Christ, his propitiatory sacrifice completed, interceding for us in heaven, just as Isaiah saw God as the royal High Priest filling the whole temple with the smoke of incense from the altar. They saw angels ascending and descending to the Son of Man, that is, girded for every kind of service, going up and down, to the right and to the left, just as Isaiah saw the Seraphim standing above and flying about on two wings toward the throne of the King, the LORD of hosts. They saw the whole earth full of the glory of Christ's priesthood, royal majesty and prophetic office, just as the prophet had seen the whole earth full of the glory of the LORD of hosts, King, Priest and Prophet. Finally they saw the blinded and unbelieving Jewish nation, where the Son of Man would discharge his threefold office, just as Isaiah saw the heart of the Jews made fat, hardened and blinded.

units.la: Geminam feré visionem Ezechiel sortitus est, quam latè exequitur cap. 1. & 10. Nempe videt 1°. quatuor animalia, quæ appellat Cherubim, Ezech. 10:20. Sed & eos uti Seraphim urentes descripsit, Ezech. 1:13. Sunt verò Cherubim simul arcæ, simul templi, Dei Angeli, 1 Pet. 1:12. Idem verò Cherubim & Seraphim appellantur varia de causa. Cherubim quidem, vel quod formam adolescentum præ se ferrent, ducta nomenclatione ex Caph nota similitudinis & רביה rabiah, quod adolescentem sonat (Unde Kimchi in Lib. rad. Rabbini nostri benedictæ memoriæ, ponunt CAPH literam servilem, & dicunt, CHERUB idem significare quod CHERUBIA, id est, quasi puer seu adolescens, quod scilicet puerorum formam habeant) vel Cherubim est à Chaldaïco & Sytiaco כרב aravit, unde כְּרוּבָא Cherubinus, seu bos arator. Ut Angeli, (quorum figuræ videbantur in loco sancto & adyto intimo, quosque oculis usurpavit Ezechiel) Cherubim dicti fuerint vel ex similitudine puerorum, vel ex labore in trahendo curru & throno Numinis, sicut Arca, Dei thronus, juvencis olim reducta fuit in Sion: iidemmet verò Seraphim urentes audierint ob zeli ardorem in capessundis & exequendis Dei mandatis ea celeritate & alacritate, quæ alis pernicibus sapientissimè adumbratur. Vidit itaque Ezechiel Angelos Dei, Cherubim simul ac Seraphim, non secus atque Jesaïas. 2°. Ezechiel Angelos videt currui & throno Dei adstantes & accinctos ad obsequium, sicuti Jesaïas. 3°. Cherubinos videt binis alis volantes: sed & binis aliis corpus suum nubentes, Ezech. 1: 11. 23. omnino sicut Jesaïas. 4°. Similitudinem throni & super throno similitudinem hominis videt, Ezech. 1: 26. hancque similitudinem hominis, igne corusco circumfusi, docet esse formam imaginis gloriæ Jehevæ, Ezech. 1: 28. non secus atque Jesaïas solium videt celsum & elevatum, & hominem veste sacerdotali indutum, & regem Jehevæ exercituum ea gloria, qua terram universam replet, præfulgentem. 5°. Deum & hominem videt in una eademque persona sicut Jesaïas, quia hominem illum, pro solio super Cherubinis sedentem, dicit esse formam similitudinis gloriæ Jehevæ. Erat ergo vir ille Rex Jehevæ gloriosissimus. 6°. Templum interius apertum videt, Ezech. 10: 4. sicuti Jesaïas. 7°. Vocem audivit è throno, qui in expanso, seu cælo, Cherubinis imminebat, Ezech. 1: 25. æque atque Jesaïas. 8°. Cherubinos seu Angelos ascendentes videt ad Jehevè sedentem pro solio, quia eorum alæ ascendebant inter volandum, Ezech. 1: 23. sed & eosdem vidit descendentes, nempe eorum alæ descendebant & demittebantur ubivis consisterent, Ezech. 1: 24. 25. Sed enim verò non nulla sunt memoranda discrimina, quibus isthæc Ezechielis visio abs visione Jesaïæ uti totidem circumstantiis distinguitur. 1°. Quidem Ezechielis Cherubim urentes quatuor faciebus insigniuntur, humanâ, leoninâ, bovinâ, & aquilinâ, Ezech. 1: 10. & 10: 14. 2°. Interstincti oculis & mirificè variegati Cherubim Ezechielis cernuntur. 3°. Currus, vectans solium Jehevè è templo intimo primùm ad limen templi, mox ad portam orientalem, volatu Cherubinorum ducitur, apud Ezechielem 10: 4. 19. sed verò nec facies multiformes, nec oculi nec quadriga rotis agitata fervidis, nec thronus Dei discedens usquam comparet in visione Jesaïæ. Contra autem nec fumus, nec ara suffitus, nec sacra solemnis propitiationis uspiam exhibentur in visione Ezechielis. Ratio discrimiuis arcescenda videtur è scopi visionum varietate. Nempe Ezechielis visio eò tendit, ut significet, Deum Messiam, qui habitat in medio Judaicæ gentis, propediem discessurum & in templum mysticum, Ecclesiam puta Christianam, ingressurum, ut inibi constituat arcam gloriæ suæ thronum, h. e. Ecclesiam spiritualem, arcâ mysticè adumbratam, Jer. 3: 16. 17. Ezech. 43: 7. Hinc quadriga rotis agitata fervidis & thronus Dei abituriens templo terreno. Itaque Ezechielis visio in tempus illud prospicit, quo Deus Messias, relicto penitus & abdicato populo Judaico, verbo Euangelii & Apostolorum preconio, quadrigâ mysticâ, Psal. 45 : 5. ita ad gentes abiit, ut templum Hierosolymitanum Romanis, flammisque exterminandum tradiderit. Contra eademmet Jesaiæ visio, qua Rex Messias simul Pontifex & Propheta contemplandus exhibetur, aliquot circumstantiis distinguitur, quia spectat directè ad tempus, quod proximè excepit ascensionem Christi in cœlum post peractam propitiationem, mystico intercessionis suæ suffitu pro nobis interpellaturi, quum primùm effudit Spiritum Sanctum è cœlo aperto, ut crearet Apostolos per orbem universum mittendos. Hinc tremor postium, & superliminarium templi. Nempe tunc commovit cœlum & terram, Agg. 2:6. Heb. 12:26. locutus simul è cœlo, simul è templo mystico novæ suæ Ecclesiæ, intereadum male feriata Judæorum natio coecutiit ad gloriam Christi, & videndo non intellexit, ne sanaretur errore Σεηλάτῳ, in extremam παιδολεθρίαν obdurata. Interim Ezechiel mystica isthæc omnia oculis Prophetiæ admirabundus palam ut intueretur, vidisse se apertum cœlum memorat Ezech. 1: 1. multis de causis.
units.tr: Ezekiel was granted a vision that was almost twofold, which he sets out at length in chapters 1 and 10. First, he sees four living creatures, which he calls Cherubim (Ezek. 10:20). He also describes them as burning Seraphim (Ezek. 1:13). The Cherubim are at once the angels of God and the attendants of the ark and of the temple (1 Pet. 1:12). The same beings are called Cherubim and Seraphim for various reasons. They are called Cherubim either because they bore the form of young men, the name being derived from the letter Caph, a mark of likeness, and rabiah [רביה], which means a young man. (Hence Kimchi, in his Book of Roots, says that our rabbis of blessed memory hold that the letter CAPH is a servile letter, and say that CHERUB means the same as CHERUBIA, that is, as if a boy or youth, because they have the form of boys.) Or the word Cherubim comes from the Chaldean and Syriac כרב, he ploughed, whence כְּרוּבָא Cherubinus, or ploughing ox. Just as the angels (whose figures were seen in the holy place and the innermost sanctuary, and which Ezekiel saw with his eyes) were called Cherubim either from their likeness to boys or from the labour of drawing the chariot and throne of the Deity, just as the ark, the throne of God, was once drawn into Zion by oxen, so the same beings were called burning Seraphim because of the ardour of their zeal in carrying out and executing God's commands with a speed and eagerness that is wisely represented by swift wings. So Ezekiel saw the angels of God, Cherubim and Seraphim alike, just as Isaiah did. (2) Ezekiel sees the angels standing about the chariot and throne of God and girded for service, just as Isaiah does. (3) He sees the Cherubim flying with two wings, but also covering their bodies with two others (Ezek. 1:11, 23), exactly as Isaiah does. (4) He sees the likeness of a throne, and above the throne the likeness of a man (Ezek. 1:26), and he explains that this likeness of a man, surrounded by flashing fire, is the form of the appearance of the glory of the LORD (Ezek. 1:28), just as Isaiah sees a lofty and elevated throne and a man clothed in priestly garments, and the King, the LORD of hosts, shining in the glory with which he fills the whole earth. (5) He sees God and man in one and the same person, as Isaiah does, since he says that the man sitting above the Cherubim upon the throne is the form of the likeness of the glory of the LORD. That man, then, was the most glorious King of the LORD. (6) He sees the inner temple opened (Ezek. 10:4), as Isaiah does. (7) He heard a voice from the throne, which stood over the Cherubim in the firmament, or heaven (Ezek. 1:25), just as Isaiah did. (8) He sees the Cherubim, or angels, ascending toward the LORD sitting on the throne, since their wings went up as they flew (Ezek. 1:23); and he also saw them descending, for their wings went down and were lowered wherever they stood (Ezek. 1:24, 25). But there are some differences worth noting, by which this vision of Ezekiel is distinguished from the vision of Isaiah through as many circumstances. (1) Ezekiel's Cherubim, the burning ones, are marked by four faces: human, lion, ox and eagle (Ezek. 1:10; 10:14). (2) Ezekiel's Cherubim are seen full of eyes and marvellously varied in colour. (3) In Ezekiel 10:4, 19 the chariot carrying the throne of the LORD is led from the innermost temple first to the threshold of the temple, then to the east gate, by the flight of the Cherubim. But in Isaiah's vision there appear neither many-formed faces, nor eyes, nor a four-wheeled chariot driven by fiery wheels, nor God's throne departing anywhere. On the other hand, neither smoke, nor the altar of incense, nor the solemn rite of propitiation is shown anywhere in Ezekiel's vision. The reason for this difference seems to be drawn from the variety of purpose in the two visions. Ezekiel's vision aims to signify that God the Messiah, who dwells in the midst of the Jewish nation, will soon depart and enter the mystical temple, that is, the Christian Church, there to establish the throne of his glory, that is, the spiritual Church mystically foreshadowed by the ark (Jer. 3:16, 17; Ezek. 43:7). Hence the fiery four-wheeled chariot and the throne of God departing from the earthly temple. So Ezekiel's vision looks forward to the time when God the Messiah, having completely abandoned and rejected the Jewish people, went out to the Gentiles by the word of the gospel and the proclamation of the Apostles, in the mystical chariot (Ps. 45:5), and handed the temple of Jerusalem over to the Romans to be destroyed by fire. By contrast, Isaiah's vision, in which the King Messiah is shown to be contemplated as both High Priest and Prophet, is distinguished by several circumstances, because it looks directly at the time that immediately followed Christ's ascension into heaven after his propitiation was accomplished, when he was about to intercede for us with the mystical incense of his mediation, at the moment when he first poured out the Holy Spirit from the opened heaven, to create Apostles to be sent throughout the whole world. Hence the trembling of the doorposts and lintels of the temple. For then he shook heaven and earth (Hag. 2:6; Heb. 12:26), speaking at once from heaven and from the mystical temple of his new Church, while meanwhile the unhappy nation of the Jews grew blind to the glory of Christ, and seeing did not understand, lest it be healed, hardened by the error [Σεηλάτῳ] into the utmost destruction of its children [παιδολεθρίαν]. Meanwhile Ezekiel, marvelling at these mystical things with the eyes of prophecy, says that he saw the heaven opened (Ezek. 1:1), for many reasons.

units.la: 1°. Ratione personæ, quam vidit; erat enim Immanuel, Jeheve Deus & homo, cujus cœlum solium est. 2°. Quia videt, quæ in adyto Sanctuarii, cœloque typico erant, nempe arcam thronum Dei & Cherubim gloriæ. 3°. Quia sub schemate templi Hierosolymorum cœlum, reale Dei domicilium, & Ecclesiam, spirituale templum, intuetur. Ezech. 43:7. 4°. Ratione personæ, quæ videt, nempe Ezechiel simul propheta, simul Sacerdos erat, Ezech. 1:3. Sicut autem Sacerdotum erat videre locum templi sanctum; ita & prophetarum sub schemate cœli typici & umbratilis cœlum reale Dei domicilium coram cernere: unde Prophetæ videntes χρηματίζοντες appellantur.
units.tr: 1. From the person whom he saw: he was Immanuel, Jehovah God and man, whose throne is heaven. 2. Because he sees what was in the inner sanctuary and in the typical heaven, namely the ark, the throne of God and the cherubim of glory. 3. Because under the form of the temple at Jerusalem he looks upon heaven, the real dwelling of God, and the Church, the spiritual temple (Ezek. 43:7). 4. From the person who sees: Ezekiel was at once a prophet and a priest (Ezek. 1:3). Just as it belonged to the priests to see the holy place of the temple, so the prophets, under the form of the typical and shadowy heaven, beheld the real heaven, the dwelling of God. For this reason prophets who see are called seeing [χρηματίζοντες].

units.la: His ita constitutis non difficilis labor est ad demonstrandum, visionem cœli aperti ad Filium hominis, ascendentibus ad eum Dei Angelis, luculentum habere visionis propheticæ implementum. Nempe isthæc Ezechielis visio illa ferè omnia habet, quæ in visione Jesaiæ Christo in cœlum apertum ascendenti convenire addiximus. Hic autem cernitur 1°. Cœlum apertum sicut Ezechieli. 2°. Deus & homo Christus 3°. Nubes, currus gloriæ Dei circumfusus, terris & templis Hierosolymitano abiens ad portam orientalem, ubi erat mons oblivarum, hincque cœlum petens. Hic Angeli ascendentes Dei & hominis, curru nubis vehentis, aurigæ & administri; hic Deus in carne manifestatus, receptusque in gloria, curru vehens verbi veritatis, Psal. 45:5. Gentibus annunannunciatus Apostolorum preconio & fides ei habita in mundo: hic denique coeli aperti visionem excipit gentis Judaeorum occaecatae destructio, quam ambae Ezechielis visiones, quas primum & decimum caput habet, interminantur.
units.tr: With these things established, it is not a difficult task to show that the vision of the open heaven, with God's angels ascending to the Son of man, has a clear fulfilment in the prophetic vision. Indeed, this vision of Ezekiel contains nearly all the features that we have said belong to the vision of Isaiah, in which Christ ascends into the open heaven. Here we see: 1. the heaven opened, as with Ezekiel; 2. Christ, God and man; 3. a cloud, the chariot of the glory of God, surrounded by the earth and the temple of Jerusalem, departing by the eastern gate, where the Mount of Olives was, and from there seeking heaven. Here are the angels of God and of man ascending, with the chariot of the cloud as their vehicle, the charioteers and attendants; here is God manifested in the flesh and received into glory, riding in the chariot of the word of truth (Ps. 45:5); here is the announcement to the nations through the proclamation of the apostles, and faith placed in him in the world. Finally, the vision of the open heaven is followed by the destruction of the blinded Jewish nation, which both visions of Ezekiel, those in the first and tenth chapters, threaten.

units.la: Ezechielis visionem excipiat apertissima Danielis visio, quae exstat cap. 7: 13. 14. Videns, inquit, in visionibus noctis, & ecce cum nubibus coeli tanquam Filius hominis veniebat, & usque ad antiquum dierum pervenit, & ei dedit potestatem, & gloriam, & regnum, & omnes nationes & lingua ei servient, potestas ei potestas aeterna, quae non auferetur, & regnum ejus, quod non corrumpetur. Visum Danieli Messiam, uno ore fatentur Rabbinorum doctissimi Saadias Gaon, Rabbi Jeschua, referente Aben Esra, Schelomo Jarchi, & Joseph Jachiades, qui omnes Filium hominis Messiam interpretantur. Sed vero Danielem vidisse coelum apertum ad Filium hominis, consecutione necessaria colligitur. 1o. Quia eum vidit vehentem in nubibus coeli. 2o. Quia vidit antiquum dierum, h. e. Deum Patrem, qui majestas in celsis dicitur. Heb. 8: 1. 3o. Quia vidit Dei Antiqui dierum apparitores, Filium hominis ad Antiquum dierum accedere facientes, utique ad coelum apertum, ubi & domicilium & thronus gloriae Dei est. Quam vero luculentum istiusmodi visionis implementum habeat visio coeli, aperti ad Filium hominis, res ipsa clamat. Nempe 1o. hic discipuli non noctu, sicut Daniel, sed interdiu Filium hominis viderunt, nube vehentem in coelum apertum. 2o. Eum viderunt adeptum nomen supra omne nomen, ut ad nomen Jesu omne genu flectatur, coelestium ac terrestrium & subterraneorum, omnisque lingua profiteatur Jesum Christum esse Dominum ad gloriam Dei Patris, Phil. 2: 9. 10. 11. 3o. Viderunt angelos Dei ascendentes ad Filium hominis, uti ipsius apparitores, eos demum visuri descendentes in futuro beati seculi complemento; sicut Daniel eos viderat Deo adstantes & obsequentes, Dan. 7: 10.
units.tr: Ezekiel's vision is followed by the very clear vision of Daniel, which stands in chapter 7:13–14: "I saw in the visions of the night, and behold, with the clouds of heaven there came one like the Son of man, and he came even to the Ancient of days, and there was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, and all peoples and nations and languages shall serve him: his power is an everlasting power, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom, which shall not be destroyed." That Daniel saw the Messiah is acknowledged with one voice by the most learned of the rabbis, Saadias Gaon, Rabbi Jeschua (as reported by Aben Ezra), Solomon Jarchi, and Joseph Jachiades, all of whom interpret the Son of man as the Messiah. But that Daniel saw the open heaven at the Son of man follows by necessary consequence. 1. Because he saw him riding in the clouds of heaven. 2. Because he saw the Ancient of days, that is, God the Father, who is called the majesty on high (Heb. 8:1). 3. Because he saw the attendants of the Ancient of days causing the Son of man to approach the Ancient of days, namely into the open heaven, where the dwelling and the throne of God's glory are. How fully this vision of the open heaven at the Son of man fulfils such a vision, the thing itself declares. Indeed, 1. here the disciples saw the Son of man, not by night as Daniel did, but by day, borne by a cloud into the open heaven. 2. They saw him obtaining the name above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, on earth and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father (Phil. 2:9–11). 3. They saw the angels of God ascending to the Son of man as his attendants, to see them again descending at the completion of the blessed age to come; just as Daniel had seen them standing before God and ministering to him (Dan. 7:10).

units.la: Denique haec coeli aperti visio implementum habet visionis, quam revelavit Deus Jacobo in divino somnio, quaeque exstat Genef. 28: 12. 13. ad 17um. Nempe vidit Jacob coelum apertum: nam expergefactus in haec verba admirabundus erumpit, quam terribilis locus iste, non est hic nisi domus Dei & porta coeli, vf. 17. Vidit Filium hominis Deum & hominem & Mediatorem coelum inter & terram, Deum quidem Abrahami & Isaaci in scalae fastigio, & hominem in Jacobo humi jacentem, & Mediatorem scala mystica, quae coelum & terram hinc inde contingebat & amice consociabat: vidit & angelos ascendentes ad filium hominis Deum, & descendentes ad Filium hominis hominem, humi jacentem, & Jacobo, in cujus lumbis erat, typicè adumbratum: vidit denique Angelos Dei, ascendentes & descendentes in scala, seu per scalam, illustrem mediationis Christi typum. Quàm verò luculentum habeat mysticæ visionis Jacobi complementum isthæc cœli aperti visio, quam Christus se demum ostensurum discipulis suis recipit, non res ipsa modò clamat: sed & nos cum bono Deo, quæstione sequenti inter explicandum typum scalæ mysticæ, haud omninò indiligenter demonstrabimus.
units.tr: Finally, this vision of the open heaven fulfils the vision which God revealed to Jacob in a divine dream, and which is recorded in Genesis 28:12–17. Jacob saw the open heaven, for on waking he breaks out in admiration with these words: "How awesome is this place! This is none other than the house of God and the gate of heaven" (v. 17). He saw the Son of man, God and man and Mediator, between heaven and earth: God indeed, the God of Abraham and Isaac, at the top of the ladder, and man in Jacob, lying on the ground, and the Mediator by the mystical ladder, which touched heaven and earth on either side and joined them in friendship. He saw also the angels ascending to the Son of man, who is God, and descending to the Son of man, who is man, lying on the ground, and foreshadowed in Jacob, in whose loins he was. Lastly, he saw the angels of God ascending and descending on the ladder, or by the ladder, a remarkable type of Christ's mediation. How fully this vision of the open heaven, which Christ receives as the thing he will at last show his disciples, completes the mystical vision of Jacob, the thing itself not only declares, but we shall also, with God's blessing, demonstrate not carelessly in the following question, when we explain the type of the mystical ladder.

units.la: Quartò. Inter tot majora, quæ brevi erat patraturus miracula, visionem cœli, sibi & aliis aperti, Christus destinato selegit, in habitudine ad Nathanaelem, quem alloquebatur, sine fraude Israelitam, vel dum plerique omnes Judæi fraudulenti forent & filii supplantatoris Jacobi, uti Numen prædixerat; Quisque ab amico cavete, & ulli fratri ne confidite: nam omnis frater omnino supplantat, & omnis amicus cum detractatione ambulat, & quisque amico suo illudunt, ac veritatem non loquuntur; docent linguam suam loqui falsum, perversè agendo defetiscuntur, Jer. 9: 4. 5. Contra Nathanael in medio fraudulentæ generationis, ita sincerè cum hominibus versabatur, alienissimus ab animo supplantatoris Jacobi parentis, & germana proles ipsius, in Israelem sincerum vorticordi gratia mutati, ut de nomine Israelitæ sine fraude, ab omnibus censeretur. Quòd igitur foret germana soboles Israelis, quem Deus visione cœli aperti & scalæ mysticæ, in qua Angeli ascendentes & descendentes videbantur, singulari prærogativa dignatus fuerat; Christus fore recipit, ut Nathanael, Israelis filius, cæterique Israelitæ fideles non in somnio quidem, sed vigilantes ac videntes, non in typo, sed in reipsa Filium hominis videant & cœlum, ad eum & cæteros fideles apertum, & Angelos Dei ministros obsequiosos ascendentes & descendentes ad Filium hominis. Quæ ut singularis erat & hactenus inusitata prærogativa, nulli mortalium facta, & argumentum luculentum præbebat, quo certissimè colligeretur, Filium hominis, Jesum, exhibere in se complementum visionis mysticæ, & esse reapse simul illum Deum, qui super fastigio scalæ præsens adstabat, & Angelorum famulantium dominum, simul filium illius hominis, qui in infimo scalæ jacebat, simul mediatorem unum, qui Deum & hominem in una persona conciliabat, suaque cœlum inter & terras mediatione, Deo & Angelis ad homines, hominibus verò ad cœlum apertum, Deum & Angelos, aditum liberrimum faceret. Unde Paulus; accessistis ad montem Sion, & civitatem Dei viri, Hierosolymam cœlestem & myriadas Angelorum, & ad judicem universorum Deum, & ad novi pacti mediatorem Jesum, & sanguinem aspersionis potiora loquentem, quam sanguis Abel, Hebr. 12: 22. 23. 24.
units.tr: Fourthly. Among the many greater miracles which he was about to perform in a short time, Christ deliberately chose the vision of the heaven opened to himself and to others, in relation to Nathanael, whom he addressed as an Israelite without guile, although almost all the Jews were deceitful and sons of Jacob the supplanter, as the Lord had foretold: "Take heed every one of his neighbour, and trust ye not in any brother: for every brother will utterly supplant, and every neighbour will walk with slanders; and they will deceive every one his friend, and will not speak the truth: they have taught their tongue to speak lies; they weary themselves to commit iniquity" (Jer. 9:4–5). But Nathanael, in the midst of this deceitful generation, dealt with men so sincerely, being most alien to the spirit of Jacob the supplanter, his father, and yet his true offspring, changed by the grace of God into a sincere Israel, that he was regarded by all as an Israelite without guile. Therefore, since he was a true descendant of Israel, whom God had honoured with a singular privilege by the vision of the open heaven and of the mystical ladder, on which angels were seen ascending and descending, Christ promises that Nathanael, an Israelite, and the other faithful Israelites should see, not indeed in a dream, but awake and seeing, not in a type, but in reality, the Son of man and the heaven opened to him and to the other faithful, and the angels of God, obedient ministers, ascending and descending to the Son of man. This privilege, being singular and hitherto unusual, granted to no mortal, provided a clear argument by which it could most certainly be inferred that the Son of man, Jesus, exhibits in himself the fulfilment of the mystical vision, and that he is in truth at once that God who stood present above the top of the ladder and the lord of the serving angels, at once the son of that man who lay at the bottom of the ladder, and at once the one Mediator, who united God and man in one person, and by his mediation between heaven and earth gave God and the angels free access to men, and to men access to the open heaven, to God and the angels. Hence Paul: "You are come to Mount Sion, and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to myriads of angels, and to God the judge of all, and to Jesus the mediator of the new covenant, and to the sprinkling of blood, which speaks better things than that of Abel" (Heb. 12:22–24).

units.la: Quintò. Inter majora & singularia Messiae miracula, quae palam propediem editurus erat, sapienter selegit futuram coeli aperti visionem, in habitudine ad Judaeos, coelum nempe, quod olim experiebantur sibi apertum frequenti Numinis cum Prophetis & Pontificibus summis commercio, somniis, visionibus, oraculo Urim & Thummim, illapsu Spiritus Prophetiae, crebris Angelorum apparitionibus & χρηματισμοῖς divinis, ubi Deus eos alloqueretur πολυμερῶς ἢ πολυτρόπως, partitis vicibus & multimodis, Hebr. 1: 1. tunc temporis ab Haggaeo & Malachia Prophetis, praeclusum sibi & impervium dolebant & lamentabantur. Hinc ab ultimis Prophetarum Zacharia, Haggaeo & Malachia Spiritum Sanctum recessisse ab Israele, in utroque Talmude fatentur Hebraeorum magistri. Hinc Discipuli, qui Johannis baptismate tincti fuerant, quaerenti Paulo, num Spiritum Sanctum accepissent, postquam baptisati fuerant, uno ore respondent; Imò, sitne Spiritus Sanctus, ne audivimus quidem, Actor. 19: 2. 3. Utique Johannis discipuli non erant Spiritus Sancti nescii (Johannes enim inter baptizandum discipulos Spiritum Sanctum specie columbae coelitus in Christum delapsum oculis palam usurpaverat, & Judaeis pervia erat Joelis Prophetia de effusione Spiritus Sancti in omnem carnem, Joel. 2: 28. & nihil crebrius apud Judaeos, quam רוח הקדש, Spiritus sanctitatis, & Spiritus misericordiarum à facie Domini, Targ. Hierof. in Gen. 1: 2.) Non itaque esse Spiritum Sanctum discipuli Johannis ignorabant, sed verò interceptam pluribus retrò seculis donorum Spiritus Sancti effusionem extraordinariam, restitutam in integrum tunc temporis penitus nesciebant. Nempe Johannes aqua, Christus verò spiritu & igne discipulos baptizabat, Matth. 3: 11. Re enim vera Judaeorum magistri contestantur summo consensu, secundum Templum, quod exstabat tempore Christi, quinque caruisse praerogativis, quibus primum Salomonis Templum decorabatur. Hae verò in Talmude Hierosolymitano tractatu Sanhedrin censentur hoc ordine, 1°. Ignis, 2°. Arca, 3°. Urim & Thummin, 4°. Oleum Unctionis, 5°. Spiritus Sanctus. Verum in Talmude Babylonico tractatu Joma, cap. 1. sub finem. mutatis nonnihil simul ordine, simul rebus ita numerantur; Arca, Propitiatorium & Cherubim, Ignis, Dei Majestas, & Spiritus Sanctus, & Urim & Thummim. Kimchius in Aggaei cap. 1: 8. nonnihil mutato ordine ita recenseт; Arca, & Urim & Thummin, & Ignis coelestis, & Dei Majestas, & Spiritus Sanctus. Midrasch in Cantic. 8. c. com. 9. iterum aliter, dum infit; quinque res habuit prima domus, quibus secunda caruit ; nempe Ignem superne delapsum, Oleum unctionis, Arcam, Spiritum sanctitatis, Urim & Thummim. Ut minus consentiant, vel in ordine recensionis, vel in rebus recensendis, aliis Oleum unctionis, aliis Dei majestatem in quinario numero cimeliorum primi Templi recensentibus ; omnes tamen summo consensu conspirant in censu quatuor, nempe Ignis cælestis, Arca, Spiritus Sancti, & Urim & Thummim, quorum tria e cœlo erant, Ignis, Spiritus Sanctus, & Oraculum Urim & Thummim. Cœlum itaque sibi clausum in Templo secundo Judæi experiebantur, quando nec ignem demittebat, nec Spiritum Sanctum impertiebatur, nec reddebat oraculum Urim & Thummim. Eccur vero? Nempe in expectationem Messiæ, omnia isthæc eminentiorem in modum restituturi, animi eorum ut erigerentur. Etenim Numen summum prædixerat fore, ut gloria secundæ Domus, in quam Angelus fœderis, & idem Dominus, quem ipsi requirebant, erat ingressurus, Mal. 3: 1. longè excelleret gloriam primæ, Hagg. 2: 9. Quam sapientissimè igitur Christus, solidè ut demonstraret, se esse illum Dominum & Regem Messiam, quem Judæi avidè præstolabantur, fore recepit, ut gens Judæorum videret cœlum apertum, ignem & Spirirum Sanctum effusum, linguisque igneis oracula fundentem,& arcam veram,puta Ecclesiam in cœlo aperto exponentem, Apoc. 11: 19. & reale propitiatorium & Cherubim gloriæ, Angelos Dei ascendentes & descendentes ad Filium hominis.
units.tr: Fifthly. Among Messiah's great and singular miracles, which he was about to display openly, he wisely chose the coming vision of the open heaven, with regard to the Jews. They knew that heaven as once open to them, through the frequent dealings of the Deity with the Prophets and the high priests: by dreams, visions, the oracle of Urim and Thummim, the descent of the Spirit of prophecy, frequent appearances of angels, and divine oracles (χρηματισμοῖς), in which God spoke to them "in many parts and in many ways" (πολυμερῶς ἢ πολυτρόπως), in divided portions and manifold ways, Heb. 1:1. After the Prophets Haggai and Malachi, they grieved and lamented that this heaven had been closed and made impassable to them. Hence the masters of the Hebrews confess in both Talmuds that the Holy Spirit withdrew from Israel after the last Prophets, Zechariah, Haggai and Malachi. Hence the disciples who had been baptized with John's baptism, when Paul asked whether they had received the Holy Spirit after they believed, answered with one voice: Nay, we have not so much as heard whether there is a Holy Spirit, Acts 19:2, 3. Certainly John's disciples were not ignorant of the Holy Spirit. John, while baptizing, had openly seen the Spirit descend from heaven upon Christ in the form of a dove, and the prophecy of Joel about the outpouring of the Spirit upon all flesh was open to the Jews, Joel 2:28. Nothing was more common among the Jews than רוח הקדש, Spirit of holiness, and Spirit of mercies from the face of the Lord, Targ. Hieros. on Gen. 1:2. So they did not fail to know that there is a Holy Spirit. What they utterly did not know was that the extraordinary outpouring of the gifts of the Spirit, interrupted for many centuries past, had now been fully restored. John baptized with water, but Christ baptized the disciples with Spirit and fire, Matt. 3:11. For the Jewish masters agree with the greatest unanimity that the second Temple, which stood in Christ's time, lacked five privileges with which the first Temple of Solomon had been adorned. In the Jerusalem Talmud, tractate Sanhedrin, these are listed in this order: (1) fire, (2) the ark, (3) Urim and Thummim, (4) the oil of anointing, (5) the Holy Spirit. In the Babylonian Talmud, tractate Joma, chapter 1, near the end, the order and the items are changed somewhat, and they are numbered thus: the ark, the propitiatory and cherubim, fire, the majesty of God, the Holy Spirit, and Urim and Thummim. Kimchi, on Haggai 1:8, gives a list with the order slightly changed: the ark, and Urim and Thummim, and heavenly fire, and the majesty of God, and the Holy Spirit. The Midrash on Canticles 8, comment 9, differs again, beginning: the first house had five things which the second lacked, namely fire sent down from above, the oil of anointing, the ark, the Spirit of holiness, and Urim and Thummim. They do not agree either in the order of the list or in the things listed, some counting the oil of anointing and others the majesty of God among the five treasures of the first Temple. Yet all agree with the greatest consensus on the four: heavenly fire, the ark, the Spirit of holiness, and Urim and Thummim. Of these, three came from heaven: the fire, the Holy Spirit, and the oracle of Urim and Thummim. Thus the Jews experienced heaven as closed to them in the second Temple, since it neither sent down fire, nor imparted the Holy Spirit, nor gave the oracle of Urim and Thummim. Why was this? It was so that their minds would be lifted up in expectation of the Messiah, who would restore all these things in a more eminent manner. For the supreme Deity had foretold that the glory of the second house, into which the Angel of the covenant, and the same Lord whom they sought, would enter, Mal. 3:1, would far surpass the glory of the first, Hag. 2:9. Most wisely, then, Christ undertook, so that he might solidly demonstrate that he was that Lord and Messiah King whom the Jews eagerly awaited, that the nation of the Jews should see the heaven opened, fire and the Holy Spirit poured out, oracles uttered with tongues of fire, the true ark, that is the Church, set forth in the open heaven, Rev. 11:19, and the real propitiatory and cherubim of glory: the angels of God ascending and descending to the Son of man.

units.la: Sextò. Simul in habitudine ad Judæos, simul in habitudine ad se ipsum Filium hominis, inter majora omnia, quæ de se videnda erat propediem exhibiturus, sapienter selegit visionem cœli aperti. Et quidem in habitudine ad Judæos: quando enim ὁ ναὸς, qui locum sanctum & sanctum sanctorum nomenclatione sua significabat, expressa erat cœli imago, authore Paulo, ubi cœlum vocat sanctuarium & verum tabernaculum, quod fixit Dominus & non homo, Hebr. 8: 1. 2. & simul tabernaculum, simul omnia vasa tabernaculi exemplaria eorum, qua sunt in cœlo, appellat, Hebr. 9: 23. & extemplò apertius, dum infit: non enim in manu factum sanctuarium, quod sit exemplar vero respondens, ingressus est Christus; sed in ipsum cœlum, ut compareat nunc apud faciem Dei pro nobis, Hebr. 9: 24. Nemini non compertum est, cœlum istud typicum & umbratile Judæos velo gemino perpetuò clausum numquam vidisse, excepto uno Pontifice summo, qui semel quotannis intra velum cum sanguine propitiationis ingrediebatur: sed tunc temporis nemini cuiquam è plebe, vel è familia Sacerdotum cœlum istiusmodi coram apertum sibi, vel Pontifici, oculis usurpare fas, jusve erat. Nempe edicto Numinis summè cautum fuerat, ne mortalium quispiam præsens tabernaculo adesset, cum Pontifex intra velum per sanguinem propitiationis ingre-deretur, Lev. 16:17. Eccur vero? Arcanum aperuit Paulus, myste-riorum regni cœlorum scriba peritissimus, dum infit: hoc declarante Spi-ritu Sancto, nondum factam fuisse manifestam ad loca sancta viam, priore Ta-bernaculo adhuc consistente, Hebr. 9:8. Quamobrem & cœlum umbra-tile clausum, & quo itur ad verum cœlum medium, Judæis omnibus ignotum erat. Sed enimverò, fuso Christi sanguine propitiatorio, quàm primum sanctam efflavit animam, velum ϛ [?]ναῦς [?], h. e. templi interio-ris, quod locum sanctum & sanctum sanctorum habebat, fissum est in duas partes à summo usque ad imum, Matth. 27:51. ut simul Judæorum Natio ab atrio sancti populi, simul Levitæ & Sacerdotes è loco sancto cœlum mysticum apertum viderint & sanguine Christi, veri propitiatorii, viam h. e. medium opportunum, quo unico in cœlum, τὰ ἅγια ἀχειροποίητα [?], tutissimè itur, apertum sibi & expositum, si mens non læva fuisset, perspicere potuerint. Christum verò quod attinet, merito sacrificii sui, quo Judæi apertum viderant cœlum typicum mundani sanctuarii, cœlum, reale sanctuarium, ita sibi aperuit, ut eum eò ascendentem stipantibus Angelis clara in luce diei homines propriis ocu-lis viderint & obstupuerint. Isthac verò cum cœli typici, tum cœli tertii apertione mortalium oculis exposita, Jesus evidentissimè de-monstravit, esse se summum & realem Pontificem, qui scissione veli ϛ [?]ναῦς terreni, figuras Legis impleverat & cultum Leviticum aboleve-rat, & cœli apertione aditum & accessum sibi & universo Dei populo liberrimum fecerat, pontifice Levitico longè excellentior, qui vel ipso propitiationis sanguine pro omnibus suis popularibus fuso, mor-talium nemini cœlum umbratile aperiebat, nedum liberum ad Deum, pro solio Majestatis in arca sedentem, aditum & accessum faciebat. Hinc liquidò patet quàm sapientissimè Christus tot inter majora mi-racula sua, cœli aperti visionem selegerit. Ita enim cùm discipulis, tum Judæis cæteris, oculis usurpanda majora longè promittit iis, quæ summo Pontifici quotannis semel videre fas, jusque erat. Nam summus Pontifex cœlum umbratile sibi uni semel apertum videbat; verum Na-thanael, cæterique discipuli cœlum, Numinis reale domicilium, thro-numque gloriæ apertum palam videbunt. Summus Pontifex Cherubim gloriæ, h. e. Angelorum nuda symbola expansis alis super arca con-templabatur; at Nathanael, cæterique discipuli ipsos Dei Angelos Filii hominis ministros obsequiosos visuri erant; Amen, amen dico vobis; in posterum cœlum apertum videbitis & angelos Dei ascendentes & descendentes ad Filium hominis. Signanter dixit ascendentes & descendentes, quia summus Pontifex Cherubinos gloriæ simul ascendentes, simul descendentes in Sanctuario terreno videbat: ascendentes quidem ad Filium hominis, symbolo nubis sedentem in throno Majestatis, ex alis Cherubinorum sursum expansis, affabré concinnato; descendentes vero & cernuos ad Filium hominis, propitiatorio adumbratum: ascendentes & descendentes simul in velo sanctuarii, quod typus erat carnis Christi, Hebr. 10: 20. (Erat enim arte mirifica interstinctum figuris Cherubinorum, qui alis expansis sursum, deorsum; dextrorsum, siniストrorsum super velum volare videbantur) simul in parietibus sanctuarii, qui pariter figuris Cherubinorum, quoquoversum volantium, arte divina fuerant variegati, Exod. 26: 31. 1 Reg. 6: 29. 32. 2 Chron. 3: 7. 14. Sicuti autem velum typus erat carnis, h. e. naturæ humanæ Christi, templi quoque parietes eandem Christi naturam typice adumbrabant, Joh. 2: 19. 21.
units.tr: Sixthly. At once with regard to the Jews, and with regard to himself, the Son of man, among all the great things which he was soon to display of himself, he wisely chose the vision of the open heaven. And indeed with regard to the Jews: since the temple (ὁ ναὸς), which by its name signified the holy place and the holy of holies, was an expressed image of heaven. Paul, its author, calls heaven the sanctuary and the true tabernacle, which the Lord pitched and not man, Heb. 8:1, 2. He calls both the tabernacle and all its vessels copies of the things which are in heaven, Heb. 9:23, and more plainly at once, when he begins: For Christ did not enter a sanctuary made with hands, which is a copy corresponding to the true one, but into heaven itself, to appear now before the face of God for us, Heb. 9:24. Everyone knows that the Jews never saw that typical and shadowy heaven, which was always shut off by a double veil, except for the one high priest, who once a year went within the veil with the blood of propitiation. At that time, however, no one of the common people, nor anyone of the priestly family, was permitted or had the right to see such a heaven open to himself, or to the high priest. Indeed, by the decree of the Deity, it was most carefully provided that no mortal should be present at the tabernacle when the high priest entered within the veil with the blood of propitiation, Lev. 16:17. Why was this? Paul, the most skilled scribe of the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, disclosed the secret when he begins: the Holy Spirit signifying this, that the way into the holy places was not yet made manifest while the former tabernacle still stood, Heb. 9:8. Therefore the shadowy heaven was closed, and the way by which one goes to the true heaven was unknown to all the Jews. But when Christ's blood had been poured out as the propitiation, as soon as he breathed out his holy soul, the veil (ναῦς) of the earthly temple, that is, of the inner temple which had the holy place and the holy of holies, was torn in two from top to bottom, Matt. 27:51. So the Jewish nation from the court of the holy people, and the Levites and priests from the holy place, could have seen the mystical heaven opened. And if their minds had not been perverse, they could have perceived the way, that is, the suitable middle by which alone one goes most safely into heaven, opened and set forth for them by the blood of Christ, the true propitiatory: the holy things not made with hands (τὰ ἅγια ἀχειροποίητα). As for Christ himself, by the merit of his sacrifice, through which the Jews had seen the typical heaven of the earthly sanctuary opened, he opened for himself the heaven, the real sanctuary, so that men saw him ascending there, with angels attending him, in the clear light of day, with their own eyes, and were astonished. Indeed, Jesus most clearly demonstrated, by the opening both of the typical heaven and of the third heaven, set before the eyes of mortals, that he is the highest and real High Priest. By the tearing of the veil of the earthly sanctuary he had fulfilled the figures of the Law and abolished the Levitical worship. By the opening of heaven he had made access and approach to God freely available to himself and to the whole people of God. He is far superior to the Levitical priest, who, even when the blood of propitiation had been shed for all his people, opened the shadowy heaven to no mortal, much less made a free access and approach to God, who sits on the throne of majesty over the ark. Hence it is plain how most wisely Christ, among so many great miracles, chose the vision of the open heaven. For he promises to those who were disciples, as well as to the other Jews, that they will see with their eyes things far greater than what it was lawful and right for the high priest to see once a year. The high priest saw the shadowy heaven opened to him alone, once. But Nathanael and the other disciples will plainly see heaven, the real dwelling of God and the throne of glory, opened. The high priest gazed upon the cherubim of glory, that is, the bare symbols of angels with wings spread over the ark. But Nathanael and the other disciples were to see the very angels of God, the obedient ministers of the Son of man: Amen, amen I say to you, hereafter you will see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending to the Son of man. He said pointedly ascending and descending, because the high priest saw the cherubim of glory in the earthly sanctuary both ascending and descending: ascending indeed toward the Son of man, sitting on the throne of majesty, represented by a cloud skilfully fashioned from the cherubim's wings spread upward; descending and bowed down toward the Son of man, shadowed by the propitiatory. They were seen ascending and descending together on the veil of the sanctuary, which was a type of the flesh of Christ, Heb. 10:20. For it was woven with marvellous art with figures of cherubim, who seemed to fly with wings spread up and down, to right and left, over the veil. And they were also seen together on the walls of the sanctuary, which likewise had been variegated by divine art with figures of cherubim flying in every direction, Exod. 26:31; 1 Kings 6:29, 32; 2 Chron. 3:7, 14. But just as the veil was a type of the flesh, that is, of the human nature of Christ, so the walls of the temple also typically shadowed the same nature of Christ, John 2:19, 21.

units.la: Septimo: Admirandam istam cœli aperti visionem sapienter selegit in habitudine ad Judæos malè præconceptis opinionibus, fœdisque erroribus liberandos. Illi enim primo errore gloriam personæ Messiæ turpiter fœdabant, rati, eum fore merum hominem, ut ipsum filium Dei adoptionis prærogativa more Regum cæterorum, & cum primis Salomonis crederent. Atenim visio cœli aperti ad Filium hominis, eò ascendentem cum lauto famulorum Dei famulitio, purgandis illis fœdo illo errore peropportuna fuit, nempe eos docuit, Christum esse verùm Deum, cui creaturarum nobilissimæ Angeli Dei serviunt, & apertum cœlum, Dei domicilium, sedem beatam & Deo dignam præbet. Secundo errore gloriam Messiæ Judæi deterebant rati eum fore Regem terrenum, qui victis ad πανολεθρίαν gentibus, Judæis infensis, sedem suam & thronum Hierosolymis figeret, latè illinc in orbem terrarum dominaturus. Atenim visio cœli aperti ad Filium hominis, eò ascendentem in nube, eos contrà docuit, Christum esse Regem cœlestem, qui terræ incolatu relicto, cœlum in nube cælesti peteret, ad dexteram Majestatis sessurus, quique non in homines solum, sed & in Angelos Dei cœlicolas dominaretur. Tertio errore Judæi superbiæ suæ ut vehificarentur, dignam rege Messia bonitatem magnificam obscurabant, rati satum sanguine Judæ Messiam unius gentis Judaicæ Regem futurum. Atenim cœli aperti ad Filium hominis, eò penetrantem, visio, Judæos contrà rrà docuit, Messiam, Regem esse omnium gentium, linguarum & populorum, utpote qui in cœlo aperto & throno gloriæ regnaret in terras omnes subditas, & è cœlo aperto simul regalia Spiritus sui munera, simul Apostolos, gloriæ suæ præcones, in omnia mundi climata mitteret, qui populos omnes suæ ditionis facerent, & jura Christi dicerent & voluntatem docerent, & regnum diaboli, falsorumque delusæ gentilitatis Numinum pessundarent.
units.tr: Seventh: He wisely chose this wonderful vision of the open heaven with regard to the Jews, who were held back by badly preconceived opinions and foul errors, and who needed to be freed from them. At first they shamefully disfigured the glory of the Messiah's person, supposing that he would be a mere man, adopted as Son of God by privilege, like other kings and especially like Solomon. But the vision of the open heaven, with the Son of man ascending there in the splendid retinue of God's servants, was very well suited to cleanse them of that foul error. It taught them that Christ is true God, whom the noblest of creatures, the angels of God, serve, and that the open heaven, the dwelling of God, offers a blessed seat worthy of God. Second, the Jews debased the glory of the Messiah, thinking that he would be an earthly king who, having conquered the nations hostile to the Jews and reduced them to utter destruction [πανολεθρίαν], would set his seat and throne at Jerusalem and rule far and wide over the world from there. But the vision of the open heaven, with the Son of man ascending there in a cloud, taught them on the contrary that Christ is a heavenly King. Having left his earthly sojourn, he would go up to heaven in a heavenly cloud, to sit at the right hand of Majesty, and he would rule not only over men but also over the angels who dwell in heaven. Third, in order to bolster their pride, the Jews obscured the magnificent goodness that befits a king, thinking that the Messiah, born of the blood of Judah, would be king of the one Jewish nation. But the vision of the open heaven, with the Son of man penetrating there, taught the Jews on the contrary that the Messiah is King of all nations, tongues and peoples. He reigns from the open heaven, on a throne of glory, over all the lands subject to him. From the open heaven he sends out both the royal gifts of his Spirit and the apostles, heralds of his glory, to all the climes of the world, to make all peoples of his dominion, to proclaim the laws and teach the will of Christ, and to overthrow the kingdom of the devil and the false gods of the deluded Gentile world.

units.la: Octavò. In habitudine ad omnes homines. Nempe cœli aperti ad Filium hominis eò ascendentem, & mox illinc Spiritum S. effusurum, visio, Apostolorum Christi præconio, omnes homines, Judæos, Græcos, barbarosque ea omnia clarè docuit, quæ cœlum typicum habebat ab hominum cognitione procul remota, ut nunc in aperta luce Novi fœderis omnia illa sanctuarii terreni oculis nostris expósita & obvia sint; simul omnia revelavit regni cœlorum mysteria, quæ oculus non vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in cor hominis ascenderunt. Illa autem aperire, ac docere homines unus Messias, adeò poterat, ut Prophetæ rerum illarum, captu naturali hominum exemptarum, revelationem uni illi addixerint; quod & ipsi Samaritani, usi solo Pentateucho, noverant. Unde Samaritana muliercula; scio, Messiam venturum, qui dicitur Christus; cum venerit ille, nobis annunciabit omnia, Joh. 4: 25. & ipsi Judæi, quia Eliam Messiæ anteambulonem præstolantur, cathedram Eliæ erigunt in Synagogis, ubi adsit præsens invisibilis, ad adventum Eliæ visibilem; mysteriorum revelationem conferunt & dicto isthoc crebro se solantur. Elias veniet & revelabit omnia. Nempe Messias, Sol justitiæ est, Malach. 4: 2. Quia Solis instar omnia, vel umbrâ noctis profundâ demersa, in clara luce diei ponit. Unde & Paulus jure docuit, Christum produxisse in lucem vitam & immortalitatem per Evangelium, 2 Tim. 1: 10.
units.tr: Eighth. With regard to all men. The vision of the open heaven, with the Son of man ascending there and soon to pour out the Holy Spirit from there, taught clearly, through the preaching of Christ's apostles, to Jews, Greeks and barbarians alike, all those things which the typical heaven kept far from human knowledge. Now, in the clear light of the New Covenant, all those things of the earthly sanctuary are set out and open to our eyes. At the same time it revealed all the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven: what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man. Now one Messiah alone could open up and teach these things, which lie beyond natural human grasp, so fully that the prophets assigned the revelation of those things to him alone. The Samaritans too, who used only the Pentateuch, knew this. Hence the little Samaritan woman: I know that the Messiah is coming, who is called Christ; when he comes, he will tell us all things, John 4:25. The Jews themselves, since they await Elijah as the forerunner of the Messiah, set up Elijah's chair in the synagogues, where he is present but invisible until Elijah comes visibly. They look for the revelation of mysteries and often console themselves with this saying: Elijah will come and reveal all things. Indeed the Messiah is the Sun of righteousness, Mal. 4:2, because, like the sun, he brings all things into the clear light of day, even those sunk in the deep shadow of night. Hence Paul rightly taught that Christ brought life and immortality to light through the gospel, 2 Tim. 1:10.

units.la: Nonò. In habitudine ad discipulos, Apostolatu ad orbem terrarum propediem vestiendos. Quando enim cœli aperti visio implementum est mystici insomnii Patriarchæ Jacobi, & illius refricabat memoriam, & pernecessariam consolationem animis eorum ingenerabat, & Filium hominis fore ut in cœlo aperto viderent, Angelorum Dominum & summum totius orbis possessorem, pollicebatur, spemque certam faciebat. Reapse enim, sicut Jacob domo paterna exul & profugus, & avita illa, quæ domi paternæ stabulabatur, benedictione spoliatus, dum frater profanus Esau eâ tranquillus potiebatur; mystica visione Dei, innixi cacumini scalæ, dominique Angelorum, eum alloquentis, indiguit in solatium exilii & futurorum laborum, quos exantlandos habebat in medio Chaldæorum idololatrarum. Nempe Dominum audivit è cœlo aperto dicentem; ego sum Dominus, Deus Abraham patris tui, & Deus Isaac; terram, in qua dormis, tibi dabo & semini tuo, eritque semen tuum quasi pulvis terræ: dilataberis ad orientem & occidentem & septentrionem & meridiem & ecce, ego tecum sum & ero custos tuus, quocunque perrexeris, Gen. 28:12. 13. 14. 15. Fato non absimili, quos palam Christus alloquebatur discipulos, apostolatu donandos, relictâ sede patriâ mittendi erant per orbem terrarum, passi persecutionem Judæorum fratrum suorum, ut innumera subirent pericula & labores ferè infinitos inter gentes, idololatriæ mancipatas, quo amplum ovile Domino colligerent, & Christi gregem pascerent. Unde eos audias paria loquentes atque Jacob: in periculis fluminum, periculis latronum, periculis à Gentibus, periculis in solitudine, periculis inter falsos fratres, in labore & arumna, in vigiliis sape, in fame & siti, in jejuniis sape, in frigore & nuditate. 2 Cor. 11:26. 27. Deus enim, puto, nos ultimos Apostolos spectandos proposuit, ut morti addictos. Nam spectaculum facti sumus mundo & Angelis & hominibus; utique sicut Jacob, fugitivus, dormiens ad scalam, & vigilans inter Aramæos 1 Cor. 4:9. Undenam solamen & levamen commodum mediis in angustiis, unde robur & firmamentum opportunum ferendis tot laboribus expectabunt? Inposterum videbitis cœlum apertum & Angelos Dei ascendentes & descendentes ad Filium hominis. Nolite amabo despondere animum, ponite metum, charissimi; me, Filium hominis, Angelorum & orbis Dominum, in cœlo aperto videbitis vos alloquentem & spiritu meo corroborantem. Ecce sum vobiscum ad seculorum consummationem. Matth. 28:20. Angelos Dei videbitis mihi adstantes ad obsequium omne genus, vobis profuturum; ascendentes ad me pro solio majestatis in cœlo sedentem; & iterum descendentes ad me præsentem vobis immensa mea, efficacissima & gratiosissima divinitate. Terram simul Judæorum simul Gentium idololatrarum vobis dabo, mihi summo Domino, subigendam. Semen vestrum, quod femine vivo & incorruptibili verbi, mihi generabitis, erit instar pulvis terræ & dilatabitur ad orientem & occidentem, septentrionem & meridiem. Nolite igitur cunctari, ad iter vos accingitote alacres. Ego è cœlo meo aperto dux ero & custos vester, quocumque perrexeritis; vos cumulatè mactabo omni benedictione spirituali, quæ est in cœlis.
units.tr: Ninth. With regard to the disciples, who were soon to be clothed with apostleship for the whole world. When the vision of the open heaven fulfilled the mystical dream of the patriarch Jacob, it both renewed the memory of that dream and instilled in their minds a most necessary consolation. It promised and assured them that they would see the Son of man in the open heaven, the Lord of the angels and supreme possessor of the whole world. For indeed, Jacob, an exile and fugitive from his father's house, stripped of that ancestral blessing which was kept at home while his profane brother Esau quietly enjoyed it, was comforted in his exile and in the labours to come, which he had to endure among the idolatrous Chaldeans. He was comforted by a mystical vision of God, as he leaned on the top of the ladder, and of the Lord of the angels speaking to him. He heard the Lord from the open heaven saying: I am the Lord, the God of Abraham thy father, and the God of Isaac; the land whereon thou liest, to thee will I give it, and to thy seed; and thy seed shall be as the dust of the earth; and thou shalt spread abroad to the west, and to the east, and to the north, and to the south; and behold, I am with thee, and will keep thee in all places whither thou goest, Gen. 28:12-15. By a not dissimilar lot, those whom Christ openly addressed as disciples, to be endowed with apostleship, were to leave their ancestral home and be sent through the world. They would suffer persecution from their Jewish brethren and undergo countless dangers and nearly endless labours among the nations given over to idolatry, that they might gather a wide fold for the Lord and feed the flock of Christ. Hence you hear them speaking in words like Jacob's: in journeyings often, in perils of waters, in perils of robbers, in perils by my own countrymen, in perils by the Gentiles, in perils in the wilderness, in perils among false brethren, in labour and toil, in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, in cold and nakedness, 2 Cor. 11:26-27. For I think that God has set us forth the last of the apostles, as men condemned to death; for we have become a spectacle to the world, and to angels, and to men, 1 Cor. 4:9. They were like Jacob, a fugitive, sleeping at the ladder and keeping watch among the Syrians. Where, then, would they look for consolation and relief in the midst of straits, and for the strength and firm support needed to bear so many labours? Hereafter you will see the open heaven and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man. Please, dear ones, do not lose heart; put aside fear. You will see me, the Son of man, Lord of the angels and of the world, in the open heaven, addressing you and strengthening you with my Spirit. Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age, Matt. 28:20. You will see the angels of God standing by me, ready for every service that will profit you, ascending to me, who sit on the throne of majesty in heaven, and descending again to you, while I am present with you by my immense, most effective and most gracious divinity. I will give you the land, both of the Jews and of the idolatrous Gentiles, to be subdued for me, your supreme Lord. Your seed, which you will beget to me by the living and incorruptible seed of the word, will be like the dust of the earth and will spread abroad to the east and west, north and south. Do not hesitate, then; set out on the journey with eagerness. I, from my open heaven, will be your leader and keeper wherever you go, and I will bless you abundantly with every spiritual blessing that is in the heavens.

units.la: QUAESTIO X.
units.tr: QUESTION X.

units.la: Quomodo, quam Iacob in somnio vidit scalam, typus fuerit Filii hominis?
units.tr: In what sense was the ladder that Jacob saw in his dream a type of the Son of man?

units.la: Mysticum planè Jacobi insomnium, quod exstat Gen. 28: 12. &c. Moyses sacer tergemino ecce, quod rem novam & admirandam significat, sapientissimè commendavit, quo lectoris animum eò potenter pertraheret & attentum redderet: & somniavit, inquit, & ecce scala erecta super terram, &c. & ecce, angeli Dei ascendentes & descendentes in ea; & ecce Jeheve stans super ea, Gen. 28: 12. 13. Divinum inquam Jacobi insomnium, aliò quovis, quàm in Christum referunt Hebraeorum magistri. Philo Judaeus, lib. de somniis, scalam hanc quatuor adumbrasse docet, 1°. aërem, cujus basis terra, caput autem coelum est; pulchrè, inquit, scala, terra infima sui parte haerens, figurat aërem. Exhalationes enim, ex terra exspirantes, tenuantur in aërem, ut terra quasi radix, coelum verò quasi caput sit aëris. Substrato isthoc fundamento pergit ad Angelos ascendentes, & descendentes per scalam, & docet esse primùm animas, quibus plenum aërem esse autumat. Harum, inquit, alia descendunt illigandae corporibus mortalibus, quotquot viciniores sunt terra, amantioresque corporum; alia sursum redeunt, separata denuò post praefinitos à natura terminos. Postmodum docet, Angelos esse illas animas purissimas, optimasque omnium ministras omnipotenti, tanquam magni regis aures, & oculos, quas genios Philosophi, Angelos vocant sacra litera: sunt enim, inquit, internuncii, patris mandata perferentes ad filios, & ad illum vicissim preces filiorum. Ideò inducuntur ascendere & descendere, quoniam id conducit nobis mortalibus, habere mediatores illos, & arbitros, quo magis revereamur rerum omnium praesidem. En tibi Philonem authorem erroris de mediatione & intercessione Angelorum. 2°. Scalam illam praefigurasse animam: sibi splendidè contradicens asseveranter pronunciat; quia, inquit, anima basis est penè corporea, & tanquam terrea, scilicet sensus: caput verò tanquam coeleste, mens illa purissima, per eam sursum deorsumque feruntur indesinenter divinae intelligentiae quoties ascendunt, trahentes eam secum, divellentesque à rebus mortalibus, & pro dignitate tantum ostendentes ei spectacula: sed non detrahentes secum, quando descendunt. 3°. Vitam meditatoris: est enim, inquit, naturaliter in aquaæqualis res meditatio, nunc proficiens in altitudinem, nunc deficiens in contrarium, & tanquam navis nunc secundis, nunc adversis ventis navigans. 4°. Denique scalam illam res humanas præfigurasse asserit: res humana, inquit, habent naturalem quodammodo scala imaginem propter cursum inaequalem inconstantemque; una enim dies alium de fastigio detrahit, alium tollit in altum, cum nihil in eodem statu apud nos perpetuo maneat: sed cuncta variis omnifariisque mutentur vicissitudinibus. An non ex plebeis principes, plebei fiunt ex principibus: pauperes ex divitibus, & pauperibus locupletissimi, honorati & contemptis, ex obscuris clarissimi? Hac est via rerum humanarum acclivis, & declivis, incertis obnoxia casibus. Somnium autem ostendit innixum summa scala principem Angelorum Dominum, credendum est enim sicut in curru aurigam, aut in navi gubernatorem, ita rebus omnibus superstare eum qui est: totum enim ille mundum ex se pendentem regit. Hactenus Philo.
units.tr: Jacob's dream is certainly mystical, and it is recorded at Genesis 28:12 etc. Moses, a sacred writer, wisely introduced it with the threefold behold, which signals something new and wonderful, so that he might draw the reader's mind more strongly to it and hold his attention: and he dreamed, he says, and behold a ladder set up on the earth, etc. and behold, the angels of God ascending and descending on it; and behold, Jehovah standing above it, Genesis 28:12, 13. I say that the rabbis refer this divine dream of Jacob to anything rather than to Christ. Philo the Jew, in his book On Dreams, teaches that this ladder prefigured four things: (1) the air, whose base is the earth and whose head is the heavens. Fitly, he says, the ladder, fixed to the earth by its lowest part, represents the air. For the exhalations breathed out from the earth are thinned into the air, so that the earth is as it were the root of the air and the heaven its head. On this foundation he goes on to the angels ascending and descending by the ladder, and teaches that they are first souls, by which he thinks the air is full. Of these, he says, some go down to be bound to mortal bodies, all those who are nearer the earth and more fond of bodies; others return upwards, separated again after the limits set by nature. Afterwards he teaches that the angels are those purest souls, the best servants of the Almighty of all, like the ears and eyes of a great king, whom the philosophers call genii and the sacred letters call angels: for they are, he says, messengers, carrying the Father's commands to the sons, and the sons' prayers back to him in turn. They are therefore introduced as ascending and descending because it serves us mortals to have these mediators and arbiters, so that we may revere more deeply the ruler of all things. Behold Philo, the author of the error about the mediation and intercession of angels! (2) That the ladder prefigured the soul: contradicting himself splendidly, he confidently declares: because, he says, the soul is a base that is almost bodily and as it were earthly, namely the senses; but the head is as it were heavenly, that purest mind, through which the divine intelligences are carried up and down unceasingly whenever they ascend, drawing the soul with them and tearing it away from mortal things, showing it sights only as fits its dignity; but they do not drag it with them when they descend. (3) The life of the mediator: for, he says, meditation is by nature a thing in water that is level, now advancing to a height, now failing into the opposite, and like a ship sailing now with favourable and now with adverse winds. (4) Lastly, he asserts that the ladder prefigured human affairs: human affairs, he says, have in some way a natural image of a ladder because of their unequal and inconstant course; for one day pulls one man down from his height and lifts another on high, since nothing among us remains perpetually in the same state, but all things are changed by various and manifold vicissitudes. Do not princes come from commoners, and commoners from princes; the poor from the rich, and the rich from the poor; the obscure become most famous, and the honoured and despised? This is the way of human affairs, rising and falling, subject to uncertain chances. But the dream shows that the Lord, the Prince of the angels, stood leaning on the top of the ladder; for we must believe that, as the charioteer stands in the chariot or the pilot at the helm of a ship, so he who is stands over all things, for he governs the whole world, which hangs from him. So far Philo.

units.la: Targum Hierosolymitanum ascensum, & descensum Angelorum duntaxat interpretatur, hac paraphrasi; & ecce Angeli qui deducebant eum de domo paterna, ascendebant ad praedicandum Angelis supernis dicendo, Venite videte Jacobum virum sanctum, cujus imagines sunt in Throno gloriae, quem intueri desiderastis. Et ecce Angeli Sancti e praesentia domini ascendebant & descendebant, eumque intuebantur. Hic autem mirari subit vanam Targumistae παραφραστὴν: ille enim relicto miraculoso scalae insomnio, ficta quinque miracula comminiscitur, quae Jacobo contigerint, quo tempore exiit e Beercheba. Primum, quod abbreviata illi fuerint hora diei, propterea quod Angelus dux itineris ejus cum eo colloqui desideravit. Secundum, quod terra subsiluerit coram eo, & in Harana sedens repertus est. Tertium, quod lapides vesperi, quos capiti suo substraverat, mane invenit in lapidem unum coaluisse, quem miraculosum lapidem in statuam erexit stabilem, & oleum super caput illius fudit. Quartum, quod lapidem ab ore putei una manuum amoverit, ut oves Labanis potaret. Quintum, quod dimoto lapide puteus ille exundaverit annos viginti continuos, toto scilicet tempore quo habitavit in Harana. Rabbi Salomon imitatus Targumistam Hierosolymitanum super visionem Angelorum, ita commentatur. Angeli, qui deduxerunt eum in terra Canaan, non egrediuntur extra terram; propterea ascenderunt in coelum, & descenderunt Angeli regionis extra terram, ut eum deducerent. Maimonides in Misna in Jesud. Hathorah, cap.7. scalam istam quatuor Monarchias parabolice adumbrasse hariolatur. Res, inquit, revelata Propheta per visionem propheticam, illi revelabantur per modum parabola, & statim interpretatio parabola cordi ipsius inscribebatur, & ille cognoscebat quid rei esset, ut scala, quam Jacob parens noster vidit, & Angelos ascenascendentes & descendentes super eam, & hac erat parabola quatuor monarchiarum. Omnium optime & vero proxime Rabbi Jechua referente Aben Ezra, docuit hanc scalam id significasse, per quod oratio Jacobi ascendebat in coelum, & salus ejus descendebat de coelo. Quid rei vero illud fuerit, penitus ignoravit. Unus Christus arcanorum revelator aperte declaravit, nempe scalam mysticam Filium hominis adumbrasse: ille ipse enim est, per quem sacrificia laudis, scil. fructus labiorum, & nominis ipsius confessionem, seu invocationem offerimus, Hebr. 13:15. Nec est in alio quoquam salus: nec enim aliud nomen est sub coelo, quod datum sit inter homines, per quod oporteat nos servari, Act. 4: 12. Re enim vera dum infit, Amen Amen dico vobis imposterum coelum apertum videbitis, & Angelos Dei ascendentes & descendentes ad Filium hominis: usque adeo gemina dixit iis, quae in Jacobi narrantur insomnio, ut praejudicatarum opinionum vacuus, nemo non fateatur visionem coeli aperti, & Angelorum Dei ascendentium, & descendentium ad Filium hominis, insomnii Jacobi luculentum inplementum habere. Nempe Jacobus vidit in somnio coelum apertum, unde isthaec admirabundi Patriarchae exclamatio. Non est hic aliud nisi domus Dei, & porta coeli! Vidit scalam, quae ima parte terram, summa vero coelum contingeret: vidit Dominum innixum scalae dicentem, ego sum Dominus Deus Abraham patris tui, & Deus Isaac, terram in qua dormis tibi dabo, & semini tuo: vidit Angelos Dei ascendentes & descendentes per eam: ascendentes nempe ad Dominum stantem super cacumen scalae, & descendentes ad se dormientem ad partem infimam scalae. Hinc necessaria consecutione colligitur, scalam fuisse typum Filii hominis, ad quem Angelos Dei ascendentes & descendentes, discipuli ut in posterum videant, Christus fore recipit. In id amice conspirant ore uno Theologi. Atenim ubi propius accedunt ad explicationem scalae mysticae, non una est eorum sententia. Plerique omnes existimant scalam nudam praefigurasse personam Christi Ἀνθρώπου quatenus Mediator est, ut scalae fastigium, quo coelum pertingebat divinam Christi naturam, ejusdem vero pars infima, qua stabat super terram, naturam ipsius humanam, & usus scalae mediae coelum inter, & terram, conjungenda, officium ipsius mediatorium adumbraverit: nempe quo fungitur unus Mediator Deum inter & homines, ut Jeheve innixus scalae persona Dei Patris fuerit, & Jacobus ad pedem scalae dormiens, humanum genus, & cumprimis Ecclesiam ex Jacobo oriundam praefiguraverit. Scalam officium Christi mediatorium adumbrasse optime dictum putamus: sed scalam summa, & infima fima sui parte divinam, & humanam Christi naturam significasse, vel Jeheve stantem super summam scalæ partem, fuisse personam Dei Patris, à veritatis tramite longè abesse existimamus, hisce de causis.
units.tr: The Jerusalem Targum explains only the ascent and descent of the angels, with this paraphrase: And behold, the angels who were escorting him from his father's house were going up to proclaim to the supernal angels, saying, "Come and see Jacob, the holy man, whose images are on the throne of glory, whom you have desired to behold." And behold, the holy angels were ascending and descending from the presence of the Lord, and gazing upon him. Here, however, one is moved to wonder at the vain paraphrase [παραφραστήν] of the Targumist. For, leaving aside the miraculous dream of the ladder, he invents five miracles that happened to Jacob at the time when he left Beersheba. The first: that the hours of the day were shortened for him, because the angel who was leader of his journey desired to converse with him. The second: that the earth leapt up before him, and he was found sitting in Haran. The third: that the stones he had placed under his head in the evening he found in the morning fused into one stone, which miraculous stone he set up as a firm statue, and he poured oil over its head. The fourth: that he moved the stone from the mouth of the well with one hand, so that Laban's sheep could drink. The fifth: that when the stone was moved that well overflowed for twenty continuous years, that is, for the whole time he lived in Haran. Rabbi Solomon, imitating the Jerusalem Targumist, comments on the vision of the angels thus: The angels who had escorted him in the land of Canaan did not go out beyond the land; therefore they went up into heaven, and the angels of the region descended outside the land in order to escort him. Maimonides, in the Mishnah, in Yesodei ha-Torah, chapter 7, guesses that this ladder allegorically foreshadowed the four monarchies. The matter, he says, was revealed to the prophet through a prophetic vision; it was revealed to him in the manner of a parable, and immediately the interpretation of the parable was inscribed on his heart, and he knew what the matter was, like the ladder which our father Jacob saw, and the angels ascending and descending on it; and this was the parable of the four monarchies. Best of all, and very nearly the truth, Rabbi Joshua, as reported by Aben Ezra, taught that this ladder signified that by which Jacob's prayer ascended into heaven, and his salvation descended from heaven. But what the thing really was he did not at all know. Christ alone, the revealer of secrets, has plainly declared that the mystical ladder prefigured the Son of man: for it is he through whom we offer the sacrifice of praise, that is, the fruit of lips, and the confession, or invocation, of his name, Hebrews 13:15. Nor is there salvation in any other: for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved, Acts 4:12. Indeed, when he begins, Verily, verily I say to you, hereafter you shall see the heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man: he so closely echoed the things recorded in Jacob's dream that anyone free of prejudiced opinions must confess that the vision of the open heaven and of the angels of God ascending and descending to the Son of man is the clear fulfilment of Jacob's dream. Namely, Jacob saw in his dream the open heaven, whence came that exclamation of the amazed patriarch: This is none other than the house of God, and the gate of heaven! He saw a ladder which touched the earth at its lowest part and reached heaven at its top; he saw the Lord leaning on the ladder saying, I am the Lord God of Abraham your father, and the God of Isaac; the land on which you lie I will give to you and to your seed; he saw the angels of God ascending and descending by it: ascending, of course, to the Lord standing at the top of the ladder, and descending to him sleeping at the lowest part of the ladder. From this a necessary consequence is drawn: that the ladder was a type of the Son of man, to whom the angels of God ascend and descend, which Christ says his disciples will see hereafter. The theologians agree on this with one voice. But when they come closer to explaining the mystical ladder, their opinion is not single. Most of them think that the bare ladder prefigured the person of Christ as Man [Ἀνθρώπου], insofar as he is Mediator: that the top of the ladder, by which it reached heaven, prefigured the divine nature of Christ; its lowest part, which stood upon the earth, his human nature; and that the function of the middle of the ladder, which joins heaven and earth, foreshadowed his mediatorial office, namely what the one Mediator between God and men performs. Thus Jehovah standing on the ladder would be the person of God the Father, and Jacob sleeping at the foot of the ladder would prefigure the human race, and above all the Church descended from Jacob. We think it has been very well said that the ladder foreshadowed Christ's mediatorial office; but we consider it far from the path of truth to hold that the ladder signified the divine and human natures of Christ by its top and bottom parts, or that Jehovah standing on the top part of the ladder was the person of God the Father, for these reasons.

units.la: Primò, quia Christus simul visionis Jacobi implementum, simul interpres infallibilis, integrum Jacobi insomnium ad se unum Filium hominis refert, Joh. 1: 51. Contrà verò Clarissimi Theologi partes insomnii principes, Deum nempe & Jacobum, alio quàm ad Christum referunt: nempe ad Deum Patrem, & genus humanum, vel Ecclesiam ex Jacobo oriundam. Unde fit, ut Deus Jacobum compellans pollicitis magnificis, & ipse Jacobus contemplator admirabundus, nec ad personam Christi, nec ad naturas, nec ad munus ipsius mediatorium spectent: & Jacobus viderit Angelos Dei ascendentes ad Deum Patrem, & descendentes ad se, contrà quam Christus verbotim docet, nempe discipulos visuros Angelos Dei ascendentes, & descendentes, non ad Deum Patrem: sed ad Filium hominis.
units.tr: First, because Christ is both the fulfilment of Jacob's vision and its infallible interpreter, he refers the whole of Jacob's dream to himself alone, the Son of Man (John 1:51). The most distinguished theologians, on the other hand, refer the principal parts of the dream, namely God and Jacob, to something other than Christ: to God the Father and to the human race, or to the Church descended from Jacob. As a result, God addressing Jacob with magnificent promises, and Jacob himself marvelling as he watches, look neither to the person of Christ, nor to his natures, nor to his mediatorial office. Jacob is said to have seen the angels of God ascending to God the Father and descending to himself. This is contrary to what Christ expressly teaches, namely that his disciples would see the angels of God ascending and descending, not to God the Father, but to the Son of Man.

units.la: Secundò, quia ex quo peccatum hominem separavit abs Numine, Es. 59: 2. Deus Pater vetante ipsius sapientia, & justitia haut se manifestavit præsentem hominibus, nisi ubi primum fœdus legale percussit cum Israëlitis, spectatis, quales sibi videbantur justi & sanƈti, peccati sui, mortisque commeritæ nefaria vituli adoratione, quàm conscii fierent priùs, Exod. 23: 20. 21. & 32: 34. & 33: 3. 14. Et ubi Danieli visus est Antiquus dierum, ad quem accedit Filius hominis in nubibus cœli, Dan. 7: 13. Cæterum filius Dei incarnationi praeludens Patribus apparuit, & cum iis verba identidem commutavit. Ille est qui Abrahamum allocutus est, & tectum ipsius adiit, epulis accubuit, sermones cum illo inter ambulandum seruit, Gen. 18: 1. &c. Unde Christus, Abrahamus diem meum vidit, & gavisus est, Joh. 8: 56. Ille ipse est, qui Moysi in rubo flammente apparuit, Exod. 3: 2. 6. 7. 8. coll. cum Act. 7: 30. 31. 32. Ille ipse est, qui Israelem eruit è servitute Ægyptiaca, nam appellatur Jeheve, & Angelus Jeheve, Jud. 2: 1, 4. 5. Ille ipse est, qui in columna nubis, & ignis per omnium solitudinum Arabiæ tractus Israelem duxit, eumque tandem in beatas, sedes terræ Canaan intromisit, sicuti Deus Pater receperat, Exod. 23: 20. 21. & 32: 34. & 33: 3. 14. Hinc palam docet divinus Paulus Israëlitas Christum tentasse in deserto, 1 Cor. 10: 9. Ille ipse est, qui armatus gladio, eoque vultu & habitu, qui principem exercituum Jeheve decebat, verba commutavit cum summo Imperatore Josue, Jos. 5: 13. 14. 15. coll. cum Exod. 3: 5. Ille ipse est, qui DaDanieli præsens adstitit, eo habitu & ornatu, qui summum Pontificem novi fœderis decet, Dan. 10: 5. 6. Sed verò constantem istam apparitionum filii Dei dispensationem violant, qui Deum Patrem scalæ innixum Jacobo apparuisse contendunt.
units.tr: Secondly, since sin separated man from the Deity (Isa. 59:2), God the Father, as his wisdom and justice forbade, did not manifest himself present to men, except where he first made a legal covenant with the Israelites. They regarded themselves as just and holy, yet they had committed the wicked worship of the calf, a deed that deserved death, and they did not realise this until later (Exod. 23:20–21; 32:34; 33:3, 14). Likewise, the Ancient of Days appeared to Daniel, and to him came the Son of Man in the clouds of heaven (Dan. 7:13). Moreover, the Son of God, preluding the incarnation, appeared to the Fathers and exchanged words with them repeatedly. It was he who spoke to Abraham, came to his tent, reclined at his meal, and conversed with him as they walked (Gen. 18:1ff.). Hence Christ says, Abraham saw my day and rejoiced (John 8:56). It was the same one who appeared to Moses in the flaming bush (Exod. 3:2, 6–8; compare Acts 7:30–32). It was the same one who rescued Israel from Egyptian slavery, for he is called Jehovah and the Angel of Jehovah (Judg. 2:1, 4–5). It was the same one who led Israel through all the wildernesses of Arabia in a pillar of cloud and fire, and at last brought them into the blessed land of Canaan, just as God the Father had promised (Exod. 23:20–21; 32:34; 33:3, 14). Hence the divine Paul plainly teaches that the Israelites tempted Christ in the wilderness (1 Cor. 10:9). It was the same one who, armed with a sword and bearing the look and dress that befit the leader of the armies of Jehovah, conversed with the supreme commander Joshua (Josh. 5:13–15; compare Exod. 3:5). It was the same one who stood present with Daniel, in the dress and adornment that befit the high priest of the New Covenant (Dan. 10:5–6).
