But those who maintain that God the Father appeared to Jacob leaning on the ladder violate this consistent pattern of the appearances of the Son of God.

units.la: Tertiò. Ille ipse, qui Jacobo apparuit in Bethel, Gen. 28: 19. iterata visione, quæ exstat, Gen. 31: 10. 11. 12. 13. Jacobum his verbis compellat, ego sum ille Deus Bethel, ubi unxisti statuam, & vovisti mihi votum, comm. 13. Quæritur, quisnam ille Deus est, num Pater, num Filius? Sed enim ipse Jacobus respondet, illum Deum Bethel esse Angelum Dei, & Angelus Dei dixit mihi in somnio, Jacob, &c. comm. 11. Erat igitur Dei Filius: is enim unus Angelus Dei est, qui à Patre mittitur; non contrà Deus Pater; is enim nusquàm totà Scripturâ Angelus Dei appellatur: nempe nunquàm à Filio, vel Spiritu Sancto mittitur.
units.tr: Thirdly. The one who appeared to Jacob at Bethel (Gen. 28:19), in a vision repeated and recorded in Gen. 31:10–13, addresses Jacob with these words: I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed the pillar and made a vow to me (v. 13). The question is, who is that God? Is he the Father or the Son? But Jacob himself answers that the God of Bethel is the Angel of God: And the Angel of God said to me in a dream, Jacob, etc. (v. 11). He was therefore the Son of God. For he is the one Angel of God who is sent by the Father, not God the Father; for nowhere in the whole of Scripture is God the Father called the Angel of God, since he is never sent by the Son or by the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Quartò. Ille ipse qui Jacobo somnianti apparuit, ipsi iterum ex Mesopotamia patrios lares repetenti visus est, Genes. 35: 9. 10. Unde Hoseas, In ipso utero calcaneum tenuit fratris sui, & robore suo principem se gessit cum Deo, principem, inquam, se gessit cum Angelo, & potentia valuit, flevit & supplex oravit eum, in Bethel invenit eum, & ibi locutus est nobiscum. Hos. 12: 4. 5. Ex locis illis parallelis abundè liquet personam illam divinam, quæ Jacobo apparuit appellari hominem, Gen. 35: 9. Deum & Angelum, Hos. 12: 5. Hæc autem in Deum Patrem nulla ratione competere possunt: nam Deus Pater nunquàm missus in forma hominis memoratur; quemobrem homo, vel Angelus dici nequit. Unus Dei Filius simul homo, simul Deus, simul Angelus est: homo quidem & Deus naturarum communione: Angelus verò faciei Jehovæ, Jes. 63: 9. Angelus fœderis; sed & qui Deus est ingressurus in templum suum, Malach. 3: 1. Angelus, inquam, ratione officii, munerisque mediatorii.
units.tr: Fourthly. The one who appeared to Jacob in his dream appeared to him again when he returned from Mesopotamia to his ancestral home (Gen. 35:9–10). Hence Hosea says: In the womb he held his brother's heel, and by his strength he acted as a prince with God; yes, he acted as a prince with the Angel, and he prevailed by his power; he wept and begged him in supplication; he found him at Bethel, and there he spoke with us (Hos. 12:4–5). From these parallel passages it is clear enough that the divine person who appeared to Jacob is called a man (Gen. 35:9), and God and an Angel (Hos. 12:5). But these titles can in no way belong to God the Father, for God the Father is never mentioned as sent in the form of a man; therefore he cannot be called man or Angel. The one Son of God is at once man, at once God, and at once Angel: man and God by the communion of the natures, but Angel as the face of Jehovah (Isa. 63:9), the Angel of the covenant, and also he who is God and will come into his temple (Mal. 3:1). He is Angel, I say, by reason of his office and mediatorial function.

units.la: Quintò. Quia, etsi Numen sapientissimum corpora naturalia, nubem, ignem, aquam, ventum, rorem, & cætera id genus bene multa, in symbola præsentiæ suæ adhibuit, ei tamen repræsentandæ artefacta, quæ ex arbitrio libituque humano pendent, adhiberi noluit: nempe ut longè se discerneret à falsis gentium Numinibus, quæ artefactis corporibus, cippis, statuis, pictisque lapidibus, oculis delusæ gentilitatis obversabantur; unde Psaltes, simulachra eorum, aurum & argentum opus manuum hominis, Psalm. 115: 4. Quod verò Deus adumbratur imagine clypei, & ensis, Deut. 33: 29. nihil causæ incomcommodat: aliud enim est Deum, quam præbet Ecclesiæ protectionem, & defensionem, artefactis clypeo & gladio adumbrare; aliud vero adhibere symbola præsentiæ suæ: illa enim Numinis sunt effecta voluntaria, quæ ex uno ipsius libitu, & arbitrio pendent: hæc vero signa sunt præsentiæ Numinis omnis dependentiæ ab arbitrio & voluntate hominum immunis. Fac vero divinam Christi naturam parte scalæ summa fuisse adumbratam; utique quod æternum, & summè necessarium in Christo est, artefacto humano fuerit adumbratum. Dispar equidem ratio est unionis hypostaticæ geminæ in Christo naturæ; sicut & officii Mediatorii, ut enim utrumque opus est unius beneplaciti, & multiformis Dei sapientiæ, artefacto, nempe scalâ adumbrari potuit, sicut & propitiatorio, quod tegmen erat arcæ aftabrè elaboratum ex auro, Exod. 25: 17.
units.tr: Fifthly. Although the most wise Deity used natural bodies, such as cloud, fire, water, wind, dew, and many other things of that kind, as signs of his presence, he was unwilling that artificial objects, which depend on human choice and whim, should be used to represent him. He wished, in this way, to distinguish himself clearly from the false deities of the nations, which the blinded heathen worshipped in material forms: bodies made by hand, pillars, statues and painted stones. Hence the Psalmist says, Their idols are silver and gold, the work of human hands (Ps. 115:4). As for the fact that God is pictured by the image of a shield and a sword (Deut. 33:29), this causes no difficulty. It is one thing to picture God, who gives the Church protection and defence, under the artificial images of a shield and a sword; it is another to employ symbols of his presence. The former are voluntary works that depend entirely on his own pleasure and choice; the latter are signs of the presence of God, free from all dependence on the choice and will of men. Suppose, however, that the divine nature of Christ was pictured by the upper part of the ladder. Then what is eternal and most necessarily in Christ would have been pictured by a human artefact. Indeed, the case of the hypostatic union of the two natures in Christ is not the same, nor is that of the mediatorial office. For both are the work of one good pleasure and of the manifold wisdom of God, and so both could have been pictured by an artefact, such as the ladder, just as the mercy-seat, which was the lid of the ark, was skilfully made of gold (Exod. 25:17).

units.la: Sextò. Quid causæ est cur divinam Christi naturam summa scalæ parte adumbratam hariolentur? Nempe quia sicuti scala erecta illa sui parte cælum tangebat, ita Christus excelsa sui divinitate cælo præsens, & proximus est. Sed enim nos pari facilitate & specie rationis dixerimus totam scalam divinam Christi naturam adumbrasse; ea enim infinita atque immensa, non minus terræ præsens quam cælo est, quod Numen hoc edicto significavit, cœlum ipsum solium meum est, & terra scabellum pedum meorum, Jef. 66: 1. Ex quo intelligitur divinam Christi naturam infima scalæ parte æquè adumbrari potuisse ac summâ. Quid quod absurdum sit, divinam Christi naturam ea re adumbrari, quæ cum cælum contingat longè distat à terra, nec terræ immediatè præsens, adesse potest. Verum est, fatebor enim, omne simile esse, & alia ratione dissimile, quia diversum est à simili suo; sed verò nullum simile eo ipso quo simile est, dissimile esse potest. Id verò incommodi hic palam cernere est; etenim quòd summa scalæ pars cælum contingeret, ea ratione, ut ferunt, naturæ divinæ similis, ea ipsa ratione dissimilis plane erat: nam eo ipso quod summa illa pars cælum contingeret, nullo modò terram contingere poterat, quod à natura divina vehementer abhorret, quæ eo ipso, quo in cælo est, & terræ præsens sistitur, nempe sua immensitate, quæ finem, & terminum omnem procul arcet à sese.
units.tr: Sixthly. Why do they guess that the divine nature of Christ was pictured by the top of the ladder? Because, they say, just as the ladder, standing upright, touched heaven with its upper part, so Christ, by his lofty divinity, is present to heaven and near it. But with equal ease and equal plausibility we could say that the whole ladder pictured the divine nature of Christ. For that nature, being infinite and immense, is present to the earth no less than to heaven, as God signified by this decree: Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool (Isa. 66:1). From this it follows that the divine nature of Christ could have been pictured by the lowest part of the ladder as well as by the highest. Moreover, it is absurd to say that the divine nature of Christ was pictured by something which, while it touches heaven, lies far from the earth and cannot be immediately present to the earth. It is true, I grant, that every likeness is in some respect unlike, because it differs from what it resembles; but no likeness can be unlike in that very respect in which it is like. And this inconvenience is plainly visible here. For the fact that the upper part of the ladder touched heaven, which they say makes it like the divine nature, is the very point in which it was plainly unlike it. For by the very fact that the upper part touched heaven, it could in no way touch the earth; yet the divine nature, far from being hindered in this way, is by the very fact that it is in heaven also present to the earth, being set there by its immensity, which keeps every limit and boundary far away from itself.

units.la: Septimò. In Patriarchæ insomnio divinam Christi naturam scalæ cacumine adumbrari, nihil quicquam opus fuit, quando ipse Dei Filius, uti Deus & dominus Angelorum est, simul præsens videbatur, simul præsentem Jacobum amicè compellabat.
units.tr: Seventhly. In the patriarch's dream there was no need at all for the top of the ladder to shadow the divine nature of Christ, since the Son of God himself, as God and Lord of the angels, was seen to be present, and kindly addressed Jacob who stood there.

units.la: Octavò. Cùm Filius Dei quatenus Deus est, & Dominus Abraha-mi, Isaaci, & Angelorum, summæ parti scalæ innixus Jacobo cerni-tur, ut suprà perspicuis Scripturæ locis addiximus; si pars scalæ sum-ma eum adumbraverit, quatenus Deus est, hinc unusquisque facile intelligit Filium Dei visum fuisse sibi ipsi Deo scalæ fastigio adum-brato, innixum vel adstantem. Id verò quis sobrius asserere sustinue-rit? Astitit quidem Filius Dei rupi quam Moyses percussit præsens, ut significaret se Deum, & hominem virgâ Moysis fuisse percussum: sed verò rupi percussæ astitit præsens, quatenus rupes sicca & aquis fundendis impar suapte natura, vilem & despectum hominem plagâ percussum propter populum suum significabat, etsi omninò impar, ad aquas consolationis & sanctificationis sitibundis peccatoribus funden-das, videretur.
units.tr: Eighthly. Since the Son of God, insofar as he is God and Lord of Abraham, Isaac and the angels, is seen by Jacob leaning on the top of the ladder, as we showed above from clear passages of Scripture, if the top of the ladder shadowed him insofar as he is God, then anyone can easily see that the Son of God would have appeared to Jacob as God himself, shadowed by the summit of the ladder, leaning on it or standing beside it. But who of sound mind would venture to assert this? The Son of God did indeed stand present by the rock which Moses struck, to signify that he, God and man, was struck with Moses' rod. But he stood present by the struck rock insofar as the rock, dry and by its own nature unable to pour out water, signified the lowly and despised man struck with blows for his people, although it seemed altogether unfit to pour out waters of consolation and sanctification for thirsty sinners.

units.la: Nonò. Quando apud omnes in confesso est, ascensum, & descen-sum Angelorum Dei ad Filium hominis, eorum obsequium in capes-sendis, & exequendis ipsius mandatis omnino significare, utique ne-cesse est ut Jacob in insomnio Angelos Dei ascendentes, & descenden-tes hoc est obsequiosos Filio hominis in capessendis ipsius mandatis viderit. Fac vero nudam scalam Filium hominis adumbrasse, utique Jacob viderit Angelos ascendentes & descendentes Deo stanti in summitate scalæ obsequiosos, ipsi verò scalæ quipote? quando scala in insomnio merè passivè se habet, uti organum & medium, quo utantur Angeli, ut per eam mediam ascendant ad Deum & ad Jacobum descen-dant. Scalam itaque mysticam solide interpretaturis, haut quaquam com-mittendum est, ut mentis perceptione divellant, quæ in mystico Ja-cobi insomnio, conjuncta Numen esse voluit. Integrum igitur pii Pa-triarchæ insomnium, ut sancto suo ambitu Deum Abrahami, & Isaa-ci, Jacobum humi jacentem & dormientem, scalam intermediam cœ-lum, & terram copulantem, Angelos Dei ascendentes, & descenden-tes, complectitur, ad Filium hominis uti typus ad ποπωσῆν suum, omni-nino referendum est. Ut Jeheve è capite scalæ Jacobum compellans Filius Dei fuerit, Jacobus vero dormiens, & denuo expergefactus cum adumbraverit: sed futurum hominem, moriturum & è mortuis excitandum, ut foret sponsus, caput, & parens universæ Ecclesiæ, scala vero intermedia cœlum inter & terram in summo Deum, in imo vero Jacobum habens, geminæ in Christo naturæ unionem, & officium ipsius mediatorium adumbraverit. Cœlum vero ubi Filius Dei videbatur, quodque scalæ pars summa contingebat Deum Patrem, terra autem, quam parte infima tangebat genus humanum, seu mundum peccato suo abs Deo remotum significaverit. Hæc verò ne ingratiis dicta cuipiam videantur, demonstrata sigillatim damus.
units.tr: Ninthly. Since it is agreed by all that the ascending and descending of the angels of God to the Son of man signifies their obedience in receiving and carrying out his commands, it is surely necessary that Jacob in his dream saw the angels of God ascending and descending, that is, obedient to the Son of man in receiving his commands. But suppose the bare ladder shadowed the Son of man. Then Jacob would have seen the angels ascending and descending, obedient to God standing at the top of the ladder; but what of the ladder itself? In the dream the ladder is purely passive, like an instrument and means which the angels use, passing through it to ascend to God and descend to Jacob. Therefore those who wish to interpret the mystical ladder soundly must by no means be allowed to separate in their understanding what God in Jacob's mystical dream willed to be joined together. The whole dream of the pious patriarch, then, which in its holy compass embraces God of Abraham and Isaac, Jacob lying on the ground and sleeping, the ladder standing between joining heaven and earth, and the angels of God ascending and descending, must wholly be referred to the Son of man as the type to its antitype [ἀντίτυπον]. Jehovah, addressing Jacob from the top of the ladder, was the Son of God; Jacob, sleeping and afterwards roused again, shadowed the man who was to come, to die and be raised from the dead, so that he would be the bridegroom, head and father of the whole Church. The intermediate ladder, with God on top and Jacob at the bottom, shadowed the union of the two natures in Christ and his mediatorial office. The heaven where the Son of God was seen, which the top of the ladder touched, signifies God the Father; and the earth, which the lowest part touched, signifies the human race, or the world removed from God by its sin. Lest these things seem to anyone to have been said without reason, we give the proofs of each one separately.

units.la: Primò quidem Jeheve Jacobum blande compellantem esse Filium Dei liquet, eum enim iisdem verbis compellat, quibus deinceps Moysem, Ego sum Deus Patris tui, Deus Abrahami, Deus Isaaci, & Deus Jacobi, Exod. 3: 6. Eum vero esse Dei Filium Stephanus, non finit nos dubitare dum ipsum vocat Angelum Domini, & Dominum ipsum, Act. 7: 30. 31. 32. At enim Deus Pater, nusquam de nomine Angeli Domini censetur. Nec plura in hanc rem afferre libet, id enim supra perspicuis Scripturæ locis, solidisque rationibus addiximus. 2°. Jacobum dormientem, & mox excitatum è somno Christum hominem moriturum, è morte exiturum, & parentem Ecclesiæ adumbrasse liquet, quia Christus homo in lumbis Jacobi erat ipsius semen in quo Filius Dei fore recipit, ut omnes orbis familiæ benedicantur. Gen. 28: 14. Gal. 3: 8. 16. & Jacobus illustri μονομάχις factus Israël, hoc est Dei bellator, & princeps, typus fuit Christi singularis. At enim quicquid typo competit uti typus est, suam habet veritatem plenumque implementum in prototypo, ut in agno Paschali palam cernere est, ejus enim ne ullum os frangeretur edicto Numinis cautum erat, nempe quia nullum os Christi ipsius prototypi frangendum erat, ut vel morte intermeratum ipsius robur adumbraretur, & spontanea mors, qua sanctissimam animam volens lubensque efflavit, palam significaretur Exod. 12: 46. Joan. 19: 36. Verum ne Jacobum, Christi hominis fuisse typum, gratis suppositum videamur, id momentosi negotii solido fultum fundamento, (habet enim summum operæ nostræ pretium) clara nunc in luce, loceimus.
units.tr: First, it is clear that Jehovah, addressing Jacob kindly, was the Son of God, for he speaks to him in the same words he afterwards used to Moses: I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, Exod. 3: 6. That he is the Son of God Stephen does not let us doubt, when he calls him the Angel of the Lord and the Lord himself, Acts 7: 30, 31, 32. But God the Father is nowhere named the Angel of the Lord. Nor is it my wish to bring more on this point, since we have already added it above from clear passages of Scripture and solid arguments. Second, it is clear that Jacob, sleeping and soon roused from sleep, shadowed Christ the man, who was to die, come forth from death, and become the father of the Church, because Christ the man was in Jacob's loins, his seed in whom the Son of God would receive flesh, so that all the families of the earth would be blessed, Gen. 28: 14; Gal. 3: 8, 16. And Jacob, made Israel by an illustrious wrestling, that is, God's fighter and prince, was a singular type of Christ. But whatever befits a type as a type has its truth, and for the most part its fulfilment, in the prototype, as is plainly seen in the Passover lamb. Concerning this lamb God's decree forbade that any bone of it be broken, namely because no bone of Christ, the prototype, was to be broken, so that his strength, unimpaired even by death, might be shadowed, and his voluntary death, by which he willingly and gladly breathed out his most holy soul, might be plainly signified, Exod. 12: 46; John 19: 36. But lest we seem to have supposed without warrant that Jacob was a type of Christ the man, let us now set this weighty matter, which rests on a solid foundation (for it is of the highest importance to our work), in clear light.

units.la: Res, vel persona, perinde est, genuinam typi ideam ut induat, duorum alterutrum, vel utrumque requiruntur. 1°. Nomen typi, exemplari suo, sacra Scriptura tribuat: vel rem in typo momentosam, efferat de ipsomet exemplari illius, quod liquido patet in Davide & Salomone Christi typis, ut Christus nomine Davidis sæpe veniat, & quæ momentosa contigere Davidi, in Christo luculentiori ratione impleta fuere Psalm. 22: 1. 8. 9. 17. 19. Matth. 27: 35. 39. 43. &c. Ita Christus princeps pacis dicitur. Esa. 9: 3. Et quod Deus Salomoni promittit: Ero ipsi Pater, & ille mihi erit Filius. 2 Sam. 7: 14. Christo tribuitur. Hebr. 1: 5. Iterum prædixit Deus fore, ut Schelomo templum ædificet 2 Sam. 7: 13. 1 Reg. 5: 5. & 6: 12. Idemmet de Christo sto asseritur Zach. 6: 12. 13. Non secus & agnus paschalis Christi typus fuit illustris, simul quia Christus agnus, sine macula, dicitur, cujus sanguine pretioso redempti fuimus. 1 Petr. 1: 19. Et Pascha nostrum immolatum pro nobis. 1 Cor. 5: 7. Simul quod Deus edixerat de agno paschali, ne ullum ipsius os frangeretur. Exod. 12: 46. Num. 9: 12. Idem met Christo tribuitur. Joh. 19: 36. Solido illo nixi fundamento statuimus, Jacobum illustrem fuisse Christi hominis typum, nempe, quod de Jacobo dicitur, quodque illi momentosum contigit, Christo homini tribuitur. Primum quidem dixit Deus de Jacobo, Jacobum dilexi infantem. Malach. 1: 2. Rom. 9: 12. 13. Et vocavi Filium meum ex Ægypto. Hos. 11: 1. Sed & idemmet Christo homini tribuitur, Matth. 2: 15. Iterum de Jacobo dicitur, quod cœlum apertum viderit, & Angelos Dei ascendentes ad Deum in scala fastigio, & descendentes ad eum ad pedem scala jacentem. Gen. 28: 12. Totum id quantum quantum est in Christo homine in terra versante, plenum habuit complementum. Joh. 1: 51. Sed & idem liquidò patet, Christum scilicet respexisse ad Jacobi visionem, ubi de se hæc verba habet ad Judæos; Nemo ascendit in cœlum, nisi qui descendit è cœlo, scilicet, Filius hominis qui est in cœlo. Joh. 3: 14. Nempe ascendere in cœlum stylo Moisis & Pauli, omnino significat, mysteria fidei, regnique cœlorum nosse & docere homines. Deut. 30: 12. Rom. 10: 6. Id merito jure sibi Christus tribuit ut Filius hominis est, quia simul erat in cœlo, simul in terra, Judæos ut docëret mysteria regni cœlorum, sicut ipse Filius Dei in cœlo erat, dum mysteria fidei, & regni cœlorum Jacobum doceret è cœlo. Gen. 28: 13. 14. Sed simul erat in terra per mediam scalam Jacobo junctus.
units.tr: Whether a thing or a person takes on the genuine idea of a type, one or both of two things are required. First, Holy Scripture ascribes the name of the type to its exemplar, or it sets forth from the exemplar itself something weighty in the type. This is clearly seen in David and Solomon as types of Christ: Christ often comes under the name of David, and what happened weightily to David was fulfilled in Christ in a more brilliant way, Psalm 22: 1, 8, 9, 17, 19; Matt. 27: 35, 39, 43, etc. So Christ is called the Prince of Peace, Esa. 9: 3. And what God promised Solomon, I will be his Father, and he shall be my Son, 2 Sam. 7: 14, is ascribed to Christ, Heb. 1: 5. Again, God foretold that Solomon would build the temple, 2 Sam. 7: 13; 1 Kings 5: 5; 6: 12, and the very same thing is asserted of Christ, Zech. 6: 12, 13. In the same way the Passover lamb was an illustrious type of Christ, both because Christ is called a lamb without blemish, by whose precious blood we have been redeemed, 1 Pet. 1: 19, and our Passover sacrificed for us, 1 Cor. 5: 7; and because God had decreed concerning the Passover lamb that not a bone of it should be broken, Exod. 12: 46; Num. 9: 12. The very same thing is ascribed to Christ, John 19: 36. Resting on that solid foundation, we establish that Jacob was an illustrious type of Christ the man: namely, what is said of Jacob, and what happened to him in a weighty way, is ascribed to Christ the man. First, God said of Jacob, I loved Jacob as an infant, Mal. 1: 2; Rom. 9: 12, 13; and I called my son out of Egypt, Hos. 11: 1. But this too is ascribed to Christ the man, Matt. 2: 15. Again, of Jacob it is said that he saw heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending to God at the top of the ladder, and descending to him, lying at its foot, Gen. 28: 12. All of that, to its full extent, found its complete fulfilment in Christ the man dwelling on earth, John 1: 51. And it is also plain that Christ indeed had in view Jacob's vision, where he says of himself to the Jews: No one ascends into heaven except he who descended from heaven, namely the Son of man who is in heaven, John 3: 14. To ascend into heaven, in the idiom of Moses and Paul, certainly means to know and teach men the mysteries of faith and of the kingdom of heaven, Deut. 30: 12; Rom. 10: 6. Christ rightly claims this for himself as Son of man, because he was at once in heaven and on earth, to teach the Jews the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, just as the Son of God himself, in heaven, taught Jacob from heaven the mysteries of faith and of the kingdom of heaven, Gen. 28: 13, 14. Yet at the same time he was on earth, joined to Jacob through the intermediate ladder.

units.la: Reapse enim gemino nomine Christus homo Judæis voluit manifestari, despicabili altero, vermis non homo, hemo dolorum & contemptus, Galilæus, & Nazarenus per contemptum ob infirmitatem dierum carnis. Mox conspicuo ac glorioso; Ea propter enim eum Deus summè evexit, dedit que nomen supra omne nomen, Philip. 2: 9. 10. Non secus atque Jacobus gemino nomine, primum quidem despicabili supplantatoris Jacobi; Ne timeas vermis Jacob, Jef. 41: 14. Sed mox exuto despicabili, gloriosò nomine Israël, victor & princeps Dei fortis, conspicuus fuit. Gen. 32: 28.
units.tr: Indeed, Christ wished to be shown to the Jews as man under a twofold name: one despised, "a worm and not a man, a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief," "the Galilean" and "the Nazarene", used by way of contempt on account of the weakness of the days of his flesh; and then one conspicuous and glorious. "For this reason God has highly exalted him and given him a name above every name," Phil. 2: 9. 10. Not otherwise than Jacob, who had a twofold name: first a despised one, the name of the supplanter Jacob, "Fear not, you worm Jacob," Isa. 41: 14. But soon, with the despised name laid aside, he appeared conspicuous under the glorious name Israel, victor and prince of God. Gen. 32: 28.

units.la: Secundò. Christus homo despectus tanquam fratrum minimus, Dei Patris benedictione factus est Regum terra primogenitus. Psalm. 89: 28. Et primogenitus inter multos fratres, Rom. 8: 29. Non secus atque Jacobus, cobus, tanquam minor natu despectus, factus fuit Esaui primogenitus electione Dei, & paterna Isaaci benedictione, Gen. 27: 29. Israël est filius meus & primogenitus meus. Exod. 4: 22.
units.tr: Secondly. Christ as man, despised as the least of his brothers, was made by the blessing of God the Father "the firstborn of the kings of the earth," Ps. 89: 28, "and the firstborn among many brothers," Rom. 8: 29. Not otherwise than Jacob, despised as the younger by birth, was made the firstborn in place of Esau by the election of God and the paternal blessing of Isaac, Gen. 27: 29. "Israel is my son, my firstborn," Exod. 4: 22.

units.la: Tertiò. Christus homo utpote primogenitus inter fratres, fuit Sacerdos, Propheta, & Rex. Non secus atque Jacob primogenituram sortitus sacerdos fuit, & sacerdotium, tribuum suarum primogenitis jure successionis reliquit Exod. 24: 5. Sed et Propheta fuit, & sortem futuram filiis suis, ultimis praecipuè temporibus, vaticinatus est senex moribundus. Gen. 49: 1. Demum Rex à patre constitutus, vel in fratrem Esauum. Dominare in fratres tuos, & incurvent se tibi filii matris tuae. Gen. 27: 29. 30. 31.
units.tr: Thirdly. Christ as man, being the firstborn among brothers, was priest, prophet and king. Not otherwise than Jacob, who obtained the birthright, was a priest, and by right of succession left the priesthood to the firstborns of his tribes, Exod. 24: 5. But he was also a prophet, and as a dying old man foretold the lot awaiting his sons, especially in the last times, Gen. 49: 1. Finally he was made king by his father over his brother Esau: "Be lord over your brothers, and let your mother's sons bow down to you," Gen. 27: 29. 30. 31.

units.la: Quartò. Christus homo sortitus est nomen supra omne nomen, quia cibum Deo gratum obtulit, bonae scilicet fragrantiae sacrificium. Ephes. 5: 2. Sicuti Jacob primogenituræ gloriam, sorte divina obtinuit, quia cibum gratum palato ex haedis mactatis Isaaco parenti, obtulit.
units.tr: Fourthly. Christ as man obtained "the name above every name" because he offered to God a sacrifice pleasing to him, namely a sacrifice of sweet fragrance, Eph. 5: 2. Just as Jacob obtained the glory of the birthright by divine lot, because he offered to his father Isaac food pleasing to the palate, made from slaughtered kids.

units.la: Quintò. Christus homo exosus fratribus suis Pharisæis, Sacerdotibus, legisque Doctoribus fuit, ob excellentissimas praerogativas stupendæ sapientiæ, miraculorum, ac summæ auctoritatis, quibus se eorum primogenitum luculenter demonstravit, cum ea propter ut neci, præconcepta malitia destinaverint. Sicuti Jacobus Esauo fratri ad mecem exosus fuit, quòd illi jus eximium primogenituræ praeripuisset.
units.tr: Fifthly. Christ as man was hated by his brothers the Pharisees, the priests and the teachers of the law, on account of his most excellent prerogatives of astonishing wisdom, of miracles and of supreme authority, by which he plainly showed himself to be their firstborn. Therefore they plotted his death with premeditated malice. Just as Jacob was hated to death by his brother Esau, because he had snatched away from him the special right of the birthright.

units.la: Sextò. Fratrum Judæorum odium, Christum hominem templo, domo Dei patris, sanctaque Jerusalem, magni illius regis civitate, ad desertum Calvariæ expulit, ubi somno profundo mortis correptus, in petra sepulchri ad diem resurrectionis dormivit. Non secus atque Jacobus, fratris Esaui odio domo paterna pulsus in deserto medio, super petra pro cervicali, dormivit.
units.tr: Sixthly. The hatred of his Jewish brothers drove Christ as man from the temple, the house of God his Father, and from holy Jerusalem, the city of that great king, into the desert of Calvary, where, seized by the deep sleep of death, he slept in the rock of the sepulchre until the day of resurrection. Not otherwise than Jacob, driven from his father's house by the hatred of his brother Esau, slept in the middle of the desert, upon a rock for a pillow.

units.la: Septimò. Christus è coelo, placidoque sinu Dei patris in terram descendit, venitque apud Judæos fratres secundum carnem laboribus, & miseriis omne genus expositus, praecepto patris ut pareret: Ecce me, inquit, veni ut faciam voluntatem tuam. Ps. 40: 8. 9. Sicut Jacobus domo patris exiit, & in Mesopotamiam ad sanguineos suos ivit, laboribus & miseriis, longi, durique itineris conflictatus, parentis Isaaci voluntati ut pareret obsequiosus. Gen. 28: 1. 2. 5.
units.tr: Seventhly. Christ came down from heaven and from the peaceful bosom of God the Father to earth, and came among the Jews, his brothers according to the flesh, exposed to labours and miseries of every kind, obedient to the command of the Father to obey: "Behold, I come, he says, to do your will," Ps. 40: 8. 9. Just as Jacob left his father's house and went to his kinsmen in Mesopotamia, struggling with the labours and miseries of a long and hard journey, dutifully obedient to the will of his father Isaac, Gen. 28: 1. 2. 5.

units.la: Octavò. Christus homo ad pugnam sese accinxit cum Deo forti, ubi nox ingrueret, & potestas tenebrarum, ut vinceret principatus & potestates, principesque tenebrarum saeculi, Judaeos, scilicet, fratres suos secundum carnem, viam sibi ut sterneret, & ascensum in coelum, patris sui domicilium. Sicut Jacob totam noctem luctatus est cum Deo forti, fratrem suum, milite armatum ut vinceret sibique conciliaret, & victor gloriosus rediret ascendens ad relictum pridem patris Isaaci domicilium. Gen. 32: 24. 25. 28.
units.tr: Eighthly. Christ as man girded himself for battle with God the strong, when night was pressing in and "the power of darkness," so that he might conquer the principalities and powers and the rulers of the darkness of this age, that is, the Jews, his brothers according to the flesh; so that he might clear a way for himself and an ascent into heaven, the dwelling of his Father. Just as Jacob wrestled the whole night with God the strong, armed like a soldier, that he might conquer his brother and win him over, and returned a glorious victor, ascending to the dwelling of his father Isaac, which he had left long before, Gen. 32: 24. 25. 28.

units.la: Nonò. Pugnavit Christus in diebus carnis sua, vicitque Deum fortem armatum tremenda justitiae suae vindicta, sed humilitate, precibus, & lachrymis, deprecationibus, & supplicationibus oblatis, cum clamore valido & lachrymis apud eum qui poterat ipsum servare a morte, & exauditus fuit ex metu. Heb. 5: 7. Sicut Jacob Deum fortem vicit precibus & lachrymis, principem se gessit cum Angelo, & potentia valuit, flevit, & supplex oravit eum. Hose. 12: 5.
units.tr: Ninthly. Christ fought "in the days of his flesh" and overcame God the strong, armed with the dreadful vengeance of his justice, but by humility, prayers and tears, "with entreaties and supplications offered, with strong crying and tears to him who was able to save him from death," and "he was heard because of his fear," Heb. 5: 7. Just as Jacob overcame God the strong with prayers and tears: "he prevailed with the angel," and "had power," "wept," and "made supplication to him," Hos. 12: 5.

units.la: Decimò. Christus homo post reportatam de Deo forti, ac hominibus gloriosam victoriam, plagarum cicatrices in corpore suo retinuit, & ostentavit pugnae cruentae, notas illustres. Joh. 20: 27. Sicut Jacob post reportatam victoriam de Deo forti, impressam pugnae suae notam in luxato femore habuit ut claudicaret super femur suum, idcirco non comedunt filii Israelis, nervos mutuos ad acetabulum femoris, quia Angelus laserat nervos mutuos ad acetabulum femoris Jacobi. Gen. 32: 31. 32.
units.tr: Tenthly. Christ as man, after his glorious victory over God the strong and over men, kept the scars of his wounds in his body and displayed the famous marks of his bloody battle, John 20: 27. Just as Jacob, after his victory over God the strong, bore the mark of his struggle impressed on his dislocated thigh, so that he "limped on his thigh," "therefore the sons of Israel do not eat the sinew of the hip," "the sinew of the hip," "because the angel struck the sinew of Jacob's hip," Gen. 32: 31. 32.

units.la: Sed enim acutum intuenti in rem praesentem, gravissima hic emergit difficultas, unde tota typi Jacobaei ratio labefactari, & convelli videtur. Nempe, ille qui totam noctem cum Jacobo strenuè luctatus est vir, angelus, simulque Deus fuit. Vir lacertorum, corporisque robore, Jacobo ut colluctaretur: Deus fatente ipso luctatore, Jacobum ubi compellat his verbis: principem te gessisti apud Deum & apud homines, & praevaluisti, ideo Israel tibi nomen in posterum erit. Sed & ipso Jacobo fatente, ubi benedictionem a viro illo collucatore efflagitat, & locum pugnae Penielem, vel Panuelem appellitat, quia Deum facie ad faciam conspexit. Gen. 32: 24. 28. 30. Demum fuit Angelus docente Hosea. In ipso utero calcaneum tenuit fratris sui, & robore suo principem se gessit cum Deo: Principem, inquam, se gessit cum Angelo, & potentia valuit, flevit, & supplex oravit eum, Bethele invenit eum, & ibi locutus est nobiscum. Atqui Deus exercituum, memoriale ejus. Hos. 12: 4. 5. 6. Persona illa cum Jacobo luctata, nec Deus pater erat, quia nunquam Angelus est, vel dicitur tota scriptura, scilicet nunquam a Filio, vel Spiritu Sancto mittitur praerogativa primatus ordinis, & originis & potestate, summaque auctoritate in foederali trium personarum adoranda pactione. Nec erat Spiritus Sanctus, ille enim nunquam ac nusquam tota Scriptura homo, vir, ve, audit. Itaque adorandus randus ille luctator Christus Dei filius fuit; ille enim Immanuel, Deus & homo hypostatica unione divinae & humanae naturae est: simul Angelus, & Angelus Foederis officio & missione a patre. Qui igitur luctatus cum ipso Jacobus, typus ipsius esse potuit? Nisi statuas, imaginariam ac fictitiam fuisse isthanc Jacobi cum Angelo dimicationem, qua Jacobum, non cum persona a sese distincta, sed cum seipso luctatum fuisse, hinc evidenter sequatur.
units.tr: But when one looks sharply at the matter at hand, a most serious difficulty emerges here, by which the whole reasoning of the Jacob type seems to be shaken and overturned. Namely, the one who wrestled the whole night with Jacob was a man, an angel, and at the same time God. A man in the strength of his arms and the vigour of his body, so that he could wrestle with Jacob; God, as the wrestler himself admits, when he addresses Jacob with these words: "You have striven with God and with men, and have prevailed; therefore Israel shall be your name from now on." But Jacob himself also admits it, when he begs a blessing from that man who wrestled with him, and names the place of the struggle Peniel or Penuel, because he saw God face to face, Gen. 32: 24. 28. 30. Finally, he was an angel, as Hosea teaches: "In the womb he took his brother by the heel, and in his strength he strove with God. He strove, I say, with the angel, and prevailed; he wept and made supplication to him. He found him at Bethel, and there he spoke with us. But the LORD God of hosts, his memorial." Hos. 12: 4. 5. 6. That person who wrestled with Jacob was not God the Father, because in the whole of Scripture he is never and nowhere called an angel, or sent by the Son or the Holy Spirit, with the prerogative of primacy of order and origin, power and supreme authority in the covenant of the three persons who are to be worshipped. Nor was it the Holy Spirit, for he is never and nowhere in all Scripture heard of as a man, or husband. Therefore that wrestler to be worshipped was Christ, the Son of God; for he is Immanuel, God and man in the hypostatic union of the divine and human natures, at once "the Angel," and "the Angel of the covenant" by office and by mission from the Father. How then could he who wrestled with Jacob be a type of himself? Unless you hold that this wrestling of Jacob with the angel was imaginary and fictitious, from which it would evidently follow that Jacob wrestled not with a person distinct from himself but with himself.

units.la: Gravissimam difficultatem sipote ut enodemus. Primum Jacobum cum Christo Dei filio collutatum fuisse ultro confitebimur: sed & secundo atteximus Christum Dei filium in hac solemni μονομαχίᾳ, personam Dei patris substinuisse pro ratione officii mediatorii, quo functus est apud homines, vel ab ipso ortu peccati, modo personam rei hominis adversus Deum ut sustineat, modo personam Patris summi numinis adversus hominem reum, sicut in isto sacro duello. Nempe Deus pater vetante ejus sapientia & justitia nunquam immediate agit cum hominibus laesae-majestatis reis confitentibus, sicuti ipse declaravit Moysi post confessam vituli aurei a populo idololatriam. Exod.33:1.2.3. Agit igitur cum ipsis per filium mediatorem missum suo nomine, tanquam Angelum suum ad ipsos personam suam ut referat & sustineat apud ipsos. Id magni momenti ad Scripturam illustrandam, liquido patet ex historia datae & promulgatae legis secunda vice, Deus enim legem promulgasse fertur in monte Sinai, ubi quadraginta dies prostratus Moyses peccatorum veniam, & poenae remissionem pro populo idololatra efflictim deprecabatur. Illa autem persona, quae Mosem alloquebatur, etsi verus Deus, & Deus Israelis erat, non Pater, sed Dei filius, Patris personam sustinens erat, quia Angelus appellatur, Act. 7:38. nomine illo de quo nunquam ac nusquam Deus Pater censetur, iis de causis quas supra memoravimus. Caetera, quae ad plenam hujus typi elucidationem pertinent, cum bono Deo inferius persequemur. Nunc e momentoso diverticulo, in viam ut redeamus.
units.tr: Let us now try to untie this most grave difficulty. First, we will readily confess that Jacob wrestled with Christ, the Son of God. But secondly, we add that Christ the Son of God, in this solemn single combat [μονομαχίᾳ], sustained the person of God the Father, in accordance with the character of the mediatorial office which he discharged among men, and which he took up from the very beginning of sin: sometimes to sustain the person of the guilty man against God, and sometimes the person of the Father of the supreme deity against the guilty man, as in this sacred duel. For God the Father, since his wisdom and justice forbid it, never deals directly with men who confess themselves guilty of treason against his majesty, as he himself declared to Moses after the people had confessed their idolatry in worshipping the golden calf, Exod. 33: 1. 2. 3. He therefore deals with them through the Son, sent as mediator in his name, as his Angel, to represent and sustain his person before them. This is of great importance for illuminating Scripture, and it is clear from the history of the law given and promulgated a second time. For the law is said to have been promulgated on Mount Sinai, where Moses, lying prostrate for forty days, pleaded earnestly for pardon of sins and remission of punishment for the idolatrous people. But that person who addressed Moses, though he was true God and the God of Israel, was not the Father but the Son of God, sustaining the person of the Father; for he is called an Angel, Acts 7: 38, a name of which God the Father is never and nowhere said to be, for the reasons we have mentioned above. The remaining matters that pertain to the full explanation of this type we will pursue further on, with God's good help. Now let us return from this important digression to our path.

units.la: Observamus 3°. Coelum in Scriptura passim Deum significare Pf. 73:9. Dan. 4:26. Matth. 21:25. Luc. 15:18.21. Joan. 3:27. Hinc regnum coelorum apud Matthaeum passim, apud alios Euangelistas regnum Dei dicitur. Matth. 4:17. Marc. 1:15. Matth. 5:3. Luc. 6:20. Matth. 11:11. Luc. 7:28. Matth. 13:11. Luc 8:10. Hinc Rabbini in Dei nominibus םיָמַשָּׁה recenseresolent, & Talmudici passim adjutorium coeli, cultum coeli, mortem per manum coeli, pro adjutorio Dei, cultu Dei, mortem per manum Dei, usurpant. Non modo, quod coelum illustre sit Dei domicilium; sed & ipsius splendidissimus typus capacitatis, lucis, puritaritatis, durationis & influxus efficacissimi ergo. 4°. Terra naturam humanam, seu mundum hominum significat. Pf. 60: 4. Jef. 49: 8. Hof. 1: 2. Matth. 13: 4. Heb. 6: 7. Apoc. 13: 3. 5°. Scalam simul Filium Dei inter, & Jacobum, mediam, simul coelum inter, & terram, adumbrasse primum unionem Filii Dei cum natura humana, seu Christum Immanuelem Θεάνθρωπον Deum simul, & hominem, secundo ipsius officium mediatorium liquet; ipse enim unus est mediator Deum inter & homines, tum naturarum communione quia ille ipse unus & Deus & homo, tum officio nempe quà Pontifex Propheta & Rex coelum, seu Deum, & terram, seu homines efficacissimè reconciliat. Ut Angeli Dei per eum descendant in terram ad homines, & iterum ad Deum & in coelum redeant exactam Deo & domino suo rationem ministerii sui perhibituri. Integrum igitur Jacobi insomnium in Christum filium hominis unicè collineabat olim in plenitudine temporum luculentum in eo implementum, scrtiturum.
units.tr: We observe, thirdly, that heaven in Scripture everywhere signifies God (Ps. 73:9; Dan. 4:26; Matt. 21:25; Luke 15:18, 21; John 3:27). Hence "the kingdom of heaven" is used throughout Matthew, while the other Evangelists say "the kingdom of God" (Matt. 4:17; Mark 1:15; Matt. 5:3; Luke 6:20; Matt. 11:11; Luke 7:28; Matt. 13:11; Luke 8:10). Hence too the rabbis count hashamayim [השָּׁמַיִם] among the names of God, and the Talmudists everywhere use "the help of heaven," "the worship of heaven," and "death by the hand of heaven" for the help of God, the worship of God, and death by the hand of God. This is not only because heaven is the illustrious dwelling of God, but also because it is the most splendid type of capacity, light, purity, and enduring and most effective influence. Fourthly, earth signifies human nature, or the world of men (Ps. 60:4; Isa. 49:8; Hos. 1:2; Matt. 13:4; Heb. 6:7; Rev. 13:3). Fifthly, the ladder, standing between the Son of God and Jacob and between heaven and earth, at once foreshadowed the first union of the Son of God with human nature, Christ Immanuel, God-man [Θεάνθρωπον], both God and man, and secondly it makes clear his mediatorial office. For he is "one mediator between God and men" (1 Tim. 2:5), both by the communion of natures, since he himself is one God and man, and by office, namely as Priest, Prophet and King, by whom he most effectively reconciles heaven, that is God, and earth, that is men. Through him the angels of God descend to men on earth and return again to God and heaven, to render an exact account of their ministry to God their Lord. Therefore Jacob's whole dream was aimed solely at Christ, the Son of man, and was in the fullness of time to find its clear fulfilment in him.

units.la: Ita ut sentiamus Christus ipse nobis author est geminis in locis, quæ huc penitus respiciunt. Primus extat Joan. 1: 51. Amen Amen dico vobis in pesterum videbitis coelum apertum, & Angelos Dei ascendentes & descendentes ad Filium hominis. Utique igitur visuri erant discipuli, quod Jacobus in somnio viderat. At non viderat Angelos Dei ascendentes, & descendentes ad Filium hominis, nisi semel statueris simul Jeheve, simul Jacobum hinc inde supra, & infra scalam, Filium hominis in carne manifestandum, moriturum, e morte exiturum, in coelum ascensurum, & e coelo demum descensurum; Angelis Dei ascendentem & descendentem comitantibus, patriarchæ præfigurasse; secus enim Jacobus Angelos Dei viderit, non ad Filium hominis, sed contra ad Deum patrem ascendentes, & ad se distinctum à Filio hominis descendentes. Locus alter extat Joan. 3: a versu 12. ad 19. Hic enim loci, mystici insomnii luculenta interpretatio est. Hic cernas Filium hominis coelestia docentem, quia is unus ascendit in coelum hoc est phrasi Moysis, Deut. 30: 12. apprimè novit coelestia, quæ captum hominum naturalem immane superant, sicut Jacobus Filium hominis videbat, coelestia de semine nascituro Jacobi, de benedicendis in eo omnibus terræ gentibus, hoc est de mundo per eum salvando docentem. Hic cernas Filium hominis qui e coelo descenderat, in coelo existentem, vel dum erat in terra verf. 13. Non secus atque Jacobus Filium Dei videbat in coelo, vel dum e coelo descenderat, ut foret cum eo. Ecce ego tecum sum Gen. 28: 15. Et ut nasceretur ab eo semen ipsius benedicturum omnibus terrae nationibus. Hic cernas Filium hominis agitantem in terra Israëlis: sed & missum in mundum & mundo datum non ut perderet, sed ut mundum perditum servaret. Nempe Judaei orbem in partes ambas dividebant, quarum alteram vocabant Terram Israëlis: alteram extra terram, nimirum Israëlis, & orbem iterum in populos ambos, quorum alterum Israëlem: alterum nationes mundi. Christus igitur agitans inter Israëlitas, & in terra Israëlis, docet se Filium unigenitum Dei datum esse propter mundum, & missum in mundum, hoc est datum & missum propter omnes nationes mundi, quia Judaei in ea erant sententia, ut opinarentur Filium Dei Messiam venturum in salutem unius terrae, & populi Israëlis; idem docuit & Joannes dum infit, Ipse nempe Jesus Christus justus est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris, nec pro nostris solum, sed etiam pro totius mundi peccatis, 1 Joan. 2: 2.
units.tr: Christ himself is our authority for this in two places which bear directly on this matter. The first is John 1:51: "Verily, verily, I say unto you, hereafter you shall see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man." Assuredly, then, the disciples were to see what Jacob had seen in his dream. But Jacob would not have seen the angels of God ascending and descending to the Son of man, unless you decide that Jehovah and Jacob both stood, one above and the other below the ladder, and that the Son of man, to be manifested in the flesh, to die, to rise from death, to ascend into heaven and at last to descend from heaven, was prefigured to the patriarch, with the angels of God accompanying him as he ascended and descended. Otherwise Jacob would have seen the angels of God ascending not to the Son of man but to God the Father, and descending to one distinct from the Son of man. The second place is John 3:12–19. Here is a clear interpretation of the mystical dream. Here you see the Son of man teaching heavenly things, because he alone "ascended into heaven" (in the phrase of Moses, Deut. 30:12), and knows the heavenly things that far exceed natural human understanding, just as Jacob saw the Son of man. He teaches heavenly things concerning the seed of Jacob that was to be born, and concerning the blessing of all the nations of the earth in him, that is, concerning the world to be saved through him. Here you see the Son of man who had come down from heaven, existing in heaven, or while he was on earth (v. 13). Just as Jacob saw the Son of God in heaven, or as he came down from heaven, so that he might be with him: "Behold, I am with you" (Gen. 28:15), and that from him should be born the seed that would bless all the nations of the earth. Here you see the Son of man living on earth in the land of Israel, but also sent into the world and given to the world, not that he might condemn it, but that he might save the lost world. For the Jews divided the globe into two parts, one of which they called "the land of Israel," the other "outside the land," that is, of Israel; and again they divided the globe into two peoples, one "Israel," the other "the nations of the world." Christ, therefore, living among the Israelites and in the land of Israel, teaches that he is the only-begotten Son of God given for the world, and sent into the world, that is, given and sent for all the nations of the world. The Jews held the view that the Son of God would come as the Messiah for the salvation of one land and the people of Israel alone. John taught the same when he said that Jesus Christ the righteous "is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world" (1 John 2:2).

units.la: Sed vero & ratio, ut in hac sententia perstemus jubet: Nam 1°. Quidquid Filius hominis divite sua nomenclatione complectitur, Jacobi insomnium juxta hanc mentem explicatum, habet. Etenim Filius hominis, quia idem atque Christus est, 1°. persona est Filii Dei, 2°. Immanuel Deus & homo, divinae simul ac humanae naturae communione, 3°. cum naturarum communione, tum officio Mediator, coelum inter & terram, Deum & homines, 4°. Christus unctus in Pontificem, & Prophetam, & Regem omnium creaturarum & comprimis fidelium, 5°. denique Jesus hoc est mundi Salvator. Haec vero omnia, non in una scala sorsim a Jeheve, & Jacobo spectata; sed integrum Jacobi insomnium abunde complectitur. Hic enim 1°. cernitur persona Filii Dei, Jacobum compellans. 2°. Immanuel Deus & homo, natura Filii Dei juncta per scalam mediam, naturae humanae Iacobi, ut idem, qui Iacobum alloquitur sit ipsius semem nasciturum sc. ex eo secundum carnem, ut in eo omnes terrae gentes benedicantur. Galat. 3. 3°. hic cernitur Mediatorium Filii Dei officium per scalam parte summa, & infima coelum & terram Deum & mundum conjungentem. 4°. Hic cernuntur terna Filii hominis, seu Christi munia, cernitur enim praeclare fungens officio Pontificis, qui pacem, & communionem conciliat coelum inter & terram, nam quatenus Pontifex sanguine sui sacrificii, pacem fecit per sanguinem crucis, & reconciliavit omnia in ipsum, tum qua in terra, tum qua in coelis, Coloss. 1: 20. Cernitur exercens propheticum munus, praedicit enim fore, ut in Iacobo & semine ipsius, omnes nationes terrae benedicantur, sitque Iacobi posteritas numeromerosissima latè per orbem, quà patet, ad Orientem & Occidentem, Septentrionem & Meridiem, diffundenda: cernitur denique Rex summus totius orbis, qui terram Canaan dono dat Iacobi posteris, & Angelos habet ministros obsequiosos, qui ad ipsius nutum ascendunt, & descendunt. 5°. Denique Iesus, hoc est Salvator cernitur in insomnio, multifariam, est enim Deus Abrahami, & Isaaci parentum, atque adeo Deus Iacobi vi foederalis formulae Gen. 17:7. 8. Deum vero ubi se profitetur docet se esse potentissimum ab omni malo, vel ab ipsa morte liberatorem, & munificentissimum in coelestem & aeternam foelicitatem remuneratorem. Est denique futurum Iacobi semen in quo benedicentur omnes nationes terrae, hoc est mundus universus. Scala verò seorsim spectata, nec personam Filii Dei viventem, loquentem, promittentem, & Angelis imperantem, nec ipsius naturam divinam, & humanam, nec ipsius salutem: sed unionem naturarum duntaxat, & mediationem coelum inter & terram, adumbrare potest.
units.tr: Moreover, reason also bids us persist in this view. For, first, whatever the Son of man comprehends in his rich name is contained in Jacob's dream, when it is explained in this sense. For the Son of man, since he is the same as Christ, is (1) the person of the Son of God; (2) Immanuel, God and man, by the communion of divine and human nature; (3) by the communion of natures and by office, the Mediator between heaven and earth, between God and men; (4) Christ anointed as Priest, Prophet and King of all creatures, and especially of believers; and (5) finally Jesus, that is, the Saviour of the world. All these are seen not separately, on a ladder alone, by Jehovah and Jacob, but are fully embraced by Jacob's whole dream. Here, first, the person of the Son of God is seen, addressing Jacob. Second, Immanuel, God and man, is seen, with the nature of the Son of God joined by the middle of the ladder to the human nature of Jacob, so that he who speaks to Jacob is the one who would be born of his seed, that is, from him according to the flesh, so that in him all the nations of the earth would be blessed (Gal. 3). Third, the Mediatorial office of the Son of God is seen, through the ladder, whose upper and lower parts join heaven and earth, God and the world. Fourth, the three offices of the Son of man, or Christ, are seen here. For he is seen clearly discharging the office of Priest, who brings peace and communion between heaven and earth, since as Priest, by the blood of his sacrifice, "he made peace through the blood of his cross, and reconciled all things to himself, whether things on earth or things in heaven" (Col. 1:20). He is seen exercising the prophetic office, for he foretells that in Jacob and his seed all the nations of the earth will be blessed, and that Jacob's posterity will become very numerous and spread abroad widely over the world, extending to the east and west, north and south. Lastly, he is seen as the supreme King of the whole world, who gives the land of Canaan to the posterity of Jacob, and has obedient angels as ministers, who ascend and descend at his nod. Fifth, Jesus, that is, the Saviour, is seen in the dream in many ways: he is the God of Abraham and Isaac, the parents, and so the God of Jacob by the force of the covenant formula (Gen. 17:7–8). When he declares himself God, he teaches that he is most powerful to deliver from all evil, even from death itself, and most bountiful as the rewarder with heavenly and eternal happiness. Finally, the seed of Jacob is to come, in whom all the nations of the earth, that is, the whole world, will be blessed. But the ladder, considered by itself, can represent neither the living, speaking, promising person of the Son of God who commands the angels, nor his divine and human nature, nor his salvation, but only the union of the natures and the mediation between heaven and earth.

units.la: Age nunc demonstremus paulo fusius, quàm divinè haec integra visio personam Christi Θεάνθρωπος, mediatorium officium, ejusque efficacium & effecta salutaria, adumbraverit.
units.tr: Let us now show, a little more fully, how this whole vision divinely foreshadows the person of Christ, the God-man [Θεάνθρωπος], his mediatorial office, and its efficacy and saving effects.

units.la: Christi personam quod attinet, ille Immanuel Deus nobiscum Θεάνθρωπος Deus & homo in unitate personae est, nempe Deus misit Filium suum factum ex muliere. Gal. 4:4. Sed enim in hac visione 1°. Deus & homo cernitur conjunctis per scalam mediam natura divina celsissima personae Filii Dei innixi fastigio scalae, & infima natura humana Jacobi humi jacentis ad pedem scalae. 2°. Sicut in visione Jacobi Deus in coelo supremo est יהוה excelsus, sed homo Deo conjunctus humilis humi jacens. Non secus & in Christo Deus in coelo & homo simul humilis atque despectus in terra fuit Joh. 3:13. 3°. Ut in visione mystica Deus apparet summâ majestate conspicuus supremus mundi dominus, qui & terram, Jacobo ubi dormit, se dono daturum recipit, simul benedictionem salutarem omnibus mundi gentibus; Atenim gloriosus ille Deus cum homine est אנכי עמך Ego tecum sum: sed cum homine exule domo parentis, profugo, paupere, ope omni humana destituto, & summè in deserto afflicto. Nihilo secius in Filio hominis Christo Apostoli contemplati sunt Dominum gloriae & gloriam unigeniti ex Patre dominantis in mare & ventos, diabolos, sepulchrum & mortem, condonantis peccata, caecorum oculos aperientis, leprosos purgantis, mortuos excitantis, coelum & Paradisum latroni promittentis. Sed enim Dominum illum gloriae Deumque benedictum concontuiti sunt in homine pauperrimo ipsis cœli avibus, & vulpeculis pauperiore, ut non haberet, ubi caput reclinaret, sed & despectissimo verme, fratribus suis Judæis exoso, funestis ipsorum minis obnoxio, & in locis desertis versanti, furorem inimicorum suorum ut declinaret. 4°. Ut in mystica visione simul Deum viventem, loquentem & immensæ majestatis insignia præ se ferentem cernimus; simul hominem humi jacentem & dormientem, cujus tamen anima cum Deo versatur, & in medio somno numerosam prolem à se oriundam intuetur; non absimili ratione in diebus carnis Christi Israëlitarum natio vidit simul Deum viventem, simul hominem mortuum terram concutientem, sepulchra aperientem, rupes dividentem, profundâ eclipsi solem ferientem, benedictum cœli Paradisum latroni promittentem, numerosam prolem è somno suæ mortis producentem, cujus anima apud Deum versatur in cœlo, dùm corpus exsangue humi jacet mortuum. 5°. Ut in Jacobæa visione Deum cernimus & hominem, Deum quidem Luzæ incolis & accolis incognitum; sed notum Jacobo & Angelis famulantibus: hominem verò, qui vel exosus, exul, profugus & propter odium fraternum miserrimus, Patriarchalis tamen familiæ primogenitus est, paternaque benedictione mactatus: parili plane modo in Filio hominis Christo verum Deum cernimus Judæis ignotum, sibi ipsi modò, Angelisque Dei perspectum & honoratum: sed & in ipso hominem, qui etsi pauperrimus, despectus & exosus omnibus est, primogenitus tamen est omnis creaturæ & inter multos fratres.
units.tr: As for the person of Christ, that Immanuel, "God with us" [Deus nobiscum], the God-man [Θεάνθρωπος], "God and man," is one person, namely: "God sent his Son, made of a woman" (Gal. 4:4). In this vision, first, God and man are seen joined by the middle ladder: the supreme nature of the divine person of the Son of God rests on the top of the ladder, and the lowest nature, the human nature of Jacob lying on the ground, is at the foot of the ladder. Second, as in Jacob's vision God is high in heaven, יהוה [Jehovah] "exalted," while the man joined to God lies low on the ground, so too in Christ God was in heaven while man was at the same time lowly and despised on earth (John 3:13). Third, as in the mystical vision God appears, conspicuous in supreme majesty, the supreme lord of the world, who also receives the land where Jacob sleeps to give to him, and at the same time a saving blessing to all the nations of the world; and yet that glorious God is with the man, אנכי עמך [I am with you]: but he is with a man exiled from his parents' home, a fugitive, poor, deprived of all human help, and greatly afflicted in the wilderness. Nonetheless, in the Son of man, Christ, the Apostles beheld the "Lord of glory" and "the glory of the only-begotten from the Father," ruling over the sea and winds, demons, the grave and death, forgiving sins, opening the eyes of the blind, cleansing lepers, raising the dead, and promising heaven and Paradise to the thief. But they saw that Lord of glory and blessed God in a most poor man, poorer than the birds of the heavens and the foxes, so that he "had nowhere to lay his head," and also in a most despised worm, hated by his Jewish brethren, exposed to their deadly threats, and moving about in deserted places to avoid the fury of his enemies. Fourth, in the mystical vision we see God living, speaking, and bearing the marks of immense majesty, and at the same time a man lying low and asleep, whose soul nevertheless is with God, and who in the midst of sleep sees a numerous offspring descended from himself. By a not dissimilar reasoning, in the days of Christ's flesh the Israelite nation saw at once the living God, and at once a dead man shaking the earth, opening the tombs, splitting the rocks, striking the sun with a deep eclipse, promising the thief the blessed Paradise of heaven, and bringing forth from the sleep of his death a numerous offspring, whose soul is with God in heaven while his lifeless body lies dead on the ground. Fifth, in Jacob's vision we see God and a man: God indeed, unknown to the inhabitants and sojourners of Luz, but known to Jacob and to the Angels who serve him; and a man who, though hated, exiled, a fugitive and most wretched because of his brother's hatred, is nevertheless the firstborn of the patriarchal family and is blessed by his father's blessing. In just the same way, in the Son of man Christ, we see the true God, unknown to the Jews, now known and honoured by himself and by the Angels of God; and in him we see a man who, though most poor, despised and hated by all, is nevertheless the firstborn of every creature and among many brethren.

units.la: 6°. Uti cœlum ad scalam visionis Jacobææ aperitur, quia Deum habet summa ex parte viventem actionibusque vitæ divinæ præclarè fungentem, hominem verò ex parte infima dormientem. Ita & cœlum reapse apertum fuit tùm ut Deus hinc blandè alloqueretur homines, Angelos mitteret, lætos nuntios, & munera Spiritus Sancti in homines sibi reconciliatos effunderet, tùm vota eorum & preces ut exaudiret, eos demum integros ad beatas Paradisi sedes ut admitteret, sed ea propter cœlum apertum est, quod Christus simul fuerit Deus æternùm vivens dominusque gloriæ, simul homo mortuus, ut uno merito viventis simul atque mortui, cœlum hominibus Deo reconciliatis & admittendis reseratum fuerit, libertatem habemus ingrediendi sacrarium per sanguinem Jesu, ea via, quam dedicavit nobis recentem & vivam per velum hoc est, per carnem suam, Hebr. 10: 19.20.
units.tr: Sixth, as heaven is opened at the ladder of Jacob's vision, because it has God living in its highest part and fulfilling the functions of divine life in an excellent way, while man lies asleep in its lowest part, so also heaven was truly opened, both so that God might from there speak kindly to men, send Angels as joyful messengers, and pour out the gifts of the Holy Spirit upon men reconciled to himself, and so that he might hear their vows and prayers and at last admit them whole into the blessed seats of Paradise. Heaven was opened for this reason, that Christ was at once God, living eternally and Lord of glory, and at once a dead man, so that by the one merit of him who is both living and dead, heaven was unlocked for men reconciled to God and to be admitted: "We have confidence to enter the sanctuary by the blood of Jesus, by the way which he has consecrated for us, new and living, through the veil, that is, through his flesh" (Heb. 10:19, 20).

units.la: 7°. Sicut Angeli è cœlo aperto descendentes moxque ad cœlum ascendentes afflictum & in solitudine versantem Jacobum solantur, suoque illo descensu & ascensu de providentia & amore Dei faciunt quàm certissimum. Non secus & Angelus ex cœlo aperto descendit, ut Christum in agone mortis afflictissimum soletur colloquio videlicet opportuno, quo in memoriam revocet, nec quicquam obstante potestate tenebrarum, maledictione legis, horrore mortis tremendique justitiæ vindicatricis calicis, eum esse unigenitum & unicè charum Patris Filium, qui se miserit, illi ut annuntiet fore ut in gloriam cœli aperti triumphalem in modum evehatur.
units.tr: Seventh, just as the Angels descending from the open heaven and immediately ascending again comfort Jacob, afflicted and dwelling in solitude, and by that descent and ascent make the providence and love of God most certain to him, so too an Angel descends from the open heaven to comfort Christ, most afflicted in the agony of death. He does so by a fitting conversation, calling to mind that, despite the power of darkness, the curse of the law, the horror of death and the dreadful cup of avenging justice, he is the only-begotten and uniquely beloved Son of the Father, who sent him, and he announces to him that he will be lifted up in triumph into the glory of the open heaven.

units.la: 8°. Sicut in visione Jacobæa Jacobus ille, qui in deserto obdormierat in petra pro cervicali, expergefactus cognoscit se versari in domo Dei & ad portam cœli, eodem plane pacto Christus somno profundo mortis maledictæ correptus extra portam Hierosolymorum in Calvaria deserto horrido, ingruentibus geminæ noctis tenebris, illinc corporeis ex solis deliquio, hinc spiritualibus ex potestate tenebrarum, demum resurrectione expergefactus, heu quantum se ab illo statu mutatum miratur, conscius versari sese ad portam cœli, viventem gloriosum & immortalem, dignumque qui cum applausu Angelorum & jubilatione in sanctuarium cœleste intromittatur.
units.tr: Eighth, as in Jacob's vision, Jacob, who had fallen asleep in the wilderness with a stone for a pillow, on waking knows that he is in the house of God and at the gate of heaven, so in exactly the same way Christ, seized by the deep sleep of accursed death outside the gate of Jerusalem, on Calvary, a desolate place, while the twofold darkness of night gathers, on one side from the failing of the sun's bodily light and on the other from the power of spiritual darkness, is at last awakened by the resurrection. Alas, how greatly he marvels at how changed he is from that state, knowing that he is now at the gate of heaven, living, glorious and immortal, and worthy to be brought into the heavenly sanctuary with the applause and rejoicing of the Angels.

units.la: 9°. Sicuti missus à parente Isaaco Jacobus, ut è conditione quieta domo parentis in Mesopotamiam descenderet, ad iter laboriosum se accinxit non splendido stipatus famulitio servorum, decem camelorum, nec instructus pretiosissima supellectile vestium, annulorum, armillarum cæterorumque id genus monilium aureorum uti Eliezer abavi Abrahami servus, sed omnibus opibus vacuus, fultus uno tantum baculo. Non secus & Christus missus à Deo, non in illa Dei forma, in qua prius erat stipatus æternæ majestatis radiis & divitiis, sed in forma illa servi abjectissimi, sese tamen &Ιῶν viator, ad iter laboriosum accinxit, ut è beatissima Dei parentis domo ad desertum hocce nostrum descenderet somno mortis maledictæ corripiendus: Ecce veni Deus ut faciam voluntatem tuam, Psalm. 40: 8. Ego pono animam meam ut eam rursus assumam, potestatem habeo deponendi eam & potestatem rursus eam assumendi, hoc præceptum accepi à patre meo, Joh. 10: 17. 18.
units.tr: Ninth, as Jacob, sent by his father Isaac to go down from his father's quiet home into Mesopotamia, girded himself for a laborious journey, not attended by a splendid retinue of servants, nor with ten camels, nor furnished with the most precious household goods of garments, rings, bracelets and other such golden ornaments, as Eliezer, the servant of Abraham's grandfather, was, but empty of all wealth and supported only by a single staff; so too Christ, sent by God, not in that form of God in which he was previously surrounded by the rays and riches of eternal majesty, but in the form of a most abject servant, girded himself as a traveller [ἰών, going] for a laborious journey, so that he might descend from the most blessed house of God the Father to this wilderness of ours, to be seized by the sleep of accursed death: "Behold, I come, O God, to do your will" (Ps. 40:8). "I lay down my life that I may take it again. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. This command I have received from my Father" (John 10:17, 18).

units.la: 10°. Sicut Jacobus domo paterna exire & in Mesopotamiam descendere jussus est à patre Isaaco, uxorem ut duceret, simili planè pacto jussus à Deo Patre è cœlo Christus descendit venitque in mundum dum sibi Ecclesiam ut desponsaret in saeculum fide, justitia, judicio, benignitate ac misericordia, Hose. 2: 19. 20.
units.tr: Tenth, as Jacob was ordered by his father Isaac to leave his father's house and go down into Mesopotamia to take a wife, in just the same way Christ, ordered by God the Father, came down from heaven and entered the world, in order to betroth to himself the Church "forever, in righteousness, judgment, kindness and mercy, and in faithfulness" (Hos. 2:19, 20).

units.la: 11°. Uti Jacob ducturus uxorem Rachelem, primogenitam prius Leam, Rachelem tandem natu minorem duxit, ut pro una duas uxores sorores habuerit. Nihilo secius Christus sibi Ecclesiam gentium desponsaturus, natu majorem primum Judæorum Ecclesiam, postmodum & natu minorem sororem gentium Ecclesiam sibi desponsavit, ut ex duabus gentibus unam sibi duxerit Ecclesiam sponsam legitimam, nunc autem per Jesum Christum vos qui ante longinqui fuistis propinqui facti estis per sanguinem Christi, ipse enim est pax nostra, qui fecit ambos unum, nempe veniens evangelizavit pacem vobis longinquis & propinquis. Eph. 2: 13. 14. 17.
units.tr: Eleventh, as Jacob, about to take Rachel as wife, first took Leah, the elder, and afterwards took Rachel, the younger, so that he had two wives, sisters, for one; so Christ, about to betroth to himself the Church of the Gentiles, first betrothed to himself the elder, the Church of the Jews, and afterwards also the younger sister, the Church of the Gentiles, so that from two peoples he made one Church his lawful bride: "But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ. For he himself is our peace, who has made the two one, and he came and preached peace to you who were far off and to those who were near" (Eph. 2:13, 14, 17).

units.la: 12°. Quemadmodum missus a patre Jacobus ea lege uxorem duxit, ut pastorem ageret & longam servitutem ac laboriosam illam serviret, ut interdiu eum absumeret æstus & gelu noctu, profugeretque somnus ab oculis ejus. Gen. 31: 40. duris illis perpetuisque laboribus uxorem sibi ut comparaverit. Eodem plane pacto Christus a Patre missus in mundum eâ lege Ecclesiam duxit, ut pastorem ageret obnoxius potestati tenebrarum & horrori funestæ noctis, ut Ecclesiam in hæc verba compellaverit: aperi mihi soror mea, nam caput meum oppletum est rore, capilli mei aspersionibus nocturnis, Cantic. 5: 2. mortique certissimæ sese exponeret bonus pastor daturus animam suam pro ovibus suis, Deusque in sæculum benedictus proprio sanguine Ecclesiam sibi acquireret Act. 20: 28. quod & lubens præstitit, cujus amor, flammâ vehementissimâ morte ipsa, fortior fuit Cantic. 8: 6. 7. Nempe Christus dilexit Ecclesiam (sicut Jacob Rachelem suam) & tradidit semetipsum pro ea oblationem ac victimam Deo in odorem bonæ fragrantiæ, ut eam sanctificaret & sisteret sibi gloriosam, non habentem maculam aut rugam, aut quicquam ejusmodi, sed ut sit sancta & inculpata, Eph. 5: 2. 26. 27.
units.tr: 12. Just as Jacob, sent by his father, took a wife on the condition that he would tend the flocks and serve that long and laborious servitude, so that by day the heat consumed him, and by night the frost, and sleep fled from his eyes (Gen. 31:40), and by those hard and unending labours he won his wife for himself. In exactly the same way, Christ, sent by the Father into the world, took the Church on that condition: that he would act as shepherd, subject to the power of darkness and the terror of the deadly night, so that he addressed the Church in these words, open to me, my sister, for my head is wet with dew and my locks with the drops of the night (Cant. 5:2). He exposed himself to certain death, the good shepherd who gives his life for his sheep (Acts 20:28), and God, blessed for ever, acquired the Church for himself with his own blood. This he also did willingly, and his love, fiercer than death itself, was stronger than the flame (Cant. 8:6, 7). Indeed, Christ loved the Church (as Jacob loved his Rachel), and gave himself up for her as an offering and a sacrifice to God, a fragrant aroma, so that he might sanctify her and present her to himself in glory, not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but that she might be holy and blameless (Eph. 5:2, 26, 27).

units.la: 13°. Sicut expergefactus Jacobus super visionem admirabundus exclamavit, quàm reverendus est hic locus, hic locus domus Dei est & porta cœli, Genes. 28: 17. nempe propter cœlum apertum, erectam scalam, cœlum & terram conjungentem, Deum alloquentem & Angelos ascendentes & descendentes. Non secus & quisquis attento animo Christum Mediatorem contemplatus, optimo jure admirabundus in hæc verba eruperit, quam reverendus iste est, quam admirabilis atque tremendus Deus æternus & homo temporarius, Abrahamo junior & antiquior, quem omnes Angeli Dei adorant, hæc est porta cœli & domus Dei, nempè tota plenitudo divinitatis in Christo habitat corporaliter, non in umbra, sicut illa nubes שכינה in tabernaculo templove Hierosolymorum, quippe λόγος sermo ille Dei æternus ἐσκήνωσεν ἐν ἡμῖν inter nos habitavit tanquam in tabernaculo, Joh. 1: 14. ut de se homine absque blasphemia, vel sacrilegio jure dixerit: dissolvite hoc templum & intra triduum excitabo illud, Joh. 2: 19. scilicet in Christo grata Deo & accepta sunt omnia fidelium sacrificia spiritualia, in eo communionem habemus cum Deo, in eo verba commutamus cum Numine, illique jubenti, quærite faciem meam, respondemus: quaram faciem tuam Domine: in eo, demum Deus benedixit nobis omnibus benedictionibus spiritualibus è locis cœlestibus, uti populo Israeli solemnem benedictionem impertiebatur in templo.
units.tr: 13. When Jacob woke from his sleep, he cried out in wonder over the vision, how awesome is this place! This is the house of God and the gate of heaven (Gen. 28:17). That is because heaven stood open, the ladder was set up joining heaven and earth, God spoke, and the angels went up and down. In the same way, whoever contemplates Christ the Mediator with an attentive mind may rightly break out in wonder: how awesome is he, how admirable and terrible is this eternal God and temporal man, younger and older than Abraham, whom all the angels of God worship. This is the gate of heaven and the house of God, for all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily in Christ, not in a shadow, as that cloud, the Shechinah [שכינה], dwelt in the tabernacle or temple at Jerusalem. Indeed, the eternal Word of God, the λόγος [logos], became flesh and dwelt among us (ἐσκήνωσεν ἐν ἡμῖν [eskēnōsen en hēmin]) as in a tabernacle (John 1:14). So too he could rightly say of himself, without blasphemy or sacrilege, destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up (John 2:19). In Christ, then, all the spiritual sacrifices of the faithful are pleasing and acceptable to God; in him we have fellowship with God; in him we exchange words with the Deity. When he bids us, seek my face, we answer, your face, Lord, I will seek. In him, at last, God has blessed us with every spiritual blessing from the heavenly places, just as in the temple he gave the solemn blessing to the people of Israel.

units.la: Sed & hæc Jacobæa visio, scalâ illâ admirandâ, officium Christi mediatorium, quam divinissimè adumbravit.
units.tr: But this Jacobean vision, with that wonderful ladder, also set forth very divinely the mediatorial office of Christ.

units.la: Primò. Sicut scala media nihil quicquam obstante immensa distantia 1°. Deum innixum fastigio, Jacobo humi jacenti ad pedem consociavit. Non secus ineffabilis unio immensam Filii Dei personam, naturæ humanæ inculo haud solubili sociavit, nec quicquam obstante intercapedine infinitâ. 2°. Sicut divina illa scala cœlum & terram utrinque contingebat, quia altera ex parte erat Filius Dei, Deo Patri proximus intimusque, altera vero ex parte homo Jacobus. Nihilo secius Christus Mediator Deum inter & homines, cœlum & terram, Deum & homines pace æternâ & vinculo inviolabili conciliavit & conjunxit, quia Deus & homo est, Deo proximus & hominibus, ut opportunus Mediator naturarum communione & officio.
units.tr: First. Just as the ladder, though an immense distance lay between, joined God, resting on its summit, to Jacob lying on the ground at its foot, so the ineffable union joined the immense person of the Son of God to human nature, by a bond that cannot be dissolved, with no infinite gulf standing in the way. Second. Just as that divine ladder touched heaven and earth at either end, because at one end was the Son of God, very near and most intimate with God the Father, and at the other end was the man Jacob, so Christ the Mediator has reconciled and joined God and men, heaven and earth, God and men, in an eternal peace and an inviolable bond, because he is God and man, near to God and near to men, a fitting Mediator by his communion in both natures and by his office.

units.la: Secundò. Sicut scala Jacobæa cœlum inter & terram media, una est & unica memoratur in Scriptura. Non absimili modo Christus unus est Mediator Deum inter & homines, 1 Tim. 2: 5. ut in nullo alio quoquam sit salus, Act. 4: 12. Quàm blasphematorium in modum ergò Legendarius Antoninus agens de morte Dominici ait, Brixiensem (alii Leonem) charissimum Dominici discipulum eadem horâ, quâ Dominicus obiit, vidisse hiatum in cœlo, per quem summittebantur duæ scalæ candidissimæ, alii (quia perplexa & inconstans superstitio res est) alteram ferunt fuisse rubram, cujus fastigio innixus Christus, Dominici discipulos ad se vocaret; albam alteram, cui innixa virgo mater eosdem compellaret; illi autem positi in medio, quasi alter Masius Sylvaducensis Episcopus, quo se verterent nescii, monente Dominico per scalam rubram in cœlum ascendere aggressi & repulsam casumque misemiserum passi, tanto demum periculo cauti & justi meliora abs Domi-nico eorum miserto, per scalam albam beatæ virginis in cœlum exultabundi ascenderunt. Quis horrendam adeo blasphemiam tacitus ferat?
units.tr: Second. The ladder of Jacob, set between heaven and earth, is mentioned in Scripture as one and unique. In a not dissimilar way, Christ is one Mediator between God and men (1 Tim. 2:5), so that there is salvation in no one else (Acts 4:12). How blasphemously, then, the legend-writer Antoninus, speaking of the death of Dominic, says that Brixiensis (others say Leo), the dearest disciple of Dominic, saw at the same hour in which Dominic died a gap opened in heaven, through which two most white ladders were let down. Others (since superstition is a tangled and unstable thing) report that one was red, and Christ, standing on its top, called Dominic's disciples to himself; the other was white, and the Virgin Mother, leaning on it, summoned the same disciples. Those placed in the middle, like another Masius, bishop of Silvaducum, did not know where to turn. When Dominic urged them to climb to heaven by the red ladder, they set out, but were repulsed, and suffered a wretched fall. Finally, made cautious by so great a danger, and set right by Dominic's pity for them, they climbed exultantly to heaven by the white ladder of the blessed Virgin. Who could bear such a horrible blasphemy in silence?

units.la: Tertio. Sicut scala exquisitæ industriæ hominum arte factum opportunum est, quo ex imo se gradatim tollant in altum, & ex alto sensim atque gradatim ad imum descendant. Eodem plane pacto Christus Mediator naturarum divinæ & humanæ communione & officio, adorandæ Dei sapientiæ opportunum medium est, quo simul Angeli lucis ministri spiritus, ad eos descendant, quos Deus ex asse conscripsit hæredes salutis, simul omne bonum omnisque perfecta donatio à Patre luminum jugiter ad eos descendat Jac. 1:17.
