Unum quoque opportunumque medium est, quo fideles fide atque fiducia ad Deum accedant τὰ ἄνω φρονεῖτε Eph. 3:12. Hebr. 4:16. Col. 3:1. Demum integri corpore & animo ad cœlum rapiantur & Deum; ample subministrabitur vobis introitus in æternum regnum Domini nostri & Salvatoris Jesu Christi 2 Pet. 1:11. Nam Christus semel pro peccatis passus fuit, justus pro injustis, ut nos ad Deum adduceret 1 Pet. 3:18.
units.tr: Third. A ladder, made by the skill of men with exquisite craftsmanship, is a convenient means by which people raise themselves step by step from the bottom to the top, and descend gradually from the top to the bottom. In exactly the same way, Christ the Mediator, by his communion and office in the divine and human natures, is a fitting means of the adorable wisdom of God. By him the angels of light, the ministering spirits, descend to those whom God has enrolled entire as heirs of salvation, and at the same time every good thing and every perfect gift from the Father of lights continually descends to them (James 1:17). He is also the one fitting means by which the faithful draw near to God by faith and trust, setting their minds on things above (Eph. 3:12; Heb. 4:16; Col. 3:1). Finally, whole in body and soul, they are caught up to heaven and to God: an entrance will be richly supplied to you into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ (2 Pet. 1:11). For Christ suffered once for sins, the just for the unjust, so that he might bring us to God (1 Pet. 3:18).

units.la: Quarto. Sicuti Scala distinctis gradibus constat, unde κλίμαξ Græcis appellatur, ut sit acclivis ascendentibus, descentibus declivis. Ita & in Christo mediatore gradus distincti spectandi in Scriptura proponuntur, sive ipse Christus officio mediatorio functus spectetur, sive Deus in Christo Mediatore ad homines descendens, sive homines ad Deum per Christum accedentes & ascendentes considerentur. Primus gradus Christi Mediatoris in mundum descendentis ipsius nativitas & in carne manifestatio est, Deus misit Filium suum in forma carnis peccati Rom. 8:3. Ea enim descendit ad partes infimas terræ h. e. in terram partem mundi infimam Eph. 4:9. Secundus descensus Christi gradus, mors maledicta ejus est, ea enim descendit in abyssum maledictionis, ne dixeris in corde tuo, quis descendet in abyssum? Hoc est Christum ex mortuis reducere Rom. 10:7. Gradus tertius, descensus Christi est ad sepulchrum, hic enim est descensus Christi ad inferos, quo de Symbolum Apostolicum loquitur. Sed & Mediatorium Christi officium distinctis gradibus constat, quibus ad gloriæ fastigium è miseria summa conscendit. Primus gradus ejus resurrectio est, ut è diametro opponatur primo illi gradui descensus, quæ ejus nativitas est, sicut enim factus ex muliere filius hominis fuit, ita & mortuorum per resurrectionem primogenitus definitus est filius Dei in potentia Rom. 1: 4. Secundus, qui morti, seu descensui in abyssum maledictionis opponitur, ejus in cœlum ascensus est. Tertius, qui & descensui in sepulchrum statumque mortuorum, respondet e diametro, ejus sessio est ad dextram Patris: ne dixeris in corde tuo, quis ascendet in cœlum? Hoc est Christum ex alto deducere Rom. 10: 6. Qui descenderat, ipse est qui etiam ascendit longè supra omnes cœlos, ut impleret omnia. Eph. 4: 10. In habitudine ad Deum per Christum Mediatorem ad nos gratiosè descendentem distincti pariter gradus conspiciendi proponuntur. Primus Electio est, quos Deus prænovit, prædestinavit, ut conformes fierent imagini filii sui, ut sit primogenitus inter multos fratres Rom. 8: 28, 29. Secundus Vocatio efficax: quos prædestinavit, eos etiam vocavit. Tertius Justificatio quos vocavit, justificavit. Quartus Glorificatio, quæ ambitu suo gloriosò adoptionem, sanctificationem, corporum resurrectionem & beatam immortalitatem complectitur. Demum in habitudine ad nos Christi mediatio distinctis gradibus ex infima miseria ad beatam Dei communionem nos evehit. Primus gradus fidei est, qua Deo vocanti in salutem respondemus: fiat mihi secundum verbum tuum ô Deus. Secundus spes, quam uti firmam anchoram animæ habemus ingredientem intra velum, quo præcursor pro nobis ingressus est Jesus Hebr. 6: 19. 20. Tertius ardens animæ desiderium bonorum cœlestium, quo è mortuis excitati cum Christo quærunt quæ superna sunt, ubi Christus sedet ad dextram Dei Col. 3: 1. Quartus adversus Deum pietas & charitas, qua transformamur ex gloria in gloriam ad imaginem Dei & proximè ad eum accedimus facti natura divina participes 2 Cor. 3: 18. 2 Petr. 1: 4. Quintus Vota & preces. Sextus Corporis in vitam immortalem resurrectio. Septimus triumphalis ascensus in nubibus ad occursum Domini. Octavus in throno Christi sessio & regni æterna cum ipso possessio.
units.tr: Fourth. Just as a ladder consists of distinct rungs, and is therefore called klimax [κλίμαξ] by the Greeks, so that it slopes upwards for those climbing and downwards for those descending, so too in Christ the Mediator, distinct degrees are set forth in Scripture, whether Christ himself is considered as exercising his mediatorial office, or God is considered as descending to men in Christ the Mediator, or men are considered as coming to God through Christ and ascending. The first degree of Christ the Mediator descending into the world is his birth and manifestation in the flesh: God sent his Son in the form of sinful flesh (Rom. 8:3). For he descended into the lower parts of the earth, that is, into the lowest part of the world (Eph. 4:9). The second degree of Christ's descent is his accursed death, for he descended into the abyss of the curse: do not say in your heart, who will descend into the abyss? That is, to bring Christ back from the dead (Rom. 10:7). The third degree, Christ's descent, is to the sepulchre; this is indeed Christ's descent into hell, of which the Apostles' Creed speaks. But the mediatorial office of Christ also consists of distinct degrees, by which he climbs from the depths of misery to the height of glory. His first degree is the resurrection, which stands directly opposite the first degree of descent, which was his birth; for just as he became the Son of man from a woman, so he was declared the Son of God in power as the firstborn from the dead by the resurrection (Rom. 1:4). The second, which is opposed to death, or to the descent into the abyss of the curse, is his ascension into heaven. The third, which answers directly to the descent into the sepulchre and the state of the dead, is his session at the right hand of the Father: do not say in your heart, who will ascend into heaven? That is, to bring Christ down from above (Rom. 10:6). He who descended is the same who also ascended far above all the heavens, so that he might fill all things (Eph. 4:10). In relation to God, through Christ the Mediator graciously descending to us, distinct degrees likewise present themselves for consideration. The first is election: those whom God foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers (Rom. 8:28, 29). The second is effectual calling: those whom he predestined, these he also called. The third is justification: those whom he called, he also justified. The fourth is glorification, which, in its glorious compass, embraces adoption, sanctification, the resurrection of the body, and blessed immortality. Finally, in relation to us, the mediation of Christ raises us through distinct degrees from the lowest misery to blessed communion with God. The first degree is faith, by which we answer God's calling to salvation: let it be to me according to your word, O God. The second is hope, which we hold as a firm anchor of the soul, entering within the veil, where Jesus has entered as a forerunner for us (Heb. 6:19, 20). The third is the burning desire of the soul for heavenly goods, by which those raised with Christ from the dead seek the things that are above, where Christ sits at the right hand of God (Col. 3:1). The fourth is piety and love towards God, by which we are transformed from glory to glory into the image of God, and by which we draw near to him, having become partakers of the divine nature (2 Cor. 3:18; 2 Pet. 1:4). The fifth is vows and prayers. The sixth is the resurrection of the body into immortal life. The seventh is the triumphal ascent in the clouds to meet the Lord. The eighth is the session on the throne of Christ and the eternal possession of the kingdom with him.

units.la: Quintò. Intercessio Officii Mediatorii Christi pars memorabilis est: sed & illa efficacissima divinè adumbratur scalâ, illa visionis mysticæ. Nempè sicut in Scala filius Dei cernitur vivens, loquens & benedictionem impertiens Scalæ fastigio innixus & cœlum vertice tangens: Sed & ipse conjunctus conspicitur homini Jacobo jacenti & dormienti in ima illa parte Scalæ, quâ terram proximè tangit. Etiam paulò acriùs intuiti in Christum munere Mediatorio functum liquidò perspicimus Filium Dei ad dextram Majestatis in cœlo viventem & pro nobis intercedentem, ut affatim in nos defluant Spirituales Dei reconciliati benedictiones. Atenim eum cernimus pro nobis interpellantem, tem, quatenus fuit in carne mortificatus Apoc. 5: 6. Ut Christi intercessio uno mortis suæ merito nitatur, unde sancta Pauli gloriatio: quis intentabit crimina adversus electos Dei? Deus is est qui justificat; quis est qui condemnet? Christus is est qui mortuus est & qui surrexit, qui etiam est ad dextram Dei & interpellat pro nobis Rom. 8: 33. 34. Unus Deus est, unus etiam mediator Dei & hominum, homo Christus Jesus, qui seipsum dedit redemptionis pretium pro omnibus 1 Tim. 2: 5. 6. Eadem mens Johanni: si quis peccarit advocatum apud Patrem habemus Jesum Christum justum, ipse enim est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris &c. 1 Joh. 2: 1. 2. Ut intercessio advocati Christi eo fundamento nitatur apud Paulum & Johannem, nempe quòd mortuus sit, quòd seipsum pro omnibus redemptionis λύτρον dederit; quòd sit demum propitiatio pro peccatis totius mundi. Hanc Christi intercessionem uno nixam mortis ipsius Sacrificio, visione cœlesti adunde confirmatam dedit Deus Johanni Apoc. 5: 6. Aspexi, inquit, & ecce inter thronum & quatuor illa animalia & inter seniores illos agnus stans tanquam mactatus habens cornua septem & oculos septem, qui sunt septem Spiritus Dei emissi in omnem terram.
units.tr: Fifthly. The intercession of Christ's mediatorial office is a notable part of it, and that most effective intercession is also divinely foreshadowed by the ladder, in that mystical vision. For in the ladder the Son of God is seen living, speaking and bestowing a blessing, leaning on the top of the ladder and touching heaven with its summit. He is also seen joined to Jacob, who lies and sleeps at the bottom of the ladder, where it touches the earth. If we look a little more keenly at Christ discharging his mediatorial office, we clearly see the Son of God living at the right hand of the Majesty in heaven and interceding for us, so that the spiritual blessings of a reconciled God may flow down upon us abundantly. Indeed, we see him interceding for us, inasmuch as he was put to death in the flesh (Rev. 5:6). Christ's intercession rests on the single merit of his death, whence comes Paul's holy boast: who shall bring any charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies; who is he who condemns? It is Christ who died, and who rose again, who is also at the right hand of God and makes intercession for us (Rom. 8:33, 34). There is one God, and also one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself a ransom [λύτρον] for all (1 Tim. 2:5, 6). John has the same mind: if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; for he is the propitiation for our sins, etc. (1 John 2:1, 2). So the intercession of Christ as advocate rests on this foundation, according to Paul and John, namely that he died, that he gave himself a ransom [λύτρον] for all, and that he is finally the propitiation for the sins of the whole world. God gave John this intercession of Christ, resting on his one sacrifice of death and abundantly confirmed by a heavenly vision (Rev. 5:6): I looked, he says, and behold, between the throne and the four living creatures, and among the elders, stood a Lamb as though it had been slain, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven Spirits of God sent out into all the earth.

units.la: Accedimus ad efficaciam & effecta salutaria officii Mediatorii Σεωτ. Θεωπτ Christi, illa enim hac visione mystica præclare etiam adumbrantur.
units.tr: We come now to the efficacy and saving effects of the mediatorial office of Christ, the Saviour and God-man, for these too are clearly foreshadowed in this mystical vision.

units.la: Primo. Sicut Filius Dei & ipse homo in lumbis Jacobi eoque adumbratus cœlum inter & terram per scalam, medius utrumque contingit atque conjungit, nihil quicquam obstante immensa utrinque distantia. Non secus & Christus Σεαν Θεωπ funetus officio mediatorio cœlum & terram, Deum & homines propter peccatum dissitos immensum & separatos Esai. 59: 2. amicè conciliauit, quia in eo Pater voluit omnem plenitudinem habitare & per eum omnia sibi reconciliare, tùm quæ in terrâ, tum quæ in cœlis, pace per sanguinem crucis ejus facta Col. 1: 19. 20.
units.tr: First. Just as the Son of God, himself man, descended from the loins of Jacob and so foreshadowed, touches and joins heaven and earth by the ladder, standing between them, although there is an immense distance on either side, so Christ, discharging his mediatorial office as Saviour and God-man, has kindly reconciled heaven and earth, God and men, who were separated and set far apart by sin (Isa. 59:2), because the Father willed that all fullness should dwell in him, and through him to reconcile all things to himself, whether things on earth or things in heaven, making peace through the blood of his cross (Col. 1:19, 20).

units.la: Secundò. Sicut scala, quæ Deum hominemque habet in extremis suis, cœlum aperuit simul Filio Dei, simul Jacobo: Filio Dei, ut se Jacobo conspiciendum è cœlo aperto præberet: Jacobo, ut admirabundus in hæc verba erumperet: hæc est porta cæli & domus Dei. Eodem plane pacto Officium Christi Mediatorium cœlum clausum aperuit, simul Filio Dei, ut ad nos descenderet manifestatus in carne, iterumque ad cœlum ascenderet novi fœderis Pontifex pro nobis interpellaturus coram facie Dei in excelsis; simul Jacobo cæterisque fidelibus, is enim via est, veritas & vita, ut nemo possit ad Deum accedere nisi per Christum Joh. 14: 6.
units.tr: Second. Just as the ladder, which has God and man at its extremities, opened heaven at once for the Son of God and for Jacob: for the Son of God, so that he might show himself to Jacob, to be seen from the open heaven; for Jacob, so that in wonder he might break out in these words: this is the gate of heaven and the house of God. In exactly the same way, the mediatorial office of Christ has opened the closed heaven, both for the Son of God, so that he might come down to us, made manifest in the flesh, and ascend again to heaven, to intercede for us as the high priest of the new covenant before the face of God on high; and for Jacob and the other faithful, for he is the way, the truth and the life, so that no one can come to God except through Christ (John 14:6).

units.la: Tertiò. Sicut Mediâ illâ admirandâ Scalâ, Dei Filius ipsi innixus Iacobo abundè adeò benedixit, ut qui uno instructus baculo pauperrimus domo parentis descenderat, redux ascendat in patriam, ampla instructus divitiarum copia. Parili plane pacto Christus officio suo mediatorio præclarè adeò functus est, ut omnes benedictiones spirituales fidelibus suis impertierit Eph. 1: 3. Nempe Deus suscitatum Filium suum Iesum misit, qui nolas benedicere, unoquoque se avertente à pravitatibus suis Act. 3: 26.
units.tr: Third. Just as on that wondrous ladder the Son of God, leaning on it, blessed Jacob so abundantly that he who had gone down from his parents' house most poorly equipped, with only a single staff, went back up to his homeland richly supplied with an ample abundance of riches, so Christ, by his mediatorial office, has done so excellently that he has bestowed all spiritual blessings upon his faithful people (Eph. 1:3). For God, having raised up his Son Jesus, sent him to bless you, by turning each of you away from your iniquities (Acts 3:26).

units.la: Quartò. Sicut Jacobæa Scala extremis suis Deum hominemque conjungens, Angelis Dei descensum præbet ad terram & è terra ascensum in cœlum, ut commercium cœli & terræ jamdiu interceptum restituat. Similem utique in modum Christi θεανθρωπικῆς[?] mediatio, ita alienos Angelos & justitiæ vindicatricis adversus Adamum ministros exosis hominibus æterno pacis vinculo ita conciliavit amicos, ut omnes nunc administri sint Spiritus, qui mittuntur in ministerium propter eos, qui hereditatem consecuturi sunt salutis Heb. 1: 14.
units.tr: Fourth. Just as the ladder of Jacob, joining God and man at its extremities, offers to the angels of God a descent to earth and an ascent from earth to heaven, so as to restore the intercourse between heaven and earth that had long been broken off. In a similar way, the mediation of Christ, the God-man [θεανθρωπικῆς], has so reconciled to men who were hateful to it, with an eternal bond of peace, the angels who had been strangers, and the ministers of avenging justice against Adam, that all of them are now ministering spirits, sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation (Heb. 1:14).

units.la: Nec plenè visionem Jacobæam explanaturis nobis committendum est, ut ejus circumstantias silentio prætereamus.
units.tr: Nor should we, in explaining Jacob's vision fully, pass over in silence its circumstances.

units.la: Primò. Sicut cœlestis visionis copia Jacobo pastori facta est. Nihilosecius nativitas Filii Dei venientis in mundum, ut foret Christus Dominus, pastoribus Bethlehemiticis cum multitudine exercituum cœlestium h. e. Angelorum ascendentium & descendentium ad Filium hominis, revelata est.
units.tr: First. Just as the abundance of the heavenly vision was given to Jacob the shepherd, so nonetheless the birth of the Son of God coming into the world, that he might be Christ the Lord, was revealed to the shepherds of Bethlehem, together with a multitude of the heavenly army, that is, of angels ascending and descending upon the Son of man.

units.la: Secundò. Sicut data est in loco deserto, Jacobo Scalæ mysticæ visio. Non secus & revelatio Immanuelis ex virgine nati, in montibus Bethlehemiticis pastoribus forte divina contigit.
units.tr: Second. Just as the vision of the mystical ladder was granted to Jacob in a desert place, so the revelation of Immanuel born of a virgin came by divine chance to the shepherds in the hills of Bethlehem.

units.la: Tertiò. Ut Visio Scalæ nocte concubia mediisque in tenebris animo Jacobi vigilantis lapidisque pro cervicali recumbentis aperta fuit. Non secus & noctu Josepho in somnio Matth. 1: 20. Et pastoribus in eadem regione excubantibus & agentibus vigilias noctis super gregem suum, Christi mediatoris natales, Angelus Domini revelavit Luc. 2: 8. 10. 11.
units.tr: Third. Just as the vision of the ladder was opened in the night, in the midst of darkness, to Jacob's waking mind, as he lay with a stone for a pillow, so also in the night the Angel of the Lord revealed to Joseph in a dream (Matt. 1:20), and to the shepherds keeping watch in the same region and guarding their flock by night, the birth of Christ the Mediator (Luke 2:8, 10, 11).

units.la: QUAESTIO XI. Cur Christus solemni isthac loquendi formula, Amen, Amen, dico vobis, &c. promissionem visionis cœli aperti, cæterasque passim roborare voluerit?
units.tr: QUAESTIO XI. Why did Christ, by this solemn form of speech, Amen, Amen, I say to you, etc., wish to confirm the promise of the opened heaven and other things throughout his teaching?

units.la: Quid Christus isthac solemni formula loquendi Amen, Amen, dico vobis, significare voluerit, non una est Theologorum sententia. Patres, cum Græci, tum Latini, non pauci, ut Origines in Matth. 26. Chrysostomus Hom. 11. in Epist. ad Hebræos. Hieronymus in Ezech. 16. Augustinus Tract. 41. in Johannem, quandam juramenti speciem esse docent: sed & multi ex recentioribus in eam sententiam pedibus eunt. Hos dum refellit doctissimus Fullerus hoc argumento, In jurisjurandi religione semper interponitur Deus & testis & judex: at in formula illa Christi Amen non est attributum divinum, quo Deus ipse, seu increata veritas significetur. Immani incuria lapsus nobis videtur: nam Amen illustre est Numinis attributum, omnis benedicens in terra, benedicet per Deum Amen, & omnis jurans in terra, jurabit per Deum Amen, Jes. 65: 16. Et nomen אמן quod plane geminum est τῷ Amen, illustre pariter Dei attributum est, 2 Chron. 15: 3. Psalm. 31: 6. & Jerem. 10: 10.
units.tr: What Christ meant by this solemn form of speech, Amen, Amen, I say to you, is not a matter on which the theologians agree. Many of the Fathers, both Greek and Latin, teach that it is a kind of oath: Origen on Matthew 26, Chrysostom in Homily 11 on the Epistle to the Hebrews, Jerome on Ezekiel 16, and Augustine in Tractate 41 on John. Many of the more recent writers also go along with this view. The most learned Fuller refutes them with this argument: In the religion of an oath, God is always called in as witness and judge; but in that formula of Christ, Amen, there is no divine attribute by which God himself, or uncreated truth, is signified. He seems to us to have slipped through a huge carelessness, for Amen is a famous attribute of the Godhead: whoever blesses himself in the land will bless himself by the God of Amen, and whoever swears in the land will swear by the God of Amen, Isaiah 65:16. And the name אמן, which is plainly the same word as Amen, is likewise a famous attribute of God: 2 Chronicles 15:3, Psalm 31:6, and Jeremiah 10:10.

units.la: Alio igitur pugione sententia istiusmodi conficienda videtur. Et 1°. quidem juramenti formula solemnis est, & eorum, apud quos obtinet, unicuique obvia, nempe continetur verbis conceptis, quorum significatio & valor tum jurantibus, tum spectantibus innotescit. Unde cum Romani jurarent per templa Tonantis, h. e. per Capitolium, seu Jovem Capitolinum; Judæi vero aliâ juramenti formulâ uterentur, Martialis sic uerpum Poëtam aggreditur, lib 9. Epigr. 95.
units.tr: A different dagger, then, seems needed to bring down this view. First, the form of an oath is solemn, and it is familiar to everyone among those who use it; it consists of set words whose meaning and force are known both to those who swear and to those who witness. So when the Romans swore by the temples of the Thunderer, that is, by the Capitol or Jupiter of the Capitol, while the Jews used a different oath formula, Martial attacks the poet Verpus in this way, Book 9, Epigram 95:

units.la: Ecce negas, jurasque mihi per templa Tonantis,
units.tr: You deny it, and you swear to me by the temples of the Thunderer,

units.la: Non credo jura, verpe, per Anchialum.
units.tr: I do not believe your oaths, you Verpus, by Anchialus.

units.la: Missis doctissimorum virorum istius per Anchialum interpretationibus, nobis cum doctissimo Seldeno sono verborum linguæ barbaræ, h. e. Hebraicæ seu Syro-Chaldaicæ falsus Poëta videtur. Nam cum formula jurisjurandi verborum, h. e. Judæorum tribus constaret vocibus אמן אמן ... peran peram chi olam, h. e. ulciscatur, aut vindicatam sumat, is qui vivit in aeternum, nempe si pejeraverim. Martialis voces miserè luxavit & dispescuit pro libitu, ut ex prima syllaba præpositionem per fecerit. An, verò cum chi & olam copulato, suum illud Anchialum composuerit. Nunc ut è diverticulo in viam. Quando omnibus compertum est jusjurandum conceptis notissimisque verbis apud jurantes, aut audientes pronunciari solitum esse, utique Christus usus esset juramenti formula apud Judæos, Syros, & Chaldæos plane barbara, nunquam enim ac nusquam in toto veteri Instrumento isthæc juramenti formula, Amen, Amen dico vobis, usurpata memoratur. Incassum igitur juraret Christus, nec suo illo incognito juramento dictis fidem apud auditores suos fecisset, quod indignum mediocri sapientia, nedum immensa Christi sapientia nemini sano non videtur. 2°. Jurisjurandi religio vetat ne crebrò juramentum adhibeatur: sed in justitia, judicio & veritate. Jerem. 4: 2. Nempe Deus juramentum in hanc finem instituit, ut lites obscurae de facto dirimantur, ubi testes idonei desiderantur: tunc enim jusjurandum, quo Deus testis & judex appellatur litigantium defertur alterutri. Unde Paulus, hominibus omnis controversiæ finis est jusjurandum ad confirmationem adhibitum, Hebr. 6: 16. Hinc Numen ipsum rarissimè juratum legitur, atque in rebus maximi momenti, nempe cum agitur de constituendo æterno Christi sacerdotio juxta ordinem Melchisedec, Psalm. 110: 4. Ubi immutabilitatem consilii æterni atque magnarum, pretiosarumque promissionum salutarium confirmare dignatur, Hebr. 6: 17. Ubi necessarium justitiæ suæ vindicatricis exercitium adversus incredulos & impœnitentes demonstrare intendit, Psalm. 95: 11. Hebr. 4: 3. Ezech. 33: 11. Ubi denique voluntatem suam de servandis improbis, quotquot pœnitudine ducti, seria conversione ad thronum misericordiæ confugiunt. Ezech. 33: 11. Fitne autem verisimile Christum Dei Filium non rarenter quidem: sed passim hac solemni formula, Amen, Amen dico vobis! juratum fuisse? Anne suo illo creberrimo jurejurando accusandi ansam præbuisset Judæis, atque adeò eum arguendi contemptus Numinis æterni? 3°. Jurarunt quidem Judæi hac formula, ut Deus vivit, vel per Deum viventem: jurati verò Deus Amen, vel per Deum Amen, nunquam ac nusquam memorantur. Novitiâ igitur, incognitâ, atque adeo plane inutili, Christus usus esset jurejurandi formula, quæ propter ignorantiam Judæorum invincibilem, momenti nihil ad fidem dictis adstruendam, habuisset.
units.tr: Setting aside the explanations of this by Anchialus offered by very learned men, it seems to me, with the most learned Selden, that the poet, through the sounds of a barbarous tongue, that is, Hebrew or Syro-Chaldaic, is speaking falsely. For the Jewish formula of oath consisted of three words, אמן אמן ... peran peram chi olam: may he who lives for ever avenge it, or take it as vengeance, namely if I have sworn falsely. Martial wrenched and cut these words badly and as he pleased, and from the first syllable he made the preposition per. Then, joining chi and olam, he composed that Anchialum of his. But to return from this detour to the road. Since it is known to all that an oath was usually uttered in set and very familiar words by those who swore or heard it, Christ would surely have used a form of oath among Jews, Syrians and Chaldeans that was utterly barbarous, for this formula of oath, Amen, Amen, I say to you, is never once mentioned as used anywhere in the whole Old Testament. Christ would therefore have sworn in vain, and by that unknown oath of his he would not have won belief for his words among his hearers. This seems unworthy of ordinary wisdom, let alone of Christ's immense wisdom, to anyone who is not foolish. Second, the religion of an oath forbids that an oath be used often, but only in justice, judgment and truth (Jeremiah 4:2). God instituted the oath for this purpose: to settle obscure disputes about matters of fact when suitable witnesses are lacking. For then the oath, in which God is called on as witness and judge, is handed to one of the litigants. Hence Paul says: men swear by a greater, and an oath for confirmation is an end of all strife among them, Hebrews 6:16. Hence we read that the Godhead itself was very rarely sworn by, and only in matters of the greatest moment, namely when the eternal priesthood of Christ according to the order of Melchizedek was to be established, Psalm 110:4, where he deigns to confirm the immutability of his eternal counsel and of the great and precious promises of salvation (Hebrews 6:17). He also intends to show the necessary exercise of his avenging justice against the unbelieving and the impenitent (Psalm 95:11, Hebrews 4:3, Ezekiel 33:11). Finally, he declares his will to spare the wicked, as many as, led by repentance, flee to the throne of mercy by serious conversion (Ezekiel 33:11). But is it likely that the Son of God swore, not seldom indeed but throughout his teaching, with this solemn formula, Amen, Amen, I say to you? Would he not by that very frequent swearing have given the Jews an occasion for accusing him, and so for charging him with contempt of the eternal God? Third, the Jews swore with the formula as God lives, or by the living God; but there is never any mention of swearing God Amen or by God Amen. Christ would therefore have used a new, unknown, and so entirely useless form of oath, which, because of the Jews' invincible ignorance, would have had no weight at all in establishing belief in his words.

units.la: Alio igitur ad quæstionem dirimendam animum ut appellamus, observa 1°. Hanc vocem Amen, sive sola compareat, sive geminata in Veteri Testamento, usurpari duntaxat in fine precum, votorum, vel maledictionum, aliorumve dictorum, in symbolum, vel vehementis desiderii, vel assensus, & confirmationis, nunquam vero ac nusquam ab initio alicujus affirmationis. Contrà vero in Novo Instrumento nunquam usurpata memoratur in fine sermonum Christi, quando loquitur ex sese, sed ubi formulam orandi docet discipulos suos, quâ scilicet illi, non Christus, utantur, in precum & votorum suorum assensum & confirmationem: sed verò ubi Christus ex sese ac pro sese loquitur, sive affirmet, sive promittat, hanc vocem Amen ab initio sermonis sui adhibet.
units.tr: So, to settle the question, let us turn our minds to another line. Observe, first, that this word Amen, whether it appears alone or doubled in the Old Testament, is used only at the end of prayers, vows or curses, or of other utterances, as a sign of earnest desire, or of assent and confirmation; it is never used at the beginning of any affirmation. In the New Testament, by contrast, it is never mentioned at the end of Christ's sayings when he speaks on his own authority. It is used when he teaches his disciples the form of prayer, which they, not Christ, use to express assent and confirmation of their own prayers and wishes. But when Christ speaks on his own authority and for himself, whether he affirms or promises, he uses this word Amen at the beginning of his speech.

units.la: Observa 2°. Hanc vocem Amen, ubi occurrit in Veteri Testamento semper in fine precum, vel votorum, vel maledictionum, ut Deut. 27: 15. &c. constanter, significare, vel ardens desiderium, vel firmum assensum, & solemnem approbationem eorum, quæ in precibus, votis, minis, vel maledictionibus, continentur. Contrà vero in Novo Instrumento ab initio sermonum à Christo usurpata, nusquam desiderium aut assensum iis, quæ dicuntur ab aliis, significare: sed vehementem firmamque asseverationem, quidve aliud plane mysticum, ut infra clarius patebit.
units.tr: Observe, second, that this word Amen, where it occurs in the Old Testament, always at the end of prayers, vows or curses, as at Deuteronomy 27:15 and elsewhere, consistently signifies either an ardent desire or a firm assent and solemn approval of the things contained in the prayers, vows, threats or curses. In the New Testament, by contrast, where Christ uses it at the beginning of his sayings, it never signifies desire or assent to what others say, but a vehement and firm asseveration, or something else quite mysterious, as will become clearer below.

units.la: Observa 3°. Christum ubi sermonem haberet de iis, quorum veritas lumini naturali obvia est, quæque præconceptis Judæorum opinionibus ita erant opportuna, ut assensum eorum facile obtineret, non usurpasse hanc loquendi formulam, Amen dico vobis, eâ tantum usus est, ubi doceret regni cœlorum mysteria lumini naturali impervia; sunt enim quæ nec oculus vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in cor hominis unquam ascenderunt, 1 Cor. 2: 9. Vel ubi ea doceret, quæ sunt ad intelligendum ardua, vel præconceptis Judæorum opiniobus è diametro contraria, v. gr. mortuos audituros vocem filii hominis & victuros, Joh. 5: 25. Se nondum quadragenarium ante Abrahamum exstitisse, Joh. 8: 58. Discipulos in posterum visuros cœlum apertum, & Angelos Dei ascendentes & descendentes ad Filium hominis, Joh. 1: 51. & cætera id genus, ut cuivis acrius intendenti in locorum circumstantias, liquidum erit.
units.tr: Observe, third, that Christ never used this form of speech, Amen, I say to you, when he was speaking of things whose truth is open to the natural light, and which were so suited to the preconceived opinions of the Jews that they could easily win their assent. He used it only when he was teaching the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, which are impervious to the natural light: for these are things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have they entered into the heart of man (1 Corinthians 2:9). Or he used it when he taught things that are hard to understand, or things directly contrary to the preconceived opinions of the Jews: for example, that the dead will hear the voice of the Son of Man and will live (John 5:25); that he existed before Abraham, not yet fifty years old (John 8:58); that the disciples would see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man (John 1:51); and other things of that kind, which will be plain to anyone who attends closely to the circumstances of the passages.

units.la: Observa 4°. Quatuor Evangelistas, ut Græcè scripserint Evangelium, h. e. vitæ, sermonum & actuum Christi historiam, quia noverant Christum vernaculâ lingua, h. e. Syrâ, vel Syro-Chaldaica usum, cum cætera Christi dicta græcè scripserint, retinuisse & stylo suo græco immiscuisse phrases aliquot Christi Syriacas, Eli, Eli, vel Eloï, Eloï, lamma Sabachthani, Matth. 27: 47. Marc. 15: 34. Tabitha Kumi, Act. 9: 40. Vel cum interpretatione annexa, vel aliquot vocabula in quibus nostrum Amen sine interpretatione usurpatum, principem locum obtinet. Anne id de nihilo, nulloque adhibito consilio, casuque fortuito à sapientissimis Spiritus Sancti Amanuensibus factum videtur? Anne occurrebat τὸ ἀληθῶς vel πεπιστευμένως, vel ἐπ' ἀληθείας, quod aliquando, sed rarissime de industria Lucas fecisse videtur, ut Luc. 4: 25. & 9: 27. & 21: 3? Quid ni igitur Evangelistæ vice Amen quo Christus usus fuerat, semper scripsere ἀληθῶς, vel ἐπ' ἀληθείας, ut Ἑλληνικωτερον ἢ σαφέστερον loquerentur? Cur & ipse Lucas natione Græcus, non raro Amen retinuit, ut Luc. 4:24. & 23: 43? Certè non de nihilo, non fortuito, non linguæ græcæ penuriâ id admirandi discriminis sapientissimi Evangelistæ fecerunt. Unde liquet vocem Amen in solemni Christi formula, non modò verè, certè, constanter & fideliter: sed & aliud magis mysticum & reconditum significasse. Eccur tandem id discriminis? Nempe aliquando licebat, vel pro re enunciata, vel pro scopo & mente Christi τὸ Amen, quo servator usus fuerat, reddere per τὸ ἀληθῶς, vel ἐπ' ἀληθείας, ut Luc. 4: 25. & 9: 27. & 21: 3. Sed verò aliis in locis, nec res enunciata, nec mens & scopus Christi sapientissimo Lucæ τὸ Amen per τὸ ἀληθῶς, seu ἐπ' ἀληθείας reddere integrum fecit, ut liquet ex iisdemmet locis ubi Lucas constanter retinuit vocem Amen, quod pio eruditoque lectori examinandum relinquimus: Nempe τὸ Amen tunc ad personam Christi Dei Filii attinet, estque illius nomen proprium, ut liquet ex Is. 65: 16. & Jer. 10: 10.
units.tr: Observe, fourth, that the four Evangelists, when they wrote the Gospel in Greek, that is, the history of Christ's life, sayings and deeds, knew that Christ had used his vernacular tongue, that is, Syriac or Syro-Chaldaic. Although they wrote the rest of Christ's sayings in Greek, they kept some Syriac phrases of Christ and mixed them into their Greek style: Eli, Eli or Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani (Matthew 27:47, Mark 15:34), and Tabitha, cumi (Acts 9:40). Among these, with the explanation attached or without it, the word Amen used unexplained holds the chief place. Does this seem to have been done by the wisest amanuenses of the Holy Spirit for no reason, without any plan, by chance? Did the phrase truly [ἀληθῶς], or faithfully [πεπιστευμένως], or in truth [ἐπ' ἀληθείας] not come to mind? Luke seems to have used these occasionally, but very rarely, and on purpose, as at Luke 4:25, 9:27 and 21:3. Why, then, did the Evangelists not always write truly [ἀληθῶς] or in truth [ἐπ' ἀληθείας] in place of the Amen that Christ had used, so that they might speak more Greek-like or more clearly? Why did Luke himself, though a Greek by birth, often keep Amen, as at Luke 4:24 and 23:43? Certainly the wise Evangelists did not make this distinction for no reason, by chance, or through poverty of the Greek language. From this it is clear that the word Amen in Christ's solemn formula signified not only truly, certainly, constantly and faithfully, but also something more mysterious and hidden. Why, then, this distinction? Sometimes, indeed, it was permitted to render the Amen that the Saviour had used by truly [ἀληθῶς] or in truth [ἐπ' ἀληθείας], either because of the matter asserted or because of Christ's purpose and intent, as at Luke 4:25, 9:27 and 21:3. But in other places, neither the matter asserted nor Christ's mind and purpose permitted the wisest Luke to render Amen wholly by truly [ἀληθῶς] or in truth [ἐπ' ἀληθείας]. This is clear from the very passages where Luke consistently kept the word Amen. We leave it to the pious and learned reader to examine this. Namely, the Amen then pertains to the person of Christ, the Son of God, and is his proper name, as is clear from Isaiah 65:16 and Jeremiah 10:10.

units.la: Observa 5°. Prophetas, ubi docent, vaticinantur, promittunt, vel minantur, usos solemni isthac loquendi formula, sic dicit mnn, vel audite, nam os יהוה locutum est, nunquam verò ac nusquam usos fuisse hac solemni Christi formula, Amen dico vobis. Eccur verò si Amen ἀληθῶς, vel ἐπ' ἀληθείας verè ac certè tantum significaverit? Anne vera certaque erant Prophetarum oracula? Anne Prophetæ certò persuasi erant de veritate & certitudine eloquiorum suorum? Utique nihil vetabat, quominus singuli Prophetæ hanc loquendi formulam dictis suis præfigerent, si quidem in hac Christi formula, Amen, Amen, dico vobis, Amen istiusmodi veritatem modò & certitudinem sermonis significaret: Quando verò omnibus compertum est usos nunquam fuisse isthac ChriChristi formula, hinc argumento quàm evidentissimo colligitur, hanc solemnem propriamque Christi formulam non veritatem & certitudinem enunciationis Christi duntaxat significasse, sed & aliquid mysticum magis, magisque arduum, quo nec Prophetis, nec ipsis Christi Apostolis uti licuit. Ecquid tandem? Ut viam ad quæstionem profligandam muniamus.
units.tr: Observe, fifthly, that the Prophets, when they teach, prophesy, promise, or threaten, used the solemn formula thus says the LORD, or hear, for the mouth of the LORD has spoken, and never once used this solemn formula of Christ, Amen, I say to you. Why, then, if Amen meant only truly [ἀληθῶς] or in truth [ἐπ' ἀληθείας], that is, truly and certainly? Were the oracles of the Prophets not true and certain? Were the Prophets not persuaded of the truth and certainty of their own utterances? Nothing would have prevented each of the Prophets from prefixing this formula to his words, if in this formula of Christ, Amen, Amen, I say to you, the Amen signified merely the truth and certainty of the speech. But since it is known to all that the Prophets never used Christ's formula, it follows, by a most evident argument, that this solemn and peculiar formula of Christ signified not merely the truth and certainty of Christ's statement, but something more mystical and more lofty, which neither the Prophets nor the Apostles of Christ themselves were permitted to use. What then? Let us clear the way for settling the question.

units.la: Observa 6°. Aliud esse ipsam veritatis, sicut & mendacii, scaturiginem, aliud verò rivum, vel canalem, mendacii, vel veritatis. Diabolus fons est & scaturigo perennis mendacii, unde & mendax & pater mendacii dicitur, & Christus jure asserit, Diabolum, ubi mendacium profert, loqui ex proprio, vel ex se ipso, Joh.8: 44. Sed verò peccatores Diaboli mancipia, filiique illius patris & authoris mendacii, rivuli & canales mendacii sunt. Deus verò è diametro fons est & scaturigo perennis veritatis, imo ipsa veritas æterna, unde unus gaudet nomine אמן Jesa. 65: 16. nomine אמת Psalm. 31: 6. nomine הנאמן Deut. 7: 9. & nomine אמונה Deut. 32: 4. Christus itaque Dei Filius, & Deus in sæcula benedictus, fons est veritatis, Deusque אמת, Deus אמת ipsa veritas æterna. Prophetæ verò, Apostoli, fideles, piique omnes filii lucis, filii veritatis, rivuli & alvei veritatis sunt. Hinc factum ut Prophetæ suæ conditionis memores, quo docerent se non esse fontem veritatis, nec ex proprio loqui, ubi, vaticinarentur, promitterent, vel minarentur, hanc loquendi formulam usurparunt, Deus loquutus est, os Domini loquutum est, Spiritus Domini in me locutus est, &c. Et Apostoli, dico veritatem in Christo, non mentior. Contrà Christus Deus in sæcula sæculorum benedictus, fons & scaturigo veritatis æterna, atque adeò Deus Amen, ubi loqueretur in terra, ex proprio loquebatur. Unde factum est, ut nunquam dixerit, Audite, nam os Domini locutum est: sed Amen, Amen, dico vobis.
units.tr: Observe, sixthly, that the source of truth, as of falsehood, is one thing, and the stream or channel of falsehood or truth is another. The devil is the fountain and perpetual spring of falsehood, whence he is called a liar and the father of lies, and Christ rightly asserts that the devil, when he utters a lie, speaks from his own [ex proprio], that is, from himself, John 8:44. But sinners, the servants of the devil and sons of that father and author of lies, are the streams and channels of falsehood. God, on the other hand, is directly the fountain and perpetual spring of truth, indeed eternal truth itself, whence he rejoices in the name אמן, Isa. 65:16; in the name אמת, Ps. 31:6; in the name הנאמן, Deut. 7:9; and in the name אמונה, Deut. 32:4. Christ, therefore, the Son of God, and God blessed for ever, is the fountain of truth, and God of truth [Deus אמת], God the eternal truth itself. The Prophets, the Apostles, and all the faithful and pious, the sons of light and sons of truth, are the streams and channels of truth. Hence it came about that the Prophets, mindful of their own condition, so as to teach that they were not the fountain of truth nor spoke from themselves, when they prophesied, promised, or threatened, used this formula: God has spoken; the mouth of the Lord has spoken; the Spirit of the Lord has spoken in me, and so on. And the Apostles: I speak the truth in Christ, I do not lie. On the contrary, Christ, God blessed for ever and ever, the fountain and perpetual spring of eternal truth, and therefore God Amen, when he spoke on earth, was speaking from his own. Hence it came about that he never said, Hear, for the mouth of the Lord has spoken, but Amen, Amen, I say to you.

units.la: Observa 7°. Ubi Christus versaretur in terris, Pharisæos, Scribas, cæterosque Rabbanim traditionarios, usurpasse solitos de lege sua שבעל פה orali, blasphemum illud effatum, תורתינו אמת הכטינו ואבריהם אמת וכל-האמר כנגדן הולר מסור ויהיה בנדוי Lex nostra est veritas, sapientes nostri sunt veritas, & verba eorum sunt veritas, & omnis qui eis contradicit, filius est spurius, & erit in excommunicatione. Quasi verò homuli mendacissimi scaturigo veritatis forent, ipsaque veritas, & lex eorum, nempe Mijna, nugis nugacissimis prægnans, ipsa foret veritas.
units.tr: Observe, seventhly, that while Christ was living on earth, the Pharisees, the scribes, and the other traditional rabbis were accustomed to use, concerning their law called the oral law [שבעל פה], that blasphemous saying: Our law is truth, our wise men are truth, and their words are truth, and whoever contradicts them is a bastard son, and shall be under excommunication [תורתינו אמת הכטינו ואבריהם אמת וכל-האמר כנגדן הולר מסור ויהיה בנדוי]. As though these most lying little men were the fountain of truth, and truth itself, and their law, namely the Mishnah, pregnant with most trifling trifles, were truth itself.

units.la: Ex præmissis observationibus tam in proclivi concludere est, quam imimber dum pluit solemnem istam Christi loquendi formulam Amen, dico vobis, nec fuisse servatoris jusjurandum, nec simplicem affirmationem veritatis. 1°. Quia Christo propria est ἀκοινωνήτως, qua Prophetarum, Evangelistarum & Apostolorum nemo usquam usus in Scriptura memoratur. Contrà vero Apostoli alia usi leguntur loquendi formulâ, ubi certissimam veritatem vehementer asseruerunt, ut Petrus ἐπ' ἀληθείας καλαλαμβάνομαι, vere deprehendo, quòd Deus non est personarum acceptor, Act. 10: 34. De industria sanè non dixit, Amen deprehendo, nempe noverat visione miraculosa lintei, & admonitione Dei, & pietate Cornelii veritatem, quam ignorabat, nempe salutarem gentium ad gratisum foedus vocationem, quare non poterat dese dicere, Amen deprehendo; nam ut unus Deus Amen est, ipsa veritas, & omnia habet pervia atque πεπραχμένα. Paulus ubi veritatem certissimam erat enunciaturus, pariter legitur hac-usus formula, ἀληθείαν λέγω, veritatem enim dicam, 2 Cor. 12: 6. Veritatem dico in Christo, non mentior, Rom. 9: 1. 1 Tim. 2: 7. Nunquam verò ac nusquam dixisse legitur Amen, dico. Quidni vero, si hæc formula Amen, dico vobis, firmam ac vehementem veritatis asseverationem duntaxat significaret? 2° Quia nulla ratio legitima reddi potest, cur Evangelistæ, ubi græce scripserunt tam crebro retinuerint ex Christi sermone vernaculo, vocem Hebræam Syramve Amen; cur contrà eam non semper reddiderint per ἀληθῶς, vel ἐπ' ἀληθείας? Vel si ad duplicatum respexerint & ad vehementiam asseverationis, cur non magis hellenicè & accommodatè ad Græcorum, quibus comprimis scribebant, intelligentiam, duplicatum Amen reddiderint per ἀληθέστατως, Verissime? 3°. Cur Apostoli fideles Christi imitatores tum in verbis, tum in factis, usi familiari ipsius consortio, auriti testes formulæ Christo solemni, ejusque sermonibus assuefacti, ipsi tamen, vel dum veritatem cœlestem vehementer docent, parati eam proprio sanguine obsignare, nunquam tamen ac nusquam leguntur istâ usi formulâ, Amen dico vobis. Utique usque adeo constans Christi loquendi formula, constans verò ab eadem Prophetarum, Apostolorum, & Evangelistarum abstinentia, nemini haud segniter attendenti non persuadet, singularem atque incommunicabilem quandam χάριν ad Christum habere, quam nullam in ea reperias utut vehementem veritatis asseverationem fuisse contendas.
units.tr: From the observations set out above it is as easy to conclude as it is for it to rain while it is raining that this solemn formula of Christ, Amen, I say to you, was neither an oath of the Saviour nor a simple affirmation of truth. First, because it is peculiar to Christ, unshared [ἀκοινωνήτως], and no one of the Prophets, Evangelists, or Apostles is recorded in Scripture as having used it anywhere. On the contrary, the Apostles are read as using other forms of speech when they strongly asserted a most certain truth, as Peter: In truth [ἐπ' ἀληθείας] I perceive [καταλαμβάνομαι], that God is no respecter of persons, Acts 10:34. He deliberately did not say, I perceive, Amen; for he knew, by the miraculous vision of the sheet, by God's admonition, and by the piety of Cornelius, the truth he had not known, namely that the calling of the Gentiles to the covenant of grace was for their salvation; therefore he could not say of himself, Amen, I perceive; for as God alone is Amen, truth itself, and has all things open to him and done [πεπραχμένα]. Paul, when he was about to state a most certain truth, is likewise read as using this formula: I speak the truth [ἀληθείαν λέγω], for I will speak the truth, 2 Cor. 12:6; I speak the truth in Christ, I do not lie, Rom. 9:1; 1 Tim. 2:7. But he is never read as having said Amen, I say. Why would this formula Amen, I say to you not signify only a firm and vehement assertion of truth? Second, because no lawful reason can be given why the Evangelists, when they wrote in Greek, so often retained from Christ's vernacular speech the Hebrew or Syriac word Amen, and why, on the other hand, they did not always render it by truly [ἀληθῶς] or in truth [ἐπ' ἀληθείας]? Or if they looked to the doubling and to the vehemence of the assertion, why did they not render the doubled Amen more in the Greek manner and more suited to the understanding of the Greeks, for whom they chiefly wrote, as most truly [ἀληθέστατως], very truly? Third, why do the Apostles, faithful imitators of Christ both in word and deed, who enjoyed his familiar company, were ear-witnesses of his solemn formula, and were accustomed to his sayings, yet, even when they teach heavenly truth vehemently and are ready to seal it with their own blood, are nowhere ever read as using this formula, Amen, I say to you? Surely this formula of Christ, so constant, and so constant an abstention from it by the Prophets, Apostles, and Evangelists, does not fail to persuade anyone who attends to it with no sluggishness that Christ has a singular and incommunicable grace, which you would not find in it, however vehement you might claim the assertion of truth to be.

units.la: Quæstioni igitur propositæ plane satisfieri posse nobis videtur, si respondeamus, Christum solemni isthac loquendi formula usum esse, ut Judæos multa doceret, 1°. Se esse Deum Amen, seu אמן de quo David, Psf. 31: 6. Jer. 10: 10. If. 65: 16. Hoc ipse Johannes, qui unus inter Evangelistas Christum exhibet constanter ingeminantem, Amen, Amen, dico vobis, evidenter asserit, Christum ipsum id docuisse hic verbis, scribe ad Angelum Ecclesiæ Laodicensis, Amen testis fidelis & verax hæc dicit, Apocal. 3: 14. Fac Christum mutasse personam, & de se ipso locutum esse, nonne isthac formula usus esset, ego Amen testis fidelis & verax hæc dico? quæ gemina plane est atque ista, Amen Amen dico vobis. 2°. Ut Judæos doceret Prophetarum vaticinia prope diem impletum iri, & tempus vocationis gentium, quo omnis benedicens in terra per nomen Dei Amen benedicturus erat, & omnis jurans in terra, per Deum Amen juraturus erat, in proximo esse. 3°. Ut frequenti isthoc proprio suo nomine Amen Dei fidelitatem in implenda promissione, qua se simul populo Israelitico, simul gentibus obstrinxerat solemni isthoc sui indigitamento יהיה Erit, Judæos aperte doceret. 4°. Ut solemni isto nomine proprio Amen, ac singulari loquendi formula ab omnibus Prophetis, Apostolis, Evangelistis singularem in modum sese discerneret. 5°. Ut solemni isthac sua loquendi formula vanitatem carperet superciliosorum gentis judaicæ doctorum, quasi dixisset cur ausu nefario πολυθρύλλητον [?] istud crepatis, Lex nostra est veritas, doctores nostri sunt veritas, verba eorum sunt veritas. Unus ego Propheta sicut Moyses, unus Messias, unus Deus Amen, dignus sum quem audiatis dicentem Evangelium meum est veritas, verba mea sunt veritas, ego Deus Amen dico vobis. 6°. Ut dictis suis, quæ homo animalis non capit, fidem faceret apud auditores suos. Quando enim Deus non homo est ut mentiatur, nec filius hominis, ut pœniteat eum, utique Deus Amen indigitatus nomine Dei Amen, & in carne manifestatus, mentiri non potest aut fallere, ut grandia, & a captu hominum remota loquatur atque promittat. An vos in stuporem dabit, si dixero, venisse horam & nunc esse, quâ mortui audient vocem filii Dei, quique eam audiverint, victuros? Nolite percelli, obsecro, vel in animum incredulum vos dedere, attendite modo quis tantum promittat miraculum, ego Deus Amen, in quem non cadit, vel umbra levitatis, nedum mendacii: ita, Amen, Amen, dico vobis, venit hora & nunc est, &c. Joh. 5: 25. Num in stuporem vos dabit si dixero, me vix triginta & tres annos natum ante Abrahamum fuisse? Nolite turbari, obsecro, vel male sana incredulitate labi, reputate modo apud vos quis est, qui vos nunc alloquitur, ego Deus Amen, in quem nec umbra mumutationis, nec umbra mendacii cadit, næ, Amen, Amen, dico vobis quàm Abraham exstaret prius, ego sum, Joh. 8: 58. Vos ne in stuporem dabit si dixero, vosmet in posterum visuros cœlum apertum, & Angelos Dei ascendentes & descendentes ad filium hominis ? Nolite percelli amabo, putate modò quis loquitur & futurum istiusmodi miraculum recipit, ego Amen, ille Deus Amen, de quo vester Isaïas retro vaticinatus est, næ Amen, Amen, dico vobis, in posterum videbitis cœlum apertum, &c.
units.tr: It seems to us that the question proposed can be fully answered if we reply that Christ used this solemn formula of speech in order to teach the Jews many things: first, that he is God Amen, or אמן, of whom David speaks, Ps. 31:6; Jer. 10:10; Isa. 65:16. John himself, who alone among the Evangelists constantly presents Christ as repeating Amen, Amen, I say to you, clearly asserts that Christ himself taught this, when he says: Write to the angel of the church of the Laodiceans: Amen, the faithful and true witness, says these things, Rev. 3:14. Suppose Christ had changed his person and spoken of himself: would he not have used this formula, I, Amen, the faithful and true witness, say these things? which is plainly twin to that other, Amen, Amen, I say to you. Second, to teach the Jews that the prophetic oracles were about to be fulfilled soon, and that the time of the calling of the Gentiles was at hand, when every one who blesses on earth will bless by the name of God Amen, and every one who swears on earth will swear by God Amen. Third, that by this frequent use of his own proper name Amen, he might openly teach the Jews the faithfulness of God in fulfilling the promise by which he bound himself at once to the Israelite people and to the Gentiles, through this solemn designation of himself as יהיה, I shall be. Fourth, that by this solemn proper name Amen, and by his singular formula of speech, he might distinguish himself in a unique way from all the Prophets, Apostles, and Evangelists. Fifth, that by this solemn formula of his own he might mock the vanity of the haughty teachers of the Jewish nation, as if he were saying: why do you dare to chant so often that notorious [πολυθρύλλητον] saying, Our law is truth, our teachers are truth, their words are truth? I alone, like Moses, am the one Prophet, the one Messiah, the one God Amen, and I am worthy to be heard saying: My gospel is truth, my words are truth; I, God Amen, say to you. Sixth, that he might make his sayings, which the natural man does not grasp, credible to his hearers. For since God is not a man that he should lie, nor the son of man that he should repent, surely God Amen, designated by the name of God Amen, and manifested in the flesh, cannot lie or deceive, even when he speaks and promises great things remote from human comprehension. Will it astonish you if I say that the hour is coming, and is now, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear it will live? Do not be struck dumb, I beg you, nor give yourselves over to an unbelieving mind; only consider who it is that promises such a miracle: I, God Amen, in whom not even a shadow of levity falls, much less of falsehood: so, Amen, Amen, I say to you, the hour comes and now is, and so on, John 5:25. Will it astonish you if I say that I, who am scarcely thirty-three years old, was before Abraham? Do not be troubled, I beg you, nor fall into sickly unbelief; only reflect among yourselves who it is that now addresses you: I, God Amen, in whom falls neither a shadow of change nor a shadow of falsehood. Yes, Amen, Amen, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am, John 8:58. Will it astonish you if I say that you yourselves will see the heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man? Do not be struck dumb, I beg you; consider only who is speaking and is promising such a miracle to come: I, Amen, that God Amen of whom your Isaiah prophesied long ago. Yes, Amen, Amen, I say to you, hereafter you will see the heaven opened, and so on.

units.la: Quòd Evangelistæ Spiritus Sancti Amanuenses Christi Amen sive simplex, sive geminatum in serie græci sui idiomatis, ut ut Hebræum Syrumve, retinuerint sine interpretatione adjecta, sicut & alia multa, V. Gr. Gethsemane, Matth. 26: 36. Hosanna, Matth. 21: 9. 15. Bethesda, Joan. 5: 1. Beelzeboul, Matth. 10: 25. Bethlehem, Matth. 2: 1. Bethania, Matth. 21: 17. Alleluja, Apoc. 19: 1. & cætera id genus alia. Cum tamen aliquando, sed rarenter admodum, nominibus propriis interpretationem subjunxerint, ut Immanuel, Matth. 1: 23. Tabitha Act. 9: 36. Hinc colligimus non satis caute fecisse interpretes, qui sacra istiusmodi solemniaque nomina, & comprimis Christi Amen lingua reddidere vernaculâ: hoc enim est sapere præter quod scriptum est 1 Cor. 4: 6. Quando enim Spiritus Sanctus, quæ Christus dixit egitque scribere voluerit, nec ipsi visum est græcè interpretari τὸ ἀμήν, Hosanna, Alleluja, Gethsemane, & cætera id genus. Eccur visum est Vernaculis interpretibus hujusmodi sacra & solemnia interpretari vocabula? Præterea lubens sciscitarer ab ipsis, cur non interpretati sunt Gethsemane, Hosanna, Alleluja, Amen. 2 Cor. 1: 20. Quando utrinque eadem est ratio, nam omnia illa nomina hebræa sunt. Quid causæ, obsecro est, nisi quia, vel nomina sunt propria, vel solemnes acclamationum laudumque formulæ, vel excommunicationum, quale est horrendum Maranatha, 1 Cor. 17: 22. Alterutrum, utrumve dixerint illibatum Christi Amen servandum erat, quando Spiritui Sancto non visum fuit illud Syro-Chaldaici sermonis Christi Amen græcè reddere per ἀληθῶς, vel πεπληρωμένως, vel per ἀληθεστάτως: nam & Amen nomen Dei Christique proprium est, & solemnis loquendi formula ipsi propria ἀκοινωνήτως, ut supra demonstravimus.
units.tr: That the Evangelists, the Holy Spirit's amanuenses, kept Christ's Amen, whether single or doubled, in the Greek form of their own idiom, untranslated, even though it was Hebrew or Syriac, just as they kept many other words, for example Gethsemane, Matt. 26:36; Hosanna, Matt. 21:9, 15; Bethesda, John 5:1; Beelzeboul, Matt. 10:25; Bethlehem, Matt. 2:1; Bethania, Matt. 21:17; Alleluja, Rev. 19:1; and others of that kind. Yet they only rarely added a translation to proper names, as with Immanuel, Matt. 1:23, and Tabitha, Acts 9:36. From this we conclude that those interpreters did not act with sufficient caution who rendered such sacred and solemn words into the vernacular, and above all Christ's Amen. For this is to be wise beyond what is written, 1 Cor. 4:6. When the Holy Spirit wished to have written what Christ said and did, it did not seem good to him to translate into Greek τὸ ἀμήν, Hosanna, Alleluja, Gethsemane, and the like. Why did it seem good to the vernacular translators to translate such sacred and solemn words? I would also gladly ask them why they did not translate Gethsemane, Hosanna, Alleluja, Amen, 2 Cor. 1:20, since the reason is the same on either side, for all those names are Hebrew. What is the reason, I ask you, except that they are either proper names, or solemn formulas of acclamation and praise, or of excommunication, such as the dreadful Maranatha, 1 Cor. 16:22? Whichever of these it was, Christ's Amen had to be kept intact, since the Holy Spirit did not see fit to render that Syro-Chaldaic word of Christ, Amen, into Greek by ἀληθῶς, or πεπληρωμένως, or ἀληθεστάτως. For Amen is both a proper name of God and of Christ, and a solemn formula of speech peculiar to him alone, ἀκοινωνήτως, as we have shown above.

units.la: QUAESTIO XII. Cur Johannes Christum constanter exhibuerit ingeminantem Amen, Amen, cùm contrà cæteri Evangelistæ Christum uno Amen perpetuò usum memoraverint.
units.tr: QUAESTIO XII. Why John constantly presented Christ as repeating Amen, Amen, whereas the other Evangelists recorded that Christ always used a single Amen.

units.la: Πολυθρύλλητον Rabbinorum effatum est, [?] אין בתורה אפילו אות אחת שאין הרים גדולים תלויים בה, Non est in lege vel litera una, à qua non montes magni dependeant. Quod superciliosi Magistri de literis Scripturæ, & cumprimis de literis majusculis, suspensis & inversis crepant, de uno nomine Amen haud immeritò pronuntiare possumus: ex eo enim magni montes divinæ sapientiæ, & mysteriorum salutis dependent, quod & demonstrandum persequimur in quæstione propositâ perstringenda: nemo enim paulò acrius animi aciem contendens iverit infitias; simul memorabile esse discrimen, quod Johannem inter cæterosque Evangelistas in referenda loquendi Christi formula solemni intercedit, simul nostrâ dignum admiratione, quòd cæteri Christum unum Amen usurpantem perpetuò exhibuerint, Johannes contrà eum ingeminantem Amen, Amen dico vobis, perpetuo exhibuerit.
units.tr: A much-repeated saying of the rabbis is this [Πολυθρύλλητον] : there is not in the law even one letter from which great mountains do not hang [אין בתורה אפילו אות אחת שאין הרים גדולים תלויים בה]. What the haughty masters cry out about the letters of Scripture, and especially about the enlarged, suspended and inverted letters, we may quite rightly say of the single word Amen. For from it great mountains of divine wisdom and of the mysteries of salvation depend. We shall pursue this point in the question proposed here for discussion. No one who applies his mind with some keenness will deny it. At the same time there is a notable difference between John and the other Evangelists in reporting Christ's solemn formula of speech, and it is worthy of our wonder that the others consistently presented Christ as using a single Amen, whereas John consistently presents him as repeating Amen, Amen, I say to you.

units.la: Dextrè quæstionem propositam soluturis, observare operæ pretium nobis videtur.
units.tr: It seems worth our while to observe the following, so that we may rightly resolve the question proposed.

units.la: 1º. Ut summa sit apud Evangelistas divinaque planè harmonia, quod rei summam & historiæ veritatem attinet, nonnullam tamen apud eos in aliquot circumstantiis occurrere varietatem, ita sapienter procurante Spiritus Sancti, cujus Amanuenses fuere, providentiâ, ut simul ejusdem spiritus veritatis ductu, eos lato regionum limite dissitos, vera scripsisse & tribus testibus oculatis, uno aurito per omnia momentosa consentientibus confirmata, simul non scripsisse ex compacto & collatis consiliis: sed tamen conscio & duce eodem spiritu, quando alter memorat, vel distinctius explicat, quod alter è circumstantiis præterierat, vel minus distinctè literarum monumentis scriptum reliquerat, ut ex quatuor collatione seria, testimonii veritas in clara luce constituta appareret, simul os hereticorum obturaretur, v. gr. cum Lucas retulerit, Christum dixisse de poculo cum gratias egisset, accipite hoc & partimini vobis ipsis: dico enim vobis me non bibiturum ex fructu vitis usque quo regnum Dei venerit, Luc. 22: 17. 18. Ne μετανάστῳ respónsarent, Christum quidem liquorem contentum in poculo paschali convivii fructum vitis appellasse, non vero poculum Eucharistiae, Matthaeus quam sapientissime annotavit, Christum dixisse de poculo Eucharistiae, bibite ex eo omnes, &c. dico autem vobis, non bibam ab hoc tempore ex hoc fructu vitis, Matth. 26: 27. 29.
units.tr: 1. There is a complete and divine harmony among the Evangelists as to the substance of the matter and the truth of the history. Yet there is some variety among them in certain circumstances. The Holy Spirit, whose amanuenses they were, providentially arranged this so wisely that, under the guidance of the same Spirit of truth, they wrote truthfully although they were separated by a wide stretch of country. They were confirmed by three eyewitnesses and one earwitness, who agreed in all important points. Yet they did not write by agreement or by joint counsel, but with the same Spirit as their knowing guide. So when one reports, or explains more distinctly, what another had passed over from the circumstances, or had left in writing less distinctly, the truth of the testimony appears in clear light from a careful comparison of the four, and the mouths of the heretics are stopped. For example, when Luke reports that Christ, after giving thanks over the cup, said: Take this and share it among yourselves; for I tell you, I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes, Luke 22:17-18. Lest the heretics should answer that Christ indeed called the liquid in the cup of the Passover meal the fruit of the vine, but not the cup of the Eucharist, Matthew most wisely noted that Christ said of the cup of the Eucharist: Drink of it, all of you, etc., but I tell you, I will not drink from now on of this fruit of the vine, Matt. 26:27, 29.

units.la: 2o. Quando Johannes Evangelistarum ultimus & superstes scripserit, prae caeteris omnibus plura memorat, quae caeteri praeterierant, sive quod historias attinet, sive rerum circumstantias, sive nomina personarum, ut eas nominatim designaverit, quas caeteri generatim indicaverant. Historiam si spectaverimus, Johannes historiam habet piscinae, quae vocabatur Bethesda, & miraculum descendentis Angeli, & sanationem cujusvis generis in unoquoque, qui primus in aquam turbidam descenderet, Joh. 5: 1. Historiam adulterae productae in medium, & Christi bis digito in pulvere templi scribentis: Joh 8: Historiam excitati e mortuis Lazari, Joh. 11: Explicatam creationis historiam mysticam, & sermonis imperii, quo septies Deus omnia creans singularem prorsus in modum a sacro Moyse narratur, Joh. 1: 1. Promissionem visionis coeli aperti, & Angelorum Dei ascendentium & descendentium ad Filium hominis, Joh. 1: 51. Personas quod attinet, cum caeteri Euangelistae generatim narraverint unum ex iis, qui erant cum Jesu extensa manu distrinxisse gladium suum, & percussisse servum Pontificis maximi, Matth. 26: 51. Marc. 14:47. Luc. 22: 50. Johannes nomen tum percutientis, tum percussi nos docet: Simon autem Petrus cum gladium haberet, eduxit eum, & feriit servum Pontificis Maximi, & abscidit auriculam ejus dextram, erat autem nomen servo Malchus, Joh. 18: 10.
units.tr: 2. John, the last and surviving of the Evangelists, when he wrote, relates more than all the others things that they had passed over. This holds whether we look at the histories, the circumstances of events, or the names of persons, for he names by name those whom the others had indicated only in general terms. If we consider the histories, John has the story of the pool called Bethesda, and the miracle of the angel descending, and the healing of whatever disease there was in whoever first went down into the troubled water, John 5:1. He has the history of the adulteress brought into the midst, and of Christ twice writing with his finger in the dust of the temple, John 8. He has the history of Lazarus raised from the dead, John 11. He has the mystical account of creation, and the word of command by which God, creating all things seven times, is narrated by holy Moses in a quite singular manner, John 1:1. He has the promise of the opened heaven, and of the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man, John 1:51. As to persons: whereas the other Evangelists had reported in general terms that one of those who were with Jesus stretched out his hand, drew his sword, and struck the servant of the high priest, Matt. 26:51; Mark 14:47; Luke 22:50, John teaches us the name both of the one who struck and of the one struck: Simon Peter, having a sword, drew it and struck the servant of the high priest, and cut off his right ear. Now the servant's name was Malchus, John 18:10.

units.la: Ex praemissis observationibus quaestioni propositae respondemus, Johannem exhibuisse Christum constanter ingeminantem, Amen, Amen, dico vobis, ut explicaret clarius mentem Christi, & caeterorum Evangelistarum unum Amen. Quando enim reliqui Christum exhibuerint dicentem Amen dico vobis, nequis existimaret istud Christi Amen significare tantum ἀληθῶς, vere, vel ἐπ' ἀληθείας in veritate, Johannes Christum exhibuit dicentem Amen, Amen, dico vobis, ut nos doceret, Amen esse nomen Christi proprium, ut se illo nomine proprio prio designaverit, postremum vero Amen ad sequentem sententiam esse referendum, & significare ἀληθῶς vere, quasi Christus dixisset, ego Amen, vere dico vobis, h, e. ego qui sum Deus ille Amen, per quem Jesaias vaticinatus est, fore ut omnis benedicens in terra benedicat, & per quem omnis jurans in terra, juret, Jesa. 65: 16. Vobis dico vere, ut nulli dubitare debeatis, vos in posterum visuros coelum apertum, & Angelos Dei ascendentes & descendentes ad Filium hominis.
units.tr: From the foregoing observations we answer the question proposed: John presented Christ as constantly repeating Amen, Amen, I say to you, in order to explain more clearly the mind of Christ and the single Amen of the other Evangelists. For when the others presented Christ as saying Amen, I say to you, lest anyone should think that this Amen of Christ signified only ἀληθῶς, truly, or ἐπ' ἀληθείας, in truth, John presented Christ as saying Amen, Amen, I say to you, to teach us that Amen is the proper name of Christ, and so that he designated himself by that proper name. The last Amen*, however, is to be referred to the following sentence and to signify ἀληθῶς, truly, as if Christ had said: I, the Amen, truly say to you; that is, I who am that God Amen, through whom Isaiah prophesied that everyone who blesses himself in the land shall bless himself and everyone who swears in the land shall swear, Isa. 65:16. I say to you truly, so that you ought to have no doubt that you will in future see the heavens opened and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man.

units.la: Sed regeras jure merito, qua ratione solida efficitur, ut in solemni Christi formula primum Amen, nomen sit Christi, desumptum ex Jesa. 65:16. potius quam secundum Amen ? ut ingeminatum istud sit adverbium, & significet ἀληθῶς vere, quandoquidem utrumque ex aequo Christus pronunciavit, & nihil quicquam apparet inter utrumque discriminis, nec ratione soni, nec ratione significationis. Pari enim ratione quivis dixerit, primum Amen significare ἀληθῶς vere, sed secundum, nomen esse Christi desumptum ex laudato Jesaiae capite, ut Christo dicere mens fuerit, vere ego Deus Amen dico vobis. Quamobrem praecedente responsione ex sententia doctissimi Lighfouti deprompta, solidior haec nostra magisque ad rem & mentem Christi, nobis videtur. Nempe utrumque Amen, nomen esse Christi desumptum ex Jesa. 65: 16. Sed a Christo sapientissimè geminatum multis de causis. 1°. Ut indicaret Judaeis Scripturae veteris locum, ubi propheta Jesaias Messiam fore Deum Amen praedixerat, nam Jesa. 65: 16. geminatum legitur Amen. Qui se benedicet in terra, se benedicet in Deo Amen, & qui jurabit in terra, jurabit per Deum Amen. Ut Christus significare voluerit primo Amen, se esse Deum illum Amen, in quo se benedicat quisquis se benedicens in terra, & secundo Amen, se esse quoque illum Deum Amen, per quem jurans in terra jurare debeat juxta prophetiam Jesaiae in sese Deo Amen impletam. 2°. Ex affectus vehementia, & indubia rei certitudine, sicuti ipse Christus (is enim Angelus est, qui Moysem alloquebatur in monte Sinai Actor. 7: 38.) ubi secundas Legis tabulas Mosi tradidit, recipitque se vocaturum nomen יהוה coram Mose. Exod. 33: 19. ubi suam promissionem impletam dedit, dum transiret coram eo ingeminando clamavit יהוה יהוה Exod. 34: 5. 6. 3°. Quia Deus Amen gloriosum est implementum nominis יהוה ut quaestione sequenti faciemus compertum. Quamobrem sicut Angelus Dei Filius & Christus, ubi gloriam suam a tergo Mosi ostenderet in monte, clamando ingeminavit יהוה יהוה, utique par erat ut ingeminaret Amen Amen implementum gloriosi nominis Tetragram, matimati, ubi gloriam suam, gloriam unigeniti ex Patre Judæis, Mosis discipulis non à tergo, sed facie ad faciam, contemplandam præberet. Idem esto cæterarum Christi sententiarum, prædictionum, vel promissionum, quibus præfigitur istud geminatum Amen judicium. Eccur verò Christus Dei Filius tam sedulo, tam frequenter illhoc singulari proprioque nomine Amen sese insignire voluerit, quæstione sequenti Scriptura sacra prælucente, examinatum imus.
units.tr: But you may rightly object: on what solid reasoning is it established that in Christ's solemn formula the first Amen is the name of Christ, taken from Isa. 65:16, rather than the second? Why should the doubled word be the adverb signifying ἀληθῶς, truly, since Christ pronounced both equally and no difference appears between them, either in sound or in meaning? For by the same reasoning anyone could say that the first Amen signifies ἀληθῶς, truly, but the second is the name of Christ taken from the chapter of Isaiah we have cited, so that Christ meant to say: truly I, the God Amen, say to you. Therefore, following the preceding answer drawn from the opinion of the most learned Lightfoot, this view of ours seems to us the sounder, and more to the point and to the mind of Christ. Namely, that both Amens are the name of Christ taken from Isa. 65:16, but that Christ doubled it most wisely, for many reasons. (1) To show the Jews the place in the Old Testament where the prophet Isaiah foretold that the Messiah would be the God Amen, for Isa. 65:16 is read with the doubled Amen: He who blesses himself in the land shall bless himself in the God Amen, and he who swears in the land shall swear by the God Amen. Christ meant the first Amen to signify that he is that God Amen in whom whoever blesses himself in the land blesses himself, and the second Amen to signify that he is also that God Amen by whom whoever swears in the land ought to swear, according to Isaiah's prophecy fulfilled in himself, the God Amen. (2) From the vehemence of his affection and the undoubted certainty of the matter, just as Christ himself (who is the Angel who spoke to Moses on Mount Sinai, Acts 7:38) when he gave the second tablets of the Law to Moses, and promised that he would proclaim the name יהוה before Moses, Exod. 33:19, and when he gave the fulfilment of his promise, as he passed before him, cried out, repeating, יהוה יהוה, Exod. 34:5-6. (3) Because God Amen is the glorious fulfilment of the name יהוה, as we shall show in the following question. Therefore, just as the Angel of God, the Son and Christ, when he showed his glory on the mountain to the back of Moses, cried out repeating יהוה יהוה, so it was fitting that he should repeat Amen, Amen, the fulfilment of the glorious name, the Tetragrammaton, when he offered the Jews, the disciples of Moses, to behold his glory, the glory of the only-begotten of the Father, not from behind but face to face. The same holds for the other sayings, predictions or promises of Christ, before which this doubled Amen stands as a judgment. Why, however, the Son of God Christ so diligently and so often wished to distinguish himself by this singular and proper name Amen, we shall examine in the following question, with holy Scripture shedding light upon it.

units.la: QUAESTIO XIII.
units.tr: QUESTION XIII.

units.la: Cur Christus Dei Filius dictus fuerit o Amen. Apoc. 3: 14.
units.tr: Why Christ the Son of God was called the Amen. Rev. 3: 14.

units.la: ANnulus Regis Persarum adeò fuit augustus, ut quicquid cœlaturâ annuli obsignatum fuerit, ratum atque irrevocabile haberetur. Hest. 8: 8. Geminam planè vim Imperatorum Regumque sigillis obsignatoriis inesse quotidiană experientiâ paret, unde vis & authoritas omnibus influat Regum diplomatis, unde Magistratus ad munera publica obeunda creentur, ut sigillo Regio anima quædam admirabilis stabulari videatur. Deus Rex Regum ac Dominus dominantium, etsi prima est & intemerata veritas, benignâ tamen æternùmque laudandâ hominibus σνγκαταβάσει edicta sua, atque placita, ad hominum salutem comparata, firma, rata esse voluit, adhibitis variis sacratissimæ suæ divinitatis sigillis. 1°. Quidem pretiosas salutis promissiones sigillo spiritus sui, nulli mortalium violando, electorum ac fidelium cordibus obsignare dignatus est, ἐν ᾧ καὶ ὑμεῖς, ἀκούσαντες τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον, τῆς σωτηρίας ὑμῶν, ἐν ᾧ καὶ πιστεύσαντες ἐσφραγίσθητε τῷ Πνεύματι τῆς ἐπαγγελίας τῷ ἁγίῳ. In quo & vos, cum audiveritis verbum veritatis, Evangelium salutis vestræ, in quo & credentes obsignati estis Spiritu promissionis Sancto. Ephes. 1: 13. Nempe ut electi atque fideles Christo Dei Filio forent quàm simillimi, (hunc enim ὁ πατὴρ ἐσφράγισεν ὁ Θεὸς, Joh. 6: 27.) nec non hoc charactere insigni benedictos suos in filios per Christum adoptatos, ab Abrahamitis ac Judæis carnalibus, quos externo circumcisionis signaculo populum sibi fecerat peculiarem, longè secerneret benignissimum Numen. men. Insuper Deo visum est placita sua salutaria variis, iisque momentosis externis sigillis, rata facere ac indubia, splendidis scilicet miraculis, donis Spiritus Sancti extraordinariis, in symbolo aliquo aspectabili coelitus collatis, ambobus adhibitis sacramentis, jurejurando tandem per se ipsum solemni, juravit enim per seipsum volens ostendere haeredibus promissionis voluntatis suae immutabilitatem, Hebr. 6: 18. Sua igitur velut impressa divinitate vivente, ut earum firmitatem immutabilem, omnique exceptione majorem certitudinem omnibus contestatam faceret, obsignatas voluit. Denique ne quid earum complemento deesse videretur, seipsum in carne nostra manifestatum nomine Amen appellare voluit τὸ δὲ λέγει ὁ Ἀμήν, ὁ μάρτυς, ὁ πιστὸς καὶ ὁ ἀληθινὸς, hac verò dicit Amen, testis, fidelis, & verax.
units.tr: The signet ring of the kings of Persia was so august that whatever was sealed with its engraving was held to be valid and irrevocable. Esth. 8: 8. Daily experience shows that royal seals carry a twofold force, and from them the authority and validity of all royal documents flow, and by them magistrates are appointed to discharge public offices, so that some wonderful life seems to dwell in the royal seal. God, the King of kings and Lord of lords, although he is the first and inviolable truth, nonetheless, by a gracious condescension (synkatabasis) deserving of eternal praise toward men, willed that his decrees and pleasures, prepared for the salvation of men, be firm and valid, employing various seals of his most sacred divinity. (1) Indeed he has deigned to seal the precious promises of salvation on the hearts of the elect and faithful with the seal of his Spirit, which violates no mortal: in whom also you, having heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, in whom also, having believed, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise [en ho kai hymeis... esphragisthēte tō Pneumati tēs epangelias tō hagiō]. Eph. 1: 13. Namely, that the elect and faithful might be made as much like Christ the Son of God as possible (for God the Father sealed him, John 6: 27), and that the most benign Deity might set apart his blessed sons, adopted through Christ, by this distinguishing mark, far from the Abrahamites and the carnal Jews, whom he had made a peculiar people by the outward seal of circumcision. Moreover, God has seen fit to make his saving decrees sure and certain by various and weighty outward seals, namely by splendid miracles, extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit, conferred from heaven in some visible symbol, by both sacraments, and finally by a solemn oath sworn by himself: for he swore by himself, wishing to show to the heirs of the promise the immutability of his will, Heb. 6: 18. Therefore, as it were impressed with his own divinity, he willed that they be sealed, so that he might make their immutable firmness and a certainty greater than any exception attested to all.
