Finally, lest anything seem lacking to their completion, he willed to call himself by the name Amen, manifested in our flesh: these things says the Amen, the faithful and true witness [tade legei ho Amēn, ho martys, ho pistos kai ho alēthinos], Rev. 3: 14.

units.la: Cur verò Christus Dei Filius hoc solemni nomine indigitari voluerit, quaestio est sedula disquisitione haud indigna, quamque si allucente Scriptura Sacra tanquam in trivio circumspicientes, perstrinxerimus, lucem ut foeneremus, variis, tum Veteris tum Novi Instrumenti illustribus, nec satis hactenus spectatis locis, fore speramus. Agedum ad momentosam quaestionem aggrediamur sub ductu & auspiciis Dei in Scriptura loquentis.
units.tr: Why the Son of God willed to be designated by this solemn name is a question not unworthy of careful inquiry. If, with Holy Scripture shining upon it, we examine it as men looking about at a crossroads, we hope it will yield light, and that various passages of both the Old and New Testaments, illustrious and hitherto not sufficiently considered, will be made clear. Come, let us approach this weighty question under the guidance and auspices of God speaking in Scripture.

units.la: Observare 1°. Nonnullius operae pretium erit, Amen esse ab אמן nutrivit, & quia alimentum causa est roboris, atque firmitatis nutriti, hinc factum ex consequenti, ut אמן significet firmavit, & quia veracitas atque fidelitas constantia est ac firmitudo animi, hinc tertio factum ut significet verax ac fidelis fuit. Denique quia fidem adhibere solemus, verbis ac promissis, quae vera ac fidelia judicamus, iisque spem nostram alere atque fovere, hinc factum iterum ut אמן significet credidit, speravit: unde tandem deductum affine τῷ אמן ὁ אמן nutritius, alumnus, & artifex, quod sit velut artis nutritius. אמן igitur veritatem ac fidelitatem significat, quatenus est animae rationalis pabulum, fomentum, & robur.
units.tr: Observe first: it will be worth some effort to note that Amen comes from 'mn [אמן], to nourish; and since nourishment is the cause of strength and firmness in what is nourished, it follows that 'mn means to make firm; and since truthfulness and faithfulness are the constancy and firmness of mind, it follows thirdly that it means to be true and faithful. Finally, since we are accustomed to give credence to words and promises which we judge to be true and faithful, and so to nourish and foster our hope in them, it follows again that 'mn means to believe, to hope. From this is finally derived the related noun 'omen [אמן], a nurse, foster-father, and craftsman, as it were the nurse of an art. Thus 'mn signifies truth and faithfulness, insofar as they are the food, nourishment and strength of the rational soul.

units.la: Observa 2°. אמן seu אמת, quod plane geminum est, nomen esse Dei Opt. Max. Psalm. 31: 6. In manu tua commendo spiritum meum redimisti me יהוה אל אמת Domine Deus fortis אמת. & Jerem. 10: 10. יהוה אלהים אמת הו אלהים & Jehovah Deus, אמת ipse Deus, & Jes. 65: 16. Qui se benedicet in terra se benedicet באלהי אמן in Deo Amen, & jurans in terra, jurabit באלהי אמן in Deo Amen.
units.tr: Observe second: 'mn or 'mt [אמת], which is clearly the same word in a double form, is a name of God Most Good and Greatest. Ps. 31: 6: Into your hand I commit my spirit; you have redeemed me, O Lord, God of truth [YHWH 'el 'emet]. And Jer. 10: 10: Jehovah God, God of truth [YHWH 'elohim 'emet, hu' 'elohim], and Isa. 65: 16: He who blesses himself in the land shall bless himself by the God of Amen [be'elohei 'amen], and he who swears in the land shall swear by the God of Amen [be'elohei 'amen].

units.la: Observa 3°. Vocem Amen complementum promissionum & minarum marum significare, dum voculæ ναι, vel ἀμήν consociata legitur, ut Apoc. 1:7. Ecce venit cum nubibus, & omnis oculus eum videbit, & qui eum confoderunt, & omnes terræ tribus super eum plangent ναὶ Ἀμήν. Doctissimis viris voculæ ejusdem plane valoris sunt atque significationis, sicut Abba, Pater, quia vaticinium de ultimo Christi adventu ad Judæos spectat atque gentiles, unde factum, si iis crediderimus, ut ναὶ in gratiam gentilium, Ἀμὴν vero in gratiam Judæorum appositum fuerit. Nobis alia mens ex phrasibus Novi Instrumenti quam similllimis. Audiatur Christus dum jurejurandum per creaturas levissimis de causis præfractè vetat, Matth. 5:37. Ἔστω δὲ ὁ λόγος ὑμῶν ναὶ, ναὶ, οὒ, οὒ. Sit vero sermo vester ita, ita, non, non. Non equidem Christo mens jurejurandum penitus exterminare: sed sinceritatem ac fidelitatem promissionum, quà affirmantium, quà negantium commendare. Si verò constantia in dictis, seu promissis semel obtineat inter homines, nihil opus erit juramentis frequentissimis, quibus levissimis abutuntur de causis, ut mendacii & infidelitatis suspicionem à sese amoliantur. Sensus igitur Christi est, quum vos aliquid facturos receperitis, state promissis, sitque vestrum ναὶ, ναὶ, unde liquet secundum ναὶ significare complementum primi, h.e. promissionis affirmantis: Cum verò vos non facturos receperitis, state pariter promissis, sitque vestrum οὒ, οὒ, unde liquet postremum οὒ, primi complementum significare, h.e. negationem promissionis. Audiatur Jacobus in loco plane gemino, cap. 5:12. ἔστω δὲ ὑμῶν τὸ ναὶ, ναὶ, καὶ τὸ οὒ, οὒ, ἵνα μὴ ὑπὸ κρίσιν πέσητε, sit vestrum nè, nè, & vestrum non, non, ne in condemnationem incidatis. Et Paulus, 2 Cor. 1:17. ubi constantiam prædicationis suæ commendavit, ut sermo ejus non fuerit apud Corinthios ναὶ καὶ οὒ, etiam & non, quòd Dei Filius Jesus Christus inter eos prædicatus, per eum, Silvanum, ac Timotheum, non fuit, ναὶ καὶ οὒ, etiam & non, (unde liquet Paulum pro eodem usurpare τὸν λόγον atque Jesum Christum Dei Filium) ut rationem perhibeat constantiæ sermonis sui apud Corinthios, illico attexuit commate 20. Quotquot enim sunt promissiones Dei, in ipso, nempe Jesu Christo, sunt, ναὶ etiam, καὶ ἐν αὐτῷ τὸ ἀμήν, & in ipso sunt amen. Hinc efficitur ναὶ καὶ ἀμήν, non significare idem, ut alterum Græcum, propter Græcos, seu gentiles: alterum verò Hebræum, propter Judæos, scriptum fuerit: sicuti Doctissimi Viri non pauci opinantur, ut Paulus docere voluerit, omnes Dei promissiones esse veritatem, & firmitatem, seu veras & firmas in Christo. Nobis alia mens est: si enim ναὶ & ἀμὴν, apud Apostolos idem plane significarent, Paulus quà erat divina sapientiâ, non distinxisset membra suae orationis per articulum τὸ geminatum, τὸ ναί, τὸ ἀμὴν: nec'conjunxisset per particulam copulativam καὶ: sed contrà dixisset, omnes Dei promissiones in Christo sunt ναὶ ἀμὴν, unde liquet, τὸ ἀμὴν, τῷ ναί copulatum & superadditum aliquid ab eo distinctum significare, nempe implementum promissionum, ut intelligentia loci sit, omnes Dei promissiones in Christo & propter Christum peccatoribus factae sunt, & in Christo & propter Christum implementum sortitae sunt, ut τὸ ναί respondeat hominum petitionibus, τὸ ἀμὴν earum significet factum à Deo implementum, quasi diceret Apostolus, Age miseri peccatores quid ex conscientia peccati & miseriae vestrae petitis à Deo? num peccatorum remissionem? Deus in Christo & propter Christum vobis annuit, dicitque ναί, etiam: in Christo & propter Christum sanctè vobis promitto peccatorum remissionem? Petitisne Filiorum Dei adoptionem? Annuit Deus, dicitque ναί, etiam; me in Christo & propter Christum vos in Filios adoptaturum sanctè promitto. Petitisne sanctificationis & consolationis Spiritum? vobis Deus annuit, dicitque ναί, etiam: Sanctè polliceor vobis in Christo & propter Christum Spiritum adoptionis, qui contestatur Spiritui vestro, vos esse Dei Filios, haeredes Dei, & cohaeredes Christi. Rom. 8: 16. 17. simul Spiritum sanctificationis & consolationis me in Christo collaturum promitto. Petitisne à morte liberationem & vitam aeternam? vobis Deus annuit, dicitque ναί etiam: in Christo & propter Christum, qui est resurrectio & vita, Joh. 11: 25. vobis resurrectionem & vitam aeternam sanctè polliceor. Sed verò & istud ναί extendi debet ad omnes aeterni Numinis promissiones factas in Veteri Testamento, ut omnes in Christo & propter Christum olim factae fuerint. Attexuit verò Apostolus, καὶ τὸ ἀμὴν, ut significet factas illas Dei in Christo promissiones suum omnes habuisse, vel demum habituras implementum. Denique Johannes ubi vaticinatus est ultimum Christi adventum formidandum impiis: contrà, piis omnibus amandum & expetendum, illicò subtexuit, ναί ἀμὴν, Apoc. 1: 7. ut ναί promissi adventus certitudinem significet, ἀμὴν vero ipsius infallibile implementum.
units.tr: Observe third: the word Amen signifies the fulfilment of promises and threats, when it is read joined with the particle nai or amēn, as in Rev. 1: 7: Behold, he comes with the clouds, and every eye shall see him, and those who pierced him; and all the tribes of the earth shall mourn over him [nai, Amēn]. To learned men these particles have exactly the same value and meaning, as Abba and Father do; and because the prophecy of Christ's final coming concerns both Jews and Gentiles, it has come about, if we believe them, that nai was added for the sake of the Gentiles and amēn for the sake of the Jews. For us the meaning drawn from the very similar phrases of the New Testament is different. Let Christ be heard, when he sternly forbids swearing by creatures for the lightest reasons, Matt. 5: 37: Let your word be yea, yea; no, no [Estō de ho logos hymōn nai, nai, ou, ou]: let your speech be so, so, not, not. Christ does not intend to banish oaths altogether, but to commend the sincerity and fidelity of promises, both those affirming and those denying. If constancy in words or promises once prevails among men, there will be no need for the very frequent oaths by which, for the lightest causes, they abuse God's name in order to remove from themselves the suspicion of lying and faithlessness. The sense of Christ's words, therefore, is this: when you have received that you are going to do something, let your promise stand, and let your word be yea, yea; from which it is clear that the first yea signifies the fulfilment of the first, that is, the affirming promise. When you have received that you are not going to do something, likewise let your promise stand, and let your word be no, no; from which it is clear that the final no signifies the fulfilment of the first, that is, the denial of the promise. Let James be heard in a passage that is exactly parallel, ch. 5: 12: Let your yea be yea, and your no no, lest you fall into condemnation [estō de hymōn to nai nai kai to ou ou, hina mē hypo krisin pesēte]. And Paul, 2 Cor. 1: 17, where he commended the constancy of his preaching, so that his word was not among the Corinthians yea and no [nai kai ou], because the Son of God Jesus Christ, who was preached among them by him, Silvanus and Timothy, was not yea and no [nai kai ou] (whence it is clear that Paul uses the word and Jesus Christ the Son of God for the same thing). In order to give the reason for the constancy of his word among the Corinthians, he immediately added in verse 20: For however many are the promises of God, in him they are yea [nai], and in him they are Amen [kai en autō to amēn]. From this it follows that nai and amēn do not mean the same thing, as if one were written in Greek on account of the Greeks, or Gentiles, and the other in Hebrew on account of the Jews, as not a few learned men suppose, so that Paul meant to teach that all God's promises are truth and firmness, or true and firm in Christ. Our view is different. For if nai and amēn meant exactly the same thing among the Apostles, Paul, being wise with divine wisdom, would not have divided the members of his sentence with the repeated article, the yea, the amen, nor would he have joined them with the conjunction and; he would rather have said, all God's promises in Christ are yea amen. From this it is clear that the amen, joined to the yea and added to it, signifies something distinct from it, namely the fulfilment of the promises, so that the sense of the passage is: all God's promises were made to sinners in Christ and on account of Christ, and in Christ and on account of Christ have obtained their fulfilment; so that the yea answers to men's petitions, and the amen signifies the fulfilment accomplished by God. It is as if the Apostle said: Come, wretched sinners, what do you ask of God out of the consciousness of your sin and misery? Forgiveness of sins? God in Christ and on account of Christ assents to you and says yea: I, in Christ and on account of Christ, solemnly promise you the remission of sins. Do you ask for adoption as sons of God? God assents and says yea: I solemnly promise that in Christ and on account of Christ I will adopt you as sons. Do you ask for the Spirit of sanctification and consolation? God assents to you and says yea: I solemnly promise you in Christ and on account of Christ the Spirit of adoption, who bears witness with your spirit that you are the children of God, heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ (Rom. 8: 16, 17), and at the same time I promise to bestow on you in Christ the Spirit of sanctification and consolation. Do you ask for deliverance from death and eternal life? God assents to you and says yea: in Christ and on account of Christ, who is the resurrection and the life (John 11: 25), I solemnly promise you resurrection and eternal life. But this yea must also be extended to all the promises of the eternal Deity made in the Old Testament, so that all were made in Christ and on account of Christ in former times. The Apostle has added and the amen, to signify that those promises of God made in Christ either have had, or will at last have, their fulfilment. Finally, John, when he prophesied the final coming of Christ, which is to be dreaded by the impious but to be loved and desired by all the pious, immediately added yea, amen (Rev. 1: 7), so that yea signifies the certainty of the promised coming, and amen its infallible fulfilment.

units.la: His praemissis ad quaestionem perstringendam propiùs accedimus. Respondemus igitur Jesum Dei Filium nomine Dei proprio Amen insignitum fuisse, ut Ecclesiam suam doceret se esse verum illum Deum Amen, de quo Jesaias vaticinatus fuerat, cap. 65: 16. ubi gentium vocationem & ad verum Deum conversionem relictis idolis suis, his verbis praedixerat, qui se benedicet in terra, se benedicet in Deo Amen, & qui jurabit in terra, jurabit per Deum Amen.
units.tr: Having set out these points, we come closer to the question itself. We answer, then, that Jesus, the Son of God, was marked with the proper name of God, Amen, so that he might teach his Church that he is that true God Amen, of whom Isaiah prophesied in chapter 65, verse 16, where, foretelling the calling of the Gentiles and their conversion to the true God away from their idols, he spoke these words: He who blesses himself in the land shall bless himself in the God Amen, and he who swears in the land shall swear by the God Amen.

units.la: 2°. Hoc nomine proprio Amen Jesus Dei Filius gaudet multis de causis. 1°. Propter aeternae naturae suae inviolabilem firmitatem, absque vel levissima mutationis umbra: est enim Ens summe perfectum, in quo nulla est non-entis mixtura. 2°. Quia fons est & scaturigo perennis entitatis & veritatis realis, quam in creaturis cernere est: nam per eum condita sunt omnia, qua in coelis sunt & qua in terra, visibilia & invisibilia, & throni, & dominatus, & imperia & potestates, omnia per eum & propter eum condita sunt, estque ipse ante omnia, & omnia per eum subsistunt, Col. 1:16. 17. 3°. In habitudine ad omnes creaturas, vel praestantissimas, Seraphim & Cherubim, quorum esse, si cum aeterna Filii Dei divinitate contendatur: umbra est levissima entitatis & veritatis. 4°. In habitudine ad falsos gentium Deos, qui nec in se naturae firmitatem inviolabilem obtinuere: nec suam divinitatem fictitiam sartam tectamque tueri sustinuere: sed velut umbrae fugaces, vacuaque phantasmata evanuerunt, quum primum Filius Dei o ἀμλω, gloriosissimo splendore divinitatis suae, suique Evangelii orbem terrarum illustravit. Hinc factum ut Apostoli Deum viventem & verum appellaverint, eum ubi cum idolis contendunt, converti estis ad Deum relictis idolis ut serviretis Deo viventi & vero. 1 Thess. 1:9. Novimus autem Filium Dei venisse & dedisse nobis intelligentiam ut cognoscamus verum & summum in vero, in Filio ejus Jesu Christo, ipse est verus Deus & vita aeterna. 1 Joan. 5:20. 5°. In habitudine ad promissiones falsorum Deorum fidem spemque, quam idololatrae Gentiles in iis jam repositerunt, simul ad vanam religionem, qua eos prosecuti sunt; nam Christus o ἀμλω adventu suo in clara luce demonstravit, ea omnia fuisse non veritatem, sed vanitatem & mendacium. Hinc factum ut suo nomini Amen extemplo attexuerit o μαρτυς, ο πιστος και αληθινος, testis fidelis & verax.
units.tr: Second, Jesus the Son of God rejoices in this proper name Amen for many reasons. (1) On account of the inviolable firmness of his eternal nature, without even the slightest shadow of change; for he is a Being most perfectly complete, in whom there is no admixture of non-being. (2) Because he is the fountain and perennial spring of the real being and truth that we see in creatures: for by him were all things created, that are in heaven and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers; all things were created by him and for him; and he is before all things, and by him all things consist, Col. 1:16, 17. (3) In relation to all creatures, even the most excellent, Seraphim and Cherubim: if their being is set against the eternal divinity of the Son of God, it is the faintest shadow of being and truth. (4) In relation to the false gods of the Gentiles, who had neither a firm and inviolable nature in themselves, nor were able to maintain their fictitious divinity intact and covered; but, like fleeting shadows and empty phantoms, they vanished as soon as the Son of God, the Amen [ὁ ἀμήν], illuminated the world with the most glorious splendour of his divinity and of his Gospel. Hence it is that the Apostles called God living and true, when they set him against idols: you turned to God from idols, to serve the living and true God, 1 Thess. 1:9. And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, that we may know him who is true; and we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God and eternal life, 1 John 5:20. (5) In relation to the promises of false gods, and to the faith and hope which idolatrous Gentiles had placed in them, and likewise to the empty religion by which they pursued them: for Christ, the Amen [ὁ ἀμήν], by his coming, showed in clear light that all these were not truth but vanity and falsehood. Hence it is that he added immediately to his name Amen the words the witness, the faithful and true [ὁ μάρτυς, ὁ πιστὸς καὶ ἀληθινός], the faithful and true witness.

units.la: 3°. Christus Dei Filius appellatur o ἀμλω in habitudine ad foedus operum, quia veritas est, finis & implementum legis, Rom. 10:4. & Johannes, lex data est per Moysen; gratia & veritas per Jesum Christum praestita est, Joh. 1:17. Hic loci manifesta instituitur oppositio Moysem inter & Christum, Legem & Evangelium, quod gratia & veritas appellatur. Eccur vero gratia & veritas prout legi opponitur? Si viros ros doctos plerosque audiveris, Evangelium gratia est in habitudine ad Gentiles, quibus non annunciata erat ἐπαγγελία, promissio Evangelii, seu gratiosi foederis: Unde factum est, cum primum Gentibus Evangelium annunciatum fuit, ut sub idea merae gratiae iis apparuerit: Veritas vero in habitudine ad Judaeos, quibus per Prophetas ἐπαγγελία, promissio gratiosi foederis, identidem annunciata fuit: ut cum primum Evangelium per Christum & Apostolos fuit Judaeis annunciatum sub idea veritatis h. e. complementi promissionis, illis apparuerit. Sed vero ut res ita habeat, quaeritur num haec fuerit mens Evangelistae, & explicatio doctorum virorum apprime cohaereat cum oppositione, quam Evangelista instituit Christum inter & Moysem, Evangelium, ut gratia & veritas est, & legem: nam si Evangelium veritas est, juxta mentem Evangelistae, quia complementum est promissi gratiosi foederis, utique Evangelium, quatenus est veritas distinguitur a Lege, tum quatenus Lex significat universam Veteris Testamenti doctrinam, quae & promissiones gratiosas continet permixtas formulis foederis operum: tum quatenus lex significat ministerium mortis & condemnationis scriptum literis, & insculptum lapidibus, quod Moyses detulit e monte ad Israelitas. Quominus vero lex hic loci usurpetur prout significat universam doctrinam veteris dispensationis, multa vetant, 1°. Quia sub hac nomenclatura lex non modo data est per Moysem, sed & per caeteros Prophetas. 2°. Quia lex sub hac notione gratiam proprie dictam complectitur, nempe favorem gratuitum, erga merentem malum contrarium puta odium, & effecta gratuiti istiusmodi favoris, quorum maxime illustria fuere οἱ ἐπαγγελίαι Messiae, frequentissimae declarationes divinae misericordiae in condonandis peccatis, in corde circumcidendo, in pangendo novo foedere, & in scribendo leges Dei in carneis cordis tabulis. Unde in expedito concludere est, Evangelistam non appellasse Evangelium gratiam in habitudine ad Gentiles, & veritatem in habitudine ad Judaeos, quia istiusmodi interpretatio legitimam subvertit oppositionem, quam Evangelista sacer instituit Moysem inter & Christum, legem & Evangelium. Superest igitur, ut Lex proprio & presso significatu ab Evangelista usurpetur, quatenus sonat foedus operum Evangelio oppositum e diametro, nempe ut est ministerium condemnationis & mortis, exaratum literis, & inscriptum lapidibus, litera occidens, non spiritus vivificans, 2 Cor. 3: 6. 7. 9. ut Evangelium sit gratia & veritas, quatenus vicissim legi opponitur. Est vero Evangelium lium gratia, quatenus opponitur justitiæ vindicatrici, quæ viget in lege, maledictioni & morti terrificæ, quam lex in sui violatores stringit, absque ulla spe veniæ aut remissionis peccatorum: nam Euangelium gratiam, h. e. favorem Dei gratuitum adversus peccatores merentes Dei odium blanda voce annunciat, & effecta illius gratiæ, quæ & mera gratia sunt, nempe remissionem peccatorum promittit & confert Deo fœderatis per fidem. Præterea Evangelium veritas est multifariam dum legi opponitur. 1°. Quia cum Lex justificationis, & felicitatis obtinendæ spem fœderatis suis facere videatur, spem vanam & vacuam sine re & veritate facit, non suo quidem vitio: sed propter inolitam cordis humani malitiam, est enim infirma in carne, Rom. 8: 3. Nec data est δυναμένῳ ζωοποιῆσαι, potens vivificare, Gal. 3: 21. Contra Evangelium veritas est, ut enim promittit Dei gratiam, peccatorum remissionem, conscientiæ pacem, & salutem, non spem facit vacuam sine re & veritate: Sed & reapsa salutem confert fœderatis Dei fidelibus, unde jure merito veritas est. 2°. Evangelium veritas est, ubi contenditur cum umbris typisque bonorum legis: nam Christus veritas est cujus Moses fuit typus & umbra, quatenus fuit liberator populi Israelitici & fœderis legalis Mediator. Salus Evangelii veritas est, cujus liberatio è servitute Ægyptiaca, mel & lac, cæteræque benedictiones terræ Canaan, figuræ fuere & umbræ. Christus igitur Amen est, veritas & complementum totius legis, unde Paulus, legemne cassam reddimus per fidem? absit, imo legem stabilimus, Rom. 3: 31. & Christus quærenti Philippo, ostende nobis patrem, & sufficit nobis, sapienter reponit, ego sum via, veritas & vita, via, qua itur ad Patrem, veritas legis, & omnium Patris promissionum implementum; vita, h. e. causa vitæ, quam vos Judæi in visione Dei Patris sitam esse, merito quidem putatis. Joh. 14: 6. Denique Christus est Amen, veritas & implementum fœderis legalis, si istiusmodi fœdus spectetur secundum partes ex quibus efflorescebat: secundum justitiam suam, & denique secundum finem externum, mentem & consilium Dei Sapientissimi Legislatoris. Legem ceremonialem si spectaverimus, Christus illius Amen est, veritas & implementum: nam omnes typi & ceremoniæ, vel in persona Christi, vel in muneribus Christi, vel in beneficiis & salute Christi, suam habent veritatem, suumque corpus: nam illa omnia umbra erant rerum futurarum, at corpus est Christi, Col. 2: 17. Si spectaverimus legem moralem, quando ejus summa est perfecta sanctitas, sita in amore summo Dei & proximi : utique Christus illius est Amen, veritas & implementum : est enim imago Dei invisibilis, perfecte dilexit justitiam, & miquitatem odio habuit, Psalm. 45: 8. Deum amavit toto corde, & proximum, ut vitam pro eo posuerit, sanctitatis consummatae absolutissimum exemplar fuit, sanctus, innocens, sine macula, a peccatoribus separatus, Hebr. 7: 26. Legem politicam si spectaverimus, Christus illius est Amen, veritas & implementum; nam corpus & veritas est Regum, Legislatorum & judicum, penes quos erat legis politicae authoritas, rempublicam habet spiritualem, nempe Ecclesiam, quae veritas corpusque est reipublicae Israelis lege politica constitutae, quia est Ecclesia primogenitorum, quorum nomina scripta sunt in coelis, sicut nomina tribuum carnalis reipublicae scripta erant in archivis templi Hierosolymitani, gens sancta, regale sacerdotium, sicut politeia Israelitica. Habet denique in se quicquid erat boni moralis in lege politica, corpus & veritatem illius, quod in hujusmodi lege typicum fuit ac ceremoniale. Nec minus Christus Amen est, veritas & implementum foederis legalis, si spectetur juxta foederalem justitiam suam, quando enim legis justitia sita fuit, hinc in sanctitate perfecta, juxta hanc formulam, qui hac faciet; illinc vero in maledictione, quam lex in sui violatores stringebat, juxta hanc formulam, maledictus quisquis non permanserit in omnibus, qua scripta sunt in libro legis, ut faciat ea, Deut. 27: 26. Galat. 3: 10. Utique Christus Amen est, veritas & implementum totius justitiae legalis: nempe perfecte implevit omnia legis opera, moralia, ceremonialia, politica, perfecte justus & sanctus Deum amavit toto corde, & proximum sicut seipsum, ut jure nullius peccati reus peragi potuerit. Joh. 8: 48. Maledictionem vero alteram legalis justitiae partem, quod attinet, utique Christus illius Amen, veritasque est: nos enim redemit ab execratione legis, dum pro nobis factus est execratio, juxta legem, scriptum est enim execrabilis est quisquis pendet in ligno, Deut. 21: 23. Gal. 3: 13. Sed vero unus Christus potuit esse Amen, veritas & implementum maledictionis legis: nam maledictio legis infinita esse debet simul positive simul negative. Positive in habitudine ad infinitam Numinis Majestatem legis violatione laesam: negative vero, h. e. tanta quantacunque creatura capax est, ut major excogitari nequeat, tum ob infinitam negative, peccatoris malitiam, tum ob criminis atrocitatem: nemo vero philos, anthropos, nudus homo, utpote finitus, capax est ferendae poenae, seu maledictionis infinitae, simul positive simul negative. Non positive, quia non habet dignitatem infinitam, paremve dignitati infinitæ Numinis, quam peccatum læddit: non negative, quia pœna & dolore, quibus afficitur mera creatura, major cum ratione infamiæ, tum ratione acrocitatis sensusque doloris, utique excogitari potest, & ferri: nempe pœna, supplicium, infamia, & dolor, quæ tulit Christus Θεάνθρωπος, Deus & homo. Unus igitur Christus Immanuel esse potuit Amen, quod Israëlitæ pronunciarunt ad finem maledictionum legis, Deuter. 27: 15. &c. Nam ipse unus, plenè implevit maledictionem legis, eam enim tulit & positive & negative infinitam: positive propter infinitam dignitatem personæ suæ parem dignitati Dei Patris: negative ob atrocitatem infamiæ supplicii, sensusque doloris, quâ major, ne mente quidem cogitari potest. Si legem spectaverimus juxta finem & consilium Dei legislatoris, Christus illius est Amen, veritas & implementum: nam Christus est finis legis in justitiam omni credenti, Rom. 10: 4. & Lex fuit paedagogus ad Christum, Galat. 3: 24. Nempe Deus legem iteraverat prospicientem in Christum: ducebat enim fœderatos legales ad Christum 1°. suâ impotentiâ ad eos vivificandum, h. e. justificandum & sanctificandum; erat enim litera mortua, non spiritus efficax, 2 Cor. 3: 6. infirma in carne, Rom. 8: 3. 2°. Suâ maledictione & severitate inexorabili fœderatos ad quærendum Christum liberatorem cogebat, Rom. 7: 24. 3°. Figuris & umbris legis ceremonialis. 4°. Lege politica, nempe posita erat ad constituendam & confervandam rempublicam Israëlis, tanquam in finem proximum: sed ipse finis proximus, hoc est conservatio reipublicæ in Christum prospiciebat, uti medium in finem suum ultimum, nempe ut distincta suis tribubus per legem politicam Israëlis respublica conservaretur, quò ex ipsius sinu in complemento temporis oriretur Messias, & ortus pro vero Messia haberi posset, insignitus propriis & germanis characteribus, quibus à Prophetis delineatus fuerat, nempe oriundus è semine Abrahami, è tribu Judæ, è familia Davidis, & ex virgine è vico Bethlehem, quæ distincta & impermixta exstare non poterant, absque lege politica fuisset, unde, moribundus Vates divinus Jacob, sceptrum non discedet è Juda, nec Legislator è pedibus ejus, donec Schilo venerit, Genes. 49: 10. Nam sive per שׁבט sceyet, sceptrum intelligat, sive tribum, perinde est: nam sceptrum, hoc est, summa imperii Majestas, penes Judam, hoc est Judæos, distinctos ab Israëlitis fuit, (quicquid contrà sentiant viri Doctissimi) usque dum Schilo, hoc est MesMessias, venerit, & tribus Judæ mansit pariter impermixta ad Christi adventum: unde duxere originem ambæ genealogiæ Christi, quas pertexuerunt Matthæus & Lucas, ille ab Abrahamo ad Christum, hic verò à Christo ad Adamum.
units.tr: Third, Christ is called the Son of God the Amen in relation to the covenant of works, because he is the truth, the end and fulfilment of the law (Rom. 10:4). And John says: the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ (John 1:17). Here a clear contrast is set up between Moses and Christ, between Law and Gospel, the latter being called grace and truth. But why are grace and truth opposed to the law in this way? If you listen to most learned men, the Gospel is grace in relation to the Gentiles, to whom the promise of the Gospel, that is, the gracious covenant [ἐπαγγελία], had not been announced. So when the Gospel was first preached to the Gentiles, it appeared to them under the aspect of pure grace. But truth is the Gospel in relation to the Jews, to whom the gracious covenant, the promise, had been announced again and again through the prophets. So when the Gospel was first preached to the Jews through Christ and the apostles, it appeared to them under the aspect of truth, that is, the fulfilment of the promise. But whether the matter really stands thus is open to question. Does this explanation agree with the contrast the evangelist draws between Christ and Moses, the Gospel and the law, when he calls the Gospel grace and truth? For if, according to the evangelist's mind, the Gospel is truth because it is the fulfilment of the gracious covenant's promise, then the Gospel, insofar as it is truth, is surely distinguished from the Law in two ways: first, insofar as the Law signifies the whole doctrine of the Old Testament, which contains gracious promises mixed with the forms of the covenant of works; and second, insofar as the law signifies the ministry of death and condemnation, written in letters and engraved on stones, which Moses brought down from the mountain to the Israelites. But that the law should be taken here in the sense of the whole doctrine of the old dispensation is forbidden by many things. (1) Because under this name the law was not given only through Moses but also through the other prophets. (2) Because in this sense the law embraces grace properly so called, namely free favour, opposed to the hatred felt towards one who deserves evil, and the effects of such free favour, of which the most illustrious were the messianic promises, the most frequent declarations of divine mercy in forgiving sins, in circumcising the heart, in establishing a new covenant, and in writing the laws of God on the fleshly tables of the heart. Hence it is easy to conclude that the evangelist did not call the Gospel grace in relation to the Gentiles and truth in relation to the Jews, because such an interpretation destroys the legitimate opposition which the sacred evangelist sets up between Moses and Christ, the law and the Gospel. It remains, therefore, that the Law is used by the evangelist in its proper and strict sense, insofar as it signifies the covenant of works, which is diametrically opposed to the Gospel: namely as the ministry of condemnation and death, written in letters and inscribed on stones, the letter that kills, not the Spirit that gives life (2 Cor. 3:6, 7, 9). So the Gospel is grace and truth, insofar as, in turn, it is opposed to the law. Now the Gospel is grace insofar as it is opposed to the avenging justice which reigns in the law, the curse and the terrifying death which the law inflicts on its violators, without any hope of pardon or forgiveness of sins. For the Gospel announces grace, that is, God's free favour towards sinners who deserve God's hatred, with a gentle voice, and it promises and bestows, through faith, the forgiveness of sins to those who are in covenant with God, which are effects of that grace and are themselves pure grace. Moreover, the Gospel is truth in many ways when it is opposed to the law. (1) Because, while the Law seems to promise justification and the hope of obtaining happiness to those in its covenant, it makes that hope vain and empty, without substance and truth. This is not its own fault, but because of the deeply rooted malice of the human heart, for it is weak through the flesh (Rom. 8:3). Nor was it given to be [δυναμένῳ ζωοποιῆσαι], able to give life (Gal. 3:21). By contrast, the Gospel is truth: for when it promises God's grace, the forgiveness of sins, peace of conscience and salvation, it does not make hope empty and without substance and truth, but in fact bestows salvation on the faithful who are in covenant with God, and so it is rightly called truth. (2) The Gospel is truth when it is set against the shadows and types of the good things of the law. For Christ is the truth, of whom Moses was the type and shadow, insofar as Moses was the deliverer of the Israelite people and the mediator of the legal covenant. The salvation of the Gospel is the truth, of which the deliverance from Egyptian bondage, the honey and milk, and the other blessings of the land of Canaan were figures and shadows. Christ, therefore, is the Amen, the truth and the fulfilment of the whole law. Hence Paul says: Do we then make void the law through faith? God forbid; yea, we establish the law (Rom. 3:31). And when Philip asks, Show us the Father, and it is enough for us, Christ wisely answers: I am the way, the truth and the life (John 14:6). He is the way, by which one goes to the Father; the truth of the law and the fulfilment of all the promises of the Father; the life, that is, the cause of the life which you Jews rightly think lies in the vision of God the Father. Finally, Christ is the Amen, the truth and fulfilment of the legal covenant, if such a covenant is considered according to its parts from which it grew: according to its justice, and finally according to its external end, the mind and purpose of God the most wise Legislator. If we consider the ceremonial law, Christ is its Amen, truth and fulfilment, for all the types and ceremonies, whether in the person of Christ, or in the offices of Christ, or in the benefits and salvation of Christ, have their own truth and their own body: for all those things were a shadow of the things to come, but the body is of Christ (Col. 2:17). If we consider the moral law, whose sum is perfect holiness, placed in the highest love of God and neighbour, then surely Christ is its Amen, truth and fulfilment. For he is the image of the invisible God, he loved righteousness perfectly and hated iniquity (Ps. 45:8). He loved God with his whole heart and his neighbour, so that he laid down his life for him; he was the most perfect pattern of consummate holiness, holy, innocent, undefiled, separate from sinners (Heb. 7:26). If we consider the political law, Christ is its Amen, truth and fulfilment. For kings, lawgivers and judges, in whose hands was the authority of the political law, were the body and truth of it; but Christ has a spiritual commonwealth, namely the Church, which is the truth and body of the Israelite commonwealth established by political law, because it is the Church of the firstborn, whose names are written in heaven (Heb. 12:23), just as the names of the tribes of the carnal commonwealth were written in the archives of the temple at Jerusalem; a holy nation, a royal priesthood (1 Pet. 2:9), just as the Israelite polity. Finally, Christ has in himself whatever was good in a moral sense in the political law, its body and truth, and whatever in such a law was typical and ceremonial. Christ is no less the Amen, truth and fulfilment of the legal covenant, if he is considered in relation to its covenantal justice. For the justice of the law lay, on the one hand, in perfect holiness, according to this formula: the man who does these things; on the other hand, in the curse which the law inflicted on its violators, according to this formula: cursed is whoever does not continue in all the things written in the book of the law, to do them (Deut. 27:26; Gal. 3:10). Christ, then, is surely the Amen, truth and fulfilment of the whole legal justice. He perfectly fulfilled all the works of the law, moral, ceremonial and political; perfectly just and holy, he loved God with his whole heart and his neighbour as himself, so that he could be pronounced guilty of no sin at all (John 8:46). As for the other part of legal justice, the curse, surely Christ is its Amen and truth: for he redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us, according to the law: for it is written, cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree (Deut. 21:23; Gal. 3:13). But only Christ could be the Amen, the truth and fulfilment of the curse of the law. For the curse of the law must be infinite, both positively and negatively. Positively, in relation to the infinite majesty of the Godhead, injured by the violation of the law; negatively, that is, as great as a creature is capable of bearing, so that a greater cannot be imagined, both because of the infinite malice of the sinner and because of the atrocity of the crime. But no mere man, psilos anthropos, a naked human being, being finite, is capable of bearing the punishment, or the infinite curse, both positively and negatively. Not positively, because he does not have an infinite dignity, or a dignity equal to the infinite dignity of the Godhead which sin injures; not negatively, because the punishment and pain with which a mere creature is afflicted, greater both in respect of infamy and in respect of the atrocity and sense of pain, can indeed be imagined and borne. But the punishment, the torment, the infamy and the pain which Christ, the Theanthropos, God and man, bore were such. Therefore only Christ Immanuel could be the Amen, which the Israelites pronounced at the end of the curses of the law (Deut. 27:15, etc.). For he alone fully fulfilled the curse of the law, for he bore it both positively and negatively infinite: positively, on account of the infinite dignity of his person, equal to the dignity of God the Father; negatively, on account of the atrocity of the infamy, the punishment and the sense of pain, than which a greater cannot even be conceived in the mind. If we consider the law according to the end and purpose of God the lawgiver, Christ is its Amen, truth and fulfilment. For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes (Rom. 10:4), and the law was our schoolmaster to bring us to Christ (Gal. 3:24). God had indeed so ordered the law that it looked forward to Christ. For it led those in the legal covenant to Christ: (1) by its own inability to give them life, that is, to justify and sanctify them, for it was a dead letter, not an effective spirit (2 Cor. 3:6), weak through the flesh (Rom. 8:3); (2) by its curse and inexorable severity it compelled those in the covenant to seek Christ as their deliverer (Rom. 7:24); (3) by the figures and shadows of the ceremonial law; (4) by the political law, which was established to constitute and preserve the commonwealth of Israel as its immediate end. But this immediate end, that is, the preservation of the commonwealth, looked forward to Christ, as a means looks to its ultimate end: namely, so that the commonwealth, distinct by tribes under the political law of Israel, might be preserved, and from its bosom, in the fullness of time, the Messiah might arise, and the one who arose might be held to be the true Messiah, marked with his own proper and genuine characters by which the prophets had described him: namely, born of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Judah, of the family of David, and from a virgin in the village of Bethlehem. These things could not exist distinct and unmixed without the political law. Hence the dying divine prophet Jacob said: The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor the lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh comes (Gen. 49:10). For whether one understands by [שׁבט], shebet, the sceptre or the tribe makes no difference. For the sceptre, that is, the supreme majesty of rule, remained with Judah, that is, the Jews, distinct from the Israelites (whatever the most learned men think to the contrary), until Shiloh, that is, the Messiah, should come; and the tribe of Judah remained equally unmixed until the coming of Christ. Hence both genealogies of Christ, which Matthew and Luke wove together, derived their origin: the former from Abraham to Christ, the latter from Christ back to Adam.

units.la: 4°. Christus Amen est in habitudine ad Prophetarum vaticinia, quæ in Christo habent suum Amen & complementum: ille enim Messias est, cujus nativitatem ex virgine, miracula, passiones, mortis genus, resurrectionem, ascensionem in cœlum, sessionem ad dexteram Dei, missionem & effusionem Spiritus Sancti in omnem carnem, Apostolorum ministerium, Euangelii prædicationem, gentium vocationem, Prophetæ vaticinati fuerant, ut Scriptura vetus in totum, suum Amen & complementum in Christo obtineat. Ut Christus opportuisse Messiam pati, & intrare in gloriam suam ex lege, Prophetis & Psalmis, hoc est ex tota Scriptura Veteri, sub tribus illis capitibus, vulgari apud Judæos divisione contentâ, probaverit. Luc. 24: 44.
units.tr: 4°. Christ is the Amen in relation to the prophets' predictions, which find their Amen and fulfilment in Christ. For he is the Messiah whose birth from a virgin, miracles, sufferings, manner of death, resurrection, ascension into heaven, session at the right hand of God, sending and outpouring of the Holy Spirit on all flesh, apostolic ministry, preaching of the Gospel, and calling of the Gentiles the prophets foretold, so that the whole of the Old Scripture obtains its Amen and fulfilment in Christ. Thus Christ proved that the Messiah ought to suffer and enter into his glory, from the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms, that is, from the whole of the Old Scripture, under those three heads which the Jews commonly use in dividing it. Luke 24:44.

units.la: 5°. Christus Dei Filius Amen est votorum & precum omnium, quo claudebantur, & veluti facta anacephalæosi continebantur, preces fidelium, vota & desideria Angelorum, & 1º. quidem Amen est, veritas & implementum votorum Angelicorum: ex quo enim Angelis revelatum est fore, ut Filius Dei fuerit Immanuel, Deus in carne manifestatus, ad destruenda opera diaboli, & genus humanum redimendum, gestierunt desiderio videndi πολυποικίλον Dei sapientiam, & gloriosum redemptionis opus, & ipsum θαυμαστὸν, ut flagrantissimum Angelorum desiderium in Christum collineans, sapientissimè Deus adumbraverit in ambobus Cherubim, ita comparatis in Arca, ut admirabundi, & sese contuerentur mutuò, & velut ex compacto vultus oculosque in propitiatorium, Christi typum converterent. Unde Petrus salutis mysteria ait ea esse, in qua Angeli incurvati avidè intueri desiderant, 1 Petr. 1: 12. & Paulus in memorandis mysterii pietatis articulis & hunc memorat, nempe Deum in carne manifestatum visum fuisse ab Angelis. 1 Tim. 3: 16. 2°. Christus Amen est veritas atque complementum votorum Regum, atque Prophetarum, quando enim regibus, Davidi, Salomoni, & Prophetis revelatum fuerat venturum Messiam Dei Filium, summa cum expectatione adventum ejus præstolati sunt, unde Christus, beati sunt oculi vestri quòd percipiant, & aures vestræ, quòd audiant, Amen enim dico vobis, multos Prophetas & justos desiderasse videre, qua vos videtis, nec tamen vidisse, & audiaudire, qua vos auditis, nec tamen audisse, Matth. 13: 16 Luc. 10: 14. & Petrus, Propheta diligenter inquisiverunt, quando & quo tempore Spiritus propheticus, qui erat in ipsis, antea testimonium perhibens, declarabat passiones futuras, qua Christum manebant, & glorias hinc secuturas, 1 Petr. 1: 11. & Ecclesia, enarra mihi, quem dilexit anima mea, ubi pascas, ubi recubare facias gregem tuum in meridie, Cant. 1: 7. Utinam disrumpens coelos descenderes, & montes difluerent e conspectu tuo, Ies. 64: 1.
units.tr: 5°. Christ the Son of God is the Amen of all vows and prayers, in whom they are all closed and, as it were, summed up: the prayers of the faithful, and the vows and desires of the angels. First, indeed, he is the Amen, the truth and fulfilment of the angelic vows. For when it was revealed to the angels that the Son of God would be Immanuel, God manifested in the flesh, to destroy the works of the devil and redeem mankind, they longed with desire to see the manifold [πολυποικίλον] wisdom of God, and the glorious work of redemption, and the wonderful [θαυμαστὸν] thing itself. God, most wisely, set this as the eager desire of the angels aimed at Christ, when he shadowed it forth in the two cherubim placed on the Ark, so that they looked in wonder at each other, and, as if by agreement, turned their faces and eyes toward the mercy seat, the type of Christ. Hence Peter says that the mysteries of salvation are those things into which the angels long to look, 1 Peter 1:12. And Paul, in recounting the articles of the mystery of godliness, also mentions this, namely that God manifested in the flesh was seen by the angels, 1 Tim. 3:16. Second, Christ is the Amen, the truth and fulfilment of the vows of kings and prophets. For when it had been revealed to kings, David and Solomon, and to the prophets, that the Messiah, the Son of God, would come, they awaited his coming with the greatest expectation. Hence Christ says: Blessed are your eyes, for they see, and your ears, for they hear. For truly I say to you, many prophets and righteous men desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it, Matt. 13:16; Luke 10:24. And Peter: The prophets searched diligently, inquiring when and at what time the prophetic Spirit, which was in them, bearing witness beforehand, declared the sufferings that were to come upon Christ, and the glories that would follow them, 1 Peter 1:11. And the Church says: Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you feed, where you make your flock lie down at noon, Song 1:7. Oh that you would rend the heavens and come down, that the mountains might flow down at your presence, Isa. 64:1.

units.la: 3°. Christus Amen est novae Ecclesiae sponsae suae: quotquot enim vivunt fideles in Christum prospiciunt, uti in finem & complementum omnium votorum, omnes dissolvi cupiunt, & esse cum Christo, ut Paulus, Philip. 1: 23. Nempe, quamdiu sumus in hoc corpore, absumus a Domino: sed quando absumus a corpore, sumus apud Dominum, 2 Cor. 5: 6. 8. omnes gestiunt pra desiderio gloriosi ipsius adventus & eorum πολιτευμα in coelis est; unde etiam Servatorem expectant Dominum Iesum Christum, qui transfigurabit corpus nostrum humile, ut conforme fiat ejus corpori glorioso, &c. Phil. 3: 20. 21. Unde Spiritus & sponsa dicunt & ingeminant, veni igitur Domine Iesu veni, & ipse votis annuit, dicitque, vai etiam, venio cito, Amen: ubi Amen promissionis implementum significat, sicut praecedens vai voti & postulati exauditionem & concessionem, Apoc. 22: 17. 20.
units.tr: 3°. Christ is the Amen of his new bride, the Church. For all the faithful who live look to Christ as the end and fulfilment of all their vows, and all desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ, as Paul says, Phil. 1:23. Indeed, while we are in this body we are absent from the Lord, but when we are absent from the body we are present with the Lord, 2 Cor. 5:6, 8. All long with desire for his glorious coming, and their citizenship is in heaven. Hence they also await the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform our lowly body to be conformed to his glorious body, etc., Phil. 3:20, 21. Hence the Spirit and the bride say and repeat: Come, therefore, Lord Jesus, come; and he himself assents to their prayers and says: Yes, I am coming quickly. Amen. Here Amen signifies the fulfilment of the promise, just as the preceding yes signifies the hearing and granting of the vow and request, Rev. 22:17, 20.

units.la: 6°. Christus Dei Filius Amen est Ecclesiae, quia pabulum est animarum, robur & firmamentum, causaque perseverantiae, seu constantiae in fide, & professione cultus Dei. Amen enim ut ducit originem ex אמן nutrivit, ita & veritatem significat, proprium animae rationalis pabulum. Christus vero Deus in carne manifestatus pabulum animae peccatoris conscii, reatus & miseriae suae luculentum est, quem male habet impiorum prosperitas, spera in יהוה Domino, & fac bonum, & pasce אמונה veritatem, & delectare in יהוה Domino, Psalm. 37: 3. 4. Ubi divinus vates delectare in Domino, subtexuit explicationis ergo istius mandati, pasce veritatem, ut אמונה pro יהוה velut ἰσοδυναμοῦντα nomina usurpaverit: est enim nomen Dei proprium, Deut. 32: 4. sicut אמת Psalm. 31: 6. & אמן Isai. 65: 16. Re enim vera, uti flagrantissimum veritatis obtinendae desiderium, quo aestuant miseri mortales, luculentissime fame & siti in Scriptura adumbratur, quia ut fames & sitis, vehementissimum est desiderium commune omnibus hominibus, naturale, & ad conservationem propriam & singularem, singulorum hominum opportunum, ita & unus Christus stus Dei Filius, mortuus, & e mortuis excitatus, Amen est & unum sedandæ famí spirituali sitiqúe restinguendæ opportunum pabulum. Nempe quicquid peccator salutis & felicitatis desiderio æstuans, quærere potest, vel efflagitare id totum quantum quantum est in uno Christo, velut in τυμεῖω refertissimo, fonteque perenni repositum habet. Sititne desiderio obtinendæ liberationis à condemnatione, & peccatorum remissionis? Nulla est condemnatio iis, qui sunt in Christo Jesu, Rom. 8: 1. & per Christum annunciatur peccatorum remissio, Act. 13: 8. In Christo habemus redemptionem per sanguinem ejus, nempe remissionem peccatorum, Ephes. 1: 7. Colos. 1: 14. Sititne desiderio pacis & tranquillitatis animæ ex sensu reconciliationis cum Deo? Justificati per fidem pacem habemus apud Deum, per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum, Rom. 5: 1. Sititne adoptionem & dignitatem Filiorum Dei? Quotquot in eum crediderunt iis dedit ἐξουσίαν Filiorum Dei, Joh. 1: 12. & factus est legi obnoxius, ut nos acciperemus adoptionem Filiorum, Gal. 4: 5. Æstuatne desiderio imaginis Dei, quæ sita est in vera justitia & sanctitate? nos qui contemplamur detecta facie gloriam Domini, in eandem imaginem transformamur ex gloria in gloriam, tanquam à Domini spiritu, 2 Cor. 3: 18. Sititne liberationem à tyrannide diaboli, mortis imperatoris, & ab ipsa morte? Christus morte sua destruxit diabolum, penes quem erat imperium mortis, Hebr. 2: 14. destruxit ipsam mortem, vitam & immortalitatem in lucem produxit per Euangelium, 2 Tim. 1: 10. Nempe Christus est resurrectio & vita, h. e. causa resurrectionis, & vitæ, Joh. 11: 25. Sititne desiderio obtinendæ vitæ æternæ? Stipendium peccati mors est, donum autem Dei vita aterna in Christo Jesu Domino nostro, Rom. 6: 23. Est igitur Christus Amen, abundans animæ pabulum, quo fames & sitis ejus vehementissima extinguatur: in eo enim sunt aperti & expositi thesauri omnes scientiæ & intelligentiæ salutaris, qui priscis retrò seculis fuerant abscondití, Colos. 2: 3. Hinc Christum audias, ego sum verus panis, qui è cœlo descendit, panis vivus, seu vivificus, caro mea verus cibus, sanguis meus verus potus est, Joh. 6: 51, 55. si quis sitiat, veniat ad me, & bibat, Joh. 7: 37. qui venit ad me, nequaquam esuriet, & qui credit in me, non sitiet unquam, Joh. 6: 35.
units.tr: 6°. Christ the Son of God is the Amen of the Church, because he is the food of souls, the strength and support, and the cause of perseverance or constancy in faith and in the profession of the worship of God. For Amen, as it derives its origin from אמן [aman], to nourish, so also signifies truth, the proper food of the rational soul. Now Christ, God manifested in the flesh, is the food of the sinner who is aware of his guilt and misery. This is plain from the case of those whom the prosperity of the wicked troubles: Trust in the LORD, and do good; feed on faithfulness [אמונה, emunah], and delight yourself in the LORD, Ps. 37:3, 4. Here the divine poet, after delight yourself in the Lord, added, to explain this command, feed on faithfulness, so that he used אמונה [emunah] for יהוה [Jehovah] as if they were equivalent names, since it is a proper name of God, Deut. 32:4, just as אמת [emet] in Ps. 31:6 and אמן [aman] in Isa. 65:16. Indeed, just as hunger and thirst are the most vehement and common desire of all men, natural and suited to the preservation of the self and of each individual, so the intense desire of miserable mortals to obtain truth is most clearly shadowed forth in Scripture by hunger and thirst. So too the one Christ, the Son of God, dead and raised from the dead, is Amen, and the one food suited to satisfy the spiritual hunger and quench the spiritual thirst. Indeed, whatever the sinner, burning with the desire for salvation and happiness, can seek or demand, all of it, however great, lies stored up in Christ alone, as in a most full storehouse and perpetual fountain. Is he thirsty with the desire to obtain deliverance from condemnation and the forgiveness of sins? There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, Rom. 8:1; and through Christ the forgiveness of sins is proclaimed, Acts 13:38. In Christ we have redemption through his blood, namely the forgiveness of sins, Eph. 1:7; Col. 1:14. Is he thirsty with the desire for peace and tranquillity of soul, from the sense of reconciliation with God? Justified by faith, we have peace with God, through our Lord Jesus Christ, Rom. 5:1. Is he thirsty for adoption and the dignity of the sons of God? To as many as believed in him he gave the power of becoming sons of God, John 1:12; and he was made subject to the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons, Gal. 4:5. Is he burning with the desire for the image of God, which consists in true righteousness and holiness? We all, beholding the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as from the Spirit of the Lord, 2 Cor. 3:18. Is he thirsty for deliverance from the tyranny of the devil, the lord of death, and from death itself? Christ by his death destroyed the devil, who had the power of death, Heb. 2:14; he destroyed death itself, and brought life and immortality to light through the Gospel, 2 Tim. 1:10. Christ himself is the resurrection and the life, that is, the cause of the resurrection and of life, John 11:25. Is he thirsty with the desire to obtain eternal life? The wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord, Rom. 6:23. Christ, then, is the Amen, an abundant food for the soul, by which his most vehement hunger and thirst are quenched: for in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge of salvation, which had been hidden in former ages, Col. 2:3. Hence hear Christ: I am the true bread which came down from heaven, the living bread, or life-giving, my flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink, John 6:51, 55. If anyone thirst, let him come to me and drink, John 7:37. Whoever comes to me will never hunger, and whoever believes in me will never thirst, John 6:35.

units.la: 7°. Christus Amen est, non modò quia finis & complementum est omnium Dei promissionum, 2 Cor. 1: 20. sed & cumprimis quia finis & complementum est magnæ illius mysticæque promissionis, quâ Deus olim sub Veteri Instrumento proprio suo solemni, gloriosò & incommunicabili nomine πτεραγραμμάτων Ecclesiæ & mundo universo verso fidem suam obstringere voluerat: nempe יהוה tertia persona est futuri verbi היה, & significat Erit. Christus autem Deus in carne manifestatus Amen est, אמן, seu אמנה veritas, & implementum promissionis mysticae, quae in nomine proprio Dei יהיה Erit, continebatur: nam in Christo & per Christum Deus sub Euangelio est, quod se futurum recipiebat proprio suo nomine היה Erit. Unde Christus ad Judaeos, nisi credideritis ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι, quod ego sum, in peccatis vestris moriemini. Joan. 8: 24. Signanter sane & sapienter dixit, Ego sum. Eccur vero ut significaret se existere? minime gentium, nemo enim Judaeorum dubitabat de praesentia & existentia ejus, nec credere illum hominem, qui Jesus Nazarethanus dicebatur, existere tunc in mundo, salutare fuit. Quid igitur? quod ego sum, nempe ille ipse qui ab initio constitutae reipub. Israelis, vocabatur היה Erit: nempe quod me futurum recipiebam proprio meo nomine היה Erit. Hinc factum, ut, etsi Deus sancte asseruerit, hoc est nomen meum in seculum, & memoriale meum de generatione in generationem, Exod. 3: 15. nominari tamen יהוה palam desierit, ubi adventus Christi propius accederet, ut confessus septuaginta viralis id nominis in gratiam Graecorum per κύριον fere semper verterint, aliquando & rarenter per θεόν. Et Josephus e prosapia sacerdotali quadraginta praeter propter annis post Christum natum, negaverit sibi fas esse pronunciare id Dei nomen, lib. 2. Antiq. cap. 5. Et summus Rabbinorum Maimonides lib. 1. more Nevochim cap. 60. asseruerit, Ex quo mortuus est Simeon justus, desiisse fratres ejus sacerdotes, benedicere in nomine י הי ה ו ה, sed benedicebant, inquit, cum nomine duodecim literarum. Nec tamen Christus aut Apostoli Judaeos abstinentes a pronunciando nomine ἀνεκφώνητον usquam superstitionis arguisse memorantur. Contra ipsi constanter abstinuerunt ab illo nomine pronunciando, ut pro eo, sicut septuaginta constanter vel κύριον, vel θεὸν dixerint, ut Matth. 4: 4. Rom. 4: 3. Jacob. 2: 23. Hebr. 2: 13. Quia pro יהוה in locis parallelis septuaginta habent θεὸς, ut Deut. 8, 3. Genef. 15: 6. Jesa. 8: 18. Eccur vero? Nempe quia sub Euangelio Deo in carne manifesto, Deus implevit promissionem, quam prae se ferebat nomen יהוה Erit, & veritatem illius exhibuit, estque in Christo & per Christum, quod se tunc futurum recipiebat. Hinc factum, ut in Veteri Instrumento nomen יהוה prae se ferat habitudinem ad nomen Dei, אהיה vel יאה vel אמנה, ut illa tria nomina plane ἑρμηνείαν (interpretationem) exhihibeant nominis יהוה, vel pro eo substituantur, quod exemplis liquido parebit, ita 2 Chron. 15: 3.4. & dies multi fuerunt Israëli absque Deo Emet: sed revertetur in angustia sua ad יהוה אֱלֹהֵי אֱמֶת Dominum Deum, Israëlu. Ubi Deus אֱמֶת & יהוה pro uno & eodem evidentissimè habentur: & Psalm. 19:10. timor יהוה Domini, mundus permanens in perpetuum, judicia אֱמֶת יהוה Domini Emet, justificata sunt pariter. Ubi nomen אֱמֶת non significat veritatem; sed nomen Dei est, & interpretamentum nominis πτεαρχεαμμάτε יהוה ut textum intuenti liquet: & Psalm. 31:6. in manu tua commendo Spiritum meum, redemisti me יהוה אֵל אֱמֶת Domine Deus Emet. Ubi אֱמֶת nomen est Dei proprium, & interpretamentum nominis יהוה, quia eo nomine יהוה Erit, Deus significabat, se futurum & habendum Deum verum, cùm idola, quæ Gentiles colebant, nihil essent nisi vanitas & mendacium, quod David significat, ubi extemplò attexit, commate 7°. Odio habui observantes vanitatem mendacii, h. e. colentes idola, sed ego in יהוה Dominum speravi. Nam Dii gentium nihil aliud erant nisi mendacium & vanitas, quod liquet ex Jerem. 16: 19.20. יהוה Domine, fortitudo mea, & robur meum, & refugium meum in die angustiæ, ad te gentes venient à finibus terræ & dicent, utique שֶׁקֶר mendacium, possederunt patres nostri, הֶבֶל vanitatem, & non est in eis profectum faciens; numquid faciet sibi homo Deos? & ipsi non sunt Dii. Ubi liquet Deum vocatum fuisse יהוה in oppositione ad Deos gentium, qui non sunt Dii, sed שֶׁקֶר & הֶבֶל mendacium & vanitas, quibus opponitur nomen Dei אֱמֶת Veritas increata & constans, atque adeò subtexitur nomini יהוה, ut ejus interpretamentum & complementum, & Psalm. 117. Laudate יהוה Dominum, omnes gentes, laudate eum omnes populi, quoniam roborata est super nos misericordia ejus, וֶאֱמֶת־יהוה & Emet Dominus, in seculum. Ubi liquet אֱמֶת & יהוה pro uno & eodem usurpari, ut אֱמֶת sit interpretamentum יהוה Erit. Nempe Deus omnium gentium, quia manebit in perpetuum omnium gentium Deus, ubi idola gentium, sicut umbræ fugaces, evanuerint. Ita Jerem. 10: 10. 11. & יהוה Deus אֱמֶת ipse Deus vivens, & Rex æternus ab ira ejus contremiscet terra, & non sustinebunt gentes indignationem ejus; secundum hoc dicetis eis, Dii qui cælum & terram non fecerunt, ipsi peribunt è terra, & de sub cælo. Unde iterum liquidò paret, אֱמֶת esse nomen proprium Dei, & interpretamentum nominis יהוה per oppositionem ad falsos gentium Deos, quos Deus va-vaticinatur peritulos, & fore ut sicut phantasmata evanescant, cum ipse futurus sit Deus אמת verus, constans & perpetuus non modo in sese: sed & in habitudine ad gentes, h. e. ab iis ut verus Deus cognoscendus, habendus, atque colendus. Nempe in Christo Deo in carne manifestando & per Evangelium & fœdus gratiosum gentibus annunciando. Concludamus igitur, Christum esse ὁ ἀμὴν[?], seu, quod idem est, Deum אמת quia implementum est, exhibetque in sese tremendi Dei nominis יהוה Erit. Momentosa hæc veritas clara in luce ut constituatur, age nonnullas de antiquo illo ac glorioso numinis indigitamento, quam fieri poterit brevissime, quæstiones perstringamus.
units.tr: 7. Christ is the Amen, not only because he is the end and fulfilment of all God's promises (2 Cor. 1:20), but above all because he is the end and fulfilment of that great and mystical promise by which God long ago, under the Old Testament, wished to bind his faith to the Church and to the whole world, by his own solemn, glorious and incommunicable name, the Tetragrammaton [πτεραγραμμάτων]. Namely, יהוה is the third person of the future of the verb היה, and it means "He will be." Christ, God manifested in the flesh, is the Amen, אמן, or אמנה, that is, truth and the fulfilment of the mystical promise contained in God's proper name יהיה, "He will be." For in Christ, and through Christ, God is under the Gospel what he declared himself to be by his own name היה, "He will be." Hence Christ says to the Jews: "Unless you believe that ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι [that I am], you will die in your sins" (John 8:24). He spoke significantly and wisely when he said "I am." But why did he say it, to signify that he exists? By no means, for none of the Jews doubted his presence or existence, nor was it useful to tell them that the man called Jesus of Nazareth was then existing in the world. What then? "That I am," that is, he himself who from the beginning of the constituted commonwealth of Israel was called היה, "He will be," namely, that I, by my own name היה, "will be," am the one who will come. Hence it happened that, although God solemnly declared, "This is my name for ever, and my memorial from generation to generation" (Exod. 3:15), the name יהוה nevertheless openly ceased to be pronounced as the time of Christ's coming drew nearer. The Seventy, as is well known, translated that name for the sake of the Greeks almost always by κύριον [Lord], and sometimes, but rarely, by θεόν [God]. And Josephus, of a priestly family, about forty years after the birth of Christ, declared that it was not lawful for him to pronounce that name of God (Antiquities, book 2, chapter 5). And Maimonides, the greatest of the rabbis, in book 1 of the Guide of the Perplexed, chapter 60, asserted: "From the time that Simon the Just died, his brothers the priests ceased to bless in the name י הי ה ו ה, but they blessed," he says, "with the name of twelve letters."* Yet we are nowhere recorded to have charged Christ or the Apostles with superstition for abstaining from pronouncing the unpronounceable name [ἀνεκφώνητον]. On the contrary, they themselves consistently abstained from pronouncing that name, so that, in its place, as the Seventy consistently did, they said either κύριον or θεόν, as in Matt. 4:4, Rom. 4:3, James 2:23, Heb. 2:13. For in parallel passages the Seventy have θεὸς in place of יהוה, as in Deut. 8:3, Gen. 15:6, Isa. 8:18. But why? Namely, because under the Gospel, in God manifested in the flesh, God fulfilled the promise which the name יהוה, "He will be," carried in front of it, and he displayed its truth; and what he then declared he would be, that he is in Christ and through Christ. Hence it happens that in the Old Testament the name יהוה carries with it a relation to the name of God, אהיה or יאה or אמנה, so that those three names plainly offer an interpretation [ἑρμηνείαν] of the name יהוה, or are substituted for it. This will be clear from examples, such as 2 Chron. 15:3–4: "For a long time Israel was without the true God, and without a teaching priest, and without law; but in their distress they turned to the Lord God of Israel, יהוה אֱלֹהֵי אֱמֶת, and sought him." Here God is evidently regarded as one and the same, אֱמֶת and יהוה. And Psalm 19:10: "The fear of the Lord (יהוה) is clean, enduring for ever; the judgments of the Lord, אֱמֶת יהוה, are altogether righteous." Here the name אֱמֶת does not mean truth, but is a name of God and an interpretation of the name יהוה, as anyone looking at the text can see. And Psalm 31:6: "Into your hand I commit my spirit; you have redeemed me, יהוה אֵל אֱמֶת, O Lord God of truth." Here אֱמֶת is a proper name of God and an interpretation of the name יהוה, because by that name יהוה, "He will be," God signified that he would be and would be held the true God, when the idols which the Gentiles worshipped were nothing but vanity and falsehood. David points to this, for right after, in verse 7, he adds: "I hate those who observe vanity of falsehood," that is, who worship idols, "but I have trusted in יהוה, the Lord." For the gods of the nations were nothing other than falsehood and vanity, as is clear from Jer. 16:19–20: "O Lord (יהוה), my strength and my stronghold and my refuge in the day of trouble, the nations will come to you from the ends of the earth and say: surely our fathers have inherited שֶׁקֶר, falsehood, הֶבֶל, vanity, and there is no profit in them. Can a man make gods for himself? And they are not gods." Here it is plain that God was called יהוה in opposition to the gods of the nations, who are not gods but שֶׁקֶר and הֶבֶל, falsehood and vanity, to which the name of God אֱמֶת, uncreated and constant truth, is opposed, and so it is added to the name יהוה as its interpretation and completion. Likewise Psalm 117: "Praise the Lord (יהוה), all nations; praise him, all peoples; for his mercy is strong over us, וֶאֱמֶת־יהוה, and the truth of the Lord endures for ever." Here it is clear that אֱמֶת and יהוה are used for one and the same thing, so that אֱמֶת is the interpretation of יהוה, "He will be." That is, God of all nations, because he will remain for ever the God of all nations, when the idols of the nations have vanished like fleeting shadows. So also Jer. 10:10–11: "But the Lord (יהוה) is the true God, אֱמֶת; he is the living God and the eternal King; at his wrath the earth will tremble, and the nations will not endure his indignation. Thus you shall say to them: the gods who did not make heaven and earth will perish from the earth and from under heaven." Hence it is again made clear that אֱמֶת is a proper name of God, and an interpretation of the name יהוה by way of opposition to the false gods of the nations, whom God foretells will perish, and that they will vanish like phantoms, since he himself will be the true God, אמת, constant and perpetual, not only in himself but also in his relation to the nations, that is, to be known, held and worshipped by them as the true God. Namely, in Christ, God manifested in the flesh, and through the Gospel and the gracious covenant proclaimed to the nations. Let us conclude, therefore, that Christ is ὁ ἀμὴν [the Amen], or, which is the same, the God אמת, because he is the fulfilment and displays within himself the meaning of the awesome name of God, יהוה, "He will be." So that this weighty truth may be set in clear light, let us now briefly touch upon some questions about that ancient and glorious designation of the divine name, as briefly as possible.

units.la: QUÆSTIO XIV. Vtrum nomen יהוה Dei proprium, Moïsi primum innotuerit, ut ante Moïsem ignotum, & inauditum fuerit?
units.tr: QUESTION XIV. Whether the proper name of God, יהוה, was first made known to Moses, so that it was unknown and unheard of before Moses?

units.la: Quæstioni occasionem dedere loca ἐναύλοφανὴς[?]. Nempe Deus Moïsem compellat his verbis, Et aparui Abrahamo, Isaaco, & Jacobo בְּאֵל שַׁדַּי in Deo omnipotenti, seu sufficienti: Sed nomine meo יהוה non notus fui ipsis. Exod. 6: 3. Contrà sanctissimum illud Dei indigitamentum Abrahamo ante Moïsem notum fuisse videtur: nam Abraham invocavit nomen יהוה Gen. 13: 4. Et Deus Abrahamum in hæc verba alloquitur. Ego יהוה. Ego sum יהוה qui te eduxi ex Ur Chaldaorum. Genef. 15: 2. 7. Isaac invocavit nomen יהוה Genef. 26: 25. Jacobus Isaaco parenti respondet. Quia יהוה Deus tuus occurrere fecit ad faciem meam. Genef. 27: 20. Sed & nobis grassantibus ad demonstrandum nomen Dei Amen, quo sese insignivit. Jesa. 65: 16. ut unum jurisjurandi objectum, & fontem perennantem benedictionis in universa terra, explosis gentium idolis, complementum esse nominis Tetragrammati, necessario perstringenda occurrit, quod deinceps dicenda compertum dabunt.
units.tr: The question arises from passages such as these. God addresses Moses with the words: And I appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob [El Shaddai, בְּאֵל שַׁדַּי] as God Almighty, or All-sufficient; but by my name [יהוה] I was not known to them. Exod. 6:3. On the other hand, that most holy designation of God seems to have been known to Abraham before Moses. For Abraham called upon the name יהוה, Gen. 13:4. And God addresses Abraham in these words: I am יהוה. I am יהוה who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans, Gen. 15:2, 7. Isaac called upon the name יהוה, Gen. 26:25. Jacob answers his father Isaac: Because יהוה your God caused it to come before me, Gen. 27:20. We must also, as we press on, show that the name of God Amen [אמן], by which he marked himself out (Isa. 65:16), as the one object of oaths and the perpetual fountain of blessing throughout the earth, with the idols of the nations cast out, is the fulfilment of the Tetragrammaton. This the things to be said later will show.

units.la: In concilianda apparente contradictione, non una mens interpretibus. Quotquot enim sentiunt tremendum יהוה nomen, sibi Deum vendicasse, proprium ad significandum æternam essentiam suam, ut causa est & fons essendi rebus omnibus. Dum suæ serviunt ὁ ἀμὴν[?]. uno ore asserunt, Deum Patriarchis innotuisse in nomine suo יהוה. Eadem mens Rabbi Eliezero in Capit Patrum. cap. 3. Docet enim ante creatum mundum, Deum, & nomen ejus tantum extitisse. Hinc Rabbi Menasseh ben-Israel, in Conciliatore suo. Quaest. 3. in Exod. existimat nomen Tetragammatum Adamo, & Patriarchis fuisse notum. Dominus, inquit, cum Adamo collucutus, praecepta sua, & postea sanctum suum nomen ei, ille Caino, & Hebelo tradidit, a quibus ad posteros ipsumque tandem Noachum, a Noacho ad Abrahamum, Isaacum, & Jacobum, denique & ad Mosem, ad posteritatem reliquam pervenit. Sed enim vero Deus ipse verbotim contrarium asserit, sed nomine meo יהוה non notus fui ipsis. Exod. 6: 3. Apparentem illam contradictionem intactam praetermisit novitius conciliator Amstelodamensis. Buxtorfius hunc in modum eam conciliare conatur, dum asserit Deum non tam loqui de nomine, quam de re ipsa per nomen significata. Eccur Buxtorfi? Quia, inquit, nulli ante de facie ad faciem apparuit. Parum caute Buxtorfius, id asserere nobis videtur. 1°. Quia directe & proprie, de nomine Dei agitur in toto Moisis cum Numine colloquio. Exod. 3: 13. 14. 15. Unde certo certius colligitur, Deum non fuisse Abrahamo, Isaaco, & Jacobo per nomen יהוה notum: Sed & id solide confirmatur, quia Deus nomen suum שדי opponit nominit יהוה, quod tunc sibi proprium, novumque vendicabat, illo innotuisse Patriarchis ut asserat, isthoc contra indigitamento suo יהוה, illis notum fuisse expresse neget. Nec plus habet ponderis, quam attexuit rationem, scilicet quia nemini ante Moisem de facie ad faciem apparuit. Nempe haec non dixit Deus Moisem ut distingueret a Patriarchis: Sed ab Aharone, Maria, caeterisque Prophetis, quibus se tunc temporis in Israele revelabat. Numer. 12: 6. 7. 8. Re enim vera Deus Abrahamo ante Moisem modo clarioriri, & magis familiari sese pridem revelaverat, apud eum diversatus, pedes suos ipsi lavandos tradiderat, mensae epulisque ejus ut conviva accubuerat, cum eo amice deambulaverat, consilium de perdenda Sodoma ipsi ut summo amico aperuerat. Gen. 18: 4. 8. 17. 18. 19. Ut Christus inde collegerit Abrahamum vidisse diem suum, & prae gaudio exultasse. Quin vero ita clare perspexisse ut potuerit eum lapidibus impetere si mens ipsi laeva fuisset, sicut degeneribus filiis suis Judaeis. Joan. 8: 40. 56.
units.tr: In reconciling the apparent contradiction, interpreters do not agree. For all who hold that the awesome name יהוה belongs to God, as a proper name signifying his eternal essence as the cause and source of being for all things, while they serve their own view, with one voice assert that God made himself known to the patriarchs in his name יהוה. Rabbi Eliezer in the chapter of the Fathers (ch. 3) holds the same view: he teaches that before the world was created, God and his name alone existed. Hence Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel, in his Conciliator, question 3 on Exodus, thinks that the Tetragrammaton was known to Adam and the patriarchs. The Lord, he says, spoke with Adam, gave him his precepts and afterwards his holy name; he passed them to Cain and Abel, from whom they came to their posterity, and finally to Noah, from Noah to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and at last to Moses and the rest of posterity. But God himself asserts the very opposite: but by my name יהוה I was not known to them. Exod. 6:3. The novice conciliator of Amsterdam passed over this apparent contradiction without touching it. Buxtorf tries to reconcile it in this way, asserting that God is speaking not so much of the name as of the thing itself signified by the name. Why Buxtorf? Because, he says, no one before had seen him face to face. Buxtorf seems to me to assert this rather carelessly. First, because the whole conversation of God with Moses in the passage (Exod. 3:13, 14, 15) deals directly and properly with the name of God. From this it is most certainly inferred that God was not known to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob by the name יהוה. And this is also firmly confirmed, because God sets his name שדי against the name יהוה, which he claimed as his own and new at that time. He asserts that he was made known to the patriarchs by the former, and by his designation יהוה he expressly denies that they knew him. Nor does the reason he adds carry more weight: that no one before Moses saw him face to face. For God did not say this to distinguish Moses from the patriarchs, but from Aaron, Miriam, and the other prophets, to whom he then revealed himself in Israel (Num. 12:6, 7, 8). Indeed God had revealed himself to Abraham long before Moses in a clearer and more familiar way: he dwelt with him, handed over his feet to be washed, reclined at his table and feasts as a guest, walked about with him in friendship, and disclosed to him, as to his greatest friend, his plan to destroy Sodom (Gen. 18:4, 8, 17, 18, 19). So Christ rightly inferred that Abraham saw his day and rejoiced exceedingly. Nay, he so clearly perceived it that he could have stoned him, had his mind been evil, as his degenerate Jewish sons did (John 8:40, 56).

units.la: Prima sua responsione fretus parum Buxtorfius, & hanc commiscitur. Verba Hebraea, inquit, sic verti possunt. Apparui Abrahamo, Isaa co, & Jacobo in El Schaddaï, & nomine meo יהוה, neque tamen notus factus sum iis.
units.tr: Relying on his first answer, Buxtorf weakly mixes in another: The Hebrew words, he says, can be rendered thus: I appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in El Shaddai, and by my name יהוה, yet I was not made known to them.

units.la: Causæ præjudiciis, quàm miserè occœcentur, vel viri doctissimi, nimiùm hîc dolendum est: Nam textum introspicienti nimis liquidum fit accentum Athnach in El Schaddaï, sensum absolvere, & particulam, Vau, in ושמי sequente, esse adversativam, ut tota enunciatio sequens hunc sensum fundat. Sed nomine meo יהוה non sum notus ipsis. Unde liquet Buxtorfium de suo infarsisse tamen. Fac enim, nullam esse habendam rationem accentus Athnach distinctivi, ut ita interpreteris, Apparui Abrahamo, Isaaco, & Jacobo in El Schaddaï, & nomine meo יהוה: non sum notus ipsis. Sensus erit suspensus, ut cum Buxtorfio extra textum supplendum sit tamen. At enim tunc falsa erit Numinis propositio. 1°. Habita ratione revelationis, per utrumque nomen El Schaddaï & יהוה. Qui enim obsecro fieri potuit, ut Deus revelatus utroque nomine Patriarchis, ipsis tamen ignotus fuerit? 2°. Habita ratione ipsius rei, & veritatis historiæ. Qui enim fieri potest, ut Deus Abrahamo ignotus fuerit, & simul Abrahamus singulari prærogativa diem Domini viderit, & eum judicem universæ terræ noverit, & confessus fuerit? Gen. 18: 25. Et in eum fide salutari crediderit, ut per fidem suam justificatus fuerit. Gen. 15: 6. Et præ majestate Dei secum familiaria verba commutantis, pulverem & cineremque confessus fuerit? Gen. 18: 27.
units.tr: It is much to be lamented here how blindly even very learned men are blinded by their prejudices. For anyone who looks closely at the text sees that the accent Athnach after El Shaddai clearly completes the sense, and that the particle Vav in the following ושמי is adversative, so that the whole following statement rests on this sense: But by my name יהוה I was not known to them. From this it is plain that Buxtorf slipped in yet on his own. Suppose, however, that no account is to be taken of the distinctive accent Athnach, so that you read: I appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in El Shaddai and by my name יהוה: I was not known to them. The sense will then be left hanging, so that, with Buxtorf, yet must be supplied from outside the text. But then the divine statement will be false. First, given that God was revealed by both names, El Shaddai and יהוה, how could it possibly happen that God, revealed to the patriarchs by both names, was nonetheless unknown to them?
