Second, considering the matter itself and the truth of the history: how can it be that God was unknown to Abraham, and yet Abraham, by singular privilege, saw the day of the Lord, knew and confessed him as the judge of all the earth (Gen. 18:25), and believed in him with saving faith, so that he was justified by his faith (Gen. 15:6), and, in the majesty of God who spoke with him in familiar words, confessed himself dust and ashes (Gen. 18:27)?

units.la: Alii aliò se vertunt, docentque nomen יהוה tria distinctè & per se significare. 1°. Essentiam æternam, & immutabilem Dei, Ego sum יהוה nec mutor. Malach. 3: 6. 2°. Essentiam Dei in habitudine ad creaturas, quatenus fons & causa est, quæ dat cæteris rebus ut sint & existant. Jesa. 42: 5. Amos. 5: 9. Actor. 17: 28. Utroque modo asserunt Deum innotuisse Abrahamo, Isaaco, & Jacobo, in nomine suo יהוה. Addunt demum tremendum istud nomen, 3°. significare fidelitatem Dei in præstandis promissis, & exequendis judiciis suis. Jesa. 49: 23. & 52: 6. & 60: 16. Ezech. 28: 22. 23. 24. 26. & 30: 19. 25. 26. Atque hoc tertio modo docent, Deum ex parte & comparatè non fuisse notum Patriarchis in nomine suo יהוה. Quemadmodum legis ministerium, ut gloriosum fuerit, dicitur non fuisse in gloria, comparatè scilicet ad excellentem gloriam ministerii justitiæ. 2 Cor. 3: 10.
units.tr: Others take a different course and teach that the name יהוה signifies three things distinctly and in themselves. First, the eternal and unchangeable essence of God: I am יהוה, I do not change (Mal. 3:6). Second, the essence of God in relation to creatures, insofar as he is the source and cause that gives all other things their being and existence (Isa. 42:5; Amos 5:9; Acts 17:28). In both ways they assert that God was made known to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob by his name יהוה. Finally they add that this awesome name, third, signifies the faithfulness of God in fulfilling his promises and executing his judgments (Isa. 49:23; 52:6; 60:16; Ezek. 28:22, 23, 24, 26; 30:19, 25, 26). And in this third sense they teach that God was not known to the patriarchs in his name יהוה in part, or comparatively. Just as the ministry of the law is said not to have been glorious in glory, meaning comparatively to the excelling glory of the ministry of righteousness (2 Cor. 3:10).

units.la: Multa quidem, fatebor enim, in Scriptura absolutè negari videntur, quæ comparatè tantum negantur: Sed ne hujusmodi distinctio hîc loci obtineat, præter rationes quibus infrà ambas sententias confutabimus, multa vetant. 1°. Quidem, ubivis Scripturarum absoluta videtur, quæ tamen comparativa negatio est, ex ipsis locorum circumstantiis comparativa negatio ultro emergit, hic verò, nec vola, nec vestigium comparationis apparet: Sed præfracta, & absoluta negatio. Notus, quidem fui, Abrahamo, Isaaco, & Jacobo, in El Schaddai: Sed nomine meo יהוה non notus fui illis. Reapse enim, vel Deus significat se plenè & perfectè notum fuisse Patriarchis & ratione nominis El Schaddai, & ratione rei, illis nominibus significatæ, cum contrà perfectè & plenè ipsis non fuerit notus per nomen יהוה, nec ratione nominis, nec ratione rei significatæ: Sed obscurè tantum, & imperfectè. Prius verè affirmari nequit, nempe nulla mens finita, nedum mortalium hominum, infinitam Dei potentiam, vel sufficientiam immensam plenè, ac perfectè assequi potest. Itaque superest ut Deus asseruerit se notum fuisse Patriarchis nomine El Schaddai, notitia imperfecta, & semi plena, ut negare non potuerit, se non fuisse notum Patriarchis in nomine יהוה, notitia pariter imperfecta, & semi plena, quæ unam Dei fidelitatem haud excepe-rit, quandoquidem ex sententia adversariorum in utraque Patriarcharum cognitione, ignorantia locum obtinuerit, nec Deus potuerit comparatè negare se Patriarchis fuisse notum in nomine יהוה, quòd notus plenè, & perfectè illo nomine ipsis non fuerit, quandoquidem pari ratione ipsis sub nomine El Schaddai plenè, ac perfectè notus non fuit. 2°. Quia Deus nihil novi suo illo nomine יהוה Moïsi vel Israëlitis revelasset, & Moïsi percontanti, quo nomine Deus parentum suorum erat appellandus, promptum erat, Deo respondere, nomen novum de te tantum opus moliente mihi aut Israëli non revelas, ut tibi & mihi gloriosam liberationem promittenti fidem habeant, noverunt enim pridem Patriarchæ nostri, & nos pridem novimus te esse יהוה. Novum tamen & hactenus inauditum fuisse nomen Dei יהוה, abundè liquet ex circumstantiis textus, quia Moïsi præ diffidentia legationem detractanti, & quærenti, Si à me petierint filii Israël, quodnam est nomen Dei patrum nostrorum, qui te misit ad nos, quid respondebo? Utique Deo promptum erat repo-nere, ut quid Moses stultam confingis Israëlitarum petitionem? An Israëlitæ ignorant nomen meum proprium, quo & patribus eorum, & ipsis innotuit, anne tumet pariter atque ipsi nomen meum & memoriale perpetuum esse יהוה apprime nosti? Sed verò Deus non ita ta respondit contrà voto Moïsis annuit, dixitque : Dices eis יהוה misit me ad vos, hoc est nomen meum perpetuò, & memoriale meum in omnem ætatem. Exod. 3: 15. Et rationem attexuit, apparui Abrahamo, Isaaco, & Jacobo in El Schaddai: Sed nomine meo יהוה non fui notus ipsis. Exod. 6: 3. Ut sit finis, omnem vitilitigandi causam. 3°. Deus præripit ubi Israelem bis alloquitur his verbis. Ego sum יהוה, Deus tuus è terra Ægypti. Hos. 12: 10. & 13: 4. Quod nobis suppeditat firmum istud argumentum. Vel Deum esse יהוה, Deum Israelis è terra Ægypti, refertur tantum ad hanc enuntiationis partem: Ego sum Deus tuus è terra Ægypti, ut antea non fuerim Deus tuus. Sed id alienum est à veritate, erat enim Deus Israelis ab Ur Chaldæorum, vi formulæ fœderalis cum Abrahamo, Ero Deus tuus, & posterorum tuorum. Genes. 17: 7. ut ex illo tempore, nempe ante exitum ab Ægypto, pluribus retro sæculis, Israelitæ circumcisione, signo fœderis sui cum Deo, obsignarentur. Integrum igitur enuntiationis attributum, nempe sum יהוה Deus tuus è terra Ægypti, ad subjectum ego, referendum est, ut fatendum sit Deum asserere, se esse יהוה, Deum Israelis ab Ægypto. Fuitne igitur יהוה Deus Israelis ab Ur Chaldæorum. Affirment necesse est adversarii, si vera sit eorum hypothesis id tamen Deus nusquam dixit Israelitis. Ut quid verò noluit illis dicere. Ego sum יהוה Deus tuus ab exitu ex Ur Chaldæorum? Ut quid expresse exordium fecit ab Ægypto? Nulla utique legitima assignari poterit ratio, nisi quod ut Deus foret Israelitarum Deus abs fœdere inito cum Abrahamo, vel ante primam ingressionem in Ægyptum, non erat tamen ipsis Deus sub nomine יהוה ante missionem Moïsis in Ægyptum, quia non innotuerat Abrahamo, Isaaco, & Jacobo, nomine suo יהוה.
units.tr: I will admit that many things in Scripture seem to be denied absolutely when they are denied only comparatively. But several considerations prevent this kind of distinction from applying here, besides the arguments by which I will refute both opinions below. (1) Elsewhere in Scripture a negation that looks absolute is in fact comparative, and the comparison emerges of its own accord from the circumstances of the passage. Here, however, there is no trace or hint of any comparison, but a blunt and absolute denial: I was known to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as El Schaddai, but by my name יהוה I was not known to them. For either God means that he was fully and perfectly known to the Patriarchs both by the name El Schaddai and by the reality signified by those names, while by the name יהוה he was not fully and perfectly known to them, neither by the name nor by the reality signified, but only obscurely and imperfectly. The first cannot be affirmed, since no finite mind, let alone mortal men, can fully and perfectly grasp the infinite power of God or his immense sufficiency. It remains, then, that God has declared he was known to the Patriarchs under the name El Schaddai with an imperfect and half-full knowledge, and that he could not deny he was not known to the Patriarchs under the name יהוה, which would be an equally imperfect and half-full knowledge. That denial would not except God's faithfulness at all, since on the opponents' view both kinds of knowledge the Patriarchs had were partial, and God could not say comparatively that he was not known to them in the name יהוה because he was not fully and perfectly known by that name, when by the same reasoning he was not fully and perfectly known to them under the name El Schaddai either. (2) God had revealed nothing new to Moses or the Israelites by that name יהוה. When Moses asked by what name he was to be called the God of their fathers, God could easily have replied: "You are making up a new name, which I do not reveal to you or to Israel, so that they may trust you and me as we promise a glorious deliverance; for our fathers knew long ago, and we have known long ago, that I am יהוה." Yet that the name יהוה was new and hitherto unheard of is abundantly clear from the circumstances of the text, where Moses, timid about his mission, asks: If the sons of Israel ask me, what is the name of the God of our fathers who sent you to us, what shall I answer? God could surely have replied at once: "Why do you invent this foolish request of the Israelites? Do the Israelites not know my proper name, by which it has become known both to their fathers and to them? Do you not know very well that my name and my everlasting memorial is יהוה?" But God did not answer like that. He granted Moses' wish and said: "You shall say to them, יהוה has sent me to you. This is my name forever, and my memorial to all generations." (Exod. 3: 15.) He also added the reason: "I appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as El Schaddai, but by my name יהוה I was not known to them." (Exod. 6: 3.) So the matter ends and every cause of empty dispute is removed. (3) God anticipates the objection when he addresses Israel twice with these words: I am יהוה your God, from the land of Egypt. (Hos. 12: 10; 13: 4.) This gives us a firm argument. Either the statement that God is יהוה, the God of Israel from the land of Egypt, refers only to this part of the sentence, I am your God from the land of Egypt, as though he had not been their God before. But this is false, for he was the God of Israel from Ur of the Chaldeans, by virtue of the covenant formula with Abraham: I will be your God and the God of your descendants (Gen. 17: 7), so that from that time, many centuries before the exodus from Egypt, the Israelites were sealed with circumcision, the sign of their covenant with God. The whole predicate of the sentence, namely I am יהוה your God from the land of Egypt, must therefore be referred to the subject I, so that we must concede that God asserts that he is יהוה, the God of Israel from Egypt. Was יהוה, then, the God of Israel from Ur of the Chaldeans? If their hypothesis is true, the opponents must say so, yet God nowhere told the Israelites this. And why did he not wish to tell them, I am יהוה your God from the going out from Ur of the Chaldeans? Why did he expressly begin from Egypt? No legitimate reason can be given except this: although he was the God of the Israelites from the covenant made with Abraham, and even before their first entry into Egypt, he was not their God under the name יהוה before Moses was sent into Egypt, because he had not been made known to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob by his name יהוה.

units.la: Nos igitur expressis Dei verbis ἀπεμαστάςως addicti, ore rotunda pronuntiamus, nomen יהוה, quod Deus sibi vendicavit proprium, non innotuisse Abrahamo, Isaaco, & Jacobo, quia nomine suo יהוה non fuit notus ipsis. Exod. 6: 3. atque adeo fuisse inauditum, & incognitum usque dum Moïses in Ægyptum ad liberandos Israelitas missus fuit. Nobis astipulatur Josephus historicorum summus & accuratissimus, sed & è prosapia sacerdotali ipse sacerdos Judæus, ita enim commentatur, lib. 2. Antiquitat. cap. 5. Καὶ ὁ Θεὸς αὐτῷ σημαίνει, τὸν ἑαυτοῦ προσηγορίαν, ὃ πρότερον εἰς ἀνθρώπους παρελθεῖν. Et Deus apperit ei, putà Moïsi, suum nomen nunquam antea hominum ulli auditum, vel cognitum. Quod verò Abrahamus, Isaacus, Jacobus nominasse, vel invocasse nomen ṁṁ à Moïse memoran-tur, prolepsis est, Moïsi cæterisque Prophetis solemnis præcipuè in nominibus propriis, ut Bethel. Genef. 12: 8. vel dum appellare-tur Luz, usque dum Jacobus eam Bethel appellaverit ob admiran-dam scalæ mysticæ visionem. Genef. 28: 19. Ita urbecula per pro-lepsim dicitur Soar. Genef. 13: 10. & 19: 22. cum tamen, quam Lothus eam parvam nominasset prius, Bela appellaretur. Genef. 14: 2. Ita locus ubi ablata fuere ab Israëlitis præputia Guilgal di-citur Γαλγαλα. Josu. 4: 19. collato cum Josu. 5: 9. Et Eben-ezer, id est, lapis auxilii, per anticipationem appellatur. 1 Sam. 4: 1. col-lato cum 1 Sam. 7: 12. Ratio figuræ in promptu est, nempe cum sacri Historici animum ad scribendum appulere, res retrò præteritas, locorum, vel personarum nomina nova jam obtinuerant, ut si an-tiquis, & oblivione sepultis nominibus loca, vel personas insigni-visset, à popularibus suis quibus scribebant, intelligi vix ac ne vix quidem potuissent. Quando igitur certò certius est Moïsem in de-serto ad scribendum historiam Patriarcharum animum suum appulisse, nihil quicquam mirari subit, si Deum fere semper ṁṁ nominaverit; & Abrahamum, Isaacum, & Jacobum nomen ṁṁ invocasse memo-raverit, nempe ubi Moïses historiam litterarum monumentis consi-gnavit, illo suo nomine proprio Deus Israëli innotuerat, inclarue-rat, & tanquam monumento gloriosó & perpetuo sese insignierat, in omnem ætatem colendum, appellandum, & invocandum. Fac enim Moïsem in pertexenda historia Abrahami, Isaaci, & Jacobi scripsisse, Abrahamum, Isaacum, & Jacobum invocasse nomen El Schaddai. Utique Moïses nefariè, vel temerè violasset præceptum istud Dei de nomine suo ṁṁ hoc est nomen meum in perpetuum, & me-moriale meum in omnem ætatem.
units.tr: We therefore, bound without hesitation to the express words of God, pronounce with a round mouth that the name יהוה, which God claimed as his own proper name, was not made known to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, because by my name יהוה I was not known to them (Exod. 6: 3), and so it was unheard of and unknown until Moses was sent into Egypt to free the Israelites. Josephus, the greatest and most accurate of the historians, and himself a Jewish priest born of a priestly family, agrees with us. In book 2 of the Antiquities, chapter 5, he writes: "And God made known to him, that is to Moses, his own name, which had never before come to the knowledge of men [τὸν ἑαυτοῦ προσηγορίαν, ὃ πρότερον εἰς ἀνθρώπους παρελθεῖν]." That Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are recorded as having named or invoked the name יהוה is a proleptic usage, which is common to Moses and the other Prophets, especially in proper names. Thus Bethel (Gen. 12: 8) is so called, though it was called Luz until Jacob named it Bethel because of the wonderful vision of the mystic ladder (Gen. 28: 19). Likewise the little town is called Zoar by prolepsis (Gen. 13: 10; 19: 22), although Lot had first given it a small name and it was called Bela (Gen. 14: 2). So the place where the Israelites removed the foreskins is called Gilgal [Γαλγαλα] (Josh. 4: 19, compared with Josh. 5: 9), and Ebenezer, that is stone of help, is named in anticipation (1 Sam. 4: 1, compared with 1 Sam. 7: 12). The reason for this figure is obvious. When the sacred historians set themselves to write, the names of places or persons from the past had already taken new forms. If Moses had pointed out places or persons by their old names, now buried in oblivion, his fellow countrymen, for whom he was writing, could scarcely have understood him at all. Since it is quite certain that Moses, in the wilderness, set his mind to writing the history of the Patriarchs, there is no reason to be surprised that he has nearly always named God יהוה, and recorded that Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob invoked the name יהוה. When Moses committed the history to the written monuments, God had already made himself known to Israel by that proper name, had become famous by it, and had marked himself by it as a glorious and perpetual monument, to be worshipped, named, and invoked in all generations. For suppose that Moses, in weaving the history of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, had written that Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob invoked the name El Schaddai. Then Moses would have wickedly and rashly violated God's command concerning his name: this is my name forever, and my memorial to all generations.

units.la: QUÆSTIO XV.
units.tr: QUESTION XV.

units.la: Vtrum nomen יהוה sit ita Deo proprium, ut nulli nisi Deo competat?
units.tr: Whether the name יהוה is so proper to God that it belongs to no one but God?

units.la: AJunt 1°. Rabbini omnes, quibus ea propter dicitur שם המיוחד nomen proprium : nempe habet nominum proprietates: Nam 1°. non assumit He Haiedia demonstrativum, quod præfigitur aliis Dei nominibus האל האלהים 2°. Non recipit affixa pronomina sicut alia Dei nomina. 3°. Non admittit formam constructam, & ubi legitur יהוה צבאות Ellipsis est pro יהוה אלהי צבאות, ut Hos. 12:6. 4°. Non flectitur è numero singulari in pluralem, unde dicitur שם המפורש, hoc est, nomen explicatum, vel separatum, explicatum & lectum per שם הנכבד והנורא, separatum verò ab aliis Dei nominibus, unde nomen gloriosum & tremendum dicitur. Deut. 28:58. & שם הנרול nomen magnum. Jerem. 44:26. & καθ' ἐξοχὴν השם nomen. Lev. 24:11. 2°. Orthodoxi Theologi uno ore confitentur, nomen יהוה Deo viventi ita esse proprium ut nulli homini nudo, nulli Angelo creato, nulli falso numini, nulli demum creaturæ, in Scriptura tribuatur, quia illo nomine tanquam proprio sui indigitamento Deus Israëlis distinguit sese, & separat ab idolis, vanisque gentium numinibus, Angelis finitis, omnibusque creaturis.
units.tr: They say, first, that all the rabbis, who for this reason call it שם המיוחד, the proper name, indeed have the properties of a name: for (1) it does not take the demonstrative He (ה הידיעה), which is prefixed to the other names of God, האל and האלהים; (2) it does not receive affixed pronouns, as the other names of God do; (3) it does not admit the construct form, and where יהוה צבאות is read, it is an ellipsis for יהוה אלהי צבאות, as in Hos. 12:6; (4) it is not inflected from the singular into the plural. Hence it is called שם המפורש, that is, the explicit name or the separated name: explicit, because it is read as שם הנכבד והנורא, and separated, because it is set apart from the other names of God; hence it is called the glorious and terrible name, Deut. 28:58, and שם הגדול, the great name, Jer. 44:26, and by way of eminence השם, the Name, Lev. 24:11. (2) Orthodox theologians with one voice confess that the name יהוה is so proper to the living God that in Scripture it is attributed to no bare man, to no created angel, to no false deity, and finally to no creature at all, because by that name, as its own proper designation, the God of Israel distinguishes and separates himself from idols, from the vain deities of the nations, from finite angels, and from all creatures.

units.la: Reclamant contra Photinianî, & Sociniani hæretici, ut gloriam Divinitatis Jesu Christo vero Messiæ detrahant, illo, nempe, nomine proprio veri Dei indigitamento, Jesu Christo Messiæ in veteri fœdere, & vicario χύριος ipsi passim in novo tributo, eo identidem ut gloriosè insigniatur, nefariam hæresim suam, æternam Divinitatem ipsi detrahentem, jugulatam, & confossam cernunt.
units.tr: The Photinians and the Socinian heretics object to this, in order to take away from Jesus Christ, the true Messiah, the glory of divinity. They see that their impious heresy, which denies him eternal divinity, is struck down and pierced through by this, namely that the proper name, the designation of the true God, is given to Jesus Christ the Messiah in the Old Covenant, and that he is everywhere in the New Covenant called κύριος (the Lord) as its equivalent, so that he may be honoured with it.

units.la: Reponunt itaque hæretici. 1°. Nomen יהוה Arcæ à Mose tributum. Num. 10:35.36.
units.tr: The heretics therefore reply: (1) the name יהוה was given by Moses to the Ark, Num. 10:35, 36.

units.la: Respondemus, id factum, per Synecdochen, & per Metonymiam signi, quia nubes sedens in throno ex alis Cherubim super Arca, symbolum erat Divinæ majestatis præsentis, unde Ecclesia Deum invocat his verbis: Sedens inter Cherubim irradia. Psalm. 80:2.
units.tr: We answer that this happened by synecdoche and by metonymy of the sign: because the cloud sitting on the throne, between the wings of the Cherubim above the Ark, was a symbol of the present majesty of God. Hence the Church invokes God in these words: You who sit between the Cherubim, shine forth, Ps. 80:2.

units.la: Reponunt 2°. Moïsem vocasse Altare quod erexit, יהוה נסי Dominus vexillum meum. Exod. 17:15. Et Gedeonem pariter altare quod erexerat isthoc elogio insigniisse יהוה שלום Jud. 6:24.
units.tr: They reply, (2) that Moses called the altar he erected יהוה נסי, The Lord is my banner, Exod. 17:15; and that Gideon likewise marked the altar he had erected with this title, יהוה שלום, Judg. 6:24.

units.la: Respondemus cum Aben-Ezra supplendum esse מזבח Altare, ut illa nomenclatio hunc sensum fundat, Altare יהוה Domini vexilli mei, & iterum, Altare יהוה Domini pacis mea. Non secus atque Paulus dixit Athenien-sibus, se invenisse altare cui inscriptum erat Ἀγνώστῳ Θεῷ, ubi supplendum reliquerant Athenienses βωμὸς altare, ignoto Deo dicatum, quod & familiare simul Græcis, simul Latinis, ut ΠΑΤΡΙΟΤ ΑΠΟΛΛΩΝΟΣ Patrii Apollinis, subintellecta ara, notante Servio ad Æneid. 3. Patriasque obtruncat ad aras.
units.tr: We answer, with Aben Ezra, that מזבח, altar, must be supplied, so that the wording means: the altar of the Lord is my banner, and again, the altar of the Lord is peace. Just as Paul told the Athenians that he had found an altar inscribed To the unknown God, where the Athenians had left βωμός, altar, to be understood, dedicated to an unknown god; which is a usage common to both Greeks and Latins, as ΠΑΤΡΙΟΣ ΑΠΟΛΛΩΝΟΣ, of the ancestral Apollo*, with the altar understood, as Servius notes on Aeneid 3, and he slaughters them at the ancestral altars.

units.la: Et de Ænea ΠΑΤΡΟΣ ΘΕΟΥ ΧΘΟΝΙΟΥ. Patri Deo indigeti, subintelligendum cultoribus, sacellum indicabant. Dionys. Halicarn. Antiq. Rom. lib. 1. Ubi ad Diana veneris ito ad dextram. Terent. Adelph. delubrum subintelligit. Volo ad Serapis ferri mane. Catul. de Vari scor-to. Rapinas scribus ad Opis fieri. Cicer. ad Attic. lib. 14. Et ad eundem lib. 6. Epist. Atqui nihil habuit inscriptum, nisi censor, ea statua, quae ad Opis aperte posita in excelso est. Et Oratione pro Cluent. Sicut in statuis inauratis, quas ad Juturna posuit. Ædem perpetuo subintelligit. Ventum erat ad Vesta.
units.tr: And for ΠΑΤΡΟΣ ΘΕΟΥ ΧΘΟΝΙΟΥ, of the father god of the underworld, the sanctuary is meant, with the worshippers understood. See Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Roman Antiquities, book 1. Where you go to the temple of Venus, to the right. Terence, Adelphi, understands the shrine. I want to be carried to the temple of Serapis early in the morning. Catullus, on Varus' mistress: the robberies are made to the temple of Ops. Cicero to Atticus, book 14; and to the same, book 6 of the letters: Yet that statue, which stands openly on high at the temple of Ops, had nothing inscribed on it except the censor's name. And in the speech for Cluentius: As in the gilded statues which he set up at the temple of Juturna. He understands aedes, the temple, constantly: They had come to the temple of Vesta. Horace, Satires, book 1, satire 9.

units.la: Horat. lib. 1. Satyr. 9.
units.tr: Horace, Satires, book 1, satire 9.

units.la: Reponunt 3°. Angelum illo elogio יהוה insignitum Genes. 31:11. 13. Exod. 3:2. 6.
units.tr: They reply, (3) that the Angel was marked with that title יהוה, Gen. 31:11, 13; Exod. 3:2, 6.

units.la: Respondemus Angelum illum esse Dei Filium, & Mediatorem, qui ea propter nomine יהוה insignitur, ut secernatur ab Angelis creatis comitibus, unde dicitur Angelus, homo & Deus, in celebri illa luctatis cum Jacobo. Hos. 12:4.5. collato cum Genes. 32:24.30. Angelus officio utpote missus à Deo Patre, homo & Deus, quia Immanuel, [?]Θεάνθρωπος Deus & homo in unitate personæ.
units.tr: We answer that this Angel is the Son of God and Mediator, who for this reason is designated by the name יהוה, so that he is distinguished from the created angels who are his companions. Hence he is called Angel, man and God in that famous wrestling with Jacob, Hos. 12:4, 5, compared with Gen. 32:24, 30. He is Angel by office, as one sent by God the Father; man and God, because he is Immanuel, θεάνθρωπος, God and man, in the unity of person.

units.la: Reponunt 4°. Hierusalem insigniri eo nomine יהוה. Jerem. 33:16.
units.tr: They reply, (4) that Jerusalem is marked with that name יהוה, Jer. 33:16.

units.la: Respondemus Hierusalem non appellari יהוה: Sed Prophetam aferere יהוה vocaturum Hierusalem, textus enim verbotim ita sonat. Ille qui vocabit eam est יהוה justitia nostra.
units.tr: We answer that Jerusalem is not called יהוה; rather the Prophet says that he who will call her יהוה, that is, the Lord, will be our righteousness; for the text reads word for word: He who will call her is יהוה, our righteousness.

units.la: Reponunt 5°. Ezechielem vocasse Hierusalem יהוה שמה Dominum ibi. Ezech. 48:45.
units.tr: They reply, (5) that Ezekiel called Jerusalem יהוה שמה, the Lord is there, Ezek. 48:45.

units.la: Respondemus 1°. Supplendum esse nomen הָעִיר urbs שמה יהוה Domini ibi, nam verba Prophetæ sic sonnant, Et nomen civitatis ex die illo יהוה שמה, ut inde liquidò pareat Prophetam reliquisse subintelligendum nomen הָעִיר, quod proximè expresserat, & clarè docuisse Hierusalem vocatum iri הָעִיר יהוה שמה, urbs Domini ibi, hoc est præsentis, & inhabitantis. 2°. Si supplere noluueris הָעִיר Prophetam tribuisse nomen יהוה insigne Jesu Christi Mediatoris elogium, Ecclesiæ mysticæ Hierusalem, propter unionem, quam cum illa colit æternùm inviolabilem, quia sponsus ejus est, ut sponsi nomen tribuatur sponsæ suæ fideli, pro more apud omnes gentes solemni, sicut pari ratione Ecclesia dicitur Christus. 1 Cor. 12: 12. Ita Propheta prædicit fore, ut Ecclesia mystica Jerusalem appelletur יהוה שמה Dominus ibi, quia Christus Dominus in ea habitat, est enim Christus in nobis. Coloss. 1: 27. is enim habitat in cordibus nostris per fidem. Ephes. 3: 17.
units.tr: We answer, first, that the noun הָעִיר, city, must be supplied: שמה יהוה, the Lord is there, for the Prophet's words sound thus: And the name of the city from that day will be יהוה שמה. From this it clearly appears that the Prophet left the noun הָעִיר, which he had just expressed, to be understood, and clearly taught that Jerusalem would be called הָעִיר יהוה שמה, the city of the Lord is there, that is, present and dwelling in it. Second, if you refuse to supply הָעִיר, the Prophet attributed the name יהוה, the distinctive title of Jesus Christ the Mediator, to the mystical Jerusalem, the Church, on account of the union which he maintains with her, inviolable for ever, because he is her bridegroom; just as the name of the bridegroom is given to his faithful bride, as is customary among all nations on solemn occasions. Likewise, by the same reasoning, the Church is called Christ, 1 Cor. 12:12. Thus the Prophet foretells that the mystical Jerusalem will be called יהוה שמה, the Lord is there, because Christ the Lord dwells in her: for Christ is in us, Col. 1:27, for he dwells in our hearts through faith, Eph. 3:17.

units.la: QUÆSTIO XVI. Quomodo nomen יהוה primitus fuerit pronuntiatum & lectum? Item quomodo hodie sit legendum, & pronuntiandum?
units.tr: QUESTION XVI. How was the name יהוה originally pronounced and read? Likewise, how is it to be read and pronounced today?

units.la: RESPONDENT uno ore Hebræorum Magistri, quibus adstipulatur clarissimus Buxtorfius filius, germanam nominis Tetragrammati pronuntiationem hodie esse ignotam, & cum reliqua Judæorum gloria, Urbe, Regno, Templo, & Sacerdotio, interiisse. Antiqui Doctores Ecclesiæ Græcæ, atque Latinæ in eandem ire sententiam unanimi consensu videntur, quia nomen istud vocant ἄῤῥητον, ἀπόῤῥητον, ἀνεκφώνητον, ἄλεκτον, ἀφθέγκτον, ineffabile, non quod omninò non possit pronuntiari: Nam & perpetuò promiscuèque pronuntiatum fuit, ex quo Deus id proprium sibi fecit indigitamentum, & perpetuum sui monimentum. Exod. 3: 15. fuitque ter prolatum in solemni benedictione. Numer. 6: 26. Sed quòd posterior ætas germanam ejus pronuntiationem ignoraverit, quia sub secundo Templo, & ante Christum
units.tr: The Hebrew masters speak with one voice, and the most distinguished Buxtorf the son agrees with them, that the genuine pronunciation of the Tetragrammaton is unknown today and has perished along with the rest of the Jews' glory: their city, kingdom, temple and priesthood. The ancient doctors of the Greek and Latin Church seem by unanimous consent to share this view, since they call the name ἄῤῥητον [arrhēton], ἀπόῤῥητον [aporrhēton], ἀνεκφώνητον [anekphōnēton], ἄλεκτον [alekton], ἀφθέγκτον [aphthengkton], ineffable. This is not because it could not be pronounced at all. For it was pronounced constantly and commonly, from the time when God made it his own designation and perpetual memorial (Exod. 3:15), and it was uttered three times in the solemn blessing (Num. 6:26). But that a later age was ignorant of its true pronunciation, because under the second Temple, and before Christ

units.la: Respon. stum natum præstractè vetuerunt Judæorum principes, ne vel ipsi Sacerdotes nomen illud pronuntiarent. Hinc Josephus è prosapia sacerdotali, sibi nefas esse scripsit de nomine isto quicquam efferre. Antiq. lib. 2. cap. 5. & Maimonides primi Nevochim. cap. 62. asserit ex quo mortuus est Simeon Justus, cessasse fratres ejus Sacerdotes benedicere cum nomine יהוה: Sed benedicebant, inquit, cum nomine duodecim litterarum. Simeon Justus summus fuit Sacerdos, nepos Jaddua, ex filio Onia, qui floruit ante Christum natum anno 298. Unde septuaginta interpretes, qui trecentis præter propter annis ante Christum floruerunt, id nomen constanter reddiderunt per Κύριον Dominum, vel Θεὸν Deum. Eccur verò reverendum illud nomen pronuntiare vetuerunt? Num ducti quadam superstitione, quod usu quotidiano vilesceret & profanaretur? Ita quidem sentiunt plerique Doctissimi viri. Sed nostram non impetrarunt sententiam, quia abusus hominum, vel nefarius, usum legitimum munerum, nominumve Dei non debet abolere, quod liquidò paret, quia filius Israëlitidis sanctum illud nomen blasphemaverat. Levit. 24: 11. 14. 16. Attamen nefarius hujusmodi abusus, gloriosi nominis pronuntiationem, tunc temporis non abolevit. Præterea Christus & Apostoli, qui præstractè Pharisæorum, popularium��que suorum traditiones & superstitiones palam damnarunt, utique & hanc præcepti Divini temerariam violationem & superstitionem damnassent. Sed non adeo damnarunt, ut Judæorum morem calculo suo, praxique perpetua confirmaverint, ubi nomen Tetragrammatum in locis veteris testamenti juxta versionem septuagintaviralem per Κύριον, vel Θεὸν constanter reddidere.
units.tr: was born, the leaders of the Jews strictly forbade even the priests themselves to pronounce that name. Hence Josephus, from a priestly family, wrote that it was unlawful for him to say anything about that name (Antiq. book 2, ch. 5). And Maimonides, Part 1 of the Guide, ch. 62, asserts: From the time Simeon the Just died, his brothers the priests ceased to bless with the name יהוה; but they blessed, he says, with the name of twelve letters. Simeon the Just was high priest, grandson of Jaddua and son of Onias, who flourished about 298 years before Christ was born. Hence the Seventy interpreters, who flourished roughly 300 years before Christ, consistently rendered that name by Κύριον [Kyrion], Lord, or Θεὸν [Theon], God. But why did they forbid the pronunciation of that revered name? Were they moved by some superstition, fearing that it would grow cheap and be profaned through daily use? Many very learned men think so. But they have not won our view. For the abuse of men, however wicked, ought not abolish the lawful use of God's offices or names, as is clear from the fact that the son of the Israelite woman had blasphemed that holy name (Lev. 24:11, 14, 16). Yet such a wicked abuse did not at that time abolish the pronunciation of the glorious name. Moreover, Christ and the apostles, who openly and expressly condemned the traditions and superstitions of the Pharisees and of their people, would surely have condemned also this rash violation of a divine precept and this superstition. But they did not condemn it so far as to confirm the custom of the Jews by their own judgment and by constant practice, since in the places of the Old Testament, following the Septuagint version, they consistently rendered the Tetragrammaton by Κύριον or Θεὸν.

units.la: Ut quid igitur præstracta istiusmodi prohibitio? Respondemus divinam providentiam, silentium sacri sui nominis sapienter procurasse, vel per ministros nefarios, sicuti procuravit ut Caiphas summus Pontifex salutarem istam, ut læva mente, sententiam proferret: Vos nihil scitis, nec cogitatis conducere nobis ut unus homo moriatur pro populo, & tota gens non pereat: Nam quia erat Pontifex Maximus, prophetavit fore, ut Jesus pro gente moreretur, nec tantum pro ea gente: sed ut etiam filios Dei dispersos congregaret in unum. Johan. 11: 49. 50. 51. 52. Non secus sapientissima numinis providentiâ dirigente lævam mentem Principum Judaici sæculi, Divina sorte contigit, ut Deus nomine suo Tetragrammato nominari desierit, quamprimùm tempus accessit, & denuo impletum est, quo vaticinium, & salutaris promissio, quam nomen יהוה Erit, præ se ferebat, implementum suum, per adventum Jesu Christi Messiæ, divinissime sortiretur.
units.tr: Yet it is not likely that its lawful pronunciation was unknown, because Josephus, when about forty years after Christ's ascent into heaven he was writing his Jewish Antiquities, does not obscurely hint that he knew it. For when he related that God had revealed his name to Moses, a name "never before heard or known by any man," he added, by way of example, ὡς ἐξ ὧν ἐμοὶ ῥῆσις εἰπεῖν [what it is not lawful for me to speak]: "which it is neither lawful nor right for me to utter" (Antiq. 2.5). He could certainly have said, "which is unknown to me." On the contrary, he plainly implies that it was known to him, but that it was wrong to speak or pronounce it.

units.la: Ignotam tamen fuisse legitimam ipsius pronunciationem non sit verisimile, quia Josephus non obscurè innuit sibi esse notam, ubi annis quadraginta præter propter à Christi in cœlum ascensu, historiam pertexeret Antiquitatum Judaicarum, is enim ubi narravit Deum Moïsi aperuisse nomen suum, numquam antea hominum ulli auditum aut cognitum, exemplo attexuit ὡς ἐξ ὧν ἐμοὶ ῥῆσις εἰπεῖν. Quod mihi eloqui nec jus est, nec fas. Antiquit. Jud. lib. 2. cap. 5. Promptum utique illi erat dicere, quod mihi ignotum est. Contrà palam innuit sibi esse notum; sed nefas esse eloqui, seu pronunciare.
units.tr: Yet it is not likely that its lawful pronunciation was unknown, for Josephus not obscurely hints that it was known to him. When he was writing his Jewish Antiquities, about forty years after Christ's ascension into heaven, and related that God revealed his name to Moses, a name never heard or known by any man before, he added by way of illustration the words ὡς ἐξ ὧν ἐμοὶ ῥῆσις εἰπεῖν [hōs ex hōn emoi rhēsis eipein], which it is neither lawful nor right for me to utter (Antiq. Jud. book 2, ch. 5). He could easily have said, which is unknown to me. On the contrary, he openly implies that it was known to him, but that it was wrong to utter or pronounce it.

units.la: Percontanti quomodo primitus fuerit pronunciatum, Clemens Alexandrinus respondet, λέγεται δὲ Ἰάω ὁ μεθερμηνευόμενος ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἐσόμενος. Dicitur autem Iaou quod vertitur qui est, & qui erit. lib. 5. Stromat. pag. mihi 562. ad finem. Iræneus lib. 1. cap. 34. Origenes contra Celsum lib. 6. Cyrillus in cap. 1. Aggæi. & Theodoretus, Quæstione 15. in Exodum, in veteri editione, καλέσι δὲ αὐτὸ Σαμαρεῖται μὲν Ἰαβὲ, Ἰουδαῖοι δὲ Ἰάω. Vocant autem illud Samaritæ Jabe, Judæi, verò Iao. Hieronymus ipsis astipulatur in Psalmum 8. juxta veterem Editionem, quam habemus præ manibus. Primum nomen Domini apud Hebræos quatuor litterarum est, Jod, He, Vau, He, quod proprie Dei vocabulum sonat, & legi potest Iaho. Clementi, Irænèo, Origeni, Theodoreto, Cyrillo, Hieronymo, concinunt Ethnici, Diodorus Siculus lib. 1. Macrobius lib. 1. Saturnal. cap. 18. ex Oraculo Apollinis Clarii.
units.tr: Asked how it was originally pronounced, Clement of Alexandria answers: λέγεται δὲ Ἰάω ὁ μεθερμηνευόμενος ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἐσόμενος [legetai de Iaō ho methermēneuomenos ho ōn kai ho esomenos]. Iaou is said, which is interpreted: he who is and he who will be. (Stromata, book 5, p. 562 of my edition, near the end.) So also Irenaeus, book 1, ch. 34; Origen against Celsus, book 6; Cyril on Haggai, ch. 1; and Theodoret, Question 15 on Exodus, in the old edition: καλέσι δὲ αὐτὸ Σαμαρεῖται μὲν Ἰαβὲ, Ἰουδαῖοι δὲ Ἰάω [kalousi de auto Samareitai men Iabe, Ioudaioi de Iao]. The Samaritans call it Jabe, the Jews Iao. Jerome agrees with them on Psalm 8, according to the old edition which we have before us: The first name of the Lord among the Hebrews has four letters, Jod, He, Vau, He, which properly sounds as the name of God, and may be read Iaho. The pagans agree with Clement, Irenaeus, Origen, Theodoret, Cyril and Jerome: Diodorus Siculus, book 1; Macrobius, Saturnalia, book 1, ch. 18, citing the oracle of Apollo Clarius.

units.la: Φεγέζεο τ πάντων ὕπατον Θεὸν ἐμμέλῃ Ἰάω.
units.tr: Φεγέζεο τ πάντων ὕπατον Θεὸν ἐμμέλῃ Ἰάω.

units.la: Dic omnium summum Deum esse Iao.
units.tr: Say that Iao is the highest God of all.

units.la: Concinunt Hæretici Gnostici, Ophiani, Valentiniani, Phibionitæ, & Basilidiani. Nam reperiuntur Basilidianorum πλεσμαλισοι lapides, cum Decanorum figuris, & Ἰάω illis subscriptum, ut annotavit Cl. Salmasius in libro de annis Climactericis, pag. 570. Sed Porphyrius sanctum Dei nomen pronunciavit Ἰᾱω, apud Eusebium Euangelicæ præparationis lib. 1. Sed & cæteri Ethnici Ἰᾱω in sacris pronuntiasse videntur, quod comprobat Græcorum Pæan hymnus sacer Diis omnibusferè communis, nempe fieri solebat cum isthac ὠαναφωνήσει Eleleu ie, ie, quæ nihil aliud erat, quam usitatus Hebræorum Hymnus Alleluia, vel Alleluie. Ie autem est decurtatum Ievὼ. Concinit Athæneus, lib. Deipnosoph. οἱ πύλαιοι, inquit, τὸ δαιμόνιον ἀξιῶνἀξιῶντες γνέσθαι σεσιφωνῶν ἰη, ἰη. Veteres Deum celebrantes proclamabant ἰη, ἰη. Hinc factum ut Græci omnia sacra vocaverint Ἰεγῷ deducta ut liquet nomenclatione ex יהיה Ihieh, vel Ieuω. Ex eo autem quòd Græci nomen Tetragrammatum Ἰαω, vel Ἰἁω pronunciaverint Doctissimus Bochartus colligit Ægyptios, cæterosque Ethnicos in hanc fuisse adductos sententiam, ut crediderint Judæos asinum adorasse, & asini caput in templo suo posuisse, quod audirent Moïsem, cæterosque Prophetas passim dicentes כי יהוה Pi ieω, os Domini loquutum est, quasi dixissent, Asinus loquutus est, quia Pieω apud Ægyptios, Asinum significat.
units.tr: The Gnostic heretics agree: the Ophians, Valentinians, Phibionites and Basilidians. For stones of the Basilidians are found, the πλεσμαλισοι [plesmalisoi], with figures of the Decani and with Ἰάω inscribed beneath, as the illustrious Salmasius noted in his book on the Climacteric years, p. 570. Porphyry, in Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, book 1, pronounced the holy name of God as Ἰᾱω [Iāō]. But the other pagans also seem to have pronounced Ἰᾱω in their sacred rites, as the Greek paean confirms, a sacred hymn almost common to all the gods. It was customarily sung with that shout, Eleleu ie, ie, which was nothing other than the usual Hebrew hymn, Alleluia or Hallelujah. Ie is truncated from Ievō. Athenaeus agrees in the Deipnosophists: οἱ πύλαιοι, inquit, τὸ δαιμόνιον ἀξιῶντες γνέσθαι σεσιφωνῶν ἰη, ἰη [hoi palaioi ... iē, iē], the ancients, wishing to honour the divine power, used to cry out ἰη, ἰη. Hence it came about that the Greeks called all sacred things Ἰεγῷ, derived, as the nomenclature clearly shows, from יהיה [Ihieh] or Ieuō. From the fact that the Greeks pronounced the Tetragrammaton as Ἰαω or Ἰἁω, the most learned Bochart infers that the Egyptians and other pagans were led to this opinion: that they believed the Jews adored an ass and set up an ass's head in their temple. For they heard Moses and the other prophets everywhere saying כי יהוה [ki YHWH], Pi ieō, that is, the mouth of the Lord has spoken, as if they had said, the ass has spoken, since Pieō means ass among the Egyptians.

units.la: Sed enim verò ut nemo negare potest, יהוה tertiam esse personam futuri היה fuit, ad formam cæterorum nominum propriorum, ut Itskach, ridebit, & Jaacob supplantabit, quod & fatetur doctissimus Buxtorfius. Anne vero simillimum sit? antiquitus, quam Mazorethæ nomini יהוה puncta, Adonai substituerent prius, lectum fuisse & pronuntiatum יְהוָה Jehove, vel per crasim יָהוָה Jeve. Ita sentiunt Mercerus, in Genes. 2: 4. Capellus, in Orat. de Nomine Tetragrammato, Drusius, in Exod. 3: 15. Etsi prætulit Jave. Ita Crellius, Episcopius, Placæus, ut ex Jeve facile apud Græcos profluxerit Ἰεω, & Ἰἁω. Ita Sandfortius lib. 1. de descensu Christi ad inferos. Ita doctissimus Grotius in Matth. 22: 44. Videsis, nec te pigebit. Ita Owenus lib. 3. c. 8. de progressu Idololat.
units.tr: But indeed, as no one can deny, יהוה is the third person future of היה, he was, on the pattern of other proper names such as Itskach, he will laugh, and Jaacob, he will supplant, as the most learned Buxtorf also admits. But is it really so similar? That in ancient times, before the Masoretes put on the name יהוה the vowel points of Adonai, it was read and pronounced יְהוָה Jehove, or by contraction יָהוָה Jeve. So think Mercer, on Gen. 2:4; Capellus, in his oration on the Tetragrammaton; and Drusius, on Exod. 3:15, although he preferred Jave. So Crellius, Episcopius and Placaeus, from whom Jeve could easily have passed among the Greeks into Ἰεω and Ἰἁω. So Sandfortius, book 1, de descensu Christi ad inferos. So the most learned Grotius, on Matt. 22:44. See them, and it will not irk you. So Owen, book 3, ch. 8, on the progress of idolatry.

units.la: Ad quæstionem secundam de nomine יהוה nunc legendo & efferendo plerique omnes respondent legendum omnino Jehova, hac imprimis ratione fulti, quod propria virorum nomina componantur ex יהו Jeho, ex nomine Jehova, & verbis Nathan, vel Chanan, vel Kun in hiphil ut Jehonathan, Jehochanan, Jehoiakim. Sed qua facilitate asseritur nomina illa propria esse composita ex nomine Jehova, eadem facilitate negatur. 1°. Quia non perpetuò scribuntur Jehonathan, Jehoiada, Jehoiaphad &c. Sed etiam non raro Jonathan, Joiadah, Josaphad, &c. ut formæ illorum nominum deductæ sint ex futuro Hiphil cum Jod formativo nominum propriorum, & littera ה epenthetica euphoniæ causa inserta, quia prisca lingua Hebræa aspirationes crebras amavit. 2°. Quia non raro legitur Joakin, unde per epenthesin litteræ ה formatur Jehoiakin; nam vel ante Moïsem cum nemini nomen Dei quadrilitterum innotuerat, ut supra addiximus, invectam videmus formam illam nominum propriorum, quorum prima sylsyllaba est Jo, ut Jochebed mater Moïsis. Exod. 6: 20. Et Joseph cui insertum legitur n. Psalm. 81: 6. testimonium in Jehoseph. 3°. Quia lectio Jehova novitia est χΘές καὶ πεῶλω, ut parentem habeat Galatinum è familia Minoritarum monachum, qui superiori sæculo vixit. De arcanis Religionis Christianæ lib. 2. cap. 9. etsi ipsemet neget legendum esse Jehova, vel Marsilium Ficinum. Nemo enim ante Marsilium & Galatinum, vel Judæorum, vel Doctorum Christianorum qui Hebraicè calluerunt, scilicet Origenes, & Hieronymus legerunt Jehova, ut ex uno Galatino cacoëthes illud irrepserit, pronuntiandi Jehov?. Id enim certo experimento probatur, quia apud Clementem Alexandrinum loco laudato & in veteri editione operum Hieronymi in Psalm. 8. hæc legas: Prius nomen Domini apud Hebraos quatuor litterarum est Jod, He, Vau, He, quod proprie Dei vocabulum sonat & legi potest Jaho. Verum in recentibus Hieronymi editionibus legas, quod proprie Dei vocabulum sonat, & legi potest Jehova. Eadem mutatio apud Clementem.
units.tr: For the second question about the name יהוה, most people now answer, in reading and pronouncing it, that it must altogether be read Jehovah. They rely chiefly on this reason: proper personal names of men are compounded from יהו Jeho, from the name Jehovah, and from the verbs Nathan, Chanan or Kun in the hiphil, as Jehonathan, Jehochanan, Jehoiakim. But the same ease with which those proper names are said to be compounded from the name Jehovah can be used to deny it. First, because they are not always written Jehonathan, Jehoiada, Jehoiaphad and so on, but also not rarely Jonathan, Joiadah, Josaphad and so on. So the forms of those names are derived from the future hiphil with the formative yod of proper names, and a letter ה is inserted as an epenthetic for the sake of euphony, because the early Hebrew language loved frequent aspirations. Second, because Joakin is not rarely read, whence by epenthesis of the letter ה comes Jehoiakin. For either before Moses, when the four-letter name of God was known to no one, as we noted above, we see that form of proper names introduced, whose first syllable is Jo, as Jochebed, the mother of Moses (Exod. 6:20). And Joseph, to whom an n is said to be inserted, has the testimony of Psalm 81:6 in Jehoseph. Third, because the reading Jehovah is a novelty of only yesterday and the day before [χθὲς καὶ πρῴην], so that its parent is Galatinus, a monk of the Franciscan order who lived in the previous century (On the Secrets of the Christian Religion, book 2, chapter 9), although Galatinus himself denies that Jehovah should be read, as does Marsilius Ficinus. For no one before Marsilius and Galatinus, either among the Jews or among Christian teachers skilled in Hebrew, namely Origen and Jerome, read Jehovah. So that itch of pronouncing "Jehov" crept in from Galatinus alone. This is proved by a sure piece of evidence: in Clement of Alexandria, in the passage cited, and in the old edition of Jerome's works on Psalm 8, you may read these words: "The earlier name of the Lord among the Hebrews has four letters, Yod, He, Vav, He, which properly sounds as God's word and can be read Jaho." But in the recent editions of Jerome you read: "which properly sounds as God's word, and can be read Jehovah." The same change has been made in Clement.

units.la: Alii litteraturæ Hebraicæ peritissimi, & longè celeberrimi Buxtorfii, Drusius, Erpennius, Capellus, &c. potioribus longè rationibus fulti, astipulantibus ipsis omnibus Hebræorum magistris, ore rotundo pronuntiant omninò legendum esse Adonai.
units.tr: Other men most expert in Hebrew literature, and far the most celebrated, namely Buxtorf, Drusius, Erpenius, Capellus and others, supported by far stronger reasons, and with all the Hebrew masters agreeing, pronounce with full voice that it must altogether be read Adonai.

units.la: Primò, quia puncta nominis יהוה vocales sunt nominis Adonai, quod liquet, quia vel præcedente, vel sequente Adonai, nomen יהוה habet vocales nominis Elohim in hunc modum יְהוִה, ne bis legatur Adonai. At enim יהוה utique invariatum maneret, si legendum foret Jehova, quia nullum sequeretur incommodum præcedente, vel sequente Adonai, ut commodè legeretur Adonai Jehova. Quod verò adversarii regerunt sub Jod nominis יהוה esse Scheva simplex, non Scheva compositum Catephpatach, quod est sub ʾ in nomine Adonai, utique levissimum est. 1°. Quia apud priscos Scheva simplex pronuntiatum fuit instar Scheva rapti, seu Catechpatach. 2°. Mutatio Scheva compositi in Scheva simplex facta est compendii causa, quia nomen Tetragrammatum creberrimè occurrit in Scriptura. 3°. Quia mutatio Schevaïm compositorum in Scheva simplex passim occurrit, in aliis dictionibus Hebraicis, ut norunt Grammaticorum filii.
units.tr: First, because the vowel points of the name יהוה are the vowels of the name Adonai. This is clear, because when the name יהוה is either preceded or followed by Adonai, it takes the vowels of the name Elohim, in this way יְהוִה, so that Adonai is not read twice. But יהוה would certainly remain unchanged if it were to be read Jehovah, since there would be no inconvenience whether Adonai preceded or followed it, so that one could conveniently read "Adonai Jehovah." As for the opponents' reply, that under the yod of the name יהוה there is a simple sheva, not the compound sheva khatef-patah which stands under the aleph in the name Adonai, this is utterly trivial. First, because among the ancients the simple sheva was pronounced like a hurried sheva, or khatef-patah. Second, the change of the compound sheva into a simple sheva was made for the sake of brevity, because the Tetragrammaton occurs very frequently in Scripture. Third, the change of compound shevas into a simple sheva occurs everywhere in other Hebrew words, as the sons of the grammarians know.

units.la: Secunda ratio, quâ nititur lectio Adonai ob puncta ejus vocalia in nomine יהוה, hæc est, quia litteræ serviles, & præfixæ ב, כ, ל, מ, ו, sub se habent Patach, vel Tsere ubivis præfiguntur nomini יהוה: SciScilicet ex nomine Adonai, quia gutturalis punctat se & praecedentem, ut ליהוה, מיהוה, ויהוה, ביהוה. Verumtamen si legendum foret Jehova, regulariter scribendum esset ביהוה ליהוה מיהוה, sicut scribitur מיהודה ביהודה. Quia quoties duo Scheváim concurrunt ab initio dictionis, primum mutatur in Chirec, & posterius si fuerit sub Iod, eliditur.
units.tr: The second reason on which the reading Adonai rests, on account of its vowel points in the name יהוה, is this: the servile letters prefixed, ב, כ, ל, מ, ו, have under themselves a patah or a tsere wherever they are prefixed to the name יהוה. That is, they take this from the name Adonai, because the guttural points itself and the preceding letter: ליהוה, מיהוה, ויהוה, ביהוה. But if it were to be read Jehovah, it would regularly have to be written ביהוה, ליהוה, מיהוה, just as מיהודה and ביהודה are written. Because whenever two shevas come together at the beginning of a word, the first is changed to a hireq, and the second, if it stands under a yod, is elided.

units.la: Tertia ratio est, quia litterae Begadkephad, post nomen יהוה recipiunt Dagech lene, ut solent post litteram mobilem Jod, in nomine Adonai. Attenim si legendum foret Jehova non haberent Dagech lene, quia post litteram quiescentem, qualis est He in Jehova, aspiratae manent.
units.tr: The third reason is that the letters begadkephat, after the name יהוה, receive a lene dagesh, as they usually do after a moveable yod in the name Adonai. For if it were to be read Jehovah, they would not have a lene dagesh, since after a quiescent letter, such as the He in Jehovah, they remain aspirated.

units.la: Quarta ratio est, quia confessus Septuagintaviralis constanter legit Adonai, nam nomen Tetragrammatum fere ubivis per κύριον reddidere.
units.tr: The fourth reason is that the Seventy constantly read Adonai, for they almost everywhere rendered the Tetragrammaton by κύριον [kyrion].

units.la: Quinta, quia Chaldaei Paraphrastae Onkelos, & Jonathan in suis Targumim, sicut & Targum Hierosolymitanum nomen יהוה perpetuò reddunt per nomen Adonai.
units.tr: Fifth, because the Chaldee paraphrasts Onkelos and Jonathan in their Targumim, as also the Jerusalem Targum, always render the name יהוה by the name Adonai.

units.la: Sexta, quia Christus & Apostoli quorum summa auctoritas & omni major exceptione, sequuti lectionem, & versionem Septuagintaviralem ubi loca laudant veteris foederis in quibus Deus appellatur יהוה, semper habent vicarium ipsius Κύριον, & aliquando Θεὸν.
units.tr: Sixth, because Christ and the Apostles, whose authority is supreme and above all exception, followed the reading and the version of the Seventy wherever they cite passages of the Old Covenant in which God is called יהוה. There they always have as its substitute κύριον [kyrion], and sometimes θεὸν [theon].

units.la: Septima, quia Origenes in Hexaplis, ubi in una ex sex columnis textum Hebraicum scripsit Graecis characteribus loco יהוה semper scripsit Adonai. Et Hieronymus doctorum Christianorum alter, qui linguam Hebraeam calluit, etsi nomen quadrilitterum & sonare, & legi posse Jaho in Psalm. 8. antiquae editionis dixit, semper tamen pro יהוה habet Adonai, vel Dominus, unde versio Vulgata in Exod. 6: 3. ita legit: Nomen meum Adonai, non indicavi eis.
units.tr: Seventh, because Origen in the Hexapla, where in one of the six columns he wrote the Hebrew text in Greek characters, always wrote Adonai in place of יהוה. And Jerome, the other Christian teacher who was skilled in the Hebrew language, although he said in Psalm 8 of the old edition that the four-letter name both sounds and can be read Jaho, nevertheless always has Adonai or Dominus for יהוה. Hence the Vulgate translator reads in Exod. 6:3: "My name Adonai I did not make known to them."

units.la: Quaeras nunc haut immeritò cur Septuaginta nomen Dei proprium יהוה per Κύριον Dominum reddiderint? Eccur etiam Massoretae nomen יהוה punctis vocalibus Adonai instruxerint? Demum cur Christus & Apostoli in laudandis veteris foederis locis ubi occurrit nomen Tetragrammatum, versionem Septuagintaviralem sequuti Adonai, vel Κύριον, vel Θεὸν pronuntiaverint? Quaestionibus illis ritè satis ut faciamus, quaestio sequens perstringenda nobis videtur.
units.tr: You may now not unreasonably ask: why did the Seventy render the proper name of God יהוה by κύριον, Lord? Why also did the Masoretes furnish the name יהוה with the vowel points of Adonai? Finally, why did Christ and the Apostles, in citing passages of the Old Covenant where the Tetragrammaton occurs, follow the version of the Seventy and pronounce Adonai, or κύριον, or θεὸν? Before we have duly satisfied those questions, it seems to us that the following question must be touched upon.

units.la: QUÆSTIO XVII.
units.tr: Question 17.

units.la: Quid proprie, directe, & per sese Deus significaverit, & de se revelare voluerit nomine proprio יהוה?
units.tr: What did God properly, directly and in himself signify, and wish to reveal of himself, by the proper name [יהוה]?

units.la: GRassantibus ad rectam mysteriorum salutis interpretationem, quæ Deus benignissimus in Novo Instrumento nobis revelare dignatus est, multa eaque gravissima necessariam faciunt quæstionis propositæ solutionem.
units.tr: As we apply ourselves to the correct interpretation of the mysteries of salvation that the most gracious God has deigned to reveal to us in the New Testament, many and very weighty considerations make a solution of the question proposed necessary.

units.la: Primò, divini illius indigitamenti excellentia gloriosa, præ cæteris omnibus Dei nominibus, dicitur enim שם הגדול הנכבד והנורא Nomen gloriosum, & terribile. Græcis Interpretibus, ὄνομα ἔνδοξον, καὶ θαυμαστόν. Nomen gloriosum & admirabile. Deuteron 28: 58. שם הגדול Nomen magnum. Jerem. 44: 26. & καὶ ἐξοχῳ ὠ את־השם Nomen. Levit. 24: 11.
units.tr: First, the glorious excellence of that divine designation, above all other names of God. It is called [שם הגדול הנכבד והנורא], "the glorious and terrible name." The Greek translators render it [ὄνομα ἔνδοξον καὶ θαυμαστόν], "the glorious and admirable name." Deut. 28:58, "the great name" [שם הגדול]. Jer. 44:26, and Lev. 24:11, "the Name" [את־השם].

units.la: Secundò, quòd novum, & ignotum Patriarchis Abrahamo, Isaaco, & Jacobo. Notus fui Abrahamo, Isaaco, & Iacobo, ut Deus fortis & omnipotens, & nomine meo יהוה non sum cognitus eis. Exod. 6: 3.
units.tr: Second, it was new and unknown to the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac and Jacob: I was known to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob as God Almighty, but by my name יהוה I was not known to them. Exod. 6:3.

units.la: Tertiò, quia Deus nomen יהוה sibi proprium fecit, ut Mosi dixerit: hoc est nomen meum in seculum, & memoriale meum de generatione in generationem. Exod. 3: 15.
units.tr: Third, because God made the name יהוה his own, as he said to Moses: This is my name for ever, and my memorial from generation to generation. Exod. 3:15.

units.la: Quartò, quia Deus proprium illud sibi fecit indigitamentum, cum miraculosam populi Israël è servitute Ægyptiaca liberationem, Mosis ministerio moliretur. Exod. 3: 14. & 6: 3. Ubi è cœlo descenderat ad montem Horeb, & è rubo ardenti Moysem alloqueretur. Sed id totum mysticum erat, sive respexeris ad personam, quæ descenderat, illa enim Angelus Dei dicitur, quod de Deo Patre, qui nunquam missus, Angelus, vel legatus dicitur, intelligi nequit. Sed & ipse Angelus verbotim asserit se esse Deum Abrahami, Isaaci, & Iacobi, parentum Moysis. Exod. 3: 6. Non erat igitur Angelus creatus: sed Deus ipse Filius, à Deo Patre missus. Deum fuisse, Angelum Dei in medio rubi, ultrò fatetur Rabbi Eliezer in Pirke Avot. c. 40. his verbis. Ibi autem revelatus est Sanctus benedictus è medio rubi juxta illud. Apparuit illi Angelus Domini in flamma ignis è medio rubi. Sive rubum spectaveris, ille enim symbolum fuit afflictionis Angeli יהוה, (ille autem Dei Filius est, à Patre missus). Ita sentit Rabbi Eliezer libro & capite laudatis, dum ita disserit de Angelo Domini Deseruit autem totum montem, & descendit in rubum, atque illic commoratus est. Rubus autem tribulat, vel pungit, & totus est ex spinis & tribulis. Cur autem habitabat in angustia & tribulatione. Quia videbat Israelitas in magna afflictione, ipse quoque cum ipsis habitavit in afflictione. Hinc illud, in omni afflictione illorum, erat ipsi afflictio. Jesa. 63: 9. Hic germanam habemus hypotypolim filii Dei in carne manifestati, afflicti, & egeni, ut non haberet ubi caput reclinaret, invidiae aculeis, injuriisque Judaeorum lacessiti, felle poti, & spinis coronati.
units.tr: Fourth, God made that designation his own when he was undertaking the miraculous deliverance of the people of Israel from Egyptian slavery through the ministry of Moses. Exod. 3:14 and 6:3. There he had come down from heaven to Mount Horeb and spoke to Moses from the burning bush. But all of this was mystical, whether you look to the person who came down, who is called the Angel of God, which cannot be understood of God the Father, who was never sent and is never called an angel or envoy. Moreover, the Angel himself states word for word that he is the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the fathers of Moses. Exod. 3:6. Therefore the Angel was not a created angel, but God the Son himself, sent by God the Father. Rabbi Eliezer, in the Pirke Avot, chapter 40, freely admits that God was the Angel of God in the middle of the bush, in these words: But there the Holy One, blessed be he, was revealed from the middle of the bush, according to that text: The Angel of the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire from the middle of the bush. Whether you look to the bush, which was a symbol of the affliction of the Angel יהוה (and that Angel is the Son of God, sent by the Father). Rabbi Eliezer thinks this way in the book and chapter cited, when he speaks thus of the Angel of the Lord: He left the whole mountain and went down into the bush, and dwelt there. The bush, however, afflicts or pricks, and is entirely of thorns and briars. Why then did he dwell in narrowness and affliction? Because he saw Israel in great affliction, he too dwelt with them in affliction. Hence that text: In all their affliction he was afflicted. Isa. 63:9. Here we have a true picture of the Son of God manifested in the flesh, afflicted and needy, who had nowhere to lay his head, assailed by the stings of envy and the injuries of the Jews, given gall to drink, and crowned with thorns.

units.la: Demum id totum mysticum est, si in finem prospexeris, cujus ergò descenderat Deus, missus à Deo, Angelus in rubum ardentem, populum, scilicet, Israelem ut liberaret è servitute Ægyptiaca: illa enim typus fuit liberationis spiritualis è servitute diaboli, peccati, & mortis, nec non libertatis gloriosae in quam nos asseruit, Deus sanguine Filii, agni inculpati, nos in haereditatem coelestem, terrâ Canaan adumbratam, ut transferret. Unde Paulus, Deus nos eruit è potestate tenebrarum, & transtulit in regnum filii sui dilecti, in quo habemus redemptionem per sanguinem ipsius, idonei facti ad participandam haereditatem sanctorum in luce. Colos. 1: 12. 13. 14.
units.tr: Finally, all of this is mystical if you look to the end: the reason God's Angel, sent by God, came down into the burning bush was to deliver the people of Israel, that is, from Egyptian slavery. That deliverance was a type of spiritual liberation from the slavery of the devil, sin and death, and of the glorious liberty into which God, by the blood of his Son, the spotless Lamb, has brought us, to transfer us to a heavenly inheritance, foreshadowed by the land of Canaan. Hence Paul: God has rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son, in whom we have redemption through his blood, made fit to share the inheritance of the saints in light. Col. 1:12–14.

units.la: Quintò, quia recta יהוה gloriosi indigitamenti intelligentia, lucem luculentam faenerat, universo foederi Mosaico, rationes & causas apperit, cur Deus sese abstinuerit abs glorioso illo indigitamento, ad Mosem usque? Cur toto primo capite Geneseos, ubi historia creationis pertexitur nusquam Deus ab sapientissimo Mose יהוה appellatur? Cur post Adami creationem, ejusque lapsum & rebellionem, illo nomine insignitur? Cur identidem conqueritur Deus Israelitas nomen suum יהוה, & perpetuum monumentum profanasse, ubi idolis serviunt? Cur demum, sexcenta alia ut praetereamus, sapientissimum numen recipit fore, ut gentes idololatrae, ipsique Israelitae noverint se esse יהוה, ubicumque, justitiam vindicatricem exercet in poenas, vel gratiam in effundendas benedictiones suas?
units.tr: Fifth, because a correct understanding of the glorious designation יהוה sheds a clear light on the whole Mosaic covenant and sets out the reasons and causes why God held back from that glorious designation until Moses. Why in the whole first chapter of Genesis, where the history of creation is set out, does the most wise Moses nowhere call God יהוה? Why after the creation of Adam, and his fall and rebellion, is God marked with that name? Why does God repeatedly complain that Israel has profaned his name יהוה and his perpetual monument when they serve idols? Why finally (to pass over six hundred other things) does the most wise deity declare that the idolatrous nations and the Israelites themselves shall know that he is יהוה, wherever he exercises avenging justice in punishments, or grace in pouring out his blessings?

units.la: Sextò, altum perpetuumque gloriosi simul ac tremendi nominis יהוה toto Novo Instrumento silentium, contrà quod Deus receperat fore, id nomen suum in perpetuum, & momoriale in omnem aetatem. Exod. 3: 15. Ut quid igitur id sui indigitamentum non retinuit in Euangelio, novoque foedere? Ut quid appellari disiit nomine illo Tetragrammato, memoriali suo perpetuo ab aetate in aetatem duraturo? An oblivione sepelienda est in Euangelio Dei liberatoris, & salvatoris memoria, quam recentem, vivamque, tremendum יהוה nomen faciebat? Utique hic mirari subit, cur Deus nomen proprium יה, quod sui fore memoriale perpetuum nusquam receperat, in voce ἀλληλούια retinuerit. Apoc. 19: 1. 3. 4. 6. Et nomen Tetragrammatum sibi proprium, suique monumentum aeternum in foedere novo ita abdicaverit, ut in Euangelio nunquam ac nusquam יהוה appelletur? Nam quod Apocal. 1: 4. nominatur ὁ ὢν, καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος, qui est, qui erat, & qui venturus est, non significat Deum esse sub Euangelio יהוה: sed implesse, quod antiquo illo, proprioque suo indigitamento, se futurum recipiebat. Nempe sub Euangelio Deus est, quod se futurum promittebat illo suo nomine, quodque erat, Israelitis sua promissione contenta isthoc nomine: sua liberatione typica, è servitute Ægyptiaca: sua liberatione & salute reali, collata in fideles veteres, per fidem adhibitam τῇ ἐπαγγελίᾳ venturi Messiae: quod denique erat in Christo sibi mundum reconcilians. 2 Cor. 5: 19. Sed & venturus est. Ubi notasse operae pretium erit Johannem non dixisse ὁ ἐρχόμενος, vel ὁ ἐσόμενος futurus, quod exactè respondebat nomini יהוה, quod proprie, & per se significat, Erit, ut infra demonstratum dabimus: sed signanter dixisse, & iterasse, ὁ ἐρχόμενος, qui venturus est. Apoc. 1: 4. 8. &c.
units.tr: Sixth, the whole of the New Testament is silent about the lofty and perpetual name יהוה, which is at once glorious and terrible, though God had said it would be his name for ever, and his memorial for all ages. Exod. 3:15. Why, then, did he not retain that designation of himself in the Gospel and the new covenant? Why did he cease to be called by that Tetragrammaton, his perpetual memorial that was to last from age to age? Or is the memory of God as Deliverer and Saviour to be buried in oblivion in the Gospel, when the awesome name יהוה made it fresh and living? Here one is surely amazed why God retained the proper name יה in the word [ἀλληλούια], Hallelujah, though he had nowhere declared it to be his perpetual memorial. Rev. 19:1, 3, 4, 6. And why did he so renounce the Tetragrammaton, his own proper name and eternal monument, in the new covenant, that in the Gospel he is never and nowhere called יהוה? For what is said in Rev. 1:4, that he is named [ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος], "who is, who was, and who is to come," does not mean that God under the Gospel is יהוה, but that he has fulfilled what he promised under that ancient proper designation, that he would be. Indeed under the Gospel God is the one who promised to be by that name, and who was, content with that name in his promise to the Israelites: by his typical deliverance from Egyptian slavery, by his real deliverance and salvation granted to the faithful of old through faith in the promise of the Messiah to come, and finally by what he was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself. 2 Cor. 5:19. But he is also to come. Here it will be worth noting that John did not say [ὁ ἐρχόμενος] or [ὁ ἐσόμενος], "future," which would have exactly matched the name יהוה, which signifies properly and in itself he will be, as we shall show below. Rather, John deliberately said and repeated [ὁ ἐρχόμενος], "who is to come." Rev. 1:4, 8, etc.

units.la: Nec quicquam juvat respondere cum Doctissimo Buxtorfio ex Elia in Thisbi, Hebraeos futurum exprimere, quandoque per עתיד simpliciter, quandoque per לבוא לעתיד futurum venire, vel venturum, hac tamen cum differentia, quòd hoc לבוא לעתיד venturum, plerumque adhibeatur in fine sententiae, ut in loco laudato Apocalypseos potius dicatur ὁ ἐρχόμενος, quam ὁ ἐσόμενος, quia adhibetur in fine sententiae. Hinc concludit ἐρχόμενος venturus, idem plane esse atque ἐσόμενος futurus, quod probare contendit ex Apocal. 16: 15. ubi Beza ex antiquo, & fide digno exemplari manuscripto restituit καὶ ὁ ἐσόμενος, Et qui futurus est, pro ὁ ὅσιος, sanctus. Multa, quae reponamus hic nobis occurrunt. 1°. Recta ratio jubet omnibus aliis exemplaribus, in quibus constanter legitur ὁ ὅσιος, fidem potius ut adhibeamus, quàm uni exemplari Bezae. 2°. Quia scopo textus, magis opportunum est ὁ ὅσιος, sanctus, quod perfecte respondet sententiae ὅτι τῶν ἐκδικιῶν, quod hac judicaveris. Agitur enim de judicio in vindictam justo & sancto, quod Dominus exercuit in homicidas Prophetarum, quàm ὁ ἐσόμενος futurus. Nam Deus sanctitate sua commendatur, ubi exercet judicia sua in impios, tribuitque victoriam sanctis. Exod. 15: 11. Apocal. 15: 4. Sed non commendatur sua futuritione, quia jam dudum venit, pugnam cruentam ut pugnaret, gloriosamque reportavit victoriam de peccato, diabolo, mundo, morte, & sepulchro, venturus demum ut judicet vivos atque mortuos. 3°. Quia nulla potest reddi ratio legitima, cur Spiritus Sanctus constanter alibi addiderit, ὁ ἐρχόμενος venturus, ut Apocal. 1: 4. 8. & 4: 8. & 11: 17. Hic verò adeò insolenter pro ἐρχόμενος venturus, dicere voluerit, ὁ ἐσόμενος futurus. Sed ratio in promptu est, cur pro ὁ ἐρχόμε-νος substituerit ὁ ὢν sanctus. Nempè agitur de justitia, & sanctitate judiciorum Domini, qui hîc loci venisse dicitur, ut sancta sua judicia exerceat. Sed ad id, quid obsecro conduceret, ὁ ἐσόμενος futurus? Ut sit finis, si Spiritus Sanctus in locis quatuor laudatis Apocalypseos, dixisset ὁ ἐρχόμενος, qui venturus est eadem mente eodemque significatu atque ὁ ἐσόμενος, quia phrasim Hebræorum, judice Buxtorfio, imitatur, qui in fine sententiæ dicere solent לבוא יבוא id est, ὁ ἐρχόμενος, venturus, seu futurus venire. Utique in loco laudato Apocal. 16: 5. dicendum erat ὁ ἐρχόμενος, qui venturus est, quandoquidem evidentissimè paret, conferentibus locum istum cum cæteris, ubi extat ὁ ἐρχόμενος, non minus esse in fine sententiæ, quàm in aliis. Concludimus igitur retinendum esse ὁ ὢν, juxta fidem omnium exemplarium, & Johannem Deum Patrem istis elogiis ὁ ὢν, καὶ ὁ ἦν, καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος insignivisse, seque sapienter abstinuisse abs participio ὁ ἐσόμενος, vel futuro ἔσται, quod tamen sermonis series exigere videbatur, atque adeo exquisitissima sapientia Deum noluisse vocare, futurum, vel, eum, qui Erit. Nempè, quia sub Euangelio Deus non est amplius appellandus יהוה, qui Erit. Est enim reapse, quod se futurum recipiebat in veteri & antiquato fœdere: sed appellandus est ὁ ἐρχόμενος, qui venturus est, nempè, ut sit in Ecclesia triumphante & gloriosa, alio atque alio modo, quam olim fuit in Ecclesia Judaïca. Olim enim in ea fuit, sua שכינה umbratili nubis præsentia, & expanso velo, remotus in sanctuario suo: longèque alio modo atque nunc est in Ecclesia Christiana militante, verbo scilicet Euangelii, Sacramentorum symbolis & Spiritus sui præsentiâ, corpore absens, & procul habitans in cœlo. Sed enim venturus est, ut sit intimè præsens victrici & triumphanti Ecclesiæ, tota plenitudine præsentiæ suæ gloriosæ, qua sit omnia in omnibus. 1. Cor. 15:28.
units.tr: Nor does it help to answer, with the most learned Buxtorf, from Elias of Tishbi, that the Hebrews express the future sometimes by [עתיד] simply, and sometimes by [לבוא לעתיד], the future coming or the one about to come, with this difference: that [לבוא לעתיד], "about to come," is usually used at the end of a sentence, so that in the passage of the Apocalypse cited it is said [ὁ ἐρχόμενος] rather than [ὁ ἐσόμενος], because it stands at the end of the sentence. From this he concludes that [ἐρχόμενος], "coming," is plainly the same as [ἐσόμενος], "future," which he tries to prove from Rev. 16:15, where Beza, from an ancient and trustworthy manuscript, restored [καὶ ὁ ἐσόμενος], "and who will be," in place of [ὁ ὅσιος], "holy." Many objections occur to us here. First, right reason bids us trust all the other copies, in which [ὁ ὅσιος] is constantly read, rather than the single copy of Beza. Second, [ὁ ὅσιος], "holy," is more suitable to the purpose of the text, and fits perfectly the sentence [ὅτι τῶν ἐκδικιῶν], since you would judge it so: the passage speaks of a judgment exercised in vengeance, just and holy, which the Lord carried out against the murderers of the prophets, rather than of [ὁ ἐσόμενος], "future." For God commends himself by his holiness when he exercises his judgments against the wicked and gives victory to the saints. Exod. 15:11; Rev. 15:4. But he is not commended by his future coming, since he came long ago, fought a bloody battle, and won a glorious victory over sin, the devil, the world, death and the grave, and will come at last to judge the living and the dead. Third, no legitimate reason can be given why the Holy Spirit should elsewhere constantly add [ὁ ἐρχόμενος], "coming," as in Rev. 1:4, 8; 4:8; and 11:17, and yet here should so unusually wish to say [ὁ ἐσόμενος], "future," in place of [ἐρχόμενος], "coming." But the reason is ready to hand why he put [ὁ ὢν], "holy," in place of [ὁ ἐρχόμενος]. Namely, the passage concerns the justice and holiness of the Lord's judgments, who is said to have come there in order to exercise his holy judgments. But what, I ask, would [ὁ ἐσόμενος], "future," contribute to that? Suppose the Holy Spirit, in the four passages of the Apocalypse cited, had said [ὁ ἐρχόμενος], "who is to come," with the same mind and the same meaning as [ὁ ἐσόμενος], "who will be," because he imitates the Hebrew idiom, which, in Buxtorf's judgment, is used at the end of a sentence in the form [לבוא יבוא], that is, [ὁ ἐρχόμενος], "coming," or "about to come." Surely in the passage cited, Rev. 16:5, it had to be [ὁ ἐρχόμενος], "who is to come," since it is most evident, on comparing that passage with the others where [ὁ ἐρχόμενος] occurs, that it stands at the end of the sentence no less than in the others. We conclude, therefore, that [ὁ ὢν], "who is," must be retained, in accordance with the agreement of all the copies, and that John marked God the Father with these titles, [ὁ ὢν, καὶ ὁ ἦν, καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος], "who is, who was, and who is to come"; and that he wisely abstained from the participle [ὁ ἐσόμενος], or the future [ἔσται], "will be," though the course of the sentence seemed to require it. Thus, by the most exquisite wisdom, he did not wish God to be called "future," or "he who will be." For under the Gospel God is no longer to be called יהוה, "he who will be." He is indeed what he promised to be in the old and abrogated covenant, but he is to be called [ὁ ἐρχόμενος], "who is to come," namely so that in the triumphant and glorious Church he may be present in a different and better way than he once was in the Jewish Church. For there he was present in his Shekinah, in the shadowy presence of a cloud, with a veil spread out, remote in his sanctuary; and in a way far different from how he is now in the militant Christian Church, by the word of the Gospel, the signs of the sacraments and the presence of his Spirit, absent in body and dwelling afar off in heaven. But he is to come, so that he may be intimately present to the victorious and triumphant Church in the full richness of his glorious presence, in which he will be all in all. 1 Cor. 15:28.

units.la: Septimò, quia septuaginta Interpretes, qui trecentis præter propter annis ante Christum floruerunt, nomen quadriliterum הוהי per τὸν Κύριον, vel Κύριον sine articulo, fere semper reddidere. Christus autem, & Apostoli, vel usi versione consessus septuagintaviralis, vel suo calculo & auctoritate, verisionem illiusmodi confirmantes, pro nomine tetragrammato Κύριον usurpavere ubivis locorum Veteris Instrumenti, quæ nomen Dei tetragrammatum habent, ut ne latum quidem unguem, hac in parte à septuaginta, discessisse videantur. Sed enim vero, quia in Veteri Instrumento nomen יהוה nonnunquam explicatur per הָאֱלֹהִים ut 2 Sam. 7:3. יהוה tecum, redditur 1 Chron. 17:2. הָאֱלֹהִים tecum. Et 2 Reg. 11:10. in domo יהוה redditur 2 Chron. 23:9. in domo הָאֱלֹהִים. Non secus & septuaginta nonnunquam nomen quadriliterum יהוה non ex more per Κύριον, sed per Θεὸν reddidere, quos & Christus & Apostoli imitati sunt, ut Deut 8:3. per os יהוה, ῥήματι Θεοῦ. Matth. 4:4. Genef. 15:6. Et Abram credidit יהוה septuaginta & Paulus Rom. 4:3. Et Jacobus 2:23. reddidere, Ἀβραὰμ ἐπίστευσεν τῷ Θεῷ. Et Esa. 8:18. Ecce me & pueros, quos dedit mihi יהוה. Septuaginta & Apostolus Hebr. 2:13. reddidere ἰδοὺ ἐγὼ καὶ τὰ παιδία ἃ μοι ἔδωκεν ὁ Θεός. Unde non levi, sed solida conjectura colligere est, nomen Dei proprium יהוה Erit, continuisse vaticinium, quo Deus promittebat se fore Κύριον Dominum, & Deum, nempe Deorum. Nam, quia non raro nomen proprium Dei יהוה in Veteri Instrumento, explicationis ergò adjunctum habet nomen אֱלֹהִים ut Genef. 1:4, 7, 8, 9, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19. & 3:1, 8, 9, 13, 14, 21, 22, 23. & 24:31. Josu. 22:22. Psalm. 50:1. Esa. 26:4. Amos 6:8. Aben-Ezra, & Buxtorfius notarunt nomen proprium יהוה, nunquam esse in regimine, sed immutatum perpetuò manere, & sicubi conjungitur cum nomine appellativo, ex. gr. cum צבאות esse Ellipsim pro יהוה אלהו צבאות Dominus Deus exercituum: sed & cum Deus dicitur אלהים Ellipsis est nominis אל ut liquet ex Jos. 22:22. יהוה אל אלהים, Dominus Deus Deorum. Quando igitur frequentissimè יהוה quitur אֱלֹהִים Ellipsis est nominis אל. Quod vel hinc liquidissimè patet, quia nomen אֱלֹהִים construitur cum verbo singulari, ut בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים creavit Deus. Gen. 1:1. h. e. Deus Deorum creavit, sicut Prov. 9: 1. חָכְמוֹת בָּנְתָה sapientia ædificavit, h. e. חָכְמֹת הַכְמֹות sapientia sapientiarum ædificavit. Numen igitur sapientissimum, quod nomini suo יהוה extemplò non raró subtexuerit, vel nomen אֲדֹנָי, vel nomen אֵלִין, ut Jos. 3: 13. &c. vel אֵל אֱלֹהִים Deus Deorum, vel simpliciter per Ellipsim, אֱלֹהִים: glorioso illo sui indigitamento, significabat, se futurum in plenitudine temporum universæ terræ Dominum, & Deum Deorum. Quam sapientissimè igitur septuaginta, Christus, & Apostoli nomen Tetragrammatum ubivis in Veteri Instrumento occurrit, per Κύριον, vel Θεὸν perpetuò reddidere.
units.tr: Seventhly, the Seventy interpreters, who flourished roughly three hundred years before Christ, almost always rendered the four-letter name יהוה by τὸν Κύριον, or by Κύριον without the article [τὸν Κύριον; Κύριον]. Christ and the Apostles, either using the version of the Seventy or confirming such a rendering by their own judgment and authority, used Κύριον for the tetragrammaton wherever it occurs in the Old Testament, so that they seem not to have departed from the Septuagint by so much as a hair's breadth in this respect. Indeed, since in the Old Testament the name יהוה is sometimes explained by הָאֱלֹהִים, 2 Sam. 7:3, "יהוה be with you," is rendered in 1 Chron. 17:2 as "הָאֱלֹהִים be with you"; and 2 Kings 11:10, "in the house of יהוה," is rendered in 2 Chron. 23:9 as "in the house of הָאֱלֹהִים." In the same way the Seventy sometimes did not render the four-letter name יהוה by Κύριον as usual, but by Θεὸν, and Christ and the Apostles imitated them. Deut. 8:3, "by the mouth of יהוה," is rendered ῥήματι Θεοῦ in Matt. 4:4; Gen. 15:6, "Abram believed in יהוה," is rendered by the Seventy, by Paul in Rom. 4:3 and by James in 2:23 as Ἀβραὰμ ἐπίστευσεν τῷ Θεῷ. Isa. 8:18, "Behold, I and the children whom יהוה has given me," is rendered by the Seventy and by the Apostle in Heb. 2:13 as ἰδοὺ ἐγὼ καὶ τὰ παιδία ἃ μοι ἔδωκεν ὁ Θεός. Hence it can be gathered, by no slight but by solid conjecture, that the proper name of God, יהוה, contained the prophecy by which God promised that he would be Κύριος, Lord, and Θεός, God, that is, the God of gods. For since the proper name of God יהוה in the Old Testament often has the name אֱלֹהִים added to it for explanation, as in Gen. 1:4, 7, 8, 9, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19; 3:1, 8, 9, 13, 14, 21, 22, 23; 24:31; Josh. 22:22; Ps. 50:1; Isa. 26:4; Amos 6:8, Aben Ezra and Buxtorf have observed that the proper name יהוה never stands in the construct state but always remains unchanged; and wherever it is joined with an appellative noun, for example with צבאות, it is an ellipsis for יהוה אלהי צבאות, "the Lord God of hosts." But also when God is called אלהים, it is an ellipsis of the name אל, as is clear from Josh. 22:22, יהוה אל אלהים, "the Lord God of gods." Therefore, when יהוה is very frequently followed by אֱלֹהִים, this is an ellipsis of the name אל. This is most clearly evident from the fact that the noun אֱלֹהִים is construed with a singular verb, as in בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים, "God created," Gen. 1:1, that is, the God of gods created; just as in Prov. 9:1, חָכְמוֹת בָּנְתָה, "wisdom built," stands for חָכְמֹת הַכְמֹות, "the wisdom of wisdoms built."
