Christ keeps the Septuagint version, Mark 12:29: [Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν, Κύριος εἷς ἐστι] The Lord our God, the Lord is one God. Zechariah prophesies the same; but he also explains the name Jehovah by Erit. And Erit Jehovah King over all the earth. [ויהיה יהוה אחד ושמו אחד] [Ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ ἔσται Κύριος εἷς, καὶ τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ ἕν] On that day Jehovah will be one, and his name one. Zech. 14:9. The God of Israel has always been, is, and is to come, one God: for it is impossible that there should be several gods properly so called, that is, supreme, infinite and independent beings, which Socrates, Seneca, and all the philosophers who have been among the pagans have admitted, not from whim or from a mind blinded by prejudice, but from true philosophy. But in the midst of the polytheism of a deluded paganism, one God was neither regarded nor worshipped, much less the one God of Israel. Therefore he prophesied at once by his proper name Erit, and at the same time by oracles repeated again and again, that when all false gods were overthrown, he himself would be regarded and worshipped as one God, King and Lord over the whole earth, from the east to the setting of the sun. If therefore, my people Israel, and you Gentiles who do not know me and have no part in my covenants, you ask me why I wished to be called Ero, and why, speaking of myself in the third person, I am called Erit, take this answer from me myself: I am called Ero and Erit, Erit, one God, King and Lord, when I have shown the destruction and abolition of false gods, which I most rightly wished to be called Erit, the destroyer and overthrower of false gods.

units.la: Nec quicquam veritati assertæ officit, quòd tres, Pater, Filius & Spiritus Sanctus in veteri Instrumento de nomine יהוה Erit, censeantur. Pater utique, Prophetam è medio tui, & fratribus tuis suscitabit tibi יהוה Deus tuus, illum audietis. Deut. 18: 15. Propheta ille Filius Dei est Jesus Christus. Jehove igitur eum suscitaturus Deus Pater est. Astiterunt reges terra & principes consilium inierunt adversus יהוה, & adversus משיחו unctum ejus, Psalm. 2: 2. Dixit יהוה Domino meo sede à dextris meis &c. Sceptrum fortitudinis tua mittet יהוה ex Sion, dominare in medio inimicorum tuorum. Juravit יהוה & non penitebit eum, tu es Sacerdos in aternum secundum morem Melchisedech. Psalm. 110: 1, 2, 4. Ubi antiqui Judæorum Doctores fatentur verba esse Dei Israelis ad Messiam. Spiritus Domini יהוה super me, eo quod unxit me יהוה &c. Jef. 61: 1. Verba illa sibi dicta à יהוה asserit Christus. Luc. 4: 18, 21. Christus pariter Dei Filius nomine יהוה passim insignitur in Veteri Instrumento. Attollite portæ postes vestros, elevate vos portæ æternæ & introibit Rex gloriæ. Quis est iste Rex gloriæ, יהוה fortis & potens, יהוה potens in prælio &c. Psalm. 24: 7, 8, 9, 10. Illa autem antiphone ascensum Christi Filii in cœlum evidentissime respicit, ea propter Christus in novo Instrumento nomine Κύριος vicario nominis יהוה passim insignitur. Matth. 22: 43, 44, 45. Luc. 2: 11. Joh. 20: 13. Rom. 10: 12.
units.tr: Nor does it detract from the truth asserted that the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are all counted under the name Jehovah [יהוה] in the Old Testament. The Father himself says: The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet from among you, from your brethren; him you shall hear. Deut. 18:15. That prophet is the Son of God, Jesus Christ. Therefore it is God the Father who will raise him up, Jehovah. The kings of the earth stood up, and the rulers took counsel together against the LORD and against his anointed, Ps. 2:2. The LORD said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, etc. The LORD will send the sceptre of your strength out of Zion; rule in the midst of your enemies. The LORD has sworn and will not change his mind: you are a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek, Ps. 110:1, 2, 4. Here the ancient teachers of the Jews confess that these are the words of the God of Israel addressed to the Messiah. The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me, etc. Isa. 61:1. Christ claims that these words were spoken to him by the LORD, Luke 4:18, 21. Likewise Christ, the Son of God, is everywhere in the Old Testament marked with the name Jehovah. Lift up your heads, O gates; lift yourselves up, O everlasting doors, and the King of glory shall come in. Who is this King of glory? The LORD strong and mighty, the LORD mighty in battle, etc. Ps. 24:7, 8, 9, 10. That antiphon most clearly refers to the ascension of Christ the Son into heaven; for this reason Christ is everywhere marked in the New Testament with the name Kyrios [Κύριος], which stands in place of the name Jehovah. Matt. 22:43, 44, 45; Luke 2:11; John 20:13; Rom. 10:12.

units.la: Sed & Spiritus Sanctus etsi non adeo frequenter, nomine tamen יהוה insignitur. Præterquam enim sæpe sæpius appellatur Spiritus יהוה Jef. 61: 1. & 63: 14. etiam יהוה dicitur Jef. 6: 9, 11. his verbis: Et audivi vocem Domini dicentis quem mittam, & quis ibit nobis? Et dixit, vade, & dicas populo huic, audite audiendo, & ne intelligatis; & videte videndo, & ne cognoscatis, & dixi usque quo Domine &c. Hic loci loquenti tribuitur nomen Domini illius, scilicet de quo Jesaias dixit. Viderunt oculi mei Regem יהוה exercituum. verf. 5. Sed Paulus apud Lucam dictum illud Domini יהוה exercituum Spiritui Sancto tribuit. Optime, inquit, Spiritus Sanctus loquutus est per Jesaiam Prophetam ad Patres nostros dicens. Vade ad populum istum, & dic, audiendo audietis, & non intelligetis: Et videndo videbitis & non cernetis. Act. 28: 25, 26. Nec regerant Socia ni sermonem esse sedentis super solio excelso, qui Dominus & יהוה exercituum dicitur, quique juxta eorum sententiam Deus Pater est, reclamante tamen, eorumque os impuimpurum cohibente Johanne, dum verbotim asserit Jesaiam vidisse gloriam Christi Filii Dei & de eo loquutum esse. Joh. 12: 41. Nec iterum regerant ergo Christo Filio Dei hæc verba, Vade ad populum istum &c. Propheta Jesaias tribuit, non Spiritui Sancto. Horrenda Hæreticorum audacia ! Eccuinam igitur potius credendum est, num Hæreticis Socinianis, num Paulo, sacrarum Scripturarum interpreti infallibili, qui dictum illud יהוה & Domini exercituum expresse tribuit Spiritui Sancto Actuum Apostolorum loco laudato? Sed ne tu, pie lector, hic hæsites & percontetur, qui fieri potest, ut dictum illud, Vade ad populum istum, Spiritui Sancto tribuatur, quandoquidem omnia, quæ illo capite Jesaiæ narrantur præcepto & edicto fiunt יהוה exercituum, sedentis pro solio excelso &c. Hæsitatio tua ut amoveatur, pie Lector, attendas 1°. oportet ad fœdus trium personarum transactum super negotio redemptionis generis humani. Juxta fœdus illud divinum Pater mittit Filium, summâ sua & ἀνδ-ξύνῳ majestate, qua jus sustinet & exercet divinitatis, ut mittat Filium, & Spiritum Sanctum. Sed enim juxta pactum illud fœderale, Filius ἀγγελ-ος nuncius, & missus à Patre, functus munere sacerdotali, & placata sui sanguinis λύτρον vice hominum mediator justitia Patris, merito obedientiæ suæ, sedit ad majestatem Patris in excelsis. Hebr. 1: 3. Officio Prophetico, & regali adversus homines functurus pro Patre, ut auctoritate & majestate Patris Spiritum Sanctum mittat, qui Prophetas & Apostolos ipse inspiret & mittat ut sint θεοδίδακτοι, divinitus edocti, doceatque eorum ministerio homines, mysteria regni coelorum, idque totum quantum quantum est, etsi præstat à Filio missus, id tamen totum peragat sua auctoritate, & majestate divina, quia ipse Deus est, cui mentiti sunt Ananias & Saphira Act. 5: 4. Etsi ex spontanea pactione fœderali missus est à Patre, & Filio. 2°. Attendas oportet, pie lector in illustri illa visione Jesaiæ oportunè distinguendum esse inter objectum visionis, illa enim persona est Filii Dei fungentis officio sacerdotali, & regio simul. Sacerdotali, quia domus repleta est, interior scilicet, fumo nimirum altaris suffitTuum; Sed & regio simul, quia sedet pro solio suo excelso, rex exercituum, ut simul sit Rex & sacerdos, juxta prophetiam Zach. 6: 13. Sed & distinguas oportet personam illam, quæ intus Prophetam afflavit pro officio suo fœderali, & personali, eam intus ut alloquatur, supremoque suo mandato mittat ad Judæos rebelles, illa autem persona Spiritus Sanctus est missus à Filio pontifice, regeque summo, sedente pro solio suo. Ea propter optimè Paulus prophetiam Jesaiæ interpre-tatus, dicta præcepta Jeshiæ prophetæ spiritui sancto tribuit, eum-que jure merito, quia unus Deus est in sæcula benedictus cum Patre & Filio, nomine Jeheve & Domini, insignivit.
units.tr: But the Holy Spirit too, although not so often, is nevertheless marked with the name Jehovah. For apart from the fact that the Spirit is very often called Jehovah's Spirit, Isa. 61:1; 63:14, he is also called Jehovah in Isa. 6:9, 11, in these words: And I heard the voice of the Lord saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? And he said, Go, and say to this people: Hear indeed, but do not understand; and see indeed, but do not perceive. And I said, Lord, how long, etc. Here the name of the Lord is given to the speaker, namely the one of whom Isaiah said: My eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts, v. 5. But Paul, in Luke's account, attributes that saying of the Lord of hosts to the Holy Spirit: Well, he says, the Holy Spirit spoke through the prophet Isaiah to our fathers, saying: Go to this people and say, You will indeed hear but not understand; and you will indeed see but not perceive. Acts 28:25, 26. Nor may the Socinians reply that it is the speech of one seated on a high throne, who is called the Lord and Jehovah of hosts and who, according to their opinion, is God the Father; for John refutes them, and silences their impudent mouths, when he expressly states that Isaiah saw the glory of Christ the Son of God and spoke of him. John 12:41. Nor again may they reply that the words Go to this people, etc. were ascribed by the prophet Isaiah to Christ the Son of God and not to the Holy Spirit. What horrible audacity of the heretics! Whom ought we rather to believe: the Socinian heretics, or Paul, the infallible interpreter of the sacred Scriptures, who expressly attributes that saying of Jehovah, the Lord of hosts, to the Holy Spirit in the passage of the Acts of the Apostles which I cited? But lest you, kind reader, hesitate here and ask how it can be that the saying Go to this people is attributed to the Holy Spirit, since everything narrated in that chapter of Isaiah is done by the command and edict of Jehovah, the Lord of hosts, seated on a high throne, etc.: so that your hesitation may be removed, kind reader, you should first attend to the covenant of the three persons made concerning the business of the redemption of the human race. According to that divine covenant, the Father sends the Son, in his supreme and co-equal majesty, by which he holds and exercises the right of deity, that he should send the Son and the Holy Spirit. But indeed, according to that federal pact, the Son, as the angel, the messenger sent by the Father, having performed the priestly office and, as the ransom-price of his blood, having appeased the justice of the Father as mediator on behalf of men by the merit of his obedience, sat down at the majesty of the Father on high. Heb. 1:3. About to perform the prophetic and kingly office toward men on behalf of the Father, he was to send the Holy Spirit by the authority and majesty of the Father, who himself would inspire and send the prophets and apostles, that they might be taught of God, divinely instructed, and that by their ministry he might teach men the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven; and all of this, however far it extends, although it is accomplished by the Son as one sent, he nevertheless accomplishes it all by his own authority and divine majesty, because he is God, to whom Ananias and Sapphira lied, Acts 5:4, even though he was sent by the Father and the Son through a voluntary federal agreement. Second, kind reader, you should attend to the fact that in that famous vision of Isaiah one must rightly distinguish between the object of the vision and the one who sees it: the object is the person of the Son of God performing the priestly office and at the same time the kingly office. He is priestly, because the house was filled, namely the inner part, with the smoke of the incense-altar; and at the same time kingly, because he sits upon his high throne as King of hosts, so that he is at once King and priest, according to the prophecy of Zech. 6:13. You must also distinguish that person who inwardly breathed upon the prophet, for the performance of his federal and personal office, so that he might speak inwardly and send him by his supreme command to the rebellious Jews; that person is the Holy Spirit, sent by the Son, the high priest and supreme King, who sits upon his throne. Therefore Paul rightly interpreted the prophecy of Isaiah, attributed the commands spoken by the prophet Isaiah to the Holy Spirit, and marked him with the name Jehovah and Lord, as is right, because he is the one God blessed for ever together with the Father and the Son.

units.la: Haut immerito igitur Deus Pater, Filius, & Spiritus Sanctus nomine tribus communi, sed & proprio יהוה Erit, in veteri Instrumento insigniuntur, illo discrimine, quod ex pactione fœderali, trium personarum arcesc est, ut patet יהוה fuerit, & appellatus qui erit, quia pro sua majestate fœderali totum negotium redemptionis, con-stituit, misitque Filium & Spiritum Sanctum, ut pro illa sua majestate fœderali dictus fuerit יהוה qui erit, scilicet Deus & Dominus Filii, Spiritus Sancti, Angelorum, Prophetarum, orbisque terrarum universi, falsorum Deorum eversor, & redemptor generis humani. Filius pariter Deus æternum benedictus nomine יהוה Erit, indigitatus fuit, quia futurus erat semen mulieris contriturum caput serpentis, & conterendum in calcaneo suo, Immanuel, Deus & homo, Sacerdos, Propheta, & Rex, qui obedientia sua, meritoque λύτρα sanguinis sui infinito, vindicatricem numinis justitiam, plenè placaturus erat, & efficacia verbi sui, suique Spiritus vorticordia debellaturus, & profligaturus Satana, Deosque nihili, & idololatriam pessundaturus ad extremos terræ fines, habendus & colendus, ut revera erat Deus, Rex, & Dominus Judæorum, & Gentium. Sed & Spiritus Sanctus indigitamento glorioso יהוה Erit, Dominus & Deus ab Jesaia & Paulo jure legitimo indigitatus fuit. Ille enim juxta fœderalem trium personarum pactionem, immediata sua virtute personali afflaturus erat Prophetas, & postmodum Apostolos, eaque debellaturus, & profligaturus Dæmonas, falsosque Gentium Deos per illos ministros fideles amanuenses & præcones, ut Deus unus natura & majestate immensus, sed & personis trinus, Deux Rex & Dominus foret Judæorum & gentium, digna vero Deo adoratione adorandus & celebrandus abs redemptis populis suis in sempiterna sæcula. Regi illi sæculorum, uni Deo sapienti, im-mortali, invisibili, laus, honos, & gloria, in sæculorum sæcula
units.tr: Rightly, therefore, God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are marked in the Old Testament with the name common to the three, but also with a proper name: Erit, that is, he who will be. The difference lies in this: the name springs from the federal agreement of the three persons, as is clear: he was Jehovah and was called he who will be, because by his federal majesty he set up the whole business of redemption and sent the Son and the Holy Spirit; so by that federal majesty he was called he who will be, namely the God and Lord of the Son, the Holy Spirit, the angels, the prophets, and the whole world, the destroyer of false gods and the redeemer of the human race. Likewise God the Son, blessed for ever, was designated by the name Erit, because he was to be the seed of the woman who would crush the head of the serpent and be bruised in his heel, Immanuel, God and man, priest, prophet and king, who by his obedience and the merit of his infinite blood-ransom was to fully appease the avenging justice of the divinity, and by the efficacy of his word and his Spirit was to subdue and overthrow Satan, to destroy the gods of nothing and idolatry to the ends of the earth, to be had and worshipped, as he truly was, as God, King and Lord of Jews and Gentiles. And the Holy Spirit too was rightly designated by Isaiah and Paul with the glorious title Erit, Lord and God. For he, according to the federal pact of the three persons, was to inspire the prophets, and afterwards the apostles, by his immediate personal power, and by them to subdue and overthrow the demons and the false gods of the Gentiles, through those faithful ministers, scribes and heralds, so that he, one God immense in nature and majesty but three in persons, might be the God, King and Lord of Jews and Gentiles, and be adored and celebrated with the worship due to God by his redeemed peoples for everlasting ages. To the King of the ages, the one God, immortal, invisible, be honour and glory for ever and ever.

units.la: Veteres Ecclesiæ Doctores Jesum, se titulo Filii Hominis, insigniis-se, ut ostenderet se vere esse Hominem, asseveranter pro-nunciant, sed male. | p. 4. 5
units.tr: The early Church teachers confidently assert that Jesus used the title Son of Man to show that he was truly man, but they are wrong. | p. 4. 5

units.la: Plerique, Orthodoxi & Pontificii existimant, Jesum hoc titulo Fi-lii Hominis se passim designasse, ad suam abjectionem & for-mam servilem significandam, improbatur. | p. 5. 6
units.tr: Many Orthodox writers and Papists think that Jesus used this title Son of Man of himself throughout, to signify his abjection and servile form. This view is rejected. | p. 5. 6

units.la: Quidam, Filium Hominis numquam dici de Christo per contemptum, volunt, sed constanter significare illustrem Christi perso-nam, sublimi munere Mediatorio ornatam, rejicitur. | p. 9
units.tr: Some hold that the Son of Man is never said of Christ contemptuously, but always signifies the illustrious person of Christ, adorned with the lofty mediatorial office. This is rejected. | p. 9

units.la: Filium hominis, Jesus Dei filius se fere semper appellavit, ut Judæis indigitaret se verum esse Messiam; seu Christum promissum. | p. 10.
units.tr: Jesus, the Son of God, called himself the Son of Man almost always, to show the Jews that he was the true Messiah, or the Christ who had been promised. | p. 10.

units.la: Filii Hominis, nomenclatio, Jesum verum fuisse Hominem, & ex Homine oriundum nos docet. | p. 13.
units.tr: The name Son of Man teaches us that Jesus was truly man and descended from man. | p. 13.

units.la: Filium Hominis Deus gloria & Honore coronavit, omnia pedibus ejus subje-cit; ô eximiam Humanæ naturæ sortem! ô gloriosam homi-nis in Christo conditionem! | p. 14. 17
units.tr: God crowned the Son of Man with glory and honour and put all things under his feet. O the remarkable lot of human nature! O the glorious condition of man in Christ! | p. 14. 17

units.la: Filius Hominis cum sit Christus, quanto in pretio Homo sit habendus, luculenter docemur. | p. 15
units.tr: We are taught plainly how highly man is to be esteemed, since the Son of Man is Christ. | p. 15

units.la: Cum Filius Hominis, Homo scilicet ex homine oriundus, sit Christus, ad studium sanctitatis perpetuò invigilare, argumento omni exceptione majore, docemur. | p 16
units.tr: We are taught, by an argument admitting no exception, that since the Son of Man, that is, man born of man, is Christ, we must constantly watch over our pursuit of holiness. | p 16

units.la: Filius Hominis non foret Christus, ni Idemmet pariter foret Filius Dei. | p. 17
units.tr: The Son of Man would not be Christ unless he were at the same time the Son of God. | p. 17

units.la: Filius Hominis Christus, lamentabilem ruinam, quam mundo intulit Adam, reparavit. | p. 19
units.tr: The Son of Man, Christ, repaired the lamentable ruin that Adam brought upon the world. | p. 19

units.la: Jesus se non quidem Τὸν ἀνθρώπων: sed τὸν Υὸν τῦ ἀνθρώπου, Illum Filium illius Hominis, constanter κατ' ἐξοχὴν, appellat; nec mirum. | p. 22
units.tr: Jesus does not call himself "the man" [τὸν ἄνθρωπον] but "the Son of the Man" [τὸν Υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου], that Son of that Man, constantly and pre-eminently (kat' exochēn); nor is this surprising. | p. 22

units.la: Jesum sua frequenti τῆς Υἱῆς τῦ ἀνθρώπυ nomenclatione, ad pri-mam de semine mulieris propheticam promissionem respe-ctasse, vel hinc evidentissime liquet, quòd nimirum se Filium
units.tr: It is most clearly evident from this, that Jesus, by his frequent use of the name "the Son of Man" [ὁ Υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου], looked back to the first prophetic promise concerning the seed of the woman, since he called himself the Son

units.la: lium Hominis dixerit, ubi ea se præstiturum, vel passurum recipit, quæ aperte continentur in solemni isthac promissione. | p. 42
units.tr: ...when he says "the Son of Man," where he undertakes to do or to suffer those things which are plainly contained in that solemn promise. | p. 42

units.la: Frequentissima Filii Hominis nomenclatio, tota in animos Judæorum ad primam de Messia promissionem dirigendos comparata, erat quam maximè opportuna, ad sistendam fluctuationem Judæorum, de origine ac modo adventus Messiæ. | p. 43
units.tr: The very frequent designation of the Son of Man, wholly suited to direct the minds of the Jews to the first promise concerning the Messiah, was most especially fitting for quieting the Jews' wavering about the origin and manner of the Messiah's coming. | p. 43

units.la: Solemnis Filii Hominis emphatica nomenclatio, quam opportunum erat remedium, ad Judæorum errorem de gemino Messia curandum. | p. 44
units.tr: The solemn emphatic designation of the Son of Man: how opportune a remedy it was for curing the Jews' error about a twofold Messiah. | p. 44

units.la: Allucente primæ promissionis veritate, in cujus intuitum tutò dirigit solemne Filii Hominis elogium, cispellitur vægrandis error, quo etiamnum laborat universa Judæorum natio, de Messia Rege præpotenti terreno, &c. | p. 45
units.tr: With the truth of the first promise shining forth, toward which the solemn title of the Son of Man rightly directs our gaze, the great error is dispelled, the error by which the whole Jewish nation still labours, concerning a mighty earthly Messiah-King, &c. | p. 45

units.la: Primæ promissionis intuitus, inquem duxit Judæorum animos insignis Christi, Filii Hominis appellatio, opportunum erat remedium, ad errorem de gentibus, regno cœlorum Messiæ æternùm exterminandis, curandum. | p. 45.46
units.tr: Looking to the first promise, which led the minds of the Jews, the distinctive appellation of Christ, the Son of Man, was a fitting remedy for curing the error concerning the Gentiles, who were to be eternally excluded from the kingdom of the Messiah in heaven. | p. 45.46

units.la: Frequens Filii Hominis nomenclatura, ad curandos omnes errores, quibus in Jesum Nazarethanum præpediti Judæi impotenter debacchabantur, quam opportunum fuit. | p. 46.47
units.tr: How fitting was the frequent designation of the Son of Man for curing all the errors by which the Jews, hostile to Jesus of Nazareth, raged without restraint. | p. 46.47

units.la: Filii Hominis nomenclatio, præ cæteris Messiæ elogiis, ad momentosa quævis super Messia capita, Judæos docenda, omnium erat maximè opportuna. Præcipue tria Filii Hominis Christi munera, propheticum, nempe, sacerdotale, & regale, haud obscurè ob oculos Judæorum exponebat. | p. 48.49
units.tr: The designation of the Son of Man, above all the other titles of the Messiah, was most especially fitting for teaching the Jews every weighty point concerning the Messiah. Above all, it set before the eyes of the Jews the three offices of Christ the Son of Man: the prophetic, the priestly, namely, and the regal. | p. 48.49

units.la: Cur Scriptura Prophetarum & Apostolorum ministerio multa memoret edita miracula, quæ & Christus edidit, hæc verò tria nominatim, nempe cæcos illuminare, surdorum aures patefacere, mutorumque linguas solvere, uni Christo propria adixerit? p. 183

units.la: MItto ad te, vir optime, præstantissimi Ecclesiæ Gallicanæ Theologi N. . . . Epistolam, ut eam in publicum edi cures. Illa, ut tu ipse judicabis, plurimas easque difficiles Criticæ Sacræ quæstiones accuratè explicat. Autor quoque tibi sim ut ejusdem Theologi CASTIGATIONES, quæ ante paucos menses in Anglia editæ sunt ad calcem DISQUISITIONUM CRITICARUM, huic Epistolæ præmittas, quæ nondum lucem aspexit. Et ut nova tua illius Opusculi editio sit accuratior, mitto ad te exemplar manu exaratum, quod edito videtur castigatius. Est etiam operæ pretium ut his adjungas ea Disquisitionum Criticarum Capita, in quibus Isaaci Vossii assertiones de Codice Ebraico Judæorum, de Septuaginta Interpretibus & Hexaplis Origenis refelluntur: nam ista ad præsens argumentum pertinent. Hæc Opuscula, vir optime, fidei tuæ committo, qui sciam te sacrarum Literarum amantissimum. Vale.
units.tr: I send you, excellent sir, a letter from the most distinguished theologian of the French Church, N. . . . , and ask you to see that it is published. As you yourself will judge, it explains with great care many difficult questions of sacred criticism. I also ask you to prefix to it the same theologian's CASTIGATIONES, which were published in England a few months ago at the end of the DISQUISITIONES CRITICAE, to this letter, which has not yet seen the light. So that your new edition of that little work may be more accurate, I send you a copy written out by hand, which seems more correctly done than the printed one. It is also worth your while to add those chapters of the Critical Disquisitions in which Isaac Vossius's assertions about the Hebrew codex of the Jews, the Seventy interpreters and Origen's Hexapla are refuted, since those points bear on the present subject. I entrust these little works to your good faith, knowing you to be a great lover of the sacred Letters. Farewell.

units.la: CASTIGATIONES ad Opusculum ISAACI VOSSII de Sibyllinis Oraculis & Responsionem ad Objectiones nuperæ CRITICÆ SACRÆ.
units.tr: CASTIGATIONES on Isaac Vossius's little work on the Sibylline Oracles, and a Reply to the Objections of the recent CRITICA SACRA.

units.la: AUctor Criticæ Sacræ in Vetus Testamentum Simonius in Isaaco Vossio, quem nimio Græcæ versionis affectu abreptum existimabat, moderationem requisierat. Sed vir doctus, qui Christum in Apocalypsi tepidos evomere novit, nihilque Deum amare quod medium sit, animo longè obstinatiori accessit ad scribendum opusculum de Sibyllinis Oraculis, in quo ad id unum respexisse videtur, ut elevatis pro suo more Judæorum codicibus, Græcos Interpretes in majus extolleret. Ita etiam respondet Simonio, ut eum potiùs animo à Rabbinis præoccupato ad scribendum se accinxisse scribat, exemplo Hieronymi, qui primus Christianorum Rabbinicam condidit versionem, & alios ad idem audendum signifer præcessit. Profitetur Vossius se non Rabbinos, sed Christum sequi Magistrum, & in ea quam Christus ipse approbavit versione acquiescere; Simonioque auctor est ut cessset novam sacrarum literarum moliri versionem, quòd purior magisque genuina introduci nequeat Scriptura quàm illa quæ à Christo & Apostolis nobis tradita est. Placet quidem in hoc Vossius quod Græcis Interpretibus plurimum tribuat; plus etiam placiturus, si non eos ab omni prorsus errore immunes affirmaret, atque ab illis ne quidem in minutioribus recedendum esse, utpote qui Prophetæ,non Interpretes, ipsi videantur. Laudo præterea eximii illius viri diligentiam in asserenda à maledicentissimorum hominum calumniis LXX. Seniorum tralatione, & in expurgandis eorum codicibus. Verùm ubi de rebus Judæorum eorumque libris agitur, summam præ se fert in his vir doctus inscitiam, falsaque passim pro veris conatur obtrudere. Totum istud negotium exemplis aliquot fiet illustrius. Quare nonnulla ex clarissimi illius viri opusculo de Sibyllinis Oraculis & Responsione ad Objectiones Criticæ Sacræ
units.tr: The author of the Critica Sacra on the Old Testament, Simon, had asked Isaac Vossius to show moderation, since he thought Vossius was carried away by an excessive attachment to the Greek version. But this learned man, who knows that Christ vomits the lukewarm out of the Apocalypse, and that God loves nothing that is halfway, approached the writing of his little work on the Sibylline Oracles with a much more stubborn spirit. In it he seems to have aimed at one thing only: to disparage the Jewish codices, as is his custom, and to exalt the Greek interpreters above all. He answers Simon in such a way as to write that Simon had set about writing with a mind already preoccupied by the rabbis, after the example of Jerome, who was the first of the Christians to compose a rabbinical version, and went before others as their standard-bearer in daring the same thing. Vossius declares that he follows not the rabbis but Christ as his Master, and that he rests content with that version which Christ himself approved; and he advises Simon to cease attempting a new version of the sacred letters, since no purer and more genuine Scripture can be introduced than that which Christ and the Apostles have handed down to us. I am indeed pleased with Vossius in this, that he attributes very much to the Greek interpreters. I would be even more pleased if he did not declare them altogether free from every error, and if he did not hold that one must not depart from them even in the smaller matters, since they seem to be prophets themselves rather than mere interpreters. I also praise that distinguished man's diligence in defending the translation of the Seventy Elders against the calumnies of the most abusive men, and in purging their codices. But where he treats of the affairs of the Jews and their books, the learned man displays great ignorance and everywhere tries to foist falsehoods upon us in place of truths. The whole matter will be made clearer by a few examples. Accordingly I shall select some passages from that most illustrious man's little work on the Sibylline Oracles, and from his Reply to the Objections of the Critica Sacra, from which it will be plain that he has pronounced judgments on matters little known to him. I shall therefore begin with the Epistle which he prefixed to the little work on the Sibylline Oracles.

units.la: Voss. in Resp. ad Obj. nup. Critic.
units.tr: Vossius, in Reply to the recent Objections to the Critica.

units.la: Idem Voss. Sacrę seligam, ex quibus manifestum erit illum de rebus parùm sibi compertis decreta tulisse. Sumam itaque exordium ab Epistola quam opusculo de Sibyllinis Oraculis præmisit.
units.tr: The same Vossius. I shall select some passages, from which it will be clear that he pronounced judgments on matters little known to him. I shall therefore begin with the Epistle which he prefixed to his little work on the Sibylline Oracles.

units.la: Primâ fronte in hac Epistola Vossius virum Hebraicè doctum miris modis traducit veluti fatuum, Semi-Rabbinum & insignem nebulonem, qui verba Hieronymi nequissimè interpolata produxerit. Verùm ex hoc potiùs B. Hieronymi loco qui in controversiam vertitur, Semi-Rabbini isti Sibyllistam Vossium tanquam falsificum injus vocabunt, qui doctissimi illius Patris verba à se minimè intellecta perverterit, protuleritque tum editos tum manu exaratos Hieronymi codices perpaucis cognitos. Locus de quo agitur extat his verbis conceptus in Quæstionibus seu Traditionibus Hebraicis in Genesim ejusdem Hieronymi. Hebræi quod sequitur, Et nescivit cùm dormisset cum ea, & cùm surrexisset ab ea, appungunt desuper quasi incredibile & quod rerum natura non capiat, coire quempiam nescientem. Testatur Vossius complura se consuluisse exemplaria MSS. & in omnibus scriptum invenisse apponunt pro appungunt. Verius dixerit in nullis qui probæ notæ fuerint codicibus se invenisse apponunt. Quis enim sensus ex his verbis formari posset, si pro appungunt repositum fuerit apponunt? Unde autem codices illos sumpserit non refert.
units.tr: At the very outset of this Epistle, Vossius treats the man who knows Hebrew with extraordinary scorn, calling him a fool, a half-rabbi and a notorious scoundrel, who has brought forth the words of Jerome most wickedly corrupted. But from this passage of blessed Jerome, which is now in dispute, these half-rabbis will rather call Vossius, the Sibyl-man, a forger, who has perverted the words of that most learned Father, which he did not understand at all, and who has produced copies of Jerome, both printed and handwritten, known to very few. The passage in question stands in Jerome's Hebrew Questions or Traditions on Genesis, in these words: The Hebrews note above what follows, "And he did not know when he had lain with her, and when he had risen from her," as incredible and contrary to the nature of things, that someone should lie with a woman without knowing it. Vossius testifies that he consulted many manuscript copies and found in all of them apponunt ("they add") in place of appungunt ("they mark"). One might more truly say that he found apponunt in no manuscripts of good standing. For what sense could be made of these words if apponunt were put in place of appungunt? But where he obtained those codices does not matter.

units.la: Sed ut veniamus ad rem, nihil causæ fuit cur Vossius verba contextûs Hebraici perverteret, veritus scilicet ne ex ista dictione appungunt punctorum antiquitas inde jam à temporibus Hieronymi defenderetur. Fatentur enim saniores Critici, ejusmodi puncta Hieronymi ætate longè recentiora esse, qui tamen haud inviti agnoscunt istud punctorum genus quorum hoc loco meminit Hieronymus, quæque supra dictiones aliquot Hebraici contextûs apponuntur, eâdem ferme ratione quâ Samaritæ & Syri lineolas quasdam transversas super quædam vocabula appingunt, quæ haud dubiè à Grammaticis seu Criticis inventæ sunt. Judæos tum antiquos tum recentiores habet sibi consentientes hac in parte Hieronymus: de his mentio fit in Talmude in Medraschim, seu Commentariis Judæorum Allegoricis in Scripturam, & in Masora. Ea quoque repræsentant hodierna Bibliorum exemplaria non secus atque Hieronymi ætate, & in plerisque ad dictionem בקומּרּ de qua in præsentia disputatur, ad oram codicum hæc additur notatio punctum super literam Vau. In Bibliis Venetis editis in minori forma à Petro Bragadino, Genesis Capite 37. ubi simile punctum occurrit ad dictionem את extat in margine hæc nota, חד מן טו׳ נקודות בתורה unum ex punctis 15. quæ sunt in Lege. Rationes ejusmodi punctorum quales redduntur à Judeis, quorum anima est ineptiendi pruritus, silentio prætermitto, quia ineptę sunt. Satis est annotasse Judeos ejusmodi puncta ex paterna traditione in exemplaribus suis dudum retinere.
units.tr: But to come to the point: there was no reason why Vossius should pervert the words of the Hebrew text, fearing, of course, that the antiquity of the vowel points would thereby be defended from the time of Jerome onward, by this very word appungunt. For the saner critics admit that points of this kind are far more recent than Jerome's age; yet they readily acknowledge that the kind of point Jerome mentions in this place, which are placed above certain words of the Hebrew text, are made in much the same way as the Samaritans and Syrians place little transverse strokes above certain words, and these were undoubtedly invented by grammarians or critics. In this matter Jerome finds the Jews, both ancient and more recent, in agreement with one another. Mention of them is made in the Talmud, in the Midrashim (that is, the allegorical commentaries of the Jews on Scripture), and in the Masora. Today's copies of the Bible also present them, no less than in Jerome's time; and in most of them, at the word bequmo [בקומּרּ], which is under discussion at present, this note is added in the margin of the codices: a point above the letter Vav. In the Venetian Bible printed in small format by Pietro Bragadin, at Genesis chapter 37, where a similar point occurs at the word et [את], this note stands in the margin: one of the 15 points that are in the Law [חד מן טו׳ נקודות בתורה]. The reasons for such points which the Jews give, whose very soul is a itch for trifling, I pass over in silence, because they are trifling. It is enough to have noted that the Jews have long retained such points in their copies by ancestral tradition.

units.la: Deplorat deinde in eadem Epistola Vossius miserum hoc tempore in Germania Academiarum statum, ubi tam impune grassatur Rabbinismus, nullaque excolitur Theologia nisi Rabbinica. Fieri non posse existimat vir doctus, ut humaniores literæ tractentur ubi Rabbinismus regnat, strigesque Rabbinicæ latè dominantur. Nec in his secum dissidentem me habebit Vossius. Auctor quoque fuerim ut nugivendi isti Theologastri, qui spretis literis Græcis & Latinis, nihil præter Rabbinorum commenta admittunt, ex Theologorum albo expungantur. Verùm ut his etiam adscribantur viri eximiè docti, qui exemplo Origenis, Hieronymi, Chrysostomi, Theodoreti, aliorumque Patrum frequentant Judæorum limina, vix ferre possum. Nugas quidem easque maximas plerique Judeorum libri præferunt: at non pauci sunt ex eorum classe Magistri qui Sacras Literas mirè illustrârunt. Rem ita esse aperte docent unius Hieronymi in Prophetas Commentarii, qui doctissimos ætatis suæ Judæos consulere non erubuit. Delicatulo Vossio Hieronymus vilis est & Theologorum Semi-Rabbinorum princeps. Semi-Rabbinus tamen iste, etsi suos quoque nævos habeat, reliquos Ecclesiæ Patres in exponendis Sacræ Scripturę libris longo intervallo superavit. Optârim quoque ut in Semi-Rabbinorum castra prius transeat Vossius, quàm res illorum tractet: vix enim à risu temperant Semi-Rabbini isti, cùm legunt in Epistola quam præmisit libello de Sibyllinis Oraculis, ne sex quidem effluxisse secula ex quo primùm usurpari cœperunt puncta ista vocalia, quibus hodierni Judæorum codices onerantur: hos tria vel quatuor secula acerrimè inter se conflixisse, dum alii sic, alii aliter inducendas esse vocales censerent; & ne nunc quidem controversiam hanc fore sopitam, nisi Daniel Bombergus litem istam diremisset conductis aliquot Judæorum centuriis; atque ita demum istas vocales primùm Venetiis ex officina Bombergi in lucem prodiisse. Habuit profectò vir doctus Bibliothecam Rabbinorum libris bene instructam, ex qua hausit commenta
units.tr: Next, in the same Epistle, Vossius laments the wretched state of the Academies in Germany at this time, where Rabbinism rages with such impunity, and where no theology is cultivated except rabbinical theology. The learned man thinks it impossible that the more humane letters should be studied where Rabbinism reigns and rabbinical witches hold wide sway. Nor will Vossius find me disagreeing with him in these things. I would also advise that these trifling peddlers of theology, who, scorning Greek and Latin letters, admit nothing but the fictions of the rabbis, be struck from the roll of theologians. But that men of very great learning, who, after the example of Origen, Jerome, Chrysostom, Theodoret and other Fathers, frequent the thresholds of the Jews, should be counted among them, I can scarcely bear. Most Jewish books indeed present trifles, and very great ones; but not a few masters of that class have greatly illuminated the Sacred Letters. That this is so is plainly shown by the commentary of Jerome alone on the Prophets, who did not blush to consult the most learned Jews of his age. To the dainty Vossius, Jerome is worthless, and the prince of half-rabbinical theologians. Yet this half-rabbi, though he too has his blemishes, surpassed the rest of the Fathers by a long interval in expounding the books of Sacred Scripture. I would also wish that Vossius would pass over into the camp of the half-rabbis before he treats of their affairs. For these half-rabbis can scarcely restrain their laughter when they read, in the Epistle he prefixed to his little work on the Sibylline Oracles, that not even six centuries have elapsed since these vocal points, with which the present codices of the Jews are burdened, first began to be used; that for three or four centuries they fought most bitterly among themselves, some holding that the vowels should be introduced in one way, others in another; and that this controversy would not even now have been put to rest, had not Daniel Bomberg settled the dispute by hiring a number of Jewish centuries; and that only then did these vowels first come forth into the light at Venice from Bomberg's press. Certainly the learned man had a library of rabbinical books well stocked, from which he drew these fictions

units.la: unum ex punctis 15. quæ sunt in Lege.
units.tr: one of the 15 points that are in the Law.

units.la: commenta ista plusquam Rabbinica. Primò siquidem nôrunt qui sunt in Judæorum libris volutati, jam ante Bombergianas Bibliorum Hebraicorum editiones in aliis Italiæ partibus, maximè Brixiæ, edita fuisse Biblia Hebraica punctis vocalibus adornata. Reperiuntur etiam Bibliorum exemplaria inde à CCCC. aut D. annis manu exarata quæ eadem puncta præferant, laudanturque à Rabbinis antiquoribus Biblia Hebraica quæ puncta ista exhibeant. Similiter non à DC. solùm, sed à DCCCC. & ampliùs annis usurpata sunt ista puncta. Rabbi Saadias Gaon librum scripsit de re Grammatica sub annum DCCCC. in quo de punctis vocalibus, quæ longè ante illius ætatem apud Judæos in usu fuerant, multis disputat. Præterea ficta sunt ea omnia quæ de gravissimo inter Judæos conflictu affert Vossius, quonam scilicet modo apponendæ essent vocales contextui Hebraico. Ex eadem quoque officina prodiit quod habet vir doctus de editionibus Bombergianis, quæ ex complurium Judæorum sententia mendis scatent. Spernunt quidem Judæi primam Bibliorum Hebraicorum Bombergianam editionem cui præfuit Felix Pratensis, quia scilicet notationes Masorethicæ ad oram illius exemplaris summâ rei illius inscitiâ adjectæ sunt. Verùm secundam & tertiam Bibliorum Bombergianorum editiones laudant & venerantur. De addendis quidem notis Masorethicis ad Bombergianas editiones maximæ suborte sunt difficultates, quia pauci sunt etiam inter Judæorum Magistros qui artem Masorethicam bene calleant; quas tamen improbo ac duro labore superavit R. Jacob Ben Hajim, primus Masoræ instaurator. Utrùm autem in alendis Judæorum, quos conduxerat Bombergus, centuriis patrimonium dilapidaverit, uti contendit Vossius, non anquiro, neque de hoc nunc agitur negotio. Complura iis quæ jam à me allata sunt facile adjici possent, forsan nec ab instituto aliena; sed vereor ne vir doctus me tanquam Semi-Rabbinum ac Judæorum fautorem trahat in judicium. Quare ad illius de Oraculis Sibyllinis opusculi examen transeo, ubi eruditiùs de Judeis eorumque libris disputat.
units.tr: these fictions more than rabbinical. For, in the first place, those who are versed in Jewish books know that before the Bomberg editions of the Hebrew Bible there had been printed in other parts of Italy, especially at Brescia, Hebrew Bibles furnished with vowel points. Copies of the Bible written by hand from four or five hundred years ago are also found which display these same points, and the older rabbis praise Hebrew Bibles which exhibit these points. Likewise these points were in use not only for six hundred years, but for more than nine hundred. Rabbi Saadia Gaon wrote a book on grammar about the year 900, in which he discusses at length the vowel points, which had been in use among the Jews long before his time. Moreover, everything that Vossius brings forward about the most serious conflict among the Jews, namely in what manner the vowels were to be added to the Hebrew text, is invented. From the same workshop also came what the learned man says about the Bomberg editions, which, in the opinion of many Jews, are full of errors. Indeed the Jews despise the first Bomberg edition of the Hebrew Bible, over which Felix Pratensis presided, because the Masoretic notes were added in the margin of that copy with the greatest ignorance of the subject. But they praise and venerate the second and third Bomberg editions of the Bible. Certainly great difficulties arose about adding the Masoretic notes to the Bomberg editions, because there are few even among the Jewish masters who have a good grasp of the Masoretic art; yet R. Jacob ben Hayyim, the first restorer of the Masora, overcame these with unremitting and hard labour. Whether Bomberg squandered his patrimony in maintaining the Jewish centuries he had hired, as Vossius maintains, I do not inquire, nor is that matter now under discussion. Many more things could easily be added to those I have already brought forward, perhaps not foreign to my purpose; but I fear that the learned man may drag me before the court as a half-rabbi and a friend of the Jews. Therefore I pass on to the examination of his little work on the Sibylline Oracles, where he disputes more learnedly about the Jews and their books.

units.la: Nonnulla affert statim ab initio operis vir inexhaustæ eruditionis de Sibyllinis Oraculis, quibus in Hispania præsertim abusi fuerint Judæi adversus Christianos. Hæc quæ minùs à commento quàm à vera historia videntur abesse, præmonet inserenda paginæ 19. vel 26. ubi tractat illud argumentum. Verùm cùm jam demonstratum fuerit Chronologiam ex Judæorum codicibus petitam minùs favere vere Judæis ipsis quàm quæ ex Græcis Interpretibus sumitur, non est cur refellendis hac in re doctissimi Vossii inventis amplius detineamur. Jam quidem vir perspicacissimus animadverterat Judæos sub Aquilæ tempora Hebræos codices dedita opera corrupisse, & bis mille annorum expunxisse tempus, ut tempus Messiæ necdum advenisse obtinerent: at hoc loco, longè oculatior, putat depravationis istius spatium utplurimum viginti duobus posse determinari annis, idque ex verbis Ignatii in Epistola ad Philadelphienses rectè confici. Scribit sanctissimus ille Martyr, referente Vossio, se audiisse nonnullos dicentes, si ea quæ in Euangeliis continentur non etiam in Archivis, seu antiquis inveniantur monumentis, nolle se iis credere. Cùm ipse respònderit, inquit Vossius, illi verò negaverint, manifestum Judæos jam tùm aut depravâsse sua exemplaria, aut recessisse à sensu quem Septuaginta tradidere Interpretes. Sed quâ ratione Ignatii responsum, qui asserit Christum sibi esse pro Archivis, ad suam de corruptis circa illud tempus à Judæis codicibus Hebraicis posset trahere sententiam vir doctus, fateor me non assequi. Neque etiam in germanis Epistolarum Ignatii exemplaribus, quæ in lucem ipse edidit Vossius, reperiuntur verba illa, Christo velut summo Sacerdoti credendum potius quam aliis Sacerdotibus; quæ tamen quasi ad Ignatii responsum pertineant, profert vir doctus. Juvat hic afferre ipsissima Ignatii verba. Ἠκουσα γὰρ τινῶν λεγόντων, ὅτι ἐὰν μὴ ἐν τοῖς ἀρχείοις εὕρω ἐν εὐαγγελίῳ, οὐ πιστεύω. Τοῖς δὲ τοιούτοις ἐγὼ λέγω ὅτι ἐμοὶ ἀρχεῖα ἐστιν Ἰησοῦς ὁ Χριστός. Audivi enim quosdam dicentes, Nisi invenero in Archivis Euangelium, non credo. His autem respondeo, mihi loco Archivorum esse Jesum Christum. Ibi de Veteri Testamento non agitur cum Novo comparato, ut existimavit Vossius, sed de Hæreticis qui ab Ecclesiæ infantia orti fidem quam præmonstrabat Euangeliorum codex respuebant: unde factum fuit ut prisci Ecclesiæ Patres, Tertullianus, Irenæus & alii ejusmodi Hæreticos non tam ex sacris codicibus refellerent, quàm ex certa traditione, seu ex Christi doctrina per Apostolos eorumque successores viros Apostolicos in Ecclesiis diversarum gentium propagatâ. Quo sensu asserit Ignatius Christum, seu illius doctrinam, sibi Archivorum antiquorumque monumentorum loco esse. Is est, ni fallor, Ignatii verborum intellectus, qui unitatem doctrinæ in Christo commendat, cujus spiritus quibuslibet Archivis debet anteferri.
units.tr: At the very start of his work on the Sibylline Oracles, the man of inexhaustible learning sets out some points about how the Jews, especially in Spain, misused those oracles against Christians. These seem to belong more to fiction than to real history. He says he will insert them on page 19 or 26, where he treats that subject. But since it has already been shown that the chronology taken from the Jewish codices favours the Jews themselves less than the chronology taken from the Greek Interpreters does, there is no reason to linger further over refuting the learned Vossius's discoveries on this point. The most perceptive man had already noted that the Jews had deliberately corrupted the Hebrew codices around the time of Aquila, and had erased two thousand years of time so that they could maintain that the time of the Messiah had not yet come. But here, far sharper-sighted, he thinks the span of this corruption can mostly be fixed at twenty-two years, and that this follows rightly from the words of Ignatius in the Epistle to the Philadelphians. That most holy martyr, Vossius reports, wrote that he had heard some people say that if they did not find the things contained in the Gospels in the archives, or ancient records, they would not believe them. When he himself replied, Vossius says, and they denied it, it is clear that the Jews had already by then either corrupted their copies or departed from the sense the Septuagint Interpreters had handed down. But I confess I do not see how the learned man can draw from Ignatius's answer, which asserts that Jesus Christ is his archive, a view that the Hebrew codices were corrupted by the Jews around that time. Nor do those words appear in the genuine copies of Ignatius's Epistles, which Vossius himself published, namely that one should believe Christ, as the highest Priest, rather than other priests; yet the learned man presents them as if they belonged to Ignatius's reply. It helps to quote Ignatius's exact words here. Ἠκουσα γὰρ τινῶν λεγόντων, ὅτι ἐὰν μὴ ἐν τοῖς ἀρχείοις εὕρω ἐν εὐαγγελίῳ, οὐ πιστεύω. Τοῖς δὲ τοιούτοις ἐγὼ λέγω ὅτι ἐμοὶ ἀρχεῖα ἐστιν Ἰησοῦς ὁ Χριστός. For I heard some saying, Unless I find the Gospel in the archives, I do not believe. To such people I answer that for me the archives are Jesus Christ. Ignatius is not there comparing the Old Testament with the New, as Vossius thought, but speaking of heretics who, arising from the infancy of the Church, rejected the faith which the book of the Gospels set before them. Hence it came about that the early Fathers of the Church, Tertullian, Irenaeus and others, refuted such heretics not so much from the sacred books as from the certain tradition, that is, from the doctrine of Christ spread through the Apostles and their successors, the apostolic men, in the churches of various nations. In this sense Ignatius says that Christ, or his doctrine, is for him in place of the archives and ancient records. This, unless I am mistaken, is the meaning of Ignatius's words, which commends the unity of doctrine in Christ, whose Spirit must be preferred to any archives whatever.

units.la: B. Ignat.
units.tr: B. Ignat.

units.la: Multa etiam hoc loco affert Vossius de vocis Æra origine, sentitque cum iis qui Æram & Hegiram Arabum idem vocabulum arbitrantur; nec id videtur extra probabilitatem: sed quod mox subjungit de nomine Hegiræ Arabicæ, quasi ductum fuerit ex Hebraeo הגר hagger, proselytus, non est ita probabile. Putat vir doctus complures Judæos è secta Herodianorum relicto suo Messia Herode, qui semper ab ipsis vocatus fuerit הגר peregrinus, ad Mahometum transiisse, & ab iis quoque dictum hagger. Cùm Judæi, inquit Vossius, Messiam peregrinum seu proselytum fore crederent. Ista profecto à commentis Rabbinicis minùs recedunt. Deinde ex quo Sibyllarum oraculo didicit vir doctus Judæorum Messiam ex ipsorummet Judæorum sententia proselytum fore & peregrinum: hanc enim assertionem Prophetarum vaticiniis & Euangelicæ historiæ contrariam esse nemo nescit. Unum quidem præ cæteris Messiam Judei exspectant, de quo in præsentia loquitur Vossius: at iste ex Judæorum omnium consensu futurus est natione & ritibus Judæus. Verùm alios præterea Messias exspectant, eoque nomine insigniunt Reges quoslibet qui erga illos bene affecti sunt. Quâ ratione Cyrus Judæorum Messias appellatus est. Sic quoque Herodes & Mahometus Messiæ nomen à Judæis reportare potuerunt. Parati sunt etiam hâc nostrâ ætate Regem illum aut Principem quemcunque qui res illorum & ritus patrios tueri voluerit, tanquam Messiam suum salutare. Verùm ista ad nomen Hegiræ, quod constat Arabicum esse, non Hebraicum, minimè pertinent. Magis ad veritatem accedit quod post nonnulla interjecta subjicit vir doctus de genuina vocis ἀπόκρυφος significatione, ita ut ἀπόκρυφος idem sit quod κρύφιος, librique Apocryphi iidem fuerint qui arcani & inaccessi. Sed quis cum Vossio inde conficiat scripta illa Apocrypha, quæ ex ejus sententia olim Veteris Testamenti libris conjuncta fuêre, & à prisci Judæis approbata, digna fuisse quæ cum cæteris libris Propheticis in Scripturarum Canonem referrentur? hodiernum tum Synagogæ tum Ecclesiæ Canonem mutilum & decurtatum esse, qui Enochi, Eliæ aliosque ejusdem naturæ libros non complectatur? Vili veneunt apud Vossium Prophetæ, qui non modò LXX. Interpretes inter Prophetas recenseat, sed & his quoque adscribat celeberrimos impostores, qui ementitis Patriarcharum & Prophetarum, nec non virorum aliquot magnæ apud Gentiles existimationis nominibus, libros Adami, Enochi, Abrahami, Moysis, Esaiæ, Hieremiæ, Hystaspis, Mercurii Trismegisti, Zoroastris, Sibyllarum, Orphei, Phocyllidæ & complurium aliorum libros in lucem protulerunt. Brevi, si superis placet, etiam inter Prophetas Vossius tanto Prophetarum stipatus agmine nova procudet vaticinia, non secus ac famosus ille impostor Guilhelmus Postellus, qui scribit Chaldæos doctrinam etiam revelatam habuisse in sua prima Monarchia, & continuè instar sacræ doctrinæ per decem Sibyllas esse instauratam, ut esset omnino apud spiritum Dei inexcusabilis mundus, Christusque sacrarum & Sibyllinarum doctrinarum Rex ab universo orbe adorandus innotesceret. Hisferè similia de Sibyllinis Oraculis affert Vossius. Oculatior tamen adhuc Postellus Propheticam istam doctrinam asserit ortum habuisse à fœmina principe totius Orientis proximâ sanguine ipsi Noacho. Quis credat Isaacum Vossium, qui nihil non virulenti paslim in operibus suis adversus Judæos eorumque Talmudem evomit, recensuisse etiam inter Prophetas Doctorem Talmudicum? Si res ita sit, miror illum tanto contentionis æstu abreptum fuisse in virum Hebraicè doctum, quòd è Talmude Euangelia exposuerit. Minus mihi peccaturus videtur, inquit Vossius, qui ex Alcorano, quam qui ex Talmude exponat Euangelia. Sed de his satis superque; ad libros Apocryphos unde diverti tempus est ut redeam.
units.tr: Vossius also offers much here on the origin of the word Æra, and agrees with those who think Æram and the Arabic Hegiram are the same word. That seems not to lie beyond probability. But what he adds soon after, about the name of the Arabic Hegira, as if it were derived from the Hebrew הגר hagger, meaning proselyte, is not so probable. The learned man thinks that many Jews of the Herodian sect, having abandoned their Messiah Herod, who had always been called by them הגר peregrinus, passed over to Muhammad, and that they too called him hagger. Since the Jews, Vossius says, believed that the Messiah would be a foreigner or proselyte. Those claims, certainly, depart little from rabbinic fictions. Next, from which oracle of the Sibyls did the learned man learn that the Jewish Messiah, by the Jews' own opinion, would be a proselyte and a foreigner? For that assertion, as everyone knows, is contrary to the prophetic predictions and to the Gospel history. The Jews indeed look for one Messiah above all others, and it is of him that Vossius is speaking at present; but that Messiah, by the agreement of all Jews, is to be by nation and rites a Jew. Yet the Jews also look for other messiahs, and they give that name to any kings who have been well disposed towards them. In this way Cyrus was called the Messiah of the Jews. Thus Herod and Muhammad too could have received the name Messiah from the Jews. Even in our own age they are ready to hail as their saviour whatever king or prince will be willing to protect their affairs and ancestral rites. But these things have nothing to do with the name Hegira, which is known to be Arabic, not Hebrew. Closer to the truth is what the learned man, after some intervening remarks, says about the genuine meaning of the word ἀπόκρυφος, namely that ἀπόκρυφος means the same as κρύφιος, and that apocryphal books are the same as secret and inaccessible ones. But who with Vossius would infer from this that those Apocryphal writings, which in his view were once joined to the books of the Old Testament and approved by the ancient Jews, deserved to be counted among the Scriptures alongside the other prophetic books? That the present canon, both of the synagogue and of the Church, is incomplete and cut short, because it does not include the books of Enoch, Elijah and others of that kind? According to Vossius the Prophets are of little value. He not only counts the Seventy Interpreters among the Prophets, but also ascribes to them the most famous impostors, who, under the false names of Patriarchs and Prophets, and of several men of great reputation among the Gentiles, brought to light books of Adam, Enoch, Abraham, Moses, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Hystaspes, Mercurius Trismegistus, Zoroaster, the Sibyls, Orpheus, Phocylides and many others. In short, if it pleases the gods above, Vossius, surrounded by such a host of Prophets, will soon also forge new prophecies, just as that notorious impostor Guillaume Postel did, who writes that the Chaldeans had also possessed revealed doctrine in their first monarchy, and that this doctrine was continually renewed like sacred teaching through ten Sibyls, so that the world would be wholly inexcusable before the Spirit of God, and so that Christ, king of sacred and Sibylline doctrines, would become known as one to be worshipped by the whole world. Vossius offers things much like these about the Sibylline Oracles. Yet Postel, even more sharp-sighted, asserts that this prophetic doctrine arose from a female ruler of the whole East, closely related by blood to Noah himself. Who would believe that Isaac Vossius, who everywhere in his works pours out venom against the Jews and their Talmud, has also counted a Talmudic teacher among the Prophets? If that is so, I marvel that he was carried away by such a heat of contention as to call a man learned in Hebrew one who expounded the Gospels from the Talmud. He would seem to make fewer mistakes, says Vossius, who explains the Gospels from the Qur'an than he who explains them from the Talmud. But enough and more than enough of these matters. It is time for me to return to the Apocryphal books, from which I digressed.

units.la: Apocryphos appello Scriptores, ubi de rebus Biblicis agitur, illos quos in suum Canonem neque Ecclesia neque Synagoga receperunt. Hinc factum est ut olim Hieronymus Judæorum personam induens, & novissimè Cajetanus, libros complures inter Apocryphos retulerint, antequàm manifesto Ecclesiæ decreto tanquam Divini & Prophetici recepti fuissent. Hoc sensu Hieronymus affirmat Danielem non habere apud Hebræos Susannæ historiam, nec hymnum trium puerorum, nec Beli Draconis fabulas; Quas nos, inquit, quia in toto orbe dispersæ sunt, vero antepositò easque jugulante subjecimus, ne videremur apud imperitos magnam partem voluminis detruncasse. Haud absimiliter alio loco, postquàm Scripturæ libros qui in Judæorum Canone erant protulit, mox addit, Quidquid extra hos est intra Apocrypha ponendum esse; nimirum Sapientiam, quæ vulgò Salomonis inscribitur, & Jesu filii Sirach librum, & Judith, & Tobiam & Pastorem. Africanus etiam simili ratione adductus, Susannæ historiam à Scriptore Græco confictam putavit: alii duos Danieles nieles finxerunt; quorum primus Vaticinii, quod sub ejus nomine legitur, auctor fuerit; alter vero historiae istius Scriptor, quae in antiquis Graeci exemplaris editionibus Prophetiae Danielis praemittebatur: primus siquidem Hieronymus hanc historiam ad calcem ejusdem libri rejecit, quod eam Judaeorum codex, quem Latinum faciebat, non repraesentaret. Sententiam suam de Susannae historia confirmat Hieronymus aliorum Patrum testimoniis. Miror, inquit, quosdam μεμψιμοίρως indignari mihi, quasi ego decurtaverim librum, cum & Origenes & Eusebius & Apollinarius aliique viri Ecclesiastici & Doctores Graeciae has, ut dixi, visiones non haberi apud Hebraeos fateantur, nec se debere respondere Porphyrio pro his quae nullam Scripturae sanctae auctoritatem praebeant. Gregorius Nazianzenus, Melito Sardensis, & auctor Synopseos quae sub nomine Athanasii circumfertur, ulterius progressi librum Estheris inter Apocryphos collocârunt, quòd linguam Hebraicam non callentes, ex eo solum quòd antiquae Estheris historiae nonnulla a Graeco Scriptore assuta fuerint, opus integrum expunxerunt. Accidit, inquit Sixtus Senensis, ut propter has appendicum lacinias hinc & inde quorundam Scriptorum temeritate insertas, liber ille quamvis Hebraicus apud Christianos auctoritatem canonicam non receperit. Nicolaus quoque de Lyra, Cajetanus, & alii nonnulli haec additamenta pro Canonicis non habuere, similibus haud dubie rationibus adducti.
units.tr: I call Apocryphal those writers who deal with biblical matters and whom neither the Church nor the Synagogue has received into its canon. Hence it happened that formerly Jerome, speaking in the person of the Jews, and more recently Cajetan, placed several books among the Apocrypha, before they were received by a clear decree of the Church as divine and prophetic. In this sense Jerome affirms that Daniel does not have among the Hebrews the story of Susanna, nor the hymn of the three boys, nor the tales of Bel and the Dragon. These we have added, he says, because they are scattered through the whole world, placing them after the true text and marking them with an obelus, lest we should seem to have cut away a large part of the book before the unlearned. Somewhat similarly, in another place, after he had set out the books of Scripture that were in the Jewish canon, he immediately adds: Whatever lies outside these must be placed among the Apocrypha; namely the Wisdom which is commonly ascribed to Solomon, the book of Jesus son of Sirach, Judith, Tobit and the Shepherd. Africanus too, moved by a similar reasoning, thought that the story of Susanna had been invented by a Greek writer. Others have made two Daniels: the first, they say, was the author of the prophecy that is read under his name; the second was the writer of that story, which in the older editions of the Greek text was placed before the Prophecy of Daniel. Indeed Jerome was the first to put this story at the end of the same book, because the Jewish codex which he was turning into Latin did not contain it. Jerome confirms his view about the story of Susanna by the testimony of other Fathers. I marvel, he says, that some [μεμψιμοίρως] are indignant with me, as if I had cut down the book, since Origen, Eusebius, Apollinarius and other ecclesiastical men and teachers of Greece themselves admit, as I have said, that these visions are not found among the Hebrews, and that they need not answer Porphyry for things which give no authority to Holy Scripture. Gregory Nazianzen, Melito of Sardis, and the author of the Synopsis that circulates under the name of Athanasius, going further, placed the book of Esther among the Apocrypha, because, not knowing the Hebrew language, and only because some parts of the old history of Esther had been added by a Greek writer, they struck out the whole work. It happens, says Sixtus of Siena, that because of these patches of additions inserted here and there by the rashness of certain writers, that book, although Hebrew, has not been received by Christians as canonical. Nicholas of Lyra, Cajetan and some others likewise did not hold these additions to be canonical, undoubtedly moved by similar reasons.

units.la: Haec paulo fusius quidem allata sunt, ut manifestum esset omnibus quinam libri ex vetustiorum Ecclesiae Patrum sententia inter Apocryphos repositi fuerint. Apocryphorum siquidem vocabulo abusus Vossius, libros suppositititios & adulterinos veteribus Apocryphis adscribit, sicque fucum facit incautis & simplicioribus. Quod enim contendit vir doctus, libros Sibyllinos aliosque quos appellat fatidicos olim cum libris Veteris Testamenti conjunctos fuisse, lectos in primitiva Ecclesia, & a Paulo aliisque Apostolis commendatos, otiosi hominis est figmentum. Non alii enim in Ecclesia primitiva lecti sunt libri Apocryphi caeterisque Veteris Instrumenti libris adjecti in Graecis Bibliorum exemplaribus, quàm illi qui a Patribus recensentur; etsi interdum Patres nonnulli, ut Judaeos, Gentilesque presssius urgerent, vocaverint etiam in auxilium libros Sibyllarum aliosque ejusdem rationis, quos tamen nemo paulo cordatior inter Apocryphos, de quibus hoc loco agitur, numerabit. Dolet Vossius libros Sibyllinos & alios fatidicos, postquàm publico blico edicto prohibiti sunt, factos fuisse Apocryphos, interdictos, à nemine legendos, cùm antea palàm & religiosè non secus ac reliqui Veteris Instrumenti libri à Judæis legerentur: tum factum fuisse ut arctiori compendio quàm antea sæpe libri sacri constringerentur, & ex eo tempore Apocryphi vocabulum in sequiorem sensum acceptum fuisse, quasi idem esset liber Apocryphus qui spurius & dubiæ fidei. Interim Scriptores non laudat à quibus lepida ista commenta hauserit, quæ tamen parùm absunt à fabulis Judaicis. Lubens à viro docto quæsierim, quod olim festivus ille Cardinalis Hippolytus Atestensis ab Ariosto; Dove ha trovato tante coglioneric? Illi tamen assentior in eo quod scribit de Apocryphis, si per libros Apocryphos non alios intelligat quàm illos qui à Judæis ad Christianos cum reliquis Veteris Testamenti libris transierunt, quippe partem maximam in Ecclesia Romana, in primis post Synodi Tridentinæ decretum, tanquam Canonici leguntur. Fieri potuit ut libri isti qui inter Apocryphos olim recensiti fuere, quòd illos Canon Judaicus minimè approbaret, Prophetas etiam habuerint auctores. Nec contra ista pugnat Josephi auctoritas, qui affirmat à temporibus Artaxerxis certam non fuisse apud Judæos Prophetarum successionem, adeoque qui ab eo tempore conscripti sunt libris Propheticis non debere adnumerari. Nam Prophetarum munus tunc omnino Judæis sublatum fuisse verisimile non est: quamdiu enim stetit Judæorum Respublica, tamdiu fuêre apud eos Scribæ publici qui res ætatis suæ chartis committerent, iique Prophetæ appellabantur, quia Spiritûs Sancti numine afflati erant, quanquam non fatidici. Imò ne quidem necesse est illos qui tunc temporis res Judaicas scriptis complectebantur Prophetas fuisse, quia Synedrii magni assessores, quos à Deo inspiratos novimus, illorum opera recognoscebant. Verùm cùm publica Senatûs Judaici auctoritas ejusmodi libros in Canonem librorum sacrorum nunquam retulerit, mirum videri non debet Patres plerosque non recepisse illos tanquam Divinos, sed ut Apocryphos & dubiæ fidei, comparatè scilicet ad alios sacri codicis libros qui certæ erant fidei. Idem enim illis non fuit liber dubiæ fidei qui spurius atque adulterinus, ut existimare videtur Vossius; sed certa ab incertis hoc titulo signare voluerunt: aliàs libri isti prisicis Patrum nostrorum seculis in Ecclesia lecti non fuissent, si quid spurii & adulterini in illis deprehensum fuisset. Minoris tantùm illi erant momenti quàm libri bri sacri, eosque idcirco Ecclesiasticos, potius quam Divinos, Patres appellabant. Legi quidem, inquit auctor Expositionis Symboli quod tribuitur Ruffino, in Ecclesiis voluerunt, non tamen proferri ad auctoritatem ex his fidei confirmandam. Qua etiam ratione eosdem libros in suis coetibus legit Ecclesia Anglicana. Non puto tamen quemquam hactenus cogitasse, si Vossium excipiamus, de introducenda in Ecclesiam librorum Sibyllinorum lectione.
units.tr: These matters have been set out here at some length, so that it may be plain to everyone which books were placed among the Apocrypha according to the judgment of the older Fathers of the Church. Vossius, however, abuses the word "Apocrypha": he ascribes to the old Apocrypha books that are spurious and counterfeit, and so deceives the unwary and the simpler sort. As for his learned claim that the Sibylline books and the others he calls prophetic were once joined to the books of the Old Testament, read in the primitive Church, and commended by Paul and the other Apostles, it is the invention of an idle man. The books read in the primitive Church, and added to the other books of the Old Testament in Greek copies of the Bible, were no others than those the Fathers list. Some Fathers, it is true, when they pressed Jews and Gentiles harder, did sometimes call in the Sibyls and other books of that kind as support; yet no reasonably sensible person would count these among the Apocrypha with which we are dealing here. Vossius laments that the Sibylline and other prophetic books, after a public edict forbade them, became Apocryphal, forbidden, and read by no one, although before this they were openly and devoutly read by the Jews just as the other books of the Old Testament were; and that from that time the sacred books were often confined within a narrower compass than before, and from that time the word Apocryphi came to be taken in a looser sense, as if an Apocryphal book were the same as a spurious book of doubtful faith. Meanwhile he does not name the writers from whom he drew these charming fictions, which in fact differ little from Jewish fables. I would gladly ask the learned man what the witty Cardinal Hippolytus of Este said to Ariosto: Where did you find so many fooleries? Yet I agree with him in what he writes about the Apocrypha, if by Apocryphal books he means none other than those which passed from the Jews to the Christians together with the other books of the Old Testament, since most of them are read as canonical in the Roman Church, above all after the decree of the Council of Trent. It may be that those books which were once listed among the Apocrypha, because the Jewish canon did not approve them, also had prophets as their authors. Nor does the testimony of Josephus contradict this, when he affirms that from the time of Artaxerxes there was no certain succession of prophets among the Jews, and therefore that books written since that time should not be counted among the prophetic books. For it is not likely that the office of prophet was then entirely taken away from the Jews: as long as the Jewish commonwealth stood, there were public scribes among them who committed the affairs of their own age to writing, and these were called prophets, because they were inspired by the power of the Holy Spirit, though they were not foretellers of the future. Indeed, it is not even necessary that those who then set down Jewish affairs in writing were prophets, since the assessors of the Great Sanhedrin, whom we know to have been inspired by God, reviewed their work. But since the public authority of the Jewish Senate never placed books of this kind in the canon of the sacred books, it ought not to seem strange that most of the Fathers did not receive them as divine, but as Apocryphal and of doubtful faith, when compared with the other books of the sacred codex, which were of certain faith. For the book of doubtful faith was not the same as the spurious and counterfeit book, as Vossius seems to think; rather, they wished by this title to distinguish the certain from the uncertain. Otherwise these books would not have been read in the Church in the earliest ages of our Fathers, if anything spurious and counterfeit had been detected in them. They were of lesser weight than the sacred books, and for this reason the Fathers called them ecclesiastical rather than divine. They were willing, says the author of the Exposition of the Creed attributed to Rufinus, that they be read in the churches, but not that they be brought forward to confirm faith by their authority. It is on this same principle that the Church of England reads these books in her assemblies. Yet I do not think anyone, Vossius excepted, has so far thought of introducing the reading of the Sibylline books into the Church.

units.la: Novi quidem Patrum nonnullos librum qui inscribitur Pastor, multum veneratos fuisse; Tertullianum quoque Enochi libellum quasi Divinum obtrudere conatum; imo contendisse Judaeos a contextu Scripturarum libros complures semovisse, qui Religionem Christianam illustrabant. Cui etiam sententiae adhaerere visus est Origenes, qui in epistola quam scripsit Africano de historia Susannae, asserit Judaeos multa a suis libris sustulisse, ne legerentur illa a plebeiis hominibus. Verum ista & alia id genus, quae perpaucorum sunt, quaeque ab iis proferuntur ut suae potius hypothesi quam veritati serviant, communi Patrum sententiae apponi nequeunt. Nam ipse Tertullianus commune illud Ecclesiae placitum verbis suis hoc loco videtur confirmare. Scis, inquit, Scripturam Enoch non recipi a quibusdam, quia nec in armarium Judaeorum admittitur. Itaque temporibus illis judicabatur istud Apocryphum, seu dubiae fidei, quod Judaei in suum Canonem non admiserunt. Aliud etiam sentit aliis locis Origenes, quam quod scripsit Africano. Verum hoc loco Susannae historiam & alia additamenta quae praefert Graeca LXX. Interpretum editio, non alia ratione tueri potuit, quam recurrens ad libros Apocryphos, ac supponens Judaeos in exscribendis suis codicibus non paucos a plebeiorum cognitione removisse quae in istis Apocryphis expressa fuerint. Didicerat forsan Origenes a Judaeis, quorum frequenti commercio utebatur, Esdram ejusque socios non omnes qui tunc extabant libros in publicum edidisse, & hinc confici posse existimabat, Graecos Interpretes ea sumpsisse quae in Hebraeis codicibus non leguntur. Sed haec sententia a communi priscorum Judaeorum consensu recedit, qui perfectam & in omnibus accuratam contextus Hebraei concordiam agnoverunt. Neque aliam ob causam inventa fuisse videtur ab Origene & aliis nonnullis, quam ut veritas Hebraica cum Graecis exemplaribus, de quorum sinceritate non parva erat dubitandi ratio, conciliaretur. His accedit, Origenem non tam ex sua mente in hac ad Africanum epistola loquuttum loquutum fuisse, quam ut codices qui tunc in Ecclesiis legebantur, defenderet.
units.tr: I know indeed that some of the Fathers greatly esteemed the book entitled The Shepherd; Tertullian too tried to thrust forward the little book of Enoch as if it were divine; indeed, he contended that the Jews had removed from the text of the Scriptures many books that illustrated the Christian religion. Origen also seems to have adhered to this opinion, who in his letter to Africanus on the history of Susanna asserts that the Jews removed many things from their books, so that these would not be read by common people. But these and similar statements, which are few in number and which are offered to serve their authors' theories rather than the truth, cannot be set alongside the common judgment of the Fathers. For Tertullian himself, in this passage, seems to confirm by his own words the common view of the Church: You know, he says, that the Scripture of Enoch is not received by some, because it is not admitted into the chest of the Jews. Thus in those times that Apocryphal book, or book of doubtful faith, was judged to be one the Jews did not admit into their canon. Origen also thinks otherwise in other places than in what he wrote to Africanus. In this passage, indeed, he could defend the history of Susanna and the other additions which the Greek edition of the Seventy Interpreters presents in no other way than by appealing to the Apocryphal books, and by supposing that the Jews, in copying out their codices, removed from the knowledge of common people much that was expressed in those Apocrypha. Origen had perhaps learned from the Jews, with whom he had frequent dealings, that Ezra and his companions did not publish all the books that then existed, and from this he thought it could be concluded that the Greek translators took up things not found in the Hebrew codices. But this opinion departs from the common agreement of the ancient Jews, who acknowledged a perfect and exact harmony throughout the Hebrew text. Nor does it seem to have been devised by Origen and some others for any other reason than to reconcile the Hebrew truth with the Greek copies, about whose trustworthiness there was no small ground for doubt. In addition, Origen in this letter to Africanus spoke not so much from his own mind as in order to defend the copies that were then read in the Churches.

units.la: Objicit præterea doctissimus Vossius, virum inexhaustæ doctrinæ Clementem Alexandrinum scribere Apostolum Paulum remisisse ad Sibyllas & Hystaspis vaticinia, & commendasse eorum lectionem. Si quæratur autem à Vossio, ubinam hoc dixerit Paulus, statim respondet sufficere nobis debuisse hoc Clementem virum sanctum & cum multis viris Apostolicis conversatum affirmasse: verum si responsionis istius habeatur ratio, priscos Ecclesiæ Patres ab omni prorsus errore immunes fuisse necesse est; quo nihil absurdius fingi potuit. Norunt quippe qui aliquam rerum Ecclesiasticarum cognitionem habent, quam vafre prisci illi Patres, atque in primis Clemens Alexandrinus, cum Judæis ac Gentilibus disputarint. Contendit etiam Vossius, librum Enochi aliosque similes libros fatidicos ex eo solum rejiciendos non esse, quod in Fragmentis aliquot quæ supersunt multa superstitiosa & magica contineantur, cum Balaamus Magus & Incantator fuerit, qui tamen futura Christi mysteria manifeste prædixit: quasi vero ea quæ de Balaamo in Scriptura referuntur, ad præsens institutum trahi possent, & hoc exemplo libros quos non solum mendaciis superstitionibusque & fabellis refertos esse constat, sed & ab impostoribus qui clarissimorum virorum ementiti sunt nomina, profectos tueri liceret. Eadem arte febricitantium Judæorum somnia in Zohare, Rabboth & Midras ab eodem spiritu quo profectum est Euangelium, inspirata fuisse auctor est Guilhelmus Postellus, qui affirmare veritus non fuit, ex doctrina Zoharis, tanquam quæ à Spiritu sancto & spiritualibus auctoribus pendet eductum esse Euangelium. Chalanni, inquit idem Postellus, Syri, Indi, Chaldæi, Magi, Gymnosophistæ, Ægyptii & Prophetæ eădem sunt origine. A quo non multum discedere videtur optimus Vossius, cui auctor fuerim ut Zorobabelis etiam vaticinium, quod de Messia clare loquitur, fuitque à Judæis sermone haud impuro & prophetico editum, in fatidicorum suorum classe collocet. Sed his valere jussis, id quod nostri est instituti persequamur.
units.tr: Moreover, the most learned Vossius objects that Clement of Alexandria, a man of inexhaustible learning, writes that the Apostle Paul referred to the Sibyls and the prophecies of Hystaspes and commended the reading of them. If Vossius is asked where Paul said this, he immediately replies that it ought to be enough for us that Clement, a holy man who had lived with many Apostolic men, affirmed it; but if this answer is accepted, the early Fathers of the Church must be assumed to have been wholly free from every error, which nothing could be more absurd to suppose. Those who have some acquaintance with ecclesiastical history know how cunningly those early Fathers, and especially Clement of Alexandria, argued against Jews and Gentiles.
