Vossius also contends that the book of Enoch and other similar prophetic books ought not to be rejected merely because some surviving fragments contain much that is superstitious and magical, since Balaam was a magician and enchanter, and yet he clearly foretold the mysteries of Christ: as if what is related of Balaam in Scripture could be drawn into the present argument, and by this example it were permissible to defend books which are known to be full not only of lies, superstitions and fables, but also to have come from impostors who falsely assumed the names of most distinguished men. By the same method, William Postel, who did not hesitate to affirm it, is the authority for the claim that the dreams of feverish Jews in the Zohar, the Rabbot and the Midrashim were inspired by the same Spirit from which the Gospel proceeded; he said, from the teaching of the Zohar, as if the Gospel had been brought forth from the Holy Spirit and spiritual authors depending on it. The Chalanni, says the same Postel, Syrians, Indians, Chaldeans, Magi, Gymnosophists, Egyptians and Prophets are of the same origin. The excellent Vossius seems not far from this, and I would advise him to place also the prophecy of Zerubbabel, which speaks clearly of the Messiah and was published by the Jews in a not unsuitable prophetic style, in the class of his prophetic writings. But, bidding these things farewell, let us pursue what belongs to our present purpose.

units.la: Præter hactenus allata de libris Apocryphis, animadvertendum est non solum Judæos sibi Canonem Scripturarum condidisse, sed & suum quoque Canonem habere Ecclesiam, quæ auctoritate sua communivit plures libros quos Judæi expunxerant, Ita Augustinus stinus asserit libros Maccabæorum non à Judæis, sed ab Ecclesia pro Canonicis accipi: quod de duobus tantùm primis Maccabæorum libris intelligendum est: tertium enim Ecclesia non minùs quàm Synagoga respuit. Cui etiam sententiæ videtur accessisse Hieronymus; etsi passim in suis operibus strenuissimum Canonis Judaici defensorem se præbeat. Ruffino enim objicienti, Hieronymum nullam Scripturæ Sacræ auctoritatem tribuisse in sua Bibliorum editione Susannæ historiæ, hymno trium puerorum ac Beli Draconis narrationibus, quas appellaverat fabulas, respondet doctissimus Pater, non se quid sentiret dixisse, sed quid Judæi contra Christianos dicere soleant explicâsse. Dixerat tamen Hieronymus, Origenem, Eusebium, Apollinarium & alios Græciæ Doctores pro his visionibus, quæ nullam Scripturæ auctoritatem præbeant, Porphyrio noluisse respondere. De libro quoque Judith hæc scribit idem Hieronymus: Hunc librum Synodus Nicena in numero Sanctarum Scripturarum legitur computâsse: ad quæ hæc animadvertit Erasmus: Non affirmat approbatum hunc in Synodo Nicena, sed ait legitur computâsse. Revera Hieronymus Præfatione in librum Regum, tum Judith tum Tobiam in Canone esse negaverat. An contraria his locis loquitur Hieronymus, qui secum etiam in hoc dissidere videtur, quòd eosdem Tobię & Judith libros apud Hebræos inter Hagiographa legi affirmet, qui & jam alibi scripserat hosce libros non exstare in Canone Judæorum, adeoque inter Apocrypha reponendos? Quæ sint illa Hebræorum Hagiographa, de quibus his locis loquitur Hieronymus, fatetur se ignorare Josephus Scaliger, quia Hagiographa à Judæis longè ante Hieronymi seculum in Scripturarum Divinarum Canonem recepta fuerint. Sed in hoc decipi Scaligerum putat D. Huëtius, quòd nulla Hagiographa extra Canonem Hebræos habuisse censuerit, affertque adversus Scaligerum famosam illam Bath kol, seu Filiam vocis, cujus ope Judæi scriptiones Hagiographas & à Deo inspiratas ediderint. Verùm mera sunt otiosorum hominum somnia, quæ Doctores recutiti de Bath kol commenti sunt. Deinde constat illos nunquam in suum Canonem recepisse libros Judith & Tobiæ. Itaque ficta sunt ea quæ de duplici apud Hebræos Hagiographorum genere à D. Huëtio & aliis proferuntur, refellique possunt non solùm Josephi & Hieronymi testimoniis, qui Tobiam, Judith aliosque libros Græcè editos, quos nunc Canon Ecclesiæ Romanæ comprehendit, neque Propheticis neque Hagiographis à Judæis adscribi palàm testantur; verùm etiam Judæorum recentiorum auctoritate, qui in recensendis libris sacris nullam planè illorum mentionem faciunt, sed eos tantùm laudant tanquam scripta sententiosa, quibus tamen nihil divini inesse crediderunt. Si igitur hac nostra ætate, imò jam priscis Ecclesiæ seculis, inter Canonicos numerati fuerint, id tribuendum est Ecclesiæ judicio, non Synagogæ. Quare duplex Canon statuendus est, Ecclesiæ scilicet & Synagogæ: à primo non malè dici possunt Ecclesiastici libri illi quos Ecclesia, non habitâ ratione Judaici Canonis, in suum Canonem voluit admitti & legi in suis coetibus. Constat enim indè jam ab ipsis nascentis Ecclesiæ primordiis legi & cani consuevisse in congregationibus fidelium libros hosce, quos miratur Erasmus hodie passim legi & cani in templis. Sed rem ita esse discere potuit Erasmus ex libro Invectivarum Ruffini adversus Hieronymum.
units.tr: Besides what has been cited so far about the Apocryphal books, it should be noted that the Jews did not merely draw up their own canon of Scripture; the Church also has its own canon, and by its authority it confirmed several books that the Jews had struck out. Thus Augustine asserts that the books of the Maccabees are received as canonical not by the Jews but by the Church. This must be understood of only the first two books of the Maccabees, for the Church rejected the third no less than the Synagogue did. Jerome also seems to have agreed with this view, although throughout his works he presents himself as a most vigorous defender of the Jewish canon. When Rufinus objected that in his edition of the Bible Jerome had assigned no authority to the history of Susanna, the hymn of the three boys, and the stories of Bel and the Dragon, which he had called fables, the learned Father replied that he had not said what he himself thought, but had explained what the Jews were accustomed to say against the Christians. Yet Jerome had said that Origen, Eusebius, Apollinarius and other teachers of Greece refused to answer Porphyry about these visions, which have no authority in Scripture. Jerome also writes this about the book of Judith: The Council of Nicaea is read to have counted this book among the holy Scriptures. Erasmus comments on this: He does not affirm that this book was approved at the Council of Nicaea, but says it is read to have been counted. Indeed, in his Preface to the Book of Kings, Jerome had denied that both Judith and Tobit are in the canon. Or does Jerome speak in these passages in a way contrary to himself, since he also seems to disagree with himself here, when he affirms that these same books of Tobit and Judith are read among the Hagiographa by the Hebrews, although he had already written elsewhere that these books are not found in the canon of the Jews and so must be placed among the Apocrypha? Joseph Scaliger confesses that he does not know what those Hebrew Hagiographa are, of which Jerome speaks in these places, because the Hagiographa were received by the Jews into the canon of the divine Scriptures long before Jerome's time. But M. Huet thinks Scaliger is mistaken in this, since he judged that the Hebrews had no Hagiographa outside the canon, and against Scaliger he brings forward that famous Bath kol, or Daughter of the Voice, by whose help the Jews are said to have published Hagiographa which were written and inspired by God. But the fancies which the recent doctors have invented about the Bath kol are mere dreams of idle men. Further, it is certain that the Jews never received the books of Judith and Tobit into their canon. Therefore what M. Huet and others put forward about a twofold kind of Hagiographa among the Hebrews is fictitious, and it can be refuted not only by the testimony of Josephus and Jerome, who openly declare that Tobit, Judith and the other books written in Greek, which the canon of the Roman Church now includes, are ascribed by the Jews neither to the Prophets nor to the Hagiographa, but also by the authority of the more recent Jews, who in listing their sacred books make no mention of these at all, but praise them only as sententious writings, in which they nevertheless believed there was nothing divine. If, therefore, in our own age, or indeed in earlier ages of the Church, these books have been numbered among the canonical, this must be attributed to the judgment of the Church, not of the Synagogue. Hence a twofold canon must be established, namely that of the Church and that of the Synagogue. The books which the Church, without regard to the Jewish canon, wished to be admitted into its own canon and read in its assemblies may fitly be called ecclesiastical books. For it is established that from the very beginnings of the nascent Church these books were customarily read and sung in the assemblies of the faithful, and Erasmus marvels that they are today commonly read and sung in the churches. But Erasmus could have learned that this is so from the book of Rufinus's Invectives against Jerome.

units.la: Hæc omnia egregiè illustrat Sixtus Senensis ab initio Bibliothecæ suæ, ubi libros Scripturæ Sacræ in duas classes partitur. In prima eos recenset, quos Protocanonicos seu Canonicos primi ordinis appellat; & hi sunt qui ex communi tum Judæorum tum Christianorum consensu extra controversiam recepti sunt: in altera autem classe eos reponit quos vocat Deuterocanonicos, seu Canonicos secundi ordinis, qui olim, inquit, Ecclesiastici vocabantur: illi nimirum de quibus inter Catholicos aliquando fuit anceps sententia, quique ferò ad notitiam totius Ecclesiæ pervenerunt. Primi generis libris adscribit in Veteri Instrumento eos solùm quos in suum armarium admisit Synagoga; ad alterum verò genus revocat illos qui priscis Ecclesiæ seculis inter Apocrypha scripta à plerisque numerabantur; quibus etiam adscribit volumen Esther, quòd de illius auctoritate nonnulli Patres dubitaverint, uti jam annotatum fuit. Sola de auctoritate Hieronymi restat difficultas, qui contra Judæorum omnium fidem, imò & sui ipsius testimonium scripserit, libros Tobiæ & Judith apud Hebræos inter Hagiographa extare. Miror viros rei criticæ peritos non animadvertisse in Hieronymi Præfationibus in Tobiam & Judith legendum non esse Hagiographa, uti nunc legitur, sed Apocrypha. Licet enim desint codices manu exarati quibus lectionem hanc suffulciam, ipsamet Hieronymi verba illam manifestè ostendunt. Librum utique Tobiæ, inquit doctissimus Pater, quem Hebraei de catalogo Divinarum Scripturarum secantes, his quæ Hagiographa memorant mancipârunt. Quis non statim deprehendat legi debuisse Apocrypha, non Hagiographa, cum liquido constet Judæos de catalogo Divinarum Scripturarum Hagiographa nunquam recensuisse? Similis prorsus ratio est Præfationis Hieronymi in Judith, ubi etiam pro voce Hagiographa reponi debet Apocrypha: sic enim in ea hodie legimus. Apud Hebræos liber Judith inter Hagiographa legitur, cujus auctoritas ad roboranda illa quæ in contentionem veniunt minus idonea. Si idonea non est libri istius auctoritas ad res fidei stabiliendas, haud dubie non est e libris Hagiographis, qui extra controversiam Canonici & inspirati apud Judæos habentur; sed ex Apocryphorum numero, seu scriptorum qui sunt dubiæ & incertæ fidei, quales existimavit libros Judith & Tobiæ Hieronymus. Hactenus de Apocryphis, quæ quidem fusius quàm postulabat instituti ratio, explicavimus. Sed rem disputantium contentionibus valde implicatam enodare à proposito nostro alienum non duximus.
units.tr: Sixtus of Siena illustrates all these points admirably at the beginning of his Bibliotheca, where he divides the books of Holy Scripture into two classes. In the first he lists those which he calls Protocanonical, or canonical of the first order, and these are the books received beyond controversy by the common consent both of Jews and Christians. In the second class, however, he places those which he calls Deuterocanonical, or canonical of the second order, which, he says, were formerly called ecclesiastical: namely those about which there was at one time doubt among Catholics, and which came only late to the knowledge of the whole Church. To books of the first kind he assigns in the Old Testament only those which the Synagogue admitted into its storehouse; to the second kind he refers those which in the earlier ages of the Church were counted by many among the writings of the Apocrypha. To these he also assigns the book of Esther, because some of the Fathers doubted its authority, as has already been noted. The only remaining difficulty concerns the authority of Jerome, who, against the faith of all the Jews and even against his own testimony, wrote that the books of Tobit and Judith are found among the Hagiographa of the Hebrews. I wonder that men skilled in textual criticism have not noticed that in Jerome's Prefaces to Tobit and Judith we ought to read not Hagiographa, as is now read, but Apocrypha. For although manuscripts written by hand that would support this reading are lacking, Jerome's own words clearly show it. Indeed, says that most learned Father, the book of Tobit, which the Hebrews, cutting it off from the catalogue of the divine Scriptures, have assigned to those things which they record as Hagiographa. Who would not immediately perceive that it ought to be read Apocrypha, not Hagiographa, since it is clearly established that the Jews never listed the Hagiographa in the catalogue of the divine Scriptures? The reasoning of Jerome's Preface to Judith is quite similar, where for the word Hagiographa the word Apocrypha must likewise be put back: for so we read it today in that passage. Among the Hebrews the book of Judith is read among the Hagiographa, whose authority is less suitable for confirming those matters which come into dispute. If the authority of that book is not suitable for establishing matters of faith, it is doubtless not one of the Hagiographa, which among the Jews are held to be canonical and inspired beyond controversy, but belongs to the number of the Apocrypha, that is, of writings of doubtful and uncertain credibility, which is how Jerome judged the books of Judith and Tobit. So far I have explained the matter of the Apocrypha, more fully than the plan of this work required. But I did not think it foreign to our purpose to unravel a question made very intricate by the disputes of the controversialists.

units.la: Satis non fuit eruditissimum Vossium novos Prophetas finxisse veteribus longè oculatiores, novum jam librorum Scripturæ Sacræ ordinem hactenus inauditum procudit. Libri Mosis, ipso auctore, quinque constituunt volumina, non vero unum, ut Judæis visum est: & ut id à nemine posset vocari in controversiam, novæ illius distributionis rationes evidentissimas profert. Constat autem, inquit, vel ex ipsis sacris literis, ut alias gentes, ita quoque veteres Hebræos non in codicibus, quod serum demum factum, sed in voluminibus & continuatis pellibus libros suos descripsisse. Quid necesse fuerit ut ad veteres Hebræos recurreret Vossius minimè capio, cum etiam ætate nostrâ Judæi in libris qui Synagogarum usui serviunt, ejusmodi voluminibus utantur: nec ideo tamen Legem in quinque partiuntur volumina; sed eam ex antiquo more, quem etiam Christi temporibus obtinuisse crediderim, unico volumine comprehendunt. Mox ulterius progressus vir doctus, affirmat ætate Aquilæ, quem vocat futilissimum Interpretem, Judæos, vel ipsum Aquilam, nequissimam & ineptissimam sacrorum librorum divisionem odio hebdomadum Danielis commentos esse, eosque pervertisse sensus & ordinem Scripturæ, inducendo novam distributionem, Legis videlicet, Prophetarum & Hagiographorum. Utrum nova librorum distributio, modo libri integri sint, illorum sensum pervertat, judicent perspicaciores. Verum ne minutiora consectari videar, dico longè probabilius esse Aquilam in vertendis sacris codicibus sequutum fuisse ordinem dinem librorum quem ætatis illius exemplaria Hebraica præferebant, cùm mutationis illius ratio nulla appareat. Sed id fecit, inquit Vossius, odio Hebdomadum Danielis, quem rejecit extremo penè inter Hagiographos loco: quasi verò Judæi non æquè fidem habeant Danielis de Messia vaticiniis, ac Christiani. Miratur illorum simplicitatem Vossius, qui Rabbinis credunt asserentibus Cetuvim, seu libros Hagiographos, Spiritûs Sancti afflatu conscriptos. Si Rabbinos, inquit, consulas, ridebunt, utpote gnaros quid per Spiritum Sanctum intelligant. Cur jam factus Rabbinista Vossius Rabbinos istos non laudavit, ut ex illis cognoscamus quid per Cetuvim intelligant? Novi quidem Judæos de germana vocis illius significatione inter se non convenire; etsi omnes sentiant Cetuvim seu Hagiographos non minùs Divinos esse & Canonicos quam reliquos Veteris Instrumenlibros. Negotium istud ita explicat subtilissimus Abravanel. Dicti fuere Cetuvim, quia scripti fuere in Spiritu Sancto: si verò ita sit, nomen Cetuvim ad id institutum non est, ut denotet sermones hosce scriptos fuisse in libro, non verò ex ore exceptos; verum ut denotet scriptos fuisse in Spiritu Sancto & in illo gradu, neque fuisse cum ipsis Spiritum Divinum nisi in ipsa sua scriptione in hac lingua & sapientia. Prophetiam in diversos gradus dividi, quorum unus alterum superet, affirmat R. David Kimchi: quos gradus subtilius explicat R. Moses Ben Maimon. Sed valere jussis ejusmodi subtilitatibus, quæ ex Philosophia Aristotelis & Averrois desumptæ sunt, constat Judæos hac in re cum Josepho consentire, quòd libri omnes qui extant in illorum Canone verè Divini sint ac Prophetici, quia scilicet à Prophetis conscripti fuère. Unde R. Don Joseph Ben Jechaia, qui Commentariis suis Psalmos illustravit, eosque cum Patribus suis ad Cetuvim, seu Hagiographorum classem revocat, illos cum Lege Mosis comparat, maximamque inde colligit Psalmorum dignitatem. Idcirco, inquit Magister iste, dignitas libri illius maxima est, quòd sequatur Legem Divinam, ejusque formam ac perfectionem imitetur. Illud confirmat Patrum suorum auctoritate, qui Psalmos Prophetis ipsis videntur anteposuisse, quandoquidem illos Mosis Pentateucho adjungunt. Itaque, fatentibus ipsis Rabbinis, neque Danielis neque Davidis minuitur auctoritas, etsi in Prophetarum classe non recensentur. Hæc enim eodem loco mox subjungit R. iste Joseph modò laudatus: Neque mirum est librum Psalmorum multa continere vaticinia de tempore Messiæ, cùm etiam in Spiritu Sancto interdum extent de rebus futuris vaticinia. Hàc arte te Judæi cum Christianis facili negotio conciliabuntur. Quodque videtur dignum animadversione, Talmudici Doctores librum Jobi volunt ab ipso Mose scriptum, qui tamen in classe Cetuvim, seu Hagiographorum, collocatur.
units.tr: It was not enough for the most learned Vossius to have fashioned new Prophets, far keener-sighted than the old ones; he has also devised a new order of the books of Holy Scripture, hitherto unheard of. The books of Moses, according to his account, make up five volumes, not one, as the Jews thought; and so that no one could call this into question, he brings forward the most evident reasons for this new division. It is certain, he says, from the sacred letters themselves, that just as other nations, so also the ancient Hebrews wrote their books not in codices, which was a later invention, but in rolls and continuous skins. I do not see why Vossius needed to go back to the ancient Hebrews, since even in our own age the Jews use such rolls in the books that serve the use of their synagogues; yet they do not divide the Law into five volumes, but, following the ancient custom, which I believe prevailed even in Christ's time, they contain it in one volume. The learned man then goes further and affirms that in the age of Aquila, whom he calls a most trifling interpreter, the Jews, or Aquila himself, devised that most wicked and most inept division of the sacred books out of hatred for the weeks of Daniel, and that by introducing a new distribution, namely of the Law, the Prophets and the Hagiographa, they perverted the senses and the order of Scripture. Whether a new distribution of the books, provided the books are complete, perverts their sense, let the more discerning judge. But lest I seem to pursue trifles, I say that it is far more probable that Aquila, in translating the sacred codices, followed the order of the books which the Hebrew copies of that age presented, since no reason for that change appears. But, says Vossius, he did this out of hatred for the weeks of Daniel, whom he placed almost at the last place among the Hagiographa, as if the Jews did not have the same faith in Daniel's prophecies about the Messiah as Christians do. Vossius marvels at the simplicity of those who believe the rabbis when they assert that the Cetuvim, or Hagiographa, were written under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. If you consult the rabbis, he says, they will laugh, as being experts in what they understand by the Holy Spirit. Why, now become a rabbinist, did Vossius not cite those rabbis, so that we might learn from them what they understand by Cetuvim? I do know that the Jews do not agree among themselves about the true meaning of that word, although all of them judge that the Cetuvim, or Hagiographa, are no less divine and canonical than the remaining books of the Old Testament. The most subtle Abravanel explains this matter thus: They were called Cetuvim because they were written in the Holy Spirit. But if it is so, the name Cetuvim was not given for this purpose, namely to denote that these discourses were written in a book and not taken down from the mouth; rather to denote that they were written in the Holy Spirit and in that degree, and that the Divine Spirit was not with them except in the very writing of them in this language and wisdom. Rabbi David Kimchi affirms that prophecy is divided into different degrees, one of which surpasses another; these degrees are explained more subtly by Rabbi Moses Ben Maimon. But setting aside subtleties of this sort, which are drawn from the philosophy of Aristotle and Averroes, it is established that the Jews in this matter agree with Josephus, that all the books that exist in their canon are truly divine and prophetic, because they were written by Prophets. Hence Rabbi Don Joseph Ben Jechaia, who illustrated the Psalms in his commentaries, and who restores them, together with their fathers, to the class of the Cetuvim, or Hagiographa, compares them with the Law of Moses and draws from this the greatest dignity of the Psalms. For this reason, says that teacher, the dignity of that book is greatest, because it follows the divine Law and imitates its form and perfection. He confirms this by the authority of his fathers, who seem to have placed the Psalms even above the Prophets themselves, since they join them to the Pentateuch of Moses. Thus, as the rabbis themselves confess, the authority of neither Daniel nor David is diminished, although they are not listed in the class of the Prophets. For in the same place the Rabbi Joseph just mentioned adds shortly after: Nor is it surprising that the book of Psalms contains many prophecies about the time of the Messiah, since prophecies about future things are sometimes also found in the Holy Spirit. By this method the Jews will easily be reconciled with the Christians. And what seems worthy of notice: the Talmudic doctors want the book of Job to have been written by Moses himself, though it is placed in the class of the Cetuvim, or Hagiographa.

units.la: Quis credat Vossium è Rabbinista fieri Doctorem Talmudicum? Contendit Judæos, etiam fatentibus antiquis Rabbinis, multa sacrarum literarum loca expunxisse, utilitate suadente, & verba & sensus immutásse. Nihil à me, inquit vir ille Talmudicus, hic fingi cognoscet, si quis Talmudicos adeat libros, in quibus pluribus locis hæc legas; Bonum est ut evellatur litera de Lege, & ut sanctificetur nomen Domini. Verùm non licet omnibus adire libros Talmudicos, uti doctissimo Vossio. Crediderim decretum istud Talmudistarum rectè explicari posse verbis R. Mosis Ben Maimon, qui cum plerisque Judæorum Magistris ita Legis Mosaicæ immutabilitatem defendit, ut quasdam illius constitutiones Synedrii magni auctoritate ad tempus rescindi posse existimet. Asserit Magister ille Talmudicus, Deum quidem prohibuisse Deuter. 4. ne quid ad verbum suum adderetur, neque etiam quidpiam ex eo detraheretur; verùm permisisse omnium temporum & ætatum sapientibus, seu domui judicii magni, sepes constituere ad judicia Legis stabilienda in rebus quibusdam quas volunt innovare ad sartam tectam conservandam Legis auctoritatem: Deum præterea facultatem illis sapientibus concessisse quædam præcepta Legis tollere, & quædam prohibita permittere in certa quapiam re & casu, non autem in perpetuum. Hæc sumpta sunt ex Latina libri More Nevochim editione à Buxtorfio publicatâ. Similia his habet auctor libri cujus nomen Cozri, quique Hebraicè & Latinè etiam à Buxtorfio editus. Roganti enim Cozri, quomodo potestas illa innovandi quidpiam in Lege Divina stare posset cum verbis illis Deuteronomii, Non ei addes, nec quidpiam ab ea detrahes; respondet Judæus, hæc verba dici solùm de multitudine, ne quid ex suo ingenio innovet, sapiatque ex sua scientia; non verò de Senatoribus Synedrii magni, quia scilicet non unius fuit Mosis sanctiones condere, sed & aliorum quoque Prophetarum Sacerdotumque & Judicum, quibus idem Spiritus Dei interfuit. Is est, nisi fallor, genuinus Talmudicæ doctrinæ sensus, quæ in eversionem verborum contextûs sacri trahi non potest, cùm de tollenda litera, imò dictione necnon sententia aliqua inter explicandum contextum illic agatur, minimè verò de mutandis eradendisque ejusdem contextûs literis aut dictionibus.
units.tr: Who would believe that Vossius has turned from a rabbinist into a Talmudic doctor? He contends that the Jews, even as the ancient rabbis admit, have struck out many passages of the sacred letters when expedience urged it, and have changed both words and meanings. "Nothing that I say here," says that Talmudic man, "will be found invented by me, if anyone consults the Talmudic books, where in many places you will read this: It is good that a letter be plucked out of the Law, so that the name of the Lord may be sanctified." But not everyone is free to consult the Talmudic books, as the most learned Vossius is. I would believe that this decree of the Talmudists can be rightly explained by the words of Rabbi Moses ben Maimon, who, with most of the Jewish masters, defends the immutability of the Mosaic Law in such a way that he thinks certain of its ordinances may for a time be annulled by the authority of the great Sanhedrin. That Talmudic teacher asserts that God indeed forbade, in Deut. 4, that anything be added to his word or taken away from it; but he permitted the wise men of every time and age, that is, the house of the great judgment, to set up fences to secure the judgments of the Law in certain matters which they wish to innovate, in order to keep the authority of the Law whole and intact. Moreover, God granted those wise men the power to remove some precepts of the Law and to permit some prohibited things in a certain matter and case, but not for ever. These things are taken from the Latin edition of the book More Nevochim published by Buxtorf. The author of the book whose name is Cozri has similar views, and he too was published by Buxtorf in Hebrew and Latin. For when Cozri was asked how that power of innovating anything in the Divine Law could stand together with those words of Deuteronomy, You shall not add to it, nor take anything away from it, the Jew replies that these words are said only of the multitude, lest it innovate anything from its own wit and be wise by its own knowledge; but they are not said of the senators of the great Sanhedrin, since it was not for Moses alone to frame ordinances, but also for other prophets, priests and judges, in whom the same Spirit of God was present. This, unless I am mistaken, is the genuine sense of the Talmudic doctrine, which cannot be drawn into the overthrow of the words of the sacred context, since it deals with the removal of a letter, indeed of a word or a sense, in the course of explaining the context, and by no means with changing or erasing letters or words of that same context.

units.la: Morinus, à quo Iiaacus Vossius id omne quod Rabbinologiam sapit in suis operibus mutuatus est, postquàm nihil non commentus fuit ut ostendat sacros codices à Judæis dedita operà corruptos fuisse, demum B. Augustini sententiam his verbis amplectitur: S. Augusti-ni sententiam de libris Judæorum ab ipsis de industria non depravatis lubentes amplectimur. A quo tamen se in eo discedere profitetur, quòd Augustinus actionem illam incredibilem judicaverit, quia fieri non potuit gentem tam longè latèque diffusam conspirasse in pervertendis codicibus tam multis & tam longè latèque dispersis; ipse verò Morinus Augustino perspicacior contendit actionem istam non modò Judæis esse credibilem, sed etiam ab iis haberi alterum fidei fundamentum. Utrum autem illud à Morino firmis probationibus demonstratum fuerit, non est hujus loci expendere: satis enim est ostendisse Morinum, à quo in plerisque dependet Vossius, adduci non potuisse ut crederet Scripturæ Sacræ libros à Judæis de industria depravatos fuisse; etsi Talmudistarum de evellenda litera è Lege pronunciatum non ignoraverit.
units.tr: Morinus, from whom Isaac Vossius has borrowed everything in his works that smells of rabbinology, after he had invented everything he could to show that the sacred codices were corrupted by the Jews on purpose, at last embraces the opinion of St Augustine in these words: We gladly embrace the opinion of St Augustine about the books of the Jews, which were not corrupted by them on purpose. Yet he professes that he departs from Augustine on this point, because Augustine judged that act incredible, since it could not have happened that a people so widely spread should conspire to pervert so many codices so widely scattered; but Morinus, keener-sighted than Augustine, contends that this act is not only credible to the Jews but is also held by them to be a second foundation of the faith. Whether this was demonstrated by Morinus with firm proofs is not for this place to weigh. It is enough to have shown that Morinus, on whom Vossius depends in most things, could not be brought to believe that the books of Holy Scripture were corrupted on purpose by the Jews, although he was not unaware of the Talmudists' pronouncement about plucking a letter out of the Law.

units.la: Jam Vossius relictis Talmudistis ad Græcos Interpretes venit, totuisque est in asserendo id omne quod superest linguæ Hebraicæ acceptum ferri debere LXX. Interpretibus; absque illis ne unum quidem verbum rectè exponi posse; nullas omnino versiones à Judæis, seu ad mentem Judæorum factas, bonas inveniri, quæ non sint à LXX. desumptæ Interpretibus; ubicunque ipsi deseruntur, ipsam quoque ibi deseri veritatem; demum ab illis Judæis petendam esse sacrarum literarum interpretationem, qui florente & superstite etiamnum linguâ Hebraicâ sacros verterunt libros, sed non ab iis Judæis qui Christianæ fidei sunt hostes, quïque sponte suâ fatentur se nescire Hebraicè. Jam his ferè similia pro evertendis hodiernis codicibus Hebraicis, & stabiliendâ veterum Interpretum auctoritate produxerat Joannes Morinus, quæ cùm à Ludovico Cappello, teste in præsenti materia locupletissimo, quem haud immeritò plurimi facit Vossius, gravissimis argumentis castigata fuerint, malim verbis doctissimi illius viri, quàm meis, optimo Vossio respondere. Primò itaque de Morino ait Cappellus, (nos verò de Vossio) facile esse ignaræ plebi fumos vendere, & ad populum phaleras jactare. Deinde veniens ad LXX. Interpretes, negat contra Vossii mentem, linguam Hebraicam fuisse illis vernaculam, quæ scilicet in captivitate Babylonica, à qua plusquàm CC. annis distabant, deperdita fuerit.
units.tr: Now Vossius, leaving the Talmudists aside, comes to the Greek interpreters, and his whole effort is to maintain that everything that remains of the Hebrew language must be credited to the Seventy interpreters; that without them not even one word can be rightly explained; that no good versions made by the Jews, or in the mind of the Jews, can be found that are not derived from the Seventy interpreters; that wherever they are abandoned, truth too is abandoned there; and finally that the interpretation of the sacred letters must be sought from those Jews who translated the sacred books while the Hebrew language was still flourishing and surviving, but not from those Jews who are enemies of the Christian faith and who of their own accord confess that they do not know Hebrew. Now John Morinus had already brought forward much the same kind of arguments to overthrow the present Hebrew codices and to establish the authority of the old interpreters. These arguments were refuted with the gravest reasoning by Ludovicus Cappellus, a most abundant witness in the present matter, whom Vossius holds in very high esteem and not undeservedly; so I prefer to answer Vossius in the words of that most learned man rather than in my own. First, then, Cappellus says about Morinus (and we say it about Vossius) that it is easy to sell smoke to an ignorant crowd and to make a show of trappings before the people. Next, coming to the Seventy interpreters, he denies, contrary to Vossius' view, that Hebrew was their native language, since it had been lost during the Babylonian captivity, from which they were more than two hundred years distant.

units.la: Addit illos ex Chaldaicæ & Syro, Chaldaicæ quâ Judæi tum utebantur, linguæ affinitate potuisse studio, labore ac frequenti sacrorum Scriptorum lectione atque diligenti examine linguæ Hebraicæ non mediocrem sibi comparare scientiam. Multa etiam potuisse illos ad linguæ illius & sacrorum librorum intelligentiam ex Patrum suorum traditione habere necessaria. At eos, inquit Cappellus, omnia vidisse, omnia intellexisse, nullibi lapsos esse aut allucinatos nemo dixerit, nisi qui Hebraicè nihil scit, & qui eorum translationem cum Hebraeo textu non contulit, etiam in iis locis in quibus illi non secus quàm nos hodie legerunt, ubi videre est frequentes eorum pueriles & pudendos lapsus, sæpè lapsus à genuina vocum & phraseon significatione, & sacrorum Scriptorum mente atque scopo. Hæc & alia ejusdem generis plurima Criticæ suæ Sacræ inseruerat Cappellus, quæ expungi curavit Morinus, quia ad illius palatum non faciebant. Illa autem sumpsimus ex sermone apologetico ejusdem Cappelli adversus Bootium. Quid autem ad hæc respondeat Vossius non video, cùm & ipse noverit Cappellum ad scribendum opus suum Criticum non accessisse animo à Rabbinis præoccupato. Imò Semi-Rabbini isti quos sæpius traducit Vossius, de Cappello ejusque libro gravissimè conquesti sunt. Audiamus iterum verba ejusdem viri docti & in hoc studii genere exercitatissimi, quibus diversum planè & à Vossii sententia alienum fert judicium de versionibus illis quæ post LXX. Interpretes ex Hebraeo factæ sunt. Tribuatur sanè veteribus illis translationibus, ait Cappellus, sua cuique laus, gloria & honor ob earum antiquitatem & perpetuum Ecclesiæ usum, at ne tamen ubi manifesto vitiosæ sunt, aut manca & imperfectæ, præponatur earum vitium ipsi originariæ veritati atque authentico textui, neve præferantur illæ perversæ quâdam & iniquâ ac jurgiosâ & contentiosâ prorsus invidiâ, aut potius damnandâ quâdam καινοῦ θεία, aliis longè melioribus atque accuratioribus translationibus. Potuit igitur melior & accuratior fieri sacrorum codicum translatio, auctore Cappello, quàm sit Græca illa LXX. Interpretum versio. His & alia complura possent adjici, quibus in præsentia supersedeo, ne sim molestus. Deinde cùm Cappellus non sit ex eorum hominum secta quos facetissimus Vossius appellat asellos cassos lumine & intellectu, togulâ cinctos Professoriâ, pro clypeo gestantes Biblia Masorethica cum omnibus suis punctis, facilè crediderim eum sine ullo negotio ad viri tam eximii sententiam de Græca LXX. Interpretum versione accessurum.
units.tr: He adds that they could, from the affinity of the Chaldee and Syriac languages, and from the Chaldee which the Jews then used, acquire no small knowledge of the Hebrew language by zeal, labour, frequent reading of the sacred writers and careful examination. He also says that they could have had from the tradition of their fathers many things necessary for understanding that language and the sacred books. But that they saw everything, understood everything, and nowhere slipped or went astray, no one will say," says Cappellus, "except one who knows nothing of Hebrew and who has not compared their translation with the Hebrew text, even in those places where they read no differently from what we read today; where one can see their frequent childish and shameful slips, often departures from the genuine meaning of the words and phrases, and from the mind and purpose of the sacred writers. Cappellus had inserted these and many other things of the same kind in his Sacred Criticism, and Morinus took care to have them struck out, because they did not suit his taste. We have taken those passages from Cappellus' own apologetic letter against Bootius. What Vossius replies to these things I do not see, since he himself knows that Cappellus did not come to writing his critical work with a mind preoccupied by the rabbis. Indeed those half-rabbis whom Vossius so often cites complained most bitterly of Cappellus and his book. Let us hear again the words of that same learned man, very well practised in this kind of study, in which he gives a judgment quite different from Vossius' view about those versions which were made from the Hebrew after the Seventy interpreters: Let those ancient translations, says Cappellus, be granted their own praise, glory and honour for their antiquity and continual use in the Church; but let not their faults, where they are manifestly defective, or maimed and imperfect, be set above the original truth itself and the authentic text, nor let those perverse, unjust, quarrelsome and contentious prejudices, or rather that damnable novelty-worship [καινοῦ θεία], be preferred to other far better and more accurate translations. Therefore, on Cappellus' authority, a better and more accurate translation of the sacred codices could have been made than that Greek version of the Seventy interpreters. Many other things could be added to these, but for the present I forbear, lest I be tiresome. Then, since Cappellus is not of that sect of men whom the most witty Vossius calls empty asses without light or understanding, girded with a little professorial gown, carrying the Masoretic Bibles with all their points as a shield, I could easily believe that he would come, without any difficulty, to the opinion of so distinguished a man about the Greek version of the Seventy interpreters.

units.la: Iterum instat Vossius, contenditque omnes Judæos qui Christi præ-
units.tr: Vossius presses the point again, and contends that all the Jews who lived before Christ, in whose synagogues no language was heard except Greek.

units.la: Ludov. Capp. in Apol. adversus Boot.
units.tr: Ludov. Capp. in Apol. adversus Boot.

units.la: Voss. in Epist. ad Andr. Colv. precessêre tempora agnovisse hanc solam versionem velut legitimam; usque ad tempora Aquilæ nullam aliam lectam fuisse in omnibus Judæorum Synagogis præter illam LXX. Interpretum, ut in Ægypto, Asia & reliqua Syria, ita quoque in Judæa à temporibus nimirum Alexandri Magni, nullam præter Græcam auditam fuisse linguam, in urbibus præsertim oppidisque; ne in Hierosolymitanis quidem Synagogis aliam præter Græcam personuisse linguam; si Hebræa prælegeretur Scriptura, accessisse interpretationem Græcam. Quot verba protulit Vossius, tot effudit commenta. Primò enim ante conditam LXX. Seniorum versionem ab Esdræ temporibus constat non aliam in Judæorum Synagogis lectam fuisse Scripturam quàm contextum Hebraicum. Non enim ita linguæ suæ obliti fuêre Judæi in exilio Babyloniensi, quin illa penès Prophetas, Sacerdotes ac viros principes remanserit, uti rectè monuit Josephus Albo præstantissimus Judæorum Theologus: & id haud invitus agnoscet Vossius, qui putet LXX. Interpretes sacros vertisse libros florente & superstite etiamnum Hebraicâ linguâ. Jam etiam post conditam LXX. Seniorum translationem saltem in aliquot Synagogis lectum fuisse contextum Hebræum, nec dissiteri poterit vir doctus, qui scribat Fl. Josephum Legem Moysis in Synagoga Hebraicè interpretatum esse, historiam belli Judaici, antequàm Græcè scriberet, lingua Hebræâ edidisse; quo argumento refellit Vossius illos qui objecerant nescisse patrium sermonem, neque unquam codicem Hebraicum inspexisse, quibus opponit ipsamet Josephi verba, qui scribat excelluisse se in disciplinis patriis præ cæteris Hebræis, Græcam verò linguam non nisi per Grammaticam addidicisse, accuratâ verò pronunciandi ratione caruisse. Ergo etiam teste ipsomet Vossio qui pugnantia loquitur, non modò vilis popellus & ii solùm qui rure & in pagis versabantur dialecto utebantur Syriacâ; sed & viri principes, inter quos Josephus, qui linguam Hebraicam, aut magis Syriacam, vocat sermonem patrium, cujus pronunciandi ratio, quia erat paulò horridior, testatur se pronunciare vix potuisse Græcum sermonem, qui Hebraico, seu Syriaco, longè politior erat. Si lingua Græca in urbibus & oppidis erat vernacula, cur Josephus qui rure & in pagis educatus non fuerat, hanc per Grammaticam didicit? Sileo Christum & Apostolos Hierosolymis Syriacè loquutos, uti manifestum est ex libris Novi Testamenti. Quare figmentum est quod asserit Vossius de Hierosolymitanis Synagogis,
units.tr: Voss. in Epist. ad Andr. Colv. First, it is established that from the time of Ezra, before the Septuagint version was made, no Scripture other than the Hebrew text was read in the synagogues of the Jews. The Jews did not forget their language so completely during the Babylonian exile that it did not remain with the prophets, priests and leading men, as the most excellent Jewish theologian Josephus Albo rightly observed. Vossius himself will readily admit this, since he thinks the Seventy translated the sacred books while the Hebrew language was still flourishing and surviving. Moreover, even after the Septuagint translation was made, the Hebrew text was at least read in some synagogues. The learned man cannot deny this, since he writes that Flavius Josephus interpreted the Law of Moses in the synagogue in Hebrew, and that he published his history of the Jewish War in the Hebrew language before writing it in Greek. With this argument Vossius refutes those who objected that Josephus did not know his native tongue and never looked at a Hebrew codex. Against them he sets Josephus's own words, where he writes that he excelled in the learning of his fathers beyond other Hebrews, but had learned Greek only through grammar and lacked a precise pronunciation of it. So, by the testimony of Vossius himself, who speaks inconsistently, it was not only the common folk, and those who lived in the countryside and villages, who used the Syriac dialect. Leading men too, among them Josephus, who calls the Hebrew, or rather Syriac, language his native tongue, used it. He testifies that, because his pronunciation of it was somewhat rougher, he could scarcely pronounce Greek, which was far more refined than Hebrew or Syriac. If Greek was the vernacular in the cities and towns, why did Josephus, who had not been brought up in the countryside or villages, have to learn it through grammar? I say nothing of Christ and the Apostles speaking Syriac in Jerusalem, as is clear from the books of the New Testament. Therefore the claim Vossius makes about the synagogues of Jerusalem, that no language but Greek was heard in them, is a fiction.

units.la: in quibus non alia audita fuerit lingua quàm Græca. Quod si, inquit vir doctus, Hebraea prælegeretur Scriptura, accedebat interpretatio Græca; à solis quippe doctis intelligebatur vetus Hebraica lingua. Mirus sanè ratiocinator Vossius, qui ex eo quòd docti solùm linguam Hebraicam intellexerint, concludit etiam Hierosolymis accessisse Græcam interpretationem. Longè verius dixisset, his locis ubi lingua Syriaca apud Judæos erat vernacula accessisse lectioni Hebraicæ sacri contextûs interpretationem Syriacam; in iis verò locis ubi apud Judæos vigebat sermo Græcus accessisse Græcam interpretationem. Sic etiam Hierosolymis in Synagoga Alexandrinorum qui Græcè loquebantur, non dubito quin sacer contextus primò Hebraicè pro antiquo Synagogarum usu non lectus fuerit, deinde Græcè ab aliquo interprete ex antiquâ etiam consuetudine Judæorum, qui inde jam à reditu exilii Babylonici, postquàm lingua Hebraica desiit esse vernacula, sibi præpositos habuerunt Interpretes qui verba Hebraica in patrium sermonem converterent, ut ab omnibus etiam plebeiis intelligerentur. Quo sensu exponenda esse Justiniani verba putaverim, quibus probant viri docti prisцis temporibus in Synagogis Judæorum qui vulgò Hellenistæ appellantur, lectam fuisse publicè Græcam LXX. Interpretum versionem. Si enim verba Novellæ Justiniani pensiculatius considerentur, manifestum erit in iis Synagogis Græcam translationem venisse tantùm in auxilium contextûs Hebraici & velut illius interpretationem, quomodo Hierosolymis aliisque locis vicinioribus lectioni Hebraicæ adjungebatur interpretatio Chaldaico-Syriaca. Minimè tamen reluctans agnosco cum Vossio, etiam in Judæa linguam Græcam aliquâ ratione obtinuisse, maximè apud viros primarios & magistratus, ita tamen ut sermo Chaldaico-Syriacus, quem eorum Majores è Babylone reportaverant, prævaluerit: & ut ita credam non solùm adducor Josephi auctoritate, sed & compluribus Novi Testamenti testimoniis, ex quibus liquidò constat Christum & Apostolos Syriacè loquutos fuisse. Verùm de his infrà iterum locus erit differendi. Sunt & alia quædam quæ in opusculum suum de Sibyllinis Oraculis adversus Judæos eorumque codices Vossius conjecit: verùm cùm ea rursus inculcet vir doctus in Responsione sua ad Objecta nuperæ Criticæ, satius erit ista omnia in unum collecta expendere. Videndum itaque an hac in parte felicior successus ei fuerit.
units.tr: in whose synagogues no language was heard except Greek. "But if," says the learned man, "the Hebrew Scripture was read aloud, a Greek interpretation was added; for the old Hebrew language was understood only by the learned." Vossius is a strange reasoner indeed, who from the fact that only the learned understood Hebrew concludes that a Greek translation was also brought in at Jerusalem. He would have put it much more truly by saying that in those places where Syriac was the vernacular of the Jews, a Syriac interpretation was added to the reading of the Hebrew sacred text, and in those places where Greek was the common speech of the Jews, a Greek interpretation was added. So too in Jerusalem, in the synagogue of the Alexandrians who spoke Greek, I do not doubt that the sacred text was first read in Hebrew, as was the ancient custom of the synagogues, and then rendered into Greek by some interpreter, following also the older custom of the Jews. From the return from the Babylonian exile onward, when Hebrew had ceased to be the vernacular, they had interpreters set over them who would turn the Hebrew words into the native tongue, so that they could be understood even by the common people. I think the words of Justinian must be explained in this sense, the words by which learned men prove that in ancient times the Greek version of the Seventy Interpreters was publicly read in the synagogues of the Jews called, in common parlance, Hellenists. For if the words of Justinian's Novel are weighed more carefully, it will be clear that in those synagogues the Greek translation came only as an aid to the Hebrew text, as its interpretation, just as in Jerusalem and the nearer places the Chaldaic-Syriac interpretation was joined to the reading of the Hebrew. Yet I do not hesitate to acknowledge with Vossius that the Greek language also held some place in Judea, especially among the leading men and magistrates; but the Chaldaic-Syriac speech, which their ancestors had brought back from Babylon, prevailed. I am led to believe this not only by the authority of Josephus, but also by many testimonies of the New Testament, from which it is plain that Christ and the Apostles spoke in Syriac. But I shall have occasion to discuss these things again below. There are also certain other points which Vossius has raised in his little work on the Sibylline Oracles against the Jews and their codices; but since the learned man repeats them in his Reply to the Objections of the recent Critica, it will be better to collect all of them together and weigh them. Let us see, then, whether he has been more successful on this point.

units.la: Primâ fronte laudat Vossius auctorem Criticæ Sacræ, quam Simonio
units.tr: At first sight Vossius praises the author of the Critica Sacra, which he attributes to Simon,

units.la: {Justin. Nov. 146.} monio tribuit, quòd prisci Interpretes, LXX. scilicet & Cappelli Observationes, ei placuerint. Diligentiam quoque ejusdem Simonii, seu potiùs patientiam, in evolvendis Rabbinorum scriptis laudat & admiratur: sed quòd illorum expositionibus traditionibusque solo auditu propagatis aliquid solidi existimet subesse, & quidem tantum, ut eas sæpè non dubitet LXX. Interpretum præponere versioni, in eo se cum illo consentire non posse palàm profitetur; nec putat quemquam cordatum cum Simonio hac in parte consensurum. Cordatus tamen est Cappellus ille quem tanti facit Vossius, & quidem merito; at in hoc de quo agitur negotio ne tantillum quidem Simonius discessit à Cappello, qui Morinum ejusque simiam Vossium perstringit tanquam homines intemperantes, qui perversâ quâdam & damnandâ κακοηθείᾳ[?] antiquas translationes aliis longè accuratioribus præferant. In hoc præterea Vossio displicet Simonius, quòd scripserit Hieronymum rectè aliquando recessisse ab antiquis Interpretibus,quasi verò antiqui illi ab omni prorsus errore immunes extitissent. Neque etiam in hoc Cappellum deseruit Simonius: ubi enim Cappellus loco jam suprà laudato pueriles lapsus in Gręca LXX. Interpretum versione haud infrequenter deprehendi annotavit, hanc & Hieronymianam inter se comparat, præfertque Hieronymianam, utpote quę meliorem sensum pariat; ac demùm ista subjungit: Sexcenta possent, imò innumera ejusmodi proferri loca, in quibus ex eadem cum hodierna planè lectione Hieronymus longè aliter & felicius multo mentem sacrorum Scriptorum expressit, quàm LXX. quia nempe eorum laboribus & translatione adjutus & aliorum, Aquilæ nimirum, Symmachi, Theodotionis, &c. versionibus sublevatus, illorum hominum σφάλματα, def- pitationes, allucinationes & aberrationes deprehendere potuit. Nec aliud profectò de Hieronymo sentiunt qui Gręcę & Hebraicę eruditionis habent aliquid, si unum excipiamus Vossium, qui exemplo Rufini Hieronymum Judaico & à Rabbinis prœoccupato animo ad cudendam novam contextus Hebraici versionem accessisse existimat. Dudum evanuit, auctore in primis Hieronymo, illa Grę-corum Interpretum Prophetia quam Majores nostri nimium venerati sunt. Verum ad id quod è re nostra est redeamus.
units.tr: {Justin. Nov. 146.} because he approved of the early interpreters, namely the Seventy and the Observations of Cappellus. He also praises and admires the diligence, or rather the patience, of the same Simon in unrolling the writings of the rabbis; but he openly declares that he cannot agree with him in thinking that something solid lies beneath their interpretations and traditions, handed down by hearing alone, and that indeed so much that Simon does not hesitate often to prefer them to the version of the Seventy. Yet Cappellus, whom Vossius holds in such esteem, was a sound man, and rightly so; but in the matter under discussion Simon did not depart in the least from Cappellus, who censures Morinus and his ape Vossius as men intemperate, who, from a certain perverse and condemnable malignity [κακοηθείᾳ], prefer the ancient translations to others far more accurate. Vossius is further displeased with Simon in that he has written that Jerome rightly at times departed from the ancient interpreters, as though those ancient men had been wholly free from every error. Nor did Simon desert Cappellus on this point either. For where Cappellus, in the passage already cited, notes that childish slips are not infrequently detected in the Greek version of the Seventy, he compares this with Jerome's version and prefers Jerome's, as the one that yields the better sense, and at last adds these words: "Six hundred, or rather countless such passages could be brought forward, in which, from the same text as we have today, Jerome expressed the mind of the sacred writers far differently and much more happily than the Seventy did, because he was aided by their labours and by the translation of others, namely Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, and so on, and so was able to detect the blunders, oversights, mistakes and aberrations of those men." Indeed, those who have some knowledge of Greek and Hebrew scholarship think no differently about Jerome, with the single exception of Vossius, who, following Rufinus, thinks that Jerome came to the new Hebrew version of the text with a mind already prejudiced by the Jews and the rabbis. That prophecy of the Greek interpreters, which our forefathers venerated too much, has long since vanished, chiefly through the authority of Jerome. But let us return to what concerns our present purpose.

units.la: Recentium Rabbinorum expositionibus & eorumdem traditionibus solo auditu propagatis nihil inesse solidi contendit Vossius, eo præsertim adductus argumento, quòd traditiones quæ solo auditu propagantur, raro solent ad duo vel tria perstare secula. Si res ita sit, quâ ratione fieri potuit ut LXX. Interpretes post deperditam à duobus seculis linguam Hebraicam, sacri codicis versionem fecerint in omnibus absolutam, qualem fingit Vossius? Dicet haud dubiè nihil hac in re mirabile esse, cùm illi Prophetæ fuerint. Sed cuinam credemus, an Vossio affirmanti Græcos Interpretes fuisse Prophetas, an Hieronymo neganti? Verùm, inquies, Semi-Rabbinus est Hieronymus, qui novam & Judaicam contra communem Ecclesiarum consensionem ausus est translationem cudere. At Sibyllista est Vossius, qui novos Prophetas & Fatidicos hactenus incognitos commentus est. Judaica illa & Rabbinica Hieronymi versio suos habet approbatores, & quidem innumeros, eosque pietate & eruditione conspicuos. Nemo autem est ætate nostrâ qui sententiam Vossii de unica LXX. Interpretum versione recipienda amplectatur, si demas quosdam Socini discipulos, qui avidè illius opinionem arripiunt. Juvat rem ipsam penitius introspicere, naturamque traditionis cui contextus Hebraici lectio innititur manifestam facere.
units.tr: Vossius contends that the recent rabbis' explanations, and their traditions passed down by word of mouth alone, contain nothing solid. He is especially moved by the argument that traditions handed down by word of mouth alone seldom last beyond two or three centuries. If this is so, how could the Seventy, two centuries after the Hebrew language had been lost, have produced a version of the sacred codex that was perfect in every respect, as Vossius imagines? He will no doubt say there is nothing remarkable in this, since they were prophets. But whom shall we believe: Vossius, who affirms that the Greek translators were prophets, or Jerome, who denies it? "But," you will reply, "Jerome is a semi-Rabbinist, who dared to produce a new translation that is Jewish and against the common consensus of the Churches." Yet Vossius is a Sibyllist, who has invented new prophets and seers hitherto unknown. Jerome's Jewish and Rabbinical version has its approvers, and indeed innumerable ones, distinguished for piety and learning. Nobody in our age embraces Vossius's opinion that the version of the Seventy alone should be accepted, except some disciples of Socinus, who eagerly seize upon it. It is worth looking more deeply into the matter itself and making clear the nature of the tradition on which the reading of the Hebrew text rests.

units.la: Res quidem Religionis, maximè quæ ad doctrinam à sensibus paulò remotiorem pertinent, unius traditionis ope absque scriptis per plura secula vix servari posse facilè concesserim. De rebus verò quas vocant disciplinæ & ceremoniarum, diversum planè ferri debet judicium, quia scilicet res istæ ferme quotidie in usum veniunt. Hoc potissimùm traditionis genus prisci Ecclesiæ Patres suis suffragiis approbant. Jam dico eamdem omnino esse linguarum rationem, quæ licet emortuæ nec amplius vernaculæ sint, adhuc apud Doctores obtinent, vigentque in Scholis. Ad hanc traditionis speciem revocamus linguæ Hebraicæ apud Judæos traditionem. Ex hac proculdubio factum est, ut etiam hodiernis temporibus Samaritæ eosdem Legis Mosaicæ codices habeant atque Judæi, si paucula excipias. Demum ex illa quoque traditione ortum, ut Judæi non modò Orientales & Occidentales de contextûs Hebraici lectione inter se consentiant; sed & illi qui Carraim apud illos nomen ex eo reportarunt, quòd, rejecto Talmude aliisque traditionibus parùm constantibus, Scripturæ adhæreant, & cum reliquis Judæis de ratione legendi sacri codicis in omnibus concordent. Explodenda igitur non est temerè traditio illa quam Carræi, qui plerasque Judæorum traditiones respuunt, integram amplexati fuêre. Huc quidem multa possem congerere sumpta ex Judæorum libris, quibus probant Majores suos inde jam à Zorobabelis & Esdræ temporibus Scholas habuisse, buisse tum apud Babylonios, tum apud Hierosolymitanos; sed his & aliis ejusdem generis prudens supersedeo, quòd non sint ad palatum doctissimi Vossii, cui Rabbinologia multùm displicet. Non ignoro complures Judæos, illos maximè qui sunt è classe Grammaticorum, existimare non solùm sacros codices in exilio Babylonico variè distractos ac miserè depravatos fuisse, uti sentiunt RR. Kimchi & Ephodæus, sed & linguam fere deperditam. Et cum his consentiunt etiam Judæi qui sunt è secta Carraeorum. Ita enim scribit de hoc argumento Aaron Ben Joseph, doctissimus Carraeus. Exules fuerunt Israelitæ ex terra sua in aliena, obsignataque est visio ac Prophetia, parumque abfuit quin lingua Hebraica deperdita fuerit. Surrexerunt sapientes Israelitæ quibus Deus addidit Spiritum, & pertractarunt Scripturam quæ apud nos libros XXIV. complectitur. Ex quibus manifestum est linguam Hebræam antiquitus omnino sepultam non fuisse, etsi post reditum Judæorum è Babylone Hierosolymis non amplius vernacula fuerit; sed à Legis tantum Doctoribus conservata. Sic dicitur Esdras Scribæ peritissimi munus præstans legisse ex pulpito Legem coram multitudine virorum & mulierum. Ex eo potissimum tempore suos ducunt Paraphrastas Judæi, qui Legis verba sermone patrio exponerent ut ab omnibus intelligerentur; nec aliunde suam duxisse originem crediderim Græcam LXX. Interpretum versionem, de quibus postea mira commenti sunt Judæi; eorumque somnia tam avidè arripuit Vossius, ut existimaverit illos solùm à Christianis audiendos esse. Tùm in Synagogis & Scholis locorum ubi lingua Græca erat vernacula, lecta est Græca illa Judæorum Alexandrinorum translatio, quæ in brevi temporis spatio ad reliquos Judæos qui Græcè loquebantur pervenit, quòd lingua Græca esset lingua dominantium. Non ideo tamen relicta est contextûs Hebraici lectio, ad cujus duntaxat auxilium veniebat Græca interpretatio. Neque id diffitebitur Vossius, qui asserat Josephum & Philonem, qui erat Alexandrinus, Hebraicè doctos fuisse. Quandonam igitur periit lingua Hebraica? An tempore Aquilæ, quem futilissimum vocat Interpretem Vossius? Verum ipse etiam agnoscit, Origenis tempore Alexandriæ, & Hieronymi ætate Tiberiade, celeberrimas fuisse linguæ Hebraicæ Scholas. Conservatas autem fuisse post Hieronymum Tiberiadis Scholas, nemo ignorat, ex quibus tandem Criticorum illorum familia, qui vulgò Masorethæ appellantur, nata est. Masoretharum autem nomen obtinuerunt, quod Masoram, seu legendi contextûs Hebraici traditionem, ab omnibus Judæis tunc receptam beneficio notarum quarumdam, seu punctorum vocalium, intra certos limites clauserunt. En traditio Judaica, cui plurimum quidem tribuit Simonius; sed à qua non totus dependet, cum non parvi etiam faciat traditionem, seu lectionem contextûs Hebraici, quam Græci Interpretes sequuti sunt. Imò eam interdum Masorethicæ præferre non dubitat, quia scilicet neque à Græcis Interpretibus, uti Vossius; neque à Latino, uti plerique Ecclesiæ Romanæ Theologi; neque à Judæis, ut turba Protestantium, præoccupato ad scribendum animo accessit.
units.tr: I would readily concede that the matters of religion, especially those doctrines that lie somewhat further from the senses, can scarcely be preserved for many centuries by oral tradition alone without writings. But concerning what they call matters of discipline and ceremonies, a quite different judgement must be made, because those things come into use almost every day. Above all, the early Fathers of the Church approve this kind of tradition with their suffrages. Now I say that the principle of languages is entirely the same: although they are dead and no longer vernacular, they still hold sway among the teachers and flourish in the schools. To this kind of tradition we refer the tradition of the Hebrew language among the Jews. From this, without doubt, it has come about that even in our own times the Samaritans have the same codices of the Mosaic Law as the Jews, apart from a few small exceptions. Finally, from this same tradition it has also arisen that the Jews, not only the Eastern and Western, agree with one another about the reading of the Hebrew text; but also those who are called Karaites among them, a name they took from this, that, rejecting the Talmud and other traditions of uncertain standing, they cling to Scripture and agree with the rest of the Jews in all points concerning the manner of reading the sacred codex. That tradition, therefore, which the Karaites, who reject most of the traditions of the Jews, embraced whole, is not to be rashly discarded. I could heap up many proofs here, drawn from Jewish books, by which they show that their forefathers had schools from the times of Zerubbabel and Ezra onward, both among the Babylonians and among the Jerusalemites; but I deliberately pass over these and other things of the same kind, because they are not to the taste of the most learned Vossius, who finds Rabbinical learning very displeasing. I am not unaware that many Jews, especially those of the class of grammarians, think that the sacred codices were not only variously scattered and wretchedly corrupted during the Babylonian exile, as Rabbis Kimchi and Ephodaeus hold, but that the language was also almost lost. And the Jews who belong to the sect of the Karaites agree with them. For thus Aaron ben Joseph, the most learned Karaite, writes on this subject: The Israelites were exiles from their land into a foreign one, and the vision and prophecy were sealed up, and it was a little short of the Hebrew language being lost. Wise Israelites arose, to whom God gave the Spirit, and they handled the Scripture, which among us comprises twenty-four books. From these things it is clear that the Hebrew language was by no means utterly buried in antiquity, although after the return of the Jews from Babylon at Jerusalem it was no longer vernacular, but was preserved only by the teachers of the Law. Thus Ezra is said, performing the office of a most skilled scribe, to have read the Law from the pulpit before a multitude of men and women. From that time especially the Jews trace their Paraphrasts, who explained the words of the Law in the native speech so that they might be understood by all; nor do I believe that the Greek version of the Seventy Interpreters had any other origin, concerning which the Jews have devised marvellous fables; and Vossius seized upon their dreams so eagerly that he thought they alone were to be heard by Christians. Then, in the synagogues and schools of places where the Greek language was vernacular, that Greek translation of the Alexandrian Jews was read, which in a short space of time reached the other Jews who spoke Greek, because the Greek language was the language of the rulers. Yet the reading of the Hebrew text was not on that account abandoned; the Greek interpretation came only as an aid to it. Nor will Vossius deny this, though he asserts that Josephus and Philo, who was an Alexandrian, were learned in Hebrew. When, then, did the Hebrew language perish? In the time of Aquila, whom Vossius calls the most worthless of interpreters? But he himself acknowledges that at Alexandria in the time of Origen, and at Tiberias in the age of Jerome, the Hebrew schools were most celebrated. That the schools of Tiberias were preserved after Jerome, no one is ignorant, and from them at last arose that family of critics who are commonly called Masorites. Now they obtained the name Masorites because they confined the Masora, that is the tradition of reading the Hebrew text, received then by all Jews, within certain limits by means of certain signs, that is the vowel points. Here is the Jewish tradition, to which Simon indeed attributes very great weight, but on which he does not wholly depend, since he also sets no small store by the tradition, or reading, of the Hebrew text, which the Greek interpreters followed. Indeed he does not hesitate sometimes to prefer it to the Masoretic reading, because he came to the task with a mind not preoccupied either by the Greek interpreters, as Vossius was, or by the Latin, as most theologians of the Roman Church were, or by the Jews, as the crowd of Protestants was.

units.la: Verùm, inquit optimus Vossius, Judæi Christiani nominis sunt inimici, adeoque ab istis peti non debuit sacri codicis lectio. Quasi verò ars aliqua ab aliis sumi posset, quàm ab illis qui artem illam tractant. Sed iterum instat Vossius, fateturque lectionem hanc à Judæis quidem petendam esse, verùm à priscis illis qui Christi tempora præcesserunt; minimè verò à recentioribus Rabbinis, qui illam penitus ignorant. Et in hoc etiam cum Vossio consentit Simonius, quòd traditionem lectionis Hebraicæ sumat quoque ab illis antiquis Judæis; in hoc verò ab eo discedit, quòd non ab iis solùm, sed & ab Aquila, Symmacho, Theodotione, Hieronymo aliisque omnibus Interpretibus sacrarum literarum hauriendam illam esse putaverit: quia nimirum ars quælibet ex uno aut altero perfici nequit, sed ex omnibus simul collectis. Nullius Magistri legibus addictum se profitetur Simonius; negat ex vulgaribus Grammaticorum regulis perfectam haberi posse linguæ Hebraicæ cognitionem, quia sunt specialiores, & intra angustos nimiûm præceptionum limites clauduntur. Censet præterea ad vetustos recurrendum esse Interpretes exemplo Hieronymi, qui non modo ætatis suæ Magistros consuluit; sed & modò LXX. Interpretes, modò Aquilam, modò Theodotionem & quemlibet alium sequitur, cujus interpretatio sibi videatur commodior. De nova instituenda versione, etiam ætate nostrâ, quæ cæteras omnes superet, non desperat. Neque enim verum est, ut sæpius inculcat Vossius, unum duntaxat Hieronymum à LXX. Interpretibus recedere ausum fuisse. Imò reliquos Patres sæpius videas ad Aquilæ, vel Theodotionis, vel Symmachi versiones recurrere, quòd hæ meliorem interdum sensum pariant. Longiùs profectò recedunt à Vossio, qui putet sublatis LXX. Interpretibus simul quoque tolli omnem quæ superest linguæ Hebraicæ cognitionem; absque que illis ne unum quidem verbum rectè exponi posse; Aquilam & alios Interpretes peccâsse ubicunque à vetere recesserunt versione; illum futilissimum esse Interpretem, qui ex Græca tantùm LXX. Seniorum translatione Hebraicè doctus non novas potestates vocibus Hebraicis affinxerit, sed eas solùm retinuerit significationes à Græcis illis interpretationibus positas, diverso tamen ordine, & alias notiones aliis locis accommodans. Istum tamen Aquilam, cujus versionem plenam futilibus vocabulis affirmat Vossius, haud infrequenter laudavit Origenes, qui de Aquila loquitur tanquam de homine qui verborum proprietates investigans, eorumque significationibus diligenter inhærens, eadem aptissimè interpretari studuerit. ὁ κυφιώτατος ἑρμηνεύειν φιλομαθὴς Ἀκύλας. Si autem eadem Aquila linguæ Hebraicæ notiones diversis locis diversâ tantùm ratione applicuerit, expendenda sunt illa loca, judicandumque an rectè ab illis Interpretibus discesserit. Constat Hieronymum aliquando prætulisse Aquilam LXX. Senioribus, quòd hi Judæis favere sibi viderentur. Similiter Origenes putavit Aquilam locis compluribus dictiones contextûs Hebraici convenientius expressisse quàm LXX. nec ab eo dissentit Theodoretus. Commentum igitur est quod fingit Vossius, inter omnes scilicet antiquos Christianos neminem fuisse cui non majus Hebraicæ veritatis lumen affulserit, quàm omnibus seculi nostri Rabbinis & Semi-Rabbinis Christianis: nam ut optimè à Ludovico Cappello annotatum fuit, nihil est simul cœptum & perfectum. Septuaginta Interpretum translatio ab Aquila, Symmacho, Theodotione & ab Hieronymo emendata est, & quotidie emendatur, non secus ac Hieronymiana, à viris Græcè & Hebraicè doctis. Illa reliquis Scripturæ Sacræ versionibus in eo solùm præstat, quòd prima sit omnium translationum, à qua proinde qui postea sequuti sunt Interpretes non pauca ad instituti sui rationem hauserint. Nec dubito quin Philonis tempore, Alexandriæ aliisque locis ubi floruit lingua Græca, dictionum Hebraicarum Lexica extiterint sumpta ex versione LXX. Interpretum. His etiam adjutum fuisse Aquilam in cudenda nova sua translatione non inficias ierim: sed ut credam illum qui ab Origene, Hieronymo aliisque Patribus diligentissimi Interpretis cognomentum reportavit, Judæos ætatis suæ non consuluisse, vix adduci possum; & ut ita sentiret Vossius non aliunde permotus fuisse videtur, quàm ex præsumpta opinione, solos nimirum audiendos esse LXX. Interpretes, quibuscum linguæ Hebraicæ cognitio sepulta fuerit. Id omne quod in Aquilam regerit Vossius, de Hieronymo etiam dici potest, quem tamen constat Doctores Judæos ætatis suæ in condenda versione sua ex Hebræo in Latinum sæpius consuluisse, imò & ab istis sæpius quàm à Græcis Interpretibus dependere voluisse. Ubique enim testatur in operibus suis Hieronymus, se à doctissimis Judæorum Magistris ætatis suæ institutum fuisse. Similis est prorsus Aquilæ ratio, quem contentiosum aliquando appellat Interpretem idem Hieronymus, quòd dictionibus Hebraicis pressius adhærens, verba potius quàm sensum exprimat. Unde illum κακοζηλίας quidem, seu pravæ affectationis accusat, minimè verò ignorantiæ; cùm hanc potius affectationem tribuat Origenes nimiæ illius diligentiæ. Verùm his diutius quàm par erat immorati sumus.
units.tr: But, says the excellent Vossius, the Jews are enemies of the Christian name, and therefore the reading of the sacred codex ought not to be sought from them. As if any art could be learned from others rather than from those who practise that art! But Vossius again presses the point, and admits that this reading is indeed to be sought from the Jews, but from those ancient ones who preceded the times of Christ, and by no means from the more recent Rabbis, who know it not at all. And in this too Simon agrees with Vossius, that he takes the tradition of the Hebrew reading also from those ancient Jews; but in this he departs from him, that he thought it was to be drawn not only from them but also from Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, Jerome, and all the other interpreters of the sacred letters: because, of course, no art can be perfected from one or another source, but only from all of them gathered together. Simon professes that he is bound to the laws of no master; he denies that a perfect knowledge of the Hebrew language can be had from the common rules of the grammarians, because they are too particular and are confined within the narrow limits of precepts. He thinks, moreover, that we must have recourse to the ancient interpreters, following the example of Jerome, who consulted not only the teachers of his own age, but sometimes follows the Seventy Interpreters, sometimes Aquila, sometimes Theodotion, and any other whose interpretation seems to him more suitable. He does not despair of a new version, even in our own age, that will surpass all the others. For it is not true, as Vossius repeatedly insists, that Jerome alone dared to depart from the Seventy Interpreters. Indeed you will often see the other Fathers too having recourse to the versions of Aquila, or Theodotion, or Symmachus, because these sometimes yield a better sense. Vossius surely departs much further from the truth, since he thinks that if the Seventy Interpreters are removed, all the remaining knowledge of the Hebrew language is removed with them, and that without them not even one word can be rightly explained; that Aquila and the other interpreters erred wherever they departed from the old version; and that he is a most worthless interpreter who, learned in Hebrew only from the Greek translation of the Seventy Elders, did not invent new powers for the Hebrew words but retained only the meanings those Greek renderings gave them, though in a different order, and adapted other notions to other places. Yet this Aquila, whose version Vossius asserts is full of worthless words, was praised not infrequently by Origen, who speaks of Aquila as a man who, investigating the proper senses of words and diligently adhering to their meanings, strove to translate them most aptly. Aquila, the most diligent translator, eager for learning. If, however, that same Aquila applied the senses of the Hebrew language in different places in different ways only, those passages must be weighed, and it must be judged whether he rightly departed from those interpreters. It is established that Jerome once preferred Aquila to the Seventy Elders, because the latter seemed to favour the Jews. Likewise Origen thought that Aquila had in many places expressed the words of the Hebrew text more suitably than the Seventy, and Theodoret does not differ from him. It is therefore a fiction that Vossius invents, that among all the ancient Christians there was none on whom the light of Hebrew truth did not shine more brightly than on all the Rabbis and semi-Rabbinical Christians of our age: for, as Louis Cappel has very well observed, nothing is begun and perfected at the same time. The translation of the Seventy Interpreters has been corrected by Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, and Jerome, and is corrected daily, no less than Jerome's version, by men learned in Greek and Hebrew. In this alone it surpasses the other versions of Holy Scripture, that it is the first of all translations, from which therefore those interpreters who came later drew not a few things for the purpose of their own undertaking. Nor do I doubt that in the time of Philo, at Alexandria and in other places where the Greek language flourished, lexicons of Hebrew words were drawn up from the version of the Seventy Interpreters. I will not deny that Aquila too was helped by these in forging his own new translation; but that the man who gained from Origen, Jerome and other Fathers the surname of most diligent interpreter did not consult the Jews of his own age, I can hardly be brought to believe; and Vossius seems to have been moved to think so by nothing except a presumed opinion, namely that only the Seventy Interpreters are to be heard, with whom the knowledge of the Hebrew language was buried. Everything that Vossius charges against Aquila can also be said of Jerome, who nevertheless is known to have often consulted the Jewish teachers of his age in making his version from Hebrew into Latin, and indeed to have wished to depend on them more often than on the Greek interpreters. For Jerome bears witness throughout his works that he was instructed by the most learned Jewish masters of his age. The reasoning about Aquila is entirely similar; Jerome himself calls him at one point a contentious interpreter, because, adhering too closely to Hebrew words, he expresses words rather than sense. Hence he accuses him of kakozelia, that is, of a wrong affectation, but by no means of ignorance; whereas Origen rather attributes this affectation to his excessive diligence. But we have dwelt on these matters longer than was fitting.

units.la: Nunc ad alia transit Vossius. Negat Scripturæ sensum erui posse ex codice muto, quem nec legere, nedum intelligere quisquam sciat, utpote trunco mediâ sui parte, nec aliis, quàm quas Christianæ fidei inimici appositæ, instructo vocalibus. Satis non fuit Interpretes sacri codicis traduxisse, nunc ipsosmet codices accusat Vossius. Passim & usque ad nauseam in opusculo objicit mutum esse codicem Hebræum; quasi verò LXX. Interpretum temporibus minùs mutus fuerit quàm ætate nostrâ. Hæc est nimirum Orientalium scribendi ratio, ut sectentur compendia; neque illud vitium magis cadit in sermonem Hebraicum quàm in Arabicum, Chaldaicum & Syriacum, quorum etiam scribendi ratio compendiaria est. Exemplarium quibus usi sunt LXX. Interpretes melior non fuit conditio; verum erat apud Hebræos, ut & apud reliquos Orientales, certa quædam legendi ratio usu confirmata, maximè apud Magistros, qualis etiam nunc extat. Nam etiam post inventa puncta vocalia plerique Orientalium libri absque istis editi sunt; neque tamen minùs eos legunt qui eorum linguas callent, quàm si punctis omnibus instructi editi fuissent. Samaritæ codicem suum ejusmodi punctis nunquam onerârunt, imò neque ea exhibent Judæorum exemplaria, seu volumina, quæ publico Synagogarum usui inserviunt. An ideo isti codices muti sunt? Suas quoque habent vocales Judæi quæ ab istis punctis minimè dependeant, ut & ipse Vossius non diffitetur: verùm istas Scribæ pro arbitratu suo modò adjiciunt, modò omittunt. Quare optimè animadvertit sapiens Aben Esra, vanum esse hac in parte Masoretharum laborem, qui nimis anxiè annotant quoties dictio aliqua plenè scribatur, & quoties deficiat; id est, quandoquam cum suis vocalibus repræsentetur. Scriba, inquit doctus Aben Esra, interdum scribendo exprimit dictionem plenam, interdum verò deficientem, idque causâ compendii. Si quis tum antiquos tum recentiores Interpretes inter se conferre voluerit, deprehendet ex illa vocalium præsentia vel absentia aliquid diversitatis in contextu transferendo contigisse. Neque etiam hodie hac in parte consentiunt secum invicem Judæorum Magistri, uti compluribus ostendit Simonius, qui non ob hanc causam de Judæorum codicibus detrahit; sed vitium illud, si quod sit, in linguarum Orientalium naturam rejicit. Hâc arte Doctores Mahumetani lectionem Alcorani adjectis ejusmodi notis, seu punctis vocalibus, constantem fecerunt, ne in varias partes pro cujusque arbitrio trahi posset. Laudanda est profectò Judæorum hac in parte diligentia, qui punctorum beneficio sacrorum codicum lectioni in posterùm consuluerunt. Certum est in qualibet ætate fuisse Masoram aliquam saltem apud linguæ Hebraicæ Doctores aspectabilem, quia semper certa fuit contextûs Hebraici legendi ratio; etsi illa nonnihil pro diversis ætatibus variaverit, ut ex diversarum translationum collationibus licet judicare. Quare totum istud negotium nunquam videtur intellexisse Vossius, qui scribat propter vocalium defectum eò miseros Judæos redactos fuisse inscitiæ, ut ne legere quidem scirent, nisi Hebraica verba Græcis expressa literis adscriberentur, quibus vocalium resarciretur defectus.
