Hunc scribendi morem, inquit, à Judæis acceptum, in Tetraplis & Hexaplis sequutus est Origenes, Hebraicis & Samariticiis opponens eadem Hebraica & Samaritica Græcis expressa literis, additis tantùm vocalibus, ut commodè legi possent. Mira sanè hoc loco, ut & alibi passim, commentus est doctissimus Vossius: ut enim sileam merum illud esse figmentum quod affert de contextu Hebræo qui literis Samariticiis insertus fuerit Hexaplis Origenis, nemo sanus exristimaverit Origenem haussisse à Judæis rationem exprimendi contextûs Hebraici Græcis literis; verùm ipse potiùs, ut linguæ suæ hominibus se accommodaret, verba Hebraica primùm Hebraicis literis, deinde Græcis characteribus expressit, ut etiam Hebraica legere possent qui nihil scirent Hebraicè. Judæi siquidem illis temporibus, ut & hodiernis, contextum suum absque punctis voca-
units.tr: Vossius now turns to other matters. He denies that the sense of Scripture can be drawn from a mute codex, which no one knows how to read, let alone understand, since it is mangled in its middle part and furnished with vowels only by those whom the enemies of the Christian faith have added. It was not enough for him to have criticised the translators of the sacred codex; now Vossius accuses the codices themselves. Throughout his little work, and to the point of nausea, he objects that the Hebrew codex is mute, as if it were less mute in the times of the Seventy interpreters than in our own age. This is certainly the manner of writing of the Orientals, who favour abbreviations, and this fault attaches to the Hebrew language no more than to Arabic, Chaldee and Syriac, whose way of writing is also abbreviated. The copies used by the Seventy interpreters were in no better condition. But among the Hebrews, as among the other Orientals, there was a certain established way of reading, confirmed by use, especially among the masters, and it still exists today. For even after vowel points were invented, most Oriental books have been published without them, yet those who know their languages read them no less than if they had been published with all the points. The Samaritans never burdened their codex with such points; indeed, the Jewish copies or scrolls that serve public use in the synagogues do not show them either. Are these codices therefore mute? The Jews too have their own vowels, which do not depend on these points, as Vossius himself does not deny; but scribes add or omit them at their own discretion. Hence the wise Aben Ezra rightly observed that the labour of the Masoretes in this respect is vain, since they anxiously note how often a word is written full and how often defectively, that is, whether it is represented with its vowels. "A scribe," says the learned Aben Ezra, "sometimes expresses a word by writing it in full, sometimes defectively, and that for the sake of brevity." If anyone wishes to compare the ancient and more recent translators with one another, he will find that some difference arose in transferring the text, owing to the presence or absence of vowels. Nor do the masters of the Jews agree with one another even today in this respect, as Simon has shown in many places; yet he does not on that account disparage the Jewish codices, but puts the fault, if there is one, on the nature of the Oriental languages. By this same art the Mahometan doctors made the reading of the Alcoran constant, adding such marks or vowel points so that it could not be dragged in various directions at each reader's whim. Truly the Jews' diligence in this respect deserves praise, since by means of the points they provided for the future reading of the sacred codices. It is certain that in every age there was at least some Masora visible among the doctors of the Hebrew language, since the manner of reading the Hebrew text was always fixed, although it varied somewhat in different ages, as may be judged from comparisons of various translations. Therefore Vossius never seems to have understood this whole matter, when he writes that because of the lack of vowels the unhappy Jews were reduced to such ignorance that they could not even read unless the Hebrew words were written out in Greek letters, which would make up for the lack of vowels. "This manner of writing," he says, "received from the Jews, Origen followed in the Tetrapla and Hexapla, setting the same Hebrew and Samaritan words, expressed in Greek letters, against the Hebrew and Samaritan, adding only the vowels so that they could be read conveniently." At this point Vossius has invented something truly remarkable, as he does everywhere else. For, to pass over the sheer fiction he brings forward about a Hebrew text inserted in Samaritan letters in Origen's Hexapla, no sane person would think that Origen took from the Jews the method of expressing the Hebrew text in Greek letters. Rather, to accommodate himself to the people of his own language, he expressed the Hebrew words first in Hebrew letters and then in Greek characters, so that even those who knew no Hebrew could read them. For the Jews, in those times as in ours, read their text without vowel points,

units.la: vocalibus facili negotio legebant, nec aliis adjuti literis quàm Hebraicis non solùm Rabbinorum libros legunt, sed & alia quaelibet opera diversis sermonibus concepta. Sic habent Bibliorum versiones Graecas & Hispanicas non Graecis & Hispanicis exaratas characteribus, sed Judaicis, quarum specimina aliquot hic subjiciam, ut peritiores inde judicent, an ita miseri sint Judaei, ut linguae suae dictiones exprimere nequeant nisi externarum linguarum characteribus; cum & ipsi aliarum gentium linguas Judaicis literis haud infeliciter exprimant. Ita in Graeca Pentateuchi interpretatione à Judaeis Constantinopolitanis edita, legimus Hebraicis literis, אן קיריוש ὁ Κύριος, או תאוש ὁ Θεὸς, פרוש ... ἐκεῖνη, קי ..., & alia ejusdem generis innumera, quibus Judaei quidem puncta vocalia adjiciunt, sed quae videntur inutilia; cum etiam sine his vix aliter legi possint. Eadem planè ratio est sermonis Hispanici, à quo puncta quoque vocalia possint abesse sine ullo germanae lectionis detrimento: quo pacto legimus, און איל מונטי En el monte, ואישטאר Estar, טיירד Veedi à delante de vos à la tierra, איל גרנדי ריאו El grande rio, ואישטריש פרריש A vuestros padres. Ex his manifestum est linguam quoque Hebraicam suis non carere vocalibus: possemque huc congerere alia diversarum linguarum specimina Judaicis expressa characteribus sine ullis punctis vocalibus, queque ope literarum in primis או, seu Aleph, Vau & Jod, quas vulgò lectionis matres Judaei appellant, facilè & promptè leguntur. Contigit tamen ut Scribae pro suo arbitrio, uti jam annotatum fuit, haud infrequenter vocales istas praetermiserint: unde tandem orta est non minima inter codices Bibliorum manu exaratos discrepantia, quae adhuc conspicitur in exemplaribus optimae notae, longeque major erat ante criticas Masoretharum notationes, ad quas plerique codices castigantur.
units.tr: with easy effort, and aided by no letters other than Hebrew ones; they read not only the books of the Rabbis but any other works composed in various languages. So too the Greek and Spanish versions of the Bible are written not in Greek or Spanish characters but in Jewish ones. I will set out some specimens of these here, so that more skilled readers may judge whether the Jews are so wretched that they cannot express the words of their own language except in the characters of foreign tongues, since they themselves express the languages of other nations in Jewish letters, and not unsuccessfully. Thus in the Greek translation of the Pentateuch published by the Jews of Constantinople we read, in Hebrew letters, an kyrios [ὁ Κύριος], "the Lord"; o theos [ὁ Θεὸς], "God"; ... [ἐκεῖνη], "that one"; ki ..., and countless others of the same kind. To these the Jews indeed add vowel points, which seem useless, since without them the words could hardly be read otherwise. The Spanish is exactly the same case, and vowel points could be absent from it without any loss to the genuine reading. So we read, in Hebrew letters: en el monte, "on the mountain"; estar, "to be"; vedi delante de vos a la tierra, "see before you upon the earth"; el grande rio, "the great river"; a vuestros padres, "to your fathers." From these examples it is clear that the Hebrew language too is not without its own vowels. I could heap up other specimens of various languages expressed in Jewish characters without any vowel points, which are read easily and promptly by means of the letters aleph, vau and yod, which the Jews commonly call the mothers of reading. It happened, however, that the scribes, as has already been noted, not infrequently omitted these vowels at their own discretion. From this there finally arose no small discrepancy among the Bible codices written by hand, which is still seen in copies of the best quality, and was far greater before the critical notations of the Masoretes, to which most codices are now corrected.

units.la: Res etiam ista exemplo aliarum linguarum, quae Hebraicae affines sunt, Arabicae nimirum, Chaldaicae & Syriacae, potest illustrari. Non aliis dudum utuntur literis Persae & Turcae, quàm Arabicis, quas ad usum suum nationes istae accommodârunt. De Persis haec habet Texeira. Quando los Arabes entraron la Persia y la senorearon, introduxeron en ella sus characteres y modo de escrivir, al qual los Persios se applicaron y accommodaron, de suarte que olvidaron y se perdio totalmente el proprio suyo. Sed frustra his immoramur: nemo enim
units.tr: This matter can also be illustrated by the example of other languages akin to Hebrew, namely Arabic, Chaldee and Syriac. The Persians and Turks have long used no other letters than the Arabic, which those nations adapted to their own use. Texeira says this about the Persians: "When the Arabs entered Persia and ruled it, they introduced their characters and manner of writing into it, to which the Persians applied and adapted themselves, so that they forgot, and their own script was totally lost." But we linger over these things in vain, for no one is ignorant that the Persians and Turks use no characters other than Arabic, which in the matter under discussion wholly resemble the Hebrew.

units.la: Texeir. Histor. Persf. cap. 22. enim ignorat Persas & Turcas non aliis uti characteribus quàm Arabicis, qui in negotio de quo agitur Hebraicos omnino referunt. Nec quidquam ad propositum facit quod mox subjungit exemplum Vossius, petitum ex scriptis Homeri & Virgilii operibus, si vocalibus destituta ad nos usque pervenissent; quandoquidem maximum est discrimen inter linguas Græcam & Latinam, atque inter Hebraicam, Chaldaicam, Syriacam & Arabicam; cùm hæ punctis vocalibus destitutæ non idcirco vocalibus penitus destituantur. Adjicit & aliud commentum vir doctus, rationem hanc scribendi, Græcis scilicet literis, viguisse apud Judæos per annos fere mille, nempe usque ad tempus Masoretharum, qui ante sexcentos fere annos, neglectâ hâc duplici scripturâ, sequuti Syros & Arabes apices, & puncta invexêre quibus vocalium loco uterentur. Verùm inde jam ab octingentis annis scripsit R. Saadias opuscula quædam de re Grammatica, ex quibus constat etiam ante illa tempora ejusmodi puncta vocalia Bibliorum codicibus adjecta fuisse. Quorsum meminit Masoretharum, quos punctorum inventores fuisse non diffiteor, cùm & ipsi diu ante Magistrum Saadiam floruerint? Verùm, inquit Vossius, adeo recentia esse puncta vel ex eo satis est manifestum, quòd nullus liber, nullumque appareat monumentum, quod quidem quingentis annis sit vetustius, in quo ista compareant. Simili ratione dixerim ante sexcentos annos nulla fuisse Hebraica Bibliorum exemplaria, quòd non inveniantur ætate nostrâ quæ majorem præferant antiquitatem: sed pudet in his refellendis, quæ apertè falsa sunt, longiùs detineri. Monumenta produxit Simonius longè antiquiora in quibus puncta compareant. Invehitur præterea in Judæos Vossius, eosque pravas & perversas vocales plerisque vocabulis aptâsse colligit ex propriis nominibus quæ in Euangeliis & in veterum Judæorum passim occurrunt monumentis; ut necesse sit, inquit vir doctus, aut ineptissimè & nullo judicio hodierna esse appósita puncta, aut Christum & Apostolos, omnesque adeò veteres Judæos, Prophetarum & proavorum ignorâsse nomina. Verùm non animadvertit optimus Vossius, illa eadem nomina hodiernis etiam temporibus à Judæis diversarum nationum diversâ ratione efferri ac scribi, si in patrium sermonem transferantur. Ea siquidem aliter scribunt Itali, aliter Hispani, & aliter Germani. Ad antiquam tum scribendi tum pronunciandi rationem magis accedunt Hispani, quia simplicior est illorum pronunciatio; Judæi verò Germani à genuina nuina tum scriptione tum pronunciatione caeteris omnibus longiùs recedunt: idque manifesto colligitur ex libris quos Italicè, vel Hispanicè, vel demum Germanicè conscripserunt, in quibus dictiones Hebraicæ diverso planè modo & aliis literis exprimuntur. Constat tamen illos hanc scriptionis diversitatem ex diversis Hebraicorum exemplarium lectionibus non hausisse. Sed pronunciationis vitium, quod ex vulgari sermone oritur, secum etiam trahit scripturę vitium; unde factum est ut plerique Hebraistarum, qui ex Grammatica Hebręa Buxtorfii Hebraicè sciunt, pravè quoque & more Germanorum dictiones Hebraicas scribant. Illud omne jam à Leone Modena verbis paucioribus annotatum fuit, qui ut genti suæ faveret, Italorum pronunciationem cæteris præfert. Nella pronuncia di essa lingua Hebrea, ait Magister ille, sono talmente poi tra di loro differenti, che à pena sono intesi; Todeschi da gl' Italiani e Levantini ne vi è chi più chiaro & conforme alle regole della vera Grammatica Favelli, che Italiani. Eamdem fuisse linguarum omnium sortem, discere possumus ex priscis Grammaticis; illudque argumentum optimè tractavit Erasmus Dialogo de rectâ Latini Græcique sermonis pronunciatione, ubi observat Maximilianum Cæsarem ab aliquot diversarum nationum oratoribus se præsente Latinè salutatum, omnes tamen qui aderant hisce orationibus credidisse nullam Latinè pronunciatam fuisse, sed vulgari quamlibet sermone. Galli orationem non malè Latinam adeo Gallicè pronunciatam fuisse testatur idem Erasmus, ut Italis aliquot eruditis qui tum aderant, Gallicè non Latinè dicere crederetur. Ad quam Galli orationem Doctor aulicus tam Germanicè respondit, ut nemo vulgari linguâ dicere potuisset magis Germanicè: in hunc enim modum exorsus est, Cæsarea Maghcstas, pene caudet fidere fos, & horationem festram lipenter audifit. Haud absimiliter Judæi Germani sermonem Hebraicum Germanicè pronunciant & scribunt, & inde maximè orta est nominum propriorum diversitas quæ in Pagnini, Munsteri, aliorumque recentiorum Interpretum versionibus deprehenditur, si cum Euangeliis & antiquioribus monumentis illa comparentur. Sed tempus est ut ad alia cum Vossio transeamus.
units.tr: Texeira, History of Persia, ch. 22. For no one is unaware that the Persians and Turks use no other characters than the Arabic ones, which in the matter under discussion wholly reproduce the Hebrew. Nor does what Vossius next adds bear on the point, the example taken from the works of Homer and Virgil, supposing they had come down to us without vowels. There is the greatest difference between the Greek and Latin languages on the one hand and the Hebrew, Chaldee, Syriac and Arabic on the other, since these, though they lack vowel points, are not for that reason entirely without vowels. The learned man adds another fiction: that this method of writing, namely with Greek letters, flourished among the Jews for nearly a thousand years, that is, until the time of the Masoretes, who about six hundred years ago, neglecting this double writing and following the Syrians and Arabs, introduced signs and points to be used in place of vowels. But already eight hundred years ago R. Saadias wrote certain treatises on grammar, from which it is clear that such vowel points had been added to the codices of the Bible even before those times. Why does he mention the Masoretes, whom I do not deny were the inventors of the points, since they too flourished long before Master Saadias? But, says Vossius, that the points are so recent is sufficiently clear from this: no book and no monument appears, at least five hundred years older, in which they occur. By a similar argument I would say that six hundred years ago there were no Hebrew copies of the Bible, because none are found in our own age which show greater antiquity. But I am ashamed to dwell longer on refuting things that are plainly false. Simonius produced far older monuments in which the points appear. Vossius moreover attacks the Jews, and infers from the proper names which occur in the Gospels and throughout the ancient Jewish monuments that they attached wrong and perverse vowels to most words: so that it must be, says the learned man, either that the present points were put in with the greatest folly and no judgment, or that Christ and the Apostles, and indeed all the ancient Jews, were ignorant of the names of the Prophets and their forefathers. But the excellent Vossius does not notice that those same names are even now pronounced and written in different ways by Jews of different nations when they are transferred into their native speech. For Italians write them one way, Spaniards another, and Germans another. The Spaniards come closer to the ancient manner of both writing and pronouncing, because their pronunciation is simpler; but German Jews depart furthest of all from the genuine writing and pronunciation. This is clearly gathered from books which they have written in Italian, in Spanish, or lastly in German, in which Hebrew words are expressed in quite a different way and with other letters. It is certain, however, that they did not derive this diversity of spelling from different readings of the Hebrew copies. But a fault of pronunciation, which arises from common speech, also brings with it a fault of writing; whence it happens that most Hebraists, who know Hebrew from Buxtorf's Hebrew Grammar, also write Hebrew words badly and in the German manner. All this was noted in a few words long ago by Leone Modena, who, to favour his own people, prefers the Italian pronunciation to all others. In the pronunciation of this Hebrew language, says that master, they differ among themselves so much that they are scarcely understood; among the Germans... there is none clearer, or more in accordance with the rules of true grammar, than among the Italians and Levantines. We can learn from the old grammarians that all languages shared this same lot, and Erasmus treated this argument excellently in his dialogue on the correct pronunciation of Latin and Greek. There he observes that when the Emperor Maximilian was greeted in Latin in his presence by orators of several different nations, all who were present nevertheless believed that nothing was pronounced in Latin, but that each spoke in his own vernacular. The same Erasmus testifies that the French orator's speech, which was not badly Latin, was so pronounced in French that some learned Italians who were present thought he was speaking French and not Latin. To that French speech a court doctor replied in German so thoroughly that no one could have spoken more German in the vernacular. For he began in this manner: Caesarean Majesty, I almost fear your gracious words, and gladly hear your speech. In much the same way German Jews pronounce and write Hebrew in German, and from this above all has arisen the diversity of proper names found in the versions of Pagninus, Münster and other more recent interpreters, when these are compared with the Gospels and older monuments. But it is time to pass on with Vossius to other matters.

units.la: Incertam esse vocum Hebraicarum expositionem propter defectum vocalium contendit vir doctus, in eaque etiam sententia Simonium esse existimat, qui etiam crediderit inde factum ut Rabbini codices Hebreos 72. facies habere affirment. Verum quidem est SimoSimonium interpretationum contextûs Hebraici diversitatem ex parte tribuisse vocalium, quæ modò adsunt, modò absunt, inconstantiæ. Sed 72. facies illas, quas codices Hebręi præse ferant, ex Judæorum opinione longè aliter explicavit; nec est profecto cur illud Judæorum pronunciatum adeo frequenter objiciat Vossius, quod non videtur intellexisse. Unus enim simplexque Scripturæ Sacræ sensus non minùs à Judæis quàm à doctissimo Vossio comprobatur. Nomine autem 72. facierum veniunt tantùm sensus allegorici, qui tot sunt, quot otiosi Magistri possunt comminisci. Commune enim est effatum non modò apud Judæos qui sunt è secta Carræorum, sed & apud Rabbanistas, quibus inest eruditionis aliquid & judicii, אין מקרא יוצא מידי פשוטו, Scripturam non abire extra sensum simplicem, seu, ut vocant, literalem, quem unicum amplexari se profitetur doctissimus Aben Esra, spretis illis 72. faciebus, seu sensibus allegoricis & Cabbalicis, quos plerique Judæorum, maximè qui incolunt regiones Orientis, sectantur. Quare Judæis ipsis illi mihi videntur ineptiores, qui ex Rabbinorum libris varia fabularum monstra congerunt, ut Doctoribus istis recutitis creent invidiam. Ejusmodi portentis pleni sunt libri Talmudis & antiqui Medraschim, seu Commentarii allegorici. Hoc sensu dicunt Magistri Mosem non esse mortuum; R. Simeonis Ben Jochai & Regis Ezechiæ temporibus visum non fuisse arcum cœlestem, quia justi erant; eo tempore quo Jonathan Paraphrasi Chaldaicæ operam dabat, aviculas super eum volitantes momento exustas fuisse. Sexcenta ejusdem generis præterea, quę Judæi sapientiores כרך הדרש, sensu allegorico dici existimant. Ad quam etiam classem revocanda sunt ea omnia quę de 72. Scripturæ faciebus commenti sunt Magistri. Cessèt itaque Vossius illis objicere veritatem constare non posse ubi adeo multiplex est sensus.
units.tr: The learned man contends that the exposition of Hebrew words is uncertain because of the lack of vowels, and he thinks Simonius holds the same opinion, who also believed that this is why the rabbis assert that Hebrew codices have seventy-two faces. It is true that Simonius attributed the variety of interpretations of the Hebrew text in part to the inconstancy of vowels, which are sometimes present and sometimes absent. But he explained those seventy-two faces which Hebrew codices display very differently from the opinion of the Jews. Nor is there any reason why Vossius should so often throw up at us that Jewish saying, which he does not seem to have understood. For a single and plain sense of Holy Scripture is approved by the Jews no less than by the most learned Vossius. By the name of the seventy-two faces are meant only allegorical senses, and there are as many of these as idle teachers can invent. For there is a common saying, not only among the Jews who belong to the sect of the Karaites but also among the Rabbanites, who have some learning and judgment: Scripture does not depart from its plain sense [אין מקרא יוצא מידי פשוטו], that is, from its literal sense, as they call it. This is the one sense the most learned Aben Ezra professes to embrace, rejecting those seventy-two faces, or allegorical and Cabbalistic senses, which most Jews, especially those who live in the regions of the East, follow. Therefore those Jews seem to me more foolish who gather from the books of the rabbis various monstrous fables, so as to create envy for those teachers who are uncircumcised. The books of the Talmud and the old Midrashim, or allegorical commentaries, are full of such portents. In this sense the teachers say that Moses did not die; that in the times of R. Simeon ben Jochai and King Hezekiah the rainbow was not seen, because they were righteous; and that at the time when Jonathan was working on the Chaldee paraphrase, little birds flying over him were burned up in an instant. Besides these there are six hundred more of the same kind, which the wiser Jews think should be called sensu allegorico, in the allegorical sense, which is the Midrash. To this same class must be assigned all that the teachers have invented about the seventy-two faces of Scripture. Vossius therefore ceased to object to them that truth cannot exist where the sense is so manifold.

units.la: Tergiversatus eodem loco vir doctus multa affert de nomine Prophetę quę sunt extra propositum planèque inutilia: quasi enim illum puduerit Græcos Interpretes Prophetis adscripsisse, illos affirmat verè Prophetas esse qui rectè Scripturas interpretantur, cùm Propheta idem sit quod Interpres, & ἑρμηνεύειν idem quod interpretari. Quasi verò de hoc Prophetię genere in præsentia agatur. Derisus fuerat à Simonio Vossius, qui rancidam de LXX. Interpretum terpretum Prophetia sententiam renovare studebat, non aliis ad id permotus argumentis, quàm ex odio illorum quos vocat Semi-Rabbinos. Quò autem tendant illa quæ verbosius comminiscitur vir acutissimus, ut ostendat non apud Græcos tantum, sed & Ægyptios somniorum, furtorum & similium interpretes vel indices appellatos fuisse Prophetas, non ita sum oculatus ut videam. Contendit etiam idolorum cultoribus Deum sæpè contulisse donum Prophetiæ. Sed quid hæc faciunt ad presens institutum? Græcam versionem divinitus inspiratam appellat, & illius auctores Spiritu Sancto aut Prophetico afflatos, earumque ℨεοπνευστίαν multis conatur adstruere. Non male igitur Simonius objecit Vossio, Prophetiam illam jampridem & ab Hieronymi temporibus à LXX. Interpretibus sublatam esse. Imponit ipse potius Simonio, cùm illum in jus vocat, quasi crediderit Stephanum Protomartyrem non Græco aut plebeio Syriaco, sed Hebraico sermone ultimam suam absolvisse concionem. Quid integrum in Euangeliis supererit, inquit vir ad superstitionem usque religiosus, si ejusmodi admittamus commenta? Verùm fingendis commentis ita assuetus est Vossius, ut nova cudere hoc loco veritus non fuerit, quę postea commentitiis rationibus refelleret. Verisimilem putavit Simonius Hieronymi opinionem, qui scripsit credibile non esse Stephanum in sua ad Judæos Hierosolymitanos concione testimonia Veteris Instrumenti aliunde produxisse quàm ex Hebręorum codicibus. De verbis concionis, quę constat sermone Syriaco expressa fuisse, non loquitur Simonius, sed de Scripturę locis quæ in illa concione à Stephano laudata sunt. Quare Vossii commentum est quod Simonio tribuit, eum existimâsse plebem tempore Apostolorum gnaram fuisse veteris linguæ Hebrææ, cùm ipse potiùs affirmet plebem Hierosolymitanam Syriacè loquutam; in Synagogis Hierosolymitanis, ubi Syriacus sermo vigebat, lectam non fuisse Legem Græcè, sed Hebraicè, cui statim adjungebatur interpretatio Syriaca, non verò Græca, uti commentus est Vossius: at de his jam suprà fusiùs dictum fuit.
units.tr: In the same place the learned man, turning aside, brings forward much about the name of Prophet which is beside the point and quite useless. As if he were ashamed that the Greek interpreters had ascribed the title of Prophets to themselves, he asserts that those are truly prophets who interpret the Scriptures correctly, since Prophet is the same as Interpreter, and [ἑρμηνεύειν] is the same as to interpret. As if this kind of prophecy were under discussion at present! Vossius had been mocked by Simonius, who tried to revive the stale opinion about the prophecy of the Seventy Interpreters, moved to it by no other arguments than by hatred of those whom he calls the Semi-Rabbis. But what that most acute man is aiming at in the many words he devises, in order to show that not only among the Greeks but also among the Egyptians those who interpreted dreams, thefts and similar things were called prophets or indicators, I am not sharp-sighted enough to see. He also contends that God has often granted the gift of prophecy to worshippers of idols. But what do these things have to do with the present subject? He calls the Greek version divinely inspired, and asserts that its authors were moved by the Holy Spirit or the prophetic breath, and he tries to establish their [θεοπνευστία] with many arguments. Simonius therefore objected to Vossius not without reason, that this prophecy was long ago, and from the time of Jerome, taken away from the Seventy Interpreters. Vossius himself rather accuses Simonius, when he summons him to court, as if he had believed that Stephen the protomartyr delivered his last sermon not in Greek or in plebeian Syriac, but in Hebrew. What will remain whole in the Gospels, says the man who is religious even to superstition, if we admit such inventions? But Vossius is so accustomed to making up fictions that he did not hesitate here to coin new ones, which he would afterwards refute with fictitious reasons. Simonius thought the opinion of Jerome probable, who wrote that it is not credible that Stephen, in his sermon to the Jerusalemites, drew the testimonies of the Old Testament from any source other than Hebrew codices. Simonius does not speak of the words of the sermon, which is known to have been delivered in Syriac, but of the passages of Scripture which Stephen cited in that sermon. Therefore it is Vossius' own invention that he attributes to Simonius the view that the common people in the time of the Apostles knew the ancient Hebrew language, when Simonius himself rather affirms that the Jerusalem populace spoke Syriac; that in the Jerusalem synagogues, where the Syriac speech flourished, the Law was read not in Greek but in Hebrew, to which a Syriac interpretation was immediately added, and not a Greek one, as Vossius has invented. But these things have already been discussed more fully above.

units.la: Iterum maligne Simonio objicit Vossius, ab eo scriptum Aristæi inter commentitia ob id repositum fuisse, quòd Judæis solenne fuerit fingere & scribere incredibilia, cùm ea quæ Moysis & Prophetarum scriptis continentur magis sint incredibilia; ac si ex eo solùm quòd Judæis solenne sit fingere incredibilia, probaverit Simonius commentitiam esse Aristæi historiam. Firmissimas & ex ipso Aristęi Aristæi opusculo desumptas rationes profert, ostenditque Philonis Herennii testimonio, quod refert Origenes, Judæos illius temporis multa confinxisse parùm verisimilia. Nec miror Vossium ejusmodi impostores cum Moyse & Prophetis conferre non dubitasse, qui jam illos inter Prophetas retulerit. Scribit tamen vir doctus in eodem opusculo, ubi, ut & fere semper, parùm consentanea loquitur, in Judæorum scriptis peregrinam rem esse veritatem, tantam infici-tiam & barbariem, tantam figmentorum copiam in iis occurrere, ut nihil verius sit illo Satyrici dicto,
units.tr: Again Vossius maliciously objects to Simonius that Simonius placed Aristeas's work among the fabrications because it was customary for Jews to invent and write incredible things, when the things contained in the writings of Moses and the Prophets are themselves more incredible. As if Simonius had proved the story of Aristeas to be fabricated merely because it is customary for Jews to invent incredible things! Simonius brings forward very firm arguments drawn from Aristeas's own little work, and he shows from the testimony of Philo Herennius, which Origen reports, that the Jews of that time invented many things that were hardly credible. I am not surprised that Vossius did not hesitate to compare such impostors with Moses and the Prophets, since he had already counted them among the Prophets. Yet the learned man writes in the same little work, where, as nearly always, he speaks inconsistently, that the truth is a stranger among Jewish writings, that there is such unbelief and barbarity, and such an abundance of fictions meets us in them, that nothing is truer than that saying of the satirist:

units.la: Ære minuto Qualiacunque volunt Judæi somnia vendunt.
units.tr: For a paltry coin the Jews will sell you whatever dreams you like.

units.la: Maligne similiter & contra mentem Simonii alia nonnulla subjungit Vossius, quibus inutile est respondere, cùm Simonii liber nunc Latinè & Gallicè omnium teratur manibus, etsi Gallica recens editio, quæque ex eo sumpta est Latina, innumeris scateat erroribus. Jam ut fortius premat Simonium Vossius, rogat unde suam de Regibus Judæorum hauserit historiam Demetrius Phalereus, si hujus ætate nulla extiterit Græca versio. Istud quoque comminiscitur Vossius, ut fingat sibi adversarium. Demetrii historiam è Græca versione quæ LXX. Senioribus vulgò tribuitur, desumptam fuisse facilè agnoscet Simonius, qui de ætate auctorum versionis illius nusquam disputat, verùm de ipsismet illius auctoribus, putatque ea quæ de illis ab Aristeo referuntur non abesse à commento. De tempore quo illa instituta & perfecta fuerit à Judæis Alexandrinis, dissentientem non habebit Simonium Vossius; sed ut credat tot fabellis quæ de illis Interpretibus vulgò circumferuntur, vix adduci potest. Suo interim fruatur judicio delicatissimus Vossius, qui somnia plusquàm Rabbinica tam avidè arripit; & quia jam factus oculatior vir doctus ad scribendum se accinxit, non solùm Moysis Pentateuchum à LXX. Interpretibus, sed & libros Historicos & Propheticos Græcè fuisse redditos nunc non dubitat, etsi olim se dubitâsse profiteatur. Gravissimę tamen sunt dubitandi rationes, in primis quę ex Josephi, Hieronymi & priscorum Judæorum testimoniis peti possunt. Negaverat Simonius verba Aristei à Vossio intellecta fuisse; nunc ad illorum qui Græcè sciunt judicium provocat vir doctus, quorum etiam decretis penitus standum esse arbitror, velimque ut ea quo-que que expendant illi judices quę ex Eusebio aliisque Scriptoribus Græcis in opus suum transtulit Vossius cum nova Gręcorum verborum translatione; adeo in omnibus novator est vir ille incomparabilis, qui iterum nova comminiscitur Origenis Hexapla, quæ nemini hactenus visa fuerint. Probabiliora sunt quæ mox subjicit de eodem Origene, qui integram LXX. Interpretum versionem & fideliter descriptam Hexaplis suis inseruerit; non vero locis aliquot immutatam, uti suspicatur Simonius. Licet tamen suspicari cum Simonio, Origenem Gręcam interpretationem, quę ipsomet teste innumeris erroribus tunc referta erat, ita integram non restituisse, quin plura loca sub prætextu castigationis immutaverit, quandoquidem non eam solum ad probatos versionis illius codices recognovit, sed & ad Hebraeos, & Aquilę, Symmachi, Theodotionis aliorumque translationes. Quod vix assequi potuit, quin antiquam illam versionem in multis vitiârit, maximè cum Origenes veritatem Hebraicam longè pluris æstimaverit quàm putat Vossius, si credamus Hieronymo, qui ingenium doctissimi illius Patris probè noverat.
units.tr: Vossius likewise adds several other remarks, maliciously and contrary to Simonius's meaning, to which it is pointless to reply, since Simonius's book is now in everyone's hands in Latin and French, although the recent French edition, and the Latin one taken from it, teem with countless errors. Now, to press Simonius harder, Vossius asks where Demetrius Phalereus got his history of the kings of the Jews, if no Greek version existed in his time. Vossius also invents this, so as to make up an opponent for himself. Simonius will readily recognise that Demetrius's history was taken from the Greek version commonly attributed to the Seventy Elders, and he nowhere disputes the date of the authors of that version, but he does think that what Aristeas reports about those authors is not free of fable. Vossius will not disagree with Simonius about the time when that version was produced and completed by the Alexandrian Jews; but he can scarcely be brought to believe the many fables that are commonly circulated about those translators. Meanwhile let the most fastidious Vossius enjoy his own judgment, he who so eagerly seizes on dreams more than Rabbinic; and because, now made more clear-sighted, the learned man has girded himself to write, he now does not hesitate to say that not only the Pentateuch of Moses but also the historical and prophetical books were rendered into Greek by the Seventy translators, although he once professed that he had doubts. Yet there are very serious grounds for doubt, above all those which can be drawn from the testimony of Josephus, Jerome, and the early Jews. Simonius had denied that Vossius had understood the words of Aristeas; now the learned man appeals to the judgment of those who know Greek, whose decisions I think must also be fully accepted, and I wish that those judges would also weigh what Vossius has carried over into his work from Eusebius and other Greek writers, together with his new translation of the Greek words; so thoroughly is that incomparable man an innovator in everything, who again invents new Hexapla of Origen, which no one has seen up to now. More probable are the things he next adds about the same Origen, that Origen inserted the entire version of the Seventy translators, faithfully copied, into his Hexapla, and did not change it in some places, as Simonius suspects. Yet one may suspect with Simonius that Origen did not restore the Greek version, which by his own testimony was then full of countless errors, so entire, but that he changed many passages under the pretext of correction, since he revised it not only by the approved manuscripts of that version but also by the Hebrew text and the translations of Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion and others. Having done this, he could hardly avoid spoiling that ancient version in many places, especially since Origen valued the Hebrew truth far more highly than Vossius thinks, if we believe Jerome, who knew well the mind of that most learned Father.

units.la: rat. De Adamantio autem, inquit Hieronymus, sileo, qui cùm in Homiliis suis quas ad vulgum loquitur communem editionem sequatur, in Tomis, id est, in disputatione majori, Hebraicâ veritate stipatus & suorum circumdatus agminibus, interdum peregrinæ linguæ quærit auxilia. Aliter igitur se habuit Origenes cum hominibus eruditis, aliter cum imperita multitudine, &, ut aiunt, cum paucis sapiens ea quæ multorum erant loquebatur. His consentiunt quæ scribit adversus Celsum: postquàm enim ex libro Exodi produxit nonnulla secundùm vulgata Græcæ versionis exemplaria, statim contextûs Hebraici lectionem subjicit cum hac animadversione: ᾿Αλλὰ τοῦτο μὲν ᾧ ἐξηγόμεθα πως ἐναι δοκεῖν, ἢ ἐν τῷ τὰ πολλὰ ἀκριβῶ. Sed hæc quæ videntur esse curiosiora, nec satis apta vulgi auribus, &c. Errat itaque vir doctus, qui existimat Origenem non alios probâsse codices quàm Græcos LXX. Interpretum. Ignorat œconomiæ illius leges quas plerique Patrum, in primis Origenes, sequuti sunt, ut jam receptis à multitudine opinionibus se accommodarent. Quam etiam Origenis œconomiam, seu prudentiam, imitantur ętate nostrâ præstantissimi Ecclesiæ Romanæ Theologi, qui usum Latinæ editionis populo concedentes, veritatis Hebraicę cognitionem sibi reservant. Quia portentosis Aristæi de LXX. Interpretum versione sermonibus fidem non habet Simonius, causam reddere conatus cur illa LXX. Senioribus attributa fuerit, testatur se ad eorum sententiam accedere, qui putant à LXXII. Synedrii Hierosolymitani Senatoribus, qui hanc suffragiis suis & auctoritate comprobârunt, nomen istud reportâsse. Nihil tamen affirmat, sed de re tam obscura & à nostris temporibus ita aliena conjecturam facit: in eum tamen modestè sentientem acriter insurgit Vossius, rogatque si ab universo approbata fuerit Synedrio Græca illa interpretatio, quî fieri potest ut mendosa minimèque exacta fuerit; ac si necesse fuerit ut auctoritas Synedrii magni, quam versioni illi accessisse suspicatur Simonius, ut publicè in Synagogis & Scholis legeretur, hanc ab omni prorsus errore eximere debuerit? Non major illi ἀνθενλία ex Senatorum Hierosolymitanorum decreto accedere potuit, quàm Latinæ editioni tributa est, postquàm Tridentini Patres illam Constitutione suâ fecerunt authenticam. An idcirco Latinus Interpres à mendis quibus antea scatebat repurgatus fuit? Minimè. In hoc etiam decreti utriusque videtur maxima paritas, quòd sicut in Occidentis Ecclesia ex linguarum Græcæ & Hebraicæ ignorantia factum est ut Biblia sermone Latino conversa & lecta fuerint; ita etiam linguæ Hebraicæ apud Judæos Hellenistas imperitia fecit ut Judæi Alexandrini sacros codices in usum suum Græcè verterint, quę deinde translatio Græca apud omnes Judæos qui Græcè sciebant obtinuit, eaque forsan à Senatoribus Hierosolymitanis approbata: dixi forsan, quia opus non est ad illorum auctoritatem recurrere, ut ratio exponatur cur versio ista LXX. Senioribus attributa fuerit; sed observanda tantùm est loquutio Judæis admodùm familiaris, quâ res omnes quæ alicujus momenti sibi esse videntur, referre soleant לאנשי כנסת הגדולה, ad viros Synagogæ magnæ. Quod genus loquutionis plurimos eosque eruditissimos in varios errores perduxit, dum Judæorum libros non satis cautè evolvunt: cùm non tam quid loquantur Magistri, quàm quomodo & quibus de causis ita loquantur animadvertendum sit. Ita plerique Rabbini contendunt sacri codicis apices & alia similia suam ducere originem à viris Synagogæ magnæ, de more scilicet gentis suæ, non verò ex rei ipsius veritate. Hoc quoque modo Græcam versionem tributam fuisse LXX. Senioribus conjicere longè satius est, quàm Aristæi commentis cum Vossio fidem adhibere.
units.tr: But I say nothing of Adamantius, says Jerome, who, while in his Homilies, which he delivers to the common people, he follows the common edition, in his Tomes, that is, in his greater disputation, surrounded by the Hebrew truth and by crowds of his own people, sometimes seeks the aid of a foreign language. Origen therefore behaved one way with learned men and another way with the unlearned multitude, and, as they say, being wise among the few, he spoke what belonged to the many. What he writes against Celsus agrees with this: after he has quoted some passages from the book of Exodus according to the common copies of the Greek version, he at once adds the reading of the Hebrew text with this remark: But these things which seem to us somewhat more curious, and not well suited to the ears of the crowd, [Ἀλλὰ τοῦτο μὲν ᾧ ἐξηγόμεθα πως εἶναι δοκεῖν, ἢ ἐν τῷ τὰ πολλὰ ἀκριβῶς] etc. The learned man is therefore wrong who thinks that Origen approved no manuscripts other than the Greek ones of the Seventy translators. He does not know the rules of that economy which most of the Fathers, above all Origen, followed, so that they might adapt themselves to opinions already accepted by the multitude. The most outstanding theologians of the Roman Church in our own age also imitate this economy or prudence of Origen, who, while they allow the people the use of the Latin edition, keep for themselves the knowledge of the Hebrew truth. Because Simonius does not believe Aristeas's extravagant accounts of the version of the Seventy translators, he tries to give a reason why that version was ascribed to the Seventy Elders, and he states that he inclines to the opinion of those who think that the name was obtained from the seventy-two senators of the Jerusalem Synedrium, who approved this version by their votes and authority. Yet he affirms nothing, but makes a conjecture about a matter so obscure and so remote from our times. Vossius, however, fiercely attacks him even though he expresses this modestly, and asks: if that Greek translation was approved by the whole Synedrium, how can it be that it was faulty and not very accurate? And as if it were necessary that the authority of the Great Synedrium, which Simonius suspects was added to that version so that it might be publicly read in the synagogues and schools, ought to have freed it entirely from every error? No greater authority could have come to it from the decree of the Jerusalem senators than was given to the Latin edition after the Fathers of Trent made it authentic by their constitution. Was the Latin translator for that reason cleansed of the errors with which he had previously been full? By no means. In this respect there seems to be the greatest parallel between the two decisions: just as in the Western Church, through ignorance of the Greek and Hebrew languages, the Bibles translated into Latin came to be read, so also among the Hellenistic Jews, through ignorance of the Hebrew language, the Alexandrian Jews translated the sacred books into Greek for their own use; and that Greek translation then prevailed among all the Jews who knew Greek, and perhaps it was approved by the Jerusalem senators. I say "perhaps," because there is no need to appeal to their authority in order to explain why that version was ascribed to the Seventy Elders; one need only observe the manner of speaking very familiar to the Jews, by which they are accustomed to refer to all things that seem to them of any importance, to the men of the Great Synagogue [לאנשי כנסת הגדולה]. This manner of speaking has led very many, and very learned, men into various errors, when they unfold the Jewish books too carelessly; for one should consider not so much what the Masters say as how and for what reasons they say it. Thus most of the Rabbis contend that the vowel points of the sacred text and other similar things derive their origin from the men of the Great Synagogue, in accordance with the custom of their nation, and not from the truth of the matter itself. It is much better to conjecture that the Greek version was in this way also ascribed to the Seventy Elders, than to place faith in the fictions of Aristeas together with Vossius.

units.la: Displicet præterea viro docto, quòd Simonius reducere conatus tus fuerit Hellenisticam linguam à viris doctis explosam, eamque obtrudere sub nomine linguæ quæ in Synagogis potissimùm obtinebat, ac si in illis peculiaris aliqua fuerit lingua quæ nec Græca nec Hebraica fuerit, ut hâc ratione efficiat LXX. Interpretes & Græcè & Hebraicè nescivisse. Noverat profectò Simonius quid jam à Salmasio adversus linguæ Hellenisticæ defensores scriptum fuerat: sed pace viri illius docti dixerim eum de umbra asini disputantem lites de nomine tantùm concitâsse. Imperitiam Hebraici & Græci sermonis Græcis Interpretibus non tribuit Simonius, sed κακοζηλίαν tantùm, seu pravam affectationem Judæis Interpretibus familiarem, maximè in vertendis Scripturis, qui verba Hebraica dum curiosiùs & ad literam volunt exprimere, à communi magisque recepto sermone paululùm deflectunt, specialesque notiones & à vulgaribus distinctas interdum vocibus quibusdam tribuunt. Ista licet animadvertere in omnibus ferme Scripturæ Sacræ versionibus quæ à Judæis conditæ sunt, uti rectè ostendit Simonius, à quo etiam optimè annotatum fuit, Græcam LXX. Seniorum interpretationem plerisque Patribus Græcis vix intellectam fuisse, quòd illa Syriacæ vel Hebraicæ linguæ aliquid retineret: sicut translatio Hispanica Ferraræ edita quæ Judæos habet auctores, ab iis qui Hebraicè nesciunt vix legi potest, etsi Hispanicè docti sint. Id etiam in causa fuit cur antiquus Græcæ versionis Interpres Latinus non paucas dictiones Græcas malè expresserit, vim illarum non assequutus. Aliquas etiam non videtur intellexisse ipsemet Hieronymus, licet Hebraicè & Græcè doctus, dum magis ad Græca, quàm ad Hebraica unde Græca sumpta fuerant, attendit. Simonio etiam objicit Vossius, eum nescivisse quinam fuerint Hellenistæ. Fateor nescivisse antea Simonium quoque contra communem doctissimorum virorum sententiam commentus est eruditissimus Vossius, qui ut ostentet Græcam eruditionem, ἑλληνίζειν esse asserit partes Græcorum sequi, ut Ῥωμαΐζειν, Περσίζειν, Μηδίζειν, Ἀντιγονίζειν, imitari mores & ritus, aut stare à partibus Romanorum, Persarum, Medorum & Antigoni, & illis quomodocunque favere. Verùm perinde est ac si dixerim in præsenti negotio, ubi de re critica lis movetur cum Vossio, non modò Vossium esse rei criticæ peritissimum, sed & Canonicum Winsoriensem, qui Liturgiam Anglicanam in templo bellè decantet. Constat duplicis generis fuisse Judæos, & Ἀλεξανδρεῖς ἢ Ἑλλήνων distinctam stinctam fuisse ab iis Judæis qui tùm in Judæa, Samaria, Babyloniâ aliisque regionibus vicinis Syriaco utebantur sermone & Hebraicis codicibus. Illi, quia dispersi erant inter nationes quibus lingua Græca erat vernacula, Græcè etiam loquebantur, & Scripturam Græcè legebant, appellanturque in Actis Apostolorum Ἑλληνισταί. De iisdem quoque exponenda sunt hæc verba Judæorum in Euangelio Joannis: Μὴ εἰς τὴν Διασπορὰν τῶν Ἑλλήνων μέλλει πορεύεσθαι; Numquid in dispersionem Gentium iturus est? Jam Simonius quod erat instituti sui referens, asserit Græcam LXX. Interpretum versionem à Judæis maximè Hellenistis approbatam, quia Græcè callebant; secus verò à reliquis Judæis quibus lingua Græca non erat domestica, quales erant Babyloniæ, Palestinæ, Syriæ & Judææ incolæ, quibus omnibus sermo Chaldaicus sive Syriacus communis fuit. Non inficiatur tamen Simonius, etiam inter hos extitisse Hellenistas aliquot; nimirum Hierosolymis erat Synagoga Alexandrinorum, & Antiochiæ reperiebantur quoque Judæi Hellenistæ, uti constat ex Actibus Apostolorum. Cùm de contextu Hebræo tantùm & Græcâ illius interpretatione hoc loco ageretur, necesse non fuit ut Simonius extra viam currens exemplo Vossii, Judæos illos vocaret Hellenistas qui pacatiori erant animo & sine cunctatione veƈtigal pendebant, monebantque jugum à Deo impositum æquo ferendum animo, istos Græcorum partes sequutos fuisse: quasi verò etiam Hierosolymis aliisque locis ubi Judæi Hellenistarum nomine insigniti non fuerunt, nulli fuerint Judæi qui æquo animo & sine cunctatione veƈtigal penderent. Quare igitur etiam isti dicti non sunt Ἑλληνισταί seu φιλέλληνες; Verùm suâ frustratur conjecturâ Vossius, & Hellenismum ad solum non referri sermonem judicet. Modò aliquâ ratione ad hunc referatur, satis est. Hellenista quoque fuit Christus, si credamus Vossio, non quòd Græci sermonis peritus fuerit, sed quia jubet ut Cæsari detur quod est Cæsaris. Quod verò mox subjungit vir doƈtus de depravatis Judæorum codicibus dedita operâ in rebus chronologicis, non est cur iterum illud ad examen revocemus, cùm jam superiori scripto fusiùs demonstratum fuerit in hoc Vossium gravissimè allucinatum esse; nec ea similiter quæ de Danielis Prophetia etiam Judæis cognita jam quoque allata sunt, hic opus est repetere. Juvat nunc ea excutere quæ tanquam minùs commodè à LXX. Interpretibus reddita carpserat Simonius, eademque obstinato animo Vossius tuetur. Expendens verba illa primi Capitis Geneseos, Εἰς ἀρχὰς ἢ ἡμέρας, dicit Simonius ancipitem sibi videri hanc expositionem, quia vox ἀρχή, principatum & principium significat. Miratur Vossius Simonium non etiam reprehendisse vocem Hebraeam, quae & ipsa duplicem habet potestatem. Sed diligentis est Interpretis vitare amphiboliam. Locum hunc ante Simonii censuram, tanquam convenientius ab Aquila expressum quam a LXX. Interpretibus, notaverat doctissimus Origenes. Deinde animadverterat Simonius ad haec verba Capitis 3. Geneseos, Ἐπικαλῶ ἐχθρὸς οὖ ὑπὸ πάντων τῶν ζῴων, praepositionem ὑπὸ huic loco non convenire, nec videri ullum constituere sensum: at longe perspicacior Vossius non potuisse locum hunc melius & exactius reddi contendit, nullumque esse Graecum Scriptorem qui non sic loquatur. Graeca quidem esse haec verba, & praepositionem Hebraicam בְּ recte exprimi per Graecam ὑπό, non inficias ierit Simonius; verum quaestio est, utrum hoc loco, ubi de comparativo agitur, uti loquuntur Grammatici, illa praepositio per Graecam ὑπὸ bene reddita fuerit. Graecus Scriptor appositisset ὑπὲρ ubi saepius LXX. & Aquila vertunt ὑπό. Tertio ad idem Caput conjecerat Simonius, pro πεψόμ & πεψόσεις legendum τεψόμ & τεψόσεις. Sed delicatior Vossius hoc non esse Graecum objicit, quia non dicitur τέψω, sed πίψω, unde futurum πεψῶ. Minus tamen delicatus Grotius futurum τεψόσω non improbavit, quod etiam legit Complutensis editio. Praeterea a τείψω non modo fieri in futuro πεψῶ, sed & πέψω nõrunt Grammaticorum filii. Caetera, quia sunt ejusdem generis & parvi momenti, visum est praetermittere, ne minutiora consectari videar. Silere tamen non possum quod peritus naupegus Vossius annotat ad haec verba Capitis 6: 14. Geneseos, Ποίησον σεαυτῷ κιβωτὸν ἐκ ξύλων τετραγώνων, Fac tibi arcam ex lignis quadratis. Negat, contra mentem Simonii, ex asseribus aut tabulis ullum construi navigium, sed ex arboribus quadratis aedificari, quae aptissimae sunt fabricae navali, utpote quae materiem & simul resinam seu picem ad unguendas exhibeant naves. Quadratas illas arbores quales fingit Vossius, cedrum videlicet, abietem, piceam, pinum & sapinum, construendis navibus aptissimas esse facile crediderim; sed cur neget illas deinde aedificari ex plancis, sive asseribus, ad costas ligneas applicatis, minime assequor. Nunc ad alia quae majoris sint momenti veniamus.
units.tr: The learned man is also displeased that Simonius tried to restore the Hellenistic language, which learned men have long rejected, and to pass it off as the language that chiefly prevailed in the synagogues, as if there were among them some peculiar language that was neither Greek nor Hebrew, so that by this reasoning he could show that the Seventy translators knew neither Greek nor Hebrew. Simonius certainly knew what Salmasius had already written against the defenders of the Hellenistic language, but with all respect to that learned man, I would say that Simonius, in disputing about a shadow of an ass, merely stirred up quarrels over a name. Simonius does not attribute to the Greek translators any ignorance of the Hebrew or Greek language, but only κακοζηλίαν [kakozēlia], that is, a perverse affectation familiar to the Jewish translators, especially in rendering the Scriptures. In wishing to express the Hebrew words more carefully and literally, they depart somewhat from common and more accepted usage, and sometimes attach special meanings to certain words that differ from the ordinary ones. This can be observed in nearly all the versions of Holy Scripture made by Jews, as Simonius rightly shows, and he also noted very well that the Greek version of the Seventy elders was scarcely understood by most of the Greek Fathers, because it retained something of the Syriac or Hebrew language. The same is true of the Spanish translation printed at Ferrara, which has Jews as its authors: those who do not know Hebrew can hardly read it, even if they are learned in Spanish. This also explains why the ancient Latin translator of the Greek version rendered not a few Greek expressions badly, failing to grasp their force. Some of them, it seems, were not understood even by Jerome himself, though he was learned in Hebrew and Greek, since he paid more attention to the Greek than to the Hebrew from which the Greek had been taken. Vossius also objects to Simonius that he did not know who the Hellenists were. I admit that Simonius did not know this before, but the very learned Vossius has devised something contrary to the common opinion of the most learned men. In order to display his Greek learning, he asserts that ἑλληνίζειν [hellēnizein] means to follow the party of the Greeks, as Ῥωμαΐζειν [rhōmaizein], Περσίζειν [persizein], Μηδίζειν [mēdizein] and Ἀντιγονίζειν [antigonizein] mean to imitate the manners and customs of the Romans, Persians, Medes and Antigonus, or to take the side of the Romans, Persians, Medes and Antigonus and favour them in whatever way. But this is just as if, in the present business, where the dispute with Vossius concerns a critical matter, I were to say that Vossius is not only most skilled in critical learning but also a canon of Windsor who sings the Anglican liturgy finely. It is established that there were two kinds of Jews, and that the Ἀλεξανδρεῖς [Alexandreis] or Ἑλλήνων [Hellēnōn] were distinguished from those Jews who, at that time, in Judea, Samaria, Babylonia and other neighbouring regions, used the Syriac speech and Hebrew codices. Because the former were scattered among nations whose native tongue was Greek, they also spoke Greek and read the Scripture in Greek, and in the Acts of the Apostles they are called Ἑλληνισταί [Hellēnistai]. These words of the Jews in John's Gospel must also be explained of the same people: Μὴ εἰς τὴν Διασπορὰν τῶν Ἑλλήνων μέλλει πορεύεσθαι; [Mē eis tēn diasporan tōn Hellēnōn mellei poreuesthai?] "Is he about to go to the dispersion of the Greeks?" Now Simonius, keeping to his purpose, asserts that the Greek version of the Seventy translators was approved chiefly by the Jews who were Hellenistae or φιλέλληνες [philhellēnes], since they knew Greek, but not by the other Jews, to whom Greek was not the native tongue, such as the inhabitants of Babylonia, Palestine, Syria and Judea, among whom the Chaldee or Syriac speech was common. Yet Simonius does not deny that some Hellenists existed among these as well: Jerusalem indeed had a synagogue of the Alexandrians, and Antioch also had Hellenist Jews, as is clear from the Acts of the Apostles. Since at this point only the Hebrew text and its Greek translation were under discussion, there was no need for Simonius, running beyond the path, to imitate Vossius and call those Jews Hellenists who were of a more peaceable spirit and paid tribute without hesitation, and who advised that the yoke imposed by God should be borne with an even mind, as if these had followed the party of the Greeks. As if, indeed, there were no Jews at Jerusalem or elsewhere, where Jews were not given the name of Hellenists, who bore the tribute with an even mind and without hesitation! Why, then, are these men not also called Ἑλληνισταί [Hellēnistai] or φιλέλληνες [philhellēnes]? Vossius, however, is disappointed in his conjecture, and he judges that the word Hellenism does not refer solely to language. It is enough that it be referred to this in some way. Christ also was a Hellenist, if we believe Vossius, not because he was skilled in the Greek language, but because he commands that Cæsari detur quod est Cæsaris ["render to Caesar what is Caesar's"]. As for what the learned man next adds about the corrupted codices of the Jews, deliberately made in chronological matters, there is no reason to call it up again for examination, since it has already been shown at length in my earlier writing that Vossius was most grievously mistaken in this. Nor is there any need to repeat here what has been brought forward about the prophecy of Daniel, which was also known to the Jews. It is now worth examining the points that Simonius criticised as rendered rather inappropriately by the Seventy translators, and that Vossius defends with stubborn spirit. Considering the words of the first chapter of Genesis, Εἰς ἀρχὰς ἢ ἡμέρας [Eis archas ē hēmeras], Simonius says that this rendering seems doubtful to him, because the word ἀρχή [archē] signifies both principatum [sovereignty] and principium [beginning]. Vossius marvels that Simonius did not also reprehend the Hebrew word, which itself has a double meaning. But it is the mark of a careful translator to avoid amphiboliam [ambiguity]. Before Simonius's criticism, the most learned Origen had noted this passage, observing that it was expressed more fittingly by Aquila than by the Seventy translators. Then Simonius observed, on the words of Genesis chapter 3, Ἐπικαλῶ ἐχθρὸς οὖ ὑπὸ πάντων τῶν ζῴων [Epikalō echthros hou hypo pantōn tōn zōiōn], that the preposition ὑπὸ [hypo] does not suit this place, nor does it seem to yield any sense at all. But the far more perceptive Vossius contends that this passage could not have been rendered better and more exactly, and that there is no Greek writer who does not speak in this way. Simonius will not deny that these words are Greek and that the Hebrew preposition בְּ [beth] is correctly rendered by the Greek ὑπό [hypo], but the question is whether, in this place, where a comparative is in view (as the grammarians speak), that preposition has been well rendered by the Greek ὑπό. A Greek writer would have used ὑπὲρ [hyper], where the Seventy and Aquila more often translate by ὑπό. Thirdly, on the same chapter, Simonius had conjectured that for πεψόμ and πεψόσεις one should read τεψόμ and τεψόσεις. But the more fastidious Vossius objects that this is not Greek, because one does not say τέψω but πίψω, whence the future is πεψῶ. Grotius, however, who was less fastidious, did not disapprove of the future τεψόσω, which the Complutensian edition also reads. Moreover, from τείψω there comes not only the future πεψῶ, but also, as the sons of the grammarians say, πέψω. The rest, since it is of the same kind and of little importance, I have decided to pass over, lest I seem to hunt after trifles. Yet I cannot be silent about what the skilful sailor Vossius notes on the words of Genesis 6:14, Ποίησον σεαυτῷ κιβωτὸν ἐκ ξύλων τετραγώνων [Poiēson seautō kibōton ek xylōn tetragōnōn], Fac tibi arcam ex lignis quadratis ["Make yourself an ark of squared timbers"]. Contrary to Simonius's view, he denies that any vessel is built from planks or boards, but says it is constructed from square trees, which are most suitable for shipbuilding, since they supply both timber and resin or pitch for smearing ships. I could easily believe that those square trees, of the kind Vossius imagines, namely cedar, fir, spruce, pine and larch, are most suitable for building ships. But I cannot at all see why he denies that they were then built up from plancis [planks], or boards, fitted to wooden ribs. Now let us come to other matters of greater importance.

units.la: Denique, ut finem dicendi faciam, Vossius maligno adversus SimoSimonium animo invidiam illi creare conatur, dum eum parem facit Spinosę Judęo in iis quę habet de incertitudine Scriptorum Veteris Testamenti. Mox tamen, seipsum veluti castigans Vossius, fatetur ingenuè merito damnatum à Simonio Spinosam velut indoctum & futilibus nimium argumentis quoscunque ferè S. Scripturę libros abjudicantem ab illis quibus semper attributi fuère auctoribus. Verùm indoctiores ipso Spinosâ se ostendunt, qui libros Scripturæ Sacræ statim tribuendos iis esse existimant quorum nomina præferunt. Damnanda quidem Spinosæ malignitas ; sed non statim ea omnia quæ habet de sacris Scriptoribus damnanda sunt, quòd in aliquibus cum viris pietate & eruditione conspicuis consentiat. Verùm cùm hac in parte Simonius non solùm doctissimo Vossio displicuerit, sed & viris haud inferioris notę, qui nihil non virulenti adversus illius Criticam Sacram evomuerunt, juvat hoc argumentum fusiùs texere.
units.tr: Finally, to bring my discussion to a close: Vossius, with ill will toward Simonius, tries to make him odious by putting him on a level with the Jew Spinoza in what he says about the uncertainty of the Old Testament writings. Soon afterward, however, Vossius seems to correct himself and frankly admits that Spinoza, who was rightly condemned by Simonius, is an unlearned man who, on rather feeble arguments, denies almost all the books of Holy Scripture to the authors to whom they have always been ascribed. Yet those who think that the books of Holy Scripture must at once be assigned to the men whose names they bear show themselves more unlearned than Spinoza himself. Spinoza's malice deserves condemnation, but not everything he says about the sacred writers must be condemned at once, since on some points he agrees with men distinguished for piety and learning. But since on this point Simonius has displeased not only the most learned Vossius but also men of no lesser standing, who have poured out everything venomous against his Critical Sacred, it is worth treating this subject at greater length.

units.la: Displicuit in primis beatulis istis & delicatulis id omne quod scripsit Simonius de publicis gentis Hebraicæ Notariis, quos cum Josepho & quibusdam Ecclesiæ Patribus vocat Prophetas, qui non solùm res gestas suis temporibus chartę commendabant, sed & ea quæ à prioribus Prophetis scripta fuerant servabanturque in scriniis publicis, recognoscebant, eâdem fermè ratione quâ Esdras post Judęorum è Babylone reditum sacros codices recognovisse, & illi quam nunc obtinent formæ restituisse, vulgò tum à Judæis tum à Christianis creditur. Nihil est in hac Simonii assertione quod non à plerisque Patribus iisdemque doctissimis approbatum fuerit. Adeatur unius Theodoreti, præstantissimi Ecclesię Orientalis Theologi, Præfatio in libros Regum, ubi totum istud negotium explicat, liberèque ac nullatenùs dubitans asserit complures apud Hebræos fuisse Prophetas, quorum unusquisque scribere consueverit quæ suę erant ætatis ; partem maximam librorum qui ab ipsis conscripti sunt nunc desiderari, idque disci ex Paralipomenon historia. Addit illos quos nunc vocamus libros Regum, ex scriptis illis longo post tempore desumptos fuisse. Theodoreto consentiunt Diodorus, Procopius & alii non pauci. Similiter doctissimus Masius, quem sequuti sunt Pererius, Sanctius, Cornelius à Lapide aliique Jesuitæ in libris sacris diu multùmque versati, quorum rum verba hic afferre non est operę pretium, cùm illorum libri omnibus sint obvii. Verùm ut res ista fiat illustrior, in singulos Scripturæ Sacræ libros speciatim incurrere forsan non erit à proposito alienum.
units.tr: Above all, those pious and delicate men took offence at everything Simonius wrote about the public scribes of the Hebrew nation, whom, with Josephus and certain Fathers of the Church, he calls prophets. These scribes not only committed the deeds of their own times to writing, but also reviewed the writings of the earlier prophets, which were kept in public archives, in much the same way as, commonly believed by Jews and Christians alike, Ezra after the return of the Jews from Babylon reviewed the sacred codices and restored them to the form they now have. There is nothing in this assertion of Simonius that has not been approved by most of the Fathers, and by the most learned of them. Let one consult the Preface of Theodoret, the outstanding theologian of the Eastern Church, on the Books of Kings, where he explains this whole matter and, freely and without any doubt, asserts that there were many prophets among the Hebrews, each of whom was accustomed to write what belonged to his own age; that the greater part of the books written by them is now lost, and that this is known from the history of the Chronicles. He adds that the books we now call Kings were drawn from those writings after a long time. Diodore, Procopius and not a few others agree with Theodoret. Likewise the very learned Masius, whom Pererius, Sanctius, Cornelius à Lapide and other Jesuits who have long and deeply studied the sacred books have followed. It is not worth while to quote their words here, since their books are available to everyone. But to make the matter clearer, it may not be out of place to go through the individual books of Holy Scripture one by one.

units.la: Primus in aciem prodibit Moyses, quem quinque librorum Legis auctorem esse constans est tam Judæorum quàm Christianorum traditio. In eo tamen religiosiores fuisse videntur Judæorum Magistri, qui ne quidem dictionem unam, imò nec syllabam, extare in Lege contendunt, quæ à Deo profecta non fuerit & Moysi dictata; secus Christianorum plerique, qui aliqua libris Moysis vel ab Esdra, vel ab aliis qui eos recognoverunt, longo post tempore adjecta fuisse liberè affirmant. Nec ipse Hieronymus singula Pentateuchi verba, qualis nunc extat, Moysi tribuere ausus est, sequutus hac in re communem Doctorum Ecclesiæ sententiam, qui Legem universam ab Esdra Scriba peritissimo recensitam recognitamque fuisse constanter asseverant. Sive Moysem dicere volueris, inquit Hieronymus, auctorem Pentateuchi, sive Esdram ejusdem instauratorem, non recuso. Verùm utrùm Moyses ipse eam quam sub ejus nomine habemus historiam totam literis mandárit, vel ex parte à Notariis illis qui res ætatis suæ conscribebant, chartis excipi jusserit, major est difficultas. Tamen in quamcunque partem res cadat, Moyses totius Legis auctor & scriptor censebitur, ut optimè à Simonio jam annotatum fuit, quia Scribæ illi, si qui jam à Moysis tempore extiterunt, ab eo in omnibus pendebant. Nihil quidem in universa Lege reperias, quod ejusmodi Scribarum auctoritatem stabiliat. Sed nisi jam ab illis temporibus ab ipso Mose constituti fuissent, aliquid Hebræorum Reipublicæ defuisset, quo nec Ægyptii, nec aliæ Orientis nationes caruêre. Jam à Moysis temporibus fuisse apud Hebræos Annalium scriptores, Sanctius Jesuita doctissimus non dubitavit asserere his verbis. Sentio fuisse in superioribus seculis verba dierum, Commentarios, Ephemerides & curam diligentem & sedulam, ne obscuraretur temporum oblivione quos quisque natales & posteros haberet: quod à tempore Moysis mihi videtur omnino certum. Parco recensendis aliorum nominibus qui eadem sentiunt. Miror tamen nuperum Scriptorem ex ordine Seraphicorum zelo plusquàm Seraphico accensum, sententiam hanc in Disquisitionibus Biblicis tanquam impiam damnâsse, illiusque auctoribus dira imprecatum. Verùm, ut audio, Seraphicus ille Doctor, cùm nihil sciat Hebraicè neque Græcè, audacissimæ tamen est inscitiā, & ex eorum secta qui quæ- cunque ignorant, blasphemant. Offendit prætera nonnullos, & fortasse delicatulum Vossium, in Critica Sacra Simonius, quòd aliqua libris Moysis postea adjecta fuisse affirmaverit. Sed non etiam hac in re novator est Simonius, qui consentientes sibi habet peritissimos Scripturæ Sacræ Interpretes Masium, Pererium-que, qui hujus verba fere integra in Præfationem suam in Genesim transtulit, Bonfrerium, Cornelium à Lapide, & alios bené multos. Placet etiam mihi, inquit Pererius, eorum sententia, qui existimant Pentateuchum longo post Mosem tempore interjectis multifariàm verborum & sententiarum clausulis, veluti sarcitum & explicatiùs redditum, & ad continuandam historiæ seriem melius esse dispositum. Simili ratione Bonfrerius expendens verba quædam Geneseos quæ suspicatur à Moyse scribi non potuisse, hæc habet: Malim dicere aliquem alterum Scriptorem Hagiographum nonnulla postea addidisse, quàm Moysi Prophetam agenti omnia adscribere. Haud absimiliter ad eundem locum Cornelius à Lapide ait: Hæc verba videntur addita post Mosem ab eo qui Moysis diaria digessit. Quid quòd & ipsemet D. Huetius Spinosæ objicienti libris Mosis nonnulla assuta fuisse, ita respondet ut ab eo vix discedere videatur. Fatemur, inquit, Scripturæ reparatorem Esdram, sicubi se darent obscuriores aut difficiliores loci, huc & illuc de suo nonnulla in libros sanctos explicationis causâ infarsisse. Præterea, cùm tot disputationibus propagati sint codices sacri, ut nullius unquam libri tot exstiterint exemplaria, quid mirum, si quod aliàs sæpè evenit, factum hic quoque sit, & adtexta ad oram à viris piis ac doctis notæ, in ipsum forte contextum irrepserint? Denique illa quæ ad calcem Deuteronomii habentur de Moysis morte & sepultura à Josua, vel potiùs à Synedrii magni Senatoribus, quorum dux fuit Josue, reliquo contextui vulgò creduntur adjecta. Ea siquidem quæ tunc gerebantur in Acta publica referri mos erat ab iis quorum fuit illa describere; quo sensu dicitur Josue nonnulla scripsisse in volumine Legis Domini, fœdus scilicet quod cum populo percusserat. Multa quidem in ipsomet Pentateucho extant quæ Legis libros à Moyse scriptos fuisse manifestè ostendunt: sic in Exodo legimus, Scripsit Moyses universos sermones Domini: & in Deuteronomio, Postquam ergo scripsit Moyses verba Legis. Sed hæc & alia ejusdem generis complura de quibusdam tantùm Legis partibus, bus, quarum in his locis fit mentio, exponenda esse demon- stravit Simonius: unde & Hieronymus Oleaster, vir Hebrai-cè doctus & in sacris literis apprimè versatus, negat posse ex Scripturis probari efficacissimè Moysem ipsum Legis quam sub ejus nomine habemus Scriptorem fuisse. Hactenus de Moyse & ejus libris; nunc reliquos historię sacrae libros expendamus.
units.tr: First into the field will come Moses, who is held, by the constant tradition of both Jews and Christians, to be the author of the five books of the Law. Yet the Jewish masters seem to have been more scrupulous in this, since they contend that not even a single word, nor indeed a single syllable, is found in the Law that did not proceed from God and was not dictated to Moses. Most Christians, on the other hand, freely affirm that some additions were made to the books of Moses by Ezra, or by others who revised them, after a long time. Nor did Jerome himself dare to ascribe to Moses each single word of the Pentateuch as it now stands, following in this the common opinion of the teachers of the Church, who constantly assert that the whole Law was reviewed and revised by Ezra, a most skilled scribe. "Whether you wish to call Moses the author of the Pentateuch," says Jerome, "or Ezra its restorer, I do not object." But whether Moses himself committed the whole history we have under his name to writing, or ordered that parts of it be taken down on paper by those scribes who recorded the events of their own age, is a greater difficulty. Yet whichever way the matter falls, Moses will be regarded as the author and writer of the whole Law, as Simonius has rightly noted already, because those scribes, if any existed from the time of Moses, were in everything dependent on him. Indeed, you will find nothing in the whole Law that establishes the authority of such scribes. But unless they had been appointed by Moses himself from those times, something would have been lacking to the Hebrew commonwealth, which neither the Egyptians nor the other nations of the East lacked. That from the times of Moses there were writers of annals among the Hebrews, the very learned Jesuit Sanctius did not hesitate to assert in these words: "I think that in earlier ages there were the words of the days, commentaries, ephemerides, and a diligent and careful concern that the names and descendants of each person should not be obscured by the forgetfulness of time; and from the time of Moses this seems to me entirely certain." I will spare the naming of others who hold the same view. I am surprised, however, that a recent writer of the Seraphic order, inflamed with more than Seraphic zeal, has condemned this opinion as impious in his Biblical Disquisitions and called down dire curses on its authors. But, as I hear, that Seraphic Doctor, though he knows neither Hebrew nor Greek, is nonetheless most audacious in his ignorance, and belongs to the sect of those who "blaspheme whatever they do not know." Simonius also offends some, and perhaps the delicate Vossius, in his Critical Sacred, by affirming that some things were added to the books of Moses afterwards. But Simonius is not an innovator even in this matter, for he has on his side the most skilled interpreters of Holy Scripture: Masius, and Pererius, who transferred nearly the whole of his words into his own Preface on Genesis, Bonfrerius, Cornelius à Lapide, and many others of good standing. "I also approve," says Pererius, "the opinion of those who think that the Pentateuch, after a long time had passed since Moses, was patched together with many clauses of words and sentences inserted into it, and was rendered more fully explained and better arranged for continuing the sequence of the history." In a similar way Bonfrerius, weighing certain words of Genesis which he suspects could not have been written by Moses, holds: "I would rather say that some other hagiographer added a number of things afterwards, than ascribe everything to Moses acting as prophet." Quite similarly, on the same passage, Cornelius à Lapide says: "These words seem to have been added after Moses by the one who arranged the diaries of Moses." What is more, the learned Huet himself, answering Spinoza, who objects that some things were sewn into the books of Moses, responds in such a way that he seems scarcely to depart from him. "We admit," he says, "that Ezra, the restorer of Scripture, wherever passages were more obscure or difficult, inserted here and there some things of his own into the sacred books for the sake of explanation. Moreover, since the sacred codices have been multiplied through so many copyings, so that no book ever had so many copies, what wonder if, as has often happened elsewhere, the notes that pious and learned men added in the margin have here too crept into the text itself?" Finally, those things found at the end of Deuteronomy concerning the death and burial of Moses are commonly believed to have been added to the rest of the text by Joshua, or rather by the members of the Great Sanhedrin, of whom Joshua was the leader. For it was the custom to record in public acts the things that were then done, by those whose task it was to write them down; and in this sense Joshua is said to have "written some things in the book of the Law of the Lord," namely the covenant he had struck with the people. Indeed, many things are found in the Pentateuch itself which clearly show that the books of the Law were written by Moses: thus in Exodus we read, "Moses wrote all the words of the Lord," and in Deuteronomy, "When therefore Moses had written the words of the Law." But Simonius has shown that these and many other things of the same kind must be explained as referring only to certain parts of the Law, which are mentioned in these places. Hence also Hieronymus Oleaster, a man learned in Hebrew and most thoroughly versed in the sacred letters, denies that it can be most effectively proved from the Scriptures that Moses himself was the author of the Law which we have under his name. So far concerning Moses and his books; now let us examine the remaining books of sacred history.

units.la: Primus post Pentateuchum occurrit liber qui dicitur Josue, quemque à Josua scriptum fuisse, non secus atque à Moyse Pentateuchum, firmissimè probare videntur verba illa, Scripsit quoque (Josue) omnia verba hæc in volumine Legis Domini. Josue nimirum defuncto Moyse, vel illius Scribæ, eo mandante, ea quæ tunc temporis gerebantur in Acta publica conjecerunt: quo sensu volumini Legis quasi addita fuisse dicuntur. Mirum tamen quàm secum dissideant qui hoc argumentum tractârunt; itâ ut ne ipse Augustinus Josuam scripti quod sub ejus nomine circumfertur, extra controversiam auctorem esse ausus sit affirmare. Si ab illo, inquit, (Josuâ videlicet) conscriptus liber qui appellatur Jesu Nave, vel si ab alio scriptus est, &c. Similiter Theodoretus auctor est hunc à Josua scriptum non fuisse, sed ex libro posteriori excerptum. E recentioribus autem doctissimus Masius pluribus ostendit, minimè dici posse ea omnia quæ in Josuæ historia nunc extant ab eo profecta fuisse, quaeque supra allata sunt de Scribis illis publicis & de illorum muneribus, gravissimis rationibus confirmat, & id ad alios etiam Scripturæ libros extendit. Talmudistarum quidem sententia est, Josuen scripsisse librum suum & octo versus Legis: sed ab his discedere veritus non est Magister acutissimus R. Isaac Abravanel, & ut ita sentiret non modò his verbis quæ referuntur ad calcem libri Josuæ, Et post hæc mortuus est Josue filius Nun, &c. adductum se fuisse asserit, sed & ob alias quæ passim in ipso Josuæ contextu reperiuntur loquutiones, quarum auctorem Josuam esse potuisse inficiatur. Hujus generis sunt primò illud quod habetur de duodecim lapidibus quos posuit in medio Jordanis alveo, de quibus nimirum dicitur, Sunt ibi usque in præsentem diem; deinde id quod refertur de circumcisione, cui statim hæc subjungit Scriptor libri Josuæ: Vocatum tum est nomen loci illius Galgala usque in præsentem diem. De quibusdam etiam populis, quos Israëlitæ penitus non deleverant, hæc leguntur: Habitaverunt in medio Israël usque in præsentem diem. Prætereo & alia multa quæ eodem planè modo enunciantur in historia Josuę, & quæ ab ipso Josua scribi non potuisse pluribus contendit idem Magister Abravanel. Si Josue, inquit Magister ille, scripsisset hæc omnia, num diceret, Usque in præsentem diem? Addit ea quæ in Josuæ historia leguntur de Danitis qui urbem Leschem expugnaverint, quæ tamen evidens est sub finem Judicum contigisse, adeoque post ipsius Josuæ obitum.
