Verùm ista & alia ejusdem rationis bene multa, quibus consultò supersedere visum est, non probant Josuam, vel illos quibus præerat Scribas, ea quæ suorum erant temporum in Acta publica non retulisse; sed tantùm alios postea Scribas eadem Acta recognovisse, interjectis aliquot connexionum & explicationis causâ.
units.tr: The first book after the Pentateuch is the one called Joshua, and the words "Joshua also wrote all these words in the book of the Law of the LORD" seem to prove most firmly that it was written by Joshua, just as the Pentateuch was written by Moses. Joshua, after Moses died, or Moses' scribe at his command, may have recorded in public records what was happening at that time, and in this sense they are said to have been added to the book of the Law. It is remarkable, however, how much those who have treated this question disagree, so that not even Augustine dared to affirm for certain that Joshua was the author of the writing that circulates under his name. "If the book called Jesus Nave," he says, "was written by him, or if it was written by another," and so on. Likewise Theodoret states that this book was not written by Joshua but excerpted from a later book. Among more recent writers, the very learned Masius shows at length that it cannot be said that all the things now found in the history of Joshua came from him, and he confirms with weighty arguments what has been said above about those public scribes and their duties, extending this also to other books of Scripture. It is indeed the opinion of the Talmudists that Joshua wrote his own book and the eight verses of the Law. But the very acute master R. Isaac Abravanel did not hesitate to depart from them. He asserts that he was led to think otherwise not only by the words that are reported at the end of the book of Joshua, "And after these things Joshua the son of Nun died," and so on, but also by other expressions found throughout the text of Joshua itself, which he denies could have been written by Joshua. Of this kind, first, is what is said about the twelve stones that he set up in the middle of the bed of the Jordan, of which it is said, "They are there unto this day"; then what is related about the circumcision, to which the writer of the book of Joshua immediately adds, "The name of that place was called Gilgal unto this day." Of some peoples also, whom the Israelites had not utterly destroyed, we read, "They dwelt in the midst of Israel unto this day." I pass over many other things that are stated in exactly the same way in the history of Joshua, and which the same master Abravanel argues could not have been written by Joshua himself. "If Joshua," says that master, "had written all these things, would he say, 'unto this day'?" He adds what is read in the history of Joshua about the Danites who captured the city of Leshem, which nevertheless clearly happened near the end of the Judges, and so after Joshua's death. But these and many other arguments of the same kind, which I have thought it best to pass over deliberately, do not prove that Joshua, or the scribes over whom he presided, failed to record in the public records the things of their own times; they show only that other scribes later revised those same records, inserting a few things for the sake of connection and explanation.

units.la: Neque aliâ profectò ratione contextus fuisse videtur liber qui Schophetim, seu Judices appellatur, quia similes in eo loquutionum formulæ apparent. Quare D. Huetius Dorothei sententiam de hoc libro amplexatur, qui Dorotheus auctor est Scribas illius temporis quæ sub Judicibus gesta fuerant, ea in Commentaria retulisse, ex quibus postea Samuel librum Judicum compos͏uerat. Quis autem fuerit Dorotheus ille in præsentia non disputo; satis est inde confecisse, nudiustertiùs natam non esse Simonii opinionem quæ Scribas publicos in gente Hebræa statuit, quorum fuit res suorum temporum describere, ex quorum postea Commentariis alii Scribæ, seu Prophetæ, qui hos exceperunt, historias contexuêre, quas legimus sub Josuæ, Judicum, Samuelis & Regum nominibus. Hanc quoque sententiam confirmant Syri: ad calcem enim historiæ Judicum in exemplari Syriaco hæc verba leguntur: Liber autem Judicum, quamvis annotatum non sit nomen ejus qui ipsum scripsit, notum tamen est quòd ab aliquo Sacerdotum filiorum Aaronis, qui temporibus Judicum istorum sacerdotio functi sunt, scriptus sit. Librum Ruth Dorotheus modò laudatus ad eosdem Scribas refert, idque videtur longè verisimilius quàm aliorum sententiæ quibus nihil inest firmitatis. De utroque hæc habet Sixtus Senensis: Dicitur Samuelem muelem librum Judicum collegisse, eique adjecisse Ruth Moabitidis historiam: sunt qui Ezechiam, & qui Esdram putent utriusque voluminis auctorem.
units.tr: Nor does the book called Shophetim, or Judges, seem to have been put together by any other method, since similar forms of expression appear in it. Hence the learned Huet adopts the opinion of Dorotheus about this book, who asserts that the scribes of that time recorded in commentaries the things done under the Judges, and that Samuel afterwards composed the book of Judges from these. I am not now discussing who that Dorotheus was; it is enough to conclude from this that the opinion of Simonius is not new, which holds that there were public scribes among the Hebrew people whose task was to describe the events of their own times, and that other scribes, or prophets, who came after them, wove together histories from their later commentaries, which we read under the names of Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings. The Syrians also confirm this opinion. For at the end of the history of Judges in the Syriac copy these words are read: "The book of Judges, although the name of the one who wrote it is not noted, is nevertheless known to have been written by one of the priests, sons of Aaron, who served as priests in the times of those judges." Dorotheus, just mentioned, refers the book of Ruth to the same scribes, and this seems much more probable than the other opinions, which have no firmness. Sixtus of Siena has this to say about both books: "It is said that Samuel gathered the book of Judges and added to it the history of Ruth the Moabitess; some think Hezekiah, and some Ezra, was the author of both volumes."

units.la: De libris autem Regum hęc annotavit Theodoretus, plurimos scilicet fuisse Prophetas apud Hebræos, quorum quisque scribebat res suę ætatis, & inde factum esse quòd primus liber Regum apud Hebræos & apud Syros nominetur Prophetia Samuelis. Deinde mox addit: Qui ergo Regnorum libros scripserunt, ex scriptis illis acceptâ occasione post plurimum tempus scripserunt. Et post nonnulla interjecta hęc affert de libris Paralipomenon. Fuerunt aliqui alii Historiographi eorum quæ ab illis fuerant prætermissa, qui de his conscriptum librum appellarunt Paralipomena. Sixtus Senensis de primo & altero librorum Regum, quos Samuelis nomine insigniunt Judæi, hęc subjicit. Liber Samuelis partim à Samuele Propheta, partim à Nathan & Gad Prophetis creditur esse conscriptus. Samuel enim collegit facta Heli, Saulis, Davidis ac sui ipsius gesta, quæ in primo Regum usque ad mortem suam referuntur. Nathan verò & Gad Prophetæ scripserunt libros Regum à morte Samuelis usque ad finem libri secundi. Quæ hoc loco scribit Sixtus Senensis, licèt à veritate minùs aliena crediderim in genere, tamen si in specie & minutatim expendantur, nequeunt esse vera ex omni parte: quandoquidem à Samuele ea omnia quæ usque ad illius mortem narrantur scribi non potuisse complura ostendunt. Vix enim credibile est eum de rebus quæ suâ ætate gerebantur, & quarum fuerit ipse testis oculatus, hęc scripsisse: Propter hanc causam non calcant Sacerdotes Dagon, & omnes qui ingrediuntur templum ejus limen Dagon in Azoto usque in hodiernum diem. Neque ea similiter quæ paulò post narrantur de arca Domini, quæ erat usque in diem illam in agro Josuæ Bethschemitis. His accedit, Samuelem hujus clausulæ quæ in illius historia legitur non videri auctorem: Olim in Israel sic loquebatur unusquisque vadens consulere Deum: qui enim Propheta dicitur hodie, vocabatur olim Videns. His tamen non obstantibus, credibile est historiam quæ nomen Samuelis præfert, ab illo verè conscriptam fuisse usque ad ea quæ de illius morte referuntur. Illa autem quæ in contrarium adducta sunt, probant duntaxat Scribæ alicujus, seu Prophetæ, puta Hieremiæ, ut quibusdam visum fuit, recognitionem accessisse, qui nonnulla
units.tr: On the books of Kings Theodoret made these observations: that there were very many prophets among the Hebrews, each of whom wrote the events of his own age, and that for this reason the first book of Kings is called among the Hebrews and among the Syrians the Prophecy of Samuel. Then he immediately adds: "Those therefore who wrote the books of the Kingdoms wrote, after a long time, taking the occasion from those writings." And after some intervening remarks he cites this about the books of Chronicles: "There were some other historians of those things which had been omitted by them, who called the book written about these things the Paralipomena." Sixtus of Siena, on the first and second books of Kings, which the Jews mark with Samuel's name, adds the following: "The book of Samuel is believed to have been written partly by the prophet Samuel, and partly by the prophets Nathan and Gad. For Samuel gathered the deeds of Eli, Saul, David and his own deeds, which are related in the first book of Kings up to his death. But the prophets Nathan and Gad wrote the books of Kings from the death of Samuel to the end of the second book." What Sixtus of Siena writes here, although I would have thought it in general not far from the truth, nevertheless, if examined in particulars and in detail, cannot be wholly true; for several things show that not everything narrated up to Samuel's death could have been written by Samuel. It is hardly credible that he wrote these things about events of his own time, of which he was himself an eyewitness: "For this reason neither the priests of Dagon nor any who enter the temple of Dagon at Ashdod tread upon the threshold, unto this day." Nor likewise what is related a little later about the ark of the LORD, which was in the field of Joshua the Beth-shemite until that day. To these is added that Samuel does not seem to be the author of this clause, which is read in his history: "Formerly in Israel a man, when he went to inquire of God, spoke thus: he who is now called a prophet was formerly called a seer." Nevertheless, notwithstanding these things, it is credible that the history which bears Samuel's name was truly written by him as far as the things that are reported of his death. But the things brought forward to the contrary prove only that some scribe, or prophet, perhaps Jeremiah, as some have thought, revised the work and added some things, who added nothing for the sake of explanation.

units.la: 1 Sam. 5: 5. nulla explicationis causâ addiderit. Alii tamen malunt tribuere has additiones Esdræ & illius Collegis. Syri librum primum & secundum Regum, qui tertius & quartus numerantur in Latinis codicibus, dicunt scriptos fuisse à Sacerdote quodam nomine Johanan.
units.tr: 1 Sam. 5: 5. Nevertheless, others prefer to attribute these additions to Ezra and his colleagues. The Syrians say that the first and second books of Kings, which are numbered third and fourth in the Latin codices, were written by a certain priest named Johanan.

units.la: De libris Chronicorum, seu Paralipomenon, à quibus illi fuerint collecti, est etiam dubitandi ratio. Judæi plerique illorum auctorem faciunt Esdram. Ita R. Salomon & R. D. Kimchi hanc esse traditionem patrum suorum afferunt, qui Esdræ quoque adjungunt socios Aggæum, Zachariam & Malachiam Prophetas; ita tamen ut illi non tam historiam de novo scripsisse dici queant, quàm vetusta Chronica Regum Judæ & Israel compilasse, rejectis iis quæ minùs suo instituto convenire videbantur, additis etiam nonnullis interdum quæ in aliis Scripturæ Sacræ libris prætermissa fuerant, unde nomen Paralipomenon ortum apud Græcos, quod ab his deinde ad Latinos transiit. Quare rectè Hieronymus appellat librum Paralipomenon Veteris Instrumenti epitomen. Sixtus Senensis affirmat libros Paralipomenon nullum habere certum auctorem. Refert tamen Judæorum ea de re sententiam, quibus etiam suffragatur Hugo Grotius, qui libros hosce scriptos fuisse ab Esdra existimat, & ab iis dictos Divre hajamim, Verba dierum, seu excerpta ex Regum diurnis. Librum qui Esdræ nomine prænotatur, partem maximam ab illo digestum & descriptum fuisse, res ipsæ quæ habentur in illius contextu videntur indicare. Nehemias autem in fronte operis auctorem se profitetur libri illius quem Judæi secundum Esdræ nominant.
units.tr: Concerning the books of Chronicles, or Paralipomenon, from which sources they were compiled, there is also reason for doubt. Most Jews make Ezra their author. So R. Solomon and R. D. Kimchi report this as the tradition of their fathers, who also join with Ezra his companions, the prophets Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi; yet in such a way that they can be said not so much to have written the history anew as to have compiled the ancient Chronicles of the kings of Judah and Israel, rejecting those things which seemed less suited to their purpose, and sometimes adding some things that had been omitted in other books of Holy Scripture. Hence the name Paralipomenon arose among the Greeks, which afterwards passed from them to the Latins. Therefore Jerome rightly calls the book of Paralipomenon an epitome of the Old Testament. Sixtus of Siena affirms that the books of Paralipomenon have no certain author. He does, however, report the opinion of the Jews on this matter, which Hugo Grotius also supports; he thinks these books were written by Ezra, and were called Divre hajamim, "Words of the Days," that is, excerpts from the daily records of the Kings. That the book which is marked with Ezra's name was for the most part arranged and written by him seems to be indicated by the facts themselves that are found in its text. Nehemiah, however, at the head of his work declares himself the author of the book which the Jews ascribe to Ezra in accordance with its name.

units.la: Liber Psalmorum à Judæis appellatur Sepher tehillim, seu liber laudum, quem Augustinus totum esse Davidis aliquando sensisse videtur, qui etiam non dubitat illos quos longo post Davidem tempore conditos fuisse manifestum est, etiam Davidi referre, quòd hic non modò Cantor, sed & Propheta extiterit. Neque etiam ab ea opinione divellere potuerunt Augustinum Asaphi, Idithi & aliorum Cantorum nomina quibus Psalmi aliquot tribuuntur, quia materiam ipsis suppeditare potuit David, quam postea adornârunt accommodâruntque ad varios cantus, quorum erant periti. Verùm longè rectius Hieronymus, qui Psalmos eorum esse asserit, qui ponuntur in titulis, David scilicet, Asaph & & Idithun, filiorum Core, Eman Ezrahita, Moysis, Salomonis & reliquorum quos Esdras primo volumine comprehendit. Hieronymo consentiunt plerique Judæi. Ita sapiens Aben Esra affirmat Psalmos eorum esse quorum nominibus prænotantur; etsi complures sint qui nullum nomen præferant. In hoc tamen castigat Hieronymum Magister ille, quòd non absolutè pronunciet Psalmos ab iis esse conditos, quorum nominibus prænotantur, sed eos qui Davidis & Salomonis præferunt nomina, vel illorum esse, vel de illis à Cantoribus compositos. Christus tamen universum Psalmorum opus tribuisse videtur Davidi, cùm ait, Ipse David dicit in libro Psalmorum. Sed communem Judæorum sententiam sequutus est Christus. Illi enim Psalmos Davidis nomine prænotabant, non quòd revera Psalmorum omnium auctorem illum agnoscerent; quandoquidem res ipsa contrarium apertè demonstrat: sed quòd præcipuus illorum Scriptor esset, & in sacris codicibus egregius Psaltes Israël appelletur. Scribit tamen jam laudatus Aben Esra, non deesse inter Magistros suos qui totum Psalterii opus Davidi tribuant, quem etiam agnoscunt Prophetam.
units.tr: The Book of Psalms is called by the Jews Sepher tehillim, that is, the book of praises. Augustine seems at one point to have thought that the whole of it was David's. He also did not hesitate to ascribe to David those psalms which it is clear were composed long after David's time, on the ground that David was not only a singer but also a prophet. Yet the names of Asaph, Idithun and the other singers, to whom some psalms are assigned, did not wholly dislodge Augustine from that opinion, since David could have supplied the material, which those men later arranged and fitted to the various melodies they were skilled in. Far more correctly, however, Jerome asserts that the psalms belong to those who are named in the titles: David, of course, Asaph, Idithun, the sons of Korah, Eman the Ezrahite, Moses, Solomon and the others whom Ezra included in the first volume. Most Jews agree with Jerome. So the wise Aben Ezra affirms that the psalms belong to those whose names they bear, although there are several which have no name at all. In this, however, that master criticises Jerome: he does not say outright that the psalms were composed by those whose names they carry, but only that those which bear the names of David and Solomon are either theirs or were composed about them by the singers. Christ, nevertheless, seems to have ascribed the whole work of the Psalms to David, when he says, David himself says in the book of Psalms. But in this Christ followed the common opinion of the Jews. For they labelled the psalms with David's name, not because they truly acknowledged him as the author of all the psalms, since the thing itself plainly shows the contrary, but because he was their chief writer, and in the sacred books he is called the outstanding psalmist of Israel. Yet the aforementioned Aben Ezra writes that among his own teachers there were not lacking those who ascribe the whole work of the Psalter to David, whom they also acknowledge as a prophet.

units.la: Liber qui vulgò dicitur Proverbiorum commendatur à nomine Salomonis quod illius frontem occupat, etsi universa operis illius ratio demonstrare videatur hoc nihil esse præter varia sententiarum excerpta, quæ cùm à Salomone, tum ab aliis Scriptoribus collectæ in unum postea corpus conjectæ fuerunt. Salomonem multas compositisse Parabolas probant ista quæ de seipso habet: Cùmque esset sapientissimus Ecclesiastes, docuit populum, & enarravit quæ fecerat, & investigans composuit Parabolas multas, quæ usque ad tria millia numerantur libro III. Regum; sed quæ hodie non extant, si paucas exceperis quas repræsentant sacri codices. Primis novem Capitibus illius operis nomen Salomonis præfigitur, deinde sequuntur & alia quindecim Capita, quæ ejusdem Salomonis nomen præferunt; & hæc secundam esse illius Parabolarum, sive sententiarum, partem existimavit Aben Esra. Pars verò tertia earumdem Parabolarum sumit initium ab his verbis Capitis 25. Gloria Dei est celare verbum: quæ distinctio ab iis profecta est qui Scripturæ Sacræ libros in ordinem quem nunc servant redegerunt. Salomonem enim ipsum nomen suum toties Parabolis lis suis præfixisse vix credibile est; sed Scribas potius qui opus illud in partes suas divisère. Ita versum hunc quem initio Capitis 25. legimus, Hæ quoque Parabolæ Salomonis, quas transstulerunt viri Ezechiæ Regis Juda, putat Aben Esra esse Sobnæ, qui Regis Ezechiæ Scriba erat. Sobnam quidem & alios qui Regi Ezechiæ erant à Commentariis, sententias istas, quarum prima est illa, Gloria Dei est celare verbum, ex integro volumine decerpsisse lubens agnosco: cùm & verba hæc, quas transstulerunt viri Ezechiæ, id aperte demonstrent. Partem quartam Parabolarum Salomonis habemus initio Capitis 30. ubi legitur in editione Latina, Verba Congregantis, & in contextu Hebraico, Verba Agur. Quis sit autem ille Agur, sive Congregans, non conveniunt inter se Scripturæ Interpretes. Prisci Judæi, teste R. Salomone, ita volunt appellatum fuisse Salomonem, quasi dixerimus colligentem sententias: id enim Hebraicè sonat dictio Agur, cujus similiter sensum expressit Latinus Interpres, dum reddidit Verba Congregantis. Eamdem opinionem illustrat R. Levi Ben Gersom, ubi ait, Videtur Salomon Aguris nomen ipse sibi imposuisse ratione habitâ sententiarum quas in hoc libro collegit. Sed forsan melius Aben Esra & eum sequutus Grotius suspicantur Agurem istum fuisse temporum illorum Theognidem, aut Phocylidem, ex cujus scriptis sententias quasdam selegerit Salomon ipse, quasque cum aliis sententiis in unum volumen conjecerit. Additur demum pars quinta Proverbiorum Salomonis, quę intra Caput 31. quod & ultimum est, clauditur, idque Regis Lamuelis nomine. Quis autem sit Lamuel ille, ignoratur. Judæi plerique existimant Salomonem indicari, non secus ac per Immanuel, ut auctor est Aben Esra, indicatur Messias; & appellationis istius rationem sumit ex eo quòd Lamuel significet illis Deus, quia nimirum Salomonis temporibus, ait idem Aben Esra, Deus unus ab Hebraeis colebatur. Sed de originatione vocis Lamuel non est cur simus soliciti, maximè cùm LXX. eam non exhibeant, & diversâ planè ratione verba contextûs Hebraici legerint ac converterint.
units.tr: The book commonly called Proverbs is commended by the name of Solomon, which stands at its head, although the whole plan of that work seems to show that it is nothing more than various excerpts of sayings, which were later gathered together into one body, both from Solomon and from other writers. That Solomon composed many parables is shown by what the book itself says about him: And since Solomon was the wisest of preachers, he taught the people, and recounted what he had done, and in investigating he composed many parables, which are counted up to three thousand, in the third book of Kings; but these no longer survive, apart from the few which the sacred books preserve. The first nine chapters of that work bear the name of Solomon as a heading; then follow fifteen more chapters which likewise carry the name of the same Solomon. Aben Ezra thought these to be the second part of his parables, or sayings. The third part of the same parables begins with these words of chapter 25: It is the glory of God to conceal a word. This division came from those who arranged the books of Holy Scripture into the order which they now keep. For it is hardly credible that Solomon himself prefixed his name so often to his parables; rather, it was the scribes who divided that work into its parts. Thus Aben Ezra thinks that the verse we read at the beginning of chapter 25, These also are the parables of Solomon, which the men of King Hezekiah of Judah copied out, refers to Shebna, who was scribe to King Hezekiah. I gladly acknowledge that Shebna and the other men who were in charge of the royal records under King Hezekiah extracted those sayings, the first of which is It is the glory of God to conceal a word, from the whole volume; the words which the men of Hezekiah copied out clearly show this. We have the fourth part of Solomon's parables at the beginning of chapter 30, where the Latin edition reads The words of the gatherer, and the Hebrew text reads The words of Agur. Yet the interpreters of Scripture do not agree about who this Agur, or gatherer, is. The ancient Jews, according to R. Solomon, wished Solomon himself to have been so called, as if we were to say one who gathers sayings: for the Hebrew word Agur has that sense, and the Latin translator likewise expressed its meaning when he rendered it the words of the gatherer. R. Levi ben Gershom supports the same opinion where he says, Solomon himself seems to have given himself the name Agur, on account of the sayings he gathered in this book. But perhaps Aben Ezra, and Grotius following him, more rightly suspect that this Agur was the Theognis or Phocylides of those times, from whose writings Solomon himself chose certain sayings, and which he then placed together with other sayings in one volume. Lastly, a fifth part of the Proverbs of Solomon is added, which closes within chapter 31, the last chapter, and bears the name of King Lemuel. Who this Lemuel is, however, is unknown. Most Jews think that Solomon is meant, just as, according to Aben Ezra, the Messiah is indicated by the name Immanuel; and he takes the reason for that name from the fact that Lemuel means to them God, because, as the same Aben Ezra says, in Solomon's time God was worshipped as one by the Hebrews. But we need not be anxious about the origin of the word Lemuel, especially since the Seventy do not give it, and they read and translated the words of the Hebrew text in a quite different way.

units.la: Librum qui Hebraicè dicitur Coheleth, & apud nos Ecclesiastes, Latinè possumus appellare Concionatorem; licèt plerique Judæi recentiores dictionem Coheleth velint significare hominem concongregantem, quòd scriptum illud multas complectatur de rebus diversis sententias. Ita sentiunt R. Salomo & R. Aben Esra, &, ut ille inquit, Salomon qui operis hujusce auctor est, in alio loco vocatur Agur ob eamdem rationem, vel ut loquitur R. David de Pomis, Titolo del libro nomato Ecclesiastes composito da Salomone significa congregatore per congregare & racorre, in quel trattato diverse opinioni de gl' huomini la maggior parte de quali sono false. Judæi tamen nonnulli, teste R. Salomone, in interpretanda voce ista Coheleth cum LXX. conveniunt; eā siquidem indicari arbitrantur hominem qui in cœtu aliquo concionatur. De Scriptore autem illius operis minimè consentiunt inter se Magistri: Talmudici enim Doctores tribuunt illud Ezechiæ; Rabbini autem recentiores Salomoni, & pro his pugnant verba contextûs, in quo multa extant quæ vix de alio quàm de Salomone exponi possunt. Itaque verisimile est Doctores Talmudicos voluisse duntaxat scriptum illud à Rege Ezechia & à viris illius confessus excerptum fuisse ex Salomonis operibus. Christiani quoque Interpretes non alium Ecclesiastę Scriptorem agnoscunt quàm Salomonem, si perpaucos excipias, inter quos est Hugo Grotius, qui serius illud scriptum compositum fuisse affirmat sub nomine Salomonis, & in illius rei argumentum habere se testatur multa vocabula ex eo collecta, quæ non alibi extant quàm in Daniele, Esdra & Chaldaeis Interpretibus. Auctor est Hieronymus, priscos Hebræos inter cætera Salomonis scripta quæ antiquata sunt, de hoc quoque obliterando cogitâsse, eò quòd vanas afferat Dei creaturas; qua in re concordat Hieronymus cum Talmudistis ac Judæis recentioribus: sed Doctores istos multa ex suo ingenio commentos esse nemo ignorat.
units.tr: The book which in Hebrew is called Qoheleth, and among us Ecclesiastes, we may call in Latin the Preacher; although most recent Jews wish the word Qoheleth to mean a man who gathers a congregation together, because that writing contains many opinions on various matters. R. Solomon and R. Aben Ezra think so, and, as the former says, Solomon, who is the author of this work, is called Agur in another place for the same reason. Or, as R. David de Pomis puts it: The title of the book called Ecclesiastes, composed by Solomon, means a gatherer, one who gathers and collects; in that treatise there are various opinions of men, most of which are false. Yet some Jews, according to R. Solomon, agree with the Seventy in interpreting this word Qoheleth; for they think it means a man who preaches in an assembly. But the teachers do not agree among themselves about the author of that book. The Talmudic doctors ascribe it to Hezekiah, while the more recent rabbis ascribe it to Solomon, and the words of the text support them, since much in it can hardly be explained of anyone but Solomon. So it is likely that the Talmudic doctors meant only that this writing was taken from the works of Solomon by King Hezekiah and the men of his council. Christian interpreters too acknowledge no other author of Ecclesiastes than Solomon, except a very few, among whom is Hugo Grotius, who affirms that it was composed later under the name of Solomon, and as proof of this he states that he has many words collected from it which are found nowhere else except in Daniel, Ezra and the Chaldee interpreters. Jerome reports that the ancient Hebrews, among the other writings of Solomon which had become outdated, even thought of removing this one too, because it presents God's creatures as vain; in this matter Jerome agrees with the Talmudists and the more recent Jews. But no one is unaware that those teachers invented much out of their own cleverness.

units.la: A quo scripta fuerit historia quam sub nomine Estheris legimus, incertum est. De tempore tamen quo illa condita fuerit, omnes fere tum Judæi tum Christiani consentiunt. Sive enim auctores illius sint viri Synagogæ magnæ, uti sentiunt Doctores Talmudici, sive Esdras, quę Patrum nonnullorum sententia est, sive Mardochæus, ut probabilius existimat R. Aben Esra, & liber ipse testari videtur, de tempore quo scripta fuerit historia Estheris lis nulla movebitur. Unde nec malè conjicit Hugo Grotius, Esdram libro suo & historię quam scripsit Nehemias, attexuisse historiam Estheris, quę medio temporum eorum quæ duobus illis libris narrantur contigerat, quam à Mardochæo quoque scriptam fuisse agnoscit idem Grotius.
units.tr: By whom the history we read under the name of Esther was written is uncertain. Yet nearly all, both Jews and Christians, agree about the time when it was composed. For whether its authors were the men of the Great Synagogue, as the Talmudic doctors hold, or Ezra, which is the opinion of some of the Fathers, or Mordecai, as Aben Ezra more probably thinks, and as the book itself seems to attest, no dispute will arise about the time when the history of Esther was written. Hence Hugo Grotius does not conjecture badly that Ezra, in his book, and in the history which Nehemiah wrote, inserted the history of Esther, which had happened in the middle of the times narrated in those two books; and Grotius also acknowledges that this was written by Mordecai.

units.la: Canticum Canticorum non alium auctorem habere quàm Salomonem, docet ipsa operis inscriptio quod illius nomine prænotatur. Constat præterea ex libro III. Regum, eumdem Salomonem Parabolas, sive sententias, & Cantica composuisse. Liber autem ille, teste R. Aben Esra, quia fuit Canticorum Salomonis præstantissimum, sortitus est nomen Cantici Canticorum, quasi dixeris excellentissimum carmen. Dubitârunt tamen nonnulli, utrùm opusculum istud quale nunc exstat, à Salomone scriptum fuerit, an verò ex integro illius Canticorum volumine excerptum. Carmen autem illud quo Salomon cum Salamitide loquens inducitur tanquam sponsus cum sponsa, explicatu difficillimum est non solùm ob loquutiones paulò audaciores, frequentioresque similitudines quæ à nostris consuetudinibus abhorrent; sed etiam quòd nomina interloquentium non annotentur, ut in libro Jobi: nam præter Salomonem & illius Sponsam interloquentes, etiam sunt duo chori Juvenum & Virginum.
units.tr: That Solomon is the author of the Song of Songs is shown by the title of the work itself, which bears his name. It is also clear from III Kings that the same Solomon composed Proverbs, or sayings, and Songs. According to R. Aben Ezra, that book, being the most excellent of Solomon's songs, received the name Song of Songs, as if one were to say the most excellent song. Some have doubted, however, whether this little work as it now exists was written by Solomon, or whether it was excerpted from his whole volume of Songs. The poem in which Solomon speaks with the Shulammite, as bridegroom with bride, is most difficult to explain. This is not only because of its rather bold expressions and frequent comparisons, which are foreign to our customs, but also because the names of the speakers are not noted, as in the book of Job. For besides Solomon and his bride who speak, there are also two choruses, of young men and of maidens.

units.la: De libro Jobi mirum est quàm secum dissideant Judæorum Magistri. Rem verè gestam in hoc opere non narrari putant Doctores Talmudici, quibus assentiuntur R. Moses Ben Maimon & alii pauci; sed esse figmentum, seu Parabolam, quæ ingens pietatis simul & patientiæ exemplum ostendat: & his suffragantur etiam Christianorum nonnulli. Imò nec defuêre qui non solùm operis istius argumentum confictum existimârunt, sed & Jobi quoque nomen volunt ex primis libri verbis desumptum, ubi legimus Jobad jom. Illa enim quæ verbis istis prævia sunt, Prologi instar addita fuisse arbitrantur. Sed Ezechielis Prophetæ testimonium, qui Noë, Danielis, Jobiquesimul meminit, demonstrat commentitium non esse Jobi nomen; & eos qui ita sentiunt acerrimè impugnat sapiens Aben Esra, qui suspicatur illum fuisse ex posteris Esau, idque denotari ex loco Huz unde ortus dicitur. Similiter rem uti narratur gestam fuisse, docent Jobi & illius amicorum nomina & alia complura quæ his adjunguntur, etsi non pauca sint quæ ad Parabolam magis quàm ad historiæ veritatem accedant. De auctore verò scripti illius longè minùs adhuc constat: alii quippe illud ad Moysem referunt, alii ad Isajam, alii ad ipsummet Jobum aut ad ejus amicos. Neque etiam inter se consentiunt qui operis hujusce auctorem ctorem faciunt Moysem: sunt enim qui ab eo solùm ex aliena lingua Hebraicè conversum putant. Sed his praetermissis, si quid etiam in re obscura licet suspicari, illos minùs recedere à verisimilitudine arbitror, qui operis illius confectionem ad tempora Captivitatis Babylonicæ revocant: dictio enim sæpiùs vix Hebraica est, scatet loquutionibus Chaldaicis, & sapit hominem qui ex alieno commercio sermonem Hierosolymitanum infecerat. Quo sensu explicanda sunt Hieronymi verba, asserentis Jobum se convertisse ex Hebraico Arabicoque sermone & Syro. Quibus omnibus accedit Judæos, quorum res tùm temporis videbantur desperatæ, magna ex illo opere tulisse solatia. Rem itaque dudum gestam Scriptor narrat: & quia Poëtam agit, licèt argumentum quod tractat non sit fictitium, orationem floridam & figuratam adhibet, verisque interdum adjicit quæ sunt tantùm verisimilia, servato tamen semper personarum loquentium decore. Jam de Prophetis nonnulla subjiciamus.
units.tr: It is remarkable how much the Jewish masters disagree about the book of Job. The Talmudic teachers think that the book does not narrate a real event, and R. Moses Ben Maimon and a few others agree with them; they hold that it is a fiction, or parable, showing a great example of piety and patience at once. Some Christians also support this view. Indeed there were some who not only judged the argument of the work to be invented, but also wished the name of Job to be taken from the first words of the book, where we read Jobad jom. For they think that what precedes these words was added as a kind of prologue. But the testimony of the prophet Ezekiel, who mentions Noah, Daniel and Job together, shows that the name of Job is not made up. The wise Aben Ezra vigorously attacks those who think so, and he suspects that Job was a descendant of Esau, as is indicated by the place Huz, from which he is said to have come. Likewise, the names of Job and his friends, and many other details joined to them, teach that the events were narrated as they happened, although there are not a few things here that belong more to parable than to the truth of history. As to the author of this writing, even less is known: some refer it to Moses, others to Isaiah, others to Job himself or to his friends. Nor do those who make Moses the author agree among themselves; for some think that he only translated it into Hebrew from another language. But setting these aside, if in an obscure matter anything may be conjectured, I think those are less far from probability who date the composition of the work to the time of the Babylonian Captivity. For the language is often scarcely Hebrew, it abounds in Chaldean expressions, and it savours of a man who had infected the speech of Jerusalem through contact with foreigners. This is the sense in which Jerome's words must be explained, when he asserts that he had translated Job from Hebrew, Arabic and Syriac. To all this must be added that the Jews, whose affairs at that time seemed desperate, drew great comfort from this work. The writer therefore narrates an event long past; and since he plays the part of a poet, although the subject he treats is not fictitious, he uses a florid and figurative style, and sometimes adds to true things what is only probable, always keeping, however, the decorum of the speaking persons. Now let us add some remarks about the Prophets.

units.la: Prophetæ à B. Augustino appellantur enunciatores verborum Dei hominibus: illi enim veluti Divinæ Legis Interpretes concionabantur ad populum, quem doctrinam à Moyse traditam docebant stabilitâ illius auctoritate. Deinde minas & promissiones quas Moyses in genere tantùm promulgaverat, hi suæ ætatis rebus accommodabant, idque Oratorum more; unde fit ut comparationum similitudinibus, metaphoris & hyperbolis abundent, simplicique ac nudâ rerum narratione haud contenti, eas verbis exaggerent. Neque enim, ut auctor est Hieronymus, simplex à Prophetis historia & gestorum ordo narratur, sed aenigmatum plena sunt omnia, aliudque in verbis sonant, aliud tenetur in sensibus, ut quae aestimaveris planâ & inoffensâ currere lectione, sequentium rursus obscuritatibus involvantur. Non ita autem futura vaticinantur Prophetæ, quin jam facta saepius referant, ut evidentissimè probari potest ex Zachariæ Prophetia, quæ magnam partem rei praeteritæ & quæ tùm gerebatur, narratio est. Quo modo diligentissimus Scripturæ Interpres Joannes Mercerus in explicandis verbis quibusdam Prophetæ Amos, Judæorum expositionem improbat, qui de rebus futuris ibi agi contendunt, cùm de re jam praeterita agatur; moxque verba ista subjungit, quæ notatu digna sunt: Laboramus penuriâ librorum sacrorum, rum, ac sæpè in Prophetis pleraque legas facta, quæ in sacris historiis quæ hodie extant non reperias. Prophetas similiter testatur Hieronymus in suis narrationibus non attendere interdum ad rerum ipsarum ordinem quo gestæ fuerint. In Prophetis, ait, historiæ ordo non tenendus, cùm inpræsentiarum sub eodem Rege priora postea, & posteriora ante dicantur. Præposterum illum ordinem tribuit Pseudo-Dorotheus Scribis qui Prophetarum vaticinia ex illorum ore excepta referebant in chartas; quasi Prophetæ ipsimet conciones quas habebant ad populum non commendassent literis. Idem observavit de Hieremiæ vaticinio Cornelius à Lapide, qui existimat Baruch Scribam illius Prophetæ omnes ejus Prophetias diverso tempore editas in unum volumen collegisse, neglecto temporis ordine quo editæ fuerant. Fatetur & ipse Joannes Calvinus, Prophetarum vaticinia eo quo decebat ordine disposita ad nos usque non pervenisse; non indè tamen illorum divinitati quidpiam detrahi arbitratur. Qui diligenter, inquit, & cum judicio versati sunt in Prophetis, mihi concedent non semper fuisse quo decebat ordine digestas illorum conciones; sed ut ferebat opportunitas, inde conflatum fuisse volumen. Existimat Sacerdotum operâ, quorum officium erat Prophetias ad posteros commendare, libros Prophetarum, etsi his infensissimi essent Sacerdotes, conservatos fuisse. Scribit præterea idem Calvinus, Prophetas postquam concionem habuêre ad populum, brevem illius summam collegisse, quæ valvis affixa ab omnibus legeretur, posteaque à ministris Templi inde ablata in thesaurum reponebatur in perpetuum rei illius monumentum: unde confectos fuisse conjicit qui nunc extant Prophetarum libros. Verùm ex verbis Isaiæ & Habacuc, quos veritatis illius testes profert Calvinus, id unum probari posse videtur, Prophetas vaticinia sua apertè ac dilucidè, ut ab omnibus intelligerentur & legi possent, super tabulas descripsisse: de valvis autem Templi, quibus illa affixa fuisse putat, nulla prorsus fit mentio. Pariter brevem duntaxat eorumdem vaticiniorum summam ab ipsis Prophetis collectam fuisse, non verò integras conciones ab iis descriptas, fingit perperam; quanquam illas quas nunc habemus Prophetias integras esse, nemo rei criticæ peritus dixerit. Verùm defectus ille, si quis sit, à Prophetis non videtur profectus. Idem Calvinus & eum sequuti Genevenses, inscriptiones quæ Prophetarum nomina, & editarum Prophetiarum annos indicant, à Sacerdotibus, quorum fuit illas in Templo aßervare, majoris lucis causâ adjectas fuisse suspicantur. Hæc siquidem sunt illorum verba: Il semble que ces titres ayent esté ajoûtez aux revelations des Prophetes par les Sacrificateurs & Levites qui avoient charge de garder les Propheties au tresor du Temple, aprés qu'elles avoient esté proposées au peuple suivant la coûtume des Prophetes. Quam Genevenßum opinionem suffragio suo comprobavit Hugo Grotius. Id tantùm inter hunc & illos est discriminis, quòd has inscriptiones non Sacerdotibus & Levitis tribuat, sed viris Senatûs magni qui Prophetarum scripta collegerunt, præno taverunt que tempora scriptionis. Hoc videtur probabilius, quia in confesso est fermè apud omnes, Senatum cui Esdras præfuit, nonnulla sacris codicibus connexionis & explicationis causâ adjecisse. Ita quoque Thomas putat inscriptiones quæ Psalmis aliquot apponuntur, eumdem Esdram auctorem habere, factasque fuisse, partim secundùm ea quæ tunc agebantur, & partim secundùm ea quæ contigerunt. Demum verisimile etiam est historias illas, quę Prophetarum quorumdam concionibus inserte reperiuntur, ab iisdem Senatoribus additas fuisse dum sacros codices recognoscerent formarentque quem nunc habemus Scripturę Canonem. Secundùm quam rationem putant nonnulli verba illa quę leguntur Hieremiæ Capite 51. Hucusque verba Hieremiæ, Prophetæ hujus vaticinium claudere, Caputque quod sequitur Prophetiam non esse, sed historiam, quæ ex fine libri IV. Regum sumpta fuerit. Et in hoc Judæorum Magistri consentiunt cum pluribus Doctoribus Christianis. Auctor est enim R. David Kimchi, verba illa, quæ usque ad finem vaticinii Hieremiæ allata sunt, ad hujus Prophetiam non pertinere; sed eum qui librum hunc descripsit, huc conjecisse deportationis historiam qualis extat in fine libri Regum. Conjicit Abravanel Esdram, seu Synagogæ magnæ Senatores, supplementi illius auctores esse, quo etiam modo Ezechiæ Regis historia ex libri II. Regum Capite 18. in Isaiæ Prophetiam translata est. Ex his omnibus facilè dignoscetur qui fuerint apud gentem Hebræam Prophetæ, quale illorum officii munus, & quę eorumdem scribendi ratio. Præterea id etiam videtur animadversione dignum, quòd Prophetę non solùm conciones ad populum habuerint, ediderintque de rebus futuris vaticinia, sed & historias suorum temporum ordine digestas in Acta publica retulerint. Quo pacto Isaias, qui Regis Oziæ gesta descripsisse dicitur, non minùs historici quàm Prophetæ nomen reportabit. Vel potiùs Prophetæ nomen apud Hebræos ista omnia complectitur; ita ut quicunque divinæ voluntatis erant interpretes, seu vaticinia ederent, sive res suorum temporum conscriberent, Prophetæ appellarentur. Ex quo haud dubiè venit ut prisci Judæi Neviim, seu Prophetarum nomine insignierint Josuæ, Judicum, Samuelis & Regum historias, quòd hæ descriptæ essent à viris qui in eorum Republica Spiritu Sancto afflati, Prophetæ nominabantur. Quo etiam sensu verè affirmavit Josephus, apud gentem suam non à quibuslibet libros componi, sed à Prophetis tantùm. Vim quoque vocis illius probè assequutus est Jonathan, qui pro dictione Hebræa Navi, Propheta, aliam quæ significat Scribam in sua Paraphrasi interdum substituit; quasi qui Prophetæ appellantur, iidem sint atque Scribæ. Neque aliud sapientissimus Esdras in sacris codicibus nomen obtinet, quàm Scribæ peritissimi. Verùm de Scriptoribus sacris satis superque hactenus dictum sit. Libros Apocryphos, seu quos non admittit Judæorum armarium, silentio præterire visum est, quia illorum auctores, ut præfert nomen Apocryphi, occulti sunt & incerti. Cesset itaque doctissimus Vossius optimum Simonium & de literis sacris benè meritum allatrare, qui de Scriptoribus Veteris Testamenti nihil in publicum edidit, quod jam à viris gravissimis iisdemque pietate & eruditione conspicuis approbatum non fuerit. In malevolam animam non introibit sapientia.
units.tr: Augustine calls the prophets the announcers of God's words to men. For they preached to the people as interpreters of the Divine Law, teaching the doctrine handed down by Moses and establishing its authority. Then the threats and promises which Moses had published only in general terms, they applied to the affairs of their own age, and this in the manner of orators. Hence it comes that they abound in comparisons, metaphors and hyperboles, and, not content with a simple and bare narration of things, they embellish them with words. For, as Jerome testifies, the prophets do not relate history simply, nor the order of events, but everything is full of enigmas; they say one thing in words and mean another in their sense, so that what you thought you were reading with a plain and smooth course is again involved in the obscurities that follow. Nor do the prophets prophesy future things without often also recounting things already done, as can be proved most clearly from the prophecy of Zechariah, which is in large part a narration of past events and of things then happening. In the same way the most diligent interpreter of Scripture, John Mercer, in explaining certain words of the prophet Amos, disapproves of the Jewish exposition, which contends that future things are treated there, whereas a past matter is being treated; and he immediately adds these words, which are worth noting: We labour under a shortage of sacred books, and often in the Prophets you may read many deeds which you will not find in the sacred histories that exist today. Jerome likewise testifies that the prophets in their narrations sometimes do not heed the order in which the things themselves were done. In the Prophets, he says, the order of history is not to be kept, since under the same king things earlier are sometimes related after things later, and later before. Pseudo-Dorotheus ascribes this disordered arrangement to the scribes who recorded in writing the prophecies taken from the prophets' mouths; as if the prophets themselves had not committed to writing the sermons they delivered to the people. Cornelius à Lapide observed the same about the prophecy of Jeremiah, and he thinks that Baruch, the scribe of that prophet, gathered all his prophecies, published at different times, into one volume, neglecting the order of time in which they had been published. John Calvin himself admits that the prophetic writings did not come down to us arranged in the order they should have had; yet he does not think that anything is taken away from their divinity on that account. Those, he says, who have dealt diligently and with judgment with the Prophets will grant me that their sermons were not always set in the order they should have had; but as opportunity offered, a volume was put together from them. He thinks that the books of the prophets were preserved through the work of the priests, whose duty it was to hand the prophecies down to posterity, even though the priests were most hostile to the prophets. Calvin also writes that the prophets, after they had preached to the people, collected a brief summary of the sermon, which was fixed to the doors and read by all; afterwards it was taken down by the ministers of the Temple and put away in the treasury as a lasting memorial of the matter; and from these, he conjectures, were made the books of the prophets that we now have. But from the words of Isaiah and Habakkuk, whom Calvin cites as witnesses of this truth, it seems only to be proved that the prophets wrote their prophecies openly and clearly on tablets, so that they could be understood and read by all; but of the doors of the Temple, to which he thinks they were fixed, there is no mention at all. Likewise, to pretend that only a brief summary of these prophecies was collected by the prophets themselves, and not the complete sermons written down by them, is a mistake; although no one skilled in criticism would say that the prophecies we now have are complete. But that defect, if there is one, does not seem to have come from the prophets. Calvin and the Genevans who followed him suspect that the headings, which indicate the names of the prophets and the years in which the prophecies were published, were added by the priests, whose task it was to keep them in the Temple, for the sake of greater clarity. Their words are these: It seems that these titles were added to the revelations of the Prophets by the priests and Levites who had charge of keeping the Prophecies in the treasury of the Temple, after they had been presented to the people according to the custom of the Prophets. Hugo Grotius confirmed this opinion of the Genevans with his approval. The only difference between him and them is that he does not assign these headings to the priests and Levites, but to the men of the Great Senate who gathered the writings of the prophets and noted the times of writing. This seems more probable, because it is almost agreed by all that the Senate over which Ezra presided added some things to the sacred codices for the sake of connection and explanation. So too Thomas thinks that the headings which are placed over some of the Psalms have the same Ezra as their author, and that they were made partly according to the things then being done, and partly according to the things that had happened. Finally, it is also likely that those histories which are found inserted in the sermons of some prophets were added by the same Senators while they were revising the sacred codices and forming the canon of Scripture that we now have. On this principle some think that the words which are read at Jeremiah chapter 51, Hitherto are the words of Jeremiah, close the prophecy of this prophet, and that the chapter which follows is not prophecy but history, taken from the end of IV Kings. In this the Jewish masters agree with many Christian teachers. For R. David Kimchi asserts that the words which are brought in up to the end of Jeremiah's prophecy do not belong to this prophet's prophecy; but that the one who wrote this book inserted here the account of the deportation, such as it stands at the end of the book of Kings. Abravanel conjectures that Ezra, or the Senators of the Great Synagogue, were the authors of that supplement, in the same way as the history of King Hezekiah from II Kings chapter 18 was transferred into the prophecy of Isaiah. From all these things it will easily be recognised who the prophets were among the Hebrew people, what was the nature of their office, and what was their manner of writing. Besides, this also seems worthy of notice: the prophets not only gave sermons to the people and published prophecies about future things, but also set down histories of their own times, arranged in order of time, in public records. In this way Isaiah, who is said to have described the deeds of King Uzziah, will be called a historian no less than a prophet. Or rather, among the Hebrews the name of prophet embraces all these things; so that whoever were interpreters of the divine will, whether they published prophecies or wrote down the events of their times, were called prophets. From this it undoubtedly came that the ancient Jews designated by the name of Neviim, that is, Prophets, the histories of Joshua, of Judges, of Samuel and of Kings, because these had been written by men who, inspired by the Holy Spirit in their Commonwealth, were called prophets. In this same sense Josephus truly affirmed that among his nation books were composed not by just anyone, but only by prophets. Jonathan also grasped well the force of that word, for in his Paraphrase he sometimes substitutes for the Hebrew word Navi, Propheta, another word which means scribe; as if those who are called prophets were the same as scribes. Nor does the most wise Ezra have any other title in the sacred codices than that of most skilled scribe. But enough and more has now been said about the sacred writers. It has seemed best to pass over in silence the Apocryphal books, or those which the Jewish library does not admit, because their authors, as the very name Apocrypha indicates, are hidden and uncertain. Let the most learned Vossius therefore cease to bark at the excellent Simon, who has deserved well of sacred literature, since he has published nothing about the writers of the Old Testament that has not already been approved by men of the greatest gravity, distinguished also for piety and learning. Wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: THE END.

units.la: EXCERPTA EX DISQUISITIONIBUS CRITICIS RICHARDI SIMONIS, Gallicanæ Ecclesiæ Theologi.
units.tr: EXCERPTS FROM THE CRITICAL DISSERTATIONS OF RICHARD SIMON, THEOLOGIAN OF THE GALLICAN CHURCH.

units.la: EXCERPTUM I.
units.tr: EXCERPT I.

units.la: OLas Judæorum Scripturas veras esse ac primigenias, communis est Theologorum, quos vulgò Protestantes vocant, opinio; qui inter disputandum cum Doctoribus Catholicis, ad codices Hebræos semper recurrunt, siquando ab his dissentiat Latinus Interpres, quem in multis errâsse arbitrantur. Inde factum est, ut Theologi illi, qui Reformatorum nomen ambiunt, antiquas Ecclesiæ versiones parvi fecerint, si perpaucos excipias, qui næ-vos etiam in contextu Judaico, non secus ac in illius Interpretibus, deprehenderunt. Verùm longè ultra progressus Isaacus Vossius à receptis Protestantium moribus recessit, ac palàm Judæos falsitatis accusavit, quòd multa è suis codicibus Christianæ Religionis odio de industria post Christi adventum & eversa Hierosolyma, expunxissent; eosque qui Judæorum causam agunt acriter suggillat, & Doctores suæ sectæ, qui hodiernam codicis Hebræi lectionem tueantur, appellat asellos cassos lumine & intellectu, togâ cinctos professoriâ, pro clypeo gestantes Biblia Masorethica cum omnibus suis punctis. Firmissimas Vossium assertionis ita liberæ rationes habere, quis non credat? At quàm graviter allucinatus ille fuerit, ex his quæ mox dicentur manifestum fiet. Quis locus, inquit, qui de Messia agat in sacris occurrit literis, quem illi non corrumpere aut sinistrâ interpretatione enervare sunt conati? Et paulò post: Cùm viderent tempus adventùs Messiæ præteriisse, expleti quippe erant anni sex mille à creatione mundi, ut lucrarentur annos bis mille, tota quatuordecim sæcula è codicibus dicibus suis expunxerunt: reliqua quinque vel sex saecula ut abolerent, decurtarunt intervalla Judicum, omittendo Anarchias, & contrahendo spatia Regum Persicorum. Hoc pacto totis bis mille annis mensuram temporis multiplicarunt. Sed haec mera sunt Vossii commenta, qui non solum Judaeos accusat, sed & a Samaritis idem facinus commissum fuisse auctor est, licet dispari ratione.
units.tr: It is the common opinion of those theologians whom people commonly call Protestants that the Jewish Scriptures are true and original. In disputes with Catholic teachers they always fall back on the Hebrew manuscripts whenever the Latin translator differs from them, since they think he has made many mistakes. As a result, those theologians who claim the name of Reformers have held the ancient versions of the Church in low esteem, with only a very few exceptions, who have also noticed blemishes in the Jewish text, just as in its translators. But Isaac Vossius went far beyond the accepted practice of the Protestants. He openly accused the Jews of falsehood, saying that, out of hatred for the Christian religion, they had deliberately removed many things from their books after Christ's coming and after the destruction of Jerusalem. He bitterly reviles those who defend the Jewish cause, and calls the teachers of his own sect, who uphold the present reading of the Hebrew text, donkeys without light or understanding, girt with a professor's gown, carrying the Masoretic Bible with all its points as a shield. Who would not believe that such a confident assertion by Vossius has firm grounds? But how gravely he was mistaken will become clear from what follows. What passage, he says, dealing with the Messiah occurs in the sacred writings which they have not tried to corrupt or weaken by a perverse interpretation? And a little later: When they saw that the time of the Messiah's coming had passed, since six thousand years from the creation of the world had been completed, they removed from their books the fourteen centuries in order to gain two thousand years. To do away with the remaining five or six centuries, they shortened the period of the Judges by omitting the anarchies, and they reduced the years of the Persian kings. In this way they multiplied the measure of time by a full two thousand years. But these are sheer inventions of Vossius, who not only accuses the Jews but also asserts that the same crime was committed by the Samaritans, though for a different reason.

units.la: Verum prisci Ecclesiae Patres Africanus, Origenes, Eusebius, Hieronymus, Augustinus & alii qui hanc Judaeorum codicis ab Hebraeis exemplaribus in rebus chronologicis discrepantiam animadverterunt, de hac depravatione Judaeis objicienda nunquam cogitarunt. Imo Augustinus hac in parte Judaeorum exemplar Graeco praeferendum esse non veretur interdum asserere, in eaque est opinione, ut ei linguae potius credatur, unde est in aliam per Interpretes facta translatio. Justinus Martyr, qui disputans adversus Tryphonem Judaeos variis modis exagitat, ut Graecam, quae tunc sola in Ecclesia auctoritatis aliquid obtinebat, LXX. Seniorum interpretationem vindicaret, de mutata ab iis Chronologia, ut causae suae patrocinarentur, ne verbum quidem protulit.
units.tr: Yet the early Fathers of the Church, Africanus, Origen, Eusebius, Jerome, Augustine and others who noticed this discrepancy in chronology between the Jewish manuscripts and the Hebrew copies, never thought of charging the Jews with this corruption. Indeed, Augustine on this point does not hesitate at times to assert that the Jewish copy should be preferred to the Greek, and he holds the view that we should rather trust the language from which the translation into another was made by the translators. Justin Martyr, who in his dispute with Trypho attacks the Jews in various ways in order to defend the Greek version of the Seventy Elders, which alone then carried any authority in the Church, did not say a single word about the change made to the chronology by them, though he could have used it to support his case.

units.la: Praeterea, si Judaeis in mentem venisset codices Hebraeos corrumpere, ne tempus quo in sacris literis venturum esse Messiam significaretur elapsum esse videretur, longe potiori titulo Danielis vaticinium, quod accuratè tempus illud observat, quàm libros Moysis aut Judicum, depravassent. Prophetiam autem Danielis, quae magnam partem Messiae tempora respicit, integram remansisse in confesso est apud omnes, & hac Judaeos valde premi negare non audet ipse Vossius. Sed latebras quaerens affirmat antiquos Judaeos non tantum Danielem a choro Prophetarum segregasse, sed & negasse fuisse Prophetam. Verum nunquam intellexit vir doctus, quo sensu Judaei Danielem Prophetarum choro minimè adscriberent. De hoc negotio, uti jam supra observatum est, frustra Christiani cum Judaeis disputant: utrique enim lubentes agnoscunt in libro Danielis multa extare de Messia venturo vaticinia, & hunc Spiritus Sancti opus esse non secus ac reliquos Scripturae Sacrae libros. De Davide eadem prorsus fingunt Judaei, atque de Daniele: non ideo tamen Spiritus Sancti afflatum ab eo removent. Contrà in Psalmis etiam multa haberi quae venturum Messiam praenunciant, palàm asserunt, & si quid sit inter illos & Christianos hac in parte discriminis, mera est de nomine, ut jam alibi probatum est, controversia: dum illi aliter Scripturae Sacrae libros partiuntur atque Christiani. Sed suo seipsum gladio jugulat Vossius, dum obres chronologicas Judæos falsitatis reos peragit; quandoquidem hodierna contextûs Hebraici Chronologia Judæos longè magis urget, quàm illa quæ ex Græca LXX. Interpretum versione ducitur; nec id Judæi ipsi diffitentur in libris Talmudicis, ubi non eunt inficias jam expletum fuisse tempus quo venturus erat Messias, sed addunt illum propter eorum iniquitates non advenisse. Hæc sunt Talmudistarum verba. Domús Eliæ traditio hæc est: Mundus constabit sex annorum millibus: annorum erunt duo millia inanitatis, seu ante Legem: duo etiam millia annorum Legis: & duo millia annorum temporis Messiæ. Sed ob iniquitates nostras, quæ multæ sunt, præteriere anni illi, qui jam elapsi sunt. Vossius, qui istud Eliæ effatum ad institutum suum trahere conatus est, in pluribus erravit: primò enim laudare videtur illud quasi revera ab Elia Propheta, aut ex ejus libro, quem olim, inquit, Veteris Testamenti scriptis annumeratum fuisse constat, desumptum fuerit. Sed Elias iste Doctor fuit Talmudicus, sicuti R. Hillel, R. Schammai, R. Johanan, & alii bene multi quorum nomina & sententiæ in Talmude referuntur. Deinde figmentum est quod ait bis mille annos qui Legem Moysis præcessêre non à principio creationis debere numerari, sed à Diluvio, vel ab illo tempore quo Noæ dixit Deus, velle se mundum perdere. Longè siquidem diversa est hoc loco Judæorum sententia de sex annorum millibus quibus mundus duraturus erat, secundùm Magistri Eliæ traditionem. Vaticinii enim illius fundamentum ex sex diebus creationis petitum est; ita ut sicuti Deus intra sex dierum spatium mundum creavit, similiter idem mundus sex annorum millibus perduraturus sit: idcirco annorum mundi supputatio inde jam à prima rerum omnium creatione sumi debet. Magistri qui Commentariis suis Talmudis libros illustrant, bis mille annorum numerant à primo homine condito usque ad tempus illud quo Abraham relicto idolorum cultu veram Dei unius Legem amplexatus est. Tunc secundùm illorum supputationem annum vitæ agebat quinquagesimum secundum. Frigida autem sunt quæ profert idem Vossius, ut probet ex B. Petri Epistola, mundi de quo agitur initium arcessendum esse à Diluvio, quòd Apostolus ille veterem mundum eum vocaverit qui Diluvium præcessit; terram verò quam nunc habitamus mundum alterum: hęc, inquam, frigida sunt & extra propositi hujusce rationem. Sed non est cur fictitiæ Doctoris Eliæ de mundi duratione Prophetiæ diutius immoremur, neque etiam ratio habenda est libri illius Prophetiarum Eliæ, quem falsò putat Isaacus Vossius, Eliæ Talmudici nomine deceptus, inter Veteris Testamenti libros olim collocatum. Alias si quæ sint majoris momenti probationes ab eodem Vossio productæ adversus Judæos, expendamus.
units.tr: Moreover, if it had occurred to the Jews to corrupt the Hebrew manuscripts so that the time in which the sacred writings signify that the Messiah is to come would not seem to have passed, they would have corrupted the prophecy of Daniel, which observes that time with great precision, with a far stronger claim than the books of Moses or of Judges. It is agreed by all that the prophecy of Daniel, which for the most part concerns the times of the Messiah, has remained intact, and Vossius himself does not dare to deny that this presses the Jews hard. Seeking a hiding place, he asserts that the ancient Jews not only separated Daniel from the company of the Prophets, but also denied that he was a prophet. But the learned man never understood in what sense the Jews did not count Daniel among the Prophets. In this matter, as has already been noted above, Christians argue in vain with the Jews. For both sides gladly acknowledge that many prophecies about the coming Messiah are found in the book of Daniel, and that it is the work of the Holy Spirit no less than the other books of Sacred Scripture. The Jews make exactly the same claims about David as about Daniel, yet they do not for that reason deny that he was inspired by the Holy Spirit. On the contrary, they openly assert that many things in the Psalms also foretell the coming Messiah. And if there is any difference between them and the Christians on this point, it is a mere dispute over a name, as has already been shown elsewhere, since they divide the books of Sacred Scripture differently from the Christians. But Vossius cuts his own throat with his own sword, when he charges the Jews with falsehood in chronological matters. For the chronology of the present Hebrew text presses the Jews far more than that which is drawn from the Greek version of the Seventy translators. Nor do the Jews themselves deny this in their Talmudic books, where they do not deny that the time in which the Messiah was to come had already been completed, but add that he did not come because of their iniquities. These are the words of the Talmudists: This is the tradition of the house of Elijah: the world will stand for six thousand years. Two thousand years will be of emptiness, that is, before the Law; two thousand years also of the Law; and two thousand years of the time of the Messiah. But because of our iniquities, which are many, those years have passed which have already elapsed. Vossius, who tried to bend this saying of Elijah to his own purpose, went wrong in several ways. First, he seems to praise it as if it had really come from the prophet Elijah, or had been taken from his book, which, he says, is known to have once been counted among the writings of the Old Testament. But this Elijah was a Talmudic teacher, as were Rabbi Hillel, Rabbi Shammai, Rabbi Johanan, and many others whose names and opinions are reported in the Talmud. Next, it is a fiction that he says the two thousand years which preceded the Law of Moses should not be counted from the beginning of creation, but from the Flood, or from the time when God said to Noah that he wished to destroy the world. For the opinion of the Jews here about the six thousand years during which the world was to last, according to the tradition of Master Elijah, is quite different. The basis of that prophecy is taken from the six days of creation, so that just as God created the world within a span of six days, so the same world is to last for six thousand years. Therefore the reckoning of the years of the world must be taken from the very first creation of all things. The masters who illustrate the Talmud in their commentaries count two thousand years from the first man who was created until the time when Abraham, having abandoned the worship of idols, embraced the true Law of the one God. According to their reckoning, he was then in his fifty-second year of life. The arguments which Vossius offers to prove from the Epistle of the blessed Peter that the beginning of the world in question must be dated from the Flood, because that Apostle called the world which preceded the Flood the old world, and the earth which we now inhabit the other world, these arguments, I say, are feeble and beside the point of our present argument. But there is no reason to dwell longer on the fictitious prophecies of the teacher Elijah about the duration of the world, nor should we take account of that book of the Prophecies of Elijah, which Isaac Vossius wrongly thinks was once placed among the books of the Old Testament, deceived by the name of the Talmudic Elijah. Otherwise let us weigh whatever proofs of greater importance have been produced by the same Vossius against the Jews.

units.la: Nonnulla deinde Vossius adversus Judæos congerit, ut conficiat illos non pauca Scripturæ Sacræ loca mutilâsse, atque in primis Justinum Martyrem opponit, qui scribat complura olim à Judæis inquinata fuisse exemplaria. Verùm jam iis omnibus quæ ex Justini auctoritate sumi possunt rationibus abundè satisfecimus. Contextum Hebræum nunquam consuluit Justinus, imò nec consulere potuit; cùm ex illius scriptis manifestum sit, eum linguam Hebræam non calluisse. Sed quos non lusus, inquit Vossius, dedisset sanctissimus Martyr Tryphoni & innumeris aliis inter quos versabatur Judæis, si non vera fuissent ea quæ illis intentat crimina? Sed hæc argumentandi ratio digna non est homine erudito, qui in evolvendis B. Justini libris deprehendere poterat multa illi excidisse. At pergit Vossius. Vaticinium de Christo quod occurrit Psalmo 22. ubi pro foderunt substitutum est tanquàm leo, fuisse ab iis depravatum fatentur plerique Christiani, exceptis Fanaticis quibusdam & sesqui-Judæis. Verum quidem est ob id à plerisque Theologis in jus vocari Judæos, quasi dedita operâ locum istum corruperint. Sed absit ut Fanaticos ac sesqui-Judæos illos esse pronunciem, qui hoc crimen à Judæis amoliuntur, cùm R. Jacob Ben Hajim Masoræ instaurator lectionem caru, foderunt, quæ Christianis favet, in nonnullis exemplaribus se invenisse palàm testetur. Neque mirum videri debet, quòd Masorethæ eam, quæ causam suam magis tuebatur, lectionem amplexati fuerint. Eam quidem quam Græci Interpretes & Hieronymus repræsentant veriorem esse agnosco; non ideo tamen accusandi sunt Judæi qui è duabus lectionibus unam selegerint, quæ ad res suas magis accommodabatur. Quin & fieri potest ut ea solùm in Masorethicis exemplaribus lectio exhiberetur, quam hodie exhibent. In lectionibus cari & caru parùm esse discriminis, nôrunt omnes qui rei criticæ periti sunt, & quàm facilis ac frequens sit literarum Jod & Vau inter se permutatio. Neque dixeris literam Aleph in dictione cari scriptam reperiri, minimè verò in dictione caru, adeoque mutationem non ita facilem fuisse. Sed alia sunt, & quidem haud infrequentia in sacris codicibus superfluæ hujusce literæ exempla, quæ Masorethis ipsis non fuêre incognita. Quare Græci Interpretes & B. Hieronymus illam veluti superfluam reticuerunt, vel ab eorum exemplaribus aberat; secus verò Masorethæ, qui illam agnoscunt.
units.tr: Next, Vossius heaps up several charges against the Jews, in order to establish that they mutilated not a few passages of Sacred Scripture. Above all, he sets against them Justin Martyr, who writes that many copies had once been corrupted by the Jews. But we have already fully answered all the arguments that can be drawn from the authority of Justin. Justin never consulted the Hebrew text, and indeed could not have done so, since it is clear from his writings that he did not have a good knowledge of the Hebrew language. But what mockery, says Vossius, would the most holy Martyr have made to Trypho and to the countless other Jews among whom he lived, if the charges they brought against them were not true? But this method of argument is not worthy of a learned man, who could have seen in reading the books of the blessed Justin that many things had escaped him. Vossius goes on: Most Christians admit that the prophecy about Christ which occurs in Psalm 22, where instead of "they pierced" there is "like a lion," was corrupted by them, with the exception of certain fanatics and half-Jews. It is true that for this reason most theologians call the Jews to account, as if they had deliberately corrupted that passage. But far be it from me to say that those who absolve the Jews of this crime are fanatics and half-Jews. R. Jacob ben Hayyim, the restorer of the Masora, openly testifies that he found in some copies the reading caru, they pierced, which favours the Christians. Nor should it seem strange that the Masoretes adopted the reading which better supported their own cause. I admit that the reading which the Greek translators and Jerome present is the truer one. Nevertheless, the Jews should not be accused for having chosen from the two readings the one which better suited their own purposes. Indeed, it is possible that only the reading which they present today was found in the Masoretic copies. Everyone who is skilled in textual criticism knows that there is little difference between the readings cari and caru, and how easy and frequent the interchange of the letters Yod and Vav is. Nor can you say that the letter Aleph is found written in the word cari, but never in the word caru, and so the change was not so easy. But there are other examples, and not infrequent ones, in the sacred codices of this superfluous letter, which were not unknown to the Masoretes themselves. Therefore the Greek translators and blessed Jerome left it out as if superfluous, or it was absent from their copies; whereas the Masoretes, who recognise it, retained it.

units.la: Vana sunt etiam quæ ex loco Zachariæ, Cap. 12: 10. objicit Vossius, quasi antiquam Judæi lectionem, quam prisci Interpretes in suis exemplaribus habuere, de industria mutaverint: at nemo non, artis criticæ peritus, judicabit hanc diversitatem ortam esse ex diversis exemplaribus, dum in aliis legitur dakeru, in aliis autem rakedu, ob facilem videlicet literarum Resch & Daleth in se invicem permutationem. Nec video cur ob id, & alia id genus sexcenta, Judæi potius in crimen falsitatis adducantur, quàm Græci, Latini, cæterarumque nationum Scribæ, qui similiter in describendis suis codicibus labuntur. Hanc literarum similium commutationem in omnibus linguis reperiri necesse est, unde postea in gens codicum nata est discordia. Qua de re consulendum est in primis Scioppii de Arte Critica opusculum, qui totum istud negotium egregiè illustravit. Leo quoque Allatius, vir in evolvendis codicibus MSS. diu versatus, varia Criticorum in rei hujusce confirmationem loca congessit: cujus verba huc referre non pigebit ex illius animadversionibus in Antiquitatum Etruscarum Fragmenta, quæ ab Inghiramio edita fuerant. Præterea, inquit, tot exscriptorum errata, tot literarum, tot nominum in antiquorum monumentis mutationes, si ingenuè agimus, à nullo alio quàm à capitalibus hisce corrivârunt, ob literarum similitudinem quam inter se capitales, non autem minusculæ, servant. Exemplis, sed paucissimis, ex aliorum animadversionibus agamus, ne ista curiosius ipse perquirere, ab inficeto nescio quo, dicar. Josephus Scaliger in Varronem de Re Rustica, lib. 2. cap. 3. Mediam non Meliam propter familiarem veteribus τὴ L in D mutationem, ut Melicæ contra gallinæ dictæ, quæ Medicæ dici debebant; & alibi librarios imperitos sæpe pro I, L, & contrà scribere. Godeschalcus Stewichius in libro 1. Appuleii ait, sæpe in mutuum locum immigrâsse has literas, D & T; & in libro 5. causam depravandi sententiam asserit similitudinem literarum B & P; nam & has, ut & R, non semel ex affinitate commutatas, testes Quintilianum & Plinium adducens, quorum verba & monita de majusculis & Romanis literis accipienda, quòd iis antiquis in libris describendis usi fuissent. Joannes Isacius Pontanus in Glossario prisco Gallico, non in dissimili argumento, B & P mutationem, solennem metastasin
units.tr: Equally groundless is what Vossius objects from the passage of Zechariah, chapter 12, verse 10: that the Jews deliberately changed the ancient reading which the early translators had in their copies. Anyone skilled in textual criticism will judge that this variation arose from different copies, since in some the reading is dakeru, in others rakedu, owing to the easy interchange of the letters Resch and Daleth. I do not see why, on account of this and countless other things of the same kind, the Jews should be accused of falsification rather than the Greeks, the Latins and the scribes of other nations, who make similar slips in copying their manuscripts. Such interchange of similar letters must occur in every language, and from it the variety of manuscripts has arisen. On this matter one should consult above all the little work of Scioppius on the art of criticism, who treated the whole business admirably. Leo Allatius, a man long engaged in working through manuscripts, also gathered various passages of critics in confirmation of this matter. It is worth quoting his words from his observations on the Fragments of the Etruscan Antiquities published by Inghirami: Moreover, he says, if we are honest, the many errors of copyists and the many changes of letters and names in ancient monuments have come about from nothing other than capital letters, on account of the similarity which the capitals keep among themselves, but not the minuscules. Let us proceed by examples, though very few, taken from the observations of others, lest I be called an ignoramus for not having sought these out myself. Joseph Scaliger, on Varro's De Re Rustica, book 2, chapter 3, notes that Media was written instead of Melia, because of the change of Τ-like L into D, familiar to the ancients, just as Melica was said for Medica, which should have been called so; and elsewhere he notes that unskilled scribes often wrote I for L and L for I. Godeschalcus Stewichius, in book 1 on Apuleius, says that these letters, D and T, often passed into each other's place; and in book 5 he asserts that the similarity of the letters B and P was the cause of the corrupted sense; for these, like R, were not once interchanged through affinity, as he shows by citing Quintilian and Pliny, whose words and warnings are to be understood of capital and Roman letters, since the ancients used these in writing books. Johannes Isacius Pontanus, in his Old Gallic Glossary, on a not dissimilar subject, calls the customary change of B and P a metastasis, or stafis.

units.la: Leo Allat. in Antiq. Etrusc. pag. 55. stafin vocat. Scioppius de Critica tradit, exemplisque ex variis fuse probat, C in G, D in L, F in E, P in B & R; & vice versa, L in D, E in F, R & B in P, ob similitudinem commigrasse. Habent quoque inter se quamdam similitudinem majusculæ Græcorum literæ. Ita facillima est literarum Græcarum β, γ, ρ, necnon τ & τ, atque Δ & Λ commutatio. Quibus addi posset non tantum inter literas etiam minusculas reperiri discrepantiæ, quin sæpius ob earum quam servant inter se similitudinem, aliquid confusionis oriatur. Quo pacto, ut innumera sileam, quando apud Græcos legendum sit ὑμῖν, quando ὑμῖν, & apud Latinos orbis vel urbis, sæpè in incerto est. Varias codicum suorum lectiones sibi objiciunt Chronographi, Historici & alii passim, quorum exempla ubique prostant: exempli causâ, hactenus Dagobertum Francorum Regem Nanthildem, puellam elegantis formæ, è Monasterio raptam, totius gentis consilio uxorem duxisse communiter receptum fuerat. Verùm ætate nostrâ viri clarissimi, Jacobus Sirmondus, Adrianus Valesius & alii in codices MSS. inciderunt, qui non habeant, Nanthildem, unam ex puellis de Monasterio, in matrimonium accipiens Reginam sublimavit, uti pravè Fredegardi contextum Aimonius laudaverat; sed, Nantechildem unam ex puellis de ministerio accipiens, &c. sicut in MS. Fredegardi codice à se lectum fuisse animadvertit Sirmondus. Ejusmodi allucinationes, quæ non solùm ex literarum similitudine, sed & ex innumeris aliis causis nascuntur, reperire est in omnibus manu exaratis, cujusque linguæ sint ac conditionis. Unde postea lectionum monstra orta sunt, quæ Criticorum ingenia valdè contorquent, & gravissima inter Grammaticos dissidia excitant. Ita qui se germanos Ciceronis imitatores jactitant, suam sibi interdum Ciceronianismi imperitiam exprobrant, non aliam sæpè ob causam, quàm quòd diversis in evolvendis Ciceronis operibus codicibus usi fuerint, quorum indolem bellè notavit Henricus Stephanus.
units.tr: Leo Allatius, on the Antiquities of Etruria, page 55. Scioppius in his work on criticism teaches, and proves at length by examples from various sources, that C passed into G, D into L, F into E, P into B and R, and vice versa, L into D, E into F, R and B into P, through similarity. The capital letters of the Greeks also have a certain resemblance to one another. Thus the interchange of the Greek letters β, γ and ρ, and also of τ and τ, and of Δ and Λ, is very easy. To these could be added that not only among the minuscule letters are there differences, but often, owing to the resemblance which they keep among themselves, some confusion arises. By this means, to pass over countless other cases, it is often uncertain whether ὑμῖν or ὑμῖν should be read among the Greeks, or orbis or urbis among the Latins.
