The chroniclers, historians and others everywhere raise objections from the variant readings of their manuscripts, and examples of this are found on every page. For instance, it has hitherto been commonly accepted that King Dagobert of the Franks took to wife Nanthild, a girl of elegant beauty, carried off from a convent, with the consent of the whole nation. But in our own time the most distinguished men, Jacques Sirmond, Adrien de Valois and others, have come upon manuscripts which do not have Nanthild, taking as wife one of the girls from the convent, raised her to the queenship, as Aimoin had wrongly quoted the text of Fredegar; rather, they have Nantechild, taking as wife one of the girls from the ministry, etc., as Sirmond observed had been read in the manuscript of Fredegar which he used. Errors of this kind, which arise not only from similarity of letters but also from countless other causes, are to be found in all hand-written texts, whatever their language or condition. Hence monstrous readings have later arisen, which greatly twist the wits of critics and stir up very serious disputes among the grammarians. Thus those who boast of being true imitators of Cicero sometimes reproach themselves for their own ignorance of Ciceronian usage, often for no other reason than that they used different manuscripts in reading through Cicero's works; the nature of these Henricus Stephanus has well noted.

units.la: Sed ne ea quæ ab imperitis duntaxat ignorari possunt, prolixius annotem, unam operum Ciceronis editionem in exemplum proferam, quæ ex officina Elzeviriorum anno M. DC. LXI. accurante Schrevelio, prodiit; in qua editione diversę aliarum editionum codicumque manu exaratorum lectiones ad oram libri utilissimè relatæ sunt. Si & in Hebraicis exemplaribus idem præstitum fuisset, & ad illorum margines variantes omnes lectiones, quę ex diversis codicibus cùm MSS. tum editis, necnon ex vetustis translationibus sumi poterant, fuissent observatæ, Judæos ob hanc codicum diversitatem exemplaria sua corrupisse nemo sanus dixerit; sed ex diversis istis lectionibus meliorem quisque seligeret, ut olim Hieronymus, qui Commentariis suis in Prophetas à Græca LXX. Interpretum translatione sæpius recedit. Ita, Magistrorum suorum lectioni addictissimus, in Caput 2. Oseæ, hæc animadvertit: Pro saltu quoque, quod Hebraicè dicitur jaar, LXX. transtulerunt testimonium, Resch & Daleth literarum falsi similitudine: si enim pro Resch Daleth legatur, testimonium dicitur; ita duntaxat ut Jod litera non legatur. Iterum ad Caput 5. ejusdem Prophetæ notat LXX. Interpretes, quòd pro חודש menses, legerint חסיל rubigo. Et ad Caput 9. quærens cur ubi LXX. habent, Caro mea ex eis, ipse verterit Cùm recessero ab eis, hæc habet: In eo loco in quo nos diximus, Væ eis cùm recessero ab eis, LXX. & Theodotio transtulerunt, Væ eis caro mea ex eis; quærensque causam cur sit tanta varietas, hanc mihi videor reperisse, caro mea lingua Hebraica dicitur besari. Rursum si dicamus, recessio mea, sive declinatio mea, dicitur besuri. Simili ratione nihil causæ fuit cur Hieronymus à recepta illa LXX. Seniorum versione, πῶς ἡ δίκη σα, Ubi causa tua, recederet; quam suâ auctoritate B. Paulus confirmaverat, nisi quòd aliam lectionem præferrent ejus exemplaria, & pro אי ubi, per transformationem literarum legeret אהי ero. Similem transpositionem longè satius est observare in dakeru, transfixerunt, & rakedu, insultarunt apud Zachariam, quàm Judæos cum Vossio suggillare, quasi mutationem istam in contextum dedità operâ invexerint. Sed his aliisque ejusdem naturæ diversitatibus contexendis supersedeo, ne prolixiori eorum recensione molestus sim, maximè cùm à Theologis, qui suis explanationibus sacra volumina illustrârunt, diligenter observentur.
units.tr: But, lest I annotate at too great length things which can be ignored only by the unskilled, I shall offer as an example one edition of Cicero's works which issued from the Elzevir press in the year 1661, edited by Schrevelius, in which the different readings of other editions and of manuscripts are very usefully set out in the margin of the book. If the same had been done with the Hebrew copies, and if all the variant readings which could be drawn from different manuscripts and printed editions, as well as from the ancient translations, had been noted in their margins, no sane person would say that the Jews had corrupted their copies on account of this diversity of manuscripts; rather, everyone would choose the better of these different readings, as Jerome once did, who in his commentaries on the Prophets often departs from the Greek translation of the Seventy. Thus, most devoted to the reading of his teachers, on chapter 2 of Hosea he remarks: For the word saltu, which in Hebrew is called jaar, the Seventy translated testimonium, through the false similarity of the letters Resch and Daleth: for if Daleth is read instead of Resch, it becomes testimonium; only so that the letter Jod is not read. Again, on chapter 5 of the same prophet he notes that the Seventy interpreters read rust [chersil] instead of menses [chodesh]. And on chapter 9, asking why, where the Seventy have My flesh from them, he himself rendered When I depart from them, he says this: In the passage where we said, Woe to them when I depart from them, the Seventy and Theodotion translated, Woe to them, my flesh from them; and asking the reason for so great a variety, I seem to have found it: in the Hebrew tongue my flesh is called besari. Again, if we say my departure, or my turning aside, it is called besuri. In a similar way there was no reason why Jerome should depart from the accepted version of the Seventy Elders, πῶς ἡ δίκη σα [pōs hē dikē sa], Where is your cause, which the apostle Paul had confirmed by his authority; except that their copies had a different reading, and, for the word אי [ai], where, through transposition of letters he read אהי [ehi], I shall be. It is far better to observe a similar transposition in dakeru, they pierced, and rakedu, they trampled upon, in Zechariah, than with Vossius to heap reproach upon the Jews, as if they had deliberately introduced that change into the text. But I forbear to set out these and other differences of the same kind, lest I trouble with a longer recital of them, especially since they are carefully noted by theologians who have illustrated the sacred volumes with their explanations.

units.la: Rectè quidem Vossius Judæorum codices in multis vitiatos esse scripsit: quorum scilicet eadem omnino sors fuerit atque Græcorum Latinorumque librorum; dignusque est Georgius Hornius qui sibilis omnium excipiatur, cùm doctissimo Vossio opponit sanctiones Regum, Principum ac Magistratuum, quibus volunt ut eæ solùm in Ecclesiis contextûs Biblici versiones legantur, quæ ad exemplaria Hebraica adornatæ fuerint; quasi verò ejusmodi sanctiones Principum codices Judæorum ab omni prorsus menda integros servare potuerint. At in eo castigandus etiam Vossius, quòd nonnullos
units.tr: Vossius rightly wrote that the Jewish manuscripts are in many places corrupted: they evidently suffered the very same fate as Greek and Latin books. And Georgius Hornius deserves to be hissed off by everyone, since he sets against the most learned Vossius the decrees of kings, princes and magistrates, by which they wish that only those versions of the biblical text should be read in the churches which have been made to agree with the Hebrew copies; as if such decrees of princes could keep the manuscripts of the Jews wholly free from every blemish. But Vossius also deserves to be rebuked in this, that he contends too obstinately that certain errors of this kind were introduced by the Jews deliberately into their copies, and out of hatred of the Christian religion, and not...

units.la: B. Hieron. nullos ejusmodi errorum à Judæis consultò in sua exemplaria & ex odio Christianæ Religionis invectos fuisse pertinacius contendat. Ita ad verba ista Geneseos, Non auferetur sceptrum de Juda, & dux de femore ejus, donec veniat qui mittendus est, hæc animadvertit: Hunc locum non tantùm in versione Græca, verùm etiam in omnibus codicibus Hebræis mutilárunt Judæi, rescribendo שילוה pro שלוה, uti observatum compluribus, quorum opinionem confirmat codex Samariticus. Sed quis nesciat olim in contextu Hebraeo literam Jod ante inventa puncta vocalia, modò i, modò e vocalium locum tenuisse? & hanc non solùm, sed & alias vocales, quas vulgò Ehevi appellant, pro Scribarum arbitrio neglectas fuisse? Sive igitur scribatur שילוה, ut in hodiernis Masorethar-um codicibus, sive שלוה, uti legisse videntur LXX. Interpretes, ob id in crimen falsitatis adduci non debent Judæi, qui in suis exemplaribus vocalem Jod retinuerunt. Fieri etiam potest ut Græci Interpretes eam in suo exemplari legerint, quandoquidem idem est omnino dictionis illius sensus, sive per Jod, sive absque Jod efferatur, quia litera Jod non minùs per vocalem e quàm per i potest pronunciari. At Masorethæ, qui legendum esse schilo arbitrati sunt, priscam literam Jod retinuere, quâ non obstante, etiam hodiernis temporibus cum Græcis Interpretibus legere possumus schelo, uti revera legunt nonnulli Judæorum Magistri. Hęc non debuit ignorare Vossius, qui toties Judæos in jus vocat, quique scribit, eos qui negant hunc locum à Judæis corruptum esse, Prophetias omnes abolere. Eadem omnino codicis Hebraei ratio extitit ante & post Christi tempora; nihilque prorsus causæ est, cur depravationes, si quę fuerint in illo ante Christi adventum, illas tribuat Vossius errori & incuriæ librariorum; eas verò quæ in exemplaria Hebraica post Christi adventum intrusæ sunt, vitio animi adscribat. Masorethis etiam Tiberiensibus plus æquo detrahit Vossius, dum illos vocat homines barbaros, & in vernacula quam jactant lingua peregrinos, à quibus nihil aliud quàm vitiosum & ab omni ratione alienum proficisci potuit. Illos quidem non fuisse Prophetas cum Vossio lubens agnosco; eosdem quoque punctorum vocalium & apicum auctores esse non diffiteor: at quis inde conficiat eos barbaros fuisse, & linguæ Hebraicæ imperitos, ac demum Scripturas punctis & apicibus onerari potiùs quàm exornari. Si vera sunt quę de seipso jactitat Vossius, vidisse plures quàm bis mille codices Hebraicos manu exaratos, artis Masorethicæ sorethicę eum prorsus ignarum non fuisse credibile est. Hęc opus est Judęorum Tiberiensium, qui codicis Hebraici lectionem, qualis tunc usu publico recepta erat, adhibitis punctis vocalibus determinârunt. Masoræ nomen illi inditum est, quòd traditionem seu legendi contextûs Hebraici rationem diuturno usu comprobatam amplexati fuerint. De illorum Critica idem plane judicium ferri debet, ac de Græcis Latinisque libris, qui à viris eruditis castigati & recogniti fuêre. Celeberrimæ apud Judæos Scholę præfuerunt Magistri illi Tiberienses, qui conquisitis undique Bibliorum exemplaribus, accuratam illorum editionem evulgârunt. Nihil ab illis in hoc negotio præstitum est, quod in crimen verti possit. Et hęc illorum correctio, quantumlibet accurata, aliis non obfuit, quin eadem exemplaria adhuc recognoscerent, eademque etiam nostrâ ætate ad Græcam LXX. Interpretum versionem & Latinam Hieronymi recognosci posse existimo, in locis quibus illorum exemplaria à Masorethicis variâsse constabit. Non ideo tamen Judæos cum Vossio falsitatis accusabimus, quia illorum codices iidem omnino non sunt, atque illi quos ad condendam translationem suam adhibuêre Græci Interpretes: sed dicemus diversas lectiones non minùs reperiri in Hebræorum exemplaribus, quàm in Græcorum, Latinorum, cæterarumque gentium libris. Rabbinorum traditionibus solo auditu propagatis nihil solidi subesse putat Vossius; & quæ solo auditu propagantur traditiones, inquit, raro solent ad duo vel tria perstare sæcula. Sed quid hęc faciunt ad eam de qua in præsentia agitur traditionem? De oralibus Judæorum, ut vocantur, traditionibus, quas merito à prudentioribus explodi agnoscit, nulla est controversia; sed de ea tantùm quæ Masora appellatur, quamque Judæi Carraitę, qui plerasque Judęorum traditiones velut anilia commenta respuunt, amplexati fuêre. Si hanc rejiciat Vossius, rejiciat quoque necesse est librorum Chaldaicorum, Syriacorum & Hebraicorum, qui nonnihil antiquitatis præ se ferunt, lectionem: iis enim omnibus, simili prorsus ratione atque Hebraicis, puncta vocalia, quę certam facerent illorum lectionem, addita sunt. Traditionis itaque hoc loco nomine, nihil aliud intelligimus quàm receptam & longo usu confirmatam codicis Hebraici lectionem. Sed codex ille, inquit Vossius, mutus est, quem nec legere, nedum intelligere, quisquam sciat, utpote truncus media sui parte, nec aliis quàm quas Christianæ fidei inimici apposuêre instructus vocalibus. Minùsne truncus erat codex ille LXX. Interpretum ætate, cùm nihil omnino punctorum vocalium in eo appareret? Ea est linguæ Hebraicæ, ut & cæterarum Orientis linguarum, natura, ut paucissimas vocales repræsentet; adeo ut librorum qui sermone Hebraeo, Chaldaico, Syriaco & Arabico scripti sunt, lectio non parum ab usu dependeat, quem hic traditionem, seu Masoram, cum Judæis vocamus. Jam à quibus usus iste legendi codicis Hebraici sumi potuit, quàm à Judæis? Verùm, inquit Vossius, Judæi inimici sunt Christianæ fidei. An ideo codices suos legere dedidicerunt quia Judæi? Imò nisi Judæi essent, codices Hebreos in Synagogis non legerent: nec ab aliis quàm ab istis illorum lectio ad Christianos derivari potuit. Judæi quoque erant LXX. Seniores à quibus totus dependet Vossius, iique non aliam contextûs Hebraici lectionem sequuti sunt, quàm quæ usu publico ætatis suæ apud Judæos recepta erat. Quapropter id omne quod regerit Vossius in Hebræum codicem, quòd sit liber dimidiatus & medià sui parte truncus, affirmari etiam potest de codice Hebræo quo usi sunt Græci Interpretes: neque tam codex accusari debuit, quàm linguæ Hebraicæ ingenium; & ob eamdem rationem reliquæ linguæ Orientales accusabuntur, quasi dimidiatæ sint linguæ. Iterum tamen, & usque ad nauseam, inculcat Vossius mutum esse Hebræum codicem, &, vel ipsis agnoscentibus Rabbinis, truncum mediâ sui parte, utpote veris destitutum vocalibus. Sed quæ sint veræ codicis Hebraici vocales fingit se ignorare, dum illis eum destitutum tam fidenter asseverat. Priscæ siquidem Hebræorum vocales sunt, ut ipse alibi non diffitetur, literæ Aleph, He, Vau & Jod, quibus & alias adjungit Hieronymus. Sed quòd populi Orientales raro inter scribendum eas adhiberent, puncta vocalia excogitârunt viri Critici, quò facilior promptiorque esset librorum lectio. Verùm parum consentaneè loquitur Vossius, nec tam ex rei veritate, quàm ex præsumpta adversus Judæorum codices opinione.
units.tr: B. Hieron. Vossius maintains too stubbornly that the Jews did not deliberately introduce errors of this kind into their copies, out of hatred for the Christian religion. On the words of Genesis, "The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent," he remarks: "The Jews have mutilated this passage not only in the Greek version but in all the Hebrew manuscripts, by writing shiloh [שילוה] for shelo [שלוה], as many have observed, and the Samaritan codex confirms their opinion." But who does not know that in the Hebrew text the letter Jod once stood in place of the vowels i or e, before the vowel points were invented? And that this letter, and the other vowels which they commonly call Ehevi, were left out at the discretion of the scribes? So whether the word is written shiloh [שילוה], as in the present manuscripts of the Masoretes, or shelo [שלוה], as the Seventy translators seem to have read it, the Jews, who kept the vowel Jod in their copies, should not be charged with falsification. It is also possible that the Greek translators found it in their copy, since the meaning of the word is exactly the same whether it is pronounced with Jod or without it, because the letter Jod can be sounded as e as well as i. The Masoretes, who judged that it should be read shiloh, kept the older letter Jod; and even now, notwithstanding this, we can read shelo with the Greek translators, as in fact some of the Jewish teachers do. Vossius ought not to have overlooked this, he who so often summons the Jews to court, and who writes that those who deny this passage was corrupted by the Jews abolish all the prophecies. The very same state of the Hebrew codex existed before and after the time of Christ, and there is absolutely no reason why Vossius should attribute to the error and carelessness of copyists whatever corruptions there were before Christ's coming, but ascribe to bad faith those introduced into the Hebrew copies after it. Vossius also disparages the Tiberian Masoretes more than is fair, calling them barbarous men, foreigners to the language they boast of as their own, from whom nothing could have come but what was faulty and alien to all reason. I gladly agree with Vossius that they were not prophets; I do not deny that they were the authors of the vowel points and accents. But who could infer from this that they were barbarous and ignorant of the Hebrew language, and that the Scriptures were burdened rather than adorned with points and accents? If what Vossius boasts about himself is true, that he has seen more than two thousand Hebrew manuscripts written by hand, it is hard to believe he was wholly ignorant of the Masoretic art. This was the work of the Tiberian Jews, who fixed the reading of the Hebrew text, as it was then received in public use, by adding vowel points. They were given the name Masora because they embraced a tradition, that is, a method of reading the Hebrew text, confirmed by long use. About their criticism the very same judgment ought to be passed as about Greek and Latin books, which were corrected and revised by learned men. Those Tiberian masters presided over the most famous school among the Jews, and, having gathered copies of the Bible from everywhere, they published an accurate edition of them. Nothing done by them in this business can be held against them. And this correction of theirs, however accurate, did not prevent others from still revising the same copies; and I think that even in our own age the same copies can be revised by the Greek version of the Seventy translators and the Latin of Jerome, in those places where their copies are known to differ from the Masoretic. Yet we shall not, with Vossius, accuse the Jews of falsification merely because their codices are not the very same as those which the Greek translators used in making their version; rather, we shall say that different readings are found no less in Hebrew copies than in Greek, Latin and other nations' books. Vossius thinks there is no solid basis in the rabbinical traditions, handed down by word of mouth alone; and traditions handed down by word of mouth, he says, rarely last two or three centuries. But what does this have to do with the tradition under discussion at present? There is no dispute about the so-called oral traditions of the Jews, which he admits are rightly rejected by the wiser sort; the dispute is only about that which is called the Masora, and which the Karaites, who reject most Jewish traditions as old wives' fables, embraced. If Vossius rejects this, he must also necessarily reject the reading of the Chaldee, Syriac and Hebrew books, which show some antiquity; for to all of them, in exactly the same way as to the Hebrew, vowel points have been added, which fix their reading. Therefore by the name of tradition we understand nothing else here than the reading of the Hebrew codex, received and confirmed by long use. "But that codex," says Vossius, "is mute, and no one knows how to read it, much less understand it, since it is mutilated in its middle part and furnished with no vowels other than those which the enemies of the Christian faith added." Was that codex less mutilated in the time of the Seventy translators, when no vowel points at all appeared in it? Such is the nature of the Hebrew language, as of the other languages of the East, that it represents very few vowels; so that the reading of books written in Hebrew, Chaldee, Syriac and Arabic depends not a little on usage, which here we call with the Jews the tradition, or Masora. Now, from whom could this method of reading the Hebrew codex have been derived, if not from the Jews? "But," says Vossius, "the Jews are enemies of the Christian faith." Did they therefore unlearn how to read their own codices because they are Jews? On the contrary, if they were not Jews, they would not read the Hebrew codices in the synagogues; nor could their reading have come down to Christians from anyone but them. The Jews were also the Seventy Elders, on whom Vossius wholly depends, and they followed no other reading of the Hebrew text than that which was received by public use among the Jews of their age. Therefore everything Vossius throws against the Hebrew codex, that it is a book cut short and mutilated in its middle part, can equally be asserted of the Hebrew codex used by the Greek translators; and the fault lies not so much with the codex as with the genius of the Hebrew language. For the same reason the other Oriental languages will be accused of being, as it were, maimed. Yet again, and to the point of nausea, Vossius insists that the Hebrew codex is mute and, as even the rabbis admit, truncated in its middle part, being deprived of true vowels. But he pretends not to know what the true vowels of the Hebrew codex are, while he so confidently asserts that it is deprived of them. For the ancient vowels of the Hebrews are, as he himself admits elsewhere, the letters Aleph, He, Vau and Jod, to which Jerome also adds others. But because Eastern peoples seldom used these when writing, the learned critics devised vowel points, so that the reading of books might be easier and quicker. Vossius speaks rather inconsistently, and not so much from the truth of the matter as from an opinion he has assumed against the Jewish codices.

units.la: EXCERPTUM II.
units.tr: EXCERPT II.

units.la: IN rebus criticis non tam quid ab aliis dictum fuerit, quàm quid perspectis omnibus dicendum sit, animum debemus advertere, de hoc potissimùm soliciti, ut non modò quid quisque loquatur, sed etiam quid quisque sentiat, & qua etiam de causa quisque sentiat exactiùs inquiramus : plerique enim dum ex aliorum auctoritate mentem suam confirmant, Scriptores sæpius ex singulis vocibus, quàm ex sententiæ perpetuitate & constantia spectant. Ita quàm fœdè in hac parte erraverit Isaacus Vossius, dum Justini Martyris aliorumque Patrum testimonia in opus suum de LXX. Interpretibus transtulit, jam ostendimus, simulque illum tam in Judæos quàm in illorum codices plus æquo injuriosum esse demonstratum est. Nimirum, ut optimè aliàs à B. Hilario annotatum, Immoderata est omnis suscepturum voluntatum pertinacia, & indeflexo motu adversandi studium persistit ubi non rationi voluntas subjicitur, nec studium doctrinæ impenditur, sed iis quæ volumus rationem conquirimus, & iis quæ studemus doctrinam comparamus. Simili bus fere rationibus adductus fuisse videtur doctissimus Vossius, ut Hebræos Judæorum codices elevaret, & Græca LXX. Seniorum exemplaria assereret. Contendit igitur hos Interpretes Spiritu Sancto afflatos fuisse, qua in re sibi consentientes habet Patres omnes priscę ætatis, si unum exceperis Hieronymum, quem tam de Judæis Bibliorum corruptoribus, quàm de Prophetia & afflatu LXX. Seniorum sibi contrarium sentit. Beatus quidem Hieronymus omnium fere ætatis suæ Doctorum maledicta in se convertit, quòd viam communem & longo Ecclesiarum usu approbatam deserens, ad Judæorum castra videretur se recipere, parumque abfuit quin ab Ecclesia tanquam novator ejiceretur; imò & ætate nostrâ illius versionem damnat Vossius, eamque appellat Rabbinicam: sed doctissimus ille Pater reprehensoribus istis occurrens, qui damnare possunt, docere non possunt, Artem Criticam exercuit, & iis à quibus reclamatum est, suis libris abundè satisfecit. Nec mirum profectò si in nonnullis attentior & copiosâ linguarum supellectili instructior Hieronymus à veteribus recedere non dubitaverit: manifestos quippe errores æquitas minimè defendit. Novi quidem in rebus fidei aliquid divini præ se ferre Doctorum Ecclesiæ consensum: at ille cordatus non est nec religiosus, giosus, qui in iis rebus quæ non sunt fidei à Patrum sententia discedere reformidat, mavultque aliorum scriptis quàm oculis suis & experientiæ credere. De seipso longè aliud olim sentiebat Augustinus, qui optat ut alii de suis operibus judicent. Neminem, inquit, velim sic amplecti omnia mea, ut me sequatur, nisi in iis in quibus me non errare perspexerit.
units.tr: In critical matters we should attend not so much to what others have said as to what ought to be said once everything has been considered. We should be especially careful to examine closely not only what each person says but also what he thinks and for what reason he thinks it. Most people, while they confirm their own opinion by the authority of others, look more often at single words than at the continuity and consistency of a whole passage. So we have already shown how shamefully Isaac Vossius erred in this respect when he carried the testimonies of Justin Martyr and other Fathers into his work on the Seventy Interpreters. It has also been demonstrated that he was unduly unfair both to the Jews and to their manuscripts. Indeed, as Blessed Hilary rightly noted elsewhere: Every will that sets out to undertake things is immoderately stubborn, and the zeal for opposing persists in unbending motion when the will is not subject to reason, and study is not given to learning, but we seek reasons for what we want and gather learning to fit what we are eager for. The most learned Vossius seems to have been moved by much the same motives to raise the Hebrew manuscripts of the Jews above the Greek copies of the Seventy Elders and to defend those Greek copies. He therefore contends that these Interpreters were inspired by the Holy Spirit. In this he agrees with all the Fathers of the early age, with the single exception of Jerome, whom Vossius thinks opposed to himself both about the Jews as corruptors of the Bible and about the prophecy and inspiration of the Seventy Elders. Blessed Jerome certainly drew upon himself the curses of almost all the teachers of his own age, because, abandoning the common road approved by the long practice of the Churches, he seemed to retreat into the camp of the Jews. He came close to being cast out by the Church as an innovator. Even in our own time Vossius condemns his version and calls it Rabbinic. But that most learned Father, meeting those critics who can condemn but cannot teach, practised the critical art and amply satisfied, in his books, those by whom he had been opposed. Nor is it surprising if Jerome, who was more careful in some points and better equipped with a wide store of languages, did not hesitate to depart from the ancients, for fairness does not defend manifest errors. I know that the agreement of the Doctors of the Church carries something divine with it in matters of faith. But he is neither a wise nor a devout man who shrinks from departing from the opinion of the Fathers in matters that do not concern faith, and who prefers to trust the writings of others rather than his own eyes and experience. Augustine thought quite differently about himself long ago, when he wished that others would judge his works. I would not wish anyone to embrace all my writings so that he follows me, he says, except in those points in which he has seen that I am not mistaken.

units.la: Non est igitur cur Vossio hac in parte assentiamur, qui contra B. Hieronymum LXX. Interpretes velit divino Numine afflatos fuisse, & ab omni prorsus errore, etiam levissimo, liberos. Imò, quasi eum puduerit Interpretes illos Prophetarum nomine donasse, seipsum postea veluti castigans affirmat Prophetam vetustis Scriptoribus idem esse quod Interpres, illosque Prophetas esse, teste Apostolo, qui Scripturas rectè interpretati sunt. Sed cur latebras hic quæ̣rit Vossius, & ad profanam, ut ita loquar, eruditionem recurrit, ut demonstret in eo errare Hieronymum, cùm scribit aliud esse Prophetam, aliud Interpretem; quasi ipse contradixerit Apostolo, qui pluribus in locis προφήτης sumpsit pro interpretari? Verùm hic non errat Hieronymus, qui vocis illius proprietatem optimè noverat, quandoquidem animadvertit Poëtam Græcum à Paulo Prophetam vocatum fuisse. Sed in Responsione sua ad Objectiones nuperæ Criticæ Sacræ Vossius ubique tergiversatur. Ita quid illi causæ fuit cur non modò Apostolorum & Euangelistarum, sed & Philonis, Festi, Platonis & aliorum proferret testimonia, ut evincat eos non tantùm qui futura prædicerent dictos fuisse Prophetas, sed & qui præterita & præsentia explicarent; quandoquidem ea de re inter illum & Scriptorem Criticæ Sacræ nihil erat controversiæ? Dum negavit Hieronymus, LXX. Seniores Prophetas esse, eosdemque Interpretes duntaxat fuisse asseverat, Prophetam eo loco idem esse arbitratus est atque hominem Spiritu Sancto afflatum, quo nimirum sensu Patres omnes Græcos illos Interpretes appellaverant Prophetas; nec aliâ ratione nomen illud Prophetæ usurpavit ipse Vossius, qui tam confidenter illorum θεοπνευστίαν sive afflatum divinum asseruerit. Non sum nescius, inquit, multorum me incursurum non reprehensionem tantùm, sed & odium, quòd tam magnificè de hac versione sentiam, & adeo quidem ut vix dubitem eam divinitùs inspiratam appellare: sed quamnam rogo possit excogitari ratio, quamobrem non id ipsum credam quod jam ab Apostolorum temporibus omnes credidêre Christiani, exceptis duntaxat paucis nimio plus faventibus sequiorum rum temporum Judæis? Inter hos haud dubiè B. Hieronymum collocabit. Deinde probat fusiùs eorumdem Interpretum Θεοπνεύςειαν, argumenta eorum infringens, qui dicunt hos non potuisse afflari Spiritu Sancto aut Prophetico, quia Judæi testantur tempore Templi secundi defuisse donum Spiritús Sancti & Prophetiæ. Illud, inquit, omnino est Rabbinicum & nugatorium. Sed non minùs nugatoria sunt quæ ille affert adversus Hieronymum his verbis: Cùm itaque tam latè Prophetarum & Prophetiæ, etiam apud Hebræos, patuerit appellatio, non admittendi sunt illi qui Septuaginta Interpretes Prophetas fuisse negant, utpote præcipuos populi Judaici Sacerdotes, & non præteritarum tantùm, sed & futurarum rerum interpretes. Quasi verò illud in quæstionem venisset, utrùm Septuaginta Senibus Prophetarum nomen competeret, quatenus nomen illud Propheta idem sonat atque Interpres; cùm ipse tam multis probare conatus fuerit eos Prophetas fuisse, qui à Spiritu Sancto ac Prophetico afflati fuêre: imò existimat injurios illos esse Hieronymo, qui testimoniis ejus abutuntur ad evertendam LXX. Interpretum auctoritatem; cùm ille ætate provectior eorum errores non ipsis Interpretibus, qui afflatu Spiritús Sancti sacros libros verterunt, sed librariis imputandos censuerit. Verùm supra fusiùs ostensum est quæ fuerit de præsenti negotio B. Hieronymi sententia, quæ Vossio latuit. Jam enim profectę erat ætatis, cùm Prophetarum libros Commentariis suis illustravit. At quàm sæpè in illis non modò librarios, sed ipsos Interpretes castiget, nemo nescit.
units.tr: There is therefore no reason for us to agree with Vossius on this point, who, against Blessed Jerome, wishes the Seventy Interpreters to have been inspired by the divine power and to have been wholly free from every error, even the slightest. Indeed, as if ashamed of having given those Interpreters the name of Prophets, he afterwards seems to correct himself and affirms that among the older writers a prophet is the same as an interpreter [ἑρμηνευτής], and that those were prophets who, as the Apostle witnesses, interpreted the Scriptures rightly. But why does Vossius here seek hiding-places, and have recourse to what I may call profane learning, to show that Jerome is wrong when he writes that a prophet is one thing and an interpreter another? As if Jerome contradicted the Apostle, who in several places uses the word "prophet" [προφήτης] to mean "one who interprets"! Here, however, Jerome is not wrong, since he knew the proper sense of that word very well; for he observed that the Greek poet was called a prophet by Paul. But in his Reply to the Objections to the Recent Sacred Criticism, Vossius shifts his ground everywhere. What reason, then, did he have for citing not only the testimonies of the Apostles and Evangelists but also those of Philo, Festus, Plato and others, in order to prove that not only those who foretold the future were called prophets, but also those who explained the past and the present? For there was no dispute between him and the author of the Sacred Criticism on that point. When Jerome denied that the Seventy Elders were prophets and asserted that they were only interpreters, he thought that "prophet" in that place meant the same as a man inspired by the Holy Spirit. This is the sense in which all the Greek Fathers called those Interpreters prophets. Vossius himself used the name of prophet in no other way when he so confidently asserted their divine inspiration [θεοπνευστία]. I am not unaware, he says, that I shall incur not only the blame but also the hatred of many, because I think so highly of this version, and so much so that I hardly hesitate to call it divinely inspired. But I ask, what reason could be devised why I should not believe the very thing that all Christians have believed since the times of the Apostles, except for a few Jews of later times who were far too favourable to them? Among these, undoubtedly, he will place Blessed Jerome. Then he argues at greater length for the divine inspiration [θεοπνευστία] of the same Interpreters, refuting the arguments of those who say they could not have been inspired by the Holy Spirit or by the prophetic spirit, because the Jews testify that the gift of the Holy Spirit and of prophecy was lacking in the time of the Second Temple. That, he says, is wholly Rabbinic and trifling. But the arguments he brings against Jerome in these words are no less trifling: Since the name of prophets and of prophecy extended so widely, even among the Hebrews, those who deny that the Seventy Interpreters were prophets must not be admitted, since they were the chief priests of the Jewish people and interpreters not only of past but also of future things. As if the question were whether the name of prophet belonged to the Seventy Elders, insofar as the word "prophet" means the same as "interpreter"; when he himself has tried to prove by many arguments that they were prophets who were inspired by the Holy Spirit and by the prophetic spirit. Indeed, he thinks those are unfair to Jerome who use his testimonies to overthrow the authority of the Seventy Interpreters, since Jerome, in his later years, judged their errors to be the fault not of the Interpreters themselves, who translated the sacred books by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, but of the copyists. But it has already been shown at greater length what Blessed Jerome's opinion was on the present question, which escaped Vossius. For Jerome was already advanced in years when he illustrated the books of the Prophets with his Commentaries. Yet how often in those works he rebukes not only the copyists but the Interpreters themselves, no one fails to know.

units.la: Etsi suppositititium esse fœtum, quæ sub nomine Aristeæ circumfertur, historiam jam antea dixerim, lubens tamen agnosco hanc quæ LXX. Senibus tribuitur interpretationem sub Ptolemęo Philadelpho conditam fuisse à Judæis Alexandrinis, & ex Hebræo codice Chaldaicis sive Babylonicis literis exarato, quia non alias adhibuêre literas in describendis suis exemplaribus Judæi post suum è Babylone reditum, quàm Assyriacas. Sed versio altera Græca, quam ex eodem codice Hebrœo Samariticis literis satis negligenter descripto factam putat Vossius ab homine neque Hebraicè forsan, neque Græcè docto, merum est figmentum ex Aristobulo desumptum; qui tamen de Samariticis literis, quibus hunc exaratum fuisse contendit Vossius, ne verbum quidem protulit, & de illis præter Vossium nemo cogitavit; adeo illud ab omni veri specie alienum videvidetur. Errant quidem, ut bene à Vossio animadversum fuit, qui putant Græcam versionem ex aliqua Paraphrasi Chaldaica aut Syriaca derivatam fuisse, cùm nulla tunc esset ejusmodi, & constet Philonem linguam Hebraicam & Chaldaicam pro eadem ubique accipere. Suspicari tamen licet, Græcos illos Interpretes sermonem Chaldaicum, qui Judæis plerisque post reditum è Babylone vernaculus fuerat, respexisse. Nulla quidem erat tunc temporis Chaldaica aut Syriaca Paraphrasis ; tamen longè ante illa tempora Magistri, tam in Scholis, quàm in Synagogis, contextum Biblicum Chaldaicè non minùs quàm Hebraicè legebant, unde forsan contigit ut plures in Græca translatione voces magis ad genium linguæ Chaldaicæ aut Syriacę conversæ sint, quàm secundùm linguæ Hebraicæ proprietatem. Commentum quoque aliud finxit idem Vossius, qui asserit usque ad tempora Aquilæ nullam aliam lectam fuisse in Synagogis Judæorum Scripturam praeter illam LXX. Interpretum, quia perierat intellectus linguę Hebraeæ, quam ne ipsi quidem callerent Judæorum Rabbini: LXX. verò Interpretes, ut auctor est idem Vossius, vixerunt florente & superstite etiamnum Hebraeâ linguâ. Verùm lingua Hebræa non magis florebat tempore LXX. Interpretum, si qui fuerint illius nominis, quàm tempore Aquilæ; quippe illa post deportatos Babylonem Judæos penitus abolita est, & post illorum inde reditum ipsis non fuit amplius domestica & familiaris. Remansit apud solos Magistros, qui eam publicè in Synagogis, seu Scholis, docuerint. Si verum est usque ad Aquilæ tempora non aliam in omnibus Judæorum Synagogis lectam fuisse Scripturam quàm Græcam LXX. Seniorum interpretationem, quâ ratione fieri potuit, ut Flavius Josephus Legem Moysis in Synagoga Hebraicè interpretatus sit, ut affirmat Vossius, qui similiter asserit eumdem Josephum, omnium sui seculi Hebræorum longè eruditissimum, historiam belli Judaici antequàm Græcè scriberet, linguâ Hebraeâ edidisse? Tamen, si credamus Vossio, lingua Hebraea penitus deperdita fuerat: si res ita sit, cur hanc appellat linguam patriam Josephi? Conveniet nulli qui secum dissidet ipse. Manifestum est etiam ex ejusdem Josephi libris, Judæos Palæstinæ regionumque vicinarum tunc temporis linguam Hebraeam excoluisse, quam usu, ut nostrâ etiam ætate, discerent absque ullis præceptionibus Grammaticis, quæ non à sexcentis tantùm, ut contendit Vossius, sed à nongentis & amplius annis inventæ sunt. Quo sensu idem Josephus ait, etiam referente Vossio, excelluisse se in disciplinis patriis præ cæteris Hebræis: Græcam verò linguam non nisi per Grammaticam didicisse. Patrias vocat disciplinas studium linguæ Hebrææ ac Legis Mosaicæ, quam Judæi Hierosolymitani in Synagogis Hebraicè legebant. Si tamen audiamus Vossium, qui sæpius à seipso dissentit, Christus & Apostoli in Judæa Græcè loquebantur. Ubicunque, inquit, jam ab Alexandri Magni temporibus Græci fuêre domini, ibi etiam Græca prævaluit lingua, & absurdum est unam excipere Judæam.: & paulò post: Ut in Ægypto, Asia & reliqua Syria, ita quoque in Judæa nulla præter Græcam audiebatur lingua, in urbibus præsertim oppidisque. Imò præter linguam Græcam in Ægypto audiebatur lingua Coptica, in Syria Syriaca, & in Judæa Judaica, seu Chaldæo-Syriaca. Ex libro Euangeliorum discere potuit Vossius, sermonem Judæorum qui Hierosolyma incolebant, quæ inter urbes & oppida reponi debent, Chaldæum sive Syriacum fuisse, nec Christum Judæos urbis ullius Græcè, sed Syriacè alloquutum fuisse. Hanc etiam postea Judæi qui regionem istam incoluêre; licèt corruptam, retinuerunt, uti probari potest exemplo Talmudis, qui vulgò ab ipsis Hierosolymitanus appellatur, & lingua quâ conceptus est liber ille vocatur quoque Hierosolymitana. Judæis etiam Babylonien-sibus tunc temporis, ut & longè antea, domesticus fuit sermo Chaldaicus, qui suum pariter Talmudem habent eâdem linguâ conscriptum. Plerique etiam vetustiores libri Judæorum, exceptis paucissimis, non alio sermone conscripti sunt quàm Chaldæo impuro. Sed non est cur refellendis Vossii assertionibus, quę nihil omnino probabilitatis præ se ferunt, diutius immoremur; qualia sunt quæ affirmat de libris Deuterosëon, seu Traditionum Judaicarum, quas omnes ante Justiniani tempora sermone dùntaxat Græco concinnatas fuisse contendit, & de libro Misna qui è Græco in Hebræum sermonem circa illud tempus conversus fuerit: quia cautum fuerat edicto Justiniani, ne Judæi Deuterosës, seu librum Traditionum, in Synagogis legerent. Illi, inquit Vossius, ut edictum eluderent, scriptum hoc in Hebræum converterunt sermonem. Risum teneatis amici!
units.tr: Although I have said before that the story circulated under the name of Aristeas is a spurious product, I gladly grant that the translation attributed to the Seventy Elders was made under Ptolemy Philadelphus by the Alexandrian Jews, from a Hebrew manuscript written in Chaldaic or Babylonian letters, since Jews after their return from Babylon used no other letters for copying their books than the Assyrian. But the other Greek version, which Vossius thinks was made from the same Hebrew codex, written rather carelessly in Samaritan letters, by a man perhaps learned neither in Hebrew nor in Greek, is a pure fiction taken from Aristobulus. Yet Aristobulus did not say a single word about Samaritan letters, in which Vossius claims the codex was written, and apart from Vossius nobody has thought of them, so far is that idea from any appearance of truth. Those are certainly mistaken, as Vossius rightly observed, who think the Greek version was derived from some Chaldaic or Syriac paraphrase, since none of that kind existed at the time, and it is established that Philo everywhere takes the Hebrew and Chaldaic languages as the same. We may nevertheless suspect that those Greek translators had regard to the Chaldaic speech, which had become the vernacular of most Jews after the return from Babylon. No Chaldaic or Syriac paraphrase existed at that time; yet long before those times the teachers, both in the schools and in the synagogues, read the biblical text in Chaldaic as well as in Hebrew, and this perhaps is why many words in the Greek translation were rendered more according to the genius of the Chaldaic or Syriac tongue than according to the proper usage of Hebrew. Vossius also invented another fiction: he asserts that until the time of Aquila no Scripture other than the Greek of the Seventy Interpreters was read in the synagogues of the Jews, because the understanding of the Hebrew language had perished, a language which even the rabbis themselves did not understand; and that the Seventy Interpreters, as the same Vossius says, lived while the Hebrew language was still flourishing and surviving. But the Hebrew language was no more flourishing in the time of the Seventy Interpreters, if there were any of that name, than in the time of Aquila. Indeed it was utterly abolished after the Jews were carried off to Babylon, and after their return from there it was no longer their household and familiar tongue. It remained only among the teachers, who taught it publicly in the synagogues or schools. If it is true that until the time of Aquila no Scripture other than the Greek translation of the Seventy Elders was read in all the synagogues of the Jews, how could it happen, as Vossius affirms, that Flavius Josephus translated the Law of Moses into Hebrew in the synagogue? Vossius likewise asserts that this same Josephus, by far the most learned of all the Hebrews of his age, published his history of the Jewish war in the Hebrew language before he wrote it in Greek. Yet if we believe Vossius, the Hebrew language had been utterly lost. If that is so, why does he call it the native language of Josephus? He will agree with no one who disagrees with himself. It is also plain from the books of the same Josephus that the Jews of Palestine and the neighbouring regions at that time cultivated the Hebrew language, which they learned by use, as in our own day, without any grammatical rules, and those rules were devised not six hundred years ago, as Vossius contends, but more than nine hundred. In this sense the same Josephus says, as Vossius himself reports, that he excelled in the native disciplines beyond the other Hebrews, but learned the Greek language only through grammar. He calls the study of the Hebrew language and of the Mosaic Law his native disciplines, which the Jews of Jerusalem read aloud in Hebrew in their synagogues. Yet if we listen to Vossius, who so often contradicts himself, Christ and the Apostles spoke Greek in Judea. Wherever, he says, since the times of Alexander the Great the Greeks have been masters, there the Greek language has also prevailed, and it is absurd to make Judea an exception; and a little later: As in Egypt, Asia, and the rest of Syria, so too in Judea no language other than Greek was heard, especially in the cities and towns. Indeed, besides Greek, the Coptic language was heard in Egypt, Syriac in Syria, and Judaic, that is, Chaldeo-Syriac, in Judea. Vossius could have learned from the book of the Gospels that the speech of the Jews who lived at Jerusalem, which must be counted among the cities and towns, was Chaldaic or Syriac, and that Christ addressed the Jews of that city not in Greek but in Syriac. The Jews who afterwards inhabited that region also kept this language, though corrupted, as can be shown from the example of the Talmud, which is commonly called the Jerusalem Talmud by them, and the language in which that book was composed is also called the Jerusalem language. The Chaldaic speech was likewise the native tongue of the Babylonian Jews at that time, as it had been long before; and they too have their Talmud written in the same language. Moreover, most of the older books of the Jews, with very few exceptions, were written in no other tongue than debased Chaldaic. But there is no reason to dwell longer on refuting Vossius's assertions, which show no probability whatever; such are his claims about the books of the Deuterosis, or collections of Jewish traditions, which he contends were all composed only in Greek before the time of Justinian, and about the book Mishna, which he says was translated from Greek into Hebrew about that time, because Justinian's edict forbade the Jews to read the Deuterosis, or book of traditions, in their synagogues. They, says Vossius, in order to evade the edict, translated this writing into the Hebrew language. Could you keep a straight face, friends!

units.la: Verùm, si ad Justiniani edictum animum advertisset vir doctus, facilè deprehendisset non modò Hierosolymis, sed etiam in eorum Synagogis qui vulgò Hellenistæ appellantur, contextum Hebræum bręum breum lectum fuisse. Id enim aperte significant verba illa Constitutionis Justiniani: Didicimus quosdam solam habentes vocem Hebraam, etiam ipsa uti velle in sacrorum librorum lectione; alii vero Graecam quoque editionem assumendam esse arbitrantur, & jamdudum hac de re inter se disputant. Nos igitur his auditis, meliores judicavimus eos esse qui Graecam quoque versionem ad librorum sacrorum lectionem volunt assumere, & quamcunque linguam simpliciter quam locus commodiorem & aptiorem audientibus facit. Duplicis generis Judeos supponit illa Justiniani Constitutio, quorum alii linguae Hebraeae penitus addicti Scripturam Sacram in Synagogis sermone duntaxat Hebraeo legerent; alii vero, quia Graecas literas callebant, lectioni Hebraicae Graecam adjunxere. Justiniani autem edicto permittitur ut non solum Graece, sed in alia qualibet lingua codex sacer legeretur. Judaei igitur omnes Hellenistae, ut decreto Mosis obtemperarent, non alio unquam sermone quam Hebraeo Legis contextum in Synagogis suis legerunt, cui deinde lectioni alia mox succedebat sermone vernaculo. Neque his obstant priscorum Judaeorum Patrumque testimonia, ex quibus manifesto liquet Judeos Alexandrinos & alios omnes quibus lingua Graeca fuit vernacula, Graecam LXX. Interpretum versionem in Synagogis suis legisse. Similiter constat etiam Hierosolymis quasdam extitisse Synagogas in quibus Lex Mosis & Prophetae Graeco sermone legerentur. Sed haec & alia ejusdem rationis bene multa quae huc congeri possent, probant tantum lectioni contextus Hebraici additam fuisse explicationis causa Graecae interpretationis lectionem, sicut & nostra etiam aetate Judei ex antiquo more singulis Sabbatis legunt aliquid Scripturae Sacrae Hebraice & Chaldaice, quia scilicet antiquitus erant in Synagogis & Lectores & Interpretes, quod etiam Interpretis seu Prophetae munus a Synagoga ad primos Christianorum coetus transisse clare demonstrant verba Apostoli in Epistola prima ad Corinthios. Hinc forsan ortum est ut Graeca illa LXX. interpretatio quibusdam in locis minus accurate verba contextus Hebraici exprimat, quia scilicet illius concionatores Paraphrastarum potius quam Interpretum, locis praesertim obscurioribus, munus obierunt. Sed ea omnia quae pro tuenda LXX. Senum translatione & elevandis Judaeorum exemplaribus contra omnem probabilitatis speciem fusius retulit Vossius, in praesentia refellere nec tempus est mihi, nec animus: longe satius erit Hieronymi versionem cum Graeca locis aliquot conferre, ut inde patefiat quam vere dixerit Vossius Hieronymum nusquam rectè ab antiquis recessisse Interpretibus, eumque primum fuisse Christianorum qui Rabbinicam condiderit versionem, quique alios ad idem audendum signifer praecesserit. Longè aliud de versione Hieronymi, quæ nunc in Ecclesia Occidentali legitur, judicium tulit Augustinus Eugubinus his verbis: Hanc si cum editione Septuaginta contuleris, ausim hac uti similitudine ut lucem ac tenebras à te collatas afferam. Id quod nos toto hoc opere ostendemus. Inveniemus certè hanc adeo fuisse Ecclesiis necessariam, ut, nisi hanc operam Divinus Hieronymus nobis praestitisset, versari adhuc nos in multis erroribus certè necesse fuerit.
units.tr: But if the learned man had paid attention to Justinian's edict, he would easily have perceived that the Hebrew text was read not only at Jerusalem but also in the synagogues of those commonly called Hellenists. For those words of Justinian's Constitution clearly indicate this: We have learned that some, having only the Hebrew language, wish to use it also in the reading of the sacred books; others think that the Greek edition too should be adopted, and have long disputed this among themselves. We, therefore, having heard them, have judged better those who wish the Greek version also to be taken up in the reading of the sacred books, and whatever language is simply more convenient and suitable for the hearers. That Constitution of Justinian presupposes two kinds of Jews: some, wholly devoted to the Hebrew language, read the Sacred Scripture in the synagogues in the Hebrew tongue alone; others, because they knew Greek letters, added a Greek reading to the Hebrew. Justinian's edict permits the sacred codex to be read not only in Greek but in any other language. Therefore all the Hellenist Jews, to obey the decree of Moses, never read the text of the Law in their synagogues in any language but Hebrew, and to that reading there immediately followed another in the vernacular. Nor do the testimonies of the ancient Jews and Fathers stand in the way, from which it clearly appears that the Alexandrian Jews and all others to whom Greek was the native language read the Greek version of the Seventy Interpreters in their synagogues. Likewise it is established that at Jerusalem there were some synagogues in which the Law of Moses and the Prophets were read in Greek. But these and many other arguments of the same kind that could be gathered here prove only that a reading of the Greek translation was added to the reading of the Hebrew text for the sake of explanation, just as even in our own day the Jews, by ancient custom, read some portion of Sacred Scripture every Sabbath in Hebrew and Chaldaic; because, of course, in ancient times there were both readers and interpreters in the synagogues, and the words of the Apostle in his first Epistle to the Corinthians clearly show that the office of interpreter or prophet passed from the synagogue to the first assemblies of Christians. Hence perhaps it arose that the Greek translation of the Seventy Interpreters in some places expresses the words of the Hebrew text less accurately, because its preachers performed the office of paraphrasts rather than of translators, especially in the more obscure passages. But I have neither the time nor the inclination to refute in the present place all those things that Vossius has set out at length in defence of the translation of the Seventy Elders and in praise of the Jewish copies, against every appearance of probability. It will be far more satisfactory to compare Jerome's version with the Greek in several places, so that it may become clear how truly Vossius said that Jerome never departed from the ancient translators, and that Jerome was the first of the Christians who established the rabbinic version, and as standard-bearer led others to dare the same. Augustinus Eugubinus passed a far different judgment on the version of Jerome, which is now read in the Western Church, in these words: If you compare this with the edition of the Seventy, I would venture to use this comparison, that I bring light and darkness set side by side. This we shall show throughout this whole work. We shall certainly find that this version was so necessary to the Churches that, unless the divine Jerome had rendered us this service, we should certainly have to remain still in many errors.

units.la: Sumam itaque exempla collationis istius ex libris Prophetarum, quos ex Hebraeo vertit Hieronymus, ac Commentariis suis illustravit, & utraque adhuc extat, cùm vetus tum recens, illorum translatio in ejusdem operibus. In omnibus autem Hieronymum vindicare etiam à levissimis erroribus, sicuti Septuaginta Interpretes vindicare enixè contendit Vossius, mihi minimè propositum est: quippe non pauca Hieronymo quantumlibet erudito exciderunt, dum Judaeis aetatis suae nimium addictus Graecos Interpretes severius interdum castigat. Sed doctissimum illum Patrem toties allucinatum fuisse quoties illos deserit, ut existimat Vossius, pernego.
units.tr: I shall therefore take examples of this comparison from the books of the Prophets, which Jerome translated from the Hebrew and illustrated with his Commentaries. Both his old and his recent translations of those books still survive in his works. But it is by no means my purpose to vindicate Jerome from every slight error, as Vossius earnestly strives to vindicate the Seventy Interpreters. Not a few errors have slipped from Jerome, however learned he was, since he was too devoted to the Jews of his own age and sometimes censures the Greek interpreters too severely. But that most learned Father was deceived as often as he departs from them, as Vossius thinks, I flatly deny.

units.la: Capite secundo Commentariorum in Isajam ad haec verba, Quiescite ab homine cujus spiritus in naribus ejus, quia excelsus reputatus est ipse, miratur Septuaginta Interpretes tam perspicuam, ut ipsi videtur, de Christo Prophetiam in Graecum noluisse vertere, damnatque Judaeos, qui verbum quod in Hebraeo est ambiguum, in deteriorem partem interpretati sint. Judaeorum autem nomine ibi Aquilam notat aliosque Interpretes qui diversam à Septuaginta Seniorum versione translationem de industria considerant, ad quas Judaei, relictis vetustis Interpretibus, recurrebant. Jam utrùm hęc omissio librariis, an ipsis LXX. Senibus tribui debeat, nunc non inquiro, quam constat à Graecis exemplaribus ante Origenis tempora abfuisse, cùm verba illa sub asteriscis de editione Aquilae addita fuerint: nec disputo similiter de bonitate versionis Hieronymi, utrùm praeferenda sit Aquilae translationi, quę cum hodiernis Judaeorum codicibus hîc consentit; verùm inde conficio versionem Hieronymi malè à Vossio Rabbinicam vocari, quasi jam senex Hieronymus solis Judaeis in condenda denda sua contextus Biblici interpretatione crediderit. Ejusdem Prophetae Capite 5. ubi juxta vocum Hebraicarum proprietatem vertit Hieronymus, Et pascentur agni juxta ordinem suum, LXX. Interpretes arguit, quod nescio quid volentes, uti loquitur, transtulerint, Pascentur direpti quasi tauri, pro agnis tauros intelligentes, & pro advenis interpretantes agnos. Hebraica tamen hoc loco implicata non sunt, & sensus apertus. Reprehendit etiam Graecos Interpretes Hieronymus, quod pro his verbis, Quis ibit nobis, ut habent omnes Interpretes, quia in Hebraeo legitur lanu, ipsi posuerint, Quis ibit ad populum istum, quod penitus, inquit, in Hebraeo non habetur. Sed forsan pro lanu legerunt laam, vel eadem verba quae mox sequuntur, majoris explicationis causa hic addita sunt; quia pronomen nobis nihil ibi, ut & alibi passim, significat.
units.tr: In the second chapter of his Commentaries on Isaiah, on the words Cease ye from man, whose breath is in his nostrils, for he is esteemed highly, Jerome marvels that the Seventy Interpreters were unwilling to render into Greek a prophecy so plainly about Christ, as it seems to him. He condemns the Jews who interpreted in a worse sense the word that is ambiguous in Hebrew. By the Jews he there means Aquila and the other interpreters who deliberately offered a translation differing from the version of the Seventy Elders, and to whom the Jews, abandoning the old interpreters, were having recourse. Whether this omission should be attributed to copyists or to the Seventy Elders themselves, I do not inquire now. It is established that it was absent from Greek copies before the time of Origen, since those words were added under asterisks from the edition of Aquila. Nor do I similarly dispute about the merit of Jerome's version, or whether it is to be preferred to Aquila's translation, which agrees here with the present Jewish codices. From this, however, I conclude that Vossius wrongly calls Jerome's version Rabbinic, as if the aged Jerome, in framing his own interpretation of the biblical text, had trusted only the Jews. In the fifth chapter of the same prophet, where, following the proper sense of the Hebrew words, Jerome translates And the lambs shall feed according to their order, he rebukes the Seventy, who, wishing, as he puts it, I know not what, translated The torn shall feed like bulls, understanding bulls for lambs and interpreting lambs as strangers. Yet the Hebrew words are not entangled in this place, and the sense is plain. Jerome also censures the Greek interpreters because, for the words Who will go for us, as all the interpreters have it, since the Hebrew reads lanu, they put Who will go to this people, which, he says, is not found at all in the Hebrew. But perhaps they read laam for lanu, or the same words that immediately follow were added here for greater explanation, since the pronoun for us signifies nothing there, as it often does elsewhere.

units.la: Verum longe magis animadversione digna sunt quae refert idem Hieronymus ad haec verba quae secundum codicis sui Hebraei lectionem transtulerat, Excaeca cor populi hujus, & aures ejus aggrava: cum longe benignior videatur Graeca interpretatio in qua legitur, Incrassatum est cor populi hujus. Sed norunt linguae Hebraeae periti, hanc diversitatem ex varia punctorum vocalium notatione ortam fuisse: sequuti sunt LXX. aetatis suae lectionem, quae diversa erat ab ea quae Hieronymi aetate obtinebat; & haec eadem in exemplari Masorethico repraesentatur. Utraque lectio traditione confirmatur; sed Graeca videtur in eo Hieronymianae praeferenda, quod illam sequutus fuerit Apostolus in Actibus Apostolorum: ad haec tamen respondet Hieronymus, lectionem hanc tribuendam potius esse Evangelistae Lucae quam Apostolo. Evangelistam Lucam, inquit, tradunt veteres Ecclesiae tractatores medicinae artis fuisse scientissimum, & magis Graecas literas scisse quam Hebraeas. Unde & sermo ejus, tam in Evangelio quam in Actibus Apostolorum, comptior est & saecularem redolet eloquentiam, magisque testimoniis Graecis utitur quam Hebraeis. Itaque in ea videtur fuisse sententia Hieronymus, ut crediderit B. Paulum cum Hebraeis disputantem non juxta LXX. loquutum fuisse, sed juxta Hebraicum; Lucam vero Evangelistam, qui Graecas literas apprime callebat, legebatque Graecos codices, Graecis testimoniis usum fuisse. Similia fere his affert Hieronymus Quaestionibus Hebraicis in Genesim, ubi expendens diversitatem quae Graeca inter & Hebraea exemplaria intererat in recensendis filiis Jacobi qui cum ipso Aegyptum ingressi sunt, quaerensque ibidem cur LXX. potiús versioni Stephanus in Actibus Apostolo-rum adhęserit, quàm Hebraeo contextui, ita loquitur: Non debuit Sanctus Lucas, qui ipsius historiae Scriptor est, in Gentes Actuum Apostolorum volumen emittens, contrarium aliquid scribere adversus eam Scripturam quae jam fuerat Gentibus divulgata. Et mox: Hoc autem generaliter observandum, quod ubicunque Sancti Apostoli aut Apostolici viri loquuntur ad populos, his plerumque testimoniis abutuntur, quae jam fuerant in Gentibus divulgata. Nimirum non ideo Apostoli versionem Graecam in suis libris adhibuêre, quòd auctores illius Divino seu Prophetico spiritu afflati fuerint, vel quòd non alia Scriptura in Judaeorum Synagogis legeretur quàm Graeca illa, ut perperam existimavit Vossius; sed quia vulgò erat recepta, &, ut auctor est B. Hieronymus, dum loquuti sunt ad populos Apostoli, iis usi sunt testimoniis quae jam fuerant in Gentibus divulgata; secus vero dum homines gentis suae, qui callebant linguam Hebraicam, alloquuti sunt. Sed mentitum fuisse Lucam necesse est, inquit Vossius, si alios Stephanus in concione sua, quam ille posuit, sensus expresserit. Quasi vero illum mentiri necesse sit qui eadem diverso tantùm sermone referat, paucis quę nullius erant momenti immutatis. Neque mentem Scriptoris Criticae Sacrae assequutus fuisse videtur vir doctus, cùm de eo ita loquitur, quasi crediderit Stephanum non Graeco aut plebeio Syriaco, sed Hebraico sermone ultimam suam concionem absolvisse. An plebs, inquit Vossius, tempore Apostolorum gnara veteris linguae Hebraeae? An mentitus Euangelista? Quid demum integrum in Euangeliis supererit, si ejusmodi admittamus commenta? Sed potiùs monstra sibi fingit quae postea debellet. Syriace concionatus est Stephanus, quia sermo Syriacus tunc Judaeis Hierosolymitanis erat vernaculus: at quae profert Veteris Testamenti testimonia ea non alio sermone proferre potuit quàm Hebraico, quia Judaei Hierosolymitani Legem Mosis Hebraicè in Synagogis suis legebant, non verò Graecè; & si qua subjungebatur interpretatio, illa Syriaco pariter sermone qui plebeius erat, ut hic liberè fatetur Vossius, non verò Graeco, quo in Helenistarum duntaxat Synagogis ac Scholis utebantur.
units.tr: But things far more worth noting are those which the same Jerome reports on these words, which he had translated, according to the reading of his Hebrew codex, as Blind the heart of this people, and make its ears heavy, whereas the Greek rendering, in which we read The heart of this people has grown fat, seems far kinder. Those skilled in the Hebrew language know, however, that this difference arose from the varied notation of the vowel points. The Seventy followed the reading of their own age, which differed from the one that prevailed in Jerome's time, and this same reading is represented in the Masoretic copy. Both readings are confirmed by tradition, but the Greek seems preferable to Jerome's in this respect, that the Apostle followed it in the Acts of the Apostles. To this, however, Jerome replies that this reading ought to be attributed rather to the Evangelist Luke than to the Apostle. The ancient writers of the Church, he says, report that the Evangelist Luke was most skilled in the art of medicine, and knew Greek letters better than Hebrew. Hence his style, both in the Gospel and in the Acts of the Apostles, is more polished and smells of secular eloquence, and he uses Greek testimonies more than Hebrew. So Jerome seems to have held the view that the blessed Paul, disputing with Hebrews, did not speak according to the Seventy but according to the Hebrew, while Luke the Evangelist, who was thoroughly proficient in Greek letters and read Greek codices, used Greek testimonies. Jerome brings forward much the same in his Hebrew Questions on Genesis, where, weighing the difference between the Greek and Hebrew copies in the list of the sons of Jacob who entered Egypt with him, and asking why Stephen in the Acts of the Apostles adhered to the version of the Seventy rather than to the Hebrew text, he speaks thus: Saint Luke, who is the writer of that history, ought not, in publishing the volume of the Acts of the Apostles to the Gentiles, to write anything contrary to that Scripture which had already been published among the Gentiles. And soon after: This, however, is to be observed in general, that wherever the holy Apostles or apostolic men speak to peoples, they mostly make use of those testimonies which had already been published among the Gentiles. Certainly the Apostles did not employ the Greek version in their books because its authors were inspired by a divine or prophetic Spirit, or because no other Scripture was read in the synagogues of the Jews than that Greek one, as Vossius wrongly thought. Rather, it was commonly received and, as blessed Jerome testifies, when the Apostles spoke to peoples, they used those testimonies which had already been published among the Gentiles; otherwise, when they addressed men of their own nation who knew the Hebrew tongue. But Luke must have lied, says Vossius, if Stephen in his sermon, which he set down, expressed other senses. As if he must lie who reports the same things in a different language, with a few unimportant words changed! Nor does the learned man seem to have grasped the mind of the writer of the Critica Sacra when he speaks of him as though he believed Stephen finished his last sermon not in Greek or in plebeian Syriac, but in Hebrew. Was the common people in the time of the Apostles acquainted with the old Hebrew language? Or did the Evangelist lie? What then will remain whole in the Gospels if we admit such inventions? But he imagines monsters for himself, which he afterwards overthrows. Stephen preached in Syriac, because Syriac was then the vernacular of the Jerusalem Jews. But the testimonies of the Old Testament which he brings forward he could not have brought forward in any language other than Hebrew, because the Jews of Jerusalem read the Law of Moses in their synagogues in Hebrew, not in Greek. And if any translation was added, it was likewise in Syriac, the plebeian language, as Vossius here freely admits, and not in Greek, which they used only in the synagogues and schools of the Hellenists.

units.la: In hoc tamen corrigendum esse Hieronymum non diffiteor, quòd dicat Matthaeum & Joannem de Hebraico Veteris Testamenti testimonia sumpsisse, oblitus regulae illius quam Traditionibus Hebraicis in Genesim produxerat, nimirum, Apostolos & viros Apostolicos non aliam ob causam Graecis exemplaribus usos fuisse, quàm quia jam hæc in Gentibus divulgata fuerant: Hebraica verò in Synagogis duntaxat Judæorum asservabantur, & inter hos paucissimi reperiebantur qui ea intelligerent: contrà autem lingua Græca tunc plerisque Gentibus erat vernacula. Observandum autem est Apostolos, etsi Græcis codicibus adhæserint, non ita tamen ab iis dependisse, quin haud infrequenter ad sensum potiùs quàm ad verba attenderint. Quare Hieronymus explicans hunc locum Michæ Prophetæ, Et tu Bethlehem Ephratha, ista annotat: Sunt qui asserant in omnibus penè testimoniis quæ de Veteri Testamento sumuntur ejusmodi esse errorem, ut aut ordo mutetur, aut verba, & interdum quoque sensus ipse diversus sit, vel Apostolis vel Euangelistis non ex libro carpentibus testimonia, sed memoriæ credentibus, quæ nonnunquam fallitur. Hæc quidem paulò duriora videntur, nec ea protuli ut iis fidem adhibeat Vossius. Interea vix fidem suam abnuere poterit Joanni Calvino, qui eumdem Michææ locum illustrans, hæc animadvertit: Quid opus est torquere Prophetæ verba, cùm Euangelistæ propositum non fuerit referre quod apud Prophetam legitur, sed notare locum duntaxat? Similiter idem Hieronymus non ex aliorum, sed ex sua loquutus sententia, de hisce omnibus testimoniis, quæ ex Veteri Testamento in Novum translata sunt, hæc in genere observat. In multis testimoniis quæ Euangelistæ vel Apostoli de libris veteribus assumpserunt, curiosius attendendum est, non eos verborum ordinem sequutos esse, sed sensum. Sed nunc ad id quod est nostri instituti revertamur.
units.tr: In this, however, I do not deny that Jerome must be corrected, in that he says Matthew and John took the testimonies of the Old Testament from the Hebrew, forgetting the rule which he had himself put forward in his Hebrew Traditions on Genesis: that the Apostles and apostolic men used Greek copies for no other reason than that these had already been published among the Gentiles, while the Hebrew was preserved only in the synagogues of the Jews, and among these very few were found who understood it, whereas the Greek language was then the vernacular of most of the Gentiles. It must be observed, however, that the Apostles, although they adhered to Greek codices, did not depend on them so much that they did not quite often attend to the sense rather than the words. Hence Jerome, explaining this passage of the prophet Micah, And thou, Bethlehem Ephratah, annotates thus: There are those who assert that in almost all the testimonies taken from the Old Testament there is such an error that either the order is changed, or the words, and sometimes the sense itself is different, the Apostles or Evangelists not drawing testimonies from the book but trusting to memory, which sometimes fails. These things indeed seem rather harsh, and I have not brought them forward so that Vossius should give them credence. Meanwhile he will scarcely be able to deny his faith to John Calvin, who, illustrating the same passage of Micah, remarks: Why is there need to twist the words of the Prophet, since it was not the purpose of the Evangelist to report what is read in the Prophet, but only to note the place? Similarly, Jerome, speaking not from others' opinion but from his own, observes in general about all these testimonies which have been carried over from the Old Testament into the New: In many testimonies which the Evangelists or Apostles have taken from the old books, we must attend more carefully: they followed not the order of the words but the sense. But now let us return to what is the purpose of our undertaking.

units.la: Prima verba Capitis noni ejusdem Prophetæ vix intelligi possunt in Græca versione, cùm omnia aperta sint in translatione Hieronymi. Utramque duabus columnis distinctam hac ratione produxit Hieronymus: Primo tempore alleviata est terra Zabulon & terra Naphthalim, &c. En Hieronymiana translatio. Græca verò ita habet: Hoc primùm bibe, velociter fac regio Zabulon & terra Napthalim. Aliunde assumptam fuisse crediderim dictionem bibe, quæ mutat sensum. Paulò post eodem Capite notat Hieronymus LXX. Interpretes, quòd pro verbis istis, Vocabitur nomen ejus admirabilis, consiliarius, Deus fortis, pater futuri seculi, princeps pacis, illi majestate nominum perterriti de puero non ausi sint dicere, quòd Deus sit appellandus, sed pro his sex nominibus posuerint quod in Hebraico non habetur. Iterum manifesti erroris Græcos Interpretes arguit Hieronymus, quòd ad lectionem suorum codicum minùs attenti, pro verbum transtulerint mortem, dicendo, Mortem misit Dominus in Jacob, cùm dicendum esseт, Verbum misit, &c. ut Hieronymus interpretatus est, qui statim addidit erroris illius originem his verbis: Apud Hebraeos דבר quod per tres literas scribitur consonantes pro locorum qualitate, si legatur dabar, verbum significat; si deber, mortem & pestilentiam. Non longè ab initio Capitis 10. ejusdem Prophetæ ad hæc verba, Væ Assur, eosdem Interpretes accusat Hieronymus, quòd Hebraica minùs accuratè expresserint. Iterum sub finem ejusdem Capitis ad verba ista, Veniet in Aiath, &c. quantum illi ab Hebraeo discrepent fusè ostendit, simulque eos falsitatis arguit quòd verterint, Rama civitatem Saul: quod perspicuè falsum est, inquit, civitas enim Saul appellatur Gabaa, ut in Hebraico continetur. Præterea Hieronymus longè diversa sentit de lingua LXX. Interpretum, quàm Vossius, qui existimat in ea nihil esse nisi Græcum, frustraque eam appellari linguam natam in Synagoga. Ita enim loquitur libro sexto Commentariorum, Pro advena, id est, προσήλυτος, LXX. γηωρὰν interpretati sunt qui Hebraicè ger dicitur----ergo georas non est Græcum verbum, sed Hebraicum Græcâ consuetudine declinatum; licet quidam, Hebrai sermonis ignarus, Græcam in eo etymologiam exprimere conetur, ab eo quod terrena rei curam habeat, γῆ enim, inquit, terra appellatur, & ωεχ, Φροντίς, id est, solicitudo. Quantum à germano Scripturæ sensu deflexerint Græci Interpretes Capite 24. ejusdem Prophetæ, ubi in Latina editione legimus, Erubescet luna, & confundetur sol, rectè animadvertit Hieronymus his verbis: Pro eo quod nos interpretati sumus, Et erubescet luna, & confundetur sol, LXX. transtulerunt, Liquefieri laterem, & cadere murum: & mox erroris causam detegit, quia scilicet pro Hebraico levana, quod lunam significat, legerunt lebena; & pro hamma, id est, calore, quo sol denotatur, legerunt etiam homa, quod murum significat. Sed frustra his diutius detineor, quippe ab omnibus legi possunt Hieronymi Commentaria in Isajam, ubi passim Græcos Interpretes erroris arguit, quòd ambiguitate vocum, vel aliâ ratione decepti fuerint: aliquando tamen illis parcit, sicuti Capite 30. postquam eorum in interpretando inconstantiam damnavit, mox veluti seipsum castigans, hæc subjicit: Datur mihi suspicio non eos errâsse à principio, sed paulatim Scriptorum vitio depravatos. Et Capite 40. ubi nonnulla à Græcis Interpretibus omissa annotavit, statim addit quasi subdubitans, vel à LXX. prætermissum, vel paulatim Scriptoris vitio prætermissum. Similiter communem Græcorum exemplarium editionem ad Hebraeos codices interdum castigat, ne error in Interpretes rejiciatur, quo modo ad hæc verba Capitis 44. Hæc dicit Dominus Christo meo Cyro, rectè animadvertit non solùm Latinorum, sed & Græcorum plurimos errare, existimantium scriptum esse, Sic dicit Dominus Christo meo Domino: Neque enim, inquit, Κυρίῳ, quod Dominum sonat, sed Κύρῳ dicitur, qui Hebraicè appellatur כורש.
units.tr: The first words of the ninth chapter of the same Prophet can hardly be understood in the Greek version, whereas everything is clear in Jerome's translation. Jerome set out the two side by side in two columns in this way: "At the first time the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali was lightly afflicted, etc." Here is Jerome's translation. The Greek, however, reads: "Drink this first; quickly make the region of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali." I would think the word "drink" was taken from somewhere else, and it changes the sense. A little later in the same chapter Jerome notes that the Seventy translators, when rendering the words "his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, the mighty God, the everlasting Father, the Prince of Peace," were so terrified by the majesty of the names that they did not dare to say of the child that he is to be called God, and instead put in place of these six names something that is not found in the Hebrew. Again, Jerome charges the Greek translators with a clear error, because, being insufficiently careful in reading their copies, they rendered "word" as "death," saying "The Lord sent death upon Jacob," where it ought to have been "The Lord sent a word," etc. Jerome explains the origin of that error with these words: "In Hebrew the word דבר, which is written with three consonants, means 'word' if it is read dabar according to the nature of the place, but 'death and pestilence' if it is read deber." Not far from the beginning of the tenth chapter of the same Prophet, at the words "Woe to Assur," Jerome accuses the same translators of having rendered the Hebrew less accurately. Again, near the end of the same chapter, at the words "He shall come to Aiath, etc.," he shows at length how far they differ from the Hebrew, and at the same time charges them with falsehood in translating "Rama, the city of Saul," which, he says, is plainly false, for the city of Saul is called Gibeah, as the Hebrew contains. Moreover, Jerome thinks very differently about the language of the Seventy translators from Vossius, who holds that there is nothing in it but Greek, and that it is vainly called a language born in the Synagogue. For he speaks thus in the sixth book of his Commentaries: "For the stranger, that is, proselyte, the Seventy rendered γηωρὰν, which in Hebrew is called ger... therefore georas is not a Greek word, but a Hebrew one, declined in the Greek manner; although some, ignorant of the Hebrew language, try to express a Greek etymology in it, from the fact that it has care for earthly things; for γῆ, he says, means earth, and ωεχ, Φροντίς, that is, solicitude." How far the Greek translators strayed from the true sense of Scripture in chapter 24 of the same Prophet, where in the Latin edition we read, "The moon shall be ashamed, and the sun shall be confounded," Jerome rightly observes in these words: "For what we have translated, 'And the moon shall be ashamed, and the sun shall be confounded,' the Seventy rendered, 'The brick shall melt and the wall shall fall'"; and soon he uncovers the cause of the error, namely that for the Hebrew levana, which means "moon," they read lebena, and for hamma, that is, "heat," by which the sun is denoted, they also read homa, which means "wall." But I am detained by these matters too long in vain, since anyone can read Jerome's Commentaries on Isaiah, where he everywhere charges the Greek translators with error, because they were deceived by the ambiguity of words or by some other cause. Sometimes, however, he spares them, as in chapter 30, where, after condemning their inconsistency in translating, he soon, as if correcting himself, adds these words: "I suspect that they did not err from the beginning, but were gradually corrupted by the fault of the copyists." And in chapter 40, where he notes some things omitted by the Greek translators, he immediately adds, as if half in doubt, "either omitted by the Seventy, or gradually omitted through the fault of the copyist." Likewise he sometimes corrects the common Greek edition of the copies by the Hebrew manuscripts, lest the error be laid on the translators; so at the words of chapter 44, "Thus says the Lord to my anointed Cyrus," he rightly observes that not only many Latins but also many Greeks err, thinking it written, "Thus says the Lord to my anointed Lord." For, he says, the word is not Κυρίῳ, which sounds like "Lord," but Κύρῳ, which in Hebrew is called כורש.

units.la: Eadem videre est in Hieronymi Commentarius in Hieremiam, Ezechielem & alios Prophetas. Ita fere ubique Commentario in Hieremiam notat quæ à LXX. Interpretibus prætermissa sunt, aut saltem non amplius in Græcis illorum exemplaribus apparent. Modò enim ipsos Interpretes, modò librarios accusat. Commentario pariter in Ezechielem, ubi Græcorum codicum omissionem animadvertit, statim hæc adjicit: Melius est in divinis libris transferre quod dictum est, licèt non intelligas quare dictum sit, quàm auferre quod nescias. Capite tamen 5. ejusdem Prophetæ vix audet Græcos Interpretes accusare, ubi ait: Multo melius fuerit transferre quod scriptum est, quàm rei male translatæ patrocinium quærere.
