Nec hoc dicimus ab illis factum, quibus vetustas auctoritatem dedit; sed per multa sæcula Scriptorum atque Lectorum vitio depravatum, quanquam & Aristeas & Josephus & omnis Schola Judæorum quinque libros tantùm Moysis à LXX. translatos asserant. Neque hoc solùm loco Hieronymus, sed & aliis in locis, negare videtur cum priscis Judæis aliud quidpiam Scripturæ Sacræ à LXX. Senibus translatum fuisse præter quinque libros Moysis; sicuti ad Caput 5. Michææ, ubi hæc habet: Interpretatio LXX. (si tamen est LXX. Josephus enim scribit, & Hebræi tradunt, quinque tantum libros Legis Moysis ab eis translatos, & Ptolemæo Regi contradictos) tantum discordat in præsenti loco ab Hebraica veritate, ut nec Capita possimus ex æquo ponere, nec eorum simul sententias explicare. Verùm longè aliud sentit Vossius, qui non solùm rei male translatæ ubique patrocinium quærit, ut verbis Hieronymi utar, sed palàm testatur se non dubitare Propheticos libros à LXX. Interpretibus Græcè fuisse redditos, licèt olim dubitaverit. Et quod fidem omnem superare videtur, si Vossio credamus, Græci Interpretes in libris obscurioribus, puta Jobi ac Proverbiorum, magis accuratos se ostendunt quàm recentiores Scripturæ Interpretes. Sed neminem fore arbitror linguæ utriusque peritum, qui hac in parte illi assentiatur, adeo inepta est multis in locis istorum librorum Græca illa translatio. Non is tamen sum qui ab Hieronymo ita dependere velim, ut etiam illius errores, qui plurimi sanè sunt, approbem. Sic, ne longiùs abeam, Capite 27. Commentariorum in Ezechielem LXX. arguit quòd pro filii Dedan, filios Rhodiorum interpretati sint, decepti forte primæ literæ similitudine, ut pro Dadan legerent Radan: sed errorem hunc in Scribas potiús quàm in Interpretes rejiciendum esse demonstrant ea quæ paulò post eodem Capite sequuntur, ubi in LXX. non secus ac in Hieronymi translatione legitur Dedan, sive Dadan. Iterum in Caput 33. ejusdem Prophetæ, ubi de Gog sit mentio, observat Græcos Interpretes libri Numerorum Capite 24. pro Agag quod legitur in Hebræo, reposuisse Gog: sed manifestus est librarii error. Sed ut innumera ejusmodi taceam, longè melius idem Hieronymus Capite 40. eorumdem Commentariorum hæc observat: Omnia prope verba Hebraica & nomina quæ in Græca & Latina translatione sunt posita, nimiâ vetustate corrupta, Scriptorumque vitio depravata; & dum de inemendatis scribuntur inemendatiora, de verbis Hebraicis facta esse Sarmatica, imò nullius gentis, dum & Hebræa esse desierint, & aliena esse non cœperint. Apprime igitur distinguenda sunt & secundùm Criticæ regulas illa omnia quæ ut minùs bene à LXX. Senibus translata arguit Hieronymus: ut enim plurimos eorum errores rectè annotavit, ita & in iisdem castigat non pauca quæ minimè castiganda erant. Nec mirum, cùm ipsemet Hieronymus testetur se Explanationes suas vix implere potuisse, quia nulla hora erat, nullum momentum in quo non fratrum occurreret turbis, seque jam senem præter dictandi difficultatem Hebraeorum volumina ob literarum parvitatem haud relegere potuisse. Similiter observat se nonnulla celeritate dictandi, dum parùm attendit, non bene vertisse. Itaque nec Hieronymus, nec LXX. Senes Prophetæ fuerunt, sed Interpretes, quibus multa, quia homines erant, excidisse necesse est.
units.tr: The same may be seen in Jerome's Commentaries on Jeremiah, Ezekiel and the other Prophets. Almost everywhere in the Commentary on Jeremiah he notes what has been omitted by the Seventy translators, or at least no longer appears in their Greek copies. Sometimes he accuses the translators themselves, sometimes the copyists. Likewise in the Commentary on Ezekiel, where he notes the omission in the Greek manuscripts, he immediately adds: "It is better in divine books to translate what has been said, even if you do not understand why it was said, than to remove what you do not know." Yet in chapter 5 of the same Prophet he scarcely dares to accuse the Greek translators, where he says: "It would have been much better to translate what is written than to seek a defence for a badly translated thing. Nor do we say this was done by those to whom antiquity has given authority; but it was corrupted through many centuries by the fault of the copyists and readers, although both Aristeas and Josephus and the whole school of the Jews assert that only the five books of Moses were translated by the Seventy." Nor does Jerome seem to deny this only in this place, but also elsewhere, namely that besides the five books of Moses the ancient Jews held that nothing else of Sacred Scripture was translated by the Seventy elders; as at chapter 5 of Micah, where he has this: "The translation of the Seventy (if indeed it is the Seventy, for Josephus writes, and the Hebrews hand down, that only the five books of the Law of Moses were translated by them and approved by King Ptolemy) differs so much from the Hebrew truth in the present place that we can neither set the chapters side by side nor explain their meanings together." But Vossius thinks quite otherwise: he not only seeks a defence for the badly translated thing everywhere, to use Jerome's words, but openly testifies that he does not doubt that the prophetic books were rendered into Greek by the Seventy translators, although he once doubted it. And what seems to surpass all belief, if we trust Vossius, the Greek translators show themselves more accurate in the more obscure books, such as Job and Proverbs, than the more recent translators of Scripture. But I think there will be no one skilled in both languages who will agree with him in this matter, so inept is that Greek translation of these books in many places. I am not, however, one who wishes to depend on Jerome so much that I approve even his errors, which are indeed very many. Thus, not to go further afield, in chapter 27 of the Commentaries on Ezekiel he charges the Seventy with rendering "sons of Dedan" as "sons of the Rhodians," perhaps deceived by the similarity of the first letter, so that they read Radan for Dadan; but that this error is to be laid on the copyists rather than the translators is shown by what follows a little later in the same chapter, where in the Seventy, no less than in Jerome's translation, we read Dedan or Dadan. Again, at chapter 33 of the same Prophet, where mention is made of Gog, he observes that the Greek translators, at Numbers chapter 24, put Gog in place of Agag, which is read in the Hebrew; but this is a manifest error of a copyist. But, to pass over countless such things, the same Jerome in chapter 40 of the same Commentaries observes much better: "Almost all the Hebrew words and names which are set down in the Greek and Latin translation are corrupted through excessive antiquity and depraved by the fault of copyists; and while things that were not right are written down as still less right, the Hebrew words have become Sarmatian, indeed of no nation at all, since they have ceased to be Hebrew and have not begun to be foreign." It is therefore necessary to distinguish most carefully, according to the rules of criticism, all those things which Jerome argues were translated less well by the Seventy elders: for as he rightly noted many of their errors, so in the same places he also censures not a few things that were in no way to be censured. Nor is this surprising, since Jerome himself testifies that he could scarcely complete his explanations, because there was no hour, no moment, in which the crowds of brethren did not come upon him, and that, now an old man, apart from the difficulty of dictating, he could not reread the Hebrew volumes because of the smallness of the letters. Likewise he observes that, in the speed of his dictation, while paying too little attention, he did not translate some things well. Thus neither Jerome nor the Seventy elders were prophets, but translators, to whom, because they were men, it was necessary that many things should slip away.

units.la: Isaaci Vossii de Hexaplorum Origenis dispositione sententia refellitur.
units.tr: Isaac Vossius's opinion on the arrangement of Origen's Hexapla is refuted.

units.la: Isaacus Vossius Origenem in Hexaplis suis compingendis aliam institisse viam ac vulgò existimant, se aliquando demonstratum pollicetur: quare respondens Scriptori nuperę Criticæ, qui novam hanc viam ab illo quæsierat, contendit Tetrapla & Hexapla Origenis ita dicta non fuisse à quatuor aut sex columellis, sed Tetrapla dicta esse, quòd quadruplicem versionem; Hexapla verò, quòd sex continerent versiones; errare de Octaplis Scriptorem Criticæ, dum errantem sequitur Epiphanium, quia nulla unquam Octapla scripsit Origenes; codicem Hebraicum non venisse in censum versionum, quia priores columnas vocat Origenes τὸ Ἑβραϊκὸν ἐλλαφῷ, velut fundamentum omnium versionum. In Tetraplis, addit Vossius, sex erant columellæ, in Pentateucho etiam septem, utpote cui Samariticus adderetur codex, literis Prototypis Hebræorum expressus, ut ab Eusebio & Africano appellantur. Quia tamen in solo id factum Pentateucho, ideo Tetrapla sex tantùm columellas vulgò continere dicebantur, pari ratione atque in Hexaplis; quamvis in Psalmis septima quoque accederet versio, Hexaplorum tamen remansit appellatio, quia septima illa versio in aliis deficeret libris. Hactenus Vossius, qui non alios opinionis istius, quę nova est illa via quam se demonstraturum pollicitus fuerat, auctores laudat quàm seipsum; & ut majorem illius dictis fidem adhibeamus, hęc demum subjicit: Cùm nulla supersint, aut saltem nulla Hexaplorum aut Tetraplorum hactenus reperta sint exemplaria, velle de his nimium copiosè contendere, id demum fuerit hominis nimium intemperanter otio suo abutentis. Hâc ratione promissa solvit Vossius, qui tam confidenter pollicitus fuerat, se novam & hactenus inauditam Hexaplorum Origenis dispositionem demonstraturum esse. Sed cùm nulla illorum exemplaria unquam viderit, priscos Ecclesiæ Patres atque in primis Epiphanium, qui illa tanquam oculati testes describunt, consulere liceat.
units.tr: Isaac Vossius promises that he will someday demonstrate that Origen followed a different method in compiling his Hexapla from the one commonly believed. So, replying to a recent writer on criticism who had asked about this new method, he contends that Origen's so-called Tetrapla and Hexapla did not get their names from four or six columns, but that the Tetrapla were called so because they contained a fourfold version, and the Hexapla because they contained six versions. The writer on criticism, he says, is wrong about the Octapla, since he follows Epiphanius in his error, for Origen never wrote any Octapla. The Hebrew codex, he says, was not counted among the versions, because Origen calls the first columns τὸ Ἑβραϊκὸν ἔδαφος ("the Hebrew foundation"), as the base of all the versions. In the Tetrapla, Vossius adds, there were six columns, and in the Pentateuch seven, since a Samaritan codex was added, written in the original Hebrew letters, as Eusebius and Africanus call them. But because this was done only for the Pentateuch, the Tetrapla were commonly said to contain six columns only, for the same reason as in the Hexapla. Although in the Psalms a seventh version was also included, the name Hexapla remained, because that seventh version was missing from the other books. So far Vossius, who, in support of this opinion, which is the new method he had promised to demonstrate, cites no authorities except himself. To give more weight to his words, he finally adds this: Since no copies of the Hexapla or the Tetrapla survive, or at least none has yet been found, to argue about them at length would be the work of a man who abuses his leisure too intemperately. By this reasoning Vossius settles the matter, though he had so confidently promised to demonstrate a new and hitherto unheard-of arrangement of Origen's Hexapla. But since he never saw any of their copies, we may consult the early Fathers of the Church, and above all Epiphanius, who describe them as eyewitnesses.

units.la: Dionysius Petavius, vir è Societate Jesu doctissimus, & in Græcis cis Hebraeisque libris non minus quam Vossius exercitatus, asserit neminem Epiphanio accuratius tradidisse quaenam fuerint Origenis Tetrapla, Hexapla & Octapla; idemque Petavius miratur plerosque, qui sua ex Epiphanio hauserunt, in tam aperto ejus loco allucinatos fuisse; ac in primis notat Marianum Victorinum Scholiis ad lib. II. Apolog. adversus Ruffinum, ubi redarguit Erasmum ex Epiphanii auctoritate, ut ait, sed male. Singularum itaque editionum ordo ex Epiphanio hoc diagrammate proponitur.
units.tr: Dionysius Petavius, the most learned man of the Society of Jesus, who was no less versed in Greek and Hebrew books than Vossius, asserts that no one has given a more accurate account of Origen's Tetrapla, Hexapla and Octapla than Epiphanius. Petavius also wonders that many who drew on Epiphanius were led astray in so clear a passage of his. He especially notes Marianus Victorinus, who in his scholia on the second book of the Apology against Rufinus refutes Erasmus on the authority of Epiphanius, as he says, but badly. The order of the individual editions, then, is set out from Epiphanius in this diagram.

units.la: Verum, inquit Vossius, Tetrapla & Hexapla non a quatuor & sex columellis dicta sunt, sed a quadruplici versione, & quod sex continerent versiones: qua in re profecto gravissime allucinatur vir doctus. Nam Tetraplorum, Hexaplorum & Octaplorum nomen derivatum fuit a numero editionum, & quaelibet editio columnellam unam, sive paginam, pro antiqua describendorum voluminum consuetudine occupabat, ut aperte evincunt verba illa Ruffini: Voluit Origenes nostris ostendere qualis apud Judaeos Scripturarum lectio teneretur, & in propriis paginis vel columnellis editiones earum singulas quasque descripsit. Eadem igitur omnino erat in Hexaplis Origenis columnellarum atque editionum ratio. Nulliusque prorsus momenti sunt quae ducit Vossius ex voce ἐδαφῳ, quo nomine insignivit Origenes priores columnellas, nimirum τὸ Ἑβραϊκὸν ἐδαφῳ velut fundamentum omnium versionum. Quid, quaeso, aliud inde colligi potest, quàm Origenem voluisse distinguere hoc nomine contextum Hebraicum à versionibus quae ex eo, tanquam fundamento, deductae fuerant? Quo similiter modo Hieronymus eumdem contextum veritatem Hebraicam appellat. Minùsne ideo constat illum contextum in Hexaplis Hebraicis & Graecis literis descriptum duas columnellas occupâsse, à quibus aequè ac à versionibus, quarum quaelibet suâ quoque columnellâ exarata erat, Hexaplorum nomen derivatum fuerit? Praeterea ejusdem Vossii commentum est quod fingit de codice Samaritano prototypis literis Hebraeorum expresso, qui Pentateucho additus fuerit. Illud enim prisci Ecclesiae Patribus, Epiphanio, Hieronymo, Ruffino, etiam Eusebio & Africano, quos in suam sententiam pertrahere conatur, prorsus fuit incognitum: neque unquam pariter certissimis rationibus demonstrabit Vossius, quod tam confidenter asseverat de codice Samaritano, qui penès Origenem fuerit, frustraque ejus rei testes profert Eusebium, Africanum, Syncellum, imò & ipsummet Origenem, qui de hoc exemplari Samaritano prototypis, ut loquitur, literis exarato ne quidem per somnium unquam cogitârunt. Habuêre Samaritani Graecam Pentateuchi versionem, quae Patribus fuit probè cognita, & ex ea sumpsêre Africanus, Eusebius & Syncellus codicis Samaritani ab Hebraico diversas lectiones quas libris suis inseruerunt. Linguae Hebraicae operam dedit Origenes praeeunte sibi Huillo Judaeorum, non verò Samaritanorum, Patriarchâ: & idcirco non Hebraeis Samaritanorum, sed Judaeorum exemplaribus usus fuit. Quo sensu intelligenda sunt verba illa Eusebii: Tantam curam ac diligentiam in divinorum librorum accuratâ inquisitione adhibebat Origenes, ut Hebraicam etiam linguam didicerit, & prototypas, quae apud Judaeos erant Hebraicis literis scriptas, sibi comparaverit. Sed Eusebii verba in alium plané sensum avertit Vossius, & ut ea sententiae suae facilius accommodaret, lectionem jam vulgatam sine ope ullius codicis MS. in aliam mutare non dubitavit. Sic enim legit: Τάς τε προς τῆς Ἰσδαίοις ἐμφερομένας πεωλοτύπως αὐτῆς Εβεξίων ςυιχείοις γεαφὰς χλῆμα ἰδιον ποιήσαςθαι, cùm vulgò legatur πεωτοτύπως, non verò πεωτοτύπως, & sic vertit: Ut Hebraicam etiam linguam didicerit, ac illas quoque sibi comparaverit Scripturas quæ prototypis Hebræorum literis exarata esse dicuntur. Apud Eusebium, inquit Vossius, prototypi characteres non sunt alii quàm Samaritici, & manifestè sibi adversaretur Eusebius, si de vulgaribus Judæorum intellexisset elementis, cùm contrarium in suo scripserit Chronico. Mirror sanè Vossii ingenium, qui lectoribus suis fucum faciat in re tam aperta, quæque omnibus qui linguam Græcam vix à limine salutaverint, est obvia. Teruntur omnium manibus libri Eusebii, cui non aliud propositum fuit loco jàm citato ostendere, quàm studium indefessum Origenis laboremque ejus improbum in evolvendis Scripturæ Sacræ libris, & perscrutando illorum sensu; qui, ut id facilius obtineret, linguam Hebræam à Judæis Magistris didicit, eorum libros characteribus Hebraicis exaratos evolvit, eosdemque cum Græcis LXX. Senum, Aquilæ, Symmachi & aliorum versionibus contulit. Utrùm πεωτοτύπως, an πεωτοτύπως legendum sit in præsentia non disputo, quia servatâ etiam lectione Vossii, manifestum erit non aliud intelligendum esse per prototypas literas quàm characteres Hebræos. Contextus scilicet Hebræus in Origenis Hexaplis descriptus erat literis Hebraicis & Græcis, ut jam observatum fuit. Quare Eusebius cogitans de exemplaribus Hebraicis, quæ tunc à plerisque Hebraicè nescientibus legebantur, quia illorum characteres Græci erant, asserit Origenem sibi comparâsse exemplar Hebræum characteribus etiam Hebraeis exaratum: qui enim aliter fieri potuisset, cùm Judæos linguæ Hebraicæ Magistros habuerit, non Samaritanos? Non incognita quidem fuisse Eusebio, Origeni & aliis Patribus Pentateuchi Samaritani etiam diversis à Judaicis characteribus descripta exemplaria lubens agnosco; sed quia plerique illorum non callebant linguam Hebraicam, ubi de codice Samaritico loquuntur, haud dubiè intelligunt versionem Græcam Pentateuchi Samaritani, quæ tunc vulgata erat. Neque Eusebii verba in Chronico ullatenus Vossio favent, ubi meminit Eusebius trium Scripturæ Sacræ codicum à quibus sua hauserit; nimirum, πεὸς τ ο ἑρμηνευόντων, à Septuaginta Interpretibus; πεὸς ς πεὸς Ἰσδαίοις Εβεξίνς,
units.tr: But, says Vossius, the Tetrapla and Hexapla were not named from four and six columns, but from a fourfold version, and because they contained six versions. In this matter the learned man is seriously mistaken. For the names Tetrapla, Hexapla and Octapla were derived from the number of editions, and each edition occupied one column, or page, according to the ancient custom of writing out volumes, as the words of Rufinus clearly prove: Origen wished to show our people how the reading of the Scriptures was kept among the Jews, and he set out each of their editions in its own pages or columns. Therefore the arrangement of columns and editions in Origen's Hexapla was altogether the same. And what Vossius draws from the word ἔδαφος, by which Origen marked the first columns, namely τὸ Ἑβραϊκὸν ἔδαφος ("the Hebrew foundation"), as the base of all the versions, has no weight at all. What, I ask, can be inferred from this except that Origen wished by this term to distinguish the Hebrew text from the versions that had been derived from it as from a foundation? Jerome likewise calls the same text the Hebrew truth. Does it follow that the text, written in Hebrew and Greek letters in the Hexapla and occupying two columns, did not give the Hexapla its name, just as the versions did, each of which was also written in its own column? Moreover, the invention about a Samaritan codex written in the original letters of the Hebrews, added to the Pentateuch, is Vossius's own. The early Fathers of the Church, Epiphanius, Jerome, Rufinus, and even Eusebius and Africanus, whom he tries to draw to his opinion, knew nothing of it. Vossius will never demonstrate by any certain reasons what he so boldly asserts about a Samaritan codex that was in Origen's possession, and he vainly calls on Eusebius, Africanus, Syncellus, and even Origen himself, who, as he puts it, never even dreamed of such a Samaritan copy written in prototypal letters. The Samaritans had a Greek version of the Pentateuch, which was well known to the Fathers, and from it Africanus, Eusebius and Syncellus took the readings of the Samaritan codex that differed from the Hebrew and inserted them in their books. Origen studied the Hebrew language under Huillus, the patriarch of the Jews, not of the Samaritans, and so he used copies of the Jews, not the Hebrew copies of the Samaritans. It is in this sense that we must understand the words of Eusebius: Origen applied such care and diligence in the exact search for the divine books that he learned even the Hebrew language, and acquired for himself the prototypal copies that were written among the Jews in Hebrew letters. But Vossius turns Eusebius's words into a quite different meaning, and to fit them more easily to his own view he did not hesitate to change the reading already in use, without the help of any manuscript. For he reads: Τάς τε πρὸς τῶν Ἰουδαίων ἐμφερομένας πρωτοτύπως αὐτῆς Ἑβραΐδι στοιχείοις γραφὰς κτῆμα ἴδιον ποιήσασθαι ("and to make his own the writings that were preserved among the Jews in the original, in Hebrew letters"), whereas the common reading is different in its form of the word for prototypes, and he translates: That he learned even the Hebrew language, and acquired for himself those Scriptures which are said to have been written in the Hebrew prototypal letters. In Eusebius, says Vossius, the prototypal characters are none other than the Samaritan, and Eusebius would clearly contradict himself if he had meant the common letters of the Jews, since he wrote the contrary in his Chronicle. I am truly amazed at Vossius's cleverness, that he should deceive his readers in a matter so plain, and one that is obvious to anyone who has barely greeted the Greek language at the threshold. The books of Eusebius are worn in everyone's hands, and his purpose in the passage already cited was nothing else than to show Origen's untiring zeal and his laborious effort in going through the books of Holy Scripture and searching out their sense. To achieve this more easily, he learned the Hebrew language from Jewish masters, read their books written in Hebrew characters, and compared them with the Greek versions of the Seventy, Aquila, Symmachus and others. Whether πρωτοτύπως or the other form should be read I do not dispute here, for even if Vossius's reading is kept, it will be clear that by the prototypal letters nothing else can be understood than the Hebrew characters. The Hebrew text, as has already been observed, was described in Origen's Hexapla in both Hebrew and Greek letters. So when Eusebius speaks of the Hebrew copies, which at that time most people who did not know Hebrew read, because their characters were Greek, he says that Origen procured for himself a Hebrew copy written also in Hebrew letters. For how could he have done otherwise, since he had Jews, not Samaritans, as masters of the Hebrew language? I gladly admit that Eusebius, Origen and the other Fathers were not unaware of copies of the Samaritan Pentateuch written in characters different from the Jewish ones; but since most of them did not know Hebrew, when they speak of the Samaritan codex they undoubtedly mean the Greek version of the Samaritan Pentateuch, which was then in general use. Nor do the words of Eusebius in the Chronicle in any way favour Vossius, where Eusebius mentions three codices of Holy Scripture from which he drew his text: namely, [πρὸς τῶν ἑρμηνευόντων] from the interpreters of the Seventy; [πρὸς τῶν Ἰουδαίων Ἑβραίων] from the Hebrews of the Jews...

units.la: Ἰσδαίοις: Greek words in the printed text are reproduced as printed; further Greek marginal text is not present. Ἑβδομήκοντα, ab Hebraico exemplari Judaeorum; ᾿Ακύλας δὲ ᾿Ακύλας Σαμαρειτανῶν ab Hebraico exemplari Samaritanorum. Ibi enim nomine exemplaris Hebraei Samaritici necesse est intelligi Graecam illius versionem, non secus ac nomine Hebraici Judaeorum exemplaris plerique Patres qui Hebraicè nesciebant, Aquilae versionem, quae ex Hebraeo ad verbum sumpta fuerat, intellexêre. Noverat igitur Eusebius Samaritanos non secus ac Judaeos Pentateuchi Hebraei exemplar penès se retinere; sed quia linguae Hebraeae imperitus erat, Graecam illius versionem à Samaritanis cusam, quaeque tunc ab iisdem legebatur, consuluit. Sicut antea Justinus Martyr disputans contra Tryphonem Judaeum, Graecam Aquilae interpretationem donat nomine contextûs Hebraei; quia Judaei plerique illius temporis eâ utebantur: sed ad hęc & alia ejusdem rationis bene multa animum non advertit Vossius. Nunc tempus est ut ad id unde diverti redeam.
units.tr: The Seventy [Ἑβδομήκοντα] rendered from the Hebrew copy of the Jews, and Aquila [Ἀκύλας] from the Hebrew copy of the Samaritans. For in this case, by the name of the Samaritan Hebrew copy, the Greek version of that copy must necessarily be meant, just as by the name of the Hebrew copy of the Jews most of the Fathers, who did not know Hebrew, understood Aquila's version, which had been taken word for word from the Hebrew. Eusebius therefore knew that the Samaritans, no less than the Jews, kept a Hebrew copy of the Pentateuch; but since he was ignorant of the Hebrew language, he consulted the Greek version of it, which had been produced by the Samaritans and was then read by them. In the same way Justin Martyr, disputing with the Jew Trypho, gives Aquila's Greek translation under the name of the Hebrew text, because most Jews of that time used it. But Vossius has not noticed these and many other things of the same kind. Now it is time to return to the point from which I digressed.

units.la: In Origenis Hexaplis, ut ex allato supra diagrammate cognoscere est, primum locum obtinebat contextus Hebraeus literis Hebraicis descriptus, secundum idem contextus Graecis characteribus exaratus; quia scilicet ex illo, tanquam ex prima origine, versiones omnes Scripturae derivatae fuerant: deinde sequebatur interpretatio Aquilę, qui Hebraica ad amussim & longè melius quàm caeteri Interpretes referebat: Septuaginta verò medium locum, non verò primum, ut quibusdam visum est, occupaverunt, tanquam caeterarum omnium regula ad quam illae expendi deberent. Symmachi praeterea & Theodotionis translationes illam proximè & ex utraque parte comitabantur, quòd ei haud dissimiles essent, eademque in his tribus observaretur interpretandi methodus.
units.tr: In Origen's Hexapla, as can be seen from the diagram given above, the first place was held by the Hebrew text written in Hebrew letters, the second by the same text written in Greek characters, because, of course, all the other versions of Scripture had been derived from it as from their first origin. Next came the translation of Aquila, who rendered the Hebrew exactly and far better than the other translators. The Seventy, however, occupied not the first place, as some have thought, but the middle one, as the rule by which all the others were to be measured. Moreover, the translations of Symmachus and Theodotion accompanied it immediately on either side, because they were not unlike it, and the same method of translation was observed in all three.

units.la: Jam quia ingens illud volumen tot editiones repraesentans quasi sub una linea carè constabat, & à paucis poterat comparari, ita ut conquestus fuerit Hieronymus, chartas Alexandrinas marsupium suum evacuâsse, cogitavit Origenes, vir acutissimi ingenii & scientiae inexhaustae, de ratione aliqua quâ omnes hasce editiones veluti sub unam repraesentaret. Et quia non alia tunc temporis in omnibus Ecclesiis Scriptura recipiebatur quàm LXX. Interpretum translatio, hanc seorsim edidit cum notis quibusdam, quarum beneficio aliae omnes exhibebantur. Ita quae in contextu Hebraico deesse videbantur, supplevit ex Theodotionis nis versione, notâ addita quæ à Grammaticis vocatur asteriscus; quia scilicet illa verba contextûs nimis curta ac velut abbreviata illustrabat: si quid vero in contextu Hebræo abundare videretur atque esse supervacaneum, locis illis luxuriantibus aliam notam adjecit à Criticis dictam obelus, sive veru; quasi jugulandum illud esset quod in Græca LXX. editione veluti luxuriabat. Ad id in primis attenderat Origenes in operis illius œconomia, teste Epiphanio, ut Judæi facilius à Christianis inter disputandum revincerentur: quippe illi passim objiciebant aliter esse in exemplari Hebræo quàm in Græca LXX. versione. Idem quoque testantur Hieronymus & Ruffinus, etsi Hieronymus interdum ejusmodi notarum usum paulò aliter exponat. Alias etiam notas, putà lemniscos, huic operi adjecerat Origenes, de quorum usu inter se non consentiunt ætatis nostræ Critici, & quod à paucis adhuc explicatum est, illa editio Græca LXX. Interpretum cum omnibus hisce notis, tam illustrantibus quàm jugulantibus, etiam in Hexaplis Origenis unà cum Aquilæ, Symmachi & cæterorum Interpretum translationibus reperiebatur, uti probare videntur verba illa Ruffini: Voluit Origenes nostris ostendere, qualis apud Judæos Scripturarum lectio teneretur, & in propriis paginis, sive columnellis, editiones eorum singulas quasque descripsit, & ea quæ apud illos sunt addita, vel decerpta, certis quibusque signis additis ad versiculorum capita designavit, & in alieno non suo opere suas tantummodo notas fixit, ut sciremus non quid nobis, sed quid Judæis adversum nos certantibus aut deesse, aut abundare videretur.
units.tr: Now, since that huge volume, representing so many editions, stood, as it were, under a single line, and could be compared by only a few, so that Jerome complained that the Alexandrian sheets had emptied his purse, Origen, a man of the keenest intellect and inexhaustible learning, devised some way by which he might present all these editions, as it were, under one heading. And since at that time the Church everywhere accepted no other Scripture than the translation of the Seventy Interpreters, he published this separately with certain notes, by means of which all the others were displayed. Thus, where something seemed to be missing from the Hebrew text, he supplied it from Theodotion's version, with a mark added that the grammarians call the asterisk, since it indicated that those words of the Hebrew text were too brief and, as it were, abridged. But if anything in the Hebrew text seemed to be superfluous and redundant, he added to those overgrown places another mark, called by the critics the obelus or veru, as if what overgrew in the Greek edition of the Seventy were to be cut down. Origen had especially this in view in the arrangement of that work, as Epiphanius attests, so that the Jews might more easily be refuted by Christians in disputation, for they were constantly objecting that the Hebrew copy differed from the Greek version of the Seventy. Jerome and Rufinus also bear witness to this, although Jerome sometimes explains the use of these marks somewhat differently. Origen had also added to this work other marks, such as the lemnisci, about whose use the critics of our own age do not agree, and which few have yet explained. That Greek edition of the Seventy Interpreters, with all these marks, both those that illustrate and those that cut down, was also found in Origen's Hexapla together with the translations of Aquila, Symmachus and the other interpreters, as the words of Rufinus seem to prove: Origen wished to show our people what kind of reading of the Scriptures was held among the Jews. In separate pages, or columns, he set out each of their editions, and by means of fixed signs added to the chapters of the verses he marked what had been added or removed in their text. In a work not his own he fixed only his own marks, so that we might know not what seemed lacking or superfluous to us, but what seemed so to the Jews who contend against us.

units.la: Idem præterea Origenes ingens illud Hexaplorum opus Scholiis diversi generis, quæ ad oram codicis retulerat, illustravit, ut editioni illi LXX. Interpretum, quæ media inter alias omnes apparebat, lucis aliquid afferret. Primò enim quid esset discriminis inter antiquam seu vulgatam LXX. Interpretum editionem, & novam editionem suam beneficio notæ illius o, id est, LXX. statim deprehendi poterat. Illa quippe nota o communem lectionem exhibebat. Deinde in iisdem Scholiis Aquilæ, Symmachi ac Theodotionis diversæ interpretationes quæque per suam literam designabantur. Ita litera A'. denotabat Aquilam, Σ'. Symmachum, & Θ'. Theodotionem; Quinta quoque editio per E'. & Sexta per ϛ'. notabantur. Notas etiam ad oram sui codicis retulerat Origenes, exponendis ad literam, ut vocant, Scripturæ Sacræ verbis, quæ Origenis notæ inter ejus opera sub nomine Scholiorum indicantur. Si etiam
units.tr: Moreover, Origen illustrated that huge work of the Hexapla with scholia of various kinds, which he had set down at the margin of the codex, so that they might throw some light on that edition of the Seventy Interpreters which stood in the middle among all the others. For first, by means of his mark o, that is, the Seventy, one could immediately see the difference between the old or common edition of the Seventy Interpreters and his new edition. For that mark o indicated the common reading. Then, in the same scholia, the different translations of Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion were each designated by its own letter. Thus the letter A' denoted Aquila, Σ' Symmachus, and Θ' Theodotion. The Fifth edition was also marked by E' and the Sixth by ϛ'. Origen had also set down at the margin of his codex notes explaining the words of Holy Scripture word by word, as they say, which are listed among his works under the name of Scholia.

units.la: Epiphan. de pond. & mensur. etiam Isaacum Vossium audiamus, non improbabile est Origenem variantes codicis Samaritici lectiones in Hexaplis suis annotâsse. Si quis malit, inquit, credere Origenem non integrum codicem Samaritici-um Hexaplis & Tetraplis suis inseruisse, sed tantùm variantes annotâsse lectiones, non multùm adversabor. Ita minùs constans Vossius in sententia sua, modò ait, modò negat; & cùm antea tam confidenter asseverâsset exemplar Pentateuchi Samaritani in Hexaplis etiam literis Samaritici-s descriptum extitisse, nunc dubitans nihil in re parùm sibi comperta audet pronunciare. Verùm uti nullatenus probabile est exemplar Samariticum, quod idem prorsus erat atque Judaicum, in Hexaplis extitisse; ita verisimile est diversas exemplaris Samaritici à Judaico lectiones Origenem inter Scholia sua retulisse, quas non ex codice Samaritano prototypis illis literis descripto, uti commentus est Vossius, sed ex Græca Pentateuchi Samaritani versione à Samaritanis ipsis accuratâ descripserat.
units.tr: If we also listen to Isaac Vossius, who cites Epiphanius on weights and measures, it is not improbable that Origen noted the variant readings of the Samaritan codex in his Hexapla. "If anyone prefers to believe," he says, "that Origen did not insert the complete Samaritan codex into his Hexapla and Tetrapla, but only noted the variant readings, I shall not greatly oppose him." Thus Vossius is inconsistent in his opinion: now he says one thing, now he denies it. And although before he had so confidently asserted that a copy of the Samaritan Pentateuch, written in Samaritan letters, existed in the Hexapla, now, doubting, he dares to pronounce nothing on a matter so little known to him. But just as it is in no way probable that a Samaritan copy, which was exactly the same as the Jewish one, existed in the Hexapla, so it is likely that Origen recorded among his scholia the different readings of the Samaritan copy from the Jewish, taking them not from a Samaritan codex written in those letters, as Vossius invents, but accurately from the Greek version of the Samaritan Pentateuch made by the Samaritans themselves.

units.la: Hæc est Origenis Hexaplorum œconomia ac dispositio, quam viri etiam eruditissimi comprehendere minimè potuerunt, dum non assequuntur quomodo in uno eodemque opere Græcæ Aquilæ, Symmachi ac Theodotionis interpretationes bis repertæ fuerint; nimirum integræ in operis contextu, & ex parte in Scholiis quæ erant ad marginem. Sed Origenes, qui omnibus prodesse voluit, immensum illud opus Hexaplorum beneficio notarum & Scholiorum in compendium redegit, ut illi qui Hexapla integra non possent comparare, saltem illorum summam etiam ex ipsismet Hexaplis describerent. Et eâdem arte κοινὴν illam, seu communem, LXX. editionem simul cum nova sua editione, quam integram, quia castigatiorem illam arbitratus est, Hexaplis inseruit, in uno eodemque opere repræsentavit, adjectis scilicet ad oram codicis κοινῆς illius, seu vulgatæ diversis lectionibus sub nota o. Quapropter in eo graviter allucinantur nonnulli, dum istâ Hexaplorum dispositione non intellectâ, contendunt in illis duplicem LXX. Interpretum editionem, tam vulgatam scilicet quàm puram illam, cujus ita frequenter meminerunt Origenes & Hieronymus, sub duplici columnella fuisse collocatam, & hâc ratione Hexapla non à diversis columnellis, sed à versionibus nomen suum ducere. Sed hæc apertè falsa sunt, nec aliunde proficiscuntur, quàm ex ignoratione dispositionis Hexaplorum, ad quorum marginem vetus LXX. Senum lectio relata fuerat: & hoc modo utraque LXX. Interpretum editio in
units.tr: This is the arrangement and disposition of Origen's Hexapla, which even very learned men have been quite unable to grasp, since they do not understand how the Greek translations of Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion came to be found twice in one and the same work: namely, in full within the text of the work, and in part in the scholia that stood in the margin. But Origen, who wished to benefit all, reduced that immense work of the Hexapla to a summary by means of the marks and scholia, so that those who could not obtain the complete Hexapla might at least copy its substance from the Hexapla itself. And by the same device he presented the common edition of the Seventy, that is, the common or vulgar edition, together with his new edition, which he thought more correct and inserted in full into the Hexapla, in one and the same work, namely by adding in the margin of that common codex the different readings under the mark o. Therefore some are gravely mistaken in this matter, for, not understanding this arrangement of the Hexapla, they contend that in it there were two editions of the Seventy Interpreters, the common one and that pure one which Origen and Jerome so often mention, placed in two separate columns; and that for this reason the Hexapla took its name not from the columns but from the versions. But these claims are plainly false, and they arise from nothing but ignorance of the arrangement of the Hexapla, in whose margin the old reading of the Seventy Elders had been placed; and in this way both editions of the Seventy Interpreters appeared in the Hexapla.

units.la: Hexaplis apparebat. Jam quia pauci immensa illa Hexaplorum volumina, quæ Hieronymi marsupium evacuârant, integra poterant comparare, plerique editionem illam LXX. ab Origene interpolatam cum asteriscis & obelis aliisque notis ex ipsismet Hexaplis desumpserunt; unde postea nata est maxima Græcis exemplaribus confusio, & ex eo tempore non amplius antiqua illa LXX. interpretatio plerisque in Ecclesiis lecta est, sed Origeniana & interpolata, quæ etiam, aut saltem similis, ad Ecclesiam Occidentalem operâ B. Hieronymi postea pervenit.
units.tr: appeared in the Hexapla. Now, since few people could obtain the whole of those huge Hexapla volumes, which had emptied Jerome's purse, most took that edition of the Seventy that Origen had interpolated, together with the asterisks, obeli and other marks, from the Hexapla itself. From this arose great confusion among the Greek manuscripts, and from that time the ancient Septuagint translation was no longer read in most churches. Instead they read the Origenian, interpolated text, which later reached the Western Church through the work of St Jerome, either in this form or in one very like it.

units.la: Egi ante paucos dies, vir optime, Isaaci Vossii ad iteratas Simonii Objectiones Responsionem, quae Canonico magis digna videtur, quàm homine Critico: cùm in ea firmissimis Simonii rationibus nihil opponens praeter inanem verborum strepitum, ineptias ineptiis accumulet. Singula illius argumenta repeto & expendo, ut cognoscas illum de rebus parùm sibi compertis judicium tulisse. Objecerat Vossio Simonius, priscos Ecclesiae Patres, Africanum, Origenem, Eusebium, Hieronymum, Augustinum & alios qui Judaeorum Codicis & LXX. Interpretum discrepantias in rebus chronologicis observarunt, de ulla Codicum depravatione Judaeis objiciendâ nunquam cogitasse, ne ipsum quidem Justinum Martyrem, qui tamen est acerrimus adversus Judaeos disputator. His cùm nihil solidi habeat Vossius quod respondeat, provocat ad Arabes qui suae sententiae faveant, uniusque Abulpharaii verba refert prolixè ex Latina doctissimi Pocokii versione. Verùm cum inepto Scriptore licet ineptire Vossio, monstrosasque sequi opiniones cum homine qui tot fabulas & portenta in opus suum conjecit.
units.tr: A few days ago, my good sir, I dealt with Isaac Vossius's reply to Simon's repeated objections. It seems more fitting to a canon than to a critic, since in it he sets nothing against Simon's very firm arguments except empty noise of words, and heaps absurdity upon absurdity. I repeat and weigh each of his arguments, so that you may see that he has passed judgment on matters he knows little about. Simon had objected to Vossius that the early Fathers of the Church (Africanus, Origen, Eusebius, Jerome, Augustine and others who noted the discrepancies between the Jewish codex and the Seventy interpreters in chronological matters) never thought of charging the Jews with any corruption of their codex, not even Justin Martyr, who is nonetheless a most bitter disputant against the Jews. Since Vossius has nothing solid to answer these, he appeals to the Arabs, who favour his opinion, and quotes at length the words of Abulpharagius alone, from the Latin version of the most learned Pococke. But it is allowed Vossius to play the fool with a silly writer, and to follow monstrous opinions with a man who has thrown so many fables and portents into his work.

units.la: A
units.tr: A

units.la: Addit tamen Vossius, non defuisse olim viros qui Judaeos depravationis hujus reos peregerint, idque ex Juliano Pomerio facile cognosci. Sed non aliud de hoc negotio sentit Julianus Archiepiscopus Toletanus, quam Augustinus, cujus testimonia in suum opus verbose transtulit. Constat autem Augustinum a Vossii sententia valde alienum fuisse, eumque redarguisse aetatis suae homines, qui ubi Codices Graecos ab Ebraicis discrepare in rebus chronologicis animadvertebant, statim affirmabant Ebraica Exemplaria a Judaeis corrupta fuisse. Sed ejusmodi objectionis vanitatem saepe ostendit Augustinus, cujus haec sunt verba. Inquiunt non esse credibile LXX. Interpretes, qui uno simul tempore unoque sensu interpretati sunt, errare potuisse, aut ubi nihil eorum interesset voluisse mentiri; Judaeos vero, dum nobis invident quod Lex & Prophetae ad nos interpretando transferunt, mutasse quaedam in Codicibus suis, ut in nostris minueretur auctoritas. Hanc opinionem vel suspicionem accipiet quisque ut putaverit: certum est tamen non vixisse Mathusalem post diluvium. Eamdem iterum quaestionem tractans Augustinus de annis Mathusalem, testatur aperte se in eorum sententiam venire non posse, qui Judaeos dedita opera suos Codices depravasse asserebant. Imo negat Judaeorum gentem tam longe lateque diffusam, in hoc conscribendum mendacium conspirare potuisse, ita ut, dum aliis invideant autoritatem, sibi veritatem abstulerint. Putat diversitatem illam numerorum, qui in Graecis Latinisque Codicibus aliter se habent quam in Ebraicis, tribuendam non esse Judaeorum malitiae, sed librariorum errori: ac demum haec subjungit. Recte fieri nullomodo dubitaverim, ut cum diversum aliquid in utrisque Codicibus invenitur; quandoquidem ad fidem rerum gestarum utrumque esse non potest verum, ei linguae potius credatur unde est in aliam per Interpretes facta translatio.
units.tr: Vossius adds, however, that in former times there were men who charged the Jews with this corruption, and that this can easily be learned from Julian Pomerius. But Julian, Archbishop of Toledo, holds no other view on this matter than Augustine, whose testimonies he has wordily transferred into his own work. It is certain, however, that Augustine was far from Vossius's opinion, and he refuted the men of his own time who, whenever they noticed that the Greek codices differed from the Hebrew in chronological matters, at once asserted that the Hebrew copies had been corrupted by the Jews. Augustine often showed the emptiness of this kind of objection, and his words are these. They say it is not credible that the Seventy interpreters, who translated together at one time and with one meaning, could have erred, or wished to lie where nothing of theirs was at stake; and that the Jews, envying us that we translate the Law and the Prophets into our language, changed some things in their codices so that our authority might be diminished. Let each person take this opinion, or suspicion, as he thinks fit; it is certain, however, that Methuselah did not live after the flood. Taking up the same question again about the years of Methuselah, Augustine plainly testifies that he cannot agree with those who asserted that the Jews had deliberately corrupted their codices. Indeed he denies that a people so long and widely dispersed could have conspired to write this lie, so that while they envied others their authority, they took away the truth for themselves. He thinks that the difference in numbers, which stands differently in the Greek and Latin codices than in the Hebrew, is to be attributed not to Jewish malice but to the error of copyists; and at last he adds these words. I would never doubt that it is rightly done whenever something different is found in the two codices, since both cannot be true for the credibility of the events recorded; the language from which the translation into another was made by the interpreters should rather be believed.

units.la: Ista & alia similia ex libris Augustini in opus suum contra Judaeos transtulit Julianus Archiepiscopus Toletanus, in quo annos ab Adamo usque ad Christum ex Ebraeis Graecisque Codicibus recensitis, Graecos quidem praefert Ebraicis cum prisicis Ecclesiae Patribus; sed secutus Augustinum Judaeos depravationis reos non peragit: contra utrisque Codicibus fidem habendam esse existimat, ubi non reperitur librariorum error; quia hanc diversitatem Divino Spiritui tribuit, cum LXX. Interpretes, referente Augustino, non interpretantium munere, sed Prophetarum libertate aliter voluisse dicere credendum sit. Affirmat idem Julianus, ex brevitate annorum quae in Judaeorum libris conspicitur, nullum instare periculum fidei, nec eam brevitatem esse contrariam nativitatis Christi temporibus. Haec clara sunt & manifesta, aptissimaque refellendis Abulpharaii & Vossii commentis.
units.tr: Julian, Archbishop of Toledo, transferred these and other similar things from Augustine's books into his own work against the Jews. In it, having reviewed the years from Adam to Christ from the Hebrew and Greek codices, he prefers the Greek to the Hebrew, together with the earliest Fathers of the Church. Yet, following Augustine, he does not charge the Jews with corruption. On the contrary, he judges that both codices are to be trusted wherever no error of copyists is found, because he ascribes this difference to the Divine Spirit: according to Augustine's report, it must be believed that the Seventy interpreters wished to say something differently not by the office of translators but by the freedom of the Prophets. The same Julian affirms that from the brevity of the years found in the books of the Jews no danger threatens the faith, nor is that brevity contrary to the time of Christ's birth. These points are clear and manifest, and most apt for refuting the inventions of Abulpharagius and Vossius.

units.la: Ad Talmudicos postea transit Vossius: sed quam bene hoc succedat, tu ipse, vir optime, judicabis: tot enim hoc loco refert ineptias, ut illo videar ineptior, si singulas persequar. Haec sunt illius verba. In Talmude prolixe narratur congressus Judaeorum cum Hieronymo a Sancta Fide Rabbino Hispa-
units.tr: Vossius next turns to the Talmudic writers. But you yourself, my good sir, will judge how well this goes, for he brings forward here so many absurdities that I would seem more foolish myself if I went through each one. These are his words. In the Talmud there is a lengthy account of a meeting of the Jews with Jerome of Holy Faith, a rabbi of Hispa-

units.la: Aug. lib. 15. de Civit. Dei. Hispano , sed ante trecentos annos facto Christiano. Sed quid ista significent ne quidem Elias divinaverit. Qui enim fieri potest ut Hieronymus à Sancta Fide, qui ante trecentos annos vixit, in Talmude cum Judæis congrediatur? Hieronymus ille à Sancta Fide fuit Medicus Pontificis Benedicti, qui Petrus de Luna appellatus est. Editæ sunt rationes quas Hieronymus è libris Talmudicis desumptas propositit coram Benedicto, Cardinalibus, Magistris & Doctoribus: sed nihil prorsus eorum quæ illi tribuit Voffius in hoc scripto legitur: è contrario eadem planè ratione Judæos urget Hieronymus, quâ illos premendos esse censuit Simonius, ita ut suo seipsum gladio jugulaverit Voffius, cûm istum Scriptorem vocavit in auxilium. Riserat Simonius Voffium, qui Eliam Talmudicum Doctorem fecerat Prophetam. Jam probat & ipse Propheta Voffius ex suppositio illo Talmudistarum congressu, non certò constitisse an hic Elias sit Propheta ille antiquus, an verò alius quidam Rabbi. Sed ea de re in scripto Hieronymi à Sancta Fide ne quidem verbum extat: imò ea quæ ex Talmude affert manifestè ostendunt Eliam Rabbinum fuisse. Quare nugatur bonus Voffius, quando de Simonio sic loquitur. Simonius in gratiam Judæorum, ipsis Rabbinis Rabbinior, audacter affirmat hunc Eliam fuisse Rabbinum. Hoc quidem affirmavit Simonius, & affirmat iterum, quia clara sunt hoc loco Talmudis verba, quæ si legisset Voffius, nugatoribus Talmudistis nugacior, nugatorem in Prophetam non transformasset: illud enim de quo agitur
units.tr: Aug. lib. 15. de Civit. Dei. Spanish, but made a Christian three hundred years earlier. But what these words mean not even Elijah could have divined. For how can it be that Jerome of Holy Faith, who lived three hundred years ago, debates with the Jews in the Talmud? That Jerome of Holy Faith was the physician of Pope Benedict, who was called Peter de Luna. The arguments which Jerome drew from the Talmudic books were published before Benedict, the Cardinals, masters and doctors; but none of the things Vossius attributes to him is found in this writing. On the contrary, Jerome presses the Jews by exactly the same reasoning by which Simon thought they should be pressed, so that Vossius has cut his own throat with his own sword when he called that writer to his aid. Simon had mocked Vossius for making Elijah, a Talmudic teacher, into a prophet. Now Vossius himself, the prophet, proves from that supposed meeting of the Talmudists that it was not certain whether this Elijah was that ancient prophet or some other rabbi. But on this matter there is not a word in Jerome of Holy Faith's writing; indeed what he quotes from the Talmud clearly shows that Elijah was a rabbi. Hence the good Vossius talks nonsense when he speaks of Simon thus. Simon, more rabbinical than the rabbis themselves, boldly affirms that this Elijah was a rabbi, to win the favour of the Jews. Simon did affirm this, and affirms it again, because the words of the Talmud are clear on this point. Had Vossius read them, he would not have turned a trifler into a prophet, more trifling than the trifling Talmudists. For that prophecy of which we are speaking

units.la: vaticinium non solùm tribuitur in Talmude Eliæ, sed aliis Rabbinis qui istud etiam referunt. Autor itaque fuerim Voffio, qui tot nugatores inter Prophetas recensuit, istos etiam Rabbinos inter Prophetas & Prophetides collocet, ut longè adhuc majori Prophetarum & Prophetidum agmine stipatus bonus Voffius, nova sua procudat vaticinia. Verùm placet ipsa Talmudis verba afferre, ut ex illis quidquid nugarum de hoc Elia effutiit, facilius refellatur. Vaticinium istud in Tractatu Avoda Zara & in Tractatu Sanhedrin sic conceptum legitur: תנא רבי אליהו ששה אלפים שנה הוי העולם שני אלפים תוהו שני אלפים תורה שני אלפים ימות המשיח בעונותינו שרבו יצאו מהם מה שיצאו. Docet domus Eliæ, sex annorum millibus erit mundus: bis mille annis inanitas: bis mille, Lex: bis mille, tempus Messiæ; propter iniquitates nostras, quæ multæ fuerunt, elapsi sunt ex iis, qui præterierunt. Per domum autem Eliæ intellige ipsum Eliam & ejus discipulos. Utrùm autem vaticinium illud quod hoc loco producitur, verum sit vaticinium, non anquiro: sive enim vera sit Prophetia, sive non sit, certum est Eliam aliosque Magistros, qui vaticinium istud referunt, Rabbinos fuisse, non Prophetas: cùm in eodem Talmude paulò ante hæc verba quæ adduximus, istud etiam legatur. אמ' רב קטינא שירת אלפים שני הוו עלמא וחד חריב. Dixit Rabbi Katina, Sex annorum millibus erit mundus, & uno destruetur. Jam si velit etiam Voffius istum Rabbi Katinam cum Rabbi Elia inter suos Prophetas collocare, per me licet ut nugetur; consentientemque hac in re habebit Postellum magnum Prophetarum & Prophetidum amplificatorem, qui scribit Talmudicos aliosque ejusdem naturae libros ab eodem spiritu profectos esse atque Euangelium. Sunt Zoar, inquit Postellus, Targum, Midras, Misnajoth, Talmud utrumque & Euangelium appendices Legis Mosaicae. Attendat Vossius ad ineptias in quas se conjicit, cum obstinato animo contendit Talmudicum Eliam esse verum Prophetam, objicitque Simonio, eum nihil amare nisi quod distortum sit, eique solenne esse Prophetas in nihilum redigere. Verum est Simonium redigere in nihilum Prophetas Vossianos qui nugatores sunt & impostores. Gaudeat ejusmodi Prophetis beatulus Vossius, autorque illi sum, ut eos albo Sanctorum quos Anglicana Liturgia continet, adjiciat: multa siquidem in illius Liturgiae Calendario spatia vacua sunt relicta, quibus omnes sancti Prophetae & sanctae Prophetides Vossii facile inseri poterunt.
units.tr: is ascribed in the Talmud not only to Elijah but also to other rabbis who report it. I would therefore advise Vossius, who has counted so many triflers among the Prophets, to place these rabbis too among the Prophets and Prophetesses, so that the good Vossius, surrounded by a far larger host of Prophets and Prophetesses, may coin his new prophecies. But I am pleased to quote the very words of the Talmud, so that whatever nonsense has been babbled about this Elijah may be more easily refuted. That prophecy is read in Tractate Avoda Zara and in Tractate Sanhedrin, conceived thus: [תנא רבי אליהו ששה אלפים שנה הוי העולם שני אלפים תוהו שני אלפים תורה שני אלפים ימות המשיח בעונותינו שרבו יצאו מהם מה שיצאו]. The house of Elijah teaches: the world will last six thousand years; two thousand years of emptiness, two thousand of the Law, two thousand the time of the Messiah; because of our iniquities, which were many, some of those years have gone out. By the house of Elijah understand Elijah himself and his disciples. Whether that prophecy which is produced here is a true prophecy I do not inquire; for whether it is true prophecy or not, it is certain that Elijah and the other masters who report it were rabbis, not prophets, since in the same Talmud, a little before the words we have quoted, this also is read: [אמ' רב קטינא שירת אלפים שני הוו עלמא וחד חריב]. Rabbi Katina said: the world will be six thousand years, and in one of them it will be destroyed. Now if Vossius wishes to place this Rabbi Katina among his Prophets along with Rabbi Elijah, he may trifle as far as I am concerned; and he will have in agreement the great Postel, amplifier of Prophets and Prophetesses, who writes that the Talmudic books and others of the same kind proceeded from the same Spirit as the Gospel. The Zohar, says Postel, the Targum, the Midrash, the Mishnah, both Talmuds and the Gospel are appendices to the Mosaic Law. Let Vossius attend to the absurdities into which he throws himself, when with obstinate mind he contends that the Talmudic Elijah is a true prophet, and objects to Simon that he loves nothing but what is distorted, and that it is his custom to reduce the Prophets to nothing. It is true that Simon reduces to nothing the Vossian prophets, who are triflers and impostors. Let the blessed Vossius rejoice in such prophets; I advise him to add them to the list of saints which the English Liturgy contains, for many blank spaces have been left in the Calendar of that Liturgy, into which all the holy Prophets and holy Prophetesses of Vossius can easily be inserted.

units.la: Pergit, & ut in Talmude exercitatum se esse ostendat, asserit ne nunc quidem Rabbinos dubitare, vaticinium de duratione mundi esse Eliae Prophetae, dummodo & illius esse admittantur illa quae sequuntur verba; Sed propter peccata nostra praeterierunt anni qui praeterierunt. At unde haec sumpserit bonus Vossius, divinet Elias Talmudicus. Addit neminem qui aliquo praeditus sit judicio negaturum adjecta esse verba illa a Rabbinis: sed ego contra ausim affirmare, neminem qui sani sit sincipitis hac in re fidem habiturum rationibus quas profert Vossius ut illud adstruat. Ipsa, inquit Vossius, id satis testatur phrasis, cum Eliae vaticinium Chaldaeo, additamentum vero Hebraeo sit expressum sermone. Verum quid sit Ebraice loqui, quid Chaldaice, nescit Vossius, cum Eliae verba minus non sint Ebraica, quam ista clausula quam putat a Rabbinis adjectam fuisse vaticinio Eliae. Neque etiam ostendit se judicio praeditum, cum Eliam Prophetam Chaldaice loquentem repraesentat, Doctores vero Talmudicos Ebraice loquentes. Nugatur iterum Vossius, dum probare conatur ex alio Talmudis loco, clausulam hanc recenter additam fuisse, & ex scripto Hieronymi a Sancta Fide, in quo illud additamentum non reperitur. Verum quidem est in scripto Hieronymi quod editum habemus non legi istam clausulam, quia haec nihil faciebat ad institutum suum & ad Eliae verba quae refert. Satis fuit ex Talmude ea referre, quibus urgere fortiter poterat Judaeos ex ipsorum Chronologia, & ostendere dudum advenisse Messiam: ad quod probandum nihil plane faciebat clausula ista quae in omnibus Talmudis editionibus legitur, & a Scholiastis Talmudis ante Hieronymi a Sancta Fide tempora explicatur. Haec boni Vossii somnia aperte docent, eum a Simonio recte monitum fuisse, ut prius in Rabbinorum castra transiret, quam de illorum rebus ferret sententiam.
units.tr: He goes on, and to show that he is practised in the Talmud, he asserts that even now the rabbis do not doubt that the prophecy about the duration of the world belongs to Elijah the Prophet, provided that the words which follow are also admitted to be his: But because of our sins, the years that have passed have passed. Where good Vossius got this from, let Talmudic Elijah divine. He adds that no one with any judgement will deny that those words were added by the rabbis. But I would venture to assert the contrary: no one of sound mind will put any trust in the arguments Vossius offers to establish it. The phrase itself, says Vossius, sufficiently shows this, since Elijah's prophecy is expressed in Chaldee, but the addition in Hebrew. But Vossius does not know what it is to speak Hebrew, or what it is to speak Chaldee, since Elijah's words are no less Hebrew than that clause which he thinks the rabbis added to Elijah's prophecy. Nor does he show himself to have judgement when he represents Elijah the Prophet as speaking Chaldee and the Talmudic teachers as speaking Hebrew. Vossius trifles again, when he tries to prove from another passage of the Talmud that this clause was added recently, and from a writing of Hieronymus a Sancta Fide, in which that addition is not found. It is true that in the writing of Hieronymus which we have in print this clause is not read, because it had nothing to do with his purpose and with the words of Elijah which he cites. It was enough for him to cite from the Talmud those passages with which he could press the Jews hard from their own chronology and show that the Messiah had long since come. For proving that, that clause, which is read in all editions of the Talmud and was explained by the commentators on the Talmud before the time of Hieronymus a Sancta Fide, contributed nothing at all. These dreams of good Vossius clearly show that he was rightly warned by Simonius that he should first cross over into the camp of the rabbis before passing judgement on their affairs.

units.la: Instat deinceps Vossius, aitque Simonium a se monitum fuisse, bis mille annos qui in Eliae vaticinio dicuntur ante Legem effluxisse, accipiendos esse de tempore quod a diluvio ad Moysem & Legem datam intercessit, cùm Apostolus & pleræque Orientis gentes, quæ aliquam diluvii habent cognitionem, sic loquantur, mundi initium à diluvio arcessentes aut à Noacho. Verùm istud Vossii monitum tanquam frigidum merito explosit Simonius, cùm in præsenti negotio non agatur de B. Petri & Orientis gentium sensu, sed de Eliæ vaticinio apud Talmudicos, ac de Judæis ex ipso Talmude & eorum Chronologia refellendis. Vossium monuerat Simonius, nihil omnino probabilitatis habere argumentum quo probare nititur Judæos in suis Codicibus expunxisse quatuordecim secula; quia Messiam expectant, quem nos advenisse putamus. Id credibile non esse Simonius animadverterat, cùm Judæi ex Codicis Ebraei lectione fortius premi possint, quàm ex Græca LXX. Interpretum Versione. Quid Vossius ad hæc? Ait à diluvio, non ab Adamo arcessendos esse annos in explicando Eliæ vaticinio. Contrà ait Simonius, annos illos numerandos esse eâ ratione quâ in Talmude à Judæorum Magistris Talmudisque Scholiastis numerantur, cùm de rebus Judæorum instituatur disputatio, ipsique Judæi haud inviti agnoscant Codicum suorum Chronologiam sibi esse contrariam, tempusque quo venturus erat Messias præteriisse: & cùm nihil solidi illis subsit quod respondeant Christianis rationem hanc ex illorum Chronologia urgentibus, dilationem adventûs Messiæ in peccata sua rejiciunt. Hoc etiam argumento Judæos urget Hieronymus à Sancta Fide, neque annos mundi à Noacho arcessit, sed ab Adamo cum Judæis Talmudicis, & Rabbi Salomone, quem Talmudis glossatorem appellat; neque quemquam scio, qui in eo de quo agitur argumento annos mundi à Noacho arcessat, si unum excipiamus Vossium, qui in fingendis commentis Rabbinis Rabbinior est: nam & ipse Julianus Archiepiscopus Toletanus, qui in sua Disputatione contra Judæos LXX. Seniorum Chronologiam præfert Judaicæ, sumit initium annorum mundi ab Adamo.
units.tr: Vossius next presses on, and says that he was warned by Simonius that the two thousand years which are mentioned in Elijah's prophecy as having passed before the Law must be understood of the time which lay between the Flood and Moses and the giving of the Law, since the Apostle and most of the peoples of the East, who have some knowledge of the Flood, speak in this way, deriving the beginning of the world from the Flood or from Noah. But Simonius rightly rejected that warning of Vossius as cold, since the present matter is not about the sense of Saint Peter and the peoples of the East, but about Elijah's prophecy among the Talmudists, and about refuting the Jews from the Talmud itself and their own chronology. Simonius had warned Vossius that the argument by which he tries to prove that the Jews have expunged fourteen centuries from their codices, because they expect a Messiah whom we think has come, has no probability at all. Simonius had noticed that this is not credible, since the Jews can be pressed more strongly by the reading of the Hebrew codex than by the Greek version of the Seventy interpreters. What does Vossius say to this? He says that the years in explaining Elijah's prophecy must be counted from the Flood, not from Adam. On the contrary, Simonius says that those years are to be counted in the way they are counted in the Talmud by the Jewish masters and the commentators on the Talmud, since the dispute concerns the affairs of the Jews, and the Jews themselves, not unwillingly, acknowledge that the chronology of their own codices is contrary to them and that the time when the Messiah was to come has passed. And since they have nothing solid with which to answer Christians who press this argument from their chronology, they throw the delay of the Messiah's coming back on their own sins. Hieronymus a Sancta Fide also presses the Jews with this argument, and he does not count the years of the world from Noah, but from Adam, along with the Talmudic Jews and Rabbi Solomon, whom he calls the glossator of the Talmud. I know of no one who, in the matter under discussion, counts the years of the world from Noah, except Vossius, who in inventing rabbinic fictions is more rabbinical than the rabbis. For even Julian, Archbishop of Toledo, who in his Disputation against the Jews prefers the Chronology of the Seventy Elders to the Jewish one, takes the beginning of the years of the world from Adam.

units.la: Objicit iterum Simonio Vossius, cum pro Elia Propheta nugatorem Rabbinum substituere, ac dicere per Legem hic intelligi tempus istud quo Abrahamus relictis idolis ad veri Dei cultum accessit;, & hoc pacto subvertì penitus vaticinium. Verùm nugatore illo Rabbino nugacior est Vossius, qui pro nugatore Rabbino substituit Eliam Prophetam. Illa autem quæ attulit Simonius de tempore, sumpsit ex ipsismet Rabbinis: hæc enim sunt illius verba. Magistri, qui Commentariis suis Talmudis libros illustrant, bis mille annos numerant à primo homine condito usque ad tempus illud quo Abraham relicto idolorum cultu veram Dei unius legem amplexatus est. Hæc si facta sunt, debuit Vossius falsitatis arguere Simonium ex Talmudicis Scholiastis, quos convincendis Judæis utiles hoc loco judicavit Simonius: at Vossius, qui nihil aliud scire videtur, quàm edere inanem strepitum verborum, ait frustra Simonium conari persuadere ad convincendam Judaicam Chronologiam, se mirificum conferre beneficium. Si quis, inquit Vossius, Judæos hac ratione aggrediatur, ludibrio erit, & nihil nisi risum referet. Verùm quâ arte melius Judæorum convinci potest Chronologia pro adstruendo Messiæ adventu, quàm ex eorum libris, quos in hoc negotio sibi adversari agnoscunt; ita ut etiam inter illos non defuerint, qui Messiam non amplius expectandum affirmaverint? Ridենt quidem Judæi: sed quid ridٹent? Vossii ineptias, qui in tractandis eorum libris tam ineptum se ostendit.
units.tr: Vossius again objects to Simonius that, in place of Elijah the Prophet, he substitutes a trifling rabbi, and says that by the Law is meant here the time at which Abraham, having left off idols, came to the worship of the true God; and in this way, he says, the prophecy is wholly overturned. But Vossius is more trifling than that trifling rabbi, since in place of a trifling rabbi he substitutes Elijah the Prophet. The things Simonius brought forward about the time he took from the rabbis themselves, for these are his words: The Masters, who illustrate the books of the Talmud in their Commentaries, count two thousand years from the first man created until that time when Abraham, having left the worship of idols, embraced the true law of the one God. If this is so, Vossius ought to have charged Simonius with falsehood on the basis of the Talmudic commentators, whom Simonius judged useful for convincing the Jews at this point. But Vossius, who seems to know nothing but how to make empty noise with words, says that Simonius tries in vain to persuade him to refute the Jewish chronology, and that he himself is conferring a wonderful benefit. If anyone, says Vossius, approaches the Jews in this way, he will be a laughing-stock and will bring nothing but laughter. But by what art can the Jewish chronology be better refuted in support of the Messiah's coming than from their own books, which they acknowledge to be against them in this matter, so that among them too there have not been lacking those who have affirmed that the Messiah is no longer to be expected? The Jews do indeed laugh. But what do they laugh at? At the silliness of Vossius, who shows himself so silly in handling their books.

units.la: Pergit deinceps Vossius, cùmque nihil habeat quod respondeat ad ea quæ sequuntur, quærit effugium, nihil iis solidi esse affirmans; gravissima tamen sunt & digna quæ à Vossio expenderentur, cùm in iis de quibusdam Scripturæ locis agatur, quæ à Judæis dedita operâ & odio Christianæ Religionis corrupta fuisse contendit, eosque qui aliter sentiunt fanaticos & sesqui-Judæos pronunciat. Sed crimen illud amolitur à Judæis Simonius, putatque illas lectionum diversitates in Exemplarium discrepantiam rejiciendas esse, non in Codicum depravationem, cùm ea sors sit omnium librorum, ut scribæ in illis describendis interdum labantur. Mutos esse Codices Ebraeos quibus nunc utuntur Judæi, autor est Vossius; sed ait Simonius, simili ratione mutos fuisse Codices Ebraeos LXX. Interpretum, imò & Samaritarum Codices, quos tamen nemo sani judicii mutos appellaverit. Istud enim est nationum Orientalium ingenium, ut libros suos cum paucis vocalibus scribant per literarum compendia; siquè ob hanc causam muti sunt Judæorum libri, similiter muti erunt Samaritarum, Chaldaeorum, Syrorum & Arabum Codices.
units.tr: Vossius goes on, and since he has nothing to answer to what follows, he seeks a way out, asserting that there is nothing solid in them. Yet they are very weighty and worthy of being weighed by Vossius, since they deal with certain passages of Scripture which he maintains were corrupted by the Jews on purpose and out of hatred for the Christian religion, and he pronounces those who think otherwise fanatics and semi-Jews. But Simonius removes that charge from the Jews, and thinks that those diversities of readings should be attributed to differences among copies, not to a corruption of the codices, since this is the lot of all books, that scribes sometimes slip in copying them. Vossius is the authority for saying that the Hebrew codices now used by the Jews are mute; but Simonius says that by a similar argument the Hebrew codices of the Seventy interpreters, and indeed the codices of the Samaritans, would be mute, though no one of sound judgement would call them mute. For it is the nature of the Eastern nations to write their books with few vowels, by abbreviations of letters; and if for this reason the books of the Jews are mute, the codices of the Samaritans, the Chaldeans, the Syrians and the Arabs will likewise be mute.

units.la: Vana esse pronunciaverat Simonius ea omnia quae Vossius adversus Judæos ex Justini Martyris aliorumque Patrum testimoniis congessit, idque se jam alibi demonstrasse dixerat. Quid ad hæc Vossius? Somniabat Simonius cùm hæc scriberet. Imò tunc vigilans Simonius Vossii & ejus similium refellebat somnia, ut manifesto liquet ex Capite 9. Disquisitionum Criticarum, quas ipse Simonio tribuit. Longè plura afferri possent, quibus constaret Vossium Patrum scripta ne quidem à limine salutavisse: at satis erit hoc loco expendere quæ habet Vossius de verbis Jonæ, Cap. 3: 4. Adhuc quadraginta dies, & Ninive subvertetur. Lectionem hanc, & Græcam, in qua extat Adhuc triduum, æqualiter rejicit, aitque Augustinum conatum esse componere hanc litem, sed nihil profecisse; Theodoretum melius errorem Græcorum Exemplarium non Interpretibus, sed librariis imputare; miratum esse Hieronymum hanc diversitatem, cùm nulla aut verborum aut numerorum sit affinitas. Vossius autem illis omnibus oculatior, affirmat quæstionem hanc solvisse Justinum Martyrem, qui in Dialogo cum Tryphone ista Interpretum verba producens, dies numeret quadraginta tres: ita ut secundum Vossium, utriusque Codicis tam Græci quam Ebraei lectio corrupta fuerit, & in Græcis Codicibus olim fuerit, non ut vulgò, ἔτι τρεῖς ἡμέρας, Adhuc tres dies; sed ἔτι τρεῖς ἢ μ'. ἡμέρας, Adhuc quadraginta tres dies. Hæc quidem lectio jam à Mel-
units.tr: Simonius had declared that all the things Vossius gathered against the Jews from the testimonies of Justin Martyr and other Fathers were vain, and he had said that he had already shown this elsewhere. What does Vossius say to this? Simonius was dreaming when he wrote this. Indeed Simonius, awake, was refuting the dreams of Vossius and his like, as is clear from chapter 9 of the Critical Disquisitions, which he attributes to Simonius himself. Many more things could be brought forward by which it would be established that Vossius has not so much as greeted the writings of the Fathers from the threshold. But it will be enough here to weigh what Vossius has about the words of Jonah, chapter 3:4. Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown. He rejects this reading equally with the Greek one, in which stands Yet three days; he says that Augustine tried to settle this dispute but achieved nothing; that Theodoret better imputed the error of the Greek copies not to the translators but to the copyists; and that Hieronymus wondered at this diversity, since there is no affinity either in the words or in the numbers. Vossius, however, sharper-eyed than all of them, affirms that Justin Martyr solved this question, who, in his Dialogue with Trypho, when producing these words of the translators, counts forty-three days: so that, according to Vossius, the reading of both codices, Greek as well as Hebrew, was corrupted, and in the Greek codices there once stood, not as commonly, [ἔτι τρεῖς ἡμέρας] Yet three days, but [ἔτι τρεῖς ἢ μ'. ἡμέρας] Yet forty-three days. This reading, indeed, had already been noted by Melchior

units.la: Vossius de Tralat. 70. Interp. cap. 23. à Melchiore Cano observata fuerat; sed est monstrosa, utpote quae conflata ex duplici lectione, nimirum ex Aquilae & LXX. Interpretum Versione. Rem ita esse deprehendisset bonus Vossius, si ad Dialogum Justini Martyris animum advertisset: nam constat sanctissimum illum Patrem Scripturae verba haud infrequenter proferre ex LXX. Interpretum Versione simul & Aquilae Tralatione. Scio in hoc ipso Justini loco etiam legi ἐν ἄλλοις τρεῖς, in aliis tres. Sed manifestum est additamentum. Nodum hunc optimè solvit Theodoretus, cujus etiam verba leguntur in Scholiis Romanis. Animadvertit vir ille doctissimus, Aquilam, Symmachum & Theodotionem legisse τεσσαρακοντα, quadraginta, & cum his consentire Syrum & Ebraeum: Συμφωνεῖ ἡ ἢ τρίτος ἢ ὁ Σύρος ἢ ὁ Ἑβραῖος. Dein, nonnullis interjectis, suspicatur etiam sic ab initio scriptum fuisse in LXX. Interpretum Versione, eosque qui ab initio scripserunt, errasse, quorum postea error in omnia Exemplaria permanarit. His verbis Theodoretus non solum docet quae sit germana hujus loci lectio; sed & Vossii sententiam de Ebraeis, Graecis & Syriacis Codicibus refellit; cum non dubitaverit omnia Exemplaria Graeca ex Ebraeo, Syro, Aquila, Symmacho & Theodotione corrigere, laudaveritque Syrum Interpretem, qui cum editione Syriaca hodierna, quae ex Ebraeo sumpta est, consentit.
units.tr: Vossius, in De translatione LXX interpretum, chapter 23, was observed by Melchior Cano. But the reading is monstrous, since it is pieced together from two readings, namely that of Aquila and that of the Seventy translators. The good Vossius would have grasped the matter if he had paid attention to the Dialogue of Justin Martyr. For it is well established that that most holy Father quotes Scripture not infrequently, sometimes from the Septuagint version and sometimes from the translation of Aquila. I know that in this very passage of Justin the reading in others, three [ἐν ἄλλοις τρεῖς] is also found. But it is a clear addition. Theodoret resolves this knot very well, and his words are also read in the Roman Scholia. That most learned man observes that Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion read forty [τεσσαρακοντα], and that the Syriac and the Hebrew agree with them [Συμφωνεῖ ἡ ἢ τρίτος ἢ ὁ Σύρος ἢ ὁ Ἑβραῖος]. Then, after some intervening words, he suspects that it was also written this way from the beginning in the Septuagint version, and that those who wrote it at the start made the error, which afterwards spread into all the copies. By these words Theodoret not only teaches what the genuine reading of this place is, but also refutes Vossius's opinion about the Hebrew, Greek and Syriac copies. For he did not hesitate to correct all the Greek copies by the Hebrew, the Syriac, Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion, and he praised the Syriac interpreter, who agrees with the present Syriac edition, which is taken from the Hebrew.

units.la: Pergit dein Vossius nugari, Propheticum ensem iterum distringens. Simonius ei objecerat, extra institituti sui rationem esse, illud omne quod in Responsione ad Criticam Sacram de Prophetis verbosius adduxit; atque ubi de LXX. Interpretibus agebatur, quos verè Prophetas & divino afflatu inspiratos asserit, multa congeri inutiliter de oraculorum, somniorum, furtorum & similium interpretibus vel indicibus, qui etiam Prophetae appellati fuerint: quasi verò de ejusmodi Prophetis instituta fuerit quaestio. Rectè itaque dixit Simonius, Vossium quaerere latebras, & ab eo malè redargui Hieronymum, qui scripserit LXX. Seniores Prophetas non fuisse, sed Interpretes. Contendit siquidem Vossius, Hieronymum manifestè contradicere Apostolo, qui pluribus in locis προφητεύειν sumpsit pro interpretari; Epimenidem Cretensium Prophetam vocari ab eodem Apostolo; secundùm Platonem in Timaeo & alibi, Prophetas dici cujuscunque veritatis testes. Verùm quò tendat ista Vossii garrulitas, tu ipse judicabis, vir optime. Perinde illi est quid scribat, modò scribat. Quando negavit Hieronymus, LXX. Interpretes esse Prophetas, constat eum locutum non fuisse de aliis Prophetis, quàm de iis qui sunt Divino Spiritu afflati. De his Prophetis loquentem Hieronymum debuit refellere Vossius, non verò excurrere inaniter, ac disserere de hominibus furiosis, somniatoribus, Poëtis, aliisque ejusdem generis Prophetis; cùm isti Prophetae Vossiani nihil omnino ad rem faciant.
units.tr: Vossius then goes on trifling, once more brandishing the prophetic sword. Simonius had objected to him that everything he adduced at greater length on the Prophets in his Response to the Critica Sacra was outside the scope of his undertaking; and that where the discussion concerned the Septuagint translators, whom he asserts were truly Prophets and inspired by divine breath, he was uselessly heaping together much about interpreters of oracles, dreams, thefts and the like, or informers, who were also called prophets; as if the question concerned prophets of that sort. So Simonius rightly said that Vossius was seeking hiding places, and that Jerome, who wrote that the Seventy elders were not prophets but interpreters, was badly refuted by him. For Vossius contends that Jerome plainly contradicts the Apostle, who in several places takes prophesy to mean to interpret; that the same Apostle calls Epimenides, the prophet of the Cretans, a prophet; and that, according to Plato in the Timaeus and elsewhere, prophets are called witnesses of any truth whatever. But where this garrulousness of Vossius is heading, you yourself, best of men, will judge. It makes no difference to him what he writes, provided he writes.
