When Jerome denied that the Septuagint translators were prophets, it is clear he was not speaking of prophets other than those who are inspired by the Divine Spirit. Vossius ought to have refuted Jerome speaking of these prophets, not to run off aimlessly and discourse about madmen, dreamers, poets and other prophets of the same kind; since those Vossian prophets have nothing at all to do with the matter.

units.la: Quasi satis non fuerit Vossium tot ineptias de Prophetis in Responsionem suam ad Objectiones Criticae Sacrae conjecisse, alias iterum illis accu-
units.tr: As if it were not enough that Vossius has thrown so many absurdities about prophets into his Response to the Objections of the Critica Sacra, he piles on still other

units.la: Vossii in Resp. ad Obj. Crit. Sac. accumulat, aitque Simonium proprio seipsum gladio jugulasse, quia Hieronymus Pauli verba explicans, affirmat Epimenidem per illusionem & ironiam ab Apostolo vocari Prophetam. Sed videat bonus Vossius, an suo seipsum potius gladio Prophetico jugulaverit, cum inde manifestum sit, nomen Prophetæ esse ambiguum. At Simonius ambiguitatem illam Hieronymo cognitam fuisse indicavit, cum dixit illum vocis istius proprietatem optime novisse; sed negasse eo tantum sensu illos esse Prophetas, quo nomen Prophetæ à priscis Patribus sumitur, quando LXX. Interpretes appellant Prophetas. Sed pudet me tot ineptias Vossii, totque ejus commenta, quæ nihil ad institutum faciant, refellere.
units.tr: ...Vossius's Response to the Objections of the Critica Sacra, and says that Simonius has cut his own throat with his own sword, because Jerome, explaining the words of Paul, affirms that Epimenides was called a prophet by the Apostle through irony and mockery. But let the good Vossius see whether he has rather cut his own throat with his own prophetic sword, since it is plain from this that the name of prophet is ambiguous. Simonius, however, indicated that Jerome knew that ambiguity, when he said that Jerome understood the proper meaning of that word very well, but denied that they were prophets except in the sense in which the ancient Fathers use the name of prophet, when they call the Septuagint translators prophets. But I am ashamed to refute so many absurdities of Vossius and so many of his inventions, which have nothing to do with the subject.

units.la: Jam à Prophetia transit ad Grammaticam Vossius; & quia non solum Propheta est, sed & de gente Latina & Latinis Latinior, Simonium arguit, qui scripserit Vossio latuit, cum scribendum esset, Vossium latuit: qua in re Despauterianum magis se ostendit Vossius, quam Ciceronianum: nam Scioppius aliique præstantissimi Grammatici affirmant, Latinum non esse latet me, idemque Scioppius testis in hac materia locupletissimus præfert latet mihi; quia locutionis istius exempla non desunt in libris Ciceronis. Verum litem hanc ad Vossianos Magistellos cinctos togâ Professoriâ remittendam esse duxi; quia non placet minuta consectari. Simonius autem Vossio objecerat, ei latuisse quæ ipse Simonius de Hieronymi sententia dixerat. Sed, inquit Vossius, valde mirabitur Vossius, si quidquam hac de re scripserit Simonius, quod Vossium latuerit. Videtur tamen ignorasse Vossius, quæ Capite 9. Disquisitionum Criticarum de Hieronymo illiusque ingenio allata sunt. Si hæc Vossio non sufficiant, paratus est Simonius demonstrare Vossium fœdè errasse non in unius Hieronymi, sed & in reliquorum Patrum testimoniis recensendis.
units.tr: Now Vossius passes from prophecy to grammar; and because he is not only a prophet but also, being of the Latin race, more Latin than the Latins, he accuses Simonius, who wrote Vossio latuit [it escaped Vossius], when it ought to have been written Vossium latuit [it escaped Vossius, accusative]. In this matter Vossius shows himself more of a Despauterian than a Ciceronian. For Scioppius and other most distinguished grammarians affirm that latet me is not Latin, and the same Scioppius, a most abundant witness in this matter, prefers latet mihi, since examples of that construction are not lacking in the books of Cicero. But I have judged that this quarrel should be referred to the Vossian little masters girt with the professorial toga, since it does not please me to chase trifles. Simonius, moreover, had objected to Vossius that he had overlooked what Simonius himself had said about the opinion of Jerome. But, says Vossius, Vossius will be greatly astonished if Simonius has written anything on this matter that has escaped Vossius. Yet Vossius seems to have been unaware of what was adduced about Jerome and his genius in chapter 9 of the Disquisitiones Criticae. If these things are not enough for Vossius, Simonius is ready to show that Vossius has shamefully erred not only in citing the testimony of Jerome alone, but also in the testimonies of the rest of the Fathers.

units.la: Ait deinceps Vossius, carpi se à Simonio, ac si dixerit præcepta Grammatica à Judæis ante sexcentos demum annos fuisse completa, cum nusquam tale quid dixerit; sed puncta vocalia Judæorum non excedere sex sæculorum ætatem. Verum quæerit effugium Vossius qui duplicem distinxit Grammaticam, quam etiam agnovit Simonius, antiquam unam, novitiam alteram. Hæc cum punctis vocalibus orta est. De prima non disputavit Simonius, sed de altera tantum, cum de punctis vocalibus ageretur. Jam Vossius secutus Morinum in prima Exercitationum Biblicarum parte, existimavit ante R. Judam nullam Judæos habuisse Grammaticam, aut admodum exiguam. Contra hanc Grammaticam declamitat Vossius, eamque novitiam appellat quæ à sexcentis annis nota fuerit. Sed contendit Simonius, hanc cum punctis vocalibus ante annos 900. inventam fuisse. Imò sententiam suam Morinus in posteriori Exercitationum suarum parte retractavit.
units.tr: Vossius next says that he is being criticised by Simonius as if Simonius had said that the rules of grammar were brought to completion by the Jews only six hundred years ago, though he never said anything of the kind; but that the Jewish vowel points do not exceed six centuries in age. But Vossius seeks an escape, having distinguished a double grammar, which Simonius also acknowledged: one ancient, the other recent. The latter arose together with the vowel points. Simonius did not dispute about the first, but only about the second, since it was the vowel points that were being discussed. Now Vossius, following Morinus in the first part of his Exercitationes Biblicae, thought that before Rabbi Judah the Jews had no grammar, or only a very slight one. Against this grammar Vossius declaims, and calls it recent, a thing known for six hundred years. But Simonius contends that this grammar, together with the vowel points, was invented more than 900 years ago. Indeed Morinus himself retracted his opinion in the later part of his Exercitationes.

units.la: Contra autem illud quod scripsit Vossius, in Ægypto Syriaque tempore Apostolorum solam linguam Græcam fuisse vernaculam, excepserat Simonius, præter linguam GræGræcam in Ægypto auditam fuisse linguam Copticam, in Syria Syriacam, in Judæa Judaicam. At regerit Vossius, falli Simonium, cùm ne nomen Copticæ linguæ extiterit antequam Arabes potirentur Ægypto. Verùm pace doctissimi Vossii dixerim, eum non magis scire Copticè, quàm Ebraicè & Chaldaicè. De nomine non disputo, sed de re ipsa. Coptici sermonis nomine intelligo sermonem Ægyptiacum qui tunc apud Ægyptios vigebat praeter sermonem Græcum. De tempore autem quo Ægyptii appellati fuerint Copti, & eorum lingua Coptica, inutile est disputare, cùm id non faciat ad institutum. Dico autem sermonem Copticum sive Ægyptiacum fuisse in Ægypto antequam Arabes potirentur illis regionibus. Verùm, sicut sub Græcis Principibus Græcis vocibus auctus fuit; ita sub Arabibus Arabicis vocabulis adauctus fuit. Demum postquam lingua Arabica in Ægypto coepit esse vernacula, paulatim in desuetudinem abiit sermo ille Copticus sive Ægyptiacus, coactique sunt Copti libros suos Copticos in sermonem Arabicum convertere. Id palam testantur Biblia MSS. Copticè & Arabicè descripta. Simili ratione manuscriptæ Coptorum Liturgiæ sub duabus columnis exaratæ conspiciuntur Arabicè & Copticè. Quod autem subjicit Vossius, ex eo probari linguam Copticam non extitisse antequam Arabes potirentur Ægypto, quòd illa lingua ex Græco & Arabico sermone conflata sit, suti-lissimum est: simili enim ratione dixerim novitiam esse linguam Tur-cicam, quòd in ea multæ sint voces Arabicæ. Constat tamen linguam hanc veterem esse Scythicam, in quam postea multæ voces Arabicæ invectæ fuerunt. Quod etiam de lingua Persica dicendum est. Si quid concludat Vossius, concludat etiam nullam linguam fuisse Anglicam in Anglia antequam Normani Principes potirentur Angliâ, quia in sermone Anglico complures sunt voces Normanicæ.
units.tr: On the other hand, against what Vossius wrote, that in Egypt and Syria at the time of the Apostles Greek was the only vernacular language, Simonius had objected that, besides Greek, the Coptic language was heard in Egypt, Syriac in Syria, and Judaic in Judea. But Vossius replies that Simonius is mistaken, since the name of the Coptic language did not exist until the Arabs gained possession of Egypt. But with respect to the most learned Vossius, I would say that he knows no more Coptic than he knows Hebrew and Chaldee. I am not disputing about the name but about the thing itself. By the name of the Coptic tongue I understand the Egyptian speech which then flourished among the Egyptians, besides the Greek language. As for the time when the Egyptians were called Copts and their language Coptic, it is useless to dispute, since that has no bearing on the matter in hand. I maintain that the Coptic or Egyptian speech existed in Egypt before the Arabs gained possession of those regions. But just as under the Greek rulers it was enriched with Greek words, so under the Arabs it was enriched with Arabic vocables. At last, after Arabic began to be the vernacular in Egypt, that Coptic or Egyptian speech gradually fell into disuse, and the Copts were obliged to turn their Coptic books into Arabic. Manuscript Bibles written in Coptic and Arabic bear witness to this openly. In a similar way, manuscript Coptic liturgies are seen written in two columns, in Arabic and Coptic. But what Vossius adds, that it follows from this that the Coptic language did not exist before the Arabs gained possession of Egypt, because that language was compounded from Greek and Arabic, is most subtle nonsense; for by the same reasoning I might say that the Turkish language is recent, because it has many Arabic words in it. It is nevertheless established that this language is an old Scythian one, into which many Arabic words were later introduced. The same must be said of the Persian language. If Vossius concludes anything, let him also conclude that there was no English language in England before the Norman princes gained possession of England, because the English speech has many Norman words.

units.la: Verùm distortas conclusiunculas ita amat Vossius, ut vix aliæ in suis libris appareant. Sic eâdem ratione concludit novitiam esse Syriacam Veteris Instrumenti Versionem, quia Græcis scatet vocabulis; pariter Syriacam Novi Testamenti Translationem nuperam esse, quia in eo infimæ Latinitatis reperiuntur vocabula, quale est illud quod occurrit Matthæi Cap.27. verf.65. קסטונרא, quæstionarius. Qui facit omnia belle Vossius, bellus est quoque Criticus, quique eodem argumento conficiet Græcum Novi Testamenti Codicem novitium esse, quia multa etiam in eo reperiuntur Latina vocabula, inter quæ numerari potest illud quod infimæ Latinitatis esse pronuntiat: quippe in Syriaco legendum non est קסטונרא cum ד sive r; sed קסטונרא cum ד sive d: & est ipsa vox κουστώδια, quæ hoc ipso loco in Græco extat, sumpta ex Latina custodia. Norunt qui Syriacè legere sciunt, nihil prorsus esse discriminis inter ר & ד, sive r & d, nisi quòd ר puncto notetur desuper; idem verò punctum sit infra ד, illudque in MSS. Codicibus interdum abest. Ista autem punctorum confusio fusio in libris manu exaratis magnam quoque attulit sensuum confusionem in libris editis, cujus confusionis exempla innumera sunt in Bibliis Polyglottis, quæ primùm Parisiis edita, deinde Londini recoëta sunt. Ne autem objiciat Vossius, in voce Syriaca haberi literam ȝ sive n, quæ in Græca & Latina non extat, dico solenne esse Syris & Chaldæis literam istam suis vocabulis adjicere, illiusque additionis infinita esse exempla. Denique illud quod subjungit Vossius, Simonium quoque in eo falli, quòd Syriacam linguam Hierosolymis vernaculam fuisse dixerit, non expendo, quia plura de hoc postea se dicturum pollicetur Vossius, & ibi sententiam quoque illius de hoc argumento expendam. Nunc ad alia Voßii commenta, quæ his majora sunt, venio.
units.tr: But Vossius is so fond of twisted little inferences that scarcely any others appear in his books. By the same reasoning he concludes that the Syriac version of the Old Testament is recent, because it abounds in Greek words, and that the Syriac translation of the New Testament is recent, because it contains words of the lowest Latinity, such as the one in Matthew 27:65, קסטונרא [qastonra], quaestionarius. Vossius does everything beautifully, and he is also a fine critic. By the same argument he will prove that the Greek codex of the New Testament is recent, because many Latin words are found in it too, among which can be counted the one he pronounces to be of the lowest Latinity. For in the Syriac one must not read קסטונרא with ר (r) but with ד (d), and it is the word κουστώδια [koustōdia] itself, which stands in the Greek in this very place, taken from the Latin custodia. Those who know how to read Syriac know there is absolutely no difference between ר and ד, that is r and d, except that ר is marked with a point above; the same point sits below ד, and in manuscripts it is sometimes absent. This confusion of points in hand-written books has also brought great confusion of meaning into printed books, of which there are countless examples in the Polyglot Bibles, first published at Paris and then reprinted at London. Lest Vossius object that the Syriac word has the letter ȝ or n, which does not occur in Greek or Latin, I say it is customary for the Syrians and Chaldeans to add that letter to their words, and there are endless examples of such additions. Finally, I do not weigh what Vossius adds, that Simonius is also wrong in saying that Syriac was the vernacular language of Jerusalem, because Vossius promises to say more on this later, and there I will weigh his opinion on this question too. Now I come to the other inventions of Vossius, which are greater than these.

units.la: Dixerat Vossius, Judæorum δελτπρωσεων sive Traditiones ante Justiniani tempora sermone duntaxat Græco concinnatas fuisse, librumque Misnæ è Græco in Ebræum sermonem circa illud tempus conversum. Hanc opinionem ut portentosam riserat Simonius. Quid ad hæc Vossius? Caveat Simonius, ne intempestivo risu ipse fiat ridiculus. Sed tempestivum fuisse risum Simonii, adeoque ridiculum esse Vossium, manifestè ostendunt ea quæ iterum affert idem Vossius, ut sententiam suam defendat. Ille enim affirmat librum δευτερωσεων sive Traditionum, cujus mentionem facit Justinianus, sermone Græco conscriptum fuisse, quia tunc in Imperio Romano non alia erat lingua vernacula quàm Græca: & quia nunc longè oculatior factus est
units.tr: Vossius had said that the Jewish deuterōseis [δευτερώσεις], or Traditions, before the time of Justinian were composed in the Greek language alone, and that the book of the Mishnah was translated from Greek into the Hebrew language around that time. Simonius had laughed at this opinion as monstrous. What does Vossius say to this? Let Simonius take care lest by his ill-timed laughter he himself become ridiculous. But that Simonius's laughter was well-timed, and that Vossius is therefore ridiculous, is plainly shown by what the same Vossius brings forward again to defend his view.

units.la: Vossius, addit Aquilam primum fuisse Traditionum illarum compilatorem; δευτερωσιν esse secundam Aquilæ editionem, quæ non tantùm sacrorum librorum Versionem continuerit, sed & instructa fuerit Commentariis seu Annotationibus margini adscriptis, quas idem Aquila ex Judæorum Traditionibus compilaverat. Risum teneatis amici. Quot verba, tot ineptias effudit bonus Vossius.
units.tr: For he affirms that the book of deuterōseis [δευτερώσεων], or Traditions, of which Justinian makes mention, was written in Greek, because at that time there was no other vernacular language in the Roman Empire than Greek; and because he has now become much more keen-sighted, he adds that Aquila was first the compiler of those Traditions, and that deuterōsis is Aquila's second edition, which contained not only a version of the sacred books but was also furnished with commentaries or annotations written in the margin, which Aquila himself had compiled from the Jewish Traditions. Hold your laughter, friends. Good Vossius has poured out as many absurdities as he has words.

units.la: Et ut à nomine δευτερωσεων sumamus initium, sæpe illud occurrit in Patrum tum Græcorum tum Latinorum scriptis, à quibus non alio sensu usurpatur, quàm pro Judaicis Traditionibus. Sic Hieronymus in Epistola ad Abgasiam & alibi passim ait, Judæos suas Traditiones appellare δευτερωσεις. Similiter Augustinus & alii Patres observant Judæos hac voce suas Traditiones denotare. Idem quoque Patres, qui secundæ editionis Aquilæ mentionem fecerunt, nunquam illam δευτερωσιν appellant. Verùm ait Vossius, veterem Novellarum Interpretem δευτερωσιν rectè vertisse secundam editionem. At quid inde confici potest? An ideo secunda illa editio est secunda editio Versionis Aquilæ, quia δευτερωσιν vetus Novellarum Interpres reddidit secundam editionem? Misnam sive δευτερωσιν etiam hodie Judæi vocant secundam Legem, seu secundam Legis editionem, quòd illa, ipsis referentibus, sit Legis repetitio. Idcirco vetus Novellarum Interpres, qui verbum de verbo expressit, secundæ editionis nomine nihil aliud intelligit quàm secundam Legis Judaicæ editionem: sic enim etiam Judæi vocant suas Traditiones, quas non minùs à Deo profectas fuisse existimant, quàm ipsam Mosis Legem.
units.tr: And to begin with the name deuterōseis [δευτερώσεων], it often occurs in the writings of the Fathers, both Greek and Latin, who use it in no other sense than for the Jewish Traditions. Thus Jerome, in his letter to Abigaus and elsewhere throughout, says that the Jews call their Traditions deuterōseis [δευτερώσεις]. Likewise Augustine and the other Fathers observe that the Jews by this word denote their Traditions. The same Fathers, who mention the second edition of Aquila, never call it deuterōsis. But Vossius says that the old translator of the Novels rightly rendered deuterōsis as second edition. But what can be inferred from this? Is that second edition therefore the second edition of Aquila's version, because the old translator of the Novels rendered deuterōsis as second edition? Even today the Jews call the Mishnah, or deuterōsis, the Second Law, or second edition of the Law, because, as they themselves report, it is a repetition of the Law. Therefore the old translator of the Novels, who rendered word for word, understood by the name second edition nothing other than the second edition of the Jewish Law; for the Jews too call their Traditions by this name, and they consider them to have come from God no less than the Law of Moses itself.

units.la: Nunc ad rem ipsam veniamus. Fierine potuit ut Eusebius, Origenes, Hieronymus, aliique Patres qui utriusque Versionis Aquilæ sæpe mentionem fecerunt, ne verbum quidem dixerint de Commentariis illis Aquilæ, quos supponit Vossius illum secundæ editioni suæ adjecisse? Simili argumento utuntur plerique viri docti, imò & ipse Vossius, ut ostendant ante Origenis & Hieronymi tempora non extitisse Chaldaicam Onkelosi Paraphrasim; nec sanè invalidum est argumentum illud: sed longè validius est in præsenti materia, cùm agatur de libro qui Græco sermone tunc vernaculo scriptus fuerit: lingua autem Chaldæa perpaucis cognita fuit; cùm & ipse Hieronymus, qui Ebraicè sciebat, vix Chaldaicè sciverit.
units.tr: Now let us come to the matter itself. Could it be that Eusebius, Origen, Jerome and the other Fathers, who often mentioned both versions of Aquila, did not say a word about those commentaries of Aquila which Vossius supposes he added to his second edition? Most learned men use a similar argument, Vossius himself included, to show that the Chaldee paraphrase of Onkelos did not exist before the time of Origen and Jerome. Nor is that argument feeble; but in the present matter it is far stronger, since we are dealing with a book written in Greek, which was then the vernacular language, whereas the Chaldean language was known to very few, since even Jerome himself, who knew Hebrew, hardly knew Chaldean.

units.la: Quod verò ait Vossius, δΔιπρώσεις sive Traditiones ante Justinianum non alio sermone scribi potuisse quàm Græco, quia non alia erat lingua vernacula in toto Imperio Romano quàm Græca; illud non est ad rem, cùm ante illa tempora nullus esset Traditionum liber apud Judæos scriptus & editus, ut apertissimis verbis testatur Augustinus, qui ait, Judæos Traditiones suas non scriptas habere, sed eas memoriter tenere, alterumque in alterum loquendo illas transferre, quas δΔιπρώσεις vocant. Quare inutile est quod ibidem subjungit Vossius, Traditiones Hebraeas Hieronymi in Genesim & reliquos Scripturæ libros è Græco translatas fuisse sermone. Præterea suo etiam gladio hic seipsum jugulat bonus Vossius, qui ex eo quòd non alia in Imperio Romano audiretur lingua quàm Græca, concludit ante Justinianum Traditiones Judæorum Græcè scriptas fuisse. Si hæc ratio valeat, necesse fuit etiam Justiniani tempore illas scribi Græco sermone, cùm tunc lingua Græca fuerit vernacula. Tamen Vossius affirmat Judæorum Traditiones tunc temporis è Græco in Ebræum sermonem translatas fuisse. Sed ridiculus & ipse fiam qui tot ineptias Vossii refellam.
units.tr: As for Vossius's claim that the deuterōseis [δευτερώσεις], or Traditions, before Justinian could not be written in any language other than Greek, because Greek was the only vernacular language in the whole Roman Empire, that is beside the point, since before those times there was no book of Traditions written and published among the Jews, as Augustine testifies in the plainest words, saying: The Jews have their Traditions not written down, but hold them in memory, and pass them on to one another by speaking, which they call deuterōseis. Therefore what Vossius adds in the same place, that Jerome's Hebrew Traditions on Genesis and the other books of Scripture were translated from Greek into the language, is useless. Moreover, good Vossius here slits his own throat with his own sword, for from the fact that no language other than Greek was heard in the Roman Empire he concludes that the Traditions of the Jews were written in Greek before Justinian. If this reasoning holds, they must also have been written in Greek in Justinian's time, since Greek was then the vernacular language. Yet Vossius affirms that the Jewish Traditions were then translated from Greek into the Hebrew language. But I myself would become ridiculous if I went on refuting so many absurdities of Vossius.

units.la: Instat iterum Vossius, aitque Judæos, teste Epiphanio, δΔιπρώσεις sive Traditiones adscribere Rabbi Akibæ; Aquilam, teste Hieronymo, discipulum fuisse Akibæ; adeoque Aquilam collectorem esse Judaicarum Traditionum. Ad compescendum, inquit Vossius, Simonii hæc, ut puto, sufficient risum. Imò non dubito quin Simonius iterum risum effundat, cùm tam lepidum ratiocinatorem audiet. Quæsierim à Vossio, cur Epiphanius, qui Mosem, Akibam, alios- que Magistros profert à quibus Judæi Traditiones suas hauserint, Aquilam etiam inter illos non recensuerit, si verum est, ut existimat Vossius, illum eas Græco sermone compilasse & in publicum edidisse; maximè cùm Moses, Akiba & alii quorum mentionem fecit Epiphanius, Traditiones illas scriptis non evulgaverint?
units.tr: Vossius presses on again, and says that the Jews, as Epiphanius testifies, ascribe the deuterōseis [δευτερώσεις], or Traditions, to Rabbi Akiba; that Aquila, as Jerome testifies, was a disciple of Akiba; and therefore that Aquila was the collector of the Jewish Traditions. To check Simonius's laughter, says Vossius, these points, I think, will suffice. Indeed I do not doubt that Simonius will laugh again when he hears such a charming reasoner. I would ask Vossius why Epiphanius, who names Moses, Akiba and the other masters from whom the Jews drew their Traditions, did not also include Aquila among them, if it is true, as Vossius thinks, that he compiled them in Greek and published them, especially since Moses, Akiba and the others whom Epiphanius mentions did not publish those Traditions in writing?

units.la: Si quis autem aveat scire, cur illis temporibus cùm lingua Græca in toto Imperio Romano erat vernacula, Judæorum Magistri suas Traditiones Ebraicè scripserint, hæc accipiat. Judæi qui δΔιπρώσεις docuerunt, quique eas collegerunt, Ebraicè & Chaldaicè sciebant, ut & plerique Judæi etiam ætate Hieronymi, qui in Præfatione in Tobiam, quem ex Chaldaico Latinum fecit, hæc habet: Et quia vicina est Chaldæorum lingua sermoni Hebraico, utriusque linguæ peritissimum loquacem reperiens, unius dièi laborem arripui, & quidquid ille mihi Ebraicis verbis expressit, hoc ego & accito Notario sermonibus Latinis exposui. Si quid igitur Judæorum Magistri Traditionum suarum in adversaria retulerint, quod & eos fecisse verisimile est, scriptum fuit Ebraicè vel Chaldaicè; indeque ortum fuit ut Talmudis libri his linguis conscripti fuerint. Constat Doctores Tiberiadis ætate Hieronymi Ebraicè & Chaldaicè fuisse locutos: iidem quoque Magistri Tiberiadenses, qui postea Maforam compilarunt, usi sunt vocibus Chaldaicis.
units.tr: If anyone wishes to know why, at a time when Greek was the vernacular language in the whole Roman Empire, the masters of the Jews wrote their Traditions in Hebrew, let him take this. The Jews who taught the deuterōseis [δευτερώσεις], and who collected them, knew Hebrew and Chaldean, as did most Jews even in Jerome's time, who in his preface to Tobit, which he turned from Chaldean into Latin, has this: And because the Chaldean language is close to the Hebrew speech, finding a speaker most skilled in both languages, I undertook the work of a single day, and whatever he expressed to me in Hebrew words, I myself, with a notary summoned, set out in Latin. If therefore the masters of the Jewish Traditions noted anything in their notebooks, which it is also likely they did, it was written in Hebrew or Chaldean; and from this it arose that the books of the Talmud were written in these languages. It is established that the teachers of Tiberias, in Jerome's time, spoke in Hebrew and Chaldean; and those same masters of Tiberias, who later compiled the Masorah, used Chaldean words.

units.la: Expendit postea Vossius nonnulla Scripturæ loca, ex quibus ostenderat Simonius Hieronymum aliquando bene, aliquando malè LXX. reprehendisse Interpretes: at Vossius, qui putat illos etiam Prophetas fuisse, eosdem facit ab omni errore immunes. Verùm quàm feliciter illud Vossio successerit, quia paratus est Simonius demonstrare in libro quem editurus est, in quo Codices Ebraicos & Hieronymi Tralationem defendit, non est cur loca ista expendam, maximè cùm Simonius etiam interdum castigaverit Hieronymum, qui non Propheta, sed Interpres fuerit. Dixerim tantùm hoc loco, Interpretem quemlibet, etiam Aquilam, quem omnium Interpretum futilissimum esse Vossius existimat, eadem arte eademque facilitate defendi posse, quâ ipse LXX. tuetur Interpretes.
units.tr: Vossius afterwards examined several passages of Scripture, from which Simonius had shown that Jerome sometimes rightly and sometimes wrongly criticised the Seventy translators. But Vossius, who thinks that they were also prophets, makes them free from every error. How successful Vossius has been in this will not be considered here, since Simonius is ready to demonstrate it in the book he is about to publish, in which he defends the Hebrew manuscripts and Jerome's translation. I see no reason to examine those passages, especially since Simonius also at times corrects Jerome, who was an interpreter, not a prophet. I will only say here that any interpreter, even Aquila, whom Vossius judges the most worthless of all interpreters, could be defended by the same method and with the same ease by which Vossius defends the Seventy translators.

units.la: Objecerat præterea Simonius, Hieronymum longè aliter de lingua LXX. Interpretum sensisse, quàm ipse sentiat Vossius, qui Græcam illam prorsus esse affirmat, putatque ex verbis Hieronymi scribentis Gioram, quod habent LXX. Interpretes, Ebraicum esse, non Græcum, concludi non posse Versionem hanc Græcam non esse, cùm Euangelia, in quibus complura verba Ebræa occurrunt, non ideo desinunt esse Græca. Verùm, ut & ipse Vossius judicet quàm bene hac in parte cum Hieronymo consentiat, placet doctissimi illius Patris verba afferre ex illius Commentariis in Epistolam ad Galatas. Verbum ἀποκαλύψεως, id est, revelationis, proprie Scripturarum est, & à nullo sapientium seculi apud Græcos usurpatum. Unde mihi videntur, quemadmodum in aliis verbis quæ de Ebraeo in Græcum LXX. Interpretes transtulerunt, ita & in hoc magnopere esse conatos, ut proprietatem peregrini sermonis exprimerent nova novis rebus verba fingentes. Hæc clara & manifesta sunt, mentemque Simonii de lingua Græca LXX. Interpretum & Novi Testamenti aperte confirmant.
units.tr: Simonius had further objected that Jerome thought quite differently about the language of the Seventy translators than Vossius does. Vossius asserts that their version is entirely Greek, and he thinks that from Jerome's words, in which he writes that the Seventy have "Gioram," which is a Hebrew word, it cannot be concluded that this version is not Greek, since the Gospels, in which many Hebrew words occur, do not therefore cease to be Greek. But so that Vossius himself may judge how well Jerome agrees with him on this point, it is pleasing to cite the words of that most learned Father from his Commentaries on the Epistle to the Galatians: "The word ἀποκαλύψεως [apokalypseōs], that is, revelation, belongs properly to the Scriptures and was used by none of the wise men of the Greeks of this age. Hence it seems to me that, just as the Seventy translators in other words which they rendered from Hebrew into Greek, so in this word too they laboured greatly to express the peculiarity of a foreign speech, coining new words for new things." These statements are clear and plain, and they openly confirm Simonius's view of the Greek language of the Seventy translators and of the New Testament.

units.la: Similiter eludit Vossius Josephi testimonium, qui etiam, referente Hieronymo, testatur LXX. Interpretes solos quinque libros Mosis Græcè reddidisse. Ait nusquam hoc Josephum affirmasse, sed eos dixisse Legem tantùm vertisse, quo nomine tota Ebraica Scriptura intelligi debeat. Noverat Simonius ambiguum esse Legis nomen, nec solùm quinque libros Mosis denotare, sed & interdum universam Scripturam. Verùm ex illa ambiguitate nunquam efficiet Vossius cum Morino suo, Josephum de solis quinque libris Mosis locutum fuisse. Neque aliter de hoc argumento sentiebant prisci Judæi, quàm ipse Hieronymus.
units.tr: Vossius similarly evades the testimony of Josephus, who also, as Jerome reports, bears witness that the Seventy translated only the five books of Moses into Greek. He says that Josephus never asserted this, but only that they had translated the Law, by which name the whole Hebrew Scripture ought to be understood. Simonius knew that the name "Law" is ambiguous and denotes not only the five books of Moses but sometimes the whole of Scripture. But Vossius, with his Morinus, will never prove from that ambiguity that Josephus spoke of the five books of Moses alone. Nor did the ancient Jews think about this question differently from Jerome himself.

units.la: Negat dein Vossius, se unquam scripsisse in libris obscurioribus, veluti Jobi & Proverbiorum, LXX. Interpretes magis accuratos se ostendere; cùm sciat illos ubique optimorum Interpretum bene functos esse munere. Verùm non aliud Vossio tribuit Simonius, quàm quod ipse Vossius scripsit, nimirum hodiernos Interpretes meras promere ineptias, præsertim in obscurioribus Scripturæ libris, integraque se posse ex illis libris adducere capita, in quibus ne unicus quidem occurrit versiculus qui ab illis Interpretibus intellectus fuerit; ac demum concludit Vossius, ubicunque deseruntur LXX. Interpretes, ipsam quoque ibi deseri veritatem. Ista sunt quæ voluit refellere Simonius, & in Disquisitionibus Criticis post illa verba, magis accuratos se ostendunt, legendum est, quàm novi Interpretes; quæ verba omissa sunt. Falli itaque putat Simonius Vossium, qui scribit in libris Jobi, Ecclesiastæ, Oseæ ac similibus, LXX. Interpretes accuratiores esse novis Interpretibus; cùm illi sæpe in his libris non solùm à vocibus, sed & à sensu recesserint, ut omnibus qui Græcè & Ebraicè sciunt, statim erit obvium. Placet hîc unum è sexcentis locum proferre etiam in re minimè obscura. Proverbiorum Capite 6: 16. in Ebraicis Codicibus, quos sequuntur Hieronymus, Syrus Interpres & Chaldæus, legimus sex esse, imò septem quæ odit Deus. Ibidem sep-
units.tr: Vossius next denies that he has ever written, in the more obscure books such as Job and Proverbs, that the Seventy translators show themselves to be more accurate. Yet he knows that they everywhere acquitted themselves well in the office of the best interpreters. But Simonius attributes nothing to Vossius except what Vossius himself wrote, namely that present-day translators put forward mere absurdities, especially in the more obscure books of Scripture, and that from those books one can cite whole chapters in which not even a single verse occurs that those translators understood. Finally Vossius concludes that wherever the Seventy translators are abandoned, truth too is abandoned there. These are the points Simonius wished to refute. In the Critical Disquisitions, after the words "they show themselves more accurate," one should read "than the recent interpreters," which words have been omitted. Simonius therefore thinks that Vossius is mistaken when he writes that in Job, Ecclesiastes, Hosea and similar books the Seventy translators are more accurate than the recent interpreters; for they often departed in these books not only from the words but also from the sense, as will be obvious at once to all who know Greek and Hebrew. Let me cite here one of the six hundred examples, even in a matter that is by no means obscure. In Proverbs chapter 6, verse 16, in the Hebrew manuscripts which Jerome, the Syriac translator and the Chaldee follow, we read that there are six, indeed seven, things that God hates. In the same place

units.la: tem illa quæ Deus odit, enumerantur, quæ Codicis Ebraici lectionem apertè confirmant. In LXX. Interpretibus neque sex neque septem legitur; idque ex eo ortum est, quòd in suis Codicibus Ebraicis aliter legerint. Ratio autem contextûs & ea quæ consequuntur, hodiernam lectionem præferendam esse docent manifestè.
units.tr: the seven things that God hates are listed, which clearly confirms the reading of the Hebrew manuscript. In the Seventy translators neither "six" nor "seven" is read, and this arose from the fact that in their Hebrew manuscripts they read differently. The context and what follows show plainly that the present reading is to be preferred.

units.la: Quæ autem eodem loco addit Vossius adversus Hieronymum, de Rodanim, nihil omnino ad rem faciunt; cùm etiam annotatum fuerit à Simonio in hoc peccasse Hieronymum. Hæc enim sunt verba Simonii in hunc locum. Non is tamen sum qui ab Hieronymo ita pendere velim, ut etiam illius errores, qui sanè plurimi sunt, approbem. Quare longè satius fuisset etiam cum Simonio agnoscere in multis quoque errasse LXX. Interpretes, errorumque causas cum ipso aperire. Verùm LXX. Seniores ipsi Vossio sunt Prophetæ, adeoque necesse est eos ab omni errore immunes fuisse. Noverat Simonius etiam ætate nostrâ non deesse Theologos, qui Hieronymum quoque inter Prophetas collocent, quique doctissimi illius Patris errores tueantur: sed illos, quia non saniori judicio videntur quàm ipse Vossius, deseruit, judicavitque secundùm Criticæ regulas expendenda esse ea omnia quæ in LXX. Interpretibus carpit Hieronymus tanquam minùs bene translata, maximè cùm in pluribus veniâ dignus sit idem Hieronymus, qui testetur fieri non posse quin peccaverit in multis, fateaturque se nonnulla distandi celeritate, dum parùm attendit, non bene vertisse. Similiter quis negaverit, LXX. etiam Interpretibus, tibus, quia homines erant, multa excidisse. In eo verò quod ibidem subjicit Vossius, perire Prophetiam, si Agag legamus, ineptum se ostendit Criticum: ut enim de sensu hujus loci nihil dicam, certum est addi potuisse huic nomini literam ℵ, Aleph, quæ nihil sensûs mutet. Sic hoc loco Interpres Arabs Samarita, qui in Codice Samaritico & in Versione Samaritica legit Gog, non dubitavit in Versione sua Arabica reponere Agog.
units.tr: As for what Vossius adds in the same place against Jerome concerning the Rodanim, these points have nothing at all to do with the matter, since it has also been noted by Simonius that Jerome erred in this. For these are Simonius's words on this passage: "I am not, however, one who would wish to depend so much on Jerome that I would also approve his errors, which are certainly very many." Therefore it would have been far better to acknowledge with Simonius that the Seventy translators also erred in many things, and to disclose with him the causes of their errors. But the Seventy elders are prophets for Vossius, and so it is necessary that they were free from every error. Simonius knew that even in our own age there are no lack of theologians who count Jerome too among the prophets, and who defend the errors of that most learned Father. But he left these men aside, because they seem to have no sounder judgement than Vossius himself, and he judged that all the things which Jerome criticises in the Seventy translators as less well translated must be weighed according to the rules of criticism, especially since Jerome deserves pardon in many cases, since he himself testifies that it cannot be that he has not erred in many things, and confesses that in some places, while he was rushing and paid little attention, he did not translate well. Likewise, who would deny that many things also slipped out of the Seventy translators, since they were men? As for what Vossius adds in the same place, that prophecy would perish if we read "Agag," he shows himself to be an incompetent critic. For, to say nothing of the sense of this passage, it is certain that the letter Aleph could have been added to this name, which would change nothing in the meaning. So in this place the Arab interpreter of the Samaritans, who in the Samaritan manuscript and in the Samaritan version reads "Gog," did not hesitate to put "Agog" in his Arabic version.

units.la: Jam ad Caput XVIII. Criticarum Disquisitionum transit Vossius, in quo manifesti illius errores circa Origenis Hexapla castigati fuerant: cùmque nihil solidi habeat quod respondeat Simonii objectionibus, caninam promit eloquentiam, verbisque pugnat, non rationibus. Ait monitum à se fuisse Simonium ut caveret ab Epiphanio sibi ipsi contradicente, & ab aliis qui eum secuti fuerant. Verùm Simonius longè satius esse existimavit Epiphanio testi oculato credere, qui Tetrapla & Hexapla vidit, quàm Vossio somnianti. Falsum quoque est hac in re sibi contradixisse Epiphanium. Quia verò totus ab aliis pendet Vossius, qui ne quidem à limine Patres salutavit, Simonium ad Henrici Valesii annotata relegat. Sed non ignoravit Simonius quid ea de re à doctissimo Valesio scriptum fuerit, qui à Vossii sententia alienus est: probat enim Epiphanii & Ruffini testimoniis, in prima columna verba Ebraea Ebraicis literis posita fuisse, & in secunda columna eadem verba Ebraea Græcis literis fuisse descripta.
units.tr: Now Vossius passes to chapter 18 of the Critical Disquisitions, in which his manifest errors concerning Origen's Hexapla were rebuked. Since he has nothing solid with which to answer Simonius's objections, he brings out a snarling eloquence and fights with words, not reasons. He says that Simonius had been warned by him to beware of Epiphanius, who contradicted himself, and of others who had followed him. But Simonius thought it far better to believe Epiphanius, an eyewitness who saw the Tetrapla and the Hexapla, than Vossius, who is dreaming. It is also false that Epiphanius contradicted himself in this matter. But since Vossius depends entirely on others, and does not even greet the Fathers from the threshold, he refers Simonius to the notes of Henri de Valois. But Simonius was not unaware of what the most learned Valesius wrote on this matter, and Valesius is far from Vossius's opinion. For he proves, by the testimonies of Epiphanius and Rufinus, that in the first column the Hebrew words were written in Hebrew letters, and in the second column the same Hebrew words were written in Greek letters.

units.la: Negaverat Simonius, Origenem unquam cogitasse de Codice Samaritarum suis Hexaplis inserendo, idque firmissimis rationibus probaverat. Quid ad istas Vossius? Nihil præter voces, phrases phrasibusque accumulans dat quidem sonum, sed sine mente. Si quis, inquit, causam quærat quamobrem pulchra istiusmodi nugamenta commentus fuerit P. Simonius, nullam profectò aliam invenies, nisi ut excluso Samaritico sua concinnaret Octapla. Sed cur ineptiens Vossius inutiliter aërem diverberat? Respondeat Simonii rationibus quibus Octapla adstruxit. Pollicitus fuerat ipse Vossius, novam & hactenus inauditam Hexaplorum Origenis dispositionem se demonstraturum: cur igitur promissa sua non exsolvit? Similiter ante annos viginti pollicitus quoque fuit se instaurarurum aliquando Versionem LXX. Interpretum, in quam, adulterinis separatis, veterem & genuinam reducet scripturam: sed prius veniet Elias Talmudicus, quàm promissa sua exsolvat bellus iste LXX. Interpretum Versionis restitutor.
units.tr: Simonius had denied that Origen ever thought of inserting the Samaritan manuscript into his Hexapla, and he had proved this by the firmest reasons. What does Vossius reply to these? Nothing, but heaping up words and phrases on phrases, he indeed makes a sound, but without mind. "If anyone asks," he says, "why Father Simonius devised such pretty trifles, you will certainly find no other reason than that, with the Samaritan excluded, he might arrange his own Octapla." But why does Vossius, playing the fool, beat the air to no purpose? Let him answer the reasons by which Simonius established the Octapla. Vossius himself had promised that he would demonstrate a new and hitherto unheard-of arrangement of Origen's Hexapla: why then has he not fulfilled his promise? Similarly, twenty years ago he also promised that he would some day restore the version of the Seventy translators, in which, by separating the spurious matter, he would bring back the old and genuine text. But Elias the Talmudist will come before this fine restorer of the version of the Seventy translators fulfils his promise.

units.la: Instat, aitque clara esse Eusebii verba, cùm dicit Origenem sibi comparasse ea Ebraica Exemplaria quæ prototypis Ebræorum descripta essent literis, id est, referente Vossio, Samariticis. Clara quidem sunt & manifesta Eusebii verba: sed quia aperte destruunt commentitia Vossii Hexapla, juvat illa proferre ut exstant in Eusebii editionibus. De Origene sic loquitur Eusebius. Τοσαύτη ἡ εἰσήγελο τῷ Ωριγένει τ' Ἑβραίων λόγων ἀπηκριβωμένη ἐξήγησις, ὡς καὶ τ' Ἑξαπλῶν γλῶτταν ἐκμαθεῖν τὰς τε
units.tr: He insists, and says that Eusebius's words are clear, when he says that Origen obtained for himself those Hebrew copies which had been written out in the letters of the prototypes of the Hebrews, that is, according to Vossius, the Samaritan letters. The words of Eusebius are indeed clear and manifest, but because they openly overthrow Vossius's invented Hexapla, it is worth quoting them as they stand in the editions of Eusebius. Eusebius speaks thus of Origen: "So great was the exact explanation of Hebrew words that Origen brought in, that he learned even the language of the Hexapla, and made his own the Scriptures that were in circulation among the Jews, written in the very primitive Hebrew letters" [Τοσαύτη ἡ εἰσήγησις τῷ Ὠριγένει τῶν Ἑβραίων λόγων ἀπηκριβωμένη ἐξήγησις, ὡς καὶ τῶν Ἑξαπλῶν γλῶτταν ἐκμαθεῖν τάς τε].

units.la: ΘΔ πρὸς τοὺς Ἰουδαίους ἐμφερομένας πεσολυτικοῖς αὐτοῖς Ἑβραϊκοῖς στοιχείοις χρᾶφας κλῆμα ἴδιον ποιησαμένης. Tantum cura ac diligentia in divinorum librorum accurata inquisitione adhibuit Origenes, ut Ebraicam etiam linguam didicerit, & prototypas quae apud Judaeos erant Ebraicis literis Scripturas sibi comparaverit. Ista Eusebii verba luce meridiana clariora sunt, atque manifeste ostendunt Origenem in concinnandis suis Hexaplis vel Octaplis, non aliis usum fuisse Codicibus Ebraicis, quam illis qui tunc circumferebantur apud Judaeos. Verum qui nova facit omnia Vossius, qui novum fecit Aquilam & nova Hexapla, novum jam fingit Eusebium, & sine ullo Codicis manu exarati auctoritate sic legenda esse Eusebii verba existimat: Τὰς τε πρὸς τοὺς Ἰουδαίους ἐμφερομένας πεσολυτικοῖς αὐτοῖς Ἑβραϊκοῖς στοιχείοις χρᾶφας κλῆμα ἴδιον ποιησαμένης, quasi sensus sit Origenem illas sibi comparavisse Scripturas quae prototypis Ebraeorum literis essent exaratae. Prototyparum autem literarum nomine apud Eusebium Samariticos characteres intelligit Vossius. Sed nugas profecto agit, qui ex praesumpta suspicione, ac sine ulla Codicis MSS. autoritate receptam lectionem mutare audeat contra ipsius Eusebii mentem. Non animadvertit Vossius, Eusebium manifeste loqui de characteribus Ebraeis quibus tunc uterentur Judaei: quippe dixit πρὸς τοὺς Ἰουδαίους; minime vero πρὸς τοὺς Σαμαρείτας. Sic idem Eusebius in Chronico, ubi Judaeorum Exemplaria distinguit a Samariticis, vocat Judaicum Exemplar τὸ πρὸς Ἰουδαίους Ἑβραϊκόν,
units.tr: "...which were circulating among the Jews, written in the very primitive Hebrew letters [πρὸς τοὺς Ἰουδαίους ἐμφερομένας πρωτοτύποις αὐτοῖς Ἑβραϊκοῖς στοιχείοις γραφὰς κτῆμα ἴδιον ποιησαμένης]. So much care and diligence did Origen bring to the accurate investigation of the divine books that he learned the Hebrew language and acquired for himself the Scriptures in Hebrew characters, the originals that were among the Jews. These words of Eusebius are clearer than the noonday sun, and they plainly show that Origen, in putting together his Hexapla or Octapla, used no Hebrew manuscripts other than those then circulating among the Jews. But Vossius, who makes everything new, who made a new Aquila and a new Hexapla, now also invents a new Eusebius, and, without any authority of a manuscript, judges that the words of Eusebius should be read thus: "which were circulating among the Jews, written in the very primitive Hebrew letters," as if the meaning were that Origen obtained for himself those Scriptures which were written in the letters of the Hebrew originals. By the primitive letters Vossius understands, in Eusebius, the Samaritan characters. But he is certainly talking nonsense, since on the strength of a presumed suspicion, and without any authority of a manuscript, he dares to change the accepted reading against the very mind of Eusebius. Vossius does not notice that Eusebius clearly speaks of the Hebrew characters then used by the Jews, since he wrote "to the Jews" and not at all "to the Samaritans."

units.la: Euseb. in Chron.
units.tr: Eusebius, in the Chronicle.

units.la: quod apud Judaeos est Ebraicum; Samaritícum vero τὸ πρὸς Σαμαρείτας Ἑβραϊκόν, quod apud Samaritas est Ebraicum. Nemo itaque sano praeditus judicio existimaverit Eusebium his verbis πρὸς Ἰουδαίους, Ebraicos Samaritarum Codices denotare voluisse.
units.tr: Thus the same Eusebius, in the Chronicle, where he distinguishes the Jewish copies from the Samaritan, calls the Jewish copy "the Hebrew one belonging to the Jews" [τὸ πρὸς Ἰουδαίους Ἑβραϊκόν], which among the Jews is Hebrew; but the Samaritan copy "the Hebrew one belonging to the Samaritans" [τὸ πρὸς Σαμαρείτας Ἑβραϊκόν], which among the Samaritans is Hebrew. No one of sound judgment, therefore, will think that Eusebius, by the words "to the Jews," meant to designate the Hebrew manuscripts of the Samaritans.

units.la: Pergit dein Vossius verbis pugnare, non rationibus. Adeone, inquit, ineptus fuit Eusebius, ut postquam dixit Ebraam quoque linguam addidicisse Origenem, tanquam rem magnam addat illum quoque Hebraeum sibi comparasse Exemplar ubique inter Judaeos obvium? Non ineptus sane fuit Eusebius; sed ipse ineptus est Vossius, qui clara Eusebii verba conatur obscurare. Affirmat Eusebius, Origenem non solum a Judaeorum Magistris linguam Ebraeam addidicisse; sed etiam Ebraicum illorum Exemplar sibi comparasse, ut illud suis Hexaplis insereret. Quae verba luce meridiana clariora sunt. Tunc prisci Ecclesiae Patres Graecam Aquilae Interpretationem, quam ille verbum de verbo reddens accuratius ex Ebraicis fontibus expresserat, Ebraeum Codicem appellabant. Deinde, quando haec scripsit Eusebius, attendebat etiam ad Ebraica Exemplaria, quae tunc a plerisque Ebraice nescientibus Graecis literis expressa legebantur.
units.tr: Vossius then goes on to fight with words, not with arguments. "Was Eusebius," he says, "so foolish that, after saying that Origen had also learned the Hebrew language, he adds, as if it were a great thing, that Origen also obtained for himself a Hebrew copy found everywhere among the Jews?" Eusebius was certainly not foolish; but Vossius is foolish himself, since he tries to obscure the clear words of Eusebius. Eusebius affirms that Origen did not only learn the Hebrew language from the teachers of the Jews, but also obtained for himself their Hebrew copy, in order to insert it into his Hexapla. These words are clearer than the noonday sun. In those days the early Fathers of the Church called the Greek translation of Aquila, which he, translating word for word, had rendered more exactly from Hebrew sources, the Hebrew copy. Then, when Eusebius wrote these things, he also paid attention to the Hebrew copies, which were then read by most people ignorant of Hebrew, written out in Greek letters.

units.la: Iterum Simonio Vossius objicit, illum de Origene contraria dixisse, quasi Origenes de Ebraico Samaritarum Codice nunquam cogitaverit, qui tamen illi non fuerit ignotus. Sed imponit Vossius Simonio, qui fatetur quidem Ebraicum Samaritarum Codicem non ignotum fuisse OriOrigeni; sed addit, de illo suis Hexaplis inserendo ne per somnium quidem unquam Origenem cogitasse: cujus rei fidem faciunt jam allata Eusebii verba. Præterea Origenes Judæos habuit præceptores, non verò Samaritas; idemque Origenes de Judæis præceptoribus suis, à quibus linguam Ebræam & alia multa didicerit, interdum loquitur, nusquam verò de Samaritis. Quare ea omnia quæ ibidem subjungit Vossius de Affricano & de prototypis Samaritocis literis, vana sunt, neque quidquam ex ipsis conficiet Vossius, nisi novum etiam cudat Affricanum. Per me licet ut Affricanus fuerit vir linguæ Syriacæ, Chaldaicæ & Arabicæ peritissimus: inde tamen nihil consequitur quòd Vossii commentum de prototypis literis & Codice Samaritico Hexaplis Origenis inserto stabiliat.
units.tr: Again Vossius objects to Simonius that he said contrary things about Origen, as if Origen had never thought of the Hebrew copy of the Samaritans, which nevertheless was not unknown to him. But Vossius puts words into Simonius's mouth. Simonius does indeed admit that the Hebrew copy of the Samaritans was not unknown to Origen; but he adds that Origen never even dreamed of inserting it into his Hexapla, and the words of Eusebius already quoted make this certain. Moreover, Origen had Jews as his teachers, not Samaritans, and the same Origen sometimes speaks of his Jewish teachers, from whom he learned Hebrew and many other things, but nowhere of Samaritans. Therefore all the things that Vossius adds there about Africanus and the Samaritan characters are empty, and Vossius will prove nothing by them unless he also invents a new Africanus. Let it be granted that Africanus was a man most skilled in the Syriac, Chaldee and Arabic languages; nothing follows from this, however, that would establish Vossius's fiction about the primitive letters and a Samaritan copy inserted by Origen into his Hexapla.

units.la: Affricanum, Origenem, aliosque Patres nomine Codicis Samaritici, è quo nonnulla in suos libros transtulerunt, intellexisse Græcam Ebræi Samaritarum Exemplaris Translationem, affirmavit Simonius: sed quia Versionem hanc Græcam Samaritarum non agnoscit Vossius, negat pariter Patres illam consuluisse, putatque Affricanum & Origenem legisse ipsummet Codicem Ebraicum Samariticiis literis exaratum. Verùm ipsemet Origenes, qui Ebraicè doctus fuit, si quando de Samaritarum literis loquatur, non ex illorum libris, sed ex ipsismet Judæis quærit testimonia. Sic Cap. 9. Ezech. versf.4. ubi in Græcis Codicibus legitur σημεῖον, & in Ebraicis וֹ, observat se didicisse à quodam Ebræo, sed qui Christianus factus fuerat, in antiquis characteribus literam Thau cruci similem esse. De Samaritics literis loqui Origenem, quas τὰ ἀρχαῖα στοιχεῖα appellat, nemo negat. Qui igitur fieri potuit ut dilectus ille Affricani filius (sic Origenem Vossius appellat) ab homine Ebræo didicerit quæ esset literæ Thau apud Samaritas figura, si illorum Codices Samariticiis literis descriptos habuerit?
units.tr: Simonius asserted that Africanus, Origen and other Fathers, under the name of the Samaritan copy, from which they transferred some things into their books, understood the Greek translation of the Hebrew Samaritan copy. But because Vossius does not recognise this Greek version of the Samaritans, he likewise denies that the Fathers consulted it, and thinks that Africanus and Origen read the Hebrew manuscript itself written in Samaritan letters. Yet Origen himself, who was learned in Hebrew, when he speaks of the Samaritan letters, does not seek testimonies from their books, but from the Jews themselves. So, on Ezekiel 9:4, where in the Greek manuscripts one reads σημεῖον, and in the Hebrew תָּו, he observes that he learned from a certain Hebrew, who had become a Christian, that in the ancient characters the letter Thau is like a cross. That Origen, who calls them "the ancient letters" [τὰ ἀρχαῖα στοιχεῖα], speaks of the Samaritan letters, no one denies. How, then, could that beloved son of Africanus (so Vossius calls Origen) have learned from a Hebrew man what the form of the letter Thau was among the Samaritans, if he had their codices written in Samaritan letters?

units.la: Iterum Vossius imponit Simonio, quasi scripserit miserè hallucinatum esse Justinum Martyrem, qui Versionem Græcam Aquilæ crediderit ipsum esse Ebraicum Exemplar. Verùm hæc sunt Simonii verba: Justinus Martyr disputans contra Tryphonem Judæum, Græcam Aquilæ Interpretationem donat nomine Contextûs Ebraï; additque Simonius, Vossium ad hoc & ad alia ejusdem rationis plurima non attendisse: quomodo enim ad ista attendere potuisset bonus Vossius, qui in referendis Patrum testimoniis summam præ se fert inscitiam. Jam non solùm Justinus, sed & alii Patres Versionem Græcam Aquilæ donant nomine Codicis Ebraici; Judæique ipsi prisci illis Ecclesiæ temporibus qui Græcas noverant literas, non aliter loqui solebant in suis disputationibus cum Christianis. Quippe his objicientibus LXX. Interpretum verba, sæpius respondebant aliter esse in Ebræo, id est, secundùm illos, in Græca Versione Aquilæ. Videat igitur Vossius, quàm inepte his verbis sibi applauserit, Nos scimus non Justinum, sed Simonium miserè hallucinari, & non intellexisse verba hujus Martyris. Hallucinacinatum fuisse Justinum hac in re nunquam scripsit Simonius; sed Vossium Justini Martyris verba non legisse, adeoque mirum non esse si tam foede erraverit.
units.tr: Again Vossius charges Simonius with saying that Justin Martyr was wretchedly mistaken, because he believed the Greek version of Aquila to be the Hebrew original itself. But these are Simonius's words: Justin Martyr, disputing against the Jew Trypho, gives the Greek translation of Aquila the name of the Hebrew text; and Simonius adds that Vossius did not pay attention to this and to many other things of the same kind. For how could good Vossius have paid attention to them, when in citing the testimonies of the Fathers he displays the greatest ignorance? Now not only Justin but also other Fathers give the Greek version of Aquila the name of the Hebrew copy; and the Jews themselves in those early times of the Church, who knew Greek letters, were accustomed to speak in no other way in their disputations with Christians. Indeed, when the Christians objected the words of the Seventy translators, they often replied that it was different in the Hebrew, that is, according to them, in the Greek version of Aquila. Let Vossius see, then, how foolishly he has applauded himself with these words: We know that it is not Justin but Simonius who is wretchedly mistaken, and that he has not understood the words of this martyr. Simonius never wrote that Justin was mistaken in this matter; rather, Vossius did not read the words of Justin Martyr, and so it is no wonder if he erred so grossly.

units.la: Nunc ad solitas relabitur ineptias Vossius, scribitque Simonium ista omnia commentum fuisse, ut evinceret Hexapla non à sex appellata fuisse Versionibus; sed ea vere fuisse Octapla, & sic dicta fuisse ab octo columnis. Nihil hac in re commentus est Simonius, qui Eusebium, Epiphanium ac Ruffinum oculatos testes secutus fuerit: sed ipse potius nova commentus est Hexapla Vossius, quae Samariticum etiam Exemplar continerent. Quod vero Hexapla à sex columnellis sic dicta fuisse existimet Simonius, non illud commentus est; sed à Ruffino teste oculato accepit, qui scribit Origenem in propriis paginis sive columnellis editiones singulas descripsisse. Jam cum fuerint in illis Origenis Exemplaribus octo columnae sive paginae, ex his columnis sive paginis sua Octapla rectè confecit Simonius.
units.tr: Now Vossius slides back into his usual silliness, and writes that all of this was Simonius's invention, in order to prove that the Hexapla were not so called from six versions, but were truly an Octapla, and so named from eight columns. Simonius invented nothing in this matter, since he followed Eusebius, Epiphanius and Rufinus as eyewitnesses; rather, Vossius himself has invented a new Hexapla, which would also contain a Samaritan copy. But as for Simonius's view that the Hexapla were so called from six small columns, he did not invent that; he received it from Rufinus, an eyewitness, who writes that Origen described the separate editions in their own pages or small columns. Now since those copies of Origen had eight columns or pages, Simonius rightly made his Octapla from these columns or pages.

units.la: De eo autem quod ait Vossius, Simonium semper paginas illas vocare columnellas, non columellas, sileo; quia utrumque Latinum est, neque judicavit hac in re castigandum esse Ruffinum qui columnellas dixit, vel, ut quibusdam placet, columnulas. Sed cum difertulum Vossium deficiant rationes, de verbis disputat. Supponamus etiam cum Vossio, Hexapla sic dicta fuisse à Versionibus, non à columnis; quid inde concludet adversus Simonii Octapla, si constet Codicem Ebraeum literis Ebraicis in prima columna, & eumdem Graecis literis in secunda columna expressum fuisse? quae duae columnae, si Hexaplis sive sex Versionibus addantur, haud dubie Octapla efficient. Sive igitur Hexapla à sex Versionibus, sive à sex columnis sic dicta fuerint, perinde est; quia Versio quaelibet columnam unam occupabat. Praeterea Codex Ebraeus tanquam ἐβραϊκὸν seu fundamentum, Ebraicis & Graecis literis descriptus in duabus columnis continebatur, fateturque ipse Vossius, Origenem priores columnas appellasse τὸ Ἑβραϊκὸν ἑξάπλων, tanquam fundamentum omnium Versionum. Itaque necesse est Vossium etiam invitum recipere Petavii Jesuitae doctissimi schemata, in quibus Tetraplorum, Hexaplorum & Octaplorum dispositionem rectè exhibuit. Etsi enim Ebraeus Codex Ebraicis & Graecis literis expressus non venerit in censum Versionum, venit tamen in censum editionum, quas in propriis paginis sive columnellis descriptas fuisse affirmat Ruffinus; quae cum octo fuerint, ex his necessario Octapla confecta sunt.
units.tr: As for Vossius's claim that Simonius always calls those pages "columnellae" rather than "columellae," I say nothing, since both forms are good Latin, and Simonius did not think Ruffinus, who wrote "columnellae" (or, as some prefer, "columnulae"), needed correcting on this point. But Vossius, lacking reasons, quarrels over words. Let us grant with Vossius that the Hexapla was so called from the versions and not from the columns. What would follow against Simonius's Octapla, if it is established that the Hebrew text was written in Hebrew letters in the first column and in Greek letters in the second? If those two columns are added to the six versions, they undoubtedly make eight, the Octapla. So whether the Hexapla was named from its six versions or from its six columns makes no difference, since each version occupied one column. Moreover, the Hebrew codex, as the foundation [τὸ Ἑβραϊκὸν], written in Hebrew and Greek letters, was contained in two columns, and Vossius himself admits that Origen called the first columns "the Hebrew of the Hexapla" [τὸ Ἑβραϊκὸν ἑξάπλων], as the foundation of all the versions. It is therefore necessary that Vossius, even against his will, accept the diagrams of the most learned Jesuit Petavius, in which he rightly displayed the arrangement of the Tetrapla, Hexapla and Octapla. For although the Hebrew codex expressed in Hebrew and Greek letters did not count as a version, it does count as one of the editions which Ruffinus says were written in separate pages or columns. Since there were eight of these, the Octapla was necessarily made up of them.

units.la: Jam quis non miretur Vossium, postquam errores erroribus accumulavit, suis verbis sibi applaudentem? Longè rectius fecerit P. Simonius, si missis tot errorum ambagibus, desinat vexare antiquorum Patrum scripta, illosque admittat sensus qui primo statim sese offerunt aspectu. Egregius sanè declamator est Vossius, qui non Simonium his verbis, sed seipsum ingeniumque suum graphicè depinxit. Eusebii siquidem verba, eo modo quo in omnibus editionibus leguntur exponunturque ab Inter-prepretibus, attulit Simonius. Contrà Vossius Eusebii verba sine ullius Codicis manu exarati autoritate mutare ausus est, eaque explicare contra manifestum ipsius Eusebii sensum.
units.tr: Who would not be astonished that Vossius, having piled error upon error, still applauds himself for his own words? Simonius would have done far better, if, leaving aside so many tangles of error, he ceased to harass the writings of the ancient Fathers and accepted those senses which present themselves at first sight. Vossius is indeed a splendid declaimer, who has portrayed not Simonius but himself and his own talent in these words. For Simonius cited the words of Eusebius in the form in which they are read and explained in all the editions by the interpreters. Vossius, by contrast, has dared to alter Eusebius's words without the authority of any manuscript, and to explain them against Eusebius's own manifest meaning.

units.la: Ab Eusebii Historia ad illius Chronicum provocaverat Vossius: at ostendit Simonius, neque etiam Eusebii Chronicum illi favere, idque demonstravit allatis Chronici Eusebiani verbis. Jam quid ad hæc Vossius? Nunc provocat ad Syncellum, aitque Simonium decurtata Affricani verba è Chronico Eusebii produxisse. An Affricani verba decurtaverit Eusebius in Chronico ignoro: scio tamen Chronici illius verba, ad quæ Simonium Vossius remiserat, ipsi esse manifestè contraria.
units.tr: Vossius had appealed to Eusebius's History and then to his Chronicle, but Simonius showed that the Chronicle of Eusebius does not favour him either, and demonstrated this by quoting the words of the Eusebian Chronicle. What does Vossius say to this? Now he appeals to Syncellus and says that Simonius has taken the abridged words of Africanus from the Chronicle of Eusebius. Whether Eusebius abridged Africanus's words in the Chronicle I do not know; but I do know that the words of that Chronicle, to which Vossius had referred Simonius, are plainly contrary to him.

units.la: Sed pergit Vossius. Syncellum debuit consulere Simonius, quem non videtur legisse. Simonio difficile non fuit legere Syncellum, qui in omnium manibus versatur Græcè & Latinè editus: eum quidem legit ac perlegit, neque in eo quidquam deprehendit quod Vossii commento de Hexaplis faveat, nisi novum ipse Vossius cudat Syncellum, sicut novum finxit Eusebium.
units.tr: But Vossius goes on: Simonius ought to have consulted Syncellus, whom he does not seem to have read. It was not difficult for Simonius to read Syncellus, who is in everyone's hands, published in Greek and Latin. He indeed read it through and through, and found nothing in it that favours Vossius's fiction about the Hexapla, unless Vossius himself coins a new Syncellus, just as he invented a new Eusebius.

units.la: Jam ut de Syncello etiam aliquid dicam; ille referens Chronologiam ex Codice Samaritarum, testatur se illam ex Eusebio sumpsisse, & illius exemplo Samariticum Codicem appellat τὸ ᾿Σαμαρεϊτικὸν ῾Εβραϊκόν. Addit Judæos etiam fateri Codicem Samariticum verum esse & primigenium, descriptumque literis quæ à Judaicis discrepent, Ἀρχαιοτάτου ἐν τῇς χαρακτῆρι Ἀλλαῖου, ὃ ἐν ἀλληθῆς εἶναι ἐν πρώτῳ ῾Εβραίοι καλούμενο-
units.tr: Now, to say something more about Syncellus: when he relates the chronology from the Samaritan codex, he states that he took it from Eusebius, and following Eusebius's example he calls the Samaritan codex "the Samaritan Hebrew" [τὸ Σαμαρεϊτικὸν Ἑβραϊκόν]. He adds that the Jews too admit that the Samaritan codex is true and original, and written in letters that differ from the Jewish ones, "in the most ancient character, which they say is truly the first Hebrew" [Ἀρχαιοτάτου ἐν τῇ χαρακτῆρι ... ἐν πρώτῳ Ἑβραῖοι καλούμενον].

units.la: γῶσι. Jam nemo sanus præditus judicio ex his verbis & similibus conficiat Affricanum & Origenem Codices Samaritic os literis Samaritcis expressos consuluisse, & hunc illos in sua Hexapla conjecisse. Sed indicavit tantùm Georgius Syncellus, Samaritas uti Codicibus Ebraicis veris ac primigeniis, non secus ac Judæos; quod didicisse videntur Affricanus, Origenes & Eusebius ab ipsis Judæis, ut & ipsa Syncelli verba innuunt, non lectis tamen ipsis Codicibus Samaritarum Samaritics characteribus expressis; quo etiam modo ipse Vossius Codicis Ebraici Samaritarum mentionem interdum facit, quem tamen nunquam legisse videtur, adeo turpiter errat in referendis illius verbis, Latinâ ejusdem Codicis Versione deceptus. Præterea Origenes, uti jam supra annotatum fuit, nihil de figura literæ Thau apud Samaritas pronunciat, nisi ex relatione Judæorum. Quando igitur Affricanus, Origenes & Eusebius laudant Samaritarum Codices, laudant tantùm Græcam Samaritici Exemplaris Versionem, quæ à Samaritis ipsis ex Ebræo condita fuerat. Simili ratione, quando Patres Syrum laudant Interpretem, Græca tantùm Syriacæ Versionis laudant Exemplaria, non autem ipsamet Syriaca Syriacis expressa literis. Sed ad hæc & alia ejusdem generis plurima nunquam advertit bonus Vossius: satis illi fuit quasi ex suggestu declamare, & in eos qui non idem, quod ipse, sentiebant, caninam suam eloquentiam promere. Jam Vossio triumphanti applaudant Magistelli illi quos ipse asellos & stupidos appellat, pellat: nemo enim verè doctus unquam ipsi applaudet.
units.tr: Now no sane man endowed with judgement will conclude from these and similar words that Africanus and Origen consulted Samaritan codices written in Samaritan letters, and that Origen placed them in his Hexapla. Syncellus merely indicated that the Samaritans use true and original Hebrew codices, just as the Jews do; and Africanus, Origen and Eusebius seem to have learned this from the Jews themselves, as Syncellus's own words suggest, but they did not read the Samaritan codices written in Samaritan characters. In the same way Vossius himself sometimes mentions the Hebrew codex of the Samaritans, though he never seems to have read it, and he errs so shamefully in reporting its words, being deceived by the Latin version of that same codex. Moreover, Origen, as was noted above, says nothing about the shape of the letter Tau among the Samaritans except on the report of the Jews. Therefore, when Africanus, Origen and Eusebius praise Samaritan codices, they praise only the Greek version of the Samaritan exemplar, which the Samaritans themselves had made from the Hebrew. Similarly, when the Fathers praise the Syriac interpreter, they praise only the Greek copies of the Syriac version, not the Syriac text itself written in Syriac letters. But good Vossius never notices these things, nor the very many others of the same kind: it was enough for him to declaim as if from a pulpit and to bring out his snarling eloquence against those who did not think as he did. Now those little schoolmasters, whom he calls donkeys and blockheads, applaud Vossius in his triumph; for no one truly learned will ever applaud him.

units.la: His præterea addit Vossius, Simonium dixisse Aquilam ad amussim Ebraica reddidisse; quod nemo unquam Christianus dixit. At de Aquila nihil Simonius dixit, quod non jam antea ab Origene, Eusebio, Hieronymo & aliis Patribus dictum fuerit, qui animadverterunt Aquilam νυξιώτατα & κατ' ἀκρίβειαν Sacros Codices transtulisse. Idemque Simonius ostendit quomodo etiam κακοζηλία istius Interpretis à Patribus damnata fuerit; adeoque de Aquila nihil dixit Simonius quod ab ipsis Patribus non hauserit.
units.tr: Vossius further adds that Simonius said Aquila rendered the Hebrew with exact precision, which no Christian has ever said. But Simonius said nothing about Aquila that had not already been said by Origen, Eusebius, Jerome and other Fathers, who observed that Aquila translated the sacred books most accurately [ἀκριβέστατα] and with precision [κατ' ἀκρίβειαν]. Simonius likewise showed how the excessive literalism [κακοζηλία] of that interpreter was condemned by the Fathers. So Simonius said nothing about Aquila that he did not draw from the Fathers themselves.

units.la: Non capit etiam Vossius quomodo Origenes, referente Simonio, Hexaplorum opus sub unam repræsentaverit lineam, cùm opus dextrâ sinistrâ, sursum deorsum penè infinitis constaret lineis; atque Simonio autor est ut plerasque istas de Hexaplis & Tetraplis observationes mittat in crucem. Verùm mirificus iste homo aurem profectò habet Batavam, qui ea non capiat, quæ tam clara & manifesta sunt. Opus Hexaplorum sub una fuisse linea dicitur à Simonio, quia singulæ editiones, quæ in propriis paginis sive columnellis, ut loquitur Ruffinus, descriptæ erant, sibi invicem ita erant oppositæ, ut στίχοι στίχοις, sive lineæ lineis, versiculi versiculis responderent, ut faciliori negotio committerentur. Autor verò sim facetissimo Vossio, ut lectâ hac Hieronymi à Sancta Fide responsione, seipsum cum novis suis Hexaplis mittat in crucem, sicque cum illis faciat I longum.
units.tr: Vossius also fails to grasp how Origen, as Simonius reports, reduced the work of the Hexapla to a single line, although the work, with its columns to right and left and up and down, consisted of almost countless lines. Simonius advises him to throw most of his remarks about the Hexapla and Tetrapla into the fire. But this marvellous man must indeed have a Batavian ear if he cannot grasp things so clear and plain. The work of the Hexapla is said by Simonius to have been under one line because the individual editions, which were written in separate pages or columns, as Ruffinus calls them, were set side by side so that lines answered to lines [στίχοι στίχοις] and short verses to short verses, so that they could be compared more easily. The author would advise the most witty Vossius, after reading this reply of Jerome to Sancta Fides, to throw himself and his new Hexapla into the fire, and so make a long I with them.

units.la: Transit postea Vossius ad ea quæ Simonius in illius scripto de Sibyllinis Oraculis castigaverat. Miratur quòd cùm Simonius tam malè se defendat, alienæ tamen opem ferat nequitiæ, & patrocinetur nebuloni, sic enim virum Ebraicè doctum appellat maledicentissimus Vossius, qui solet, cùm nihil habet quod reponat, maledictis pugnare. Sed ad rem ipsam venio. Agitur de verbis Hieronymi, quæ Theologus ille ex Quæstionibus doctissimi illius Patris in Genesim produxerat, quæque ab eo nequissimè perversa contendit. Vossius, qui putat pro appungunt, ut in libris editis habetur, legendum esse apponunt, ut in quibusdam Exemplaribus MSS. se legisse testatur. Ob hanc causam clamitat Vossius, aitque hominem istum fatuum esse, Semirabbinum & insignem nebulonem, qui verba Hieronymi perverterit. Jam absit à Simonio ut bonum Vossium falsificum appellaverit; sed eum monuit amico animo, ut sibi caveret ne ipse à Semirabbinis istis in jus vocaretur tanquam falsificus, qui verba Hieronymi à se minimè intellecta perverteret. Contendit itaque Simonius, in verbis Hieronymi legendum esse appungunt, uti legit nebulo iste Vossianus cum Erasmi & Marii Victorini editionibus, qui longè plures Codices MSS. Hieronymi versarunt, quàm ipse Vossius, maximè cùm, si legatur apponunt, verba Hieronymi vix ullum sensum admittant.
units.tr: Vossius next turns to the points that Simonius had criticised in his writing on the Sibylline Oracles. He wonders that Simonius, defending himself so badly, nevertheless brings help to another's wickedness and stands up for a scoundrel; for that is how the most abusive Vossius calls a man learned in Hebrew, since he is accustomed, when he has nothing to answer, to fight with insults. But I come to the matter itself. The question concerns the words of Jerome, which that theologian quoted from the Questions on Genesis of that most learned Father, and which he wickedly claims were perverted. Vossius, who thinks that appungunt, as it is printed in the published books, should be read as apponunt, as he testifies he found in some manuscript copies, cries out on this account, and says that this fellow is a fool, a half-rabbi and a notorious scoundrel who has perverted the words of Jerome. Far be it from Simonius to have called the good Vossius a forger; he advised him in a friendly spirit to take care that he himself not be summoned before these half-rabbis as a forger, since he was perverting the words of Jerome which he had not understood at all. Simonius therefore maintains that in Jerome's words appungunt must be read, as that scoundrel Vossius reads it with the editions of Erasmus and Marius Victorinus, who handled far more manuscript copies of Jerome than Vossius himself, especially since, if apponunt is read, Jerome's words admit hardly any sense at all.

units.la: Jam quid ad hæc Vossius? Opponit nonnullos Codices manu exaratos, in quibus constanter legerit apponunt. Objicit præterea Simonio, eum nulla unquam inspexisse Exemplaria Hieronymi manu exarata. Sic miris modis sibi applaudit Vossius, etiam cum ineptit. Sciat igitur Vossius, Simonium complures evolvisse Hieronymi Codices MSS. sed fere nullos invenisse qui bonae notae fuerint, etsi magnam prae se ferrent antiquitatem: cum enim Hieronymus Graecis Ebraicisque vocibus abundet, multaque sint in eo recondita eruditionis, hinc factum fuit ut scribae in describendis Hieronymi operibus saepe lapsi fuerint. Sic in loco de quo agitur, praeter vulgatam lectionem appungunt, Exemplaria manu exarata quae legit Simonius, duas alias lectiones exhibent, nimirum apponunt & adjungunt. In omnibus tamen Codicibus MSS. constanter se legisse apponunt, testatur Vossius. In hac lectionis varietate quid faciat Criticus ut veram lectionem seligat? Attendit ad materiam quam isto loco tractat Hieronymus, & quia illa Rabbinica est, vetustos recentioresque Rabbinos consulit. Tunc in illis omnibus deprehendit eamdem quae in Hieronymo legitur annotationem, scilicet in dictione בקומה appingendum esse punctum desuper. Inde conficit in Hieronymo legendum esse appungunt, non vero apponunt, neque adjungunt. Sed quia Vossius argumentum Rabbinicum quod ibi tractat Hieronymus ignorat, mirum non est si monstrosam lectionem in Hieronymi Codicem invexerit, perverteritque doctissimi illius Patris sensum.
units.tr: Now what does Vossius say to this? He cites several manuscript codices in which he consistently found apponunt. He also objects to Simonius that he never examined any manuscript copies of Hieronymus. In this way Vossius congratulates himself in odd ways, even when he is being foolish. Let him know, then, that Simonius has gone through many manuscript codices of Hieronymus and found almost none of good quality, although they show great age. Since Hieronymus abounds in Greek and Hebrew words and contains much hidden learning, the scribes who copied his works often erred. So in the passage in question, besides the common reading appungunt, the manuscript copies that Simonius read offer two other readings, namely apponunt and adjungunt. Vossius testifies, however, that he consistently found apponunt in all the manuscript codices. Faced with this variation, what should a critic do to choose the true reading? He attends to the subject Hieronymus is treating in that place, and since it is rabbinical, he consults the older and more recent rabbis. In all of them he finds the same note that is read in Hieronymus, namely that a point must be placed above the word [בקומה] (bequmah). From this he concludes that Hieronymus should read appungunt, not apponunt or adjungunt. But because Vossius is ignorant of the rabbinical matter that Hieronymus treats there, it is no wonder that he has introduced a monstrous reading into the codex of Hieronymus and distorted the meaning of that most learned Father.

units.la: Clara itaque sunt & aperta quae hic observavit Hieronymus, eademque omnino atque illa quae dudum Judaei ex paterna Traditione in suis Codicibus retinent. Unde annotavit Masora, hoc punctum locis quindecim in libris Moisis occurrere. Ea vero quae iterum adjecit Vossius ut pravam lectionem defenderet, inepta sunt & absurda. Bene igitur Simonius monuerat Vossium, ut prius transfiret in castra Semirabbinorum, quam de illorum rebus parum sibi cognitis judicium ferret. De punctis enim quae vocant irregularia, agi hoc loco, nemo sani judicii negaverit. At Vossius rogat Simonium, ut explicet sensum verborum Hieronymi, prout ab isto nebulone depravata sunt, qui non dubitavit affirmare, Hieronymum ibi mentionem fecisse punctorum regularium. Verum de eo quod ex verbis Hieronymi concludit Vossianus iste nebulo, nunquam disputavit Simonius, qui sciat Judaeos & Hebraicas non minus quam Vossium ineptire; sed de genuina verborum Hieronymi lectione litem solum intendit, quam putat se demonstrasse. Ipse quoque eodem loco animadvertit irregularia ejusmodi puncta nihil prorsus facere pro tuendis punctis regularibus, quae constat Hieronymo esse posteriora.
