units.tr: What Hieronymus observed here is therefore clear and plain, and it is entirely the same as what the Jews have long retained in their codices from paternal tradition. Hence the Masora noted that this point occurs in fifteen places in the books of Moses. But what Vossius added again to defend his faulty reading is silly and absurd. Simonius was right, then, to advise Vossius to cross over first into the camp of the half-Rabbinists before passing judgment on matters of which he knows little. No one of sound judgment will deny that this passage concerns what are called irregular points. But Vossius asks Simonius to explain the meaning of Hieronymus's words, as this scoundrel has corrupted them, a man who did not hesitate to assert that Hieronymus there mentioned regular points. Simonius, however, never argued about what this Vossian scoundrel infers from the words of Hieronymus. Simonius knows that the Jews and the Hebrew scholars are no less foolish than Vossius; he only wished to dispute the genuine reading of Hieronymus's words, which he believes he has proved. He himself also observed in the same place that such irregular points do nothing whatever to support the regular points, which it is agreed were later than Hieronymus.

units.la: Simonius riserat Vossium, qui de Rabbinis ipse nequidem Semirabbinus judicium ferre ausus fuerit. Nunc factus Rabbinista ensem Rabbinicum distringit & aerem diverberat. Carpit Simonium, qui innixus auctoritate Saadiae Gaonis, probaverit non a sexcentis, sed a nongentis annis usurpata fuisse a Judaeis puncta vocalia. Regerit Saadiam floruisse ante annos 756. quae summa multum tùm abest à nongentis.Recta quidem est boni Voffii computatio, sed inepta illius ratiocinatio : hæc enim sunt verba Simonii. R. Saadias Gaon librum scripsit de re Grammatica sub annum 900. in quo de punctis vocalibus, qua longè ante illius tempora apud Judæos in usu fuerant, disputat. Si igitur primus punctorum repertor non fuerit ille Saadias, sed ea tantùm collegerit quæ dudum à suis patribus edita fuerant, facile erit nongentorum annorum summam attingere.
units.tr: Simonius had mocked Vossius, who dared to pass judgment on the rabbis without even being a half-Rabbinist. Now, having become a Rabbinist, he draws a rabbinical sword and beats the air. He finds fault with Simonius, who, relying on the authority of Saadia Gaon, had shown that vowel points had been in use among the Jews for not six hundred but nine hundred years. Vossius replies that Saadia flourished 756 years ago, a sum that falls well short of nine hundred. Vossius's calculation is indeed correct, but his reasoning is foolish. For these are Simonius's own words: "Rabbi Saadia Gaon wrote a book on grammar about the year 900, in which he discusses the vowel points, which had been in use among the Jews long before his time." So if Saadia was not the first discoverer of the points, but only gathered together those that had long before been published by his fathers, it will be easy to reach a sum of nine hundred years.

units.la: Jam liberalior factus bonus Voffius ait, Libenter dederim istoc tempore innotuisse puncta Rabbinis; (hoc tamen antea negaverat) verùm addit id non esse quod quæritur, sed quando puncta vocalia Scripturis apponi cœperint. Petit igitur à Simonio, ut ostendat aut indicet unum tantæ vetustatis Exemplar cui apposita fuerint puncta. Deinde ait fe in sola Chriftinæ Suedorum Reginæ Bibliotheca plures quàm septingentos numerauisse Codices Ebraicos manu exaratos. Rectè dixit fe tot Codices numerasse; quâ etiam ratione libros suos numerare solent Bibliopolæ, non legere. In tanta autem libraria suppellectili, referente Voffio, nullus comparebat Codex Ebraicus quadringentis, aut utplurimum quingentis vetustior annis cui puncta adscriberentur vocalia, uno excepto, qui contineret quidem vocales, sed alio annotatas atramento. Neque sanè id mirum videbitur iis qui sciunt non comparere hodie Codices apud Judæos, qui ante quingentos vel sexcentos annos descripti fuerint. Denique his subjungit Voffius, libros illos magna ex parte ad illustrissimi Colberti Bibliothecam migraffe, certumque se esse, si qui ad illam se conferant, facilè sibi ipsi assensuros, dummodo in tractandis membranis non rudes & parum exercitati fuerint. Ne autem bono Voffio desint plausores, sibi primus applaudit, aitque, Accipiat hæc P. Simonius quomodocunque placuerit, rideat, indignetur, faciat quidquid velit. Miror profectò belli istius Critici audaciam, qui tamen non aliam habeat librorum Ebraicorum cognitionem, quàm illam quam habere soleant Bibliopolæ. Verùm singula ista excutiamus.
units.tr: Now, having become more generous, the good Vossius says: "I would gladly grant that the points were known to the rabbis at that time" (though he had previously denied this). But he adds that this is not the question, which is when vowel points began to be applied to the Scriptures. He therefore asks Simonius to show or point out a single copy of such antiquity to which points were attached. Then he says that he counted in the library of Queen Christina of Sweden alone more than seven hundred Hebrew codices written by hand. He spoke correctly in saying that he counted so many codices, a method by which booksellers too are accustomed to count their books rather than read them. But in so great a store of books, according to Vossius, no Hebrew codex appeared that was older by four hundred, or for the most part five hundred, years and had vowel points added to it, except one, which indeed contained vowels, but marked with a different ink. Nor will this seem surprising to those who know that there are no longer any codices among the Jews that were written six or five hundred years ago. Finally, Vossius adds that most of those books have migrated to the library of the most illustrious Colbert, and that he is certain that if anyone goes there to consult them, they will readily agree with him, provided they are not unskilled and inexperienced in handling parchment. Lest the good Vossius lack applauders, he applauds himself first and says: "Let P. Simonius take these things however he pleases; let him laugh, let him be indignant, let him do whatever he wishes." I indeed marvel at the boldness of this warlike critic, who nevertheless has no other knowledge of Hebrew books than that which booksellers are accustomed to have. But let us examine these points one by one.

units.la: Non tot quidem Codices Ebraicos numeravit Simonius, sed longè plures legit quàm Voffius, ad eosque animum advertit, ne magis Bibliopola videretur quàm Criticus. De hoc enim argumento & expensis à se Codicibus Ebraicis manu exaratis scripsit ante annos septemdecim sapientissimo Magistro Claudio Cappellano Doctori & Socio Sorbonico, editaque est illius Epistola, in qua demonstrat vetustos Judæorum Codices sine punctis vocalibus plerosque descriptos fuisse, in quos postea puncta illa vocalia à Judæis ipsis invecta fuerint, multisque locis castigatos fuisse, ut illi cum Masorethicis perfectè consentirent, erasis scilicet literis Vau & Jod quæ ipsis videbantur superfluæ. Tunc Simonius Ebraica Judæorum Exemplaria MSS. non numerabat, sicuti Voffius, sed expendebat. Jam nihil ex his potest confici quod Voffii sententiæ faveat, quia constat, ut rectè à Simonio observatum fuit, etiam hodie multa superesse monumenta, quæ ostendent jam ab illa ætate, de qua lis mota est, Sacri Codicis verba à Judæis cum punctis vocalibus lecta fuisse, etsi puncta illa raro Codicibus adjicerentur, non solùm quia difficile erat & laboriosum tot minutias describere; sed & quia ista Exemplaria sic descripta à perpaucis hominibus comparari poterant. Illa autem quæ supersunt monumenta, & ex quibus patet jam ab illa ætate lectum fuisse cum punctis vocalibus Ebraicum Codicem, sunt Rabbinorum libri, maximèque Grammaticorum, qui in suis libris voces Contextûs Biblici punctis vocalibus notatas referunt, iidemque, si quæ sit lectionis diversitas circa illas vocales, ex Codicibus antiquis illam sedulò annotant. In Bibliis quoque manu exaratis interdum ad marginem referúntur lectiones Codicis Rabbi Hillelis circa vocales. Scio quidem non tantam Hilleli tribuendam esse antiquitatem, quantam illi vulgò tribuunt Judæi & plerique Ebraistæ, ut firmissimis rationibus probavit ipse Simonius: verùm constat illum vixisse saltem ante annos quingentos, ut ex Rabbinis qui eum laudant, demonstrare facile est. R. Davidis Kimhi Lexicon Scripturæ Sacræ voces punctis notatas exhibet, & aliquas varietates lectionis circa vocales complectitur ex vetustioribus Codicibus MSS. desumptas. Quid dicam de Rabbinorum Judæ & Jonæ Lexicis sermone Arabico conscriptis, in quibus eadem licet animadvertere? Rabbi autem Judam ante sexcentos annos vixisse non diffitetur Vossius. Sileo de Saadia Gaone, qui etiam, teste Vossio, ante annos 756. floruit; cùm ante illius tempora ipsi Masoretæ, qui
units.tr: Simonius did not, to be sure, count so many Hebrew codices, but he read far more than Vossius did, and he paid attention to them, so as not to appear more a bookseller than a critic. For he wrote on this subject, and on the Hebrew manuscript codices he had examined, seventeen years ago to the most wise master Claude Cappelain, doctor and fellow of the Sorbonne, and his letter was published, in which he demonstrates that most of the ancient Jewish codices were written without vowel points, and that the points were later introduced into them by the Jews themselves, and that in many places the codices were corrected so that they would agree perfectly with the Masoretic text, the letters Vav and Yod, which seemed superfluous to them, being erased. Simonius, then, did not count the Hebrew manuscript codices of the Jews as Vossius did, but weighed them. Now nothing can be inferred from these facts that favors Vossius's opinion, because it is clear, as Simonius rightly observed, that even today many monuments survive which show that from that age, about which the dispute has been raised, the words of the Sacred Codex were read by the Jews with vowel points, although such points were rarely added to the codices. This was not only because it was difficult and laborious to copy so many minute marks, but also because such copies, so written, could be obtained by very few people. The surviving monuments, however, from which it is evident that from that age the Hebrew codex was read with vowel points, are the books of the rabbis, and especially of the grammarians, who in their books report the words of the biblical text marked with vowel points, and who, if there is any variation of reading in those vowels, carefully note it from ancient codices. Also, in Bibles written by hand, the readings of the codex of Rabbi Hillel concerning the vowels are sometimes referred to in the margin. I know indeed that Hillel must not be credited with as great an antiquity as the Jews and most Hebraists commonly ascribe to him, as Simonius himself proved by very firm arguments; but it is established that he lived at least five hundred years ago, as can easily be shown from the rabbis who praise him. Rabbi David Kimhi's Lexicon of Sacred Scripture presents words marked with points and includes some variations of reading concerning the vowels, drawn from older manuscript codices. What shall I say of the Lexicons of the rabbis Judah and Jonah, written in the Arabic language, in which one may notice the same things? Vossius does not deny that Rabbi Judah lived six hundred years ago. I say nothing of Saadia Gaon, who also, according to Vossius, flourished 756 years ago; for before his time the Masoretes themselves, who were many, had codices marked with vowel points, and the rabbis Menahem de Lonzano and other Jewish critics think that the remaining codices should be corrected according to the reading of these copies.

units.la: plures fuerunt, Codices habuerint punctis vocalibus notatos, ad quorum Exemplarium lectionem R.Menahem de Lonzano & alii Judæi Critici cæteros Codices castigandos esse existimant.
units.tr: There were many of them who had codices marked with vowel points, and R. Menahem de Lonzano and other Jewish critics think that the other codices must be corrected by the reading of these exemplars.

units.la: Argumentum autem quod sumit Vossius à Græcis qui habuerint accentus ante bis mille annos, cùm tamen nullus inveniatur Codex Græcus accentibus notatus qui non mille annis sit recentior, nihil omnino facit ad rem; quia de Ebraicis, non de Græcis, disputamus: Ebraica autem ex libris Judæorum, non Græcorum, petenda sunt. Tamen difficile non fuerit ostendere etiam hodie Codices Græcos extare, qui ante annos mille accentibus notati fuerint. Sed non placet in ea excurrere quæ sunt à proposito aliena. Quare etiam de tempore, quo Alcoranî Exemplaria punctis vocalibus notari coeperint, sileo; cùm de libris Judæorum in præsentia tantùm agatur. His id unum addam; Vossium rudem plane esse & in tractandis Judæorum membranis parùm exercitatum, qui testimonio Menasse Ben Israël & aliorum duorum Rabbinorum probet, in Exemplari Ebraico Reginæ Suedorum vocales alio atramento notatas fuisse. Frustra quærit horum Rabbinorum auxilium Vossius, qui si rei criticæ peritus fuisset, ex ipsismet Judæorum Codicibus facili negotio probasset, alios sæpe scribas esse qui Codices exarent; alios qui puncta vocalia illis adjiciant, uti judicare licet ex literis Vau, Jod & similibus, quæ erasæ sunt ab iis qui vocales addunt Exemplaribus, uti leguntur in Masorethicis Codicibus. Inter-
units.tr: The argument Vossius takes from the Greeks, who had accents two thousand years ago, though no Greek codex marked with accents is found that is not at least a thousand years more recent, has no bearing at all on the question. We are disputing about Hebrew, not Greek, and Hebrew must be sought in the books of the Jews, not the Greeks. Yet it would not be difficult to show that Greek codices still exist today which were marked with accents a thousand years ago. But I do not wish to digress into matters foreign to my purpose. For that reason I also pass over the question of when copies of the Koran began to be marked with vowel points, since at present we are dealing only with the books of the Jews. I will add only this: Vossius is plainly ignorant and little practised in handling Jewish manuscripts. He proves, on the testimony of Menasseh ben Israel and two other rabbis, that in the Hebrew exemplar of the Queen of Sweden the vowels were marked with a different ink. Vossius seeks the help of these rabbis in vain. If he had been skilled in critical method, he could easily have proved from the Jewish codices themselves that some scribes wrote out the codices, and others added the vowel points to them. One may judge this from the letters vau, yod and the like, which have been erased by those who add vowels to the copies, as they are read in the Masoretic codices.

units.la: Interdum etiam in fine Codicum leguntur eorum nomina qui Exemplaria descripserint, & illorum qui vocales in eadem Exemplaria invexerint, notatis etiam interdum scriptionis temporibus. Sed Vossius, qui Codices tantùm numeravit, non legit, ista & alia bene multa quae ad Judaeorum Criticam pertinent ignorat.
units.tr: Sometimes the names are also read at the end of codices, both of those who copied the exemplars and of those who introduced the vowels into them, sometimes with the dates of writing noted as well. But Vossius, who only counted codices and did not read them, is ignorant of these and many other things that belong to Jewish criticism.

units.la: Iterum objicit, Simonium cavillari, suaque verba pervertisse, ac si puncta Ebraeorum ex Bombergi officina primùm prodiisse scripserit. Non cavillatur Simonius; sed ipsum pudet Vossium tot ineptias commentum fuisse, quas in Simonii postea cavillationes rejicere conetur. Haec enim ipsa sunt Vossii verba in Epistola quae illius Opusculo de Sibyllinis Oraculis praemittitur. Vocales seu puncta quae primùm Venetiis ex Bombergi officina in lucem prodierunt, illa ipsa sunt quae Christiani Rabbinistae tanquam coelitus delapsa suspiciunt. Illi tamen Christiani Rabbinistae diu ante Bombergianas Bibliorum editiones legebant Biblia punctis vocalibus & accentibus notata, qualia prodierunt Brixiae anno 1494. Quia verò in fingendis commentis totus est Vossius, fingit etiam Judaeos per integra tria vel quatuor secula inter se conflixisse, dum alii sic, alii aliter inducendas esse vocales contenderunt, donec tandem Bombergus litem istam diremisset. Sed quaeserim à bono Vossio, an novam habeat Bibliothecam Rabbinicam, unde ingentem illum Rabbinorum conflictum hauserit.
units.tr: Again he objects that Simon mocks and perverts his words, as if he had written that the Hebrew points first came out of Bomberg's press. Simon does not mock. Rather, it is Vossius who is ashamed that he invented so many absurdities, which he then tries to throw back at Simon's later mockery. For these are Vossius's own words in the letter prefixed to his little work on the Sibylline oracles: "The vowels or points which first came to light at Venice from Bomberg's press are those very points which Christian rabbinists regard as having fallen from heaven." Yet those Christian rabbinists were reading Bibles marked with vowel points and accents long before the Bomberg editions of the Bible, such as those that appeared at Brescia in 1494. And since Vossius is wholly given to inventing fictions, he also imagines that the Jews fought among themselves for three or four whole centuries, some contending one way and some another about how the vowels should be introduced, until at last Bomberg settled the dispute. But I would like to ask good Vossius where he has a new rabbinic library from which he drew that enormous conflict among the rabbis.

units.la: Pergit nugari Vossius, probatque Bombergum verè dilapidasse patrimonium suum in alendis aliquot Judaeorum centuriis. Rideat, inquit, Simonius istas aedes (Bombergi) perinde ac aediculas LXX. Interpretum in Pharo: temperasset tamen ab inepto risu, si Leonem Juda Mutinensem haec coram referentem audisset. Risit quidem Simonius, iterumque ridet, non quidem Bombergi aedes, sed Isaaci Vossii nugas, qui tot ineptias referat. Bombergum autem dilapidasse patrimonium non negavit Simonius; sed ineptienti Vossio respondit, illud non facere ad institutum, nec posse afferri nisi ab homine qui ineptias ineptiis accumulet: haec enim sunt verba Simonii. Utrum in alendis Judaeorum quos conduxerat Bombergus centuriis patrimonium dilapidaverit, uti contendit Vossius, non anquiro, neque de hoc nunc agitur negotio. Cur igitur eadem regerit Vossius, quae non esse ad rem jam objecit Simonius? Rem autem ita se habere probat iterum ex nugatorio libello qui sub Scaligeranorum titulo editus est, ex quo haec refert bonus Vossius. Bombergue qui étoit d'Anvers, & duquel le fils est venu à Venise, & là a tout consommé son bien, a si bien imprimé les Livres Hebreux. Les Juifs corrigeoient & presidebant à l'imprimerie. Il a imprimé des Livres pour plus de quatre millions d'or. Sed ista quàm appositè allata fuerint videat ipse Vossius; nisi quòd tam ingenti pecuniae summae inhiet, quia Bombergum inter suos progenitores numeret. Si quis igitur velit causam scire cur Vossius Judaeos & eorum sequaces tot maledictis lacesseriverit, hanc accipiat. Verpi illi pingue Bombergi progenitoris sui patrimonium consumpse-
units.tr: Vossius goes on trifling, and he proves that Bomberg truly squandered his patrimony in supporting some hundreds of Jews. "Let Simon laugh," he says, "at that building of Bomberg's, just as at the little houses of the Seventy Interpreters on Pharos. Yet he would have refrained from his silly laughter had he heard Leone Modena of Modena relating these things in person." Simon did indeed laugh, and he laughs again, not at Bomberg's building but at the trifles of Isaac Vossius, who recounts so many absurdities. Simon did not deny that Bomberg squandered his patrimony, but he answered Vossius, who was talking nonsense, that this had nothing to do with the matter in hand and could only be brought forward by a man who piles absurdity upon absurdity. These are Simon's words: "Whether Bomberg squandered his patrimony in supporting the hundreds of Jews he had engaged, as Vossius maintains, I do not inquire, nor is that the subject now under discussion." Why then does Vossius repeat the same things which Simon has already objected are irrelevant? He proves that the matter stands so once more from the trifling little book published under the title of the Scaligerana, from which good Vossius reports these words: "Bomberg, who was from Antwerp, and whose son came to Venice and there consumed all his wealth, printed the Hebrew books so well. The Jews corrected them and presided over the printing house. He printed books worth more than four million gold pieces." But let Vossius himself see how aptly these things were brought forward, except that he gapes after such a huge sum of money, because he counts Bomberg among his own ancestors. If anyone therefore wishes to know why Vossius has assailed the Jews and their followers with so many insults, let him take this as the reason: he has swallowed the fat patrimony of Bomberg, his ancestor, to his own great profit.

units.la: Voss. in Epist. ad Thom. Brun. sumpserunt. Dignus sanè miseratione est bonus Vossius, cujus patrimonium ita amplum Judæi dilapidaverint.
units.tr: Vossius in his letter to Thomas Browne. Good Vossius is certainly worthy of pity, whose ample patrimony the Jews have squandered.

units.la: Jam ad Ignatii locum, qui sumptus fuit ex illius Epistola ad Philadelphenses, venio, ex quo posse ostendi tempus quo primùm Ebraici Codices corrumpi cœperint, Vossius existimat. Sed quàm fœdè etiam in hoc à Vossio erratum fuerit demonstraverat Simonius, ipsius Ignatii mentem verbis illius claris & apertis explicans. Nunc Vossius Ignatii sensum conatur obscurare. Miratur Simonii supinitatem, qui cùm se Criticum profiteatur, spurii Ignatii verba adduxerit; affertque Vossius ipsa Ignatii verba, ut concipiuntur in Codice Florentino, nec quidquam in illis mutandum esse affirmat. Sed quàm feliciter hoc negotium illi succedat, juvat expendere.
units.tr: Now I come to the passage of Ignatius, which was taken from his letter to the Philadelphians, from which Vossius thinks it can be shown when the Hebrew codices first began to be corrupted. But Simon had already demonstrated how shamefully Vossius has erred also in this matter, explaining the mind of Ignatius himself from his clear and plain words. Now Vossius tries to obscure the sense of Ignatius. He marvels at Simon's carelessness, that when he professes to be a critic he has cited the words of a spurious Ignatius. Vossius adduces the very words of Ignatius as they stand in the Florentine codex, and he affirms that nothing in them needs changing. But it is worth weighing how happily this business turns out for him.

units.la: Simonius Ignatii verba non quidem omnino ut extant in Florentino Codice, qui manifestè hoc loco corruptus est & obscurus, protulit; sed ex interpolato Codice, qui isto loco interpolatus non est, imò simplicior est Florentino, & vetustam lectionem magis referens. Interpolatum enim Epistolarum Ignatii Codicem in omnibus interpolatum esse nemo dixerit, ne quidem ipse Vossius. Existimavit igitur Simonius, hìc Florentinum Codicem, qui multum præ se fert obscuritatis, corrigendum esse ex alio Codice qui simplicior est, cujusque verba clara sunt; cùm ipse Vossius hoc ipso loco legendum putet ἀρχαίοις, ut habet Codex interpolatus, non verò ἀρχέιοις, ut extat in Codice Florentino. Melior est, inquit Vossius, lectio Pseudo-Ignatii, quam & sequentia videntur approbare. Licuit igitur Simonio sequi Pseudo-Ignatii lectionem, ubi constat illum interpolatum non esse, melioremque sensum quàm Codex Florentinus efficit. Rem ita esse aperte demonstrat ipsius Vossii explicatio, qui miris modis se contorquet, ut Ignatii verba exponat prout concipiuntur in Florentino Codice, neque aliud reperit effugium, quàm fingere Græcæ LXX. Interpretum Versioni in iis voluminibus quæ in Alexandrinam Bibliothecam relata fuerant, accessisse quoque verba Ebraica, ad quæ hoc loco respexerit Ignatius, quia, referente Vossio, similia Exemplaria tunc in Synagogis legebantur. De hac Bibliorum dispositione cogitavit Ignatius, si Vossio, qui oculatissimus est, fidem habeamus. Sed pudet tot ineptias referre, quæ nihil prorsus faciant ad expiscandam Ignatii mentem, cujus verba clara & manifesta sunt secundùm lectionem & expositionem Simonii.
units.tr: Simon did not quote the words of Ignatius exactly as they stand in the Florentine codex, which is manifestly corrupt and obscure in this place. He quoted them from an interpolated codex which is not interpolated in this place; indeed it is simpler than the Florentine and better reflects the older reading. For no one would say that the interpolated codex of the letters of Ignatius is interpolated throughout, not even Vossius himself. Simon therefore judged that the Florentine codex, which has a great deal of obscurity about it, should be corrected from another codex which is simpler and whose words are clear, since Vossius himself thinks that in this very place one should read "ancient" [ἀρχαίοις], as the interpolated codex has it, and not "[ἀρχέιοις]", as stands in the Florentine codex. "The reading of Pseudo-Ignatius is better," says Vossius, "and what follows seems to approve it." Simon was therefore free to follow the reading of Pseudo-Ignatius, where it is certain that he is not interpolated, and it gives a better sense than the Florentine codex. That the matter is so is clearly shown by Vossius's own explanation, who twists himself in wondrous ways to expound the words of Ignatius as they stand in the Florentine codex, and finds no way out except to imagine that Hebrew words were added to the Greek version of the Seventy Interpreters in those volumes which had been carried into the Alexandrian library, and that Ignatius looked to these words in this place, because, as Vossius reports, similar copies were then read in the synagogues. Ignatius, if we may trust Vossius, who is most keen-sighted, had in mind this arrangement of the Bible. But I am ashamed to recount so many absurdities, which do nothing whatever to help us search out the mind of Ignatius, whose words are clear and manifest according to Simon's reading and exposition.

units.la: Ad alia commenta transit Vossius, qui multùm se torquet, ut illud quod Judæis tribuit, quasi Messiam peregrinum fore seu proselytum ipsi credant, explicet. Rogaverat eum Simonius, ex quo Sibyllino oraculo hausisset Judæos credere Messiam fore peregrinum: & quia eum puduit tantam ineptiam effutiisse, nunc quærit effugium. Ait Ægyptiacæ servitutis tempore omnes Judæos fuisse peregrinos ac proselytos; eos quoque nunc toto orbe dispersos esse peregrinos: unde concludit, cùm Judæi hoc tempore ubique sint peregrini, necessùm quoque esse talem fore Messiam, scilicet proselytum, sed non proseproselytum proselytorum. Si valeant ejusmodi argutiolæ, simili ratione concluserim Vossium ineptum esse, sed non ineptum ineptorum. Cur enim mirificus iste ratiocinator latebras quærit & effugia? Hic agitur de Messia qui Judæus ex Judæo nascitu-rus sit, quique futurus est, ex Judæorum consensu, natione & ritibus Judæus. Ut enim lepida sua commenta de Æra & Hegira stabiliret, probare conatus est ex Herodianorum Secta Herodem primum fuisse qui inter Judæos pro Christo fuerit habitus. Nempe, inquit, verba illa, Non deficiet Princeps è Juda, neque Dux de femoribus ejus, &c. ita accepere (Herodiani) ac si cessante Principe è stirpe Juda, necesse foret ut Messias proselytus aut alienigena esse debeat. Ista Vossii verba clara sunt & manifesta, fingitque Herodianorum Sectam, quæ forsan nulla unquam fuit, nunquam defecisse, sed revixisse apud Judæos, præsertim in Hispania. Sed per me licet ut commentis suis gaudeat bonus Vossius, nugisque chartas suas impleat, quales sunt, quas mox subjungit, fabellæ, quas à Menasse Ben Israël & Judæis Poloniæ acceperat. De eo autem quod mox addit, vocem Hegiram æquè Ebraicam esse atque Arabicam, sileo, donec illud probet ex novo Lexico quod novas potestates nominibus Ebraicis tribuat.
units.tr: Vossius turns to other fictions, and he labours greatly to explain that which he ascribes to the Jews, namely that they believe the Messiah will be a foreigner, or a proselyte. Simon had asked him from which Sibylline oracle he had drawn the notion that the Jews believe the Messiah will be a foreigner. And because he was ashamed to have uttered so great a folly, he now seeks an escape. He says that at the time of the Egyptian servitude all the Jews were foreigners and proselytes, and that they too are now scattered as foreigners throughout the whole world. From this he concludes that, since the Jews at this time are everywhere foreigners, the Messiah must necessarily be such too, namely a proselyte, but not a proselyte of proselytes. If such quibbles were valid, I could by a similar reasoning conclude that Vossius is foolish, though not a fool of fools. For why does this wonderful reasoner seek hiding-places and escapes? Here the question concerns a Messiah who is to be born a Jew of a Jew, and who, by the agreement of the Jews, will be a Jew by nation and by rites. For in order to establish his charming fictions about the Aera and the Hegira, he tried to prove from the sect of the Herodians that Herod was the first to be held among the Jews as the Christ. "Indeed," he says, "those words, 'The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet,' etc., the Herodians took in such a way that, when the prince from the stock of Judah had ceased, the Messiah must necessarily be a proselyte or a foreigner." Vossius's words here are clear and manifest, and he invents a sect of Herodians, which perhaps never existed at all, as never having failed but as having revived among the Jews, especially in Spain. But as far as I am concerned, good Vossius may rejoice in his own fictions and fill his pages with trifles, such as the fables which he immediately subjoins, which he had received from Menasseh ben Israel and the Jews of Poland. As for what he adds next, that the word Hegira is as Hebrew as it is Arabic, I pass over it until he proves it from a new lexicon which assigns new meanings to Hebrew words.

units.la: Carpit dein Simonium, qui objecerit Vossium locupletare voluisse Scripturæ Canonem novis Prophetis. At Simonius hac in re non impositit Vossio, qui docet Sibyllinos aliosque ejusdem generis libros ex antiquo Scripturæ Canone sublatos fuisse.
units.tr: He then censures Simonius, who had objected that Vossius wanted to enrich the canon of Scripture with new prophets. But in this matter Simonius did not deceive Vossius, who teaches that the Sibylline books and others of that kind were removed from the ancient canon of Scripture.

units.la: Haud sane, inquit Vossius, parum utilitatis Christianæ accederet Religioni, si etiamnum superessent scripta illa apocrypha quæ Veteris Testamenti olim conjungebantur libris, cum & approbata fuerint à Judæis antequam essent Christiani, & lecta in primitiva Ecclesia, & commendata à Paulo & Apostolis. Sic bonus Vossius autoritate primitivæ Ecclesiæ tuetur nugatorum impostorumque scripta, qui sub ementitis nominibus Patriarcharum, Prophetarum, ac virorum magnæ existimationis apud Gentiles nominibus, libros Adami, Enochi, Abrahami, Moysis, Esajæ, Hieremiæ, Hystaspis, Mercurii Trismegisti, Zoroastris, diversi generis Sibyllarum, Orphei, Phocyllidæ, aliorumque similium, in lucem protulerunt. Felix sane est Ecclesia Anglicana, quæ à dilecto filio suo Isaaco Vossio ætate nostra aucta fuerit tot Prophetis ac Prophetidibus, habeatque nunc unde longam sanctorum Prophetarum, Patriarcharum, Doctorum, Virginum & Viduarum Litaniam contexat, quæ Liturgiæ suæ inseratur.
units.tr: "Certainly," says Vossius, "it would add little Christian usefulness to religion if those apocryphal writings which were once joined to the books of the Old Testament were still extant, since they were approved by the Jews before they were Christians, were read in the primitive Church, and were commended by Paul and the Apostles." So good Vossius, on the authority of the primitive Church, defends the writings of triflers and impostors, who under the false names of Patriarchs, Prophets, and men of great repute among the Gentiles brought to light the books of Adam, Enoch, Abraham, Moses, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Hystaspes, Mercurius Trismegistus, Zoroaster, various kinds of Sibyls, Orpheus, Phocylides, and others of the same sort. Truly the English Church is fortunate, which in our own age has been enriched by her beloved son Isaac Vossius with so many Prophets and Prophetesses, and which now has material from which to weave the long litany of holy Prophets, Patriarchs, Teachers, Virgins and Widows, to be inserted into its Liturgy.

units.la: Ferre non potest Vossius, se cum Postello homine non satis sani sincipitis commissum fuisse. An sani sincipitis Postellus fuerit ignoro: sed scio ovum ovo similius non esse, quàm Postello similis est Vossius in eo de quo agitur argumento. Quod autem Simonius dixit, Postellum adhuc Vossio oculatiorem fuisse, illud non ista accipi debet ac si magis desipuerit Postelius, uti Vossius existimare videtur; sed quia Postellus majorem nugamentis suis probabilitatem conciliet, quàm ipse Vossius. Ille enim nuganugatorum istorum Prophetiam à priscis temporibus arcessit, quando in mundo erant Prophetæ; at minùs oculatus Vossius Prophetas commentus est, quando jam apud Judæos desierant Prophetæ. Sic Adami, Enochi ac Sibyllarum libros autor est Vossius à Judæis toto orbe dispersis compositos fuisse, Deo impellente ipsorum mentes; negat tamen ipsos esse antiquiores diluvio. At cur id negaverit non video, cùm ipse affirmaverit in diluvio universam terram inundatam non fuisse. Jam Guillelmum Postellum audiamus Isaaco Vossio longè oculatiorem. Ille asserit apud Brahmanes latere infinitos historiarum & librorum antediluvianorum thesauros, quos nos expectare unà cum Enochianis opus est. Ne quis autem libros illos antediluvianos in dubium revocet, addit, Scripturam Sacram fuisse ante diluvium manifestè probari ex Sabbathæ nurûs Ogygis libris ab ipsa conscriptis. Hæc autem Sabbatha, referente eodem Postello, fuit Sibylla Babylonia, quam etiam inter suas Prophetides Vossius recensuit.
units.tr: Vossius cannot bear that he was compared with Postellus, a man of not quite sound head. Whether Postellus was of sound head I do not know, but I do know that an egg is not more like an egg than Vossius is like Postellus in the matter under discussion. As for Simonius's remark that Postellus was more sharp-sighted than Vossius, it should not be taken as though Postellus was the greater fool, as Vossius seems to think, but because Postellus lends more probability to his trifles than Vossius himself does. For Postellus traces the prophecy of these triflers back to early times, when there were still prophets in the world; but the less sharp-sighted Vossius invents prophets when the prophets had already ceased among the Jews. So Vossius is the author of the view that the books of Adam, Enoch, and the Sibyls were composed by Jews scattered throughout the world, with God impelling their minds; yet he denies that they are older than the Flood. Why he denies this I do not see, since he himself has asserted that the whole earth was not flooded in the Flood. Now let us hear Guillaume Postel, far sharper-sighted than Isaac Vossius. He asserts that among the Brahmans there lie hidden "infinite treasures of histories and books from before the Flood, which we must await together with the Enochian books." Lest anyone call those pre-diluvian books into doubt, he adds that Sacred Scripture was clearly known before the Flood from the books written by Ogyges' daughter-in-law Sabbatha herself. This Sabbatha, according to the same Postel, was the Babylonian Sibyl, whom Vossius too included among his Prophetesses.

units.la: Eodem etiam loco narrat oculatissimus Postellus ejusmodi librorum historiam; quomodo scilicet ab Adamo ad Enochum, qui primus illos conscripsit, dein ab Enocho ad Noachum, & ab hoc ad alios venerint. Scholas præterea idem Postellus recenset, in quibus secretiores illæ disciplinæ, quæ in Sibyllarum aliorumque Vossii Prophetarum libris extant, traditæ fuerint. Unam scilicet Scholam Noachus ad ilicem Ogyn è regione Mamre instituit; alteram Japhetus in Armenia, cui præsecit Sabbathium Sagam. Ex hac Postelli historia, quæ clara & manifesta est, aperte refellitur Vossii sententia, qui existimat libros istos Propheticos à Judæis sub Patriarcharum & Prophetarum suorum nominibus compositos fuisse, vergentibus ad finem Danielis hebdomadis.
units.tr: In the same place the most sharp-sighted Postel also relates the history of such books: how they came from Adam to Enoch, who first wrote them, and then from Enoch to Noah, and from him to others. Postel also lists the schools in which those more secret teachings, which are found in the Sibyls' books and in the other Prophets of Vossius, were taught. One school, namely, Noah founded at the oak of Ogyges, opposite Mamre; another Japheth founded in Armenia, placing Sabbathius Saga over it. From this history of Postel, which is clear and manifest, the opinion of Vossius is plainly refuted, for he thinks those prophetic books were composed by Jews under the names of their Patriarchs and Prophets, "toward the end of Daniel's week."

units.la: Jam Vossius, quem Simonius dixerat tanto stipatum Prophetarum agmine brevi fusurum vaticinia, in Prophetam transformatus ex tripode pronunciat, Simonium, nisi stilum vertat, solis semper placiturum semidoctis. Sed ego, qui non sum vates neque Propheta, ausim affirmare, Vossium ne quidem semidoctis placere, sed sucum facere simplicioribus.
units.tr: Now Vossius, whom Simonius had said would soon pour forth prophecies surrounded by a great host of Prophets, has been transformed into a Prophet and pronounces from the tripod: "Simonius, unless he changes his style, will always please only half-learned men." But I, who am neither a seer nor a Prophet, would venture to affirm that Vossius does not even please half-learned men, but merely wins over the more simple.

units.la: Pergit dein Vossius pugnare verbis, objicitque Simonium multa congessisse de Apocryphis & millies dicta; eorum verò quæ ad rem pertineant cavisse sibi quàm diligentissimè. Nova quidem non commentus fuit Simonius Vossii exemplo; sed ea tantùm attulit quæ ad institutum facerent. Cùm enim Apocryphorum voce usus fuerit Vossius, ut nugamenta sua stabiliret, necesse fuit Simonium ostendere quid vox ista tam apud Ecclesiæ Patres, quàm apud ætatis nostræ Doctores significet. At regerit Vossius, quæstionem esse, quâ ratione Libri Sacri recondíti, cùm priùs Apocryphi dicerentur, postea factum sit ut hæc vox in pravam detorta fuerit significationem, & Libri Apocryphi habiti fuerint pro spuriis & dubiæ fidei libris: ac demum colligit Judæos fuisse qui novam vocis istius expositionem fabricarint, eo nempe consilio filio, ut destruerent autoritatem librorum qui Vetus Testamentum cum Euangeliis connectunt, & simul illorum in quibus adventus Christi clarius quàm ab antiquis annuntiaretur.
units.tr: Vossius then goes on to fight with words, and charges that Simonius has heaped up many things about the Apocrypha, said a thousand times over, and has been most careful to avoid the things that pertain to the matter. Simonius, to be sure, did not invent new things after Vossius's example; he brought forward only those things that bore on his purpose. For since Vossius had used the word "Apocrypha" to establish his trifles, it was necessary for Simonius to show what that word means both among the Fathers of the Church and among the teachers of our own age. But Vossius replies that the question is how the Sacred Books, once called hidden, afterwards came to have this word, Apocrypha, twisted into a bad sense, so that the Apocryphal books were regarded as spurious books of doubtful faith. And at last he concludes that it was Jews who devised this new explanation of the word, with the plain purpose of destroying the authority of the books which join the Old Testament to the Gospels, and at the same time of those in which the coming of Christ was announced more clearly than by the ancients.

units.la: Jam oculatissimus factus est bonus Vossius, ipsisque primitivæ Ecclesiæ Patribus sapientior, cui ob id inprimis displicet vox Apocryphorum, quæ in malam quoque partem à priscis illis Patribus interdum sumitur, quòd hâc voce nugatores illi, quos in veros Prophetas transformavit, Prophetarum albo expunguntur. Ambiguum esse nomen Apocryphi dixit Simonius, quod in sua origine reconditum significat; sumique à Patribus modò in bonam, modò in malam partem. Sive autem Aquila, sive Judæi primi illud in malam partem acceperint, nihil planè illud facit ad institutum, cùm à priscis quoque Ecclesiæ Patribus in malam partem acceptum fuerit. Sed quis inde conficiat, Judæos hanc vocem fabricasse, ut destruerent autoritatem librorum qui Vetus Testamentum cum Euangeliis connectunt? Nihil simile unquam præviderunt Patres, quibus omnibus oculatior est Vossius, qui cor solus habet, solus & ingenium; ingenium scilicet Propheticum, quod videt ea quæ non sunt tanquam ea quæ sunt, & quo impellente, judicavit novos suos Prophetas dignos esse qui cum aliis Prophetis inter Scripturæ Sacræ libros recenserentur. Ista sunt quæ merito ineptias appellavit Simonius, quæ ab Ariosti nugamentis minùs abessent. Rectè igitur quæsierat à Vossio, sicut & à nugatore
units.tr: Now good Vossius has become most sharp-sighted, wiser than the very Fathers of the primitive Church. He is especially displeased by the word "Apocrypha," which those ancient Fathers sometimes also used in a bad sense, because by this word those triflers, whom he has transformed into true Prophets, are struck off the roll of the Prophets. Simonius said that the word "Apocrypha" is ambiguous, since in its origin it means something hidden, and the Fathers took it sometimes in a good sense, sometimes in a bad. But whether Aquila or the first Jews took it in a bad sense, this has nothing at all to do with the purpose, since it was also taken in a bad sense by the ancient Fathers of the Church. But who can infer from this that the Jews fabricated this word in order to destroy the authority of the books which join the Old Testament to the Gospels? The Fathers never foresaw anything like this, and Vossius is more sharp-sighted than all of them, he who alone has "heart, and alone also wit"; that is, a prophetic wit, which sees things that are not as though they were, and by whose impulse he judged that his new Prophets were worthy to be counted among the books of Sacred Scripture alongside the other Prophets. These are the things that Simonius rightly called absurdities, things that would not be far removed from the trifles of Ariosto. Rightly, therefore, had he asked Vossius, just as Cardinal Ippolito d'Este asked the trifler Ariosto:

units.la: Ariosto Cardinalis Hippolytus Atestensis, Dove haveva pigliate tante coglionerie? Satis verniliter, reponit Vossius, sed loco non satis convenienti. Pronunciatum tamen hoc est illustrissimi Cardinalis, majoresque sunt Vossii ineptiæ, qui tot Prophetas nugatores commentus sit, quàm Ariosti, cui, quia erat Poëta, licuit fingere nugatores. Jam facetissimus Vossius Simonio autor est, ut nomen illud Coglionerie ad frontes & titulos suorum transferat librorum. Bene quidem Vossius monet Simonium, qui libris quos posthac adversus Vossium editurus est, hæc verba literis sesquipedalibus exarata præmittet,
units.tr: "Where had he picked up so many coglionerie?" Vossius replies rather coarsely, but at an unsuitable place. Yet this is the judgment of the most illustrious Cardinal, and Vossius's absurdities are greater, since he has invented so many triflers as Prophets, than those of Ariosto, to whom, because he was a poet, it was allowed to invent triflers. Now the most witty Vossius advises Simonius to transfer that word "Coglionerie" to the title pages and headings of his books. Vossius certainly does well to advise Simonius, who is about to publish books against Vossius hereafter, to prefix these words written in letters a foot and a half long:

units.la: LE COGLIONERIE DI MESSER VOSSIO, GRAN COGLIONATORE DE' LETTERATI.
units.tr: The Follies of Master Vossius, the Great Fool of the Scholars.

units.la: Transit ad alia Vossius. Quærit à Simonio, cur velit Scribas, qui res Ebræorum chartis committebant, & plerosque magni Synedrii Assessores, Prophetas fuisse, & à Spiritu Sancto afflatos; neget verò tales fuisse LXX. Interpretes? Manifesta est discriminis illius ratio: nemo enim Christianus negat Sacros Libros à Prophetis scriptos fuisse & à viris Spiritu Sancto afflatis: sed Interpretum longè alia est ratio quàm Scriptorum. Semper autem apud Judæos extitisse Prophetas qui res ætatis suæ chartis committerent, docet manifestè Josephus, qui affirmat singula quidem apud gentem suam à temporibus Artaxerxis usque ad suam ætatem scriptis comprehensa fuisse: sed illa parem cum prioribus non mereri fidem ; quia ab illis temporibus non fuit certa , ut prisciis illis temporibus, Prophetarum successio. 'Απο ῆ 'Αρταξέρξε μέχρι ῆ καθ' ἡμᾶς χρόνε γέγαπται μὴ ἑκαστε πίστεως ῆ χ ὁμοίας ηξιῶ τῆς περὶ ἑαυτῶν, ἀλλ' τὸ μὴ γεγενέσθαι τ τ Προφητῶν ἀκριβῆ ἀξιοχρέων. Illa igitur Prophetarum successio, teste Josepho, à Mose usque ad Artaxerxis tempora extitit apud Judæos, adeoque fictum non est Scribarum sive Prophetarum munus, qui res quæ gestæ fuerint in Ebræorum Republica chartis commiserint; munusque illud ad solos Prophetas pertinuisse declarat idem Josephus, cujus hæc sunt verba. Μόνων τ Προφητῶν τὰ μὲν ἀνώτατα καὶ παλαιώτατα ἢ τ ἐπίνοιαν τ ἀπὸ ἕ Θεῦ μαθόντων, τὰ ἢ καθ' ἑαυτὸς ὡς ἐγένετο σαφῶς συγγεγραφότων. Prophetarum tantùm fuisse, qui remota quidem à suis temporibus & vetustissima ex afflatu divino discerent; quæ verò sua erant ætatis uti gesta fuerant explicatè conscriberent.
units.tr: Vossius next turns to another matter. He asks Simonius why he wants the scribes, who committed the affairs of the Hebrews to writing, and most of the members of the great Sanhedrin to have been prophets, inspired by the Holy Spirit, and yet denies that the Seventy translators were such. The reason for this difference is plain. No Christian denies that the sacred books were written by prophets and by men inspired by the Holy Spirit, but the case of the translators is quite different from that of the writers. Josephus clearly shows that there were always prophets among the Jews who committed the events of their own age to writing. He affirms that the events of his nation from the time of Artaxerxes down to his own day were indeed recorded in writing, but that these accounts do not deserve the same faith as the earlier ones, because from those times there was no certain succession of prophets, as there was in earlier times. [Ἀπὸ δὲ Ἀρταξέρξου μέχρι τῆς καθ' ἡμᾶς γενεᾶς γέγραπται μέν, οὐκ ἀξιόπιστα δὲ ὁμοίως τῶν πρότερον, διὰ τὸ μὴ γεγενῆσθαι τὴν τῶν προφητῶν ἀκριβῆ διαδοχήν.] So, according to Josephus, the succession of prophets from Moses to the time of Artaxerxes existed among the Jews, and the office of writing down the events that took place in the Hebrew commonwealth was not invented; and the same Josephus declares that this office belonged to the prophets alone. His words are these: [Μόνων τῶν προφητῶν τὰ μὲν ἀνωτάτω καὶ παλαιότατα ἐκ τῆς ἐπιπνοίας τῆς ἀπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ μαθόντων, τὰ δὲ καθ' αὑτοὺς ὡς ἐγένετο σαφῶς συγγεγραφότων.] Only the prophets wrote, learning from divine inspiration what was remote and most ancient, and setting down clearly what happened in their own times as it happened.

units.la: Miror sanè repertos fuisse Parisiis ætate nostrâ Theologos, qui hanc Prophetarum apud Judæos successionem improbaverint, quasi inde sequeretur Synagogam fuisse præstantiorem Ecclesiâ, quæ tales hodie Prophetas non habet. Audio enim illud & alia similia ab illis Simonio objecta fuisse: sed pace illorum dixerim, eos non satis attendisse ad ea quæ Ecclesiam à Synagoga distinguunt. Eusebius hos non solùm Prophetas in Synagoga agnoscit; sed & alios, qui ne Pseudo-Prophetis locus daretur, Prophetarum scripta recognoscerent, suaque munirent auctoritate. Hæc sunt doctissimi illius Patris verba. Παρ' Εβραίοις τὸ παλαιὸν ἃ ἕ τλήθος ἦν τὸ κρίνειν τὰς ἐν θείου πνεύματος προφερομένας ἢ τὰς ἐνθέους ᾠδὰς· ἀλλ' ἦσαν ἐγχεῖς ἢ ἀπανίοι μέτοχοι ἢ αὐτοὶ θείᾳ πνεύματος ἀγγελικὰ τ λεγομένων, οἷς μόνοις ἐξὴν ἐγκρίνειν ἢ δὴ ἀφιερῶν τὰς Προφητῶν βίβλους, τὰς ἢ τ μὴ τιστῶν ἀποδοκιμάζειν. Apud Ebræos antiquitus non erat multitudinis de iis judicare qui Divino Spiritu afflati producebantur & de divinis Carminibus: sed perpauci erant, iidemque participes Divini Spiritûs, cujus est de eorum quæ dicuntur judicare, quibus etiam solis fas erat ea de re statuere, & Prophetarum libros consecrare; eos verò qui non erant Prophetici reprobare.
units.tr: I am truly astonished that in our own age there have been theologians at Paris who have disapproved of this succession of prophets among the Jews, as if it followed that the synagogue was superior to the Church, which today has no such prophets. I hear that Simonius was charged with this and other similar things by them. But with all respect to them, I must say that they did not pay enough attention to the points that distinguish the Church from the synagogue. Eusebius acknowledges not only that these prophets existed in the synagogue, but also others, who, so that no room would be given to false prophets, examined the writings of the prophets and confirmed them with their own authority. These are the words of that most learned Father: [Παρ᾽ Ἑβραίοις τὸ παλαιὸν οὐ πλήθους ἦν τὸ κρίνειν τὰς ἐν θείῳ πνεύματι προφερομένας ἢ τὰς ἐνθέους ᾠδάς· ἀλλ᾽ ἦσαν ἐγχώριοι ἢ ἀπαξαπλῶς μέτοχοι αὐτοὶ θείου πνεύματος, ἀγγελικὰ τῶν λεγομένων, οἷς μόνοις ἐξῆν ἐγκρίνειν ἢ δὴ ἀφιερῶν τὰς προφητῶν βίβλους, τὰς δὲ μὴ τοιαύτας ἀποδοκιμάζειν.] Among the Hebrews of old it was not the business of the multitude to judge the utterances that were brought forth under divine inspiration or the sacred songs; there were only a few, and these shared in the divine Spirit, able to discern what was said, and to whom alone it was lawful to approve and consecrate the books of the prophets, and to reject those that were not prophetic.

units.la: Quærenti autem Vossio, cur etiam munus illud Propheticum ad LXX. Interpretes non pertinuerit, respondeo illos Interpretes tantùm fuisse, non verò rerum divinarum Scriptores, neque etiam ad eorum classem revocari posse, quorum erat scripta Prophetica à non Propheticis secernere. Sic magni Synedrii Assessores scripturas illas, antequàm in publicum exirent, recognoscebant; unde Hilarius non aliâ ratione adductus fuisse videtur, ut LXX. Interpretes Prophetarum albo adscriberet, quàm quòd existimaverit illos fuisse Hierosolymitanos Senatores. Addit eodem loco Vossius, Simonium ubi loquitur de Prophetis, dixisse eos non fuisse fatidicos; at non sic loqui Christianos. Ego quoque, quia Vossius bonus est Christianus, & benè monet, autor fuerim Simonio, ut vocem fatidici retractet; modò tamen eâ uti illi liceat, ubi de Prophetis Voffianis loquetur.
units.tr: As for Vossius's question why that prophetic office did not also belong to the Seventy translators, I answer that they were only translators, not writers of divine matters, and that they cannot be counted among those whose task it was to separate the prophetic writings from the non-prophetic. Thus the members of the great Sanhedrin used to examine those writings before they were made public; and Hilary seems to have been led to enrol the Seventy translators among the prophets for no other reason than that he thought they were senators of Jerusalem. Vossius adds in the same place that Simonius, when he speaks of the prophets, said they were not soothsayers, but that Christians do not speak in this way. I too, since Vossius is a good Christian and gives good advice, would advise Simonius to retract the word soothsayers; provided, however, that he may use it when he speaks of Vossian prophets.

units.la: Dixerat Simonius, neminem hactenus, si Voffius excipiatur, cogitasse de introducenda in Ecclesiam Sibyllinorum librorum & aliorum ejusdem generis lectione. Sed negat se unquam ea de re cogitasse. Totus tamen est in Opusculo de Sibyllinis Oraculis, ut ostendat sinistram vocis ψευδεπιγραφ acceptionem in causa fuisse cur scripta illa Apocrypha, quae Veteris Testamenti olim conjungebantur libris, hodie non supersint. Item rum in eodem Opusculo vaticinium Eliae desumptum fuisse suspicatur ex libro Prophetiarum Eliae, quem olim, inquit, Veteris Testamenti scriptis annumeratum fuisse constat.
units.tr: Simonius had said that, apart from Vossius, no one until now had thought of introducing the reading of the Sibylline books and others of the same kind into the Church. But Vossius denies that he ever thought about this matter. Yet he is wholly engaged, in his little work on the Sibylline oracles, in showing that the unfortunate sense of the word pseudepigraphal was the reason why those apocryphal writings, which were once joined to the books of the Old Testament, no longer survive today. Likewise, in the same little work, he suspects that the prophecy of Elijah was taken from the book of the prophecies of Elijah, which, he says, is known to have once been counted among the writings of the Old Testament.

units.la: Jam Prophetico furore exagitatus Vossius invehitur in Simonium, qui existimaverit mentitum fuisse Clementem Alexandrinum, dixeritque vafros, id est, teste Vossio, subdolos & malitiosos priscos Patres fuisse, & imprimis Clementem, siquando cum Judaeis & Gentilibus disputarent: at sic melius, inquit, Judaei & Gentiles, quam Christiani loquantur. Verum compescat bilem furoremque suum Propheticum bonus ille Christianus Vossius, qui zelum quidem habet, sed non secundum scientiam, adeò se rudem ostendit in tractandis Patrum scriptis. Divinos esse libros Sibyllarum ex eo se confecisse putavit, quòd Clemens Alexandrinus scripserit Apostolum remisisse ad Sibyllarum & Hystaspis vaticinia, eorumque lectionem commendasse: roganti autem ubinam hoc dixerit Paulus; respondit sufficere nobis debuisse, hoc Clementem virum sanctum affirmasse. At regessit Simonius, nosse eos qui aliquam rerum Ecclesiasticarum cognitionem habent, quàm vafrè prisci illi Patres cum Judaeis & Gentilibus disputarint. Quid ad haec Vossius? Totus in furorem versus tonat, debacchatur, malignoque animo Simonii verba explicat, quasi vafrum esse idem sit quod mentiri. Verum nemo unquam pluris fecit Hieronymum, quàm Erasmus, qui tamen eadem de illo scribat, atque Simonius scripsit de Clemente. Ille siquidem nonnulla Hieronymi verba expendens quae extant Praefatione in Danielem, ait Hieronymum obliquè vafrèque respondisse. An ideo Erasmus, qui proprietatem illius vocis melius noverat quàm ipse Vossius, putavit Hieronymum malitiosum esse hominem ac subdolum qui mentitus fuerit? Absit. Alia siquidem est obliqua & vafra responsio; alia malitiosa & mendax. Sed quàm ineptè bonus Vossius Patrum scripta tractaverit exponam ex ipso Hieronymo, qui Graecos omnes & Latinos Scriptores qui praecesserant evolvit.
units.tr: Now Vossius, driven on by prophetic frenzy, rails against Simonius, who thought that Clement of Alexandria had lied, and who said that the early Fathers were crafty, that is, according to Vossius, sly and malicious, and especially Clement, whenever they disputed with Jews and Gentiles: but, he says, Jews and Gentiles speak better in this way than Christians do. But let that good Christian Vossius restrain his bile and prophetic frenzy, for he has zeal, but not according to knowledge, and shows himself so unskilled in handling the writings of the Fathers. He thought that the books of the Sibyls were divine because Clement of Alexandria had written that the Apostle referred people to the prophecies of the Sibyls and of Hystaspes, and commended reading them; but when asked where Paul said this, he replied that it ought to be enough for us that the holy Clement affirmed it. But Simonius answered that those who have some knowledge of ecclesiastical matters know how craftily those early Fathers disputed with Jews and Gentiles. What does Vossius say to this? He turns wholly to fury, thunders, rages, and explains Simonius's words with a malicious mind, as if being crafty were the same as lying. Yet no one ever valued Jerome more than Erasmus did, and yet Erasmus wrote the same things about him as Simonius wrote about Clement. For, weighing some words of Jerome found in his preface to Daniel, Erasmus says that Jerome answered obliquely and craftily. Did Erasmus, who knew the meaning of that word better than Vossius himself, therefore think that Jerome was a malicious and deceitful man who lied? Far from it. An oblique and crafty answer is one thing; a malicious and lying one is another. But I will show how unskillfully the good Vossius has handled the writings of the Fathers, using Jerome himself, who went through all the Greek and Latin writers who came before him.

units.la: Ruffino respondens doctissimus ille Pater declarat, Aliud esse γυμναστικῶς scribere, aliud διαλεκτικῶς; in priori vagam esse disputationem, & adversario respondentem nunc hac, nunc illa proponere; argumentari ut libet; aliud loqui, aliud agere. Istud scribendi genus secutos fuisse Graecos Latinosque Patres autor est idem Hieronymus. Origenes, inquit, Eusebius, Methodius, Apollinarius, multis versuum millibus scribunt adversus sus Celsum & Porphyrium. Considerate quibus argumentis & quàm lubricis problematibus Diaboli spiritu contexta subvertant; & quia interdum cogun-tur loqui, non quod sentiunt, sed quod necesse est dicunt adversus ea qua di-cunt Gentiles.
units.tr: In replying to Rufinus, that most learned Father declares: It is one thing to write gymnastically [γυμναστικῶς], another dialectically [διαλεκτικῶς]; in the former the discussion is wandering, and the one answering the opponent now puts forward this, now that; he argues as he pleases; it is one thing to speak, another to act. That the Greek and Latin Fathers followed this manner of writing is affirmed by the same Jerome. Origen, Eusebius, Methodius, Apollinarius, he says, write many thousands of verses against Celsus and Porphyry. Consider with what arguments and how slippery problems, woven by the spirit of the Devil, they overturn them; and because sometimes they are compelled to speak not what they think, but what they must say against the things the Gentiles say.

units.la: Benignè igitur, & ad eorum men-tem contra quos disputant, verba Pa-trum explicanda sunt. Illi enim haud infrequenter in exponendis Chri-stianæ Religionis mysteriis varias Græcorum historias & fabellas ora-tioni suæ admiscent, ut illa mysteria minùs à Religione aliena esse vi-deantur. Hæc in Clemente Alexan-drino ejusque discipulo Origene li-cet animadvertere. Sic Origenes, si quando loquitur de Christo Deo & homine, probat exemplo Herculis & aliorum quos Gentilium Theolo-gi in Deos translatos fuisse com-menti sunt, Christianorum hac in re persuasionem non superare ca-ptum humanum. Hæc sunt verba Origenis. Οὐδὲν ἧ ἀρχαῖον ᾧσις Ἑλληνας καὶ Ἑλληνικὰς ἱστορίας χρή-σασθαι, ἵνα μὴ δοκῶμεν μόνοι τὴν παρ-δόξω ἱστορίαν τύλην χρήσασθαι. Neque absurdum fuerit cum Græcis agentes Græcis uti historiis, ne videamur soli historiam mirificam adduxisse. Hoc loco de Christi ortu ex Virgine lo-quitur Origenes.
units.tr: Therefore the words of the Fathers must be explained kindly, and according to the mind of those against whom they dispute. For they quite often mix various Greek histories and fables into their discourse when expounding the mysteries of the Christian religion, so that those mysteries may seem less foreign to religion. This can be observed in Clement of Alexandria and his disciple Origen. Thus Origen, whenever he speaks of Christ as God and man, proves by the example of Hercules and of others whom the theologians of the Gentiles invented as having been translated into gods, that the belief of Christians in this matter does not exceed human understanding. These are the words of Origen: [Οὐδὲν ἧττον ἀρχαῖον ὂν Ἕλληνας καὶ Ἑλληνικὰς ἱστορίας χρῆσθαι, ἵνα μὴ δοκῶμεν μόνοι τὴν παράδοξον ἱστορίαν τολμᾶν χρῆσθαι.] It is not absurd, when dealing with Greeks, to use Greek histories, so that we do not seem to be the only ones to have adduced a wonderful history. Here Origen speaks of the birth of Christ from the Virgin.

units.la: Istud quoque scribendi genus illu-strat eodem loco Hieronymus exem-plo Patrum Latinorum Tertulliani, Cypriani, Minutii, Victorini, La-ctantii, Hilarii; quin etiam ipsius Pauli, his verbis: Legite Epistolas ejus, & maximè ad Romanos, ad Galatas, ad Ephesios, in quibus totus in certa-mine positus est; & videbitis eum in
units.tr: This manner of writing is also illustrated in the same place by Jerome, following the example of the Latin Fathers Tertullian, Cyprian, Minucius, Victorinus, Lactantius and Hilary; indeed, also by Paul himself, in these words: Read his Epistles, and especially those to the Romans, the Galatians and the Ephesians, in which he is wholly engaged in the contest; and you will see him in

units.la: testimoniis quæ sunt de Veteri Testa-mento quàm prudens, quàm dissimula-tor sit ejus quod agit. Hæc quidem verbosè allata sunt; sed mihi res cum homine qui verbis magis pugnat quàm rationibus, quique longo ver-borum circuitu & quasi ex suggestu declamitans, simplicioribus conetur imponere. Jam modestissimus Vos-sius in Patres tanquàm minùs Chri-stianos promat caninam suam elo-quentiam; allatret Paulum, & ipsum Christum, quem scribit Euangelista finxisse longiùs ire.
units.tr: the testimonies taken from the Old Testament, how prudent and how dissembling he is about what he is doing. These things have been said at length, but I have to do with a man who fights more with words than with arguments, and who, by a long circuit of words and as if declaiming from a platform, tries to impose on simpler readers. Now the most modest Vossius, in order to show the Fathers as less than Christian, lets loose his dog-like eloquence; he barks at Paul and at Christ himself, whom he writes the Evangelist invented, and goes further.

units.la: Objectat iterum Vossius, frustra se relegari à Simonio, ad Postelli in-eptias, quasi, inquit, non sufficiant Simonianæ. Verùm Postelli in-eptiæ Vossianæ sunt, non Simonia-næ. Jam enim supra demonstratum fuit, ovum ovo similius non esse, quàm Postello Vossius similis est: uterque simili ratione nugatores & impostores in Prophetas transfor-mavit. Addit prætera eodem loco, id omne quod Simonius adduxit de Li-bris Canonicis, Hagiographis & A-pocryphis nihil facere ad institutum, cùm debuisset ex antiquioribus Ju-dæis vel Christianis depromere te-stimonia, quibus ista Scripturarum divisio quam commentus est Aqui-la, aut Judæi qui ejus ætate vixe-runt, confirmaretur.
units.tr: Vossius objects again that he is wrongly referred by Simon to the follies of Postel, as if Simon's own arguments were not enough. But the follies are Vossius's, not Simon's. For it has already been shown above that an egg is no more like an egg than Vossius is like Postel: each in the same way turned trifling impostors into prophets. He adds, moreover, in the same place, that everything Simon adduced about the Canonical, Hagiographical and Apocryphal Books has nothing to do with the question, since he ought to have drawn from the more ancient Jews or Christians testimonies by which that division of the Scriptures, which Aquila devised, or the Jews who lived in his time, would be confirmed.

units.la: Verùm ea quæ ex prisci's Ecclesiæ Patribus de Scripturis Canonicis, Hagiographis & Apocryphis Simo-nius retulit, valde faciunt ad insti-tutum, cùm demonstrent ridiculum esse Vossium, qui Librorum Sacro-rum divisionem ab antiquis Patribus approbatam rejiciat; quia putat illam à Judæis odio Christianæ Religio-nis nis inventam fuisse. Solus igitur hoc in negotio sapit Vossius, Patresque cum Aquila judaizant. Sed etsi supponamus Aquilam accepisse hanc divisionem à Judæis, nihil planè hoc facit ad rem: à quibus enim aliis, quàm à Judæis, Librorum Sacrorum, quos ex Ebræo Græcos fecit, divisionem accipere poterat Aquila? Ille Ebræos Codices presfius secutus, eos convertit in Græcum sermonem, quales tunc à Judæis legebantur. Divisionem autem illam, postquam Græci facti sunt libri Judaici, autoritate suâ Patres approbarunt. Voces quæ antea solis Judæis cognitæ erant, ubi Græcæ factæ sunt, in usum Ecclesiæ transfierunt, quas unus Vossius respuit, quia videt illarum beneficio nugatores suos Prophetas albo Prophetarum expungi.
units.tr: But what Simon brought forward from the ancient Fathers of the Church about the Canonical, Hagiographical and Apocryphal Scriptures bears very much on the question, since it shows how ridiculous it is for Vossius to reject a division of the Sacred Books approved by the ancient Fathers, because he thinks it was invented by the Jews out of hatred for the Christian religion. Vossius alone, then, is wise in this business, and the Fathers judaize along with Aquila. But even if we suppose that Aquila received this division from the Jews, it makes nothing at all to the point: from whom other than the Jews could Aquila receive the division of the Sacred Books, which he turned from Hebrew into Greek? He followed the Hebrew manuscripts most closely and translated them into Greek, such as the Jews then read. The Fathers, however, after the Jewish books had been made Greek, approved that division by their own authority. Words which had formerly been known only to the Jews, once they had been made Greek, passed into the use of the Church; Vossius alone rejects them, because he sees that by their help his trifling prophets are struck from the roll of the prophets.

units.la: Sed regerit Vossius, admisså hac Judæorum divisione, Euangelia præcipuam Sacrarum Literarum partem libris Scripturæ non annumerari. Quasi verò Ecclesia etiam Novi Testamenti libros à Synagoga recipere debuerit. Mirificus iste homo semper ineptit, nihilque affert quod ad rem faciat. Similiter Sixti Senensis sententiam improbat, Scripturæ libros dividentis in Protocanonicos & Deuterocanonicos; quia voces istæ, autore Vossio, confictæ sunt contra usum linguæ Græcæ. Sic disertulus Vossius vocem quoque Hagiographa & alias rejicit, quæ tamen ipsis Patribus non displicuerunt. In eo verò quod subjicit, nos rectius facturos, si primam Christianorum divisionem sequamur, non habet Simonium dissentientem, qui autor est ut retineatur librorum ordo qui in Græcis & Latinis Bibliis apparet, quia prior est & melior, atque Ecclesiæ tam Orientalis quàm Occidentalis autoritate comprobatus; aitque audiendos non esse Ebraistas, qui secuti Judæorum Magistros, priscum illum ordinem in edendis Græcis Latinisque Bibliorum Exemplaribus evertunt. Sed adduci non potuit Simonius, ut crederet cum Vossio, novam à prisicis Judæis inventam fuisse eo consilio librorum Scripturæ divisionem, ut Christianæ Religioni adversarentur: nam qualiscunque fuerit librorum Scripturæ Sacræ distributio, nihil de eorum integritate minuitur.
units.tr: But Vossius retorts that, if this Jewish division is admitted, the Gospels, the principal part of the Sacred Letters, are not counted among the books of Scripture. As if the Church ought to receive the books of the New Testament from the Synagogue! This marvellous fellow always talks nonsense and brings forward nothing that bears on the matter. In the same way he disapproves the opinion of Sixtus of Siena, who divides the books of Scripture into Protocanonical and Deuterocanonical, because, on Vossius's authority, these words were coined contrary to the usage of the Greek language. So the clever Vossius also rejects the word Hagiographa and others, which nevertheless did not displease the Fathers themselves. As to his added claim that we would do better to follow the first Christian division, Simon is not in disagreement: he recommends that the order of books which appears in the Greek and Latin Bibles be kept, because it is earlier and better and approved by the authority of the Church, both Eastern and Western; and he says that the Hebraists should not be listened to, who, following the masters of the Jews, overturn that ancient order in the printing of the Greek and Latin copies of the Bible. But Simon could not be brought to believe with Vossius that this division of the books of Scripture was devised by the ancient Jews with the purpose of opposing the Christian religion; for whatever the distribution of the Sacred Scriptures may be, nothing is taken away from their integrity.

units.la: Carpit præterea. Vossius Simonium, qui in duobus Hieronymi locis vocem Hagiographa mutandam esse in Apocrypha censuerit contra omnium Exemplarium fidem. Loca autem illa sumpta sunt ex illius Præfationibus in Tobiam & Judith, ubi doctissimus ille Pater libros Tobiæ & Judith ab Ebræis inter Apocrypha recenseri affirmat. Fatetur quidem Simonius, libros manu exaratos cum vulgatis libris conspirare; sed ait lectionis vitium ex ipsius Hieronymi verbis manifestè deprehendi, qui scribat libros hosce catalogo Divinarum Scripturarum à Judæis expunctos fuisse, ac repositos inter Hagiographa. Constat autem ex ipsomet Hieronymo, à Judæis nunquam expunctos fuisse Libros Hagiographos è catalogo Scripturarum Divinarum, cum eos in tertia Librorum Sacrorum parte collocent, sitque extra controversiam Libros Hagiographos etiam à Judæis Scripturis Canonicis adscriptos fuisse. Rectè itaque Simonius observavit Hieronymi verba isto loco casticastiganda esse, licet desint Codices MSS. qui lectionem suam confirmant: quia sic legendum esse docent ipsius Hieronymi verba, si paulò attentiùs considerentur.
units.tr: Vossius also carps at Simon, who thought that in two places of Jerome the word Hagiographa should be changed to Apocrypha, against the faith of all the copies. Those passages, however, are taken from that Father's Prefaces to Tobit and Judith, where that most learned Father affirms that the books of Tobit and Judith were counted by the Hebrews among the Apocrypha. Simon does admit that the manuscript books agree with the printed books; but he says that the error of reading is clearly detected from Jerome's own words, since he writes that these books were struck by the Jews from the catalogue of the Divine Scriptures and placed among the Hagiographa. It is, however, plain from Jerome himself that the Jews never struck the Hagiographa from the catalogue of the Divine Scriptures, since they place them in the third part of the Sacred Books; and it is beyond dispute that the Jews also counted the Hagiographa among the Canonical Scriptures. Simon therefore rightly observed that Jerome's words in this place should be corrected, even though the manuscripts that confirm the reading are lacking; for Jerome's own words, if they are considered a little more carefully, teach that it must be read thus.

units.la: Instat tamen Vossius, qui ait Apocrypha mutari non potuisse in Hagiographa, quia notiora vocabula non permutantur ignotioribus. Sed voces Apocrypha & Hagiographa æqualiter notæ sunt. Illius autem mutationis ratio est evidens. Scribæ videlicet, qui libros Tobiæ & Judith etiam ab Hieronymo inter Hagiographos reponi cognoverunt, pro voce Apocrypha reposuere Hagiographa, non attendentes Hieronymum his locis non ex sua & Ecclesiæ sententia loqui, sed ex mente Judæorum.
units.tr: Vossius nevertheless presses the point, saying that Apocrypha could not have been changed into Hagiographa, because better-known words are not replaced by less-known ones. But the words Apocrypha and Hagiographa are equally well known. The reason for that change, however, is evident. Namely, the scribes, who knew that Jerome too placed the books of Tobit and Judith among the Hagiographa, put Hagiographa in place of Apocrypha, not noticing that Jerome in these places speaks not from his own opinion and that of the Church, but from the mind of the Jews.

units.la: Jam ad solitas Vossius declamationes relabitur, ut novum & hactenus inauditum Librorum Sacrorum ordinem, quem introducere voluit, adstruat. Riserat eum Simonius, quòd recurrisset ad veteres Ebraeos, ut probaret Judæorum libros olim non descriptos fuisse in Codicibus, sed in voluminibus & pellibus continuatis; cùm etiam ætate nostrâ Judæi in suis Synagogis ejusmodi voluminibus utantur; neque tamen illi Legem in quinque partiuntur volumina, uti fecit Vossius, qui nunc rogat, an soli Ebræi justam voluminum mensuram ignorarunt. De eo solùm quod in Synagogis olim à Judæis observatum fuerit Simonius locutus est, priscumque illum Synagogarum usum ex eo confirmavit, quòd eumdem ætate nostrâ retineant. Certum est autem Judæos in volumina quæ Synagogarum usui serviunt nihil ferè mutationis invexisse, cùm etiam post inventa à Tiberiadensibus Magistris puncta, quorum ope verborum Ebraicorum lectio expeditior facta est, nihil prorsus in Synagogarum voluminibus immutatum fuerit. Sed missis hisce minutiis venio ad alia quæ majoris sunt momenti.
units.tr: Now Vossius slides back into his usual declamations, in order to establish the new and hitherto unheard-of order of the Sacred Books which he wished to introduce. Simon had laughed at him because he had recourse to the ancient Hebrews to prove that the books of the Jews were once not written in codices but in continuous rolls and skins; although even in our own day the Jews use rolls of this kind in their synagogues, and yet they do not divide the Law into five rolls, as Vossius did, who now asks whether the Hebrews alone were ignorant of the proper measure of rolls. Simon spoke only of what was once observed by the Jews in the synagogues, and he confirmed that ancient custom of the synagogues from the fact that they retain it in our own day. It is certain, moreover, that the Jews introduced almost no change into the rolls which serve the use of the synagogues; for even after the points were devised by the Masters of Tiberias, by whose help the reading of the Hebrew words was made easier, nothing whatever was changed in the synagogue rolls. But setting these trifles aside, I come to other matters of greater weight.

units.la: Objecerat Vossius, ab Aquila & Judæis odio hebdomadum Danielis, illum Prophetam extremo penè inter Hagiographos loco rejectum fuisse. Respondit Simonius, de ordine quem in Judæorum libris Daniel teneat disputandum non esse; quia constat Judæos æquè fidem habere Danielis de Messia vaticiniis, atque ipsi Christiani fidem habent. Quid ad hæc vitilitigator Vossius? Profectò si hoc verum esset, non essent Judæi. Quasi verò ex eo quòd Judæi æquè ac Christiani Danielis vaticinia de Messia exponant, sequatur illa eodem modo ab utrisque explicari. Simonius firmissimis rationibus probavit, nihil à Judæis de autoritate Davidis & Danielis minui, etsi illos in Prophetarum classe non recenseant; quia in his libris, æquè ac Christiani, agnoscunt vaticinia de Christo contineri. Cur igitur Simonii rationibus, quæ ex Judæorum ipsorum libris depromptæ sunt, Vossius non respondit? Sed Hieronymus, inquit, & Theodoretus testantur Judæos negare Danielem fuisse Prophetam. At quo sensu id verum sit ostendit Simonius, qui putat litem hanc tantùm esse de nomine inter Christianos & Judæos, quæ facili negotio conciliari possit; cùm ipsemet Hieronymus testetur Danielem recenseri à Judæis inter Apocryphos Libros, qui etiam Divini sunt, inferioris tamen ordinis quàm libri Prophetici; quo etiam modo Judæi agnoscunt libros Propheticos ordine & dignitate inferiores esse libris Mosis. Nemo tamen inde conficiet, unum Mosem apud Judæos Spiritu Sancto afflatum fuisse.
units.tr: Vossius had objected that, through Aquila and the Jews' hatred of Daniel's weeks, that Prophet had been thrust almost to the last place among the Hagiographa. Simon replied that the order which Daniel holds in the books of the Jews is not to be disputed, because it is established that the Jews put as much faith in Daniel's prophecies about the Messiah as Christians themselves do. What does the quibbler Vossius answer to this? Surely, if this were true, the Jews would not be Jews. As if it followed, from the fact that the Jews, like the Christians, expound Daniel's prophecies about the Messiah, that they are explained in the same way by both. Simon proved with the firmest arguments that the Jews diminish nothing of the authority of David and Daniel, although they do not count them in the class of the Prophets, because in these books, just as Christians do, they acknowledge that prophecies about Christ are contained. Why, then, did Vossius not answer Simon's arguments, which were drawn from the Jews' own books? But, he says, Jerome and Theodoret testify that the Jews deny that Daniel was a Prophet. In what sense that is true, however, Simon shows: he thinks this dispute is only about a name between Christians and Jews, and one that can be settled with little effort; since Jerome himself testifies that Daniel is counted by the Jews among the Apocryphal Books, which are also Divine, yet of a lower order than the Prophetic books, in the same way as the Jews acknowledge that the Prophetic books are lower in order and dignity than the books of Moses. Yet no one will conclude from this that Moses alone among the Jews was inspired by the Holy Spirit.

units.la: His & aliis pluribus cùm nihil habeat Vossius quod reponat, nugas agit;& quia non alios opinionum suarum testes laudare solet, quàm nugatores, profert Montaltum Judæum affirmantem, Danielem eâdem prorsus ratione quæ scripsit vidisse, atque asinam Balaami cernentem ea quæ ipse non videret Balaamus. Viderit ipse Vossius Latinissimus, quàm ineptè loquatur: verba enim illius indicant visam esse à Daniele asinam Balaami. Sed ista non moror, quia leviora sunt. Dixerim tantùm, si Vossius plus sciret Ebraicè quàm asina Balaami, Judæorum sententiam ex eorum libris hausisset, uti fecit Simonius, non ex nugatore.
units.tr: Having nothing to answer these and many other points, Vossius trifles. He usually cites none but triflers as witnesses for his opinions, so he brings forward the Jew Montaltus, who affirms that Daniel saw what he wrote in exactly the same way that Balaam saw, when Balaam did not see, the things his ass saw. Let the most Latin Vossius see how badly he expresses himself, for his words indicate that Balaam's ass was seen by Daniel. But I will not dwell on these points, since they are trivial. I would only say this: if Vossius knew Hebrew better than Balaam's ass, he would have drawn the Jews' opinion from their own books, as Simonius did, and not from a trifler.

units.la: Addit de Cetuvim opus non fuisse ut eum moneret Simonius; quia ipse scit Judæos sorbere simul & flare, atrumque albo permutare, si res postulet. Sed si res ita sit in eo de quo agitur argumento, cur non illud ex eorum libris demonstravit, maximè cùm Simonius hoc loco Vossium remiserit ad Judæorum libros, eumque rogaverit ut ex illis aliquid proferret quod sententiæ suæ faveat? Quæ enim mox subjungit de voce Cetuvim ridicula sunt, quasi eâ Judæi scriptiunculas intelligant ne quidem nomine librorum dignas. Quid enim ad rem facit grammatica observatio de vocabulo <bl>χεαφεῖον</bl>, quo, referente Vossio, Judæi olim usi fuerint, ut libros Cetuvim seu Hagiographos expri-
