units.tr: He adds that Simonius need not have warned him about Cetuvim, since he himself knows that Jews both sip and blow, and can exchange white for black if the matter requires it. But if this is so in the argument under discussion, why did he not demonstrate it from their books? This is especially so since Simonius, in this place, referred Vossius to the Jewish books and asked him to bring forward something from them that favours his view. What he goes on to say about the word Cetuvim is ridiculous, as if the Jews understood by it little writings not even worthy of the name of books. For what bearing does the grammatical observation about the word γραφεῖον have? According to Vossius, the Jews once used this word to express the books Cetuvim, or Hagiographa,

units.la: merent, si ex ipsismet Judæis manifestè probari possit, eos <bl>χεαφεῖων</bl> nomine intellexisse libros qui ab hominibus Spiritu Sancto afflatis scripti fuerint? Cur sensum vocis illius, quam putat ineptam & ab Aquila confictam, pervertit contra illorum mentem qui eâ utuntur? Nihil enim ipsis aliud fuit <bl>χεαφεῖον</bl>, quàm Ebraicum Cetub sive Scriptum. Sic quoque Christiani universam Sacram Scripturam vocant <bl>Βιβλία</bl> & Scripturam. An ideo minùs divina est, quia non appellatur Scriptura Divina. Sed bono Vossio nihil aliud subest quod Judæis opponat, quàm subtilitates quas depromit è Grammatica.
units.tr: if it can be clearly proved from the Jews themselves that by the name γραφεῖον they understood books written by men inspired by the Holy Spirit? Why does he twist the meaning of that word, which he thinks is absurd and was coined by Aquila, against the mind of those who use it? For to them γραφεῖον was nothing other than the Hebrew Cetub, that is, Writing. Christians too call the whole of Holy Scripture "Books" and "Scripture". Is it therefore less divine because it is not called Divine Scripture? But good Vossius has nothing else to set against the Jews except the subtleties he draws from grammar.

units.la: Iterum Vossius objicit Talmudis verba, quæ sic habent. Bonum est ut evellatur litera de Lege, & sanctificetur nomen Dei. Ait Simonium, qui Talmudistam Vossium riserat, ironiis valde delectari. Sed quis non rideat hominem, qui cùm tam imperitè Rabbinorum libros tractaverit, nunc adeat libros Talmudicos paucissimis etiam Judæis cognitos? Dixerat Simonius, hanc locutionem & similes quæ occurrunt in Talmude ad Sacrorum Librorum corruptionem trahi non posse, sed ad diversas illarum explicationes. Eadem verò Talmudis verba hîc repetens Vossius, Simonii mentem ita interpretatur, ac si crediderit non licitum quidem fuisse cuilibet è plebe verba Scripturæ immutare, sed solis magni Synedrii Assessoribus. Verùm ipsa hoc loco Simonii verba evincunt illum de sanctionibus tantùm ferendis locutum fuisse, non de Sacrorum Librorum mutatione; idque manifestè apparet ex R. Ben Maimon & Autoris libri
units.tr: Again Vossius objects with words from the Talmud, which read thus: "It is good that a letter be torn out of the Law, so that the name of God may be sanctified." He says that Simonius, who mocked Vossius the Talmudist, takes great delight in irony. But who would not laugh at a man who, having handled the rabbinic books so unskilfully, now approaches Talmudic books known to very few even among the Jews? Simonius had said that this expression, and similar ones that occur in the Talmud, cannot be taken as a corruption of the Holy Books, but refer to various explanations of them. Yet by repeating the same Talmudic words here, Vossius interprets Simonius' mind as if he believed that it was lawful not for any common person to alter the words of Scripture, but only for the members of the great Sanhedrin. Simonius' own words in this place, however, prove that he spoke only of enacting decrees, not of changing the Holy Books. This is plainly evident from Rabbi Ben Maimon and the author of the book

units.la: Talmud. Bonum est ut evellatur litera de Lege & sanctificetur nomen Dei (marginal note, right) Cozri testimoniis, quibus suam ea de re sententiam illustravit. Hanc ferendarum sanctionum potestatem penès Synedrii magni Assessores fuisse, nemo nisi novator & è Socini discipulis negaverit.
units.tr: Talmud: "It is good that a letter be torn out of the Law and the name of God be sanctified" (marginal note), together with the testimonies of Cozri, by which Simonius illustrated his opinion on this matter. That the power of enacting such decrees belonged to the members of the great Sanhedrin, no one would deny except an innovator and a disciple of Socinus.

units.la: Alia dein Simonii verba subjicit Vossius, quæ ita obscura esse putat, ut ne quidem ea credat à Simonio posse explicari. Miror hominem qui spiritu Sibyllino afflatus res obscurissimas & à nostris temporibus remotissimas intueatur, ea quæ explicatu facilia sunt non intellexisse; in hunc enim locum manifesto Typographi errore irrepsit illum pro illic. Curabit Simonius ut Opusculum illud quod ipse non edidit, è suo Codice, qui castigatior est & auctior, iterum lucem aspiciat. Verborum autem Simonii is est sensus; in allato Talmudis loco agi de litera, imò de dictione vel sententia aliqua Scripturæ, ubi verba ejusdem Scripturæ exponuntur; minimè verò de mutandis eradendisque ipsius Contextûs literis aut dictionibus. Sed quia Sibyllista Vossius Talmudico spiritu afflatus non fuit, ejusmodi Talmudicas locutiones non potuit comprehendere, quæ tamen sæpius in istis libris occurrunt. Sic dicunt Talmudistæ אל תקראי כן / כן אלא תקראי. Ne legas sic; sed legas sic. Nemo judicio præditus inde concludet Judæos Sacri Codicis lectionem pervertisse: sed Magistri illi qui valde allegoriis delectantur, varias literarum Scripturæ fingunt lectiones, ut diversos ex fictis illis lectionibus sensus eliciant. Sed istæ & similes locutionum formulæ in Scripturæ Sacræ eversionem trahi non possunt, nisi ab imperitis qui Judæorum libros nunquam tractarunt. Qui in re isti homines Talmudistis ipsis sunt ineptiores. Quantum autem Judæi ab ista Sacrorum Librorum depravatione alieni fuerint, docet Trypho Judæus, quem Justinus Martyr introducit dicentem, rem istam incredibilem esse, magisque Judæos ab illa abhorrere, quàm à vituli fabricatione. ᾿Απίστω ἐοικε· φοβερώτερον γὰρ ἐςι τ̑ μοχθηρίας.
units.tr: Vossius next adds other words of Simonius, which he thinks are so obscure that he does not believe Simonius himself could explain them. I am surprised that a man who, as if inspired by a Sibyl, looks into the most obscure matters, and those most remote from our own times, did not understand things that are easy to explain. By a manifest printer's error "illum" has crept into this place in place of "illic". Simonius will see to it that that little work, which he himself did not publish, comes to light again from his own manuscript, which is more correct and fuller. The sense of Simonius' words is this: the Talmudic passage cited concerns a letter, or rather a word or some sentence of Scripture, where the words of that same Scripture are explained; it by no means concerns altering or erasing the letters or words of the context itself. But because Vossius, the Sibylline prophet, was not inspired with the Talmudic spirit, he could not grasp such Talmudic expressions, which nevertheless occur very often in those books. Thus the Talmudists say: "Do not read it so; but read it so" [אל תקראי כן / כן אלא תקראי]. No one of sound judgment will conclude from this that the Jews corrupted the reading of the Sacred Codex. Rather, those masters who greatly delight in allegories invent various readings of the letters of Scripture, so that they may draw different senses from these invented readings. But such expressions and similar formulas of speech cannot lead to the overthrow of Holy Scripture, except among the unskilled who have never handled the Jewish books. In this matter such men are more foolish than the Talmudists themselves. How far the Jews were from this corruption of the Sacred Books is shown by Trypho the Jew, whom Justin Martyr introduces as saying that such a thing is incredible, and that the Jews shrink from it more than from the making of the calf. "It seems incredible, for it is more dreadful than wickedness" [ἀπίστῳ ἔοικε· φοβερώτερον γὰρ ἔστι τῆς μοχθηρίας].

units.la: Morinum hic non moror, à quo Vossius locum hunc Talmudis & alia omnia quæ apud ipsum Rabbinologiam sapiunt, deprompsit. Laudo quidem Morini eruditionem, laboremque illius ac patientiam in evolvendis Judæorum libris admiror: sed eum fuisse judicii pauci illius scripta ostendunt. Vossius, qui multa ab illo sumpsit, illius errores multiplicavit, ut ab eo aliquâ ratione discrepare videretur. Optat ipse Vossius, ut etiam Simonius Morini similis fiat. Verùm licet Vossio μωρα̑ίνειν; quod abest à Simonio.
units.tr: I will not dwell here on Morinus, from whom Vossius drew this Talmudic passage and all the other things in him that smell of rabbinical learning. I indeed praise Morinus' erudition and admire his labour and patience in working through the Jewish books; but his writings show that he had little judgment. Vossius, who took much from him, multiplied his errors, so that he might seem to differ from him in some way. Vossius himself wishes that Simonius might become like Morinus. But although Vossius may play the fool [μωραίνειν], which is far from Simonius...

units.la: Quæ autem mox subjungit Vossius de Simonii sententia, qui cum Cappello aliisque viris doctis existimaverit, linguam Ebræam in captivitate Babylonica deperditam fuisse, ea omnia vana sunt & inutilia; cùm inde non concluserit Simonius, LXX. Interpretes linguæ Ebraicæ ignaros fuisse, uti fingit Vossius, cui profecto nihil solidi subesset quod posset reponere Simonio, nisi verba ejus perverteret. Negavit itaque Simonius, linguam Ebraicam temporibus LXX. Interpretum superstitem fuisse apud Judæos & vernaculam, cùm illam in captivitate Babylonica dedidicerint, etiam non diffitente Vossio: constat enim Judæos postea Chaldaicè
units.tr: As for what Vossius goes on to say about Simonius' opinion, that with Cappellus and other learned men he thought the Hebrew language was lost in the Babylonian captivity, all of this is empty and useless. Simonius did not conclude from it that the Seventy translators were ignorant of the Hebrew language, as Vossius pretends. Vossius has nothing solid to set against Simonius, unless he perverts his words. Simonius therefore denied that the Hebrew language survived among the Jews as a living, vernacular tongue in the time of the Seventy translators, since they had unlearned it during the Babylonian captivity, and Vossius does not deny it. For it is certain that the Jews afterwards spoke Chaldee,

units.la: Trypho apud Justin. Martyr. daicè locutos fuisse, non Ebraicè. Non inde tamen sequitur LXX. Interpretes ignorasse sermonem Ebraicum, qui, ut multis probat Simonius, in exilio Babyloniensi penes Prophetas, Sacerdotes ac viros principes remanserit, quique non solùm usque ad LXX. Seniorum tempora apud illos servatus fuerit; sed & seculis posterioribus apud Doctores: quippe Lex Mosis in Scholis & Synagogis semper Ebraicè lecta est.
units.tr: Trypho in Justin Martyr: they spoke Chaldee, not Hebrew. Yet it does not follow from this that the Seventy translators were ignorant of the Hebrew language. As Simonius proves from many sources, that language remained during the Babylonian exile among the Prophets, the priests and the leading men, and it was preserved among them not only until the time of the Seventy elders, but also in later centuries among the teachers. Indeed, the Law of Moses was always read in Hebrew in the schools and synagogues.

units.la: Jam negat Vossius, se unquam talia de Josepho somniasse quæ ipsi tribuit Simonius, quasi dixerit Josephum Legem Moysis in Synagoga Ebraicè interpretatum fuisse. Aperta tamen sunt illius verba, nec mirum est illum hominem etiam vigilantem somniare, apud quem Josephus modò Ebraicè loquitur, modò Chaldaicè, modò Syriacè, modò Arabicè. Brevi, si Vossio placet, idem Josephus loquetur Hibernicè. Quod verò addit Vossius, Josephi verba initio belli Judaici nec à Simonio nec ab aliis Interpretibus intellecta fuisse, non est ad rem, quia Simonius nihil è Josepho attulit, quàm illud quod ex eo ipse Vossius deprompserat: sed & solum Vossium verba Josephi non intellexisse mox ostendam. Dixit igitur Vossius, Josephum historiam belli Judaici, antequàm Græcè scriberet, linguâ Ebraicâ edidisse. Nunc hoc ipsum negat Vossius, qui semper loquitur pugnantia. Tamen sic ille respondet Hornio, qui objecerat Josephum Ebraicè imperitum fuisse. Ut tamen aliquid dicere vide aris, vide quàm stulta promas, Flavium Josephum omnium sui seculi Hebraeorum longè eruditissimum, qui
units.tr: Now Vossius denies that he ever dreamed the things about Josephus that Simonius attributes to him, as if he had said that Josephus interpreted the Law of Moses in Hebrew in the synagogue. Yet his words are plain, and it is no wonder that this man dreams even when awake, for in his eyes Josephus now speaks Hebrew, now Chaldee, now Syriac, now Arabic. In short, if it pleases Vossius, the same Josephus will soon speak Irish. As for what Vossius adds, that Josephus' words at the beginning of the Jewish War were understood neither by Simonius nor by other interpreters, this is beside the point. Simonius brought nothing from Josephus except what Vossius himself had drawn from him, and I will show shortly that Vossius alone did not understand Josephus' words. Vossius therefore said that Josephus published the history of the Jewish War in the Hebrew language before he wrote it in Greek. Now Vossius denies this very thing, for he always speaks in contradictions. Yet he thus replies to Hornius, who had objected that Josephus was ignorant of Hebrew: "So that you may seem to say something, see how foolish a thing you put forward: Flavius Josephus, by far the most learned of all the Hebrews of his age, who..."

units.la: Legem Moysis in Synagoga Hebraicè interpretatus est, qui historiam belli Judaici, antequàm Græcè scriberet, linguâ Hebraâ edidit, uti ipse testatur; hunc, inquam, Josephum Hebraicè nescivisse. Dein paucis interjectis hæc regerit modestissimus Vossius adversus Hornium. Ullumne majus insciitia & impudentia exemplum possit excogitari, quàm id quod hic denuò ostendere conatur, Flavium Josephum nescivisse linguam patriam, & ne quidem inspexisse Codicem Hebraicum? Tunc igitur Josephus, teste Vossio, loquebatur Ebraicè, patriusque illius sermo erat Ebraicus; de hoc enim sermone cum Hornio disputavit, qui Josephum illius fuisse imperitum assereret. Verùm illud Josephi testimonium de sermone Syriaco sive Chaldaico intelligendum esse rectè monuit Simonius, cùm tunc sermo Ebraicus apud Judæos vernaculus non esset.
units.tr: He who interpreted the Law of Moses in the synagogue in Hebrew, and who published his history of the Jewish War in the Hebrew tongue before writing it in Greek, as he himself attests: this Josephus, I say, did not know Hebrew. Then, after a few words, the most modest Vossius replies to Horn as follows: Can any greater example of ignorance and impudence be devised than what he here again attempts to show, that Flavius Josephus did not know his native language, and did not even look at the Hebrew text? So, according to Vossius, Josephus did speak Hebrew, and that was his native tongue. For it was about this language that he disputed with Horn, who asserted that Josephus was ignorant of it. But Simonius rightly pointed out that Josephus's testimony must be understood of the Syriac or Chaldee language, since Hebrew was then no longer the vernacular among the Jews.

units.la: Sapiens Vossius, qui mutatur ut luna, neminem esse affirmat qui tempore Apostolorum & Josephi in Imperio Romano linguæ Syriacæ meminerit, quia in Syria Palæstina lingua Græca erat vernacula. Sed si ita res se habet, quomodo Josephus linguam Ebræam sive Syriacam appellat sermonem patrium? Quomodo Christus, ipsomet Vossio referente, Syriacè cum muliere Samaritana collocutus est? Cuidam enim Magistello, qui Vossium reprehenderat, quòd dixisset Christum cum Samaritana muliere Ebraicè collocutum esse, objicienti debuisse dici Syriacè, sic respondet modestissimus Vossius. Nescit fatuus eamdem olim fuisse linguam Syriacam & Ebraicam: adeo- que
units.tr: The wise Vossius, who changes like the moon, affirms that no one in the time of the Apostles and of Josephus, in the Roman Empire, made mention of the Syriac tongue, because in Syria and Palestine Greek was the vernacular. But if that is so, how does Josephus call the Hebrew or Syriac language his native speech? How did Christ, as Vossius himself reports, converse in Syriac with the Samaritan woman? For when a certain little schoolmaster, who had criticised Vossius for saying that Christ spoke Hebrew with the Samaritan woman, objected that it should have been said Syriac, the most modest Vossius answered him thus. The fool does not know that Syriac and Hebrew were once the same language, and so

units.la: Voss. Castigat. ad Script. tum Hornii.
units.tr: Vossius, Castigationes against Horn.

units.la: Voss. in Epist. ad Andr. Colv.
units.tr: Vossius, in his letter to Andreas Colvius.

units.la: que nunc Josephus loquetur etiam Syriacè.
units.tr: so now Josephus will also speak Syriac.

units.la: Jam longè oculatior factus Vossius negat Josephum etiam Syriacè locutum, sed putat patrium illius sermonem fuisse quamdam linguam Chaldaicam, quam ipse ignorat, sed quæ erat lingua vernacula illorum Barbarorum qui extra fines Romani Imperii trans Euphratem viverent. Miror profectò hominis istius ingenium, qui tot commenta effutiat quæ nihil faciant ad institutum, quique suo seipsum gladio jugulet. Si enim verum est sermonem vernaculum istorum Trans-Euphratensium Chaldaicum fuisse, uti quoque verum esse existimo, necesse quoque est patrium Josephi sermonem fuisse Chaldaicum, cum non alium habuerit sermonem patrium quàm illum, quo etiam, teste Vossio, historiam suam conscripsit. Illud autem confirmat Simonii sententiam, qui nomine Syriaci sermonis, qui tunc apud Judæos vernaculus erat Hierosolymis & in locis vicinioribus, nihil aliud intellexerit quàm sermonem illum Chaldaicum, quem cum viris doctis appellat modò Syriacum, modò Chaldaicum, modò Chaldaico-Syriacum, aitque eum sermonem qui tot diversis nominibus indicatur, non alium fuisse, quàm illum quem Judæorum Majores è Babylone reportaverant; quique alius esse non potuit quàm Chaldaicus.
units.tr: Now, having become much more clear-sighted, Vossius denies that Josephus spoke Syriac, but thinks that his native speech was a certain Chaldee language, which he himself does not know, but which was the vernacular of those barbarians who lived beyond the Euphrates, outside the borders of the Roman Empire. I am truly amazed at the talent of this man, who pours out so many inventions that contribute nothing to the matter in hand, and who cuts his own throat with his own sword. For if it is true that the vernacular of those beyond the Euphrates was Chaldee, as I too think it is true, then it must also follow that Josephus's native speech was Chaldee, since he had no other native speech than that in which, as Vossius himself says, he wrote his history. This in turn confirms the opinion of Simonius, who, under the name of the Syriac language, which was then the vernacular of the Jews at Jerusalem and in the neighbouring regions, understood nothing other than that Chaldee speech, which he variously calls by learned men now Syriac, now Chaldee, now Chaldeo-Syriac; and he says that this speech, indicated by so many different names, was none other than that which the fathers of the Jews had brought back from Babylon, and which could be nothing other than Chaldee.

units.la: Quis credat Josephum libros de bello Judaico, quos se Ebraicè edidisse testatur, non scripsisse Judæis in Imperio Romano viventibus, sed solis Trans-Euphratensibus? Quasi Josephus, qui tunc de scribenda nationis suæ historia patrio & vernaculo sermone cogitabat, ad eos solùm animum suum applicuerit, qui Parthicæ Ditioni obnoxii erant. Hoc quidem viris judicio præditis minùs credibile videbitur; sed bonus Vossius nihil amat nisi quod est distortum & parum credibile. Id tamen rectè se confecisse putat, si dixerit, Josephi verba à nemine hactenus intellecta fuisse. Ineptissimè, inquit, verba Josephi Interpretes reddidere, ac si οἱ ἄνω Χάρ-Χαρροι sint Barbari qui retrò fuerunt, & Josephus in usum jam olim defunctorum istâm condidisset historiam. Sed vereor ne hîc solus ineptiat Vossius; hanc tamen addit novæ suæ interpretationis rationem, οἱ ἄνω Χάρχαροι sunt superioris Continentis Barbari: sic οἱ ἄνω ἐπαρχίαι sunt provinciæ quæ longiùs absunt à mari, ut οἱ κάτω ἐπαρχίαι mari propiores. Ex vocum ambiguitate semper quærit Vossius effugia. Notum est omnibus, Græcum ἄνω & locum & tempus denotare. Hîc Vossius illud contra manifestum Josephi sensum pro loco sumendum esse existimat: at pro tempore sumendum esse res ipsa indicat; adeoque hæc Josephi verba, οἱ ἄνω Χάρχαροι, rectè ab Interpretibus reddita sunt Barbari qui retro fuerunt. Neque tamen Josephus historiam suam condidit in usum jam olim defunctorum, sed Barbarorum, id est hominum gentis suæ, qui à prisci s temporibus Palæstinam incolebant, & quibus vernaculus erat sermo Chaldaicus sive Syriacus, quem Josephus patrium appellat. Hîc igitur dictio οἱ ἄνω tempus denotans significat antiquos Regionis illius incolas. Josephus autem eamdem Judaici belli historiam, quam primùm Chaldaico seu patrio sermone ediderat in usum gentis suæ, postea Græcè scripsit in eorum usum qui Græcè scirent, quia scilicet vix alia reperiebatur lingua in toto Imperio Romano; ita ut Romæ etiam plerique callerent Græcas Literas. Hic est genuinus Josephi verborum sensus, neque alius ea legenti primo aspectu sese offeret. In prima scilicet historiæ suæ editione Judæos instruxit, eosque magis qui in Syria Palæstina degebant, quàm Parthos, Babylonios, Arabas, Trans-Euphratenses atque Adiabenos; & ob hanc causam ait se patrio sermone scripsisse: in secunda verò editione Græco sermone conscriptâ, in animo habuit alias Imperii Romani gentes, quæ Græcè loquebantur, vel Græcè sciebant, instruere.
units.tr: Who could believe that Josephus did not write his books on the Jewish War, which he attests he published in Hebrew, for Jews living in the Roman Empire, but only for those beyond the Euphrates? As if Josephus, who was then thinking of writing the history of his nation in its native and vernacular speech, had applied his mind only to those who were subject to the Parthian dominion! This will seem less credible to men of sound judgment; but good Vossius loves nothing except what is twisted and scarcely credible. Yet he thinks he has done well if he says that no one has hitherto understood Josephus's words. Most foolishly, he says, have the interpreters rendered the words of Josephus, as if οἱ ἄνω Χάρχαροι [hoi ano Charcharoi] were the barbarians who lived back there, and as if Josephus had composed his history for the use of men long dead. But I fear that Vossius alone is foolish here; he nevertheless adds this reason for his new interpretation: οἱ ἄνω Χάρχαροι [hoi ano Charcharoi] are the barbarians of the upper continent, just as οἱ ἄνω ἐπαρχίαι [hoi ano eparchiai] are the provinces that lie farther from the sea, and οἱ κάτω ἐπαρχίαι [hoi kato eparchiai] the provinces nearer the sea. Vossius always seeks escape in the ambiguity of words. It is known to everyone that the Greek ἄνω [ano] denotes both place and time. Here Vossius thinks that, contrary to Josephus's plain meaning, it must be taken of place; but the matter itself shows that it must be taken of time, and so these words of Josephus, οἱ ἄνω Χάρχαροι [hoi ano Charcharoi], were rightly rendered by the interpreters as the barbarians who were back then. Nor did Josephus compose his history for the use of men long dead, but for barbarians, that is, men of his own nation, who from ancient times had inhabited Palestine, and for whom the vernacular speech was Chaldee or Syriac, which Josephus calls his native tongue. Here, then, the word οἱ ἄνω [hoi ano], denoting time, means the ancient inhabitants of that region. Josephus, however, after he had first published the same history of the Jewish War in Chaldee or his native speech for the use of his own nation, afterwards wrote it in Greek for the use of those who knew Greek, because scarcely any other language was to be found in the whole Roman Empire, so that even at Rome most people understood Greek letters. This is the genuine meaning of Josephus's words, and no other would present itself to one who reads them at first sight. Clearly, in the first edition of his history he instructed the Jews, and especially those who lived in Syria and Palestine rather than the Parthians, Babylonians, Arabs, those beyond the Euphrates and the Adiabeni; and for this reason he says he wrote in his native speech. But in the second edition, written in the Greek language, he intended to instruct the other peoples of the Roman Empire who spoke Greek or knew Greek.

units.la: Instat iterum Vossius, negatque Christum & Apostolos Hierosolymis Syriacè locutos fuisse: & ut audax est, ita affirmat audacter hanc sententiam semidoctorum esse & fanaticorum. Semidoctus igitur est ipse Vossius & fanaticus, quia scripsit Christum cum muliere Samaritana Syriacè collocutum fuisse, & voces quas Joannes Euangelista, Cap. 19. vocat Ebræas manifestè esse Syriacas. Verùm didicit Vossius à Judæis sorbere & flare. Fanatici, si qui sunt in Anglia qui hanc sententiam tueantur, non sunt hac in re fanatici, utpote qui cum Ecclesiæ Patribus, præstantissimis Theologis, virisque Ebraicè, Græcè ac Syriacè doctissimis hac in re consentiant. Sed fanaticus potiùs plerisque hominibus videbitur Vossius, qui solus sapiat.
units.tr: Vossius presses on again, and denies that Christ and the Apostles spoke Syriac at Jerusalem; and, being bold, he boldly affirms that this opinion belongs to half-scholars and fanatics. Therefore Vossius himself is a half-scholar and a fanatic, since he has written that Christ conversed with the Samaritan woman in Syriac, and that the words which the Evangelist John, in chapter 19, calls Hebrew are clearly Syriac. But Vossius has learned to slurp and blow from the Jews. If there are any fanatics in England who defend this opinion, they are not fanatics in this matter, since they agree in it with the Fathers of the Church, the most distinguished theologians, and men most learned in Hebrew, Greek and Syriac. But Vossius, who alone is wise, will seem to most men the fanatic.

units.la: Quod autem addit, in tota Ditione Romana nullum inveniri Scriptorem qui scripserit Syriacè, sed omnes Græcè scripsisse, vanum est ac futile: nam Josephus primam historiæ suæ editionem Syriaco sive Chaldaico sermone scriptam evulgavit: Matthæi quoque & Nazaræorum Euangelium Græcè conscriptum non fuit. Judæi qui non erant Hellenistæ nonnullos Scripturæ libros fecerunt Chaldaicos; unde etiam Hieronymi temporibus Judæi quibus utebatur præceptoribus Chaldaicè sciebant & loquebantur.
units.tr: As for his further statement, that no writer throughout the Roman Empire is to be found who wrote in Syriac, but that all wrote in Greek, it is empty and frivolous; for Josephus published the first edition of his history written in the Syriac or Chaldee language. Nor was the Gospel of Matthew and that of the Nazarenes written in Greek. Jews who were not Hellenists made some books of Scripture Chaldee; whence also in the time of Jerome the Jews who were his teachers knew and spoke Chaldee.

units.la: Iterum negat Vossius, linguam quæ Syriaca dicebatur fuisse inter Syros Romanæ Ditionis: sed rem aliter esse ostendunt manifestè complures Novi Testamenti voces. At regerit Vossius, malè in Euangelio & in Actibus Apostolorum per linguam Ebraicam intelligi Syriacam. Idem tamen Vossius contra Magistellum quemdam disputans, ineptos & fatuos eos appellat, qui nomine sermonis Ebraici in Novo Testamento alium intelligunt quàm Syriacum. Sit igitur modestissimus Vossius, seipso autore, ineptus & fatuus.
units.tr: Again Vossius denies that the language called Syriac was spoken among the Syrians of the Roman Empire; but several words of the New Testament clearly show that the matter is otherwise. Yet Vossius replies that it is wrong to understand the Hebrew language in the Gospel and in the Acts of the Apostles as Syriac. Yet the same Vossius, disputing against a certain little schoolmaster, calls foolish and stupid those who by the name of the Hebrew language in the New Testament understand anything other than Syriac. Let the most modest Vossius, then, by his own admission, be foolish and stupid.

units.la: Dein de nominibus lites intendit, cùm linguam illam dicendam esse Chaldæam asserit, quia sic Josephus & Philo locuti sunt. Verùm, ut omnem de nominibus disputationem Simonius tolleret, linguam istam modò appellat Chaldaicam, modò Syriacam, modò Chaldaico-Syriacam; ac demum ait illam esse quam Judæi è Babylone reportaverant. Syriacam eam appellavit, quia viri linguarum Orientalium callentissimi sic locuti sunt: tanta est enim inter lintlinguam Syriacam & Chaldaicam affinitas, ut etiam ætate nostrâ Syri, tam Maronitæ & Jacobitæ quàm Nestoriani, linguam quâ eorum libri conscripti sunt, quæ extra controversiam Syriaca est, Chaldaicam appellent. Sic Maronitarum Missale Romæ editum inscribitur Missale Chaldæum. Similiter Georgius Amira qui Maronita fuit, Grammaticam suam Syriacam, quæ Romæ quoque edita est, inscripsit Grammaticam Syriacam sive Chaldaicam. Neque etiam desunt in Sacris Literis exempla, quæ probent linguam Chaldæorum appellari Syriacam. Ita Danielis Cap. 2. verf. 4. Chaldæi dicuntur respondisse Regi תִּמְלְכָא, in Græca Versione Συριστὶ, & in Latina Syriacè. Chaldaicus igitur sermo sive Babylonius, de quo agitur, etiam secundùm ipsos Babylonios appellatur Syriacus. Verùm ea omnia quæ Vossius huc congessit de lingua Chaldaica, Syriacâ & Arabicâ, demonstrant illum ejusmodi linguarum minùs peritum fuisse. Neque enim aliud sibi propositum fuisse videtur, quàm inani verborum sono simplicioribus imponere. Postquàm tamen tot ineptias bonus Vossius effutiit, miris modis sibi applaudit. Valeat, inquit, Hierosolymitana ista Syriaca lingua, aquè vana ac Hellenistica. Valeant quoque cavillationes P. Simonii, cùm ex omnibus ne una quidem succedat. Sed potiori jure dixerim, Valeat & in æternum valeat bonus Vossius, qui ineptiis effutiendis ita assuetus est, ut seipso autore ineptus sit, fatuus & fanaticus; pudeat illum tot nugas & ineptias comminisci, ut ineptis & fatuis imponat.
units.tr: Then he stirs up quarrels about names, when he asserts that the language must be called Chaldean, because Josephus and Philo spoke so. But, so that Simonius might remove every dispute about names, he calls that language now Chaldee, now Syriac, now Chaldeo-Syriac, and finally says that it is the language the Jews brought back from Babylon. He called it Syriac because the men most skilled in Oriental languages have spoken so: for there is such affinity between the Syriac and Chaldee languages that even in our own age the Syrians, both the Maronites and the Jacobites as well as the Nestorians, call the language in which their books are written, which is beyond dispute Syriac, Chaldee. So the Maronite Missal printed at Rome is entitled the Chaldean Missal. Similarly, George Amira, who was a Maronite, entitled his Syriac grammar, which was also printed at Rome, Syriac or Chaldee Grammar. Nor are there lacking examples in Sacred Scripture which prove that the language of the Chaldeans is called Syriac. Thus in Daniel 2:4 the Chaldeans are said to have answered the king in Aramaic [malka, תִּמְלְכָא]; in the Greek version in Syriac [Syristi], and in the Latin in Syriac. So the Chaldee or Babylonian speech of which we are speaking is, even according to the Babylonians themselves, called Syriac. But all those things which Vossius has heaped together here about the Chaldee, Syriac and Arabic languages show that he was little skilled in languages of this kind. For he seems to have had no other aim than to impose on simple readers with the empty sound of words. Yet after uttering so many follies, good Vossius applauds himself in wonderful ways. Let, he says, that Jerusalem Syriac language be farewell, as vain as the Hellenistic. Let the cavillings of P. Simonius also be farewell, since not one of them succeeds. But with better right I would say: farewell, and forever farewell, to good Vossius, who is so accustomed to uttering follies that by his own admission he is foolish, stupid and a fanatic; let him be ashamed to invent so many trifles and absurdities in order to impose on the foolish and the stupid.

units.la: Denique Vossius his ineptiis alias accumulans addit, putare se non errare, si audacter (id est temerè) affirmaverit tempore Christi in omnibus Hierosolymitanis Synagogis, paucis forsan exceptis, quas Parthici & Arabici generis frequentarent Judæi, solas lectas fuisse quas LXX. Interpretes tradiderunt Scripturas, cùm sola iis Græca esset vernacula lingua. Sed longè verius cum Simonio dixerim, non quidem audacter, Judæos legisse Hierosolymis ex avita Patrum suorum Traditione Scripturam Ebraicè, cui prælectioni ex eadem Traditione accesserit Chaldaica sive Syriaca interpretatio, quia sermo Chaldaicus quem Majores sui è Babylone reportaverant, etiam illis temporibus Hierosolymis superstes erat, ut ex pluribus Novi Testamenti locis apertè demonstratur.
units.tr: Finally, Vossius adds yet more of these absurdities. He thinks he is not wrong if he rashly (that is, carelessly) affirms that in the time of Christ, in all the synagogues of Jerusalem, perhaps with a few exceptions, which Jews of Parthian and Arabian origin frequented, only the Scriptures that the Seventy Interpreters handed down were read, since Greek alone was their vernacular language. But I would say, with Simon, and not rashly, that the Jews in Jerusalem read Scripture in Hebrew, following the ancient tradition of their fathers, and that to this reading, by the same tradition, was added a Chaldee or Syriac translation, because the Chaldee speech which their ancestors had brought back from Babylon still survived in Jerusalem even in those times, as is clearly shown from several places in the New Testament.

units.la: His omnibus quasdam ratiunculas subjicit Vossius, quæ facilè refelli possunt. Affirmat Romanas leges non permisisse ut in templo Hierosolymitano habitæ fuerint conciones Ebraeo, aut quocunque alio sermone Græcis & Romanis ignoto; Græcæ aut Latinæ linguæ necessitatem omnibus victis impositam fuisse. Quomodo, inquit, potuisset vita miseris constare Judæis, si Hebraica, seu, ut volunt, Syriaca tantùm gnari linguæ eò redacti fuissent necessitatis, ut nec testamentum condere, nec contractus & obligationes facere & signare potuissent? Bellus sanè ratiocinator est Vossius. Romanas illas leges proferat, quibus Judæis vetitum fuerit secundùm Religionis suæ ritus vivere, ac legere in Synagogis suis Ebraicè Legem Mosis, eamque patrio sermone sermone interpretari. Si verum sit non aliam Hierosolymis auditam fuisse linguam quàm Græcam & Latinam, cur titulus quem cruci imponi jussit Pilatus, scriptus fuit Ebraicè, Græcè & Latinè ? Dicet sanè lepidulus Vossius, Ebraicè sive Chaldaicè tituli verba etiam scripta fuisse, ut à Judæis illis Trans-Euphratensibus, qui lynceos habebant oculos, legi possent.
units.tr: To all this Vossius adds some little arguments, which can easily be refuted. He asserts that the Roman laws did not permit sermons in the temple at Jerusalem to be given in Hebrew, or in any other language unknown to Greeks and Romans; that the use of Greek or Latin was imposed on all the conquered peoples. How, he says, could life have gone on for the wretched Jews if those who knew only Hebrew, or, as they wish, only Syriac, had been reduced to such necessity that they could neither make a will nor make and sign contracts and obligations? Vossius is a fine reasoner indeed! Let him produce those Roman laws by which the Jews were forbidden to live according to the rites of their religion, and to read the Law of Moses in Hebrew in their synagogues, and to interpret it in their native tongue. If it were true that no language other than Greek and Latin was heard in Jerusalem, why was the title which Pilate ordered to be put on the cross written in Hebrew, Greek and Latin? No doubt the witty Vossius will say that the words of the title were also written in Hebrew or Chaldee, so that the Jews from beyond the Euphrates, who had lynx's eyes, could read them.

units.la: Jam à Simonio annotatum fuit, linguam Græcam etiam obtinuisse Hierosolymis apud viros primarios & Magistratus, quorum erat curare ut testamenta, contractus, obligationes, aliaque acta civilia & forensia instruerentur. Etsi victores linguæ suæ necessitatem in ejusmodi rebus imponant victis, nunquam tamen linguæ illius necessitas ad plebeios homines transit, nisi post longa tempora, ut ex diversarum nationum Annalibus licet colligere. Quodque videtur animadversione dignum, Judæi qui in Palæstina commorabantur linguam illam Chaldaicam, quam à suis Patribus acceperant, adhuc Hieronymi ætate retinebant. Sic etiam hodie Judæi Hispani, qui in Oriente dispersi sunt, præter Turcarum linguam servant quoque Hispanicam, habentque Biblia Hispanicè conversa, quæ Ebraicis characteribus exarata sunt.
units.tr: Simon has already observed that the Greek language was also in use in Jerusalem among the leading men and the magistrates, whose duty it was to see that wills, contracts, obligations and other civil and legal documents were drawn up. Although victors impose the necessity of their own language on the vanquished in such matters, the necessity of that language never passes down to the common people, except after a long time, as one may gather from the annals of various nations. And, which seems worth noting, the Jews who lived in Palestine still kept that Chaldee language which they had received from their fathers, even in the time of Jerome. So too today the Spanish Jews, who are scattered in the East, keep Spanish besides the language of the Turks, and have Bibles translated into Spanish, written in Hebrew characters.

units.la: In Francia ante Francisculm Primum res forenses Latinè agebantur in Curiis : Parlamentorum arresta, ut vocant, quæque tunc judicata appellabantur, Latino sermone concepta fuerunt. Similiter alia quæcunque acta civilia eodem sermone concepta sunt. An ideo tunc miseri erant Franci, quos constat Latinè locutos non fuisse? Quomodo poterit vita miserrimo constare Vossio, si degens in Anglia ignarus linguæ Anglicæ eò redactus fuerit necessitatis, ut nec testamentum condere, nec contractus & obligationes facere & signare possit? Itaque apud Judæos Hierosolymitanos res forenses Græco vel Romano sermone peragi potuerunt; adeoque vanum est & inutile quod eodem loco subjungit Vossius, stipulationem Punico aut Assyrio conceptam sermone in Jure non posse subsistere. Sed non est cur ejusmodi Vossii ratiunculis diutius immorer.
units.tr: In France, before Francis I, legal business was conducted in Latin in the courts: the decisions of the parlements, as they are called, which were then termed judgments, were composed in the Latin tongue. Likewise all other civil documents were drawn up in that same language. Were the French then wretched, since it is certain they did not speak Latin? How could life be wretchedly sustained for Vossius if, living in England and ignorant of the English language, he were reduced to such necessity that he could neither make a will nor make and sign contracts and obligations? Therefore among the Jews of Jerusalem legal business could be carried on in the Greek or Roman language; and so what Vossius adds in the same place, that a stipulation drawn up in the Punic or Assyrian language cannot stand in law, is vain and useless. But there is no reason for me to dwell longer on such little arguments of Vossius.

units.la: Neque etiam plus habet soliditatis quod ibidem ex Theodoreto profert, qui ait pueros Ebræorum ætate suâ non statim usos fuisse linguâ Ebraicâ, sed linguâ gentium apud quas nati sunt; ubi verò adoleverint doceri literarum characteres, & per has addiscere Scripturam Sacram Ebraicam. Ista quidem vera sunt; sed nihil faciunt ad institutum: nam pueri Ebræorum Hierosolymitanorum gentis etiam suæ linguam, quæ Syriaca erat seu Chaldaica, primùm addiscebant; dein docebantur literarum Ebraicarum characteres; sicque tandem Scripturam Sacram Ebraicam addiscebant.
units.tr: Nor does what he cites from Theodoret in the same place carry any more weight. Theodoret says that in his own day Hebrew children did not at once use the Hebrew language, but the language of the nations among whom they were born; and only when they grew up were they taught the letters of the alphabet and through these learned the Hebrew Holy Scripture. These things are indeed true, but they have nothing to do with the matter in hand: for the children of the Hebrews of Jerusalem first learned the language of their own people, which was Syriac or Chaldee; then they were taught the letters of the Hebrew alphabet; and so at last they learned the Hebrew Holy Scripture.

units.la: Imponit iterum Simonio Vossius, verbaque & rationes illius pervertit, ut habere videatur aliquid quod reponat. Objicit Simonium, etsi videatur parum tribuere figmentis Rabbinicis, probare tamen illud quod est omnium figmentorum futilissimum, vocales scilicet seu puncta Moysi à Deo in monte Sinai reverevelata, à Maforethis post exacta tria annorum millia Legi adscribenda. Verùm Judaicum istud commentum passim rejicit ac refellit Simonius in suis scriptis, simulque originem illius aperit, cur videlicet Judæis nihil sit nisi Divinum & Propheticum, curve fabellas suas è monte Sinai vel è Synagoga quam appellant magnam, deducant: sed id Vossio non arrisit, quia ex eadem origine Simonius ducit LXX. Interpretum Prophetiam. A commento autem Judæorum de antiquitate punctorum adeo alienus est, ut hoc loco asserat fabellam istam de punctorum vocalium antiquitate ex eo potissimùm venire, quòd Judæi hac in re de more gentis suæ locuti fuerint, non verò ex rei ipsius veritate; illudque genus locutionis, quod Judæis familiare est, complures viros in errorem perduxisse, dum Judæorum libros non satis caute evolvunt. Quibus verbis Simonius ætatis nostræ Ebraistas notat, qui tantam punctis vocalibus tribuunt antiquitatem. Quî igitur fieri potest, ut jam Simonius in alium hominem transformatus, laudet probetque Rabbinorum commentum de punctis Mosi à Deo in monte Sinai revelatis? Sed Vossius, qui nugatores in Prophetas transformare potuit, Simonium etiam in Rabbinorum defensorem & Patronum transformavit. Quod autem mox subjicit sumptum ex libro Cozri, ut de Judæorum Traditionibus detrahat, illud non est hominis judicio præditi, cùm Scriptor illius libri ad id unum attendere videatur, ut Religionem Judaicam asstruat beneficio Traditionis contra Philosophos & Judæos Carraeos Judaicarum Traditionum contemptores.
units.tr: Vossius again accuses Simon, and distorts his words and arguments, so that he may seem to have something to reply. He charges Simon with proving, although he seems to give little credit to Rabbinic fictions, that most futile of all fictions: namely, that the vowels or points were revealed by God to Moses on Mount Sinai and were ascribed to the Law by the Masorites after three thousand years had passed. But Simon, in his writings, repeatedly rejects and refutes this Jewish invention, and at the same time reveals its origin, namely why the Jews consider nothing to be divine and prophetic unless it derives its fables from Mount Sinai or from the Synagogue they call the Great. But this did not please Vossius, because Simon derives the prophecy of the Seventy Interpreters from the same origin. Yet Vossius is so far from the Jewish invention about the antiquity of the points that in this passage he asserts that the fable about the antiquity of the vowel points arises chiefly from the fact that the Jews spoke in this matter according to the custom of their nation, and not from the truth of the thing itself; and that this kind of speech, which is familiar to the Jews, has led several men into error while they read the Jewish books too carelessly. In these words Simon is marking the Hebraists of our own age, who attribute such great antiquity to the vowel points. How, then, can it be that Simon, now transformed into another man, praises and approves the Rabbinic invention that the points were revealed to Moses by God on Mount Sinai? But Vossius, who could transform trifling men into prophets, has also transformed Simon into a defender and patron of the rabbis. As for what he next adds, taken from the book of the Kuzari, to detract from the Jewish traditions, this is not the work of a man of sound judgment, since the author of that book seems to attend to this one thing only, namely to establish the Jewish religion by the help of tradition against the philosophers and the Karaites, who despise Jewish traditions.

units.la: Pergit Vossius Simonio imponere, dum eum refellit, quasi in ea sit sententia, ut in Scripturis interpretandis soli audiendi sint Rabbini. Nam dixit Simonius, etiam referente Vossio, artem nullam ab uno & altero perfici, sed ab omnibus simul qui illam artem tractarunt; adeoque linguæ Ebraicæ cognitionem petendam non esse à recentioribus tantùm Rabbinis, sed & à vetustis Interpretibus. Parvi facit etiam Simonius recentiores Scripturæ Sacræ Interpretes, quòd Versiones suas è Rabbinis hauserint. Viderit etiam Vossius, quâ fronte eodem loco scribat à Simonio in construenda nova Scriptura adduci solos Judæos, Masorethas videlicet, Aquilam, Symmachum, Theodotionem & Hieronymum, nullâ factâ LXX. Interpretum mentione; cùm istoc loco & alibi passim LXX. Interpretes primos nominet, testeturque se hac in re non dissentire à Vossio, sed in hoc solùm quòd præter LXX. Interpretes Vossius existimet nullos alios audiendos esse: at Simonius contrà putat consulendos quoque esse Aquilam, Symmachum, Theodotionem, Hieronymum & Rabbinos; quia ars nulla ex uno & altero perfici potest, sed ex omnibus simul. Hoc etiam sensu dixit se nullius Magistri legibus addictum esse, utpote qui non solos audiendos esse LXX. Interpretes sentiat, sed & alios omnes ex quibus perfectior linguæ Ebraicæ cognitio habeatur.
units.tr: Vossius goes on imposing on Simon while he refutes him, as if Simon held the view that only the rabbis should be heard in interpreting the Scriptures. For Simon said, as Vossius himself reports, that no art is perfected by one or two men, but by all who have cultivated that art together; and therefore knowledge of the Hebrew language is to be sought not only from the more recent rabbis but also from the ancient interpreters. Simon also holds in low esteem the more recent interpreters of Holy Scripture, because they drew their versions from the rabbis. Let Vossius see with what face he writes in the same place that Simon, in constructing a new Scripture, adduces only Jews, namely the Masorites, Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion and Jerome, with no mention of the Seventy Interpreters; when in this passage and elsewhere throughout he names the Seventy Interpreters first, and testifies that he does not dissent from Vossius in this matter, except in this alone: that Vossius thinks no one else should be heard besides the Seventy Interpreters, whereas Simon holds on the contrary that Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, Jerome and the rabbis should also be consulted, because no art can be perfected by one or two men, but only by all together. In this sense he also said that he was bound by no master's laws, since he thinks that not only the Seventy Interpreters should be heard, but all the others from whom a more complete knowledge of the Hebrew language may be gained.

units.la: Fingit præterea Vossius, quia nihil hil habet quod reponat, Oralem Judæorum Traditionem propugnari à Simonio, qui tamen illam passim ridet & evertit in suis scriptis. Contendit quidem traditionem aliquam sive usum lectionis semper fuisse apud Judæos in legendis Sacris Codicibus: sed hæc traditio à Cabbala seu Orali Judæorum Traditione multùm discrepat, quam Carræi Traditionum contemptores respuunt. Illa autem lectionis traditio, cujus mentionem facit Simonius, ab iisdem Judæis Carræis approbata est. Nomine igitur traditionis nihil aliud se intelligere profitetur Simonius, quàm usum quemdam legendi Contextûs Ebraici, qui semper apud Judæorum Doctores remanserit, cùm eadem planè sit ratio linguæ Ebraicæ ac cæterarum linguarum, quæ etsi emortuæ sint nec amplius vernaculæ, vigent tamen & in Scholis & apud Doctores. Hac ratione linguam Ebraicam apud Judæos servatam fuisse demonstrat Simonius, sicut etiam hodie sermo Syriacus apud Syros retinetur. Quis hanc traditionem seu hunc lectionis usum confundet cum superstitiosa Judæorum Cabbala sive Traditione, nisi Isaacus Vossius, qui semper falsa scribit, nec unquam ferit scopum?
units.tr: Moreover, Vossius invents, because he has nothing to reply, that Simon defends the oral tradition of the Jews, although Simon repeatedly mocks and overturns that tradition in his writings. He does indeed contend that there has always been some tradition or practice of reading among the Jews in reading the sacred books; but this tradition differs greatly from the Cabbala or oral tradition of the Jews, which the Karaites, despisers of traditions, reject. Yet the tradition of reading, which Simon mentions, was approved by those same Karaite Jews. By the name of tradition, therefore, Simon professes to understand nothing other than a certain practice of reading the Hebrew text, which has always remained among the Jewish teachers; since the reasoning about the Hebrew language is exactly the same as for other languages, which, although they are dead and no longer vernacular, still flourish both in the schools and among scholars. By this reasoning Simon shows that the Hebrew language was preserved among the Jews, just as even today the Syriac speech is kept among the Syrians. Who would confuse this tradition, or this practice of reading, with the superstitious Cabbala or tradition of the Jews, except Isaac Vossius, who always writes falsehoods and never hits the mark?

units.la: Ad id quod scripserat Simonius, etiam Aquilam ab Origene laudatum fuisse, ut Interpretem qui verborum proprietates explicaret, Vossius respondet Origenem id fecisse ex opinione Judæorum, cùm seipsum interpretetur in Epistola ad Africanum. Verùm quidem est Origenem in Epistola quam scripsit Africano videri esse in ea sententia, ut soli audiantur LXX. Interpretes: sed illum hoc loco ex recepta magis opinione quàm ex sua sententia locutum fuisse manifestè demonstravit Simonius. Ipse siquidem Origenes aliis locis, ubi mentem suam exprimit, multum tribuit Aquilæ & aliis Interpretibus qui Codices Ebraicos in Græcum sermonem converterant, eosque haud infrequenter sequitur: ita ut etiam illorum ope corruptam LXX. Interpretum scripturam corrigere non reformidaverit. Sic postquàm deprehendit nomina propria in LXX. Interpretum Exemplaribus magna ex parte corrupta fuisse tam in Lege quàm in Prophetis, censet illa restituenda esse ex Ebraeorum Codicibus & ex Versionibus Aquilæ, Symmachi & Theodotionis, quas puriores esse affirmat. Hæc enim sunt Origenis verba Commentariis in Joannem, postquàm nonnulla in nominibus propriis Novi Testamenti errata correxit, & eadem in LXX. Interpretibus occurrere deprehendit. Τὸ ἢ ὁμοιον ὡς ἐν τοῖς ὀνόμασιν σφάλμα πολλάκις ἐν νόμῳ καὶ τῶν Προφητῶν ἔγιν ἰδεῖν, ὡς ἡμεῖς ἐπὶ τῶν Ἑβδομήκοντα μαθόντες ἐν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις αὐτῶν τὰ ἡμέτερα συγχέαντες μαςζυρηθέισιν ὑπὸ τῆς μη-δέτω Ἀφξραφεισῶν ἐκδόσεων Ἀκύλα ἡ Θεοδοτίωνος καὶ Συμμάχου. Corruptos igitur ætate suâ fuisse Græcos LXX. Interpretum Codices agnoscit Origenes; contrà verò incorruptum remansisse Contextum Ebræum; Græcasque Aquilæ, Theodotionis & Symmachi Versiones remansisse quoque incorruptas: quâ potissimum ratione adductus est Hic-
units.tr: Simonius had written that Aquila was also praised by Origen as an interpreter who explained the peculiarities of words. Vossius replies that Origen did this out of the Jewish opinion, since he himself explains it in his letter to Africanus. It is true that in the letter he wrote to Africanus, Origen appears to hold the view that only the Seventy translators should be heard. But Simonius has clearly shown that Origen spoke here according to the opinion then generally received, rather than his own view. In other places, where he expresses his own mind, Origen greatly values Aquila and the other translators who had turned the Hebrew codices into Greek, and he follows them quite often. So much so that with their help he did not hesitate to correct the corrupted text of the Septuagint. Thus, having found that the proper names in the copies of the Septuagint were largely corrupted, both in the Law and in the Prophets, he judges that they must be restored from the Hebrew codices and from the versions of Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion, which he affirms are purer. These are Origen's own words in his Commentary on John, after he had corrected some errors in the proper names of the New Testament and found the same in the Septuagint: "[Τὸ ἢ ὁμοιον ὡς ἐν τοῖς ὀνόμασιν σφάλμα πολλάκις ἐν νόμῳ καὶ τῶν Προφητῶν ἔγιν ἰδεῖν, ὡς ἡμεῖς ἐπὶ τῶν Ἑβδομήκοντα μαθόντες ἐν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις αὐτῶν τὰ ἡμέτερα συγχέαντες μαςζυρηθέισιν ὑπὸ τῆς μη-δέτω Ἀφξραφεισῶν ἐκδόσεων Ἀκύλα ἡ Θεοδοτίωνος καὶ Συμμάχου]." So Origen acknowledges that the Greek copies of the Seventy were corrupt in his own age, but that the Hebrew text remained uncorrupted, and that the Greek versions of Aquila, Theodotion and Symmachus also remained uncorrupted. This is the chief reason why he was led to ... [Hieronymus]

units.la: Orig. Comment. in Euang. Joann.
units.tr: Orig. Comment. in Euang. Joann.

units.la: Hieronymus, ut novam Ebraici Codicis Versionem conderet. Similiter Origenes, ubi diversas LXX. Interpretum lectiones offendit, non dubitat eam praferre quæ cum Ebraeo concordat. Cur autem interdum Græcam LXX. Interpretum Tralationem cæteris Versionibus præferat, causa evidens est; quia videlicet ea sola tunc in Ecclesiis obtinebat. Unde, si quando lectionem Codicum Ebraicorum præmonstrat, statim addit id quod jam usu receptum in Ecclesiis legebatur exponendum esse, ita tamen ut quod in Ebraicis legebatur Exemplaribus intactum non relinqueret. Δεῖ ἓν ἡ τὸ καταγεγραμμένον ἢ φερόμενον ἐν ταῖς Ἐκκλησίαις διηγήσασθαι, ἡ τὸ ἐκ τῶν Ἐβραϊκῶν χαρῶν ἀδιήγητον μὴ καλύπτειν.
units.tr: Jerome, in order to make a new version of the Hebrew codex. Likewise Origen, when he finds different readings of the Septuagint, does not hesitate to prefer the one that agrees with the Hebrew. Why he sometimes prefers the Greek translation of the Septuagint to the other versions is clear: namely, because it alone then held sway in the churches. Hence, whenever he points out a reading of the Hebrew codices, he at once adds that what was already received and read in the churches by custom must also be explained, yet in such a way as not to leave untouched what was read in the Hebrew copies. "[Δεῖ ἓν ἡ τὸ καταγεγραμμένον ἢ φερόμενον ἐν ταῖς Ἐκκλησίαις διηγήσασθαι, ἡ τὸ ἐκ τῶν Ἐβραϊκῶν χαρῶν ἀδιήγητον μὴ καλύπτειν.]" That is, one must either explain what is written or current in the churches, or not conceal what is unexplained from the Hebrew text.

units.la: Simonius dixerat, non ideo mutos fuisse Judæorum Codices tempore Origenis, quòd illos Græcis literis in suis Hexaplis expressisset; sed quia voluit, ut ii etiam qui nihil Ebraicè scirent, Ebraica possent legere. Jam Vossius, qui liberalis est, lubenter illud se concedere affirmat: sed quærit, cùm Ebræi Codices carerent vocalibus, unde & à quibus haurire potuit Origenes rationem resarciendi istum defectum vocalium, nisi à Judæis. Mirificus sanè ratiocinator est Vossius, qui nodum in scirpo quærit. Jam respondit Simonius, id habuisse Origenem ex recepta apud Judæos legendi ratione; qualem in legendis libris Syriacis, Chaldaicis & Arabicis extare apud Syros, Chaldæos & Arabas norunt linguarum Orientalium periti. Ita si quis hodie Maronita verba Syriaca libri alicujus Latinis literis velit exprimere, illa facillimè exprimit, si sciat Syriacè. Neque profecto hac in re alia fors fuit linguæ Ebraicæ, quàm linguæ Syriacæ, Chaldaicæ & Arabicæ. Quare nugas agit Vossius, & linguarum Orientalium imperitum se ostendit, quando ait legi quidem vulgò à Judæis libros à quibus absunt vocales, postquàm stabilita est lectio à Masorethis; sed ante illa tempora eos legi non potuisse, nisi illà quam Origenes tradidit ratione, apponendo nempe Ebraica Græcis literis; quæ Ebraica tunc vocalibus instructa fuerint; quà tantùm ratione Judæos compendiariam scripturam assequi potuisse contendit Vossius: sicuti nunc eamdem assequuntur beneficio Masorethicæ lectionis. Verùm à Vossio quæsierim, unde Samaritæ, qui eamdem compendiariam scribendi Codices Ebraicos rationem habent atque Judæi, vocales resarcire potuerunt, cùm Masorethica puncta non agnoscant: unde etiam Syri, Chaldæi & Arabes, quorum simili est ratio atque Judæorum, supplent in linguis suis ejusmodi vocales, cùm in paucissimis eorum libris puncta vocalia exprimantur: præterea quâ arte Judæi Talmudicorum Rabbinorumque libros possint legere & interpretari, à quibus absunt ejusmodi Masorethsarum puncta.
units.tr: Simonius had said that the Jewish codices were not mute in Origen's time because he had expressed them in Greek letters in his Hexapla, but because he wished that even those who knew no Hebrew could read the Hebrew. Vossius, who is generous, gladly affirms that he concedes this; but he asks, since Hebrew codices lacked vowels, where and from whom Origen could draw the method of supplying this lack of vowels, if not from the Jews. Vossius is a marvellous reasoner, who seeks a knot in a bulrush. Simonius has already answered that Origen had this from the method of reading received among the Jews, of the sort which, as those skilled in the Oriental languages know, exists in the reading of Syriac, Chaldee and Arabic books among the Syrians, Chaldeans and Arabs. Thus if someone today wishes to express in Latin letters the Syriac words of some book of the Maronites, he expresses them very easily, if he knows Syriac. Indeed, in this matter the lot of the Hebrew language was no different from that of Syriac, Chaldee and Arabic. Therefore Vossius is talking nonsense, and shows himself ignorant of the Oriental languages, when he says that the Jews did indeed commonly read books lacking vowels after the reading was fixed by the Masoretes, but that before those times they could not have read them except by the method Origen handed down, namely by setting the Hebrew in Greek letters, the Hebrew then being furnished with vowels; and that only by this method, he contends, could the Jews attain to the abbreviated script, just as they now attain it by the benefit of the Masoretic reading. But I would ask Vossius: how could the Samaritans, who have the same abbreviated manner of writing Hebrew codices as the Jews, supply the vowels, since they do not acknowledge the Masoretic points? Likewise the Syrians, Chaldeans and Arabs, whose practice is like that of the Jews, supply such vowels in their languages, although the vowel points are expressed in very few of their books. Besides, by what art could the Jews read and interpret the books of the Talmudists and rabbis, which lack such Masoretic points?

units.la: Pergit iterum nugari Vossius, ac quærit, si unicuique pro lubitu licitum fuit addere aut variare vocales, quomodo sibi constare potuit lectionis & pronunciationis ratio. Sed non ita pro lubitu scribarum licitum fuit variare vocales illas, quas vocant RabRabbini lectionis matres, quin aliquæ certæ remanserint, ex quibus vera discerni posset lectio. Verùm tamen est, ut annotavit Aben Esra, sæpius hac in re à scribis pro arbitratu suo variatum fuisse, adeoque inutilem esse Masoretharum laborem, qui tam anxiè vocales illas seu literas Aleph, Vau, Jod numerarunt, cùm earum præsentia & absentia sæpè nihil faciat ad sensum. Inde ortum est ut locis quàmplurimis Samaritæ idem prorsus legant in suis Codicibus, quod Judæi in Judaicis Exemplaribus; etsi vocales illæ diversâ ratione in Samariticis & Judaicis libris notentur. Simonius tamen agnoscit, hinc etiam factum fuisse ut ipsimet Judæi diversis temporibus Codices suos diversâ ratione legerint: idemque Simonius observat, frustra Judæos Masoram suam seu lectionis suæ usum opponere; cùm etiam LXX. & alii Interpretes ante illorum tempora Masoram suam sive legendi rationem habuerint. Quæ lectionis diversitas traditioni seu lectionis receptæ usui nequaquam officit; quia hæc est sors linguarum nationum Orientalium quæ scribunt per compendia: neque magis ob hanc causam accusandi sunt Judæorum Codices quòd muti sint, quàm Chaldæorum, Syrorum, Arabumque libri. Istæ enim linguæ suas quoque vocales habent, quæ sunt, ut ita loquar, lectionis matres, quæque haud infrequenter pro scribarum lubitu adjiciuntur & omittuntur; quia eas tantùm adjiciunt quas ad lectionem vocum sufficere existimant.
units.tr: Vossius goes on trifling, and asks: if it was lawful for each person to add or vary vowels at will, how could the method of reading and pronunciation remain consistent? But it was not lawful for scribes to vary at will those vowels which the rabbis call mothers of reading, without some fixed ones remaining by which the true reading could be discerned. It is true, however, as Aben Ezra observed, that in this matter the scribes varied things very often at their own discretion, and so the labour of the Masoretes, who so anxiously counted those vowel letters Aleph, Vau and Yod, was useless, since their presence or absence often makes no difference to the sense. Hence it comes about that in very many places the Samaritans read in their codices exactly what the Jews read in their Jewish copies, although those vowels are marked in different ways in the Samaritan and Jewish books. Simonius nevertheless acknowledges that from this it also happened that the Jews themselves read their codices in different ways at different times. The same Simonius observes that the Jews vainly oppose their Masorah, or their manner of reading, since the Seventy and other translators, before those Jews' time, also had their own Masorah, or manner of reading. This diversity of reading is by no means prejudicial to tradition, or to the established use of reading. This is the lot of the Oriental languages which are written by abbreviations; nor are the codices of the Jews to be blamed for being mute any more than the books of the Chaldeans, Syrians and Arabs. For those languages have their own vowels too, which are, so to speak, the mothers of reading, and which are quite often added or omitted at the scribe's pleasure, since they add only those they think sufficient for reading the words.

units.la: Præterea Simonius ex eo probaverat Judæis suas quoque non deesse voca-les,quòd aliarum gentium linguas suis characteribus exprimant. Sic habent libros Græcos, Hispanicos, Germanicos, aliòsque literis Ebraicis descriptos. Sed regerit Vossius, in istis, præter Aleph, Vau, Jod, etiam puncta vocalia exprimi. Hoc quidem verum est, & à Simonio observatum fuit, qui voces quasdam ex iisdem libris proferens sine punctis illis vocalibus, eas expeditè legi posse demonstrat, adeoque in istis vocibus inutilia esse puncta vocalia. Illud omne confirmari potest autoritate Sabaïtarum, qui in libris suis Chaldaico sermone conscriptis singulis fere consonantibus vocales adjungunt, quibus haud dubiè literæ Aleph, Vau & Jod genuinæ sunt vocales; & in hoc à reliquis Orientis populis differunt, quòd linguam suam quæ Chaldaica est minùs compendiariò scribant. Europæos quoque rident nationes illæ Orientis, quòd linguæ Græcæ, Latinæ & aliarum vocabula nequeant legere, nisi omnibus suis vocalibus instructa sint.
units.tr: Furthermore, Simonius had proved from this that the Jews also do not lack their own vowels, since they express the languages of other nations with their characters. Thus they have Greek, Spanish, German and other books written in Hebrew letters. But Vossius replies that in these, besides Aleph, Vau and Yod, the vowel points are also expressed. This is indeed true, and Simonius noted it; he shows, by producing certain words from the same books without those vowel points, that they can be read easily, and so in these words the vowel points are useless. All of this can be confirmed by the authority of the Sabaeans, who in their books written in the Chaldee language add vowels to nearly every consonant, though there the letters Aleph, Vau and Yod are undoubtedly genuine vowels; and in this they differ from the other peoples of the East, that they write their own language, which is Chaldee, less in abbreviated form. Those Eastern nations also laugh at Europeans, because they cannot read the words of Greek, Latin and other languages unless these are furnished with all their vowels.

units.la: Jam Vossius putat se efficaciter ex eo demonstrasse, puncta vocalia Codici Ebraico ineptissimè & nullo judicio apposita fuisse à Masorethis, quòd Christus & Apostoli diversâ plane ratione Patriarcharum & Prophetarum nomina legerint, atque Judæi recentiores. Sed optimè respondit Simonius, hanc scriptionis diversitatem rejiciendam esse in Judæos diversarum regionum diversarumque ætatum, qui eadem nomina Ebraica eodem plane modo scripta diversè proferunt, quæ si in patrium sermonem transferantur, scribuntur quoque diversè: & hæc sors fuit
units.tr: Now Vossius thinks he has effectively demonstrated that the vowel points were added to the Hebrew codex by the Masoretes in a most foolish way and without judgment, because Christ and the Apostles read the names of the Patriarchs and Prophets in a quite different way from recent Jews. But Simonius answered well that this diversity of spelling must be attributed to Jews of different regions and different ages, who pronounce the same Hebrew names, written in exactly the same way, differently; and if these are transferred into their native speech, they are also written differently. And this has been the lot of all languages, since not even Latin words are pronounced in the same way by different peoples.

units.la: Aben Esra. omnium linguarum, cùm ne quidem voces Latinæ à diversis populis eâdem ratione pronuncientur. Jam Vossius regerit ista quidem vera esse, sed non ad propositum, cùm non de consonnis quæstio sit, sed de vocalibus literis, in quarum pronunciatione omnes gentes conveniunt; additque nullos esse homines in quorum ore Nabuchodonosor & Nebuchadnesar eumdem efficiant sonum.
units.tr: Aben Ezra. of all languages, since not even Latin words are pronounced in the same way by different peoples. Now Vossius replies that these things are indeed true, but they are beside the point, since the question is not about the consonants but about the vowel letters, in whose pronunciation all peoples agree. He adds that there are no people in whose mouths Nabuchodonosor and Nebuchadnesar produce the same sound.

units.la: Sed aurem Batavam profectò habet Vossius, qui hanc etiam sonorum diversitatem in pronunciandis literis vocalibus non percipiat. Audiat Anglos Latinè loquentes, qui etiam in vocalibus pronunciandis magis Anglicè loqui videntur quàm Latinè, apud quos videlicet litera vocalis a sæpè sonat ut e. Galli præterea & Hispani hac etiam in re differunt. Sed ut ad Orientis nationes veniam; in uno sermone Arabico pronunciando Turcæ & Arabes diversè literas vocales pronunciant, etsi illas iisdem punctis notatas legant. Suam quoque Maronitæ habent ejusmodi vocalium propriam pronunciationem. Hanc etiam in Syriaco sermone pronunciationis literarum vocalium discrepantiam licet animadvertere: nam etsi voces notentur iisdem punctis vocalibus, tamen ubi Maronitæ legunt o, Nestoriani legunt a, imitati Chaldæos. Judæi ipsimet Grammatici certant de genuino punctorum vocalium sono: ita punctum Cames alii sono rotundiori pronunciant & quasi o; alii ore magis aperto & fere ut a. Quare facilis fuit vocis Nabuchodonosor in Nebuchadnesar permutatio in linguis Orientalibus, cùm tam inconstans sit apud Orientis populos
units.tr: But Vossius surely has a Batavian ear, if he cannot perceive this diversity of sounds even in the pronunciation of vowel letters. Let him listen to the English speaking Latin, who even in pronouncing vowels seem to speak more like Englishmen than Latinists, among whom the vowel a often sounds like e. The French and the Spanish also differ in this respect. But to come to the nations of the East: in pronouncing the one Arabic language, the Turks and the Arabs pronounce the vowel letters differently, even though they read them marked with the same points. The Maronites also have their own particular pronunciation of such vowels. In the Syriac language too one may notice this difference in pronouncing the vowel letters. For although the words are marked with the same vowel points, where the Maronites read o, the Nestorians read a, imitating the Chaldeans. The Jewish grammarians themselves dispute about the genuine sound of the vowel points: some pronounce the point Qames with a rounder sound, almost as o; others with the mouth more open, nearly as a. Hence the change of Nabuchodonosor into Nebuchadnesar was easy in the Eastern languages, since the pronunciation of vowel letters is so unsettled among the peoples of the East.

units.la: literarum vocalium pronunciatio. Sed qui hæc ignoravit Vossius ex tripode pronunciavit, Simonium nihil retulisse quod ad quæstionem faceret.
units.tr: Yet Vossius, who was ignorant of these things, pronounced from the tripod, claiming that Simonius had said nothing that bore on the question.

units.la: Objecerat Simonius, Vossium non intellexisse Judæorum pronunciatum, qui affirmant Scripturam habere LXXII. facies sive sensus; quia constat etiam Judæos agnoscere unum sensum simplicem, seu, ut vocant, literalem; alii autem sensus allegorici sunt & cabbalici, ex quibus nemo sano præditus judicio concludet inconstantem esse apud Judæos Scripturæ lectionem. At sensus allegorici, regerit Vossius, sunt etiam sensus. Verum est; sed sunt sensus allegorici, qui tot sunt, ut rectè annotavit Simonius, quot otiosi Magistri possunt comminisci. Addit, sensus etiam simplices, seu, ut vocant, literales LXXII. quoque esse, si LXXII. consulantur Magistri; neque solùm Rabbinos, sed & Christianos complures multiplicem probare interpretationem. Fateor; verùm istud nihil facit ad rem: nam ubi verba Contextûs obscuriora sunt, licet semperque licebit Interpretibus Scripturæ novas indagare expositiones, quæ in Codicis Ebraici eversionem trahi non possunt. Scriptorum enim omnium sors communis est, ut illorum verba diversis modis interdum exponi possint. Quam obscuritatem potissimùm libris Ebraicis tribuit Simonius. Sed hæc verborum obscuritas efficit tantùm interpretationis diversitatem, non varietatem lectionis.
units.tr: Simonius had objected that Vossius did not understand the Jewish claim that Scripture has seventy-two faces or senses. He pointed out that the Jews also acknowledge one simple sense, which they call literal; the other senses are allegorical and cabbalistic, and no one of sound judgment will conclude from these that the reading of Scripture is unstable among the Jews. But Vossius replies that allegorical senses are senses too. That is true; but they are allegorical senses, and there are as many of them as idle teachers can devise, as Simonius rightly observed. He adds that the simple or literal senses also number seventy-two, if seventy-two teachers are consulted; and not only rabbis but many Christians prove multiple interpretations. I grant it, but that has nothing to do with the matter. For where the words of the context are obscure, interpreters of Scripture both may and always will seek out new explanations, and these cannot overturn the Hebrew text. For the common lot of all writings is that their words can sometimes be explained in different ways. Simonius attributes this obscurity chiefly to the Hebrew books. But this obscurity of words produces only a diversity of interpretation, not a variety of readings.

units.la: Iterum in solitas declamationes relabitur disertulus Vossius, aitque in Simonii scripto nihil inveniri præter ter frigidas cavillationes sine ullo ordine & judicio. Hac ratione respondet Simonio objicienti Vossium ubique afferre quæ sint plane inutilia & extra propositum. Quippe hic contendit LXX. Seniores appellari Prophetas, quia sunt Interpretes, cùm προφητεύειν idem sit quod interpretari. At rectè illum monuerat Simonius, hîc non agi de ejusmodi Prophetis; sed de hominibus Spiritu Sancto afflatis, quales fuisse LXX. Seniores Vossius putavit: & quia nunquam ferit scopum, iterum regerit, à Christo & Apostolis omnes eos Prophetas appellari, qui S. Scripturas intelligunt & rectè interpretantur: sed pergit ineptire Vossius, cùm de hisce Prophetis non instituta fuerit quæstio.
units.tr: The glib little orator Vossius again slips into his usual declamations, and says that nothing is to be found in Simonius's writing except three cold cavils without any order or judgment. In this way he answers Simonius, who objected that Vossius everywhere brings forward things that are quite useless and beside the point. Indeed, Vossius maintains that the Seventy Elders are called prophets because they are interpreters, since prophēteuein [προφητεύειν] means the same as to interpret. But Simonius had rightly warned him that this is not about prophets of that kind, but about men inspired by the Holy Spirit, which Vossius thought the Seventy Elders were. And since he never hits the mark, he again replies that all those who understand and rightly interpret the Holy Scriptures are called prophets by Christ and the Apostles. But Vossius goes on talking nonsense, since the question was not raised about these prophets.

units.la: Præterea, ut excellentis sui judicii vim ostendat bonus Vossius, sic ratiocinatur. Si idolorum cultores sæpè in Sacris Literis appellantur Prophetæ, multò magis hoc nomen conveniet veris Dei sacerdotibus, scilicet LXX. Interpretibus. Potuit etiam addere, nugatoribus & impostoribus, quales sunt novi Prophetæ Vossiani. Sed ista nihil quoque faciunt ad institutum, cùm de veris Prophetis & Spiritu Sancto afflatis quæstio instituta fuerit. Si autem alios non agnoscit Prophetas quàm Interpretes & idolorum cultores, actum est de Prophetia & de Sacrorum Librorum divinitate. Argumentum quod sumit à Scribis qui res Ebræorum chartis committerent, quique, teste Simonio, Prophetæ fuerint & à Deo inspirati, nihil etiam facit pro adstruenda LXX. Interpretum Prophetia: quia, uti jam observatum fuit, alia est ratio eorum qui res divinas scripserunt; alia ratio eorum qui illas ex Ebraicis fecerunt Græcas. Illos Divino Spiritu afflatos fuisse necesse est; his verò linguæ Ebraicæ & Græcæ cognitio sufficiebat, ut libros Ebraicos in Græcum sermonem converterent.
units.tr: Moreover, so that the good Vossius may display the force of his excellent judgment, he reasons as follows. If worshippers of idols are often called prophets in the Sacred Letters, the name will apply much more to the true priests of God, namely the Seventy Interpreters. He could also have added: to triflers and impostors, such as the new Vossian prophets. But these things again have nothing to do with the subject, since the question was raised about true prophets and men inspired by the Holy Spirit. But if he acknowledges no prophets other than interpreters and worshippers of idols, then prophecy and the divinity of the Sacred Books are gone. The argument he takes from the scribes who committed the affairs of the Hebrews to writing, and who, according to Simonius, were prophets and inspired by God, also does nothing to establish the prophecy of the Seventy Interpreters. For, as has already been observed, the case of those who wrote down divine matters is one thing, and the case of those who turned them from Hebrew into Greek is another. The former must have been moved by the divine Spirit; but for the latter a knowledge of the Hebrew and Greek languages was enough to translate the Hebrew books into the Greek tongue.

units.la: Objectat Vossius, Simonium semper relabi in Hieronymum suum, quia non alium præter illum sistere potest testem sublatæ à LXX. Interpretibus Prophetiæ. Sed unum proferat testem Vossius è prisci s Ecclesiæ Patribus, qui artem criticam, de qua in præsentia agitur, felicius tractaverit quàm Hieronymus, qui fictas illas LXX. Interpretum æmiculas, quas Justinus Martyr & alii Patres cum Judæis admirati sunt, etiam sustulit: neque hodie inveniuntur homines qui Judaicis istis commentis fidem habeant. Cur igitur Vossius similiter non credit, rectè quoque ab eodem Hieronymo sublatam fuisse LXX. Interpretum Prophetiam, quæ non alios quoque autores habeat quàm Judæos illorum temporum? In rebus criticis paucorum qui judicio polleant sententia multorum hominum testimoniis sæpius præferenda est.
units.tr: Vossius objects that Simonius always falls back on his Jerome, because he can produce no other witness to the prophecy of the Seventy Interpreters that was taken away. But let Vossius produce one witness from the ancient Fathers of the Church who handled the critical art, which is now under discussion, more successfully than Jerome, who also removed those fictitious fables of the Seventy Interpreters which Justin Martyr and other Fathers admired along with the Jews; nor are men found today who give credence to those Jewish inventions. Why then does Vossius not likewise believe that the prophecy of the Seventy Interpreters was also rightly removed by the same Jerome, since it has no other authors than the Jews of those times? In critical matters the opinion of a few who excel in judgment is to be preferred more often than the testimony of many men.

units.la: Simonius rectè confecerat Beatum Stephanum ultimam suam concionem non Græcâ, sed Syriacâ linguâ, quæ Hierosolymis tunc erat vernacula, absolvisse; verisimilem quoque esse Hieronymi opinionem, qui existimavit Stephanum in illa concione testimonia Veteris Instrumenti produxisse ex Ebraicis Codicibus. Jam, quid ad hæc Vossius? Respondet non opus esse fingere, cùm hodie supersint ipsa Stephani verba quæ Græca sunt, & loca Scripturæ conveniant cum LXX. Interpretibus, non autem cum Judæorum libris. Miror belli istius Critici judicium. Simili ratione dixerim Christum, quem Syriacè cum muliere Samaritana collocutum esse ipse Vossius agnoscit, Græcè locutum fuisse, quia illius verba Græcè referuntur ab Euangelista. Sed quid pluribus opus est? Lucas ipse autor Actuum Apostolorum testatur se hanc historiam Græcè scripsisse, simulque sermonem Hierosolymitanorum Judæorum vernaculum fuisse Syriacum. Sic Cap. 1. Actuum, verf. 19. agri Judæ mentionem faciens, dicit illum lingua Hierosolymitanorum vernaculâ, τῇ ἰδίᾳ Ἀκελδαμάχ αὐτῶν, appellatum fuisse haceldama sive agrum sanguinis. Jam extra controversiam est, voces hacel dama Syriacas esse seu Chaldaicas.
units.tr: Simonius had rightly concluded that the blessed Stephen delivered his last sermon not in Greek but in the Syriac language, which was then the vernacular in Jerusalem; and that Jerome's opinion is probable, who thought that Stephen in that sermon brought forward testimonies of the Old Testament from Hebrew manuscripts. Now what does Vossius say to this?
