He replies that there is no need to invent anything, since the very words of Stephen, which are Greek, still survive, and the passages of Scripture agree with the Seventy Interpreters, not with the books of the Jews. I marvel at the judgment of that fine critic. By a similar argument I would say that Christ, whom Vossius himself acknowledges spoke with the Samaritan woman in Syriac, spoke in Greek, because his words are reported in Greek by the Evangelist. But why need there be more? Luke himself, the author of the Acts of the Apostles, testifies that he wrote this history in Greek, and at the same time that the vernacular speech of the Jews of Jerusalem was Syriac. So in Acts 1, verse 19, mentioning the field of Judah, he says that it was called in the vernacular tongue of the people of Jerusalem, tē idia Akeldamach autōn [τῇ ἰδίᾳ Ἀκελδαμάχ αὐτῶν], Haceldama, that is, the field of blood. Now it is beyond controversy that the words hacel dama are Syriac or Chaldean.

units.la: Rectè quoque ab Hieronymo observatum fuit, Stephanum in concione quam habuit ad Judæos Hierosolymitanos non aliis usum fuisse testimoniis Scripturæ, quàm iis quæ deprompserat ex Ebraicis Exemplaribus; quia videlicet tunc Hierosolymis, uti demonstratum fuit, Judæi Legem Mosis aliosque Scripturæ libros ex avita Patrum suorum traditione legebant Ebraicè, non Græcè.
units.tr: Jerome also rightly observed that Stephen, in the sermon he delivered to the Jews of Jerusalem, used no testimonies of Scripture other than those he had taken from Hebrew copies; because at that time in Jerusalem, as has been shown, the Jews read the Law of Moses and the other books of Scripture in Hebrew, not in Greek, from the ancient tradition of their fathers.

units.la: Instat Vossius, aitque fieri non potuisse, ut Stephanus Ebraicè vel Syriacè locutus fuerit, quia tunc Hierosolymis erant Romani & Græci generis Judæi, Libertini videlicet, Cyrenæi, Alexandrini, Cilices & Asiatici, quibus Græca lingua familiaris erat. Sed quis credat Stephanum ad Hierosolymitanos aliâ linguâ orationem habuisse, quàm illâ quæ Hierosolymis vernacula erat apud Judæos, paucorumque qui Græcè sciebant rationem habuisse? Sermonem autem Græcum Hierosolymis vernaculum apud Judæos non fuisse, sed Syriacum, præter jam allata testimonia, manifestè probant verba Tribuni, Act. 21. quem cùm Paulus vellet alloqui, eum rogat Tribunus, an sciret Græcè, quia scilicet Judæi Hierosolymitani Græcè non loquebantur. Unde etiam eodem Capite legimus Paulum, etsi Græcè sciret, quia Tarsensis erat, Ebraicè, id est Syriacè sive Chaldaicè ad Judæos Hierosolymitanos orationem suam habuisse, qui majus silentium præstiterunt, quòd Ebraicè seu patrio eorum sermone loqueretur.
units.tr: Vossius insists that Stephen could not have spoken in Hebrew or Syriac, because at that time there were Jews of Roman and Greek origin in Jerusalem, namely freedmen, Cyrenians, Alexandrians, Cilicians and Asiatics, to whom the Greek language was familiar. But who would believe that Stephen addressed the people of Jerusalem in a language other than the one that was the vernacular among the Jews there, and took account only of the few who knew Greek? That the Greek language was not the vernacular among the Jews of Jerusalem, but Syriac, is clearly shown, besides the testimonies already adduced, by the words of the Tribune in Acts 21, when Paul wished to address him, and the Tribune asked whether he knew Greek, plainly because the Jews of Jerusalem did not speak Greek. Hence also in the same chapter we read that Paul, though he knew Greek because he was from Tarsus, made his speech to the Jews of Jerusalem in Hebrew, that is, in Syriac or Chaldean; and they kept all the more silence because he spoke in Hebrew, that is, in their native tongue.

units.la: Vossium maligne Aristeam & alios ætatis illius impostores Judæos cum Mose & Prophetis contulisse merito objecit Simonius, qui de Judæis tantùm illorum temporum locutus fuerat, quibus solenne fuisse fingere ac falsa scribere nec ipse potest diffiteri Vossius, qui autor est tunc Judæos finxisse libros Adami, Enoch, Sibyllarum & alios complures sub Patriarcharum Prophetarumque nominibus. Id quoque jam olim priscis Scriptoribus suboluisse demonstraverat Simonius Philonis Herennii testimonio, quod refert Origenes. Tamen nihil tale dixisse Origenem contendit Vossius, cujus etiam hîc verba profert, quæ repetam, ut de his æqui judicent lectores. Fertur & Hecatæi Historici de Judæis liber, in quo adeo probat hujus gentis sapientiam, ut Herennius Philo in Commentariis suis primùm dubitet an hujus Historici id scriptum sit; deinde addat, siquidem
units.tr: Vossius rightly objected to Simonius that he maliciously compared Aristeas and the other impostors of that age among the Jews with Moses and the Prophets. Simonius had spoken only of the Jews of those times, among whom it was customary to invent things and write falsehoods, and Vossius himself cannot deny this, since he affirms that the Jews of that time forged the books of Adam, Enoch, the Sibyls, and many others under the names of the Patriarchs and Prophets. Simonius had also shown that earlier writers had already suspected this, from the testimony of Philo Herennius, which Origen reports. Yet Vossius contends that Origen said nothing of the kind, and he quotes Origen's own words here, which I will repeat so that the readers may judge fairly. There is also a book on the Jews by the historian Hecataeus, in which he so proves the wisdom of this people that Philo Herennius, in his Commentaries, first doubts whether this historian wrote it, and then adds, if indeed it is his

units.la: Origen. adv. Celf. dem ejus est, videri eum corruptum Judaeorum persuasionibus, probasseque illorum placita. Jam igitur ab illis temporibus suspicatus est Herennius Philo Hecataei librum de Judaeis ab ipsismet Judaeis confictum fuisse; ut etiam his verbis adductus Scaliger existimavit librum hunc supposititium esse.
units.tr: Origen, Against Celsus. ...that he seems to have been corrupted by the persuasions of the Jews and to have approved their opinions. Thus, from those times onward, Philo Herennius suspected that the book of Hecataeus on the Jews had been fabricated by the Jews themselves, and Scaliger, moved by these same words, also thought that this book is spurious.

units.la: Iterum ad Origenem venio, Scriptorem sane in praesenti materia gravissimum. Simonius dixerat in hoc errare Vossium, quod existimaverit Origenem non alios probasse Codices quam Graecos LXX. Interpretum, cum ipse Origenes, referente Hieronymo, in tomis suis Ebraicae linguae quaesierit auxilia, etsi in Homiliis suis quas ad vulgum loquitur communem editionem sequeretur. Addit Vossius, Simonium ad suum Hieronymum relabi, ex cujus tamen verbis effici non posset praelatam unquam fuisse ab Origene LXX. Interpretibus Aquilae Versionem. Sed a quo melius Origenis mentem possumus addiscere, quam ab Hieronymo qui libros illius legit ac perlegit, queque testatur chartas Alexandrinas, id est libros Origenis, marsupium suum evacuasse? Versionem Aquilae LXX. Interpretibus praelatam fuisse ab Origene non affirmavit Simonius, sed eum illis Interpretibus non ita fuisse addictum, quin etiam ex aliis saepe auxilium quaereret; idque tam Hieronymi quam ipsius Origenis verbis demonstratum fuit. Hic enim LXX. Interpretum Codices, quos putavit corruptos, ex Aquilae, Symmachi ac Theodotionis Versionibus castigare non reformidavit.
units.tr: I come back to Origen, a writer of great weight on the present subject. Simonius had said that Vossius erred in thinking that Origen had followed no manuscripts except the Greek copies of the Seventy Interpreters, whereas Origen himself, as Jerome reports, sought help from the Hebrew language in his Tomes, although in his Homilies, which he delivered to the common people, he followed the common edition. Vossius adds that Simonius falls back on his own Jerome, from whose words, however, it could not be shown that Origen ever preferred the version of Aquila to that of the Seventy Interpreters. But from whom can we better learn Origen's mind than from Jerome, who read and reread his books, and who testifies that the Alexandrian papers, that is, the books of Origen, emptied his purse? Simonius did not affirm that Origen preferred Aquila's version to that of the Seventy, but that he was not so attached to those Interpreters that he did not often seek help from others as well; and this was shown by the words of Jerome and of Origen himself. For here he did not hesitate to correct the copies of the Seventy, which he thought corrupt, by the versions of Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion.

units.la: Verum Origenes ipse, inquit Vossius, testatur contrarium in Epistola ad Africanum, in qua asserit recedendum non esse a terminis quos Christus & Apostoli posuerunt. At quale fuerit Origenis ingenium, & qua ratione exponenda sint verba illius scribentis Africano, ostendit Simonius: quippe Origenes in hac Epistola vulgares opiniones sequitur. Itaque doctissimi illius Patris auctoritate abusus est Vossius, cujus scribendi rationem non cognovit: ille enim haud infrequenter receptis apud plebem de LXX. Interpretum Versione opinionibus se accommodavit. Rem ita se habere declarat non modo Hieronymus, sed & ipse Origenes, qui Aquilae, Symmachi & Theodotionis Codices pluribus locis sinceriores esse LXX. Interpretibus subens agnovit, sique interdum plus sit in illis quam in Ebraeo, non falsitatis Ebraicum Exemplar accusat, uti facit Vossius; contra notat his locis LXX. Interpretum lectionem tanquam suspectam. Sic Commentariis in Euangelium Joannis, postquam aliquot nomina in illis restituit ex veritate Ebraica & ex Versionibus Aquilae, Symmachi & Theodotionis, addit illa suspecta debere esse loca in Graeca LXX. Interpretum Tralatione, ubi plura nomina propria enumerantur, quam in Contextu Ebraico. Haec enim sunt doctissimi illius Patris verba. Μάλιστα δ' ὑπο-πιδέτιον τῆς τόπως τ' χαφῶν, ἐνῶν καλλόγως ἐσιν ἀμα ὀνομάτων πλειόνων, ὡς ἐν τῷ Ἰησοῦ τὰ ἀεὶ τ' κληρονο-μίας ἢ ἐν τῇ πεώτη τ' Παραλειπο-μένων. At contra Vossius his ipsis locis semper declamitat in Judaeos tanquam librorum suorum corruptores, neque aliam istius depravationis tionis causam affert, quàm quia aliter habent LXX. Interpretes. Longè modestiùs in hoc negotio se gessit Origenes, qui ut hominem criticum & summo præditum judicio decebat, Ebraicos Græcosque Codices committens, plus autoritatis tribuit Ebraicis quàm Græcis qui ex illis sumpti fuerant.
units.tr: But Origen himself, says Vossius, testifies to the contrary in his Letter to Africanus, in which he asserts that one must not depart from the limits which Christ and the Apostles set. But what sort of man Origen was, and how the words he wrote to Africanus should be explained, Simonius shows: in that letter Origen follows the common opinions. Vossius, therefore, has abused the authority of that most learned Father, whose manner of writing he did not understand, for Origen not infrequently accommodated himself to the opinions held among the common people about the Version of the Seventy. That this is so is declared not only by Jerome but by Origen himself, who acknowledged, in several places, that the copies of Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion were more faithful than those of the Seventy, and when the Seventy have sometimes more than the Hebrew, he does not accuse the Hebrew text of falsehood, as Vossius does; on the contrary, in these places he marks the reading of the Seventy as suspect. Thus in his Commentary on the Gospel of John, after restoring several names from the Hebrew truth and from the versions of Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, he adds that those passages in the Greek translation of the Seventy where more proper names are listed than in the Hebrew text ought to be regarded as suspect. These are the words of that most learned Father: [μάλιστα δ' ὑποπιδέτιον τῆς τόπως τ' χαφῶν, ἐνῶν καλλόγως ἐσιν ἀμα ὀνομάτων πλειόνων, ὡς ἐν τῷ Ἰησοῦ τὰ ἀεὶ τ' κληρονομίας ἢ ἐν τῇ πρώτη τ' Παραλειπομένων.] But Vossius, on the contrary, always inveighs against the Jews, at these very places, as corrupters of their own books, and gives no other cause of this depravation than that the Seventy read otherwise. Origen conducted himself with far greater moderation in this matter; as became a critical man endowed with the highest judgment, he compared the Hebrew and Greek copies and gave more authority to the Hebrew than to the Greek copies that had been taken from them.

units.la: De loco autem Exodi quem hîc Vossius verbosè explicat, sileo, quia nihil facit ad propositum; cùm de Origenis mente quam illustravimus solùm agatur, non de genuina loci istius interpretatione. Quocunque enim modo exponantur verba Exodi, certum est Origenem in suis Commentariis etiam ex aliis Interpretibus quæsivisse auxilia, uti cum Hieronymo Simonius contendit: quodque magis ad rem facit, idem Origenes suspectam interdum LXX. Interpretum lectionem ex illis Interpretibus reformare non dubitavit.
units.tr: As for the passage of Exodus, which Vossius explains here at wordy length, I say nothing, because it has no bearing on the question; for we are concerned only with Origen's mind, which we have illustrated, and not with the genuine interpretation of that passage. However the words of Exodus are explained, it is certain that Origen in his Commentaries also sought help from other interpreters, as Simonius contends with Jerome; and what bears more directly on the point, the same Origen did not hesitate to correct, from those other interpreters, a reading of the Seventy that he judged suspect.

units.la: Jam sophistam agens Vossius, quasi ex suggestu declamat adversus Simonium, qui objecerat illum scripta Patrum imperitè tractasse, ac nescivisse quid Patres ex sua sententia affirment, quid ex vulgaribus opinionibus proferant, atque in primis Origenes. Quærit postea quinam sint portentosi illi Aristeæ sermones, cùm in illis quæ vulgò teruntur Exemplaribus nihil tale occurrat. Sed jam annotavit Simonius, ea quæ in historia sua narravit Aristeas, minùs abesse à fabellis & portentis quæ Judæi de Jonathane Chaldæo Interprete confinxerunt, quàm à vera narratione. Ille siquidem ratione haud absimili scribit, eos qui antea Legem Græcè evulgare ausi fuerant, à Deo punitos fuisse. Sic Theopompus, qui voluerat nonnulla ex Lege historiæ suæ inserere, animo turbatus fuit ultra dies triginta: cùmque Deum supplex oraret ut morbi sui causam aperiret, in somno responsum accepit, hoc ei accidisse quòd res divinas evulgare in animo habuisset. Simile quid Aristeas narrat de Theodecte Poëta, cui cùm etiam voluisset ex libro Legis aliquid in suam transferre fabulam, statim visus ablatus est. Has offas quæ crudæ sunt, bonus Vossius concoquit, quia illius stomacho aptæ; quas tamen vix concoqui posse sentiens ipse Aristeas, hæc eodem loco subjicit. ὅτι ὁμολογεῖ ἢ ἐξ ... Existimo autem fore ut iis omnibus qui hæc lecturi sunt videantur ea esse incredibilia.
units.tr: Now, playing the sophist, Vossius declaims from the pulpit against Simonius, who had charged him with handling the writings of the Fathers unskilfully, and with not knowing what the Fathers affirm from their own opinion and what they set down from common opinions, above all Origen. Vossius then asks what those portentous discourses of Aristeas are, since nothing of the kind occurs in the copies commonly in use. But Simonius has already pointed out that the things Aristeas relates in his history are less remote from the fables and portents which the Jews invented about Jonathan the Chaldee interpreter than from true narrative. For Aristeas writes, on a not dissimilar principle, that those who had earlier dared to publish the Law in Greek were punished by God. Thus Theopompus, who had wished to insert some matters from the Law into his history, was troubled in mind for more than thirty days; and when, as a suppliant, he prayed God to reveal the cause of his illness, he received an answer in a dream that this had befallen him because he had intended to publish divine things. Aristeas tells of something similar concerning the poet Theodectes, who, when he had wished to transfer some matter from a book of the Law into his own play, immediately lost his sight. Good Vossius digests these crude morsels because they suit his stomach; yet Aristeas himself, sensing that they could scarcely be digested, adds the following in the same place: [ὅτι ὁμολογεῖ ἢ ἐξ ...] I suppose that all who read these things will judge them incredible.

units.la: His & aliis similibus adductus fuit Simonius, ut fidem non haberet Aristeæ narranti minùs credibilia dignaque ætate quâ Opusculum istud à Judæis confictum est. Quare testatur sibi probabilem videri eorum sententiam, qui putant Græcam Versionem nomen LXX. Interpretum sumpsisse à LXXII. Synedrii Hierosolymitani Senatoribus qui hanc suffragiis suis comprobarunt. Quid ad hæc modestissimus Vossius? Totus versus in furorem asserit sic sentire semichristianum Talmudistam; Simonium in ea esse opinione, ut putet Versionem illam, licet approbatam à Senatoribus Hierosolymitanis, non sinceram esse & legitimam, sed dolosam, perfidam & summa cum astutia ad decipiendas concinnatam fuisse
units.tr: Moved by these and similar things, Simonius refused to believe Aristeas's account, which is less credible and less worthy of the age in which that little work was fabricated by the Jews. Hence he declares that the opinion seems probable to him of those who think that the Greek version took the name of the Seventy Interpreters from the seventy-two senators of the Jerusalem Sanhedrin who approved it by their votes. What does the most modest Vossius say to this? He declares, in a whole paragraph, that a half-Christian Talmudist thinks in this way; that Simonius holds the opinion that that version, although approved by the Jerusalem senators, is not sincere and lawful, but was contrived deceitfully, treacherously, and with the greatest cunning, to deceive

units.la: Arist. de Vers. LXX. Interp. fuisse gentes. Parcendum est ardori Prophetico quo accensus fuit bonus Christianus Vossius, qui tunc de refellendo semichristiano illo Talmudista cogitavit. Nemo est qui pluris fecerit Graecam LXX. Interpretum Versionem quàm Simonius, qui etiam Vossium laudaverit, quòd illam à maledicentissimorum hominum calumniis asserere conaretur: non eam tamen Divinam esse & Propheticam existimavit. Si semichristianus Talmudista in hoc solùm peccavit, quòd dixerit Versionem istam à Synedrii magni Sacerdotibus approbatam fuisse, non video cur tot maledictis illum lacessiverit Vossius: inde enim magna illi conciliatur autoritas. Sixtus Senensis vir doctus libri secundi Maccabaeorum divinitatem arcessit potissimùm ex illorum Senatorum suffragiis. Haec sunt illius verba. Jason Cyrenaeus natione Judaeus verax & disertus historiarum Scriptor scripsit Graecâ & copiosâ dicendi ubertate de gestis Maccabaeorum Principum libros quinque, quos ob eximiam narrationis fidelitatem Senatus Populusque Hierosolymitanus jussit in parvam redigi Epitomen, quae nunc inter caeteros Divina Scriptura libros annumeratur, parique cum eis veneratione suscipitur, & secundus Maccabaeorum inscribitur. Itaque Sibyllino furori quo tunc percitus fuit Vossius, tribuo haec quae mox subjicit verba. Quâ verò ratione factum sit, ut in perfida & fraudulenta Sacrarum Literarum procudendâ Versione conspirarint omnes isti qui Synedrium magnum constituerent Judaeorum Prophetae, id non explicat P. Simonius, sed similitudine declarat. Id
units.tr: Aristeas, On the Version of the Seventy Interpreters, the nations. We must make allowance for the prophetic zeal with which the good Christian Vossius was inflamed, when he then thought of refuting that half-Christian Talmudist. There is no one who has valued the Greek Version of the Seventy Interpreters more highly than Simonius, who even praised Vossius for trying to defend it against the calumnies of the most slanderous men; yet he did not judge it to be divine and prophetic. If the half-Christian Talmudist sinned only in this, that he said that this version was approved by the chief priests of the great Sanhedrin, I do not see why Vossius assailed him with so many abuses, since that statement actually brings him great authority. The learned Sixtus of Siena derives the divinity of the second book of the Maccabees chiefly from the votes of those senators. These are his words: Jason of Cyrene, a Jew by nation, a truthful and eloquent writer of histories, wrote in Greek and with a copious richness of expression five books on the deeds of the Maccabean princes, which the Senate and people of Jerusalem ordered to be reduced to a small epitome, on account of the remarkable faithfulness of the narration; this epitome is now counted among the other books of Divine Scripture and is received with equal veneration, and is entitled the second book of the Maccabees. Therefore I attribute to the Sibylline frenzy by which Vossius was then stirred the following words which he adds: But how it came about that all those who constituted the great Sanhedrin of the Jews, the prophets, conspired in producing a faithless and fraudulent version of the Sacred Letters, P. Simonius does not explain, but declares by a comparison. Simonius does not explain this, because he never devised anything of the kind. The comparison, however, which he takes from the common Latin version, which was wisely approved by the Fathers of the Council of Trent, serves the point admirably; for the question concerns the Greek translation, which among the Hellenistic Jews was accepted as authentic

units.la: quidem non explicat Simonius, quia tale quid nunquam commentus est. Similitudo autem quam sumit ex Versione vulgari Latina, quae sapienter à Patribus Concilii Tridentini approbata est, mirè facit ad propositum; quia de Graeca Tralatione agitur, quae apud Judaeos Hellenistas authentica facta est, postquàm talem eam declararunt Synedrii magni Assessores; sicut apud Christianos Ecclesiae Occidentalis Versio Latina facta est etiam authentica Patrum Tridentinorum decreto. Par est utrobique ratio; quia non agitur de S. Scripturarum libris, qui extra controversiam Divini sunt & Canonici; sed de illorum Versione, quae ideo Divina non est & ab omnibus mendis repurgata, quòd authentica declarata fuerit: de hoc enim nunquam cogitarunt Tridentini Episcopi, neque etiam Summi Pontifices Sixtus V. & Clemens VIII. qui curarunt tantùm ut Latinum Exemplar quàm emendatissimè ederetur. Sed certè, inquit Vossius, non consensissent Patres Tridentini in approbanda hac Versione, nisi eam optimam judicassent. Bene quidem arguit: hanc enim optimam esse existimavit Simonius; siquè idem de ea judicium ferret Vossius, non tot maledictis illius autorem Hieronymum lacesseret. Verùm, ex eo quòd Synodus Tridentina vulgarem Editionem Latinam caeteris Versionibus Latinis praetulerit, & eam definierit authenticam, non sequitur eam quoque esse Divinam; quia de Versione agitur cujus autor Propheta non fuit, sed Interpres; minimè verò de ipsius Scripturae libris, quos Divinos esse Synodus Tridentina declarare potuit, non tamen ipsos facere Divinos.
units.tr: Simonius does not explain this, because he never devised anything of the kind. The comparison he draws from the common Latin Version, which the Fathers of the Council of Trent wisely approved, is very much to the point. The question concerns the Greek translation, which was made authentic among the Hellenist Jews once the assessors of the great Synedrion declared it such, just as the Latin Version of the Western Church was made authentic by the decree of the Tridentine Fathers. The reasoning is the same in both cases, since the question is not about the books of Holy Scripture, which are beyond dispute divine and canonical, but about their translation. That translation is not divine, and it is cleared of all errors only because it has been declared authentic. The bishops of Trent never thought of this, nor did the supreme pontiffs Sixtus V and Clement VIII, who only took care that the Latin text should be published as correctly as possible. But surely, says Vossius, the Tridentine Fathers would not have agreed to approve this Version unless they judged it the best. He argues well enough. Simonius did indeed think it the best; and if Vossius held the same opinion of it, he would not assail its author Jerome with so many insults. Yet it does not follow, because the Council of Trent preferred the common Latin edition to the other Latin versions and defined it as authentic, that it is also divine. The question concerns a translation whose author was not a prophet but an interpreter, and not at all the books of Scripture themselves, which the Council of Trent could declare to be divine, but could not thereby make divine.

units.la: Ab eodem furore Sibyllino profectum est illud quod Vossius argumentum suum non prosequens ibidem Simonio objicit; eum videlicet existimare, nos non habere scripta Prophetica Veteris Testamenti integra, sed ampliata, decurtata, & variis modis pro lubitu & ratione temporum à Sacerdotibus magni Synedrii interpolata. Furor sanè Propheticus facit ut bonus Vossius tam desultorie scribat & argumentetur. Quia verò eadem nonnullis interjectis repetit, totum hoc negotium isto loco resumam. Satis erit in praesentia adversus Vossium ea regerere quae Simonio objicit, qui nihil prorsus mutationis Scripturae libris accidisse putat, ex eo tempore quo in publicum editi sunt & in Canonem relati, nisi ea quae in librariorum incuriam poterit rejici. Contrà Vossius Criticam sacram tractans sine judicio autor est, S. Literarum fontes consultò à Judaeis & Samaritis depravatos fuisse odio Christianae Religionis; genuinam Scripturam petendam esse à Graeca LXX. Interpretum Tralatione, quae jam ante Origenis tempora mutila erat, decurtata & ampliata. Viderit igitur Vossius, quâ ratione affirmare potuerit Simonium scripta Prophetica Veteris Testamenti protulisse non integra, sed decurtata & ampliata, cùm firmissimis rationibus probaverit, Judaeos nunquam suos Codices corrupisse, ostenderitque imperitum esse Criticum Vossium, qui hoc ausus sit affirmare. Constat LXX. Interpretes, in libris maximè Prophetarum, decurtatos fuisse etiam ante Origenem, qui decurtatis istis locis quaesierit auxilia seu supplementa ex sermichristianorum Versionibus. Praeterea Hieronymi tempore Daniel Propheta non ex LXX. Interpretibus, sed ex Theodotione legebatur in Ecclesiis.
units.tr: From the same Sibylline frenzy comes that objection which Vossius, not pursuing his own argument, brings against Simonius in the same place: that Simonius thinks we do not have the prophetic writings of the Old Testament whole, but enlarged, shortened, and altered in various ways, at the will of the priests of the great Synedrion and according to the needs of the times. Surely a prophetic frenzy makes the good Vossius write and argue so aimlessly. Since he repeats the same point after some intervening matter, I shall take up the whole business at this place. For the present it will suffice to answer against Vossius those things which he objects to Simonius, who thinks that nothing whatever has happened to the books of Scripture since they were published and received into the canon, except such changes as can be put down to the carelessness of copyists. On the contrary, Vossius, in treating sacred criticism, is without judgment when he asserts that the sources of the sacred Letters were deliberately corrupted by the Jews and Samaritans out of hatred for the Christian religion, and that the genuine Scripture must be sought in the Greek translation of the Seventy, which was already mutilated, shortened, and enlarged before the time of Origen. Let Vossius see how he could affirm that Simonius put forward the prophetic writings of the Old Testament not whole but shortened and enlarged, when Simonius has proved by very firm reasons that the Jews never corrupted their codices, and has shown that Vossius is an unskilled critic for daring to assert this. It is established that the Seventy translators shortened the books, especially those of the Prophets, even before Origen, who sought help and supplements for those shortened passages from the versions of the semi-Christians. Moreover, in Jerome's time the prophet Daniel was read in the churches not from the Seventy but from Theodotion.

units.la: Transit postea ad linguam Hellenisticam Vossius, objicitque Simonium linguam hanc sepultam & ad inferos missam denuò suscitare. Sed jam respondCrat Simonius, Salmasium hac in re de nominibus saepè disputasse: etsi enim pleraque voces quibus utuntur LXX. Interpretes Graecae sint, novas tamen illis potestates affingunt interdum ex praesumptis opinionibus. Similiter quando verba Ebraica ita reddunt, ut verbum de verbo exprimant, minùs Graecè loquuntur; & hoc Simonius vocavit κακοζηλίαν seu pravam affectationem Judaeis Interpretibus familiarem, quae etiam interdum in LXX. Interpretibus occurrit. Sic, dum quasdam praepositiones ex Ebraeo faciunt Graecas, retinent dictionem Ebraicam: exempli causâ, sermo Ebraicus comparativum exprimit per מִן, quod LXX. cum Aquila haud infrequenter reddunt ἀπό, ab. Tunc ista κακοζηλία sensum efficit obscurum. His accedit, LXX. Interpretes tribuere etiam interdum verbis Graecis potestates quas sumunt ex sermone Syriaco; quia sermo Syriacus seu Chaldaicus tunc Judaeis erat vernaculus, ita ut his & similibus locis difficile sit eorum mentem expiscari: unde factum est, ut ipse Vossius, qui se Graecè scire putat, miris modis se contorqueat ut explicet verbum τυρήσει, Cap. Genes. 3. accusavit enim librarios, quasi contra omnium Codicum auctoritatem legendum sit τέψαι. Demum factus oculatior vulgarem lectionem quam improbaverat, retinendam esse censet: quia jam ab aliis annotatum fuit, verbum τηρέω etiam sumi in malam partem, ac significare quoque observare, insidiari. Verum si Graecum est verbum τηρέω sumptum hoc sensu, cur Vossius qui scit Graece in re tam obvia modo ait, modo negat, secumque manifeste pugnat? Cur non alios hujusce rei profert testes, quam ipsosmet LXX. Interpretes, vel Scriptores Ecclesiasticos, qui saepius ut sensum vocum Graecarum quae occurrunt in LXX. exponant, recurrunt ad Aquilam & alios Interpretes? Hoc quidem loco existimaverim, vulgarem lectionem Graecam τυρήσει retinendam esse, sed illius sensum ex lingua Hellenistica petendum, quia LXX. Seniores tunc attenderunt ad verbum שמר, quod interdum apud Syros & Chaldaeos in malam partem sumitur. Haec, quia saepius in Graeca LXX. Interpretum Versione occurrunt, Patres Graeci tunc alios Interpretes Graecos consulunt, ut eorum beneficio LXX. Interpretum mentem facilius assequantur. Verba quidem illa Graeca esse nemo dubitat; sed quaestio est, utrum notiones quas illis affingunt LXX. semper sint Graecae.
units.tr: Vossius next turns to the Hellenistic language, and objects that Simonius raises again a language buried and sent down to the dead. But Simonius had already replied that Salmasius had often disputed about these words in this matter. For although most of the words the Seventy use are Greek, they sometimes attach new meanings to them, drawn from preconceived opinions. Likewise, when they render Hebrew words so as to express word for word, they speak less like Greeks; and Simonius called this κακοζηλία [kakozēlia], a perverse affectation familiar to the Jewish translators, which also sometimes occurs among the Seventy. Thus, while they make some prepositions Greek from the Hebrew, they keep the Hebrew idiom: for example, the Hebrew idiom expresses the comparative by מִן [min], which the Seventy, together with Aquila, not infrequently render ἀπό [apo], "from." This κακοζηλία then makes the sense obscure. To this must be added that the Seventy sometimes also give Greek words meanings which they take from the Syriac language, since Syriac or Chaldee was then the vernacular of the Jews; so that in these and similar passages it is hard to grasp their meaning. Hence it came about that Vossius himself, who thinks he knows Greek, twists himself in strange ways to explain the word τυρήσει [tyrēsei] in Genesis 3. For he accused the copyists, as if against the authority of all the codices one ought to read τέψαι [tepsai]. At last, becoming more clear-sighted, he thinks the common reading which he had disapproved must be retained, since it has already been noted by others that the verb τηρέω [tēreō] is also taken in a bad sense, and signifies observare [to watch], insidiari [to lie in wait for]. But if the Greek verb τηρέω is taken in this sense, why does Vossius, who claims to know Greek, say now yes and now no about a matter so obvious, and plainly contradict himself? Why does he bring forward no other witnesses to this usage than the Seventy themselves, or ecclesiastical writers, who very often resort to Aquila and other interpreters to explain the sense of the Greek words that occur in the Seventy? For my part, I should think that at this place the common Greek reading τυρήσει must be kept, but its sense must be sought in the Hellenistic language, because the Seventy elders then attended to the Hebrew שמר [shamar], which among the Syrians and Chaldeans is sometimes taken in a bad sense. Since these words occur very often in the Greek version of the Seventy, the Greek Fathers then consult other Greek interpreters, so that by their help they may more easily grasp the meaning of the Seventy. No one doubts that these are Greek words; but the question is whether the notions the Seventy attach to them are always Greek.

units.la: Praeterea voces esse tam in LXX. quam in Novo Testamento, quae minus Graecae sint, dudum observavit Hieronymus; adeoque nupera non
units.tr: Besides, it was long ago observed by Jerome that there are words in the Seventy as well as in the New Testament which are less Greek,

units.la: est ac ficta lingua illa Hellenistica: quippe Graece sciebat Hieronymus, qui etiam illas voces novas tuetur adversus disertulos quosdam aetatis suae homines, qui notabant LXX. Interpretes quasi minus Graece loquerentur, iisque, ut loquitur Hieronymus, de novitate & vilitate sermonis illuderent. Hos, quos Hieronymus disertos seculi appellat, ex eo in primis arguit, quod LXX. Interpretes de Ebraeis difficultatibus proprietates exprimere conati sint. Haec est καταζηλία illa quam recte Simonius cum Hieronymo tribuit LXX. Senioribus: adeoque male reprehenditur a Vossio qui scopum nunquam ferit, quasi relicta lingua Hellenistica transierit ad καταζηλίαν Judaicorum Interpretum, nec tamen addiderit de quibus Interpretibus loqueretur: nam eodem loco verbis expressis affirmat Simonius, se non tribuere LXX. Interpretibus Graeci sermonis imperitiam, sed tantum καταζηλίαν. Vossius, cui nihil solidi subest quod respondeat, semper quaerit effugia.
units.tr: and that the Hellenistic language is therefore no recent or invented thing. Jerome certainly knew Greek, and he defends those new words against certain clever men of his own age, who noted that the Seventy spoke less like Greeks and mocked them, as Jerome puts it, for the novelty and cheapness of their speech. He refutes these, whom he calls the clever men of the age, chiefly on the ground that the Seventy tried to express the peculiarities of the Hebrew difficulties. This is the καταζηλία [katazēlia] which Simonius rightly attributes with Jerome to the Seventy elders; and so Vossius wrongly criticises it, never hitting the mark, as if Simonius had left the Hellenistic language and passed over to the καταζηλία of the Jewish translators, without saying which translators he meant. For in the same place Simonius affirms in express words that he does not attribute to the Seventy ignorance of the Greek language, but only καταζηλία. Vossius, who has nothing solid to answer with, always looks for escape routes.

units.la: Neque etiam Augustino videtur ignota fuisse lingua Hellenistica: ille enim expendens verba illa Levit. Cap. 22. ut leguntur in Itala, Cum adimpleti fuerint dies purgationis ejus super filio aut super filia, haec addit: Merito quidam nostri ita interpretati sunt istum in Levitico locum, ut non dicerent super filio aut super filia, sed pro filio aut pro filia: hanc enim vim hujus praepositionis esse intellexerunt hoc loco, ubi Graecus ait ἐφ' ὑμῶν ἢ ἐπὶ ὑμῶν. Sic quidem in Vulgata reddidit Hieronymus; neque aliunde vis illa praepositionis Graecae ἐπὶ sumpta
units.tr: Nor does Augustine seem to have been ignorant of the Hellenistic language. For when he examines those words of Leviticus 22 as they are read in the Itala, When the days of her purification shall be fulfilled for a son or for a daughter, he adds: Some of our people have rightly translated that passage in Leviticus not as "upon a son or upon a daughter" but as "for a son or for a daughter"; for they understood the force of this preposition in this place, where the Greek has ἐφ' ὑμῶν ἢ ἐπὶ ὑμῶν [eph' hymōn ē epi hymōn]. Jerome also rendered it so in the Vulgate; nor was that force of the Greek preposition ἐπὶ [epi] taken from anywhere else

units.la: {y} Hieron. Comm. in Epist. ad Gal. sumpta est, quàm ex Ebraeo ⸗, quod hoc loco idem est atque ⸗: constat autem, ⸗ apud Ebraeos significare super & pro.
units.tr: Jerome, Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians. It is taken from the Hebrew word, which here means the same as the other. It is certain that among the Hebrews this word signifies both "over" and "for."

units.la: Quae autem eodem loco subjicit Vossius de verbo ἐκληνίζειν, quasi significet partes Graecorum asserere, ea non esse ad propositum recte animadvertit Simonius, cùm de hac vocis istius, quae plures habet significatus, notione minimè agatur; atque Simonius, perinde esse ac si quis de Vossio dixerit eum esse Criticum & Canonicum. Sic verbum ἐκληνίζειν potest significare partes Graecorum sequi; ita tamen ut significet etiam loqui Graecè. Hîc de prima significatione non agitur; sed de secunda. Jam fuisse Graecos qui Graecè loquerentur non inficias ierit Vossius, qui velit non aliam fuisse linguam Judaeis omnibus qui erant in Imperio Romano, quàm Graecam. Cùm autem firmissimis rationibus demonstraverit Simonius, fuisse etiam Judaeos qui Chaldaicè sive Syriacè loquerentur, maximè Hierosolymis & in locis vicinioribus, optimè confecit Judaeos illos qui ἐκληνίζονται, distingui ab aliis, quòd Graecè loquerentur.
units.tr: As for what Vossius adds at the same place about the verb ἐκληνίζειν [eklēnizein], as if it meant to take the side of the Greeks, Simonius rightly observes that this has nothing to do with the question, since we are not concerned here with that sense of a word which has several meanings. Simonius is like someone who said of Vossius that he was a critic and a canonist. The verb ἐκληνίζειν [eklēnizein] can mean to follow the Greeks, but it can also mean to speak Greek. Here the question is not about the first meaning but the second. Vossius will not deny that there were Greek-speaking Jews, though he would have it that all the Jews in the Roman Empire spoke no language but Greek. But Simonius has demonstrated by very firm arguments that there were also Jews who spoke Chaldee or Syriac, especially in Jerusalem and the nearby regions. So he has rightly concluded that those Jews who are called ἐκληνίζονται [eklēnizontai] were distinguished from the others because they spoke Greek.

units.la: Iterum in solitam λογομαχίαν relabitur Vossius, qui Simonium arguit quòd Rabbinos appellaverit Doctores recutitos, quam vocem notat ut ineptam; quia illâ denotantur Judaei qui soliti fuerint sibi praeputium adducere. Sic, quia minutus est Criticus Vossius, de verbis disputat cùm rationes desunt; cùmque sit lepidulus, rogat Simonium ut ostendat recutitos peculiarem habuisse linguam & distinctam ab aliis Judaeis. Si li-
units.tr: Vossius again slips into his usual war of words. He accuses Simonius of calling the rabbis "uncircumcised teachers," and he marks the phrase as inept, because it denotes Jews who were accustomed to draw the foreskin over. So, since Vossius is a petty critic, he argues about words when he lacks reasons, and since he is a bit of a wit, he asks Simonius to show that the uncircumcised had a language of their own, distinct from other Jews. If it

units.la: ceat cum Vossio sectari minutias; dixerim non ita certam esse vocis istius notionem, quin plerique Grammatici & Lexicographi recutitum idem esse agnoscant atque circumcisum, seu eum cui recisa est cutis vel praeputium. Miror tamen Vossium de vocibus ineptis lites intendere, cujus libri vocibus & phrasibus veré ineptis & minùs Latinis abundant, quarum amplam messem facile sit colligere. Quodque in isto homine Latino mirabilius est, vocabulum quod hodie ipsi Latinum est, cras Latinum non erit. Sed mitto ista, quia leviora sunt. Satis est dixisse Vossium in prima libri sui de LXX. Interpretibus periodo, scientias in plurali usurpare: at qui Latinè loquuntur dicunt disciplinas, vel quid simile. Caetera non lubet persequi, quòd non sint ad propositum.
units.tr: pleases me to chase trifles with Vossius, I would say that the meaning of this word is not so certain that most grammarians and lexicographers do not recognise that "uncircumcised" (recutitus) means the same as "circumcised," that is, one whose skin or foreskin has been cut away. Still, I am surprised that Vossius should bring lawsuits over inept words, when his own books abound in words and phrases that really are inept and not very Latin. It would be easy to gather a large harvest of these. What is more remarkable in this Latin man is that a word which is Latin today will not be Latin tomorrow. But I pass over these things, since they are minor. It is enough to say that in the first period of his book on the Seventy translators, Vossius uses the word "sciences" in the plural, whereas those who write Latin say "disciplines" or something similar. I do not wish to pursue the rest, since it does not bear on the question.

units.la: In verbis Genes. Cap. ⸗ dixerat Simonius ancipitem sibi videri LXX. Interpretum Versionem, quia vox ἀρχή principium & principatum significat: diligentis autem est Interpretis vitare amphiboliam sive ambiguitatem. At regerit Vossius, debuisse quoque Christum & Apostolos carpi, qui passim similiter loquantur. Sed in hoc errat Vossius, qui putet Christum & Apostolos Graecè in Novo Testamento locutos fuisse, quia eorum verba ab Euangelistis Graecè exprimuntur. Jam observaverat Simonius, Novi Testamenti phrasim non minùs esse Hellenisticam, quàm LXX. Interpretum sermonem quem imitati sunt Euangelistae. Rectè quoque animadvertit,
units.tr: On the words of Genesis chapter 1, Simonius had said that the version of the Seventy seemed ambiguous to him, because the word ἀρχή [archē] means both "beginning" and "rule." It is the task of a careful translator to avoid amphiboly, that is, ambiguity. But Vossius retorts that Christ and the Apostles should also have been censured, since they speak in the same way throughout. But Vossius is wrong to think that Christ and the Apostles spoke Greek in the New Testament simply because the Evangelists express their words in Greek. Simonius had already observed that the phrasing of the New Testament is no less Hellenistic than the language of the Seventy, which the Evangelists imitated. He also rightly noticed

units.la: Origenem hoc loco convenientiorem judicasse Aquilæ interpretationem: sic quoque passim alii Patres, maximè Græci, laudant Aquilæ, Symmachi & Theodotionis Versiones uti minùs obscuriores quàm sit LXX. Interpretum Tralatio, quos etiam relinquunt in suis Commentariis. Potuit igitur tam hîc Simonius quàm aliis locis LXX. accusare ambiguitatis & obscuritatis, præeuntibus sibi Græcis Patribus.
units.tr: that Origen judged the translation of Aquila more suitable in this place. Likewise other Fathers, especially the Greeks, often praise the versions of Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion as less obscure than the translation of the Seventy, which they even leave aside in their commentaries. So Simonius, here and elsewhere, could accuse the Seventy of ambiguity and obscurity, following the Greek Fathers who went before him.

units.la: Quod verò ait Vossius, unicum Aquilæ studium fuisse invertere ordinem verborum quem LXX. posuere, ut hac ratione sensum Scripturæ obscuraret, ac hoc loco posuisse ἐξωσίαν, quia LXX. posuere ἀρχάς, illud non facit ad institutum, imò in ipsum Vossium regeri potest, cùm Græci illi Patres, qui relictis LXX. Interpretibus sequuntur interdum Aquilam, quia his locis Versio illius clarior est, declarant manifestè eundem Aquilam non eo consilio invertisse ordinem verborum quem LXX. posuere, ut Scripturæ sensum obscuraret, sed magis ut illum redderet explicatiorem. Ineptè igitur Vossius huc transtulit duos hosce versiculos, Omnia enim stolidi magis admirantur amantque Inversis quæ sub verbis latitantia cernunt.
units.tr: As for Vossius's claim that Aquila's only aim was to invert the order of the words that the Seventy had put, so as to obscure the sense of Scripture, and that here he put ἐξωσίαν [exousian] because the Seventy put ἀρχάς [archas], this does not bear on the matter. Indeed it can be turned against Vossius himself. Those Greek Fathers who, leaving the Seventy translators, sometimes follow Aquila because his version is clearer in these places, plainly show that Aquila did not invert the order of the words, as the Seventy had them, with the purpose of obscuring the sense of Scripture, but rather to make it plainer. So Vossius has inappropriately applied to this matter two lines of verse: "For fools admire and love all the more things that are inverted, which conceal their meaning under the words."

units.la: nisi dicat ineptos esse Patres & stolidos, qui passim in suis scriptis observant Aquilam & alios Interpretes Græcos verba Ebraica clarius ac dilucidius vertisse quàm LXX.Seniores. Nugas igitur hîc ubique agit Vossius. Pergit quoque ineptire, ubi ait illum esse Aquilam quem deperit Simonius, & quo præcipuè duce novam S.Literarum meditatur editionem. Norunt qui Criticam Sacram Simonii legerunt, eum longè aliam veri Sacrarum Literarum Interpretis ideam effinxisse, quàm illam quam ei tribuit Vossius.
units.tr: Unless he means that the Fathers were inept and foolish, who throughout their writings observe that Aquila and other Greek translators rendered the Hebrew words more clearly and distinctly than the Seventy elders. So Vossius is talking nonsense here throughout. He also goes on being inept when he says that Simonius is in love with Aquila and that Simonius meditates a new edition of the Sacred Scriptures chiefly under Aquila's guidance. Those who have read Simonius's Critical History of the Sacred Texts know that he formed a very different idea of the true interpreter of the Sacred Scriptures from the one Vossius attributes to him.

units.la: Verba Genes. Cap. 3. vers. 14. Ἐπικαταράτος σὺ ὑπὲρ πάντων τῶν κτηνῶν, obscura esse notaverat Simonius, quia voces Ebraicas pressiùs exprimunt, & מן, quod apud Ebræos nota est Comparativi, vertunt ὑπὲρ, ab. Contra hæc regerit Vossius, ὑπὲρ non sumi comparativè; sed hîc esse Prosopopoiam, Deumque imprecari serpenti, ut eum animalia omnia maledictis incessant. Verùm ista dici comparativè res ipsa loquitur; unde etiam in Vulgata habetur, Maledictus es inter omnia animantia: nam præpositio מן, quam etiam retinent Chaldæus, Syrus & Arabs, significat pra, & Latini Interpretes istarum Versionum omnes cum Vulgata concordant in exprimenda hac præpositione. Fecit etiam illa præpositionis Græcæ ὑπὲρ apud LXX. ambiguitas, ut interdum Interpres qui ex Græco Scripturam fecit Arabicam, vertat ὑπὲρ plus quàm, etiam ubi illa non sumitur comparativè. Ut ista ambiguitas tollatur, melius redditur ὑπὲρ, super, uti Simonius annotavit in Castigationibus: sic enim ibi legendum est, non ἀπὸ: quo etiam modo LXX. Interpretes haud infrequenter vertunt מן Ebraicum. De verbo autem πηγνύω & πηγνύεις jam supra egimus. ex asseribus seu tabulis construi; sed ex arboribus quadratis construi affirmat, huncque esse sensum verborum Genes. Cap. 6. verf. 14. Ποίησον σεαυτῷ κιβωτὸν ἐκ ξύλων πετρασμένων. Fac tibi arcam ex lignis quadratis: & quia peritus est naupegus, solusque scit quid rei sit navis, fingit arbores quasdam quadratas fabricae navali aptissimas, quia materiem simul & resinam seu picem ad unguendas naves exhibeant. Sed manifestum est, apud LXX. Interpretes nomine lignorum quadratorum nihil aliud intelligi quàm oblongos asseres ex quibus naves construuntur; quàm expositionem confirmat Latinus Interpres, qui habet Fac tibi arcam ex lignis levigatis, id est, ex complanatis asseribus.
units.tr: Simonius had remarked that the words of Genesis chapter 3, verse 14, "Cursed are you above all the beasts" [Ἐπικαταράτος σὺ ὑπὲρ πάντων τῶν κτηνῶν, Epikataratos su hyper pantōn tōn ktēnōn], are obscure, because they render the Hebrew words too closely, and they translate the Hebrew מן [min], which among the Hebrews is the sign of the comparative, as ὑπὲρ [hyper], "above." Against this Vossius replies that ὑπὲρ [hyper] is not used comparatively here, but that this is a prosopopoeia, and God is calling down a curse upon the serpent, as all animals assail it with curses. But the thing itself shows that the words are used comparatively. That is why the Vulgate also has, "You are cursed among all living creatures." For the preposition מן [min], which the Chaldee paraphrast, the Syrian and the Arab also retain, means "above," and all the Latin translators of those versions agree with the Vulgate in rendering this preposition. The ambiguity of the Greek preposition ὑπὲρ [hyper] in the Seventy has also caused some interpreters, who made an Arabic Scripture from the Greek, to render ὑπὲρ [hyper] as "more than," even where it is not used comparatively. To remove this ambiguity it is better to render ὑπὲρ [hyper] as "over," as Simonius noted in his Castigations. For so it should be read there, not ἀπὸ [apo]. This is also how the Seventy quite often translate the Hebrew מן [min]. I have already discussed the verb πηγνύω [pēgnyō] and πηγνύεις [pēgnyeis] above. Vossius holds that the ark was built not from planks or boards, but from squared trees, and he claims this is the sense of the words of Genesis chapter 6, verse 14: "Make yourself an ark of squared wood" [Ποίησον σεαυτῷ κιβωτὸν ἐκ ξύλων πετρασμένων, Poiēson seautō kibōtον ek xylōn petrasmenōn], that is, "make an ark of squared timber." And since he is a skilled shipbuilder, and alone knows what a ship is, he imagines certain squared trees that are most suitable for shipbuilding, because they supply both timber and the resin or pitch used to smear ships. But it is plain that among the Seventy translators, by "squared timber" nothing else is meant than long planks from which ships are built. The Latin translator confirms this explanation, since he has "Make yourself an ark of planed timber," that is, of smoothed planks.

units.la: Maligne Vossius objecerat, Simonium de Veteris Testamenti Scriptoribus idem sentire quod sensit Spinosa. Nunc Simonium rogat, cur id ægre ferat, cùm eos faciat ipso Spinosa indoctiores, qui libros Scripturae Sacrae statim tribuendos esse existimant illis quorum nomina praeferunt. Quia verò Simonius sententiam suam Theodoreti aliorumque Patrum testimoniis confirmaverat, regerit Vossius nihil occurrere in Theodoreto & in aliis Patribus quod non libenter legant & approbent Christiani: qua in re iterum bonus ille Christianus malignitatem suam & imperitiam ostendit, qui de Patrum scriptis, quos nunquam ipse legit, pronunciare audeat. Constat Theodoretum & complures alios Patres, doctissimosque aetatis nostrae Theologos in ea esse sententia, ut de Autoribus multorum Veteris Instrumenti librorum nihil certi affirmari possit, uti pluribus verbis ostendit Sixtus Senensis & alii qui hoc argumentum tractarunt. De quibus libris à Gregorio Magno Summo Pontifice egregiè dictum est, Quis haec scripserit valde supervacue quaeritur, cùm tamen autor libri Spiritus Sanctus fideliter credatur. Itaque Simonius rectè observavit Spinosam imperitum esse malignumque hominem, qui ex iis quae in confesso sunt apud praestantissimos Ecclesiae Catholicae Theologos, autoritatem Sacrorum Librorum conetur evertere. Simonius censuit refellendas ac damnandas esse impias quas Spinosa inde ducit consecutiones, quaeque manifeste falsae sunt. Sic firmis demonstravit rationibus ejusdem Spinosae imperitiam in iis quae de Scriptore Pentateuchi effutiit; probavitque istum hominem S. Literas non intellexisse. Dubitavit Augustinus, an Josue sit Autor libri qui nomen ejus praefert: Theodoretus hoc ipsum negavit aperte: jam quis inde concludat Augustinum & Theodoretum consentire cum Spinosa? Similiter doctissimi Theologi ante centum annos affirmarunt plures esse in rebus chronologicis errores tam in Ebraicis Scripturae Sacrae Codicibus, quàm in Graecis & Latinis. Spinosa, qui idem quoque sentit, sumit inde malignè rationes in eversionem Sacrorum Librorum. Jam quis inde conficiat, nisi maledicentissimus Vossius, gravissimos illos Theologos in hoc negotio cum Spinosa conspirare ut Sacras Literas evertant? Rectè igitur dixit Simonius, illos esse Spinosa indoctiores, qui libros Scripturae Sacrae putant statim tritribuendos esse iis quorum nomina praeferunt. Imperitus quoque disputator est Vossius, qui hac arte Spinosæ argumentis vires addat.
units.tr: Vossius had maliciously objected that Simonius thinks the same about the writers of the Old Testament as Spinoza thought. Now he asks Simonius why he takes this badly, since it makes them less learned than Spinoza himself, who believe that the books of Holy Scripture must at once be ascribed to those whose names they bear. But since Simonius had confirmed his opinion by the testimony of Theodoret and other Fathers, Vossius replies that nothing in Theodoret and the other Fathers occurs which Christians would not gladly read and approve. In this matter that good Christian again shows his malice and his ignorance, daring to pronounce on the writings of the Fathers, which he has never himself read. It is well known that Theodoret and many other Fathers, and the most learned theologians of our age, hold the view that nothing certain can be affirmed about the authors of many books of the Old Testament, as Sixtus of Siena and others who have treated this subject have shown at length. About these books Gregory the Great, the chief Pontiff, rightly said: "It is very pointless to ask who wrote these things, since the Holy Spirit is faithfully believed to be the author of the book." So Simonius rightly observed that Spinoza is an ignorant and malicious man, who tries to overthrow the authority of the Sacred Books from things that are admitted by the most eminent theologians of the Catholic Church. Simonius judged that the impious consequences which Spinoza draws from this must be refuted and condemned, since they are manifestly false. Thus he showed by firm arguments the ignorance of this same Spinoza in what he babbled about the author of the Pentateuch, and he proved that this man had not understood the Sacred Letters. Augustine doubted whether Joshua is the author of the book which bears his name; Theodoret openly denied this very thing. Now who would conclude from this that Augustine and Theodoret agree with Spinoza? Similarly, the most learned theologians a hundred years ago affirmed that there are many errors in chronology, both in the Hebrew codices of Holy Scripture and in the Greek and Latin ones. Spinoza, who also thinks this, maliciously takes from it reasons for overthrowing the Sacred Books. Now who would infer from this, except the most slanderous Vossius, that those grave theologists conspire with Spinoza in this business to overthrow the Sacred Letters? So Simonius was right to say that those are less learned than Spinoza who think the books of Holy Scripture must at once be ascribed to those whose names they bear. Vossius is also an unskilled disputant, since by this method he gives strength to Spinoza's arguments.

units.la: Pergit Vossius invidiam creare Simonio, qui dixerit præstantissimos Ecclesiæ Theologos in hoc etiam non consentire cum Judæis, qui putent ne unam quidem vocem esse in Lege quæ non sit Mosis. Contrà certum est nonnulla libris Mosis postea addita fuisse ab Esdra vel ab aliis Prophetis qui illos recognoverunt. Rem ita esse manifestè ostendunt Theologorum illorum Commentarii in Scripturam Sacram. Sed Vossius, qui nunquam cessat maledictis suis B. Hieronymum lacessere, autor est illum esse unum ex vetustis Ecclesiæ Patribus qui id affirmare ausus fuerit, quasi libri Mosis ab Esdra interpolati fuerint. Iterum maligno carpit animo Vossius Simonii verba, qui dixerit non constare utrùm Moyses ipse eam quam sub ejus nomine habemus historiam totam literis mandarit, vel ex parte à Notariis illis publicis qui res ætatis suæ conscribebant, chartis excipi jusserit. Mirè sibi applaudit hac in re mirificus Vossius, quasi novos Scribas Prophetasque finxerit Simonius. Valeant, inquit, isti quos P. Simonius fingit Notarii : valeant quoque omnes isti commentitii Scribæ & Prophetæ interpolatores & infessores Sacrorum Librorum. Jam tempus est ut totum istud negotium excutiam, ostendamque commentitios non esse Scribas illos seu Prophetas qui apud Ebræos gesta Reipublicæ chartis commiserint, adeoque maledicum esse Vossium, qui cùm tam imperitè Patrum scripta tractaverit, audeat quoque sententiam ferre de rebus parum sibi cognitis.
units.tr: Vossius goes on to stir up ill feeling against Simonius, who said that the most distinguished theologians of the Church do not agree with the Jews on this point either, the Jews who think that not even a single word in the Law is anything other than Moses'. On the contrary, it is certain that some things were added to the books of Moses afterwards, by Ezra or by other prophets who revised them. The commentaries of those theologians on Holy Scripture make this plain. But Vossius, who never tires of assailing blessed Jerome with his slanders, asserts that Jerome was one of the ancient Fathers of the Church who dared to affirm this, as if the books of Moses had been interpolated by Ezra. Vossius again criticises Simonius' words with a malicious mind, since Simonius said it was uncertain whether Moses himself committed to writing the whole of the history that we have under his name, or whether he ordered parts of it to be recorded on paper by those public notaries who wrote down the events of their own age. The marvellous Vossius congratulates himself greatly on this point, as if Simonius had invented new scribes and prophets. "Let those notaries whom Father Simonius imagines fare well," he says, "let all those invented scribes and prophets, interpolators and assailants of the Sacred Books, fare well too." Now it is time to examine this whole business thoroughly and to show that those scribes or prophets who among the Hebrews entrusted the public affairs of the state to writing are not invented. It will also show that Vossius is a slanderer, who, though he has handled the writings of the Fathers so unskilfully, dares to pass judgement on matters he knows little about.

units.la: Scribas publicos apud Ebræorum gentem fuisse Regum suorum temporibus, notius est quàm ut probetur. De Mosis tempore longè major est difficultas, cùm de illis publicis Scriptoribus nihil in Pentateucho haberi videatur; unde factum fuisse puto, ut nonnulli ætatis nostræ Theologi, qui illos sub Regibus Ebræorum fuisse lubenter agnoscunt, negent tales Scribas extitisse sub Mose. Verùm ut credam inde jam à prisicis illis temporibus apud Ebræos fuisse Prophetas qui res gestas in Acta publica referrent, Josephi verbis adversus Apionem adducor. Ille enim ex eo potissimùm Judæorum historiis fidem conciliat, quòd apud Ebræos ab ipsius Mosis temporibus viri fuerint qui res gestas literis commendarint. Contrà, Græcos nihil firmi in suis historiis habuisse, ex eo in primis arguit, quòd illi publicos Annalium Scriptores à prisicis temporibus non constituerint, quos etiam agnoscit apud Babylonios & Ægyptios. Numenius quoque apud Eusebium, Jannem & Mambrem Ægyptiorum Magos qui olim Mosi adversati sunt, appellat ἱερογραμματεῖς, sive rerum sacrarum Scriptores. Sic etiam primis temporibus apud Romanos, referente Cicerone, Pontifex Maximus res omnes singulorum annorum chartis mandabat. Quâ ratione Josephus affirmat curam hanc penès summos Pontifices & Prophetas Ebræorum extitisse. Munus scilicet illud apud Ebræos injunctum fuit Summo Pontifici & Sacerdo-
units.tr: That the Hebrew nation had public scribes in the time of its kings is too well known to need proof. For the time of Moses the difficulty is much greater, since nothing about those public writers seems to be found in the Pentateuch. This, I think, is why some theologians of our own age, who gladly acknowledge that such men existed under the kings of the Hebrews, deny that such scribes existed under Moses. But I am led, by the words of Josephus against Apion, to believe that from those most ancient times there were already among the Hebrews prophets who recorded the deeds of their people in public registers. For Josephus wins credit for his Jewish histories chiefly on this ground: that among the Hebrews, from the time of Moses himself, there were men who committed the deeds of their people to writing. On the other hand, he argues especially from this that the Greeks had nothing firm in their histories, because they did not appoint public writers of annals from early times, although he acknowledges that such writers existed among the Babylonians and Egyptians. Numenius too, in Eusebius, calls Jannes and Jambres, the Egyptian magicians who once opposed Moses, hierogrammateis, that is, writers of sacred things. Likewise in early times among the Romans, as Cicero reports, the Pontifex Maximus committed to writing all the events of each year. By this reasoning Josephus affirms that this care rested with the high priests and prophets of the Hebrews.

units.la: Joseph. adv. Apion. — Numen. apud Eusseb. Præp. Evang. lib. 8. — Cicero. cerdotibus, qui, quòd essent Divino Spiritu afflati, vocabantur Prophetæ.
units.tr: Joseph. adv. Apion. — Numen. apud Eusseb. Præp. Evang. lib. 8. — Cicero. The office among the Hebrews was assigned to the high priest and the priests, who, because they were inspired by the Divine Spirit, were called prophets.

units.la: Ex his publicis ac Propheticis conscriptionibus excerpti sunt quinque libri Moßs, qui ex eo Moßs nomen reportarunt, quòd partim ab ipso scripti fuerint, partim eo jubente ab ætatis illius Notariis. Norunt qui Sacras versant Literas, pleraque in illis Deo & viris principibus tribui, quæ illorum mandato facta sunt; quo sensu Pentateuchus, cujus pars à publicis Scriptoribus in publicas conscriptiones relata fuit, totus Moßi tribuitur, qui etiam Propheta illis præfuit; neque minùs de Josua quàm de Moße dicitur, illum scripsisse librum suum: non ausus tamen est Augustinus asserere Josuæ historiam quæ edita est, ab ipso Josua conscriptam fuisse. Theodoretus Josuam illius autorem esse negat aperte. Quare à nonnullis Patribus rectè animadversum fuit, ex libri nomine non necessariò ejus autorem colligi, sed materiam.
units.tr: From these public and prophetic records were drawn the five books of Moses, which took the name of Moses partly because he himself wrote them, and partly because, at his command, they were written by the notaries of that age. Those who study Sacred Scripture know that many things in it are attributed to God and to leading men which were done by their command. In this sense the Pentateuch, part of which was taken from public writers and entered into public records, is attributed entirely to Moses, who also presided over them as prophet. And it is said of Joshua no less than of Moses that he wrote his own book. Yet Augustine did not dare to assert that the history of Joshua which has been published was written by Joshua himself. Theodoret plainly denies that Joshua is its author. Hence some Fathers rightly observed that the author of a book is not necessarily inferred from its title, but its subject matter is.

units.la: Simili ratione libri qui Judicum, Samuelis ac Regum nomina præferunt, à Scribis seu ætatum illarum Prophetis fuere conscripti. Quam locutionem, quæ sacris Scriptoribus familiaris est, non ignoravit Augustinus, qui explicans verba Exodi, Cap. 17. verf. 5. ubi Deus dicit Moysi ut sumat virgam quâ fluvium ipse Moses percusserat, quærit quomodo illud verum esse posset, cùm non Moyses, sed Aaron virgâ fluvium percusserit. Respondet, Quod Aaron fecit Moysi potiùs tribuendum est, quia per Moysen Deus jubebat quæ faceret Aaron, & in Moyse autoritas,
units.tr: In a similar way the books which bear the names of Judges, Samuel and Kings were written by scribes, or prophets, of those times. Augustine was not unaware of this manner of speaking, which is familiar to the sacred writers. In explaining the words of Exodus 17:5, where God tells Moses to take the rod with which Moses himself had struck the river, he asks how this could be true, since it was not Moses but Aaron who struck the river with the rod. He answers that what Aaron did is rather to be attributed to Moses, because God commanded through Moses what Aaron was to do; authority lay in Moses, and the ministry in Aaron.

units.la: in illo autem ministerium fuit. Haud abfimiliter, illud quod jubente Mose à Scribis ætatis suæ in Annales relatum fuit, Mosi potiùs tribuitur, quàm Summo Pontifici & Prophetis, quia in Mose fuit autoritas, & in illis ministerium: quo etiam modo explicanda sunt verba illa ejusdem Capitis Exod. verf. 12. quibus Mosi dixisse Deus fertur, ut victoriam quam contra Amalecitas Israelitæ consecuti fuerant, scribat in libro ob monumentum, id est, ut juberet victoriam hanc in Acta publica referri. Eodem quoque Capite dicitur Moses ædificasse altare, non quòd ipse ædificaverit, sed quòd illud jusserit ædificari.
units.tr: In a similar way, what was recorded in the annals by the scribes of his age at Moses' command is attributed to Moses rather than to the high priest and the prophets, because authority lay in Moses and the ministry in them. In this same way must be explained those words of the same chapter of Exodus, verse 12, in which God is said to have told Moses to write the victory which the Israelites had won against the Amalekites "in a book as a memorial", that is, to order that this victory be recorded in the public registers. In the same chapter it is also said that Moses built an altar, not because he built it himself, but because he ordered it to be built.

units.la: Jam quia necesse non fuit populo committere ingens Annalium volumen, illorum tantùm compendium in publicum editum est, quod Mosis nomen retinuit. Sic constat librum Sapientiæ non esse Salomonis eâ quâ nunc est formâ dispositus, etsi in hoc nonnulla sint quæ in solum cadant Salomonem, eumque Salomoni tribuant omnes antiquæ Ecclesiæ Patres, si perpaucos exceperis. Illa autem quæ in Pentateucho legimus manifestum videntur esse compendium priscorum Annalium, qui in Archivis seu publicis Tabulariis asservabantur.
units.tr: Now, since there was no need to commit to the people a huge volume of annals, only an abridgement of them was published, and this kept the name of Moses. So it is established that the Book of Wisdom is not Solomon's in the form in which it now stands, although it contains some things that can apply only to Solomon, and all the ancient Fathers of the Church attribute it to Solomon, with very few exceptions. But those things which we read in the Pentateuch appear clearly to be an abridgement of the ancient annals, which were kept in the archives or public registries.

units.la: Ampliora fuisse vetustis illis temporibus rerum gestarum Commentaria verbis apertis testatur summus vir Affricanus & rerum Ebraicarum callentissimus. Ille siquidem apud Eusebium autor est, à Mosis temporibus usque ad Herodem in Archivis descriptas fuisse Ebraicarum familiarum origines, & eorum qui ad proselytos felytos genus suum referebant. 'Ανα- ςαπλων ὁ εἰς τότε ἐν τοῖς ἀρχαίοις οὖ- τως ἐ Ἑβεργικῶν ἡμῶν ἡ ἀχεὰ ἀπο- σπλύτων ἀναφεροῦμένων. Ibidemque addit Affricanus, Herodem omnia illa vetusta familiarum monumenta concremasse. Ἐνεπῆνξεν ἀνὶων τὰς ἀναχρα-φὰς ἡ ἡμῶν. Ex quibus manifestum est, eas quæ evulgatæ sunt historias & genealogias compendiarias esse, ac remansisse integras in publicis Tabulariis. Quare Simonius recte annotavit ex Libris Sacris qui superfsunt, nihil certi de rebus chronologicis & genealogicis affirmari posse, utpote quæ in breviorem summam contractæ fuerint. Quis enim credat Annales Ebræorum qui ad nos usque pervenerunt res omnes gestas illius gentis complecti? Quod nec Augustino ignotum fuisse videtur, qui quærens quomodo Caïn potuerit condere civitatem, cùm in Scriptura duo tantùm parentes & duo filii referantur; respondet his verbis. An ideo quæstio est, quoniam qui legunt putant solos tunc fuisse homines quos Divina Scriptura commemorat, nec advertunt eos qui prius sunt conditi duos, vel eos etiam quos genuerunt tamdiu vixisse, ut multos gignerent? Non enim & Adam ipse eos solos genuit quorum nomina leguntur, cùm de illo Scriptura loquens ita concludat, quod genuit filios & filias.
units.tr: The great man Africanus, who was most skilled in Hebrew affairs, openly testifies that the commentaries on the deeds of those ancient times were fuller. For he states in Eusebius that from the time of Moses down to Herod the origins of the Hebrew families were recorded in the archives, together with those of the people who traced their lineage back to proselytes [ἀνα- ςαπλων ὁ εἰς τότε ἐν τοῖς ἀρχαίοις οὖ- τως ἐ Ἑβεργικῶν ἡμῶν ἡ ἀχεὰ ἀπο- σπλύτων ἀναφεροῦμένων]. In the same place Africanus adds that Herod burned all those ancient records of families [Ἐνεπῆνξεν ἀνὶων τὰς ἀναχρα-φὰς ἡ ἡμῶν]. From these facts it is clear that the histories and genealogies which have been published are abridgements, and that the complete versions remained in the public archives. Hence Simonius rightly observed that from the surviving Sacred Books nothing certain can be affirmed about chronological and genealogical matters, since these were condensed into a shorter summary. For who would believe that the annals of the Hebrews which have come down to us embrace all the deeds of that nation? This also seems not to have been unknown to Augustine, who, asking how Cain could have founded a city when Scripture mentions only two parents and two sons, answers in these words: "Is the question raised because those who read it think that the only men then were those whom Divine Scripture mentions, and do not notice that the first two who were created, or even those whom they begot, lived so long that they had many children? For Adam himself did not beget only those whose names are read, since Scripture, speaking of him, concludes thus: that he begot sons and daughters."

units.la: His igitur & similibus adductus Simonius, recte confecit Annalium Ebraicorum partem solùm editam fuisse, qui in publicis Tabulariis, quæ tunc consulere facile erat, integri remanserint; adeoque inania sunt & futilia quæ Simonio Voffius objicit de scriptis Veteris Testamenti pro Scribarum seu Prophetarum lubitu decurtatis: nihil enim hac in re affirmavit Simonius, quod doctioribus antiquæ Ecclesiæ Patribus cognitum non fuerit; & eas quas nunc Ebræorum habemus historias compendiarias esse res ipsa loquitur, quæ non possunt dici decurtatæ, cùm tunc in Archivis remanerent integræ, & ex iis illud solùm fuit evulgatum, quod populo sufficere visum est. Totum illud negotium juvat illustrare P. Martinii Jesuitæ verbis de Sinensium Annalibus. Fuit, inquit, & est etiamnum genti huic usitatum, ut doctissimis aliquot Philosophis Imperatoris defuncti res gestæ conscribendæ à successore mandentur, fucis & adulatione omni remotâ. Quod munus apud ipsos cum primis est honorificum & à summis quibusque viris expetitum. Hinc historia Sinica ita sibi semper similis continuatur, ut quanquam ab alio sit atque alio succedentibus annis adducta, unius tamen autoris opus esse videatur, & omnino unicum est, non ab alio quàm regio Scriptore unquam tentata, magnisque & pluribus voluminibus contenta. Inde sibi Sina pro memoriæ subsidio epitomen conficiunt, qualem his ipsis libris repræsento.
units.tr: Led by these and similar considerations, Simonius rightly concluded that only part of the Hebrew Annals was published, while the complete versions remained in the public archives, which were easy to consult at that time. So what Vossius objects to Simonius, that the writings of the Old Testament were shortened at the whim of the Scribes or Prophets, is empty and trivial. Simonius affirmed nothing in this matter that was not known to the more learned Fathers of the ancient Church. The histories the Hebrews now have are abridgements, as the facts themselves show. They cannot be called truncated, since the full versions then remained intact in the archives, and only what seemed sufficient for the people was made public. It helps to illustrate the whole matter with the words of the Jesuit Father Martini on the Chinese Annals. It was, he says, and still is, customary for this people that, after an emperor's death, some very learned philosophers are commissioned by his successor to write up his deeds, with all flattery and embellishment set aside. This task is among them especially honourable and is sought by the most distinguished men. Hence the Chinese history is continued so consistently with itself that, although it is carried forward by different writers in successive years, it seems to be the work of one author. It is altogether unique, never attempted by anyone other than a royal writer, and fills many large volumes. From it the Chinese make an epitome as an aid to memory, of the sort I here present from these very books.

units.la: Similis fuit apud Ebræos ac Sinenses scribendorum Annalium ratio, nisi quòd apud Ebræos qui Scribæ fuerunt, iidem quoque Prophetæ erant; Scriptores verò Sinensium viri fuere Philosophi veritatisque amantissimi. Distinguendi quidem sunt Sacrorum Librorum Scriptores à cæterarum gentium Scriptoribus; quia illi Spiritu Sancto impulsi Sacros Annales conscripserunt. Sed cavendum est ne hos Annales ad nos cœlitus delapsos
units.tr: The method of writing Annals among the Hebrews and the Chinese was similar, except that among the Hebrews those who were Scribes were also Prophets, whereas the writers of the Chinese were philosophers and great lovers of truth. Certainly the writers of the Sacred Books must be distinguished from the writers of other nations, because the former, moved by the Holy Spirit, composed the Sacred Annals. But we must take care not to claim that these Annals fell down to us from heaven

units.la: Augustin. Quæst. in Genes. lapsos esse affirmemus, sicut de libris Alcorani Muhammedani commenti sunt. Longè enim major erit Divinorum Librorum autoritas, & ex iis Christiani nominis inimici facilius refellentur, si dixerimus in iis nihil contineri, quod non sit certum depromptumque ex Ebraeorum Annalibus, qui inde jam à Moses temporibus apud illos extiterunt. Hinc potissimum Josephus Judaicarum historiarum veritatem commendat adversus Graecos, quibus objicit Graecarum historiarum inconstantiam, quòd illi publicos rerum suarum Scriptores non habuerint.
units.tr: Augustine, Quaest. in Genes., as they have invented about the books of the Koran of Muhammad. For the authority of the Divine Books will be much greater, and the enemies of the Christian name will be more easily refuted, if we say that nothing is contained in them that is not certain and taken from the Annals of the Hebrews, which have existed among that people from the times of Moses onward. Hence Josephus especially commends the truth of the Jewish histories against the Greeks, objecting to them the inconsistency of Greek histories, because they had no public writers of their affairs.

units.la: Judaei, quia nimii sunt rerum suarum ostentatores, affirmant ne unam quidem vocem esse in Lege, imò ne unam quidem syllabam quae à Deo Mosi dictata non fuerit. Sic Magistri illi nihil habent nisi à Deo ipso in monte Sinai profectum. Sed rem istam aliter se habuisse docet Scribarum usus inde jam à Moses tempore confirmatus. Ipse etiam Augustinus ante Mosem Scriptores fuisse apud Chaldaeos & Aegyptios videtur agnoscere: ubi enim expendit verba Capitis 21. Numerorum, verf. 14. in quibus fit mentio libri bellorum Domini, haec habet. Hic dictum est scriptum in libro, non dictum est in cujus Prophetae vel Patriarchae sancto libro; neque negandum est fuisse jam libros sive Chaldaeorum, unde egressus est Abraham, sive Aegyptiorum, ubi didicerat Moyses omnem illorum sapientiam, sive cujuscunque gentis alterius, in quorum librorum aliquo potuit hoc esse scriptum.
units.tr: The Jews, because they are too great boasters of their own things, affirm that not even one word in the Law, indeed not even one syllable, was not dictated to Moses by God. Thus those teachers have nothing that did not proceed from God himself on Mount Sinai. But the Scribes' practice, confirmed from the time of Moses onward, teaches that the matter was otherwise. Augustine himself seems to acknowledge that there were writers before Moses among the Chaldeans and Egyptians. For when he weighs the words of Numbers chapter 21, verse 14, where mention is made of the book of the wars of the Lord, he says: Here it is said "written in a book", not "said in the book of which holy prophet or patriarch". Nor should it be denied that there were already books either of the Chaldeans, from whom Abraham came out, or of the Egyptians, where Moses learned all their wisdom, or of any other nation, in one of whose books this could have been written.

units.la: Aliud igitur de Pentateuchi libris sentiebat Augustinus, quàm Judaei sentiunt; Judaeisque ipsis illi videntur ineptiores, qui eorum commenta tam avidè arripiunt, quasi non aliunde sumi posset librorum Moysis autoritas quàm ex monte Sinai, & ex eo quòd singulae illorum voces & syllabae à Deo Mosi dictatae fuerint. Satius est viris doctrinâ & judicio praeditis fidem habere, qui existimant illos qui Cap. Numer. 21. verf. 27. appellantur מש"ל, & in LXX. Interpretibus 'Αινισματισταί, fuisse aetatis illius Scriptores; à quorum etiam sententia minùs alienus Augustinus valdè laborat in explicatione vocis Aenigmatistae, quam hoc loco legebat in Itala: haec sunt illius verba. Non incredibiliter putantur illi Aenigmatistae sic tunc appellati quos Poëtas nos appellamus, eò quòd Poëtarum sit consuetudo atque licentia miscere carminibus suis aenigmata fabularum, quibus aliquid significare intelligantur.
units.tr: Augustine therefore thought differently about the books of the Pentateuch than the Jews do. And those seem to be more foolish than the Jews themselves who so eagerly seize upon their fictions, as if the authority of the books of Moses could be derived from nowhere but Mount Sinai and from the fact that each of their words and syllables was dictated to Moses by God. It is better for men endowed with learning and judgement to hold the view that those who are called מש"ל [meshalim] in Numbers chapter 21, verse 27, and in the Septuagint Ἀινισματισταί [ainismatistai], were writers of that age. Augustine, not far from this opinion, labours hard in explaining the word "riddle-makers", which he read in this place in the Old Latin. These are his words: It is not unlikely that those riddle-makers were then so called, whom we call poets, because it is the custom and licence of poets to mix riddles of fables into their songs, by which something is understood to be signified.
