units.la: Sunt etiam viri docti & in Sacris Literis versati, qui conjiciant ea quae Moses scripsit de mundi fabricatione rebusque gestis ante sua tempora, partim ex divina habuisse revelatione, partim ex privatis familiarum Commentariis, vel magis ex Majorum suorum Traditione inde ab Adamo usque ad illius aetatem fideliter transmissa, uti pluribus verbis exponitur à Pererio Jesuita doctissimo Praefatione in Pentateuchum.
units.tr: There are also learned men, versed in the Sacred Letters, who conjecture that what Moses wrote about the making of the world and the deeds done before his own time, he partly had from divine revelation, partly from the private records of families, or rather from the tradition of his forefathers, faithfully handed down from Adam to his own age, as is set out at length by the most learned Jesuit Pererius in his Preface to the Pentateuch.

units.la: Praeterea Vossius objicit, sequi ex Simonii sententia, Nos non habere scripta Prophetarum Veteris Testamenti integra, sed ampliata, decurtata, & variis modis pro lubitu & ratione temporum à Sacerdotibus magni Synedrii interpolata. Et quia paulò delicatior est Vossius, assertionem hanc ait esse crudam offam quam ipse non possit concoquere; iterumque ut se bonum demonstret Christianum addit, frustra Simonium relegare ad Patres, in quibus nihil occurrit quod non libenter legant & approbent Christiani. Sic bonus ille Christianus, qui bonus non est ratiocinator, fundit verba more Sophistarum. Nihil tamen affirmavit hac in re Simonius, quod antea à priscis Patribus, atque in primis ab Origene in Epistola ad Affricanum, scriptum non fuerit. Ille enim asserit, ex aliorum tamen magis, ut puto, opinione quàm ex sua, Judaeos à quibus Scripturas accepimus, nonnulla ex iis resecuisse ac sustulisse à cognitione populi, ἀπὸ τῆς γνώσεως ἐκ λαῶν, quae servata fuerint in libris ἀποκρύφοις seu arcanis: nomen enim ἀποκρύφων non sumit hoc loco Origenes in malam partem, sed pro libris qui in publicum non editi in armariis conservabantur. Unde libros ἀποκρύφας sive abscònditos opponit φανεροῖς, apertis & manifestis, seu iis qui evulgati fuerant.
units.tr: Moreover, Vossius objects that it follows from the opinion of Simonius: that we do not have the writings of the Prophets of the Old Testament whole, but enlarged, shortened, and altered in various ways at the will and according to the circumstances of the times by the priests of the great Sanhedrin. And because Vossius is rather more refined, he says this assertion is a raw morsel that he cannot digest; and, again, to show himself a good Christian, he adds that it is in vain for Simonius to refer us to the Fathers, in whom nothing occurs that Christians would not gladly read and approve. Thus that good Christian, who is not a good reasoner, pours out words in the manner of the Sophists. Yet Simonius affirmed nothing in this matter that had not been written earlier by the ancient Fathers, and above all by Origen in his Letter to Africanus. For Origen asserts, though I think more on the opinion of others than on his own, that the Jews, from whom we received the Scriptures, cut out and removed some parts of them from the knowledge of the people, ἀπὸ τῆς γνώσεως ἐκ λαῶν [apo tēs gnōseōs ek laōn], and that these were preserved in books ἀποκρύφοις [apokryphois], that is, hidden or secret. For Origen does not use the name of the hidden books here in a bad sense, but for books that were not published and were kept in cupboards. Hence he sets the hidden books, ἀποκρύφας [apokryphas], against the φανεροῖς [phanerois], the open and manifest, that is, those which had been published.

units.la: Jam hac ratione Origenes putavit historiam Susannae, quam nunc Graece tantum in libro Danielis scriptam habemus, Judaeorum studio sublatam fuisse à Scripturis, ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν. Multa quoque recenseт, quae existimat in priscis illis Judaeorum libris quos vocat Apocryphos extitisse, quaeque Judaei consultò in publicum non ediderint; cujusmodi sunt Christi verba, Vae vobis Scribae & Pharisaei, quia aedificatis sepulcra Prophetarum, & quae sequuntur Matth. Cap. 23. verf. 29. usque ad verf. 39. ista & alia bene multa quorum in hac ad Affricanum Epistola mentionem facit, au-tor est in antiquis Scripturis extitisse, sed σοφῶς ἢ ἀρχόντως ἢ πρεσβύτερος, Sapientes seu Doctores, Principes & Presbyteros noluisse ut ea evulgarentur, quae tamen in libris arcanis quos apud se retinent adhuc remanerent.
units.tr: On this ground Origen thought that the history of Susanna, which we now have only in Greek in the book of Daniel, was removed from the Scriptures by the zeal of the Jews, ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν [apo tōn graphōn]. He also recounts many things which he thinks existed in those ancient books of the Jews that he calls Apocryphal, and which the Jews deliberately did not publish. Of this kind are the words of Christ: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, because you build the tombs of the prophets, and what follows, Matth. 23, verse 29 to verse 39. These and many other things, which he mentions in this Letter to Africanus, he asserts existed in the ancient Scriptures, but that the σοφῶς [sophōs] or wise, ἀρχόντως [archontōs] or rulers, and πρεσβύτερος [presbyteroi] or elders, the Sages or teachers, the Princes and the Elders, did not want them made public, though they still remained in the secret books which they kept among themselves.

units.la: Libri Josuae, Samuelis ac Regum, si Theodoreto fidem habeamus, etiam decurtati & ampliati sunt, cùm illi, ipso referente, ex amplioribus Prophetarum Commentariis deprompti fuerint, quibus etiam aliquid à posterioribus Scribis additum fuerit. Sed quia Vossius est bonus Christianus, Theodoretum, Procopium, Diodorum aliosque Patres sic sentientes non recipiet. Theodoretus itaque autor est, apud Ebraeos fuisse Prophetas qui res aetatis suae conscriberent, à quibus Prophetis ortum fuisse putat, ut liber primus Regum apud Ebraeos & Syros appellatus fuerit Prophetia Samuelis. Dein addit, eos qui editi sunt Regum libros, ex scriptis illorum Prophetarum, quorum munus fuit res quae gerebantur in publicos Annales referre, longo post tempore excerptos fuisse. Profert denique aliquot exempla, quibus demonstrat ejusmodi libris nonnulla postea à Scribis adjecta fuisse. Neque aliud sentit de libris qui vulgò appellantur Paralipomena.
units.tr: The books of Joshua, Samuel and Kings, if we believe Theodoret, were also shortened and enlarged, since, as he himself reports, they were drawn from the fuller commentaries of the Prophets, to which something was also added by later Scribes. But because Vossius is a good Christian, he will not accept Theodoret, Procopius, Diodorus and the other Fathers who think this way. So Theodoret vouches that among the Hebrews there were Prophets who wrote down the events of their own age, and he thinks it was from these Prophets that the first book of Kings came to be called among the Hebrews and Syrians the Prophecy of Samuel. Then he adds that the books of Kings that have been published were excerpted, after a long time, from the writings of those Prophets, whose task it was to record the things done in the public Annals. Finally he offers several examples by which he shows that some things were afterwards added to such books by the Scribes. He holds no other view about the books commonly called Paralipomena.

units.la: Haec etiam Theodoreti verba in Scholia sua transtulit Procopius, ut ostendat Scribas illos seu Prophetas apud Ebraeos extitisse, qui priorum Prophetarum historicas conscriptiones collectas aliquot locis ampliaverint. Παλαιοι Προφῆται, inquit Procopius, γεγραμμένοι, ὧν τὰς μὲν βίβλως ἐκ ἐυρομένα τὰς ἡ περιγραφὴ ἐν τῷ Παρεχ-
units.tr: Procopius also includes these words of Theodoret in his Scholia, to show that among the Hebrews there were scribes or prophets who enlarged the historical writings of the earlier prophets in several places when they collected them. "The ancient prophets," says Procopius, "wrote [the things] of which some books..." [Παλαιοὶ Προφῆται γεγραμμένοι, ὧν τὰς μὲν βίβλους οὐκ εὑρόμενα τὰς δὲ περιγραφὴ ἐν τῷ Παραλειπομένων μεμαρτυρημένοις ἱστορίας]

units.la: Παραλειπομένων μεμαρτυρημένοις ἱστορίας. Τούτων συνέλεξεν ἕκαστος δὲ οἱ σωμάτων γίνεσθαι τὸ οἰκεῖον καιρὸν· ἀνλικὰ γὰρ καὶ ἡ πρώτη τῶν Βασιλειῶν ἡ ᾧδὴ Ἐβραίοις καὶ ᾧδὴ Σύροις περιφήμεια Σαμυὴλ ὀνομάζει. Οἱ γὰρ τῶν Βασιλειῶν συγγεγράφαντες ἐκ ἐκείνων λαβόντες τὰς ἀφορμὰς μὴ πολλὴν συνέγραψαν χρόνον· πῶς δὲ οἱ ὄντες Σαμυὴλ, τὸ τῷ Σαοὺλ ἢ ἐξ τῶ Δαυὶδ συνηγμένοις τὰ μὴ ταῦτα συγγεγράφα μέχρι τῆς Νεβουχοδονόσορ πλάστης, ὡς αἰχμάλωτον εἰλήφει τὸ Ἰσραὴλ. Theodoreto & Procopio suffragatur Diodorus, qui expendens hanc clausulam libri 1. Samuelis, Qui Prophe-ta dicitur hodie, vocabatur olim Videns, putat illam à Scribis posterioribus adjectam fuisse: hæc enim sunt illius verba. Ἐκ τούτων δείκνυ, ἐπὶ ἄπερ τῶν Προφητῶν ἕκαστος τὰ ἐν τοῖς καὶ' αὐτὸν χρόνοις ἐγραψαν, ταῦτα οἱ μὴ ταῦτα συναγάγοντες περιέσχηκαν τὸ, ὅτι ἐμπεριέθεν βλέποντα τὴν Προφήτην ἐκάλεσεν. Ex his ostenditur, quacunque Prophetæ singuli temporibus suis gesta scripserunt, ea illos qui postea extitere colligentes adjecisse istud, olim Prophetam appellabant Videntem.
units.tr: Each of them collected these things at the proper time. For the first book of Kings, which the Hebrews and the Syrians call Samuel's prophecy, takes its name from the first of the prophets. The writers of the Books of Kings took their material from those prophets and did not write over a long period. But those who came after Samuel, who had gathered the things concerning Saul and David, wrote these things down up to the time of Nebuchadnezzar, when Israel was taken captive. Diodorus supports Theodoret and Procopius. In his commentary on the first chapter of the first book of Samuel, he weighs the closing clause, "He who is now called the Prophet was formerly called the Seer," and thinks that it was added by later scribes. His words are: "From this it is shown that whatever the individual prophets wrote in their own times, those who later gathered these things added that clause, because they called the prophet 'the Seer'." [Ἐκ τούτων δείκνυ... ἐκάλεσεν]

units.la: Nihil etiam frequentius occurrit in libris Regum & Chronicorum, quàm publicarum illarum conscriptionum Acta sub his verbis, Nonne hæc scripta sunt in libro verborum dierum Regum Juda: similiter, Nonne hæc scripta sunt in libro verborum dierum Regum Israël. Ex quibus manifeste liquet, Regum historias, quæ evulgatæ sunt, in breviorem summam à Scribis seu Prophetis posterioribus contractas fuisse, easque tantùm esse compendia publicorum Annalium qui penès Ebræos in Ta-bulariis asservabantur. Præterea lib. 2. Paralip. Cap. 24. verf. 27. mentio fit libri מלכים Regum, qui diversus fuit à libro Regum qui editus est; atque ille complectebatur res gestas על מדרש, id est, diligentius, uti vertit Hieronymus in Vulgata, sive uberius. Septuaginta autem Interpretes על מדרש reddunt ἐπὶ τὴν γραφήν, quo nomine denotasse videntur Acta illa diurna Regum quæ asservabantur in Tabulariis publicis.
units.tr: Nothing occurs more often in the books of Kings and Chronicles than the record of those public chronicles under these words: "Are not these things written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?" and likewise, "Are not these things written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?" From these passages it is plainly clear that the histories of the kings that have been published were reduced into a shorter summary by later scribes or prophets, and that they are only abridgements of the public annals which the Hebrews kept in their archives. Moreover, in 2 Chronicles 24:27 mention is made of the book of the kings (מלכים, Melachim), which differed from the Book of Kings that has been published, and which contained the deeds of the kings "according to the midrash" (על מדרש, al midrash), that is, more diligently, as Jerome translates it in the Vulgate, or more fully. The Seventy, however, render "according to the midrash" as "upon the writing" [ἐπὶ τὴν γραφήν], by which they seem to have meant those daily records of the kings that were kept in the public archives.

units.la: De isto autem Regum libro Sixtus Senensis hæc scribit; In illo latiori narratione luculentius universa ac singula gesta Regum Juda & Israël digesta fuisse, & ea quæ nunc de his habemus ab incerto abbreviatore, quem alii Jeremiam, alii Esdram esse putant, brevi compendio collecta fuisse.
units.tr: Concerning this Book of Kings, Sixtus of Siena writes as follows: "In that fuller narrative the deeds of the kings of Judah and Israel, both general and particular, were set out more clearly, and those things that we now have about them were gathered into a brief epitome by an unknown abridger, whom some think was Jeremiah and others Ezra."

units.la: Psalmos quoque Davidis quos nunc legimus partem duntaxat esse eorum qui longè plures à Davide scripti fuerint, existimarunt nonnulli Patres, qui putant illos in parvum numerum à Rege Ezechia redactos fuisse. Ὁ βασιλεὺς Ἐζεχίας τὸ τ Ψαλμῶν συνήθη εἰς ὀλίγωσιν ἄσων. Quod autem illi de Rege Ezechia dicunt, de ejus Scribis intelligendum est, qui eo jubente Psalmos Davidis in certam formam redegerint: quo etiam modo Patres nonnulli putarunt Salomonis Proverbia ab iisdem Ezechiæ Scribis in breviorem summam fuisse contracta, selectis iis tantùm sententiis quæ meliores populoque utiliores esse videbantur. Qui liber Proverbiorum sic digestus ab Ezechiæ Scribis ad nos pervenit.
units.tr: Some Fathers also thought that the Psalms of David which we now read are only a part of those that David wrote, which were far more numerous, and they hold that they were reduced to a small number by King Hezekiah. [Ὁ βασιλεὺς Ἐζεχίας τὸ τῶν Ψαλμῶν συνήθη εἰς ὀλίγωσιν ἄγων.] But what they say about King Hezekiah must be understood of his scribes, who, at his command, reduced the Psalms of David into a fixed form. In the same way some Fathers thought that the Proverbs of Solomon were abridged into a shorter summary by the same scribes of Hezekiah, with only those sayings selected that seemed best and most useful to the people. The book of Proverbs, so arranged by the scribes of Hezekiah, has come down to us.

units.la: Verùm quid multis opus est? Ecclesia Catholica dudum in Libros Ca-
units.tr: But why need there be many words? The Catholic Church long ago...

units.la: Diodor. Schol. in lib. 1. Samuel. Cap. 4. verf. 4.
units.tr: Diodorus, Scholia on 1 Samuel, chapter 4, verse 4.

units.la: Sixtus Sen. in Bibl. Sanct. Canonicos retulit librum secundum Maccabæorum, quem constat amplioris voluminis esse compendium. Hæc enim sunt Scriptoris ipsius verba. Τὰ ἐπὶ Ἰάσωνος δ' Κυρηναίου διεξηλωμένα ἐκ πέντε βιβλίων ἐπιτομὴν δὲ ἑνὸς συγγράμματος ἐπιλεψαι. Doleat bonus ille Christianus Voffius Sacrorum Librorum vicem, qui sic decurtati & ampliati fuerint; modò tamen pro libris decurtatis novos Prophetas qui nugatores & impostores fuerunt, non substituat.
units.tr: Sixtus of Siena, in the Bibliotheca Sancta, counted among the canonical books the second book of the Maccabees, which is plainly an abridgement of a larger work. For these are the author's own words: "The things of Jason of Cyrene, set out in five books, we shall try to epitomise in one volume." [Τὰ ἐπὶ Ἰάσονος τοῦ Κυρηναίου διεξοδευμένα ἐκ πέντε βιβλίων ἐπιτομὴν δὲ ἑνὸς συγγράμματος ἐπιχειρῆσαι.] Let that good Christian Vossius lament the fate of the Sacred Books, which have been so cut down and enlarged, provided only that he does not substitute for the abridged books new prophets who were triflers and impostors.

units.la: Iterum tamen instat, Simoniumque reprehendit quòd dixerit, plerosque Theologos etiam in Pentateucho ampliationes aliquas agnovisse; & quia nihil amat nisi quod vetustum est, spretis illis recentioribus Theologis, objicit ex antiquæ Ecclesiæ Patribus ne unum quidem sistì posse testem, excepto uno Hieronymo, qui ultima Pentateuchi verba de morte Mosis, & illud de sepulchro Rachelis usque in hodiernum diem, existimavit ab Esdra fuisse addita. Sed illum, inquit Voffius, manifesti erroris convincit Samaritanum Exemplar, in quo totidem verbis hæc ipsa leguntur. Illud autem ab Esdra fuisse interpolatum nemo sanæ mentis dixerit.
units.tr: Yet Vossius again presses the point, and he reproaches Simon for saying that most theologians have recognised some additions even in the Pentateuch. Because he loves nothing but what is old, he sets aside those more recent theologians and objects that not even one witness from the Fathers of the ancient Church can be produced, except Jerome alone, who thought that the last verses of the Pentateuch, about the death of Moses, and the words about the sepulchre of Rachel, unto this day, were added by Ezra. "But," says Vossius, "the Samaritan copy convicts him of a manifest error, since these very words are read in it word for word. Nobody of sound mind would say that Ezra interpolated that."

units.la: Jam utrùm ipse Voffius sit sanæ mentis expendamus, qui Hieronymi testis in hac materia locupletissimi autoritatem contemnat. Hæc scripsisse Hieronymum animo à Rabbinis præoccupato non dixerit Voffius, cùm longè aliud sentiant Rabbini de libris Mosis. Verùm nihil in hoc negotio affirmavit Hieronymus, nisi quod à prisci s Ecclesiæ Patribus acceperat, qui in hanc conspirant sententiam, ut Esdras Divino Spiritu impulsus Scripturæ Sacræ libros misere deperditos, vel saltem corruptos, restituerit aut recognoverit. Itaque Hieronymus, ubi manifestum in Pentateucho additamentum deprehendit, istud merito Esdræ tribuit, qui ex constanti Patrum traditione Libros Sacros restituerat; unde fit ut ipse pronunciare non audeat, Mosem Pentateuchi, uti nunc extat, Scriptorem esse; sed verba sua emolliens sic loquitur, Sive Moysem dicere volueris autorem Pentateuchi, sive Esdram ejusdem instauratorem, non recuso. Ea verò quæ in fine Pentateuchi de morte Mosis referuntur manifestum esse additamentum fatentur ipsi Judæorum Magistri in Talmude, qui etsi singula verba Legis Mosi à Deo fuisse dictata affirment, excipiunt tamen hæc ultima, quæ libris Legis à Josua adjecta fuisse existimant.
units.tr: Now let us weigh whether Vossius himself is of sound mind, when he despises the authority of Jerome, a witness most abundant on this matter. Vossius would not say that Jerome wrote these things with a mind preoccupied by the rabbis, since the rabbis think quite differently about the books of Moses. But Jerome asserted nothing in this business except what he had received from the ancient Fathers of the Church, who agree in this opinion: that Ezra, moved by the Divine Spirit, restored or revised the Sacred Scriptures, which had been almost lost or at least corrupted. Accordingly, when Jerome found a manifest addition in the Pentateuch, he rightly attributed it to Ezra, who, by the constant tradition of the Fathers, had restored the Sacred Books. Hence he does not dare to pronounce that Moses is the writer of the Pentateuch as it now stands; softening his words, he speaks thus: Whether you wish to call Moses the author of the Pentateuch, or Ezra its restorer, I do not object. Indeed, the masters of the Jews themselves in the Talmud admit that the passages which are related at the end of the Pentateuch about the death of Moses are a manifest addition. Although they affirm that the individual words of the Law were dictated to Moses by God, they make an exception of these final passages, which they think were added to the books of the Law by Joshua.

units.la: Josephus quidem & Philo putarunt etiam illa à Mose fuisse scripta, qui spiritu Prophetico impulsus fuerit: sed reclamant præstantissimi quique Theologi, quòd Contextûs ipsius verba clara sint & manifesta, ut ostendit Abulensis. Nam, licet fingamus Mosem de seipso locutum esse Prophetico spiritu, fierine potuit, ut de seipso quoque Moses dixerit, Et non cognovit homo sepulcrum ejus usque in præsentem diem? Hæc clausula supponit Moysem jam mortuum atque sepultum fuisse: quare etiam Bellarminus de hoc additamento sic loquitur. Quæ autem post mortem ipsius Mosis scribuntur in extremo Capite Deuteronomii, addita sunt vel à Josua, vel ab Esdra, vel ab alio alio aliquo Propheta. Hæc tamen libro Legis potiùs adjecta fuisse à Josua, quàm ab Esdra, probavit ex eo Simonius, quòd Josue, seu Synedrii magni Assessores, quibus ipse præfuit, in publicas conscriptiones retulerint ea quæ post mortem Mosis gesta sunt : quo sensu explicanda censet verba illa Josuæ, Scripsit quoque omnia verba hæc in volumine Legis Domini : id est, Scribæ seu Prophetæ quorum fuit Annales illorum temporum scribere, ista in illos retulerunt, ex quibus, dein & ex aliis posterioribus, teste Theodoreto, composita est, quam nunc habemus, Josuæ historia. Denique fieri etiam potuit ut Esdras, qui ex Patrum sententia Scripturas Sacras recognovit, nonnulla explicationis vel connexionis causâ iis inseruerit. Quæ sententia tot tantorumque virorum suffragiis comprobata est, ut inutile sit istis diutiùs immorari.
units.tr: Josephus and Philo did indeed think that these passages too were written by Moses, who was moved by the Prophetic Spirit. But the most distinguished theologians object, because the words of the context itself are clear and manifest, as Abulensis shows. For even if we suppose that Moses spoke about himself by the Prophetic Spirit, could it have happened that Moses also said of himself, And no man knew his sepulchre unto this present day? This clause presupposes that Moses was already dead and buried. That is why Bellarmine also speaks of this addition as follows: What is written after the death of Moses himself in the last chapter of Deuteronomy was added either by Joshua, or by Ezra, or by some other prophet. Simon, however, proved from this that the addition was made to the Law by Joshua rather than by Ezra: Joshua, or the assessors of the great Sanhedrin over which he presided, put into the public records the things that were done after the death of Moses. In this sense, he thinks, those words of Joshua must be explained, He also wrote all these words in the volume of the Law of the Lord: that is, the scribes or prophets whose office it was to write the annals of those times recorded these things, and from these, together with other later sources, as Theodoret testifies, was composed the history of Joshua which we now have. Finally, it could also be that Ezra, who according to the opinion of the Fathers revised the Sacred Scriptures, inserted some things into them for the sake of explanation or connection. This view has been confirmed by the support of so many and such great men that it is useless to dwell on these objections any longer.

units.la: His tamen obstare videtur quod subjungit Vossius de Samaritarum Pentateucho, qui ista additamenta æquè continet, atque Judæorum Exemplar; nemo autem sani judicii dixerit libros Samaritarum ab Esdra interpolatos fuisse. Argumentum illud, quia majoris erat momenti, jamque à Judæo Albo doctissimo Rabbino propositum fuerat, Simonius expendit in sua Critica Sacra. Autor est Samaritas Legis Mosaicæ Exemplaria Ebraica à Judæis accepisse: illud enim quod vulgò objicitur, fieri non potuisse ut Samaritæ ab hominibus quos odio prosequebantur libros suos sumpserint, validum non est: quia constat illos vehementer expetivisse, ut Judæis adjungi possent, sicut ex hisce verbis Esdræ manifestum est: Et accedentes ad Zorobabel & ad Principes Patrum, dixerunt eis, ædificemus vobiscum, quia ita ut vos quærimus Deum vestrum. Hinc colligit Thorndicius, primos Samaritas idololatras fuisse, ac sub Esdra solum testari se verum Deum coluisse. Certum est eos usque ad illa tempora semper idolorum cultûs aliquid retinuisse; neque firmis rationibus ostendi potest, Legem Mosis ante Esdram ab illis usu publico receptam ac lectam fuisse. Eos autem Legis Mosaicæ Exemplaria à Judæis sumere, necesse fuisse videtur, cùm ab aliis quàm à Judæis illam mutuari non possent. Quodque animadversione dignum est, iidem Samaritæ seculis posterioribus non ita fuere religiosi, quin Arabicam Rabbi Saadiæ Versionem legerint & approbaverint, antequàm Abusaid Samarita novam Legis Mosaicæ Tralationem Arabicè in usum gentis suæ condidisset, damnatâ Saadiæ Versione ut ineptâ & Judaicâ. Itaque Esdras non interpolavit Samaritarum Pentateuchum, sed ipsi Samaritæ Legis Codices à Judæis Esdræ temporibus acceperunt: & ita sensisse Hieronymum non dubito, cui Samaritarum libri cogniti fuerunt.
units.tr: Yet what Vossius adds about the Samaritan Pentateuch seems to stand in the way, since it contains these additions just as the Jewish copy does. But no one of sound judgment would say that the books of the Samaritans were interpolated by Ezra. Simonius weighed that argument in his Critica Sacra, since it is weightier and had already been put forward by the learned Jewish rabbi Albo. He holds that the Samaritans received the Hebrew copies of the Mosaic Law from the Jews. The common objection, that the Samaritans could not have taken their books from men whom they hated, is not valid, because it is clear that they eagerly sought to be joined to the Jews, as is plain from these words of Ezra: And they came near to Zerubbabel and to the chief of the fathers, and said unto them, Let us build with you, for we seek your God as ye do. From this Thorndicius infers that the Samaritans were originally idolaters, and that under Ezra they merely professed that they worshipped the true God. It is certain that until that time they always retained some part of idol worship, and it cannot be shown by solid arguments that the Law of Moses was publicly received and read by them before Ezra. It seems necessary, however, that they got their copies of the Mosaic Law from the Jews, since they could not have borrowed it from anyone but the Jews. It is also worth noting that these same Samaritans in later centuries were not so scrupulous that they would not read and approve the Arabic version of Rabbi Saadia, before Abu Said the Samaritan made a new Arabic translation of the Law of Moses for the use of his people, rejecting Saadia's version as inept and Jewish. Therefore Ezra did not interpolate the Samaritan Pentateuch; rather the Samaritans themselves received the codices of the Law from the Jews in Ezra's time. I do not doubt that Jerome, who knew the Samaritan books, thought the same.

units.la: Iterum Vossius verba fundens in solitas declamationes relabitur, objicitque Simonium compilasse digressionem non valde bonam nec facientem ad propositum ex Rabbinis & recentibus Theologis de Sacrorum Librorum Scriptoribus. Verùm nihil dixit isto loco Simonius, quod non faceret ad propositum: nam Vossio & ejus similibus qui objecerant rant eum novatorem fuisse in eo quod de Sacrorum Librorum Scriptoribus attulit, ipse respondet nihil à se innovatum esse in hoc negotio, idque demonstrat non solùm Rabbinorum & Theologorum recentium testimoniis, sed & antiquæ Ecclesiæ Patrum autoritate. Satis tamen erat, ut novitatis suspiciones à se amoliretur, illud recentium Theologorum testimoniis comprobasse, ut ostenderet imperitè ac malignè objectam illi fuisse sententiæ suæ novitatem.
units.tr: Again Vossius, pouring out his words, falls back into his usual declamations, and objects that Simonius compiled a digression, not very good and not relevant to the question, from the rabbis and recent theologians on the writers of the sacred books. But Simonius said nothing in that place that was not relevant to the question. For to Vossius and others like him, who had objected that he was an innovator in what he set out about the writers of the sacred books, he replies that he has introduced nothing new in this matter, and he demonstrates it not only by the testimony of the rabbis and recent theologians but also by the authority of the Fathers of the ancient Church. Yet it was enough, in order to remove the suspicion of novelty from himself, to have confirmed it by the testimony of recent theologians, so as to show that the charge of novelty against his opinion was made ignorantly and maliciously.

units.la: Carpit præterea Vossius Simonium, qui dixerit libros illos esse Apocryphos, quorum autores occulti sunt & incerti. Si hæc vocis hujus, inquit Vossius, legitima sit expositio, omnino oportet ut major pars librorum Veteris Testamenti sint Apocryphi, quia scilicet ne unum certo alicui relinquit autori. Sed iterum sophistam agens Vossius cavillatur. Ut enim de eo sileam quòd nihil à Simonio dictum sit de Sacrorum Librorum Scriptoribus, quod jam antea à plerisque Patribus doctissimisque Theologis non fuerit approbatum, certum est libros appellari Apocryphos qui occulti sunt & incerti. Illos autem occultos & incertos appellavit Simonius, de quibus nihil certi pronunciavit Ecclesia vel Synagoga, an scilicet illorum autores ad scribendum Divino Spiritu impulsi fuerint. Dixit igitur Simonius, Scriptores Apocryphos esse incertos & occultos, neque à quoquam recipi posse tanquam Divinos ac Propheticos, nisi postquàm ea de re Synagoga vel Ecclesia tulit judicium. Sic Scripturas Apocryphas rejiciens Cyrillus Hierosolymitanus, autor nobis est, ut eas solùm meditemur quæ liberè leguntur in Ecclesia. Πρὸς δὲ τὰ Σαπ-νευφα μηδὲν ἔχε νεωον· πάντας μόνον (βιβλια) μελέτα ἀναγινώσκομεν, ὡς ἐν ἐκκλησίᾳ μὴ παράγεται ἀναγινώσκομεν. Cujus Sanctissimi Patris monitis si obtemperasset Vossius, impuros Scriptores non adscripsisset albo Prophetarum.
units.tr: Vossius also finds fault with Simonius for calling those books Apocryphal whose authors are hidden and uncertain. If this is a legitimate explanation of the word, says Vossius, then it must be that most of the books of the Old Testament are Apocryphal, since he attributes not one of them with certainty to any author. But Vossius, again playing the sophist, wrangles. For, to say nothing of the fact that Simonius said nothing about the writers of the sacred books that had not already been approved by most of the Fathers and the most learned theologians, it is certain that books are called Apocryphal when their authors are hidden and uncertain. Simonius, however, called those books hidden and uncertain about which neither the Church nor the Synagogue has pronounced anything certain, namely whether their authors were moved by the Divine Spirit to write. Simonius therefore said that the writers of the Apocrypha are uncertain and hidden, and that they cannot be received by anyone as divine and prophetic unless the Synagogue or the Church has first passed judgment on them. So Cyril of Jerusalem, rejecting the Apocryphal Scriptures, advises us to meditate only on those books that are read openly in the Church: "Concerning the Apocrypha, have nothing new; meditate only on the books that we read in the Church" [Πρὸς δὲ τὰ ἀπόκρυφα μηδὲν ἔχε νεώτερον· πάντα μόνα (τὰ βιβλία) μελέτα, ἃ ἀναγινώσκομεν ἐν ἐκκλησίᾳ]. If Vossius had obeyed the admonitions of this most holy Father, he would not have enrolled impure writers in the list of the Prophets.

units.la: Denique placet iterum Vossio μωεχίνειν. Simonius, qui Vossii maledicentiam ex illius scriptis noverat, hoc illum signaverat elogio, In maledicam animam non introibit sapientia; jam ut elogium istud in Simonium transferat, ait illum sibi conscium esse vitæ P. Morini. Sed quid ad rem faciat vita P. Morini, viderit ipse Vossius, nisi quòd ipsi solenne sit μωεχίνειν. Jam vitâ functus erat Joannes Morinus, quando Simonius Oratorianis Parisiensibus nomen suum dedit. Mirum non est Vossium Morini defensorem se præbere, qui illius exemplo manifestos errores obstinatè tueatur. Illud enim de Morini moribus à viris fide dignis accepi, illum tam pervicaci animo fuisse, ut exactis jam tribus annis ab expugnata Rupella, hanc revera expugnatam fuisse firmiter negaverit, dixeritque vanos esse qui ea de re vagati fuerant rumores. Similiter bonus Vossius fabellas commentaque plusquàm Rabbinica non alià defendit ratione, quàm quòd eodem atque Morinus præditus sit ingenio. Nugas verò non agebat ille qui à Vossio postulavit ut Simonium cessaret allatrare, cùm ejus scripta caninæ suæ eloquentiæ manifesta præbeant argumenta. Neque etiam Vossio responrespondens cavillatus est Simonius, qui ridens ejus ineptias validissimis easdem rationibus confutaverit. Jam precor bonam mentem firmiusque judicium optimo Vossio, ut paratior ac fortior iterum descendat in arenam cum Simonio, qui eum quocunque ierit lubens ac promptus sequetur. Hæc ad te scripsi raptim, vir clarissime. Si tamen ea judicaveris digna quæ lucem aspiciant, per me licet ut evulges.
units.tr: Finally, Vossius once again likes to carp [μωμοσχεῖν]. Simonius, who knew Vossius's slanderous temper from his writings, had marked him with this saying: Wisdom will not enter a malicious soul. Now Vossius turns this saying against Simonius, claiming that he is conscious of the life of P. Morin. But what the life of P. Morin has to do with the matter, let Vossius himself see, unless it is his habit to carp. Indeed, Jean Morin had already died when Simonius joined the Oratorians of Paris. It is no wonder that Vossius presents himself as a defender of Morin, who obstinately upholds manifest errors after his example. For I have heard from trustworthy men about Morin's character that he was so stubborn in mind that, three years after Rochelle had been taken, he firmly denied that it had really been taken, and said that those who had spread rumours about it were empty-headed. Likewise good Vossius defends fables and fictions more than Rabbinic ones on no other ground than that he has the same kind of mind as Morin. Yet he was not trifling who asked Vossius to make Simonius stop barking, since Simonius's writings provide clear evidence of his canine eloquence. Nor did Simonius, in replying to Vossius, quibble; rather he laughed at his absurdities and refuted them with the strongest arguments. Now I pray for good sense and a firmer judgment for the excellent Vossius, so that, better prepared and bolder, he may again descend into the arena with Simonius, who will gladly and promptly follow him wherever he goes. I have written these things to you in haste, most distinguished sir. If you judge them worthy to see the light, you may publish them through me.

units.la: Juliobona in Caletibus, die 12. Januarii, 1685.
units.tr: Juliobona in the country of the Caletes, 12 January 1685.

units.la: Pag. 32. post hæc verba, sed ex mente Judaorum, addenda sequentia.
units.tr: Page 32. After these words, but according to the mind of the Jews, the following is to be added.

units.la: His omnibus accedit Petri Comestoris autoritas, quem vulgò Magistrum Historiarum appellant, qui Prologo Hieronymi in Judith affirmat legendum esse Apocrypha, non verò Hagiographa; quam lectionem putat esse vitium Scriptoris. Similiter editor Bibliorum, quibus Glossa ordinaria & Lyrani Annotationes inseruntur, verba Hieronymi Prologo in librum Tobiæ profert cum duplici lectione: nam super vocem Hagiographa notavit, alias Apocrypha; unde Brito in sua Expositione probans hanc lectionem, scribit ad vocem Hagiographa, quæ vulgaris erat lectio, Alia litera habet Apocrypha, quod melius est. Plura sunt ejusdem naturæ quæ in Hieronymi libris ex ipsomet Hieronymo facilè restitui possunt sine Codicibus manu exaratis.
units.tr: To all this must be added the authority of Peter Comestor, whom they commonly call the Master of Histories. In his prologue to Jerome's preface on Judith he affirms that one should read Apocrypha, not Hagiographa, and he thinks the latter reading is a fault of the writer. Similarly, the editor of the Bibles into which the Ordinary Gloss and Lyra's Annotations are inserted gives the words of Jerome's prologue to the book of Tobit with a double reading. Above the word Hagiographa he noted that others have Apocrypha. Hence Brito, in his Exposition, approving this reading, writes at the word Hagiographa, which was the common reading: Another copy has Apocrypha, which is better. Many things of this kind in Jerome's books can easily be restored from Jerome himself, without manuscripts written by hand.
